Ages and genders reported only as bar charts, never matched or tested; accuracy alone on imbalanced classes with no baseline; feature selection over several hundred dimensions against 55 subjects with no evidence of nesting inside the LOSO folds, which perfect majority-class recall suggests leaked; clinical labels rest on unspecified prior diagnoses; no ethics or consent statement despite an identifiable facial-video and voice database. | One of the corpus's few adult-focused studies and one of even fewer to model comorbidity explicitly, with control screening that is more rigorous than its case ascertainment. It is also the corpus's clearest example of a dataset announced as a community contribution with no access conditions attached, and of an identifiable-media database published without any stated ethics or consent basis. | [RQ1.1] Four groups: controls (n=18), ASD only (n=22), ADHD only (n=4) and comorbid ADHD+ASD (n=11), totalling 55 adults. Group sizes must be inferred from the classification tables and a bar chart rather than a participant table. The ADHD-only group was explicitly too small (n=4) to train a classifier for, so the reported analyses collapse to controls-vs-condition and comorbid-vs-ASD-only. This is one of very few corpus studies with both a non-autistic clinical group and an explicit comorbid group. [RQ1.2] 'subjects who have been diagnosed with ASD', 'individuals with ADHD', 'people with ASD', 'subjects with ADHD/ASD', 'the ASD group', 'the Condition group', 'healthy controls', 'healthy individuals', 'control group'. Person-first for the clinical groups, but the comparison group is repeatedly framed as 'healthy', which implicitly positions autism as ill-health rather than difference - a framing choice worth noting against the more neutral 'typically developing' used elsewhere in this corpus. [RQ1.3] Poorly reported. Total n=55 adults over 18. Group sizes are recoverable (18 control, 22 ASD only, 4 ADHD only, 11 comorbid) but only from the results tables. Median age per group and gender distribution per group are presented solely as bar charts (Figs. 2 and 3) with no numeric values, no standard deviations and no age range. No matching procedure, and no statistical test of age or gender comparability between groups, is reported. Adults only, so no early-diagnosis relevance. [RQ1.4] Clinical groups: prior clinical diagnosis of ADHD and/or ASD, recruited through the Nottingham City Asperger Service and ADHD Clinic; the diagnostic instruments and criteria behind those prior diagnoses are not described. Controls: actively screened out using two validated instruments with stated thresholds - Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale Part A (threshold 4) and AQ-10 (threshold 6). The control screening is more rigorously specified than the case ascertainment, which is the reverse of the usual pattern in this corpus. [RQ1.5] No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive-functioning measures are reported for any group. ASRS and AQ-10 are used only as control-admission gates and their scores are never reported for the ASD, ADHD or comorbid groups. Comorbidity, by contrast, is handled seriously - ADHD+ASD co-occurrence is a defined group and the subject of the second classification task, motivated by the observation that treatment differs across the three clinical groups. [RQ2.1] Goal: a fully automatic end-to-end diagnostic aid predicting presence/absence of ADHD and ASD in adults directly from video, explicitly contrasted with prior work that only detected predefined behavioural markers. Main findings: 96.4% accuracy for controls vs condition (16/18 controls and 37/37 condition correct) and 93.9% for comorbid vs ASD-only (9/11 and 22/22 correct); head-motion speed and lip-corner depressor activity were most discriminative for the first task, inner-brow raiser, lip-corner puller and head yaw for the second. [RQ2.2] A controlled recording setting with a screen and Kinect camera, with clinical recruitment via an NHS Asperger and ADHD service. Newly collected data - the study contributes the KOMAA dataset and no existing dataset is used. [RQ2.3] A computer-mediated version of the Strange Stories task: 12 short stories displayed on screen and simultaneously read aloud by a pre-recorded voice, each followed by 2-3 questions answered aloud. The design deliberately simulates a human interviewer while removing the interviewer, so that the stimulus is identical across participants. Video was manually segmented into the 12 story periods for feature aggregation. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single ~12-minute recording per participant with no follow-up. The data are highly sensitive - identifiable RGB facial video plus depth and recorded voice responses from clinically diagnosed adults. Despite this, and despite announcing the resulting database as a contribution to the research community, the paper contains no ethics-approval statement, no participant consent statement, and no anonymization, access-control or data-protection provision. Only funding bodies are acknowledged. [RQ2.5] Hardware: Microsoft Kinect 2.0 RGBD sensor capturing high-resolution colour and depth; a computer screen with speakers for stimulus delivery. Software: Kinect v2 library for animation units and 3D head pose; a modified deep CNN facial-action-unit detector (the Jaiswal & Valstar architecture with the BLSTM removed); custom landmark-centroid head-speed computation; SVM with RBF kernel and greedy forward feature selection. [RQ2.6] Weak. The KOMAA dataset is announced as a contribution but no access conditions, licence, repository or contact route is stated - so a dataset presented as a community resource is in practice unavailable. No code release. Feature construction is described in good detail (histogram bin counts, AU list, angle ranges, smoothing window, normalisation) and would be re-implementable, but SVM hyperparameters, the feature-selection stopping criterion and the final feature-vector dimensionality are not given, and nothing states whether feature selection was nested in the cross-validation. Not reproducible as reported. [RQ2.7] No limitations section exists, so nothing is acknowledged by the authors beyond the ADHD-only group being too small to model. Identifiable in review: severe class imbalance (18 controls vs 37 condition) reported only as accuracy, where always predicting 'condition' would already score 67%; group sizes of 4 and 11 in two of the four cells; ages and genders never reported numerically and never matched or tested, so demographic confounding cannot be assessed at all; a very high-dimensional feature vector (six feature families x 12 segments) against 55 subjects with greedy forward selection not stated to be nested inside the leave-one-subject-out loop - the single most likely explanation for 37/37 and 22/22 perfect recall on the majority classes; single-site recruitment; and no ethnicity data. [RQ2.9] None proposed. The conclusion asserts high potential for facial expressions to predict ADHD, ASD 'and other neurodevelopmental disorders' but sets out no specific research programme, no validation plan and no open questions - unusual even by the standards of a short conference paper. [RQ3.1] Facial expression (FACS action units and Kinect animation units), head pose in 3D, head-motion speed and cumulative head displacement, plus response latency to spoken questions. Voice is recorded for the answers but no acoustic or linguistic analysis of it is performed - only the time taken to respond is used. [RQ3.2] Six behavioral feature families are combined by concatenation into a single normalised vector before classification - early/feature-level fusion - with temporal structure preserved by computing each family separately per story segment and concatenating across the 12 segments, which the authors describe as trading a twelvefold dimensionality increase for retained temporal information. No integration with clinical scores or demographics. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning. The diagnostic classifier is an RBF-kernel SVM with greedy forward feature selection. A deep CNN (a modified dynamic deep-learning AU architecture) is used upstream as a pre-trained facial action unit detector. The authors explicitly reject end-to-end deep learning on raw pixels because the small training set would cause severe overfitting - a deliberate and well-reasoned choice to use deep learning for representation but not for diagnosis. [RQ4.2] Histogram-based aggregation of frame-level descriptors: AU intensities, animation-unit intensities, head-pose angles and head speeds are each binned into per-segment histograms; cumulative distance and response times enter as scalars; everything is length-normalised by frame count and Z-scored. This is a handcrafted statistical representation built on top of deep-learned per-frame features rather than a learned embedding of the video. [RQ4.3] Classification accuracy only, supported by raw per-class correct/incorrect counts (which is at least transparent enough to recover the confusion matrix). No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confidence intervals - a significant gap given the 18-vs-37 and 11-vs-22 class imbalances, where the reported accuracies of 96.4% and 93.9% cannot be compared against the relevant majority-class baselines of 67% and 67% without recomputation. [RQ4.4] Greedy forward feature selection identifies the discriminative features, with the top three per task visualised and the top 30 ranked by individual classification power. Informative features: head-motion speed (stories 1-2) and lip-corner depressor (story 10) for controls vs condition; inner-brow raiser (story 1), lip-corner puller (story 3) and head yaw (story 8) for comorbid vs ASD-only. Notably the features are segment-specific, implying that particular Strange Stories items carry the signal - an interpretable finding the paper does not pursue. The direction of each group difference is never stated. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, which is subject-independent at the outer level. Overfitting is explicitly reasoned about in two places - rejecting raw-pixel deep learning, and motivating feature selection because 'any classifier trained directly on the entire feature-set is most likely to overfit'. But there is no statement that feature selection was nested within folds, no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no class-imbalance handling or metric, no statistical testing, and no deployment or real-time evaluation despite the time-saving clinical framing. The comorbid classifier is trained on 33 subjects total. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list. The paper's vocabulary: 'automatic detection', 'expressive behaviour', 'RGBD data', 'behaviomedical conditions', 'diagnostic predictions', 'facial action units', 'animation units', 'Strange Stories'. The term 'behaviomedical' - conditions that alter expressive behaviour - is distinctive to this line of work and does not recur elsewhere in the corpus. [RQ5.2] IEEE International Conference on Automatic Face and Gesture Recognition (FG) 2017 - a technology/computational venue (computer vision), not an autism or clinical venue. [RQ5.3] 2017. The paper characterises computer vision for ADHD and ASD as 'still in its infancy', with prior work confined to detecting predefined behavioural markers (AOSI markers, self-stimulatory behaviour, social games, engagement) whose 'effectiveness in predicting the actual ADHD and ASD diagnosis still remains to be seen'. It positions itself as one of the first to pose diagnosis directly as a machine-learning problem and, unusually for this corpus, targets adults rather than children. |
| S-009 | Retrospective acoustic analysis nested in the prospective EASE high-risk sibling cohort; 10 infants later diagnosed with ASD at 3 years and 10 typically developing infants, all recorded at exactly 10 months, exactly sex-balanced (5M/5F per group); 684 manually segmented vocalisations from 12-minute parent-child free-play recordings, not released. | Ceiling-mounted camcorder audio-video of naturalistic toy play; vocalisations segmented by vocal breathing group in Noldus Observer XT by an annotator blind to group, with vegetative sounds excluded and complexity annotated via SAEVD-R; 88 eGeMAPS acoustic parameters extracted with openSMILE; linear-kernel SVM (Weka SMO) and a one-layer eight-cell BLSTM (TensorFlow) compared under subject-independent 3-fold cross-validation with a genuine train/development/test split; subject-level decisions from thresholded per-vocalisation ASD ratios. | 54 of 88 features differed significantly between groups, five with \|r\| > 0.3, strongest mean spectral slope 0-500 Hz unvoiced (r = 0.3966). Vocalisation-level UAR 64.5% +/- 3.3% (SVM) and 62.9% +/- 2.0% (BLSTM). Subject-level accuracy 70% at a fixed 0.5 threshold and 75% with optimised thresholds (8/10 ASD, 7/10 TD). Volubility did not differ (p = 0.104). | Only 20 infants, so the subject-level result is 15/20 correct with a wide interval; 54 significant features reported without multiple-comparison correction; vocalisation counts unbalanced between groups and highly variable per subject (9-98); headline accuracy uses per-fold optimised thresholds; high-familial-risk sibling design is not a general screening population; no external validation; no consent or anonymization statement for infant audio-video. | The youngest sample in the corpus (10 months, with outcome 26 months later) and its methodological benchmark for speech: blinded segmentation, subject-independent folds with a real development set, UAR with confusion matrices, published partitions and thresholds, and honest reporting of a null volubility finding and a deep-learning model that did not beat a linear baseline. Its modest 75% is a useful calibration point against the 90%+ figures reported elsewhere in this corpus on comparable sample sizes. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of 10: infants at heightened familial risk (younger siblings of children with ASD) later diagnosed with ASD at 3 years, and typically developing infants from a low-risk population with normal 3-year outcome. Both groups fully specified per subject in Table 1, including vocalisation counts and cross-validation partition assignment - subject-level transparency that is rare in this corpus. No other-diagnosis group. [RQ1.2] 'children with autism spectrum disorder', 'individuals with ASD', 'individuals later diagnosed with ASD', 'infants later diagnosed with ASD', 'the ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) infants', 'TD controls', 'affected individuals'. Consistently person-first, and notably careful in using 'later diagnosed with ASD' for the infants, which correctly avoids attributing a diagnosis to a 10-month-old who did not yet have one. [RQ1.3] ASD n=10 (5 male, 5 female); TD n=10 (5 male, 5 female). All infants exactly 10 months old at recording, so age is matched by design with no variance. Gender is exactly balanced within and across groups, and the authors additionally describe the sample as family-language-balanced. This is one of the very few corpus studies with perfect sex balance - though at n=20 total it is also among the smallest. Highly relevant to early diagnosis: 10 months is the youngest recording age in the corpus, with outcome ascertained 26 months later. [RQ1.4] ASD diagnosis at 3 years of age using DSM-5 criteria within the EASE longitudinal cohort; TD status confirmed by normal outcome at the same 3-year assessment. The specific instruments used at the 3-year assessment are not named in this paper. Group membership was withheld from the annotator during segmentation. [RQ1.5] Speech-language developmental level was annotated using the Stark Assessment of Early Vocal Development-Revised (SAEVD-R), recording whether each infant produced vocalisation types more complex than single canonical syllables - 4 ASD and 4 TD infants did, so the groups were comparable on this measure. No cognitive, adaptive or IQ measures are reported, and comorbid conditions are not described. Pacifier use during recording is noted for three infants, and one misclassified TD infant is flagged as having used one - an unusually granular disclosure of a potential acoustic confound. [RQ2.1] Goal: earlier identification - characterise ASD-related acoustic specificities in pre-linguistic vocalisations and test the feasibility of automated identification. Main findings: 54 of 88 eGeMAPS features differed significantly between groups (five with \|r\| > 0.3, strongest being mean spectral slope 0-500 Hz over unvoiced segments at r = 0.3966); vocalisation-level UAR 64.5% (SVM) and 62.9% (BLSTM); subject-level accuracy 75% with optimised thresholds (70% at a fixed 0.5 threshold), correctly assigning 8/10 ASD and 7/10 TD infants. Volubility did not differ between groups (p = 0.104), a negative result reported plainly. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting - a closed recording room with ceiling-mounted cameras, deliberately arranged so parents would play as they would at home and with study personnel absent during recording. Existing data: retrospective analysis of recordings collected within the EASE (Early Autism Sweden) longitudinal high-risk sibling study. [RQ2.3] A semi-standardised free-play parent-child interaction on a mat with toys, 12 minutes per infant, with parents instructed to play as at home. No task demands were placed on the infant. Vocalisations were then manually segmented by vocal breathing groups using Noldus Observer XT, with vegetative sounds excluded, and annotated for developmental complexity against SAEVD-R by an annotator blinded to group membership. [RQ2.4] The parent study is longitudinal - infants recorded at 10 months with diagnostic outcome at 3 years, a 26-month prospective interval - but the acoustic analysis itself is cross-sectional at the single 10-month recording. Data are highly sensitive: audio-video of identifiable infants and their parents in intimate play interaction. Ethical review board approval at the participating centres is stated in a single footnote; there is no consent statement, no anonymization or de-identification procedure, and no data-protection or access-control provision despite the media type. [RQ2.5] Hardware: Panasonic HC-V700 camcorders ceiling-mounted in the room corners so infant behaviour could be captured continuously regardless of orientation; audio extracted from one camera as single-channel 44.1 kHz AAC. Software: Noldus Observer XT for video coding and segmentation; openSMILE (audEERING) for eGeMAPS extraction; Weka with sequential minimal optimisation for SVM training; TensorFlow with the Adam optimiser for the BLSTM. [RQ2.6] No data availability statement and no code release, but reproducibility of the method is comparatively strong: the feature set is a published open standard (eGeMAPS) extracted with an open-source tool (openSMILE), both classifiers use widely available toolkits (Weka, TensorFlow), the SVM complexity grid is stated, the BLSTM architecture search outcome (one layer, eight cells), time step (10 ms), optimiser and early-stopping rule are given, the exact cross-validation partitions are published per subject in Table 1, and the optimised per-fold decision thresholds are listed. This is among the most re-implementable pipelines in the corpus; only the cohort recordings are unavailable. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors: the small number of subjects limits the impact of the results, and a genuine performance difference between SVM and deep learning 'might only become evident on a dataset with a considerably higher number of vocalisations'. They also note that a proportion of ASD infants' vocalisations carry no acoustic atypicality, and disclose pacifier use as a possible source of error for one misclassified control. Identifiable in review: n=20 makes the 75% subject-level figure equivalent to 15/20 correct with a very wide confidence interval; the headline 75% uses per-fold optimised thresholds rather than the fixed 0.5 threshold (70%); vocalisation counts are unbalanced between groups (259 ASD vs 425 TD) and per subject (9 to 98), so subject-level ratios rest on very different amounts of evidence; 54 of 88 features are declared significant with no multiple-comparison correction, so a substantial share are likely false positives; and the high-familial-risk sibling design means the ASD group is not representative of general-population screening. [RQ2.9] Larger and more fine-grained studies; systematic comparison of alternative acoustic feature sets; alternative feature pre-processing such as bag-of-words representations; and other deep learning architectures. The authors also sketch the intended deployment scenario - early preventative judgements from vocalisations captured during routine paediatric examinations in the first year of life - which frames the eventual clinical target rather than a research step. [RQ3.1] Speech/voice: pre-linguistic infant vocalisations (babbling and other non-vegetative vocal breathing groups) characterised by spectral, energy and frequency-related acoustic parameters. No linguistic content, since the infants are pre-verbal. Parental voice is present in the recordings but is not analysed. [RQ3.2] Single modality; no fusion. Video was recorded but used only for segmentation and annotation, not as a modelling input - a notable choice given that the same recordings could have supported gaze or motor analysis. Within the modality, per-vocalisation decisions are aggregated into a subject-level judgement by computing an ASD ratio and thresholding it, which is a late/decision-level fusion across utterances. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning. Algorithms: linear-kernel SVM (Weka SMO) as the baseline, chosen for robustness and insensitivity to feature overfitting, and a one-layer bidirectional LSTM neural network with eight cells as the deep-learning alternative. The comparison is reported as effectively a tie, which the authors attribute to sample size rather than to the architectures. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted standardised acoustic features: the 88-parameter eGeMAPS set of statistical functionals computed over 25 smoothed low-level descriptors per vocalisation. The BLSTM additionally consumes the descriptors on 10 ms time steps, so the deep model sees a frame-level time series while the SVM sees utterance-level functionals - a representation difference the paper does not foreground. [RQ4.3] Unweighted average recall as the primary metric with weighted average recall alongside, both reported with standard deviations across folds; full vocalisation-level confusion matrices for both classifiers; and subject-level accuracy at two explicitly stated thresholds. Using UAR rather than accuracy is the methodologically correct choice for the unbalanced 259-vs-425 vocalisation split, and this is one of the few corpus studies to make it. [RQ4.4] Univariate Mann-Whitney U tests with effect size r, with the top ten features tabulated and the strongest visualised as per-group probability density estimates. Most informative features are voice-quality and spectral-balance measures over unvoiced segments - spectral slope 0-500 Hz and 500-1500 Hz, Hammarberg index, alpha ratio - together with MFCC variability, unvoiced segment length, f0 mean and range, and voiced segments per second. No model-internal importance (no SVM weights or BLSTM attribution) is reported, and the acoustic-phonetic interpretation of the differences is left undeveloped. [RQ4.5] The strongest validation design among the early speech studies here: subject-independent 3-fold cross-validation with partitions matched for gender and diagnosis and balanced for vocalisation count, and a genuine three-way train/development/test split in which the SVM complexity parameter, the BLSTM architecture and the early-stopping point are all selected on development data only. Confusion matrices and fold standard deviations are reported. Weaknesses: the headline subject-level accuracy uses thresholds optimised on the merged training and development partitions of each fold, which is defensible but should be read alongside the 70% fixed-threshold result; there is no external or independent validation and no held-out site; class imbalance is handled by reporting UAR rather than by resampling; and no real-time or deployment evaluation is performed, though a paediatric-examination scenario is proposed. [RQ5.1] Index terms: autism spectrum disorder, early identification, infant vocalisation analysis, speech-language pathology. Task vocabulary: 'earlier identification', 'automatic vocalisation-based approach', 'early acoustic markers', 'pre-linguistic vocalisations', 'feasibility', 'en-route to'. The framing is markedly more cautious than most of the corpus - the claim is feasibility and markers, not diagnosis. [RQ5.2] INTERSPEECH 2017 (18th Annual Conference of the International Speech Communication Association) - a technology/computational venue (speech science and signal processing), not an autism or clinical venue, though the author list spans developmental neuroscience, child psychiatry and machine learning. [RQ5.3] 2017. The paper notes that early speech-language development in ASD has repeatedly been characterised as delayed and deviant but that only a few studies examine vocalisation specificities at the feature level, and that most of those assessed crying with single acoustic features such as fundamental frequency or duration. It positions itself as one of the first to explore ASD-related pre-linguistic vocalisation specificities across a wide standardised parameter set - documenting the shift from single hand-picked acoustic measures to standardised high-dimensional feature sets that characterises the speech strand of this corpus. |
| S-010 | Cross-sectional four-way classification on secondary data; 102 French monolingual children with communicative verbal skills - 11 autism disorders, 10 PDD-NOS, 13 specific language impairment, 68 typically developing - from the Child Pathological and Emotional Speech Database; ~12 hours of audio segmented into 6380 utterances, access conditions unstated. | eGeMAPS (88) and ComParE (6373) acoustic features extracted with openSMILE; a GAN with a four-hidden-layer discriminator (256 units, LeakyReLU, batch normalisation) trained unsupervised, with hidden-layer activations used as representations for a linear-kernel SVM; baselines linear SVM, RBF-SVM and a four-layer MLP; fixed child-independent 60/20/20 train/validation/test partitions with all tuning on validation; one-sided z-tests for system comparison. | Against a 25% chance UAR: eGeMAPS best GAN representation 44.06% test UAR versus 39.91% linear-SVM baseline (+10.4% relative, p<0.05); ComParE best GAN representation 46.93% versus 42.83% baseline (p<0.05). Confusion matrices show autism-disorder utterances recovered at 24/149 (eGeMAPS) and 16/149 (ComParE), with most misassigned to SLI or TD. | No participant ages or sexes reported at all; matching asserted without numbers; 11 autism-disorder children against 68 controls; minimally verbal children excluded by inclusion criteria; utterance-level rather than child-level evaluation despite child-independent partitions; no feature-level interpretation; best-layer selection appears to track test performance; no recording protocol, no data access conditions, no code, and no ethics or consent statement. | The corpus's most useful negative calibration point: with a genuinely held-out child-independent test set, a language-impairment comparison group and a metric appropriate to class imbalance, speech-based autism recognition performs near floor - directly contradicting the 90%+ accuracies reported by comparably sized studies elsewhere in this corpus, and the paper says so, naming small-corpus confounds as the field's central obstacle. | [RQ1.1] Four groups: autism disorders (n=11), PDD-NOS (n=10), specific language impairment (n=13) and typically developing (n=68), totalling 102 children. Group sizes are reported. This is one of the few corpus studies to include a non-autistic clinical comparison group - and notably one (SLI) chosen to probe exactly the specificity question that most ASD-versus-TD studies leave open. It is also one of the few to separate autism disorders from PDD-NOS as distinct classes. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASC', 'children with autism', 'children suffering from ASC', 'children with AD', 'patients', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'control group'. Person-first but with an explicitly medical framing - 'patients', 'suffering from', 'pathological' (in the corpus name), 'automatic diagnosis'. The paper uses 'Autism Spectrum Conditions' rather than 'Disorders', a comparatively neutral choice, alongside otherwise clinical vocabulary. [RQ1.3] Sample sizes are given (11 AD, 10 PDD-NOS, 13 SLI, 68 TD) but no age, no age range, no standard deviation and no gender distribution is reported anywhere in the paper. Matching is asserted - patients matched among themselves for age, sex, academic grades and lexical abilities, and TD children matched to patients for age and sex at a 2:1 ratio - but with no numbers and no statistical verification. Absence of any age data makes the study impossible to place in the early-diagnosis timeline. [RQ1.4] Clinical diagnosis under DSM-IV criteria in two university departments of child and adolescent psychiatry in Paris. Control status established by teacher questionnaire excluding learning disorders. No standardised autism instrument (no ADOS, ADI-R or questionnaire measure) is reported, and no inter-rater reliability is given for the clinical diagnoses that serve as ground truth for a four-way task. [RQ1.5] Lexical abilities and academic grades are named as matching variables for the patient groups, but no scores are reported for any group and they are not used in modelling. All children are stated to have communicative verbal skills - an important inclusion constraint that excludes minimally verbal autistic children. Comorbidities are not described beyond the exclusion of learning disorders from the TD group. [RQ2.1] Goal: automatic diagnosis framed as a four-way classification, with the methodological objective of testing GAN representation learning against hand-crafted acoustic features under data scarcity. Main findings: best test UAR 46.93% with ComParE-derived GAN representations and 44.06% with eGeMAPS-derived ones, both significantly above the corresponding linear-SVM baselines (42.83% and 39.91%) at p<0.05, against a 25% chance level. The optimal discriminator layer differed by feature set (bottom layer for ComParE, third layer for eGeMAPS). The autism-disorders class was recognised at close to floor in both systems. [RQ2.2] Mixed clinic and school setting - patients recruited in two Paris university child and adolescent psychiatry departments, controls from elementary schools. Existing dataset: the Child Pathological and Emotional Speech Database (CPESD), used entirely as secondary data; no new collection. [RQ2.3] Spontaneous speech recordings designed to induce three emotional valence categories (positive, neutral, negative). The elicitation procedure itself is not described in this paper - no prompts, stimuli, interlocutor or session structure are given, only the valence categories and the resulting utterance counts. Recordings were segmented into 6380 utterances by an unspecified procedure. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; nearly 12 hours of audio in total but no per-child session duration, number of sessions or follow-up. The data are identifiable child speech recordings from a clinical population. This paper contains no ethics approval, no consent statement and no anonymization or data-protection provision, deferring entirely to the source corpus citations - a notable gap for a paper published at a digital health venue. A competing-interests declaration is present (none declared), which makes the absence of an ethics statement more conspicuous. [RQ2.5] No acquisition hardware is described - microphone, recording format, sampling rate and environment are all absent. Software: openSMILE for eGeMAPS and ComParE extraction, selected explicitly 'for transparency and reproducibility'; GAN generator and discriminator as feed-forward networks trained with SGD (mini-batch 128, LeakyReLU, batch normalisation, tanh output, binary cross-entropy); linear-kernel SVM for classification. The deep-learning framework is not named. [RQ2.6] Mixed. Strong on the modelling side: the feature sets are published open standards extracted with an open-source toolkit chosen for reproducibility, full network architectures are specified (layer counts, hidden units, activations, normalisation, objective, optimiser, batch size), the SVM complexity parameter is stated to be tuned on validation, and partition sizes are given. Weak on the data side: CPESD access conditions are never stated, the elicitation protocol and recording setup are absent, no code is released, no random seeds are reported, and the exact child-to-partition assignment is not published, so the child-independent split cannot be reproduced. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors: small corpus size in ASC research generally is the paper's motivating problem, and they cite prior work warning that high accuracies on small datasets 'may lead to potential confounds'. Identifiable in review: severe class imbalance (68 TD versus 11 AD children, 4547 versus 149 test-set utterances by the confusion matrices) with the reported UAR concealing near-floor autism recognition; no age or sex data reported at all, so demographic bias cannot be assessed; matching is asserted without numbers; single-country, monolingual, verbally able children only, which excludes minimally verbal autistic children entirely; evaluation is at utterance rather than child level; and the best-layer selection differs between feature sets in a way that suggests the layer choice is being read off test performance rather than validation - the eGeMAPS validation UARs are essentially flat across layers (39.33-40.92%) while the test UARs vary by more than a point. [RQ2.9] Apply the GAN-based system to other health tasks such as depression detection; extend GAN representation learning to other behavioural signals including video descriptors and to physiological signals such as electrocardiogram and electrodermal activity; and compare and combine GAN-based feature learning with alternative unsupervised representation-learning approaches such as bag-of-words. All the proposed directions are methodological rather than clinical - no validation, replication or population-extension work is proposed. [RQ3.1] Speech: spontaneous child vocal production analysed paralinguistically through prosodic, spectral, cepstral and voice-quality descriptors. The introduction explicitly argues that linguistic markers may be unreliable because language skills vary across spectrum subtypes, and that paralinguistic cues are better suited to automatic detection - so linguistic content is deliberately excluded. [RQ3.2] Single modality; no fusion. Two acoustic feature sets are compared rather than combined, and no combination with clinical, cognitive or demographic data is performed. The future-work section proposes extending the approach to video and physiological signals, but no multimodal work is done here. [RQ4.1] Unsupervised deep representation learning combined with supervised classification. Algorithms: a generative adversarial network whose discriminator acts as a non-linear feature extractor, with hidden-layer activations fed to a linear-kernel SVM. Baselines: linear SVM, RBF-kernel SVM and a four-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron. Notably the GAN is used purely for representation learning, not for the data augmentation that the introduction motivates - the generator's synthetic samples are never used to enlarge the training set. [RQ4.2] Two-stage representation: hand-crafted acoustic functionals (eGeMAPS 88-dimensional, or ComParE 6373-dimensional) computed per utterance, then transformed into deep embeddings by taking the activations of one of four GAN discriminator hidden layers (256 units each). The comparison across layers is itself a study of representation depth, and yields different optima for the compact and the brute-forced feature set. [RQ4.3] Unweighted average recall only, chosen explicitly because the four-class task is imbalanced - the methodologically correct choice, and reported on both validation and test partitions. Full four-by-four confusion matrices are published for the best system under each feature set, which is unusually transparent and is what makes the near-floor autism-class performance visible. One-sided z-tests compare systems. No accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 or AUC, and no per-child metric. [RQ4.4] None. No feature importance, saliency, attention or attribution analysis is performed, and no acoustic property is identified as characteristic of any group. The only interpretability-adjacent result is which discriminator hidden layer produces the most useful representation, which speaks to network depth rather than to behaviour. This is one of the least interpretable studies in the corpus, and unusually the paper makes no interpretive claim it cannot support. [RQ4.5] Generalisability is addressed by design: partitioning is 'completely child independent', with all utterances from a given child confined to one partition, and a dedicated validation partition is used for all parameter optimisation while the test partition is 'solely used for the purpose of performance evaluation on unseen children'. This is the correct structure and better than most of the corpus. Class imbalance is addressed at the metric level (UAR) but not by resampling or class weighting, and the confusion matrices show the imbalance is not in fact overcome. No external validation on a second corpus, no held-out site, no bias mitigation, no calibration, and no real-time or deployment analysis. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: Autism Spectrum Condition; automatic diagnosis; generative adversarial networks; representation learning. CCS concepts: Applied computing - Life and medical sciences, Health informatics; Computing methodologies - Neural networks. Task vocabulary: 'speech-based diagnosis', 'objective marker', 'computational paralinguistics', 'data scarcity', 'representation learning'. [RQ5.2] DH'17 - the 2017 ACM International Conference on Digital Health, London. A technology/health-informatics venue rather than an autism or clinical journal, though more health-oriented than the pure signal-processing venues elsewhere in this corpus. [RQ5.3] 2017. The paper characterises the field as showing that 'high levels of accuracy can be achieved' for discriminating typically developing children from children with ASC, but immediately qualifies that these results come from 'rather small datasets, and may lead to potential confounds', naming corpus size as 'a major obstacle in the development of robust models which are sufficiently reliable for clinical practice'. It positions itself as the first application of GAN representation learning in computational paralinguistics. This is one of the corpus's most explicit internal critiques of its own literature's headline accuracies. |
| S-011 | Cross-sectional case-control; 30 Malaysian children with mild ASD (mean age 8.63) vs 30 typically developing children (mean age 9.52), recruited from a national autism society centre, social media and the local community; 3D ground reaction force data from a single left-limb stance per child, not released. | Barefoot self-paced walking over two AMTI force plates sampling at 1000 Hz, filtered at 30 Hz; 20 time-series parameterisation features (peak/minimum forces and their relative timings across medial-lateral, anterior-posterior and vertical components), amplitude-normalised to body weight and time-normalised to stance phase; stepwise discriminant analysis with Wilks' lambda reduced these to three; ANN with scaled conjugate gradient and SVMs with linear, polynomial and RBF kernels evaluated by 10-fold cross-validation over ten iterations. | Three significant features: relative time to maximum supination (p=0.005), relative time to zero anterior-posterior force at mid-stance (p<0.001) and second vertical peak force (p<0.001). ANN 93.3% accuracy, 96.7% sensitivity, 90.0% specificity; SVM-RBF 85.0%, SVM-polynomial 83.3%, SVM-linear 78.3%. | SWDA feature selection and the full hyperparameter grid search were both run on the complete labelled dataset outside the cross-validation folds, so the 93.3% is not a generalisation estimate; best of four configurations reported; no diagnostic instrument for the ASD group; no gender data; groups not age-matched or tested despite a ~0.9-year difference in a paediatric gait study; one stance phase of one limb per child; no effect directions; no fold-level variance; no external validation. | The corpus's clearest gait-kinetics entry, and a useful contrast with the kinematic motor studies: it shows that force-plate measures alone carry group-discriminative signal concentrated in just three parameters spanning loading response, mid-stance and push-off. It is also a compact illustration of the corpus's most common validation flaw - label-informed feature selection and hyperparameter tuning performed before, rather than inside, cross-validation - made unusually visible here because the full p-value table is published. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of 30: children with ASD (all mild category) and typically developing children. Group sizes, mean age, height and body mass are reported for both. Recruitment is split within the ASD group - 14 from the National Autism Society of Malaysia centre and 16 from the local community via parents approached through social media - which is unusually specific. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD subjects', 'ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD healthy children', 'normal children', 'normal gait patterns', 'ASD population'. Person-first for the participants but the comparison condition is repeatedly framed as 'normal' rather than 'typical' - 'ASD and normal gait', 'normal children' - which positions autistic gait as pathological by contrast; the paper also groups ASD gait with 'pathological gait' alongside cerebral palsy, stroke and Parkinson's disease. [RQ1.3] ASD n=30, mean age 8.63 +/- 2.16 years, height 1.29 +/- 0.14 m, mass 31.21 +/- 14.20 kg. TD n=30, mean age 9.52 +/- 1.96 years, height 1.27 +/- 0.13 m, mass 28.03 +/- 10.57 kg. No gender distribution is reported for either group, and no age matching is claimed or statistically tested despite a ~0.9-year mean difference - material for a gait study in children, where maturation changes force profiles. Height and body mass are reported, which is appropriate since GRF amplitudes are normalised to body weight, but the large mass SD in the ASD group (14.20 kg) is not discussed. [RQ1.4] Not reported. Participants are described only as 'previously diagnosed with a mild category of ASD' with no instrument, diagnostic criteria, diagnosing clinician or confirmation procedure named. Control status is asserted rather than screened. Since diagnostic label is the classification target, this is the study's most serious reporting gap. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive-functioning measures are reported for either group, and no autism severity instrument underlies the 'mild category' description. The only functional criteria are physical - no history of lower-extremity injury and ability to walk independently. Comorbidities are not otherwise described. [RQ2.1] Goal: automated ASD gait recognition to assist diagnosis, clinical decision-making and treatment targeting, plus identification of dominant GRF biomarkers. Main findings: three of 20 GRF features were statistically significant discriminators (Tx1 p=0.005, Ty2 p<0.001, Fz3 p<0.001); a three-input ANN achieved 93.3% accuracy, 96.7% sensitivity and 90.0% specificity, outperforming SVM-RBF (85.0%), SVM-polynomial (83.3%) and SVM-linear (78.3%) as well as the authors' earlier KNN approach. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting - a dedicated human motion gait analysis laboratory with force plates embedded in an instrumented walkway. Data were newly collected within a larger institutional research project but are reused here from the authors' earlier published work, so this paper is a secondary analysis of an in-house dataset rather than a new collection. [RQ2.3] Straight barefoot walking along a 6.5-metre walkway at self-determined speed, with the two force plates positioned so that one foot strikes each. Trials were accepted only on a clean foot strike on each plate. Only a single left-limb stance phase from one selected valid trial per participant was analysed - an extremely small behavioral sample per child, and the selection criterion for which valid trial to use is not stated. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single walking session with no follow-up and no repeated measurement. The data are numeric force-plate traces rather than identifiable media, so privacy risk is minimal. Ethics approval is reported at the level of the parent project (Research Ethics Committee of Universiti Teknologi MARA), but no participant or parental consent statement and no anonymization or data-protection procedure is described. [RQ2.5] Hardware: two independent Advanced Mechanical Technology Inc. force plates embedded consecutively in a 6.5 m walkway, recording medial-lateral, anterior-posterior and vertical forces at 1000 Hz. Software: second-order low-pass Butterworth filter with 30 Hz cut-off; IBM SPSS Statistics v21 for stepwise discriminant analysis; MATLAB R2015a Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox and Neural Network Toolbox for SVM and ANN classification. [RQ2.6] No data availability statement, no code release and no random seeds. Method reporting is otherwise good: the full 20-feature definition table, the complete SWDA p-value distribution for every feature, the SWDA entry and removal criteria, the sampling rate and filter settings, the SVM kernel types with their C and gamma grids, the polynomial degree range, and the ANN architecture and training function are all specified. The pipeline is re-implementable in principle but the analysis cannot be reproduced without the data. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors: only that evaluation on a larger dataset is needed to confirm the observations - there is no limitations section as such. Identifiable in review: feature selection by SWDA used group labels on the full dataset before cross-validation, and the exhaustive hyperparameter grid search (three SVM kernels, six C values, three polynomial degrees, 21 gamma values, 50 ANN hidden-layer sizes) was likewise performed outside the folds, so 93.3% is not an unbiased generalisation estimate; the reported figure is also the best of four classifier configurations; no gender data at all, so sex bias cannot be assessed in a literature with strong male skew; groups differ by ~0.9 years in mean age with no matching test, and gait matures with age; body mass SD is large and unequal; ASD recruitment is split across a specialist centre and social-media outreach with no comparison between subgroups; only one stance phase of one limb from one trial represents each child, so within-subject gait variability - itself a reported feature of autistic movement - is entirely discarded. [RQ2.9] Two directions only: deeper exploration of kinematic and kinetic gait parameters beyond ground reaction forces, and evaluation on a larger dataset. No proposals for external validation, for comparison against other motor-affected conditions, or for addressing the demographic and methodological gaps. [RQ3.1] Motor behavior: ground reaction forces during walking - the kinetic rather than kinematic aspect of gait, measuring the forces generated against the ground in three directions rather than limb trajectories or joint angles. [RQ3.2] Single modality, but with a form of within-modality fusion: features from all three orthogonal GRF components (medial-lateral, anterior-posterior, vertical) are pooled into one candidate set, and the three surviving features happen to come one from each component - so the discriminative signal is genuinely distributed across all three force directions. No combination with clinical, cognitive or demographic data. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning. Algorithms: a three-layer feed-forward artificial neural network trained by scaled conjugate gradient backpropagation, and support vector machines with linear, polynomial and RBF kernels. Stepwise discriminant analysis serves as a statistical feature-selection stage. The authors note that comparative studies often favour SVM, which makes their ANN result a departure from expectation. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted time-series parameterisation: each GRF waveform is reduced to its local peaks, minima and the relative times at which they occur, with amplitudes normalised to percentage body weight and times to percentage of stance phase. This yields 20 scalar features, reduced to three by feature selection. No raw waveforms, time series or learned representations are used. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, reported for all four classifier configurations. Headline: 93.3% accuracy, 96.7% sensitivity, 90.0% specificity for the ANN. No AUC, F1, precision, confidence intervals or fold-level variance, despite averaging over ten folds and ten iterations where a standard deviation would have been readily available. [RQ4.4] Stepwise discriminant analysis with Wilks' lambda provides the interpretability, and the paper publishes the complete p-value distribution for all 20 candidate features - unusually transparent, since it lets a reader see exactly how sharp the separation between selected and discarded features is (three at p<=0.005, next best Fy1 at 0.084). The three retained features are interpreted anatomically as spanning loading response, mid-stance and terminal stance, and the altered second vertical peak is related to gait instability and body-weight support difficulties by analogy with cerebral palsy. The direction of each group difference is not reported. [RQ4.5] Weak. 10-fold cross-validation repeated over ten iterations is used and is explicitly motivated by small sample size, but both the label-using SWDA feature selection and the exhaustive hyperparameter grid search were performed on the complete dataset before the folds were drawn, so information from every test fold informed both the feature set and the model configuration. There is no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no class-imbalance issue (30/30), no statistical comparison between classifiers, no bias mitigation, and no real-time or deployment analysis - though clinical diagnosis and treatment evaluation are named as intended applications. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: artificial neural network, autism spectrum disorder, gait classification, ground reaction force, support vector machine. Task vocabulary: 'automated recognition', 'gait disturbances', 'prominent biomarkers', 'pathological gait', 'clinical decision-making'. The framing situates autism alongside cerebral palsy, post-stroke and Parkinson's gait as a pathological gait recognition problem. [RQ5.2] TENCON 2018 - the IEEE Region 10 Conference. A general engineering/technology venue, neither autism-specific nor clinical, and broader than the specialist computer-vision and speech venues elsewhere in this corpus. [RQ5.3] 2018. The paper notes that machine learning has been proven effective for automated gait recognition in cerebral palsy, post-stroke and Parkinson's disease, but that 'research in the area of automated recognition of ASD gait using machine learning techniques based on GRFs gait features is less prevalent' - positioning autism gait analysis as lagging behind other clinical gait populations, and its own contribution as an incremental extension of the authors' prior KNN study on the same data. |
| S-012 | Cross-sectional case-control; 8 children with ASD (2.1-4.1 years) vs 8 typically developing children (2.11-7.6 years) at an Iranian autism treatment centre; 190 s of overhead-camera interaction per child with the RoboParrot social robot, not released. | Kernelized Correlation Filter tracking of child position relative to the robot; floor partitioned into a 4x4 grid; binary Presence Vector, time-weighted Presence Vector and robot-facing-cell presence ratio computed; pairwise cosine similarities compared within and between groups by t-test and ANOVA with a random-regrouping control; decision tree, KNN, Gaussian SVM, linear discriminant and logistic regression evaluated by 8-fold cross-validation, with a second-layer classifier stacking the two feature families. | Weighted Presence Vector similarity separated groups (t-test p=0.001, ANOVA p=1.09e-05) while binary presence did not (p=0.160); presence ratio in the robot-facing cell significant at p<0.05. Final Gaussian SVM 81.3% accuracy (13/16) with 2 false positives and 1 false negative; single-feature classifiers reached 75%. Random regrouping produced no significant differences. | n=16 with 81.3% equal to 13 of 16 children; control ages span nearly double the ASD range with no matching, confounding development with diagnosis in a spatial-approach measure; no gender data; no standardised diagnostic instrument; best of a five-classifier by three-feature grid reported without nesting; stacking degraded four of five classifiers; no ethics or consent statement despite dual-camera video of young children. | The corpus's clearest robot-mediated screening entry and a rare example of a study that runs a permutation control, reports a non-discriminative feature as such, analyses each misclassification individually, and reasons explicitly about the asymmetric costs of screening errors - while simultaneously illustrating how a small unmatched sample and an unnested classifier sweep can produce a headline accuracy that means only thirteen correct children. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of 8: children with ASD and typically developing children, total n=16. Group sizes are reported; no other-diagnosis group. The predecessor study being automated (Soleiman et al.) used 32 children, so this automation paper works on half that sample. [RQ1.2] 'children with autism', 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'Typically Developed (TD) children', 'TD children', 'normal ones', 'autistic ones', 'suspicious cases'. Mixed usage - person-first in the formal descriptions, but the comparison group is called 'normal' in the hypothesis statements and misclassified controls are described as 'suspicious cases'. The paper also uses 'high-functional in autism range' when explaining errors. [RQ1.3] ASD n=8, age range 2.1-4.1 years. TD n=8, age range 2.11-7.6 years. No means, no standard deviations, and no gender distribution for either group. The groups are not age-matched and the mismatch is substantial - the control range extends to 7.6 years while no autistic child was older than 4.1 - which is a serious confound for a measure based on where a child physically positions themselves relative to a robot, since approach behaviour, mobility and social confidence all change markedly between age 2 and age 7. Very young sample, so relevant in principle to early screening. [RQ1.4] Diagnosis by a clinical team - a developmental-behavioural pediatrician and a child psychologist - with a child psychiatrist validating the psychologist's initial evaluation. This multi-clinician process is described in more detail than most corpus studies, but no standardised instrument is named (no ADOS, ADI-R, GARS or SCQ), despite the introduction reviewing exactly such instruments. Control status was established by attendance at mainstream daycare and absence of observed cognitive deficit, with no screening instrument. [RQ1.5] None reported. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive measures for either group, and no autism severity instrument. Functioning level enters only as a post-hoc anecdote - two misclassified autistic children are described as 'high-functional in autism range' - which is used to explain errors rather than as measured data. [RQ2.1] Goal: automate an existing manually-coded robot-interaction screening protocol. Main findings: the time-weighted spatial occupancy pattern (WPV cosine similarity) separated the groups significantly (t-test p=0.001, ANOVA p=1.09e-05) while the binary presence pattern did not (p=0.160); the ratio of time spent directly in front of the robot was also significant (p<0.05); a Gaussian SVM stacking both feature families reached 81.3% accuracy with 2 false positives and 1 false negative; a random-regrouping control produced no significant differences, confirming the effect was not an artefact. [RQ2.2] Clinic setting - the Center for Treatment of Autistic Disorders (Tehran Autism), with the robot placed in a cage and cameras positioned overhead and beside it. Newly recorded interaction data, but building directly on an existing robot-screening platform and protocol from the same research group. [RQ2.3] A fixed 190-second scenario of interaction with RoboParrot, beginning with a greeting from the robot followed by several communication actions designed to motivate the child to engage further. The robot speaks, blinks, sings, laughs and moves slightly, and is teleoperated from a tablet. Parents accompanied their child but were instructed not to get involved. The child is free to move within the space in front of the robot; there is no task instruction to the child. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single 190-second session per child with no repeat or follow-up. The data are highly sensitive - continuous video of identifiable young children from two angles, including a close-range facial camera, plus a published photograph of a child interacting with the robot. There is no ethics approval statement, no parental consent statement, and no anonymization or data-protection provision anywhere in the paper. Only the funding council and recruiting clinic are acknowledged. [RQ2.5] Hardware: RoboParrot, a parrot-like social robot with speech, blinking, singing, laughing and limited movement, teleoperated by tablet and placed inside a cage; two cameras, one beside the robot for facial expression and one overhead for global movement. Software: motion detection or manual tagging for initial child detection; Kernelized Correlation Filter tracking, chosen after comparison against MIL, Boosting and TLD trackers; custom grid partitioning, cosine similarity, and classifiers. No specific software packages or versions are named. [RQ2.6] Poor. No data availability statement, no code, no software versions, no hyperparameters (the Gaussian SVM kernel width and the KNN k are never given), no random seeds, and no specification of how the 4x4 grid maps onto physical space. Table 1, which holds the per-group presence ratios, is not recoverable as values. The method is describable in principle - grid occupancy, cosine similarity, standard classifiers - but no quantitative result other than the accuracies and p-values can be extracted from the paper. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors: the limited number of cases is explicitly named as a limitation, with a stated plan to run on more children; and the method is acknowledged to fail on shy typically developing children, which the authors address by arguing it should be combined with other screening methods rather than used alone. Identifiable in review: control age range (2.11-7.6 years) roughly doubles the ASD range (2.1-4.1) with no matching, confounding age with group in a spatial-approach measure; no gender data despite a strongly sex-skewed condition; no diagnostic instrument; the best of five classifiers across three feature configurations is reported with no nesting of that selection inside the 8-fold cross-validation; the stacking layer degrades four of five classifiers, so the 81.3% may reflect a fortunate combination rather than a real gain; and post-hoc explanations of the four first-layer errors (shyness, high functioning) are unmeasured narrative rather than data. [RQ2.9] Test on more children for higher accuracy and confidence; study child-parent interaction during screening sessions; develop a more robust protocol to cut image-processing cost and complexity; exploit the front camera for facial emotion and other features; and integrate with other intelligent screening approaches. The last of these follows directly from their own finding that the method misclassifies shy typically developing children, so it is a limitation-driven rather than generic proposal. [RQ3.1] Spatial/locomotor behaviour: the child's physical position and dwell time relative to a social robot, derived from overhead video tracking. Facial video is captured but not analysed. This is proxemic and approach behaviour rather than gaze, speech or fine motor kinematics. [RQ3.2] Two feature families derived from the same modality - similarity of time-weighted spatial occupancy patterns, and the presence ratio in the robot-facing cell - are each fed to separate first-layer classifiers whose outputs are combined by a second-layer classifier. The authors describe this explicitly as a form of sensor fusion, though both inputs come from one sensor; it is decision-level fusion across feature views. Notably the fusion helped only the SVM (75% and 75% to 81.3%) and hurt the other four classifiers (dropping to 68.8%). No integration with clinical scores, demographics or parent report. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning. Algorithms: decision tree, k-nearest neighbours, Gaussian-kernel SVM, linear discriminant analysis and logistic regression, each evaluated on both feature families and on the stacked combination. Gaussian SVM was selected as the final model. Statistical hypothesis testing (t-test, ANOVA) is used alongside classification to establish that the features carry group information. [RQ4.2] Symbolic/spatial-occupancy representation: continuous tracked position is discretised onto a 4x4 grid and summarised either as a 16-bit binary occupancy vector or a 16-dimensional dwell-time proportion vector, then converted into pairwise cosine similarities between children. The classification features are therefore relational - how similar this child's spatial pattern is to others' - rather than absolute, which is an unusual representation choice in this corpus and one that makes the features dependent on the composition of the sample. [RQ4.3] Accuracy only, reported for five classifiers across three feature configurations, supplemented by narrative false-positive and false-negative counts (2 and 1 for the final model). No sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, AUC or confidence intervals, though the raw counts allow them to be derived: with 8 per group, 2 FP and 1 FN gives sensitivity 87.5% and specificity 75%. [RQ4.4] Interpretability comes from statistical comparison rather than model attribution. The Weighted Presence Vector similarity is shown to separate groups (p=0.001) while the binary Presence Vector does not (p=0.160), which is an informative negative result: the discriminative signal lies in how long a child stays near the robot, not in which regions they ever visit. The presence ratio in the robot-facing cell is directly interpretable as attraction to the robot. Importantly, the authors ran a permutation-style control - randomly regrouping the children and repeating the analysis, which produced no significant differences - a check almost no other study in this corpus performs. [RQ4.5] Limited. 8-fold cross-validation is used and explicitly motivated by overfitting prevention, but with 16 children this leaves two per test fold, and neither the choice among five classifiers nor the two-layer stacking design is nested inside it. The random-regrouping control is a genuine robustness check on the statistical claim, though not on the classifier. There is no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no class-imbalance issue (8/8), and no real-time or deployment evaluation despite screening being the stated application. Generalisability is addressed only by the authors' plan to test more children, and the known failure mode (shy typically developing children) is handled by proposing combination with other methods rather than by any modelling change. [RQ5.1] Keywords as printed: 'autism screening; human robot interactions; image processing; classification' (the keyword line retains an unedited template fragment, 'Keywords-component; formatting'). Task vocabulary: 'autism screening', 'human-robot interaction', 'vision-based approach', 'Presence Vector', 'Weighted Presence Vector', 'suspicious cases'. [RQ5.2] The 6th RSI International Conference on Robotics and Mechatronics (IcRoM 2018), Tehran - a technology/robotics venue, not an autism or clinical venue. [RQ5.3] 2018. The paper situates itself against traditional questionnaire-and-expert screening (3DI, ASD-OC), noting clinical guidance that no questionnaire can be recommended as a diagnostic test and that a combination of direct behavioural observation and caregiver report is recommended instead - then frames robot-based screening as 'a new trend'. Its own contribution is explicitly the automation of a previously manual feature-extraction step in an existing robot protocol, illustrating the corpus-wide progression from manually coded behavioural observation to automated sensing of the same behaviour. |
| S-013 | Cross-sectional case-control proof of concept; 37 Chinese children with ASD (mean age 4.6, CARS 34.4, 89% male) vs 37 age- and gender-matched typically developing children (mean age 4.8) screened by a physician; newly collected eye-tracking data from a single 10 s stimulus, not released. | SMI RED250 eye tracking at 250 Hz during passive viewing of a 10 s muted video of a female mouthing the alphabet, in a dark soundproof room at fixed 65 cm viewing distance; fixation times computed for ten predefined areas of interest plus three within-face ratios; group comparisons by t-test with Bonferroni correction; SVM classification with five-fold cross-validation, with both accuracy and per-AOI discriminative weights tested by 1000-iteration permutation. | Fixation times significantly lower in ASD at eyes, mouth, nose, body, person, face and outer-person (p<0.005 corrected), but no difference in eyes-to-face, mouth-to-face or nose-to-face ratios. Only mouth (p=0.008) and body (p=0.03) carried significant discriminative weight. Classification 85.1% accuracy, 86.5% sensitivity, 83.8% specificity, above chance by permutation (p<0.001). Fixation time correlated with the Gesell large-motion subscore in ASD. | No ADOS or ADI-R confirmation (authors' own first limitation); no IQ or adaptive-behaviour measure; n=74 with single-site, ethnically homogeneous recruitment; gender 89% vs 73% male despite non-significant chi-square; nesting of AOI selection within cross-validation unstated; and two mutually inconsistent sets of accuracy figures reported for the same analysis. | The corpus's strongest demonstration that a very short paradigm - ten seconds of passive viewing - can carry usable screening signal, and one of the few studies to test feature importance with permutation rather than ranking. Its most valuable contribution is a negative one that survived reporting: the ASD group looked less overall but did not redistribute attention within the face, so the discriminative signal here is global reduced social attention rather than eye avoidance specifically. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of 37: children with ASD recruited from a hospital child mental health outpatient ward, and typically developing children recruited from a local kindergarten. Both groups fully characterised in a demographic table. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD children', 'the ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD group', 'individuals with autism', 'patients' (once, when discussing evaluation bias). Predominantly person-first with 'ASD children' used interchangeably; the comparison group is consistently 'typically developing' rather than 'normal', which is the more neutral convention. [RQ1.3] ASD n=37, 33 boys / 4 girls, age 4.6 +/- 0.7 years, CARS 34.4 +/- 7.8. TD n=37, 27 boys / 10 girls, age 4.8 +/- 0.4 years. Age matched by design with no significant difference (p = 0.17), and gender difference non-significant by chi-square (p = 0.14) - though the actual distributions are 89% versus 73% male, so the matching is statistically defensible rather than close. Narrow 4-6 year age band by inclusion criterion, directly relevant to early screening but, as the authors note, leaving open whether the finding generalises to younger children. [RQ1.4] DSM-5 diagnosis by experienced physicians plus a CARS score above 30 as an explicit inclusion criterion. The authors state directly that ADI-R and ADOS were unavailable in China and list the absence of confirmation with validated diagnostic instruments as their first limitation - an unusually forthright acknowledgement. Controls were screened by a licensed physician to exclude any psychiatric or neurological history including ASD, which is a stronger control-status procedure than most corpus studies. [RQ1.5] The Gesell Developmental Scale (Chinese version) was administered to the ASD group, with adaptation, large motion, fine motion, language and personal-social subscores all reported - one of the fuller functional characterisations in the corpus. However the authors themselves list the absence of IQ and adaptive behaviour measures as their second limitation, and no GDS or other functional data were collected for the control group. Comorbidities are not described for the ASD group. [RQ2.1] Goal: early screening, with the specific design question of whether a very short paradigm suffices, plus replication of an infant speaking-face finding in an older age group. Main findings: fixation times significantly lower in ASD at seven of ten AOIs after Bonferroni correction; no differences in any within-face ratio; only mouth (p=0.008) and body (p=0.03) fixation carried significant discriminative weight; SVM accuracy 85.1%, sensitivity 86.5%, specificity 83.8%, above chance by permutation (p<0.001); fixation time correlated with the GDS large-motion subscore (p<0.01 corrected). [RQ2.2] Clinic setting for testing (a dark, soundproof room with fixed viewing geometry) with clinical recruitment from a hospital outpatient ward and control recruitment from a kindergarten in the same city. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used. [RQ2.3] Passive viewing, deliberately minimal: five-point calibration, then eye-position correction on a dynamic pink rabbit, then a single 10-second muted video of a young Asian female mouthing the English alphabet. The brevity is the explicit design contribution - the authors argue that with young children the paradigm must be short as well as informative, since keeping such subjects focused on a monitor for long periods is difficult. The stimulus is muted, so the speaking face provides visual mouth motion without audio. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single 10-second measurement per child with no follow-up. The data are fixation durations on predefined regions - among the least identifiable data types in the corpus. Ethics approval from the hospital research committee is reported with explicit reference to the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its amendments, informed consent was obtained from parents of all participants, and a conflict-of-interest disclosure is given for one author. Ethics and consent reporting is essentially complete. [RQ2.5] Hardware: SMI RED250 portable eye tracker sampling at 250 Hz with 0.03 degree spatial resolution; 22-inch widescreen LCD at 1024x768; fixed 65 cm eye-to-monitor distance; dark soundproof room. Software: BeGaze for gaze data analysis; SPSS 22.0 for statistics, group comparisons and the SVM discriminant analysis. [RQ2.6] No data availability statement and no code release. Method reporting is nonetheless strong: eye-tracker model, sampling rate, spatial resolution, screen resolution, viewing distance, calibration procedure, stimulus content and duration, the full AOI definitions and the ratio definitions are all specified, as are the cross-validation folds and the permutation counts. The analysis is re-implementable in principle on comparable data; the specific SVM kernel and regularisation settings are not given. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors in an explicit five-point limitations list: ADOS/ADI-R unavailable so diagnoses rest on DSM-5 and CARS alone; no IQ or adaptive-behaviour measure of functional level; relatively small sample requiring larger-sample validation; unknown whether findings are specific to the 4-6 age group; and no direct comparison against or combination with other eye-tracking paradigms. Identifiable in review: gender is imbalanced in practice (89% vs 73% male) despite a non-significant chi-square on n=74; the control group has no GDS or functional data so the correlational analysis cannot be contrasted across groups; single-site recruitment with an ethnically homogeneous sample viewing an Asian female face, leaving cross-cultural transfer untested; whether AOI selection was nested inside the five-fold cross-validation is unstated; and the paper reports two mutually inconsistent sets of accuracy figures for the same analysis. [RQ2.9] Larger-sample validation; extension to other populations, particularly young infants, where early detection would matter most; determination of whether the effect is age-group specific; direct head-to-head comparison of this short paradigm against established longer paradigms; and combination of the short paradigm with other paradigms. The authors also state a general principle rather than a research step - that current ASD biomarkers including eye tracking are supplementary and not replacements for clinical assessment. [RQ3.1] Gaze: fixation duration on predefined facial and body regions during passive viewing of a speaking face. Aggregate dwell time per region rather than scanpath, saccade dynamics or pupillometry. [RQ3.2] Single modality; no fusion. Within the modality, ten regional fixation times plus three derived ratios are supplied jointly to the SVM, which is feature-level combination across regions. Gaze data are separately correlated with Gesell developmental subscores using age and gender as covariates - an integration with clinical measures for interpretation rather than for prediction. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning with a single algorithm: support vector machine, described as discriminant analysis. No comparison against alternative classifiers, which is unusual for this corpus and arguably a strength - it removes the best-of-many selection optimism that inflates other studies here. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted region-aggregated features: total fixation time per area of interest over the 10-second clip, plus three normalising ratios. Extremely low-dimensional - ten AOIs and three ratios against 74 children - which is a far healthier feature-to-sample ratio than most studies in this corpus and materially reduces overfitting risk. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, with a permutation-derived p-value establishing that accuracy exceeds chance. Headline: 85.1% / 86.5% / 83.8% (p<0.001). No AUC, F1 or confidence intervals. A contradictory second set of figures (82.8% / 79.3% / 86.2%) appears in the Discussion for what is described as the same analysis, and is never reconciled. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is handled better than in most of the corpus. SVM discriminative weights per AOI are tested by 1000-iteration permutation against the null that weights are arbitrary, so feature importance carries a p-value rather than a rank. Only mouth (p=0.008) and body (p=0.03) survive. The most informative result is a negative one: although fixation was globally reduced in ASD across seven AOIs, none of the eyes-to-face, mouth-to-face or nose-to-face ratios differed, so the group difference is in total looking rather than in the within-face distribution of attention - a finding that complicates the common eye-avoidance interpretation and which the authors report rather than suppress. [RQ4.5] Five-fold cross-validation, with two separate permutation procedures - one testing whether classification accuracy exceeds chance (1000 label permutations) and one testing whether each AOI's discriminative weight is non-arbitrary (1000 permutations). Multiple comparisons across the ten AOI group tests are Bonferroni-corrected, and the correlational analysis with GDS subscores is likewise corrected, with the authors explicitly flagging which correlations did not survive correction. What is absent: external or independent validation, held-out site, any statement of whether AOI selection is nested within the folds, class-imbalance handling (not needed at 37/37), and any deployment or real-time analysis - though the authors explicitly position eye tracking as supplementary to clinical assessment rather than a replacement. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: Autism; Eye tracking; Fixation time; Machine learning; Face. Task vocabulary: 'early detection', 'screening', 'biomarkers', 'areas-of-interest', 'discriminant analysis', 'proof of concept'. The paper's framing of biomarkers as 'supplementary' rather than diagnostic is a distinctive and unusually cautious note. [RQ5.2] Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders - an autism-specific clinical journal, not a computational venue. [RQ5.3] 2018 (published online August 2018, in the 2019 volume). The paper documents the field's trajectory in some detail: eye tracking as 'one emerging objective tool increasingly being applied in ASD clinics and research', machine learning recently applied to behaviour, brain activity and eye tracking with 'encouraging results', and ASD biomarker research having 'grown exponentially' with integration into future risk assessment 'almost certain'. It also situates itself against three specific predecessors (Shic et al. on infants, Liu et al. on face-scanning machine learning, Fujioka et al. on adults), comparing accuracies directly - one of the more explicitly cumulative papers in the corpus. |
| S-014 | 17-month naturalistic home data collection with cross-sectional classification; 35 US children recruited (18 ASD, 9 TD, 8 undiagnosed at-risk siblings), 27 analysed, aged 3 months to 17 years at recruitment with no matching; 1858 structured-test recordings (19.8 h) and 7427 monitoring recordings (890.4 h), not released. | Custom iOS app on iPod Touch with external microphone, mailed to families and used unsupervised at home; four gamified tests (picture description, word, sentence and story reading using GFTA material) plus voice-activity-triggered passive monitoring; COVAREP acoustic functionals (222-dim per recording) and LIWC plus task-specific linguistic features; feature-level fusion across five sources into 1330 dimensions with -1 padding for missing sources; CFS feature selection and an SGD-trained hinge-loss SVM; leave-one-subject-out with a separate 8-subject development set. | Unweighted average F1 0.87, accuracy 88.9% (24/27), with the three misclassified subjects identified and two attributed to low data volume. Single-source F1: story reading 0.77, word reading 0.76, monitoring 0.72, picture description 0.68, sentence reading 0.49, usage pattern 0.47.
