CFS selected features from all five sources; acoustic features (MCEP, HMPDM, quasi-open quotient) dominated linguistic ones. | No diagnostic instrument reported for any participant; 27 analysed children spanning 3 months to 17 years, entirely unmatched on age or gender, with toddlers concentrated in the ASD group and teenagers among controls - a decisive confound for voice-quality features; 1330 features against 27 subjects; data volume varying from 4 to 1968 recordings per child with no minimum threshold; the 17-month longitudinal structure collapsed to a single averaged vector; no ethics or consent statement for 890 hours of in-home audio; no external validation. | The corpus's only genuinely home-based, unsupervised, long-duration behavioral data collection, and its clearest articulation of a global health-equity motivation for automated screening. Methodologically it is the strongest demonstration that multi-source fusion beats any single elicitation task, quantified by ablation, and one of few studies to report a negative result against its own hypothesis. It is also the corpus's sharpest illustration of a confound the authors half-saw: they excluded age as a feature because recruitment might have correlated it with the label, without addressing that the same correlation exists in the sample itself. | [RQ1.1] Three groups recruited: 18 children diagnosed with ASD, 9 typically developing children, and 8 at-risk children defined as undiagnosed younger siblings of ASD children. Only the 27 with definite TD or ASD status entered the classification experiment; the at-risk group was excluded because undiagnosed, which is handled transparently. Per-subject characteristics are tabulated individually. [RQ1.2] 'ASD children', 'children diagnosed with ASD', 'affected individuals', 'affected children', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'at-risk children', and notably 'the child's health condition' when referring to diagnostic status. Predominantly diagnosis-first ('ASD children') with a medicalised framing of autism as a health condition; the paper also uses 'neurodevelopmental disability' and 'disorder' interchangeably. [RQ1.3] This is the study's weakest reporting. Sample sizes are clear (18 ASD, 9 TD, 8 at-risk) and every subject's individual age, gender and diagnosis is listed in Table 1, but no group-level age mean, SD or gender distribution is computed anywhere, and no matching or comparability test is performed. Ages span 3 months to 17 years at recruitment. Inspecting Table 1, the ASD group includes children aged 2, 3 and 4 years while the TD group includes 16-year-olds, so the groups are grossly unmatched on age - a decisive confound for acoustic voice features, which change dramatically across childhood and adolescence. [RQ1.4] Not reported at all. Children are described as 'diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, no criteria, no diagnosing professional and no date. TD status is asserted without any screening. At-risk status is defined purely by sibling relationship. Given that diagnostic label is the classification target and the paper proposes a screening tool, the complete absence of reference-standard information is the study's most serious gap. [RQ1.5] None reported. No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive-functioning measures, no autism severity instrument, and no comorbidity information for any group. The reading materials are drawn from the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, so a standardised articulation instrument supplies the stimuli, but it is not scored as an assessment. The authors note narratively that 'some non-verbal children may not able to finish the reading test' but no verbal-ability data exist. [RQ2.1] Goal: a practical, affordable, fully automatic home screening tool requiring no professional help, explicitly motivated by the scarcity of psychiatrists in South East Asia, the Western Pacific and Africa (0.21, 0.28 and 0.05 per 100,000). Main findings: unweighted F1 0.87 and accuracy 88.9% (24/27) from fused multi-source features; every single source performed worse alone (best 0.77); acoustic features dominated linguistic ones; and usage pattern was not discriminative. [RQ2.2] Home setting, and uniquely so in this corpus - devices were mailed to families and all collection occurred inside children's homes with no professional supervision, deliberately to emulate real deployment of child-specific smart devices. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used. [RQ2.3] Two complementary protocols. Structured: four gamified exercises activated by child or parent - picture description of social scenarios (9 pictures), word reading (5 lists of 10-11 words), sentence reading (2 sentences) and story reading (2 ~100-word stories), with materials drawn from the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation and reproduced in full in the appendix. Unstructured: a monitoring mode that continuously listens and begins recording on voice-activity detection, capturing everyday communication. Crucially the paper documents real-world protocol failure honestly, reproducing a transcript in which a parent prompts and speaks over the child throughout a word-reading test, and designing error-robust features (irrelevant-word and repeated-word ratios) in response. [RQ2.4] Longitudinal in collection (17 months, April 2016 to September 2017) but cross-sectional in analysis - all of a subject's recordings are averaged into one feature vector, so no temporal or developmental modelling is performed despite the long span. The data are among the most sensitive in the corpus: 890 hours of passive in-home audio from children's bedrooms, inevitably capturing parents and other household members. Two protections are described - HIPAA-compliant encryption (Sookasa over Dropbox) for cloud storage, and parent-controlled activation/deactivation of monitoring mode 'for privacy considerations'. But there is no ethics approval statement, no IRB reference, no parental or child consent statement, and no consideration of consent for third parties recorded incidentally. [RQ2.5] Hardware: Apple iPod Touch with an iRig Mic Cast external microphone (chosen to ensure data quality), sent to each family. Software: a custom iOS app implementing the four gamified tests and the monitoring mode with voice-activity-triggered recording and automatic cloud upload; Sookasa for HIPAA-compliant encrypted Dropbox storage; COVAREP for acoustic feature extraction; Google Cloud Speech-to-Text for ASR; LIWC for linguistic analysis; a custom self-adaptive SVM voice-activity segmentation using per-recording energy percentiles to handle varying background noise. [RQ2.6] No data availability statement and no code release. Method reporting is otherwise strong: all toolkits are named and are standard (COVAREP, LIWC, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text), feature dimensions are tabulated per source and per type totalling 1330, the missing-data encoding (-1 padding rather than interpolation) is stated, normalisation is described, the grid-search ranges for epochs and learning rate are given, and the complete reading and picture stimulus materials are reproduced in an appendix. The pipeline is re-implementable; the corpus is not accessible. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors, unusually thoroughly for a conference paper: large variance in data volume per subject (4 to 1968 recordings) driven by device-usage preference rather than condition; real-life data errors including interrupted tests and parents completing tests on the child's behalf, which would overestimate development level; varying background noise across subjects; absence of speaker diarization so child and parent speech cannot be separated; ASR error rates that increase precisely when child speech is atypical, undermining the linguistic features; and misclassification associated with low data volume for two of the three errors. They also deliberately excluded age and gender as features because 'in the subject recruitment process, it is possible that age and gender information have some implicit connection with the label'. Identifiable in review: that same recruitment confound is not addressed at the sample level - ages span 3 months to 17 years with toddlers over-represented in the ASD group and teenagers among the TD group, entirely unmatched, so acoustic maturation is confounded with diagnosis; 18 ASD versus 9 TD with only 27 analysed; no diagnostic instrument whatsoever; no ethics or consent statement; and the 17-month longitudinal structure is collapsed to a single averaged vector, discarding the developmental information the design was uniquely placed to capture. [RQ2.9] Develop a speaker diarization algorithm suited to everyday monitoring conditions, named as important future work because the absence of diarization degrades both acoustic and linguistic analysis; incorporate age and gender to enable age- and gender-dependent fine-grained inference; and extend beyond screening to evaluating intervention effectiveness and tracking child development over time. [RQ3.1] Speech and language jointly: acoustic/paralinguistic properties (voice quality, spectral envelope, harmonic phase distortion, F0) and linguistic content derived from ASR transcripts (LIWC categories, vocabulary size, repetition, reading accuracy, words per second). The explicit joint acoustic-linguistic framing is unusual in this corpus, where most speech studies are purely paralinguistic. [RQ3.2] Fusion is the paper's central methodological claim and is done at two levels. Across modalities: acoustic and linguistic features are extracted separately and concatenated. Across sources: features from four structured tests plus passive monitoring plus usage pattern are all concatenated into one 1330-dimensional vector, with missing sources explicitly encoded as -1 so the model can handle non-participation rather than requiring imputation. The benefit is quantified by ablation - every single source scored 0.47-0.77 alone against 0.87 fused - and confirmed by CFS selecting at least one feature from each source, which the authors correctly note implies the sources are complementary rather than redundant given CFS's redundancy penalty. No integration with clinical scores or demographics, deliberately. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning. Algorithm: binary SVM optimised by stochastic gradient descent with a hinge loss objective, preceded by correlation-based feature subset selection. No deep learning, and no comparison against alternative classifiers - the paper's contribution is the data collection and fusion scheme rather than the model. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted features at two levels of abstraction: acoustic functionals (mean, max, min over 74 COVAREP descriptors sampled at 10 ms, giving 222 dimensions per recording, then averaged across recordings) and symbolic linguistic features from ASR transcripts (LIWC psycholinguistic categories, plus task-performance counts such as correct, irrelevant and repeated word ratios and word error rate). Notably the task-specific features are designed to be robust to the real-world failure mode observed - a parent prompting the child - by counting irrelevant and repeated words rather than only correct ones. [RQ4.3] Unweighted average F1-score as the primary metric, selected explicitly because the classes are unbalanced (18 ASD vs 9 TD) - the methodologically correct choice and one only a minority of corpus studies make. Accuracy (88.9%) and a confusion matrix are also reported, along with per-single-source F1 scores enabling the fusion ablation. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confidence intervals. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is handled through three complementary analyses. CFS selection reports exactly which features were chosen from which source. Per-source correlation coefficients with the diagnostic label are tabulated with the top five features per source. Single-source ablation quantifies each source's standalone contribution. The findings are substantive: acoustic features dominate, specifically high-order Mel cepstrum envelope and harmonic model phase distortion mean coefficients plus quasi-open quotient - all voice-quality measures; only one linguistic feature (LIWC_Interrog) survives CFS, and linguistic features appear in the top-five correlations of only the picture description test, leading the authors to conclude that linguistic features are discriminative mainly when speech content is not fixed. Directions of effect are not reported, only correlation magnitudes. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-subject-out with a genuine three-way split - one test subject, 18 training and 8 development subjects, with epochs and learning rate grid-searched on development only - which is subject-independent and separates model selection from performance estimation. Class imbalance is addressed at the metric level via unweighted F1. Robustness to real-world data corruption is a design goal rather than an afterthought: missing sources are explicitly encoded, error-correcting linguistic features are designed against the observed parent-prompting failure, and voice-activity segmentation adapts per recording to differing noise levels. Age and gender are deliberately excluded to prevent the model exploiting recruitment-correlated demographics. Absent: external or independent validation, any held-out site or device, calibration, and any deployment measurement despite the app being the contribution. Whether CFS is recomputed inside each leave-one-out fold is stated only as being 'conducted in the model training', which is suggestive but not explicit. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: Autism spectrum disorders, pervasive health, data mining, speech processing, natural language processing. Task vocabulary: 'ASD screening tool', 'ASD biomarkers', 'fully automatic', 'everyday vocalizations', 'continuous and transparent monitoring', 'first ASD screening solution'. The 'pervasive health' and 'transparent monitoring' framing situates this in ubiquitous computing rather than clinical assessment. [RQ5.2] ACM-BCB'18 - the 9th ACM International Conference on Bioinformatics, Computational Biology and Health Informatics, in the mHealth session. A technology/health-informatics venue, not an autism or clinical journal. [RQ5.3] 2018. The paper characterises prior speech-based autism work as demonstrating that vocalisations contain usable biomarkers across infants, young children and teenagers, but criticises it on two specific grounds: recordings are 'mostly based on audio data obtained in very controlled environments' and are 'often manually reviewed, segmented, and processed by speech experts', which limits both practicality and recording length. It positions the emergence of affordable child-specific smart devices (Amazon Echo Kids Edition at $79, Xiaomi Kids Smartwatch at $45) as the enabling shift - documenting the corpus-wide movement from laboratory instrumentation toward consumer hardware and naturalistic settings, and framing it explicitly as a global health-equity argument. |
| S-015 | Cross-sectional case-control secondary analysis; 15 autistic adults (9M/6F, mean age 37) vs 15 AQ-screened non-autistic adults (8M/7F, mean age 33.7) in the UK; eye-tracking data over six web pages, released openly with code and stimuli. | Gazepoint GP3 at 60 Hz recording browsing (2 min/page) and searching (30 s/page, two questions each) over six web pages of graded visual complexity; per-AOI gaze features (time to first view, time viewed, time viewed %, fixations, revisits) computed under both VIPS-derived page-specific AOIs and a generic 2x2 grid, plus contextual non-gaze variables; logistic regression in R with 100-fold participant-level cross-validation (10 train, 5 test participants per group) and majority-vote aggregation to participant decisions. | Best 0.75 accuracy for Search with page-specific AOIs; Browse best 0.71 (95% CI 0.69-0.73) on the Apple and AVG pages, 0.66 across all pages. Generic AOIs matched page-specific ones for browsing (0.70 vs 0.71) but collapsed for searching (0.56 vs 0.75). Adding AOI or media ID lowered accuracy. Gender, visual complexity and correct-answer location had no significant effect. Confusion matrices showed balanced per-class performance. | No diagnostic instrument named, with case verification delegated to the recruiting charity; 30 high-functioning computer-using adults with intellectual disability excluded; stimuli were repurposed from a web-accessibility study and never designed to elicit group differences, which the authors identify as capping accuracy; unsuitable for the young children where screening would matter most; best figure selected across tasks, AOI schemes, feature sets and page subsets, though all alternatives are reported with intervals. | The corpus's reference point for methodological honesty and open science: it diagnoses segment-level rather than participant-level partitioning as a source of inflated accuracy in the prior literature, adopts strict participant-level validation in response, reports confidence intervals on every number, releases data, code and stimuli, compares its own 0.75 unfavourably against fMRI results, and raises ethical concerns about its own future application. Its finding that area-of-interest definition interacts with task type is also a transferable design lesson absent from the rest of the gaze literature here. | [RQ1.1] Two groups: adults with a confirmed clinical diagnosis of high-functioning autism or Asperger's syndrome (18 recruited, 15 analysed) and non-autistic control adults (18 recruited, 15 analysed after 2 data-quality exclusions and 1 random removal to balance classes). All recruitment, exclusion and balancing decisions are reported explicitly, including the random removal. No other-diagnosis group. [RQ1.2] 'people with autism', 'participants with autism', 'people on the autism spectrum', 'autistic individuals', 'autistic readers', 'the group with autism', 'neurotypical participants', 'control group of participants without autism', 'non-autistic control participants'. Notably mixed and deliberately so - the paper uses 'people with autism' and 'autistic' interchangeably, consistently pairs them with 'neurotypical' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy', and uses 'condition' rather than 'disorder' in its own prose. It also frames misdiagnosis in terms of harm to 'a person's self-perception', a person-centred framing absent elsewhere in the corpus. [RQ1.3] ASD n=15 analysed (9 male, 6 female), mean age 37 +/- 9.14 years, mean 16 +/- 3.33 years of formal education. Control n=15 analysed (8 male, 7 female), mean age 33.66 +/- 8.6 years, mean 18.35 +/- 2.47 years of formal education. No formal matching procedure or comparability test is reported, though age and gender are close in practice. At 40% and 47% female, this is by a wide margin the most gender-balanced sample in the corpus - most comparable studies are 80-90% male. Adults only, and the authors explicitly acknowledge that web tasks are unsuitable for the young children where early detection would matter most. Education differs by about 2.3 years in the controls' favour, which is not discussed. [RQ1.4] A confirmed clinical diagnosis of autism 'as verified by the charity organisation' through which participants were recruited - no instrument, criteria or clinician is named, and verification is delegated to a third-party organisation. By contrast, control status is established rigorously with the Autism Quotient, with an explicit threshold (none above 32) and a rationale (the AQ is used by UK general practitioners as pre-referral screening). As in several other corpus studies, the control ascertainment is better specified than the case ascertainment. [RQ1.5] Years of formal education reported for both groups; web-use frequency assessed for all participants (all daily users); familiarity with each of the six stimulus websites surveyed to rule out over-familiarity confounds. No IQ, language or adaptive-functioning measures, and no autism severity score for the autistic group. Comorbidity handled only by excluding formally diagnosed intellectual disability, which bounds the sample to high-functioning adults. [RQ2.1] Goal: accessible, unobtrusive, scalable screening from everyday behavioural data, explicitly framed as a route to a future serious game rather than as a diagnostic substitute. Main findings: 0.75 accuracy for the Search task with page-specific AOIs; 0.71 (CI 0.69-0.73) for Browse on the two most predictive pages; task type matters (search beats browse); AOI definition matters and interacts with task (generic 2x2 grid gives 0.70 for browse but only 0.56 for search); gender, visual complexity and correct-answer location had no significant influence; adding AOI ID or media ID lowered accuracy relative to gaze features alone. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting with a controlled eye tracker and fixed viewing distance. Existing data - the eye-tracking corpus was originally collected to investigate web-searching difficulties experienced by autistic users, and the authors are explicit that 'the data used in this study was not collected with this objective in mind', treating this as a limitation on achievable accuracy. [RQ2.3] Two contrasting tasks over the same six web page screenshots. Browsing: up to two minutes per page, free to read or ignore anything, moving on when ready. Searching: 30 seconds per page to answer two questions posed verbally by the researcher, with the answer read aloud - the full set of twelve questions is published in a table. Pages were presented in randomised order per participant and the two tasks were counterbalanced. Pages spanned three ViCRAM-rated visual complexity levels, giving a designed manipulation of stimulus complexity. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single session with no follow-up. Gaze data over public web pages carry low re-identification risk, which is part of why the data can be released openly. Full ethical approval was obtained from the University of Wolverhampton Faculty of Arts Ethics Committee before collection, all participants signed consent forms after being familiarised with the purpose and procedure, and participants were debriefed. Uniquely in this corpus, the authors also flag prospective ethical risk in the discussion, warning that future profiling of conditions from web-searching behaviour 'will raise ethical considerations which should not be treated lightly'. [RQ2.5] Hardware: Gazepoint GP3 video-based eye tracker at 60 Hz with 0.5-1 degree of visual angle accuracy, a 19-inch LCD monitor, and an integrated sensor controlling viewing distance at approximately 65 cm; nine-point calibration. Software: Gazepoint software for capture; the extended VIPS (Vision-Based Page Segmentation) algorithm for page-specific AOI definition; the ViCRAM tool for rating page visual complexity; R for logistic regression and cross-validation. [RQ2.6] The best in the corpus. An explicit 'Open Data' section states that the eye-tracking data, code, and materials are available at a named GitHub repository, and the abstract states the gaze data, R code, visual stimuli and task descriptions are 'made freely available for replication purposes'. Full replicability is listed as one of the paper's three stated contributions. Beyond the release, the paper publishes the complete search question set, the AOI definition methods, the eye tracker specifications, viewing distance, calibration procedure, cross-validation scheme, and confidence intervals for every configuration, and directs readers to the repository for results of page combinations not shown in the paper. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors in a dedicated Limitations subsection: the 0.75 accuracy compares unfavourably with the 71-86.7% range reported for fMRI classifiers, which they attribute partly to the data not having been collected for classification; web-searching tasks are unsuitable for the very young children in whom early detection would be most valuable, so a different task would be needed to reach them; and the sample is not large, though they note it exceeds the 12-per-group benchmark study they compare against. Identifiable in review: no diagnostic instrument is named, with verification delegated to the recruiting charity; formally diagnosed intellectual disability is an exclusion criterion so results apply only to high-functioning adults; control education exceeds autistic education by 2.3 years, undiscussed; the headline is selected across two tasks, two AOI schemes, four feature sets and multiple page subsets - though every alternative is reported with confidence intervals, making the selection auditable; and the participant-level aggregation rule (majority vote over behaviours) is a design choice whose sensitivity is not explored. [RQ2.9] Design tasks specifically intended to amplify visual-processing differences between groups, since the present stimuli were repurposed; explore capturing the same differences without an eye tracker at all, using operation logs, mouse clicks, task accuracy and miss rate, so that screening could run on ordinary hardware; develop a serious game for large-scale accessible screening; extend the gaze-classifier approach to other conditions with visual attention differences such as dementia, schizophrenia and ADHD; and confront the ethical implications of profiling for clinical conditions from web behaviour. [RQ3.1] Gaze: fixation timing, duration, count and revisit behaviour within areas of interest during naturalistic web interaction. Distinctively, the stimuli are real web pages rather than faces or social scenes, so the measured construct is general attention allocation and search strategy rather than social attention. [RQ3.2] Single modality. Gaze features are combined at feature level with non-gaze contextual variables (page identity, AOI identity, correct-answer location, gender, visual complexity), and the paper reports that these additions generally reduced accuracy relative to gaze features alone - a negative fusion result reported plainly. Behaviour-level predictions are aggregated to a participant-level decision by majority vote, a late fusion across observations. The discussion proposes future fusion with non-gaze interaction data (mouse clicks, operation logs) as a route to eye-tracker-free deployment. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning. Algorithm: logistic regression in R, chosen after testing several classification algorithms. The deliberate choice of a simple linear model with a small feature set, rather than a high-capacity model on 30 participants, is consistent with the paper's general conservatism about overfitting. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted per-AOI gaze summary features - time to first view, total and percentage viewing time, fixation count and revisit count - computed under two alternative AOI definitions (VIPS-derived page elements versus a generic 2x2 grid), plus categorical contextual variables. No raw scanpaths, time series or learned embeddings. The AOI-definition comparison effectively treats the representation itself as an experimental variable, which is unusual and produces one of the paper's most useful findings. [RQ4.3] Classification accuracy, reported with 95% confidence intervals for every single configuration in every table - the only study in the corpus to do this systematically - plus confusion matrices for the two best results showing balanced per-class performance (0.722 control, 0.706 ASD for the best browse model). No sensitivity, specificity, F1 or AUC as such, though the confusion matrices permit their derivation. [RQ4.4] No per-feature importance ranking or saliency analysis. Interpretability instead comes from systematic ablation across design variables, which yields several substantive findings: gaze features alone outperform gaze plus contextual features; page-specific AOIs are necessary for search but not for browse, because search requires locating specific elements while browse treats all screen regions as equal; the Apple and AVG pages showed the largest between-group differences during browsing; and gender and visual complexity do not matter. The authors also connect back to prior analyses of the same data identifying longer scan paths, more transitions, shorter fixations and more fixations on irrelevant elements as the underlying behavioural differences. [RQ4.5] The strongest validation reasoning in the corpus. The background section explicitly critiques two prior studies (an EEG study reporting 94% and a French speech study reporting 93.5%) for partitioning data segments rather than participants, noting that this allows segments from the same participant into both training and test sets and produces 'potentially overoptimistic results' that do 'not account for real-world scenarios where the algorithm will have the task of correctly classifying a new person'. The study then adopts 100-fold cross-validation with strict participant-level partitioning (10 training and 5 test participants per group per fold) precisely to emulate diagnosing a new person, and reports 95% confidence intervals throughout. Class balance is enforced by design, including the random removal of one control. What is absent: external validation on an independent cohort, any held-out site or apparatus, calibration analysis, and any measurement of the proposed eye-tracker-free variant. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: Autism, Eye Tracking, Web, Screening, Diagnostic Classification. CCS concepts: user characteristics, people with disabilities, user studies, web-based interaction, empirical studies in accessibility, accessibility design and evaluation methods. Task vocabulary: 'screening for risk of autism', 'marker of the condition', 'serious games for autism screening', 'accessible and unobtrusive screening method'. The accessibility-research framing is unique in this corpus. [RQ5.2] W4A '18 - the 15th International Web for All Conference (Lyon), themed 'The Internet of Accessible Things'. A technology venue, but specifically a web accessibility venue rather than a machine-learning or clinical one, which shapes the paper's framing around scalability, cost and access rather than diagnostic accuracy. [RQ5.3] 2018. The paper surveys autism classification from fMRI (71-86.7% across several studies) and EEG (94%), and argues that eye tracking 'has not been used to investigate whether it is suitable to detect autism by considering atypical visual attention patterns', claiming to be the first study to test gaze data for autism screening. It also documents an important methodological trend critically rather than approvingly - noting that several high-accuracy results in the literature rest on partitioning by data segment rather than by participant - and situates eye tracking as moving from research equipment into consumer hardware (Samsung Galaxy S4, Tobii gaming trackers, Acer notebooks), anticipating the consumer-device turn this corpus records. |
| S-016 | Cross-sectional case-control; 20 Italian children with ASD without intellectual impairment (18 male, mean age 9.8, FSIQ 98.5) vs 20 age-, gender- and IQ-matched typically developing children (16 male, mean age 9.5, FSIQ 102.8); 1837 video clips of reach-to-grasp movements, publicly released. | Standardised bottle-grasping protocol with four intention conditions and 48 trials per child, filmed laterally at 100 fps and trimmed at the moment of contact so only pre-grasp reaching is modelled; frames Gaussian-smoothed to suppress appearance; GoogLeNet convolutional features weighted by a learned 7x7 spatial attention map and fed to a 128-dimensional LSTM with binary softmax; leave-one-subject-out across 39 independently trained models; dense trajectories with HOG/HOF and VLAD as a handcrafted baseline. | 0.82 detection accuracy (32/39 subjects) with full-data training and 0.72 (28/39) per-condition; mean per-subject accuracy 0.75 +/- 0.22; ASD recall 78.95% and TD recall 85.00%; the handcrafted baseline performed at chance; detection accuracy fell to 0.67 at a 0.7 confidence threshold and below chance above 0.9; attention maps localised to hand and arm. | No limitations section; 39 children so 0.82 equals 32 correct; ASD group restricted to children without intellectual impairment and IQ-matched, so no coverage of the broader spectrum; 80-90% male; single site and single camera viewpoint with no external validation; several ASD subjects classified confidently wrong (0.15-0.31); decision rule is a 0.5 threshold on averaged frame probabilities; no training hyperparameters or code released. | The corpus's methodological reference point for deep learning on behavioral video: the only study to release its video dataset, the only one to include a handcrafted baseline that fails at chance (supporting the claim that the signal is genuinely subtle kinematics), one of very few to suppress appearance cues by design, and one of the few to publish per-subject results and a confidence-threshold sensitivity analysis showing where the model stops being trustworthy. Its finding that ASD subjects are classified less accurately and more variably than controls is also the corpus's most direct empirical statement that spectrum heterogeneity limits classifier performance. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of 20: children with ASD without accompanying intellectual impairment (18 male), and typically developing children (16 male). One ASD subject (subject 3) was discarded because all their non-corrupted videos came from a single condition, so 39 subjects enter the experiments. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'autistic subjects', 'ASD subjects', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'healthy subjects', 'patient and healthy children', 'pathological and healthy subjects', 'autism disease', 'this pathology'. Markedly medicalised framing - autism is repeatedly called a 'disease' and a 'pathology', and the comparison group is 'healthy' - which is at the opposite end of the corpus's terminological range from the identity-first, 'neurotypical' usage of studies like Li et al. (2017). [RQ1.3] ASD n=20 (18 male, 2 female), age 9.8 +/- 1.5 years, WISC-IV Full Scale IQ 98.5 +/- 11.1. TD n=20 (16 male, 4 female), age 9.5 +/- 1.5 years, Full Scale IQ 102.8 +/- 9.4. Matching is verified statistically on both age (t38 = -0.665, p = 0.510) and IQ (t38 = 1.325, p = 0.193), and gender is matched by design. This is among the best-matched samples in the corpus - age, gender and IQ all matched with tests reported - though both groups are male-dominated (90% and 80%) and the ASD group is restricted to children without intellectual impairment. [RQ1.4] DSM-5 criteria, with both ADOS-2 and ADI-R administered by two experienced professionals. This is the most complete diagnostic ascertainment encountered in the corpus to date - the two instruments that the literature identifies as having the highest sensitivity and specificity, both applied, by two independent experienced assessors. [RQ1.5] Full Scale IQ measured by WISC-IV for both groups and used as a matching variable; executive function assessed in both groups by the Tower of London test with no significant difference (TD 29.35 +/- 3.54, ASD 29.35 +/- 2.80, t38 = 0, p = 0.999); handedness assessed by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (all but two children right-handed). Comorbidity is handled by explicit exclusion of pharmacological treatment, dyslexia, epilepsy and any other neurological or psychiatric condition. This is unusually thorough functional characterisation for a computer-vision paper. [RQ2.1] Goal: automatic objective diagnostic support from video alone, framed explicitly as a first step toward a computer-aided tool usable in clinical and more open settings. Main findings: 0.82 detection accuracy (32/39 subjects) with full-data training, 0.72 (28/39) when training per intention condition; mean per-subject accuracy 0.75 +/- 0.22; ASD recall 78.95%, TD recall 85.00%; a dense-trajectories handcrafted baseline performed at chance; attention maps localised to hand and arm; per-subject variability was large and is interpreted as evidence of spectrum heterogeneity. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting - a quiet room with fixed table and chair geometry and a standardised start posture - with clinical recruitment from a hospital child neuropsychiatry unit and control recruitment from primary schools. Newly collected data, released as the first public video dataset of ASD/TD gestures. [RQ2.3] A highly standardised reach-to-grasp protocol: fixed start posture with pincer grip on a marked point, a water-filled bottle of specified dimensions at 44 cm from the child's midline, and four intention conditions (grasp-to-place, grasp-to-pour, pass-to-place, pass-to-pour) with target objects at specified distances. 12 consecutive grasps per condition (48 total), initiated at natural speed after an auditory tone, with 2 practice trials before each block, pseudo-randomised block order, and a 2-minute pause between blocks to avoid fatigue. Crucially, video is trimmed at the moment of contact, so only the pre-grasp reaching phase is analysed - testing the neuroscientific claim that intention is encoded in the earliest stages of a motor act. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single ~30-minute session per child with no follow-up. Video of identifiable children is inherently sensitive, though the analysis pipeline applies Gaussian smoothing to suppress appearance and the released clips show only a lateral view of a reaching arm. Ethics approval from the local committee (ASL3 Genovese) under the Helsinki Declaration is reported, and parents gave written informed consent after a detailed study description. No anonymization or data-protection statement accompanies the public dataset release, which is a gap given that the dataset is posted openly. [RQ2.5] Hardware: Vicon VUE video camera at 1280x720 and 100 frames per second, lateral viewpoint; height-adjustable chair and a table of specified dimensions; a plastic bottle, box and glass of specified dimensions. Software: pre-trained GoogLeNet for CNN features; a custom LSTM with soft spatial attention; dense trajectories with HOG and HOF descriptors and VLAD encoding for the baseline. Deep-learning framework and training hyperparameters are not named. [RQ2.6] Mixed but above corpus average. The dataset is publicly released at a stated URL - the only video dataset released in this corpus - and the experimental protocol is specified in exhaustive physical detail (table dimensions, object weights and positions, start posture, trial counts, block structure, camera settings, trimming rule). The model architecture is described concretely (GoogLeNet last conv layer, 7x7x1024 features, 7x7 attention map, 128-dim LSTM hidden state, 16-dim FC layer, 15-frame clips). What is missing: no code release, no training hyperparameters (learning rate, optimiser, epochs, regularisation), no random seeds, and no statement of how the model handles the 15-frame clip splitting at test time beyond averaging. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section, so nothing is formally acknowledged, though the authors do report the difficulty candidly in the results - the large per-subject standard deviation is presented as evidence that 'finding a very general pattern in the video, that could be unique in distinguishing autistic subjects, is a challenging task', and TD subjects being classified better than ASD ones is read as 'evidence of the fact that autistic spectrum disorders comprise indeed a very wide spectrum of variability'. Identifiable in review: n=39 makes 0.82 equal to 32 of 39 children; the ASD group excludes intellectual impairment and is IQ-matched to controls, so results cannot extend to the broader spectrum; both groups are 80-90% male; the per-subject table shows several ASD children classified confidently wrong (subjects 7, 17 and 20 at 0.15, 0.16 and 0.31), which a single aggregate figure would conceal; the 0.5 threshold on averaged frame probabilities is a lenient decision rule and performance collapses below chance above a 0.9 threshold; and single-site recruitment with one fixed camera viewpoint leaves transfer entirely untested. [RQ2.9] Exploit the intention labels already in the dataset to test whether intention classification itself is altered in ASD, which could provide an additional diagnostic cue; and refine the spatial attention model to more finely inspect the kinematic discriminants in the gestures. Both are concrete and grounded in the existing data rather than generic calls for larger samples. [RQ3.1] Motor behavior captured as raw video: the kinematics of a reach-to-grasp movement, with visual appearance deliberately degraded by Gaussian smoothing so that only movement information remains available to the model. No markers, no motion capture, no handcrafted kinematic parameters - the paper positions this freedom from 'invasive sensory devices (e.g., MRI, microphones, eye tracker, Motion Capture landmarks)' as its central practical advantage. [RQ3.2] Single modality, no fusion. There is a form of temporal-spatial integration internal to the model - the LSTM's learned attention map weights spatial CNN features at each time step based on its accumulated hidden state, so spatial and temporal information are combined adaptively rather than by fixed pooling. Frame-level probabilities are averaged into a per-subject decision, a late fusion across frames and clips. No combination with clinical scores, IQ or demographics, despite those being available. [RQ4.1] Supervised deep learning: a pre-trained GoogLeNet CNN as frame feature extractor feeding a recurrent LSTM with a learned soft spatial attention mechanism and a binary softmax classifier. A handcrafted alternative (dense trajectories with HOG/HOF and VLAD encoding) is included specifically as a baseline and is reported to perform at chance - an informative negative comparison that most corpus studies omit. [RQ4.2] Learned deep embeddings over raw video, with no handcrafted features at all: 7x7x1024 convolutional feature maps per frame from GoogLeNet, adaptively pooled by a learned 7x7 attention map into a 1024-dimensional vector, then consumed recursively by a 128-dimensional LSTM. Videos are split into 15-frame clips for training, with each clip treated independently and probabilities averaged across frames at test time. This is one of the few genuinely end-to-end representations in the corpus. [RQ4.3] Per-subject averaged accuracy with standard deviation, detection accuracy at a stated threshold, a full confusion matrix with per-class precision and recall (ASD 83.33% precision / 78.95% recall; TD 80.95% precision / 85.00% recall), and a threshold sensitivity curve from 0.5 to 0.95. No AUC or confidence intervals, but the reporting is more complete than accuracy-only studies and the full per-subject accuracy table is published, which allows a reader to see the distribution rather than only its mean. [RQ4.4] A learned soft spatial attention map, generated per frame by the LSTM from its hidden spatio-temporal state and visualised superimposed on the video, is the interpretability mechanism - and it is designed into the model rather than applied post hoc. The maps concentrate on the hand and arm during reaching, which the authors read as the network attending to gesture kinematics, and they propose the maps as feedback clinicians could use in interpreting a diagnosis. The interpretation stops at localisation: no kinematic property (velocity, jerk, trajectory shape) is extracted or named, so the explanation identifies where the model looks but not what it sees there. [RQ4.5] Robustness is handled unusually seriously. Leave-one-subject-out with 39 independently trained models is used deliberately, with the authors stating that it is 'more challenging than the usual cross-validation whose classification scores are always higher' and that they consider it the correct procedure for a system meant to generalise. Appearance information is removed by Gaussian smoothing so the model cannot exploit incidental visual differences. A handcrafted state-of-the-art baseline is run and reported to fail at chance. A confidence-threshold sensitivity analysis shows detection accuracy degrading from 0.82 to 0.67 between thresholds 0.5 and 0.7 and dropping below chance above 0.9, with the authors stating plainly that the model 'is not more trustable after a threshold of 0.9'. What is absent: any external or independent dataset, any held-out site or camera viewpoint, any class-imbalance issue (19/20), and any real-time or deployment measurement despite clinical use being the stated aim. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list. The paper's vocabulary: 'autism disease diagnosis', 'video gesture analysis', 'attention map', 'computer-aided diagnostic algorithms', 'objective quantitative tool', 'motor signals of Autism', 'first screening test', 'pathological vs healthy subjects'. The recurrent 'disease'/'pathology' framing is distinctive and contrasts sharply with the neurodiversity-aligned vocabulary elsewhere in this corpus. [RQ5.2] The 24th International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR) 2018, Beijing - a technology/computational venue (pattern recognition and computer vision), not an autism or clinical venue, though the author list spans a computer vision institute, a cognition and motion neuroscience group, a university psychology department and a hospital child neuropsychiatry unit. [RQ5.3] 2018. The paper surveys machine learning applied to autism across quotient-based diagnostic tools, MRI, kinematic data, eye tracking and language acoustics, and argues that these modalities are 'quite invasive or require specialized personnel, often affecting the behavior of the subjects under study', and that most rely on 'handcrafted features and simplified linear models that often fail to handle the complexity of human behaviors in less controlled settings'. It positions itself as the first to cast autism diagnosis as a video-based computational problem and as part of the shift toward deep learning - a shift this corpus documents accelerating sharply from 2018 onward. |
| S-017 | Cross-sectional case-control methods demonstration; 21 individuals with ASD (2 female, mean age 16.27, mean IQ 109.4, ICD-10 diagnosis re-confirmed with ADOS-2) vs 23 age- and IQ-matched typically developing controls (5 female, mean age 16.31, mean IQ 112.3) in Poland; 60 trials per subject across five face-perception tasks, with data and code released. | SMI RED250 at 250 Hz with chinrest; fixations assigned to the nearest of 76 AOIs from an automatic 68-point facial landmark detector plus 8 frame points; scanpaths encoded as duration-weighted character strings; ScanMatch pairwise similarity with a spatial-and-semantic substitution matrix and length normalisation; t-SNE embedding to two dimensions per eye; LightGBM classifiers compared with and without the temporal representation under 5-by-2 repeated cross-validation with subject-level fold partitioning; a permuted-character control isolating spatial information, plus a Levenshtein/non-metric-MDS benchmark. | t-SNE embedding distributions differed significantly between groups for both eyes (Cramer test p < 0.001). Spatial-only classifier 53.9%, spatial-plus-temporal 55.5%, difference significant at p = 0.032, both above chance by permutation (p < 0.001). The alternative-technique benchmark showed no significant temporal contribution (51.8% vs 51.9%, p = 0.387). Adding emotion, gender, age or task type did not improve either model. | Absolute accuracies of 53.9% and 55.5% are barely above chance, so the demonstrated temporal effect is statistically real but diagnostically negligible - a point not foregrounded; the unit of analysis is a two-second trial rather than a person, so no participant-level estimate exists; ASD ages extend to 29 against a control maximum of 21; both groups heavily male; IQ restricted above 85; trials without AOI transitions excluded, potentially disproportionately from the ASD group; no external validation. | The corpus's most important calibration point. It applies subject-level partitioning, a matched permuted control, permutation testing against chance, an alternative-method benchmark, ADOS-2-confirmed diagnosis and IQ matching - and finds that trial-level gaze scanpaths separate autistic from typically developing viewers at 55.5%. Read against the many 88-97% figures elsewhere in this corpus obtained from comparable gaze data at comparable sample sizes but with image-level or unpartitioned validation, it indicates how much of those figures may be attributable to evaluation design. It is also the only study here to make temporal scanpath ordering, rather than spatial dwell distribution, the object of analysis. | [RQ1.1] Two groups: 21 individuals with ASD and 23 age- and IQ-matched typically developing controls, total 44. Group sizes, sexes and IQ means are all reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'subjects with ASD', 'individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)', 'the ASD population', 'ASD subjects', 'autistic vs. typically-developing individuals', 'typically developing (TD) controls'. Mixed person-first and identity-first, with 'typically developing' rather than 'normal' throughout. Autism is described as 'a developmental disorder affecting social and communicative functioning and related to repetitive, limited patterns of behavior and interests' - a conventional clinical framing without pathologising language. [RQ1.3] ASD n=21 (2 female, 10%), mean age 16.27, range 11-29, mean full-scale IQ 109.4. TD n=23 (5 female, 22%), mean age 16.31, range 10-21, mean full-scale IQ 112.3. Groups are described as age- and IQ-matched and the means are indeed near-identical, though the ASD age range extends to 29 while no control exceeded 21, and no standard deviations or formal comparison tests are reported. All participants had full-scale IQ above 85, so the sample is restricted to average-or-above intellectual ability. Both groups are heavily male. Adolescents and adults, so no early-diagnosis relevance. [RQ1.4] Among the strongest in the corpus: all ASD participants had prior clinical diagnoses under WHO ICD-10 criteria, and all diagnoses were additionally confirmed by the research team using ADOS-2, described accurately as 'a standardized, validated instrument for the assessment of autism spectrum conditions'. Control status was established by absence of any history of autism spectrum or other neurodevelopmental disorders. Independent re-confirmation with a gold-standard instrument, rather than reliance on prior diagnosis alone, is uncommon here. [RQ1.5] Intelligence measured with the Wechsler Scales for all participants, with group means reported (109.4 and 112.3) and a minimum threshold of 85 applied as an inclusion criterion - so IQ is both measured and controlled by restriction and matching. Vision was normal or corrected-to-normal and neurological conditions excluded for all subjects. No language or adaptive measures, and ADOS-2 severity scores are not reported despite the instrument being administered. [RQ2.1] Goal: primarily methodological - to enable statistical comparison of two groups of scanpaths on temporal features, with autism as the demonstration domain. Main findings: t-SNE embeddings of ASD and TD scanpaths differed highly significantly for both eyes (Cramer test p < 0.001); adding the temporal representation to a spatial-only feature set raised classification accuracy from 53.9% to 55.5% (p = 0.032), establishing a genuine temporal difference beyond the known spatial one; both models were above chance by permutation test; and a benchmark using Levenshtein distance with non-metric MDS found no significant temporal contribution, indicating the effect depends on the specific ScanMatch/t-SNE combination. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting with a chinrest, fixed viewing distance and periodic data-quality monitoring. The data were collected by the authors across two experiments, with Experiment 1 data also used in a separate publication on information extraction - disclosed transparently on the grounds that 'recruiting ASD subjects and validating their diagnoses is extremely costly'. [RQ2.3] Five face-perception tasks spanning emotion recognition, a non-social perceptual judgement (brow versus lip width), free viewing, age estimation and a social evaluation ('nice' or not), across 60 trials per subject. Stimuli were 60 FACES database photographs balanced by sex and across three age bands, each shown once per subject with one randomly chosen expression from six to avoid familiarity effects and face-emotion confounds. Notably the study deliberately used images of the entire head with varying facial-feature locations, criticising the field's usual practice of using cropped images with standardised feature positions as 'somewhat unrealistic' - and solved the resulting AOI problem with automatic landmark detection. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; two experiments in a laboratory session series with no follow-up. The data are gaze coordinates over third-party stimulus faces, so re-identification risk is minimal and the public release is correspondingly low-risk. Consent handling is exemplary: ethics approval from the named Faculty Research Ethics Committee, written consent from adult subjects or from guardians of underage subjects, and additionally oral consent obtained from the underage subjects themselves - a two-tier assent procedure that only one other study in this corpus matches. [RQ2.5] Hardware: SMI RED250 Mobile remote eye tracker at 250 Hz with 0.4 degree accuracy; 15-inch Dell Precision M4800 at 1280x720; chinrest at 65 cm; 5-point calibration with 4-point validation and automated periodic quality checks prompting repositioning. Software: C# experimental program; SMI event detector (60 ms minimum fixation, 50 degrees/s velocity threshold); Wolfram Mathematica 11.3 for the facial landmark detector and LightGBM; MATLAB (van der Maaten's original code) for t-SNE; R for the Cramer test. [RQ2.6] The strongest reproducibility profile in the corpus alongside Yaneva et al. Data and code are both released as supplementary information. The method is documented exhaustively: eye tracker specifications, calibration and validation procedure, fixation detection thresholds, the 68+8 AOI construction and why the extra 8 frame points were added, the 50 ms character-repetition encoding, the substitution matrix construction with its distance and group logic and its [-1,+1] rescaling, the length normalisation rationale, the t-SNE implementation used, the LightGBM hyperparameters, the class priors, and the subject-level fold constraint. The authors also report that manipulating t-SNE settings and LightGBM defaults produced no qualitative change - an informal robustness check. [RQ2.7] The paper has no dedicated limitations section, since it is framed as a methods demonstration. It does report transparently that Experiment 1 data were reused from a companion paper and why. Identifiable in review: the absolute accuracies of 53.9% and 55.5% are barely above chance and correspond to a 1.6 percentage point improvement, so while the temporal claim is statistically supported the practical discriminability is negligible - a fact the paper does not emphasise; the unit of analysis is a single two-second trial rather than a person, so no participant-level diagnostic estimate exists; the ASD age range extends to 29 against a control maximum of 21 despite matched means; both groups are heavily male on very small female counts; all participants have IQ above 85, so the sample excludes much of the spectrum; and trials with no AOI transitions in either eye were excluded, which may remove disproportionately many ASD trials given the noted tendency toward stray fixations. [RQ2.9] No autism-specific future work is proposed. The methodological conclusion is that the technique 'could be used in other problems in which one needs to compare two sets of eye movement sequences in terms of their temporal features', positioning the contribution as a general tool for eye-movement research rather than an autism screening development. [RQ3.1] Gaze: binocular fixation sequences with duration and order, encoded relative to automatically detected facial landmarks. The distinguishing feature is that temporal ordering is preserved and made the object of analysis, whereas the corpus's other gaze studies aggregate into dwell times or fixation counts that discard sequence. [RQ3.2] Single modality, but with an unusual internal contrast: spatial-only and spatial-plus-temporal representations of the same data are constructed through identical pipelines and compared, which is a form of ablation rather than fusion. Left and right eye representations are kept separate and both included as features, motivated by a possible lateral offset with each eye directed slightly toward its own side of the face. Face emotion, gender, age and task type were tested as additional predictors and reported as not significantly improving either model. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning with unsupervised embedding: gradient boosted decision trees (LightGBM) over t-SNE embeddings of a ScanMatch similarity matrix. The Needleman-Wunsch sequence alignment underlying ScanMatch is a classical bioinformatics algorithm repurposed for gaze. A benchmark condition substitutes Levenshtein distance and Kruskal's non-metric multidimensional scaling for the ScanMatch/t-SNE pair. [RQ4.2] A distinctive three-stage representation: fixation sequences are first converted to character strings where each AOI symbol is repeated proportionally to fixation duration (one character per 50 ms), so that duration is encoded in string length; pairwise ScanMatch alignment then produces a similarity matrix incorporating spatial proximity and anatomical group membership through a purpose-built substitution matrix; and t-SNE finally embeds each scanpath as a point in two dimensions. This converts an inherently pairwise, non-vector representation into per-item coordinates that can be tested statistically - which is exactly the barrier the paper sets out to solve. [RQ4.3] Classification accuracy averaged over folds and iterations, with a paired t-test between the two models, confusion matrices for both, and permutation-based verification against chance. Group-level distributional differences are tested separately with the non-parametric Cramer test with reported statistics, critical values and p-values for each eye. The reporting is statistically thorough, though absolute accuracy is the only classification metric and no sensitivity, specificity or AUC is given. [RQ4.4] No feature-level interpretation is offered, and this is a deliberate choice: the paper establishes that temporal ordering carries group-discriminative information without claiming to characterise what the ordering difference is. The illustrative hypothesis it uses to motivate the design - that TD subjects might look at the eyes before the mouth while ASD subjects do the reverse - is offered as a possibility to be tested, not a finding. The permuted-character control is the interpretive mechanism: because it destroys order while preserving AOI frequencies, any accuracy gain over it must come from sequence. [RQ4.5] Among the best in the corpus. Subject-level partitioning is explicit and enforced, with both groups evenly split across folds and class priors set to 0.5. The 5-by-2 repeated cross-validation design is a recognised procedure for comparing classifiers. Both models are permutation-tested against chance (p < 0.001, k = 1000), which matters given accuracies near 50%. A benchmark using alternative standard techniques is run and reported as null, guarding against the conclusion being an artefact of the general pipeline. Sensitivity to algorithm settings is informally checked for both t-SNE and LightGBM. Absent: external validation on an independent sample, and any participant-level aggregation that would yield a diagnostic estimate. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: eye tracking; scanpath comparison; dimensionality reduction; machine learning; autism; face perception. Task vocabulary: 'scanpath', 'areas-of-interest', 'temporal scanpath features', 'substitution matrix', 'dimension-reduced scanpath representation'. Notably the vocabulary is that of eye-movement methodology rather than diagnosis - words like 'screening', 'detection' and 'biomarker' are absent. [RQ5.2] Sensors (MDPI) - an instrumentation and sensing journal, neither autism-specific nor clinical, consistent with the paper's methodological framing. [RQ5.3] 2019. The paper's field characterisation is methodological rather than clinical: it observes that 'most related studies rely on spatial information about which different areas of visual stimuli were looked at, without considering the order in which this occurred', and that 'even state-of-the-art analyses of this type are typically based on spatial but not temporal eye movement information'. It also criticises the prevailing stimulus convention - that existing studies 'typically use facial images with cropped peripheral regions... and such that the locations of the key facial regions are the same across images', which 'facilitates the analysis but can be seen as somewhat unrealistic'. Both observations identify structural simplifications in the gaze literature that this corpus otherwise leaves unexamined. |
| S-018 | Cross-sectional case-control; 20 Chinese children with high-functioning autism (DSM-IV, psychiatrist-confirmed, ADHD/ID/schizophrenia excluded, average non-verbal IQ) vs 23 age-matched typically developing children aged 6-13; three 60-second LeapMotion recordings per child, dataset explicitly not released. | Participants performed one-dimensional oscillatory hand movement 'as complex as possible' above a 60 cm string; palm position interpolated, filtered at 5 Hz and differentiated; Shannon entropy over 101-bin histograms and central 95% range computed for amplitude, velocity and acceleration and aggregated across trials by min, median and max (18 features); t-test screen at p<0.1 followed by forward feature selection; SVM, LDA, decision tree, random forest and KNN (k=1,3,5,7) evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation. | KNN (k=1) with four features - maximal amplitude range, minimal velocity range, median and minimal velocity entropy - achieved 88.37% accuracy and AUC 0.8815, with sensitivity and specificity of 91.3% and 85% (labels inconsistent between abstract and discussion). Nine of 18 features differed between groups at p<0.1; ASD children showed significantly greater maximal amplitude range. All classifiers except the decision tree exceeded 75% with five or fewer features. | Feature screening and forward selection both performed outside the cross-validation loop and both optimised on labelled data, so the headline is a search maximum; best of five classifiers and four k values; 1-nearest-neighbour winner on 43 participants; high-functioning-only sample with ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia excluded; no standardised diagnostic instrument; sensitivity/specificity labels inconsistent; directions not reported for the velocity features that dominate the model; demographics confined to an unreproduced table. | The corpus's only study to operationalise restricted and repetitive behaviour - the second cardinal DSM criterion - as a directly measurable motor property, by inverting the task so that participants are instructed to be maximally variable and restrictedness appears as non-compliance. It is also one of very few to state plainly that its own method cannot serve early screening, and one of the few to declare dataset unavailability explicitly rather than by omission. | [RQ1.1] Two groups: 20 children with high-functioning autism and 23 age-matched typically developing children. Group sizes are clear. No other-diagnosis comparison group - indeed ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia were explicit exclusions - though the conclusion identifies ASD-versus-ADHD classification as the needed next step. [RQ1.2] 'children with high functioning autism', 'children with ASD', 'patients with ASD', 'ASD patients', 'the patient', 'individuals with typical development (TD)', 'TD children', 'non-ASD individuals'. Consistently medicalised - 'patient' is the default noun throughout, and the framing is diagnostic rather than descriptive. [RQ1.3] ASD n=20, TD n=23, described as age-matched with an inclusion range of 6-13 years. Demographic details including ages and sexes are presented in Table 1, which is not recoverable from the extracted text, so exact means, standard deviations and sex ratios cannot be charted here. Non-verbal IQ was assessed with Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices as an inclusion criterion (average ability required) but the values are likewise in the unrecoverable table. Age matching is claimed and a demographic comparison is tabulated, which is better practice than most of the corpus. [RQ1.4] Confirmed diagnosis of high-functioning autism by a licensed psychiatrist using DSM-IV criteria, with Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices confirming average non-verbal intellectual ability and explicit exclusion of ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia. No ADOS or ADI-R. The exclusion of common comorbidities is unusually explicit and is a design strength for internal validity, though it narrows the population. [RQ1.5] Non-verbal IQ assessed by Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices and used as an inclusion criterion (average ability), so cognitive level is controlled by restriction rather than by matching or covariate adjustment. No language or adaptive-functioning measures and no autism severity instrument. Comorbidity is handled by exclusion: ADHD, mental retardation and schizophrenia ruled out for the ASD group; controls reported no physical or mental disorders. [RQ2.1] Goal: test whether restricted kinematic features derived from restricted and repetitive behaviour can identify ASD, providing an objective assessment of a symptom domain normally rated by informants. Main findings: KNN (k=1) with four features achieved 88.37% accuracy and AUC 0.8815; nine of 18 features differed between groups at p<0.1; three of the four best features derive from the velocity distribution; and all classifiers except the decision tree exceeded 75% accuracy with five or fewer features. [RQ2.2] Clinical recruitment (hospital child psychiatry department) with laboratory-style testing on a desktop LeapMotion apparatus. Newly collected data; no existing dataset used. [RQ2.3] A deliberately inverted task design: participants perform one-dimensional oscillatory hand movement 'as complex as possible', with the experimenter demonstrating the contrast between simple periodic oscillation (mono amplitude and frequency) and complex unpredictable oscillation (variant amplitude and frequency), followed by practice trials until the requirement was understood. Three 60-second trials with the subdominant hand held behind the back, breaks of 2-5 minutes between trials, and trial reinitiation if the hand left the recording zone or movement stopped. The design is the paper's key idea - restrictedness is measured as failure to comply with an instruction to be variable. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; three 60-second trials in a single session with no follow-up. Data are numeric hand-position traces, not identifiable media. Written informed consent was signed by caregivers, the study conformed to the Declaration of Helsinki, and it followed the ethical guidelines of Shenzhen University. No anonymization procedure is described, and none is materially required for this data type. [RQ2.5] Hardware: LeapMotion hand-tracking device connected to a Lenovo Legion R720-15IKBN computer, with a physical rig of two sticks and a string defining a 60 cm movement zone and a mat for comfortable hand positioning. Software: MATLAB R2017b for signal processing (piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation, second-order 5 Hz low-pass Butterworth filter, differentiation) and machine learning; SPSS 17.0 for statistical comparison. [RQ2.6] The dataset availability is stated explicitly and negatively - 'The dataset is not made publicly available' - which is at least transparent, and rarer in this corpus than silence. No code release. Method reporting is otherwise strong: apparatus, movement-zone geometry, trial structure and durations, interpolation and filter settings, noise thresholds for each kinematic quantity, the 101-bin histogram construction, the Shannon entropy and range equations, the two-stage feature-selection procedure with its p<0.1 threshold, the five classifiers with the k values tested, and the software versions. Re-implementable in principle; not reproducible without the data. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors in a dedicated Limitations section that is notably candid: only high-functioning children were recruited to ensure task compliance, and whether low-functioning patients could perform the task 'remains an open question'; and 'obviously, this motor task would not work for children less than 2 years old, which suggests that this motor task would not function for the early screening of ASD' - an explicit concession that the method cannot serve early screening, which almost no other corpus study makes. They further note that motion-capture approaches can quantify low-level stereotyped movement but not higher-level RRB such as circumscribed interest. Identifiable in review: the t-test screen from 18 to 9 features used the full labelled dataset before cross-validation, and forward feature selection then selected the combination maximising classification accuracy, so 88.37% is a maximum over a search using the evaluation criterion; the best of five classifiers and four k values is reported; sensitivity and specificity are reversed between abstract and discussion; the direction of the velocity features carrying most of the signal is not reported; exclusion of ADHD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia makes the discrimination easier than the clinical task; and demographic detail resides in a table that is not reproduced in the running text. [RQ2.9] Extend classification from ASD-versus-TD to ASD-versus-other-conditions, specifically ADHD; apply machine learning to adjacent problems such as engagement evaluation; integrate genetic, neurological, psychological and kinematic features toward automated objective diagnosis, while acknowledging the open problem of selecting relevant features from a very large pool; and develop ways to quantify higher-level restricted and repetitive behaviour such as circumscribed interest, which accelerometer and Kinect approaches to stereotyped movement cannot capture. [RQ3.1] Motor behavior: one-dimensional hand kinematics, specifically the statistical distributions of oscillation amplitude, velocity and acceleration rather than their means. The construct measured is behavioural variability/complexity rather than speed, accuracy or coordination - a different target from every other motor study in this corpus. [RQ3.2] Single modality; no fusion. Within the modality, three kinematic quantities (amplitude, velocity, acceleration) are each summarised by two complexity measures (entropy and 95% range) and three cross-trial aggregates (min, median, max), giving an 18-feature grid, and the selected model combines amplitude-range and velocity-range/entropy features - so the fusion is across kinematic derivatives and trial aggregates. The discussion proposes future integration with genetic, neuroimaging and psychological data. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning with a broad classifier comparison: SVM, linear discriminant analysis, decision tree, random forest and k-nearest neighbour with k in {1,3,5,7}. KNN with k=1 - effectively a nearest-neighbour lookup, the highest-variance choice available - gave the best result, which on 43 participants with four selected features warrants caution the paper does not express. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted distributional features: Shannon entropy over a 101-bin normalised histogram and the central 95% range, computed for amplitude, velocity and acceleration and aggregated across three trials by minimum, median and maximum. This is a distribution-shape representation rather than the point-statistic representation (peak velocity, duration, jerk) used by other motor studies in the corpus, and is well matched to the construct of restrictedness. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for the best model of each of the five classifiers, plus a confusion matrix for the winning model and a plot of accuracy against number of features for all classifiers - which usefully exposes how performance varies with model size. Headline: 88.37% accuracy, AUC 0.8815. Sensitivity and specificity values (91.3% and 85%) are reported but with their labels swapped between the abstract and the discussion, leaving the assignment formally ambiguous. No confidence intervals or significance testing against chance. [RQ4.4] Two-stage and reasonably transparent: independent t-tests identify nine discriminative features from 18, and forward feature selection then builds up the model incrementally, with the accuracy-versus-feature-count curve published for all five classifiers. The substantive interpretation is developed - three of four selected features derive from the velocity distribution, connected to prior work showing velocity distributions characterise subtle individual motor differences, and greater maximal amplitude range in ASD is linked to reported macrographia and fine motor control deficits. However the direction of the velocity entropy and range differences is never stated, so the central claim that autistic children are more restricted is not directly evidenced for the features that matter most. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-out cross-validation is applied uniformly across all five classifiers, and the comparison across classifiers and feature counts is systematic. But the two selection stages are not nested: the t-test screen used the full labelled dataset, and forward feature selection optimised the same accuracy metric that is then reported, so the headline is a maximum over a search rather than an unbiased estimate - the same failure mode that Vabalas et al. (2019) in this corpus identify and correct. There is no external or independent validation, no permutation or significance testing, no class-imbalance handling (20 vs 23 is near-balanced), and no deployment analysis. Generalisability is addressed honestly in narrative terms - high-functioning only, unusable below age 2 - but not tested. [RQ5.1] Index terms: Autism, entropy, kinematic feature, machine learning, restricted and repetitive behavior. Task vocabulary: 'restricted kinematic features', 'kinematic complexity', 'rapid diagnostic tool', 'automated and objective diagnosis', 'locked into a specific thought or behavior'. The entropy and complexity vocabulary is distinctive within the corpus's motor strand. [RQ5.2] IEEE Access - a broad open-access engineering and computing journal, neither autism-specific nor clinical. [RQ5.3] 2019. The paper characterises machine learning in autism as having concentrated on two things: shortening existing diagnostic instruments by removing redundant ADOS and ADI-R items (citing a claimed 100% accuracy from an 8-item ADOS subset, later above 95% on a larger sample), and classifying from neuroimaging, eye gaze and kinematic data - with only 'a handful' of kinematic studies, none of which targeted restricted and repetitive behaviour. Its closing argument that integrating genetic, neurological, psychological and kinematic features 'might pose a considerable challenge to the current diagnostic criteria of ASD' is one of the corpus's more ambitious claims about where the field is heading. |
| S-019 | Cross-sectional case-control with a human-rater benchmark; 35 children with ASD (mean age 11.42, FSIQ 105.5, ADOS-2 CSS 6.57) vs 35 typically developing children matched on full-scale, verbal and non-verbal IQ and sex ratio (mean age 10.57, ADOS-2 CSS 1.23), all native English speakers at a US hospital autism centre; 5-minute conversations with 22 naive confederates, not released. | Unstructured get-to-know-you conversations recorded on a dual-camera four-microphone device, transcribed verbatim under a double-annotation plus senior-review protocol with >90% gold-standard reliability; 352 openSMILE ComParE13 acoustic features and 272 LIWC/qdap text features computed for both speakers; per-fold univariate correlation filtering (p<0.025) and PCA to 10 components inside each fold; Gradient Boosting Classifier under leave-one-out cross-validation; two undergraduate raters classified a matched 12-conversation subset for comparison. | 75.71% accuracy, AUC 0.754; TD 85.71% (30/35) versus ASD 65.71% (23/35); ASD precision 0.82, recall 0.66. Human raters averaged 83.33%. Autistic children showed higher median HNR-delta, lower voicing-probability variability and reduced pitch dynamism; confederates showed higher HNR-delta and lower jitter when talking to autistic children. Adding age and sex did not help; adding IQ worsened performance. | Sex counts in the demographic table sum to 25 rather than 35 per group; part of the predictive signal comes from the conversation partner's voice rather than the child's, limiting transfer to partner-free screening; single site, native English speakers only, with no ethnicity or socioeconomic data; 19 of 22 confederates female; n=70 so 75.71% is 53 of 70; no external validation; no data or code release. | The corpus's methodological benchmark: gold-standard Clinical Best Estimate ascertainment applied symmetrically to cases and controls, IQ- and sex-matched groups with every comparison tested, feature selection and PCA correctly nested inside cross-validation folds, complete per-class metrics, and - uniquely - a human-rater comparison establishing that the task is hard for people too. Its finding that a naive conversation partner's own voice quality shifts measurably depending on whether they are talking to an autistic child is the corpus's clearest evidence that the measurable signal in social interaction is dyadic rather than located in one person. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of 35: children with ASD and typically developing children, plus 22 young adult confederates (19 female) who served as conversation partners and whose speech was also analysed. The confederates are effectively a third participant group whose data enter the model - an unusual design in this corpus. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'children on the autism spectrum', 'ASD children', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TDC', and one appearance of 'ASD patients' in the discussion. Predominantly person-first with the notable use of 'children on the autism spectrum' in the introduction, and 'typically developing' rather than 'normal' throughout. [RQ1.3] ASD n=35, mean age 11.42 +/- 2.51, full-scale IQ 105.51, verbal IQ 104.97, non-verbal IQ 104.63. TD n=35, mean age 10.57 +/- 2.82, full-scale IQ 107.14, verbal IQ 105.83, non-verbal IQ 105.97. Age difference non-significant (t=1.33, p=0.19); IQ differences non-significant on all three measures (p=0.6, 0.78, 0.68); sex ratio matched by design and non-significant (chi-square=0.06, p=0.8). This is among the best-matched samples in the corpus - matched and tested on full-scale, verbal and non-verbal IQ as well as sex. The one defect is that the printed sex counts ('13 f., 12 m.' and '11 f., 14 m.') sum to 25 rather than the stated 35 per group. [RQ1.4] The strongest reference standard in the corpus: diagnoses were confirmed for the ASD group and ruled out for the TD group using the Clinical Best Estimate process informed by ADOS-2 and adhering to DSM-5 criteria.
