Aggregate dwell time only - no scanpath, saccade, pupillometric or temporal-sequence information. [RQ3.2] Single modality, no fusion. Per-ROI mean fixation durations are concatenated into a single feature vector per participant, described as capturing the time distribution of visual attention across regions - a within-modality spatial aggregation rather than multimodal fusion. No integration with clinical scores, demographics or the medical-history data the workflow collects. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning. Algorithm: support vector machine only, selected because it is used in the cited literature and is a capable binary classifier. No paradigm comparison, no alternative algorithms, and no kernel specification. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted low-dimensional features: mean fixation duration per region of interest, assembled into one feature vector per participant. The paper describes this as incorporating both temporal and spatial information, since duration is temporal and ROI identity is spatial. No raw scanpaths, images or learned embeddings. [RQ4.3] Accuracy (88.6%), specificity (92.31%), sensitivity (86.63%) and AUC (0.96) - a reasonably complete metric set on its face, and the authors explicitly motivate reporting all four. But with no sample size reported, none of the figures carries an interpretable precision, and the two-decimal specificity (92.31%, consistent with 12 of 13) hints at a very small test set. No confusion matrix, confidence intervals or significance testing. [RQ4.4] None. No feature importance, ROI ranking or ablation is reported. The results assert that 'using ROIs as features for analysis prove clearly the levels of discrimination between ASD and non-ASD patients' but identify no specific region, direction or effect, so nothing interpretable about autistic visual attention emerges from the study itself. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-out cross-validation at the participant level is described and is an appropriate choice, with the rationale cited. Beyond that, nothing: no external or independent validation, no held-out site, no repetition, no permutation or significance testing, no class-imbalance handling or reporting, no calibration, no bias analysis, and no deployment or real-time evaluation despite clinical deployment in Saudi autism centres being the explicit goal. Generalisability is addressed only by the future-work statement that larger datasets are needed. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Intelligent, Machine Learning, early diagnoses, speed up screening, early intervention. Task vocabulary: 'intelligent screening', 'gaze-based screening', 'early biomarkers', 'automated data-driven prediction model', 'computer-aid diagnostic tool', 'transformative step'. The 'intelligent system' framing and the emphasis on speeding up screening throughput are distinctive. [RQ5.2] The 2nd International Conference on Computer Applications and Information Security (ICCAIS) 2019 - a general computing and information-security venue, neither an autism, clinical, nor machine-learning-specialist venue. [RQ5.3] 2019. The literature review is the paper's strongest section and characterises the field carefully: screening has 'evolved recently from subjective clinical assessments to objective metrics acquired from sensing devices such as gaze-tracking, motion sensors, and speech analytics'; machine learning in autism has 'largely focused on how to select the most effective features from a large feature set on the clinical diagnostic tools to shorten the diagnosis time'; and, most pointedly, 'all presented studies adopted machine learning differently yet there is no automatic prediction model integrated within a screening tool to be used in clinics'. It also documents a geographic gap - a shortage of Arabic-language autism research and uncertain prevalence estimates of 1.4, 29 and 59 per 10,000 children in Oman, the UAE and Saudi Arabia - which is a dimension of coverage bias not raised elsewhere in this corpus. |
| S-025 | Cross-sectional case-control; 24 autistic adults (9 female, mean age 31.5) vs 22 IQ-matched non-autistic adults (7 female, mean age 30.8) at a UK university; 60 kinematic and accuracy features from a 10-second pointing task per hand, not released. | Polhemus Fastrak tracking of index-finger position at 120 Hz during repetitive pointing between two markers 30 cm apart; 20 movement measures plus endpoint-scatter accuracy features, pooled across hands as means and SDs and z-scored; SVM-RBF with grid-searched C and gamma, coupled with four feature-selection methods; 10-fold nested cross-validation with the whole pipeline inside the training fold, repeated 100 times; 1000-permutation significance testing. | Best 71% accuracy (75% sensitivity, 66% specificity, p=0.021) with t-test feature selection; ReliefF 70% (p=0.027); SVM-RFE 62% and mRMR 60% both non-significant. Group-level: autistic participants slower (0.42 vs 0.37 s duration; 776 vs 912 mm/s) but roughly twice as accurate (30.87 vs 64.01 mm2 scatter), with Cohen's d from 0.69 to 0.82. | No diagnostic instrument named and no IQ values despite IQ matching being claimed; no age SDs or ranges; 46 adults so 71% is about 33 correct, with no confidence interval; outliers replaced with group means before the folds; no external validation; no data or code release. | The corpus's clearest methodological correction: it names the prior kinematic studies reporting 86.7-96.7%, attributes those figures to K-fold cross-validation on small samples, applies nested cross-validation with permutation testing instead, and reports 71% - then states the transferable lesson that large group-level effect sizes need not produce high individual-level classification. Its speed-accuracy finding, that autistic adults were slower but substantially more precise, also reframes a motor difference as a strategy rather than a deficit. | [RQ1.1] Two groups: 24 autistic adults and 22 non-autistic (typically developing) adults, IQ-matched. Both group sizes and sex counts are reported. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'autistic individuals', 'autistic adults', 'ASC participants', 'non-autistic adults', 'non-autistic individuals', 'typically developing (TD) individuals', 'affected individuals'. Predominantly identity-first ('autistic individuals') paired with 'non-autistic' rather than 'healthy' or 'normal', and the paper uses 'Autism Spectrum Condition' rather than 'Disorder' throughout - among the more neurodiversity-aligned terminology in the corpus, consistent with the same Manchester group's other entries here. [RQ1.3] ASC n=24 (9 female, 37.5%), mean age 31.5 years. TD n=22 (7 female, 31.8%), mean age 30.8 years. Groups are stated to be IQ matched, but no IQ values, no age standard deviations, no age ranges and no statistical comparisons are reported. Female representation is comparatively high for this literature. Adults only, so no early-diagnosis relevance. [RQ1.4] Not reported. Participants are described simply as autistic adults with no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or verification procedure named, and control status is asserted without screening. Given that diagnosis is the prediction target, this is the study's principal reporting gap - though the same research group's companion 2020 paper documents its ascertainment more fully. [RQ1.5] IQ matching is claimed but no IQ values are reported for either group, and no language, adaptive-functioning or autism-trait measures are given. Comorbidities are not described. This is unusually sparse given that the paper is otherwise meticulous about its analysis. [RQ2.1] Goal: predict autism diagnosis at the individual level from a short simple motor task, with the stated methodological aim of producing unbiased performance estimates. Main findings: 71% accuracy (75% sensitivity, 66% specificity, p=0.021) with t-test feature selection and 70% with ReliefF, while SVM-RFE (62%) and mRMR (60%) did not reach significance; autistic participants moved more slowly but pointed about twice as accurately; and large group-level effect sizes did not translate into high classification accuracy. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting at a UK university. Newly collected data using motion tracking; no existing dataset used. [RQ2.3] A deliberately minimal task: point between two 8 mm stickers 30 cm apart on a table with the index finger, as quickly and accurately as possible, for 10 seconds, repeated with the dominant and non-dominant hand. The brevity and simplicity are the point - the paper tests whether a task this short can carry diagnostic signal, in contrast to the longer imitation and gameplay protocols elsewhere in the corpus. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single session of a few seconds of task data per hand, with no follow-up. Data are numeric 3D position traces, not identifiable media, so sensitivity is low. Ethics approval from the University of Manchester research ethics committee is reported with the specific reference number (2017-2541-4204); no consent statement or anonymization procedure is separately described. [RQ2.5] Hardware: Polhemus Fastrak electromagnetic motion tracker with a single sensor on the distal phalange of the index finger, sampling X, Y and Z at 120 Hz; two 8 mm red target stickers on a table. Software: scikit-learn for SVM and grid search, scikit-rebate for ReliefF; outlier handling following the Van Selst and Jolicoeur non-recursive procedure. [RQ2.6] No data or code release and no random seeds, but the analytic pipeline is described in enough detail to reimplement: the full 20-measure table, the accuracy-feature definitions, the outlier-removal procedure and its citation, z-score normalisation, the four feature-selection methods with their parameters (ReliefF K=23, top 10 features for the filter methods), the SVM kernel and grid-searched parameters, the named libraries, the nested cross-validation structure with 10 folds repeated 100 times, and the 1000-permutation significance test. Analytically this is one of the more reproducible descriptions in the corpus; empirically it is not reproducible without the data. [RQ2.7] No dedicated limitations section, but the paper's entire framing is a limitation critique aimed at its own field: prior kinematic studies achieving 86.7-96.7% 'used K-fold Cross-Validation, which was demonstrated to produce overoptimistic performance estimates, especially when a sample size is small' and did not assess whether performance differed significantly from random guessing. The conclusion adds that large parametric effect sizes 'do not necessarily translate to high ML classification performance'. Identifiable in review: no diagnostic instrument named; IQ matching claimed without values; no age standard deviations or ranges; adults only; n=46 so 71% is roughly 33 of 46 correct, with no confidence interval reported though accuracy distributions are plotted; the best of four pipelines is highlighted, though all four including the two non-significant ones are reported in full; and outlier replacement with group means (1.4% of data points) uses group information, a minor leakage route not discussed. [RQ2.9] Extend the approach to kinematic data from more complex movement imitation tasks, with preliminary results described as promising - which is exactly what the same group's 2020 Scientific Reports paper in this corpus goes on to do; and validate the models on newly collected independent data to establish robustness, directly addressing the absence of external validation. [RQ3.1] Motor behavior: 3D index-finger kinematics during repetitive pointing (velocity, acceleration, deceleration, jerk, amplitude and their timings) together with spatial endpoint accuracy derived from where the finger contacted the table. [RQ3.2] Single modality, but with two distinct feature families combined - movement kinematics and endpoint accuracy - which is what allows the speed-accuracy trade-off to emerge. Features from dominant and non-dominant hands are pooled into means and standard deviations, a form of within-modality aggregation. No integration with clinical, cognitive or demographic data. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning. Algorithm: SVM with RBF kernel, with C and gamma grid-searched. Four feature-selection strategies are compared as complete pipelines: SVM recursive feature elimination (embedded), two-sample t-test (filter), ReliefF (filter with neighbour interactions) and mRMR (filter with redundancy penalty). The finding that the two simplest filters outperformed the two more sophisticated methods is reported without embellishment. [RQ4.2] Handcrafted kinematic summary features: 20 scalar movement measures per pointing movement plus spatial accuracy measures, aggregated to 60 features as means and standard deviations pooled across hands, then z-score normalised. No raw time series, images or learned embeddings. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and a permutation p-value for each of the four pipelines, plus accuracy distributions across the 100 nested cross-validation repetitions and confusion matrices for all four models. Reporting non-significant results with their p-values (0.113 and 0.148) alongside significant ones is rare in this corpus. No AUC or confidence intervals, though the plotted distributions convey spread. [RQ4.4] No per-feature importance ranking from the final models. Interpretability comes from the group-level behavioural analysis, which reports the five most discriminative measures with means, t-statistics, p-values and Cohen's d, and from averaged velocity and vertical-amplitude profiles plotted across movement progression for both groups. The substantive finding is a speed-accuracy trade-off: autistic participants were slower but roughly twice as spatially precise (30.87 vs 64.01 mm2 scatter area), which is a difference in movement strategy rather than an impairment - a framing that contrasts with most motor studies in this corpus. [RQ4.5] The strongest validation design among the motor studies here. Nested 10-fold cross-validation with normalisation, feature selection and hyperparameter tuning all performed inside each training fold, so test data never informs model development; the whole procedure repeated 100 times with random splits to yield performance distributions; and permutation testing with 1000 label shuffles to establish that accuracy differs from chance. The authors cite Varma and Simon on nested cross-validation giving 'almost unbiased' estimates and K-fold producing 'significantly overoptimistic results'. Absent: external or independent validation (explicitly named as future work), any held-out site, class-imbalance handling (24 vs 22 is near-balanced), and any deployment analysis. Outlier replacement with group means is performed before the folds, a small residual leakage path. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list in the extracted text. The paper's vocabulary: 'predict autism diagnosis', 'ASC biomarkers', 'automated algorithms assisting with ASC identification', 'nested Cross-Validation', 'overoptimistic performance estimates', 'statistically significantly different from random guessing'. The validation vocabulary is unusually prominent and is effectively the paper's contribution. [RQ5.2] The 41st Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC) 2019 - a biomedical engineering venue, technology-focused but clinically adjacent, not an autism-specific journal. [RQ5.3] 2019. The paper explicitly characterises the state of kinematic autism classification: three prior studies using tablet gameplay sensors, reach-and-throw tracking and movement imitation achieved 'high classification accuracy rates of 86.7% to 96.7%', but 'these studies used K-fold Cross-Validation, which was demonstrated to produce overoptimistic performance estimates, especially when a sample size is small' and did not test significance against chance. This is the corpus's most direct statement that its own literature's headline accuracies are methodologically inflated, and the paper's 71% is offered as the corrected estimate for a comparable task. |
| S-026 | Cross-sectional case-control with the scanpath image as the unit of analysis; 29 ASD-diagnosed and 30 non-ASD French children, whole-sample mean age 7.88 and 64% male with no per-group breakdown; 547 scanpath images plus 2,735 augmented derivatives, released publicly on Figshare. | SMI Red-m 250 Hz eye tracking during approximately 5 minutes of varied video viewing; gaze coordinates rendered as images with velocity, acceleration and jerk encoded as red, green and blue gradients, capped at a quarter of the screen diagonal and limited to 200 drawn points; images rescaled to 100x100, grayscaled and PCA-reduced to 50 components; Naive Bayes, logistic regression, SVM and random forest baselines against single- and two-layer neural networks (100 epochs, 20% dropout) under 10-fold cross-validation. | Conventional classifiers approximately AUC 0.70; all neural networks above 0.90 with the single-layer 200-neuron model best at approximately 0.92, and no gain from added depth or width. Multi-label CARS-severity classification reached approximately 83%, with non-ASD discriminated well and ASD categories at least 20% worse, especially severe ASD. | The reported AUC is image-level, from 547 images across only 59 children plus fivefold augmentation applied before splitting, with no statement of participant-independent partitioning - the principal threat to the result; no per-group age or sex data; diagnosis by unspecified clinic examination with CARS only and unscreened controls; the ASD exemplar described as looking toward the eye tracker itself; CARS used as both diagnostic characterisation and severity prediction target; commercial funder acknowledged without a competing-interests declaration. | The corpus's most inventive gaze representation - packing spatial path plus velocity, acceleration and jerk into a single colour-coded image so that generic image classifiers apply - and one of only three studies to release its dataset publicly, which is why the Figshare scanpath corpus recurs in later work. It is simultaneously the corpus's clearest illustration of image-level rather than participant-level evaluation, and of augmentation performed before rather than inside the fold split. | [RQ1.1] Two groups: 29 ASD-diagnosed children and 30 non-ASD children, total 59. Group sizes are reported. For the multi-label experiment the ASD group is further split by CARS severity into Low, Mild and Severe bands, making four classes. No non-autistic clinical comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'individuals diagnosed with ASD', 'ASD-diagnosed children', 'ASD-diagnosed participants', 'children with ASD', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'Non-ASD'. Predominantly diagnosis-first labelling driven by the classification framing, with the notable phrasing that individuals with ASD 'typically suffer from deficits' and that symptoms 'place a considerable strain on their lives and their families' - a deficit-and-burden framing. [RQ1.3] Reported only at whole-sample level: 59 children, 38 male (64%) and 21 female (36%), mean age 7.88 years and median 8.1 years, with age and CARS distributions shown as box plots. No per-group age means, standard deviations, ranges or sex breakdowns are given, and no matching procedure or comparability test is reported. This makes it impossible to assess whether the ASD and non-ASD groups differ in age or sex - a material gap since gaze behaviour changes markedly across childhood. The sample is school-aged (around 8 years), so despite the paper's early-detection framing it does not test the youngest ages. [RQ1.4] ASD-diagnosed children were examined in multidisciplinary ASD specialty clinics, with autism intensity rated by psychologists using CARS. Typically developing status rests on recruitment from mainstream schools plus careful consideration of parental reports of any possible concerns. No ADOS, ADI-R or structured screening instrument is used, and CARS serves both as the severity measure and, implicitly, as part of the diagnostic characterisation - which matters because CARS bands are later used as the multi-label prediction target. [RQ1.5] No cognitive, linguistic or adaptive measures are reported for either group, and no comorbidity information. CARS is the only clinical instrument, reported as a sample-level mean and median with a box-plot distribution. [RQ2.1] Goal: assistive diagnosis supporting early detection, achieved by converting scanpaths into images so the problem becomes image classification. Main findings: neural networks exceeded AUC 0.90 (best approximately 0.92 with a single 200-neuron hidden layer) against approximately 0.70 for Naive Bayes, logistic regression, SVM and random forests on the same data; increasing model depth or width gave no further gain; and a four-class CARS-severity model reached approximately 83% overall but performed at least 20% worse on ASD categories than on non-ASD, particularly for severe ASD. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting - a quiet university room with white barriers to reduce visual distraction, children seated alone or on a parent's lap at approximately 60 cm. Newly collected data, with the resulting image dataset released publicly on Figshare and described in more detail in an earlier publication by the same group. [RQ2.3] Passive video viewing lasting about 5 minutes on average, with scenarios deliberately varied in content and length to allow ocular activity to be analysed from different perspectives. Stimuli were designed to attract children (colourful balloons, cartoons) with elements whose position changes during the experiment, and some videos featured a human presenter speaking in French who attempts to direct the child's attention to visible or invisible elements. Additional SMI Experiment Center stimuli spanned static and dynamic naturalistic scenes with and without receptive language, joint attention stimuli, static faces or objects, and cartoons. A five-point calibration with subsequent verification procedures preceded recording. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single approximately 5-minute session per child with no follow-up. The data are gaze coordinates rendered into abstract images, so identifiability is low and the public release is correspondingly low-risk. Consent handling is reported carefully: both informed consent from parents and assent from the children themselves were confirmed for all cases, and procedures followed institutional and/or national research committee ethical standards and the 1964 Helsinki declaration with later amendments. [RQ2.5] Hardware: SMI Red-m remote screen-based eye tracker at 250 Hz mounted below a 17-inch monitor at 1280x1024, with the child approximately 60 cm away; physical white barriers around the setup. Software: SMI Experiment Center for stimulus presentation; Python with Matplotlib for scanpath rendering; Keras for image augmentation and neural network training; scikit-learn for PCA and conventional classifiers; Azure ML Studio hosting the models as web services with an ASP.NET and JavaScript front end for the demonstration application. [RQ2.6] Unusually strong on data, weaker on process. The 547-image dataset with metadata is publicly released on Figshare with the explicit intention that others reuse it, and a working demonstration application is deployed at a stated URL. The rendering procedure is described in reproducible detail - the colour-gradient encoding of velocity, acceleration and jerk, the one-quarter-diagonal cap, the vertical mirroring, the 200-point threshold and how it was chosen, the 100x100 rescaling, the grayscale luminance equation, and the PCA reduction to 50 components. What is missing: no code release, no random seeds, no statement of how cross-validation folds were partitioned, no augmentation transformation parameters beyond 'rotation, shearing', and no per-group demographics. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors in a brief limitations section: the relatively small number of participants, and the fairly short duration of the video scenarios, with longer scenarios possibly allowing a richer visual representation. Identifiable in review and more consequential: the unit of analysis is the image not the child, with 547 images from 59 children plus 2,735 augmented synthetic derivatives, and no statement that cross-validation was participant-independent - so images and their own augmented near-duplicates can span the training and test folds, which would inflate the reported AUC substantially; no per-group age or sex data at all; the qualitative observation that the ASD exemplar looked toward the bottom of the screen where the eye tracker was physically located raises the possibility of apparatus-driven signal; the multi-label experiment predicts CARS bands from data collected on children whose diagnosis was itself characterised by CARS, which is partly circular; and the work was funded by a commercial healthcare IT company, acknowledged but not declared as a competing interest. [RQ2.9] No dedicated future-work section. The limitations imply that longer video scenarios should be tested, and the conclusion suggests the scanpath-visualisation approach may generalise to comparable diagnostic problems and to other psychological disorders. No proposals for participant-level validation, larger or independent samples, or addressing the demographic reporting gaps. [RQ3.1] Gaze: raw point-of-regard coordinates over time, from which velocity, acceleration and jerk are derived and encoded chromatically. Distinctively, the representation preserves the full spatiotemporal trajectory rather than aggregating into area-of-interest dwell times, which is the dominant approach elsewhere in the corpus. [RQ3.2] Single modality, but with an internal fusion of four kinematic quantities into one image: spatial path as line geometry, velocity as the red channel, acceleration as green and jerk as blue. This packs position and its first three temporal derivatives into a single representation that a generic image classifier can consume - an elegant encoding, though the subsequent grayscale conversion collapses the three colour channels back into a single luminance value, discarding the channel separation the encoding created. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning, with the problem deliberately recast as image classification. Conventional baselines (Naive Bayes, logistic regression, SVM, random forests) are compared against feed-forward artificial neural networks of increasing capacity (single layer with 50, 200 or 500 neurons; two layers of 80 and 40), trained with 100 epochs and 20% dropout. PCA provides unsupervised dimensionality reduction. Notably no convolutional architecture is used despite the image framing, since PCA-compressed grayscale vectors are fed to fully connected layers. [RQ4.2] A two-stage engineered-then-learned representation: scanpaths are first rendered into RGB images encoding position and its derivatives via colour gradients, then compressed by rescaling to 100x100, grayscale conversion, and PCA from 10,000 dimensions to 50 components. The classifier therefore operates on a 50-dimensional linear projection of a grayscale rendering rather than on the image directly, which is a significant loss of the spatial structure the rendering was designed to create. [RQ4.3] AUC with standard deviation across cross-validation folds, plotted as ROC curves for all four neural architectures, plus a normalised confusion matrix for the multi-label severity model. AUC is a reasonable primary metric, and reporting fold standard deviations is better than corpus norm. However no accuracy, sensitivity, specificity or precision is given for the binary task, and no confidence intervals, so the per-class error profile of the main result cannot be assessed. [RQ4.4] None quantitatively. Two example visualisations are compared qualitatively, with the observation that both show high-density central regions and that the ASD exemplar tended to look toward the bottom of the screen. The confusion matrix for the multi-label model does carry an interpretable finding - that non-ASD is discriminated well while ASD categories, especially severe ASD, are at least 20% worse - which suggests the representation captures the presence of atypicality better than its gradation. [RQ4.5] This is the study's weakest dimension. Ten-fold cross-validation is reported with AUC standard deviations, and dropout and augmentation are used as regularisers, but the fundamental question of what constitutes a fold is never addressed: 547 images derive from 59 children and 2,735 further synthetic images derive from those 547, so unless partitioning is by participant - which is never stated - the test folds contain images from children whose other images, and augmented copies of whose images, were used in training. Augmentation performed before rather than within the fold split compounds this. There is no external validation, no held-out site, no participant-level reporting, no class-imbalance treatment (328 non-ASD vs 219 ASD images), and no permutation or significance testing. The deployed web application demonstrates practical delivery but not validity. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Machine Learning, Eye-tracking, Scanpath. Task vocabulary: 'assistive tools to support the diagnosis process', 'learn the eye-tracking patterns of ASD', 'visual representation', 'image classification task', 'second opinion that is considered to be less biased and reproducible'. The framing of machine learning as a less biased second opinion is a recurring justification in the corpus. [RQ5.2] HEALTHINF 2019, part of the 12th International Joint Conference on Biomedical Engineering Systems and Technologies (BIOSTEC) - a health informatics and biomedical engineering venue, technology-focused rather than clinical, though the work is described as interdisciplinary collaboration between psychology and AI research units. [RQ5.3] 2019. The related-work section surveys the eye-tracking evidence base - shorter and less frequent saccades in high autistic traits, longer fixation on dynamic geometric images in ASD toddlers, declining eye fixation in infants aged 2 to 6 months who later developed ASD, and cohort evidence for eye tracking as an objective measure of autism risk and severity - and then the machine-learning turn, citing RNN classification of Fragile X from gaze during conversation (86-91%) and the authors' own earlier saccade-feature model on 17 children. It positions the visual-representation approach as novel: 'It is claimed that such approach has not been applied before in the context of ASD, to the best of our knowledge'. The accompanying dataset release and deployed web service also document the field's move toward shared benchmarks and demonstrable tooling around 2018-2019. |
| S-027 | Perspective article with an embedded cross-sectional proof-of-principle classification; 29 high-functioning autistic adults (ICD-10 F84.0/F84.5, double-confirmed by two specialists) and 29 typically developed adults in Germany, with no ages, sexes or matching reported; 116 videos of dyadic interaction from an existing study, not shared on stated consent grounds. | Four 5-minute dyadic tasks (two debates, meal planning, roleplay) recorded under standardised camera and lighting geometry; Motion Energy Analysis over manually drawn head and body regions produced movement time series, cross-correlated in non-overlapping 60 s windows at plus or minus 5 s lag to yield 4016 intrapersonal synchrony features per participant; linear SVM in NeuroMiner with PCA (80% variance) inside the inner fold, under repeated nested cross-validation (10 outer folds x 5 permutations, 5-by-5 inner). | 75.9% accuracy, 96.6% sensitivity, 55.2% specificity, AUC 0.71, from 28 true positives, 16 true negatives, 13 false positives and 1 false negative - all but one autistic participant identified, but nearly half of controls misclassified. | No participant ages, sexes or matching reported in this paper; 58 high-functioning adults; specificity of 55.2% means the accuracy rests on over-calling autism; 4016 features against 58 participants; regions of interest drawn manually, retaining a subjective component the authors acknowledge; one entire interaction task dropped because a single dyad misunderstood instructions; no external validation or transdiagnostic specificity testing. | The corpus's clearest statement of methodological standards from inside the field: it names three distinct problems in the 2015-2019 autism machine-learning literature - circularity when training on clinician-derived features, over-optimism from simple cross-validation, and instability from leave-one-out on a heterogeneous phenotype - then implements repeated nested cross-validation and reports a deliberately conservative 75.9%. It is also the only study to refuse data sharing on an explicit consent basis and the only one to measure intrapersonal synchrony, the temporal coupling of a person's own head and body during real conversation. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of 29: high-functioning autistic adults (ICD-10 F84.0 or F84.5) and typically developed adults. Dyads were composed in three configurations - two typically developed, two autistic, or mixed - which is a design feature no other corpus study uses, since it means each participant's behaviour is measured while interacting with partners of both diagnostic statuses. No other-diagnosis group, though transdiagnostic specificity testing is named as required future work. [RQ1.2] 'autistic individuals', 'individuals with ASD', 'autistic adults', 'patients', 'typically developed (TD) individuals', 'TD adults'. Mixed identity-first and person-first, with 'typically developed' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. The paper also refers to autism as 'an umbrella term for neurodevelopmental conditions' and uses 'conditions' alongside 'disorder'. [RQ1.3] Only the group sizes are reported in this paper: 29 autistic and 29 typically developed adults. No ages, no age ranges, no standard deviations, no sex distribution, and no matching information or comparability testing - all deferred to a companion manuscript described as under revision. For a Perspective article this is understandable, but it means the classification result cannot be assessed for demographic confounding from this paper alone. Adults only, so no early-diagnosis relevance. [RQ1.4] Diagnosis confirmed independently by two medical specialists in clinical interviews according to ICD-10 criteria, supplemented by extensive neuropsychological examination, with the sample restricted to F84.0 high-functioning autism and F84.5 Asperger syndrome. Independent double confirmation by two specialists is stronger than most corpus studies, though no standardised observational instrument is named. Control status is asserted with no screening instrument reported. [RQ1.5] Extensive neuropsychological examination is stated to have supplemented the diagnostic interviews for the autistic group, but no scores are reported and none are used in analysis. No IQ, language or adaptive measures for either group, no autism severity instrument, and no comorbidity information. [RQ2.1] Goal: proof-of-principle demonstration that full-body non-verbal behaviour from naturalistic interaction can classify autistic adults, alongside a methodological argument for cross-validation standards. Main findings: 75.9% accuracy, 96.6% sensitivity, 55.2% specificity, AUC 0.71, with 28/29 autistic participants correctly identified but 13/29 controls misclassified. The authors present 75.9% as a deliberately conservative estimate produced by a rigorous validation procedure. [RQ2.2] Laboratory setting with standardised lighting and fixed camera and seating geometry, but with naturalistic unscripted conversation content. The data come from an existing study on interpersonal coordination in dyadic interactions by the same group, so this is a secondary analysis for classification purposes. [RQ2.3] Five 5-minute dyadic social interaction tasks - an ice-breaker, two debating tasks, a meal-planning task and a roleplay - with dyads composed as TD-TD, ASD-ASD or mixed. The ice-breaker task was abandoned entirely because one mixed dyad did not understand the instructions, reducing 145 videos to 116. Recording used a fixed high-definition camera 320 cm from chairs placed 60 cm apart under standardised artificial lighting. Two regions of interest per participant (head; body including legs) were drawn manually, and grayscale change within them produced two continuous movement time series per person. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; four analysed 5-minute interactions per dyad in a single session with no follow-up. The data are video of identifiable adults in extended conversation - among the most sensitive in the corpus. Handling is the most careful encountered: written informed consent under the Declaration of Helsinki, local ethics committee approval, 50 Euro compensation, debriefing, and an explicit data availability statement refusing sharing because the data are 'identifiable patient data from a sample that did not consent to their data being shared in any form'. That is a substantive privacy-protective decision rather than an unexplained absence. [RQ2.5] Hardware: Panasonic DV C Pro HD P2 high-definition video camera on a tripod at a fixed 320 cm distance, chairs 60 cm apart, standardised artificial lighting. Software: Motion Energy Analysis following the Ramseyer and Tschacher pipeline; the rMEA R package for smoothing, scaling and lagged cross-correlation; NeuroMiner for PCA, SVM training and nested cross-validation. Notably no wearable sensors are used, which the authors flag as an advantage given hypersensitivity in autism. [RQ2.6] Data sharing is refused on explicit consent grounds and no code is released, but the analysis is described in unusual procedural detail: the MEA pipeline and its source, the region-of-interest definitions, the cross-correlation window length (60 s), lag range (plus or minus 5 s) and step size (0.04 s), the non-overlapping window rule, the resulting feature counts (1004 lagged cross-correlations, 4016 features per participant), the PCA variance threshold (80%) and its placement inside the inner fold, the feature scaling range, the full nested cross-validation structure (10 folds x 5 permutations outer, 5-by-5 inner), and the eight C values searched. The named open-source tools (rMEA, NeuroMiner) further support re-implementation. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors: the sample size is 'rather limited', so the next step must be applying the algorithm to a completely new and larger dataset; transdiagnostic specificity across psychiatric conditions is untested; and Motion Energy Analysis retains 'a subjective component' because regions of interest are drawn manually, even though pixel-change detection is automatic. The paper also criticises the wider literature for circularity where classifiers are trained on clinician-derived features. Identifiable in review: no participant ages, sexes or matching information are reported in this paper at all; specificity of 55.2% means the model misclassifies nearly half of controls, so the headline accuracy rests on an unbalanced error profile; the dyadic design means each participant's synchrony was measured while interacting with partners of differing diagnostic status, a potential source of variance that is not analysed; one entire task was dropped because a single dyad misunderstood instructions; and the sample is high-functioning adults only. [RQ2.9] Apply the trained algorithm to a completely new and larger dataset, and test transdiagnostic specificity across different psychiatric disturbances; combine multiple non-verbal communication parameters with clinical data such as questionnaires to improve prediction and detect cross-domain associations; extend to eye-gaze and facial expression; and move toward fully automated computer-vision pose and gaze estimation to remove the manual region-of-interest step - while cautioning that such tools' validity against standard motion capture is not yet demonstrated and that they vary in susceptibility to tracking failure and in the video types they support. [RQ3.1] Motor behavior: whole-body non-verbal movement captured as frame-differencing motion energy in head and body regions, converted into intrapersonal synchrony - the temporal coordination between a person's own head and body movement. This is a distinctive construct in the corpus: not movement quantity, speed or trajectory, but the internal temporal coupling of one's own body segments during social interaction. [RQ3.2] Single modality in this analysis. The parent study measured interpersonal coordination between dyad members, but this classification uses intrapersonal synchrony only. Features from four separate interaction tasks are aggregated per participant, a form of fusion across contexts. The future-work section explicitly proposes multimodal fusion with eye-gaze, facial expression and clinical questionnaire data, and Box 1 lists 'combination of objective variables and standard diagnostic measures as input features' as a minimum requirement for reliable clinical application. [RQ4.1] Supervised learning: linear-kernel support vector machine, with PCA used unsupervised for dimensionality reduction. A single algorithm with no best-of-many comparison, consistent with the paper's methodological conservatism. [RQ4.2] Automatically computed high-dimensional synchrony representation: 1004 lagged cross-correlations per window between head and body motion energy time series, z-standardised and aggregated across four interaction conditions into 4016 features per participant, then projected onto principal components explaining 80% of variance within each inner fold. No handcrafted kinematic parameters and no manual behavioural coding. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC and raw true/false positive and negative counts, plus a decision-score plot showing each participant's position relative to the decision boundary. Reporting the raw counts (28/16/13/1) is what makes the error profile legible - the model's 75.9% accuracy comes with 96.6% sensitivity but only 55.2% specificity, meaning 13 of 29 controls were called autistic. No confidence intervals. [RQ4.4] None from the model - no feature importance, SVM weight inspection or ablation is reported, which is a real gap given 4016 features reduced by PCA to an uninterpretable subspace. The only interpretive output is the per-participant decision-score plot, which shows the distribution of confidence and highlights that only one autistic participant fell on the wrong side of the boundary. Substantive behavioural interpretation is deferred to the companion manuscript. [RQ4.5] The methodological centrepiece. The paper argues explicitly that most autism machine-learning studies rely on simple cross-validation, which 'increases the likelihood of choosing an overly optimistic model', and that leave-one-out validation - used by several studies it names - 'creates overly variable test sets, rendering model outcomes unstable' given autism's heterogeneity. It implements repeated nested k-fold cross-validation instead: 10 outer folds with five permutations, a 5-by-5 inner cycle, participants shuffled before each fold definition, parameter optimisation confined to the inner cycle and performance evaluation confined to the outer, with PCA fitted inside each inner fold. It then presents 75.9% as a conservative estimate obtained under this regime, and codifies the standards in a Box listing minimum requirements. What remains absent: external validation on an independent sample (named as the immediate next step), transdiagnostic specificity testing, and any deployment analysis. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: autism spectrum disorder, machine learning, nonverbal synchrony, support vector machine, motion energy analysis, classification, intrapersonal synchrony, nested cross-validation. Including 'nested cross-validation' as a keyword is itself notable and signals the paper's methodological intent. Task vocabulary: 'behavioral marker', 'automatized and objective classification', 'external validity', 'predictive psychiatry', 'transdiagnostic specificity'. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Robotics and AI, in the Human-Robot Interaction specialty section, published as a Perspective article - a technology venue, though the author list is dominated by psychiatry departments and the content is clinical-methodological rather than robotic. [RQ5.3] 2019. The paper provides one of the corpus's most explicit critical surveys of its own field. It notes that early machine-learning work in autism aimed at shortening ADOS and ADI-R administration by item reduction, 'yielding a classification accuracy of autism vs. typically-developing individuals of up to 99.9%', but warns that in such studies 'the features utilized for classification are still highly subjective and not independent of the respective clinician who bases the diagnostic decision on just those features (circularity)'. It catalogues the kinematic strand (96.7%, 92.5%, 93% from staged movement tasks) and observes that 'the movements under investigation were staged, thus, highly unnatural', arguing for a move to naturalistic interaction. And it identifies simple cross-validation and leave-one-out as sources of unstable and optimistic estimates. Together these amount to a diagnosis of three distinct methodological problems in the 2015-2019 literature that this corpus documents. |
| S-028 | Prospective, multi-site, phase III diagnostic classification study protocol, designed according to the Standards for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy Studies and registered as NCT03438994 with status 'Pre-results'. The planned sample is 760 children aged 30 months to 5 years 11 months across Glasgow and Gothenburg, allocated in a published table: 280 with a clinical diagnosis of autism (100 Glasgow, 180 Gothenburg), 280 typically developing (180 Glasgow, 100 Gothenburg) and 200 with another neurodevelopmental disorder (140 Glasgow, 60 Gothenburg) including intellectual disability, non-verbal disability, communication disability, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, Down's syndrome and cerebral palsy, with subclinical or secondary autism expressions excluded from that cohort. Recruitment runs through NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde Specialist Children's Services, other specialist children's centres, nurseries and schools, via two streams for the clinical groups. The reference standard is clinical diagnosis on DSM-5 or equivalent ICD-10 criteria, supplemented for both clinical cohorts by the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, the ESSENCE Questionnaire and either the Adaptive Behavior Assessment System-3 or the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-II. Ethics approval was obtained from the West of Scotland Research Ethics Service Committee 3 and the University of Strathclyde Ethics Committee. Funding is a subcontract from Harimata sp. z o.o. under Horizon 2020 SME Instrument grant 756079. | Each child plays two commercially available children's cartoon games from the Duckie Deck series, engineered with bespoke code to capture data from the iPad's capacitive touch screen and its triaxial accelerometer and gyroscope, for five minutes per game. The third-party Play.Care algorithm - an adaptation of the method developed and published from an 82-child Polish pilot - then classifies the sub-second movement data as positively or negatively associated with autism. The algorithm is locked before the evaluation data are collected, is applied to data obtained independently of its software engineers and commercial sponsors, and the results remain blind until data collection is complete, at which point the classifications will be compared against medical diagnosis. The primary outcome is sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing autistic from typically developing children; the secondary outcome is accuracy in distinguishing autistic children from those with other neurodevelopmental disorders. The sample size is justified by power calculation: if sensitivity or specificity is as high as 90%, the study has 80% power to show it exceeds 83.0% and 90% power to show it exceeds 81.9%; if it is only 70%, there is 91% power to show it is below 80%. | None reported. The trial is registered as pre-results and the classifications are blind until data collection closes. The only performance figure in the article is from the antecedent pilot - 93% accuracy distinguishing autistic children from age- and gender-matched controls among 82 children recruited from specialist day-care centres in Poland - which the trial exists to test under prospective, blinded, multi-site conditions. | As a protocol the article reports no results, so execution and outcome cannot be assessed. Two design points are worth recording. Recruitment through specialist services and existing diagnoses means that predictive value at population prevalence will not be directly estimable even on completion, although the primary outcome measures are the ones a screening instrument requires. And the algorithm is a commercial product applied as a black box, so a positive result would establish that the instrument discriminates without establishing what it measures - the construct-level hypothesis about movement disruption would be supported but not localised. | The methodological benchmark for this review, and the only study in the corpus that closes, by design, every failure mode the synthesis documents elsewhere. The algorithm is locked before the evaluation data exist and applied by investigators separate from its developers; results are embargoed until collection closes; sensitivity and specificity are prespecified as primary outcomes rather than accuracy; recruitment spans two countries and multiple streams to address the site-specific effects the authors identify in their own pilot; the reference standard is independent clinical diagnosis supplemented by symptom-breadth and adaptive-functioning measures; the trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and the protocol published before any result exists; and the sample size is justified with power calculations framed explicitly around detecting underperformance, with the authors stating that if the assessment is underperforming - 'which is the major concern of healthcare services' - the study has a high probability of detecting it. It is also the only powered design in the corpus to prespecify differential diagnosis as an outcome, recruiting 200 children with other neurodevelopmental disorders to test the question that the robot and free-play studies name as the hardest and that the ADOS-versus-schizophrenia study shows the field's gold-standard instrument failing at an AUC of 0.562. Its commercial-interest handling is the most complete here, separating academic investigators holding no equity from company board members with vesting options within a stated governance structure and with the analysis blinded to the developers. Beyond the design, one passage should be carried into the synthesis verbatim because it names the inferential gap that most of this corpus leaves open: of its own pilot, the protocol states that it 'employed the same dataset to train and test the machine learning algorithm. It did so with 10 repetitions of a 10-fold cross-validation procedure that is not prone to overfitting. Nevertheless, it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.' Repeated cross-validation establishes consistency within a dataset, not generalisation beyond it - and a research group took that distinction seriously enough about a 93% figure of their own to commission a 760-child prospective trial to test it. The paradigm is also the most deployable in the review: two five-minute games on a consumer tablet, requiring no professional training, no verbal instruction, no examiner and no subjective coding, with a construct - motor pattern - chosen deliberately in preference to social and emotional variables and reachable in pre-verbal children whom the language-based measures here cannot assess. | [RQ1.1] A planned sample of 760 children aged 30 months to 5 years 11 months across two countries, allocated in a published table: Glasgow 100 autistic, 140 other neurodevelopmental disorder and 180 typically developing; Gothenburg 180 autistic, 60 other neurodevelopmental disorder and 100 typically developing. The composition is the most important feature of the design for this review. Two hundred children with a diagnosed neurodevelopmental condition that is not autism - intellectual disability, non-verbal disability, communication disability, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, Down's syndrome and cerebral palsy - are recruited specifically to test whether the instrument distinguishes autism from other developmental difference rather than only from typical development. Children with subclinical or secondary expressions of autism are excluded from that cohort to keep the contrast interpretable. No participant data are reported, since the protocol was published before data collection closed and the results are embargoed. [RQ1.2] Clinical and health-economic, and unusually precise about the problem being solved. Autism is 'a childhood neurodevelopmental disorder', with UK prevalence and an aggregate annual healthcare and support cost of £28 billion cited. The diagnostic argument is specific rather than dismissive: 'Diagnosis currently relies on specialist medical expertise with diagnostic instrumentation dependent on subjectively rated scores during child observations, parent interviews and testing' - an accurate description that identifies subjectivity of scoring as the issue rather than impugning clinical judgement, and the protocol's stated ambition is to be 'an attractive and useful addition to the assessment and diagnostic toolbox', explicitly alongside ADOS-2 and ADI-R rather than in place of them. Early identification is framed in terms of what it enables for families - 'opportunity to adjust' and access to healthcare intervention and children's services - rather than in terms of treatment or cure. No autistic person or organisation is reported as involved in the design. [RQ1.3] Not reportable, since no participants had been analysed. The design nonetheless specifies more clinical characterisation than almost any completed study in this corpus: parents of children in both clinical cohorts complete the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, the ESSENCE Questionnaire, and either the Adaptive Behavior Assessment System-3 or the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-II, so behavioural difficulties, neurodevelopmental symptom breadth and adaptive functioning will all be available alongside the diagnostic label. The pilot study on which the trial builds used age- and gender-matched controls, and the age window is tightly bounded at 30 months to 5 years 11 months. [RQ1.4] Clinical diagnosis of autism made independently of the study on DSM-5 criteria or the equivalent ICD-10 framework, against which the algorithm's blinded classification will be compared once data collection closes. Two features distinguish this from every other reference standard in the review. The comparison is prospective and blinded - the classifier is locked and applied to data 'obtained independently of the Play.Care software engineers and commercial concerns', with results embargoed until collection is complete - so the index test cannot be tuned to the labels. And the standard is supplemented rather than replaced by questionnaire data: SDQ, ESSENCE and an adaptive behaviour scale are collected for both clinical cohorts, so a positive or negative classification can be examined against symptom breadth and adaptive functioning rather than only against a binary label. [RQ1.5] Planned and comprehensive. The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, the ESSENCE Questionnaire and the Adaptive Behavior Assessment System-3 or Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-II are all administered to parents of children in the autistic and other-neurodevelopmental-disorder cohorts. That combination gives a behavioural-difficulty measure, a neurodevelopmental symptom-breadth measure and an adaptive-functioning measure alongside the diagnostic label, which is the apparatus needed to ask whether the instrument's output tracks severity or only category - the analysis this review has repeatedly found missing in completed studies whose data would have supported it. [RQ2.1] The aim is to test, under phase III conditions, whether a tablet-based serious game can identify autism in preschoolers - specifically whether the 93% accuracy obtained in an 82-child Polish pilot survives prospective, blinded, multi-site evaluation against clinical diagnosis. The primary outcome is sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing autistic from typically developing children; the secondary outcome is accuracy in distinguishing autistic children from those with other neurodevelopmental disorders. No results are reported: the trial is registered as NCT03438994 with status 'Pre-results' and 'the results are blind until data collection is complete'. The protocol's substantive contribution to this review is therefore methodological, and it is considerable - it is the only study in the corpus that locks its algorithm before seeing the evaluation data, separates the analysts from the developers, prespecifies sensitivity and specificity as primary outcomes, powers the study to detect underperformance, recruits a non-autistic clinical comparison group, registers prospectively and publishes the protocol in advance. [RQ2.2] Two sites, Glasgow and Gothenburg, with recruitment through NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde Specialist Children's Services, other specialist children's centres, nurseries and schools, and via two streams for the clinical cohorts - children receiving a positive diagnosis following an NHS clinic assessment, and children already diagnosed. Multi-site international recruitment is itself a design feature aimed at the pilot's acknowledged weakness, that a sample drawn from 'a small number of specialist day-care centres in Poland' is 'prone to selection bias and site-specific effects'. The assessment is intended for use 'in the home, clinic or classroom', so the deployment envelope is broad and the trial's setting is the referral pathway rather than a research laboratory. The residual limitation, not stated, is that recruitment through specialist services and existing diagnoses means predictive value at population prevalence will still not be directly estimable. [RQ2.3] Two commercially available children's cartoon games from the Duckie Deck series, engineered with bespoke code to capture touch-screen and inertial sensor data, played for five minutes each. This is the most deployable paradigm in the review and the protocol states its properties exactly: the method 'required no professional training to deploy, no verbal instructions were required to engage the child, and only limited supervision was necessary. The result of the assessment was purely statistical; no subjective coding was required.' Four consequences follow that no other included paradigm achieves together. There is no examiner, so examiner variability is eliminated rather than merely controlled. There is no verbal demand, so the assessment reaches pre-verbal and minimally verbal children whom the language-based measures in this review cannot assess. There is no human rating anywhere in the chain, so inter-rater reliability is not a consideration. And the apparatus is a consumer tablet running a children's game, so ten minutes in a nursery or a living room produces the data. Against this, what the child is doing is playing a game rather than interacting socially, so the construct measured is motor control rather than reciprocity - which the protocol presents as a deliberate choice. [RQ2.4] Prospective and cross-sectional at the level of the index test, with each child assessed once, and prospective in the trial sense that the algorithm is fixed before any evaluation data are collected. Ethics approval was obtained from the West of Scotland Research Ethics Service Committee 3 and the University of Strathclyde Ethics Committee. The competing-interest handling is the most thorough in this review and is worth recording in full: the academic authors sit on the trial steering and management committees and declare no financial interest in the product or in the funding company, while two coauthors are board members of Harimata sp. z o.o., which intends to commercialise the technology, and hold options vesting in it. The funding is a subcontract from that company under a Horizon 2020 SME Instrument grant. A commercially sponsored diagnostic evaluation in which the analysis is blinded to the developers, the academic investigators hold no equity, and the governance structure is stated, is exactly what this review has found missing elsewhere - most notably in the commercially funded cry-analysis study, whose disclosure is comparably complete but whose design provides none of these separations. [RQ2.5] An Apple iPad and two children's games. The sensing is entirely built in - capacitive touch screen for contact kinematics, triaxial accelerometer and gyroscope for device movement - so nothing is purchased, worn, calibrated or maintained beyond a consumer tablet. Set against the eye trackers, depth cameras, thermal cameras, EEG amplifiers, force plates and MRI scanners charted elsewhere in this review, this is the lowest equipment barrier of any instrumented approach here, and it is the reason the protocol can propose deployment 'in the home, clinic or classroom'. [RQ2.6] The most complete protocol reporting in the corpus. Specified: the design and its STARD basis; the trial registration number and its pre-results status; both sites with participant allocation broken down by cohort and site in a table; inclusion and exclusion criteria for all three groups in a second table, including the exclusion of subclinical or secondary autism expressions from the comparison-disorder group; the age window; both recruitment streams; the games, their source and their duration; the sensor modalities; the third-party algorithm with its provenance in a published pilot; the questionnaire battery for the clinical cohorts; primary and secondary outcomes; the sample size justification with explicit power figures; both ethics approvals; the funding source with grant number; an itemised competing-interest statement distinguishing academic from commercial authors; and author contributions naming who performed the sample size calculations and who conducted technical development. What cannot be reported is any result. [RQ2.7] The protocol's account of its predecessor's limitations is the most methodologically literate passage in this corpus, and it names both failure modes that this review has documented repeatedly. On selection: the pilot's 82 children came from 'a small number of specialist day-care centres in Poland. Such limited subject recruitment is prone to selection bias and site-specific effects and precludes assessment of predictive value in population-based settings.' On evaluation: 'the pilot study employed the same dataset to train and test the machine learning algorithm. It did so with 10 repetitions of a 10-fold cross-validation procedure that is not prone to overfitting. Nevertheless, it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.' That second sentence is important - it concedes that repeated cross-validation, which most studies in this review treat as sufficient, does not establish generalisation beyond the dataset it is computed on. Both concerns are then addressed structurally rather than rhetorically. Two design points remain unstated: recruitment through specialist services means population-prevalence predictive value will still not be directly estimable, and the algorithm remains a commercial black box, so a positive result would show that the instrument works without showing what it measures. [RQ2.9] Completion of recruitment and comparison of the blinded classifications against medical diagnosis, with dissemination through peer-reviewed publication and conferences. For the review, the protocol's value is that it specifies in advance what a credible answer would look like, which makes any eventual result interpretable in a way that retrospective studies cannot be. [RQ3.1] Motor pattern during gameplay, chosen deliberately in preference to social and emotional variables - the protocol lists as a strength that 'a computational analysis of motor pattern variables, rather than social and emotional variables, is employed', grounded in the hypothesis that 'an underlying movement disruption may be a core component of autism spectrum disorder and a new, accessible early biomarker'. The measurement is sub-second: touch-screen contact kinematics and triaxial inertial signals sampled while a child plays. Three properties make this construct choice significant for the synthesis. Motor control is measurable without any social demand, so it does not require the child to engage with a person, which is both an advantage in accessibility and a limitation in construct coverage. It is measurable without language, reaching the pre-verbal and minimally verbal children that the transcript- and conversation-based measures in this review cannot assess. And it is measurable without human rating, so the entire chain from behaviour to classification is instrumented - the protocol notes that in the pilot 'the result of the assessment was purely statistical; no subjective coding was required'. The motor hypothesis aligns with the one-legged-standing and skeleton-movement studies charted elsewhere here, which target postural and gait control on similar reasoning. [RQ3.2] Two synchronous sensor streams from a single consumer device - touch-screen contact patterns and triaxial accelerometer plus gyroscope - capturing both what the child does to the screen and how the device moves while they do it. The fusion is inherent to the platform rather than engineered, which is part of the design's practical appeal: no synchronisation, no calibration and no additional hardware is required to obtain two complementary views of the same motor behaviour. [RQ4.1] A commercial third-party classifier, Play.Care, described as an adaptation of the algorithm developed and published from the pilot study. Its internals are not restated in the protocol, and for the trial's purposes this is by design: the point of a phase III evaluation is that the instrument is locked and applied unchanged to new data, so the algorithm's specification belongs to the development phase rather than to the evaluation. The trade-off is that the trial can establish whether the instrument works without establishing what it measures - a limitation the protocol does not name. [RQ4.2] Sub-second touch-screen and inertial time series from two five-minute gameplay sessions per child. The feature set derived from these is not enumerated, being internal to the commercial product. [RQ4.3] Sensitivity and specificity as prespecified primary outcomes for the autism-versus-typical comparison, and accuracy for the autism-versus-other-neurodevelopmental-disorder comparison as a secondary outcome. Choosing sensitivity and specificity rather than accuracy as the primary measures is correct for a diagnostic instrument and is done by almost no other study in this corpus, most of which report accuracy alone on balanced designs. The sample size justification is expressed in the same terms and is worth quoting for the synthesis: if sensitivity or specificity is as high as 90%, the study has 80% power to show it exceeds 83.0% and 90% power to show it exceeds 81.9%; and 'if the sensitivity (or specificity) is only 70%, there will be 91% power to show that it is below 80%. That is, if the Play.Care assessment is underperforming, which is the major concern of healthcare services, this study has a high probability of detecting it.' Powering a study to detect its own instrument's failure, and stating that this is the point, is unique in this review. [RQ4.4] Not addressed for the algorithm, which is applied as a commercial black box. The construct-level interpretability is nonetheless strong: the target is motor pattern rather than an aggregate behavioural impression, grounded in a specific and falsifiable hypothesis about movement disruption, so a positive result would be interpretable at the level of the construct even if not at the level of the model. [RQ4.5] The methodological benchmark for this review, and the only design in the corpus that closes every failure mode the synthesis documents elsewhere. The algorithm is locked before the evaluation data exist, so no tuning to the labels is possible. The data are collected prospectively and 'independently of the Play.Care software engineers and commercial concerns', so the developers cannot influence the evaluation. Results are embargoed - 'the results are blind until data collection is complete' - so no interim selection can occur. Recruitment spans two countries and multiple streams, addressing the site-specific effects the protocol identifies in its own pilot. Sensitivity and specificity are prespecified as primary outcomes rather than accuracy. A non-autistic clinical comparison group of 200 children is recruited specifically to test differential diagnosis, prespecified as a secondary outcome. The trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov before results exist and the protocol is published in advance. And the sample size is justified with power calculations framed around detecting underperformance rather than demonstrating success. Most significantly for this review, the protocol states explicitly why the pilot's evaluation was insufficient despite using repeated cross-validation: it 'only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset'. That sentence identifies the exact inferential gap that most studies in this corpus leave open - cross-validation within a dataset establishes internal consistency, not generalisation - and the trial exists to close it. The one residual limitation is that recruitment through specialist services and existing diagnoses means predictive value at population prevalence will not be directly estimable even on completion. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list appears in the retrieved text. Terms carried through the protocol: serious game, smart tablet, inertial sensors, movement disruption, motor pattern, biomarker, diagnostic classification, phase III, STARD, sensitivity, specificity, other neurodevelopmental disorder. [RQ5.2] BMJ Open 2019;9:e026226, Protocol section, open access under CC BY-NC; received 6 September 2018, revised 26 March 2019, accepted 1 May 2019, first published 16 July 2019. A general medical journal with a dedicated protocol section, and the venue's requirements are visible throughout: STARD-based design, trial registration with status, a Strengths and Limitations box, tabulated participant allocation and eligibility criteria, explicit power calculations, named ethics committees, an itemised competing-interest statement distinguishing academic from commercial authors, and author contributions specifying individual roles. Publishing a diagnostic protocol before results exist is the practice that makes selective reporting detectable, and this is the only instance of it in the corpus. [RQ5.3] Published July 2019 by a collaboration between the University of Strathclyde, the University of Glasgow, the University of Aberdeen, the Gillberg Neuropsychiatry Centre at Gothenburg, and Harimata sp. z o.o., funded through a Horizon 2020 SME Instrument subcontract. For this review the article is the methodological benchmark against which the rest of the corpus can be read, and it earns that position on six counts. The algorithm is locked before the evaluation data exist and applied by investigators separate from its developers, with results embargoed until collection closes - so none of the tuning, selection or leakage mechanisms documented across the other 130-odd included studies can operate. Sensitivity and specificity are prespecified as primary outcomes rather than accuracy. A 200-child cohort with other neurodevelopmental disorders is recruited to test differential diagnosis as a prespecified secondary outcome, making this the only powered study in the corpus to address the question the free-play and robot studies name as the hardest and that the ADOS-versus-schizophrenia study shows the field's gold-standard instrument failing. The sample size is justified with power calculations framed around detecting underperformance, with the protocol stating that 'if the Play.Care assessment is underperforming, which is the major concern of healthcare services, this study has a high probability of detecting it'. The commercial interest is managed structurally, with academic investigators holding no equity, company board members with vesting options identified individually, and the analysis blinded to the developers. And the protocol is registered and published before any result exists. Beyond the design, one passage deserves to be carried into the synthesis verbatim, because it states the inferential problem that most of this corpus leaves unexamined: the pilot 'employed the same dataset to train and test the machine learning algorithm. It did so with 10 repetitions of a 10-fold cross-validation procedure that is not prone to overfitting. Nevertheless, it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.' Repeated cross-validation establishes consistency within a dataset and not generalisation beyond it - and the entire trial exists because its authors took that distinction seriously about a 93% figure of their own. What the article cannot supply is a result: it is registered as NCT03438994 with status 'Pre-results', and no participant data are reported. |
| S-029 | Cross-sectional classification on a public benchmark; the Saliency4ASD dataset of 300 natural images each freely viewed for 3 seconds by 14 ASD and 14 typically developing children (ASD aged 5-12, mean 8), with no distinct participant counts, control ages or gender data reported; organiser-held blind test set of 100 further images. | Two approaches. Synthetic saccade: STAR-FC generates a simulated typical scanpath per image, aligned to each real scanpath by dynamic time warping, with aligned coordinates plus duration statistics and DTW, Hausdorff and Frechet distances fed to fully connected networks of 492 and 1.4 million parameters. Image-based: fixations rendered as 33 duration-valued Gaussian-smoothed image channels, encoded by a ResNet-18 branch and concatenated with a frozen pretrained ResNet-18 image encoding (11.3 million parameters total). Internal split by image (240 train, 60 test) plus extensive augmentation. | Internal validation: 65.41% / 63% / 61.62% accuracy with AUC 0.69 / 0.66 / 0.63. Organiser's blind test: 54.15% / 53.88% / 55.13% with AUC 0.546 / 0.545 / 0.553 and specificity falling to 0.351 / 0.282 / 0.471. Every model lost 6-11 accuracy points and 0.09-0.14 AUC between the two regimes. | No distinct participant counts, no control ages, no gender data, no diagnostic ascertainment; internal split partitioned by image rather than participant so the same children appear on both sides; unit of analysis is the scanpath not the person; blind-test specificity collapses to as low as 0.282, meaning apparent sensitivity comes largely from over-calling ASD; no ethics or provenance statement; no future work proposed. | The corpus's most direct measurement of internal-validation optimism: identical models and data evaluated first on an image-partitioned internal split and then on an organiser-held blind test set, with accuracy falling from 61-65% to 54-55% and AUC to barely above chance. It also introduces a conceptually distinctive approach - measuring deviation from a computationally simulated typical viewer rather than learning autistic gaze directly - and is one of very few papers here to explicitly discount a prior headline result (a cited 92% adult accuracy) as possibly not transferring to children. | [RQ1.1] Two groups by dataset label - ASD and typically developing - with 14 of each viewing every image. The total number of distinct participants is never stated, only the per-image viewer counts, so the actual sample size is unrecoverable from this paper. No other-diagnosis group. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'people on the autism spectrum', 'ASD subjects', 'typically developed (TD) viewers', 'neurotypical individuals', 'children who develop typically'. Mixed but generally neutral, with 'neurotypical' and 'typically developed' used rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. [RQ1.3] Sparse. 14 ASD and 14 TD children viewed each of 300 images, but the number of distinct children is not reported. Age is given only for the ASD group: 5 to 12 years, mean 8. No control age data, no gender data for either group, no matching procedure and no comparability testing. Given that gaze behaviour changes substantially between ages 5 and 12, and that no control ages are reported at all, demographic confounding cannot be assessed. [RQ1.4] Not reported. Class labels are inherited from the Saliency4ASD challenge dataset with no description of diagnostic instrument, criteria or procedure for either group. [RQ1.5] None reported. No cognitive, linguistic, adaptive or severity measures, and no comorbidity information - consistent with the absence of participant metadata in the challenge dataset as used here. [RQ2.1] Goal: an easy-to-use ASD screening tool for infants and toddlers, motivated by the gap between early symptom emergence and a mean US diagnosis age above 4 with fewer than 25% diagnosed before age 3. Main findings: internal validation accuracies of 61.62-65.41% with AUC 0.63-0.69, falling on the organiser's blind test set to 53.88-55.13% with AUC 0.545-0.553 and specificity as low as 0.282. The 492-parameter model performed best on validation and was matched by the 11.3-million-parameter CNN on the blind test. [RQ2.2] Setting not reported - entirely secondary analysis of the Saliency4ASD benchmark. The source dataset used a Tobii T120 eye tracker with a 17-inch monitor, but no room, distance, calibration or session details are given. [RQ2.3] Free viewing of 300 natural images, each shown at original full resolution for 3 seconds. The paper adds a computational task of its own: generating a synthetic 'typical viewer' scanpath for every image using STAR-FC, a multi-saccade generator that fixates centrally, applies a retinal transform with anisotropic blurring, combines peripheral low-level and central high-level conspicuity streams into a priority map with inhibition of return, and iterates. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; 3 seconds of viewing per image with no temporal or longitudinal component. The data are fixation coordinates over public stimulus images, so re-identification risk is minimal. No ethics approval, consent or data-provenance statement appears - understandable for secondary use of a released challenge dataset, but not acknowledged as such. [RQ2.5] No acquisition hardware used by these authors; the source data came from a Tobii T120 eye tracker with a 17-inch monitor. Analysis: STAR-FC for synthetic scanpath generation; dynamic time warping for alignment; ResNet-18 pretrained backbones; PyTorch on a Titan XP GPU.
