Reporting the false negative rate explicitly, and using it to disclaim diagnostic readiness, is better practice than the corpus norm of quoting accuracy alone. Training accuracy and loss are also given. No AUC, F1, confidence intervals or per-class breakdown beyond the confusion matrix, and no significance testing. [RQ4.4] None. No feature importance, saliency or ablation analysis is performed, and no behavioral characteristic is identified as distinguishing the groups - so despite using Laban movement analysis, whose weight, space and time dimensions carry established interpretive meaning, nothing is reported about how autistic and typically developing children's movement qualities differed. The study yields a classifier without a finding. [RQ4.5] The weakest dimension. A single 80/20 split with no cross-validation, no repeated splits and no separation between validation and test sets, and - decisively - no statement that partitioning occurred at child level, when the discussion makes clear the unit is the 1-second data window with approximately 18,597 per subject. Dropout at 20% across four layers is the only overfitting control described. There is no external validation, no permutation testing, no class-imbalance handling despite 5 versus 7 children, and no calibration or deployment analysis. The authors do reason about deployment readiness qualitatively, correctly declining to claim diagnostic utility, but generalisation is addressed only through the aspiration to collect more data. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: Autism spectrum disorder, child-robot interaction, multi-modal behaviors, deep learning, machine learning, diagnosis. CCS concepts span robotics, machine learning and human-centered computing user studies. Task vocabulary: 'risk detection', 'at-risk ASD', 'streamline existing diagnostic procedures', 'clinical prioritization', 'accessible layer of screening'. The triage-oriented vocabulary is consistent and the paper avoids diagnostic overclaiming. [RQ5.2] HRI '20 Companion - the Late-Breaking Report track of the 2020 ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction. A robotics and human-computer interaction venue, and specifically a short-format preliminary-results track, which bounds what can be expected of the reporting. [RQ5.3] 2020. The brief related-work statement characterises prior machine-learning approaches to ASD diagnosis as based on standardised assessment data, brain imaging datasets, and kinematic analysis of upper-body movement during specialised tasks. The paper positions its own contribution against these as using 'only behavioral data captured through video recordings of a naturalistic interaction with social robots' with unrestricted movement and no obtrusive sensors - articulating the corpus-wide trend away from constrained laboratory tasks and toward naturalistic, sensor-free observation. |
| S-039 | Cross-sectional case-control instrument-development and validation study; 27 children with autism spectrum conditions and 21 typically developing children aged 8-12 with IQ at or above 80, diagnosed by DSM-5 with ADOS-2, ADI-R and SRS-2 confirmed by research-reliable assessors at a US neurodevelopmental research centre; Kinect motion data from four one-minute imitation trials, not released. | Whole-body imitation of unfamiliar, goal-less, multi-limb dance movements shown on screen; two Kinect depth cameras at 30 fps with 20 joints extracted by iPi Motion Capture; CAMI scoring via hip-centred normalisation, automatic joint importance estimation from gold-standard displacement, DTW-aligned weighted distance, and lag and advance durations, combined by metric-learning weights learned within three-fold class-balanced cross-validation; SVM classification; comparison against human observation coding on the same children. | CAMI classified diagnostic groups at 87.2% versus 74.4% for expert human coding; a single one-minute trial reached 84.6%. CAMI-HOC construct validity r = .69-.87; test-retest reliability r = .73-.86; poorer imitation in ASC at p < .005; imitation-severity correlations of r = -0.50 with SRS-2 total and -0.34 with ADOS-2 total. | 48 children means 87.2% is roughly 42 correct, with approximately 13 training samples per class per fold; the headline is the better of two scoring methods on the same folds; sample restricted to IQ at or above 80 and ages 8-12; no external validation; sensitivity and specificity not reported; demographic table not recoverable from the extracted text; and the pipeline is not yet fully automatic, requiring manual processing to compensate for Kinect tracking imperfections. | The corpus's clearest example of an instrument-development study rather than a classification exercise: it validates construct validity against the existing expert standard, quantifies test-retest reliability, demonstrates convergent validity with two independent symptom measures, and only then reports classification - which it wins against human expert coding on the same children. It is also the only study here to make a specificity argument about its own construct, noting that prior motor classifiers cannot distinguish general motor abnormality from imitation-specific impairment, and to control for general motor ability with a dedicated instrument in order to isolate imitation. | [RQ1.1] Two groups: 27 children with autism spectrum conditions and 21 typically developing children, total 48. Group sizes are clear and participant characteristics are tabulated with group comparison test statistics, though the values are not recoverable from the extracted text. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'children with autism spectrum conditions (ASCs)', 'children with ASCs', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'TD peers'. Consistently person-first, and the paper uses 'autism spectrum conditions' rather than 'disorder' throughout - one of a minority in this corpus to do so. The framing is developmental and functional rather than pathologising, discussing imitation's role in 'social bond formation and learning' rather than deficit alone, though 'imitation deficits' and 'impairments' are used. [RQ1.3] 27 ASC and 21 TD children aged 8-12 years. Participant characteristics including means, standard deviations, ranges and group comparison test statistics are presented in Table 1, but the values are not recoverable from the extracted text, so age and sex matching cannot be independently verified in this charting. IQ is controlled by inclusion criterion - full-scale IQ of at least 80 or at least one WISC-V index score of at least 80 - which restricts the sample to children of broadly average or above cognitive ability. General motor ability was additionally measured with the Movement Assessment Battery for Children-2 specifically 'to account for autism-associated differences in general motor abilities', which is an unusually thoughtful covariate choice for an imitation study since it separates imitation-specific from general motor difficulty. [RQ1.4] The most complete diagnostic ascertainment in the corpus alongside Cho et al. (2019): DSM-5 criteria confirmed on site by research-reliable assessors using ADOS-2 (module 3 for all participants, ensuring comparability), the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised, and the parent-report SRS-2. Using all three of the field's principal instruments, applied by research-reliable assessors, and standardising the ADOS module across participants, is a materially stronger reference standard than the 'prior clinical diagnosis' that most of this corpus relies on. [RQ1.5] Extensive. Full-scale and index IQ measured with WISC-V and used as an inclusion criterion; general motor ability measured with the Movement Assessment Battery for Children-2 explicitly to separate imitation-specific from general motor differences; ADOS-2 and SRS-2 administered and used quantitatively in correlational analyses of symptom severity. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are deferred to a supplement. This is among the fullest functional characterisations in the corpus. [RQ2.1] Goal: develop an objective, continuous, scalable measure of motor imitation, validated on four fronts - construct validity, test-retest reliability, diagnostic discrimination, and clinical association. Main findings: CAMI classified diagnostic groups at 87.2% versus 74.4% for human observation coding; a single one-minute trial reached 84.6%; CAMI-HOC correlations r = .69-.87; test-retest r = .73-.86; poorer imitation in ASC (p < .005); and poorer imitation correlated with greater symptom severity on SRS-2 (r = -0.50 total) and ADOS-2. [RQ2.2] Research centre setting at a neurodevelopmental research institute, with community and school recruitment. Data were collected as part of a wider study of imitation skills in autism, so this is a focused analysis within a larger programme rather than a standalone collection. [RQ2.3] Whole-body imitation of dance-like movements performed by a young woman on a large TV screen, deliberately without music or sound. Sequences comprised 14-18 individual movement types selected to be 'relatively unfamiliar (e.g., moving arms up and down like a puppeteer)', to lack an end goal, and to require moving multiple limbs simultaneously - chosen on the basis of prior research showing that autistic imitation difficulties are most pronounced for meaningless, goal-less actions. A brief training phase preceded testing. Of 14 collected trials at varying speeds, only the 4 at 100% speed are analysed to avoid confounding by speed, comprising two sequences each presented twice, which is what enables the test-retest analysis. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; two-day visits with repeated trials within session, and no longitudinal follow-up - though repeated trials within session provide the test-retest estimate. Data are depth-camera recordings reduced to skeletal joint coordinates, so identifiability is moderate rather than high. Ethics governance is complete: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine IRB approval prior to commencement, written informed consent from all legal guardians, verbal assent from all children, and $100 compensation. [RQ2.5] Hardware: two Microsoft Kinect Xbox depth cameras at 30 frames per second positioned in front of and behind the child, requiring no sensors or special clothing - an explicit design advantage for this population; a large TV screen for stimulus display. Software: iPi Motion Capture Software for extracting 20 joint coordinates from depth recordings; a custom dynamic time warping and metric learning pipeline with equations supplied in a supplement; SVM for classification. [RQ2.6] No data or code release is stated in the extracted text, and substantial methodological detail - the CAMI equations, parameter learning formula, parameter values, full inclusion and exclusion criteria, study setup, and supplementary ten-fold replication - is deferred to a supplement. What is in the main text is precise: the five-step algorithm is described in sequence, joint importance estimation is explained, the three features are defined, the cross-validation scheme and its rationale are given, and the software and hardware are named. The approach would be reimplementable with the supplement. [RQ2.7] Reported by the authors, and addressed unusually rigorously rather than merely acknowledged. On sample size, they concede that 27 ASC and 21 TD 'can be considered relatively small' given phenotypic heterogeneity, then argue quantitatively that the method does not suffer from a sample size problem: invoking the 1-in-10 rule for the three-variable metric learning (30 samples needed, approximately 90 used), and applying Raudys's formula for SVM expected error with p=3, delta=3.83 and n=13 per class to derive a 5.9% expected error against a 2.8% infinite-sample floor. They also note their parameter-to-sample ratio is more favourable than two named prior autism motor studies (40 parameters from 30 subjects, and 7 parameters from 30 subjects). On scalability they concede that Kinect imperfections 'require some manual processing that can be time-consuming'. Identifiable in review: 48 children means 87.2% is roughly 42 correct; the headline is the better of two scoring methods evaluated on the same folds; IQ at or above 80 and ages 8-12 bound generalisability; and the demographic table is not recoverable from the extracted text so matching cannot be verified. [RQ2.9] Improve scalability by exploring capture technologies beyond Kinect, whose motion-tracking imperfections currently require time-consuming manual processing. The authors also frame CAMI as a candidate biomarker 'for defining biologically meaningful ASC subtypes and guiding intervention', and note it can 'track performance during interventions designed to improve social-communicative function through imitation training' - positioning it as a measurement instrument for intervention research rather than only a diagnostic tool. [RQ3.1] Motor behavior: whole-body 3D joint trajectories during imitation, evaluated for both spatial fidelity to a model and temporal synchrony with it. The construct measured is specifically imitation ability - the correspondence between the child's movement and a target - rather than movement quality in the abstract, which the authors argue distinguishes their approach from prior motor classifiers. [RQ3.2] Single modality, with a designed internal fusion: spatial distance and two temporal asynchrony measures (lag and advance) are combined by learned linear weights into one continuous score, so spatial and temporal aspects of imitation are integrated rather than treated separately. The authors argue this integration is necessary 'given the importance of timing in social coordination and in characterizing autism-specific imitation impairments'. Separately, the CAMI score is validated against and correlated with independent clinical instruments (ADOS-2, SRS-2, MABC-2), which is convergent validation rather than fusion. [RQ4.1] A hybrid of classical algorithm and learning: dynamic time warping provides temporal alignment, metric learning determines how the three derived features combine, and a support vector machine performs diagnostic classification. The design rationale is stated explicitly - the authors deliberately impose structure to reduce learnable parameters using expert-derived guidance, arguing that 'using expert knowledge to guide the features improved CAMI's interpretability, while deviance from HOC as a result of automatized learning processes improved CAMI's diagnostic discriminative ability'. [RQ4.2] A three-dimensional interpretable representation derived from 20-joint 3D trajectories: a joint-importance-weighted DTW distance capturing spatial fidelity, and two durations capturing how long the child lagged and led the model. Producing a continuous score in [0,1] rather than a categorical judgement is an explicit design goal, argued as necessary for populations with high behavioural variability where 'categorical outputs can only capture relatively large variations'. This is one of the lowest-dimensional and most interpretable representations in the corpus. [RQ4.3] Classification accuracy for the diagnostic comparison, but the evaluation is much broader than classification: Spearman correlations for construct validity against the expert standard, correlations across repeated trials for test-retest reliability, correlations with two independent symptom instruments for clinical validity, and group comparison significance testing. Reporting reliability alongside validity and accuracy is close to unique in this corpus and reflects a psychometric rather than purely machine-learning framing. No sensitivity, specificity or AUC is reported, which is the main metric gap. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is architectural rather than post hoc. The three features have direct behavioural meanings (spatial deviation, lag, advance), joint importance is estimated automatically from the model's own displacement so that the score reflects the joints that actually matter for each movement, and the output is a bounded continuous score interpretable as 'how well the children performed with respect to a model'. The authors explicitly contrast this with methods that 'classify children into diagnostic groups based on broad differences in movement patterns', arguing those cannot distinguish general motor abnormality from imitation-specific impairment - a specificity critique that applies to several other motor studies in this corpus. [RQ4.5] Strong. Three-fold cross-validation with class-balanced folds, and the metric-learning weights are learned only on training folds so that CAMI scores are computed 'completely independently from and without reference to' the HOC scores against which they are validated - an explicit leakage control on the validation comparison itself. The fold count is justified against the bias-variance literature and the analysis is replicated with ten folds in supplementary results. Test-retest reliability across repeated trials provides a form of stability evidence that cross-validation cannot. The small-sample concern is addressed with two quantitative arguments rather than dismissed. What is absent: external or independent validation on a separate cohort, sensitivity and specificity reporting, and any deployment evaluation - though the authors are candid that the current pipeline is not yet fully automatic. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list in the extracted text. Vocabulary: 'Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation', 'construct validity', 'test-retest reliability', 'promising biomarker', 'biologically meaningful ASC subtypes', 'scalable'. The psychometric vocabulary - validity, reliability, construct - is distinctive within a corpus dominated by accuracy-centric machine-learning language. [RQ5.2] Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging - a clinical neuroscience and psychiatry journal, neither computational nor autism-specific, and one of the more clinically prestigious venues in this corpus. [RQ5.3] 2020. The paper characterises the field precisely along two axes. On imitation assessment, it notes that human observation coding remains the standard but is 'subjective and time-consuming and requires intensive coder training', rendering it 'impractical for use in clinics and home settings', and that prior automated approaches are either rule-based with 'very limited generalizability' or DTW-based but reduced to dichotomous or categorical outputs that waste the continuous distance metric. On machine learning it makes a specificity critique that bears directly on this corpus: prior studies classifying autism from motor patterns 'did not directly assess imitation ability even when some tasks involved imitation', so 'it is unclear if the observed differences represent general motor abnormalities or specific imitation impairments' - a limitation that 'restricts the use of these methods for intervention purposes'. |
| S-040 | Retrospective secondary analysis of clinical diagnostic audio; 39 Korean infants (10 autistic aged 12-24 months, 4 male; 29 typically developing aged 6-18 months, 19 male) assessed at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital 2016-2018; 1,125 infant-only utterances (475 autistic, 650 typically developing), not released. | Session audio segmented into infant-only clips labelled into five developmental vocalisation categories; 88 eGeMAPS parameters extracted per 25 ms frame with openSMILE, normalised on training statistics and grouped into five-frame blocks; four models compared - linear SVM, eight-cell BLSTM on 88 features, the same on 54 Mann-Whitney-selected features, and a 88-70-54-70-88 stacked auto-encoder with an auxiliary ASD/TD softmax head jointly optimised with the BLSTM - trained in TensorFlow with ADAM, batch normalisation, dropout and early stopping, and evaluated by five-fold cross-validation over utterances. | AE+BLSTM best throughout: accuracy 0.6818, F1 0.5457, UAR 0.6509, versus 0.6640/0.5091/0.6302 (eGeMAPS-88), 0.6373/0.4545/0.5997 (eGeMAPS-54) and 0.6178/0.2234/0.5514 (SVM). Derived autistic-class sensitivity is 45.3%, 41.3%, 35.8% and 13.1% at specificities of 84.9%, 84.8%, 84.2% and 97.2%. Statistical feature selection degraded performance relative to using all 88 features. Autistic infants produced proportionally fewer first words (0.011 vs 0.054) and more atypical vocalisation (0.433 vs 0.249). | Cross-validation splits utterances rather than infants, so the same child appears in training and evaluation folds; group ages are near-disjoint (no autistic infant under 12 months, no typically developing infant over 18) at the developmental stage where vocalisation changes fastest; sex ratio inverted between groups; 10 autistic infants only; precision and recall labels transposed in the results table; autistic-class sensitivity below 50% even for the best model; no learning rate, batch size, dropout rate or loss weighting reported; no code or data; single site, no external validation. | The corpus's best example of diagnostic ascertainment - seven instruments including ADOS-2 and ADI-R plus psychiatrist DSM-5 best-estimate applied identically to both groups, so the typically developing label is as well evidenced as the autistic one. It is also the corpus's most candid paper about small-data conditions, naming infant anonymity requirements as a structural constraint on what data can exist and designing for that constraint rather than assuming it away. Its negative result on statistical feature selection, and its demonstration that a learned bottleneck of the same dimensionality outperforms a significance-selected subset, is a methodological finding the rest of the corpus does not test. Read against its own confusion matrices, it is also a useful corrective on headline metrics: 68% accuracy corresponds to catching fewer than half of autistic utterances. | [RQ1.1] Two groups, 39 infants: 10 diagnosed autistic and 29 typically developing, all recruited as consecutive clinical cases undergoing diagnostic assessment at one hospital between 2016 and 2018. The typically developing group is not a convenience sample - these are infants brought for assessment who were assessed as typical, which makes them a clinically relevant comparison (children of diagnostic concern who turn out not to be autistic) rather than a community control group. Analysis is at the utterance level: 1,125 utterances, 475 autistic and 650 typically developing. [RQ1.2] 'infants with autism spectrum disorder', 'children with ASD', 'children with TD', 'typical development'. Person-first and consistently paired ASD/TD. The framing is clinical-disorder oriented - 'a developmental disorder with a life-span disability' - but without the burden-of-disease register found elsewhere in the corpus. Notably the paper describes existing diagnosis as compromised by 'subjectivity and interpretive bias between professions' rather than by clinician inadequacy. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: n = 10, 4 male / 6 female, mean age 19.20 +/- 2.52 months, all aged 12-24 months. Typically developing group: n = 29, 19 male / 10 female, mean age 14.72 +/- 2.45 months, all aged 6-18 months. Age separation is near-total: every infant in the 6-12 month band is TD and every infant in the 18-24 month band is ASD, with overlap confined to the 12-18 month band. The sex ratio is inverted relative to autism's usual epidemiology (40% male in the autistic group versus 66% in the TD group) and is not addressed. Country and site are single (South Korea, SNUBH); no socioeconomic or ethnicity data. Per-infant age, sex, initial diagnosis date and definite final diagnosis date are tabulated for all 39 participants, which is unusually transparent. Note that the running text states the ASD mean age as 14.72 months, contradicting the table - an apparent transposition with the TD figure. [RQ1.4] The most thorough in the corpus. Every participant was assessed with seven instruments: ADOS-2, ADI-R, BeDevel-Interview, BeDevel-Play, K-CARS (refined from CARS-2), the Social Communication Questionnaire and the Social Responsiveness Scale. The final diagnosis was the best clinical estimate by a licensed child psychiatrist against DSM-5 criteria using all available information. Both groups received the identical procedure, so the typically developing label carries the same evidential weight as the autistic one - a property almost no other study in this corpus has. A definite final diagnosis date roughly one month after initial examination is recorded for each infant. [RQ1.5] K-CARS, SRS and SCQ were administered and could have supported severity analysis, but no severity, cognitive, language or adaptive scores are reported and no severity-stratified result is given. The five-category vocalisation labelling (single syllable, canonical babbling, non-syllabic babbling, first word, atypical voice) functions as a developmental-stage descriptor and is the only developmental characterisation reported, given per group as proportions of total vocalisation time. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether auto-encoder-based learned features, jointly optimised with the classifier, improve automated autism detection from infant vocalisations under small, unbalanced, unrefined data conditions. Main findings: the jointly optimised AE+BLSTM outperformed vanilla BLSTM and SVM on accuracy (0.6818), F1 (0.5457) and UAR (0.6509); Mann-Whitney-based selection of 54 eGeMAPS features degraded rather than improved performance; t-SNE shows eGeMAPS-88 and eGeMAPS-54 spaces nearly identical and heavily overlapped while the auto-encoder space is visibly redistributed; and at the categorical level autistic infants produced proportionally fewer first words and more atypical vocalisation. [RQ2.2] Retrospective secondary analysis of audio extracted from video recordings of clinical autism diagnostic sessions conducted at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital between 2016 and 2018, under IRB approval for use of fully anonymized data from an existing study. Recording conditions are reported: two clinical rooms of stated dimensions with ambient noise around 40 dB. [RQ2.3] No experimental task at all - and this is a deliberate methodological position rather than an omission. Audio comes from the clinical diagnostic procedure itself, so what the models see is the same behaviour a clinician sees, recorded in situ with clinician speech, parent speech, toy noise and chair scraping all present. The cost is that infant-only segments must be isolated by hand and that the recording contains no controlled elicitation; the benefit is ecological validity and the possibility of retrofitting to sessions already being recorded. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional per infant, with a definite final diagnosis recorded about a month after the initial examination. Data are clinical audio of infants, and the governance reporting is exemplary by corpus standards: two IRB approval numbers, explicit statement that analysis used fully anonymized retrospective data, and - unusually - the paper treats infant anonymity as a first-order constraint shaping what data can ever exist in this field, which is the stated motivation for the small-data method it develops. [RQ2.5] 48 kHz stereo recording downsampled and downmixed to 16 kHz mono; openSMILE for the 88 eGeMAPS parameters at 25 ms frames with 10 ms overlap; TensorFlow; t-SNE. Model components: a 88-70-54-70-88 stacked auto-encoder with an auxiliary softmax head on the latent layer, and a BLSTM with eight cells matched to prior work for comparability. [RQ2.6] Good on architecture and preprocessing, thin on training detail. Reported: layer dimensions, auxiliary output formulation with equations, frame length and overlap, five-frame grouping, normalisation fitted on training data only, batch normalisation, ReLU, dropout, ADAM, early stopping with 100-epoch patience, best-model checkpointing, and the utterance decision rule (mean frame-wise class index above 0.5). Not reported: learning rate, batch size, dropout rate, auto-encoder pretraining schedule, the relative weighting of reconstruction and auxiliary losses in the joint objective, and whether SVM hyperparameters were tuned. No code and, by design, no data. [RQ2.7] Explicitly acknowledged: the data set is insufficient, dispersed and unbalanced; performance is 'relatively poor in comparison to the general classification tasks based on deep learning'; the improvement from joint optimisation is 'only marginal'; the BLSTM was deliberately kept small (eight cells) to match prior work rather than to maximise performance; and comparison with the prior study is only indirect because feature selection did not reproduce. Not acknowledged: the near-disjoint age distributions between groups, on the variable that most strongly governs infant vocalisation; the inverted sex ratio; the utterance-level rather than infant-level splitting, which allows the same child's voice into both training and evaluation folds; and the transposed precision and recall labels in the results table. Reading the confusion matrices directly also shows that autistic-class sensitivity is only 45.3% even for the best model, a figure the accuracy and UAR headline numbers obscure. [RQ2.9] Increase the volume of infant speech data; refine the acoustic features and the auto-encoder architecture; adopt deeper and more current model structures, since the authors expect the auto-encoder's redistributed feature map to pay off more in complex models than in the deliberately small BLSTM used here; extend the approach to children aged 3-4 who can produce several sentences, adding linguistic features to acoustic ones; and generalise beyond autism to the detection of developmental delay. [RQ3.1] Infant vocalisation captured passively during clinical assessment - one syllable utterances, canonical babbling, non-syllabic babbling, first words, and atypical voice including screaming and crying. Uniquely in the corpus, the vocalisations are categorised by developmental stage before modelling, so the acoustic analysis sits on top of an explicit linguistic-development taxonomy rather than treating all speech as homogeneous. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion - audio only, and the paper notes that video recordings existed but only their audio was used. The structural comparison it does make is across feature representations of the same modality: raw eGeMAPS-88, statistically selected eGeMAPS-54, and learned auto-encoder bottleneck features. Extension to linguistic features alongside acoustic ones for older children is named as future work. [RQ4.1] Four models compared on identical data: a linear-kernel SVM baseline, a vanilla eight-cell BLSTM on 88 features, the same BLSTM on 54 statistically selected features, and a stacked auto-encoder jointly optimised with the BLSTM. The auto-encoder is semi-supervised, carrying an auxiliary binary ASD/TD softmax head on its latent layer so that the representation is shaped by the diagnostic target rather than by reconstruction alone. Joint optimisation of representation and classifier is the paper's actual contribution, and holding the BLSTM fixed at eight cells across conditions is what isolates it. [RQ4.2] eGeMAPS - all 88 parameters, per 25 ms frame with 10 ms overlap, normalised using training-set statistics and grouped into blocks of five consecutive frames so the BLSTM sees local temporal context; the SVM receives the same five frames flattened into a 440-dimensional vector. The auto-encoder compresses 88 to 54 dimensions, matched deliberately to the 54-feature statistical subset so the two dimensionality-reduction strategies are directly comparable. That comparison is the paper's cleanest result: learned compression beat statistical selection, and statistical selection was worse than no reduction at all. [RQ4.3] Full confusion matrices for all four models, plus accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and unweighted average recall - UAR explicitly adopted from the INTERSPEECH 2009 Emotion Challenge because the classes are imbalanced. Reporting UAR alongside accuracy is good practice and rare in this corpus. Two caveats: precision and recall are transposed in the table (the printed 0.4526 for the AE model is autistic-class recall, as the reported UAR confirms), and all metrics are utterance-level, so no per-infant performance can be derived. Derived from the matrices, autistic-class sensitivity is 45.3% (AE), 41.3% (eGeMAPS-88), 35.8% (eGeMAPS-54) and 13.1% (SVM), against specificities of 84.9%, 84.8%, 84.2% and 97.2%. [RQ4.4] No feature attribution or post hoc explanation. Interpretability is pursued at the representation level through t-SNE projections of the three feature spaces, which support a specific and testable claim: eGeMAPS-88 and eGeMAPS-54 are almost indistinguishable and heavily overlapped between classes, while the auto-encoder produces a more separable distribution. The authors offer a mechanistic reading - the bottleneck weights significant parameters up and ambiguous ones down - and a diagnosis of why statistical selection failed, namely that eGeMAPS contains temporal parameters relevant to vocalisation generally which confuse the ASD/TD distinction. The clinically interpretable layer is the vocalisation taxonomy rather than the model. [RQ4.5] Five-fold cross-validation with a separate randomly selected 10% test set balanced across vocalisation categories, early stopping on validation loss, and best-model checkpointing - properly structured as a protocol. The defect is the unit of division: splitting is by utterance, not by infant, so with 1,125 utterances from 39 children the same speaker appears on both sides of every fold, and the models can exploit speaker identity rather than autism-related acoustics. Given that the two classes are also near-disjoint in age, speaker-level information is doubly informative about the label. No independent test cohort, no external site, no per-infant aggregation, and no comparison against the seven clinical instruments the labels came from. [RQ5.1] Keywords: auto-encoder; bidirectional long short-term memory (BLSTM); joint optimization; acoustic feature extraction; autism spectrum disorder. Four of the five are machine-learning terms and autism appears last - the paper's identity is a representation-learning contribution demonstrated on an autism task, and its comparisons (INTERSPEECH challenge metrics, eGeMAPS, openSMILE) situate it in the computational paralinguistics community. [RQ5.2] Sensors (MDPI), published as a Letter - a short-format engineering venue rather than a clinical journal, consistent with the paper's framing as a proof of possibility rather than a diagnostic study. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing cites prevalence rising from 1 in 150 children in 2000 to 1 in 54 in 2016, and identifies the bottleneck as the gold-standard behavioural assessments themselves - time-consuming, requiring multidisciplinary teams, and unstable because of accessibility, subjectivity and 'interpretive bias between professions'. Its most distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is a data-availability argument: it names infant anonymity requirements and parental non-recognition at early developmental stages as the structural reasons the field's data is small, dispersed by sex, age and vocalisation count, and unrefined, and it observes that 'these problems were typically overlooked by previous research with controlled and small amounts of data'. The method is then designed for those conditions rather than assuming they will be solved. [RQ_funding_note] Funded by the Korean IITP grant No. 2019-0-00330, 'Development of AI Technology for Early Screening of Infant/Child Autism Spectrum Disorders based on Cognition of the Psychological Behavior and Response' - a national programme explicitly targeting AI-based early autism screening, which situates this paper within a funded state initiative rather than an isolated academic effort. |
| S-041 | Methodological comparison of two data representations; 21 subjects (12 clinically diagnosed autistic, 9 typically developed) with no demographic or diagnostic characterisation reported; Vicon motion capture at 250 Hz over at least five walking trials each, yielding 278 gait cycles (Dataset A) or 105 trial averages (Dataset B); not released. | Eight temporal gait-phase durations per cycle (step, stance, swing and step-to-step time for each leg) computed as frame-count differences between detected foot strike and foot off events, L2-normalised; SVM, KNN, random forest and decision tree each hyperparameter-tuned by grid search with precision as the selection metric and evaluated by 10-fold cross-validation over gait cycles or trials rather than participants. | Dataset A: random forest 68.75% accuracy / 76.63 F1, SVM 63.75 / 76.80, decision tree 63.75 / 72.90, KNN 58.75 / 65.98. Dataset B: random forest 76.67 / 78.79, decision tree 63.33 / 62.07, KNN 56.67 / 48.00, SVM 50.00 / 66.67 as a degenerate always-autistic predictor. Averaging visibly compressed intra-subject spread, most for the most variable subjects, and autistic subjects showed greater intra-subject variability than typically developed ones. | Cross-validation splits gait cycles rather than participants, with the authors explicitly noting the same subject and trial can appear on both sides and judging the impact limited; hyperparameter selection and performance estimation share the same cross-validation; no age, sex, site, ethics approval or diagnostic instrument is reported, so nothing excludes stature, cadence or age as the discriminated variable in features that are all durations; the two compared datasets differ in size as well as variance; no significance test accompanies the headline improvement on 105 data points. | The corpus's most explicit instance of leakage recognised and then reasoned past: the paper states plainly that training and test folds can contain data from the same subject and the same trial, and proceeds with cycle-level splitting anyway. That makes it a valuable counterpart to the Vabalas papers, which diagnose exactly this defect from the outside. It is also the only study in the corpus to treat the unit of data representation as its research question, and its incidental finding - that autistic subjects show greater intra-subject gait variability, so variance itself may be the signal rather than noise to be averaged away - is a hypothesis the rest of the gait literature here does not test. | [RQ1.1] Two groups, 21 subjects: 12 clinically diagnosed autistic and 9 typically developed. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The analysis unit is not the subject but the gait cycle (Dataset A: 167 autistic and 111 typically developed cycles) or the walking trial (Dataset B: 60 and 45), so 21 people generate 278 or 105 data points respectively. The authors themselves note that with a dataset this small 'the impact of variation in the subjects may be magnified due to the large portion of the dataset each subject represents'. [RQ1.2] 'subjects clinically diagnosed as having ASD', 'subjects with ASD', 'those with autism', 'typically developed (TD)', 'people with the condition'. Predominantly person-first, with 'typically developed' rather than 'healthy' or 'normal'. Autism is framed as 'a permanent neurological condition' rather than a disease, and the motivating argument is that objective motor measurement can supplement subjective behavioural assessment - a relatively neutral register. [RQ1.3] None reported. The paper gives group sizes (12 autistic, 9 typically developed) and nothing else: no ages, no age ranges, no sex distribution, no ethnicity, no socioeconomic information, no country of collection, and no statement about matching on any variable. This is the least participant characterisation of any included study in the corpus, and it means the reported group difference cannot be attributed to autism rather than to age, sex, height, leg length or any other determinant of gait timing - all of which the eight features measure directly. [RQ1.4] A single clause: subjects were 'clinically diagnosed as having ASD'. No instrument, no criteria, no diagnostician, no date. Typically developed status carries no stated basis at all. Given that the entire classification target rests on these labels, this is the study's most consequential reporting gap. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure is reported, and no comorbidity information. Nor are the anthropometric variables that directly determine gait phase durations - height, leg length, body mass - which for a gait study is a substantive omission independent of clinical characterisation. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine how the choice of data representation - individual gait cycles versus trial averages - affects autism classification performance, as a methodological question in its own right. Main findings: averaging reduced intra-subject variance, most for subjects with the greatest initial variance; random forest improved from 68.75% to 76.67% accuracy; decision tree and KNN showed little accuracy change but substantial F1 loss; the SVM degenerated into an always-autistic predictor; autistic subjects showed visibly greater intra-subject gait variability than typically developed subjects; and the benefit of variance reduction depends on classifier suitability, dataset size and class balance. [RQ2.2] Not stated. Author affiliations span Ulster University (Northern Ireland), Bangor University (Wales) and the University of Colombo (Sri Lanka), but no collection site, recruitment route, period or setting is identified, and no ethics approval or consent statement appears. [RQ2.3] Overground walking trials with lower-limb marker placement - a minimum of five per subject, each containing a variable number of gait cycles, with the analysis restricted to the five-trial common minimum so that every subject contributes equally. Restricting to a common trial count is a deliberate balancing decision at the subject level, and is the only such control the design applies. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single capture session per subject with no follow-up. Data are numeric marker trajectories and event timings, so low sensitivity in themselves, but no ethics approval, consent procedure or data governance statement appears anywhere in the paper. Since ages are never reported, it cannot even be determined whether the participants were adults or children. [RQ2.5] Vicon infrared motion tracking system sampling at 250 Hz for marker capture and gait event detection; the scikit-learn Python library for L2 normalisation, the four classifiers, grid search, 10-fold cross-validation and the four reported metrics. No custom software and no bespoke instrumentation. [RQ2.6] Mixed. The feature definitions are exemplary - all eight are named explicitly by their event pairs (RS-LS, LS-RS, LO-LS, RO-RS, LS-LO, RS-RO, LS-LS, RS-RS), mapped to their gait phases, with the sampling rate and the frame-difference computation stated, so the feature set is fully reproducible. The dataset construction is also precisely specified, down to the cycle and trial counts in each condition. Everything else is missing: no grid-search ranges or selected hyperparameters for any classifier, no random seed, no code or data release, no ethics statement, and no participant characteristics whatsoever. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged with unusual directness in one respect and not at all in others. The authors state that training and testing folds 'can both contain data points from the same subject and even from the same trial', judge the impact 'potentially limited', and choose 10-fold over leave-one-out on that basis - naming the leakage and then reasoning past it rather than eliminating it by splitting on participants. They also acknowledge the small dataset, the class imbalance, that averaging reduces the data available for training, and that the SVM's apparent 100% recall was a degenerate single-class predictor with 'no use in real world applications'. Not acknowledged: that grid search selected hyperparameters on the same cross-validation whose scores are reported, so every figure is optimistically biased; that no participant characteristic is reported, so nothing rules out age, sex or stature as the discriminated variable in features that are all durations; that no diagnostic instrument is named; and that no ethics approval is stated. The paper describes itself as a 'preliminary investigation', which is a fair self-assessment. [RQ2.9] Include objective measures of intra-subject gait variance directly in the feature vectors, on the basis of the observed greater variability in autistic subjects; pair variance reduction with synthetic data generation for the minority class to counter the imbalance that averaging exacerbates and the overfitting seen in the SVM; and examine more generally when the loss of dataset size outweighs the gain from reduced variance. [RQ3.1] Walking gait, reduced to the temporal structure of the gait cycle: step time, stance time, swing time and step-to-step interval, each measured separately for the left and right leg. Only timing is used - no kinematics, no joint angles, no ground reaction forces, and no spatial measures - which makes the feature set narrow but exceptionally well specified. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion. A single modality throughout. The paper's structural comparison is instead between two aggregation levels of the same modality - the gait cycle and the walking trial - which is a distinct axis from the sensor-fusion comparisons elsewhere in the corpus and arguably a more fundamental one, since it concerns what a data point is rather than what it contains. [RQ4.1] Four classical supervised classifiers held as the experimental variable: SVM, KNN, random forest and decision tree, each optimised by grid search so that comparisons are between best-configured models rather than arbitrary defaults. The selection rationale is stated per classifier - KNN as a simple baseline suited to small data, SVM as the field's default for small datasets and for autism classification specifically, and random forest and decision tree for their handling of non-linearly separable data. No deep learning, appropriately for 105 or 278 data points with eight features. [RQ4.2] Eight temporal gait-phase durations per gait cycle, computed as frame-count differences at 250 Hz between detected foot strike and foot off events, then L2-normalised per feature vector to equalise phases of naturally different duration. The two representations compared are the raw per-cycle vector (Dataset A) and its mean across all cycles within a trial (Dataset B). The averaging is the intervention under study, and the paper demonstrates its effect directly by plotting the same two features before and after for six subjects. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, recall, precision and F1, with accuracy and F1 designated primary and the other two used for extended analysis. Reporting all four is what makes the SVM's degeneration detectable - accuracy 50% with recall 100% and precision 50% is diagnostic of a single-class predictor, and the authors correctly identify it as such. Precision was also the grid-search selection metric, chosen on the stated grounds that the application is identifying autistic from non-autistic people. Missing: AUC, confusion matrices, per-fold variance, confidence intervals, and any statistical test of the difference between Dataset A and Dataset B results - so the headline improvement from 68.75% to 76.67% on 105 data points is reported without any indication of whether it exceeds noise. [RQ4.4] No model interpretability method is applied, and neither the random forest nor the decision tree feature importances are extracted, which is a missed opportunity given both were trained. Interpretation is instead pursued through direct data visualisation: scatter plots of two features for three autistic and three typically developed subjects, before and after averaging, used to show that averaging compresses within-subject spread most for the subjects who varied most, and incidentally that autistic subjects vary more than typically developed ones. This is transparency about the data rather than about the model, and it is the source of the paper's only substantive clinical observation. [RQ4.5] The weakest link, and knowingly so. Splitting is by gait cycle or by trial, never by participant, across 10 folds; the authors state outright that the same subject's and even the same trial's data can fall on both sides of a split, and proceed on the judgement that the effect is limited. With 21 subjects generating 278 cycles, and with the eight features being timing measures strongly determined by individual stature and habitual cadence, the classifiers can succeed by recognising people rather than by recognising autism - and the paper's own introduction concedes the premise, noting that gait analysis is used for 'person identification' and that 'gait representations are unique to individual people'. Compounding this, hyperparameters were grid-searched on the same cross-validation that produced the reported scores. There is no held-out participant set, no external cohort, no repeated cross-validation, and no significance testing. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Machine Learning, Autism Spectrum Disorder, automatic classification, intra-subject, variation. 'Intra-subject variation' as an indexed keyword is what distinguishes this paper - the object of study is a property of the data rather than a clinical construct or an algorithm. [RQ5.2] An IEEE conference proceedings paper (IEEE Xplore, 2020), venue name not captured in the extracted text. A short methodological contribution rather than a clinical study, which matches the depth of participant reporting. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is a shift in the field's evidential basis: research on autism detection 'traditionally focused on behavioural aspects' but has moved toward 'more objective alternatives' such as gait analysis, on the argument that instrumented measurement 'can identify ASD with more confidence when compared to behavioural assessments recorded by human beings'. The paper situates itself against a set of prior results it reports at face value - 95%, 89% and 100% for random forest, KNN and SVM on adolescent scan data, 96.2% for a PART classifier on gaze and demographic data - and against gait datasets of 60 subjects (30/30) and 44 subjects (12/32). Its own contribution is to notice that these studies differ in how each subject is represented and that this choice has not been examined, which makes it one of the few papers in the corpus whose motivation is a defect in the literature's methodology rather than a clinical need. |
| S-042 | Cross-sectional severity regression on a referred clinical cohort; 72 Hebrew-speaking children assessed at the National Autism Research Center of Israel (56 ASD, 10 other diagnoses after referral for suspected autism, 6 typically developing), each recorded during a single ADOS-2 session averaging 41.6 +/- 12.4 minutes, yielding 27,395 vocal segments; not released. | Speaker intervals manually labelled, vocal segments detected by an energy-threshold algorithm with stated parameters, 60 prosodic, acoustic and conversational features extracted using PRAAT and custom code; six models compared - linear regression with nested sequential forward selection, SVR across four kernels, three fully connected deep networks differing in input arrangement, and a CNN over a 100 x 48 sub-sample matrix per child - evaluated across 50 participant-level train/test splits balanced on the mean, SD, kurtosis and skewness of ADOS scores. | CNN best across 50 splits at mean R = 0.718 +/- 0.093 and RMSE 4.648 +/- 0.592, followed by FC-DNN model 3 (0.696, 4.952), SVR (0.510, 5.853), FC-DNN model 1 (0.501, 6.148), linear regression (0.355, 7.364) and FC-DNN model 2 (0.312, 6.393). Matrix-input models were also far more stable across splits. Twenty-one of 60 features correlated with ADOS total: higher and more variable pitch and higher ZCR with greater severity, fewer vocalisations and turns with greater severity, and shorter response latency contrary to prior English-language findings. RRB scores tracked acoustic features while SA scores tracked conversational ones. | Speaker labelling is manual, so the pipeline is semi-automated and its throughput benefit unrealised; architecture and hyperparameters appear to be selected outside the 50-split evaluation loop; RMSE 4.65 on a 0-30 ADOS scale is a large absolute error relative to the paper's 'remarkably accurate' framing; only 6 typically developing children thinly supports the low-severity end; the best models exclude the conversational features that track social affect because those require the whole recording; no ethics or consent statement for full clinical session audio; single site, single language, no external validation, no test-retest reliability despite the proposed use as a treatment outcome measure. | The corpus's benchmark for validation practice in speech work: participant-level splitting repeated 50 times with explicit distribution matching, across-split variability reported and interpreted as evidence about robustness, and feature selection nested inside training folds. It is also one of the few studies here to predict a continuous clinician-scored severity measure rather than a binary label, and to sample a realistically ambiguous population including ten referred children who received other diagnoses. Its symptom-domain dissociation - acoustic and prosodic features tracking restricted and repetitive behaviour, conversational features tracking social affect - is a substantive interpretive finding, and its architectural result (stacking many sub-samples of a child's speech into one matrix helps, treating them as independent samples hurts) is directly transferable to other small-sample behavioural modelling in this corpus. | [RQ1.1] One clinically referred cohort of 72 children treated as a severity continuum rather than as contrasting groups: 56 with an ASD diagnosis, 10 referred with suspected autism who received other diagnoses (language or developmental delays), and 6 typically developing children. Including the 10 diagnostically ambiguous referrals is unusual and important - most of the corpus either excludes such children or treats them as noise, whereas here they are the cases that make the prediction problem realistic. All 72 completed the same DSM-5 clinical assessment and ADOS-2. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'children with ASD who are deaf'. Mixed person-first and 'ASD children'; consistently 'typically developing' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. The framing is clinical and quantitative - autism as a severity dimension to be measured rather than a category to be detected - and the stated purpose includes tracking improvement and deterioration, which positions the work as an outcome measure rather than a gatekeeping test. [RQ1.3] Group sizes and diagnostic composition are given (56 ASD, 10 other diagnoses, 6 TD) and ADOS module distribution is reported (toddler module 10, module 1 19, module 2 31, module 3 12), indicating a young cohort spanning a wide language-ability range. Ages and sexes were tabulated in Tables 1 and 4 but those tables did not survive text extraction, so the numbers cannot be reported here. What can be established is that age was handled analytically rather than by matching: age was correlated against all 60 features and found to relate mainly to vocalisation rate, duration and count, with little overlap with the features predicting severity, and train and test sets were matched on age and behavioural characteristics. All participants are Hebrew-speaking children assessed at a single Israeli centre; no ethnicity or socioeconomic reporting. [RQ1.4] Strong. Every child completed a full clinical assessment against DSM-5 criteria plus an ADOS-2 with the module matched to age and language capacity, at a national autism research centre. Crucially the reference standard is not a binary label but the ADOS total score itself, decomposed into Social Affect (0-22) and Restricted and Repetitive Behavior (0-8), so the model is regressed against a graded, instrument-derived measure rather than a dichotomised clinical impression. The 10 children who were referred but received other diagnoses demonstrate that the assessment discriminated rather than confirmed. [RQ1.5] ADOS total, SA and RRB scores are the severity characterisation and are used analytically throughout, including a separate correlation analysis per subscale. No IQ, language, adaptive or cognitive measures are reported, which matters because ADOS module assignment already encodes language capacity and so the cohort spans a language range that is not otherwise quantified. Comorbid language and developmental delays are present in 10 children and identified as such but not scored. [RQ2.1] Goal: estimate continuous autism severity (ADOS total) from speech recorded during the ADOS itself, and compare regression and deep architectures for the task. Main findings: 21 of 60 features correlated significantly with ADOS total; higher and more variable pitch and higher ZCR with greater severity, fewer vocalisations and turns with greater severity, and shorter rather than longer response latency; RRB scores tracked acoustic and prosodic features while SA scores tracked conversational features; a CNN on a 100 x 48 sub-sample matrix achieved mean R = 0.72 and RMSE 4.65 across 50 balanced splits, beating SVR (0.51) and linear regression (0.36); and matrix-input models were far more stable across splits than vector-input ones. [RQ2.2] The National Autism Research Center of Israel in Beersheba, a collaboration between Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and Soroka University Medical Center. Recording used a fixed setup in a dedicated ADOS room - an AKG CHM99 microphone 1-2 m from the child feeding a TASCAM US-16x08 interface at 44.1 kHz, downsampled to 16 kHz. Funded by the Israel Science Foundation (grant 961/14) and the BGU Research Authority, with the centre itself funded by the Israeli Ministry of Science and Technology. [RQ2.3] The ADOS-2 assessment itself, with no additional or purpose-built task. This is the design's central choice and its main practical strength: the data are generated by a procedure clinics already perform, so deployment requires only recording rather than a new protocol, and the model's target and its input come from the same session. The cost is that the input is contaminated with clinician, parent and environmental sound, which is why manual speaker labelling was necessary; and that module assignment varies by child, so the speech elicited is not identical across participants. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional - a single ADOS session per child, averaging 41.6 +/- 12.4 minutes. Longitudinal follow-up is named as necessary future work precisely because the intended application (tracking severity change over time and after treatment) requires it. Data are full audio of clinical sessions including parent and clinician speech - among the most sensitive material in the corpus - yet no ethics approval, consent procedure or anonymization statement appears in the extracted text, while funding and acknowledgements are reported in detail. [RQ2.5] AKG CHM99 microphone at 1-2 m; TASCAM US-16x08 sound card; 44.1 kHz downsampled to 16 kHz; in-house GUI software for manual speaker interval labelling; PRAAT for pitch and formant analysis; custom code for energy, ZCR, spectral slope, jitter and conversational features; deep models with RMSProp and MSE loss. No commercial analysis system - the paper argues explicitly against LENA on the grounds that it is not open source, so 'it is not possible to further develop the LENA algorithms nor assess their utility in estimating ASD severity'. [RQ2.6] Among the best in the corpus for method reporting. All 60 features are enumerated individually with their computation; the segmentation algorithm is given with its equations and every threshold (40 ms frames at 10 ms rate, baseline as modal energy within +/- 20 s, onset at 90% above baseline held 50 ms, offset at 10% above baseline held 50 ms, 110 ms and 3 s duration bounds, under 1.5% excluded); the PRAAT voicing threshold is stated as 0.45; all six model architectures are specified layer by layer with epochs, batch sizes and dropout; the hyperparameter search grid is given (batch size from {4,8,16} or {32,64}, learning rate from {1e-5, 5e-5, 1e-4, 5e-4}); and the balanced-split acceptance criteria are stated numerically. Missing: code and data release, ethics documentation, and the selected hyperparameter values are relegated to a table that did not survive extraction. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged: that speaker labelling was manual and that automatic diarization is needed for a fully automated system; that recordings are short clinic sessions rather than naturalistic home recordings; that the shorter-response-latency finding contradicts prior English-language work and needs replication; that feature utility may change with age and requires longitudinal testing; and, implicitly but importantly, that single-split results overstate robustness. Identifiable in review but not stated: RMSE 4.65 on a 0-30 scale is a large absolute error against which the phrase 'remarkably accurate prediction' sits uneasily; architecture and hyperparameters were selected by trying combinations, apparently outside the 50-split evaluation, so the reported means carry model-selection optimism; only 6 typically developing children means the low end of the severity range is thinly sampled, which inflates correlation through range restriction at one end and thin support at the other; and no ethics approval is reported for full clinical session audio. [RQ2.9] Incorporate automatic speaker diarization to remove the manual annotation step and enable a fully automated system; extend from clinic recordings to long home recordings of the kind LENA collects; adopt a longitudinal design testing which speech features are informative at which developmental periods; and reassess the anomalous finding that more severely affected children responded faster rather than slower. [RQ3.1] Child speech during clinical interaction, analysed along three distinct behavioural dimensions: prosody and voice quality (pitch, formants, spectral slope, jitter), acoustic energy dynamics (normalised energy and its derivatives, zero crossing rate), and conversational behaviour (vocalisation rate, segment durations, turn-taking latency and rate, total vocalisation count). The turn-taking features are what distinguish this from purely acoustic work - they measure the child's behaviour in relation to the clinician's, requiring the whole session and both speakers, and they turn out to be the features that track social affect specifically. [RQ3.2] No cross-sensor fusion - audio only. But there is a meaningful within-modality fusion result with a clear cost: the conversational features cannot be computed on short sub-groups of segments because they require the entire recording, so FC-DNN models 2 and 3 and the CNN use only the 48 acoustic and prosodic features. The best models therefore discard exactly the feature family that correlates most strongly with social affect symptoms, and still outperform the 60-feature vector model - which suggests the gain from many sub-samples outweighs the loss of conversational information, and implies an architecture that could use both would do better still. [RQ4.1] Six models spanning linear regression, kernel regression and three deep architectures, all on identical data, which makes the comparison genuinely informative. The decisive variable turns out to be input structure rather than model family: the same 100 x 48 matrix input produces the two best models (FC-DNN 3 and CNN) while the same sub-sampled features presented as independent 48-vectors (FC-DNN 2) produce the worst model of all six. The authors draw the right conclusion - that architectures exploiting multiple simultaneous samples of a child's speech have a large advantage, and that the non-linear models' margin over linear regression and SVR shows 'the optimal ADOS prediction model is not likely to be linear'. [RQ4.2] Sixty handcrafted features across seven families, fully enumerated, computed over automatically detected vocal segments within manually labelled speaker intervals. Three input arrangements are compared: one 60-feature vector per child; 100 independent 48-feature vectors per child, each from 10 sequential vocal segments; and those same 100 vectors stacked into a 100 x 48 matrix per child. The sub-sampling is a deliberate data-augmentation strategy for a 72-child dataset, raising training samples from 51 to 5100 in model 2 - and the finding that this hurt while stacking the same samples into a matrix helped is one of the more useful negative-plus-positive results in the corpus. [RQ4.3] RMSE and Pearson correlation against clinician-assigned ADOS total, reported as mean +/- standard deviation over 50 splits and shown as histograms, plus scatter plots for one representative split. Reporting the across-split standard deviation and interpreting it is the distinguishing feature: it reveals that models with respectable means (SVR at R = 0.51, FC-DNN 2 at 0.31) were also wildly unstable (SD 0.17 and 0.25), while the two matrix-input models were stable at SD 0.09. Because the task is regression, no sensitivity, specificity or AUC applies; but no calibration analysis or error-versus-severity breakdown is given, so whether error concentrates at particular ADOS ranges is unknown, and with only 6 typically developing children the low end is thinly supported. [RQ4.4] No post hoc model explanation, but strong interpretability at the feature level and, unusually, at the symptom-domain level. Every feature's Pearson correlation against ADOS total, SA, RRB and age is reported with significance marking, sequential forward selection names the 15 features that minimise linear-model RMSE, and the resulting interpretation is specific: acoustic and prosodic features (pitch, formants, jitter, energy, ZCR) track restricted and repetitive behaviour, while conversational features (vocalisation rate, turn-taking, vocalisation count) track social affect. The authors correctly note why this matters - symptom heterogeneity means a single global severity estimate is less clinically useful than measures tied to specific domains. The age analysis serves a second interpretive purpose, showing that the severity-predictive features are largely distinct from the age-predictive ones. [RQ4.5] The strongest validation design among the corpus's speech studies. Splitting is at the participant level (51 train, 21 test), so the 100 sub-samples per child never cross the boundary - the leakage failure mode that undermines most segment-level work here is avoided by construction. The split is then repeated 50 times under explicit distribution-matching constraints (mean, SD and kurtosis of ADOS within +/-10% of the whole sample, skewness within +/-0.3), with rejection sampling until satisfied, and every model is run on all 50. Feature selection for the linear model is nested inside 5-fold cross-validation on training data only. What is missing: the architecture and hyperparameter search appears to sit outside the 50-split loop rather than nested within it, so the reported means retain some selection optimism; there is no external site, no independent cohort and no second language; and no test-retest or longitudinal reliability, which the intended use as a treatment outcome measure would require. [RQ5.1] Index terms: audio signals, autism, autism diagnostic observation schedule, autism spectrum disorder, convolutional neural network, deep neural network, early detection, outcome measure, pitch, speech, symptom severity, treatment efficacy, zero crossing rate. The presence of 'outcome measure', 'symptom severity' and 'treatment efficacy' alongside the signal-processing terms is diagnostic of the paper's position - it is proposing a measurement instrument for monitoring, not a screening test. [RQ5.2] IEEE Access, in a special section on emerging deep learning theories and methods for biomedical engineering - an open-access engineering venue (CC BY 4.0), with clinical co-authors from Soroka University Medical Center and the National Autism Research Center of Israel giving the work genuine clinical grounding. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is unusual in this corpus for arguing about tooling as much as about clinical need. It identifies LENA as the dominant platform for automated speech analysis in autism and objects on methodological grounds - LENA 'is not an open-source software and it is, therefore, not possible to further develop the LENA algorithms nor assess their utility in estimating ASD severity' - making open, inspectable pipelines part of the paper's motivation. It also notes that only a few studies had attempted severity estimation rather than binary classification, citing one that explained about 40% of the variance in Social Affect scores from 33 English-speaking children, and positions itself as the first application of these features and deep learning to Hebrew, arguing that the results 'highlight the utility of speech analyses for estimating ASD severity at very young ages, regardless of the child's spoken language or their cultural environment'. |
| S-043 | Two independent case-control eye-tracking studies with different participants, web pages and tasks; 71 UK adults recruited and 68 retained (28 autistic with documented formal diagnoses meeting ADOS criteria, 32 controls screened with the AQ-50), 15 per group analysed in Study 1 and 19 per group in Study 2; gaze data, code and materials publicly released. | Gazepoint GP3 at 60 Hz recorded fixations while participants browsed, searched or synthesised information on six (Study 1) or eight (Study 2) web pages under manipulated time limits; fixations were mapped to AOIs defined three ways (VIPS page-specific elements, 2 x 2 grid, 4 x 4 grid), giving one feature vector per AOI per page per participant; logistic regression classified each vector and each participant was assigned by majority vote, evaluated over 100 random participant-level 70:30 splits with 95% confidence intervals. | Best accuracies of 0.75 (Search), 0.74 (Browse, 120 s), 0.73 (Synthesis) and 0.65 (Browse, 30 s), each from a two-page subset selected as most discriminatory. AOI granularity mattered: 0.71 for both page-specific and 4 x 4 AOIs versus 0.66 for 2 x 2 on Browse 1. Capping browse time confirmed the groups differ in scanning strategy, not just duration. Increased task difficulty, page visual complexity, participant gender, AOI ID and Media ID all failed to improve accuracy. | Headline accuracies are maxima over task, AOI definition, feature set, split ratio and page subset, all optimised on the same 100 splits, so they should be read as upper bounds; the control group is visibly more educated than the autistic group on tasks that are fundamentally reading and search, with no adjustment; only accuracy is reported in the paper, omitting the sensitivity and specificity that determine screening utility; 68 participants is small for validation, as the authors state; no externally collected dataset was available for external validation; and the design cannot explain why particular pages discriminate better than others. | Sets the corpus's benchmark for two things at once: methodological candour and openness. It names segment-level splitting as the reason prior EEG and speech accuracies of 93-94% are overoptimistic, then splits by participant across 100 draws and votes per person; it screens its control group with the AQ-50 rather than assuming typicality; it releases data, code, stimuli, alternative-classifier comparisons and full per-configuration results; and it scopes its own claim to screening and referral rather than diagnosis. It is also one of very few studies here to address adults with high-functioning autism, and the only one using non-social, everyday stimuli - which makes its 74-75% a different and in some ways more surprising result than higher figures obtained from face-viewing paradigms in children. | [RQ1.1] Two groups across two independent collections: 71 adults recruited, 68 retained (28 autistic, 32 control), with 15 per group analysed in Study 1 and 19 per group in Study 2, and 9 participants (6 autistic, 3 control) taking part in both. Exclusions are itemised: in Study 1, three autistic and two control participants for calibration and head-movement problems plus one randomly chosen control to rebalance classes; in Study 2, five controls - one for a high AQ score, three for reported school dyslexia referrals and two for calibration. Adults with high-functioning autism are a substantially under-represented population in this corpus, which is dominated by preschool and school-age children. [RQ1.2] 'adults with and without high-functioning autism', 'participants with autism', 'people on the spectrum', 'people with ASD', 'neurotypical people', 'control group'. Mixed person-first and 'people on the spectrum'; 'neurotypical' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy'. The framing is notable for treating heterogeneity as definitional - 'the term spectrum is used to signify the different types and levels of support that different individuals might need' - and for locating the diagnostic problem in the procedure rather than the person: current diagnosis is 'a highly subjective assessment process' restricted to 'behavioural, historical, and parent-report information' that 'leads to a lack of consistency and reliability'. [RQ1.3] Group sizes and exclusions are fully itemised, and functional and educational characteristics are reported in unusual detail: all participants were highly independent adults with no caregiver; 20 autistic participants were employed or in higher education and 8 lived independently on disability benefits; among the autistic group 8 had completed high school, 8 held bachelor's and 3 master's degrees, against 3, 10 and 5 plus one PhD in the control group. All but one participant used the web daily. Ages and sex distributions were tabulated in Table I but that table did not survive extraction. The visible education imbalance favouring controls is not adjusted for, and matters for tasks that are fundamentally reading and information-search tasks. Ethnicity and socioeconomic status are not reported; recruitment was from Wolverhampton and Birmingham. [RQ1.4] Documented formal diagnosis rather than self-report: autistic participants were recruited through a UK autism charity and a university Enabling Centre, both of which require a copy of the formal diagnosis for service access, and all met ADOS diagnostic criteria. Pre-2013 diagnoses of High-Functioning Autism or Asperger's syndrome were accepted, appropriately for an adult cohort. The control group is the more distinctive part: all completed the 50-item Autism Quotient and one was excluded for a high score, so control status is positively screened rather than assumed - a step almost no other study in this corpus takes. [RQ1.5] Intellectual disability and reading disorder were formal exclusions, and three control participants were excluded for school dyslexia referrals, so reading ability is controlled at the eligibility level for a task that depends on reading. Vision not correctable by glasses or lenses was also excluded. No IQ, AQ score (for the autistic group), symptom severity or adaptive functioning measure is reported; functional level is characterised by employment, housing and education instead, which is arguably more informative for an adult cohort though not comparable across studies. [RQ2.1] Goal: test whether gaze during ordinary web-page use detects high-functioning autism in adults, and whether the effect holds across independent participants, stimuli and tasks. Main findings: all four tasks produced a discrimination signal, with best accuracies of 0.75 (Search), 0.74 (Browse, 120 s), 0.73 (Synthesis) and 0.65 (Browse, 30 s); capping browse time showed the groups differ in browsing strategy and not only in time spent; increased task complexity did not increase separability; AOI content and granularity both affect accuracy, with the 2 x 2 grid consistently worst; and page visual complexity and participant gender contribute nothing. [RQ2.2] A quiet room at the University of Wolverhampton with only researcher and participant present. Autistic participants recruited through a UK autism charity and the university's Enabling Centre; controls by snowball sampling in the Birmingham area. Ethical approval obtained from the University of Wolverhampton Ethics Committee before collection began. [RQ2.3] Real web pages under three task types drawn from a published hierarchy of information needs - browse (no goal), search (locate one element), synthesis (locate two elements and infer a third). Study 1 used six pages spanning low, medium and high visual complexity; Study 2 selected eight from the Alexa top 100 after removing duplicates, non-English pages, search engines and pages requiring authentication, then scoring visual complexity with the ViCRAM tool and randomly selecting four low- and four high-complexity home pages. The rationale for web pages is ecological: they offer mixed textual and visual stimuli organised for a semantic purpose, permitting multiple search strategies, and browsing is 'a highly familiar and naturalistic task' whose data could in principle be captured without laboratory equipment. Time limits were manipulated deliberately across studies to separate strategy differences from duration differences. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; one session per participant per study, with nine participants contributing to both. Data are gaze coordinates plus demographic questionnaire responses. Governance is properly reported - prior ethics committee approval, signed consent forms, debriefing - and the authors go further than compliance by naming ethics as an open research question for any future move to naturalistic recording. [RQ2.5] Gazepoint GP3 at 60 Hz with 0.5-1 degree accuracy, right eye, roughly 65 cm with sensor-controlled distance and nine-point calibration; 19-inch and 17-inch LCD monitors; Gazepoint's position-variance fixation algorithm; extended VIPS for page segmentation into hierarchical elements, using the fifth level (or deeper where a task could be completed by fixating a single element); ViCRAM for visual complexity; R for classification. The eye tracker is deliberately a low-cost consumer-grade device, consistent with the paper's argument that gaze hardware is already commodity technology. [RQ2.6] The best in the corpus. Data, code, materials, page screenshots, task questions, confusion matrices, comparisons against other classifiers, and full results for every data split and page configuration are all deposited at a public repository, and releasing data is stated as an explicit objective of the paper. Apparatus, calibration, viewing distance, fixation algorithm, AOI construction and split procedure are all specified in the text, and results carry 95% confidence intervals. The one gap in the paper itself is that Tables I and II - demographics and the feature list - are the two most reference-critical tables and neither survived text extraction here, though both are presumably in the deposited materials.
