[RQ2.7] Acknowledged: that web-searching tasks are unsuitable for very young children; that the sample is small, 'comparable with those of state-of-the-art fMRI studies for autism detection but smaller than the number needed for large validation studies'; that the design cannot explain why some pages discriminate better than others, nor why the harder Synthesis task did not outperform Search; that testing on independently collected data is not currently feasible because the data are task-specific and no comparable independent dataset exists; and, in a footnote, that the better accuracy under the longer browse limit might reflect the different pages and participants rather than the time limit itself. Identifiable in review but not acknowledged: the headline accuracies are maxima over a large configuration space - task, AOI definition, feature set, split ratio and every page subset - selected on the same 100 splits that produce the reported means, so the confidence intervals describe split variability but not selection uncertainty; and the control group's visibly higher educational attainment is left unadjusted in tasks that are fundamentally reading and search tasks. [RQ2.9] Develop a serious game that captures visual processing differences without a dedicated eye tracker; move to behavioural data collected in natural environments; test whether aggregating more simple Search tasks beats designing more complex ones, since complexity did not help; and apply the approach to other conditions with atypical attention patterns - dementia, schizophrenia, ADHD. The authors frame three prerequisites: what makes a good discriminating task, how to record outside the laboratory, and how to do so ethically. [RQ3.1] Visual attention during naturalistic information-seeking - fixation behaviour across web-page regions during free browsing, targeted search and inferential synthesis. This is a distinctive behavioural target for the corpus: not social attention to faces or eyes, but general visual-information-processing strategy on non-social stimuli. The paper argues this is a feature rather than a limitation, since 'atypical visual-attention patterns reflect higher-order differences in information processing', and it sidesteps the dependence on social stimuli that characterises most gaze work here. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion. Gaze only, with non-gaze metadata (AOI identity, media identity, correct-answer indicator, page visual complexity, participant gender) tested as additional variables and found in almost every case to reduce accuracy. That systematic negative result is itself the paper's fusion finding: on this data, adding non-gaze information hurt. [RQ4.1] Logistic regression, chosen after testing a set of standard classification algorithms in R with the comparison deposited publicly. A deliberately simple model, appropriate at 30-38 participants, and consistent with the paper's emphasis on characterising the signal and the data representation rather than on architecture. The experimental variables are the task, the AOI definition and the feature set, not the learner. [RQ4.2] AOI-level gaze feature vectors: one row per AOI per page per participant, under three AOI definitions - VIPS page-specific elements at the fifth hierarchical level, a 2 x 2 grid, and a 4 x 4 grid. The AOI comparison is the paper's most transferable methodological result. Page-specific AOIs suit Search tasks, where areas have differing task relevance; grid AOIs lose less for Browse tasks, where all elements are equally relevant; the coarse 2 x 2 grid is always worst; and the finer page-specific segmentation in Study 2 (26.6 AOIs per page against 18.6 in Study 1) may have added noise rather than information, since the 4 x 4 grid outperformed it for Synthesis. The authors conclude there is 'a trade-off between having sufficiently detailed AOIs and not introducing too much noise' and that the optimal number 'is best defined empirically'. Grid AOIs have the additional property that no fixation is lost. [RQ4.3] Mean accuracy over 100 random participant-level splits with 95% confidence intervals, reported for every one of the 12 task-by-AOI configurations and for individual pages and page combinations. Confidence intervals are used substantively - the authors read them as showing 'the models are robust in their predictions'. Confusion matrices exist but are deposited rather than printed, and no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1 or AUC appears in the paper. For a screening application where the cost of false negatives and false positives differ, this omission matters more than for a purely comparative study. [RQ4.4] No model-explanation method, but extensive experimental interpretation through ablation and design manipulation. The two substantive interpretive results come from controlled comparisons rather than from the model: capping browse time at 30 seconds isolates strategy from duration and shows the groups differ in how they scan, not just how long; and the AOI comparison separates the contribution of page structure from that of spatial granularity. The tentative behavioural reading offered - that autistic adults may scan elements in a different order or be drawn more to images than to text - is explicitly flagged as requiring further analysis rather than asserted from the classifier. [RQ4.5] Participant-level splitting throughout, repeated 100 times, with per-participant classification by majority vote over that participant's AOI-level predictions - and the choice is argued for explicitly against the segment-level splitting the authors identify in prior EEG and speech work. Cross-study replication with different participants, stimuli and tasks provides a form of generalisation evidence stronger than repeated splitting alone. Two gaps remain. There is no external validation on independently collected data, which the authors address directly: it 'is currently not feasible for our approach due to the task-specific nature of the data, and the unavailability of comparable data collected independently' - an honest statement of a real constraint, and part of why they released their own data. And configuration selection sits outside the validation loop: task, AOI definition, feature set, split ratio and page subset were all chosen by their performance on the same 100 splits. [RQ5.1] Index terms: autism, eye tracking, web, screening, diagnostic classification, detection. 'Screening' rather than 'diagnosis' is the operative word and the paper is careful about it - the method 'is not intended to substitute clinical diagnostic procedures where these are available. Rather, its purpose is to be used to identify autistic traits at a wider level and to provide the means to refer for further assessment those people who might be at risk.' That framing is rare in this corpus and materially changes what the accuracy figures need to support. [RQ5.2] IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering, 28(6), 1254-1261 - an engineering journal with a rehabilitation and assistive-technology orientation, consistent with the authors' backgrounds in language processing and web accessibility rather than clinical psychiatry. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is unusual in taking the measure of its own field before contributing to it. It positions resting-state fMRI as the state of the art for adult autism detection from behavioural data, quoting 79-86% under leave-one-out and 71-83% on unseen data, and notes the practical objection that fMRI is expensive, obtrusive and unsuitable for pregnant women or people with sensory issues, metal implants, claustrophobia or head trauma. It then singles out the EEG (94%) and speech (93%) results as 'potentially overoptimistic' for segment-level splitting, and observes of a comparable child eye-tracking study reporting 85.1% that there was 'no note on how the data was split'. Against that background it positions its own 74-75% as comparable to fMRI at far lower cost, and frames the adult high-functioning population as the underserved case: symptoms are less obvious, lifelong coping strategies mask presentation, and 'unlike for children, critical incidents with adults are not monitored by school staff or parents'. |
| S-044 | Case-control classification on a purpose-built dataset; 31 autistic children (1.8-8 years, mean 4.67 +/- 1.59) from a Xi'an rehabilitation centre and 43 typically developing children (2.5-7 years, mean 4.15 +/- 0.98) from mainstream schools, with 30 and 40 used in the experiments; 82 free-viewing images across facial, social, animated and synthetic categories; dataset not released. | SciEye 2.0 at 140 Hz recorded scanpaths during 3-second free viewing of each image with 1-second masks; scanpaths were segmented into overlapping pieces of one to five fixations, each fixation encoded by a pretrained two-stream CNN over centre and surround patches plus 33 low-, mid- and high-level saliency features; five scale-specific SVM regression models scored pieces, scores were averaged into scanpath and then subject scores, and children were classified against an Otsu maximum between-class variance threshold; evaluated over five random participant-level train/test permutations. | Subject-level accuracy 94.29, 91.43, 94.29, 94.29 and 91.43 percent across permutations, averaging 93.15% with sensitivity 94.66% and specificity 92.00%. Accuracy rose monotonically with aggregation: 87.16% per piece, 88.03% per scanpath, 93.15% per subject. Ablation cost 8.6 points for CNN features, 5.7 for high-level semantic, 4.0 for low-level and 2.3 for mid-level features. | The Otsu decision threshold is computed on the score distribution being classified, so test data set the boundary and the method would not transfer to assessing an individual child; the abstract's 94.28% is the best of five permutations against a 93.15% average, and one test subject is worth 2.86 points; comparisons against 89% and 92% come from different datasets; group is confounded with recruitment setting; ages differ in mean, spread and range without adjustment; sex is unreported and the control group unscreened; diagnosis rests on CCMD-3 with no instrument or diagnostician named; four recruited children are unaccounted for; and no ethics approval or consent statement appears. | The corpus's clearest demonstration that where you aggregate determines what an accuracy figure means: by reporting the same model at piece, scanpath and subject level (87.16 / 88.03 / 93.15 percent) it quantifies exactly the inflation that segment-level reporting produces elsewhere in this literature, and does so as a deliberate contribution rather than an admission. It is also a rare example of feature representation targeting what was looked at - image semantics at each fixation - rather than gaze geometry, with an ablation showing that face, person and car detector responses carry substantial weight. Against that, its Otsu thresholding illustrates a distinct and less-discussed failure mode: a decision rule that requires a population of scores to calibrate against, and therefore cannot serve the individual-assessment use case the paper's own cost and portability arguments describe. | [RQ1.1] Two groups: 31 autistic children recruited through the Children Rehabilitation Center at Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital and 43 typically developing children attending mainstream schools in Xi'an. The reported experiments use 30 and 40 respectively (15 + 20 training, 15 + 20 testing), so one autistic and three typically developing children are recruited but unaccounted for in the analysis, with no explanation given. No other-diagnosis comparison group; the authors themselves flag class balance as an issue needing attention. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'infants with ASD', 'subjects'. Mixed person-first and 'ASD children'. The framing is medical and burden-oriented - autism is 'a severe lifelong neurodevelopmental disorder', children with it 'usually struggle in school, which affects their quality of life', and families 'may also bear enormous psychological pressure and burden'. The paper also uses 'the hazards of the disease' and refers to a 'golden period' for treatment at ages 2-6. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: n = 31, aged 1.8-8 years, mean 4.67 +/- 1.59. Typically developing group: n = 43, aged 2.5-7 years, mean 4.15 +/- 0.98. Age is reported but not tested: the means differ by about half a year, the spreads differ substantially (SD 1.59 versus 0.98), and the ranges are asymmetric, with only the autistic group including children under 2.5 or over 7. Free-viewing behaviour changes rapidly across 2-8 years, and age is not entered into or controlled by the model. Sex is not reported at all for either group, nor is IQ, developmental level, socioeconomic status or ethnicity. All participants are from Xi'an. [RQ1.4] Autistic children had 'confirmed clinical diagnoses of ASD according to the Classification and Diagnostic Criteria of Mental Disorders in China-Third Edition' (CCMD-3), with no instrument, diagnostician, date or severity measure reported. Using CCMD-3 rather than DSM-5 or ADOS/ADI-R is a legitimate national standard but limits comparability with the rest of this corpus, where ADOS confirmation is the norm. Typically developing status rests on mainstream school attendance and absence of a prior autism diagnosis, with no screening instrument applied - so the control group is unscreened. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, developmental quotient, language, adaptive functioning or symptom severity measure is reported for either group, and no comorbidity information. Grading severity is named only as future work. [RQ2.1] Goal: identify autism from the dynamic structure of saccadic scanpaths rather than from static fixation statistics, using learned representations. Main findings: 93.15% mean subject-level accuracy across five participant-level permutations (94.29% maximum), with sensitivity 94.66% and specificity 92.00%; accuracy increases monotonically with aggregation from pieces (87.16%) to scanpaths (88.03%) to subjects (93.15%); CNN features contribute most and high-level semantic features next in ablation; and errors concentrate on typically developing children, attributed to distraction producing uninformative gaze. [RQ2.2] A therapy room with at most two people present besides the child. Autistic participants came from the Children Rehabilitation Center at Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital, Xi'an; typically developing participants from mainstream Xi'an schools. Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the China Postdoctoral Science Foundation and the Natural Science Foundation of Shaanxi Province. [RQ2.3] Free viewing of 82 static images across four categories - facial images, social scenarios, animated characters and synthetic patterns - each shown for 3 seconds with a 1-second mask between images to suppress carry-over, at 0.5 m from a 1920 x 1080 monitor with no instruction beyond observing. The design choice is deliberate and argued: eye-tracking protocols for this population 'usually consider the limited attention of children with ASD, with each set of experiments lasting less than 10 minutes', and the paper contrasts its short protocol against comparators requiring 10 minutes or 10-45 minutes. Note that 82 images at 4 seconds each implies roughly 5.5 minutes of presentation, against the 'approximately 2.5 minutes for recording eye movement' claimed in the comparison - an unexplained discrepancy. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single session per child with no follow-up. Data are gaze coordinates over image stimuli. No ethics committee approval, parental consent procedure, anonymization or data governance statement appears anywhere in the paper, despite participants being children as young as 1.8 years recruited through a clinical rehabilitation service. [RQ2.5] SciEye 2.0 eye tracker at 140 Hz; 1920 x 1080 monitor at 0.5 m; a pretrained two-stream CNN taken from prior published work rather than trained here; LIBSVM; a saliency pipeline incorporating Itti et al.'s conspicuity maps, Oliva-Torralba saliency, a trained horizon-line detector and face, person and car object detectors. Sampling rate, viewing distance, presentation timing and image dimensions are all specified; calibration procedure, data loss rate and fixation-detection algorithm are not. [RQ2.6] Mixed. The model is described in enough detail to reimplement - patch sizes (79 x 79 centre, 158 x 158 surround resized to 79 x 79), the full 33-dimensional saliency breakdown with dimension counts per component, the multi-scale piece construction for k = 1 to 5 with the scoring equations, the aggregation formula, the thresholding method and the toolbox used. Stimulus timing, count, categories and apparatus are given. Missing: SVM kernel and hyperparameters, calibration and data-quality procedures, the identity of the CNN's pretraining data, any code or data release, any ethics documentation, and an account of the four recruited children who do not appear in the experiments. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged and unusually specific: the sample of 31 and 43 children is small and needs large-scale replication; class balance 'is also a problem that needs attention in the validation of our machine learning based model'; severity subdivision is not addressed; and data validity is limited because distracted typically developing children 'may generate meaningless eye movement', which the error analysis identifies as the reason specificity trails sensitivity. Not acknowledged: the Otsu threshold is computed on the score distribution being classified, including at test time, so the decision boundary uses test data and would not be available when assessing a single child; the abstract's 94.28% is the best of five permutations rather than the average; comparisons against Liu and Jiang and Zhao are across different datasets and cannot establish superiority; age differs between groups in mean, spread and range without any test or adjustment; sex is unreported; the control group is unscreened; and no ethics approval is stated. [RQ2.9] Larger-scale replication with attention to class balance; extension from binary identification to severity scoring; protocol improvements to hold children's attention and increase the proportion of valid data; incorporation of fixation duration, which the authors observe 'most identification models have ignored'; replacement of fixed-length piece encoding with recurrent networks able to consume variable-length scanpaths directly; and transfer of the framework to other recognition tasks including other diseases, gender and age. [RQ3.1] Visual attention during free viewing, targeted specifically at its dynamic structure - the sequence of and transitions between fixations rather than where or how long the eye rests. This is the paper's defining choice and its stated critique of the field: existing methods 'tend to analyze the indicators based on individual static fixation, such as the fixation location and fixation duration. However, the actual eye movement is a dynamic process. The relationship between fixations also contains important information in visual attention.' Ironically, in operationalising the dynamic view the model discards fixation duration entirely, which the authors recognise and list as future work. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion - gaze only. There is within-modality feature fusion between learned CNN representations and handcrafted multi-level saliency features, and the ablation quantifies each family's contribution: removing CNN features costs 8.6 accuracy points, high-level semantic features 5.7, low-level 4.0 and mid-level 2.3. The paper closes by expressing the hope that the work 'can contribute to the development of multimodal approaches in the early detection and diagnosis of ASD', positioning gaze as one future component rather than a complete solution. [RQ4.1] A hybrid: a pretrained two-stream CNN as a fixed feature extractor (not fine-tuned on this data), scale-specific SVM regression models via LIBSVM, and Otsu thresholding for the final decision. Using a frozen pretrained CNN is a sensible response to 74 participants, avoiding the overfitting that end-to-end deep training would invite, and the SVM stage operates on a much larger effective sample because each child contributes many scanpath pieces. The multi-scale design - one model per piece length from 1 to 5 fixations - is the architectural contribution, and is explicitly contrasted with the alternative of zero-padding variable-length scanpaths to a fixed size. [RQ4.2] Scanpath pieces of one to five consecutive fixations, each fixation represented by two-stream CNN features over centre and surround image patches concatenated with 33 saliency features spanning low-level (orientation subbands, colour, Itti conspicuity, colour histograms, Oliva-Torralba saliency), mid-level gist (distance to centre, horizon line) and high-level semantic (face, person and car detector responses) tiers. Crucially, features describe what was looked at - the image content at each fixation - rather than the gaze coordinates themselves, so the representation encodes the semantics of visual attention rather than its geometry. Fixation duration is deliberately excluded and its omission acknowledged. [RQ4.3] Accuracy at three aggregation levels (piece, scanpath, subject) plus sensitivity and specificity, tabulated per permutation and per ablation condition. Reporting accuracy at all three granularities is a real methodological contribution: it makes the value of hierarchical evidence integration measurable (87.16 to 88.03 to 93.15 percent) rather than assumed, and it is the kind of reporting that would expose segment-level inflation in studies that report only the finest granularity. Missing: AUC, confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any statistical comparison between conditions - on a 35-child test set, where one subject is worth 2.86 points, the differences between permutations and between some ablation conditions amount to one or two children. [RQ4.4] No saliency maps, attention visualisation or attribution over the model's decisions, and no directional characterisation of what distinguishes the groups. Interpretability is confined to the feature-family ablation, from which the authors infer 'the importance of semantic high-level attributes in ASD recognition' - a reasonable but indirect inference, since the high-level features are face, person and car detector responses and their removal costs 5.7 accuracy points. Because the model scores image content at fixated locations rather than gaze geometry, a per-category or per-region analysis would have been straightforward and would have connected the classifier to the reduced-social-attention literature the paper reviews at length; it is not performed. [RQ4.5] Participant-level splitting into disjoint training and testing sets, repeated over five random permutations with every permutation's result tabulated rather than only the best - a sound design, and better than most of the corpus. Two qualifications. First, the classification threshold is obtained by the maximum between-class variance method applied to the score distribution being classified, so at test time the boundary is set using the test subjects' own scores; this is transductive rather than inductive, and would not transfer to assessing an individual child, which is the deployment scenario the paper's cost and portability arguments envisage. Second, no independent cohort, external site or held-out stimulus set is used, and the cross-paper comparisons against 89% and 92% are drawn from studies on entirely different datasets and populations, so they establish nothing about relative performance. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Machine Learning, Eye-Tracking, Saccadic Scanpath, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Representation Learning. 'Saccadic scanpath' and 'representation learning' together capture the contribution - the object of study is how to represent a gaze trajectory, with autism as the classification task on which the representation is evaluated. [RQ5.2] ICBRA 2020, the 7th International Conference on Bioinformatics Research and Applications (ACM, Berlin) - a computing conference, published open access with support from King's College London and Northwestern Polytechnical University. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing combines an access argument with a methodological one. On access: autism diagnosis 'usually relies on a multidisciplinary team of experts, which is relatively difficult to achieve, especially for economically underdeveloped areas', and eye trackers are 'affordable, portable, and easy to operate' so 'they can also be used in poor and remote areas'. On method: the paper's specific criticism of the existing eye-tracking literature is that models 'have usually utilized statistical analysis to discover the differences between the two classes' and so 'have high requirements for selecting the stimuli and indicators of eye movement for analysis', and that they analyse static fixations while 'the actual eye movement is a dynamic process'. Protocol duration is treated as a competitive dimension in its own right - the paper contrasts its short recording against comparators needing 10 or 10-45 minutes - reflecting a field increasingly aware that attention span, not accuracy alone, bounds what is deployable with young children. |
| S-045 | Cross-sectional case-control classification with a 5 body-region by 4 stimulus-condition factorial; 24 autistic children (5.13 +/- 1.35 years, 21 male) from a Valencia cognitive development centre and 25 typically developing children (4.86 +/- 0.91 years, 16 male) recruited by family mailing, both groups holding ADOS-2 and ADI-R assessment reports; RGB-D movement data from a 14-minute CAVE session, not released. | Children imitated avatar actions in a projected virtual street under three cumulative sensory conditions - visual waving, visual-auditory dancing, visual-auditory-olfactory muffin-biting with butter scent delivered by a wireless diffuser - each preceded by a 2-minute baseline; an Intel RealSense D435 with OpenPose extracted 25 3D joints per frame, joints below 0.5 confidence were discarded, and mean inter-frame Euclidean displacement per joint was aggregated by body region and condition; each of 24 datasets was PCA-reduced at 95% variance and classified by Gaussian-kernel C-SVM with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, training-fold normalisation and nested SVM-RFE. | Fifteen joints differed significantly between groups, with autistic children moving more at 13 of them, concentrated in head and legs. Best accuracy 89.36% (kappa 0.79) for all joints under visual stimulation and 89.36% (kappa 0.78) for head joints under full multisensory stimulation. Pooled across conditions, head, trunk and feet each reached 82.98%, arms 74.47%, legs 72.34%. Whole-body accuracy fell as sensory load increased (89.36 to 74.47 to 70.21 percent) while head accuracy rose (80.85 to 82.98 to 89.36). The all-joints all-conditions model was worst at 70.21% with 45.45% sensitivity. Every model retained three or fewer features. | Twenty-four model configurations built with hyperparameters tuned to maximise Cohen's kappa on the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result, on 47 children where one child is worth 2.13 accuracy points; groups not matched on IQ, cognitive ability or motor comorbidities, which the authors state limits attributing differences to autism; sex distributions differ by over 20 percentage points on a motor outcome, untested and undiscussed; the between-group comparison uses Wilcoxon signed-rank, a paired test, for independent groups; the measure called movement 'frequency' is in fact mean displacement, so nothing quantifies repetitiveness despite that being the target construct; results denominators imply 47 analysed children against 49 stated; stimulus order not counterbalanced; no other-disorder comparison group; no data or code release. | The corpus's most theoretically designed elicitation paradigm - a cumulative sensory ladder built directly from the autism hyper- and hypo-sensitivity literature, with olfactory stimulation delivered by hardware no other study here uses - and one of the few to assess both groups with ADOS-2 and ADI-R. Its factorial reporting of all 24 models is unusually transparent and yields a transferable negative result that cuts against the corpus's fusion orthodoxy: pooling all joints across all conditions performed worst of any configuration, so aggregating more data destroyed a localised signal. Its limitations section is also the corpus's clearest statement of the confounding problem, naming unmatched IQ, cognitive ability and motor comorbidity as directly undermining the attribution of group differences to autism, and identifying the absence of other-neurodevelopmental comparison groups as a specificity failure rather than a scope choice. | [RQ1.1] Two groups: 24 autistic children recruited through Red Cenit, a cognitive development centre in Valencia, and 25 typically developing children recruited by a management company through mailings to families. Both groups presented individual assessment reports including ADOS-2 and ADI-R, so the comparison group is instrument-assessed rather than merely unscreened. No other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify this as a specificity limitation, proposing ADHD and intellectual disability comparisons for future work. Note that the results tables imply 22 rather than 24 autistic children were analysed. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'children with typical development (TD)', 'children with typical neurodevelopment', 'ASD individuals', 'ASD population'. Mixed person-first and 'ASD children'. The framing is clinical but not burden-oriented; notably the paper's critique is directed at the assessment instruments rather than at the children - ADOS 'relies on the examiner's expertise and subjectivity' and ADI-R diagnosis 'is based on caregivers' reports rather than on objective evaluation'. The sensory-difference framing is also treated as explanatory rather than deficit-laden, with hyper- and hypo-sensitivity used to motivate the stimulus design. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: n = 24, 21 male and 3 female (87.5% male), mean age 5.13 +/- 1.35 years. Typically developing group: n = 25, 16 male and 9 female (64% male), mean age 4.86 +/- 0.91 years. Overall range 4-7 years. The age difference is small but untested and the spreads differ. The sex imbalance is substantial and unaddressed, which matters because the dependent variable is body movement magnitude. Critically, the authors state plainly that 'the experimental groups were not matched on measures related to the intelligence quotient performance, cognitive abilities, and motor comorbidities (e.g., dyspraxia)' and that this limits confidence that the observed differences are attributable to autism. No ethnicity or socioeconomic reporting; single site in Valencia. [RQ1.4] Both groups presented individual assessment reports including ADOS-2 and ADI-R, and both instruments are described in detail with their test-retest reliabilities (ADOS-2: 0.87 social affect, 0.64 repetitive behaviour, 0.88 global; ADI-R: 0.93-0.97). Applying the same instruments to both groups is a genuine strength. Two qualifications: no ADOS-2 or ADI-R scores, cut-offs or severity indices are reported for any participant, so the diagnostic evidence cannot be inspected; and ADOS-2 module 1 was used for all assessments, which is the module for children with little or no phrase speech - implying a minimally verbal autistic sample and making its application to typically developing 4-7 year olds difficult to interpret. [RQ1.5] None reported, and their absence is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation. ADOS-2 and ADI-R were administered and yield severity indices in social affect and restricted/repetitive behaviour domains, but no scores appear and no severity-stratified analysis is performed. No IQ, cognitive, language or adaptive measure, and no motor comorbidity screening despite the outcome being motor. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether body movement during multimodal VR imitation tasks discriminates autistic from typically developing children, which body regions carry the signal, and which sensory conditions best elicit it. Main findings: 15 joints differed significantly with autistic children moving more in 13 of them, concentrated in head and legs; best classification 89.36% (all joints, visual condition; and head joints, visual-auditory-olfactory condition); head is the most consistent region and improves with increasing sensory load; whole-body accuracy declines with increasing sensory load; the all-joints all-conditions model performs worst at 70.21%; and every model needed three or fewer features. [RQ2.2] A three-surface CAVE of 4 x 4 x 3 m at the Institute for Research and Innovation in Bioengineering, Polytechnic University of Valencia. Autistic participants came from Red Cenit, a Valencia cognitive development centre; controls were recruited by a management company through family mailings. Funded by the Spanish Ministry of Economy, Industry and Competitiveness ('Immersive virtual environment for the evaluation and training of children with autism spectrum disorder: T Room'), the Generalitat Valenciana REBRAND project, and ERDF Valencian Community funds. [RQ2.3] Avatar imitation in a projected virtual city street, under three cumulative sensory conditions - visual (waving), visual-auditory (dancing to a disco track), and visual-auditory-olfactory (biting a buttered muffin with a butter scent released by a wireless diffuser). The design is the most theoretically motivated stimulus escalation in the corpus: the sensory ladder follows the autism sensory literature directly, adding modalities to which autistic children are reported hypersensitive (visual, auditory) before one to which they are reported hyposensitive (olfactory), on the hypothesis that sensory load provokes repetitive behaviour. The imitation framing is also apt, since imitation deficits are independently documented. Order was fixed rather than counterbalanced, deliberately, to avoid sensory overload - a defensible clinical choice that the authors correctly flag as a methodological cost. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single 14-minute session with three 2-minute-40-second conditions each preceded by a 2-minute baseline, no follow-up. Data are depth video of identifiable children reduced to joint coordinates. Governance is properly reported: written information and written consent from family caregivers, approval by the Ethical Committee of the Polytechnic University of Valencia, and conformity with institutional and national committee standards and the 1964 Helsinki Declaration. [RQ2.5] CAVE with three ceiling ultra-short-throw projectors (100-degree image from 55 cm) and a Logitech Z906 5.1 sound system; Olorama Technology wireless scent diffuser with 12 UDP-triggered channels and programmable fan control of duration and intensity; Intel RealSense D435 depth camera with SDK 2.0; OpenPose for 25-joint pose estimation on an Nvidia GTX1060; MATLAB R2016a with LIBSVM. The scent delivery hardware is unique in this corpus and is what makes the olfactory condition possible. [RQ2.6] Good on apparatus and pipeline, thin on results provenance. Reported: CAVE dimensions and projector specification, viewing distance, condition durations and baselines, camera model and SDK, OpenPose joint indices with their anatomical mapping, the 0.5 confidence cutoff, the displacement computation, PCA variance threshold, SVM kernel and search grid, the LOSO normalisation scheme, the nested RFE with correlation bias reduction, the optimisation criterion, and the software versions. Missing: any data or code release; ADOS-2 and ADI-R scores; frame rate of the depth camera; the proportion of joints discarded by the confidence threshold; an explanation for the two autistic children apparently absent from the analysis; and any account of how the 24 reported models relate to the number actually run. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged with unusual candour: the sample is small and precludes a genuine test set; autism's heterogeneity means larger training groups would be needed for generalisation; other neurodevelopmental comparison groups are absent, so the classifier may separate neurodevelopmental difference generally rather than autism specifically; the groups were not matched on IQ, cognitive ability or motor comorbidities, which the authors say directly limits attributing the differences to autism; and the stimulus order was not counterbalanced. Not acknowledged: the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a paired test applied here to independent groups, where Mann-Whitney U is required, so the reported per-joint significances are unverified; 24 models were built and hyperparameters tuned to maximise kappa on the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result, making 89.36% a best-of-many figure on 47 children where one child is worth 2.13 points; the sex distributions differ substantially on a motor outcome; the analysed sample appears to be 47 not 49; and the quantity called 'frequency' throughout is mean displacement, a magnitude. [RQ2.9] Larger samples permitting a held-out test set and better coverage of autism's heterogeneity; comparison groups with other neurodevelopmental conditions involving movement impairment - ADHD and intellectual disability are named - specifically so that 'taking also into account different neurodevelopment conditions could improve the specificity of the classifiers for ASD rather than for neurodevelopment disorders in general'; matching on IQ, cognitive ability and motor comorbidity; and counterbalanced stimulus orders stratified by functioning level. [RQ3.1] Whole-body movement during imitation, decomposed anatomically into head, trunk, arms, legs and feet, and measured as mean inter-frame joint displacement. The behavioural target is repetitive and stereotyped motor behaviour - the DSM criterion domain the paper argues is under-studied relative to social communication - operationalised as movement magnitude under graded sensory provocation rather than as counts of identified stereotypies. Uniquely in the corpus, the behaviour is elicited by a designed sensory manipulation rather than merely observed. [RQ3.2] Multimodality here is in the stimulus rather than the sensing: a single depth camera captures movement, while visual, auditory and olfactory channels are added cumulatively to the environment. The results are informative and partly counterintuitive. For whole-body movement, discrimination is best under visual stimulation alone (89.36%) and degrades as modalities accumulate (74.47%, then 70.21%). For the head alone the pattern reverses, improving from 80.85% to 82.98% to 89.36% as sensory load rises. And pooling everything - all joints across all conditions - gives the worst result of any model at 70.21% with 45.45% sensitivity. The lesson transferable to the corpus's sensor-fusion studies is that indiscriminate aggregation across conditions and channels can destroy a localised signal. [RQ4.1] A conventional and appropriately conservative pipeline for 47 participants: PCA at 95% variance retention, then C-SVM with a Gaussian kernel, with nonlinear SVM-RFE including correlation bias reduction as a wrapper inside each training fold. No deep learning is used for classification - OpenPose supplies the deep component as a fixed, externally trained pose estimator, which is the right division of labour at this sample size. Hyperparameters were searched over seven logarithmically spaced values of cost and gamma between 0.1 and 1000. [RQ4.2] Mean inter-frame Euclidean displacement per joint, aggregated by body region and stimulus condition into a 24-cell factorial of datasets, each reduced by PCA then by RFE to three or fewer retained features. The representation is deliberately minimal - a single scalar per joint per condition - which is defensible at this sample size but discards everything about the temporal structure, rhythmicity or repetitiveness of the movement, despite repetitive behaviour being the construct the study is about. The paper's own terminology reflects the gap: it calls the measure 'frequency' throughout, but nothing in the pipeline computes a rate or a period. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, true positive rate, true negative rate, Cohen's kappa and retained feature count, tabulated for all 24 models. Reporting the full factorial rather than a selected best is good practice and is what allows an external reader to see both the multiplicity problem and the confusion-matrix imbalances - the pooled head model achieves 82.98% with 100% sensitivity but 68% specificity, while the pooled trunk model achieves identical accuracy with 63.64% sensitivity and 100% specificity, which the paper notes explicitly. Including Cohen's kappa is unusual in this corpus and appropriate given the near-balanced classes. Missing: confidence intervals, AUC, and any statistical comparison between models, which matters when adjacent accuracies differ by one or two children. [RQ4.4] No model-explanation method, but the factorial design itself is the interpretive instrument, and it yields anatomically specific conclusions: the head is the most consistently discriminative region and becomes more so under multisensory load, while arms and legs contribute less. This is supported independently by the joint-level statistical analysis showing more movement in autistic children at 13 of 15 significant joints, concentrated in head and legs, which the authors connect to documented stereotypies of head tilting and leg flapping. The interpretation is therefore anchored in observable anatomy rather than in abstract features - though the underlying group comparison uses an inappropriate paired test. [RQ4.5] The cross-validation architecture is correct: leave-one-subject-out folds, normalisation statistics computed on training folds only and applied to the held-out child, and SVM-RFE performed within each fold's training set with median ranks aggregated across folds. There is no participant-level leakage and no feature selection on the full dataset. What sits outside the loop is model selection - both the SVM hyperparameters ('the model was optimized to achieve best Cohen's kappa') and the choice of which of 24 configurations to headline were determined by the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result. On 47 children this is a large source of optimism. The authors recognise the underlying constraint, noting that larger samples 'could allow validating the ML method, providing also the possibility to test the model' - an acknowledgement that no independent test was possible here. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder; body movements; repetitive behaviors; virtual reality; machine learning. The inclusion of 'repetitive behaviors' locates the work in a specific DSM criterion domain rather than in autism generally, and the paper argues that this domain has been comparatively neglected - 'ASD studies primarily examine the weaknesses in social interaction abilities, and less on the stereotyped and repetitive motor behaviors'. [RQ5.2] Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 9(5), 1260 - an open-access clinical journal, matching the paper's clinical framing and its detailed treatment of ADOS-2 and ADI-R. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is a critique of the gold standard on two grounds simultaneously - objectivity and ecological validity. On objectivity: 'since in ADOS examiner has to judge a child's performance giving scoring and rating, evaluation relies on the examiner's expertise and subjectivity; likewise, in ADI-R ASD diagnosis is based on caregivers' reports rather than on objective evaluation'. On ecology: the limitation is 'the absence of both objective assessment methods and the ecological validity of the setting'. Virtual reality is offered as addressing both at once - a controlled, repeatable environment that is nonetheless a simulated real-life scene, with sensory content that can be manipulated in ways a clinic room cannot. The paper positions itself as 'the first attempt to discriminate ASD children from children with typical neurodevelopment using body movements parameters of an imitation VR task and machine learning', and situates repetitive behaviour as an under-studied criterion domain relative to social communication. |
| S-046 | Cross-sectional case-control with a two-stage evaluation; 41 toddlers aged 12-32 months (mean 23.34) at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, 20 diagnosed autistic and 21 non-autistic under DSM-IV, 33 boys and 8 girls overall with no group-wise breakdown; 196 stimulus samples plus a separate 15,000-clip expression database from 54 non-overlapping children; neither released. | A scripted six-stimulus Responsive Social Smile protocol (greeting, praise, hide and seek, tickle hint, tickle, parent greeting) delivered in a fixed room layout with a single camera at 24 FPS; Kaldi ASR trained on AISHELL-2 detects each stimulus keyword to locate the response window, OpenCV-DNN detects the child's face, and a two-branch 2D/3D ResNet-18 network classifies 7-frame clips as smile or non-smile with a 0.9 threshold; per-stimulus binary scores form a six-dimensional vector, mean-imputed where stimuli were missed, classified by decision tree, SVM, naive Bayes and logistic regression under leave-one-out cross-validation. | Expression recognition 89.10% on Oulu-CASIA and 92.60% for binary smile after fine-tuning; stimulus scoring 85.20% against three-clinician majority-vote ground truth; autism classification 80.49% accuracy, 85.00% sensitivity, 77.27% specificity by decision tree, against 70.73% SVM, 68.29% naive Bayes and 63.41% logistic regression. Substituting clinicians' own stimulus scores raised the decision tree only to 82.93%. Most residual scoring errors were genuine smiles judged by clinicians to be spontaneous rather than socially responsive. | Group-wise ages and sexes are never reported for a 12-32 month cohort whose outcome is age-sensitive, so age and sex confounding cannot be excluded; autism labels rest on unspecified DSM-IV clinical judgement with no instrument; the headline is the best of four classifiers on 41 children where one child is worth 2.4 accuracy points, the same margin as the human-score ablation; stimulus scoring is evaluated at trial level with the same child across folds; the system detects smiles in a time window rather than responses to a stimulus, which the failure analysis shows is the dominant error mode; no ethics approval statement despite frontal toddler video; no data or code release. | The corpus's clearest example of decomposing a screening pipeline and measuring where its error actually lives: running the same four classifiers on machine-scored and clinician-scored stimuli shows the perception stage contributes only about 2.4 accuracy points, so the ceiling is the protocol's information content, not the computer vision. Its failure analysis draws a distinction the rest of the corpus rarely articulates - between recognising a behaviour and attributing it to the stimulus that was supposed to elicit it - which bounds what any expression-based screening system can claim. It also demonstrates the right discipline for training data, building a purpose-made 15,000-clip children's expression database from 54 children explicitly disjoint from the evaluation cohort, on the correct premise that adult-derived expression corpora do not transfer to toddlers. And at 12-32 months it addresses the youngest cohort of any classification study in the corpus. | [RQ1.1] Two groups, 41 toddlers: 20 diagnosed autistic and 21 non-autistic, all assessed at the same specialist hospital. The comparison group is therefore clinically referred rather than community-recruited, which makes the discrimination task harder and more clinically realistic than most of the corpus. A separate, non-overlapping group of 54 children under six supplied 15,000 labelled expression clips for training the perception module. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'autism children', 'non-ASD', 'autistic children'. Mixed person-first and 'ASD children'; the comparison group is 'non-ASD' rather than 'typically developing' or 'healthy', which is accurate given they were clinically assessed rather than screened as typical. Autism is described as 'a mental disorder that may significantly impact people's lives' and as causing 'deficits in social lives'. The paper's stated aim is to equip clinicians rather than replace them - 'clinicians would be equipped with leading technology and rich experience and universally serve autism children'. [RQ1.3] Reported only for the pooled cohort: 41 children aged 12-32 months, mean 23.34 months, 33 boys and 8 girls. No group-wise ages, standard deviations, sex splits or matching tests are given, and an age-by-diagnosis figure is shown but its values are not tabulated. This is a material gap: with a 12-32 month range, responsive social smiling to scripted verbal prompts changes substantially with age, so an age difference between groups would directly produce the observed effect. The authors note the 4:1 male:female ratio matches autism epidemiology, which speaks to representativeness but not to between-group balance. No IQ, developmental, socioeconomic or ethnicity data; single site in Guangzhou. [RQ1.4] 'Professional doctors diagnose all these 41 children' at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, according to DSM-IV standards. No instrument (ADOS, ADI-R, CARS or otherwise), no cut-off, no diagnostician count and no assessment date are reported, and the use of DSM-IV rather than DSM-5 is not explained. Separately and more strongly, the per-stimulus ground truth is well established: three clinicians independently watched the protocol videos and labelled each trial, with majority voting used as the final score - so the intermediate outcome the system is optimised against has a genuine consensus reference standard even though the diagnostic label does not. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, developmental quotient, language, adaptive or symptom severity measure is reported, and no comorbidity information. The six behaviour scores function as a within-protocol profile but are not related to any external severity measure. [RQ2.1] Goal: automate scoring of the responsive social smile, one element of clinical screening that lacks clear behavioural benchmarks, and use the resulting scores for autism classification. Main findings: 85.20% agreement with three-clinician consensus stimulus scores; 80.49% autism classification accuracy with 85.00% sensitivity and 77.27% specificity from a decision tree; substituting clinicians' own stimulus scores raises this only to 82.93%, locating the performance ceiling in the protocol rather than the perception pipeline; 92.60% smile classification after fine-tuning on a purpose-built children's expression database; and most residual scoring errors are correctly detected smiles that clinicians judged spontaneous rather than socially responsive. [RQ2.2] A standardised low-cost room setup deployed at the collaborating Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, with a fixed seating layout for child, clinician and parent and a single camera positioned to record the child's frontal face. Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Key Research and Development Program of Jiangsu Province, the Six Talent Peaks project and a Guangzhou municipal livelihood science and technology plan. [RQ2.3] A purpose-designed protocol modelled on ADOS and organised around distinct humour mechanisms: greeting smile with the child's name, praise words, hide and seek, hints of tickling, actual tickling, and a parent-delivered greeting smile. Each stimulus opens with a scripted keyword phrase, which is what makes automatic temporal segmentation possible - the ASR system detects the phrase and thereby locates the response window, so protocol design and pipeline design are co-dependent by construction. Stimuli are repeated up to three times if the child does not respond, and children who do not complete every step contribute missing scores that are mean-imputed. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single session per child with no follow-up. Data are frontal video and audio of identifiable toddlers with a parent and clinician present - among the most sensitive material in the corpus. Governance reporting is a single clause in the acknowledgements referring to participants' consent; no ethics committee approval, formal consent procedure, anonymisation or retention policy is stated, and no data availability statement is given. [RQ2.5] A single camera at 24 FPS and a microphone in a fixed layout, explicitly framed as low-cost. Software: Kaldi with an AISHELL-2-trained Mandarin ASR model; OpenCV-DNN face detector chosen for robustness on small toddler faces; a custom 2D-3D CNN built from ResNet-18 and pretrained 3D-ResNet-18 components; standard classifiers for the final decision. Standardising the physical setup is treated as a contribution in its own right. [RQ2.6] Good on architecture, thin on protocol provenance. Reported: the full network architecture layer by layer for both branches with feature map dimensions, the 7-frame clip length and 224 x 224 input size, the 24 FPS and 20-second default window (about 480 frames per stimulus), the 0.9 smile decision threshold with its rationale, the ASR training corpus, the mean-imputation rule for missing stimuli, and the leave-one-out evaluation. Missing: decision tree hyperparameters, the smile-count threshold for stimulus scoring, group-wise demographics, ethics documentation, and any data or code release. A typographical error in the stimulus scoring description states that the score is marked 0 in both branches of the threshold test. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged: that a single protocol is insufficient - 'using the responsive social smile score alone cannot give a very comprehensive ASD classification' - and that fusing multiple protocols is needed; that autistic children are heterogeneous, making single-aspect screening hard; and, through the failure case study, that most residual errors are smiles that occurred but were not responses to the designed stimulus. Not acknowledged: that group-wise ages and sexes are never reported, so age and sex confounding cannot be excluded in a 12-32 month cohort; that the diagnostic reference standard is a bare DSM-IV clinical judgement with no instrument; that 80.49% is the best of four classifiers on 41 children where one child is worth 2.4 points - the same size as the gap the human-score ablation reveals; that stimulus scoring is evaluated at the trial level so the same child appears across folds; and that no ethics approval is reported. [RQ2.9] Fuse scores and features from multiple complementary automated protocols - response to name and joint attention are named as the natural partners - to move from a single-aspect indicator to a composite screen, and address the distinction between spontaneous and socially responsive smiling that accounts for most remaining scoring error. [RQ3.1] Responsive social smiling - whether a toddler produces a clear smile in response to a specific social overture, across five humour mechanisms plus a parent-delivered greeting. The behaviour is deliberately chosen because it is the hard case: unlike response to name or joint attention it 'is evaluated by emotion description that usually remains an ambiguous classification result', so it is the element of screening where automation has the most to offer and where a defensible ground truth is hardest to obtain. That the paper builds a three-clinician consensus for exactly this reason is a considered response to the problem. [RQ3.2] Genuinely multimodal, but with the modalities serving different functions rather than being fused as parallel evidence: audio drives temporal segmentation (locating each stimulus onset from its scripted keyword) while video drives measurement (detecting the face and classifying the expression). This division is the framework's structural idea - speech tells the system when to look, vision tells it what it sees - and it is what allows an unsegmented clinical recording to be parsed automatically. Within the vision branch there is a second fusion, between a 3D-CNN capturing temporal dynamics and a 2D-CNN capturing spatial detail, concatenated to 1024 dimensions before classification. No accuracy comparison between the branches is reported, so the contribution of each is unquantified. [RQ4.1] A cascade rather than a single model: pretrained ASR, pretrained face detection, a fine-tuned two-branch expression network, and a shallow classifier over six binary scores. The design is well matched to the data regime - deep components are trained on large external corpora (AISHELL-2, Oulu-CASIA, and the purpose-built 15,000-clip children's database) while the only model fitted to the 41-child cohort is a decision tree over six features. Four classifiers are compared, with the decision tree best by a wide margin (80.49% against 70.73% for SVM), which for a six-dimensional binary feature space is plausible. [RQ4.2] A six-dimensional binary vector, one element per stimulus. This is a deliberately clinical representation - it mirrors exactly what a clinician records on a screening sheet, so the classifier's input is inspectable and the system's intermediate output is directly usable by a human even if the final classification is ignored. The cost is that all temporal, intensity and latency information about the smile is collapsed to a single bit per stimulus, and missing stimuli are mean-imputed within the child, which for a binary feature produces values the classifier was not otherwise trained on. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity with full confusion matrices at both stages, and - most valuably - a four-classifier comparison run twice, once on predicted stimulus scores and once on clinicians' scores. That paired table is the paper's best methodological contribution: it decomposes total error into the perception stage and the protocol stage, showing the perception stage contributes about 2.4 accuracy points. No AUC, no confidence intervals, no statistical test, and no per-stimulus analysis. The cross-study comparison table against eye-movement, hand-imitation, prosody and neuroimaging methods is drawn from different populations and age ranges and cannot support relative claims, though the paper presents it as context rather than as competition, noting its own cohort is the youngest at 1-3 years. [RQ4.4] No attribution or saliency method, but the pipeline is interpretable by construction: every intermediate output is a clinically meaningful quantity - stimulus onset time, face crop, smile or non-smile, per-stimulus score - so a clinician can inspect where a decision came from without any explanation technique. The failure case study is the interpretive high point, examining all 29 misscored trials and finding that most involve genuine smiles that clinicians attributed to spontaneous emotion rather than to the social stimulus, with four examples shown. This identifies a specific conceptual limit: the system measures whether a smile occurred in a time window, not whether it was caused by the stimulus, and closing that gap requires modelling attention or gaze direction rather than better expression recognition. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-out cross-validation at both stages, with the autism classification held out at the child level. The perception module's training data is cleanly disjoint from the evaluation cohort - the fine-tuning database comes from 54 children with explicitly no overlap with the 41 participants - which prevents the most serious form of leakage in video-based work. Two weaker points: the stimulus scoring evaluation is at the trial level across 196 samples from 41 children, so the same child appears in training and test folds for that stage; and the decision tree was chosen as best of four on the same leave-one-out estimate reported as the result. There is no independent cohort, no external site, and no held-out test set, which the sample size precludes. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list. Vocabulary: 'responsive social smile', 'multimodal behavior assessment framework', 'early stage autism screening', 'standardize', 'stimulus scoring', 'temporal stimulus localization'. The recurring word is standardisation - the paper's claim is as much about making a protocol repeatable and machine-readable as about classification accuracy. [RQ5.2] Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR), Milan, pages 2240-2245 - a computer vision and pattern recognition venue, with clinical co-authorship from the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is about clinician workload and the limits of subjective scoring in a specific, unusually difficult case. The paper argues that the responsive social smile differs from other screening indicators because it lacks clear benchmarks and is 'evaluated by emotion description', that assessing 'children's emotions on small faces' while simultaneously running the experiment is error-prone, and that 'remembering every score for different social stimuli during the screening or perform the behavior scoring after the test is very subjective and labor-intensive'. Its comparison table is a useful snapshot of the 2020 field - eye movement at 88.51%, hand imitation at 86.70%, prosody at 76.00%, neuroimaging at 70.00% - and its accompanying observation is that 'cost and age requirements prevent some accurate ASD screening methods among children', with neuroimaging singled out as both expensive and impractical for young children who cannot stay still. Its own cohort at 12-32 months is the youngest in that table. |
| S-047 | Methodological study on a clinical eye-tracking cohort; 64 US children aged 76.32 +/- 16.3 months (43 male), 32 autistic and 32 non-autistic with mixed diagnoses including language delay and other developmental concerns; 109 stimuli across six paradigms yielding 9,647 features in 109 groups; ADOS severity, SRS and Vineland for 30 autistic children and Stanford-Binet IQ for all 64; data available on request, code open sourced. | Passive viewing of Activity Monitoring, Biomotion, Dyadic Bids, Dynamic Scenes, Social Referencing and Theory of Mind paradigms recorded on an EyeLink 1000 Plus at 500 Hz; fixations identified by dynamic-programming distance dispersion, oculomotor and ROI statistics computed per stimulus with expert frame-level annotation, missing values EM-imputed; lasso, group lasso and SGIN - a neural network with group l1 penalties on the input-to-first-hidden-layer parameter blocks, optimised by stochastic blockwise coordinate descent - compared on identical 10-fold splits with 100 bootstrap runs for selection stability, against non-sparse SVM, tree, forest and regression baselines. | With 99 of 109 stimuli removed, SGIN retained 78.13% accuracy and 82.91% AUC; lasso at 71 stimuli removed reached only 65.6% and 70.8%; group lasso matched SGIN on average (79.71%, 79.72%) but rarely removed intermediate numbers of groups; non-sparse baselines reached about 84% with no sparsification. Dyadic Bids was least discarded (24.96%) and Social Referencing most (72.00%). SGIN predicted IQ at r = 0.54 (p < 0.0001) but neither SGIN nor lasso fitted ADOS severity, SRS or Vineland above chance. | Group-wise ages, sexes and IQs are asserted balanced but never tabulated, which matters because IQ is the one clinical variable the features predict; sparsity operating point, hyperparameters and the choice of best method all determined against the same 10-fold estimate, which the authors acknowledge may be over-optimistic; 64 participants against 9,647 features with only 30 having full clinical measurement; no held-out cohort, external site or independent battery; the specific 11 retained stimuli are not identified; and selected paradigms are not guaranteed stable because the p > n problem may have no unique optimum. | The corpus's most direct engagement with what actually prevents eye-tracking biomarkers from reaching practice - session length rather than accuracy - and the only study to formalise stimulus selection as a grouped variable problem and report the full parsimony-versus-performance trade-off curve. Its central negative result deserves weight in the synthesis: the same features that separate diagnostic groups at 78-84% fail entirely to predict ADOS severity, SRS or Vineland, while predicting IQ at r = 0.54, suggesting that gaze-based group separation may rest substantially on general cognitive and compliance factors rather than autism-specific severity - a reading reinforced by data-quality variables appearing among the top SHAP features and explained by the authors as non-compliance during socially oriented content. Its mixed-diagnosis comparison group and its two-IRB, open-code, quality-quantified reporting also make it a benchmark for how this kind of study should be documented. | [RQ1.1] One cohort of 64 children split 32 autistic and 32 non-autistic, with the non-autistic group deliberately heterogeneous - 'typical development, language delay, and other developmental concerns'. This is one of only a few studies in the corpus whose comparison group is a clinically referred mixed-diagnosis sample rather than typically developing children, which raises the difficulty of the task and makes the result far more relevant to real screening. Clinical instrumentation is deep for a subset: ADOS severity, SRS total and Vineland-3 ABC for 30 of the 32 autistic children, and Stanford-Binet IQ for all 64. [RQ1.2] 'children with autism', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'non-ASD', 'children without ASD', 'typical development'. Consistently person-first, and the non-autistic group is named by what it is not rather than being called healthy or normal - accurate given its composition. The framing is biomarker-development rather than deficit-focused, referencing the FDA-NIH Biomarker Working Group and treating eye tracking as 'a powerful marker of cognition and human variability'. [RQ1.3] Reported for the whole cohort only: 64 children, mean age 76.32 +/- 16.3 months (about 6.4 years), 43 male and 21 female. Group-wise ages and sexes are not tabulated; the paper states there is 'no significant difference for age and sex between the ASD and non-ASD population' without giving means or test statistics. Stanford-Binet IQ was obtained for all participants, which is unusual and important, though group-wise IQ is likewise not reported - a notable gap given that IQ turned out to be the one clinical variable the eye-tracking features could predict. No ethnicity or socioeconomic reporting. The authors flag that findings 'may reflect developmental properties of ASD specific to the school-age period'. [RQ1.4] Clinician-assigned diagnostic labels supported by an unusually complete instrument battery: ADOS severity scores administered as direct assessment by trained administrators, SRS-2 caregiver questionnaire, Vineland-3 structured caregiver interview, and Stanford-Binet IQ administered directly to every child. Each instrument is described with its purpose and administration mode. The one gap is that the diagnostic decision procedure itself - which instruments determined the ASD label, against which criteria - is not stated, and ADOS, SRS and Vineland were obtained for only 30 of the 32 autistic participants. [RQ1.5] The most complete clinical characterisation in the corpus for a subset of participants: ADOS severity (autism symptom severity), SRS total (reciprocal social behaviour), Vineland-3 ABC across communication, daily living skills and socialisation (adaptive functioning), and Stanford-Binet IQ for the full cohort. Critically, these are not merely tabulated but used as regression targets, which is what allows the paper's central negative finding - that eye-tracking features predict IQ but not autism severity or adaptive functioning. [RQ2.1] Goal: select a parsimonious subset of eye-tracking stimuli that preserves discriminative and predictive power, treating selection as a grouped variable problem. Main findings: 11 of 109 stimuli retained 78.13% accuracy and 82.91% AUC; SGIN was the only method achieving sparsity and accuracy together, with lasso 15 points worse at comparable sparsity and group lasso behaving near-bimodally; Dyadic Bids was the most-retained paradigm and Social Referencing the most-discarded; and the features predicted IQ (r = 0.54) but failed above chance for ADOS severity, SRS and Vineland. [RQ2.2] Laboratory eye-tracking at Seattle Children's Research Institute and Yale University, with acquisition protocols aligned to a published multi-site standard and a delivery system providing embedded 5-point calibrations and the ability to insert video breaks for behavioural management. Funded by NIH awards K01 MH104739, R21 MH103550 and R03 MH092618, an NSF Expedition in Socially Assistive Robotics, and a Simons Foundation award. [RQ2.3] Six passive-viewing paradigms totalling 109 stimuli, each designed by clinical psychologists 'to characterize features known to be atypical or impaired in individuals with ASD' and each targeting a distinct construct: social motivation and shared play (Activity Monitoring), primitive social preference (Biomotion), sensitivity to social overtures (Dyadic Bids), naturalistic scene viewing (Dynamic Scenes), automaticity of information-seeking from others (Social Referencing), and interest in and comprehension of others' intentions (Theory of Mind). Passive viewing with no instruction is a deliberate design decision justified by the observation that autistic individuals are differentially affected by verbal instruction, so implicit-attention paradigms generalise better across ability and age. Stimuli were presented in counterbalanced orders. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single session per child with no follow-up, though the motivating application - monitoring treatment response and predicting later outcomes - is inherently longitudinal and the paper acknowledges much work remains before eye tracking can serve it. Data are gaze recordings with linked clinical scores. Governance is fully reported: IRB approval from both Yale University and Seattle Children's Research Institute covering experiments, acquisition and analysis. [RQ2.5] SR EyeLink 1000 Plus at 500 Hz binocular; Samsung SyncMaster 2233RZ 22-inch at 60 Hz, 1680 x 1050; 650 mm viewing distance; Neurobehavioral Systems Presentation with embedded calibration and behavioural management; Dynamic Programming on Distance Dispersion fixation identification; expert frame-level ROI annotation; PyTorch, sklearn and pyglmnet in Python 3.6. Quality control is quantified - 95% trimmed mean calibration error of 0.751 visual degrees - which almost no other eye-tracking study in this corpus reports. [RQ2.6] Among the best in the corpus. Reported: all six paradigms with their construct rationale, stimulus counts, durations and per-stimulus feature counts with standard deviations; the eye tracker, monitor, refresh rate, resolution, viewing distance, calibration scheme and measured calibration error; the fixation identification algorithm; the ROI annotation scheme including the non-overlap rule and composite variables; the imputation method; the network architecture, layer sizes, activation, bias handling, learning rate schedule, epochs and batch sizes; the optimisation algorithm; and the identity of every comparator method. Code is open sourced on GitHub and the data and processing pipeline are offered on request. Missing: group-wise demographics, the diagnostic decision procedure, and the specific 11 stimuli that constituted the best sparse subset. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged with unusual directness: 'We acknowledge that the validation performance might be over-optimistic and does not represent real-world performance for ASD/non-ASD classification'; only 64 participants with just 30 having full ADOS, Vineland and SRS measurement; limited power to characterise autism heterogeneity; results possibly specific to the school-age period; selected paradigms not guaranteed stable across runs because the p > n problem may have no unique optimum; and that much remains before eye tracking can be used practically for treatment optimisation or long-term outcome prediction. Identifiable in review but not stated: group-wise ages, sexes and IQs are asserted as balanced but never tabulated, which matters greatly given that IQ is the one variable the features do predict; the sparsity operating point, the hyperparameters and the identification of SGIN as best were all determined against the same 10-fold estimate; and the non-autistic group's heterogeneity, while a design strength, means the classifier's target is 'autism versus other developmental presentations', which is not the same construct as 'autism versus typical development' and complicates comparison with the rest of this corpus. [RQ2.9] Extend group sparsity to bi-level, hierarchical, tree-structured and overlapping group definitions so that paradigms can be organised into nested subgroups; replace expert-annotated event windows with data-driven identification of the informative time periods within stimuli; expand the sample to characterise heterogeneity, since limited power constrains severity prediction; design stimuli specifically for predicting ADOS, SRS and Vineland rather than reusing paradigms built for group separation, and develop modelling techniques suited to those outcomes; and test the robustness of selected stimuli on larger unseen data. [RQ3.1] Passive visual attention across six distinct social-cognitive constructs, decomposed into oculomotor mechanics (fixation counts and durations, saccade durations, first-saccade timing, exploration order), region-of-interest allocation (bodies, heads, eyes, mouths, activities, distractors), event-locked response latency, and data-quality measures (percentage of gaze on screen, missing data, proportion of events meeting quality requirements). Including quality metrics as candidate features rather than as exclusion criteria is a distinctive choice, and it pays off - one such feature appears third in the SHAP ranking, which the authors interpret as non-compliance during socially oriented content being itself informative. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion; the study is gaze-only. What it does instead is the inverse of fusion and arguably more useful: it asks how much of a large multi-paradigm battery can be discarded. The result is that 89.9% of stimuli can be removed with modest accuracy loss, and the paradigm-level analysis shows the retained signal concentrates in Dyadic Bids and Theory of Mind, both of which include visual response latency features, while Biomotion also has latency features but lacks discrete ROI measures on heads, faces, eyes and bodies. The authors hypothesise that Dyadic Bids and Theory of Mind features subsume information available in the other paradigms - a redundancy argument that is the mirror image of the fusion arguments elsewhere in this corpus. [RQ4.1] Three sparsity-inducing methods compared on identical splits - lasso, group lasso and the paper's SGIN - against a panel of non-sparse baselines (linear and RBF SVM, decision tree, random forest, linear and logistic regression) run 100 times each. SGIN extends group l1 regularisation to a multi-layer non-linear network by penalising the Frobenius norm of the parameter block connecting each input group to all first-hidden-layer neurons, and introduces a Stochastic Blockwise Coordinated Gradient Descent optimiser that converges faster and finds more sparse groups than plain SGD. The comparison is informative precisely because the winner is not the most accurate model: non-sparse linear baselines reach about 84% accuracy against SGIN's 78-80%, but they remove nothing, so they cannot shorten the battery at all. [RQ4.2] 9,647 features organised into 109 groups, one per stimulus - the grouping is the methodological point, since acquisition cost is incurred per stimulus and not per derived variable, so selection must respect that structure. Group sizes are unequal by paradigm (41 to 177 features per stimulus) and group lasso's square-root-of-group-size weighting accounts for this. The regime is p >> k > n, with 9,647 features and 109 groups against 64 participants, which the paper states explicitly as the reason standard variable selection is inapplicable. Missing values imputed by unsupervised Expectation-Maximization. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and AUC, all plotted as functions of the number of sparsified groups rather than reported as single points - so the deliverable is a trade-off curve between battery length and discriminative power, which is exactly the quantity a biomarker designer needs. Pearson correlation for the four regression targets, likewise plotted against sparsity, with random guessing anchored at r = 0. Selection stability is quantified as discard probability per paradigm over 100 bootstrap runs. No confidence intervals on the accuracy curves and no statistical test between methods. [RQ4.4] Two complementary interpretability layers. At the paradigm level, bootstrap discard probabilities rank the six paradigms and reveal a surprise the authors flag themselves - Social Referencing, designed to probe automaticity of information-seeking from others, is the most discarded. At the feature level, SHAP values over the trained network yield a top-10 list spanning gaze duration to activities and to eyes, latency to biological and non-biological motion, exploration timing (start times of the 4th, 9th and 10th fixations or regions), and data quality. The interpretation offered for the quality feature is candid and important: autistic children 'can provide poorer quality data due to non-compliance and attention issues during presentation of socially-oriented scene content', so a variable normally treated as measurement noise is functioning as behavioural signal. [RQ4.5] 10-fold cross-validation with identical splits across all methods and training-set-fitted normalisation per fold, plus 100 bootstrap runs to assess selection stability. Two limitations, one acknowledged and one not. Acknowledged: the authors state directly that validation performance may be over-optimistic and does not represent real-world performance. Not stated: the operating point on the sparsity curve, the hyperparameters and the conclusion that SGIN is best were all determined against that same 10-fold estimate, and no held-out cohort, external site or independent battery was used. The paper's own framing is careful about this - it describes the work as setting 'the stage for concerted techniques designed around engines to iteratively refine and define next-generation biomarkers' rather than as delivering a validated biomarker. [RQ5.1] Keywords: eye-tracking, feature selection, group selection, stimuli selection, paradigm selection, neural network, autism. Four of seven concern selection and only one names autism - the paper is a methods contribution to biomarker refinement, with autism as the application domain.
