[RQ5.2] ETRA '20, the ACM Symposium on Eye Tracking Research and Applications (Stuttgart), full papers track - the field's dedicated eye-tracking venue, published open access with support from the University of Washington, Yale and Seattle Children's. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is explicitly regulatory and infrastructural rather than clinical-need-driven: it situates itself among 'large-scale ongoing efforts in progress to develop next generation biomarker applications', cites the FDA-NIH Biomarker Working Group, and identifies validation studies aimed at markers of treatment response, predictors of later outcomes and subgrouping for intervention response. Its diagnosis of the field's practical bottleneck is precise and rarely stated elsewhere in this corpus: 'the longer the session associated with a biomarker, the more burdensome that biomarker becomes, and the less likely it will be to see practical implementation', with long batteries 'often stressful for young children and infants' and shorter sessions reducing burden, improving data quality and requiring less staff time. It also criticises current selection practice - 'straightforward winnowing of experimental batteries based on independent trial discriminability' - for ignoring interrelationships between trials that machine learning can capture, while warning that overfitting risk in the large-p small-n regime demands specialised techniques. |
| S-048 | Cross-sectional case-control with a modality comparison; 97 Chinese children aged 3-6, 49 autistic (4.29 +/- 1.07 years, 39 male) diagnosed by experienced psychiatrists using PEP-3 and DSM-5, and 48 typically developing kindergarten children (4.26 +/- 1.00 years, 36 male), matched on age and sex; resting EEG plus face-viewing gaze data, available on request. | Six minutes of eyes-open resting EEG on a 128-channel HydroCel net at 1000 Hz with 62 electrodes retained, preprocessed by mastoid re-referencing, 0.5-45 Hz filtering, downsampling, notch filtering, ICA artefact removal and 4-second epoching, then Welch relative power in five bands; Tobii TX300 eye tracking at 300 Hz during 12 ten-second presentations of own-race and other-race female faces, with fixation-time proportions computed for eight AOIs under a 60 ms threshold; mRMR feature selection feeding a linear SVM, with accuracy swept across one to forty-five selected features. | EEG alone 68%; gaze alone 72.33% (AUC 0.827) for own-race faces, 66.67% (AUC 0.746) for other-race, 75.89% (AUC 0.865) combined; EEG plus gaze 85.44% with AUC 0.93 at 32 features. Autistic children fixated the background far more (19.40% versus 3.27% own-race) and the face, nose and mouth less; eye-region differences were non-significant. EEG showed group differences in theta, beta and gamma but not delta or alpha. | No validation scheme of any kind is described - no split, cross-validation, held-out set or repetition - and supervised mRMR selection is applied with no stated nesting over a feature pool much larger than the 97-participant sample; the headline accuracy is the maximum of a feature-count sweep chosen on the same data; the 32 selected features are never identified so the source of the fusion gain cannot be verified; no sensitivity, specificity or confidence intervals; recruitment routes differ systematically between groups; no severity or functioning measure despite heterogeneity being central to the paper's own argument; and the tabulated theta means contradict the text's stated direction. | Provides the corpus's cleanest modality ladder - 68% EEG alone, 75.89% gaze alone, 85.44% fused - and, unusually, a principled reason to expect complementarity rather than a generic appeal to more data: EEG abnormalities are inconsistent across the spectrum and especially absent in high-functioning autism, whereas atypical face processing appears across presentations, so the modalities should fail on different subgroups. Its own-race versus other-race manipulation is also rare in this literature and yields an interpretable result. All of this is undercut by the complete absence of a stated validation procedure, which makes the study a useful illustration for the review's methodological synthesis: a well-designed, well-matched, properly governed experiment whose reported accuracies nonetheless cannot be read as out-of-sample performance. Its gaze finding is also worth carrying forward substantively - the dominant group difference was excess fixation on the background rather than avoidance of the eye region, with eye-region differences non-significant, which sits awkwardly against the eye-avoidance framing the paper adopts. | [RQ1.1] Two groups, 97 children: 49 with confirmed autism diagnoses and 48 typically developing children recruited from a local kindergarten. No other-diagnosis comparison group. At 97 participants this is one of the larger single-site cohorts in the corpus, and the authors note they 'recruited a relatively large sample size for the sake of classification'. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'autistic children', 'ASD children', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'normal children', 'patients with autism', 'healthy children'. Mixed and inconsistent - person-first in places, 'autistic children' elsewhere, and 'normal' and 'healthy' both used for the comparison group. Autism is framed as 'a very complex neurodevelopmental disorder' and once as 'this complex disease', with aetiology attributed to 'biological factors such as genetic defects, brain inflammation, and abnormal conditions during pregnancy'. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: n = 49, 39 male and 10 female, mean age 4.29 +/- 1.07 years. Typically developing: n = 48, 36 male and 12 female, mean age 4.26 +/- 1.00 years. The authors state there were no statistical differences in age or gender between groups, and the reported means and SDs bear that out - this is among the best-matched pairs in the corpus, on the two variables most likely to confound gaze during face viewing at this age. Both groups span 3-6 years. No IQ, developmental level, socioeconomic or ethnicity data; recruitment routes differ between groups (clinical for autism, a local kindergarten for controls), which is not addressed. [RQ1.4] Diagnosis by 'experienced Chinese psychiatrists based on the psychoeducational profile (Third Edition)' and DSM-5 criteria. PEP-3 is a developmental and autism-characteristic assessment rather than a diagnostic instrument in the ADOS or ADI-R sense, so the ascertainment is weaker than the corpus norm for well-documented studies, though DSM-5 clinical judgement by experienced psychiatrists is a reasonable standard. Control status rests on kindergarten recruitment and the absence of 'genetic history of autistic family members', with no screening instrument applied. [RQ1.5] None reported. PEP-3 yields developmental scores that could have supported severity or functioning analyses, but no scores appear and no stratification is performed. This is a substantive gap given the paper's own explanation for inconsistent EEG findings in the literature - that 'autism can be divided into low function and high function according to behavioral ability' and that heterogeneity is why 'using only EEG evaluation may be insufficient'. Having advanced that argument, the study is unable to test it in its own data. [RQ2.1] Goal: test whether fusing resting-state EEG spectral power with face-viewing gaze features improves autism identification over either modality alone. Main findings: EEG alone 68%, gaze alone 75.89% (AUC 0.865) combining own- and other-race faces, and fused 85.44% with AUC 0.93 at 32 selected features; autistic children fixated the background far more (19.4% versus 3.3%) and the face, nose and mouth less; own-race faces classified better than other-race faces; and EEG showed differences in theta, beta and gamma but not delta or alpha. [RQ2.2] A shielded room for EEG recording and a separate eye-tracking station, with autistic children recruited clinically and typically developing children from a local kindergarten. Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the National Key Research and Development Program of China. [RQ2.3] Two distinct paradigms in one session. Resting-state EEG for about 6 minutes with eyes open, with the child kept as still and quiet as possible. Then passive viewing of face photographs - a young girl of the child's own race or of another race, each type presented 6 times for 10 seconds in random order, with a dynamic kitten and sound between trials to re-engage attention and no response required. The own-race/other-race manipulation is uncommon in this literature and yields a directly interpretable comparison; the attention-recapturing interstimulus is a practical design detail for this age group that few papers describe. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single session per child with no follow-up. Data are EEG traces and gaze coordinates over face photographs, low in identifiability. Governance reporting is complete: conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki, approved by the ethics committee of Beijing Normal University, with parental informed consent obtained before participation, and a data availability statement offering the data on request. [RQ2.5] 128-channel HydroCel Sensor Net (Electrical Geodesics) at 1000 Hz, with 62 electrodes selected and re-referenced to linked ears; Tobii TX300 at 300 Hz with a five-point calibration required to pass with small error vectors before the experiment proceeded, at roughly 60 cm; MATLAB R2016a with EEGLAB for preprocessing and pwelch for spectral estimation. [RQ2.6] Good on signal processing, absent on evaluation. Fully reported: electrode count and selection, sampling rates, referencing scheme, filter bands, downsampling, notch filtering, ICA artefact removal, visual rejection, epoch length, Welch parameters (eight segments, 50% overlap, Hamming window), the five frequency bands with their boundaries, the eight AOIs, the fixation-proportion index definition, the 60 ms fixation threshold, viewing distance, calibration procedure, stimulus counts and durations, and the interstimulus attention device. Entirely absent: any statement of how the classifier was trained and evaluated - no split, no folds, no repetition - together with SVM hyperparameters, the identity of the 32 selected features, and any code release. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged: that the cohort begins at age 3 and that 'diagnosis of autism at earlier ages is a pressing clinical need', with a stated plan to recruit children aged 2 or younger; and that more features should be extracted from both modalities. The paper also usefully concedes a limitation of its own EEG modality, noting that 'no differences in EEG were found in some previous studies, especially for high functioning autism' and concluding that 'using only EEG evaluation may be insufficient to identify children with this complex disease'. Not acknowledged, and decisive: no validation scheme of any kind is described, so the reported accuracies have no established out-of-sample interpretation; mRMR uses class labels with no indication of nesting within any resampling; the headline 85.44% is the maximum of a curve swept over one to forty-five features, so the operating point was selected on the reported data; the identity of the selected features is never given; recruitment routes differ systematically between groups; and no severity or functioning measure is reported despite heterogeneity being central to the paper's own argument. [RQ2.9] Recruit younger children, aged two years or under, to address the clinical need for earlier diagnosis; and extract additional features from both EEG and eye tracking, since 'multi-modal, multi-feature fusion will likely improve classification accuracy further'. [RQ3.1] Two behavioural-adjacent targets of different kinds. The behavioural measure proper is visual attention allocation during face viewing, decomposed across eight regions from whole-face down to individual eyes, and manipulated by face race. The EEG measure is neurophysiological rather than behavioural - resting-state cortical rhythm power - and the paper interprets it in behavioural terms, linking theta to working memory encoding and retrieval, beta to alertness and motor behaviour, and gamma to sensory processing, working memory, attention and arousal. [RQ3.2] The clearest and most cleanly reported fusion result in the corpus, precisely because both single-modality baselines are given: EEG alone 68%, gaze alone 75.89%, fused 85.44% with AUC rising from 0.865 to 0.93. That is close to a 10-point gain over the better single modality, and the authors' rationale for expecting it is specific rather than generic - EEG abnormalities are inconsistent across the autism spectrum, particularly in high-functioning presentations, whereas 'atypical face processing' has been found 'for all types of ASD', so the modalities should fail on different subgroups. There is a second, within-modality fusion as well: own-race faces alone gave 72.33% and other-race faces 66.67%, but combining both face types gave 75.89%, better than either. The caveat is that with no validation scheme and feature selection over a much larger EEG feature pool, the size of the fusion gain cannot be taken at face value, and the identity of the 32 selected features is not disclosed so complementarity cannot be verified. [RQ4.1] A single linear SVM throughout, preceded by mRMR feature selection based on mutual information, chosen for jointly maximising relevance to the class label and minimising redundancy among features. No model comparison is performed - the experimental variable is the modality and the number of selected features, not the learner. This is a defensible focus given the paper's question, but it means there is no evidence about whether the linear SVM is the right choice for these features. [RQ4.2] Two feature families of very unequal size. EEG contributes relative power in five bands across 62 electrodes - potentially over 300 features, though the paper reports an EEG-only classification 'using the five frequency bands' relative power', suggesting channel-averaged values were used there. Eye tracking contributes 16 features (eight AOIs by two face races) as fixation-time proportions. The relative power formulation is a considered choice, expressing each band as a share of total spectral power to expose 'abnormalities in the rhythmic fluctuations' independent of overall amplitude. The 60 ms fixation threshold on the gaze side is a similarly considered detail, excluding gaze too brief to be conscious. The asymmetry in pool size between modalities is not addressed and matters for interpreting which features the mRMR selection favoured. [RQ4.3] Accuracy and AUC only, but reported for every modality and stimulus condition separately, which is what makes the fusion ladder legible. Missing: sensitivity, specificity, confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any statistical test of the differences between modality conditions - so whether 85.44% is significantly better than 75.89% on 97 children is not established. The accuracy-versus-feature-count curve is plotted, which is transparent about the sweep but also makes explicit that the headline is a maximum rather than a pre-specified operating point. [RQ4.4] No model-explanation method and no disclosure of which features mRMR selected, which is the paper's main interpretive gap - having established that fusion helps, it cannot say what the fused model is using. Interpretation instead comes from a parallel descriptive analysis: independent t-tests on each band and AOI, with the resulting differences read against established theory. The gaze findings are interpreted through the eye avoidance hypothesis, that autistic people avoid eye contact because they 'may consider it an unbearable social threat and experience uncomfortable physiological responses', making avoidance 'an adaptive strategy' that nonetheless degrades processing of facial identity and intention. The EEG findings are mapped onto cognitive functions band by band. Notably, the descriptive analysis found the strongest gaze effect on background fixation rather than on the eye region, and eye-region differences did not reach significance - a result that sits somewhat awkwardly with the eye-avoidance framing the discussion adopts. [RQ4.5] The study's decisive weakness. No train/test split, cross-validation, held-out sample or repetition procedure is described anywhere in the methods or results. mRMR feature selection uses class labels and there is no statement that it was nested within any resampling scheme. The reported 85.44% is explicitly the maximum of a curve swept across one to forty-five selected features, so both the feature count and the reported figure were chosen against the same data. With 97 participants and an EEG feature pool potentially exceeding 300 variables, this is exactly the configuration in which unnested supervised selection produces substantial upward bias. There is no independent cohort, no external site and no replication. The accuracies should therefore be read as in-sample separability rather than as estimates of predictive performance. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism; Typically developing children; EEG; Eye-tracking. Purely descriptive of the design, with no methodological or clinical framing term - consistent with a paper whose contribution is presented as the combination of two established measurement modalities rather than as a modelling advance. [RQ5.2] Computers in Biology and Medicine, 120, article 103722 - an Elsevier biomedical engineering journal, appropriate for a signal-processing-plus-classification contribution. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is the standard objectivity argument - 'clinical diagnosis is mainly based on behavioral scale tests including the autism behavior checklist and Childhood Autism Rating Scale' and 'due to subjectivity, evaluation results may not be very accurate' - but with a more specific biomarker orientation than most: biomarkers are defined as objective indicators of biological processes used 'for diagnosis, outcome predictions, and treatment prediction', with high accuracy, reliability and validity named as prerequisites for clinical use. The paper's distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is its argument for why single-modality approaches fail: it cites a review finding a U-shaped profile of EEG power alterations in autism (excess low- and high-frequency power, deficient alpha), then notes that other studies found no EEG differences at all, particularly in high-functioning autism, and concludes that heterogeneity makes EEG alone insufficient. Eye tracking is added specifically because 'atypical face processing' has been found across all presentations. That is a heterogeneity-driven rationale for fusion rather than a generic more-data-is-better argument, and it is unusual in this literature. |
| S-049 | Cross-sectional case-control feasibility and classification study; 16 autistic (12.13 +/- 3.31 years, 81% male, SCQ 18.86, SRS-2 78.85, ABIQ 102.75) and 17 neurotypical children (11.53 +/- 2.48 years, 53% male, SCQ 1.82, SRS-2 44.41, ABIQ 108.94) at Stanford, from 43 enrolled with 10 itemised exclusions; wearable eye and world video plus emotion responses across 125 CAFE stimuli, not released. | Google Glass fitted with a US $35 modified-webcam eye tracker on a 3D-printed prism mount recorded gaze while children identified emotions on centrally presented child faces flanked by two validated nonsocial distractors, across three trials with audio feedback in trial 2 only; hybrid pupil tracking and four per-participant polynomial calibrations produced per-frame gaze coded as face, left distractor, right distractor or nowhere; 219 features per trial in four blocks (emotion confusion matrix, per-face correctness, gaze statistics, age and gender) were classified by elastic net with leave-one-participant-out cross-validation and Monte Carlo shuffling significance tests across a 60-cell ablation grid. | Mean distraction ratio was higher in autism (0.0433 +/- 0.0911 versus 0.0139 +/- 0.0215) but not significantly at participant level (P = .12). The full model reached 71.0% - identical to an age-and-gender-only baseline of 71.0%. Gaze features alone reached 83.9% on trial 1 and all trials (P = .00, .002) but did not survive Bonferroni correction; emotion confusion matrices alone fell to 6.5% and 35.5% in trials 2 and 3. Discrimination was best in trial 1, before any feedback or task adaptation. | Authors' own list: age range 6-17 misses the critical developmental window; sex imbalance of 81% versus 53% male on tasks with known gender effects; only 3 of 16 autistic participants below ABIQ 80 so the cohort is predominantly high-functioning; a chinrest added after four participants while more autistic children were tested later, a confound the authors say 'may be exploited by the classifiers'; and a custom eye tracker never validated against a standard device, requiring extensive manual annotation and occluding about 15% of the lower visual field with possible differential effects on children with tactile sensitivities. Additionally no data or code release and no external cohort. | The corpus's definitive negative result and its methodological benchmark for interpreting accuracy. By including an age-and-gender-only baseline that reached exactly the same 71.0% as the full behavioural model, it demonstrates what almost every other study here leaves untested - whether reported accuracy exceeds what trivial demographics achieve. It reports permutation-based significance for all 60 ablation cells, applies multiplicity correction, and declines to claim a gaze-only 83.9% at P = .002 as a finding. Its explicit revision of a field assumption - that facial attention differences in autism are clear enough to exploit, now judged subtle - is the kind of correction the synthesis should carry forward, alongside its disclosure that later generations of the same system abandoned wearable eye tracking altogether on practical grounds. Its participant characterisation, including drug-level medication reporting and control screening on sibling diagnosis, sets the standard against which the rest of the corpus can be measured. | [RQ1.1] Two groups: 16 autistic and 17 neurotypical children, from 43 enrolled (23 autistic, 20 neurotypical). Exclusions are itemised with reasons: 4 controls received an early prototype version with visual rather than audio cues and could not read the cues or complete the task; 5 autistic participants received images in a different randomised order because of a stimulus ordering error; and 1 autistic participant had an unrelated health issue mid-session. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The cohort is predominantly high-functioning - only 3 of 16 autistic participants had an abbreviated IQ below 80. [RQ1.2] 'children with autism', 'children with ASD', 'ASD participants', 'neurotypical controls (NCs)', 'individuals with autism'. Consistently person-first, and 'neurotypical' rather than 'normal', 'healthy' or 'typically developing' - the neurodiversity-aligned term. The framing acknowledges theoretical uncertainty rather than asserting deficits: 'There are several leading theories about facial processing in ASD, and the underlying biological mechanisms are not fully understood.' Autism is nonetheless introduced as 'one of the most important public health challenges we face today'. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: n = 16, 13 male (81%) and 3 female, mean age 12.13 +/- 3.31 years, range 6-17; SCQ 18.86 +/- 6.43; ABIQ 102.75 +/- 19.54 (range 55-133); SRS-2 total 78.85 +/- 11.13. Neurotypical group: n = 17, 9 male (53%) and 8 female, mean age 11.53 +/- 2.48, range 8-17; SCQ 1.82 +/- 1.07; ABIQ 108.94 +/- 9.58 (91-129); SRS-2 total 44.41 +/- 8.11. Comorbidities and current medications are itemised for the 11 autistic participants who completed the survey - methylphenidate in 3, sertraline in 2, and single instances of arginine vasopressin, guanfacine, carbamazepine, aripiprazole and dexmethylphenidate, with only 4 of 11 unmedicated against 15 of 17 controls. This is the most complete participant characterisation in the corpus. The sex imbalance (81% versus 53% male) is named by the authors as a limitation, and the ABIQ distribution shows the autistic cohort is predominantly high-functioning with wider spread than controls. [RQ1.4] Official autism diagnosis confirmed via medical record, with parent-reported diagnosis corroborated by SCQ above 16, and syndromic autism excluded on the basis of genetic, metabolic or infectious aetiology in the record. The control group is screened more rigorously than anywhere else in the corpus, excluded on SCQ above 14, history of mood or personality disorder, a sibling diagnosed with autism or schizophrenia, history of seizures or neurological disorder, and vision impairment. Excluding on sibling diagnosis controls for the broader autism phenotype - a step no other study here takes. Stanford-Binet ABIQ was administered by a trained research assistant and SRS-2 completed by parents for every participant. [RQ1.5] Complete. SCQ, SRS-2 total and Stanford-Binet ABIQ for every participant in both groups, plus itemised comorbid psychological conditions and current medications for those who completed the survey. Uniquely in this corpus, the medication data are reported at drug level rather than as a summary count, which matters because several of the drugs listed - methylphenidate, guanfacine, aripiprazole - have documented effects on attention and eye movement. [RQ2.1] Goal: test the feasibility of wearable gaze tracking during an emotion recognition task and whether the resulting data distinguish autistic from neurotypical children. Main findings: autistic children showed a higher mean distraction ratio (0.0433 versus 0.0139) but not significantly at the participant level (P = .12); the full classifier reached 71.0%, exactly matching an age-and-gender-only baseline; gaze features alone reached 83.9% but did not survive Bonferroni correction; performance was best on trial 1 before feedback and worst on trial 2 during audio cueing; and the authors conclude the differences are too subtle and the data too noisy for reliable machine exploitation. [RQ2.2] In-lab at Stanford University, with families recruited between 25 February 2015 and 26 January 2016 through the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Research Registry, referrals to the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Clinic, the Developmental Behavioral Unit of Lucile Packard Children's Hospital, and academic presentations. Funded by NIH grants 1R01EB025025-01 and 1R21HD091500-01 plus multiple foundation and Stanford programme grants. The senior author declares founding Cognoa, a company building digital child-health solutions. [RQ2.3] Emotion recognition under competing attentional demand - a face at centre flanked by two validated high-autism-interest nonsocial distractors, so that gaze allocation and emotion identification are measured in the same trial. The paper's rationale for combining them is theoretical rather than opportunistic: emotion recognition and social attention 'have mostly been studied in isolation' and both have been proposed separately as diagnostic indicators, so the authors 'hypothesized that they are deeply linked and studied them together'. The three-trial structure with feedback in trial 2 only is designed to emulate the Superpower Glass intervention, and it produces an unanticipated result - discrimination was best in trial 1, before any feedback or task adaptation. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; one 20-minute session per child with no follow-up, though the stated goal of continuous phenotyping is inherently longitudinal. Data include eye and world video of identifiable children with extensive manual annotation by independent labellers. Governance is reported: written informed consent from both parents and children under an approved Stanford IRB protocol. The conflict of interest is declared. [RQ2.5] Deliberately low-cost and open-hardware derived: Google Glass with a custom 3D-printed prism mount holding a Microsoft LifeCam HD-6000 webcam whose infrared filter was removed and whose indicator LEDs were replaced with infrared emitters, adapted from the open-source Pupil Project, at about US $35 for the add-on. Multiple mount variants were printed so the best eye view could be chosen per participant. Stimuli came from the CAFE dataset of child faces, balanced across five racial groups and by gender and emotion within each trial - the most carefully balanced stimulus set in the corpus. [RQ2.6] Very good, with implementation detail deferred to a supplementary appendix rather than omitted. Reported in the paper: recruitment window and channels, all inclusion and exclusion criteria for both groups, every excluded participant with the reason, hardware construction and cost, screen size, resolution and viewing distance, stimulus source and balancing, image counts per trial, display durations, feedback modality and timing, the calibration validation device, the four-calibration scheme with per-calibration polynomial regression, the four-way gaze coding scheme, all four feature blocks with their dimensionalities, the classifier and its rationale, the cross-validation scheme, the shuffling test with iteration count and convergence checking, and a full 60-cell ablation grid. Pupil tracking algorithms, inter-labeller reliability and outlier exclusion criteria are in Multimedia Appendix 1. Not released: data or code. [RQ2.7] The most complete limitations section in the corpus, with five named items. Age range 6-17 'is not representative of children who are in critical periods of development for cognition and speech'. Gender imbalance of 13:3 in the autistic cohort against 9:8 in controls, with the authors noting that gender differences exist on emotion recognition and gaze tasks and 'may have been exacerbated by our imbalanced cohorts'. Limited spectrum coverage, since only 3 of 16 autistic participants had ABIQ below 80 so 13 are high-functioning. A chinrest added after the first four participants because of head movement, with the explicit admission that 'more ASD subjects took part in the study later on. This confound may be exploited by the classifiers'. And nonstandard eye tracking - the custom system was never evaluated against a standard tracker, the mount shifted requiring recalibration and extensive manual annotation, and it 'occluded roughly 15% of the field of view in the lower region for most participants, which may have had a greater distracting effect on participants in the ASD group with tactile sensitivities'. The discussion adds an ethological caution: static 6-second photographs are 'quite divergent from real-life social interactions with moving children and fleeting displays of facial emotion', and the field 'does not have enough information to know how divergent our experimental data might be from the ecologically valid situations'. [RQ2.9] Move acquisition into the home, with four named prerequisites: large-scale in-home data acquisition, augmented reality platforms with robust native eye tracking, game design for at-home analysis platforms, and clearly defined measurable experimental parameters. Extend feasibility testing to younger children. Balance cohorts for age and gender. And solve a human-computer interaction problem the authors state precisely - producing 'appropriate user interfaces and games that homogenize use in ways so as to lower the natural variability of measurement', since follow-up Superpower Glass studies showed heterogeneity in less-restricted collection. They also note that later generations of the system dropped the eye tracker entirely because of bulkiness and calibration issues, and expect native gaze tracking in commercial AR devices to resolve this. [RQ3.1] Two behaviours measured simultaneously and by design: visual attention allocation between a central social stimulus and flanking nonsocial distractors, and emotion recognition accuracy and error structure. The distraction ratio - proportion of gaze frames on distractors rather than the face - is the primary behavioural measure, with a variant excluding frames coded 'nowhere in particular' to give a more direct face-versus-distractor comparison. Emotion responses are captured both as a 7 x 7 confusion matrix and as a per-face correct/incorrect sequence preserving performance over time. [RQ3.2] The fusion result is negative and instructive. Gaze features alone gave the best behavioural performance (83.9% on trial 1 and on all trials), emotion confusion matrices alone performed at or below chance in two of three trials (6.5% and 35.5%), and combining all feature blocks gave 71.0% - worse than gaze alone. Adding emotion features to gaze reduced accuracy in most cells of the ablation grid. This is a rare demonstration in the corpus that multimodal combination can degrade rather than improve performance when one modality carries little signal and the feature-to-participant ratio is extreme. The critical comparison, though, is not between modalities but against the metadata baseline: age and gender alone reached 71.0% with P = .04, the same accuracy as the full model with a marginally better P value, so no combination of behavioural features demonstrably beat two demographic variables. [RQ4.1] Elastic net as the primary classifier, chosen explicitly for the data regime: 219 features per trial against 33 participants means 'regularization was important to prevent model overfitting', and elastic net combines lasso and ridge penalties. Logistic regression with grid-searched l1 or l2 regularisation serves as an ablation comparator, included on the technical grounds that elastic net optimisers can be unstable at the edge cases where one penalty vanishes. Elastic net outperformed logistic regression in most tasks, which the authors read as confirming 'a need for regularization in this dataset'. No deep learning, correctly - the discussion notes that a larger, more balanced corpus 'would also enable the use of more complex statistical models, such as artificial neural networks', which is a statement of what the data cannot currently support. [RQ4.2] 219 features per trial in four clearly separated blocks, which is what makes the ablation grid possible: a row-normalised 7 x 7 emotion confusion matrix flattened to 49 features; a per-face binary correctness sequence of 41 or 42 features preserving temporal structure; three gaze features per face (proportion of frames on the face rather than a distractor, proportion of fixation changes directed to the face, and frames elapsed before first looking at the face) giving 123 or 126; and two metadata features, age and gender. Including metadata as an explicit feature block rather than as covariates is the design decision that makes the paper's central finding visible. [RQ4.3] Leave-one-participant-out accuracy paired with a Monte Carlo shuffling P value for every one of 60 grid cells (15 feature combinations by four trial conditions), plus cross-validation confusion matrices for the full model. Shuffling tests ran 2,500 iterations and were checked for convergence. Bonferroni correction is applied when interpreting significance across the grid, and the authors note which results survive it and which do not. Reporting a permutation-based significance test for every reported accuracy is unique in this corpus and is precisely what distinguishes an accuracy from a finding at this sample size. No sensitivity, specificity or AUC. [RQ4.4] No model-explanation method, but the ablation grid functions as a structured interpretability analysis at the block level, and its results are interpreted carefully. Two patterns are drawn out. First, discrimination is best in trial 1 - 'the first trial conducted which was before receiving any feedback or adjusting to the task' - implying the signal is strongest on first exposure and attenuates as children adapt, which has direct implications for protocol design. Second, emotion confusion matrices alone collapse to below chance in later trials, so the emotion-response signal is unstable. The behavioural interpretation is explicitly bounded: the authors note that classical eye-tracking studies have found subtler effects such as increased mouth relative to eye attention, and state that 'the gaze data collected by our system was too noisy to test for these subtler effects'. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-participant-out cross-validation throughout, with Monte Carlo shuffling tests establishing significance against chance for every reported accuracy, hyperparameters grid-searched on training folds only, and Bonferroni correction applied when interpreting the grid. Most importantly, the design includes a null-model baseline using only age and gender, which is the element almost every other study in this corpus lacks and which is what converts a nominal 71% accuracy into an interpretable finding. What remains absent is an independent cohort or external validation, which the sample size precludes, and the acknowledged possibility that the mid-study chinrest change is confounded with group and could be exploited by the classifiers - a validity threat the authors identify but cannot remove. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder; translational medicine; eye tracking; wearable technologies; artificial intelligence; machine learning; precision health; digital therapy. The recurring frame is 'continuous social phenotyping' - measurement carried out repeatedly in natural settings rather than episodically in clinics - which positions the work as infrastructure for longitudinal characterisation rather than as a diagnostic test. [RQ5.2] Journal of Medical Internet Research, 22(4), e13810 - a digital health venue, appropriate for a wearable feasibility study, and one whose remit makes a negative feasibility result publishable in a way that a pure machine learning venue might not. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is the gap between where social skills are practised and where they are measured: emotion recognition and eye contact skills 'are important to improve social functioning, but the methods currently used to measure and track such skills are delivered in clinical settings or via trained administrators outside the social context where these skills are practiced'. The proposed remedy is mobile and wearable machine learning platforms enabling continuous phenotyping during natural social interactions. The paper's most valuable contribution to the field's self-understanding is its retraction of a prior assumption, stated explicitly: 'The prevailing belief in the literature was that facial attention differences are very clear in ASD, so we hypothesized that distraction ratios across an emotion recognition task alone were enough to distinguish ASD vs NC reliably. We now believe that integrating further subtlety through robust gaze-tracking hardware will be required to design a phenotyping marker from this effect.' It also reports that later generations of the same research group's system abandoned the eye tracker entirely because of bulkiness and calibration problems - a rare disclosure of a technology's practical failure trajectory. |
| S-050 | Two-part study - a facial EMG preparatory study in 40 healthy males for feature selection, then a cross-sectional case-control classification with clinician benchmarking; 37 autistic adults without intellectual disability (36.89 years, 49% female, ADOS in 35, ADI-R in 21) from a Berlin specialist clinic and 43 controls (33.14 years, 51% female) screened for psychiatric history; video and audio withheld for privacy but available on request, code public, instrument scheduled for open release. | A 7-minute Simulated Interaction Task in which a prerecorded actress conducts a food-preferences conversation structured into neutral, positive and negative segments while displaying empathic listening; OpenFace extracted action units and gaze angles with confidence thresholding, Librosa and Praat extracted voice features, and summary statistics per conversation segment gave 715 facial, 85 gaze and 58 voice features plus gender; a 1,000-tree random forest was evaluated by leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with nested three-fold hyperparameter tuning, one aggregate vector per participant, and benchmarked against a majority vote and eight expert clinicians. | Combined AUC 0.78, accuracy 73%, sensitivity 67%, specificity 79% - significantly better than majority vote (p = 0.014) and not significantly worse than clinicians, whose mean accuracy was 0.71 with a range of 0.56-1.00 correlating with experience (rs = 0.72). Voice AUC 0.77, facial expression 0.74 (all action units) or 0.65 (domain-selected), gaze 0.63 with no group differences surviving correction. Autistic adults smiled less (AU12 occurrence 0.09 versus 0.40), mimicked the actress's AU6 less (0.08 versus 0.19), frowned more during negative content, and spoke at higher fundamental frequency. Predicted probability correlated with ADOS (rs = 0.48) and with age (rs = 0.35). | Groups are not age-matched and the classifier demonstrably exploits this, with the authors identifying an age bias they do not correct for; the reported direction of the harmonics-to-noise ratio effect contradicts the paper's own table; the autistic cohort is high-functioning adults with existing diagnoses, so camouflaging is present in the classified population; gaze contributes almost nothing and its null result cannot be distinguished from measurement imprecision; the prerecorded actress cannot adapt to answer length; no independent cohort or external site; and no comparison group with other psychiatric conditions despite the targeted deficits being transdiagnostic. | The only study in the corpus to benchmark its classifier against practising clinicians on identical material, and the result cuts two ways: the model matched expert performance, and the experts ranged from 0.56 to 1.00 with accuracy scaling with experience - an empirical measurement of exactly the inter-rater variability the tool is designed to reduce. It is also one of very few studies to show that a diagnostic classifier's continuous output tracks clinical severity (rs = 0.48 with ADOS) rather than merely separating groups, and simultaneously one of very few to detect and name a demographic confound in its own model (rs = 0.35 with age), concluding that this 'points to the strong need of careful testing for confounders and biases in training data for all kind of machine-learning diagnostic methods'. Methodologically it sets the corpus benchmark for elicitation design - standardising a social interaction by prerecording one side, then verifying the stimulus by running the same computer vision pipeline over the actress - and for validation, with nested hyperparameter tuning, an explicit statement that no repeated measures enter the feature representation, and a majority-vote baseline. Its near-even sex distribution in both groups is unique in this corpus and enables a per-gender finding that women were detected more accurately. | [RQ1.1] Two groups in the main study: 37 autistic adults without intellectual disability recruited via the autism outpatient clinic of Charite Universitatsmedizin Berlin, and 43 healthy controls, with one autistic participant excluded from the combined classifier for missing audio. A separate preparatory study used 40 healthy males with facial EMG to select regions of interest before the main analysis - a two-stage design in which feature selection is performed on an entirely different sample, which is stronger than any within-study selection procedure. No other-psychiatric-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors identify testing 'in larger clinical samples with different psychiatric conditions' as necessary since the social interaction deficits targeted are common to many disorders. [RQ1.2] 'individuals with ASD', 'adults with ASD', 'autism spectrum disorder', 'healthy controls (HC)', 'neurotypical (NT)', 'individuals without autism'. Consistently person-first, with both 'healthy controls' and 'neurotypical' used. The framing locates the problem in clinical practice rather than in patients: clinicians rely on 'the so-called clinical gaze, the implicit knowledge based on experience', which is 'difficult to verbalize, teach, quantify, standardize, and validate', and 'interrater-variability may account for inconsistencies regarding diagnostic accuracy'. Camouflaging is described neutrally as a strategy adults develop to compensate, and is identified as a reason for late diagnosis rather than as a deficit. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: n = 37, 18 female (49%), mean age 36.89 years, range 22-62. Control group: n = 43, 22 female (51%), mean age 33.14 years, range 18-49. The sex balance is the most striking feature - essentially even in both groups, against the 4:1 male predominance typical of autism cohorts including most in this corpus - and it enables the paper's per-gender analysis showing better detection of women (33 of 39 versus 25 of 40, p = 0.048), which the authors interpret through the finding that women require more severe symptoms to receive a diagnosis. Age is not matched, with the autistic group 3.75 years older and extending 13 years further, and the classifier demonstrably picks this up (class probability correlated with age at rs = 0.35, p = 0.001). Verbal intelligence was confirmed sufficient by the Wortschatztest but no IQ values are reported. No ethnicity or socioeconomic data; single clinic recruitment. [RQ1.4] Prior ICD-10 diagnoses of Asperger syndrome, atypical autism or childhood autism, made through a specialist autism outpatient clinic, with ADOS administered to 35 of 37 participants and ADI-R to the 21 for whom parental informants were available. Autism-Spectrum Quotient was collected for all participants in both groups and the Wortschatztest confirmed verbal intelligence. Control status was established prospectively by excluding any history of psychiatric disorder, with three participants excluded on that basis. Both groups were also screened for current antipsychotic and anticonvulsant medication and comorbid neurological disorders. This is among the more rigorous ascertainments in the corpus, and the ADOS scores are used analytically rather than merely reported. [RQ1.5] ADOS scores for 35 participants, Autism-Spectrum Quotient for all participants in both groups, and Wortschatztest verbal intelligence as an inclusion screen. The ADOS data are used substantively: the classifier's predicted class probability correlates with ADOS score at rs = 0.48, p < 0.0001, establishing that the model's output tracks symptom severity and not merely group membership. No full-scale IQ, adaptive functioning or comorbidity scores are reported. [RQ2.1] Goal: build and validate a standardised, automatically scored measure of social interaction behaviour capable of supporting autism diagnosis in adults. Main findings: combined AUC 0.78 with 73% accuracy, 67% sensitivity and 79% specificity; voice was the strongest modality (0.77), facial expression next (0.74), gaze weakest (0.63) with no differences surviving correction; autistic adults showed less social smiling and less mimicry and higher fundamental frequency; the classifier beat a majority vote and matched eight clinical experts whose own accuracy ranged from 0.56 to 1.00 and scaled with experience; and predicted probability correlated with both ADOS severity (rs = 0.48) and age (rs = 0.35), the latter identified as a confound. [RQ2.2] A quiet laboratory with constant lighting at Humboldt-Universitat zu Berlin, with participants recruited through the autism outpatient clinic of Charite Universitatsmedizin Berlin. The experimenter left the room before the task began, so the participant was alone with the screen. Ethics approval from the Charite ethics committee, Helsinki conformity, written informed consent from all participants and separate consent for figure publication. [RQ2.3] The Simulated Interaction Task - the corpus's most carefully constructed elicitation paradigm. A prerecorded actress conducts a small-talk conversation about food preferences and dinner preparation, structured into neutral, positive and negative segments of 24-26 seconds each, alternating between her speaking and the participant answering while she displays empathic listening (nodding, social smiling). The design reasoning is stated in unusual detail: food preferences were chosen because they elicit positive and negative emotion quickly without personal or sensitive content, and because response lengths vary less than for topics such as favourite films, which aids standardisation. To generate natural behaviour, the actress actually conversed with the film director during shooting rather than reading to camera. Naturalness was supported by informing participants the actress's part was prerecorded, by instructing and rehearsing three-to-four-sentence answers, and by opening with a practice exchange. Crucially, the actress's own behaviour was then verified with the same OpenFace pipeline, confirming she expressed more disgust and less joy when discussing disliked food and smiled more when listening than speaking - so the stimulus is quantified rather than assumed. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; one session per participant with no follow-up, though the stated applications include monitoring disorder course and treatment outcome. Data are video and audio of identifiable adults. Governance is complete and includes an unusual element - explicit separate consent from individuals appearing in published figures - and the data availability statement withholds the dataset specifically 'due to privacy restrictions of the video data' while making it available on reasonable request. The discussion also engages the downstream consequences of deployment, noting that 'especially screenings and unsupervised feedback might result in more individuals seeking care and lead to higher costs for the health system' and that 'it is warranted to carefully define the area of use and evaluate benefits, costs, and risks' - one of very few papers in the corpus to consider system-level effects of its own tool. [RQ2.5] Deliberately minimal: a standard computer with a camera and microphone, which the paper contrasts against comparators using 'high-cost apparatus, not suited for large-scale testing'. Analysis used OpenFace for action units, landmarks and gaze with a trained confidence network, Librosa for MFCCs and energy, Parselmouth Praat scripts for fundamental frequency, jitter and shimmer, and scikit-learn. The preparatory study used facial EMG over zygomaticus major, corrugator supercilii and levator labii to establish which action units to target. [RQ2.6] Among the best in the corpus. Reported: all recruitment, inclusion and exclusion criteria; the full SIT structure with segment durations and the reasoning behind topic choice; the actress's verified non-verbal behaviour; frame- and participant-level tracking confidence thresholds (0.75 confidence, 90% of frames) with actual achieved tracking rates (99% of frames, mean confidence 0.99, no group difference at p = 0.97); feature construction at both primary and secondary levels with counts per modality; the classifier, ensemble size and full hyperparameter grids; the nested cross-validation scheme with an explicit statement about the absence of repeated measures; the expert rating protocol; and all statistical tests with effect sizes. Analysis code is public on GitHub, and the SIT instrument was scheduled for open release from 2024 under a Creative Commons licence at a named repository. Video data are withheld for privacy but available on request. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged with unusual thoroughness. On the age bias: 'older participants in both groups were more often labeled as autistic than young participants by the machine-learning classifiers, as the classifier was probably picking up a tendency of higher age in the ASD group. This age bias points to the strong need of careful testing for confounders and biases in training data for all kind of machine-learning diagnostic methods.' On gaze: the null result is attributed to appearance-based estimation being 'not sensitive enough to detect the subtle gaze dysfunctions present in ASD', with a caution that the null 'has to be interpreted with caution'. On the paradigm: the prerecorded actress cannot adapt to answer length, and future versions should provide tailored responses and partners matched on gender, age or ethnicity since similarity enhances mimicry. On the HNR finding: interpretation 'is not straightforward, given the lack of reference studies', with conflicting prior findings acknowledged and the possibility raised that groups differ in speaking-to-pause ratios. On multiplicity: the authors note that automated analysis 'allows the comparison of many different aspects of behavior' so 'the problem of multiple testing remains', which is why they favour the multivariate machine learning approach. Not acknowledged: the reported direction of the HNR effect contradicts the tabulated medians, which are lower rather than higher in autism; and the age confound, though identified, is not adjusted for in the headline accuracy. [RQ2.9] Compare SIT behaviour against a live face-to-face condition with the same topic and script to validate the simulation; make the actress's responses adaptive to participants' answer lengths; provide interaction partners matched on gender, age or ethnic background since similarity enhances mimicry; add automated camera and microphone checks and evaluate accuracy in home settings, since self-administration often diminishes accuracy; use state-of-the-art eye tracking to establish whether gaze carries information in this paradigm; and test sensitivity and specificity in larger clinical samples spanning other psychiatric conditions, since social interaction deficits are common to psychosis, depression, bipolar disorder and substance use disorders. [RQ3.1] Three behavioural channels measured simultaneously during a single interaction: facial expression (action unit occurrence and intensity, and critically mimicry - the time-shifted correlation between the actress's and participant's expression time series), gaze (angle, deviation from personal median, speed and acceleration), and voice (fundamental frequency, jitter, shimmer, energy, harmonics-to-noise ratio and MFCCs). Measuring mimicry rather than expression alone is the distinctive choice: it captures a dyadic property that requires both partners' behaviour, and it is only possible because the partner's behaviour is identical for every participant. [RQ3.2] A clean modality comparison with an informative asymmetry. Voice alone reached AUC 0.77, facial expression 0.74 with all 17 action units and 0.65 with the domain-selected subset, gaze 0.63, and all three combined 0.78 - so fusion added essentially nothing over voice alone, and the combined result is carried by the two strong modalities. The gaze failure is diagnosed rather than glossed: appearance-based estimation from a webcam is judged insufficiently precise for the subtle differences reported in the eye-tracking literature, and the authors explicitly recommend state-of-the-art eye trackers to test whether gaze carries information in this paradigm. The comparison between domain-selected facial features (0.65) and all available action units (0.74) is also instructive - constraining features for interpretability cost about 9 AUC points, a trade-off the authors accepted deliberately for 'transparent and explainable diagnostic decisions'. [RQ4.1] A single random forest of 1,000 trees with maximum depth and minimum samples per leaf tuned over seven values each, applied identically to each modality and to the combination. Model choice is deliberately conservative given 80 participants, and an earlier conference paper by the same group compared alternative approaches. The more consequential modelling decision is what enters the model: features were restricted 'strictly to features based on domain-knowledge or on the EMG preparatory study' for the primary analyses, which is a principled constraint that sacrifices accuracy for interpretability and is quantified by the parallel all-action-unit result. [RQ4.2] Primary features chosen a priori from theory and from an independent EMG study, then expanded into secondary summary statistics (mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, time of maximum, skewness, kurtosis) computed separately for each of the seven conversation parts - yielding 715 facial, 85 gaze and 58 voice features. Segment-wise computation preserves the paradigm's designed structure, so the representation encodes not just how much a participant smiled but when relative to the emotional content of the conversation. Each participant contributes exactly one feature vector, which the authors state explicitly rules out nested repeated measures. Gender is included as a feature throughout so that the model can weight sex-dependent voice features appropriately. [RQ4.3] AUC per modality and combined, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at a stated threshold, McNemar tests against a majority-vote baseline and against expert raters, correlations of predicted class probability with ADOS severity and with age, per-gender classification breakdowns, and supplementary confusion matrices and ROC curves for every classifier. Two of these are almost unique in the corpus. Comparing against a majority-vote baseline establishes that the accuracy exceeds trivial prediction. Correlating predicted probability with ADOS establishes that the model's continuous output has clinical meaning beyond the binary decision - and correlating it with age reveals the confound. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is designed in rather than added afterwards. Features were restricted to those with prior theoretical or EMG-based justification specifically 'for transparent and explainable diagnostic decisions', so every input has a stated behavioural meaning. Each is then reported as a univariate group comparison with effect size, so the multivariate result can be read against the individual behaviours: less social smiling in mouth and eye regions, reduced mimicry of the actress's cheek-raise, more intense frowning during negative content, higher fundamental frequency. The cost of this constraint is measured - all 17 action units reached AUC 0.74 against 0.65 for the selected subset. The clinical validity of the model's output is separately established by its correlation with ADOS score, and its principal bias by its correlation with age. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with nested three-fold cross-validation inside each training set for hyperparameter tuning, and an explicit assurance that no test-participant data entered training. The paper states directly that each participant contributes a single aggregate feature vector so that 'the data for the machine-learning analysis did not include any nested repeated measures' - an explicit repudiation of the segment-level splitting that inflates results throughout this literature. Beyond internal validation, the study adds two external reference points that most of the corpus lacks: a majority-vote baseline, beaten significantly, and eight practising clinicians rating the same videos, whose performance the classifier matched. What remains absent is an independent cohort or external site, and the age confound is detected but not corrected in the reported figures. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list. Vocabulary: 'social biomarkers', 'simulated interaction task', 'clinical gaze', 'camouflaging', 'social phenotypes', 'time-effective and cost-effective'. The framing term that does most work is 'clinical gaze' - the implicit expertise the tool is designed to externalise and standardise. [RQ5.2] npj Digital Medicine 3:25 - a Nature Portfolio digital health journal, open access, with authorship spanning psychology, computer science and psychiatry across Humboldt-Universitat, University of Potsdam, Hasso Plattner Institute and Charite. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is distinctive in locating the problem in the measurement instrument rather than in access or cost alone. For general cognition, standardised tests exist - the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, the Mini Mental State Examination - but 'quantifying social interaction deficits is still in its infancy', so clinicians rely on the clinical gaze, which 'practitioners need many years of training to acquire' and which is 'difficult to verbalize, teach, quantify, standardize, and validate'. The paper's own expert-rating data then substantiate this claim empirically: eight experienced clinicians rating the same videos ranged from 0.56 to 1.00 accuracy, with performance correlating with months of experience. The population argument is equally specific - adults with average or above-average intelligence are diagnosed late because they develop camouflaging strategies, and 'to the best of our knowledge, no existing approach focuses on adults with ASD and normal intelligence levels despite the high need for access to diagnosis'. The paper is also careful about its own claim, stating that the SIT 'is not meant to substitute traditional clinical assessment but rather to allow additional information about the client's social communication abilities at an early stage of the diagnostic process'. |
| S-051 | Secondary analysis of an unidentified saccade dataset; 65 autistic and 43 non-autistic participants with no reported ages, sexes, recruitment, diagnostic instruments or provenance; 19 tabular eye-tracking attributes from one block of 30 gap trials and one block of overlap trials per participant. | All processing in Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio: missing-value cleaning, removal of ethnicity, blood type and eye colour leaving 16 inputs, mutual-information filter-based feature selection reducing to 6, then k-fold cross-validation (k unstated) of a Two-Class Boosted Decision Tree selected over linear regression, logistic regression, multiclass neural networks, support vector algorithms and quantile regression. | 88% accuracy (abstract: 88-91%) with an ROC curve whose AUC is not given and no sensitivity or specificity. Retained features named as mean primary saccade amplitude, absolute saccade error and latency plus three unidentified others. Descriptively and without statistics: comparable mean saccade latency but greater trial-to-trial variability in autism, larger and more variable absolute saccade error amplified at higher target amplitudes, and lower peak velocity with longer time to peak. | Mutual-information feature selection applied to the whole dataset before cross-validation splitting, so supervised selection sits outside the validation loop; no participant characteristics of any kind, so no confound can be excluded on a measure that varies strongly with age; the dataset is never named or cited so its provenance, diagnostic basis and collection ethics are untraceable; only accuracy is reported for a proposed diagnostic test, on a 60:40 sample where majority-class prediction scores 60%; k, hyperparameters, seed and comparator results all unreported; the abstract and text give different accuracies; and every descriptive group difference is asserted without a single statistic. | Included on the criteria rather than on merit, and useful to the review mainly as a boundary case. It is a clear instance of the failure mode in which cross-validation is invoked as protection against overfitting in the same passage that describes the supervised feature selection which defeats it - the pipeline order is set out explicitly and reproduced as a workflow diagram, making it one of the corpus's most legible examples of pre-split selection leakage. It is also the corpus's clearest example of secondary data used without provenance, with no citation, no diagnostic basis and no ethics trail. Its one substantive contribution is a hypothesis worth carrying into the synthesis and testing against better-instrumented studies: that the oculomotor signature of autism lies in elevated trial-to-trial variability rather than in shifted central tendency, a pattern it reports for latency, saccade error and time-to-peak-velocity alike. | [RQ1.1] Two groups totalling 108 participants: 65 with autism and 43 without. No other-diagnosis comparison group. Nothing further is reported about either group, and because the dataset is secondary and unidentified, no additional characteristics can be recovered. The class imbalance (60:40) is never addressed in the modelling, and with accuracy as the only reported metric a classifier predicting the majority class throughout would score 60%. [RQ1.2] 'patients with ASD', 'ASD participants', 'affected patients', 'healthy patients', 'children with ASD'. Consistently medicalised - participants are 'patients' throughout and autism is repeatedly framed by severity, opening with the claim that 'symptoms range from completely debilitating to manageable'. The one nuanced observation concerns sex: the paper notes that 'patients with less noticeable symptoms, often girls, who are found to be better at copying stereotypical social patterns, are much harder to accurately diagnose, and often grow into adulthood without ever being diagnosed', which correctly identifies camouflaging as a diagnostic problem - though the study then reports no sex data at all. [RQ1.3] None reported. The entire participant description is 'a total of 65 participants with ASD and 43 with no autism present; these were closely related in terms of patients of similar ages and genders'. No ages, no age ranges, no sex counts, no ethnicity, no socioeconomic information, no country, no recruitment route and no statistical test of the asserted matching. This is the least participant characterisation of any included study in the corpus. It matters directly here because saccade latency, peak velocity and accuracy all change substantially across childhood and adolescence, so an unreported age difference would reproduce every group difference the paper describes. [RQ1.4] Participants are described as 'confirmed to have ASD' with no further detail - no instrument, no criteria, no diagnostician, no date. Non-autistic status is asserted as 'no autism present' with no screening described. Because the dataset is secondary and is never named or cited, the diagnostic basis cannot be traced to a source publication either. The paper's own introduction emphasises that diagnosis requires a multidisciplinary team conducting in-depth neurological, cognitive and language testing, which makes the absence of any account of how these 108 labels were obtained more conspicuous. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure, and no comorbidity information. Given the paper's opening claim that autism symptoms 'range from completely debilitating to manageable', the absence of any severity characterisation means nothing can be said about where on that range the classified sample sits. [RQ2.1] Goal: build a machine-learning classifier on saccade features to shorten and simplify autism diagnosis. Main findings: a Two-Class Boosted Decision Tree reached 88% accuracy (88-91% per the abstract); mutual-information filtering selected six of sixteen attributes, including mean primary saccade amplitude, absolute saccade error and latency; and descriptively, autistic participants showed comparable mean saccade latency but greater trial-to-trial variability, larger and more variable absolute saccade error amplified at higher target amplitudes, and lower peak velocity with longer time to reach it. [RQ2.2] Not stated. No collection site, period, recruitment route or ethics approval appears, because the data are secondary and their origin is never identified. All modelling was performed in Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio. [RQ2.3] The gap/overlap paradigm, which is a well-chosen task for this question even though the paper does not explain why: extinguishing the fixation point before target onset (gap) versus leaving it visible (overlap) separates attentional disengagement from saccade execution, and the paper correctly reports that overlap latencies were substantially longer than gap latencies, confirming the manipulation worked in the source data. Each participant completed one block of 30 gap trials and one block of overlap trials. The paradigm is described but not motivated, and the gap-minus-overlap difference that gives it its diagnostic interest is never analysed as such. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. No ethics approval, consent procedure, anonymisation statement, data governance policy or data provenance is reported anywhere. Since the dataset is neither named nor cited, it cannot be established under what approvals the original collection took place or whether this reuse was authorised - a governance gap that is qualitatively different from simply failing to report approval for one's own collection. [RQ2.5] Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio for the entire pipeline - data ingestion, column selection, missing-value cleaning, filter-based feature selection, train/validation splitting, model training and evaluation - with a screenshot of the workflow reproduced as a figure. No eye-tracking hardware is identified. The paper notes that the Studio limited its ability to tune the model, being unable to 'adjust the number of nodes, leaves, and depth', which is an unusual admission that the tooling constrained the science. [RQ2.6] Poor. The workflow diagram and the named Azure modules make the pipeline order legible - which is how the feature-selection leakage becomes visible - but almost nothing else is reproducible. Not reported: the dataset's identity or citation, k for the k-fold cross-validation, any hyperparameters, the random seed, the identity of three of the six retained features, performance figures for any comparator algorithm, the AUC value behind the plotted ROC curve, and any statistic supporting any descriptive claim. No code and no data. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged: that only 108 individuals were used and more would produce a more diverse and robust classifier with better performance on edge cases; that restricting to six features may have cost accuracy; and that Azure ML Studio prevented direct hyperparameter tuning. Not acknowledged, and decisive: mutual-information feature selection was applied to the full dataset before splitting, so supervised selection sits outside the cross-validation loop; no participant characteristics are reported so no confound can be excluded; the dataset's provenance, diagnostic basis and collection ethics are entirely unstated; only accuracy is reported for a proposed diagnostic test, with no sensitivity or specificity and an unlabelled ROC curve; the 60:40 class imbalance means a majority-class predictor scores 60%; the abstract's 88-91% range is unexplained against the text's single figure of 88%; the comparator set includes regression methods that are not binary classifiers; and every descriptive group difference is asserted without a statistic. [RQ2.9] Retain more than six input features, since filtering may have discarded useful signal; move the model out of Azure ML Studio to permit tuning of node count, leaf count and tree depth; and expand beyond 108 participants for a more diverse and robust classifier better able to handle edge cases. [RQ3.1] Saccadic eye movement - specifically latency, accuracy (absolute error), amplitude, peak velocity, acceleration and the trial-to-trial variability of each, measured under gap and overlap conditions, together with fixation-proportion and pupil-area measures carried in the dataset. The rationale offered for targeting saccades rather than social gaze is worth noting and is not made elsewhere in this corpus in quite these terms: sensorimotor abnormalities are said to be detectable 'prior to the identification of social and cognitive deficits', so an oculomotor marker could in principle precede the social behaviours on which clinical diagnosis depends. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion - a single modality throughout, and no within-modality condition comparison is exploited either. The gap and overlap blocks are described and their latency difference noted, but the paradigm's defining contrast is never used as a feature or analysed as a group-by-condition interaction, which is the main analytic opportunity the design offers and the paper leaves unused. [RQ4.1] A Two-Class Boosted Decision Tree, selected after comparing linear regression, logistic regression, multiclass neural networks, support vector algorithms and quantile regression models within Azure ML Studio. The stated justification - that ensemble boosting suits small tabular data better than the bagging of random forests or the hierarchical structure of neural networks - is reasonable in outline, and choosing a shallow tabular model over deep learning at n = 108 is the right instinct. But no performance figure is given for any comparator, so the selection cannot be assessed, and including linear and quantile regression in a binary classification comparison indicates the model set was not well matched to the task. [RQ4.2] Nineteen tabular attributes reduced to sixteen by dropping ethnicity, blood type and eye colour, then to six by mutual-information filtering. The features arrive pre-computed, so no representation design was performed here. Two observations about the feature set are worth recording: the presence of blood type and eye colour in a saccade dataset is unexplained and suggests the source was not well understood; and dropping ethnicity as 'unrelated to tracking eye movement' removes the one variable that would have permitted any check on demographic confounding, which given the total absence of participant characteristics is a consequential deletion. [RQ4.3] Accuracy alone, at 88% in the text and 88-91% in the abstract, with a plotted ROC curve whose AUC is never stated. For a paper proposing to replace multidisciplinary diagnostic assessment with a single test, the absence of sensitivity and specificity is the critical omission - these are the quantities that determine whether such a test would be usable, and with 60% of the sample autistic, accuracy alone cannot distinguish a useful classifier from one biased toward the majority class. No confusion matrix, no confidence interval, no per-fold variability and no statistical comparison against any baseline. [RQ4.4] The mutual-information filter is presented partly as an interpretability device - it 'communicates the attributes in the dataset which have the most predictive power in the model to drive future experimentation' - and three of the six retained features are named: mean amplitude of primary saccades, absolute saccade error and latency. The other three are never identified, and no model-derived importances, tree structure or decision rules are shown despite the classifier being a decision tree ensemble, which is among the more inspectable model families. The behavioural interpretation offered is that variability rather than central tendency distinguishes the groups, but the paper twice states that the implications are unclear - 'it is uncertain what further implications it has on sensorimotor activity' and 'it is still uncertain what the connections are between these dynamics and saccade error or latency'. [RQ4.5] k-fold cross-validation with k unstated, and with supervised feature selection performed on the complete dataset before the split. The paper sets out the sequence unambiguously - pass in data, select columns, apply filter-based feature selection, then split - and reproduces the Azure workflow confirming it. Because mutual information is computed against the class labels, every fold's feature set was chosen using information from that fold's test data, which biases the reported accuracy upward by an amount that cannot be estimated from what is reported. The paper's own description of cross-validation as a method that has 'been shown to lower bias and overfitting' sits directly alongside the step that defeats it. There is no held-out test set, no independent cohort, no external validation and no repetition. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list. Vocabulary: 'saccades', 'sensorimotor activity', 'predictive machine learning model', 'novel method of diagnosis', 'shorten time, resources, and uncertainty'. The register is throughput-oriented - the claim is about reducing the professionals, resources and waiting time required for diagnosis rather than about mechanism or accuracy per se. [RQ5.2] 2020 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference (URTC) - an undergraduate research venue, which is relevant context for the depth of methodological scrutiny the work received. [RQ5.3] 2020. The framing is access and throughput: CDC prevalence of 1 in 54, an estimate of 'two undiagnosed cases for every three accurately diagnosed', and a description of comprehensive developmental evaluation as requiring 'a multidisciplinary team consisting of a psychologist, neurologist, psychiatrist, speech therapist, and may include others' conducting in-depth neurological, cognitive and language testing, with no single medical test available. Two framing points are distinctive within this corpus. First, the sex argument - girls with subtler presentations who are 'better at copying stereotypical social patterns' go undiagnosed into adulthood - correctly identifies camouflaging as a diagnostic failure mode, although the study then reports no sex data. Second, the rationale for choosing saccades over social gaze is temporal rather than practical: sensorimotor abnormalities are said to be present 'prior to the identification of social and cognitive deficits', which would make an oculomotor marker earlier-detectable in principle than the social behaviours clinical diagnosis relies on. The paper also states that saccades in autism are an under-researched area, which is broadly consistent with this corpus, where gaze studies overwhelmingly examine where people look rather than how their eyes move. |
| S-052 | Prospective intervention study with severity categorisation and no comparison group; 12 autistic children (11 male, 4.2-7.5 years, mean 6.5) at an Islamabad autism resource centre, split 8 for training (72 sessions over 9 weeks) and 4 for testing (25 sessions over 6 weeks); CARS severity categories assigned by centre clinicians; data not released. | Two modules of an existing Multi-Robot-mediated Intervention System with two NAO robots: joint attention with least-to-most escalating visual, speech and motion cues, gaze scored by the robots' cameras via ALGazeDetection; and imitation, activated only after five seconds of sustained gaze on a chosen robot, with four gross motor actions scored by Kinect skeletal tracking. Session success percentages were binned into three ordinal levels each at 50% and 80% thresholds and fed to a two-state Hidden Markov Model whose hidden states are the minimal and mild severity levels, with posteriors computed as the product of two conditional probabilities. | The model matched clinician CARS categories in 19 of 25 test sessions (76% accuracy) with Cohen's kappa 0.52 (p = 0.009), described as moderate agreement. Errors were symmetric - three false-mild and three false-minimal.
