The resulting interpretation is concrete and clinically legible: autistic children move their heads through larger angles and accumulate more rotation per minute while making the same gestures with the same frequency. The blind human coding provides an independent check on the frequency null, with Spearman reliabilities of 0.787 for nodding and 0.895 for shaking. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-out cross-validation at the participant level, correctly implemented and explicitly motivated as overfitting protection. The weakness is the search: the random feature combination approach deliberately tests every subset of the six features, and the authors justify it on the grounds that exhaustive search 'typically yields equal or higher classification accuracy simply owing to the fact that all features and feature combinations could be tested' - which is precisely the property that makes the resulting maximum optimistic. Sixty-three subsets across five classifiers gives 315 fits, all scored on the same leave-one-out estimate, with no outer loop and no held-out set. The mixed-effects feature screening also used all participants, though since all six features passed and all were retained, this contributed no additional selection. There is no independent cohort or external replication. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism, Biomarkers, Diagnosis, Head movement, Machine learning. 'Head movement' is the novel term and the paper's claim to priority - the authors state theirs is 'the first to use head movement related features to detect ASD'. [RQ5.2] Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 52, 3038-3049 - a specialist autism journal rather than an engineering venue, which is consistent with the paper's substantive engagement with the motor-atypicality literature and its careful covariate handling. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing combines diagnostic delay with a specific argument for motor markers. On delay, it cites more than a year on average between initial screening and confirmed diagnosis in the United States, and a 35-country meta-analysis giving a mean diagnosis age of 60.48 months, falling to 43.18 months among children aged ten or under. On motor markers, it assembles evidence of atypical motor function in postural control, gait stability, arm movements and gross and fine motor control, and of delayed motor development in infancy that 'could subsequently contribute to the social impairments' - so motor features are argued to be developmentally upstream of the social criteria, not merely correlated with them. It then identifies head movement specifically as documented but unexploited, citing stereotyped head rolling, shaking and banging, greater head turning displacement and velocity when viewing social stimuli, and slower and less frequent head turning in response to name. Its closing claim is notably strong: 'the current diagnostic system of ASD, which are established on behavioral evaluation of social communication and restricted and repetitive behavior, would be greatly challenged' by combining features across neuroimaging, eye tracking, EEG and motion capture. |
| S-065 | Secondary computational analysis of a publicly released scanpath image dataset; 547 images (219 autistic, 328 non-autistic) from 59 French children aged approximately 3-13, 64% male, with diagnosis conveyed only as CARS severity classification; no new data collected. | Images were converted to greyscale, brightened and resized to 128 x 128, then partitioned by k-means into four clusters fitted on the full image set; decision tree, gradient boosting, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression, multilayer perceptron, naive Bayes, random forest, SVM and XGBoost were each applied to every cluster and to the pooled data under ten-fold cross-validation over images, with accuracy, AUC, F-measure, G-mean, sensitivity, specificity, fall-out and miss rate reported for all 45 combinations. | Best result 88.89% accuracy with a multilayer perceptron in cluster 1 (AUC 0.792, sensitivity 88.9%, specificity 69.4%), against 74.2% for random forest on the pooled dataset. Remaining clusters reached 70.7%, 75.8% and 77.8%. Several cells are near-degenerate, with naive Bayes and SVM in cluster 1 both returning 73.3% accuracy at 26.7% specificity and exactly 0.500 AUC. | Ten-fold cross-validation operates over 547 images from 59 children with no statement that a child's images were kept together, reproducing the configuration that the dataset's originating study showed inflates accuracy by roughly 19 points on these exact images; k-means clustering was fitted on the full image set including test images, so the partition producing the headline improvement is not independent of the evaluation; the reported figure is the best of 45 cells with no multiplicity correction or confidence intervals; the abstract and table disagree (87% versus 88.89%); cluster composition and participant-to-cluster mapping are never reported; raw pixel vectors are a poor representation for the classifiers used; and no limitations, behavioural interpretation or cluster characterisation is offered. | Valuable to the review mainly as a documented instance of what happens when an openly released dataset is reanalysed without the validation discipline its originators applied. The source study released these images to serve as a benchmark and reported both configurations - approximately 90% pooling scanpath images and approximately 71% holding out participants, at 9.27 images per child. This reanalysis runs ten-fold cross-validation over the images without that correction and reports a pooled best of 74.2% and a within-cluster best of 88.89%. The pairing of the two papers therefore gives the synthesis a clean illustration that open data does not by itself propagate methodological standards, and that a benchmark released with a caveat can be reused without it. The paper's one substantive observation is candid and worth carrying forward: that 'these scanpath images were almost similar for normal and autistic children', a plain statement that the raw visual separation between groups is small. | [RQ1.1] Two groups inherited from the source dataset: 30 autistic and 29 non-autistic children, contributing 219 and 328 scanpath images respectively. The analysis operates on images rather than children throughout, and the 59 participants are never treated as the unit of anything. Following k-means partitioning, the effective analysis units become four image clusters of unstated composition - the paper does not report how many images, or how many children, fall in each cluster, nor the class balance within them, which makes the per-cluster metrics difficult to interpret. [RQ1.2] 'autistic children', 'ASD children', 'normal children', 'ASD patients', 'control instances'. The comparison group is 'normal' and autistic children are described as showing 'an unbearable social attitudes and unable to present regular physiological responses' - phrasing that is both pathologising and unclear. Autism is characterised in the abstract as 'reducing concentration on social activities and improving interest in non-social tasks', which restates a contested empirical claim as a definition. [RQ1.3] Reported entirely at second hand and only for the whole sample: 59 participants, 38 male (64%) and 21 female (36%), aged approximately 3 to 13 years, recruited from schools in the Hauts-de-France region. No group-wise ages, sexes, means or standard deviations appear, and no matching is discussed. The source study reports mean ages of 7 years 7 months and 8 years 0 months by group, so the information exists but is not carried over. [RQ1.4] Inherited and incompletely transmitted. The paper states only that 'the severity of autism were classified by the psychologists using the Childhood Autism Rating Scale' - describing a severity instrument rather than a diagnostic procedure. The source study reports diagnosis confirmed by health professionals using ADI-R and ADOS-G in multidisciplinary clinics, which is stronger ascertainment than this paper conveys. Non-autistic status is not described at all. [RQ1.5] None used. CARS is mentioned as having been applied in the source study but no scores are reported, no severity stratification is performed, and no cognitive, language or adaptive measures appear. Since the source dataset's accompanying publication reports CARS and ECSP scores, the omission is a choice of this reanalysis rather than a constraint of the data. [RQ2.1] Goal: improve classification on an existing scanpath image dataset by clustering it first into more homogeneous subgroups. Main findings: best accuracy of 88.89% with a multilayer perceptron in cluster 1, against 74.2% for the best classifier on the pooled dataset; the other three clusters reached 70.7%, 75.8% and 77.8%; and the authors conclude that clustering produced groups in which classes were more separable. [RQ2.2] No data collection. The source data were gathered from schools in Hauts-de-France; all analysis here was performed in Google Colaboratory using scikit-learn, by authors at institutions in Bangladesh and Australia. [RQ2.3] Not described. The paper does not report what the children were looking at, how long the stimuli lasted, or how scanpaths were rendered into images - all of which are documented in the source publication and all of which bear on what the classifiers are learning. A reader of this paper alone cannot tell whether the images encode gaze position only or, as in the source, gaze velocity through colour gradient. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis of publicly released images. No ethics statement appears, which is largely defensible for reuse of open data, though the paper does not discuss the terms of that reuse. The Figshare repository is cited with its URL, and the originating study is credited. [RQ2.5] scikit-learn in Python on Google Colaboratory. No hardware, hyperparameters, random seeds or software versions are reported. [RQ2.6] Poor for a computational paper. Reported: the source dataset with its repository link and originating citation, the preprocessing chain (greyscale, brightness increase, resize to 128 x 128), the number of clusters, the nine classifier names, ten-fold cross-validation, the eight evaluation metrics, and a complete 45-row results table. The k-means algorithm is set out in full mathematical detail, which is unnecessary for a standard method. Not reported: how many images or children fall in each cluster and their class balance; any hyperparameter for any classifier; the random seed; the rationale for choosing four clusters; whether images from a child were kept together; and any code. The mathematical exposition of k-means occupies more space than the entire account of how the classifiers were configured. [RQ2.7] None. There is no limitations section and no caveat on sample size, validation design, cluster interpretation or generalisability. Identifiable in review: ten-fold cross-validation operates over 547 images from 59 children with no statement that a child's images were confined to one fold, and the source study demonstrated on these same images that participant-level splitting reduces accuracy from approximately 90% to approximately 71%; k-means clustering was performed on the full image set before classification, so cluster membership was determined using test images; the headline is the best of 45 cluster-by-classifier cells with no multiplicity correction or confidence intervals; the abstract quotes 87% against the table's 88.89%; several reported cells are near-degenerate single-class predictors that are not flagged; and no clinical or behavioural interpretation of any result is offered. [RQ2.9] None stated. [RQ3.1] Inherited from the source dataset: visual scanning behaviour rendered as a spatial trace. This paper adds no behavioural analysis of its own and does not characterise the target behaviour beyond the assertion in its introduction that autistic children show reduced attention to social content. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion. The only combination performed is unsupervised partitioning followed by supervised classification, which is a pipeline rather than a fusion. The result - higher accuracy within one cluster than on the pooled data - is presented as evidence that clustering helps, but no cluster is characterised, no analysis explains what makes cluster 1 different, and the improvement is a maximum over 36 cluster-by-classifier combinations, so it cannot be distinguished from selection across the grid. [RQ4.1] Nine classifiers spanning trees, ensembles, kernel methods, neural networks and probabilistic models, applied uniformly across all five datasets. Breadth is the only principle - no rationale is given for any individual choice, no hyperparameters are reported, and the winning algorithm differs by cluster (multilayer perceptron in cluster 1, random forest in clusters 3 and 4, three classifiers tied in cluster 2), which at these sample sizes is consistent with noise rather than with any property of the clusters. [RQ4.2] Raw 128 x 128 greyscale pixels with brightness increased - 16,384 features per image, with no engineered representation, no dimensionality reduction and no convolutional structure. Applying classifiers such as naive Bayes, k-nearest neighbours and logistic regression directly to raw pixels of spatially structured images is a poor match of method to data, and is likely why the pooled results plateau around 74%: none of these models can exploit spatial locality. The source study used a convolutional network on the same images for exactly this reason. [RQ4.3] Eight metrics for all nine classifiers on all five datasets, which is comprehensive in coverage and is the paper's strongest feature. Reporting specificity and fall-out alongside sensitivity is what makes the degenerate cells visible: in cluster 1, naive Bayes and SVM both show 73.3% accuracy with 26.7% specificity and exactly 0.500 AUC, and the best model itself pairs 88.9% sensitivity with only 69.4% specificity. Missing: confidence intervals, confusion matrices, cluster composition, and any statistical comparison - so whether 88.89% differs meaningfully from 77.8% is not established. [RQ4.4] None. No feature importance, no saliency, no cluster characterisation and no behavioural interpretation. The paper does not state what the four clusters correspond to - whether they separate stimulus types, participants, image quality or something else - which leaves its central claim uninterpretable: the reader cannot tell whether clustering identified clinically meaningful subgroups or simply partitioned the images in a way that happened to make one subset easier. Given that images from the same child are visually similar, one plausible explanation is that clusters partly track individual participants, which would make the within-cluster accuracy gain a direct consequence of increased within-fold similarity. [RQ4.5] The decisive weakness, and unusually well documented because the source study performed the missing check. Ten-fold cross-validation is applied over 547 scanpath images drawn from 59 children, with no statement that a child's images were confined to a single fold. The study that released these images ran both configurations and reported approximately 90% accuracy pooling images against approximately 71% holding out participants - so the inflation attributable to image-level splitting on this exact dataset is known and is roughly 19 points. This reanalysis does not repeat that check. Separately, k-means clustering used the entire image set, so the partition determining each model's training and test pool was fitted on data including the test images. There is no held-out set, no participant-level analysis, no confidence intervals and no independent cohort. [RQ5.1] Index terms: ASD, Eye Tracking, K-Means Clustering, Classifier, Machine Learning. Three of five name generic methods, which reflects a paper whose contribution is a pipeline applied to someone else's data. [RQ5.2] 2021 2nd International Conference on Robotics, Electrical and Signal Processing Techniques (ICREST), pages 383-387 - a general engineering conference with no clinical or autism-specific remit. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is brief and largely a literature enumeration, cataloguing prior eye-tracking autism work including the source dataset's own publications, web-page gaze studies, video-based screening paradigms, geometric-preference subtyping and autism risk indices. Its stated motivation is that 'there are needed a elaborated work that can explore significant factors of eye-signs for detecting autism', though the analysis performed does not in fact explore any factors. Its most interesting incidental observation is the honest one that motivates the clustering: 'these scanpath images were almost similar for normal and autistic children', which is a candid statement that the raw visual difference between groups is small - consistent with the source study's finding that participant-level accuracy sits near 71%. |
| S-066 | Cross-sectional case-control combining group comparison, severity correlation and single-subject classification; 26 Italian preschoolers - 13 autistic (66.2 +/- 11.6 months, 5 female, ADOS 8-23, four with comorbid language disorder and one with epilepsy) from an outpatient neurodevelopmental clinic and 13 typically developing (60.1 +/- 9.5 months, 9 female, ADOS 0-3) from a kindergarten, age-matched by t-test; 40 reaching-grasping trials per child on three-camera optoelectronic capture at 200 Hz; data not released. | Children reached for and grasped a felt-tip pen in one of four orientations to complete a printed figure; eleven markers defined a five-segment, nine-joint-angle upper-limb model, with trial-wise PCA applied to time-normalised and z-scored angular displacements to extract variance accounted for by the first three components as a motor synergy index; mixed-effects ANOVA compared groups on movement time, relative time to peak velocity, trajectory-length variability and synergy, with permutation confirmation for non-normal measures; Spearman correlations related each measure to ADOS total within the autistic group; and an RBF support vector machine on 17 trial-level features was evaluated by leave-one-subject-out with training-fold normalisation and per-iteration grid search. | Autistic children moved faster (743.7 versus 839.5 ms, p = 0.008), showed larger relative time to peak velocity (0.503 versus 0.463, p = 0.031), greater trajectory-length variability (45.96 versus 34.22 mm, p = 0.0034) and lower cumulative variance accounted for by three components (97.53% versus 98.20%, p = 0.009). Only the synergy measure correlated with ADOS total (rho = -0.650, p = 0.016); movement time, velocity-profile symmetry and spatial variability did not. Classification gave trial-level accuracy 0.739 and subject-level AUC 0.947 with sensitivity 0.846 and specificity 0.923 at the optimal operating point, with five of 26 children classified below 0.6. | Thirteen children per group, acknowledged as insufficient for autism's heterogeneity; sex imbalanced at 38% versus 69% female, tabulated but never tested or discussed; no IQ or cognitive measures, which the authors name as a priority given intellectual disability's known impact on motor planning; the severity correlation rests on 13 observations with a visibly influential high-ADOS point; the abstract reports the subject-level AUC of 0.947 as classification accuracy when trial-level accuracy is 0.739; sensitivity and specificity are taken at an operating point optimised on the evaluation ROC; no other-diagnosis comparison group; and no data or code release. | The corpus's clearest example of classification serving a mechanistic question rather than replacing one. It proposes a specific substrate for autistic motor difficulty - weakened co-control of redundant degrees of freedom, measured as the variance three principal components absorb across nine joint angles - and supplies the evidence that distinguishes mechanism from epiphenomenon: only the synergy index correlates with ADOS severity, while movement speed, velocity-profile shape and endpoint variability do not. Its explicit criticism that standardised assessments in this literature 'are often only used to assign group labels', preventing any understanding of how motor differences relate to symptom heterogeneity, applies to most of the corpus and should inform the synthesis. Methodologically it also sets several benchmarks: ADOS administered to both groups with individual scores published, per-participant tabulation of diagnosis subtype, comorbidity and handedness, leave-one-subject-out with normalisation and hyperparameter search confined to training folds, permutation confirmation of non-normal results, per-child accuracy distributions rather than means alone, and robustness analyses framed around the concrete constraint that autistic children may not tolerate a full marker set. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of 13 children each. The autistic group spans three ICD-10 diagnoses - six with F84.9 pervasive developmental disorder unspecified, six with F84.0 autistic disorder and one with F84.5 Asperger syndrome - and includes four children with comorbid mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and one with epilepsy, all reported per participant rather than excluded. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the authors identify developmental coordination disorder and ADHD as necessary additions for establishing whether the motor finding is autism-specific or shared across neurodevelopmental conditions. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'typically developing (TD) children', 'neurotypical subjects', 'participants with ASD'. Consistently person-first with 'neurotypical' used for the general comparison. The framing is developmental and mechanistic rather than deficit-cataloguing - autism's heterogeneity is described at length, aetiology is acknowledged as 'far from being understood', and the theoretical argument runs from low-order sensorimotor processing upward to social cognition rather than treating social impairment as primary. [RQ1.3] Autistic group: 13 children, 8 male and 5 female, aged 44-82 months, mean 66.23 +/- 11.56. Typically developing group: 13 children, 4 male and 9 female, aged 43-71 months, mean 60.08 +/- 9.54. Age matching is formally tested and confirmed (t(24) = 1.480, p = 0.152). Sex is not: 38% female against 69% female, an inversion of the usual direction, reported per participant but never tested or mentioned. Handedness was assessed behaviourally by asking children to draw and confirmed by caregivers or clinicians, with two left-handed children and two of unclear handedness, and left-hand trials from three autistic children were discarded because markers could not be placed on their left arms due to compliance problems. Per-participant ADOS totals, modules, ages, sexes, ICD-10 codes, comorbidities and handedness are all tabulated - the most complete individual-level characterisation in the corpus. No IQ or cognitive measures, which the authors name as a limitation. [RQ1.4] Diagnosis by an experienced clinician under both ICD-10 and DSM-5, with specific ICD-10 subcodes reported per child. ADOS was then administered to every participant in both groups, with autistic children meeting the diagnostic cut-off and typically developing children scoring below it - ten of the thirteen scored zero, and the highest comparison score was 3. Applying the gold-standard instrument to both groups and publishing individual scores is stronger practice than almost anything else in the corpus. The authors also report ADOS's own published operating characteristics (sensitivity 0.94, specificity 0.80 across 12 studies) and use them as the benchmark against which to judge their classifier. [RQ1.5] ADOS total scores individually reported for all 26 participants with the module used, plus ICD-10 diagnostic subtype and comorbid diagnoses per child. Severity is used analytically rather than descriptively - correlated against all four kinematic outcomes - which is what produces the paper's key dissociation. The acknowledged gap is intellectual functioning: no IQ or developmental level was measured, and the authors state that future research 'will have to evaluate intellectual disability, which is an important source of inter-subject variability in ASD that seems to impact motor planning and coordination'. [RQ2.1] Goal: test whether motor synergies - the co-control of redundant degrees of freedom - are impaired in autism, and relate this to symptom severity. Main findings: autistic children moved faster with more symmetrical velocity profiles, showed greater trial-to-trial spatial variability, and showed significantly reduced variance accounted for by the first three principal components across nine joint angles; only the synergy measure correlated with ADOS severity (rho = -0.650, p = 0.016); and leave-one-subject-out SVM classification reached AUC 0.947 with 0.846 sensitivity and 0.923 specificity at the optimal operating point, on trial-level accuracy of 0.739. [RQ2.2] Laboratory motion capture at the University of Ferrara and the Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia's Center for Translational Neurophysiology of Speech and Communication, with autistic children recruited from a local outpatient neurodevelopmental clinic and comparison children from a local kindergarten. Funded by two Italian Ministry of Health young-researcher grants and an EU H2020 project. No competing interests declared. [RQ2.3] Reaching for and grasping a felt-tip pen to complete a printed figure - a task chosen because it is ecological and needs no explanation to a preschooler, with pen orientation varied across four positions specifically to prevent stereotyped movement. Forty trials per child across eight blocks in two sessions, with block order randomised and free choice of hand and grip. The design decisions are all in service of the mechanistic question: enough trials to estimate trial-to-trial variability and to fit trial-wise PCA, enough orientation variation to require genuine motor parameter selection rather than a rehearsed movement, and enough naturalness that task comprehension is not a confound. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; two sessions per child with no follow-up. Data are numeric marker trajectories, with per-participant clinical data published in tabular form but no identifiers. Governance is complete: written informed consent from parents or legal guardians, Helsinki-compliant design, and local ethical committee approval with a full reference number. [RQ2.5] Qualisys optoelectronic motion capture with three infrared cameras at 200 Hz - the highest-fidelity motion measurement in the corpus - with ten passive markers on the upper limbs and one on the sternum, low-pass filtered at 10 Hz with a third-order Butterworth filter. Marker labelling was verified by offline visual inspection, and the movement onset and offset criteria were themselves validated by visual inspection of individual trials. The robustness analysis using only the ulnar marker is a direct response to the practical constraint that autistic children may not tolerate a full marker set. [RQ2.6] Excellent. Reported: task geometry with all distances, stimulus dimensions, block structure and randomisation; camera count, sampling rate, filter type and cutoff; marker placement anatomy; the five-segment kinematic model with all nine joint angles and their derivation including the pronosupination computation; movement onset and offset criteria with their thresholds and durations; PCA preprocessing including time-normalisation to 200 points and per-trial z-scoring with its stated rationale; the justification for retaining three components; the full ANOVA model with both factors; permutation testing for non-normal outcomes with iteration count; all 17 classifier features defined individually in a table; the SVM kernel and full hyperparameter grid; the leave-one-subject-out procedure including how normalisation was applied across the split; and per-participant clinical data. Supplementary material covers pronosupination derivation, trial-count robustness, feature-restricted robustness and per-participant feature importance. Missing only: data or code release, and IQ measures. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged: the sample was 'relatively small and likely not able to capture the full heterogeneity of ASD'; intellectual disability was not measured despite being a known source of variability affecting motor planning and coordination; and only autism and typical development were contrasted, whereas motor difficulties occur across neurodevelopmental disorders so additional diagnostic classes would 'facilitate a dimensional acknowledgment of atypical development'. Practical constraints are also disclosed, including that left-arm markers could not be placed on three autistic children due to compliance problems. Not acknowledged: the abstract reports 0.947 as classification accuracy when it is the subject-level AUC, with trial-level accuracy being 0.739; the sensitivity and specificity are taken at an operating point optimised on the same ROC used to characterise performance; the sex imbalance of 38% versus 69% female is tabulated but never tested or discussed; and the severity correlation rests on 13 observations with a visibly influential high-ADOS point. [RQ2.9] Measure intellectual disability as a source of inter-subject variability affecting motor planning and coordination; include developmental coordination disorder and ADHD comparison groups to test whether impaired synergies represent 'a common pathogenetic mechanism for these conditions' rather than an autism-specific marker; and extend the synergy framework to speech and language, on the argument that 'speech and language coordination share key similarity with upper limb action' and that language difficulties are common in autism. [RQ3.1] Upper-limb reaching and grasping, analysed at two levels. Conventional kinematics capture the surface properties of movement - speed, velocity-profile shape, endpoint variability. The synergy analysis captures something different in kind: how tightly the nine joint angles covary, indexed by how much of their joint variance three principal components can absorb. That second level is the paper's contribution, and it targets a construct - co-control of redundant degrees of freedom - that no other study in this corpus measures. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion. What the study combines is levels of description within a single modality, and it does so to informative effect: the 17 classifier features include both conventional kinematics and the three synergy measures, and the per-participant feature importance analysis finds that spatial displacement measures and the cumulative variance accounted for by three components both contribute. The authors note that this 'substantially confirmed the results obtained with univariate statistics', so the classifier's internal weighting agrees with the group-level analysis - a convergence that few studies in the corpus check and that here supports treating the classification as reflecting the same phenomenon as the hypothesis test rather than an unrelated pattern. [RQ4.1] A single radial-basis-function SVM with hyperparameters grid-searched at each leave-one-subject-out iteration. No model comparison is reported, which is appropriate given that classification is explicitly secondary to the mechanistic question and the paper makes no claim about optimal architecture. The design decision that matters is aggregation: the classifier operates on trials, and subject-level inference is obtained by taking each participant's proportion of positive trial responses as an estimate of diagnosis probability, from which the ROC is built. [RQ4.2] Seventeen trial-level features, each defined explicitly in a table, spanning movement timing, peak dynamics and their relative timing, spatial displacement at both peak velocity and movement offset, trajectory length, and the three cumulative variance-accounted-for measures. The representation is compact, physically interpretable and includes the theoretically motivated coordination variables alongside the descriptive ones. The PCA preprocessing is carefully specified - trial-wise application after time-normalisation to 200 points and per-trial z-scoring, the latter adopted specifically to account for the differing ranges of motion across joints, with the choice of three components justified by reference to prior work on three-dimensional movement. [RQ4.3] Trial-level accuracy reported as a mean and in bands across participants, plus a subject-level ROC with AUC and the sensitivity and specificity at its optimal operating point. Reporting the distribution of per-child accuracy rather than only the mean is valuable - it shows five of 26 children classified below 0.6, which a summary figure would hide. The weakness is presentational: the abstract's 'classification accuracy reached up to 0.947' conflates AUC with accuracy, no subject-level accuracy is given directly, and the operating point yielding 0.846 sensitivity and 0.923 specificity is selected on the same curve. Comparison against ADOS's own published sensitivity and specificity is a useful external anchor that few studies provide. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is the paper's organising purpose. Every feature is a physical quantity with a motor-control meaning, the group differences are reported with effect directions and interpreted against specific literatures on feedforward versus feedback control, and the synergy result is developed into an explicit mechanistic account - that impaired co-control forces either learning motor commands for each degree of freedom separately, which is prohibitively slow, or mapping each behavioural goal to a whole set of muscle activations, which prevents generalisation, with either extreme producing the idiosyncratic and fragmented motor strategies observed clinically. The correlation analysis then provides the discriminating evidence, showing that only the synergy measure tracks severity. Per-participant feature importance is computed and reported, and the authors verify that it agrees with the univariate findings. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-subject-out, correctly implemented and explicitly motivated as simulating 'the diagnosis of a new patient in everyday life clinical settings'. Normalisation is fitted on training folds and applied to test data using training statistics, and hyperparameters are grid-searched at each iteration rather than fixed globally. Two robustness analyses extend the validation usefully - varying the number of trials available in the test set, and restricting features to those derivable from the ulnar marker alone - both framed around deployment constraints rather than as statistical exercises. The residual issues are that the ROC operating point is chosen on the evaluation curve, and that no independent cohort or external site is tested, which the small sample precludes. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism spectrum disorder, Motor synergies, Machine learning, Kinematics, Early diagnosis, Neurodevelopmental disorders. 'Motor synergies' is the novel term and the paper's claim - the authors state their result indicates 'for the first time, that motor synergies are impaired in ASD'. [RQ5.2] Cognition, 213, article 104652, published open access in a special issue honouring the journal's founding editor - a cognitive science venue rather than a clinical or engineering one, which explains the depth of theoretical development relative to the modelling. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is developmental and causal rather than diagnostic-efficiency driven. It argues that 'low-order impairments of sensory processing and motor coding during the early stages of life may impact the acquisition of more complex abilities, including socio-communicative skills and cognitive functions', and assembles evidence of pervasive sensorimotor impairment across posture, balance, gait, aiming movements, eye-hand coordination, force control and handwriting - proposing that these 'scattered disturbances presumably arise from a limited number of common dysfunctional mechanisms'. Its most distinctive contribution to the corpus's framing is a methodological criticism aimed at its own field: that standardised symptom assessments 'are often only used to assign group labels (i.e. ASD vs. neurotypical)', and that 'this approach has prevented understanding the impact of motor differences in the heterogeneous expression of ASD symptoms'. The paper then acts on that criticism by correlating every kinematic measure against ADOS totals within the autistic group, which is what yields its central dissociation. |
| S-067 | Single-arm clinical pilot and longitudinal intervention study conducted at an autism rehabilitation centre in Al Ain, United Arab Emirates, by a group at UAE University with Al Ain Hospital and collaborators in Japan, Australia and Malaysia. Eleven autistic boys took part, all with CARS2 scores of 30-36.5 indicating mild to moderate severity, all under 16 years with a mean age of 9.03 years (SD 2.56), and all required to understand verbal communication and respond at least with yes or no. Six of the eleven continued into the long-term study; no reason is given for the other five. There is no comparison group. The study was approved by the Social Sciences Research Ethical Committee of UAE University and by Al Ain Hospital, with signed parental consent letters. | A NAO humanoid robot was fitted with a purpose-designed chest mount holding a mobile phone that displayed facial expressions through an Emotions Selector application, with the mount engineered so that the added mass 'barely affects the center of mass of the robot body' and the robot's balance and built-in behaviours were preserved. The phone camera was configured as an IP camera. Children took part in a semi-autonomous adaptive interaction scenario of 13 sections presenting emotional cues and soliciting emotional responses, with the scenario adapting across sessions according to each child's attention score history. An attention score was accumulated in real time at approximately 1 Hz from three rule-based components: Haar cascade face detection incrementing the score by 5 when the child faced the robot and decrementing it by 1 when not; joint attention detected through left or right ear detection, with a head turn matching the robot's directed gaze incrementing the score by 15; and a sound-response increment computed from speech-onset latency by a fixed linear formula. All increments are operator-adjustable per patient. No model was trained and no data were fitted at any point. The system's session-level attention trend was compared against the treating therapist's 0-100 attention ratings across 34 sessions. | The automated attention score agreed with the therapist's assessment on 28 of 34 sessions, giving 82.4%, described in the conclusion as 'matching over 80% of therapist assessments'. Across a seven-week course of sessions, attention scores rose in most of the six children who continued, which the authors present as support for their stated hypothesis that 'a properly designed robot intervention system can increase the attention levels' of autistic children. No autism classification is attempted and no diagnostic metric is reported. | There is no comparison group and no control condition, so the seven-week rise in attention scores cannot be separated from familiarisation with a novel robot, practice on a repeated task, maturation or the attention of participating in a study - and every component of the score rewards orienting toward and responding to the robot, so all of these would raise it. Attrition is substantial and unexplained: 5 of 11 children did not continue, and if disengagement drove that then the trajectory is computed on a self-selected subgroup already engaging. The 82.4% agreement is an uncorrected proportion over 34 sessions clustered within 6 children, with no adjustment for clustering, no chance-corrected statistic such as Cohen's kappa, and no confidence interval; and no reliability estimate exists for the therapist ratings serving as the standard, so the achievable ceiling is unknown and a measure agreeing at this level could be tracking one particular therapist rather than the construct. The scoring constants are operator-adjustable per child, so scores are not comparable across children and agreement may partly reflect tuning. Equating a Haar-detected face with attending is a strong assumption for a child who may attend without orienting. And the population is male, mild to moderate and verbally capable, despite the abstract describing the target group as having minimal verbal capabilities. | Contributes to the review as its only closed-loop system and one of its very few longitudinal ones. The automated attention measure does not terminate in a classification: it feeds back into the interaction scenario, which adapts across sessions to each child's score history, so measurement serves the intervention directly. Nothing else in the corpus implements that loop, and it reframes what behavioural computation is for - the paper's stated problem is not detection but the cost of repeated assessment during therapy, with the argument that if assessment could be repeated frequently enough to trace symptom development, therapists could adapt treatment and families would be better sustained through long courses. The study also demonstrates how much is achievable without any learned model: three transparent rules with stated constants, running at 1 Hz on a camera mounted to the robot the child is attending to, agreeing with the treating therapist on 28 of 34 sessions. Every score is readable and adjustable by the clinician using it, which is the opposite design point from the deep models charted throughout this review and a defensible trade for a system running inside a live session. Its evidential limits should be stated plainly: no comparison group and no control condition for the intervention claim, unexplained attrition of 5 of 11 children, an uncorrected agreement statistic over sessions clustered within six children, a validation standard of unknown reliability, and a narrow population. The authors' own restraint is notable - the causal claim is labelled a hypothesis rather than a conclusion, the system is positioned as a tool for therapists rather than a diagnostic instrument, and a practical failure encountered during the study (children handling the chest display, depressing scores) is reported along with its fix. | [RQ1.1] Eleven autistic boys recruited from Al Ain Hospital in the United Arab Emirates, all with CARS2 scores between 30 and 36.5 - the mild-to-moderate band - under 16 years of age with a mean of 9.03 years (SD 2.56), and all required to have at least minimal verbal capability, being able to understand verbal communication and answer yes or no. Six of the eleven continued into the long-term study, with no explanation given for the other five. There is no comparison group of any kind, which is consistent with the design: the study measures attention within an intervention rather than discriminating between populations. Two features of the sample are worth recording for the review. Reporting a CARS2 range as an eligibility criterion is more severity characterisation than most included studies provide, and it bounds the population precisely - but because only the range is given rather than per-child scores, within-sample severity variation cannot be related to any outcome. And the eligibility requirements taken together - male, mild to moderate, verbally responsive - define a narrow population, so the system's behaviour with non-speaking or more severely affected children is untested despite the abstract describing the target group as having 'minimal verbal capabilities'. [RQ1.2] Predominantly medical, with 'ASD patients' used throughout and 'recovery progress' appearing in the discussion of what current systems cannot track - a framing that treats autism as something one recovers from. Against this, the introduction opens with a genuinely thoughtful question about what social robots are for, asking whether robots might help people 'establish richer relationships with other humans, fulfilling their inherent empathic potential', and framing the issue as most pressing for 'individuals who are prevented by clinical factors from establishing typical social relations with others'. The clinical reasoning is also person-centred in a practical way: the authors note that assessment is usually done at enrolment and repeated occasionally, that more frequent assessment would let therapists adapt treatment and would help 'patients and their parents ... be better motivated to withstand long, repetitive therapy sessions', and that success depends on knowing which stimuli hold a particular child's attention. That is an argument for measurement in service of individualised therapy rather than for classification, and it is why the study has no diagnostic target. No autistic person is reported as involved in the design. [RQ1.3] Age is reported as a mean with standard deviation and severity as a CARS2 eligibility range, both of which exceed the corpus norm. Sex is not a variable, since all eleven participants are male. What is absent is cognitive and language measurement: the verbal-response criterion is a functional floor rather than an assessed level, so the children's language ability is bounded below and not otherwise characterised, and no IQ, adaptive or developmental measure was obtained. Since the outcome is attention during a verbally mediated robot interaction, and the sound-response component of the score is a speech-latency measure, language ability is directly implicated in the measurement and is unmeasured. No socioeconomic, ancestry or comorbidity information is reported. [RQ1.4] Clinical diagnosis established through the recruiting hospital, with severity quantified by CARS2 and reported as a 30-36.5 range for all participants. This is genuine clinical ascertainment, and specifying the severity band is a real strength - it makes the population interpretable in a way that a bare 'diagnosed with ASD' does not, and it bounds the claims to children with mild-to-moderate presentation. What is not reported is the instrument set beyond CARS2, the assessors, or the dates. Because the study makes no diagnostic claim, the reference standard's role here is to define the population rather than to serve as a target, and for that purpose it is adequate. [RQ1.5] CARS2 is used as an eligibility range rather than as a per-child variable, so no severity gradient is available for analysis - a missed opportunity, since relating attention trajectories to baseline severity across six children in a seven-week course would have been the natural individualisation question and the data existed to ask it. The study's own outcome measure, the automated attention score, functions as a repeated within-child measure and is used that way: its whole design rationale is that assessment could be 'repeated more frequently to trace the severity and development of symptoms'. That is a severity-tracking argument, and it is the clearest statement in this review of why continuous behavioural measurement might matter clinically for reasons other than diagnosis. [RQ2.1] The aim is a robot-mediated therapy and assessment system that measures a child's attention automatically, adapts its own interaction scenario to that measurement, and thereby increases engagement over a course of sessions. Two results are reported. The automated attention score agreed with the treating therapist's assessment on 28 of 34 sessions, giving 82.4%, which the conclusion describes accurately as 'matching over 80% of therapist assessments'. And attention scores rose across a seven-week course in most of the six children who continued, from which the authors draw an explicitly hypothetical conclusion - 'our hypothesis is that a properly designed robot intervention system can increase the attention levels'. Neither claim concerns autism detection: all participants are autistic, there is no comparison group, and no classification is attempted. For this review the study contributes a different kind of evidence - a demonstration that an automated behavioural measure can track a clinician's judgement of the same construct well enough to be usable in a therapy loop, which is the closed-loop application that most of the corpus's detection-oriented work does not consider. [RQ2.2] An autism rehabilitation centre, with participants recruited from Al Ain Hospital - a clinical service setting, and the same setting in which the system would be deployed. That alignment between study setting and intended use setting is shared by only a few studies in this review. The clinical framing is specific: the authors note that assessment is typically performed at enrolment and repeated during long-term therapy, and that if it 'could be repeated more frequently to trace the severity and development of symptoms, then therapists could implement more efficacious diagnostic and therapeutic options' - so the setting defines the problem, which is the cost in expert time of repeated assessment. [RQ2.3] A semi-autonomous adaptive scenario in 13 sections, delivered by a NAO robot with a mobile phone mounted on a purpose-built chest holder that displays facial expressions through an Emotions Selector application, presenting emotional cues and soliciting emotional responses. The paradigm's distinctive property is that it is closed-loop: the scenario adapts across sessions according to each child's attention score history, so the measurement feeds back into the intervention. No other study in this review implements that loop - the rest measure behaviour and stop. The engineering description is also careful in a way that matters practically: the chest mount was designed so that the added weight 'barely affects the center of mass of the robot body, hence the changes in the moment of inertia are negligible', preserving the robot's balance and its built-in interactive behaviours, which is the kind of detail that determines whether a modified platform actually works in a clinic. What is not reported is the session duration or the content of the 13 sections, so the paradigm cannot be reproduced from the paper. [RQ2.4] Longitudinal in design - a seven-week course of sessions per child, with 34 sessions contributing to the agreement analysis - which distinguishes it from the almost uniformly cross-sectional remainder of this review. Repeated measurement within children is the study's methodological point rather than an incidental feature. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the Social Sciences Research Ethical Committee of UAE University and by Al Ain Hospital, with signed parental consent letters. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text. Attrition is substantial and unexplained: 6 of 11 children completed the long-term study. [RQ2.5] An Aldebaran/SoftBank NAO robot with a custom-designed chest mount holding a mobile phone, the phone camera configured as an IP camera through a mobile application, and Haar cascade classifiers performing face and ear detection at approximately 1 Hz. The design point worth recording is that the sensing is the robot's own - the camera that measures the child is mounted on the thing the child is attending to - so the measurement apparatus and the social stimulus are the same object. That is more elegant than the arrangements charted elsewhere in this review, where a separate camera observes a child interacting with something else, and it means the face-detection geometry directly encodes orientation toward the robot. The cost is that the measure is only as good as the assumption behind it, and a low-frame-rate Haar cascade detecting a face is a coarse proxy for attending. [RQ2.6] Strong on the system and incomplete on the study. Reported: eligibility criteria including the CARS2 band and the verbal-response requirement, mean age with standard deviation, recruitment site, both ethics approvals, the parental consent procedure, the robot and the custom chest-mount with its mass-distribution justification, the phone-as-IP-camera configuration, the detector types, all three scoring rules with their exact constants (+5, -1, +15 and a linear latency function), the 1 Hz update rate, the 13-section scenario structure, the adaptive personalisation mechanism, the number of sessions in the agreement analysis and the exact number of mismatches, and a practical failure mode with its fix. Not reported: session duration, the content of the 13 sections, why 5 of 11 children did not continue, the therapist rating procedure and its reliability, funding and competing interests. A reader could rebuild the scoring system and could not reproduce the study. [RQ2.7] The introduction contains an unusually clear analysis of the field's constraints, which functions as a limitations discussion of the wider literature: most preprogrammed robot systems 'have fixed behavior (i.e., they are unable to autonomously perform adaptable closed-loop interactions), are not tailored to the individual needs of patients, and cannot keep track of their recovery progress', while adaptive systems 'need high-performance hardware, such as GPUs chips, to process real-time data' and 'are not yet reliable outside controlled research' settings. The discussion reports a practical failure - children handling the chest display in early sessions, depressing scores, addressed by fixing the display - and the causal claim about attention improvement is labelled a hypothesis. What is not addressed: there is no control condition, so the seven-week rise in attention scores cannot be separated from familiarisation with the robot, task practice, maturation or study attention, and the score's own components would be expected to rise as a child grows comfortable with the apparatus. Attrition of 5 of 11 children is unexplained, and if disengagement drove it then the trend is computed on the children who were already engaging. The 82.4% agreement is computed over sessions clustered within children with no adjustment, no chance-corrected statistic and no confidence interval, and no reliability estimate exists for the therapist ratings serving as the standard. Scoring constants are operator-set per child, so scores are not comparable across children. And equating a detected face with attending is a strong assumption for children who may attend without orienting. [RQ2.9] The authors propose sharing assessment data 'locally, within the same team or clinic, or globally as integrated clinical dataset sharable by professionals in different places through interoperable systems', and continued development of semi-autonomous adaptive robots that recognise behavioural cues and respond accordingly. The steps the study most needs are a control condition to separate intervention effect from familiarisation, an account of attrition, a chance-corrected agreement statistic with clustering adjustment, and reliability data for the therapist ratings. [RQ3.1] Attention and engagement, decomposed into three operationally defined components with explicit rules. Face attention: orientation toward the robot's chest display, detected by Haar cascade, scoring +5 when the face is detected and -1 when it is not. Joint attention: a head turn matching the robot's directed gaze, detected through left or right ear detection, scoring +15 - the largest weight in the system, and appropriately so, since joint attention is the more specific construct. Sound response: latency from prompt to vocal response, converted by a fixed linear formula. The construct choice is well matched to the clinical purpose the paper sets out, which is not diagnosis but therapy targeting: the authors argue that 'one of the most important preconditions for the success of these interventions is the knowledge and availability of the kinds of stimuli that usually draw the attention of the child and increase his or her engagement over time'. Attention is what a therapist needs to know moment by moment to steer a session, and it is the quantity the system measures and feeds back. The weakness is the operationalisation of face detection as attention, which equates orienting with attending and will misclassify a child who listens without looking. [RQ3.2] Three streams combined into one running score - face detection, ear-based head orientation, and speech-response latency - fused by weighted accumulation with operator-set constants rather than by a learned combiner. The weights encode a clinical judgement about relative importance (joint attention worth three times face attention, non-attention penalised lightly), which is transparent and adjustable but not empirically derived. No ablation examines what each stream contributes to the 82.4% agreement, which would have been informative about whether the joint-attention component - the most clinically specific and the hardest to detect from ear cascades - is carrying its weight. [RQ4.1] No model is trained. The system is rule-based throughout: off-the-shelf Haar cascade classifiers perform face and ear detection as measurement infrastructure, and the attention score is accumulated by hand-specified increments with operator-adjustable constants. There is no training set, test set, cross-validation or fitted parameter anywhere. For a review of computational approaches this is a useful boundary case, because it shows what can be achieved without learning: a transparent, adjustable, real-time measure that tracks a clinician's judgement on 82.4% of sessions and closes a therapy loop. The corresponding limitation is that the constants are asserted rather than derived, so the score's calibration rests on the operator's judgement rather than on evidence. [RQ4.2] A scalar attention score accumulated at approximately 1 Hz across a session, with session-level trends used both for the agreement analysis and for adapting the next session's scenario. Every increment is traceable to a detection event and a stated constant. [RQ4.3] One agreement figure - 82.4%, from 6 mismatches in 34 sessions against the therapist's 0-100 attention ratings - plus session-by-session attention scores for the longitudinal arm. The metric is the right kind for the claim, since concurrent agreement with a clinician's judgement of the same construct is what a therapy-support measure needs to demonstrate, and the paper describes it correctly as matching therapist assessments rather than as diagnostic accuracy. Three gaps: no chance-corrected statistic such as Cohen's kappa, so the proportion of agreement attributable to the marginal distribution of therapist ratings is unknown; no adjustment for the clustering of 34 sessions within 6 children; and no reliability estimate for the therapist ratings themselves, so the achievable ceiling is unknown. [RQ4.4] Complete and by design. Every component of the score is a stated rule with a stated constant, adjustable per child by the operator, so a therapist can read the derivation of any score directly and can tune the measure to a particular patient. Against the learned models charted throughout this review, this is the opposite design point: nothing is fitted, so nothing requires post-hoc explanation, and the trade-off is that calibration is asserted rather than derived. For a system intended to run inside a clinical session and inform a therapist's next move, that trade is defensible. [RQ4.5] Not applicable in the classification sense - no model is trained, no individual is assigned a class, and no autism prediction is attempted. The relevant validation question is whether the automated attention measure tracks the construct it claims to measure, and the study answers it with concurrent validation against an independent human standard: agreement with the treating therapist's 0-100 attention ratings on 28 of 34 sessions, reported as 82.4%. That is the right design for the claim and it is described accurately, with the conclusion stating that the system matches 'over 80% of therapist assessments' rather than presenting the figure as diagnostic performance. Four qualifications bound it. The 34 sessions come from 6 children and are therefore clustered, with no adjustment reported, so the effective sample is closer to 6 than to 34. No chance-corrected agreement statistic is given, so how much of the 82.4% reflects the marginal distribution of the therapist's ratings is unknown. No reliability estimate exists for those ratings, so the ceiling on achievable agreement is unknown - and a measure agreeing 82.4% with a standard of unknown reliability could be tracking either the construct or that particular therapist. And the scoring constants are operator-adjustable per child, which is clinically sensible but means the score is not a fixed instrument and its agreement with a clinician may partly reflect tuning. The separate longitudinal claim - that attention rose across seven weeks - has no control condition at all, so it cannot be separated from familiarisation with a novel robot, practice on a repeated task, maturation, or the attention of being in a study; and with 5 of 11 children not completing and no reason given, the trend is computed on a self-selected subgroup. The authors label the causal claim a hypothesis, which is the correct standing for it. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism, Robotics, Assessment, Attention, Therapy. Accurate and complete - naming the population, the technology, the purpose, the construct and the application. Unusually, the keyword set correctly signals that the study is about assessment within therapy rather than about diagnosis, which is not true of several titles in this corpus. [RQ5.2] International Journal of Social Robotics 13:67-82, 2021; accepted 25 February 2020, published online 6 March 2020. A social robotics venue, and the article reads accordingly - the system engineering, the chest-mount mass distribution, the detector configuration and the scoring rules are all specified precisely, while the clinical evaluation carries no control condition, no chance-corrected agreement statistic and no account of attrition. The venue's orientation also explains the study's most valuable feature, the closed measurement-intervention loop, which is a robotics design idea rather than a clinical-trial one. [RQ5.3] Published 2021 by a group at United Arab Emirates University with Al Ain Hospital, and collaborators at RIKEN, the University of New South Wales, Western Sydney University and the University of Malaya. The framing separates it from most of this corpus: the problem identified is not detection but the cost of repeated assessment during therapy - assessment 'is typically performed at the time of enrollment and repeated during long-term therapy to measure progress', and if it 'could be repeated more frequently to trace the severity and development of symptoms, then therapists could implement more efficacious diagnostic and therapeutic options, and patients and their parents would be better motivated to withstand long, repetitive therapy sessions'. For this review the study contributes three things that the detection-oriented literature does not. It closes the loop: the automated attention measure feeds back into the interaction scenario, which adapts to each child's score history across sessions, so measurement serves intervention rather than terminating in a classification - no other study in the corpus implements this. It demonstrates what is achievable without any learned model: three transparent rules with operator-adjustable constants, running at 1 Hz on a phone camera mounted to the robot the child is attending to, agreeing with the treating therapist's judgement on 28 of 34 sessions. And it is longitudinal, tracking six children across a seven-week course, in a corpus that is otherwise almost entirely cross-sectional. Its evidential weight is nonetheless limited in ways that should be stated: there is no comparison group and no control condition, so the observed rise in attention cannot be separated from familiarisation, practice or maturation; 5 of 11 children did not complete and no reason is given; the 82.4% is an uncorrected agreement rate over sessions clustered within six children, against a therapist standard of unknown reliability; and the population is narrow - male, mild to moderate, verbally capable - despite the abstract describing the target as children with minimal verbal capabilities. The authors' own restraint is worth noting: the causal claim is presented as a hypothesis, and the system is positioned as a tool for therapists rather than as a diagnostic instrument. |
| S-068 | Cross-sectional case-control classification on a purpose-built questionnaire; 200 children in Lahore - 100 autistic recruited from Mayo Hospital's child psychiatry department and a private autism school, and 100 described as healthy with no stated source - with no diagnostic instrument, ages, sexes or matching reported; dataset not released. | A 21-item caregiver questionnaire covering child sex, age and birth order, six retrospective behavioural and developmental items, five perinatal history items and eight parental and family background items, administered on paper and via Google Forms, binary- and one-hot-encoded, then reduced by SelectKBest (k = 17), a 0.8 variance threshold and SelectFromModel, and classified by nine algorithms under a single 80/20 train-test split. | Best accuracy 95%, achieved by six of 27 algorithm-by-selection cells, with the remainder between 90% and 92.5%. Confusion matrices under SelectKBest show random forest and SVM each detecting 18 of 20 autistic children with all 20 comparison children correctly classified. No feature importances or selected feature sets are reported. | No diagnostic instrument for either group and no screening for the comparison group, so the classified label has no stated basis; no ages, sexes or matching reported while sex, age and birth order are model features; a single unrepeated 80/20 split giving a 40-child test set with SelectKBest's k tuned to give the best results and the maximum quoted across 27 cells; no ethics approval or consent statement for sensitive family data; most items are retrospective caregiver recollections with no treatment of recall bias; the selected feature sets are never disclosed so the stated aim of identifying important factors is unmet; and conclusions present single-group frequencies about maternal vaccination and parental smoking without comparison rates or tests. | Included at the boundary of the review's behavioral-data criterion and flagged as such: only about six of 21 items concern the child's behaviour and all are retrospective caregiver recollections, with the remainder perinatal, familial and parental variables - a composition that should separate this record from the corpus's directly instrumented studies in the per-group analysis. Its durable contribution is documentary rather than methodological: a concrete account of research conditions in a setting where autism cases are not tracked nationally, the only government child psychiatry department averages two patients a day, and no records existed in storable form, so a dataset had to be built from scratch. Its closing caution that the dataset is local and should not be applied elsewhere without consultation is more scoping discipline than most of the corpus offers. Against that, it is the corpus's clearest instance of an aetiological claim outrunning a design - the abstract promises to identify causes so lifestyle changes can be made, while the conclusions offer uncontrolled single-group frequencies including maternal vaccination rates, a juxtaposition that a review of this literature should note explicitly. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of 100 children each: 100 autistic children recruited from the Child Psychiatry Department at Mayo Hospital Lahore and a private autism school, and 100 children described as healthy whose recruitment source is never stated. The comparison group was collected specifically 'to ensure that our model is trained without any class imbalance problem', so its purpose is stated as statistical rather than clinical. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'children with autism', 'autistic children', 'ASD individuals', 'healthy children'. The comparison group is 'healthy', and autism is introduced as 'a severe condition related to brain development that impairs communication and interaction with others'. The framing is disease-oriented, and the stated purpose of identifying 'common causes leading up to it so that appropriate lifestyle changes can be made accordingly' implies modifiable aetiology in a way the design cannot support. [RQ1.3] Essentially none. No ages, means, standard deviations, sex counts or matching statistics are reported for either group. The age eligibility is stated inconsistently - under 12 in the abstract and under 10 in the methods. Sex, age and birth order are model features while remaining undescribed at group level, so the classifier's reliance on demographic separation cannot be assessed. Histograms of the distributions are presented as figures but no counts are given in text or table. No socioeconomic data beyond parental education, which is itself a model feature. [RQ1.4] None. The autistic group is defined by recruitment from a child psychiatry department or a specialist school, with no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or date reported anywhere. The comparison group has no stated screening or source. The label is simply a questionnaire field, 'ASD diagnosed', answered yes or no. This is the weakest ascertainment among included records, and it is consequential because the entire study is a supervised classification of that label. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive measure. Family history of cognitive disability is collected as a predictor rather than as a characterisation. [RQ2.1] Goal: build the first autism prediction model for Pakistan from a purpose-collected questionnaire and identify commonly associated background factors. Main findings: 95% best accuracy across several algorithm-and-selection combinations, with 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity in the best confusion matrices on a 40-child test set; and a set of narrative single-group observations about birth order, sex, family history, sensory reactivity, maternal vaccination and parental smoking, none accompanied by control comparison or statistical test. [RQ2.2] The Child Psychiatry Department at Mayo Hospital Lahore, described as the only government-run child psychiatry department in Pakistan and seeing on average two patients daily, together with a private school for autistic children in Lahore. Questionnaires were administered on paper at the school and via Google Forms otherwise. No setting is described for the comparison group. [RQ2.3] No behavioural task and no observation of any kind. All data are caregiver responses to a 21-item questionnaire, most of it retrospective - the age at which a child first walked or spoke, whether they rocked in a crib as a baby, whether they were ever thought deaf, and maternal behaviours during a pregnancy that occurred years earlier. Recall accuracy for such items is known to be limited and to differ systematically between parents of diagnosed and undiagnosed children, since a diagnosis reframes recollection of early development. The paper does not address recall bias. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional; a single questionnaire per family with no follow-up, though the items ask retrospectively about the perinatal period and early childhood. Data include maternal substance use, antidepressant use and miscarriage history - sensitive material about identifiable families collected partly through a commercial web form. No ethics committee approval, consent procedure, anonymisation policy or data-handling statement appears anywhere in the paper. [RQ2.5] Paper questionnaires and Google Forms for collection; Python with scikit-learn for encoding, feature selection and classification. No hardware, versions, seeds or hyperparameters are reported. [RQ2.6] Poor. Reported: the full 21-item questionnaire with each item's type and wording, the encoding scheme, the three feature-selection methods with their parameters, the nine algorithms with brief descriptions, the 80/20 split ratio, a complete 27-cell accuracy table, and confusion matrices for all nine algorithms under one selection scheme. Absent: any diagnostic instrument, ethics approval, group demographics, recruitment source for the comparison group, the identity of features retained by any selection method, all hyperparameters, the random seed, sensitivity and specificity values despite being said to have been computed, and any data or code. The questionnaire itself is the one element documented well enough to be reused. [RQ2.7] Acknowledged: the dataset should be enlarged for reliability; the model 'should be used with care and under supervision of some professional'; and 'this is a local dataset which should not be applied elsewhere in the world without consultation'. The last two are genuine scoping cautions that most of the corpus omits. Not acknowledged: no diagnostic instrument for either group; a single 80/20 split with a 40-child test set and no cross-validation; SelectKBest's k tuned to give the best results; the maximum reported across 27 cells; no group demographics despite sex, age and birth order being model features; no ethics approval; recall bias in retrospective caregiver report, which differs systematically between parents of diagnosed and undiagnosed children; and, most consequentially, the presentation of single-group frequencies about maternal vaccination and parental smoking as observations about autism without any control comparison or base rate. [RQ2.9] Expand the dataset; build a mobile application for clinicians; maintain historical records and raise mental health awareness; and strengthen trait correlations with more data. The authors add two cautions that function as recommendations - that the model requires professional supervision in use, and that the dataset is local and should not be transferred to other populations without consultation. [RQ3.1] No behaviour is observed. Six of 21 items concern the child's behaviour as recalled by a caregiver - crib rocking, suspected deafness, insistence on particular music, reaction to bright lights, colours or unusual sounds, age of walking and age of first words - which together sample early sensory reactivity, repetitive movement and developmental milestone timing. The remaining fifteen items are perinatal, familial and parental variables that are not behavioural at all. This composition is the principal reason the record sits at the boundary of the review's scope and should be distinguished in the per-group analysis from directly instrumented behavioural studies. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion. What the study does combine is heterogeneous variable types within one questionnaire - child behaviour, perinatal history, family history and parental lifestyle - but no analysis separates their contributions, no feature importances are reported, and the retained feature sets under each selection scheme are never disclosed. Since the design's stated purpose is to identify which factors matter, this omission removes the paper's principal claimed contribution: a reader cannot tell whether classification rests on the developmental items, on demographics such as sex and birth order, or on parental background variables. [RQ4.1] Nine classifiers spanning probabilistic, instance-based, linear, tree, ensemble and kernel families, each described in a sentence with no rationale for inclusion and no hyperparameters. Breadth substitutes for justification. That six of the 27 cells reach 95% while the rest cluster between 90% and 92.5% - a spread of two test cases - indicates the comparison is not resolving real differences between algorithms. [RQ4.2] Twenty-one questionnaire items binary- or one-hot-encoded, reduced by three alternative selection schemes. The representation is transparent and the questionnaire is fully documented, which makes it reproducible as an instrument even though the analysis is not. The critical gap is that the outcome of selection is never reported: SelectKBest retained 17 of the features, but which 17 is not stated, and the variance-threshold and model-based schemes likewise report no retained sets. [RQ4.3] Accuracy for all 27 combinations, confusion matrices for nine algorithms under one scheme, and ROC curves. Providing the confusion matrices is what allows sensitivity and specificity to be derived - random forest and SVM both achieve 18 of 20 autistic children detected with all 20 comparison children correctly classified - even though the paper states these were calculated but does not tabulate them. Missing: confidence intervals, any statistical comparison, and any acknowledgement that a 40-child test set makes each case worth 2.5 accuracy points. [RQ4.4] The paper's stated aim includes helping 'visualize common causes leading up to' autism, and interpretability is therefore central to its purpose - but no interpretability analysis is performed. No feature importances, no selected feature lists, no coefficients, no decision rules. What is offered instead is a list of narrative observations in the conclusion, each a frequency within the autistic group presented without the corresponding control-group frequency. Two of these are actively hazardous as written: 'most of the mothers were vaccinated during pregnancies' and 'almost 50 percent of the parents smoked before giving birth to children with autism' both appear in a list introduced as observations about autism, in a paper whose abstract promises to identify causes so that lifestyle changes can be made. Without a comparison rate these statements are uninformative, and in the vaccination case the juxtaposition risks reinforcing a well-documented and thoroughly refuted misattribution. [RQ4.5] The weakest element. A single 80/20 split of 200 children gives a 40-child test set, with no cross-validation, no repetition across splits and no separate tuning set. SelectKBest's k was chosen as 17 'as it gave the best results', which tunes a selection parameter against the reported evaluation. Twenty-seven algorithm-by-selection combinations were evaluated and the maximum quoted in the abstract. There is no independent cohort, no external validation and no confidence interval, so the reported 95% cannot be distinguished from the 90% cells by anything the paper provides. [RQ5.1] Index terms: autism, autism spectrum disorder, machine learning, predictive analysis, ASD. Four of five are generic; 'predictive analysis' is the operative framing and signals an aetiological ambition the design does not support. [RQ5.2] 2021 International Conference on Frontiers of Information Technology (FIT), pages 305-309 - a general computing conference with no clinical remit. [RQ5.3] 2021. The framing is about data absence rather than methodological gap, and on that point it is informative and specific.
