The mSVM-RFE analysis then delivers a genuinely useful negative result - the optimal eight-feature subset (0.9344) did not significantly outperform the full 17-feature model (0.9235, p = 0.1592), so feature selection bought nothing, and the authors report this rather than promoting the higher figure as their headline. [RQ4.2] One 17-dimensional vector per participant, produced by averaging frame-level acoustic measures across the task and computing transcript-level language measures over the same interval, then normalising all features to [0,1]. The unit is therefore the participant throughout, which is what makes leave-one-subject-out cross-validation meaningful. One representational property is worth noting because the authors use it defensively and correctly: almost every measure is length-normalised, being either an average over frames or c-units or a proportion computable on any sample length, the sole exception being number of distinct word roots. This lets them rebut the objection that the nine missed autistic participants escaped because their unusually long transcripts broke the measures - 'it is highly unlikely that the measures did not perform well for high language output, and more likely that high IQ and older children had fewer communication difficulties, making them harder to detect'. That is an argument about measurement invariance made from the construction of the features rather than from post hoc testing. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC with 95% confidence intervals for all three models, with DeLong tests for every pairwise AUC comparison - the appropriate test for correlated ROC curves derived from the same participants, and one that almost no other study in this corpus uses. The confidence intervals do real work: the voice model's interval (0.7076-0.8525) and the combined model's (0.8768-0.9641) do not overlap, so that comparison is visibly supported, whereas the language and combined intervals do overlap and the DeLong test is correspondingly marginal at p = 0.033. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately is what makes the complementarity finding legible - the voice model's specificity of 0.6857 is the weakness that the language model repairs, and the combined model's unchanged specificity alongside raised sensitivity is the signature of the two modalities catching different people. The misclassification analysis adds a class of evidence absent elsewhere: Mann-Whitney comparisons of age, IQ, two CCC-2 scales, two ADOS domains and three task indices between detected and missed participants, for each of the three models separately, with the counterpart analysis for non-autistic participants in supplementary material. No chance or trivial baseline is reported, which is the one gap. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is built into the design rather than added afterwards, and it operates at three levels. The features are individually meaningful by construction - mean length of utterance, filled-pause ratio, disfluency proportion, F0, shimmer, loudness - so any model weight is directly interpretable, in contrast to the learned representations used by the deep-learning speech studies elsewhere in this corpus. mSVM-RFE ranks them and identifies an optimal eight, evenly split between modalities, though the selection is honestly reported as producing no significant gain. And the misclassification analysis functions as the deepest interpretive layer, answering not 'which features matter' but 'which children does this measure see', which is the question that determines clinical utility. Its findings are specific and consequential: the language model is biased toward younger children with poorer language and less output; the voice model is unbiased with respect to language level; the residual misses have the highest IQ and most language output; and neither ADOS severity nor IQ predicts misclassification in any model - from which the authors draw the appropriately hedged conclusion that 'if replicated, this result could confirm that our voice and language measurement methodology specifically taps aspects of communication skills that are not confounded by autism severity or developmental delay'. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, and uniquely in this corpus the choice is justified by citation to the methodological literature on exactly this issue - Saeb et al. (2017) on subject-wise versus record-wise validation - with the rationale that it approximates 'the clinically relevant use-case of diagnosis in unseen participants'. Because each participant contributes a single averaged feature vector, there is no possibility of the within-subject leakage that inflates results throughout this review. Robustness was checked against 10-fold cross-validation, giving 0.9235 against 0.9205 with p = 0.9219, confirming the estimate is not an artefact of the resampling scheme. Comparisons between models use DeLong's test rather than informal inspection. Sex-stratified models were fitted to test whether the sex imbalance drove the result. The confounding variables were tested rather than acknowledged. What remains: the soft-margin constants were chosen per model on performance and the linear configuration was selected for reporting over tuned non-linear alternatives, so some selection optimism is present though bounded by the small hyperparameter space; feature selection was performed under 10-fold rather than leave-one-out for software reasons; and there is no independent replication cohort - the sample is a single site and overlaps with the two prior papers whose findings are being replicated, so the 'replication' is of models rather than of data. The authors' own framing is appropriately cautious about all of this, describing the results as 'preliminary but very encouraging'. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism, automated measures, communication, disfluency, natural language processing, pragmatic language, prosody, voice. Six of eight are linguistic or communicative constructs rather than computational methods - 'disfluency', 'pragmatic language' and 'prosody' name specific behavioural phenomena - which accurately signals a paper whose subject is communication measurement with machine learning as instrument, rather than the reverse. [RQ5.2] Autism Research 15(7):1288-1300 (2022), the journal of the International Society for Autism Research - a specialist autism venue with clinical and behavioural-science readership rather than an engineering one. Authorship spans OHSU's Department of Psychiatry, the Institute on Development and Disability and the Department of Pediatrics, with the senior author being a prominent autism epidemiologist and the two first authors marked as contributing equally, one from the language side and one from computation. Funding is from NIH and specifically the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders. The venue and authorship explain the paper's balance: full clinical characterisation, careful terminology, statistical inference appropriate to a clinical audience (DeLong tests, confidence intervals, non-parametric group comparisons), and modelling that is deliberately conservative. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is unusual for this corpus in three respects. First, it declines the diagnostic frame outright: 'This work (past and current) is not currently intended to be employed for diagnostic or screening purposes. Rather, our methodology uses already-established diagnosis as an external criterion against which we can validate (in the sense of discriminant validity) these voice and language measures.' The target is outcome measures for trials and longitudinal studies, and the paper closes on that application. Second, the critique of existing instruments is specific rather than generic - conventional tests like the CELF-4 and PPVT 'evaluate structural aspects of language' and must be augmented by natural language sampling; parent-report instruments such as the CCC-2 have validity limits 'as illustrated in treatment studies that have shown caregiver reports to be susceptible to the placebo effect'; and, echoing the group's companion paper, the ADOS and SRS 'include only one item each on voice quality' despite prosodic difference being a cited characteristic of autism. Third, the epidemiological framing is calibrated rather than alarmist, citing a worldwide prevalence range of 0.043% to 2.68% and noting that 'reasons for the increasing prevalence rate are uncertain' - written by an author who has published extensively on exactly that question. The comparison against prior work is likewise careful, noting that Tanaka et al.'s sample of four autistic and two typically developing participants made its findings 'unreliable', and that the sampling contexts of the compared studies differed from this one so that 'examination of contextual effects should be vigorously pursued'. |
| S-081 | Prospective cross-sectional study in four Duke pediatric primary care clinics: 457 toddlers aged 17-36 months recruited during routine well-child checkups, of whom 41 were subsequently diagnosed with autism (70.7% male, 24.38 +/- 4.73 months, ADOS-2 CSS 7.56, Mullen Early Learning Composite 63.64) and 416 classified neurotypical (50.2% male, 20.59 +/- 3.18 months); 12 with non-autism diagnoses were excluded. Diagnosis followed enrolment via M-CHAT-R/F screening, referral on positive screen or raised concern, and ADOS-2 Toddler Module with DSM-5 determination by research-reliable licensed psychologists. Groups differ significantly on age, sex, ethnicity and caregiver education. Data are tablet front-camera video; not released. | An iOS app on a tripod-mounted tablet 60 cm from the child, held on a caregiver's lap, presented four social and three nonsocial movies while the front camera recorded. Computer vision extracted 49 facial landmarks with human-supervised face tracking, and analysis was restricted to attending segments verified by a \|yaw\| < 20 degree criterion and independent gaze estimation. Head movement rate was the Euclidean displacement of three central landmarks normalised by inter-eye distance and smoothed over 1/3 s; acceleration its frame-to-frame difference; complexity the sample entropy across 30 coarse-grained scales (m = 2, r = 0.15 x population-wide sigma) integrated over the first 10. Participants with under 40% valid data per movie were excluded from that movie. Inference used Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, 2x2 mixed ANOVA and ANCOVA with age and missing data as covariates; classification used an RBF-kernel SVM with leave-one-out cross-validation, Hanley-McNeil confidence intervals and a variance-based model-comparison criterion. | Autistic toddlers showed significantly higher rate (F(1,427) = 42.48), acceleration (F(1,427) = 38.65) and complexity (F(1,427) = 29.68), all p < .0001, with significant movie-type main effects and no interaction. Effect sizes were medium to large for social movies (rate r = 0.39-0.73; entropy r = 0.40-0.68) and small to medium for nonsocial; Mechanical-Puppy showed no group difference. Neurotypical toddlers moved more, faster and less predictably during social than nonsocial movies (r = 0.47, 0.62, 0.51) while autistic toddlers showed no content-dependent difference. Classification reached AUC 0.85 for acceleration combined across the four social movies and 0.80 for entropy; the eight-dimensional combination gave 0.73. Per-movie AUCs were 0.67-0.73 with wide confidence intervals. Attention was 95% and 93%. Age and missing data did not affect the group comparisons. | The groups differ significantly on age, sex, ethnicity, caregiver education and cognitive ability, with only age and missing data covaried; the authors state that the contribution of cognitive differences is unclear and that the sample lacked power to examine sex. Mullen data exist only for the autistic group, so the cognitive gap cannot be quantified. The 12 children with non-autism diagnoses were excluded, so the discrimination tested is against typical development rather than against developmental concern. Inspection of videos revealed that the movement extends to trunk and shoulders, which the face-only algorithm does not capture, so the construct may be whole-body postural instability rather than head movement. Per-movie AUC confidence intervals are wide (one runs 0.53-0.75). The Results and Discussion contradict each other on the direction of the Mullen-movement correlation. No data or code release. Five authors have a licensed financial interest in the app. | The corpus's benchmark for translational realism, and the study whose performance figure should be read most literally. Alone among the classification studies here, it recruits consecutively from routine primary care rather than from diagnosed cohorts, ascertains diagnosis after enrolment through a screen-and-refer pathway, and reports performance at a 41:416 class ratio that approximates real screening prevalence - so its AUC of 0.85 is estimated under something close to the base rate a deployed tool would face, whereas the balanced designs that dominate this corpus report figures that would translate into far worse positive predictive value in practice. It is also one of only two studies here to cite the methodological literature on validation bias directly (Vabalas et al.), and it pairs participant-level leave-one-out cross-validation with confidence intervals on every AUC and a formal criterion for comparing classifier configurations. Three findings should carry into the synthesis independently of the classification result. The within-group content contrast - neurotypical toddlers modulate head movement by social content while autistic toddlers do not - is stronger evidence than any between-group difference and is used to argue against a competing published interpretation, illustrating what a behavioural study can establish that an accuracy figure cannot. Aggregating one feature across four movies raised AUC from roughly 0.70 to 0.85 while adding a second correlated feature type reduced it to 0.73, which is a concrete demonstration that more stimulus sampling beats more feature types on a moderate dataset. And the authors' own report that the movement extends to trunk and shoulders is the corpus's clearest instance of a group naming, unprompted, that their measured signal may not be the construct they set out to measure. | [RQ1.1] Three groups identified, two analysed. Of 457 toddlers recruited during well-child checkups at four pediatric primary care clinics, 41 were subsequently diagnosed with autism under DSM-5 and 416 were classified neurotypical. A third group of 12 who screened positive on the M-CHAT-R/F and received a non-autism diagnosis - language delay without autism is the example given - was excluded from analysis because of small sample size. That exclusion is the design's one substantive omission, since those 12 are precisely the children against whom a screening tool must discriminate, and their removal means the reported AUC reflects autism versus typical development rather than autism versus developmental concern. The neurotypical group is nonetheless better ascertained than most comparison groups in this corpus, being formed of two subsets - children with a negative M-CHAT-R/F and no caregiver or physician concern, and children who screened positive or raised concern but were then judged on the ADOS-2 and psychologist clinical judgment to have no developmental or autism-related concerns. The 41:416 ratio is the study's most consequential structural feature: it approximates the base rate a deployed screening tool would encounter, in contrast to the balanced designs that dominate this review. [RQ1.2] 'autistic toddlers', 'autistic children', 'autistic individuals', 'young autistic children', consistently identity-first including in the title, against 'neurotypical toddlers'. 'Patients' never appears and 'typically developing' is replaced throughout by 'neurotypical'. The framing of the phenomenon is descriptive rather than deficit-oriented - head movements are 'differences' in 'dynamics', autism is 'characterized by differences in social communication', and the interpretive discussion entertains the possibility that the movements 'might also serve a regulatory function' rather than treating them as symptoms to be catalogued. This is among the most careful terminology in the corpus and is consistent with the senior authorship's position in the autism research community. [RQ1.3] Reported in full and tested, and the picture is one of multiple significant imbalances. Autistic group: 41 toddlers, 70.7% male, 24.38 +/- 4.73 months. Neurotypical group: 416 toddlers, 50.2% male, 20.59 +/- 3.18 months. Age differs significantly by ANOVA, sex by chi-squared. Two further significant differences appear in the demographic table and are less commonly reported elsewhere in this corpus: Hispanic ethnicity (29.3% versus 7.5%) and caregiver education, where 85.6% of neurotypical caregivers held a four-year college degree or more against 53.7% of autistic caregivers. Age and the proportion of missing data were entered as ANCOVA covariates and did not affect the between-group results; sex was not covaried, with the authors stating that the sample 'did not offer sufficient power to determine the influence of biological and demographic characteristics, such as sex'; ethnicity and caregiver education are reported but never revisited. The last is worth attention in this particular paradigm, since the measurement is of a toddler sitting on a caregiver's lap with 'no special instructions given regarding how to hold the child', so any systematic difference in how caregivers positioned or settled their children would enter the signal directly. Cognitive ability differs markedly - the autistic group's Mullen Early Learning Composite averages 63.64 - and no Mullen data were collected for the neurotypical group, so the difference cannot be quantified or adjusted. [RQ1.4] A genuine prospective screening pathway, which is rare in this corpus and is the study's principal methodological asset. Every participant received the M-CHAT-R/F as part of routine clinical care. Referral for diagnostic evaluation was triggered by a total score of 3 or more initially, 2 or more after follow-up questions, or developmental concerns raised by the pediatrician or parent. Referred children received the ADOS-2 Toddler Module from research-reliable licensed psychologists who determined DSM-5 status, supported by the Mullen Scales of Early Learning. Diagnosis therefore followed rather than preceded enrolment, and the mean interval between diagnosis and app administration was 0.7 months, so the behavioural measurement and the diagnostic determination are close in time. The comparison group's status is partly instrumented rather than assumed, since screen-positive children judged to have no concerns are retained in it. The one gap is that children with a negative M-CHAT-R/F and no raised concern were not directly assessed, so the neurotypical group will contain some proportion of children whose autism was not detected by screening - which biases toward underestimating the group difference rather than inflating it. [RQ1.5] Comprehensive for the autistic group and absent for the comparison group. ADOS-2 Toddler Module calibrated severity scores average 7.56 +/- 1.67 across a range of 2-10, so the sample spans the severity spectrum. The Mullen Scales of Early Learning provide an Early Learning Composite of 63.64 +/- 10.17 alongside Expressive Language (T = 28.08), Receptive Language (T = 23.14), Fine Motor (T = 34.11) and Visual Reception (T = 33.94) T-scores - all substantially below average, indicating a group with considerable developmental delay, and the Fine Motor score is directly relevant since the outcome is a motor measure. The Mullen composite is used analytically, correlated against all three head movement measures. Because no Mullen data exist for the neurotypical group, the cognitive difference between groups cannot be estimated or adjusted, and the authors list this among their limitations: 'The autistic and neurotypical group differed in cognitive ability and, thus, it is not clear the degree to which differences in cognition contributed to our findings.' Comorbidity is not otherwise characterised, and the 12 children with non-autism diagnoses were removed. [RQ2.1] Goal: replicate a prior head-movement-rate finding in a larger sample with redesigned stimuli, and extend it to acceleration and multiscale-entropy complexity, testing whether differences are more pronounced for social content and whether the measures can be combined for classification. Main findings: autistic toddlers showed significantly higher rate (F(1,427) = 42.48), acceleration (F(1,427) = 38.65) and complexity (F(1,427) = 29.68), all p < .0001, with medium to large effect sizes for social movies and small to medium for nonsocial; a significant main effect of movie type with no group-by-type interaction; neurotypical toddlers modulated all three measures by content while autistic toddlers did not; classification reached AUC 0.85 for acceleration across the four social movies and 0.80 for entropy, with the eight-dimensional combination performing worse at 0.73; and neither age nor missing data affected the group comparisons. [RQ2.2] Four Duke pediatric primary care clinics during routine well-child checkups - the only truly point-of-care setting in the corpus. The description of environmental control is unusually honest: a quiet room with few distractions was identified at each clinic, but 'although it was quiet and without a lot of distraction, it was not otherwise controlled as in a laboratory setting', with the four rooms noted as similar in size, lighting and presence of distractions. The social arrangement is specified in detail and matters for the measurement: the caregiver held the child on their lap with no instructions on how to do so, sat quietly, and was asked not to guide the child's behaviour or give instructions, while siblings and the administering assistant stayed behind both caregiver and child to reduce distraction. The tablet sat on a tripod approximately 60 cm in front of the child. That the caregiver's holding is uninstructed is a deliberate choice for ecological validity and an uncontrolled source of variance for a measure of postural movement. [RQ2.3] Seven brief movies totalling about five minutes, split four social and three nonsocial by explicit design, each described with its duration and content. The social movies feature actors smiling, frowning, gesturing and using limited verbal expression; the nonsocial movies feature bubbles moving randomly, a mechanical toy puppy and a puppy appearing at screen positions in a fixed right-right-left pattern. The social/nonsocial split is the analytic instrument rather than a background feature: it enables the within-group contrast that produces the paper's most informative result, and it permits the group-by-content interaction test that adjudicates against Martin and colleagues' interpretation. The paradigm requires nothing of the child beyond sitting and watching, which is what makes it viable at 17 months in a clinic waiting room, and the near-equivalent attention rates of 95% and 93% across groups indicate that it holds toddlers' attention in both groups - an important equivalence, since differential attention would otherwise confound any movement measure. One movie, Mechanical-Puppy, showed no significant group difference on any of the three measures, and this is reported consistently rather than omitted. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional in analysis but embedded in a prospective screening pathway, with diagnosis ascertained after app administration at a mean interval of 0.7 months (range -0.1 to 5.9). No longitudinal follow-up of the measures themselves, and the authors identify the developmental course of head movement differences as a future direction. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: written informed consent from caregivers and approval by the Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board under two named protocol numbers. Conflicts of interest are declared at length and are substantial: five authors developed technology related to the app which has been licensed, with both they and Duke University benefiting financially; the senior clinical author sits on four scientific advisory boards, consults for three companies including Apple and receives book royalties; both senior authors have invention disclosures and patent applications registered with Duke's licensing office; and the senior engineering author is affiliated with Apple, with a note that the work was done before and independently of that affiliation. The disclosure is exemplary in its completeness, and the commercial interest in the app is relevant context for a paper reporting the app's discriminative performance. [RQ2.5] Deliberately minimal and entirely commodity: an iOS tablet on a tripod, using its own front-facing camera, running a purpose-built app. No external camera, depth sensor, marker, wearable or motion capture. That is what permits administration in a primary-care room by a non-specialist assistant with a caregiver holding the child. The analytic chain is specified in detail - face detection with human-supervised tracking to ensure only the participant's face is followed, 49 2D facial landmarks, head pose angles relative to the tablet, an automatic gaze estimation algorithm, and Python with pingouin for all statistics. Two engineering decisions deserve note because they neutralise obvious confounds. Landmark displacement is normalised by a one-second running average of inter-eye distance, which removes the effect of the child moving closer to or further from the camera - a variance source that would otherwise dominate in a lap-held toddler. And the sample-entropy tolerance uses the population-wide standard deviation rather than each participant's own, chosen explicitly so that 'this choice defined a distance threshold r consistent across participants', which prevents children with more variable movement from being scored on a correspondingly wider tolerance and hence appearing artificially regular. [RQ2.6] Among the most completely reported studies in the corpus. Specified: recruitment setting and inclusion and exclusion criteria; the full screen-and-refer diagnostic pathway with M-CHAT-R/F cut-points; instrument names and administrator qualifications; the demographic table with race, ethnicity, caregiver education and statistical tests; all seven movies with durations and content descriptions; the physical setup including tripod distance, caregiver instructions and positioning of other people; the landmark count and pose angles; the \|yaw\| < 20 degree attention criterion with its theoretical justification and the additional gaze-based confirmation; the inter-eye normalisation with its rationale; the 10-frame smoothing window; the complete multiscale entropy formulation with the coarse-graining equation, the sample entropy definition, m = 2, r = 0.15 sigma, the use of population-wide sigma with its rationale, integration across the first 10 scales, and the missing-data handling; the 40% data-quality threshold with its justification and the resulting per-movie sample sizes shown in every figure; every statistical test with its Python function; the classifier, kernel, cross-validation scheme and confidence-interval method; and the model-comparison criterion. Missing: no data or code release, no random seeds, and no reporting of how many of the 457 were excluded per movie in aggregate, though per-movie counts are given. [RQ2.7] Three limitations are stated and each is substantive. The sample, though large overall, contained only 41 autistic children and therefore 'did not offer sufficient power to determine the influence of biological and demographic characteristics, such as sex'. Data from all participants were not used in every analysis because of the 40% attendance threshold. And 'the autistic and neurotypical group differed in cognitive ability and, thus, it is not clear the degree to which differences in cognition contributed to our findings' - a direct acknowledgement that the study's most likely alternative explanation is unresolved. A fourth limitation appears not in the limitations section but in the discussion, and is arguably the most important: inspection of videos from high-movement toddlers 'revealed that the movement involves not just the head but also the upper body including trunk and shoulders, which were not captured by our computer vision algorithm, as we focused solely on the face in this study'. That reframes the construct from head movement to whole-body postural instability, and the authors follow it with a serious engagement with the postural-sway literature. What goes unaddressed: the significant ethnicity and caregiver-education differences, never revisited after the demographic table; the exclusion of the 12 children with non-autism diagnoses, which removes the clinically decisive contrast; the wide confidence intervals on the per-movie AUCs; and the internal contradiction between the Results' positive Mullen correlations and the Discussion's statement that lower-ability children moved more. [RQ2.9] Three directions, each following from a stated limitation. Explore the developmental course of head movement differences and 'elucidate their nature and neurobiological basis', with several concrete hypotheses already advanced - that the movements modulate sensory information generally rather than social perception specifically, that they reflect postural control difficulties that increase with sensory demand, or that like some repetitive behaviours they serve a regulatory function when stimuli are arousing. Extend the computer vision beyond the face to the trunk and shoulders, following directly from the observation that the movement is not confined to the head. And combine head movement 'with other behavioral biomarkers such as gaze, facial dynamics, and response to name' toward a multimodal digital phenotyping tool - which is the group's programmatic direction and is supported here by the demonstration that a single behavioural channel reaches AUC 0.85 in a prevalence-realistic sample. [RQ3.1] Head movement dynamics during passive viewing, decomposed into three levels: how much the head moves (rate), how sharply that movement changes (acceleration, motivated as relating 'to the magnitude of the instantaneous forces involved in head movement'), and how predictable the movement time series is across temporal scales (multiscale entropy, indexing 'the level of predictability and stability'). The complexity measure is the study's conceptual contribution and is well chosen: rate and acceleration are magnitude measures that could be produced by any source of extra motion, whereas entropy captures the structure of the movement over time and licenses the specific claim that autistic toddlers' movements were 'less predictable and less stable'. The behaviour is explicitly sensorimotor rather than social, and the paper situates it in a substantial literature on motor differences in autism - stereotypies, fine and gross motor impairment, motor planning and coordination, asymmetry in home-video studies of infants later diagnosed, and difficulties in gait, balance, postural control, movement accuracy, manual dexterity and praxis. The authors' own inspection finding, that trunk and shoulders move too, suggests the underlying construct is postural rather than cephalic. [RQ3.2] Single modality, with the fusion result confined to combining features within it - and that result is a clean negative. Two features (acceleration, entropy) across four movies gives an eight-dimensional space and AUC 0.73, worse than either feature alone combined across the same four movies (0.85 and 0.80). The authors report this plainly and explain it correctly as the expected behaviour of a moderate-sized dataset as dimensionality grows. Two aspects make the negative result more useful than most. The two features are moderately correlated (r = 0.4-0.5), so combining them adds dimensionality without much independent information - which is the situation in which such degradation is predicted, and the authors report the correlation that makes it interpretable. And combining a single feature across movies did help substantially, lifting acceleration from around 0.68-0.71 on individual movies to 0.85 across four - so aggregation over stimuli was worth far more than aggregation over feature types. The paper's stated future direction is genuine multimodal fusion with gaze, facial dynamics and response to name, which is the group's programme; this study establishes what one channel contributes. [RQ4.1] A single SVM with RBF kernel on two or three interpretable features, chosen because it 'is popular when used on relatively smaller datasets' and paired with leave-one-out cross-validation explicitly 'to minimize the risk of overoptimistic classification', citing Vabalas et al. (2019) - one of only two studies in this corpus to cite the methodological literature on validation bias directly. The modelling is deliberately subordinate to the statistical analysis: the paper's primary evidence is a set of mixed ANOVAs, Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests with effect sizes and ANCOVA covariate control, and classification is used to answer a specific supplementary question - whether the measures 'can be integrated to distinguish autistic and neurotypical toddlers'. That ordering is appropriate for a study whose contribution is a behavioural finding rather than a screening product, and it is unusual in this corpus, where classification accuracy is typically the primary and often the only evidence. Classifier configurations are compared by a formal variance-based true-difference criterion, so the claim that combining across movies beats single movies is tested rather than asserted. [RQ4.2] One scalar per feature per movie per child, so the unit of analysis is the participant throughout and no segment-level inflation is possible. Three representational decisions do substantial confound-neutralising work. Displacement is normalised by a running average of inter-eye distance, removing the effect of a lap-held toddler moving toward or away from the camera, which would otherwise dominate the raw landmark displacement signal. The entropy tolerance uses the population-wide standard deviation rather than each child's own, so a child with more variable movement is not scored against a correspondingly wider tolerance and thereby made to appear more regular - a subtle and correct choice, with a prior paper cited for its detailed justification. And analysis is restricted to segments where the child is attending, established by two independent criteria: a head-yaw threshold justified by central-bias theory for gaze estimation, and an automatic gaze estimation algorithm confirming the child was looking at the screen. That restriction is what allows the authors to argue that the differences 'do not appear to reflect the degree of attention to the movies', and it is reinforced by the near-equal attention rates of 95% and 93%. [RQ4.3] The most complete statistical reporting in the corpus for a study of this kind. Every group comparison carries an effect size r alongside its p value; the mixed ANOVAs report F with degrees of freedom for group, movie type and their interaction; entropy comparisons are reported per scale across all 30 multiscale resolutions rather than only for the integrated summary; every AUC carries a Hanley-McNeil 95% confidence interval; and classifier configurations are compared by a stated variance-based criterion with the explicit rule that models are 'considered not significantly different' if the interval spans zero. The confidence intervals are essential to reading the result honestly and the paper does not hide what they show: for Blowing-Bubbles the entropy AUC interval runs 0.53 to 0.75, so that single-movie result barely excludes chance, and the intervals on the individual-movie AUCs are uniformly wide because only about 30 autistic children contribute to each. The headline 0.85 is correspondingly better supported than the per-movie figures. Also reported are the attention rates for both groups and the per-movie participant counts after the data-quality gate, both of which bear on whether the measurement was equally successful in the two groups. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is pursued through the design of the measures rather than through model attribution, and the analysis that carries most weight is the within-group contrast. Because the measures are three physically meaningful quantities, the finding can be stated directly in behavioural terms. The decisive analysis compares social against nonsocial movies within each group: neurotypical toddlers moved more, faster and less predictably during social content (r = 0.47, 0.62, 0.51), while autistic toddlers showed no content-dependent difference at all. That single contrast does three things a between-group difference cannot. It shows the effect is not simply 'autistic children move more' but that neurotypical children modulate movement by content and autistic children do not. It adjudicates directly against Martin and colleagues' published interpretation that increased head movement in autism serves to modulate perception of social stimuli, since on that account the difference should be confined to social content, and here it is not. And it rules out the reading that the measure indexes social engagement, since the group difference persists for nonsocial content. The paper then engages seriously with alternative mechanisms - general sensory modulation, postural control under multisensory demand, a regulatory function analogous to repetitive behaviour - rather than settling on one. The Mullen correlation analysis is the interpretively weakest element and contains an internal contradiction: the Results report positive correlations between Early Learning Composite and all three movement measures during social movies (r = .36, .39, .34), implying higher cognitive ability accompanied more movement, while the Discussion asserts that 'autistic children with lower cognitive abilities showed higher levels of head movement rate, acceleration, and complexity' and builds an interpretation on that reading. [RQ4.5] Sound in every respect that this corpus commonly gets wrong, with the residual weakness being confounding rather than leakage. The unit is the participant, since all features are per-child summaries; leave-one-out cross-validation is used and justified by citation to Vabalas et al. on overoptimistic classification; AUCs carry Hanley-McNeil confidence intervals; and classifier configurations are compared by a formal criterion rather than by inspecting point estimates. Two further design properties strengthen the estimate beyond what the cross-validation alone provides. The class ratio of 41:416 approximates real screening prevalence, so the AUC is not estimated under an artificially balanced design - a distinction that matters enormously for translation, since the same AUC implies very different positive predictive value at 9% prevalence than at 50%. And diagnosis followed rather than preceded enrolment, so the sample is not conditioned on already being diagnosed, removing the referral filter that shapes almost every other study here. What remains unaddressed: age and missing data were covaried but sex was not, on stated power grounds; ethnicity and caregiver education differ significantly and are never revisited; cognitive ability differs and cannot be adjusted because Mullen data exist only for the autistic group; the 12 children with non-autism diagnoses were excluded, so the discrimination tested is against typical development rather than against developmental concern; and there is no independent replication cohort, though this study is itself a replication and extension of the group's earlier rate-only finding in a larger sample with redesigned stimuli. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism; head movements; computer vision; complexity analysis. Four terms, two naming the behavioural construct and two the method - a compact and accurate description of a paper that measures one behaviour precisely rather than surveying many. [RQ5.2] Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry 64(1):156-166 (2023, published online 2022), a clinical child mental health journal rather than an engineering venue. Authorship spans Duke's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Center for Autism and Brain Development, Global Health Institute, Office of Information Technology, and Department of Biomedical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Sciences, with two co-senior authors - one clinical, one engineering. Funded by an NIH Autism Centers of Excellence award and two NIMH R01s, with additional support to the engineering authors from NSF, the Department of Defense and industry gifts. The genuinely joint clinical-engineering leadership is visible throughout: the statistical inference is what a clinical journal would require (effect sizes, mixed ANOVA, ANCOVA covariates, non-parametric tests), the measurement engineering is what a computer vision group would produce (landmark normalisation, population-wide entropy tolerance, dual attention criteria), and neither is subordinated to the other. The paper includes a 'Key points' box in the journal's clinical format. [RQ5.3] 2022-2023. The framing is developmental and mechanistic rather than diagnostic, positioning head movement as 'one of the early sensorimotor signs associated with autism' and situating it within an established literature on motor differences - stereotypies, fine and gross motor impairment, motor planning and coordination, asymmetry in home videos of infants later diagnosed, and documented difficulties in gait, balance, postural control, movement accuracy, manual dexterity and praxis. What distinguishes the positioning is that the paper engages directly with a competing published interpretation and produces evidence against it: Martin and colleagues found head movement differences only during social stimuli and proposed that autistic children use head movements to modulate their perception of social scenes, whereas this study finds differences during both content types and states plainly that 'our data do not support the hypothesis that the head movements of the autistic toddlers were used to modulate the perception of social stimuli, per se'. It then offers alternatives without overclaiming, noting that 'the nature of these differences in head movement dynamics is not fully understood'. The translational claim is correspondingly modest - computer vision 'offers a scalable means of detecting subtle differences' that 'may be helpful in identifying early behaviors associated with autism' - and the stated endpoint is a multimodal digital phenotyping tool combining this channel with gaze, facial dynamics and response to name, not a standalone diagnostic. Given the disclosed commercial interest in the app, that restraint is notable. |
| S-082 | Cross-linguistic case-control classification across two sites: American English participants drawn from a family-genetic autism study in the United States and Hong Kong Cantonese participants recruited via social media, schools, autism organisations and employment programmes. Recruited 55 English autistic, 39 English comparison, 28 Cantonese autistic and 24 Cantonese comparison; analysed 33, 33, 24 and 24, with the shortfall unexplained. English autistic 87.9% male, 15.96 +/- 7.38 years, IQ 104.13, ADOS-2 CSS 7.02; English comparison 45.5% male, 19.31 +/- 5.35 years, IQ 111.03. Cantonese groups matched on age and sex. Diagnosis confirmed by research-reliable ADOS-2; comparison participants screened for personal and family history of autism. IQ measured with Wechsler scales in English and TONI-4 in Cantonese. Minimal dataset and analysis scripts deposited on OSF. | Participants narrated the wordless picture book Frog, Where Are You? page by page while being audio recorded; recordings were transcribed and segmented at natural pauses and 20 utterances per participant retained. Two feature classes were extracted with the MATLAB Audio Toolbox and published scripts: rhythm, comprising the envelope spectrum, intrinsic mode functions and temporal modulation spectrum, giving 8,640 features per participant; and intonation, comprising 20 time-normalised f0 values per utterance concatenated to 400 features. Analysis was at the utterance level on the argument that the intonational phrase is universal across languages. Linear-kernel SVMs were trained on principal components under repeated 10-fold cross-validation with PCA and hyperparameter tuning nested inside folds, and significance established by permutation with 5,001 iterations. | Within language, rhythm classified successfully in both: English median AUC 0.900 (accuracy 0.819, sensitivity 0.788, specificity 0.849) and Cantonese 0.962 (accuracy 0.880, sensitivity 0.917, specificity 0.833), both p < 0.001. Intonation classified significantly in English only (AUC 0.695, accuracy 0.683, sensitivity 0.758, specificity 0.606, p = 0.007) and not in Cantonese (0.620, p = 0.507). With languages pooled, rhythm remained robust (AUC 0.886, accuracy 0.835) while intonation fell to near chance (0.559, p = 0.509). Rhythm models were balanced across classes; the significant English intonation model showed good sensitivity but poor specificity. | Forty percent of the English autistic sample and 15% of the English comparison sample were dropped between recruitment and analysis with no reason stated, and the demographic table conflicts with the analysis counts for the Cantonese autistic group. The English groups differ by 42 percentage points in proportion male and by three years in mean age, and this imbalance falls on the one intonation classification that reached significance, where f0 is strongly sex-dependent; a post-hoc analysis is reported only in supplementary material. Diagnostic confirmation rests on ADOS-2 alone with no ADI-R or best-estimate procedure, and part of the Cantonese sample came from employment programmes where the original diagnosis is of unknown provenance. IQ was measured with different instruments in the two language groups, so cognitive level is not comparable across them, and no language ability measure was obtained - which the authors identify as material given that language ability influences pitch. No recording equipment, sampling rate or acoustic condition is reported for either site, a substantive gap for envelope-based features collected at two locations. No confidence intervals on any AUC and no formal test comparing feature classes. The ASPM allele speculation rests on population genetics with no genetic data collected. | The only study in the corpus to test whether a behavioural marker of autism generalises across languages, and its answer is a dissociation that the rest of this review should absorb: rhythm-based prosodic classification survived pooling across a stress-timed Indo-European non-tone language and a syllable-timed Sino-Tibetan tone language at AUC 0.886, while intonation-based classification failed to exceed chance in Cantonese and collapsed to 0.559 when languages were combined. Since almost every other speech study here derives its features and reports its accuracy from a single language and cultural context, this result establishes that such figures carry an untested language-specificity assumption - and identifies exactly which prosodic dimension is most vulnerable to it. The explanation offered is mechanistic rather than post hoc: in tone languages pitch carries lexical meaning, so f0 is phonologically constrained, and the account simultaneously reconciles the standing discrepancy between English studies reporting higher f0 and wider range and Thai and Japanese studies reporting the opposite. Two methodological practices should also carry forward. Dimensionality reduction and hyperparameter tuning are nested inside cross-validation folds - the correct handling with 8,640 features and 66 participants, and the direct contrast with Liao and colleagues, who selected features on the full sample before cross-validating. And permutation testing rather than an assumed chance level is what converts two weak positive-looking AUCs (0.620 and 0.559) into properly reported null results, mirroring the role the empirical chance level plays in Keles and colleagues. Against this, the study is also a reminder that validation discipline cannot repair selection problems: the unexplained loss of 40% of the English autistic sample and the 42-point sex imbalance concentrated on the significant intonation model are not addressed by any amount of nested cross-validation. | [RQ1.1] Four groups across two languages, with recruitment and analysis counts that do not match. Recruited: 55 English-speaking autistic, 39 English-speaking comparison, 28 Cantonese-speaking autistic, 24 Cantonese-speaking comparison. Analysed: 33, 33, 24 and 24 respectively, stated in a parenthesis within the narrative-elicitation section - so 22 of 55 English autistic participants (40%) and 6 of 39 English comparison participants (15%) do not appear in the analysis, with no reason given, no flow diagram, and no comparison between retained and dropped participants. The demographic table reports 28 for the Cantonese autistic group where the analysis text says 24, a further inconsistency. The English participants come from a larger family-genetic study of autism that also enrolled parents and controls; the Cantonese participants were recruited via social media, schools and organisations serving autistic people, and employment programmes for adults previously diagnosed with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism. No other-diagnosis comparison group in either language. [RQ1.2] 'individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'individuals with typical development (TD)' throughout, and uniquely in this corpus the choice is explained rather than defaulted: 'We acknowledge the variability in preferences related to person-first and identity-first terminology (i.e., individuals with ASD versus autistic individuals). We do not endorse one style over the other. For the purpose of this manuscript, to ensure that language is parallel when referencing both participant groups, we remain consistent with the following terminology.' The stated reason - parallelism across the two groups so that neither is described in a grammatically different form from the other - is a considered linguistic argument rather than a convention, and no other paper in the corpus addresses the question at all. Substantively, prosodic variation is framed as 'differences' rather than deficits throughout, including in the title, though the paper does report that such differences 'can contribute to an impression of oddness reported by listeners' when reviewing prior work. [RQ1.3] Tabulated with within-language significance testing, and the picture differs sharply between the two language groups. Cantonese: autistic 19 male : 9 female, 17.83 +/- 9.24 years, IQ 108.54 +/- 10.92; comparison 17 male : 7 female, 18.88 +/- 8.70 years, IQ 115.08 +/- 10.13 - well matched on sex and age, with an IQ gap. English: autistic 29 male : 4 female, 15.96 +/- 7.38 years, IQ 104.13 +/- 14.34; comparison 15 male : 18 female, 19.31 +/- 5.35 years, IQ 111.03 +/- 13.79 - a 42-percentage-point sex imbalance in opposite directions, a three-year age gap, and an IQ gap. The authors identify this asymmetry themselves, referring to 'differences in gender and age observed between the English (but not Cantonese) groups', and run a post-hoc analysis in supplementary material to rule them out as confounds in the English f0 classification. That the confounds are concentrated in the English sample matters because the English intonation model is the only intonation classification that reached significance, and f0 is strongly sex-dependent: an autistic group that is 88% male compared against a group that is 55% female differs in mean pitch for reasons unrelated to diagnosis. Age ranges are wide in every group (6-35 years overall), spanning pre- and post-pubertal voice change. IQ was assessed with Wechsler scales in English and the TONI-4 in Cantonese, so cognitive level is not comparable across languages even though both language groups show a difference favouring comparison participants. [RQ1.4] ADOS-2 with research-reliable administration and scoring, using Overall, Social Affect and Restricted and Repetitive Behavior calibrated severity scores. This is a real observational instrument correctly administered, but it is the only diagnostic evidence described - there is no ADI-R, no DSM criterion application, no clinician best-estimate procedure and no statement of who made the final determination. For a subset of the Cantonese sample recruited through 'employment programmes particularly designed for adults previously diagnosed with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning Autism', the original diagnosis was made elsewhere under unknown procedures and the ADOS-2 serves as confirmation. The comparison groups are handled more stringently than in most studies here, screened for personal or family history of autism or related genetic disorders such as fragile X - a criterion that follows from the English cohort's family-genetic origins and that excludes the broader autism phenotype in relatives. General exclusions of brain injury, major psychiatric disorder, known genetic syndrome and other neurodevelopmental disorders were applied to all participants. [RQ1.5] IQ was measured in every participant, but with different instruments by language group: the WASI, WAIS-III/IV or WISC-IV for English participants and the TONI-4 for Cantonese participants. The TONI-4 is a nonverbal reasoning measure while the Wechsler scales yield full-scale IQ incorporating verbal subtests, so the two sets of scores are not interchangeable and cross-language comparison of cognitive level is not possible. Within each language group the comparison participants score higher (111.03 versus 104.13 in English; 115.08 versus 108.54 in Cantonese). ADOS-2 calibrated severity scores are reported for both autistic groups (7.02 English, 6.00 Cantonese) with full ranges spanning 3-9.5 and 3-10, so both samples cover the severity spectrum. No language ability measure was administered, and the authors identify this as a limitation that matters specifically for their outcome: 'future studies should employ more comprehensive assessments of language abilities for group matching, since baseline language ability may covary with age and autism severity, influencing prosody and pitch in particular'. No adaptive functioning or comorbidity data. [RQ2.1] Goal: identify prosodic differences in autism that span typologically distinct languages and those shaped by language-specific properties, by comparing rhythm-relevant and intonation-relevant acoustic feature classes within English, within Cantonese and across both combined. Main findings: rhythm classified successfully in English (median AUC 0.900), Cantonese (0.962) and combined (0.886), all p < 0.001; intonation classified significantly only in English (0.695, p = 0.007), failing in Cantonese (0.620, p = 0.507) and falling near chance when combined (0.559, p = 0.509). The dissociation is attributed to the phonological role of pitch in tone languages and is used to reconcile the conflicting f0 literature, where higher f0 and wider range are reported in English but lower f0 range in Thai and Japanese. [RQ2.2] Two sites in different countries with different recruitment routes - a research setting in the United States, where participants came from an established family-genetic study of autism, and community recruitment in Hong Kong through social media, schools, autism organisations and employment programmes. The recording setting itself is described minimally: pages presented on a computer monitor with narration audio recorded, and no information about room, microphone, distance or recording equipment in either site. For a study whose primary features are the amplitude envelope and its spectral structure, the absence of any acoustic-recording specification is a genuine reproducibility gap, and it is compounded by the two-site design: if recording conditions differed systematically between the United States and Hong Kong, that difference would be absorbed into the envelope features. The combined-language model would be sensitive to this, though the fact that rhythm classification succeeds within each language separately - where recording conditions are presumably homogeneous - substantially mitigates the concern. [RQ2.3] Narration of Frog, Where Are You?, a 24-page wordless picture book, presented one page at a time on a monitor with no examples given. The choice is the study's enabling methodological decision. Because the book contains no words, the identical stimulus can be administered in any language without translation, and it elicits connected spontaneous narrative rather than repetition, reading or single-word production - so the speech is naturalistic while the content is controlled across participants and across languages. The task has a long history in narrative discourse research in autism and in cross-linguistic work, which the authors cite. Twenty utterances per participant, segmented at natural pauses, were selected for analysis. The analytic level is deliberately the utterance rather than the syllable, on the grounds that 'the utterance is associated with the intonational phrase, the most fundamental unit of prosody argued to be universal across all languages' - the linguistic argument that makes English and Cantonese commensurable, since syllable-level units (final-syllable excursion in English, sentence-final particles in Cantonese) are language-specific and had been the focus of the group's prior work in each language separately. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, one narration per participant, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is adequate but generic: informed assent and consent from all participants and guardians as applicable, approval by each institution's ethics committee, and conformity with the Declaration of Helsinki, without naming the committees or protocol numbers. Data sharing is a genuine strength and rare in this corpus - 'The minimal dataset and analytic scripts are available from the OSF database' with a working URL, so the analysis is independently verifiable even though raw audio is not shared, which is the appropriate handling of identifiable speech. A competing interest is declared: one author owns a startup company supported by a Hong Kong government technology scheme, with a statement that the reported research is not associated with it. [RQ2.5] Essentially nothing on the acquisition side - no microphone, recording device, sampling rate, room or distance is specified for either site, which for a study built on amplitude-envelope spectra is the most consequential reporting omission. Analysis tools are named: the MATLAB Audio Toolbox together with scripts from four prior published studies for the envelope spectrum, intrinsic mode function and temporal modulation spectrum extraction, with further technical detail relegated to supplementary material. The intonation pipeline extracts time-normalised f0 contours at 20 points per utterance. Principal component analysis and a linear-kernel SVM complete the chain. The reliance on published scripts rather than bespoke implementations, together with the OSF deposit of the analysis code, makes the computational half of the pipeline substantially more reproducible than the acquisition half. [RQ2.6] Split sharply between the computational and the empirical. Fully specified or deposited: the two feature classes with their theoretical motivation, the counts (8,640 rhythm features, 400 intonation features), the utterance selection rule and count, the analytic level with its linguistic justification, the classifier and kernel with an argument for the choice, the nested structure of dimensionality reduction and hyperparameter tuning within cross-validation, the permutation testing with 5,001 iterations, and the analysis scripts on OSF. Not specified: any recording equipment or acoustic condition; the reason 22 English autistic and 6 English comparison participants were dropped between recruitment and analysis; how the 20 utterances per participant were selected from the full narrative; who performed transcription and segmentation, with what training or reliability; the number of principal components retained; and the SVM hyperparameter ranges searched. The supplementary file carries the post-hoc confound analysis, the technical feature-extraction detail and a supplementary demonstration that the rhythm features do contain systematic cross-linguistic differences - the last being an important internal check that the combined-language rhythm result is not simply detecting language. [RQ2.7] Three limitations are stated, each substantive. The wide age range across groups and the small number of females are raised together, with the authors arguing that robust classification despite these may indicate 'aspects of prosodic profiles of ASD which are relatively age and gender invariant', supported by the post-hoc analysis, while conceding that 'future studies with larger samples are needed to confirm whether findings reported here extend to both males and females and different age ranges where prosodic abilities may vary'. The absence of language ability measures for group matching is identified with a precise mechanism - baseline language ability covaries with age and autism severity and influences pitch in particular. And the restriction to two languages is named, with specific proposals for extension. What goes unaddressed: the unexplained loss of 40% of the English autistic sample between recruitment and analysis; the discrepancy between the demographic table and the analysis counts for the Cantonese autistic group; the absence of any recording specification; the use of different IQ instruments across language groups, which makes the two samples non-comparable on cognitive level; and the fact that the sex imbalance falls precisely on the English intonation model, the one f0 classification that reached significance. [RQ2.9] Five directions, four of them well grounded. Larger samples covering both sexes and wider age ranges. Comprehensive language-ability assessment for group matching, with the mechanism stated. Extension to further typological classes, with named candidates chosen for their position relative to the two languages studied - German and Dutch as rhythmically similar to English, Japanese as distant from both. Neurophysiological investigation of prosody production across language groups, building on existing findings of increased right inferior frontal gyrus and right caudate activation during prosody comprehension in autism, with the observation that such findings 'would be particularly compelling if replicated in individuals with ASD who are speakers of languages other than English'. The fifth is a proposal to examine the ASPM gene as a marker for prosodic differences, on the basis that most Han Chinese people carry a T allele favouring linguistic pitch processing which 'may implicate a role of genetic factors in contributing to cross-linguistic differences of ASD phenotypes'. This last is speculation built on a population-genetic association applied to a null classification result, with no genetic data collected in the study, and it is the one place where the paper's interpretive discipline lapses - it offers an ancestry-based genetic explanation for a language-based finding when the language explanation the authors themselves give (that lexical tone constrains f0) is sufficient. [RQ3.1] Prosody decomposed into its two canonical components and operationalised as multivariate structure rather than summary statistics. Rhythm is captured through the amplitude envelope - its spectrum, its intrinsic mode functions and its temporal modulation spectrum - with a neurobiological rationale that envelope rhythmicity in the 2-8 Hz band 'is crucial in the neural processing of intelligible speech as it aligns with brain areas in the spoken language processing pathway that oscillate at a similar rate'. Intonation is captured as the full time-normalised f0 contour across each utterance, on the argument that the contour 'encompasses the dynamicity of speech intonation which varies across time within the most fundamental utterance-sized linguistic unit known as the intonational phrase'. The theoretical framing distinguishes affective prosody, which expresses emotion and intent and is broadly recognisable across cultures with possible evolutionary homologies in other mammals, from linguistic prosody, which encodes lexical and grammatical structure and varies drastically across languages - and this distinction predicts the study's result, since rhythm carries more affective and less linguistic load than pitch does in a tone language. [RQ3.2] Not multimodal, but the study performs the corpus's most informative feature-class comparison, which serves an analogous function. Two feature classes representing the two components of prosody are tested on identical participants and identical utterances, within each language and combined, giving six models whose pattern is interpretable as a whole. The result is a dissociation rather than a fusion gain: rhythm classifies in both languages and survives pooling, intonation classifies in one language and collapses on pooling. Crucially the authors do not attempt to combine the two feature classes into a single model - which would have been the obvious accuracy-maximising move and would have obscured the dissociation. That restraint is what makes the study informative: the purpose is to determine which prosodic dimension is cross-linguistically robust, and combining them would have answered a different and less useful question. A supplementary analysis reported in the paper demonstrates that the rhythm features do contain systematic cross-linguistic differences, which is the necessary check that the successful combined-language model is separating diagnosis rather than exploiting language as a proxy - though with the two languages recruited at different sites through different routes, that check carries real weight and would ideally have appeared in the main text. [RQ4.1] A single linear-kernel SVM applied consistently across all six configurations, with the kernel choice argued from the structure of the problem rather than selected empirically: linear kernels are 'preferable to non-linear kernels because theoretically it is always possible to find a linear decision boundary that separates data, in spite of high data dimensionality and small sample size', with precedent cited in neuroimaging and gene expression, where features routinely outnumber samples. Holding the model fixed across all six configurations is the right design for a study whose question is about features rather than about learners - any performance difference between rhythm and intonation, or between English and Cantonese, is attributable to the data rather than to differential model tuning. No alternative classifier is compared, which is appropriate given that no classification-performance claim is being made against competing methods. [RQ4.2] One feature vector per participant, formed by concatenating measures across the 20 selected utterances - so the unit of analysis is the participant and there is no possibility of the utterance-level leakage that would arise if each utterance were treated as an independent sample. Given 8,640 rhythm features against 66 English or 48 Cantonese participants, dimensionality reduction is unavoidable, and the handling is the correct one: principal component analysis is performed inside each cross-validation training fold rather than once on the full dataset, so the components are not informed by test-fold participants. The representational commitment that distinguishes the study is retaining trajectories rather than summaries - a full f0 contour instead of mean and range, an envelope spectrum instead of a speech rate. The cost is interpretability, since no directional statement about any acoustic quantity can be recovered from a principal component of an envelope spectrum, and the paper accordingly reports no group means or effect sizes for any feature. That is a defensible trade for a study whose question is about generalisation across languages rather than about characterising a difference. [RQ4.3] Median AUC across 5,001 iterations with permutation-derived p values, reported alongside accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for every one of the six configurations, with the full AUC distributions displayed as boxplots and aggregated confusion matrices provided. Reporting the median across iterations with its distribution rather than a single point estimate is the correct summary for a repeated cross-validation, and it makes the stability of each result visible. The permutation testing is what carries the paper's central negative claims - without it, a Cantonese intonation AUC of 0.620 and a combined intonation AUC of 0.559 might have been reported as weak but positive results, whereas the permutation p values of 0.507 and 0.509 establish them as indistinguishable from chance. The sensitivity and specificity breakdown adds a further observation the authors draw out: the significant English intonation model has good sensitivity (0.758) but poor specificity (0.606), so it tends to call typically developing participants autistic, while the rhythm models are balanced across classes. No confidence intervals accompany the AUCs, and no formal test compares one model against another - the rhythm-versus-intonation contrast rests on one being significant and the other not, rather than on a test of their difference. [RQ4.4] No feature-level interpretability, and none is possible given principal components of 8,640-dimensional envelope representations - the paper reports no group means, no effect sizes and no directional statements. What it provides instead is interpretability at the level of theoretical construct, which is the level its question operates at. The rhythm-versus-intonation contrast is itself the interpretive result, and the authors connect it to the existing descriptive literature ('the ML algorithms identified in this study appeared to capture patterns from acoustic features that were representative of these prosodic characteristics, paralleling such descriptive observations by clinicians and researchers') and to prior objective measures of speech rate, lexical stress and cross-syllabic durational variability. The Cantonese intonation failure is then given a mechanistic account grounded in phonology - pitch carries lexical meaning in tone languages, so f0 is under phonological constraint - and used to reconcile conflicting prior findings across English, Thai and Japanese. That is a stronger form of interpretation than a feature-importance ranking would have provided, because it generates a testable prediction: intonational differences in autism should be attenuated in tone-language speakers generally. The one interpretive overreach is the ASPM allele speculation, which substitutes a population-genetic explanation for a linguistic one that the paper has already established. [RQ4.5] The strongest aspect of the study, and stated in the terms that matter: 'Several procedures were performed in the classification pipeline to further avoid overfitting and optimistic bias due to limited sample size and the high-dimensionality of data'. Three properties follow. Repeated 10-fold cross-validation is used rather than a single split. Dimensionality reduction into principal components and hyperparameter tuning are both performed 'in a nested fashion' inside the cross-validation, so neither the components nor the hyperparameters are informed by held-out data - the single most common source of optimistic bias in high-dimensional small-sample classification, and one that Liao and colleagues elsewhere in this corpus violate directly by selecting features on the full sample before cross-validating. Significance is established by permutation rather than assumed from a nominal chance level, with 5,001 iterations, and the resulting p values are what license the paper's negative claims. The unit is the participant throughout. What remains: no independent replication cohort, though the two-language design provides a form of internal generalisation test that is arguably stronger for the question at hand; no confidence intervals on the AUCs; no formal test comparing feature classes; and the unexplained 40% attrition from the English autistic sample, which is a selection concern that no amount of validation discipline can address. The combined-language model's validity also rests on the supplementary demonstration that language differences in the rhythm features do not account for the classification, a check that is performed but reported outside the main text. [RQ5.1] No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is cross-linguistic, prosody, rhythm, intonation, tone language, machine learning classification, and autism phenotype - a register that places the work in linguistics and communication science with machine learning as instrument, which matches its actual contribution. [RQ5.2] PLOS ONE 17(6):e0269637 (2022), open access. Authorship spans the Roxelyn and Richard Pepper Department of Communication Sciences and Disorders at Northwestern University, the Department of Linguistics and Modern Languages and Brain and Mind Institute at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Chongqing University, and St. John's University - a genuinely bi-national collaboration, which is what the design requires and which is unique in this corpus. Funding comes from NIH grants in the United States and the Health and Medical Research Fund and two private foundations in Hong Kong. The communication-sciences provenance is visible throughout: the theoretical framing of prosody, the choice of a standard narrative elicitation task, the distinction between affective and linguistic prosody, and the interpretation of results in phonological terms all reflect a speech-language rather than an engineering orientation. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is unusual for this corpus in being about scientific generalisation rather than about diagnostic deployment. The stated problem is not that clinicians are subjective or that diagnosis is slow, but that 'most studies have concentrated on studying prosody in English-speaking groups' while 'language is fundamentally cultural, and how specific aspects of prosody are used can vary substantially across languages' - so the field's evidence base may describe an English-specific phenotype without knowing it. The paper documents the concrete consequence: higher f0 and larger f0 range are reported repeatedly in English-speaking autistic groups, yet a Thai study found lower f0 range and a Japanese study likewise, and the existing cross-linguistic comparisons have all been between closely related languages (English and Danish, both Germanic; Cantonese and Mandarin, both Sinitic). The clinical implications drawn are correspondingly framed around intervention and cultural sensitivity rather than screening - that cross-linguistic differences 'may also help to optimize culturally sensitive diagnostic and intervention practices', and that if extensive pitch experience ameliorates intonational differences then pitch is 'a fruitful target for speech interventions in ASD for those who do not speak a tone language'. Diagnostic application is mentioned only in the conclusion and hedged: 'although further study with larger samples, and with additional language comparisons, is needed to support adaptation of the current models into clinical use'. The methodological argument against scalar summaries - that averaging or taking extreme values discards the dynamics that constitute prosody - is also a positional claim about how the field measures, and it is the study's most transferable methodological contribution. |
| S-083 | Cross-sectional case-control study in Poland: 25 participants with a prior multidisciplinary ICD-10 diagnosis of idiopathic autism (14.55 +/- 5.46 years, non-verbal IQ 109.08, verbal IQ 106.62, ADOS-2 overall 13.60, SCQ 22.19) and 25 typically developing comparisons (14.38 +/- 5.83 years, non-verbal IQ 114.64, verbal IQ 113.12, ADOS-2 2.48, SCQ 3.60), matched on age (p = 0.92), sex and ethnicity and near-matched on both IQ measures. All required non-verbal IQ of 80 or above, fluent Polish and no sensory or mobility impairment; comparisons additionally excluded for personal or family autism history, developmental disorders and psychiatric or genetic conditions. Narratives elicited during ADOS-2 administrations by research-reliable clinicians; transcripts not publicly released on privacy grounds. | Participants narrated the 15-page wordless picture book Tuesday during the ADOS-2 Telling a Story from a Book task, producing on average 22 sentences and 323 tokens over 4 minutes 24 seconds. Video recordings were transcribed independently by two blind transcribers in CHAT format with 91% word-level reliability and discrepancies resolved against video. Text was encoded by Polish ELMo (1024 dimensions) and Universal Sentence Encoder large v3 (512 dimensions) under three schemes: one vector for the whole narration; page-level vectors concatenated with zero vectors for the roughly 15% of pages with no utterance; and page-level vectors with neural masking. XGBoost, SVM with radial and linear kernels, and a tuned single dense layer were applied, with leave-one-out cross-validation over participants. Two psychiatrists independently classified participants from the same transcripts, and ADOS-2 and SCQ performance was computed on the same sample. | Best computational configurations - ELMo with page-level zero-vector representation and SVM, and USE with the same representation and XGBoost - both reached sensitivity 0.72, specificity 0.68, PPV 0.69 and NPV 0.71. ELMo with a single whole-narration vector gave the highest sensitivity (0.76) at the lowest specificity (0.60). The two psychiatrists reading identical transcripts reached sensitivity 0.56 and 0.60 with specificity 0.60 and 0.64. ADOS-2 on the same sample reached sensitivity 1.00 and specificity 0.92; SCQ reached 0.92 and 0.96. Page-level representation with zero vectors beat both whole-narration and masked representations, and the two structurally different encoders reached identical top scores. | Only the best classifier per input combination is reported, across three families and a 27-point hyperparameter grid, selected on the same leave-one-out folds used for reporting. No AUC, confidence interval or significance test accompanies any figure, so a sensitivity of 0.72 rests on 18 of 25 cases with an interval spanning roughly 0.51-0.88. The sample is restricted to fluent speakers with non-verbal IQ of 80 or above and, as the authors concede, was 'carefully selected with clear signs of ASD' with no developmental problems in comparisons - which also inflates the instrument ceiling relative to real clinical practice.
