Sex composition is claimed as matched but never reported. Page-level segmentation was manual and is acknowledged as sometimes ambiguous, requiring video to resolve. No non-spectrum clinical comparison group, only one narrative context, no interpretability, and transcripts not publicly deposited. | The corpus's most useful calibration study, and it earns that role through a design choice rather than a result. By placing six model configurations, two experienced psychiatrists and two standardised instruments in one table with identical metrics on the same 50 participants, it supplies both bounds that a single-model accuracy figure cannot: a floor, since clinicians reading the same transcripts performed near chance and the models beat them, establishing that narrative text carries extractable signal; and a ceiling, since ADOS-2 reached 1.00 sensitivity and 0.92 specificity on the same people while the best model reached 0.72 and 0.68. That gap - roughly 28 points of sensitivity between an automated narrative classifier and the observational instrument it might supplement - is the single most useful quantity in this review for calibrating what the corpus's other reported accuracies would mean clinically, and almost no other study provides it. The interpretation drawn is correspondingly disciplined: the authors state that beating psychiatrists on isolated transcripts 'does not indicate that neural networks can replace clinical judgment' because clinicians do not work from isolated statements, and that automated narrative analysis 'may only be complementary or supportive'. Two further practices transfer. Transcription reliability is quantified at 91% word-level agreement between blind independent transcribers, the only such figure in the corpus and a necessary precondition for any text-based measure. And the single-vector representation is recommended for clinical use over the marginally better page-level one because the latter cannot be automated - a deployability argument allowed to override a performance argument, which is the reasoning the rest of this literature almost never performs. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of 25, recruited through a university clinic, diagnostic or therapeutic centres and schools, and 'matched for age, sex and ethnicity, and nearly matched for intelligence quotients'. The autistic group required a prior clinical diagnosis of idiopathic autism from a multidisciplinary team including a psychiatrist under ICD-10 criteria; the comparison group was excluded for personal or family history of autism, history of developmental disorders, and neurological or psychiatric conditions or suspected genetic syndromes. No other-diagnosis comparison group, which the authors identify as a limitation and propose for future work: 'as we compared individuals with ASD and controls with TD, future studies should include individuals with non-spectrum disorders and other psychiatric conditions'. The design's distinguishing feature is that two further comparators operate on the same 50 participants - two standardised instruments and two human raters - so the study contains four independent classification approaches on one sample rather than one model evaluated in isolation. [RQ1.2] 'individuals with ASD', 'participants with ASD', 'people with ASD', 'individuals with typical development', 'participants with TD' - consistently person-first, with 'controls with TD' used for the comparison group. 'Patients' appears once in a general statement about clinical practice. The framing acknowledges heterogeneity explicitly at the outset - 'the clinical expression of the disorder is heterogeneous, and symptoms may vary widely from person to person. The cognitive abilities of people with ASD can range from gifted to severely challenged' - and describes autistic people as those who 'may communicate, interact, behave and learn differently from most other people', which is a difference rather than deficit construction. Narrative characteristics are nonetheless described in deficit terms throughout the literature review ('poor narrative skills', 'struggle with conveying the gist', 'deficits in pragmatic language'), reflecting the source literature. [RQ1.3] Reported with tests for every variable. Autistic group: 25 participants, 14.55 +/- 5.46 years (7.1-24.6), non-verbal IQ 109.08 +/- 13.04 (80-140), verbal IQ 106.62 +/- 19.70 (72-131). Comparison group: 25 participants, 14.38 +/- 5.83 years (7.3-25.3), non-verbal IQ 114.64 +/- 12.50 (80-134), verbal IQ 113.12 +/- 14.33 (85-141). Age matches closely (p = 0.92) and both IQ measures are non-significant (p = 0.13 and p = 0.20), though the authors describe the match as 'nearly matched' and list imperfect IQ matching among their limitations - an appropriately cautious reading, since a five-to-six point gap in both verbal and non-verbal IQ at n = 25 per group is underpowered to detect. Verbal IQ matters particularly here because the outcome is narrative language. The one reporting gap is sex: the groups are stated to be matched on sex and ethnicity, but no counts, proportions or test are given for either, so the claim cannot be verified. The age range is wide (7 to 25 years), spanning most of narrative development, and the authors note they could not stratify by age, sex or IQ at this sample size. [RQ1.4] Two-stage and well structured. Entry required a prior clinical diagnosis of idiopathic autism made by a multidisciplinary team including a psychiatrist under ICD-10 criteria - so ascertainment is clinical and independent of the research team. For the study itself, ADOS-2 was administered by research-reliable clinicians under the supervision of an author who is an ADOS-2 trainer, and parents completed the SCQ. The critical design detail is stated explicitly: 'Prior to this study, participants were not evaluated using SCQ and ADOS-2 measures.' That independence is what makes the instruments usable as comparators rather than as circular confirmations - though not entirely, since group membership was determined by the prior clinical diagnosis and the instruments are then evaluated against that same clinical determination. The Polish versions of both instruments have published psychometric validation, and the SCQ's reported agreement with clinical diagnosis (kappa 0.84) and with ADI-R (kappa 0.81) is cited. The comparison group's negative status is established by three separate exclusions plus fresh ADOS-2 and SCQ administration. [RQ1.5] Both verbal and non-verbal IQ measured in every participant using age-appropriate Wechsler scales - the WISC-R for those aged 6.0-16.11 and the WAIS for those older - with means, standard deviations, ranges and t-tests reported for both. Reporting verbal and non-verbal IQ separately is appropriate and uncommon, and matters directly for a narrative-language outcome. Non-verbal IQ of 80 or above was an inclusion criterion, so the sample is confined to participants without intellectual disability, which the authors identify as limiting generalisation: 'our study included only fluently speaking participants with ASD with no intellectual disability and might not apply to everyone on the autism spectrum'. ADOS-2 overall and SCQ overall scores characterise severity in both groups. No adaptive functioning or language-specific standardised measure was administered, and no comorbidity information is reported beyond the idiopathic-autism inclusion requirement. [RQ2.1] Goal: evaluate deep neural text encoders for detecting autism from narrative transcripts and compare them against standardised instruments and human expert judgement on the same participants. Main findings: best computational configurations reached sensitivity 0.72 and specificity 0.68; two psychiatrists reading identical transcripts achieved 0.56-0.60 sensitivity and 0.60-0.64 specificity, close to chance; ADOS-2 achieved 1.00 sensitivity and 0.92 specificity and SCQ 0.92 and 0.96 on the same sample; page-level representation with zero vectors for skipped pages outperformed whole-narration representation; and ELMo and USE reached identical top scores despite different architectures, suggesting representation granularity matters more than encoder choice. [RQ2.2] Poland, with participants contacted through a university clinic, diagnostic or therapeutic centres, or schools, and assessed as part of a research evaluation. The narratives themselves come from ADOS-2 administrations conducted by research-reliable clinicians, so the elicitation context is a standardised clinical assessment rather than a naturalistic setting. This has the same double edge noted in the OHSU studies: the standardisation makes narratives comparable across participants and the data are a by-product of an assessment already being conducted, but the assessment is specifically designed to elicit autism-related behaviour, so performance may not transfer to spontaneous narration. The authors raise the related point about narrative context, citing evidence that 'participants with ASD exhibit lower performance in less structured tasks (i.e., narratives of personal experiences, conversation) than more structured picture book tasks' - which implies, though the authors do not draw the inference explicitly, that a less structured elicitation might yield stronger rather than weaker classification. [RQ2.3] The ADOS-2 Telling a Story from a Book task using Tuesday by David Wiesner, a 15-page wordless picture book in which frogs float on lily pads and fly over a town at night. The choice is substantively motivated: the book presents 'unreal and humorous situations, and several mental and emotional states of the characters', so producing a coherent narrative requires inference about characters' internal states, causal linking of unusual events, and management of a fantastical premise - exactly the pragmatic demands the narrative literature identifies as difficult in autism. Being wordless, it supplies no linguistic scaffolding, so the entire narrative is the participant's construction. The resulting samples are short: on average 22 sentences, 323 tokens and 4 minutes 24 seconds, with participants producing utterances for a mean of 13.6 of 15 pages. That brevity is the practical constraint on the whole study - a few hundred words per person is a thin basis for a 15,360-dimensional representation - and the paper's honest performance figures should be read against it. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, one narration per participant, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is complete and unusually granular on consent, which was obtained separately from three parties as applicable: parents of participants under 16, parents of participants aged 16 and older, and the participants themselves - a structure that respects the assent of older adolescents and adults alongside parental consent. Approval came from the Faculty of Psychology, University of Warsaw Research Ethics Committee, with Declaration of Helsinki conformity stated. Data are withheld from public deposit on an explicit and appropriate privacy rationale - narrative transcripts of identifiable clinical assessments 'containing information that could compromise the privacy of the research participants' - with availability on request from the named authors. No competing interests, with Polish National Science Centre and University of Warsaw funding declared. [RQ2.5] No specialised acquisition equipment - narratives were video recorded during ADOS-2 sessions already being conducted. The methodological weight sits on transcription, which is described more carefully than in any other study here: two experienced transcribers worked independently and blind to diagnosis, following the Codes for Human Analysis of Transcripts convention, achieving word-level reliability averaging 91%; one trained transcriber then compared the two transcripts word for word and resolved discrepancies by reference to the video. Reporting an actual reliability figure for transcription is unique in this corpus - MacFarlane and colleagues describe extensive transcriber training and consistency checks but state explicitly that they have no reliability results. Computational tools are named precisely: the Polish ELMo from ELMoForManyLangs pre-trained on 20 million words from Wikipedia and Common Crawl, at default settings; Universal Sentence Encoder large v3; XGBoost with default settings; scikit-learn NuSVC; and TensorFlow 2, with package URLs given in footnotes. [RQ2.6] Good on the computational pipeline and the language sample, thinner on the participants. Reported: inclusion and exclusion criteria for both groups; the ADOS-2 task and the specific book; the transcription protocol with its convention, blinding, reliability figure and discrepancy resolution; descriptive statistics of the transcripts (sentences, tokens, duration, pages narrated); all three representation schemes with their vector dimensions and the 15% missing-page rate; every encoder with its version, pre-training corpus and settings; the classifier families with the dense layer's full hyperparameter grid; the leave-one-out scheme; and package URLs. A footnote even records that recurrent classifiers were tried and performed substantially worse. Not reported: sex composition despite matching being claimed; how the narrative was divided into page-level subsets, described only as done manually and acknowledged as 'sometimes ambiguous, especially when a participant skips one of the pages'; the number of trials or seeds; and any AUC, confidence interval or significance test. Data are available on request rather than deposited, for stated privacy reasons; no code release. [RQ2.7] Six limitations are stated, all substantive. The sample is small with a wide age range and imperfect IQ matching, so 'we were not able to divide our sample into subgroups based on age, sex or IQ level'. The sample includes only fluently speaking participants without intellectual disability, so results 'might not apply to everyone on the autism spectrum' - followed by an unusually thoughtful observation that this may mean the figures 'show the upper limit of diagnostic possibilities from the closed text data only'. Only one narrative context was tested, with the authors noting prior evidence that less structured tasks are harder for autistic participants. No non-spectrum clinical comparison group was included. The approach requires high-quality transcription, which remains difficult to automate for spontaneous speech. And the models offer no interpretability. The authors additionally volunteer, when discussing why their instruments outperformed published validation figures, that 'participants in our sample were carefully selected with clear signs of ASD among individuals in the ASD group and lack of developmental problems among individuals in the TD group' - a candid acknowledgement that the sample is easier than a clinical population, which qualifies their own headline comparison. Not addressed: that only the best classifier per input combination is reported, over three families and a 27-point grid; the absence of any confidence interval on figures derived from 25 cases per class; and the unreported sex composition. [RQ2.9] Six directions, each following from a stated limitation. Larger samples permitting stratification by age, sex and IQ. Inclusion of non-spectrum and other psychiatric groups. Other narrative contexts, with the specific prediction that less structured elicitation may behave differently. Model explanation techniques applied to word-level contributions, with the goal that 'giving meaning to collections of important words may lead to discovering new dimensions of language relevant to ASD' - which frames explainability as a route to linguistic discovery rather than only to trust. Combination of text with speech and extra-linguistic features, citing Asgari and colleagues and Fusaroli and colleagues. And automatic speech-to-text to eliminate the transcription bottleneck. The authors also express a clear preference between their own representations for translational purposes: 'the single vector approach, rather than the pages approach, seems to have the greatest possible clinical utility', because page segmentation is ambiguous and manual whereas the single vector 'enables full automation and objectification of the measurement' - choosing the marginally worse-performing option on deployability grounds, which is the right kind of reasoning and rare in this corpus. [RQ3.1] Narrative discourse as linguistic content, deliberately abstracted from acoustics. What is modelled is the semantic and syntactic structure of what the participant said, encoded by language models pre-trained on general Polish text - so the target is pragmatic and structural narrative ability rather than prosody or voice quality. The literature review specifies the constructs at stake: conveying the gist of a story, appropriate use of referential devices, coherence and causal connection, avoidance of irrelevant components, lexical diversity, and internal state language describing characters' perceptions, emotions and cognitive states. None of these is measured directly; the embeddings are expected to capture them implicitly, which is the study's bet and also the source of its interpretability gap. The complement to this design is Asgari and colleagues elsewhere in this corpus, who model the acoustics of the same kind of ADOS-derived speech while discarding the content, and MacFarlane and colleagues, who show that the two channels detect different participants. [RQ3.2] Single modality - text only, with no acoustic or extra-linguistic input, and combination with speech features named as future work. Within the modality the study performs a systematic representation comparison that functions as its main experimental variable: two encoders crossed with three representation schemes, reported as six configurations. The pattern is informative. Page-level representation with zero vectors beat whole-narration representation for both encoders, which the authors attribute to information loss in aggregation - 'the aggregation that occurs in the single vector approach for the whole narration causes some key information to be lost' - and to the possibility that particular pages matter more than others. The zero-vector scheme also beat masking, which is the more interesting of the two comparisons: masking tells the model to ignore pages the participant skipped, while zero vectors leave a marked absence, and the better performance of the latter supports the authors' reading that 'even missing out certain pages may provide clues to identify ASD participants'. Silence is treated as signal rather than as missing data. And the two encoders reaching identical top scores despite one being a bidirectional LSTM and the other a transformer suggests the architecture is not the limiting factor at this sample size. [RQ4.1] Frozen pre-trained encoders feeding conventional classifiers, rather than end-to-end fine-tuning - the appropriate choice for 50 participants and roughly 300 words each, and justified on exactly those grounds: 'Thanks to the properties of embedding vectors, classification algorithms can successfully learn from relatively small labelled data sets.' Three classifier families were tried (XGBoost, SVM with two kernels, and a single dense layer with a 27-point hyperparameter grid), and a footnote records that recurrent classifiers were also tested and performed substantially worse. Reporting the failed recurrent experiments is good practice. The problem is the reporting rule for the successful ones: 'For each input combination we only report the results of the best performing classifier', so each of the six reported figures is the maximum over at least three classifier configurations and, for the masking rows, over a 27-point grid - all selected on the same leave-one-out folds used for reporting, with no held-out estimate of the selection cost. [RQ4.2] One feature vector per participant in every configuration, so the unit is the person and leave-one-out cross-validation is genuinely participant-level. The representation question is the study's actual experiment, and it is framed as a trade-off rather than an optimisation. The page-level scheme carries far more information - 15,360 dimensions for ELMo against 1024 for the single vector - and performs marginally better, but requires manually segmenting the narrative by book page, which the authors describe as 'sometimes ambiguous, especially when a participant skips one of the pages during storytelling' and which they were only able to resolve because they had video recordings; with audio alone it 'may require arbitrary decisions whether the utterance should be assigned to one page or the next'. They then recommend the single-vector approach for clinical use despite its slightly lower scores, because it is fully automatable. That is a deployability argument overriding a performance argument, made explicitly, and it is the kind of reasoning almost absent from the rest of this corpus. [RQ4.3] Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value - clinically appropriate metrics reported identically for all ten rows of the comparison table. Reporting PPV and NPV alongside sensitivity and specificity is uncommon here and is meaningful in this design because the class balance is 25:25, so the predictive values are directly interpretable as performance at 50% prevalence. The table's real contribution is its scope: six model configurations, two human raters and two standardised instruments, all evaluated on the same 50 participants with the same four metrics, which allows the reader to locate the models between a human floor and an instrument ceiling rather than against an absent baseline. What is missing matters at this sample size. There is no AUC, no confidence interval and no significance test anywhere, so a sensitivity of 0.72 represents 18 of 25 correct and carries a binomial confidence interval running from roughly 0.51 to 0.88 - wide enough that the differences among the six configurations, and between the models and the raters, are not established. Nor is any chance or trivial baseline reported, though the balanced design makes 0.50 the natural reference and the human raters serve a similar function empirically. [RQ4.4] None, and the authors treat this as the study's principal scientific shortcoming rather than a minor gap: 'Neural network encoders followed by classifiers can take into account a wide variety of utterance characteristics but does not help to identify which particular aspects of language are crucial.' They frame the remedy as a route to discovery rather than to trust, proposing LIME-style word-level attribution so that 'giving meaning to collections of important words may lead to discovering new dimensions of language relevant to ASD', and connecting it to their own prior work identifying sentiment and language abstraction as relevant dimensions - while noting 'it is very likely that this list is not exhaustive'. That framing is correct: for a study whose motivating literature is entirely about specific narrative constructs (coherence, causal connection, referential devices, internal state language), a classifier that cannot say which of these it is using contributes no linguistic knowledge. The one indirect interpretive finding is that skipped pages carry signal, inferred from zero-vector representation outperforming masking. [RQ4.5] Leave-one-out cross-validation with the participant as the held-out unit, chosen deliberately for small-sample efficiency, and correctly described. Because each participant is represented by a single vector there is no possibility of utterance-level leakage. What is not controlled is selection: only the best classifier per input combination is reported, across three families and, for the masking configurations, a 27-point hyperparameter grid, all evaluated on the same folds that produce the reported numbers. With 50 participants and six reported configurations each maximised over several classifiers, the optimism is unquantified and could plausibly account for a substantial part of the 12-point gap between the best models (0.72) and the human raters (0.60). No permutation test, confidence interval or AUC is reported to bound this. Set against that, the study's benchmarking design provides a form of validation that internal resampling cannot: the human raters constitute an empirical performance floor obtained on identical input, and the standardised instruments an empirical ceiling obtained on identical participants, both of which anchor the model figures in a way no single-model study can achieve. The authors themselves qualify the ceiling, noting that their instruments exceeded their own published validation figures because the sample was selected for clear-cut cases while the validation sample included non-spectrum clinical participants. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorders (ASD), deep neural networks, deep learning, language processing, narrative. The inclusion of 'narrative' alongside three method terms signals the study's dual location in computational linguistics and communication disorders, and the journal's structured 'What this paper adds' box frames the contribution in clinical rather than technical terms. [RQ5.2] International Journal of Language and Communication Disorders 57(5):948-962 (2022), published on behalf of the Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists - a speech and language therapy journal, so the readership is clinical rather than computational. Authorship pairs the Institute of Computer Science of the Polish Academy of Sciences with the Faculty of Psychology at the University of Warsaw, with equal contribution declared, and the psychology author is an ADOS-2 trainer who supervised the assessments. That composition explains the study's shape: the clinical measurement is handled to research standards (research-reliable ADOS-2 administration, blind dual transcription with reliability, three-tier consent) while the computational work is competent but modest, and the interpretation is oriented toward what a speech and language therapist could use. The journal's format requires an explicit statement of clinical implications, which the authors use to state the supportive rather than replacement role of the method. [RQ5.3] 2022 (submitted October 2020, accepted April 2022). The framing is unusual in this corpus for beginning from the strength of existing practice rather than its weakness: 'the validity and reliability of diagnosis of ASD improves considerably when diagnostic evaluation is carried out using standardized tools with good psychometric properties', and computational models are positioned as tools that 'may provide tools that, similarly to psychological testing, support clinicians in their decision-making'. The limiting statement follows immediately - 'due to the multidimensionality and complexity of the diagnosis problem, the role of such automatic analyses of narratives may only be complementary or supportive' - and the paper then proves its own point by measuring the gap between its models and the standardised instruments. The specific clinical gap it identifies is narrower and better argued than the usual appeals to cost or delay: hand-coding of narratives 'is time and labour intensive, and requires extensive training for coders to achieve reliability', which 'limit[s] sample sizes and may be difficult to implement across different research sites', while 'objective, valid and reliable measures of narration ability among individuals with ASD with no clear structural language deficits are limited' and 'standardized tests often miss evident-in-naturalistic-settings differences'. The target population is therefore explicitly the group for whom current instruments are least sensitive - 'participants with less severe autism spectrum-related symptoms, more advanced language, and no intellectual disability' - and the sample is constructed to match, with non-verbal IQ of 80 or above and fluent speech required. |
| S-084 | Cross-sectional case-control study in Ankara: 61 toddlers with a clinical DSM-5 autism diagnosis from licensed child psychiatrists (34.85 months, 37:24 male:female, Bayley cognitive 77.79, language 67.70, 55 M-CHAT high risk) and 72 typically developing toddlers (32.90 months, 38:34, Bayley cognitive 98.0, language 101.27, all M-CHAT no risk), aged 26-36 months. Groups matched on age (p = 0.07) but differing significantly on sex (p = 0.00) and on both Bayley scores (p < 0.001). Comparison children required no autism in any first- or second-degree relative. No observational diagnostic instrument administered. Machine-learning data publicly posted; no ethics statement. | A paired preferential-viewing paradigm presented social interaction videos against non-social competitors side by side, six pairs of 16-second videos with 2-second central fixation dots between and left-right position counterbalanced, split into a social-versus-toys set and a social-versus-animations set. Gaze was recorded on an SMI RED250 at 250 Hz at approximately 60 cm, with five-point calibration repeated until deviation fell below one degree. Thirteen area-of-interest metrics were computed for both the social and non-social regions and averaged across the three videos in each set. ReliefF, Information Gain and Wrapper feature selection were applied, and decision tree, naive Bayes, random forest and SVM classifiers trained on each resulting set under participant-based 10-fold cross-validation on class-balanced data. | Best accuracy 87.5% with ROC area 0.888 (random forest) and 0.875 (SVM), both with ReliefF features on the animation dataset, at true positive rates of 0.800 for autistic and 0.950 for comparison toddlers. Best on the toys dataset 85.0% (naive Bayes with Information Gain). Across all 24 configurations accuracy ranged 67.5-87.5%, with animations outperforming toys on average (84.37% versus 78.12%). Mean looking times: animation AOI 6.061 s for autistic against 3.204 s for comparisons; people AOI in the animation set 5.679 s against 10.370 s; the toys set showed much smaller separations. Net dwell time, diversion duration and first fixation duration on the social AOI were selected by all three algorithms. Net dwell time alone gave 70.67% and 79.17%, below the multivariate sets. | The number of participants entering classification cannot be reconciled with the 133 recruited: every reported accuracy falls on a 2.5-point grid and every true positive rate on a 0.05 grid, arithmetically consistent with roughly 20 per class, and the statement that classes were balanced gives no size or selection rule. The groups differ by 20 Bayley cognitive points and 34 language points, neither adjusted for nor mentioned outside the demographic table, with the authors justifying non-matching on the ground that passive viewing does not require cognitive or language skills. The 87.5% is the maximum across 24 configurations preceded by feature selection including an accuracy-driven Wrapper method whose nesting is asserted but not described. No confidence intervals, significance tests, classifier hyperparameters or trivial baselines. Sensitivity for the autistic class is the weaker side throughout, at 0.800 in the best model. No ethics approval or consent statement appears anywhere. The claim that above-80% accuracy on balanced data indicates the system can handle class imbalance does not follow. | Two contributions transfer regardless of the reliability of the headline figure. The first is a directly usable design finding: by testing two classes of non-social competitor as separate datasets on the same children, the study shows that spinning animations expose the attentional bias substantially better than familiar toys, with autistic toddlers looking at animations for nearly double the comparison group's duration while looking at people for roughly half - divergences that largely disappear when toys are the competitor. Anyone constructing a preferential-viewing paradigm for this age group has an empirical basis for stimulus choice that the rest of this corpus does not supply. The second is featural: diversion duration, a measure of the cost of disengaging from an area of interest, was selected as discriminative by all three feature-selection algorithms, and the authors note against their own published systematic review that this metric is essentially absent from an eye-tracking literature dominated by fixation count, fixation time, average fixation duration and dwell time. Their single-feature ablation, showing that multivariate selection beats the best individual metric, is the check that supports treating this as a real finding rather than a ranking artefact. The study is also notable for the quality of its critique of the surrounding literature - surveying prior accuracies, identifying the sources of their variance, citing meta-regression evidence that poorly designed studies overestimate group differences, and dissecting a widely cited geometric-preference result to point out that only 40% of autistic participants showed the effect. That makes its own unexplained sample reduction and its silence on a 34-point language gap the more instructive: the study demonstrates that awareness of the field's methodological failures does not by itself prevent reproducing them. | [RQ1.1] Two groups recruited: 61 toddlers with a clinical DSM-5 autism diagnosis and 72 typically developing toddlers, all aged 26-36 months, from a university-based research centre in Ankara. Recruitment was multi-source for the autistic group - a research centre database, speech and language clinics, and child psychiatrists at accredited hospitals, across both metropolitan and rural areas - and community-based for comparisons. No developmental-delay comparison group, which the authors identify as needed: future work should include 'children with developmental delays'. The critical unresolved issue is that the classification analyses do not appear to use all 133 recruited children. The paper states that 'we used balanced datasets in our study in terms of ASD and TD children distribution... in which all classes had the same number of training samples', and every reported accuracy across all six results tables falls on a 2.5-percentage-point grid while every per-class true positive rate falls on a 0.05 grid - a pattern arithmetically consistent with roughly 20 participants per class and inconsistent with 61 and 72. No exclusion count, flow accounting or subsampling rule is given anywhere, so the number of children behind the headline 87.5% and the basis on which they were selected are both unstated. [RQ1.2] 'young children with ASD', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', against 'TD children' and 'typically developing children'. Consistently person-first, with 'young children' rather than 'subjects' or 'patients' throughout, which suits a toddler sample. The framing is deficit-oriented in describing attention - 'diminished attention to social stimuli', 'social orienting impairment', 'attentional bias toward non-social stimuli may compete with social cognition development' - but the paper is notably even-handed in one respect that most of this corpus is not: it repeatedly frames the phenomenon as involving 'both diminished and superior processing', treating heightened attention to animations and objects as a positive preference rather than only as a failure to attend socially. Autism is described as 'a spectrum rather than a distinct clinical disorder... which means that the symptoms can present in various combinations and range from mild to severe', invoked specifically to explain the study's false negatives. [RQ1.3] Reported with tests, and the picture is one of a single successful match against two large failures. Age: 34.85 months for the autistic group against 32.90 for comparisons, p = 0.07 - matched, though marginally, and matching on age was the stated design intention. Sex: 37:24 against 38:34, reported as p = 0.00, acknowledged in the limitations. Development: Bayley-III cognitive scores of 77.79 against 98.0 and language scores of 67.70 against 101.27, both p < 0.001. The language gap of 33.6 standard score points is the largest developmental difference reported in any study in this corpus, and the cognitive gap of 20 points places the autistic group's mean more than one standard deviation below the comparison group's. Neither is adjusted for, stratified on, or listed as a limitation. The authors' stated reason for matching only on age is that 'the study involved a passive viewing paradigm and did not require cognitive or language processing skills', which conflates task demands with developmental sensitivity: no response was required, but where a 30-month-old looks when a conversing adult and child compete against a spinning animation is itself a developmental milestone, and a group averaging a 34-point language deficit would be expected to attend differently to a social interaction scene for reasons that are not specific to autism. Standard deviations are not reported for age or for either Bayley score. [RQ1.4] Clinical diagnosis by licensed child psychiatrists under DSM-5 criteria, established before study entry and applied as an eligibility criterion, with subsequent exclusion of comorbid conditions including seizure disorder, known genetic disorder and uncorrectable sensory impairment. No observational diagnostic instrument - no ADOS, ADI-R or CARS - was administered, so ascertainment rests on clinical judgement whose procedures are not described beyond the practitioners' qualification. The M-CHAT-R/F was administered and its distribution reported by group (55 high risk and 6 medium risk among autistic participants; all 72 comparisons at no risk), which provides useful confirmation that the groups separate on a standardised screener but is not itself a diagnostic instrument, and the authors are clear-eyed about its limits, citing evidence of 'low to moderate accuracy' and explaining their use of it on the practical ground that it 'is the only available standardized screening instrument in the participants' native language'. The comparison group's negative status is established more stringently than the autistic group's positive status: no autism in any first- or second-degree relative, and no sibling with developmental, behavioural or emotional symptoms. [RQ1.5] Developmental level was measured properly, with the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition - an age-appropriate instrument covering 1 to 42 months, cited with its psychometric properties - administered to both groups and reported separately for cognition and language. That both groups were assessed is a genuine strength relative to studies here that measure cognition in the autistic group only or not at all. The problem is that the resulting data are used descriptively and never analytically: the 20-point cognitive gap and 34-point language gap are tabulated and then absent from every subsequent analysis, with no covariate adjustment, no matched subsample, and no mention in the discussion or limitations. No autism severity instrument was administered, so the model's outputs cannot be related to a severity gradient and the false-negative analysis the authors themselves call for - assessing 'the symptom profiles of false-negative children' - is not possible with the data collected. No comorbidity or medication information beyond the exclusion criteria. [RQ2.1] Goal: develop and test a decision support system for early autism screening in toddlers, and determine whether toys or animations are the more effective non-social competitor in a preferential-viewing paradigm. Main findings: best accuracy 87.5% with ROC area 0.888 (random forest and SVM with ReliefF features on the animation dataset); animations outperformed toys across most configurations, with mean looking times showing autistic toddlers viewing animations for 6.06 s against 3.20 s for comparisons and people for 5.68 s against 10.37 s; diversion duration, net dwell time and first fixation duration on the social area of interest were selected as discriminative by all three feature-selection algorithms; multivariate feature sets beat net dwell time alone (78.12% and 84.37% against 70.67% and 79.17%); and 12.5% of autistic toddlers were false negatives even in the best model. [RQ2.2] A purpose-built eye-tracking laboratory at a university research centre for children with special needs, with lighting described as optimised for tracking. The acquisition arrangement is described with the care a toddler paradigm requires: children sat approximately 60 cm from the screen either alone or on a parent's lap, screen distance and height adjusted individually, a researcher accompanying each parent-child pair throughout, a five-point calibration using a crying cartoon as the attention-catching target, and calibration repeated for each child until deviation in both x and y fell below one degree. Repeating calibration to a stated tolerance rather than accepting the first attempt is a discipline few studies here report. The setting is a controlled laboratory rather than a clinic or home, which the authors implicitly acknowledge as a limitation of the field when they call for 'less intrusive screening instruments that do not require tightly controlled environments' - a requirement their own paradigm does not yet meet. [RQ2.3] A paired preferential-viewing paradigm with social and non-social content presented simultaneously on either side of a central dividing line, six pairs in total, each a 16-second video preceded by a 2-second central red fixation dot, with the 2-second segments excluded from analysis and left-right position counterbalanced. The design's distinctive feature is treating the non-social competitor as an experimental variable rather than a fixed choice. Two competitor classes were used, both selected on empirical rather than theoretical grounds - toys 'selected because many young children with ASD highly preferred these toys during their free play activities at the university-based research center', and spinning animations chosen because 'many young children with ASD's parents report that their children are highly interested in screen time compared to playtime and reading together'. The social videos were deliberately naturalistic, filmed in a playroom with a colourful carpet, shelves and toys, 'to observe how children view a natural environment' - which raises the competitive demand, since the social scene itself contains objects. The comparison then answers a design question the rest of the eye-tracking literature leaves implicit: which competitor best exposes the attentional bias. The answer, that animations beat toys, is directly usable by anyone constructing such a paradigm. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. The most conspicuous reporting omission in the paper is ethical: no ethics committee approval, protocol number, consent or assent statement appears anywhere in the extracted text, despite the participants being toddlers with clinical diagnoses recruited through hospitals and clinics. Funding by the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey is acknowledged and a conflict-of-interest declaration is present, so the absence is not a matter of missing front matter. Against this, data sharing is handled well: an open practices statement provides a URL at which 'the study data for all machine learning experiments are available', which is more than most studies here offer and which would in principle allow the sample-size discrepancy to be resolved externally. [RQ2.5] Fully specified and appropriate to the age group. An SMI RED250 remote eye tracker at 250 Hz - remote rather than head-mounted, which is necessary for toddlers - mounted below a 17-inch LCD at 1680x1050 resolution, with stimuli presented via SMI Experiment Suite and data collected and stored in Experiment Center 3.6. Viewing distance approximately 60 cm with both distance and screen height individually adjusted, five-point calibration with a crying cartoon target repeated until x and y deviation fell below one degree, and a researcher present with each parent-child pair. Areas of interest were drawn in BeGaze, and all analysis performed in WEKA. Reporting the calibration tolerance and the repeat-until-criterion rule is important for a study whose features are all derived from gaze position, and it is done here where most studies in the corpus simply state that calibration was performed. [RQ2.6] Strong on acquisition and stimulus design, weak on the analytic sample and the modelling. Reported in full: recruitment sources; inclusion and exclusion criteria for both groups; the complete stimulus structure with durations, pairing, counterbalancing and the rationale for each non-social class; tracker model, sampling rate, monitor, resolution, viewing distance, calibration procedure and tolerance; all thirteen features with definitions for the less familiar ones; the three feature-selection algorithms with their selections tabulated feature by feature and area by area for both datasets; all 24 classifier-by-selection-by-dataset results with seven metrics each; a worked decision tree with split thresholds; group mean looking times per area of interest per stimulus set; and a public data URL. Not reported: how many participants entered the classification analyses and how the balanced subset was formed; any hyperparameters for any of the four classifiers; standard deviations for age or Bayley scores; the number of participants excluded for tracking failure; ethics approval; and how feature selection was nested within cross-validation beyond the assertion that only training data were used. [RQ2.7] Four limitations are stated. Class balance is treated most carefully and is the best-argued passage in the paper: the authors note that 'we need the true ratio of children with ASD to TD children, 1 in every 54 children, to test the usefulness of the DSS for predicting how DSS would perform on a sample representative of the population' - correctly identifying that a balanced design overstates deployment performance, which very few studies in this corpus acknowledge. They then undercut it with a non-sequitur: 'Despite missing this class imbalance, our results show over 80% accuracy and AUC ROC values (for SVM and RF) which indicates that the proposed DSS can also handle class imbalance.' Performance on balanced data carries no information about performance under 1-in-54 prevalence, where positive predictive value would collapse. The sex imbalance is acknowledged. The 12.5% false-negative rate is acknowledged and attributed to clinical heterogeneity, with a call to characterise those children's symptom profiles. Sample size is acknowledged. Not acknowledged: the 20-point cognitive and 34-point language gaps between groups; the discrepancy between recruited and analysed sample sizes; that 87.5% is the maximum across 24 configurations; the absence of an observational diagnostic instrument; the laboratory setting relative to the paper's own call for less intrusive screening; and the absence of any ethics statement. [RQ2.9] Five directions, the first two substantive. Recruit a developmental-delay comparison group alongside autistic and typically developing children - the specificity test that the paradigm currently cannot support, and which matters particularly for a preferential-viewing task since developmental delay would be expected to affect social attention. Test at true population prevalence rather than balanced classes, to establish deployment performance. Characterise the symptom profiles of false-negative children, on the hypothesis that the 12.5% miss rate reflects clinical heterogeneity - though this requires severity data the study did not collect. Address the sex imbalance with reference to the established prevalence gap. And develop the system into 'an off-the-shelf and ready-to-use software package'. The last sits uneasily against the preceding four: a system that has not been tested at realistic prevalence, against developmental delay, or with characterised failure modes is not ready for packaging, and the paper does not sequence these. [RQ3.1] Competitive social attention - specifically, how a toddler allocates looking when social interaction and an attractive non-social alternative are visible simultaneously. This is a stronger operationalisation than measuring attention to social content alone, because it makes the measurement relative rather than absolute and therefore less sensitive to overall engagement or tracking success. The theoretical framing is explicitly two-sided, distinguishing 'diminished' from 'superior' processing and noting that autistic attention 'is captivated by non-social stimuli such as objects, lights, and geometric shapes' - so the target behaviour is a preference rather than only a deficit. The thirteen area-of-interest metrics then decompose that preference into how long (dwell time, net dwell time, fixation time), how often (fixation count, glances count, revisits, appearance count), how quickly (time to first appearance, entry time), how sustained per visit (average fixation duration, first fixation duration, glance duration) and how the eye leaves (diversion duration). That last dimension is the one the authors highlight as novel, and it captures something the others do not - the temporal cost of disengaging from an area, which connects to the attention-disengagement literature in early autism that the introduction reviews. [RQ3.2] Single modality, and no cross-modal fusion is attempted. Two within-modality combinations are studied instead, and both are informative. The first is the stimulus comparison: two competitor classes tested as separate datasets so that toys and animations can be compared directly, with animations winning on both raw looking times and classification. The second is a feature-combination test structured as a genuine ablation - net dwell time alone, the single most consistently selected feature, was used to classify and reached 70.67% and 79.17% on the two datasets, against 78.12% and 84.37% for the multivariate selected sets, and the authors report having 'made similar observations for all other single features as well'. That comparison establishes that the multivariate combination contributes real information beyond the best individual metric, which is the check that distinguishes a feature-selection claim from a dimensionality claim and which most studies here omit. What is not tested is combining the two stimulus sets, so whether toys and animations elicit complementary information from different children remains open. [RQ4.1] Four conventional classifiers spanning distinct inductive biases - a decision tree, naive Bayes, random forest and SVM - each run on each of three feature-selection outputs for each of two datasets, giving 24 configurations all of which are reported. Running the full grid and publishing all of it is good practice and exposes the spread: accuracy ranges from 67.5% to 87.5%, an 20-point range on the same participants, and no single classifier dominates across configurations (naive Bayes wins on the toys dataset, random forest and SVM on the animation dataset). The authors read this correctly as indicating that decision trees overfit small data while noting the tree's compensating virtue - it 'can be visualized' and traversed by a clinician, which they illustrate with a worked example walking through the split on social interaction fixation time at 5,879 ms. Choosing conventional classifiers over deep models is appropriate at this sample size. No hyperparameters are stated for any of the four, so the comparison cannot be assessed for equal tuning effort. [RQ4.2] One value per feature per area of interest per participant, averaged across the three videos within each stimulus set - so 26 values per participant per dataset, and the unit of analysis is the child. Features were min-max normalised to [0,1]. Averaging across the three videos within a set discards between-video variability, which is defensible for a screening measure but means the paradigm's internal consistency is never examined. Computing every metric for both the social and the non-social area of interest is the representational choice that makes the design work: it lets the classifier use the relationship between the two halves of the display rather than absolute looking at either, which is what a preferential paradigm is for. The two stimulus sets are kept as separate datasets throughout, so no participant contributes to a combined model. [RQ4.3] Seven metrics per class per configuration - true positive rate, false positive rate, precision, recall, F-measure, ROC area and accuracy - across six full tables, plus two summary tables and two figures. This is among the most complete metric reporting in the corpus, and reporting per class rather than only overall is what makes the study's central asymmetry visible: across every configuration the true positive rate for the autistic class is lower than for comparisons, and in the best model it is 0.800 against 0.950, so the system misses one autistic toddler in five while correctly clearing nineteen comparisons in twenty. For a screening instrument that asymmetry is the wrong way round, and the authors flag the 12.5% false-negative rate explicitly. What is missing: no confidence intervals on any of the 24 accuracy figures, no significance test between configurations, and no chance or demographic baseline - the last being consequential given the 34-point language gap, since a classifier using Bayley language score alone would likely perform comparably and would establish how much of the 87.5% is attributable to gaze rather than to development. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is pursued at two levels and both are useful. At feature level, the selections of all three algorithms are tabulated feature by feature and area by area for both datasets, with agreement across algorithms used as the criterion for calling a feature discriminative - a more conservative approach than trusting any single ranking. The resulting claim is specific and checkable: net dwell time, diversion duration and first fixation duration on the social area were selected by all three algorithms in both stimulus sets. The authors then situate this against their own published systematic review of eye-tracking features in autism, noting that fixation count, fixation time, average fixation duration and dwell time dominate the literature while diversion duration is essentially absent - so the finding is that the field's default feature set may not contain its most discriminative member. At model level, the decision tree is reproduced with its thresholds and its traversal explained in clinical terms, presented as a transparency argument rather than a performance one. What is absent is any link between model output and clinical characteristics: no severity measure was collected, so the authors' own proposal to examine the symptom profiles of false negatives cannot be executed on these data. [RQ4.5] Two claims are made and both are the right ones to make, but neither can be verified from what is reported. The cross-validation is stated to be participant-based - 'the data is divided into ten subsets based on participants... ensuring that all participants' data appeared either in the training or test set' - which forecloses within-participant leakage, though since each child contributes a single feature vector the safeguard is structural rather than earned. Feature selection is stated to use training data only. Against these, three issues remain. The analysed sample cannot be reconciled with the 133 recruited: the accuracy grid across all six results tables is consistent with roughly 20 per class and inconsistent with 61 and 72, and the balancing statement acknowledges that classes were equalised without saying how or how much was discarded. The Wrapper feature-selection method is by definition driven by classification accuracy, and while WEKA's attribute-selection mode can be run under cross-validation, the description does not establish that selection was refitted inside each classification fold rather than performed once and then used throughout - a distinction that determines whether the reported figures carry selection optimism. And the headline 87.5% is the maximum over 24 reported configurations, with no correction, no confidence interval and no held-out confirmation. The public data posting is the mitigating factor: it is the only route by which an external reader could resolve the sample question. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorders, eye tracking, visual attention, screening, machine learning, biomarker. The presence of both 'screening' and 'biomarker' signals the applied framing, and 'visual attention' rather than 'gaze' or 'fixation' indicates that the construct rather than the measurement is the intended subject. [RQ5.2] International Journal of Psychophysiology 173:69-81 (2022), a psychophysiology journal with a methods-oriented readership. Authorship pairs two special education departments (Hacettepe and Gazi Universities) with two computer engineering departments (Pamukkale and Hacettepe), and the pairing shows in the paper's shape: the paradigm design, stimulus rationale, calibration discipline and literature critique are of special-education quality while the machine learning is competent but conventional and under-specified. Funded by the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey. The authors' own prior systematic review of eye-tracking features in autism is cited and used substantively to position the diversion-duration finding. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is the standard early-screening argument but with more specific and better-sourced grounding than most in this corpus. The clinical problem is stated in concrete terms: 'many clinicians adopt a wait and see approach during the early years, delaying their diagnosis'; assessments are 'time-intensive processes that make many children are waitlisted for a long time'; and access depends on 'financial resources available to a child, the number of clinicians in a region, and governmental policy around access to resources'. The instrument critique is quantitative rather than rhetorical, citing the M-CHAT-R/F's reported positive predictive value of 54% for autism against 98% for developmental delay in a low-risk group, and noting that 'currently, no screening instrument can identify young children with ASD from non-ASD peers with high accuracy'. What most distinguishes the framing, though, is a genuinely critical reading of the machine-learning literature the paper is contributing to. The introduction surveys eight prior studies with their reported accuracies and then observes that 'the results of the reviewed studies indicated a large variance in prediction of ASD diagnosis', attributing it to 'the age of the participants, validation methods, and sample size but also... processing of noise, training dataset imbalances, feature selection, ranking, and data cases that overlap in features', and concluding that 'the variability of ASD classification performance require a careful reading of improvements in ML research related to ASD classification'. The discussion goes further, noting that many machine-learning studies in autism are 'limited by diverse methodological problems such as unreliable evaluation measures, small sample size, class imbalances in data, and invalid diagnostic procedures', citing Frazier's meta-regression that poorly designed and poorly reported studies overestimate group differences, and dissecting Pierce's geometric-preference finding to point out that only 40% of the autistic participants actually showed the preference and that the number of repeated trials was never reported. That level of critical engagement with the surrounding literature is unmatched in this corpus - which makes the study's own unreported sample reduction and unaddressed developmental confound the more striking. |
| S-085 | Cross-sectional two-cohort case-control study in Shenzhen: a toddler cohort of 55 autistic children (2.4 +/- 0.5 years, 50 boys, CARS 32.3) and 40 typically developing children (2.2 +/- 0.6 years), and a preschool cohort of 37 autistic children (4.6 +/- 0.5 years, CARS 33.0) and 41 comparisons (4.8 +/- 0.3 years), with both cohorts matched on age and gender. Diagnosis by DSM-5 plus CARS above 30 without ADOS or ADI-R confirmation; comparison children screened on three developmental instruments by a study physician. No developmental or cognitive measure in either group. Raw data available on request. | Five short paradigms totalling around 40 seconds paired social against non-social content: a mouthing face (eyes versus mouth), upright versus inverted point-light biological motion, a mouthing face versus a moving dot, a moving duck and helicopter, and an infant face versus an electric fan, with the biological motion and face-versus-dot paradigms presented in both left-right arrangements and averaged. Gaze was recorded on an SMI RED250 at 250 Hz at 65 cm in a dark soundproof room, with five-point calibration and exclusion of children who could not follow the target, and a second exclusion of children whose fixation deviated from the screen. Fixation time percentage per area (fixations over 100 ms, displacement under one degree) was analysed by ANCOVA with diagnosis, age group and their interaction, covarying age and gender, with Levene's testing, weighted least squares where required, Tukey correction and multivariate-t adjustment. SVM classification used leave-one-out cross-validation separately per cohort, with single-area accuracies tested against permutation. | Autistic children showed reduced fixation time percentage in nine of ten areas, with a main effect of diagnosis significant at p < 0.001 for six. A diagnosis-by-age interaction reached significance for the eye area (p = 0.048): toddler groups did not differ (15.4% versus 17.6%, p = 0.93, d = 0.12) while preschool groups did (15.1% versus 29.2%, p = 0.006, d = 0.74). The mouth showed the reverse pattern (d = 0.81 in toddlers, 0.44 in preschoolers). Classification reached 80% accuracy, 80% sensitivity and 82% specificity in toddlers, and 71% accuracy, 81% sensitivity and 61% specificity in preschoolers. Single-area rankings largely inverted between cohorts. Only preschool comparison children preferentially attended to upright over inverted biological motion (p = 0.01). No fixation measure correlated with CARS (p = 0.13-0.99). | Diagnosis rests on DSM-5 and CARS without ADOS or ADI-R, acknowledged as due to limited access in China, and CARS was not administered to comparison children. Two quality-control steps exclude children who fail calibration or look off-screen, both of which plausibly operate differentially by group, with no exclusion counts reported. Fixation percentages are normalised by total stimulus duration rather than by valid tracked time, so a child looking away accrues a lower percentage on every area at once - which is consistent with the observed reduction on non-social areas including a moving dot and an electric fan, and is left uninterpreted. No developmental or cognitive measure in either group. No independent validation cohort and no classifier specification. The preschool cohort is 78 in the results table but N = 74 in the leave-one-out description. The authors additionally identify spectrum bias from comparing clear-cut cases against thoroughly screened comparisons. | The most valuable single contribution this study makes to the review is arithmetic rather than empirical. Declining to report predictive values, the authors explain why and then perform the calculation: at 80% sensitivity and 82% specificity with 1% population prevalence, positive predictive value is approximately 4.2% while negative predictive value exceeds 99%. No other paper in this corpus performs that translation, and it is the number against which every other reported accuracy should be read - a classifier performing at the level most studies here report would be wrong about roughly 24 of every 25 children it flagged in an unselected population. The paper pairs this with an equally direct statement of spectrum bias, naming the mechanism and stating that discriminative ability 'may be overestimated in medical practice'. Two substantive findings also transfer. The developmental dissociation on the eye area - no group difference before age three, a large difference after, because typical eye-looking rises while autistic eye-looking stays flat - implies that the field's most cited gaze marker is age-dependent in a way that single-age-band studies cannot detect, and it supplies a concrete reason why paradigms optimised in preschoolers may fail in toddlers. And the reported nulls are instructive: no fixation measure tracked CARS severity, converging with the same finding in Keles and colleagues that gaze measures separating groups on average need not index individual severity. Against these, the study also illustrates a measurement issue that recurs across the eye-tracking studies here: because fixation percentage is normalised by stimulus duration rather than by successfully tracked time, a group that looks away more will show reduced percentages on every region simultaneously - which is exactly the pattern observed, extending to a moving dot and an electric fan, and which the paper does not consider as an alternative to a social-attention account. | [RQ1.1] Two cohorts, each with two groups. Toddler cohort: 55 autistic children (aged 1.5-3, including eight aged 1.6-1.8) and 40 typically developing. Preschool cohort: 37 autistic children (aged 3-5) and 41 typically developing. Autistic participants came from the Child Mental Health and Rehabilitation Center of a maternity and child healthcare hospital; comparison children from a local kindergarten or from routine annual check-ups in the same hospital's outpatient ward. No developmental-delay or other-diagnosis comparison group, and the authors identify the consequence explicitly as spectrum bias. The two-cohort structure is the study's design contribution: rather than treating age as a covariate to be adjusted away, the cohorts are analysed both jointly through a diagnosis-by-age-group interaction and separately through cohort-specific classifiers, which is what permits the finding that different areas of interest discriminate at different ages. A discrepancy sits unreconciled between the 37 + 41 = 78 preschoolers reported in the results and the 'N = 74 for preschool' stated in the leave-one-out description, and exclusion counts from the two quality-control steps - calibration failure and off-screen fixation - are not reported for either cohort. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'ASD children' and 'toddler ASD' used interchangeably, against 'TD children' and 'typically developing individuals'. The acronym is frequently used adjectivally and occasionally as a bare group label ('toddler ASD, and TD is similar'). The framing is conventional and deficit-oriented - autism 'involves deficits in face processing', gaze is 'aberrant', and the literature on 'gaze abnormalities' is reviewed at length - but the paper is careful about the state of the evidence in a way that softens this: it notes that 'the precise nature of these deficits and the relationships between anomalous face processing and atypical socio-emotional function in ASD remain unclear', and cites a review finding that 'the excessive mouth and diminished eye gaze hypothesis of ASD is not generally supported'. That willingness to report that a widely repeated claim lacks support is uncommon in this corpus. [RQ1.3] Reported per cohort with tests, and both cohorts are matched on both variables. Toddlers: autistic 2.4 +/- 0.5 years and 50 boys to 5 girls, comparison 2.2 +/- 0.6 years and 33 boys to 7 girls, with p = 0.27 for age and p = 0.22 for gender. Preschoolers: autistic 4.6 +/- 0.5 years and 33 boys to 4 girls, comparison 4.8 +/- 0.3 years and 33 boys to 8 girls, with p = 0.11 and p = 0.29. Age and gender were then additionally entered as covariates in every ANCOVA despite already being matched, which is belt-and-braces and appropriate. What is absent is any measure of developmental or cognitive level in either group - no Mullen, Bayley, Griffiths or equivalent - and the authors address this directly rather than omitting it, arguing that 'predominant ASD studies used chronological age instead of developmental age' and that 'in practice, a child transition from Toddler to preschooler is typically based on the chronological age without developmental testing', while conceding that 'future studies may also need to consider adding a developmental test'. The argument is reasonable for defining the cohorts but does not address the confound: two groups matched on chronological age but differing in developmental level would differ in where they look for reasons unrelated to diagnosis, and nothing in the data can separate these. [RQ1.4] DSM-5 diagnosis by experienced physicians with a CARS score above 30 required for children aged 2 and over, described as 'in line with the ADOS standard'. The absence of an observational instrument is stated as the study's first limitation together with its cause - limited access to ADOS and ADI-R in China - which is a candid acknowledgement of a resource constraint rather than a methodological choice. The comparison group is screened more thoroughly than in most studies here: three instruments (the Ages and Stages Questionnaires Chinese Version, the Chinese children warning signs checklist, and the Developmental Screening Parent Questionnaire for Children Aged 0-6) covering communication and language, physical ability, social skills, problem solving and intelligence, administered by a study physician through onsite assessment and parent interview, with exclusion of any psychiatric or neurological history. The authors nonetheless flag the asymmetry: 'we did not assess the CARS in TD Children', so comparison participants were screened on general development but never on autism-specific symptomatology with the same instrument used to establish the cases. [RQ1.5] CARS scores were obtained for the autistic groups only and only for children aged 2 and over, at 32.3 +/- 1.5 in toddlers and 33.0 +/- 2.1 in preschoolers - both close to the cut-off of 30, so the samples sit at the milder end of the CARS range with narrow standard deviations, which limits the severity gradient available for correlation. The severity data are nonetheless used analytically, in a multiple regression of fixation time percentage on CARS with age and gender as covariates across all autistic children, returning no significant association on any area of interest (p values from 0.13 to 0.99). That null is reported without qualification and is important: it means the gaze measures separate the groups on average without tracking how autistic an individual child is, which converges with the same finding in the Keles adult study and bears on whether such measures could serve as severity or outcome measures rather than only as classifiers. No cognitive, language or adaptive measure was collected for either group, and no comorbidity or medication information. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether eye-tracking differences between autistic and typically developing children are the same in toddlers and preschoolers, and identify which paradigms discriminate at which age. Main findings: reduced fixation time percentage in nine of ten areas of interest with a main effect of diagnosis, but a main effect of age group on only one area; significant diagnosis-by-age interaction on the eye area, where toddlers did not differ (p = 0.93) but preschoolers did (p = 0.006); single-area classification rankings that largely invert between cohorts, with mouth, upright walking, moving dot and baby face discriminating toddlers and eyes, duck, infant face and fan discriminating preschoolers; full-model accuracy of 80% in toddlers and 71% in preschoolers; only preschool comparison children showing the expected preference for upright biological motion; and no association between any fixation measure and CARS severity. [RQ2.2] A hospital-based child mental health and rehabilitation centre in Shenzhen, with testing conducted in 'a dark and soundproof room' at a fixed 65 cm viewing distance with the child's centre of vision aligned to the monitor centre. This is a tightly controlled laboratory environment rather than a point-of-care setting, which suits the measurement but limits the deployment claim - a dark soundproof room with a calibrated remote tracker is not a paediatric waiting area. The recruitment asymmetry is present but mitigated: autistic children came from the hospital's rehabilitation centre while comparison children came either from a local kindergarten or from routine check-ups at the same hospital's outpatient ward, so a proportion of the comparison group was recruited within the same institution. [RQ2.3] Five short paradigms totalling roughly 40 seconds, each pairing a social element against a non-social competitor within a single display, and each with a stated theoretical rationale drawn from a specific prior literature. The design's strongest feature is its use of position-switched replicates: both the biological motion and the face-versus-dot paradigms were presented twice with left and right positions swapped and the fixation percentages averaged, which controls for any lateral gaze bias - a source of artefact that most paired-display studies in this corpus do not address. The paradigms also span a graded range of social content, from a full face with moving mouth, through point-light biological motion, to a still infant face, against competitors ranging from an abstract moving dot to an electric fan to clipart animals - which is what makes the age-specific ranking analysis informative, since it identifies which level of social content carries signal at which age. The brevity is a practical virtue for 18-month-olds and a limitation for reliability: a 5-second still-image trial yields one fixation percentage per child with no within-child replication from which stability could be estimated. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional with two age cohorts sampled independently rather than followed longitudinally - so the developmental claim rests on a cross-sectional age contrast, which the design cannot distinguish from cohort effects, though this is a standard and reasonable compromise. Ethics reporting is complete: approval by the Ethics Committee of Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital, written informed consent from legal guardians, and separate written consent obtained specifically for publication of potentially identifiable images or data. Partial overlap with a prior publication by the same group is disclosed rather than concealed: 'A portion of preschool data using paradigm (video clip) data had been used in a previous study... However, this study used more comprehensive paradigms and the findings presented in this study have never been published before.' Raw data are offered on request. [RQ2.5] An SMI RED250 remote tracker at 250 Hz with 0.03 degree spatial resolution, viewing a 22-inch LCD at 1024x768 from 65 cm in a dark, soundproof room, with the child's centre of vision aligned to the screen centre. Calibration used five points with a dynamic pink rabbit as the target, and - importantly - 'those who failed to follow the dynamic pink rabbit fixation did not continue in the experiment', so calibration failure was an exclusion rather than a tolerated source of noise. A second quality step used Gaze Replay path playback before analysis 'to exclude the subjects whose fixation point deviates from the screen to reduce systematic errors'. Both steps are good practice for a toddler paradigm and both are likely to remove children differentially by group, since compliance with a calibration target and sustained on-screen looking are themselves plausibly reduced in autism - yet no exclusion counts are given for either step in either group, which is the most consequential reporting omission in the paper. Fixation detection thresholds are stated (duration above 100 ms, displacement below one degree) and analysis used BeGaze and R-studio 3.5.2. [RQ2.6] Strong on statistics and stimuli, weak on flow and on the classifier. Fully reported: recruitment sources and screening instruments for both groups; the diagnostic basis with its acknowledged limitation; demographics per cohort with tests; every paradigm with duration, content, area-of-interest definition and rationale; the position-switching and averaging procedure; tracker model, sampling rate, spatial resolution, monitor, resolution, viewing distance, room conditions and calibration procedure with its exclusion rule; fixation detection thresholds; the complete statistical model including covariates, variance assumption testing, the weighted least squares substitution, post-hoc correction method and the multivariate-t adjustment for interaction contrasts; means and standard deviations for all ten areas in all four groups; F statistics and p values for all three ANCOVA effects on all ten areas; Cohen's d for every contrast; and the leave-one-out procedure. Not reported: exclusion counts at either quality-control step; the SVM kernel, hyperparameters or implementation; the reconciliation between 78 and 74 preschoolers; and any code. Raw data are offered on request. [RQ2.7] Five limitations are stated and each is substantive, but two passages go considerably beyond the corpus norm. The prevalence discussion is the most valuable: rather than reporting predictive values, the authors explain why they will not, and then calculate the answer - 'using the above toddler values of 80% sensitivity and 82% specificity, and assuming 1% prevalence in the population, the PPV is approximately 4.2%. On the other hand, using these same values, NPV is greater than 99%.' They note that readers can perform the calculation themselves and that omitting predictive values 'is consistent with previous ASD studies on this topic', citing three. The spectrum bias passage is equally direct, naming the phenomenon, identifying its cause in the exclusion of psychiatric and neurological histories from the comparison group, and stating its direction: discriminative ability 'may be overestimated in medical practice'. The other three limitations are the absence of ADOS/ADI-R confirmation with its stated cause, the absence of CARS in comparison children, the small sample without independent validation, and the absence of developmental assessment with a reasoned defence of using chronological age. What is not addressed: that fixation reduction appears across non-social as well as social areas and may therefore index general attention rather than social attention; that the off-area residual is never reported by group; that the two quality-control exclusions may operate differentially by group and their counts are unreported; and the 78-versus-74 discrepancy. [RQ2.9] Five directions, tightly tied to the stated limitations. Validate on independent datasets. Recruit 'a broad spectrum of the ASD and non-ASD participants' to address spectrum bias - the direct remedy for the acknowledged overestimation. Add developmental assessment alongside chronological age.
