No age, diagnostic instrument, severity or cognitive information; a 43-percentage-point sex imbalance restated without comment; a single fixed split with no repetition, confidence intervals, significance tests or baseline; internal inconsistencies between reported accuracies, AUCs and per-class rates; no ethics statement; no code; and no limitations section. | Charted principally as the second of two studies in this corpus analysing the identical 547-image Carette dataset, and the pair together make the point more forcefully than either alone. Gaspar and colleagues report 98.8% having augmented the testing data as well as the training data and described no split at all; this paper reports 99.8% having correctly confined augmentation to training but partitioned by image rather than by child; the dataset's own originators, applying a participant-level correction, reported approximately 71%. Three independent analyses of the same images therefore span 27 percentage points, and the entire range is attributable to validation design rather than to method. That comparison is the cleanest available demonstration in this review that reported accuracy on a shared dataset is determined by how the evaluation is constructed. Two further observations transfer. This paper's restatement of the source sex composition - 86.2% male in the autistic group against 43.3% in the comparison group - supplies information Gaspar omitted entirely, and reveals that the dataset carries a large uncontrolled demographic confound that neither reusing study addresses. And the finding that generic image texture descriptors outperform fine-tuned ResNet-18 and GoogleNet on these images, presented here as a positive result, is more naturally read as evidence that the discriminative information lies in low-level plot morphology rather than in anything a visual network would recognise as content - which is consistent with the complete absence of any behavioural finding in 27 pages. | [RQ1.1] Two groups inherited from the Carette et al. dataset: 29 autistic children contributing 219 images and 30 typically developing children contributing 328 images, 547 images from 59 children in total. This paper is more informative than Gaspar and colleagues on the same data, which reported only image counts, since it restates the participant counts and sex composition from the source publication. But the participant structure is then entirely disregarded in the analysis: the 80/20 partition operates on images, so children are not the unit at any stage and images from the same child necessarily span the training and test sets at roughly nine images per participant. No other-diagnosis or developmental-delay comparison group. The class imbalance of 219 to 328 is addressed by differential augmentation of the training and validation partitions - sevenfold for the autistic class, tenfold for the comparison class - rather than by any participant-level consideration. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'children with autism', 'people with autism', against 'TD' and 'typically developing children'. Person-first in the main, though 'patients with autism spectrum disorder' appears and autism is once described as 'autism disease' and elsewhere as something requiring 'effective treatments to improve responses in children with autism'. The framing is medical and treatment-oriented in a way that misdescribes the condition, referring to 'the heterogeneous response to treatment and the search for effective treatments' and to children 'who are less responsive to the currently available treatment methods'. The introduction also contains a confused clinical passage - 'Many symptoms of ASD appear, such as genetic, cognitive, neurological and cognitive factors' - listing aetiological factors as symptoms and repeating 'cognitive' twice, which is symptomatic of the paper's general disengagement from the clinical subject matter. [RQ1.3] Sex composition is restated from the source publication and is the only demographic information given: the autistic group comprises 25 males and 4 females (86.2% male) and the comparison group 13 males and 17 females (43.3% male). That 43-percentage-point difference, running in opposite directions between groups, is reported in a single sentence and never mentioned again - not analysed, not covaried, not listed as a limitation, and not discussed anywhere in a 27-page paper. It matters because the classifier operates on rendered scanpath images, and any systematic difference in viewing behaviour, screen coverage or trace density associated with sex would be absorbed directly into the texture features. No ages, no age range, no IQ, no language level, no severity and no matching of any kind. Given that the same dataset elsewhere in this corpus is analysed by Gaspar and colleagues with no participant information at all, the restatement here is an improvement in reporting that is not accompanied by any improvement in analysis. [RQ1.4] Nothing. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role, setting or timing is reported, and the source dataset's ascertainment procedure is not summarised even in a sentence. The class labels are treated as file attributes throughout. Under this review's classification this is dataset-label-only ascertainment in its least documented form. The omission is compounded by the paper's framing, which repeatedly describes the systems as tools for 'diagnosis' and 'early diagnosis' and proposes that they 'could help experts and autism treatment centres in the early detection of autism in children' - claims about diagnostic utility made against a reference standard whose nature is entirely unknown to the reader. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, language, adaptive, severity, comorbidity or medication information for either group, and no exclusions described. Nothing therefore relates model output to any clinical dimension, and the possibility that the classifier separates developmental level rather than diagnosis cannot be examined. [RQ2.1] Goal: compare three artificial-intelligence approaches - shallow neural networks on hand-engineered texture features, transfer-learned CNNs, and CNN-plus-SVM hybrids - for classifying autism from gaze-path images. Main findings: FFNN and ANN on concatenated LBP and GLCM features reached 99.8% overall accuracy (98.7% at test phase); ResNet-18 reached 97.6% and GoogleNet 93.6%; the hybrids reached 95.5% and 94.5%; and the hand-engineered pipeline was concluded to be 'the best performance amongst the proposed systems'. No behavioural finding, group difference or gaze characteristic is reported. [RQ2.2] Not reported. The paper describes neither the room, the country, the recruitment route, the eye tracker nor the acquisition protocol for the source recordings. The only settings named are the four institutions where the analysis was carried out and the hardware on which it ran - a fifth-generation i5 processor with 8 GB RAM and a 4 GB GPU, specified more precisely than anything about the children. [RQ2.3] Entirely absent. Unlike Gaspar and colleagues on the same dataset, who at least state that participants 'were shown different videos containing stimulating scenarios for the movement of the eye in the entire screen', this paper reproduces nothing at all about what was viewed, for how long, or under what conditions. The reader is given no basis on which to judge what behaviour the scanpaths represent. Since the analysis proceeds by treating the resulting plot as a texture image, the absence is internally consistent with the method - the pipeline does not require knowing what generated the trace - but it means the study cannot connect its result to any behavioural construct, and the paper accordingly makes no attempt to. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a public dataset; no follow-up. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere, and no pointer is given to where the source dataset's approvals were obtained. A data availability statement supplies the figshare URL for the source images with an access date, funding is acknowledged from the Najran University Scientific Research Deanship under a named grant, and a conflict-of-interest declaration is present - so the absence of an ethics statement is not a matter of missing front matter but of the section not being written. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment is described at any point. The analysis chain is specified in unusual mathematical detail: the average filter with its 5x5 window and neighbour-averaging equation, the Laplacian operator, the subtraction combining them, the active contour formulation including the level-set function, the energy terms, the Heaviside and Dirac delta smoothing functions, the sign convention determining whether the contour shrinks or expands, and the stopping criterion comparing successive masks. Morphological operations are named, LBP is given with its neighbourhood size and feature count, and the CNN training options are tabulated with optimiser, mini-batch size, epochs, learning rate, validation frequency and execution environment for both networks. The asymmetry is total: every arithmetic step is documented and nothing about the measurement is. [RQ2.6] Reproducible as an image-processing pipeline, not as a study. Fully specified: all filtering, segmentation and morphological steps with equations; LBP neighbourhood and feature count; the 216-dimensional concatenated vector; the network architectures with layer counts; both CNNs' complete training hyperparameters; the augmentation operations and the resulting counts before and after; the exact split into 350 training, 88 validation and 109 test images with per-class breakdowns; the evaluation formulae; and the compute hardware. Not reported: anything about the participants beyond counts and sex; the stimuli; the eye tracker; the diagnostic procedure; the final chosen contour parameters; whether the split was stratified or randomised and with what seed; and any code. The data availability statement points to the public source images. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section, and no limitation is stated anywhere in the paper. Nothing is acknowledged about the image-wise split, the pooled headline accuracy, the absence of participant information, the sex imbalance restated in the methods, the lack of diagnostic provenance, the absence of any behavioural interpretation, or the single fixed split without repetition or confidence intervals. The conclusion instead asserts that all three systems 'achieved superior results' and 'promising results', and the future work proposes only to concatenate the feature families - an architectural extension that would address none of the above. This is the least self-critical paper in the corpus. [RQ2.9] One direction: 'to extract features using CNN models and combine them with features extracted by LBP and GLCM algorithms into a single feature vector for each image and classify it using all three ANN, FFNN and SVM algorithms.' This proposes more feature concatenation on the same 547 images with the same split, and addresses none of the study's substantive weaknesses. No proposal is made to group by participant, obtain demographic or diagnostic metadata, validate externally, interpret the features behaviourally, or test on an independent dataset. [RQ3.1] Nominally visual attention, but no behavioural construct survives the pipeline. The source dataset encodes gaze coordinates and their derivatives as a rendered plot; this study then applies average filtering, Laplacian edge enhancement, active contour segmentation of the trace region, morphological hole-filling, and finally local binary pattern and grey-level co-occurrence texture descriptors. What reaches the classifier is a 216-dimensional summary of the local texture statistics of a processed image of a line drawing. No fixation, saccade, dwell time, area of interest, coverage measure or any other quantity with a gaze interpretation is computed at any stage, and consequently the paper reports no group difference in viewing behaviour, no effect direction and no interpretation. The introduction's extensive discussion of social versus non-social orientation, social attention deficits and visual biomarkers has no connection to anything the method actually measures - a gap of several sections between the stated construct and the operationalisation. [RQ3.2] Single modality with no cross-modal fusion. Two within-pipeline combinations are performed. The first concatenates LBP and GLCM outputs into a single 216-dimensional vector, justified on the general ground that 'extracting the features from several methods and combining them are two of the most important recent methods that have an effect on accurate diagnosis' - an assertion rather than an argument, with no ablation showing what either family contributes alone. The second replaces each CNN's classification head with an SVM operating on its deep feature maps. That second comparison is the more informative because it is properly controlled: the same features are classified two ways, and the result is mixed - the SVM head improves GoogleNet from 93.6% to 95.5% but degrades ResNet-18 from 97.6% to 94.5%. The paper reports both directions without comment. Across all six configurations the pattern that hand-engineered texture beats learned representation is presented as the headline conclusion but never examined, though it is the observation most consistent with the discriminative signal residing in low-level plot morphology rather than in anything a pretrained visual network would find semantically salient. [RQ4.1] Six configurations spanning three families, all reported, which is a reasonable comparative design in itself. The shallow networks use 216 input neurons and 10 hidden layers, an unusually deep configuration for a fully connected network on 216 features and 547 samples, with no justification, no hidden-layer widths and no regularisation described. The CNN training is more conventionally specified with full hyperparameters for both networks. The SVM is unspecified as to kernel or parameters. What is missing throughout is any baseline: no chance level, no permutation test, no simple comparator such as image mean intensity or trace pixel count, and no repetition across splits - so a 6.2-point spread between the best and worst configuration is reported without any means of judging whether it exceeds split-to-split variation on 109 test images. [RQ4.2] The representational chain is the study's core and its central problem. Four preprocessing stages precede feature extraction - average filtering, Laplacian enhancement, active contour segmentation, morphological cleaning - each documented with equations and each progressively removing information that might have carried gaze meaning. Segmentation isolates 'the eye-tracking path region', converting a trajectory into a binary or near-binary shape; morphological cleaning then modifies that shape further. LBP and GLCM are then computed over the result. Local binary patterns encode the relative intensity of a pixel against its neighbours and were developed for texture and face recognition; grey-level co-occurrence matrices summarise second-order intensity statistics. Neither has any relationship to where a child looked. The consequence is visible in the paper's own output: 27 pages containing six accuracy tables, multiple confusion matrices and ROC curves, and not one statement about what distinguishes autistic children's scanning from that of their peers. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for all six configurations, with confusion matrices and, for the neural network pipeline, separate training, validation and test figures. Reporting the three phases separately is genuinely useful and is what allows the headline to be diagnosed: the ANN achieved 100% on training and validation and 98.7% at test, and the abstract's 99.8% is described as 'the overall accuracy' - so it pools performance on data the model was fitted to with performance on held-out data. The correct held-out figure is 98.7%, on 109 images. Two internal inconsistencies also appear: GoogleNet is reported with 93.6% accuracy but 99.48% AUC while ResNet-18 has higher accuracy (97.6%) and lower AUC (97.56%), a pattern that would require explanation and receives none; and GoogleNet's per-class accuracies of 97.7% and 90.9% are difficult to reconcile with its stated 94.5% sensitivity and 94.5% specificity. No confidence intervals, no repeated splits, no significance tests and no baseline of any kind accompany any figure. [RQ4.4] None, and none is possible. There is no feature importance, attribution, saliency or ablation, and the representation - texture codes over a segmented, morphologically cleaned rendering of a gaze trace - admits no behavioural interpretation even in principle. No group means, effect sizes, directions or descriptive statistics about viewing behaviour appear anywhere. The paper therefore contributes six accuracy figures and no knowledge about autism, gaze or visual attention, despite an introduction devoting several pages to social orientation, attention biomarkers and the clinical significance of atypical visual attention. That disconnection between the stated motivation and the delivered content is the study's defining characteristic. [RQ4.5] Two distinct problems, one shared with several studies in this corpus and one specific to this paper. The shared problem is the unit of analysis: 547 images come from 59 children at roughly 9.3 images each, and the 80/20 partition is by image with no participant grouping described, so images from the same child appear in both training and test. Cilia and colleagues, who produced this dataset, measured the consequence directly, reporting image-level accuracy near 90% falling to approximately 71% when recomputed per child; that correction is neither cited nor applied here. The specific problem is that the headline figure pools phases: the abstract and conclusion report 99.8% while the results text states the same model achieved 100% in training and validation and 98.7% in testing, and describes 99.8% as 'the overall accuracy'. One element is handled correctly and deserves credit - augmentation by flipping, rotation, displacement and shearing was applied only to the training and validation partitions, expanding them from 175 and 262 to 1,750 and 1,834 images, while the test set remained unaugmented at 44 and 66. This is the correct discipline and is precisely what Gaspar and colleagues violated on the same dataset by augmenting the testing data as well. Against that, there is a single fixed split with no repetition, no cross-validation, no confidence intervals and no external validation, so the reported differences among six configurations rest on one partition of 109 test images. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, eye tracking, machine learning, neural networks, convolutional neural network, GLCM, local binary pattern. Five of seven are computational and two of those name specific texture descriptors, which accurately identifies the paper as a texture-classification study that happens to use autism-labelled images. [RQ5.2] Electronics 11(4):530 (2022), an MDPI open-access engineering journal. Authorship spans the Applied College at Najran University in Saudi Arabia, Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar Marathwada University in India, Bournemouth University in the UK and the University of Malaya in Malaysia, with no clinical, psychological or autism-research affiliation among the seven authors. The review timeline is compressed - received 15 January 2022, accepted 6 February, published 10 February, twenty-six days from submission to publication - and the paper contains no limitations section, no ethics statement and several internal inconsistencies in its reported metrics. Funded by the Najran University Scientific Research Deanship. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is the standard early-detection argument with the usual supporting claims: prevalence of one in 160 per WHO, diagnosis typically delayed to age 4 despite symptoms appearing earlier, and eye tracking recommended as 'fast, inexpensive, easy to analyse and applicable to all ages'. The related-work section is a list of prior studies with their reported accuracies and no critical assessment, and it includes an error that indicates limited engagement with the clinical literature - the ADOS is attributed to Lord et al. as 'a method... for assessing autism' consisting of 'unstructured observational tasks', when the instrument is explicitly semi-structured and standardised, and the CARS is described as being 'based on the doctor's assessment of children's behaviour through two scales, a social communication questionnaire and a social responsiveness scale', which conflates three distinct instruments. One passage is worth noting because it states a caveat the paper then ignores: 'evidence regarding positive eye-tracking outcomes as a strong predictor of long-term outcomes in children with ASD is lacking'. Having noted that the predictive validity of the modality is unestablished, the paper proceeds to report 99.8% accuracy and to propose the systems as aids for diagnosis and early detection without returning to the point. |
| S-089 | Cross-sectional analysis of a crowdsourced home-video corpus collected via the GuessWhat mobile charades app: 449 videos from 95 children recruited through social media and research email lists from approximately 1,000 app downloads - 68 with parent-reported autism (53 male, 15 female, 380 videos) and 27 neurotypical (18 male, 9 female, 69 videos), aged 2 to 15 with no group-specific ages reported. Mean 4.7 videos per child, 11.1 hours, 1,084,267 frames. Diagnostic status by unverified parent survey; no cognitive, language or severity measures; dataset not released. Stanford IRB approval. | Parents held a smartphone on their forehead with the front camera on the child during 90-second charades, then chose whether to share. Annotation was fully automated to avoid human viewing: Amazon Rekognition supplied 30 facial landmarks and bounding boxes with frames containing zero or more than two faces discarded, and OpenFace supplied per-frame gaze direction as a camera-relative coordinate pair with frames below 75% confidence discarded, reducing 1,084,267 frames to 619,620. Gaze was discretised into a 4x4 grid of 16 areas of interest. Fixation profiles and 16x16 transition adjacency matrices were compared by two-sided permutation tests with 100,000 permutations and Bonferroni correction (thresholds 0.0031 and 0.0008). One-hot encoded gaze sequences were windowed (50-500 frames, shift 10-100) and fed to an LSTM with Adam, learning rate 0.001, batch size 5 and weighted binary cross-entropy, on a child-disjoint split of 324 training, 71 validation and 54 held-out test videos. | One of 16 fixation regions differed significantly after correction (region BC, p < .001) and one of 61 transition pairs (BB-BC, p < .001), with comparison children making 13% of gaze shifts between these regions against 9.4% for autistic children. Children of both groups fixated predominantly on the four central regions nearest the camera. The best LSTM configuration (window 100, shift 10) reached weighted-average precision 0.661, weighted-average recall 0.656, macro-averaged precision 0.595 and macro-averaged recall 0.598 on the held-out set; the two other configurations performed comparably or slightly worse. The authors characterise this as mild predictive power and note the macro-weighted divergence as evidence of class-dependent accuracy. | Diagnostic labels are unverified parent report with no instrument or clinician contact, and unlike the companion speech study from the same group this is not acknowledged. The sample spans ages 2 to 15 with no group means, medians or tests reported in the text and no age covariate or stratification, despite gaze behaviour and gameplay engagement changing radically across that range. Cases outnumber controls more than five to one at video level, and the held-out test set of 43 autistic against 11 comparison videos means a majority-class predictor would achieve weighted-average recall of about 0.80, above the reported 0.656 - a comparison the paper does not make, and no baseline, permutation null or confidence interval accompanies any classification result. The areas of interest are camera-relative directions from a phone on a moving head and, as the authors concede, cannot be matched to facial regions, so the single significant finding cannot be connected to eye contact or any other construct. No cognitive, language or severity measures; no dataset or code release. | Useful to the synthesis principally as a controlled demonstration of what survives when every experimental constraint is removed at once. The related-work section sorts prior video-based studies into three categories and identifies a cost for each - manual annotation is expensive and compromises privacy, eye trackers require inaccessible hardware, and structured-environment studies control lighting and camera distance in ways that leave translation untested - and the study then removes all three simultaneously. The answer, reported without inflation, is a single significant fixation region from 16 and a single significant transition pair from 61 under 100,000-permutation Bonferroni-corrected testing, and a classifier with macro-averaged recall of 0.598. That figure belongs in the review's lower bound alongside the Saliency4ASD challenge band of 0.53-0.62, and for a related reason: both represent gaze-based classification evaluated without the design choices that inflate results elsewhere. Three practices transfer independently of the result. The split is child-disjoint and stated as such even though the sliding-window construction generates thousands of overlapping sequences per video. The group comparisons are permutation-tested with Bonferroni correction and the 15 and 60 negative results are reported alongside the two positives, which is what makes the positives credible. And the metric choice is reasoned from the class structure rather than defaulting to accuracy. Set against these, the paper illustrates two failure modes the review should note: a reference standard weaker than the companion paper from the same group acknowledges, and a measurement frame that the authors correctly identify as uninterpretable, meaning the study can establish that gaze distributions differ without being able to say what they differ about. | [RQ1.1] Two groups from a crowdsourced app population: 68 children with parent-reported autism (53 male, 15 female) contributing 380 videos and 27 neurotypical children (18 male, 9 female) contributing 69 videos, 95 children and 449 videos in total, from approximately 1,000 individuals who downloaded the app. The imbalance is substantial and runs opposite to the direction usual in this corpus - cases outnumber controls by more than two to one at child level and by more than five to one at video level, which the authors identify as the reason for choosing macro- and weighted-average metrics over accuracy. After frame filtering the imbalance is similar (520,536 autistic frames against 99,084), so per-video frame retention was comparable between groups, which is a useful check that the automated quality filters did not operate differentially. No other-diagnosis comparison group. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', 'the ASD cohort', against 'neurotypical (NT) children'. Person-first throughout, and 'neurotypical' rather than 'typically developing' or 'normal', which is the more neurodiversity-aligned term. Autism is described conventionally as 'characterized by social impairments, communication difficulties, and restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior', and the behavioural framing is deficit-oriented in places ('impaired social interactions', 'difficulty with maintaining eye contact'), though the analytic language is neutral and descriptive - differences in fixation distribution and transition frequency rather than abnormality. The privacy framing is notable for treating participants as people with interests to protect rather than as data sources. [RQ1.3] Reported only in aggregate and incompletely. Sex is given as 53 male and 15 female in the autistic group against 18 male and 9 female in the comparison group - 77.9% versus 66.7% male - with no test and no discussion. Age is reported only as an overall range of 2 to 15 years, with the distribution shown in a figure and no group means, medians, standard deviations or tests in the text, and one comparison-group child not providing an age at all. That is the study's most consequential reporting gap: gaze allocation, sustained attention, and willingness to engage in a charades game with a parent all change enormously between a 2-year-old and a 15-year-old, and the analysis pools the entire range without stratifying, covarying or reporting whether the groups are comparable. No IQ, language, adaptive or severity measure for either group, and no exclusion criteria described. [RQ1.4] Parent report alone. Parents who chose to share videos 'completed a survey to provide the age, sex, and diagnostic status of their children'. No instrument, no clinician involvement, no record verification, and no description of how diagnostic status was elicited. The companion study from the same group using the same app for speech analysis concedes this directly, noting that such labels 'are self-reported and thus unverified' and describing the mitigating design of offering diagnostic options unfamiliar to families who have not been evaluated. Neither the concession nor the mitigation appears here, and the limitations section does not mention the reference standard at all. Comparison-group status likewise rests on parental assertion with no screening. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, language, adaptive, severity or comorbidity measure for either group. Nothing therefore relates the gaze findings to any clinical dimension, and with an age span of 2 to 15 years and no developmental measure, neither age nor ability can be separated from diagnosis as an explanation for the observed differences. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether gaze fixation and visual scanning differences associated with autism can be detected from unstructured home video on consumer phones, without eye trackers, manual annotation or structured tasks. Main findings: one of 16 gaze regions (BC, p < .001) and one of 61 transition pairs (BB-BC, p < .001) differed significantly after Bonferroni correction across 100,000-permutation tests, with comparison children making 13% of transitions between these regions against 9.4% for autistic children; an LSTM on the discretised gaze sequences reached macro-averaged recall 0.598 and weighted-average recall 0.656 on a child-disjoint held-out set, described by the authors as mild predictive power; and the entire pipeline operated without any human viewing participant video. [RQ2.2] Participants' own homes with no researcher present, no environmental control and no equipment standardisation - and the paper's positioning depends on this. The related-work section is unusually specific in critiquing prior computer-vision studies on precisely this point, noting that Hashemi and Chang 'controlled the room lighting and distance of the camera from the participant's face' and concluding that 'the ability of these techniques to translate to natural nonclinical environments and unstructured tasks remains to be explored'. The consequences are then reported rather than hidden: 'excessive camera movement and poor lighting conditions rendered some frames in our data set too blurry for use', and 'other adults or siblings would often join in gameplay, resulting in multiple faces in the frame'. Roughly 43% of frames were discarded by the automated quality filters. This is the most uncontrolled acquisition setting in the corpus and the paper treats that as its subject rather than as noise. [RQ2.3] Ninety-second charades within a mobile game, with the child acting out prompts - emotions, sports, animals, chores - while the parent guesses, and the phone held on the parent's forehead with the front camera facing the child. The design achieves something specific: because the parent must watch the child to guess, the game creates a genuine dyadic social interaction in which the child's gaze toward the parent's face is functionally motivated, rather than a passive viewing task. The authors describe this as supplying 'inherent structure' in camera position, child location and interaction type while leaving the child free of hardware. The corresponding weakness is that the phone is mounted on a moving head, so the coordinate frame in which gaze is measured drifts continuously - which is why the resulting regions cannot be mapped to facial features. The prompts also vary between videos, so the elicited behaviour is not held constant across children. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, with videos accumulated opportunistically as families played and chose to share; no follow-up. Ethics approval from the Stanford IRB under a named eProtocol number, with parental consent to share each recording built into the app flow. Privacy is treated as a design constraint rather than a compliance step, and is one of the paper's three stated contributions: annotation was performed entirely computationally so that no human annotator ever viewed the footage, and the discussion explicitly contrasts this with prior manual-annotation work that 'may compromise the privacy of participants by providing annotators with access to video footage'. The senior author declares founding Cognoa and a co-author declares part-time consulting for the same company. [RQ2.5] No specialised hardware at all - participants' own phones, with no model, camera specification, resolution or frame rate reported. The analytic chain uses two off-the-shelf systems applied without task-specific training: Amazon Rekognition for 30 facial landmarks and bounding boxes, and OpenFace for gaze direction. Both are used as noisy annotators with explicit quality gates - frames with zero or more than two faces removed, and frames with OpenFace gaze confidence below 75% removed - and the authors are appropriately cautious about what survives, stating that 'we expected the final annotations to be of high quality, but the presence of some noise and incorrect labels was to be expected'. Using general-purpose vision tools as automated annotators rather than training bespoke models is what makes the privacy-preserving claim credible and the pipeline reproducible, and it is a deliberate architectural choice rather than a convenience. [RQ2.6] Good on pipeline, weak on participants. Fully reported: the app, game format, 90-second limit and recording arrangement; video and frame counts before and after filtering, broken down by group; both annotation tools with their outputs and the exact exclusion rules including the 75% confidence threshold; the gaze coordinate convention with its sign meanings; the 4x4 discretisation; the graph construction and normalisation for the transition analysis; the permutation test specification with 100,000 permutations and both Bonferroni thresholds; the sliding-window parameterisation with the ranges explored; the LSTM architecture, optimiser, learning rate, batch size and loss function; the three-way split with per-group video counts and the child-level constraint; and the metric choice with its rationale. Not reported: group-specific ages; any statistical comparison of demographics; the diagnostic elicitation; phone models or video specifications; the number of children excluded at any stage; and any data or code release. [RQ2.7] Two limitations are stated and both are real. Class imbalance is identified as the reason macro-averaged and weighted-average statistics diverge, with dataset augmentation proposed as the remedy. More importantly, the interpretability of the areas of interest is conceded directly: 'due to camera motion and variation in the location of the smartphone relative to the parent's face, the gaze fixation maps are difficult to interpret qualitatively, and AOIs cannot be definitely matched to a parent's specific facial regions'. That is the central caveat on the whole study and the authors state it plainly rather than gesturing at eye contact or mouth-looking. What is not acknowledged: that diagnostic labels are unverified parent report, conceded by the same group in their companion speech paper but absent here; that the sample spans thirteen years of childhood with no age reporting, matching or covariate adjustment; that weighted-average recall of 0.656 falls below the roughly 0.80 a majority-class predictor would achieve on a test set of 43 autistic and 11 comparison videos; and that no confidence intervals, permutation tests or baselines accompany the classification results, in contrast to the rigour applied to the group comparisons. [RQ2.9] Four directions, of which two are unusually practical. Expand the population and correct the class imbalance by augmentation. Analyse additional motion features such as limb movements and coordination, which the charades format would support naturally since the child is acting out prompts with their whole body. And - the most substantive - 'performing qualitative human-centered investigations or pragmatic randomized controlled trials to evaluate clinical usability' and 'evaluating the real-world diagnostic capabilities of our approach across diverse environmental settings'. Proposing a pragmatic randomised trial and human-centred usability work as the next step, rather than a larger dataset or a better architecture, is a translational rather than technical research agenda and is rare in this corpus. [RQ3.1] Two constructs drawn deliberately from clinical instruments: gaze fixation, 'which represent[s] regions of an individual's visual focus', and visual scanning, 'which refer[s] to the ways in which individuals scan their surrounding environment', both described as 'included in standard clinical diagnostic instruments'. The theoretical grounding is specific - fixation on the eyes signals communicative intent in dyadic interaction, and autistic individuals are reported to fixate instead on the mouth or other regions; scanning is grounded in Pelphrey's finding that neurotypical viewers transition between core facial features while autistic viewers scan non-feature areas such as the forehead and cheeks. Both constructs are then operationalised in a coordinate frame that cannot distinguish eyes from forehead from background, which the authors concede. The scanning analysis is nonetheless the more original contribution: modelling gaze shifts as a weighted graph and comparing adjacency matrices captures the sequential structure of looking rather than only its aggregate distribution, and it is what yields the interpretable finding that comparison children move between two adjacent central regions 13% of the time against 9.4% for autistic children. [RQ3.2] Single modality, and no fusion is attempted, though the companion speech study from the same group and app processes audio from the same recordings - so the two papers together represent an unexploited multimodal opportunity on a shared corpus, which neither notes. Within the modality, two representations of the same annotation are compared: a static fixation profile and a dynamic transition graph. Both yield exactly one significant finding after correction, and interestingly they converge on the same location - fixation differs at region BC and the significant transition is between BB and BC - which is a form of internal corroboration the paper does not draw attention to. Only the fixation representation is carried into the classifier; the transition matrices, which encode sequence and might plausibly carry more information, are used only descriptively. [RQ4.1] An LSTM chosen to exploit temporal structure, with the architecture kept minimal - w cells each taking a 16-dimensional one-hot vector, a single fully connected output and a sigmoid - and a weighted binary cross-entropy loss to handle the class imbalance. Only window size and shift are varied, explored across 50 to 500 frames and 10 to 100 respectively on the validation set, with the three best carried to the held-out test set. No alternative architecture, no baseline classifier and no chance comparator is reported, which is the main gap: given the imbalance, a majority-class predictor and a permutation null are both necessary to interpret a macro-averaged recall of 0.598, and neither is provided. The restraint in model complexity is appropriate for 95 children, but the absence of any comparator makes the modest result harder to situate than the group-difference analysis, where permutation testing does exactly that job. [RQ4.2] The representation is where the study's tradeoff is concentrated. Frame-level gaze is discretised from continuous (x, y) direction estimates into a 4x4 grid, then one-hot encoded and windowed. Discretisation is defensible given noisy estimates from uncalibrated phone video, and the sliding window with shift smaller than window generates overlapping samples, which multiplies the effective training set from 449 videos into many thousands of sequences - a legitimate augmentation given that the split is child-disjoint so the overlap cannot cross the partition. The decisive property, however, is the coordinate frame: gaze is expressed relative to the camera, which sits on the parent's forehead and moves with them. A region in this space is a direction, not a target, and the authors state that it cannot be matched to facial anatomy. The consequence is that the representation supports detecting that gaze distributions differ but not saying what they differ about - which is precisely the distinction between a signal and a behavioural finding, and the paper is clear about which it has. [RQ4.3] Two very different standards are applied to the two halves of the paper, and the contrast is instructive. The group comparisons are analysed with exemplary conservatism: two-sided permutation tests with 100,000 rearrangements at every location, Bonferroni correction applied to both families, and the correction's stringency explicitly noted as reducing Type 1 error at the cost of power. Reporting one significant region from 16 and one transition from 61 under that regime is a credible finding precisely because 15 and 60 negatives are reported alongside. The classification results receive no equivalent treatment - four metrics for three configurations with no confidence intervals, no permutation null and no baseline. The metric choice is nonetheless well reasoned, with macro- and weighted-average precision and recall selected over accuracy because of the imbalance and the divergence between them correctly interpreted as class-dependent performance. What is missing is the comparison that would locate the result: with 43 autistic and 11 comparison videos in the test set, always predicting autism yields weighted-average recall around 0.80, above the reported 0.656. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is pursued through the design of the analysis rather than through model attribution, and the outcome is honest about its own limits. The two group-comparison analyses are fully interpretable in their own terms - which regions, which transitions, what percentages - and the graph representation adds a sequential dimension that a fixation profile alone would miss. The reported effect is concrete: 13% of comparison children's gaze shifts occur between two adjacent central regions against 9.4% for autistic children. What is missing, and is conceded, is the mapping from those regions to anything in the world. Because the phone moves with the parent's head, region BC is a direction relative to a moving camera, not the parent's eyes or mouth, so the finding cannot be connected to eye contact, mouth-looking, or the Pelphrey and Chawarska results the introduction builds on. The LSTM receives no attribution analysis at all. The net position is that the study establishes a difference exists without being able to characterise it, and says so. [RQ4.5] The split is child-disjoint and stated as such, which is the single most important property and is applied correctly even under a feature construction that generates heavily overlapping windows: 324 videos to training, 71 to validation and 54 to a held-out test set, 'ensuring that all videos corresponding to a single child were assigned to the same set'. Hyperparameters were selected on validation and only the three best configurations evaluated on the test set, so the held-out estimate is not tuned. Group comparisons are protected by permutation testing with Bonferroni correction across both feature families. Three limits remain. There is no independent cohort. There is no baseline or null for the classification results, which matters acutely given a test set of 43 autistic and 11 comparison videos where the majority-class weighted-average recall of roughly 0.80 exceeds the reported 0.656 - a comparison the paper does not make. And the split is by video within child rather than being balanced on any covariate, so with an unreported age span of 2 to 15 years the training and test partitions could differ substantially in age composition without this being detectable. The overall picture is a study that validates its statistical claims rigorously and its predictive claim only loosely, while describing the latter as mild. [RQ5.1] Keywords: mobile health, autism spectrum disorder, social phenotyping, computer vision, gaze, mobile diagnostics, pattern recognition, autism, diagnostic, pattern, engagement, gaming, app, insight, vision. The presence of 'social phenotyping' alongside 'mobile health' and 'gaming' locates the work in digital phenotyping delivered through consumer software rather than in vision research or clinical assessment. [RQ5.2] Journal of Medical Internet Research 24(2):e31830 (2022), a digital health venue. Authorship spans Stanford's Departments of Computer Science, Bioengineering, Pediatrics and Biomedical Data Science, and Neuroscience, from the same group that produced the crowdsourced speech study on the same GuessWhat corpus. Funding is extensive, listing four NIH grants, an NSF award and numerous foundations. The senior author declares founding Cognoa and a co-author declares part-time consulting for the same company - relevant context given that the corpus's FDA pivotal trial paper evaluates a Cognoa device, and that the present study's honest reporting of a weak result sits in a portfolio that also contains a regulated commercial product. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is the standard access and delay argument - 1 in 44 prevalence, lengthy parent questionnaires and clinical observation producing 'long waiting times for results', and a goal of 'mitigating the problems associated with limited diagnostic resources for neurodevelopmental disorders, especially in regions where access to care is limited'. What distinguishes the positioning is the structure of the related-work critique, which sorts prior video-based work into three categories and identifies a specific cost for each: manual annotation 'require[s] large numbers of trained annotators when implemented on a large scale, which is expensive and time-consuming' and 'may compromise the privacy of participants'; eye trackers 'require custom hardware that can often be expensive and inaccessible, especially for individuals living in resource-limited regions'; and structured-environment studies controlled 'room lighting and distance of the camera from the participant's face', leaving translation to natural settings untested. The study then removes all three constraints simultaneously and reports what remains, which is a small but statistically defensible difference and a weak classifier. Read that way the paper is a deliberate test of how much signal survives the removal of every experimental control - and the answer, reported without inflation, is not much. |
| S-090 | Secondary analysis of the public Carette et al. gaze-path image dataset: 547 scan path images of 640x480 from 59 children - 29 autistic contributing 219 images and 30 typically developing contributing 328. No ages, sexes, diagnostic procedure, severity or cognitive information is reported for either group, though the literature review notes that CARS-based severity accompanies the source data. No ethics statement; dataset publicly available; no code release. | Images were converted to greyscale by equal channel weighting, resized to 100x100 and flattened to 10,000-element vectors. Principal component analysis on the resulting array supplied 500 features for boosted decision tree, deep SVM and decision jungle classifiers in Azure ML Studio Classic. A purpose-built convolutional network - four convolutional layers of 16, 32, 64 and 128 filters at 3x3 with interleaved 2x2 max pooling, 4,608 flattened features, dense layers of 256 and 128, sigmoid output - was trained with Adam, learning rate 0.001, batch size 16, 50 epochs, with architecture and hyperparameters selected iteratively on performance. Three data conditions were run: the original 547 images under a 70:30 split with five-fold cross-validation; a rotation-augmented set of 2,566 images (45, 60, 90 and 180 degrees) under the same protocol; and a 'mini batch' of one image per participant (59 images) under leave-one-out cross-validation. Augmentation and PCA were both applied before partitioning. | Original images: deep SVM AUC 51.50%, decision jungle 60.40%, boosted decision tree 67.60%, convolutional network 78.00% (sensitivity 78.57%, specificity 75.47%). Augmented images: boosted decision tree AUC 74.60%, convolutional network 97.00% (sensitivity 93.28%, specificity 91.38%, PPV 94.46%, NPV 90.06%) - the abstract's headline. Participant-level subset: the same network achieved 72.88% accuracy, correctly classifying 17 of 29 autistic children (sensitivity 58.62%) and 26 of 30 comparison children (specificity 86.67%), with PPV 80.95% and NPV 64.00%. | Rotation augmentation and principal component analysis were both applied to the complete dataset before partitioning, and images from the same child span the split at roughly 9.3 per participant, so the 97.00% and 78.00% figures are contaminated - the first of these diagnosed by the authors themselves. The abstract, keywords and conclusion nonetheless lead with the 97.00% figure that the discussion attributes to contamination. Rotation by 45 and 60 degrees produces gaze trajectories no eye could generate on a rectangular screen. Greyscale conversion discards the colour channel encoding velocity, acceleration and jerk. Architecture and hyperparameters were selected on performance without held-out confirmation. The participant-level analysis rests on 59 samples with one arbitrarily selected image per child and no confidence interval, and Table 6 labels its 72.88 as AUC while the text describes it as accuracy. No participant demographics, diagnostic procedure, ethics statement or code. | The single most useful paper in the corpus for quantifying how much reported accuracy depends on validation design, because it runs all three conditions on the same images with the same network and reports every one. The sequence - 97.00% AUC with pre-split rotation augmentation, 78.00% without augmentation but still image-wise, and 72.88% accuracy with 58.62% sensitivity restricted to one image per child - brackets the inflation within a single study. The participant-level figure agrees closely with the roughly 71% that Cilia and colleagues obtained by applying the same correction to the same data, so an independent group with a different architecture has effectively replicated the corrected estimate; that convergence is stronger evidence for the corrected figure than either study alone provides. The authors also name the mechanism in the right terms, attributing the augmented result to 'possible data contamination as similar replicates are entered into the training set, as seen in the testing dataset', and generalise it in their limitations into the sharpest statement in this review of what is wrong with the available data infrastructure: open eye-tracking datasets 'combine multiple ETSP images from a small set of participants rather than a single trial from a large group, making them unsuitable for reliable ASD screening'. Two secondary observations transfer. Conventional classifiers on principal components of the same images reached AUC 51.50% and 60.40%, near chance, which localises whatever signal exists in the convolutional representation and provides a useful internal control absent from the other two reuses of this dataset. And the paper's structure - abstract leading with a figure its own discussion attributes to an artefact - illustrates how such numbers propagate: a reader who stops at the abstract takes away 97.00%, and the corrected 72.88% appears only in a table two-thirds of the way through the results. | [RQ1.1] Two groups inherited from the Carette dataset: 29 autistic children contributing 219 images and 30 typically developing children contributing 328 images, 547 images from 59 children. The participant structure is not merely restated but actually used, which distinguishes this paper from the other two reuses of the same data in this corpus: a 'mini batch dataset that encapsulated only single trials from each of 59 participants' is constructed and evaluated separately. That analysis is the study's most valuable output. The main analyses nonetheless proceed at image level, so in the 70:30 split of 547 images and in the augmented analysis of 2,566 images, images from the same child appear in both training and test at roughly 9.3 images per participant. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The class imbalance of 219 to 328 is not corrected in the original analysis and is partly amplified by uniform augmentation, which preserves the ratio at 1,047 to 1,519. [RQ1.2] 'autistic children', 'children with ASD', 'individuals with ASD', against 'typically developing (TD)' and 'TDs'. Person-first and identity-first are used interchangeably, and the comparison group is frequently reduced to the bare plural acronym 'TDs'. Autism is described as 'a chronic illness that lasts a lifetime' and elsewhere as a 'disease' and a 'condition' one may 'have', a framing that misdescribes a neurodevelopmental condition as a progressive illness. The introduction does include one observation that is clinically apt and rarely made in this corpus, noting that autism 'is diagnosed four times more frequently in boys than in girls; compared to boys, many girls with ASD show fewer visible signs' - though the study collects no sex data and cannot examine this. [RQ1.3] Nothing. No ages, no sexes, no group sizes beyond the participant and image counts, no IQ, no language level and no matching of any kind for either group. The literature review mentions in passing that a different Carette study involved children aged 8 to 10, but no demographic information is given for the participants whose images are analysed here. This is a lesser omission than in the two companion reuses of the same data only in that participant counts are stated and, uniquely, used; on every other demographic variable the study is silent. [RQ1.4] Not reported for the analysis. The literature review does note that the source group 'developed a four-level severity-based classifier model for ASD, with classes such as TD, low, medium, and severe based on Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) score', which establishes that CARS scores accompany the source dataset - so this paper is aware that a severity instrument exists and does not use it. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role or setting is stated as applying to the participants analysed, and the class labels are treated as image attributes. Under this review's classification this is dataset-label-only ascertainment, though better documented in its literature review than in its methods. [RQ1.5] None used. CARS-based severity exists in the source data and is referenced in the literature review, but no cognitive, language, adaptive, severity or comorbidity measure enters the analysis, and no exclusions are described. Consequently nothing relates model output to any clinical dimension, and the paper's speculation that 'ML models could quantify heterogeneities in ASD symptoms, allowing for accurate ASD severity grading using ET data' is untested despite the severity data being available in the source. [RQ2.1] Goal: identify an accurate model for autism screening from scan path images and determine whether performance survives restriction to one image per child. Main findings: conventional classifiers performed at or near chance on the original images (deep SVM AUC 51.50%, decision jungle 60.40%, boosted decision tree 67.60%); the convolutional network reached AUC 78.00% on the same images; rotation augmentation raised the network to AUC 97.00%, which the authors attribute to data contamination; and the participant-level subset of 59 images evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation yielded 72.88% accuracy with sensitivity 58.62% and specificity 86.67%. [RQ2.2] Not reported for the data collection. The literature review states, summarising the source publication, that recordings used 'an SMI RED series mobile eye tracker' while participants 'watched a series of videos to stimulate eye movement across the screen', but nothing about the room, country, recruitment or protocol is restated in the methods. The only settings named are the two analysing institutions and the compute environments - Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio Classic, Google Colaboratory, and a specified Dell laptop. [RQ2.3] Not described. The methods section begins from the images and never states what the children viewed. The literature review's one-line summary of the source study is the only information available, and it is not carried into the analysis or used to interpret any result. The limitations section does return to the acquisition question with a substantive recommendation - 'the clinician must ensure that the child is staring at the eye tracker throughout the trials and that the recording environment is free from any distractions that may impact the child's attention' - which correctly identifies attention and environmental control as determinants of data quality, but this is offered as guidance for future collection rather than as a characterisation of the data analysed. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a public dataset; no follow-up. No ethics statement, consent statement or IRB approval appears anywhere, and no pointer is given to the source dataset's approvals - an omission that is common for benchmark reuse in this corpus but is not acknowledged. Funding is not declared in the extracted text. The dataset is described throughout as publicly available but no URL or accession is given in the extracted portion. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment is described beyond a literature-review mention of the source study's SMI RED tracker. The analytic environment is specified in unusual detail for a computational paper: Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio Classic for the conventional models, Google Colaboratory for the neural network, and a Dell XPS 15 9500 with an Intel i7-10750H at 2.60 GHz with six cores. Model hyperparameters are stated - binary cross-entropy loss, 50 epochs, batch size 16, learning rate 0.001 with Adam - along with the full convolutional architecture layer by layer with filter counts, kernel sizes, pooling dimensions and output feature dimensions. [RQ2.6] Reproducible as a pipeline, silent on the data. Fully reported: greyscale conversion with its channel weighting; resizing to 100x100 and flattening to 10,000 elements; the resulting array dimensions; the number of principal components retained in each condition; the complete convolutional architecture with all layer dimensions; the hyperparameters and the tuning procedure; the 70:30 split with exact image counts; the five-fold cross-validation; the augmentation rotations and the resulting class counts; the mini-batch construction and its leave-one-out protocol; the compute platforms and hardware; and full performance tables for every model in every condition. Not reported: participant demographics, diagnostic procedure, stimulus, acquisition protocol, the criterion by which one image per child was selected for the mini batch, random seeds, ethics approval, or any code. [RQ2.7] Two limitations are stated and the first is the most substantive limitation statement in this part of the corpus. It identifies the structural problem with the available data infrastructure: 'A few open-access ET datasets are available; however, they combine multiple ETSP images from a small set of participants rather than a single trial from a large group, making them unsuitable for reliable ASD screening.' That is a correct and generalisable diagnosis, and it is reinforced in the discussion where the authors attribute their own augmented result to 'possible data contamination as similar replicates are entered into the training set, as seen in the testing dataset'. The second limitation concerns collection quality, recommending that clinicians ensure the child attends to the tracker in a distraction-free environment. What is not acknowledged: that the abstract, keywords and conclusion all lead with the 97.00% figure the discussion attributes to contamination; that images from the same child span the training and test partitions even without augmentation; that principal component analysis was fitted on the full dataset before splitting; that rotation by 45 and 60 degrees produces physically impossible gaze traces; that the participant-level result rests on 59 samples with no confidence interval; and that greyscale conversion discards the colour-encoded derivative information the source images carry. [RQ2.9] Four directions. The first follows directly from the stated limitation and is the right one: obtain a dataset of single trials from a large group rather than multiple images from few participants. The second concerns collection quality - ensuring attention to the tracker and a distraction-free environment. The third proposes electrooculography as an alternative signal. The fourth is a deployment proposal that outruns the evidence considerably: 'a mobile app with an incorporated DNN-based ASD classifier and an extensive ET dataset of children aged 6 to 24 months may assist parents in independently screening their toddlers for ASD using a mobile device' - proposed for an age band entirely outside the analysed data, using a modality that requires an eye tracker, on the basis of a participant-level sensitivity of 58.62%. [RQ3.1] Nominally atypical visual preference, with the introduction grounding this in the claim that autistic individuals 'pay less attention to faces and other social stimuli such as the human voice and hand gestures when compared to nonsocial stimuli' and that 'this unique pattern of eye movements appears in autistic children well before behavioral symptoms of ASD start showing'. Nothing of this construct survives into the analysis. The images are converted to greyscale - discarding the colour channel through which the source dataset encodes velocity, acceleration and jerk - resized to 100x100, and either flattened into pixel vectors for principal component analysis or passed through convolutional layers. No fixation, saccade, dwell time or area-of-interest quantity is computed at any stage, and no group difference in looking behaviour is reported anywhere. The construct discussed in the introduction and the quantity modelled in the methods are unconnected. [RQ3.2] Single modality with no fusion. The paper's comparative structure is instead across model families and, more importantly, across data conditions, and the second of these is the study's real contribution. Running the same convolutional network across three data conditions - original, rotation-augmented, and one image per participant - constitutes an ablation over validation design rather than over features, and it is the only such experiment in the corpus. The model-family comparison is also informative as an internal control: deep SVM on principal components of the same images reached AUC 51.50% on the original data, indistinguishable from chance, and decision jungle 60.40%, so the conventional pipeline extracts essentially nothing. That places whatever signal exists in the convolutional representation and simultaneously indicates that the pixel statistics captured by principal components carry no class information - a useful negative result that the authors note but do not pursue. [RQ4.1] Four algorithms across two families. The three conventional models were run in a graphical cloud environment with 'minimal settings, making them lightweight and suited for low-power computers', which is a deployment argument rather than a methodological one. The convolutional network was arrived at by iterative search - 'we continued modifying configurations of the above model, such as various combinations of convolutional, pooling, and dense layers until we found an optimal model' - and its hyperparameters likewise tuned 'until the model produced the highest score', so both architecture and hyperparameters were selected on performance with no held-out confirmation of that selection. The authors do report an honest interim observation, that 'we found that all models were overfitting, which could be due to two factors: model complexity or the limited size of the dataset', and their response - augmenting the data - is a reasonable inference that turns out to have created a worse problem, which they then diagnose correctly. [RQ4.2] Two representations of the same images, both stripped of behavioural content. For the conventional models: greyscale conversion by equal channel weighting, resizing to 100x100, flattening to a 10,000-element vector, then principal component analysis retaining 500 components (1,750 after augmentation). For the network: the same greyscale 100x100 image passed through four convolutional stages producing 4,608 features. The greyscale step is the most consequential and passes without comment: the source dataset's distinguishing property is that gaze velocity, acceleration and jerk are encoded as colour gradients, and averaging the three channels equally discards precisely that information, leaving a monochrome trace of position only. Both this study and Gaspar and colleagues make the same conversion on the same images, so the two independent reuses of this dataset both destroy the derivative encoding it was constructed to carry. [RQ4.3] The metric panel is a deliberate improvement on the field's convention and is argued as such: 'In contrast to the previously reported studies, we evaluate the model performance using the area under the ROC curve (AUC), specificity, sensitivity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative prediction value (NPV).' Reporting PPV and NPV alongside sensitivity and specificity is uncommon here and is what makes the participant-level result legible - sensitivity 58.62% against specificity 86.67% shows immediately that the model detects comparison children far better than autistic ones, which a single accuracy figure would conceal. All four models are reported in every data condition with all five metrics, so the deterioration of the conventional models and the improvement of the network under augmentation are both fully visible. Two gaps: no confidence intervals accompany any figure, which matters most for the 59-sample participant-level result; and Table 6 labels 72.88 as AUC while the discussion describes it as 'an overall accuracy of 72.88%', with the arithmetic (17 + 26 correct of 59) confirming it is accuracy, so the participant-level table header is mislabelled. [RQ4.4] No feature-level interpretability of any kind, and none possible given that the features are principal components of pixel arrays or convolutional activations over a rendered plot. No group means, effect sizes, directions or descriptive statistics about gaze appear anywhere. What the paper offers instead is interpretability at the level of experimental design: by running the same model across three data conditions it makes visible what each condition contributes, which is a more useful form of insight for this review than a saliency map would be. The discussion also contains speculation not supported by anything done here - that 'by leveraging the capabilities of complex CNN-based algorithms, ML models could quantify heterogeneities in ASD symptoms, allowing for accurate ASD severity grading using ET data' - which is notable because the source dataset contains CARS-based severity labels that would have permitted a direct test. [RQ4.5] This is simultaneously the study's weakest and its most valuable dimension, because it fails and then measures its own failure. Three separate contaminations affect the headline analyses. Rotation augmentation was applied to all 547 images before partitioning, so rotated copies of the same source image appear in training and test. Principal component analysis was fitted on the complete 547x10,001 array (and later the 2,566x10,000 array) before splitting, so the components for the conventional models are informed by test images. And images from the same child span the partition regardless of augmentation, at roughly 9.3 per participant. The authors identify the first of these explicitly - 'possible data contamination as similar replicates are entered into the training set, as seen in the testing dataset' - and respond by constructing a one-image-per-participant subset evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation, which removes both the augmentation and the within-child duplication. The result is 72.88% accuracy with 58.62% sensitivity, against 97.00% AUC in the contaminated condition. That within-study drop of roughly 24 points, produced by the same architecture on the same source images, is the cleanest quantification of validation-induced inflation available in this review, and its close agreement with the approximately 71% Cilia and colleagues obtained by the same correction on the same data amounts to an independent replication of the corrected figure. The remaining weakness is that the participant-level analysis itself is thin - 59 samples, one arbitrarily selected image per child, leave-one-out, no confidence interval - so 72.88% is 43 correct classifications and carries a wide interval. [RQ5.1] Keywords: ASD screening, autism spectrum disorder, machine learning, convolutional neural network (CNN), eye-tracking scan path images. The use of 'screening' rather than 'diagnosis' in the first keyword matches the paper's explicit positioning that the model 'is meant to be used for ASD screening' rather than as a diagnostic tool - a scope statement that several higher-profile studies in this corpus do not make. [RQ5.2] Diagnostics 12(2):518 (2022), an MDPI open-access clinical diagnostics journal. Authorship is from the Schools of Electronics and Electrical Engineering at Vellore Institute of Technology in India and the Department of Biomedical Engineering at Ajman University in the UAE, with no clinical or autism-research affiliation. The review timeline is compressed - received 27 January 2022, accepted 12 February, published 17 February, twenty-one days from submission to publication - and no ethics statement appears. The literature review is nonetheless the most substantive of the three studies reusing this dataset, summarising six prior works with their samples, equipment, stimuli and reported figures, and correctly identifying which prior study reported what. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is the standard screening argument with the usual claim that current procedures 'are highly subjective, leading to misdiagnoses or missed diagnoses' and that an objective biomarker 'would substantially impact current diagnosis practices'. Two features of the positioning are better than that suggests. The scope is explicitly bounded - a dedicated Clinical Implications subsection states that 'rather than being a diagnostic tool, the research model we proposed in this work is meant to be used for ASD screening using ET data' - which is the correct claim for what the evidence supports and is stated before any results are discussed. And the literature review engages with prior figures specifically rather than generically, comparing its own augmented AUC of 97.00% against 'the performance (AUC: 90%) reported in the research work on the same dataset with augmentation' - that is, against the source authors' own result on the same images. What the paper does not do is carry its own contamination diagnosis into that comparison: having established that the augmented condition is contaminated, it compares its contaminated 97% favourably against another group's similarly obtained 90%, when the informative comparison is between its own participant-level 72.88% and the source group's participant-level result of approximately 71%. |
| S-091 | Cross-sectional classification on a remotely recruited convenience sample: 49 children aged 3 to 12 - 28 with a parent-reported formal autism diagnosis (19 male, 9 female) and 21 neurotypical (10 male, 7 female, 4 unspecified) - recruited via the GuessWhat user base, the Hartwell Foundation KidsFirst database, ResearchMatch.org and Facebook, with data collected between April 2017 and February 2021. Diagnostic status by parent report, safeguarded by requiring confirmation of formal medical assessment, selection from a specific diagnostic menu, and reporting of therapies received. No group-specific ages; the whole-sample figure of 7.10 +/- 5.82 years is arithmetically implausible. No cognitive, language or severity measures. Stanford IRB approval; dataset not released. | The app recorded four fields per trial - prompt start time, end time, correct flag and skip flag - during 90-second charades sessions in which the parent held the phone to their forehead, the child enacted a displayed prompt, and the parent guessed and labelled by tilting. Analysis was restricted to the 17 most frequently presented prompts, CAFE facial-emotion photographs. Thirty-four features were derived: percentage correct and mean prompt duration for each of the 17 emotions. XGBoost, random forest, logistic regression and linear SVM were evaluated by repeated nested cross-validation - inner four-fold grid search selecting hyperparameters by AU-ROC, outer held-out fold for estimation, seven repetitions giving 28 estimates - with outlier removal, k-nearest-neighbour imputation, standardisation and SMOTE upsampling all performed inside each split to prevent leakage. Feature importances were inspected across all 28 iterations and models retrained on the duration-only subset. | Full feature set: XGBoost AU-ROC 0.74 and recall 0.76; random forest 0.73 and 0.76; linear SVM 0.70 and 0.70 with precision 0.70; logistic regression 0.67 and 0.67. Duration-only subset: random forest best at AU-ROC 0.75, recall 0.77, accuracy 0.72, precision 0.67; linear SVM 0.71 and 0.74; logistic regression 0.69 and 0.69; XGBoost fell to 0.70 and 0.72. Duration features were significantly more important than accuracy features (t = 5.15, p = 1e-5), and three of four classifiers improved or held when accuracy features were dropped. Accuracy features clustered at ceiling in both groups. Among duration features, disgust was consistently most important, followed by surprise and sadness. | The duration feature - which carries nearly all the signal - spans prompt onset to the parent's tilt, so it may measure the parent's recognition and labelling speed rather than the child's enactment, as the authors state; the parent is also unblinded and generates every accuracy label. Diagnostic labels are unverified parent report. Demographic reporting is minimal: no group-specific ages, an arithmetically impossible whole-sample age standard deviation, four comparison children not reporting sex, and no demographic comparison; the authors acknowledge the sample is too small to assess performance across gender, ethnicity, nationality, age or co-occurring diagnoses. The unit of analysis is not stated - features are described as per-session while the sample is described as 49 children - so child-disjointness of the folds cannot be confirmed. Feature-family selection used importances from all cross-validation iterations before retraining. No confidence intervals despite bootstrapped distributions, and no chance baseline. No data or code release. | Two contributions carry into the synthesis. Methodologically, this is one of very few papers in the review to name data leakage explicitly and design against it, performing outlier removal, imputation, standardisation and SMOTE inside each cross-validation fold with the reason stated, and pairing that with genuine nested cross-validation over 28 repetitions. The contrast with Liao and colleagues, who select features on the full sample before cross-validating, and with Kanhirakadavath and colleagues, who fit principal components before splitting, is direct and instructive. That this careful design yields AU-ROC 0.745 rather than a figure in the nineties is itself part of the evidence. Substantively, the study defines the minimal end of the data-modality spectrum in this review: four event fields per trial, no video, no audio, no imagery, no sensor and no annotation, yielding a signal that is weak but real and that raises no privacy question at all. Set against the FDA pivotal trial at the other extreme - three inputs including expert-scored home video and a specialist consensus reference standard - the pair brackets what is achievable at each end of the cost and intrusiveness range. Two further observations transfer. The feature ablation is a model of how to do one, showing by three convergent methods that response latency rather than task accuracy carries the signal and diagnosing the ceiling effect that renders accuracy uninformative. And the authors' own caveat, that the latency they measure runs from prompt onset to the parent's tilt and so may index the parent rather than the child, is the kind of confound identification that several higher-performing studies in this corpus would have benefited from applying to themselves. | [RQ1.1] Two groups from a remotely recruited convenience sample: 28 children with a parent-reported formal autism diagnosis (19 male, 9 female) and 21 neurotypical children (10 male, 7 female, 4 not reporting sex), 49 in total, with data accumulated between April 2017 and February 2021. Recruitment ran through four channels - the app's existing user base, the Hartwell Foundation's KidsFirst autism research database, ResearchMatch.org and Facebook advertisements - which is a more diverse sampling frame than the single-channel recruitment typical here, though all routes select for families with smartphones, internet access and English literacy, and the last two select for research-engaged families. No other-diagnosis comparison group, though the diagnostic menu presented to parents included ADHD/ADD, anxiety and speech and language delay, so children with those labels would presumably have been identifiable had they been recruited. The class imbalance is modest (28 to 21) and is handled by SMOTE upsampling applied within each cross-validation split rather than to the whole dataset.
