[RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'children with autism', 'individuals with ASD', against 'neurotypical (NT) children'. Person-first throughout, with 'neurotypical' preferred over 'typically developing'. The framing is oriented toward access and equity rather than deficit: the introduction is organised around rural and low-socioeconomic disparities in identification, the observation that 'up to 80 pct. of counties in the U.S. lack sufficient diagnostic resources', and the argument that questionnaire-based screening performs worse for non-white and lower-education caregivers. The game itself is described as 'a gamified therapeutic intervention' designed to be 'an engaging and fun way for parents and children to interact', so the data collection is framed as a by-product of something intended to benefit the family rather than as extraction. The paper also engages briefly with the ethics of framing, noting 'some disagreement about the patient as a consumer model' before arguing that user experience nonetheless matters for engagement. [RQ1.3] The weakest demographic reporting relative to the paper's methodological care elsewhere. Sex is given as 19 male and 9 female among autistic children and 10 male, 7 female and 4 unspecified among comparison children - so 67.9% versus 47.6% male among those reporting - with no comparison or discussion. Age is reported only as a whole-sample figure of 7.10 +/- 5.82 years, with no group-specific means, and that figure is arithmetically implausible: with inclusion restricted to ages 3 to 12, a standard deviation of 5.82 cannot arise, since the entire range spans nine years. Whether this is a transcription error or a computation over a different variable cannot be determined. No IQ, language, adaptive or severity measure for either group. The authors identify the consequence in their limitations - 'the sample size was too small to evaluate the predictive power of our models across various demographic dimensions, including gender, ethnicity, nationality, age and other diagnosis' - and commit to demographic fairness validation as recruitment expands, which is the right commitment but does not substitute for reporting what was collected. [RQ1.4] Parent report, with a described mitigation that is more substantive than most. Caregivers were required to confirm that the diagnosis 'came from a formal medical assessment', to select a diagnostic label from a menu including several distinctions that a family without evaluation experience would be unlikely to navigate - Autism Spectrum Disorder, Autistic Disorder, PDD-NOS, Asperger Syndrome, ADHD/ADD, anxiety, speech and language delay - and to report the specific therapies their child was receiving, on the reasoning that 'this information requires a specialized understanding of the autism diagnosis and subsequent treatment prescriptions'. That is a coherent design: it uses the specificity of diagnostic and treatment vocabulary as an indirect check on whether a formal evaluation occurred. It remains parent report, with no instrument, clinician contact or record verification, and the therapy information collected as part of the check is never described or analysed. Comparison-group status rests on parental assertion with no screening at all. [RQ1.5] None analysed. No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure was obtained for either group, and no comorbidity data are reported despite the diagnostic menu having captured alternative labels and despite therapy type having been collected. The absence matters for the specific construct at issue: response latency in an emotion-enactment task depends on receptive language, processing speed and motor planning, none of which is measured, and the sample spans ages 3 to 12 with no age reported by group. The authors list co-occurring diagnoses among the dimensions they cannot examine at this sample size. [RQ2.1] Goal: determine whether the GuessWhat game generates a signal separating autistic from neurotypical children using only objective gameplay metadata, as a step toward an easily deployed remote screening tool. Main findings: AU-ROC 0.745 with recall 0.769 for the best model (random forest on duration features); duration features significantly more important than accuracy features (t = 5.15, p = 1e-5); accuracy features uninformative because they cluster at ceiling in both groups; three of four classifiers improved or held when accuracy features were removed; and disgust, surprise and sadness prompts carried the most importance among duration features. [RQ2.2] Participants' own homes with no researcher present, no equipment provision and no environmental control - 'this study was conducted remotely' - which is the design's entire point. The equity argument is developed at length and with specifics rather than as a gesture: prevalence is similar in rural (0.9%) and urban (1.0%) areas but rural communities face limited access to identification and intervention services; up to 80% of US counties lack sufficient diagnostic resources; and existing questionnaire-based screening 'require[s] literacy and perform[s] worse with non-white and lower education caregivers', so digitising those questionnaires 'risks exacerbating current disparities'. The proposed alternative - deriving signal from behaviour rather than from caregiver report - would in principle be insensitive to caregiver literacy, though the game itself still requires a smartphone, internet access and English. [RQ2.3] A 90-second charades game in which the parent holds the phone against their forehead displaying a prompt they cannot see, the child acts it out, and the parent guesses and labels the outcome by tilting the phone. The prompts analysed are 17 CAFE facial-emotion photographs spanning anger, fear, sadness, happiness, surprise, disgust and neutrality, so the task requires the child to recognise an emotion and enact it recognisably to another person - a compound demand the authors characterise carefully as 'a complex interaction between child performance and parent interpretation', functioning as 'a proxy for emotion recognition' that 'likely captures components of theory of mind, metacognition and many other phenomena, as well'. The design's strength is that the parent's guessing behaviour makes the child's enactment functionally consequential rather than performed for a camera. Its corresponding weakness, which the authors state, is that the parent is inside the measurement loop: they set the end of every timed interval and they generate every accuracy label. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, with data accumulated opportunistically across nearly four years as families played and shared. Stanford Institutional Review Board approval is stated, though without a protocol number, and recruitment channels are named. The privacy position is a genuine design property rather than a claim: because the analysis uses only four event fields per trial - start time, end time, correct flag, skip flag - no imagery, audio or identifiable content is involved at all, which the authors present as enabling screening 'in a privacy-preserved manner' and contrast with computer-vision approaches where 'privacy concerns are at the forefront'. Among the three GuessWhat studies in this corpus, this is the only one whose modality raises no confidentiality question. [RQ2.5] None beyond a smartphone the family already owns - iOS or Android, with internet access, and no model, sensor or specification requirement, because the data are event timestamps rather than recordings. This is the most minimal data-collection footprint in the review and it is the paper's principal translational argument: a screening signal derived from four fields per trial imposes no bandwidth cost for video upload, no storage burden, no annotation pipeline and no privacy exposure. Analysis used Python with scikit-learn and XGBoost, with hyperparameter grids tabulated for all four classifier families. [RQ2.6] Strong on modelling, weak on participants, with one substantive ambiguity. Fully reported: the game mechanics including the tilt-labelling convention; the four event fields recorded; the rationale for restricting to CAFE prompts; both feature definitions with their formulae; the complete preprocessing sequence with its ordering, the three-standard-deviation outlier rule, k = 3 for imputation, and SMOTE; the explicit statement that preprocessing occurs within each split; the nested cross-validation structure with outer and inner fold counts and the seven repetitions; the selection criterion of AU-ROC in the inner loop; hyperparameter grids for all four classifiers; the deliberate bias of the search space toward regularisation; and all sixteen performance figures across two feature conditions. Not reported: group-specific ages; any demographic comparison; the therapy information collected as a diagnostic check; whether a child contributing multiple sessions supplies multiple rows to the dataset; the IRB protocol number; and any data or code release. The unit-of-analysis ambiguity is the most consequential gap given the paper's otherwise careful leakage handling. [RQ2.7] Two limitations are stated and both are substantive, and one further caveat appears in the discussion that is arguably more important than either. The stated limitations are that the sample is too small to evaluate performance across demographic dimensions - gender, ethnicity, nationality, age and co-occurring diagnoses - with a commitment to demographic fairness validation as recruitment expands; and that the study should be reproduced 'in a clinical setting in which the person displaying the prompts to the child is neither a parent nor informed of the child's diagnosis', which would remove both parental leniency in labelling and the unblinding of the person generating the labels. The discussion caveat is the one that bears on the headline: 'the duration-based measures in this study could capture the speed with which a parent marks a prompt as correct as opposed to the speed with which it takes the child to answer the prompt' - so the feature family carrying nearly all the signal may be measuring the parent. The authors also diagnose why the accuracy features failed, attributing the ceiling effect to 'parents incorrectly labeling or a game design that was too easy for the majority of children regardless of diagnosis'. Not acknowledged: the implausible age standard deviation; the absence of any group-specific demographics; and the unit-of-analysis ambiguity. [RQ2.9] Four directions, two of which would directly test the study's own weaknesses. Reproducing the paradigm with an examiner who is neither the parent nor informed of the diagnosis would isolate the child's contribution to the duration measure from the parent's and would blind the labeller - addressing the confound and the unblinding in a single design change, and it is the right experiment. Expanding recruitment to permit demographic subgroup validation follows directly from the equity framing that motivates the study, since a tool proposed to reduce disparities must be shown not to perform differentially across the groups it is meant to serve. The remaining two are extending prompts beyond CAFE images to video, and investigating how the parent-child dyadic relationship shapes the signal - the latter framed as scientific rather than merely methodological. [RQ3.1] Emotion recognition, targeted through a compound behaviour whose composite nature the authors are unusually careful about. The stated construct is grounded in prior work showing that autistic and neurotypical children differ both in 'the ability to correctly identify an emotion and the reaction time required to do so', and the two feature families map onto exactly those two components. But the measured behaviour is not the child's recognition alone: it is the child recognising the emotion, planning and executing an enactment, and the parent interpreting that enactment and responding. The paper states this rather than eliding it, describing the process as 'a complex interaction between child performance and parent interpretation' and noting that treating it as a proxy for emotion recognition risks 'an oversimplified understanding', since it 'likely captures components of theory of mind, metacognition and many other phenomena, as well'. That is the right level of caution for a construct that no single measurement isolates, and it is rarer in this corpus than it should be. [RQ3.2] Single modality with no fusion, but the feature-family comparison functions as a well-executed ablation and yields the study's clearest finding. Two families of seventeen features each - accuracy and duration - are compared in three ways: by model-derived importance across all 28 cross-validation iterations for all four classifiers, by a statistical test of the difference in mean importance (t = 5.15, p = 1e-5), and by retraining on the duration subset alone. All three converge: duration dominates, and removing accuracy improves or maintains performance in three of four classifiers, with XGBoost the only exception. The diagnosis of why is equally clean - accuracy scores cluster at ceiling in both groups, so the feature carries no variance to exploit - and the authors offer two candidate explanations, lenient parental labelling or a game too easy for most children, either of which would be actionable in redesign. This is what a feature ablation should look like, and it is more informative than the several fusion claims elsewhere in this corpus that rest on an accuracy delta alone. [RQ4.1] Four classifier families selected on three reasoned criteria rather than by convention: no a priori assumption about linearity, so both linear and non-linear families are tested; the small sample, motivating families 'that offered considerable flexibility to prevent overfitting through regularization'; and interpretability, 'to gain insight into the specific aspects of gameplay that predict ASD'. The hyperparameter grids are tabulated in full and were deliberately restricted 'to include hyperparameters that would lead to more regularization and less overfitting' - so the search space itself was biased against complexity because of n = 49, which is a considered decision rather than a default. The spread across families is informative: tree-based methods reach AU-ROC 0.73-0.75 while linear methods reach 0.67-0.71, and linear SVM achieves the highest precision at 0.70 while tree methods achieve the highest recall, so the choice among them is a genuine operating-point decision. Model selection is stated as 'the simplest model resulting in the highest average of AU-ROC and Recall', a criterion declared before the comparison rather than fitted to it. [RQ4.2] Thirty-four scalar features per child, derived directly from four event fields with no signal processing, feature learning or dimensionality reduction. The representation is maximally interpretable - each feature is 'percent correct on the disgust prompt' or 'mean response duration on the surprise prompt' - which is what makes the feature-importance analysis meaningful and what allows the finding to be stated in behavioural terms. Restricting to the 17 most commonly presented prompts 'in order to minimize missing-data imputation' is a sensible data-quality decision that is stated and justified. The one unresolved representational question is aggregation: features are described as computed 'for a single session of gameplay' while the sample is 49 children, and the paper does not state whether a child playing several sessions contributes several rows. If it does, the nested cross-validation would not be child-disjoint and the estimates would inherit the within-subject leakage that the paper is otherwise careful to avoid. [RQ4.3] Mean AU-ROC, recall, accuracy and precision reported for all four classifiers under both feature conditions - sixteen complete result rows - with the values being means across 28 nested cross-validation iterations rather than single-split point estimates, and with distributions bootstrapped from those 28 sets. Reporting the full grid rather than only the winner exposes the tradeoff structure: linear SVM has the best precision on the full feature set while tree methods have the best recall, and XGBoost is the only model that degrades on the reduced set. The metric-selection reasoning is also made explicit, with the authors arguing for choosing 'the model that results in the highest average of AU-ROC and Recall' and undertaking to discuss the practical considerations of each metric. What is missing: no confidence intervals are printed despite distributions having been bootstrapped, and no chance or trivial baseline is reported - which matters at n = 49, where an AU-ROC of 0.745 estimated over 28 folds of roughly 12 held-out children each carries substantial uncertainty. [RQ4.4] The most thorough feature-importance analysis in the corpus relative to the size of the study. Importances are extracted from the best model at each of the 28 cross-validation iterations for each of the four classifier families and displayed as per-iteration heatmaps, so stability across folds is directly visible rather than asserted from a single fit. The two feature families are then compared statistically, yielding a large and significant separation (t = 5.15, p = 1e-5), and importances are aggregated by emotion category to give an interpretable ranking. The finding that disgust prompts carry the most importance, followed by surprise and sadness, is then connected to independent evidence that 'younger children are worse at discriminating facial expressions of disgust and surprise when images of these expressions are presented alongside specific other emotions', suggesting these emotions require more cognitive development to process - a mechanistic account that generates a testable prediction rather than a post hoc rationalisation. The authors immediately temper it, warning against 'an oversimplified understanding of these features'. The one weakness is that no direction of effect is reported: it is not stated whether autistic children took longer or shorter on disgust prompts, so the finding is that the feature discriminates without saying how. [RQ4.5] Among the best-handled in the corpus on the dimensions the paper controls. Leakage is named explicitly and designed against: 'To avoid incorporating information from the distribution of the training data into the test set (i.e., data leakage), we carried out the following preprocessing steps separately for each test-train split of the data' - covering outlier removal, k-nearest-neighbour imputation, standardisation and SMOTE upsampling. Performing imputation and resampling inside the fold rather than on the full dataset is the correct handling and is violated by several studies here, including Liao and colleagues who select features on the whole sample and Kanhirakadavath and colleagues who fit principal components before splitting. The validation structure is genuine nested cross-validation - inner four-fold grid search selecting hyperparameters by AU-ROC, outer held-out fold estimating performance, repeated seven times for 28 estimates - so hyperparameter selection cannot contaminate the reported figures. Two residual issues. Feature selection was performed by inspecting importances across the 28 iterations and then retraining on the duration subset, so that selection used information from all folds; the effect is likely small since the selection is a binary family choice made on a large and statistically tested difference, but it is not nested. And the unit of analysis is not stated, so whether the folds are child-disjoint cannot be confirmed. Set against the corpus, the reported AU-ROC of 0.745 is modest precisely because these controls are in place, and the paper presents it as feasibility rather than accuracy. [RQ5.1] No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is digital phenotyping, gamified therapeutic, remote screening, telehealth and health equity - a digital-health and access register rather than a machine-learning one, matching a paper whose contribution is a deployment argument supported by a modest classifier. [RQ5.2] Intelligence-Based Medicine 6:100057 (2022), an Elsevier open-access journal. Authorship spans Stanford's Departments of Biomedical Data Science, Bioengineering, Pediatrics and Electrical Engineering, from the same group and the same GuessWhat platform as the crowdsourced speech study and the gaze study elsewhere in this corpus - three papers analysing three different data streams from one app. No competing-interest declaration appears in the extracted text, though the senior author declares founding Cognoa in both companion papers. The paper carries some marks of light editing, including a placeholder left in the methods ('need figure/graphic showing this') and a misspelling in the introduction. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is a health-equity and access argument built around the COVID-19 transition to remote care, and it is more specific than the corpus norm at each step. Prevalence is similar in rural (0.9%) and urban (1.0%) areas, but rural communities face limited access to identification and intervention, and 'up to 80 pct. of counties in the U.S. lack sufficient diagnostic resources'. The critique of existing screening is where the paper is sharpest, and it is a critique this review should record: caregiver-report questionnaires 'require literacy and perform worse with non-white and lower education caregivers', so 'naively deploying digitized versions of diagnostic questionnaires risks exacerbating current disparities in the early identification of ASD'. That argument - that digitising an instrument inherits and can amplify its demographic bias - is made by no other paper here, and it motivates the study's choice to derive signal from a child's behaviour rather than a caregiver's report. The paper also engages with adoption as a design problem, noting that 'delays in the adoption of telehealth have been attributed to unengaged and resisting users' and that 'simply providing the current physician interaction through a smartphone may not be the best way of providing remote care', which is why the data collection is embedded in a game with progression mechanics rather than an assessment. Whether the resulting AU-ROC of 0.745 supports the deployment ambition is a separate question, and the abstract is appropriately hedged, claiming feasibility and 'potential' rather than accuracy. |
| S-092 | Cross-sectional case-control study in Anhui, China: more than 80 autistic children and more than 60 comparison children recruited through Anhui Medical University, the Anhui Autism Association and special education schools, contributing roughly 4,000 and 3,000 speech recordings respectively over about two years. Fewer than one third were usable, the loss attributed to autistic children's pronunciation difficulty, and 511 autistic and 506 comparison one-second recordings at 48 kHz were randomly selected. No ages, sexes, diagnostic procedure, severity or cognitive data are reported for either group; no ethics statement; corpus not released. | Recordings were framed, windowed and transformed by STFT with window 512 and offset 256, producing 256 frequency sequences, and complex-valued ICA was applied at each frequency point using negative entropy as the independence criterion with a fixed-point update, followed by permutation sorting and amplitude compensation. Three feature constructions were compared: Method 1 concatenating the row vectors of the 2x2 unmixing matrix across frequency points; Method 2 using the separated component sequences directly; and Method 3 reconstructing time-domain speech and extracting MFCC, LPCC and PLP features. An SVM with RBF kernel and cross-validated C and gamma, and an unspecified CNN, were trained on a single 80:20 split of recordings (408 autistic and 428 comparison for training). The two observation channels required by the ICA are never described; the mixing equations state that they are 'the ASD children's speech signal and the normal children's speech signal, respectively'. | Method 1: SVM 98.51% accuracy, 97.36% precision, 98.15% recall, 97.25% F1; CNN 95.59%. Method 2: SVM 59.71% and CNN 55.19%, this being the best of 256 frequency sequences. Method 3: PLP features gave SVM 92.89% and CNN 90.43%; LPCC gave 91.47% and 85.92%; MFCC gave 91.00% and 89.34%. SVM outperformed CNN under every condition, attributed by the authors to the small dataset. | The 80:20 split is over recordings rather than children, with roughly six one-second utterances per child randomly distributed across training and test, so utterances from the same speaker appear on both sides. The two-channel structure required by time-frequency ICA is never described, and the paper's own equations state that the two observation channels are an autistic and a comparison speech signal - under which reading each unmixing matrix would be estimated from a label-dependent pairing, invalidating Method 1's features as a classification input. Method 2's 59.71% is the maximum over 256 frequency sequences, uncorrected, and its near-chance value is not reconciled with Method 1's 98.51% despite both deriving from the same separation. No participant ages, sexes, diagnostic procedure, severity or cognitive data; no recording configuration; no CNN specification; no confidence intervals, repetitions or chance baseline; no ethics or consent statement; and no limitations section beyond noting the dataset is small. | Charted chiefly as a cautionary case with one transferable observation and one framing issue worth recording. The cautionary value lies in the combination of a near-perfect headline with a feature construction whose validity cannot be assessed: the unmixing matrix carrying the 98.51% is meaningful only in terms of what the two ICA observation channels are, and the paper describes them in a way that, taken literally, would make the features depend on a label-dependent pairing. Read alongside the recording-wise split - roughly six one-second utterances per child distributed randomly across training and test - the figure cannot be compared with participant-level results elsewhere in this review. The transferable observation is the paper's own Method 3 result: ordinary MFCC, LPCC and PLP features on the same recordings under the same split reach 91-93%, which is the range other speech studies here report under similar recording-level splits, and which offers a more plausible reading of what the corpus actually supports. The paper also documents, unusually and to its credit, that fewer than one third of collected recordings were usable because 'some ASD children can't pronounce normally, or it's difficult for them to pronounce as required' - a differential data-loss mechanism that speech studies in this corpus rarely quantify and that systematically restricts such samples to the more verbally able. Finally, the study is the corpus's clearest instance of normative framing embedded in method rather than prose: autistic speech is formally modelled as neurotypical speech convolved with 'filter banks representing the dysfunctional factors', so the comparison group's production is the undistorted reference signal and the feature of interest is the inverse of a hypothesised deficit filter. That assumption is not incidental - it is the stated justification for the feature construction that produces the headline result. | [RQ1.1] Two groups described only in aggregate: 'more than 80 ASD children and more than 60 normal children', from whom about 4,000 and 3,000 recordings respectively were collected in cooperation with Anhui Medical University, the Anhui Autism Association and special education schools. After quality exclusion 'less than 1/3 of the data was usable', and 511 autistic and 506 comparison recordings were randomly selected for analysis. Participant counts are given imprecisely ('more than'), no exact numbers are stated, and the mapping between children and recordings is never specified - so the analysed sample is roughly six recordings per child but the actual distribution is unknown. No other-diagnosis comparison group. The critical structural fact is that all analysis, splitting and reporting operates on recordings, and children are never used as a unit at any stage. [RQ1.2] 'ASD children' throughout, against 'normal children' - the comparison group is called normal in the title framing, the abstract, every table and every figure caption, with 'typically developing' never used. That alone would place the paper at the normative end of this corpus, but the framing goes further and is embedded in the method rather than only in the wording. The generative model states that 'we consider the speech data of a ASD children as the convolution of pure normal children's speech data with all the filter banks representing the "dysfunctional" factors', so neurotypical speech is formally the undistorted source signal and autism is a distortion applied to it, alongside noise. The discussion repeats this, describing autistic speech as 'formed by the convolution of normal children's speech signals and all filter sets representing physiologically dysfunctional factors'. This is the only study in the corpus in which the deficit framing is a mathematical assumption of the model rather than a descriptive choice, and it determines the feature construction: Method 1's features exist only because the unmixing matrix is interpreted as the inverse of a hypothesised dysfunction filter. [RQ1.3] Nothing whatsoever. No ages, no age ranges, no sexes, no IQ, no language level, no matching and no statistical comparison of any kind for either group. Even the participant counts are approximate. This is the least characterised sample in the corpus among studies that collected their own data rather than reusing a public benchmark - the benchmark-reuse papers at least have the excuse of inheriting an undocumented dataset, whereas this group recruited the children themselves over roughly two years and reports none of what they must have known. For a speech study the omission of age is especially consequential, since fundamental frequency, formant structure and articulatory precision change substantially across childhood and would separate any two groups differing in age composition. [RQ1.4] Nothing. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician role, setting or timing is reported anywhere in the paper. The only relevant information is the recruitment route - cooperation with a medical university, an autism association and special education schools - which establishes that participants were engaged with autism services but not how their diagnoses were made or verified. The comparison group's status is likewise unestablished, with 'normal children' asserted and no screening described. The paper's introduction observes that 'ASD diagnosing can be difficult because there are no standard and quantified medical tests like blood tests to diagnose the disorder', which makes the absence of any account of how the reference labels were obtained more conspicuous rather than less. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, language, adaptive, severity, comorbidity or medication information for either group, and no exclusion criteria. One relevant observation is made in passing and is important: 'the quality of children's word pronunciation was poor because some ASD children can't pronounce normally, or it's difficult for them to pronounce as required, finally, less than 1/3 of the data was usable'. That establishes that expressive speech ability varied substantially within the autistic group and that data loss was driven by it, but no measure of that ability was collected and the retention rate is not reported separately by group. [RQ2.1] Goal: compare three acoustic feature constructions derived from time-frequency ICA for distinguishing autistic from comparison children's speech. Main findings: unmixing-matrix features reached 98.51% accuracy with SVM and 95.59% with CNN; separated frequency-point sequences reached only 59.71% and 55.19%, this being the best of 256 sequences; cepstral features on separated signals reached 91.00-92.89% with SVM, with PLP best and MFCC worst; and SVM outperformed CNN under every condition, which the authors attribute to the small dataset. [RQ2.2] China, with collection organised through Anhui Medical University, the Anhui Autism Association and special education schools. The recording environment is not described in text at all - a figure is referenced showing the collection setup, but no room, distance, microphone or channel configuration is stated. This gap is not merely a reporting deficiency here but a methodological one, because time-frequency ICA is a multichannel technique: it requires at least two observation channels to separate sources, and which two signals constitute those channels determines entirely what the unmixing matrix represents. Without the recording configuration the paper's central feature construction cannot be reconstructed or evaluated. [RQ2.3] Elicited single-word production, with words constituting 95% of the corpus and phrases and sentences the remainder, each analysed sample trimmed to exactly one second at 48 kHz - a duration chosen because it 'not only ensured the integrity of the speech signal but also reduced the computational effort'. No prompt list, elicitation script, examiner instruction or session structure is described. Single-word production is the most constrained speech paradigm in the corpus, which has one methodological advantage - lexical content can in principle be held constant across children, removing a source of acoustic variation - and one significant cost, that prosodic, pragmatic and conversational features cannot be measured at all, so the study cannot address the prosodic constructs that motivate most speech work in autism. Whether lexical content was in fact matched between groups is not stated. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, with recordings accumulated over roughly two years and no follow-up. No ethics committee approval, consent statement or institutional review is mentioned anywhere, despite the study having purpose-collected approximately 7,000 speech recordings from more than 140 children recruited through special education schools and an autism association. Funding from two Anhui provincial science programmes is acknowledged. The dataset is presented as a contribution, with the authors noting that 'currently, there is no available public speech dataset for ASD children, which creates a big obstacle for related research', but no release, access route or sharing commitment is offered. [RQ2.5] The most consequential reporting gap in the paper. No microphone, recording device, sampling arrangement beyond the 48 kHz rate, room, distance or channel count is described; a photograph is referenced in place of a methods description. This matters because the entire analysis rests on a two-input two-output convolutive mixing model, and the paper's own equations describe the two observation channels ambiguously. Equation 1 sets up a general M-receiver model, which implies multiple microphones. Equation 2 then simplifies to two channels and states that 'x(n) are the ASD children's speech signal and the normal children's speech signal, respectively' - which describes not two microphones recording one speaker but one recording from each group. Under that reading each ICA would operate on a paired autistic and comparison utterance, and the resulting unmixing matrix would depend on the pairing, which requires the labels. The analytic chain is otherwise well specified: STFT with window 512 and offset 256 giving 256 frequency sequences, negative entropy as the independence criterion with the definition given, a fixed-point update rule, and permutation sorting with amplitude compensation before reconstruction. [RQ2.6] Mathematically detailed and empirically opaque. Fully specified: the convolutive mixing model, the frequency-domain formulation, the negative-entropy independence criterion with its definition, the fixed-point update equation, the STFT window and offset, the resulting number of frequency sequences, the three feature constructions and the SVM kernel with its cross-validated parameter search. Not reported: recording equipment or channel configuration; participant ages, sexes, diagnoses or severity; the elicitation protocol or prompt set; whether lexical content was matched between groups; the CNN architecture, depth, training regime or any hyperparameter; how the 1,017 analysed recordings map to children; the retention rate by group; the criterion for selecting the 126th frequency sequence beyond it performing best; ethics approval; and any data or code release. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section and only one limitation is acknowledged anywhere - that the dataset is small, offered as the explanation for the CNN underperforming the SVM and as the motivation for the sole future direction. Not acknowledged: that recordings from the same child are distributed across training and test; that the sample is entirely uncharacterised demographically and clinically; that no diagnostic procedure is reported; that the 59.71% figure for Method 2 is the maximum over 256 frequency sequences; that Method 2's near-chance result is difficult to reconcile with Method 1's near-perfect one; that the two-channel configuration underpinning the whole method is never described; that less than a third of collected recordings were usable and the loss was driven by the autistic children's pronunciation difficulty, so the analysed autistic sample is the more verbally able subset; and that no ethics approval is reported. [RQ2.9] One direction: 'One of our main tasks in future is to further enrich the dataset', motivated by the observation that the CNN needs more labelled data than are available. No proposal is made to group by child, characterise the participants, document the diagnostic procedure, describe the recording configuration, or validate on independent data. [RQ3.1] Nominally the acoustic properties of autistic children's speech, but the construct is defined by a generative assumption rather than by any behavioural theory. The paper's model is that an autistic child's utterance equals a neurotypical utterance convolved with a filter bank representing 'all the dysfunctional factors', plus noise - so the target is whatever linear transfer function distinguishes the two groups' vocal production, treated as a property of 'the vocal system' rather than of prosody, articulation, phonation or pragmatics. Nothing in the analysis identifies which acoustic dimension is involved, and no group difference in any interpretable quantity is reported. The paper opens with a figure asserting 'noticeable distinctions' between an autistic and a comparison child's waveform, spectrum and spectrogram for the same content, but this is a single illustrative pair with no quantification. Compared with the other speech studies in this corpus - which measure pitch, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio, rhythm or disfluency and report directions of effect - this study contributes no characterisation of speech at all. [RQ3.2] Single modality with no fusion, but the three-method comparison is the paper's structure and its internal inconsistency is the most informative thing in it. Methods 1 and 2 are two views of the same computation: the ICA produces an unmixing matrix, which is applied to the observations to produce separated components. Method 1 uses the matrix, Method 2 uses its outputs. The reported results are 98.51% and 59.71%. If the separation were extracting genuinely different vocal sources for the two groups, the separated signals should carry that difference, yet they classify barely above chance even after the most favourable of 256 frequency sequences is selected. Method 3, which reconstructs time-domain speech from those same separated components and extracts standard cepstral features, then recovers 91-93% - which suggests the discriminative information is present in the reconstructed audio but not in the individual frequency-point sequences, and is consistent with ordinary speaker- and speech-level acoustic differences. Taken together the three results do not form a coherent picture, and the paper's explanation - that the unmixing matrix captures 'the essential distinctions between the two types of children's speech' - does not address why the separation those same matrices perform yields near-chance signals. [RQ4.1] Two classifiers applied uniformly across all three feature methods, which makes the method comparison interpretable in that respect. The SVM is specified - radial basis function kernel with C and gamma selected by cross-validation, with the search surface plotted - and justified on small-sample grounds, that it 'still has good generalization ability under finite small samples'. The CNN is not specified at all: no layer count, filter sizes, depth, optimiser, learning rate, batch size or epoch count appears, only the general claim that convolution 'provides translation invariant convolution in time and space'. It underperforms the SVM under every one of the six conditions, by margins from 2.9 to 5.6 percentage points, which the authors attribute to insufficient training data. No baseline, chance level or permutation test is reported for any condition, which matters most for Method 2 where 59.71% needs to be judged against both chance and the 256-way selection that produced it. [RQ4.2] Three representations of the same recordings, differing in where they intercept the ICA pipeline, and the choice among them is the paper's contribution. Method 1's representation is the unusual one and the one carrying the headline: the coefficients of the 2x2 unmixing matrix at each of 256 frequency points, concatenated. These are not properties of the child's voice in any direct sense - they are the parameters of a linear demixing operator estimated from the observation channels - and their interpretation depends entirely on what those channels are, which the paper does not establish. Method 2's representation is the separated component sequences, one per frequency point, of which the single best-performing was reported. Method 3's is conventional: MFCC, LPCC and PLP computed on reconstructed audio, and the authors note that separation 'eliminates the influence of certain noises and makes the speech data more pure', while sensibly cautioning that speech processing 'need not overly pursue the complete elimination of noise' since aggressive denoising distorts speech. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 reported for both classifiers under all six feature conditions - a complete and consistently applied panel, and the metric definitions are given. Reporting all three methods including the near-chance one is to the paper's credit, since Method 2's 59.71% could easily have been omitted. What is missing bears directly on how the numbers should be read. There is no confidence interval anywhere, on a test set of 181 recordings where a single reclassification moves accuracy by half a percentage point. There is no chance or trivial baseline, so Method 2's result is uninterpretable as stated - especially given that it is the maximum over 256 candidate frequency sequences, a selection that would elevate the apparent performance of pure noise. And there is no per-child aggregation, so the reported figures describe how well one-second recordings are classified rather than how well children are. [RQ4.4] None. No feature importance, attribution, group comparison, effect size or acoustic characterisation appears anywhere, and Method 1's representation admits none in principle - an unmixing-matrix coefficient at frequency point k has no interpretation as a property of a child's voice. The one interpretive claim offered is theoretical rather than empirical: that because autistic speech is modelled as neurotypical speech convolved with dysfunction filters, 'the unmixing matrix can be regarded as the inverse matrix of these filter banks', so extracting it 'is equivalent to extracting the inherent distinguishing features representing the vocal system of both, reflecting the essential distinctions between the two types of children's speech'. This is an argument from the assumed generative model to the meaning of the features, not evidence that the features mean what is claimed, and it is not tested. Method 3, using standard cepstral features, would have supported conventional acoustic interpretation and none is attempted. [RQ4.5] The weakest dimension, with three compounding problems. The split is by recording: 408 autistic and 428 comparison recordings train, the remainder test, described as randomly selected from 511 and 506 recordings originating in more than 80 and more than 60 children - so approximately six utterances per child are randomly assigned between the two sets and utterances from the same child appear on both sides. For one-second single-word samples from the same speaker in the same session, this approaches speaker identification rather than group classification, and it is the same failure that Kanhirakadavath and colleagues quantified on gaze images as a fall from 97% to 73% when the unit was corrected. There is no cross-validation of the classifier, no repetition and no confidence interval, so the reported figures come from one partition of 181 test recordings. And Method 2's headline of 59.71% is the best of 256 frequency sequences, chosen after inspecting all of them, with no correction and no report of the distribution across the other 255. Layered over all of this is the unresolved question of what the two ICA observation channels are: if the equations mean what they say, each unmixing matrix is estimated from a paired autistic and comparison utterance, so Method 1's features would be functions of a label-dependent pairing and the 98.51% would not measure classification at all. The paper provides no information with which to exclude that reading. [RQ5.1] Index terms: Autism Spectrum Disorders, Independent Component Analysis, Deep Learning, Time-Frequency Feature. Three of four are signal-processing or machine-learning terms and none is clinical, which accurately identifies a paper whose contribution is a feature-construction comparison rather than a finding about speech. [RQ5.2] Proceedings of the 2022 IEEE 34th International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI), DOI 10.1109/ICTAI56018.2022.00164. All three authors are from the School of Computer Science and Technology at Anhui University, with no clinical, psychological or speech-science affiliation, though the data collection is credited to cooperation with Anhui Medical University, the Anhui Autism Association and special education schools. Funded by two Anhui provincial science programmes. The venue is an artificial intelligence tools conference, and the paper's profile matches: the signal-processing derivation is developed at length with full equations while the participants, the diagnostic basis, the recording configuration and the ethics are absent. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is a comparative argument for acoustic screening over the alternatives, and it is made concretely: methods based on eye movement, EEG and gut microbiome analysis 'all require expensive equipment, and the detection process is complex', while 'the scale based method highly depends on the subjective experience of doctors', so acoustic analysis 'provides a new path which is more simple and reliable for autism screening'. The related work is engaged specifically rather than generically, contrasting the study's use of speech against a prior study using infant cry - 'they focused on cry which is more random than the speech voice' - which is a reasonable methodological distinction. The paper also identifies a genuine infrastructure gap that this review can corroborate: 'currently, there is no available public speech dataset for ASD children, which creates a big obstacle for related research', a statement consistent with the fact that no speech study in this corpus shares its recordings, in contrast to the eye-tracking literature where a single public image dataset supports at least three of the charted studies. The paper's own corpus, roughly 7,000 recordings from over 140 children, would have been a substantial contribution to that gap had it been released. |
| S-093 | Cross-sectional regression study at the Azrieli National Centre for Autism and Neurodevelopment Research, Israel: 132 Hebrew-speaking children recorded during ADOS-2 assessments administered by a clinician with research reliability - 105 autistic (3.7 +/- 1.3 years, 80.0% male, ADOS 14.6 +/- 6.5) and 27 non-autistic (3.1 +/- 1.5 years, 77.8% male, ADOS 3.2 +/- 3.7) comprising children with language or developmental delays alongside typically developing children. Cohort aged 1 to 7 and described as mostly not verbally fluent. Approximately 11 hours of child vocalisation from sessions averaging 41.96 +/- 11.51 minutes; no cognitive or language measures; no ethics statement; data not released. | Sessions were recorded with a single AKG CHM99 microphone 1-2 metres from the child at 44.1 kHz, downsampled to 16 kHz, at an average child-speech signal-to-noise ratio of 12 +/- 5 dB, and manually labelled into six categories. Two diarization feature sets - 13 MFCCs plus pitch with first derivatives, and 512-dimensional x-vectors - were fed to a fully connected network with dual softmax layers followed by Viterbi decoding, evaluated by leave-one-out. Detected child segments were split into vocalisations and each recording summarised as a 100x48 matrix, each row comprising 48 prosodic and acoustic features computed over a random run of 10 sequential vocalisations. A convolutional network with linear output regressed the ADOS raw score, trained with RMSprop and per-condition hyperparameters selected by random search under five-fold cross-validation. Evaluation used 80:20 participant-level splits constructed to match the ADOS distribution on mean, standard deviation, kurtosis and skewness, repeated 50 times. | Diarization: MFCC plus pitch achieved the lowest diarization error rate at 26.91%; x-vectors achieved 73.42% recall, 74.06% precision and 89.84% accuracy on child segments. Detected child speech totalled 10.85 hours under manual labelling, 11.11 under MFCC plus pitch and 10.72 under x-vectors. Severity estimation: manual baseline Pearson R 0.567 +/- 0.120 with NRMSE 0.261 +/- 0.036; MFCC plus pitch R 0.606 +/- 0.099 with NRMSE 0.248 +/- 0.028; x-vectors R 0.581 +/- 0.115 with NRMSE 0.254 +/- 0.032. Automatic diarization therefore matched or slightly exceeded manual annotation, and the more accurate segment classifier produced the worse severity estimate. | The correlation of 0.606 is computed across a sample containing two well-separated clusters - autistic children averaging ADOS 14.6 and comparison children 3.2 - so an unquantified part of it reflects group membership rather than graded severity, and no within-autism correlation is reported. No cognitive or language measure was collected in a cohort defined by limited verbal fluency, leaving expressive language as an unmeasured mediator between acoustic predictors and a communication-weighted outcome. The system requires at least 20 seconds and 50 vocalisations of child speech, excluding an unreported number of the least verbal children. Audio quality is limited by a single distant microphone at 12 +/- 5 dB, acknowledged. The 48 features, vocalisation segmentation method and CNN architecture are deferred to prior publications. Whether hyperparameter tuning sat inside the 50 outer splits is not stated. No ethics or consent statement, no data or code release, and no test-retest assessment of the severity estimate's stability. | Important to the synthesis as the corpus's clearest instance of severity estimation rather than binary classification, and it names the gap in the terms this review has repeatedly encountered: prior speech studies 'reported high classification performance' but 'did not estimate the severity of autism symptoms in individual children'. Keles and colleagues and Kong and colleagues both report as negative findings that their gaze measures fail to correlate with ADOS or CARS severity; MacFarlane and colleagues note the same limitation of classification generally. This study takes that correlation as its endpoint and achieves 0.606, explaining roughly 37% of ADOS variance from speech acoustics alone. The qualification is that the correlation spans two diagnostic clusters and no within-autism figure is given, so the review should treat it as an upper bound on genuine severity grading rather than as an estimate of it - the same caution applied to Kojovic and colleagues' clinical-validity correlations. Three methodological features transfer. Splits are participant-level, repeated 50 times, and constructed to match the outcome distribution on four moments including skewness and kurtosis, which is the appropriate control for a bimodal regression target and is attempted nowhere else here. The three-way segmentation comparison isolates a pipeline stage cleanly and produces a counterintuitive result - automatic diarization matching manual annotation, explained by manual labelling being itself unreliable for quiet child speech in a reverberant room at 12 dB. And the dissociation between x-vectors' superior segment-classification accuracy and their inferior downstream severity estimate is a concrete demonstration that optimising an intermediate metric can select the worse end-to-end system. Finally, the cohort is one of the few in this review drawn from the less verbally fluent end of the spectrum, which the authors contrast explicitly against prior work on 'verbally fluent children' - and it adds Hebrew to a corpus otherwise dominated by English. | [RQ1.1] One cohort of 132 children recorded during routine ADOS-2 assessments, partitioned by diagnosis into 105 autistic and 27 non-autistic. The comparison group is the design feature worth noting: it comprises children 'diagnosed with language or developmental delays or were defined as typically developing', so it is a clinically referred population rather than a screened-typical one. That means the model is fitted across the range of children who actually present for autism assessment, and the regression target spans a continuum from ADOS 0 to 30 rather than two discrete classes. The proportion of the 27 who were developmentally delayed rather than typically developing is not reported, which limits how far the specificity claim can be pushed. No exclusion criteria are stated beyond the downstream requirement of at least 20 seconds and 50 vocalisations of child speech, and how many children that requirement removed is not reported. [RQ1.2] 'children with ASD', 'ASD children', 'verbal children with ASD', against 'non-ASD' and 'typically developed (TD)'. Person-first and acronym-adjectival usage alternate. The clinical description is conventional and largely accurate, and one passage is notably careful about heterogeneity: autistic children 'exhibit speech and expressive language abnormalities, which range from a total lack of speech (i.e., non-verbal children) to those who develop normal vocabulary and syntax, but exhibit difficulties with the use of appropriate prosody and pragmatics'. Speech is described as 'abnormal' and 'strange prosody' is quoted from prior work, so the register is deficit-oriented, but the paper is precise about the range rather than treating autistic speech as a single phenotype - and that precision matters here, because the sample is drawn from the less verbal end of that range, which the authors state explicitly when comparing their corpus against prior work on 'verbally fluent children'. [RQ1.3] Reported compactly and adequately for both groups: 105 autistic children aged 3.7 +/- 1.3 years, 80.0% male, ADOS 14.6 +/- 6.5; and 27 non-autistic children aged 3.1 +/- 1.5 years, 77.8% male, ADOS 3.2 +/- 3.7. The groups are close on sex (a 2.2-point difference) and reasonably close on age (0.6 years), though neither is formally tested and matching is not claimed. The overall age range of 1 to 7 years is given in the discussion. What is absent is any cognitive, language or adaptive measure, which is a real gap for a study whose predictor is speech and whose sample is described as 'mostly do not speak fluently or use little or no phrase speech' - expressive language level would be the obvious covariate, and it plausibly mediates both the acoustic features and the ADOS score. Ethnicity and socioeconomic information are not reported. [RQ1.4] The reference standard is the ADOS-2 itself, administered by a clinician with ADOS-2 research reliability, and it functions here as a continuous outcome rather than a categorical label - raw scores on the 0-30 scale are the regression target. That is a defensible use of the instrument and is more demanding than binary classification, since it requires the model to track a graded clinical judgement rather than a dichotomy. Two caveats. The categorical diagnoses used to describe the groups - autistic versus language delay, developmental delay or typical development - are stated without describing who assigned them or under what criteria, so the group composition rests on unspecified clinical judgement even though the regression target does not. And using a single instrument as both the sole clinical characterisation and the prediction target means the system is validated against one clinician's scoring on one occasion, with no second rater, no test-retest interval and no independent confirmation of the score's stability. [RQ1.5] ADOS raw scores are reported for both groups and are the dependent variable, so severity is characterised more centrally here than anywhere else in the corpus. Nothing else is measured: no IQ, developmental quotient, language level, adaptive functioning or comorbidity data for either group. The omission is consequential for interpretation because the sample is explicitly a young and largely non-fluent one, so expressive language ability varies widely and is not quantified. Since the predictors are acoustic properties of speech and the outcome is a clinical score that itself weights communication heavily, an unmeasured language-ability variable sits between the two and could account for a substantial part of the reported correlation without any autism-specific acoustic signal being involved. [RQ2.1] Goal: build an end-to-end system that locates child speech within a full ADOS recording and estimates autism severity from it, and determine whether automatic diarization can replace manual annotation. Main findings: MFCC-plus-pitch diarization achieved a 26.91% diarization error rate against x-vectors' 89.84% child-segment accuracy; severity estimation reached Pearson R 0.606 +/- 0.099 with NRMSE 0.248 with automatic diarization, against 0.567 +/- 0.120 and 0.261 with manual segmentation; and automatic diarization therefore matched or slightly exceeded manual annotation, which the authors attribute to imperfect manual labelling of quiet child speech in a reverberant room. [RQ2.2] The ADOS examination room at a national autism research centre, with recording conditions described honestly rather than idealised: a single microphone 1-2 metres from the child, in an environment with 'background noise, reverberation, and overlapping speech', and with both child and therapist free to move during the session. The resulting average signal-to-noise ratio of child speech is reported as 12 +/- 5 dB and named as a limitation. The authors position this deliberately against better-equipped prior work, noting that another group 'applied a diarization method for speech signals using four microphones, including a beamforming algorithm that improved their recordings' SNR' and that 'even though our proposed diarization methods achieved higher DER values, we used only one distant microphone recorded in a noisy environment'. Accepting worse acquisition in exchange for deployability in an ordinary clinic room is a defensible trade and is argued as such. [RQ2.3] No purpose-built task - the speech analysed is whatever the child produced during a standard 45-minute ADOS-2 administration. This is the design's principal translational strength: any clinic already recording ADOS sessions holds the raw material, no additional child burden is imposed, and the sampling context is by construction the one in which the reference score is generated. The corresponding limitation is the one the review has noted for other ADOS-derived studies: the assessment is designed to elicit autism-related behaviour, so acoustic differences observed within it may not generalise to spontaneous conversation. The paper does not raise this. A second, more specific constraint is imposed downstream: the severity model requires at least 20 seconds of child speech comprising at least 50 vocalisations, so children who spoke less than this could not be analysed - and in a cohort described as mostly not verbally fluent, that threshold plausibly excludes a meaningful proportion, though the number is not given. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, one recorded session per child, with no follow-up and no test-retest assessment of the severity estimate's stability. The absence of any ethics, consent or institutional review statement is the most conspicuous reporting gap: the study analyses audio recordings of clinical diagnostic assessments involving young children, their parents and clinicians, manually labelled by researchers, and no approval is mentioned in the extracted text. Funding from the Israel Ministry of Science and Technology is acknowledged with a grant number. No data availability statement and no code release. [RQ2.5] Fully specified and deliberately minimal: a single AKG CHM99 microphone at 1-2 metres, 44.1 kHz downsampled to 16 kHz, in the ADOS room. Reporting the microphone model, its distance, the sampling and downsampling rates, the mean session duration and the achieved signal-to-noise ratio is more complete acquisition reporting than most speech studies in this corpus provide, and it matters here because the paper's central claim - that automatic diarization matches manual annotation - depends on the audio being genuinely difficult. Analysis tools are named specifically: the Brno University of Technology x-vector system with its window size and rate, the dscore tool with a 0.25-second collar, and RMSprop with random-search tuning under five-fold cross-validation, with the selected batch size, epoch count and learning rate tabulated separately for each of the three segmentation conditions. [RQ2.6] Good within the constraints of a four-page conference paper, with one systematic deferral. Reported: microphone model, distance, sampling and downsampling rates, session duration, signal-to-noise ratio; the six manual labelling categories; both diarization feature sets with dimensionality and, for x-vectors, window size and rate; the shared network structure with its dual softmax and Viterbi post-processing; the vocalisation splitting including the treatment of segments over 3 seconds; the 100x48 matrix construction with its 10-vocalisation sampling rule; the optimiser and per-condition hyperparameters; the diarization error decomposition with its collar and the rationale for ignoring silence errors; the split construction with its four matched distributional moments and 50 repetitions; and the total detected duration under each segmentation condition. Deferred to a prior publication: the identity of the 48 features beyond four examples, the vocalisation separation method, and the CNN architecture details. Absent: ethics approval, data or code release, and the number of children excluded by the 20-second threshold. [RQ2.7] Two limitations are stated, both technical and both substantive. The audio quality achieved with a single distant microphone in a reverberant room, quantified as 12 +/- 5 dB signal-to-noise ratio for child speech, is named and contextualised against prior work using four microphones with beamforming. And the requirement for a minimum of 20 seconds of child speech comprising at least 50 vocalisations is acknowledged as a constraint of the deep-learning approach. What is not acknowledged is the more consequential interpretive issue: the correlation of 0.606 is computed across a sample containing two well-separated clusters, with the autistic group averaging ADOS 14.6 and the comparison group 3.2, so a large part of the association reflects group membership rather than graded severity within either group. No within-autism correlation is reported, and without it the claim to estimate severity rather than to detect diagnosis is not established. Also unaddressed: the absence of any language or cognitive measure in a cohort defined by limited verbal fluency; the use of a single ADOS administration as both the only clinical characterisation and the prediction target; and the absence of an ethics statement. [RQ2.9] No dedicated future-work section, but both stated limitations imply directions and one is developed comparatively. Improving acquisition - the authors' contrast with a four-microphone beamforming setup indicates that better signal-to-noise ratio is the obvious lever, though it would trade against the deployability that a single-microphone setup buys. And relaxing the 20-second, 50-vocalisation minimum, which is framed as a constraint of the deep-learning architecture and which currently excludes the least verbal children. The paper also positions its result against two prior severity-estimation studies - one on Japanese-speaking adolescents using support vector regression and one on English-speaking children achieving a correlation of 0.634 in 33 children - and notes that it achieves 'a similar correlation value (0.606) while using a larger dataset of 132 children', which implicitly frames sample size as the axis along which the field should progress. [RQ3.1] Prosodic and acoustic properties of spontaneous child speech during clinical assessment, grounded in a specific prior literature that the introduction summarises accurately: autistic children have been reported to show 'strange prosody', 'increased pitch variability and pitch range', 'slower speech rate, and prolonged word production', with the observation that 'these studies used manual annotation and inspection of the audio recordings' - which is precisely the dependency the present work is designed to remove. The 48 features are named only in part (pitch, formants, zero-crossing rate, duration), so the operationalisation cannot be fully evaluated from this paper. The construct that the model actually targets, though, is not an acoustic property but a clinical score: the system predicts ADOS raw scores, which aggregate social affect and restricted repetitive behaviour ratings across a 45-minute observation, most of which concerns behaviour the microphone cannot capture. That the model recovers 37% of the variance in such a score from speech acoustics alone is the substantive finding, and it is also the reason the result is hard to interpret mechanistically. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion, but the study performs a well-designed three-way comparison of segmentation inputs feeding an identical downstream model - manual annotation, MFCC-plus-pitch diarization, and x-vector diarization - which isolates the contribution of the segmentation stage cleanly. The result is the paper's most interesting finding and runs against expectation in two ways. Automatic diarization matched or slightly beat manual annotation (R 0.606 and 0.581 against 0.567), which the authors explain rather than merely report: 'the manual segmentation is not perfectly accurate, especially for the child segments. The child speech is often quiet and is sometimes masked by noises, especially when using a distant microphone in a reverberant environment.' And the more sophisticated representation lost: 512-dimensional x-vectors achieved better child-segment accuracy (89.84%) than MFCC plus pitch, yet produced worse downstream severity estimation - so segment-classification accuracy and downstream utility diverge, and optimising the intermediate metric would have selected the worse system. That dissociation between an intermediate objective and the end-to-end outcome is a transferable lesson for any pipeline architecture. [RQ4.1] Two networks in sequence, each matched to its task. Diarization uses a fully connected network with two stacked softmax layers, the second added on cited grounds that it improves final classification, followed by Viterbi decoding to impose temporal coherence on the frame-level outputs - a sensible structure for a sequence-labelling problem. Severity estimation uses a convolutional network with a linear output for regression, trained with RMSprop and hyperparameters selected by random search under five-fold cross-validation, with the selected values reported separately for each segmentation condition. Reporting per-condition hyperparameters is a small but meaningful detail: it shows the comparison between segmentation methods was made with each given its own tuned configuration rather than one set imposed across all three. Neither architecture is described in enough depth to reimplement, with details deferred to a prior publication. [RQ4.2] The representation choice is the study's most considered technical decision. Rather than reducing each recording to a single averaged feature vector - which is what most speech studies in this corpus do - the system builds a 100x48 matrix per child, where each row summarises 48 features over a randomly drawn run of 10 sequential vocalisations. This preserves within-session variability, which matters for a construct like prosodic atypicality that is expressed as inconsistency rather than as a shifted mean, and it supplies a two-dimensional input that a convolutional architecture can exploit. Because the matrix is the input and one prediction is produced per recording, the unit of analysis remains the child despite the internal resampling, so no leakage arises from the 100 correlated rows. The design also implicitly handles variable session length: a child with more vocalisations contributes more distinct draws, but every child yields the same fixed-size matrix. [RQ4.3] Appropriate to a regression problem and reported with variability. Severity estimation uses Pearson correlation and normalised RMSE, each as a mean and standard deviation across 50 repeated splits - so the reader sees not only that R is 0.606 but that its standard deviation is 0.099, which places the manual baseline of 0.567 +/- 0.120 well within the automatic method's variation and correctly supports the paper's cautious claim of 'equivalent or slightly better' rather than a claim of superiority. Diarization is evaluated with the standard diarization error rate, decomposed into substitution, false-accept and missed-detection components with the collar specified, plus recall, precision and accuracy on child segments, and with a stated and reasonable justification for excluding silence errors. The most useful supplementary figure is the total detected vocalisation duration under each condition - 10.85, 11.11 and 10.72 hours - which demonstrates that the three segmentation methods recovered comparable amounts of speech and so that the downstream differences are not simply a matter of one method finding more data. No confidence intervals on the correlations beyond the across-split standard deviations, and no significance test between conditions. [RQ4.4] No feature-level interpretability: the 48 features are not individually reported, no importance analysis is performed, and no acoustic characterisation of severity is offered, so the study contributes a prediction system rather than a finding about how autistic children's speech varies with symptom level. The interpretability that is present operates at the level of the pipeline. The three-way segmentation comparison establishes which stage contributes what, and the finding that automatic diarization outperforms manual annotation is given a mechanistic account grounded in the recording conditions. The dissociation between x-vectors' better segment accuracy and their worse severity estimate is reported without explanation, but it is reported, and it is the kind of intermediate-versus-final metric divergence that a paper optimising only for diarization performance would never have surfaced. [RQ4.5] Among the better-designed validations in the corpus for a regression problem, with one important limitation that is interpretive rather than procedural. The split is by child and repeated 50 times, and - distinctively - each split is constructed so that the ADOS score distribution matches the full sample on four moments: 'we divided the children into training and testing datasets while balancing the distribution of ADOS scores (mean, standard deviation, kurtosis, and skewness) in each dataset'. Matching skewness and kurtosis as well as mean and variance is the right control for a bimodally distributed target, since an unlucky split could otherwise place most of the low-scoring comparison children on one side and inflate or deflate the correlation. Reporting means and standard deviations across the 50 repetitions rather than a single split follows properly. Hyperparameters were tuned by random search under five-fold cross-validation, though whether that tuning sat inside the 50 outer splits or was performed once beforehand is not stated - which leaves some selection optimism unquantified. The substantive limitation is what the correlation measures rather than how it was estimated: computed across a sample where the autistic group averages ADOS 14.6 and the comparison group 3.2, R = 0.606 conflates between-group separation with within-group severity grading, and no within-autism correlation is reported. That is the analysis that would distinguish a severity estimator from a diagnostic classifier expressed on a continuous scale, and it is the same conflation this review has flagged in Kojovic and colleagues. [RQ5.1] No keyword list appears in the extracted text. The operative vocabulary is speaker diarization, severity estimation, diarization error rate, ADOS score and prosodic features - a speech-engineering register applied to a clinical regression target, which accurately describes a paper contributed to a biomedical engineering venue by a signal-processing group working with a clinical centre. [RQ5.2] Proceedings of the 2022 44th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC), DOI 10.1109/EMBC48229.2022.9871523. All authors are at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, spanning biomedical engineering and the Azrieli National Centre for Autism and Neurodevelopment Research, so signal-processing and clinical autism expertise are co-located in a single institution - which shows in the study's access to research-reliable ADOS administration and in the realism of its recording setup. Funded by the Israel Ministry of Science and Technology with a grant number. The work builds explicitly on the same group's prior publications for the vocalisation segmentation method, the 48-feature set and the CNN architecture, so this paper reports an increment - the substitution of automatic diarization for manual labelling - rather than a standalone system. [RQ5.3] 2022. The framing is unusually precise about what the field has and has not done. Prior speech studies 'reported high classification performance' but 'did not estimate the severity of autism symptoms in individual children', and the two exceptions are named and characterised - one on Japanese-speaking adolescents using support vector regression, one on English-speaking children reaching a correlation of 0.634 in 33 participants. The paper also identifies the specific practical dependency it is removing: the earlier acoustic findings on prosody, pitch variability and speech rate all 'used manual annotation and inspection of the audio recordings', which is what makes them non-scalable. Its comparative positioning is likewise concrete rather than promotional: it acknowledges achieving worse diarization error than a four-microphone beamforming study, explains why, notes that a prior 499-hour corpus comprised verbally fluent children whereas this cohort 'mostly do not speak fluently or use little or no phrase speech', and describes its own correlation as 'similar' to the 0.634 of a smaller study rather than as an improvement. Adding a Hebrew-language cohort also extends the linguistic coverage of this corpus, which is otherwise dominated by English with single studies in Italian, Polish, Cantonese and Chinese. |
| S-094 | Small controlled observational comparison conducted by a Polish-British collaboration spanning robotics, cognitive and applied psychology, education and rehabilitation medicine. Ten children aged 5.5 to 6.5 years (mean 6.08, SD 0.4) took part, recruited through the kindergartens they attended: five diagnosed with autism and five typically developing, each group comprising four boys and one girl. Diagnoses were recorded in kindergarten files and had been delivered by a multidisciplinary team of a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a pedagogue; the instruments and criteria are not stated. The study was approved by the local research ethics committee at the University of Lower Silesia, guardians were informed of the aims and procedures, and signed consent was obtained both for participation and, separately, for filming. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is reported. | Each child took part in two sessions. A five-minute familiarisation session had NAO introduce itself and perform two short rhythmic dances; after a short break the main experiment followed, comprising the 'Touch me' game with a stationary robot issuing voice commands and then the 'Dance with me' game with a moving robot inviting imitation, each lasting about five minutes. The two scenarios were designed to dissociate routes to the same observable behaviour: a child touching the robot during 'Dance with me' cannot be a response to a voice command and is read instead as imitation, while 'Touch me' precludes spontaneous reactions because the robot does not move. NAO was operated remotely by an experimenter through its standard graphical interface and its onboard sensing was not used for measurement. Sessions were recorded and rated by six competent raters from special education, who counted movement activities and scored interest in the robot and additional movements on 0-5 severity scales at each of a set of defined positions, with the full scale published in an appendix. Analysis used Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis and chi-squared tests; no computational model was fitted and no individual received a predicted class. | Autistic children produced significantly fewer turn-taking behaviours than typically developing children in both game scenarios. Group differences also emerged on interest in the robot and on additional movements, which the authors read as confirming that autistic characteristics were present during the interaction and as supporting the initial diagnoses. Inter-rater reliability across the whole scale was satisfactory at Kendall's W = 0.65 (p < 0.001), and the Additional movements subscale returned Cronbach's alpha of 0.77.
