The complementarity has a physical basis rather than a statistical one: the two sensors disambiguate states that either alone would confuse, since a stationary car with spinning wheels and a car carried through the air with static wheels are distinguishable only by looking at both signals together, and the new roll/pitch features are themselves derived by short-time Fourier transform of the accelerometer specifically to characterise what the body is doing during wheel play. The caution is that the ablation shares the sample and the feature-selection procedure with the final model, so the gains are measured under the same optimistic conditions as the headline accuracy; and that the largest single-feature contributor from the encoder side may be the not-playing ratio, which indexes engagement rather than rotation interest. [RQ4.1] Classical machine learning throughout, with three algorithms compared: a linear-kernel SVM as the primary model, a random forest, and a multilayer perceptron trained with unspecified data augmentation. The SVM was retained because it outperformed the others on overall accuracy, and the linear kernel was chosen after testing three kernel types. No deep learning, no sequence model, no probabilistic or Bayesian approach; the whole session is collapsed to one fixed-length feature vector per child before any model sees it. The choice is defensible at n = 46 and the authors implicitly acknowledge the sample-size constraint by noting that 'the size of the training set is small compared to the size of the feature vector' as the motivation for aggressive feature reduction. The most interesting modelling observation in the paper is the discussion of the SVM/random forest trade-off: the random forest is 4.7 points worse on accuracy but better on both sensitivity and specificity, and the authors state plainly that a user may prefer it because it would miss fewer autistic children and mislabel fewer typically developing ones - an error-profile argument that most studies in this corpus never make. [RQ4.2] A single 54-dimensional hand-crafted feature vector per child, reduced to 10 by feature selection. The 44 inherited acceleration features are per-axis means, variances, the five dominant frequencies and their amplitudes, signal energies, pairwise inter-axis correlations, a jolt count and the playing-time duration - i.e. a mix of time-domain statistics and coarse spectral descriptors computed over the whole session. The 10 new features are of two kinds: seven state-occupancy ratios derived from the joint encoder/accelerometer signature (fractions of total and of interactive playtime spent not playing, on wheels only, on the ground and in the air) plus the total wheel turn rate, and two tilt-count features (about X and about Y) obtained by short-time Fourier transform of the acceleration signal to recover the car's roll and pitch during wheel play. The representation is therefore entirely aggregate: no temporal ordering, no sequence, no windowing, and no per-episode analysis, so a child who spins the wheels once for ninety seconds and one who spins them thirty times for three seconds each are indistinguishable. The final selected set was seven acceleration features (Y-direction jolt, tilt about Y, X-direction energy, X-Y acceleration correlation, the fourth-highest X frequency, the fifth-highest Z frequency, and the relative amplitude of the highest Y frequency) and three encoder features (wheels-only play ratio, not-playing ratio, total wheel turn rate). [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and precision, reported for all six classifier/feature configurations in a single table, plus a confusion matrix for the best model. Reporting four metrics across a full ablation grid rather than one number for one model is better practice than much of this corpus. What is missing: AUC or ROC, F1, any confidence interval or standard deviation across the five folds, calibration, and any translation of the operating point to a screening context - no PPV or NPV at a plausible population prevalence, despite the paper's entire argument being about population-level screening access. At the study's own 60.9% prevalence a precision of 87.67% is unremarkable; at a 1-2% community prevalence, sensitivity 81.7% with specificity 81.0% would give a positive predictive value in the low single digits, which is the number that matters for a device proposed for home and daycare use. There is also an internal consistency problem: for several rows the reported accuracy cannot be recovered from the reported sensitivity and specificity given the 28:18 class ratio - row 6 implies about 81.4% rather than 85.56%, row 4 about 72.3% rather than 78.61%, and row 1 about 77.3% rather than 71.11% - so the columns appear not to be computed on a common basis. [RQ4.4] Good, and grounded in physics rather than post-hoc attribution. Every feature is a named, humanly meaningful quantity, and the four play states are defined by an explicit and checkable sensor logic: encoder moving with accelerometer static means wheel spinning; accelerometer moving with encoder static means the car is airborne; both moving means floor play; neither means no play. The selected 10 features are listed individually so a reader can see exactly what the model uses, and the three encoder features that survived - wheels-only ratio, not-playing ratio, total wheel turn rate - map directly onto the behavioural hypothesis that motivated the hardware change. The mechanism itself came from observation of children playing with version 1, not from a literature-driven guess, which is a legitimate and transparent route to a feature. What is absent is any quantitative feature-level analysis: no group means or effect sizes for the wheels-only ratio or any other feature, no statistical test that autistic children actually spin the wheels more, no feature importances or coefficients, and no error analysis. So the paper can say which features the classifier used but cannot say by how much the groups differ on them, which is why the not-playing-ratio confound cannot be assessed from the reported results. [RQ4.5] Better than most on the split unit, weaker on everything downstream. The unit of splitting is the child - one aggregate feature vector per participant - so the segment-level leakage that inflates results throughout this corpus is impossible here by construction, and the paper deserves credit for that even though it is a consequence of the aggregate representation rather than a deliberate safeguard. The reported scheme is an 80/20 division with 5-fold cross-validation rotating which 20% is held out, giving fold test sets of about 9 children and averaged metrics. The problems lie elsewhere. First, feature selection: two consecutive rounds of backward elimination were run over the feature set, described in a section that precedes the results and with the surviving 10 features named as a fixed outcome, with no indication that the procedure was repeated within each training fold. Selecting 10 of 54 features on all 46 children and then cross-validating the chosen subset is a well-characterised source of optimism, and it is most severe exactly in this regime of many features and few samples - the regime the authors themselves identify as the reason feature reduction was needed. Second, model selection: three algorithms, three SVM kernels and four feature configurations were evaluated on the same 46 children, and the maximum of that grid is the abstract's claim. Third, no chance baseline: the majority class alone gives 60.9%, and no permutation test or confidence interval is reported, so with roughly 9 children per test fold a single child's label moves fold accuracy by 11 percentage points and the difference between the 78.61% and 85.56% configurations is a handful of children. Fourth, prevalence: 61% autism in the modelled sample against a population rate near 1-2%, with no prevalence-adjusted metric. The corrective design is straightforward and worth stating for the synthesis - move both backward-elimination rounds and the kernel/algorithm choice inside the training folds, report the mean and spread across folds rather than the best cell of the grid, add a majority-class and a permutation baseline, and retain the CP and fragile X children as a differential-diagnosis check. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: autism spectrum disorder (ASD); sensorized toy; machine learning; IoT. The inclusion of 'IoT' rather than a clinical term signals where the paper locates itself - in connected-device engineering, not diagnostics - and 'sensorized toy' is the contribution rather than a topic. Neither 'screening', 'diagnosis' nor any behavioural term appears, despite screening being the stated purpose. Terms carried through the body: playing patterns, attention to details, interest in rotating objects, repetitive behaviors, shaft encoders, multi-modal features, early screening, sustainable development. [RQ5.2] Sustainability 15(10), article 7790, MDPI, in a section handled by an academic editor from the image-processing field. This is an open-access multidisciplinary sustainability journal rather than a clinical, autism-specialist or biomedical-engineering venue, and the fit is achieved through an explicit framing device: the paper argues that low-cost widespread screening advances the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals by extending access to under-served and rural populations, and the argument recurs in the abstract, discussion and conclusion. That framing explains several features of the report - the emphasis on device cost and expert-independence, the comparison table of competing modalities by accessibility and cost, and the near-absence of clinical detail such as diagnostic criteria. Received 28 December 2022, revised 13 March 2023, accepted 25 April 2023, published 10 May 2023, CC BY. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 from the University of Tehran (Mechanical Engineering and ECE) with co-authors then at the University of Minnesota and UC Riverside, with no external funding. The framing is health-equity engineering rather than diagnostics: the opening premise is that many cases remain undiagnosed 'due to the limited access to experts, especially in low and middle-income societies', and the proposed answer is a device cheap enough to deploy in homes and daycares. Version 2 of an existing platform, so the framing is explicitly incremental - the contributions are stated as introducing a new modality and suggesting new features, and the authors state that they do not wish to compare their accuracy against other modalities in the literature but only against their own version 1. That restraint is unusual and appropriate. The paper is also of its moment in treating multimodality as an answer to within-spectrum heterogeneity - different autistic children show different symptoms, so a comprehensive screen needs several sensing channels - an argument that recurs across the 2022-2023 papers in this corpus. |
| S-097 | Cross-sectional case-control classification study in Campania, Italy, remodelling a dataset the same group had previously analysed descriptively without achieving significant group separation. Sixty children aged 5-10 participated: 30 autistic, mean age 7 +/- 1.4 years, recruited from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, all diagnosed under both DSM-5 criteria and ADOS-2 with comorbidity excluded; and 30 typically developing, mean age 6 years 8 months +/- 1, recruited from a primary school and excluded for any suspected autism sign, developmental abnormality or psychiatric or neurological history, with any child about whom a clinician or teacher was uncertain excluded outright. Leiter-3 IQ ranged 59-109 in the autistic group, six children scoring 59-70, and 74-110 in the comparison group; no means, SDs or comparison are reported, and sex is not reported for either group. Ethics approval came from the University of Naples Federico II and guardians gave written informed consent; two authors are employed by the recruiting rehabilitation centre and declare it. | A Unity/C# Android tablet application reimplemented five subtests of the Leiter-3 Cognitive Battery, presenting up to five draggable cards and eight placeholders per scene with distractors and detail increasing across five difficulty levels; each child completed 25 tasks, five per level, seated opposite the examiner at a standardised table with the tablet 20 cm from the edge. Finger position was logged at 40 Hz. Each trajectory - first tap to finger lift - yielded 12 features computed in RStudio with the traj package: mean, max, min and SD of speed and of acceleration, plus straightness (STH), directional change (DC), its standard deviation (sdDC) and mean trajectory count. Only trajectories from correctly performed tasks were analysed. Trajectory features were averaged per task, giving 60 x 25 = 1,500 twelve-dimensional observations, each labelled with the child's diagnosis. A variational autoencoder mapped these to a diagonal-Gaussian latent space, with a symmetric decoder and a jointly trained predictor MLP (tanh hidden layer, softmax output); the loss summed mean squared reconstruction error, KL divergence to a standard normal, and binary cross-entropy, all equally weighted. Ten-fold cross-validation was run over the 1,500 observations. PCA on a 10-dimensional latent space showed two components carrying 95% of its variance, so analysis proceeded in two dimensions. For interpretation the predictor was replaced by bivariate Gaussians fitted to each class's latent cloud, and each feature was Monte Carlo resampled 100 times with the other eleven held fixed to trace how it moves a participant's latent projection. | Mean cross-validated accuracy was 91.2% +/- 5.6% at the task-observation level - the only performance metric reported anywhere in the paper. The latent space separated the two groups into distinct regions, with separation visibly cleaner when each participant was plotted as the mean of their 25 tasks than when tasks were plotted individually, and the latent structure was stable across weight initialisations up to a rotation. Monte Carlo perturbation identified sdSpeed, MaxAcceleration, MinAcceleration and sdAcceleration as the features most able to displace a participant across the latent space and reverse their assigned class, while sdDC, MeanSpeed, MaxSpeed and MeanLength mapped preferentially into the typically developing region and were judged marginal. The fitted class densities yielded signed rules offered as candidate clinical thresholds: higher MaxAcceleration and sdAcceleration, and lower MaxSpeed and MinAcceleration, increase the probability of autism assignment. The group's earlier descriptive analysis of the same data had found high MaxSpeed in autistic trajectories, so the speed direction here is partly reversed. | The dataset is 60 children expanded to 1,500 rows at 25 tasks each, and the reported 10-fold cross-validation partitions those rows with no indication that a child's rows were kept together - so each test observation is accompanied into training by roughly 22-23 siblings from the same child, session and hand. Movement kinematics function close to an individual motor signature, so 91.2% substantially measures within-child consistency rather than generalisation to an unseen child; the paper's own observation that clustering is clearer after averaging a participant's tasks, combined with the absence of any participant-level accuracy, points the same way. Accuracy is the only metric given - no sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confusion matrix - so the error profile is unknown. The latent dimensionality and the class-conditional Gaussians proposed as clinical thresholds were both fitted on the full dataset. Analysis was restricted to correctly performed tasks, conditioning the retained data on cognitive success in a group pair whose IQ ranges differ and six of whose autistic children fall below the control floor, with no per-group error rates reported. Sex is not reported for either group. And the autistic children were receiving psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre while controls were not, confounding motor-training history with diagnosis in a study whose entire signal is motor. The single stated limitation - that supervision was required so the ground truth still comes from clinical assessment - does not touch any of these. | Important to this review on three counts. It is the only variational autoencoder in the corpus and shows what a generative latent-variable model offers over a discriminative classifier: because the KL term forces the latent space towards a known analytic form, class-conditional densities can be fitted and probability, not just a score, can be computed for any point - and the authors then use this deliberately, discarding the predictor network at inference so that a participant landing in an unpopulated region is treated conservatively rather than confidently misassigned. That is the most thoughtful handling of out-of-distribution inputs anywhere in this corpus. Its Monte Carlo feature-perturbation analysis is likewise the corpus's most sophisticated interpretability work, tracing not merely which features matter but at what values the classification flips, and expressing the result as candidate clinical thresholds rather than as feature importances. Second, the paradigm is unusually translatable: kinematics are captured as a free by-product of administering a standardised cognitive test a child might undergo anyway, so the marginal burden of the index test is zero - a property no other study here shares. Third, it is a clean illustration of the corpus's dominant methodological failure appearing in a study that is otherwise careful: a strong dual-criterion reference standard including ADOS-2, documented ethics, standardised acquisition and thoughtful modelling, all reported through a single accuracy figure computed by splitting 1,500 rows that came from 60 children. The corrective experiment - participant-disjoint folds with sensitivity and specificity reported at the child level - is available within this dataset and would be worth more than the current headline number. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of 30, total 60 children aged 5-10 years. ASD group: 30 children, mean age 7 years +/- 1.4, recruited from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, all diagnosed under both DSM-5 criteria and ADOS-2, with no existing comorbidities as an inclusion requirement. TD group: 30 children, mean age 6 years 8 months +/- 1, recruited from a primary school, with no confirmed neurodevelopmental disorder and excluded for suspected autism signs, developmental abnormalities, or any current or past psychiatric or neurological history. All 60 had normal vision and no sensory or motor deficits, and any child about whom a clinician or teacher was uncertain was excluded. No attrition or exclusions after enrolment are reported. The modelled dataset, however, is not 60 rows but 1,500: each child contributed 25 task observations (five tasks at each of five difficulty levels), and it is these observations, not the children, that are the unit of the reported cross-validation. [RQ1.2] 'Children with autism', 'autism spectrum disorder (ASD)', 'ASD group', 'typically developing (TD) group'. Person-first phrasing predominates but slips into group-as-noun usage in the results and discussion ('classify ASD and TD individuals', 'ASD trajectories', 'the ASD one'). The framing is firmly medical: autism is 'a by-birth neurodevelopmental disorder', characterised by 'communication and social impairment and restricted, repetitive, and stereotyped behaviours', and the target construct is 'motor abnormalities' throughout - abnormality rather than difference. One usage requires comment: the six autistic children with IQ 59-70 are described as having 'mild mental retardation', with the WHO (2016) cited as the source of the classification. That terminology is outdated in English-language practice, where intellectual disability is standard, and its appearance in a 2023 paper is worth noting even allowing for translation from Italian and for the cited WHO/ICD source. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement, though the stated purpose - to give clinicians objective quantitative indicators to supplement a process the authors criticise as subjective and examiner-dependent - is a clinician-support rather than a replacement agenda. [RQ1.3] Partial. Reported: group sizes (30/30), mean and SD of age per group (7 +/- 1.4 versus 6 years 8 months +/- 1), age range 5-10, and IQ ranges per group from the Leiter-3 (ASD 59-109, TD 74-110), with the note that six autistic children scored between 59 and 70 and that no severe or profound impairment was present. Recruitment source is given for both groups. Not reported: sex distribution for either group - a striking omission in a 60-child study where sex ratio is both clinically salient and trivially available; race or ethnicity; socioeconomic status; parental education; language level; medication; and any positive comorbidity data, since comorbidity was an exclusion criterion. Two features of what is reported deserve emphasis. First, IQ is given only as a range, with no mean or SD, so the distributions cannot be compared - yet the ranges are visibly asymmetric and six autistic children sit below the TD group's floor of 74, which matters because the index task is a reimplementation of a cognitive test and the analysis is restricted to correctly performed trials. Second, the two groups differ systematically in more than diagnosis: the autistic children were recruited from a rehabilitation centre and were actively receiving psychomotor therapy, i.e. motor intervention, while the controls came from a mainstream school, so exposure to motor training is confounded with group membership in a study whose outcome is motor kinematics. [RQ1.4] Among the better-specified in this corpus. Autism required satisfaction of two independent criteria - DSM-5 clinical criteria and the ADOS-2 - with diagnoses made by 'qualified doctors and professionals in the sector', and the absence of comorbidity was an explicit inclusion requirement. This is a dual-criterion standard including a gold-standard observational instrument, which places it above the single-clinician, registry-label or unspecified approaches seen elsewhere here. Typically developing status was established negatively rather than by instrument: no confirmed neurodevelopmental disorder, no suspected signs of autism, no developmental abnormality, no psychiatric or neurological history, plus an unusual and sensible catch-all whereby 'any child whose clinician or teacher was uncertain about the child's diagnosis or health was excluded'. That conservative rule reduces the risk of undetected autistic traits in the control group, though no screening instrument (SCQ, SRS, CAST) was administered to confirm it. Three details limit the standard's usefulness. The ADOS-2 module, algorithm scores and comparison scores are never reported, so the instrument is used as a gate and then discarded as data. Diagnosing clinicians are described only generically. And there is no statement of the interval between diagnosis and testing. [RQ1.5] Cognitive ability was measured in every participant with the Leiter-3 International Performance Scale, a non-verbal instrument appropriate for this population, and reported as a per-group range (ASD 59-109, TD 74-110) with the six autistic children in the 59-70 band identified. No means, SDs or statistical comparison are given. Autism severity was not measured or reported at all: ADOS-2 was administered for diagnosis but no severity, comparison or algorithm score is carried into the paper, so the position of these 30 children on the spectrum is unknown, no analysis relates model output to symptom severity, and it cannot be checked whether the model succeeds preferentially on more affected children. No language, adaptive-functioning or motor-competence measure was obtained, the last being a notable gap in a study whose entire signal is motor. There is also a structural entanglement peculiar to this design: the Leiter-3 serves simultaneously as the cognitive measure and, in tablet form, as the experimental task, so the kinematic features are recorded while children perform the very test used to characterise their cognitive ability, and only trials they completed correctly are analysed. Cognitive ability is therefore not an independent covariate here - it conditions which trajectories exist in the dataset. [RQ2.1] Goal: to move beyond descriptive comparison of touchscreen motion features - which the group's own earlier work (Simeoli et al., 2020) had found insufficient to distinguish the groups significantly - by using a variational autoencoder to learn a low-dimensional latent distribution of movement, and then to interrogate that latent space to identify which kinematic features drive classification and at what values. The framing is explicitly dual: not merely a diagnostic classifier but 'a new quantitative method to assess ASD', with the theoretical grounding in embodied cognition and predictive coding and the claim that motor abnormality is an underrated defining feature of autism. Findings: task-level cross-validated accuracy 91.2% +/- 5.6%; a latent space in which the two groups occupy distinct, approximately Gaussian regions, with cleaner separation when participants are plotted as the mean of their 25 tasks than task by task; latent structure stable across initialisations up to rotation; and, from Monte Carlo perturbation of one feature at a time, the finding that sdSpeed, MaxAcceleration, MinAcceleration and sdAcceleration have the largest capacity to move a participant across the latent space and reverse their classification, while sdDC, MeanSpeed, MaxSpeed and MeanLength map preferentially into the TD region and are judged marginal. The fitted class densities give signed rules - higher MaxAcceleration and sdAcceleration, and lower MaxSpeed and MinAcceleration, increase the probability of ASD assignment - which the authors offer to clinicians as candidate threshold values. [RQ2.2] Two sites in Campania, Italy, and the pairing is itself a confound. Autistic children came from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, which is also the employer of two of the four authors, and were undergoing psychomotor and speech therapy there. Typically developing children came from a mainstream primary school. Testing conditions were standardised across both groups - the same tablet, a table 65-70 cm high with the tablet within 20 cm of the edge, the examiner seated opposite, the same instruction protocol - so the acquisition chain does not differ by group in the way it does in some other studies in this corpus. But the recruitment geometry is the classic case-control one at 50% prevalence, and it carries a specific extra risk here: the autistic group's ongoing psychomotor therapy is an intervention directed precisely at the motor system whose kinematics constitute the study's entire feature set. Whether that therapy makes autistic movement more or less like typical movement, it makes the two groups differ in motor training history as well as in diagnosis. [RQ2.3] A tablet reimplementation, built in Unity and C#, of five subtests of the Leiter-3 Cognitive Battery, administered following the original test's instruction procedure with the examiner switching between subtests as the manual prescribes. Each scene shows up to five draggable cards at the bottom and up to eight placeholders at the top that capture cards dragged nearby, with distracting stimuli and image detail increasing across five difficulty levels; each child completed 25 tasks, five per level. Instructions were delivered by pointing and gesture without vocal aid, after which the child worked unaided. The design has real strengths: it is a standardised, clinically meaningful task rather than an ad hoc game, it varies difficulty systematically, and it captures fine motor behaviour as a by-product of a cognitive assessment the child would plausibly undergo anyway - which is the most translationally attractive property of the whole approach, since it means no additional testing burden. Two design decisions constrain interpretation. A task counted as complete when all cards had been placed regardless of correctness, but only correctly performed tasks were analysed 'to avoid the noise of the cognitive mistakes for the classification process'. This conditions the analysed sample on cognitive success and, if the groups differ in error rate - which is likely given the IQ ranges and six autistic children below the TD floor - removes trials differentially by group, changing what the retained trajectories represent. No error rates per group are reported, so the size of this effect cannot be assessed. And features are averaged to task level, so within-task temporal structure and trial-to-trial variability, both plausibly informative about motor control, are discarded before modelling. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, no test-retest reliability for any kinematic feature - which matters for a proposal to use feature values as clinical thresholds, since a threshold is only useful if the measurement is stable within a child across occasions. Ethics reporting is complete and appropriate: the study was reviewed and approved by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities, University of Naples Federico II, and written informed consent was obtained from participants' legal guardians. The conflict-of-interest statement discloses that two authors were employed by Neapolisanit S.R.L., the rehabilitation centre from which the autistic participants were recruited - a material disclosure, correctly made. Funding is not reported. [RQ2.5] Hardware and capture: an Android 6.0 tablet, 241.9 x 149.5 x 8.5 mm with a 9.6 inch 1280 x 800 screen at 60 Hz refresh, running custom software written in Unity and C# that logged finger position at 40 Hz. Cognitive assessment: Leiter-3 International Performance Scale. Feature extraction: RStudio with the traj package, citing Leffondree et al. (2004) and Sylvestre et al. (2006) - a specific, checkable toolchain. Modelling software is not named at all: no TensorFlow, PyTorch, Keras or equivalent, and no architecture details beyond 'a simple multilayer perceptron' predictor with a tanh intermediate layer and softmax output. The imbalance in the Methods is conspicuous - roughly two pages explain what a feed-forward neural network and backpropagation are, at textbook level, while the actual network used in the experiments has no stated layer sizes, learning rate, optimiser, batch size or epoch count. [RQ2.6] Split, in the same pattern as several engineering-led studies in this corpus. Reproducible: the tablet specification, the 40 Hz sampling, the seating and table geometry, the five Leiter-3 subtests and 25-task structure, the definition of a trajectory (first tap to finger lift), all 12 features with their formulas or plain definitions in Table 1, the extraction package, and the three-term VAE loss written out in full with the equal weighting stated. Not reproducible: the network architecture and every training hyperparameter, the fold assignment procedure, random seeds, the Monte Carlo perturbation's sampling distribution parameters beyond 'N(mu_fi, sigma_fi)', and any code. Raw data are offered on request without undue reservation, which is a genuine commitment though weaker than deposition. The paper also reports no participant-level accuracy despite plotting participant-level latent means, so the single most useful number for a reader wanting to compare against other studies is absent. [RQ2.7] The stated limitation is real but tangential: that supervision was required at the outset, so the ground truth still comes from traditional assessment, whereas an ideal VAE application would organise the latent space unsupervised. The unstated limitations are more consequential. The decisive one is the validation unit. The dataset is described unambiguously as 1,500 x 12 observations built from 60 children x 25 tasks, and 10-fold cross-validation is applied to those observations. Nothing indicates that a child's 25 rows were kept together, so in a standard k-fold split roughly 22-23 of each test observation's sibling rows - same child, same hand, same session, adjacent difficulty levels - are in the training set. A model with a 12-dimensional input and a 2-dimensional latent bottleneck can readily encode a child's individual motor signature, and the reported 91.2% is therefore substantially a measure of within-child consistency rather than of between-child generalisation. The tell is in the paper's own figures: Figure 3, which averages a participant's 25 tasks to a single point, shows cleaner separation than the task-level Figure 2, yet no accuracy is computed at that level, which is exactly the number a participant-disjoint evaluation would produce. Beyond validation: accuracy is the only metric reported, with no sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confusion matrix; the reduction from 10 to 2 latent dimensions was chosen by PCA on a latent space fitted to all the data; the analysis is restricted to correctly performed tasks, conditioning on cognitive success in a way that plausibly differs by group and is never quantified; IQ ranges are asymmetric with six autistic children below the TD floor and no means, SDs or test reported; sex is not reported at all; and the autistic group was in active psychomotor therapy while controls were not, confounding motor training with diagnosis in a study of motor kinematics. [RQ2.9] Four directions. Enlarge the dataset in both size and feature relevance so that the latent space organises without supervision, which is the authors' stated ambition and would remove their reliance on clinical labels as ground truth. Generate as many candidate features as possible so a globally optimal feature set for autism identification can be determined, citing Zhao et al. (2021). Collect more clinical data so the latent space is more densely covered and new participants are less likely to fall into unvisited regions - a coverage argument that follows directly from their decision to classify by fitted density rather than by the predictor network. And combine these kinematic measures with traditional behavioural and cognitive scales into a multimodal risk indicator supporting clinicians rather than replacing them. Absent from the list, and more pressing than any of these, are participant-level validation, an independent cohort, a clinical comparison group, and test-retest reliability for the features proposed as clinical thresholds. [RQ3.1] Fine motor control during goal-directed touchscreen dragging - specifically the kinematic profile of moving a finger from a card to a target placeholder, characterised along three dimensions. Speed: mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation. Acceleration: mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation. Path geometry: STH (straightness, the ratio of start-to-end distance to actual path length, an index of linearity), DC (directional change over time, an index of nonlinearity), sdDC (its standard deviation, a measure of irregularity), and MeanLength (the number of finite trajectories drawn per task). The behavioural hypothesis, grounded in embodied cognition and predictive coding, is that impaired active perception in autism produces abnormalities in planning and in serial and prospective coordination, which should surface as measurably different movement kinematics even in a simple drag. The group's earlier descriptive work had found autistic trajectories to show low linearity, high maximum speed and acceleration, and low minimum speed and acceleration, but without significant group separation; the present analysis partly reverses the speed direction, finding that lower MaxSpeed increases ASD probability while higher MaxAcceleration does. Note what is not modelled: no social behaviour, no gaze, no language, no gross motor activity - this is one of the most narrowly motoric behavioural targets in the corpus, and deliberately so. [RQ3.2] None - a single modality with 12 features from one sensor stream. The study is nonetheless relevant to the fusion question in two ways. First, the authors' explicit future direction is to combine these kinematic measures with 'the traditional behavioural and cognitive scale' into a multimodal risk measure - a clinician-facing rather than sensor-facing conception of fusion, in which the computational signal supplements standardised assessment rather than being fused with another sensor. Second, and more interestingly, the design already contains an implicit two-channel structure that goes unexploited: the tablet records both what the child does cognitively (which cards go where, and whether the answer is correct) and how the child moves while doing it. The paper deliberately discards the first channel, analysing only correctly performed tasks so that cognitive errors do not contaminate the motor signal. Since Leiter-3 performance is itself diagnostically informative and the two groups' IQ ranges differ, the discarded channel is not noise but a second modality that the design chose to suppress rather than fuse. [RQ4.1] A variational autoencoder with an attached supervised predictor - the only VAE in this corpus and one of few genuinely generative models here. The encoder maps the 12 features to the parameters (mean and standard deviation) of a diagonal Gaussian latent distribution; a latent vector is sampled and passed both to a symmetric decoder that reconstructs the input and to a predictor MLP with a tanh intermediate layer and a softmax output over the two classes. The composite loss has three equally weighted terms: mean squared reconstruction error, the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the learned latent distribution and a zero-mean unit-variance diagonal Gaussian, and binary cross-entropy on the prediction. The architectural rationale is stated clearly and is the paper's conceptual contribution: the KL regularisation forces a well-behaved latent geometry, and the predictor loss forces the two classes into separable regions of it, because if the class-conditional latent distributions overlap too much the stochastic sampling makes the prediction loss stagnate. The result is a latent space in which classification and generative description coexist. At inference the predictor is then set aside in favour of two fitted bivariate Gaussians over the latent points, on the explicit grounds that density-based assignment is more conservative for inputs that land in unvisited regions - a deliberate outlier-aware design choice that is unusual and clinically sensible. [RQ4.2] Twelve hand-crafted scalar features per task observation: four speed statistics (mean, max, min, SD), four acceleration statistics (mean, max, min, SD), and four path-geometry descriptors (STH straightness, DC directional change, sdDC directional-change variability, MeanLength). Features are computed per trajectory - one dragging movement from first tap to finger lift - using the R traj package, then averaged across the trajectories within a task, giving one 12-vector per child per task and 1,500 rows overall. The 40 Hz raw coordinate stream is therefore reduced twice before the network sees anything: once to per-trajectory summary statistics, once again by averaging across trajectories. No sequence model, no raw-signal input, no learned front end, and no representation of within-task variability across trajectories except through the SD features. The bottleneck is 10 latent dimensions at training, reduced to 2 for analysis after PCA showed the first two components carried 95% of the latent variance - so the effective representation of a child's movement on a task is a point in a plane. [RQ4.3] Accuracy alone: 91.2% +/- 5.6% across 10 folds. This is the thinnest metric reporting of any study charted in this review that reports a headline number at all. There is no sensitivity, no specificity, no precision or recall, no F1, no AUC or ROC curve, no confusion matrix, and no per-class breakdown, so it is impossible to tell whether errors fall preferentially on autistic or typically developing observations - which is precisely the information a clinician evaluating a screening aid needs. The +/- 5.6% is a fold standard deviation, not a confidence interval, and with observation-level folds it does not carry the meaning it would under participant-level splitting. There is also no participant-level accuracy at all, despite Figure 3 plotting exactly the per-participant aggregation that would yield one, and despite the paper's own observation that the separation is clearer at that level. The balanced design (750 versus 750) at least makes 50% the unambiguous chance floor, so no prevalence adjustment is needed to read the number - but nor is any positive or negative predictive value offered for the screening use the discussion proposes. [RQ4.4] The best interpretability work in this corpus, and it is not an add-on but the paper's purpose. Three techniques are layered. First, the latent space is made analytically tractable by construction: the VAE's KL term drives it towards a diagonal Gaussian, so two-dimensional class-conditional Gaussians can be fitted to the ASD and TD point clouds and a genuine probability density function evaluated for any point rather than a black-box score. Second, feature influence is measured causally within the model rather than by correlation: for each participant, each of the 12 features is resampled 100 times from a Gaussian while the other 11 are held fixed, and the resulting displacement of that participant's latent projection is tracked, identifying not only which features move a subject but at which values the class assignment flips. Figure 5 aggregates this into per-feature density maps over the latent space and Figure 6 into class-probability curves against raw feature values. Third, the outputs are expressed in clinically usable form: signed, feature-specific rules (higher MaxAcceleration and sdAcceleration, lower MaxSpeed and MinAcceleration increase ASD probability) explicitly offered as candidate threshold values for joint use by clinicians. The design also embeds an interpretability-motivated safety property, replacing the predictor with density evaluation at inference so a participant in an unpopulated region is not confidently misassigned. The caveats are that no uncertainty is attached to any of these feature effects, no group-level statistics on the features themselves are reported (the earlier descriptive paper failed to find significant differences, which is the stated motivation for this analysis), and the whole latent geometry was learned on data containing the test observations, so the thresholds are in-sample. [RQ4.5] The critical weakness, and it is unacknowledged. The dataset is stated plainly: 60 participants x 25 tasks = 1,500 observations of 12 features, with a parallel 1,500-element label vector repeating each child's diagnosis 25 times. Cross-validation is 10-fold over that observation set, giving 91.2% +/- 5.6%. There is no statement that a child's 25 rows were assigned to a single fold, and the description ('we used the k-fold cross-validation with k = 10 and returning the average accuracy', applied to 'the collected dataset') implies observation-level partitioning. Under that scheme every test observation has roughly 22-23 siblings from the same child, same session and same hand in the training data, differing only in Leiter-3 subtest and difficulty level. Movement kinematics are strongly individual - speed and acceleration profiles are close to a motor signature - so a 12-input, 2-latent model can separate children rather than groups and score highly, exactly the leakage Keles et al. quantified directly elsewhere in this corpus by identifying individuals from behaviour at many times chance. Two internal signals support this reading: the authors themselves note that the clustering is 'even more evident' when participants are plotted as the mean of their tasks than task by task, which is what one expects when within-child consistency is high; and they never compute the participant-level accuracy that this observation invites. Secondary issues compound it. The choice of two latent dimensions was made from PCA on a latent space learned from the entire dataset. The class-conditional Gaussians used for the interpretability analysis and proposed as clinical thresholds are fitted to all 1,500 points. Only accuracy is reported. And the balanced 50/50 design, while making chance interpretable, is 25-50 times the population prevalence at which the proposed screening support would operate. The corrective is straightforward and would be a genuinely valuable result: split the 60 children into folds, train on one set of children and test on unseen children, report participant-level sensitivity and specificity as well as accuracy, and refit the latent Gaussians within training folds only. Given 60 children and a well-specified reference standard including ADOS-2, that study is within reach of this dataset. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: machine learning, autism spectrum disorder, ASD, motor abnormalities, deep learning, early detection, diagnosis. Unusually, both 'early detection' and 'diagnosis' appear, which is a stronger clinical claim than the paper's own discussion supports - the text positions the method as supplying 'additional indicators of disorder or suspected diagnosis' and supporting clinicians rather than diagnosing. 'Motor abnormalities' is the theoretical stake, asserting that motor difference is a hallmark rather than an incidental correlate. Terms carried through the body: variational autoencoder, latent variable model, latent space, generative model, kinematics, touch-based functions, trajectory, straightness, directional change, embodied cognition, predictive coding, threshold values. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Psychology 14, article 1194760, Original Research, in a psychology rather than an engineering or clinical venue - which shows in the structure. Roughly two pages of the Methods are a textbook exposition of artificial neural networks and backpropagation aimed at a psychology readership, while the network actually used has no reported layer widths, learning rate, optimiser or epoch count; conversely the theoretical framing in embodied cognition and predictive coding is developed at length. Editorial and review handling is disclosed by name, as Frontiers requires. Received 27 March 2023, accepted 21 April 2023, published 18 May 2023 - a 25-day review turnaround - under CC BY. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 from the Department of Humanistic Studies, University of Naples Federico II, in collaboration with the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, where two of the four authors were employed and from which the autistic participants were recruited - disclosed appropriately in the competing-interests statement. No funding is reported. The framing is a critique of existing assessment: the authors list four specific constraints of gold-standard tools - no explicit sensory-functioning assessment, dependence on examiner expertise and subjective evaluation, limited ecological validity, and the time demanded - and position quantitative motor measurement as the remedy. The paper is explicitly a second pass at the group's own earlier dataset, whose descriptive analysis had failed to separate the groups significantly, which makes it an unusually transparent instance of a common pattern in this corpus: conventional statistics find nothing, a deep model is applied to the same data, and separation appears. The stated ambition is to move eventually to unsupervised latent organisation so that the model no longer depends on clinical labels for ground truth - a 2023-era aspiration that the paper's own sample size prevents it from testing. |
| S-098 | Method-development and agreement study conducted inside routine clinical practice at The First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, China, with engineering from Jilin University. Four fixed RGB cameras were installed in the assessment room and video plus audio were captured during live ADOS-2 screening sessions, leaving the clinical protocol unmodified. Thirty children participated - 29 autistic and 1 typically developing, mean age 3.65 years - selected as those assessed with ADOS-2 modules TM, M1 or M2, which cover children from 12 months upward with little or no fluent language. No other demographic or clinical data are reported: no sex, no age range, no IQ, no language measure, no ADOS-2 scores. Each child received up to five name calls under the standard press, giving 109 test events. The reference standard for the study's outcome is an experienced clinician's 0-5 response-to-name score for each child, and Table 2 shows that 17 of the 30 children scored 5, meaning no response after all five calls. Ethics review is asserted without naming a committee; parental informed consent was obtained before each session and faces are mosaicked in published figures. | Audio was transcribed by a commercial deep convolutional ASR service (iFlytek) to timestamp each name call automatically, avoiding manual annotation error, and the following 3 s of video was extracted as the response window. Body pose came from the front-left camera: YOLOv3, retrained on more than 1,700 images of the study's own 30 subjects rather than using COCO weights, detected people; HRNet estimated 2-D joints; OSNet re-identification tracked identities across frames, which is necessary because the scene contains the child, the clinician and an unrestricted number of parents. From the child's shoulder joints, the rotation angle at each frame was computed as the arccosine of the normalised dot product between the left-right shoulder vector at that frame and at the first frame after the call. Head pose came from whichever rear camera faced the child - two are needed because the clinician may stand on either side - with OpenFace supplying facial landmarks and 3-D Euler angles, of which yaw indexes turning. The decision is a hand-written cascade with five asserted constants: shoulder rotation above 90 degrees on more than 10 of the 75 frames (0.4 s, derived by doubling a 0.2 s gaze-fixation figure to allow for timing error) gives a positive response; rotation below 20 degrees on every frame gives a negative response; in the intervening band, more than 8 frames of detected head yaw gives a positive response. No model is trained on the behaviour, and no training/test split, cross-validation or held-out set exists anywhere in the pipeline. | Body pose alone agreed with the clinician for 25 of 30 children (83.3%) and 104 of 109 name calls (95.4%). Adding head pose raised agreement to 28 of 30 children (93.3%) and 107 of 109 calls (98.2%), with sensitivity 84.6% and specificity 100% under an explicitly inverted convention in which the positive class is failure to respond. The 6 x 6 confusion matrix of clinician against predicted scores is published, with the modal cell being clinician 5 / predicted 5 in 17 children. Both residual participant-level errors are diagnosed concretely: one child responded too slowly to accumulate the required 10 frames above the shoulder threshold and was also wearing a mask, which blocked facial landmark detection and hence the head-pose fallback; the other turned their head too quickly for 8 frames of yaw to be registered. The authors state in the methods that the experiment 'is an assessment of the response to name, not an assessment of autism risk'. | There is no validation of any kind. All five decision constants were set by hand and reported on the same 30 children, and the one trained component - the YOLOv3 person detector - was retrained on more than 1,700 images of those same 30 children, so no part of the pipeline was ever exercised on a participant it had not seen. No chance-agreement baseline is computed, although the data demand one: with 17 of 30 children scoring 5 and each such child contributing five non-response events, an always-predict-non-response rule would already agree with the clinician on a majority of children and on a considerably larger share of the 109 calls, which makes the 98.2% event-level figure uninterpretable without a weighted kappa - and none is reported for what is an ordinal agreement task. The 109 events are treated as independent although they cluster within 30 children and are serially dependent by the protocol's own logic. The reference standard is a single unblinded clinician, scoring in real time while conducting the assessment, with no second rater and no reliability statistic. The shoulder angle is a 2-D image-plane measurement from an uncalibrated fixed camera, so seating position confounds it. Demographic reporting is limited to a single mean age. And the framing is internally inconsistent: the methods' correct disclaimer that this is not an autism-risk assessment is contradicted by the abstract's report of 93.3% consistency with 'clinical diagnosis' and by the conclusion's proposal of deployment for early autism screening in remote areas - in a sample containing one non-autistic child. | This is the corpus's only attempt to automate the scoring of an individual item of a standardised diagnostic instrument, and that makes it worth charting despite its methodological weakness, because it defines a category distinct from the diagnosis-prediction studies that dominate this review. The target is not a diagnosis but an ADOS-2 response-to-name score, the comparator is a clinician's judgement of that item, and the deployment vision is a clinician-facing scoring aid rather than a screening classifier. Three features recommend it to the synthesis. It is one of very few studies here recorded inside live clinical assessment with the protocol left untouched, deliberately accepting variable parental presence and uncontrolled child behaviour as the target distribution - the authors argue this explicitly and are right to. Its multimodal design is justified by named behavioural failure modes rather than by accuracy search: body pose is added because head-pose-only methods miss children who turn only the head and falsely flag children who shift while playing, and the reported ablation is consistent with that reasoning, though it rests on three children. And it is the most fully interpretable system in the corpus, reducing every judgement to two angles and a frame count that can be replayed against video. Against this, it is also the clearest illustration in the review of a specific reporting hazard: an agreement figure computed against a reference in which one category holds a large majority, reported as raw accuracy with no chance correction, and then described in the abstract as consistency with clinical diagnosis. The contrast with Wawer and Chojnicka's three-way benchmarking of models, psychiatrists and instruments on the same participants is instructive - both concern the relationship between automated output and clinician judgement, but only one measures it in a way that survives the base rate. | [RQ1.1] Thirty children in total: 29 with autism and 1 typically developing, mean age 3.65 years. Selection was by ADOS-2 module - only children assessed with the TM, M1 or M2 modules were included, i.e. children from 12 months upward with little or no fluent oral expression, excluding the M3 and M4 modules used for verbally fluent older children and adults. There is no comparison group in any meaningful sense; the single typically developing participant cannot support a between-group contrast and the paper never attempts one. A second and more relevant unit of analysis exists: 109 individual name-call test events, since each child receives up to five calls (three in natural tone at about 3 s intervals, then up to two reinforced calls by clinician or parent). These 109 events are the denominator for the study's highest reported figure of 98.2%, but they are not independent - they cluster within 30 children and are strongly serially dependent, because a child who ignores the first call usually ignores the remaining four. Table 2 shows the consequence: 17 of the 30 children scored 5, meaning they did not respond to any of the five calls. [RQ1.2] 'Autistic children' and 'children with ASD' are both used, with 'autistic children' predominating in the title, abstract and conclusion - identity-first language, which is unusual in this corpus and may reflect translation from Chinese as much as a deliberate stance. Other usages are less careful: 'the number of autistic patients has been rising', 'more than 10 million people have been diagnosed with ASD', and 'children with autism have a low quality of life, require family care, and bring huge economic costs to society'. That last sentence, in the opening paragraph, frames autistic children primarily as a burden and is the starkest instance of deficit-and-cost framing encountered so far in this review. Clinically the vocabulary is standard medical-model: 'neurodevelopmental disorder', 'incidence rate', 'RTN deficiency', 'symptoms', 'no medicine can reliably relieve the symptoms of ASD'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. Set against this, the study's practical stance towards children is respectful in a way several others here are not: it works within a real clinical assessment rather than imposing an experimental protocol, accepts a flexible number of accompanying parents, and mosaics participants' faces in published figures for privacy even at the cost of obscuring the detected landmarks. [RQ1.3] The thinnest demographic reporting of any included study charted so far. What is given: n = 30, of whom 29 autistic and 1 typically developing; a single overall mean age of 3.65 years; and the ADOS-2 modules from which participants were drawn (TM, M1, M2), which implies limited or absent fluent language across the sample. What is absent: sex distribution, age range or standard deviation, per-group age, IQ or developmental quotient, language level beyond the module implication, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, comorbidity, medication, and any ADOS-2 total, algorithm or comparison score. Because the sample is 29 autistic children and 1 control, the usual concern about group matching does not arise, but a different problem does: without age spread, sex, or developmental level it is impossible to judge for whom the vision pipeline works. Body proportions, head size, motor control and sitting posture all vary sharply across the 12-month to roughly 5-year span that modules TM through M2 encompass, and a shoulder-rotation threshold of 90 degrees measured in 2-D image coordinates is not obviously age-invariant. All data come from one hospital in Changchun, so the sample is also geographically and culturally homogeneous. [RQ1.4] Two distinct reference standards operate in this study and the paper does not clearly separate them. For group membership, the 29 autistic children were assessed by professional clinicians using ADOS-2 at the Department of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics of a university teaching hospital, with module assignment reported; but no ADOS-2 score, no DSM or ICD criteria, no diagnosing-clinician description and no diagnostic date are given, and the single typically developing child's status is not characterised at all. For the study's actual outcome, the reference is an experienced clinician's 0-5 response-to-name score, assigned during the same session under an explicitly stated rule set. This second standard is well defined operationally - the rule tree in Fig. 2 is unambiguous - and it is the appropriate comparator for what the system does. Its weaknesses are that a single clinician scored each child, that this clinician was necessarily unblinded (they were conducting the assessment and calling the child's name), that no second rater or reliability statistic exists, and that the score is therefore an individual judgement rather than a consensus. Since response to name is exactly the kind of item where a clinician standing behind a child must judge in real time whether a head turn counted as a response with eye contact, the absence of any inter-rater reliability is a real gap: the paper's headline number is agreement with one person's uncorroborated judgement. [RQ1.5] No cognitive, language, adaptive or global severity measure was administered or reported. The only quantitative symptom measure in the study is the response-to-name score itself, and it is genuinely informative: Table 2 shows that 17 of the 30 children failed to respond after all five calls, with the remainder distributed across the lower scores. That distribution is a symptom-severity profile for one ADOS-2 item, and it is reported honestly. But it is also the paper's undoing statistically, because a majority of children and a larger majority of the 109 calls fall into the single 'no response' category, and no chance-corrected agreement statistic is computed against that floor. Beyond this item, nothing: no ADOS-2 calibrated severity score despite ADOS-2 having been administered in full to every child, no developmental quotient, no language measure beyond the coarse module assignment, and no motor assessment - the last being relevant since the system's primary signal is torso rotation and children in this age and module range vary widely in postural control. [RQ2.1] Goal: to automate the judgement of response to name during real clinical ADOS-2 assessments, by combining automatic speech recognition (to timestamp the name calls) with human pose tracking (to measure shoulder rotation) and head pose estimation (to measure head yaw), and to show that adding body pose to the head-pose-only approach used in prior work improves agreement with clinicians. Three contributions are claimed: a four-camera multi-view capture rig; a 'Response to name Dataset' drawn from live ADOS-2 screening rather than a controlled laboratory protocol, with more natural child behaviour and an unrestricted number of accompanying parents; and the finding that combining shoulder rotation angle, head pose and response duration improves accuracy over pose alone. Findings: shoulder pose alone agreed with the clinician for 25 of 30 children (83.3%) and 104 of 109 calls (95.4%); adding head pose raised this to 28 of 30 (93.3%) and 107 of 109 (98.2%), with sensitivity 84.6% and specificity 100% under an inverted convention in which the 'positive' class is non-response. The two residual participant-level errors are diagnosed concretely: one child responded too slowly to accumulate the required 10 frames above the shoulder threshold and was also wearing a mask, which blocked the facial-landmark fallback; the other turned their head too fast for 8 frames of yaw to be detected. The score-level confusion matrix shows the modal outcome to be clinician 5 / predicted 5 in 17 children. [RQ2.2] Single site: the Department of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics, The First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, with engineering from Jilin University's School of Communication Engineering. The setting is the study's most distinctive feature and is used deliberately rather than incidentally. Recording took place during actual ADOS-2 screening sessions rather than in a purpose-built experiment, with four fixed cameras installed in the assessment room and the clinical protocol left untouched: the clinician stands where the protocol requires, calls in a natural tone, repeats and reinforces as the manual specifies, and an unspecified and varying number of parents may be present. The authors argue explicitly that this yields 'less laboratory control, more realistic child response, and a flexible number of accompanying parents', and they are right that this is the correct target distribution for a tool meant to sit inside a clinic. It also creates the engineering problem the pipeline is built to solve - the scene contains multiple adults, so person re-identification is needed simply to know which skeleton belongs to the child. The countervailing point is that the sample is a referred clinical series at a tertiary hospital with 29 of 30 children already autistic, which is the opposite of the community screening population the conclusion invokes when it proposes deployment 'in remote areas with underdeveloped medical care'. [RQ2.3] The ADOS-2 response-to-name press, executed as the manual prescribes and left unmodified. The child sits at a table absorbed in toys; the clinician stands behind and to one side and calls the child's name in a natural voice; if the child turns and makes eye contact the item ends, otherwise the call is repeated up to three times at roughly 3 s intervals; then up to two reinforced calls follow, delivered with a changed tone or by a parent. Scoring runs 0 (responds to the first call) through 5 (no response after all five). Two properties make this paradigm unusually well suited to automation. It has a precise onset - the moment the name is spoken - which the ASR component recovers automatically and which the authors correctly identify as removing a source of manual-annotation error; and it has a precise, short response window of 3 s fixed by the protocol itself. Two properties make it hard. The clinically defined response is 'turn and face the implementer with eye contact rather than glance to the side', which is a conjunction of orientation and gaze that no single sensor captures, and which the cascade approximates rather than measures - eye contact per se is never assessed, only head yaw and whether a face was detected by the rear camera. And the caller's position varies between left and right rear, which is why two rear cameras are required and why the head-pose channel depends on the child turning towards whichever camera happens to be behind the caller. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional single session with no follow-up and no test-retest assessment. Since the pipeline is proposed as a clinical scoring aid, the absence of any repeat measurement means nothing is known about whether the same child assessed twice would receive the same automated score. Ethics reporting is minimal but present in both required elements: 'these experiments have passed an ethical review', with no committee, institution or approval number named, and informed consent obtained from the children's parents before each session. A privacy measure is also implemented and disclosed - participants' faces are mosaicked in the published figures, with the authors noting that this may obscure the facial joints they wish to illustrate - and the data are declared confidential rather than released. For video recorded on preschool children with disabilities during clinical assessment, the consent and privacy handling is appropriate; the ethics statement is thinner than the norm and would not satisfy most journals' current reporting requirements. [RQ2.5] Capture: four Hikvision RGB cameras with 2.8 mm lenses mounted at a common height of 1.44 m, recording 1280 x 720 at 25 fps, of which three are used - C1 at the child's left front for body pose and C3/C4 at left and right rear for head pose, the pair being necessary because the clinician may stand on either side. Audio is captured alongside and converted to 16 kHz 16-bit PCM for the speech service. Software stack, all named and all off-the-shelf except for retraining: iFlytek (HKUST Xunfei) real-time speech transcription, a deep fully-convolutional ASR that returns timestamped text and thereby locates each name call; YOLOv3 for person detection, deliberately retrained on more than 1,700 images from the study's own 30 subjects rather than using COCO weights, on accuracy grounds; HRNet for top-down 2-D pose estimation, chosen for its high-resolution feature maintenance and repeated multi-scale fusion; OSNet person re-identification to associate detections across frames and assign a stable ID, without which the child's skeleton could not be distinguished from the clinician's and the parents'; OpenFace for face detection, landmarks and 3-D head Euler angles. Implementation in Python and PyTorch. What is missing is any calibration: the cameras' geometry is fixed and stated but no intrinsic or extrinsic calibration is performed, and the shoulder rotation angle is computed directly in 2-D image coordinates, so a given physical torso rotation maps to different measured angles depending on where the child is seated and how they are oriented with respect to C1. [RQ2.6] Strong on specification, absent on artefacts. Every decision constant is stated numerically - the 3 s response window, the 90 degree and 20 degree shoulder thresholds, the 10-frame (0.4 s) and 8-frame duration thresholds - and the angle computation is written out as three equations from the shoulder vector through the arccosine to the degree conversion. The camera rig, frame rate, resolution, focal length and mounting height are given, as are the roles of each camera, the clinical protocol and its full scoring rule, the exact third-party models used, and the size of the custom detection training set. A competent group could rebuild the system from the paper. What cannot be reproduced is any number in it: the data are declared confidential, the retrained YOLOv3 weights and the 1,700-image annotations are not released, no code is available, and the ASR component is a commercial service whose behaviour may change. There is also no preregistration and no independent evaluation of the perception components (detection, tracking, landmark) in isolation, so their error rates on this population are unknown and are folded silently into the end-to-end figure. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section, though the discussion analyses the two residual errors carefully and the methods contain an important and creditable scope disclaimer - 'although RTN deficiency is closely associated with ASD, our experiment is an assessment of the response to name, not an assessment of autism risk'. The unaddressed limitations are substantial and several are structural. First, there is no validation of any kind: the five decision constants were chosen by hand and reported on the same 30 children, and the one trained component, YOLOv3, was retrained on 1,700 images of those same 30 children, so the detector has seen every participant it is evaluated on. Nothing in the paper estimates performance on an unseen child. Second, no chance baseline is computed, and the sample makes one essential: 17 of 30 children scored 5, so a rule that always predicted non-response would agree with the clinician on a majority of children and on a still larger majority of the 109 calls, since each non-responding child contributes five non-response events. For an ordinal agreement problem of this shape the natural statistic is a weighted kappa, and none is reported. Third, the 109 events are treated as independent for the headline 98.2% although they cluster within 30 children and are strongly serially dependent. Fourth, the reference standard is one unblinded clinician with no second rater and no reliability statistic, on an item that requires a real-time judgement about eye contact from behind the child. Fifth, the shoulder angle is a 2-D image-plane measurement from an uncalibrated fixed camera, so it confounds true rotation with seating position and posture. Sixth, the demographic reporting is too thin to establish for whom the method works. Finally, the framing is inconsistent: the abstract reports agreement with 'clinical diagnosis' and the conclusion invokes early autism screening in underserved regions, while the actual comparator is one clinician's score of one behavioural item in a sample that contains a single non-autistic child. [RQ2.9] No future-work section is provided. The conclusion's forward-looking claims are about deployment rather than research: that the method reduces the professional-knowledge requirement for assessment, provides efficient and objective computer-aided screening, and could support early autism screening in remote areas with underdeveloped medical care. Judged against the evidence, the research steps that would need to come first are clear and unstated: evaluation on children not used to train the detector; a balanced sample containing a meaningful number of non-autistic children so that the item score's discriminative value can be assessed; a second, blinded clinician rater with reported reliability so the reference standard is not one person's judgement; chance-corrected agreement statistics appropriate to an ordinal score; and threshold selection on a development set separate from the evaluation set. The wider point this study raises for the review, and does not itself pursue, is whether automating individual ADOS-2 items one at a time is a viable route to instrument automation - it is the only paper in this corpus attempting it, and the answer depends on error rates the paper cannot currently estimate. [RQ3.1] One behaviour, examined more closely than any other single behaviour in this corpus: response to one's own name. The clinical definition adopted is precise - the child should turn and face the caller with eye contact rather than glance to the side - and the paper's decomposition of it into measurable components is the substantive contribution. Torso orientation is captured as the angle between the left-right shoulder vector at each frame and the same vector at the first frame after the call, so the measurement is relative to the child's own starting posture rather than to an absolute frame. Head orientation is captured as the yaw Euler angle from facial landmarks, with the mere detection of a face by the rear camera also serving as evidence that the child turned towards the caller. Response latency is captured by the ordinal 0-5 score, which encodes how many calls and reinforcements were needed. The authors are explicit about why body pose is needed alongside head pose, and the reasoning is behavioural rather than technical: prior work used head pose and gaze only, but some responsive children turn only the head with little shoulder movement, while some unresponsive children rotate slightly while manipulating toys, so neither channel alone separates response from non-response. What is not measured, despite being in the clinical definition, is eye contact itself - gaze is approximated by head direction on the stated assumption that the two agree, an approximation that is reasonable in general but is exactly the point at which a glance to the side, which the protocol says does not count as a response, becomes indistinguishable from a genuine orienting response. [RQ3.2] Three-stream fusion with a clearly reported ablation, and the fusion architecture is a hand-written cascade rather than a learned combination. Audio and video are fused at the segmentation stage: the ASR stream supplies timestamps for each name call, which cut the video into 3 s response windows, and the authors note that this removes the manual-annotation error that would otherwise attach to onset marking. Body pose and head pose are then fused at the decision stage in a three-branch rule: shoulder rotation above 90 degrees for more than 10 frames gives a positive response outright; shoulder rotation below 20 degrees on every frame gives a negative response outright; and only in the ambiguous 20-90 degree band does head yaw adjudicate, with more than 8 frames of detected yaw giving a positive response. The ablation is reported for the two visual streams and is the paper's central quantitative claim: pose alone gives 83.3% of participants and 95.4% of events, pose plus head pose gives 93.3% and 98.2%. In participant terms that is three additional children correctly scored out of 30, so the confidence interval on the improvement is wide even though the direction is plausible. Two features of this fusion design are worth carrying into the synthesis. It is complementary by explicit behavioural argument rather than by empirical search - each stream is introduced to cover a named failure mode of the other - which is a more defensible basis for multimodality than the accuracy-chasing seen in several other studies here. And the multi-view arrangement is itself a form of fusion driven by the clinical protocol: two rear cameras are required because the caller may stand on either side, so which camera contributes the head-pose evidence depends on the geometry of the assessment rather than on a fixed sensor assignment. [RQ4.1] A hybrid that is unusual in this corpus: four deep neural networks are used as perception front ends, but no model is trained on the behaviour and the decision itself is a hand-written rule. The deep components are YOLOv3 for person detection (retrained on the study's own images rather than using COCO weights, on accuracy grounds), HRNet for top-down 2-D pose estimation (selected for its high-resolution feature maintenance and repeated multi-scale fusion), OSNet re-identification for multi-object tracking (necessary because the scene contains the child, the clinician and a variable number of parents, so the child's skeleton must be identified and followed), OpenFace for facial landmarks and 3-D head Euler angles, and a commercial deep fully-convolutional ASR for name-call timestamps. Above these sits a three-branch threshold cascade with five hand-set constants. The architectural choice is defensible for the task - the clinical scoring rule is itself a deterministic decision tree over observable orienting behaviour, so encoding it directly rather than learning it from 109 examples is the right call at this sample size, and it makes every judgement auditable. The cost is that nothing adapts: the thresholds cannot accommodate a child whose habitual posture or motor control differs, the paper's own two error cases are both threshold-boundary failures, and there is no probability or confidence attached to any judgement, so no case can be flagged as uncertain and referred back to the clinician - which is precisely what an assistive scoring tool ought to do. [RQ4.2] Two scalar angle time series per 3 s response window, each sampled at 25 fps and therefore up to 75 frames long, reduced to threshold-crossing frame counts before the decision. The shoulder rotation series is computed frame by frame as theta_t = arccos(v_0 . v_t / \|v_0\|\|v_t\|) converted to degrees, where v_t is the vector from the right to the left shoulder joint at frame t and v_0 is the same vector at the first frame after the name call - so the measurement is self-referenced to the child's posture at call onset rather than to any absolute frame, which is a sensible choice that removes dependence on how the child happened to be sitting. The head series is the OpenFace yaw Euler angle, accompanied by an implicit binary of whether a face was detected at all by the relevant rear camera. Both series are then summarised only by counting frames that satisfy a threshold, so the representation discards the shape of the movement entirely: peak angular velocity, smoothness, whether the turn was completed or aborted, and whether the child returned to the toys are all invisible. Nothing is learned from the raw joint coordinates, and no representation of the temporal profile of orienting survives into the decision.
