The importance analysis is done at two levels and, critically, against the right baseline: individual top-10 features are named, and the four anatomical categories are compared with their proportion of the full 6,272-feature pool, so the conclusion that mouth features matter is not an artefact of there being many mouth features (25.5% of the pool, 40% of the top 10) and the pose finding is stronger than it looks (5.3% of the pool, 13.3% of the top 10). Findings are then related to independent literature on blinking, nodding, social orienting and backchannel feedback rather than left as bare weights. The authors are equally explicit about the ceiling: they cannot distinguish upper lip from mouth corner, a fuller account would require 3D versions of localised bases, and 'further analysis to uncover why these features are important is beyond the scope of this study'. Finally, the discussion argues that interpretability is a precondition for the assistive use case the paper proposes - a clinician cannot rationally weigh a dissenting AI opinion without knowing which behaviours produced it - which correctly makes explanation a functional requirement rather than a courtesy. [RQ4.5] The strongest validation design encountered so far in this review, with one important caveat about how the result should be read. Each participant contributes exactly one feature vector, so the unit of splitting is the person by construction and the segment-level leakage that inflates most studies in this corpus is structurally impossible. Validation is nested cross-validation with a single tuned hyperparameter, the correlation window Tw over four candidate values, optimised inside the inner loop; the SVM's regularisation is left at its default rather than tuned, further reducing researcher degrees of freedom; and no feature selection is performed at all, so selection bias cannot arise despite 6,272 features. The outer evaluation is 10-fold cross-validation repeated 100 times with participant order shuffled between repetitions, which addresses fold-assignment variance - a source of instability that very few studies here even acknowledge. The identity-modelling step deserves separate credit as leakage control of a different kind: because the 3DMM estimates and removes facial identity, the representation is explicitly stripped of the individual-appearance information that, elsewhere in this corpus, silently drives high accuracy. The caveat is the base rate and the operating point. At 15 autistic and 27 neurotypical participants, majority-class prediction yields 64.3%, so 80.5% is a 16-point improvement rather than the 30 points a reader assuming balance might infer, and no permutation test or confidence interval is offered. The class imbalance also shapes the classifier: at sensitivity 0.55 and specificity 0.95 the model has learned to be conservative, so its accuracy is carried disproportionately by correctly identifying neurotypical participants. None of this undermines the study's actual claim - which concerns the non-overlap of AI and human errors, evaluated per participant - but it does mean the headline accuracy should not be read as evidence of a strong autism detector. [RQ5.1] Author keywords: autism; assistive healthcare technologies; digital phenotyping. The choice is revealing. 'Digital phenotyping' locates the work in a measurement tradition rather than a diagnostic one, and 'assistive healthcare technologies' states the intended role explicitly - neither 'diagnosis', 'screening', 'classification', 'machine learning' nor 'deep learning' appears, even though the paper performs classification with machine learning. Terms carried through the body text include computational behavior analysis, 3D morphable model, windowed cross-correlation, monadic versus dyadic analysis, Clinical Best Estimate, Contextual Assessment of Social Skills, and neurodiverse samples. [RQ5.2] CEUR Workshop Proceedings volume 3359, the ITAH (Intelligent Technologies for Assistive Healthcare) track of the Joint Proceedings of the ACM IUI 2023 Workshops, pages 48-57 - a workshop paper at a human-computer interaction venue rather than a clinical or machine-learning journal. The venue choice fits the contribution: the question of whether AI predictions add anything beyond human judgement is an interaction question, and the paper's framing around assistive rather than autonomous use is native to the IUI community. It also explains some of the reporting compression, since workshop papers are short. The article is deposited as an HHS Public Access author manuscript, reflecting the NIH funding, and is available under CC BY 4.0. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 (author manuscript available in PMC from November 2023), from the Center for Autism Research at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania, funded by four NIH grants (R01MH118327, R01MH122599, 5P50HD105354-02, R21HD102078). The framing is deliberately corrective rather than promotional. The opening premise is that psychiatry, unlike the rest of medicine, relies almost exclusively on observational and paper-and-pencil instruments, and that computational behaviour analysis could supply the missing instrumentation - with the explicit acknowledgement that clinical assessment reliability is currently limited, citing the DSM-5 field trial kappa of 0.69 for autism. The central rhetorical move is to identify a gap the field has left open: 'to our knowledge, no study has directly compared AI algorithms and human raters with respect to overall predictive capacity or specific decisions on individual cases'. That reframing - from 'can AI classify autism?' to 'does AI tell a clinician anything they did not already know?' - is the paper's real contribution and is the question most of this corpus does not ask. The positioning is consistently augmentative: AI as an assistive tool that could prompt a clinician to re-evaluate when the two disagree, with the caveat that this is only workable if the algorithm can say why. |
| S-101 | Cross-sectional case-control classification study with multi-centre recruitment across Shaanxi and Fujian provinces in China, chosen by the authors because medical provision there is relatively poor and screening in such areas is understudied. Three hundred and thirty-three children aged 3-6 participated: 140 with autism (112 boys, 28 girls; mean age 4.66 +/- 1.00 years) and 193 typically developing (122 boys, 71 girls; mean age 4.77 +/- 0.92 years), all with normal or corrected vision, recruited from multiple hospitals and schools. Ages are well matched; sex is not, at 80.0% male in the autistic group against 63.2% in the comparison group, a difference never tested or discussed. The main text describes no diagnostic instrument, criteria or process for either group, and reports no IQ, developmental, language or severity measure. Testing took place in a therapy room with the child seated 0.5 m from a monitor accompanied by at most the mother and one researcher, and data collection ran through 2021. The study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Northwestern Polytechnical University under protocol 202002032 with Declaration of Helsinki conformity; no consent statement appears. | Children freely viewed 82 static images drawn from four categories - facial images, social scenarios, animated characters and synthetic patterns - presented in two roughly three-minute sessions, each image for 3 s separated by a 0.5 s grey mask, with no instruction other than to observe. Gaze was recorded on a SciEye 2.0 infrared eye tracker at 140 Hz, with device-level noise suppression merging points closer than 0.02 in normalised coordinates and deleting merged points shorter than 0.1 s. Each stimulus was segmented into SLIC superpixels; for every fixation, the containing superpixel's bounding box was resized and passed through a deep autoencoder pretrained on 10,000 MS COCO images to yield a compressed semantic code, concatenated with four low-level descriptors (position, duration, saccade amplitude, saccade orientation). The resulting per-fixation sequence for each stimulus entered an LSTM with fully connected and regression heads, trained by backpropagation through time under weak supervision: because it is unknown which specific stimuli elicit atypical viewing in a given child, each child's diagnostic label was propagated to all 82 of their patterns. At test time the 82 stimulus scores were averaged per child and binarised with Otsu's maximum between-class variance threshold. Evaluation used a 50% subject-level random split repeated over five permutations. Two baselines were reimplemented for comparison - a fixation-count histogram with SVM, and stacked deep features of up to 10 fixations with SVM - and ablations removed the semantic or low-level feature families in turn. | Subject-level accuracy was 96.73% with sensitivity 96.85% and specificity 96.63% on 165 test children, and all five random splits exceeded 95.76%. Ablation showed semantic features contributing more than low-level ones (semantic alone 94.85%/97.14%/93.16%; low-level alone 93.33%/90.71%/95.26%), with the combination improving both sensitivity and specificity rather than trading them; both fixation-based baselines underperformed the sequence model, and a variant discarding sequence structure fell to 90.91%. The pre-modelling descriptive analysis reproduced the expected group differences - fewer fixations, longer saccades, less looking at faces and other salient objects, slower first fixation on objects, more dwelling on background and on the grey mask, with the largest between-group difference in facial areas - but the authors state that these hand-crafted differences are insufficient for direct classification. A time-delay embedding analysis showed between-group distance increasing with the length of pattern used and with the number of stimuli pooled, and that for sections shorter than five fixations the within-autism variability exceeds the between-group difference. Ranking all 82 stimuli by discriminative power put facial images first (499.59), then synthetic patterns (443.60), social scenarios (366.48) and animated characters (356.27), and showed that a well-chosen 60-image subset loses no accuracy while a random 60 loses considerably. Subgroup analysis found higher error rates in boys, lowest sensitivity in 5-6 year olds - attributed to rehabilitation training having taught them to attend to social information - and lowest specificity in 3-4 year olds, attributed to younger children failing to sustain attention and producing meaningless fixations on the grey mask. | The main text never states how autism was diagnosed in the 140 autistic children or how typical development was established in the 193 others, so the quantity predicted with 96.73% accuracy is undefined - a gap made more conspicuous by Table IV, which tabulates comparator studies' diagnostic instruments while leaving the study's own blank. The groups differ by 17 percentage points in the proportion of boys, unmatched and unmentioned, in a paper that separately reports higher error rates in boys. No cognitive, developmental or severity measure exists, so an autism-specific viewing signature cannot be separated from a general attentional or developmental one - and the authors' own explanation of why specificity is lowest in 3-4 year olds, that younger children cannot stay engaged and produce meaningless grey-mask fixations, shows the two are confusable, since grey-mask drift is one of the three factors they identify as driving model scores. The Otsu decision threshold is computed on subject scores from training and test subjects together, so the operating point is chosen with sight of the test distribution and would be unavailable in the sequential-arrival deployment the paper envisages. Network size, epoch count, batch size, learning rate, the minLength lower bound and the 60-stimulus shortened protocol were all selected by comparison on the evaluation data with no development set. No majority-class baseline (57.6%), confidence interval, or prevalence-adjusted predictive value is reported despite the paper proposing population-scale screening. And the finding that sensitivity falls in children who have received rehabilitation training - reported candidly, and prompting the statement that the model suits children who have not been trained - indicates that the measured signal is modifiable by intervention, which bears on what the proposed AI-marker represents. | The most computationally careful study charted in this review to date, and the one that most directly confronts the corpus's structural weaknesses. Four contributions matter for the synthesis. Its sample of 333 children across multiple hospitals and schools in two provinces is by a wide margin the largest and most site-diverse here, and the paper makes an explicit methodological argument from it, showing through visualisation that group separability degrades as subjects accumulate and stating that 'when the number of subjects is less than 100, the test cannot accurately reflect the performance of the model' - an indictment of much of the surrounding literature that a study of this size is entitled to deliver. Its time-delay embedding analysis is unique in the corpus for treating separability as a quantity to be measured rather than assumed, and yields a specific and transferable finding: with short gaze sections the within-autism variability exceeds the between-group difference, so classification requires pooling temporal and stimulus context. That reframes multi-stimulus aggregation, used implicitly everywhere in this literature, as a measurable necessity rather than a convenience. Its analysis of the minLength preprocessing parameter is a model of a kind of care almost absent elsewhere: raising the minimum fixation count would improve nothing and would preferentially discard autistic children's data, because autistic children produce fewer fixations - recognition that a preprocessing threshold can interact with the very group difference it is meant to measure. And its stimulus-discriminability ranking, showing that 60 well-chosen images match the full 82 while 60 random ones do not, is a concrete contribution to protocol design. Two findings should be carried into the discussion as cautions rather than results. Sensitivity is lowest in 5-6 year olds who had undergone rehabilitation training, so the signal is erased by intervention; specificity is lowest in 3-4 year olds who could not sustain attention, so the signal is mimicked by ordinary disengagement. Together with the fact that drift to the blank grey mask is one of three named drivers of the model's scores, these suggest that a substantial part of what this pipeline measures is task engagement - which is genuinely informative and genuinely non-specific. Set against all of this, the paper reports a 96.73% accuracy against a target it never defines, which is the sharpest illustration in the corpus of engineering rigour outrunning clinical specification. | [RQ1.1] Two groups, with a corpus considerably larger than most in this review. Total recruited: 333 children aged 3-6, comprising 140 with autism (112 boys, 28 girls; mean age 4.66 +/- 1.00 years) and 193 typically developing (122 boys, 71 girls; mean age 4.77 +/- 0.92 years), all with normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Recruitment was multi-centre, from several hospitals and schools across Shaanxi and Fujian provinces. The evaluation set is 165 subjects - 70 autistic and 95 typically developing - formed by a 50% subject-level random split, with robustness checked over five permutations. The paper explicitly frames sample size as a methodological argument rather than a logistical fact: Fig. 14(a) visualises how group separability degrades as more subjects are added, and the discussion states that 'when the number of subjects is less than 100, the test cannot accurately reflect the performance of the model' - a direct criticism of the small-sample studies that dominate this corpus, and one this study is entitled to make. A second unit of analysis exists and is handled correctly: each child contributes 82 stimulus-based viewing patterns, and these are scored individually before being aggregated to a subject-level decision, but the split is by child so the 82 patterns never straddle training and test. [RQ1.2] 'Children with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD) children' are the working terms, used consistently and person-first. But the surrounding framing is the most burden-oriented in this corpus. The introduction states that 'most patients diagnosed with ASD cannot independently live, study and work when they grow up, which places a heavy burden on their families and society', and autistic children are referred to throughout as 'patients' - including in the abstract, where the aim is 'to screen patients with ASD'. Early intervention is motivated by 'reducing the harm caused by the disorder'. Elsewhere the vocabulary is that of deviation from a norm: 'atypical performance', 'abnormalities in ASD', 'abnormal distribution values', and children whose viewing is 'passive in the information exploration process'. Set against this, the study's practical orientation is genuinely equity-driven and its design is respectful of children in a way several others here are not - six minutes of passive viewing, no instructions, no restraint, mother present, stimuli chosen partly to hold attention. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. One passage complicates the picture in an interesting way: the finding that 5-6 year olds who had undergone rehabilitation training scored lower and were more often missed is reported neutrally as a limitation of the model, without remarking that it implies the measured signal is modifiable by intervention - which is a substantive point about what the 'AI-marker' is actually marking. [RQ1.3] Reported: group sizes, sex counts and mean and standard deviation of age for both groups, plus normal or corrected vision as the only participant criterion. Age is well matched (4.66 +/- 1.00 versus 4.77 +/- 0.92). Sex is not: the autistic group is 80.0% male (112 of 140) and the comparison group 63.2% male (122 of 193), a difference of nearly 17 percentage points that is neither tested, matched, adjusted nor mentioned. This omission is more consequential here than in most studies because the paper's own subgroup analysis reports that 'the groups of boys presented higher error rates than the groups of girls' - so sex is demonstrably related to model performance and is also unequally distributed between the classes. Not reported at all: IQ or developmental level, language ability, socioeconomic status, comorbidity, medication, and any autism severity measure. Recruitment sites are described qualitatively as areas 'where medical conditions are relatively poor', which is the closest the paper comes to a socioeconomic characterisation and is offered as a strength of external validity rather than as a demographic variable. The absence of any cognitive measure is a real limitation for a passive-viewing task in 3-6 year olds, since the capacity to sit still and attend to a screen for six minutes varies sharply with developmental level - and the paper's own analysis of why specificity is lowest in the youngest children turns on exactly that capacity. [RQ1.4] Not described. This is the study's most serious reporting gap and it sits oddly alongside the sophistication of everything else. The Data Acquisition section states only that 140 children with autism and 193 typically developing children were recruited and that all had normal or corrected vision; no diagnostic instrument, no DSM or ICD criteria, no clinician, no assessment procedure and no diagnostic date appears anywhere in the main text for either group. Two clinical co-authors are affiliated with the Children Healthcare Department of the Affiliated Hospital of Northwest University and the Children Rehabilitation Center of Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital, so clinical diagnosis is clearly implied, and the multi-centre recruitment from hospitals suggests service-identified children - but none of this is stated. The irony is sharpened by Table IV, in which the authors tabulate the diagnostic instruments used by comparator studies in the literature - Autism Behaviour Checklist, M-CHAT, ADOS, ADI-R - as a characteristic worth reporting, while leaving their own blank. Typically developing status rests on school recruitment with no screening instrument reported. Supplementary material was not retrieved and may contain more; on the main text alone, the quantity the model predicts with 96.73% accuracy is not defined. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, developmental, language, adaptive or severity measure was administered to any of the 333 children, and no autism severity score of any kind is reported. Three consequences follow that the paper does not address. First, the autistic sample cannot be positioned on the spectrum, so it is unknown whether the model's performance would hold in a less clearly affected group - a particular concern given that the discussion itself observes that adding subjects makes 'more unclear and atypical cases' appear. Second, the paradigm demands six minutes of sustained attention to a screen from 3-6 year olds, and the ability to comply is developmentally graded; without a cognitive measure it is impossible to separate an autism-specific viewing signature from a general attentional or developmental one, and the authors' own explanation of why specificity is lowest in 3-4 year olds - younger children 'find it difficult to focus on the screen the entire time, resulting in meaningless fixations that fall on the gray mask' - shows that this is not hypothetical. Third, the conclusion proposes that dynamic viewing patterns 'can also be employed to quantitatively assess subjects' ASD risk', but with no severity instrument in the study there is nothing against which such a continuous risk score could be calibrated or validated. [RQ2.1] The goal is explicitly infrastructural rather than merely methodological: to build a screening method that works where the constraints are affordability, child-friendliness and the absence of professionals, which the authors identify as the three barriers to autism screening in remote areas. The technical contribution is the dynamic viewing pattern - gaze treated as an ordered trajectory over both viewing time and the stimulus set, rather than as a static distribution of fixations - together with a pipeline that encodes each fixation semantically via an autoencoder, scores each stimulus sequence with an LSTM, and aggregates 82 stimulus scores into a subject decision. Findings: subject-level accuracy 96.73% with sensitivity 96.85% and specificity 96.63% on 165 test children, stable above 95.76% across five random subject-level splits. The supporting analyses are more informative than the headline. Conventional hand-crafted features reproduce the expected group differences - autistic children make fewer fixations with longer saccades, look less at faces and other salient objects, take longer to notice them, and dwell more on background and on the grey mask - but the authors state plainly that these differences are 'not sufficiently significant to directly use these hand-crafted features for classification'. A time-delay embedding analysis then shows that between-group distance grows with the length of the pattern section used and with the number of stimuli included, and that for sections shorter than five fixations the within-autism variability exceeds the between-group difference - a quantitative argument that separability is manufactured by using more temporal and more stimulus context, not merely asserted. Ablation confirms both feature families contribute (semantic 94.85%, low-level 93.33%, combined 96.73%) and that sequence modelling beats fixation-histogram and stacked-fixation baselines. [RQ2.2] Multi-centre, and deliberately so: children were recruited from multiple hospitals and schools in Shaanxi and Fujian provinces, chosen because 'medical conditions are relatively poor' there. This is one of only a few studies in this corpus with genuine site diversity, and the framing is consistent throughout - the paper's entire motivation is that screening in remote and low-income areas is understudied, and the design constraints follow from that premise rather than being retrofitted to it. Recording took place in a therapy room with the child 0.5 m from the monitor and at most two other people present, the mother and one researcher, which is a realistic community-clinic arrangement rather than a laboratory. The counterweight is the usual one: recruitment pairs hospital- or rehabilitation-identified autistic children against school-recruited comparison children at 42% prevalence, so the geometry remains case-control and the accuracy does not transfer to a community screening population. The authors do not compute what their operating point would mean at population prevalence, which for a proposed universal screening tool is the omission that matters most. [RQ2.3] Passive free viewing of 82 static images, presented in two sessions of roughly three minutes each with each image shown for 3 s and a 0.5 s grey mask between images, with the only instruction being to observe. Four stimulus categories were chosen 'according to the behavioural characteristics of children with ASD': facial images, social scenarios, animated characters and synthetic patterns. Three properties make this among the better-designed paradigms in the corpus. It is short and undemanding by explicit design, because the authors treat children's limited sustained attention as a constraint on the method rather than as a nuisance. It varies stimulus type systematically, which permits the study's most practically useful analysis - a ranking of all 82 images by discriminative power, showing facial images strongest (499.59) and animated characters weakest (356.27), and demonstrating that dropping to the best 60 images costs no accuracy while dropping to a random 60 costs a great deal. That result is a concrete contribution to protocol design that most eye-tracking studies here are not positioned to make. And the grey mask, introduced as a simple inter-stimulus interval, turns out to carry signal, since fixations landing on it are one of the three factors the authors identify as driving model scores. That last point is also the paradigm's weakness: dwelling on a blank grey screen is at least as much a measure of disengagement from the task as of atypical social attention, and the paper's own observation that 3-4 year olds in the comparison group generate 'meaningless fixations that fall on the gray mask' concedes that the same behaviour arises from ordinary inattention. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, and no test-retest reliability - which is a real gap for a tool proposed for repeated community screening. The nearest thing to a temporal analysis is Fig. 8, which tracks how the sample and the classification results evolved across the four quarters of 2021, showing 2-4 misclassified cases in an initial 40-child phase and stable results thereafter; this is a development log rather than a validation, but it is unusually transparent about how the model matured alongside the dataset. Ethics reporting is complete for approval and thin for consent: the study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Northwestern Polytechnical University under protocol 202002032, with all procedures conducted in accordance with the latest revision of the Declaration of Helsinki - a named committee and a protocol number, better than most reports here - but no parental consent or child assent statement appears, despite the participants being 3-6 year olds. Funding from three National Natural Science Foundation of China grants is itemised. No competing-interests statement appears. [RQ2.5] A SciEye 2.0 eye tracker sampling at 140 Hz, using infrared illumination with corneal and retinal reflection, feeding a 1920 x 1080 monitor on which 1040 x 780 images were centred; the child sat 0.5 m away. The device's own preprocessing is specified numerically and is a genuine reporting strength: gaze points separated by less than 0.02 in normalised coordinates were merged, and merged points shorter than 0.1 s deleted, to suppress noise. No calibration procedure is described, which is the notable gap in an otherwise well-specified acquisition chain. On the analysis side: SLIC superpixel segmentation, a deep autoencoder trained layer-wise then fine-tuned globally with a cross-entropy reconstruction loss on 10,000 MS COCO images, and an LSTM with fully connected and regression heads trained by backpropagation through time, with the full gate equations reproduced. Otsu's maximum between-class variance method supplies the decision thresholds. Two baselines were reimplemented for comparison rather than merely cited - a fixation-count histogram with SVM, and stacked deep features of up to 10 fixations with SVM - which is more effort than most papers here expend on their comparators. Software frameworks and hardware for training are not named. [RQ2.6] Strong on method, absent on artefacts, with an unusual amount of parameter transparency. Reproducible from the text: the complete stimulus protocol including image count, categories, display and mask durations, session structure and viewing distance; the eye tracker, its sampling rate and its exact noise-suppression rule; the superpixel step; the autoencoder's external training corpus, loss function and two-stage training strategy; the full LSTM equations; the feature concatenation; the weak-supervision label assignment; the aggregation and Otsu thresholding; and a sensitivity table spanning hidden units, fully connected size, epochs, mini-batch size, learning rate and the minLength lower bound. The finding that the resized superpixel bounding box outperforms a centred patch is reported as a negative result, which is rare and useful. Not available: code, data, the 82-image stimulus set, the specific final architecture dimensions, and - most importantly - the diagnostic procedure that generated the labels. Ten supplementary figures and three supplementary tables exist but were not retrieved. As an IEEE TBME paper the reporting standard is engineering-first, which shows in the asymmetry between an exhaustively specified pipeline and an unspecified clinical protocol. [RQ2.7] The stated limitations are concrete and unusually specific about failure modes: the model is trained only on 3-6 year olds and applies only there; natural scenes with small between-group differences and few training examples are hard; small objects defeat the semantic encoder; and images with objects near the edge cause false positives because typically developing children's exploratory fixations also land on the grey mask. Two further constraints appear as subgroup findings rather than caveats and are more interesting than either: sensitivity is lowest in 5-6 year olds because some had undergone rehabilitation training teaching them to attend to social information, prompting the statement that 'the model is more suitable for the initial screening of children who have not undergone rehabilitation training'; and specificity is lowest in 3-4 year olds because they cannot sustain attention to the screen. Taken together these say that the measured signal is erased by intervention at one end of the age range and mimicked by ordinary inattention at the other, which bears directly on what the proposed 'AI-marker' represents - a point the paper reports but does not draw out. The unstated limitations are led by the absence of any described diagnostic reference standard, without which the target of a 96.73% accuracy is undefined. Others: sex is imbalanced between groups by 17 percentage points and never mentioned, despite the paper's own finding that error rates differ by sex; the Otsu decision threshold is fitted on training and test scores together, so the operating point is chosen with sight of the test distribution; architecture, learning parameters and the minLength value were compared on the evaluation data with no separate development set; the stimulus-discriminability ranking used to justify a shortened protocol is derived from the same data on which accuracy is reported; there is no majority-class baseline (57.6%) or confidence interval; and no prevalence-adjusted metric is offered despite the paper proposing population-scale screening. [RQ2.9] Four directions, all substantive. Collect data from other age bands both to extend the model beyond 3-6 years and to characterise how dynamic viewing patterns change developmentally. Investigate diversity and individuality within the autistic group through subcategory classification and, notably, through explicit comparison of children who have and have not undergone rehabilitation training - which would convert the study's incidental finding about trained attention into a proper analysis. Predict stimulus discriminability directly with deep models, so that screening image sets can be designed rather than curated, building on the study's own demonstration that 60 well-chosen images match the full 82 while 60 random ones do not. And fuse gaze with fMRI, EEG, facial expression and observation-scale scores, described as an important and understudied challenge. What is missing from the list is the step that would matter most for the stated purpose: prospective evaluation in an unselected community population at realistic prevalence, with a described diagnostic reference standard. [RQ3.1] Visual attention during passive free viewing, reconceived as a temporally ordered process rather than a spatial distribution. The paper's construct - the dynamic viewing pattern - encompasses where each fixation lands, in what order, for how long, and with what saccade amplitude and direction connecting it to the next, across all 82 stimuli. The descriptive analysis identifies the component behaviours: autistic children make fewer fixations with larger saccade amplitudes; they fixate faces less than typically developing children, with the largest between-group difference of any region appearing in facial areas; they fixate other salient objects less across food, animals, toys, gazed objects and touched objects; they are slower to notice most object types; and they spend more time on background regions and on the inter-stimulus grey mask. The mechanistic account offered is information-theoretic rather than social-motivational: typically developing children are described as fixating regions of continuous salient information under an information-maximisation principle, while autistic children are 'passive in the information exploration process'. The temporal analysis locates the difference at the extremes of each trial - autistic children's first fixation is often random or outside the image while typically developing children's lands near salient objects, the middle of the trial shows convergence, and the final stage diverges again as autistic children drift to non-salient background. One measured behaviour deserves separate flagging because the authors identify it as a top-three driver of model scores: whether the fixation pattern stays on the image or moves to the grey mask. This is as much a measure of task engagement as of visual preference, and the paper's own age analysis shows the same behaviour arising in typically developing 3-4 year olds from ordinary inattention. [RQ3.2] No cross-sensor fusion - a single eye tracker - but two feature families are combined within the modality and their contributions are separately quantified, which is more than most multimodal papers here achieve. The semantic stream encodes what the child is looking at, by locating each fixation in a SLIC superpixel and passing that region through an autoencoder pretrained on MS COCO to yield a compressed code; the low-level stream encodes the mechanics of looking - position, duration, saccade amplitude and saccade orientation. The ablation is clean and reported in the discussion: semantic features alone give 94.85% accuracy with 97.14% sensitivity and 93.16% specificity, low-level features alone 93.33% with 90.71% and 95.26%, and the combination 96.73% with 96.85% and 96.63%. The two are therefore complementary in a specific and interpretable way - semantic content drives sensitivity while movement mechanics drive specificity - and combining them raises both rather than trading one against the other. That is a more informative fusion result than the usual report of a single accuracy gain. A second, structural form of integration operates at the stimulus level: 82 per-stimulus scores are aggregated into one subject decision, and the paper shows both that individual stimulus scores are unreliable (Fig. 9(a) shows typically developing children scoring high on particular images) and that between-group separation grows with the number of stimuli pooled, so multi-scene aggregation is doing work analogous to multimodal fusion. On genuine cross-modality, the authors list fMRI, EEG, facial expression and observation-scale scores as future work and describe the problem of relating data across modalities as important and understudied. [RQ4.1] A three-stage deep pipeline with an unsupervised front end, a weakly supervised middle and an unsupervised decision rule. Stage one is a deep autoencoder used purely as a nonlinear dimensionality reducer, trained layer-wise then fine-tuned globally with cross-entropy reconstruction loss on 10,000 MS COCO images - so the semantic encoder never sees participant data, which is a clean separation and removes one potential leakage path. Stage two is an LSTM over the per-fixation feature sequence for each stimulus, chosen for its capacity to model sequential dependence and to avoid the vanishing-gradient problems of plain recurrent networks, ending in a fully connected layer and a single-neuron regression head that scores the pattern. Stage three aggregates the 82 stimulus scores into a subject average and binarises it with Otsu's maximum between-class variance threshold. The weak supervision is explicit and correctly reasoned: the authors note that an autistic child's viewing will be atypical on only some stimuli but that labels for which specific stimuli are unavailable, so each child's diagnostic label is propagated to all 82 of their patterns and the aggregation step is relied upon to recover the subject-level decision from noisy per-stimulus targets. This is the appropriate formulation for the problem and is stated as such rather than adopted implicitly. Two baselines are reimplemented for comparison - a fixation-count histogram with SVM and stacked deep features of up to 10 fixations with SVM - and both underperform, which is the study's evidence that sequence structure, not merely deep features, carries the signal. [RQ4.2] Per fixation: a c-bit semantic code obtained by locating the fixation's SLIC superpixel, resizing that superpixel's bounding box to d x d and passing it through the pretrained autoencoder, concatenated with four low-level descriptors - normalised position, duration, saccade amplitude and saccade orientation. A viewing pattern of m+1 fixations on one stimulus becomes a length-m sequence of these vectors, and each child yields 82 such sequences. The defining property is that no aggregation precedes the model: sequences enter the LSTM in their original order and length, in deliberate contrast to the histogram baseline (which discards order entirely) and the stacked-feature baseline (which fixes the fixation count at 10 by zero-padding or truncation). The authors' analysis of the minLength parameter is a good illustration of how carefully this was handled - raising the minimum sequence length from 2 to 4 fixations improves nothing and causes 'significant data loss in the ASD group', because autistic children produce fewer fixations, so filtering by pattern length would systematically discard the very participants the model must detect. Recognising that a preprocessing threshold interacts with the group difference it is meant to measure is a subtlety absent from most of this corpus. One reported negative result adds to the representation's credibility: using a fixed patch at each superpixel's centre performed worse than the resized full bounding box. [RQ4.3] Accuracy at two levels of aggregation (A1 for stimulus-based patterns, A2 for subjects), sensitivity, specificity, ROC analysis and AUC, with results additionally broken down by sex and by age band and by ablation condition. Reporting sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy is the minimum this literature should meet and is met here; adding subgroup breakdowns, and reporting them honestly when they are unflattering, goes beyond it. Robustness is addressed by repeating the subject-level split five times and reporting the minimum (95.76%) rather than only the mean. What is missing: confidence intervals; a majority-class baseline, which at 42.4% autism in the test set would be 57.6%; and any prevalence-adjusted metric such as positive predictive value, which is the number that matters for the community-screening application the paper proposes. At a population prevalence near 1-2%, sensitivity 96.85% with specificity 96.63% would yield a positive predictive value in the range of roughly 22-37% - far better than most operating points in this corpus, and a calculation the paper would have benefited from making explicit given how strongly it frames itself as a universal screening tool. The 82 stimulus-level scores are also not independent within a child, which affects the interpretation of A1 though not of A2. [RQ4.4] The paper does substantial interpretive work, but almost none of it is attribution on the trained model. Three strands. First, an extensive pre-modelling descriptive analysis with low-level and semantic gaze features, region-of-interest labelling, first-fixation timing and object-category breakdowns, which establishes the expected group differences and then concludes candidly that they are 'not sufficiently significant to directly use these hand-crafted features for classification' - an honest admission that the interpretable features do not do the work. Second, and most distinctive, a quantitative analysis of separability itself using time-delay embedding to compute Hausdorff and mean-minimal distances, showing how between-group distance and within-group variability change as a function of how much temporal context and how many stimuli are used. The finding that with pattern sections shorter than five fixations the within-autism variability exceeds the between-group difference is a genuinely useful result about the structure of the problem, and it turns the paper's architectural choices into consequences of measurement rather than assertions. Third, qualitative inspection of model scores, from which three drivers are named: whether the pattern stays on the image or drifts to the grey mask, whether fixations on salient objects are missing, and whether fixation order and duration are reasonable - each illustrated with worked successful and failed cases against the two baselines. The gap is that no attribution method is applied to the LSTM: there is no saliency analysis, no gate inspection, no per-fixation contribution, and no way to say for an individual child which of their 82 patterns or which fixations produced their score. For a system proposed as an aid to non-specialists in remote clinics, per-child explanation is exactly what would be needed, and the paper's own emphasis on an 'AI-marker' makes its absence more noticeable. [RQ4.5] Among the stronger validation designs in this corpus at the level of splitting, with two specific weaknesses further down the pipeline. The split unit is the subject: 50% of the 333 children are held out, so all 82 stimulus-based patterns from a child stay together and within-child leakage is structurally impossible - which matters here more than usual, because the model scores individual stimuli and a naive pattern-level split would have placed 41 of each test child's own patterns in training. The procedure is repeated over five random permutations with the minimum reported (95.76%), addressing split-assignment variance. The semantic autoencoder is trained on MS COCO rather than on participant data, so the representation learning introduces no leakage. Two ablation baselines are implemented on the same data rather than cited from other papers. Against this: first, the decision threshold is fitted transductively. The paper states that subject average scores were computed 'for each subject in training and testing' and the Otsu maximum between-class variance threshold selected on that combined distribution, and the same is described for the stimulus-level threshold. Otsu does not use labels, so this is not label leakage, but the operating point is nonetheless chosen with sight of the test subjects' score distribution, and in a deployment where children arrive one at a time no such distribution exists - the threshold would have to be fixed in advance from training data alone, and no result is reported under that constraint. Second, several choices were compared on the evaluation data with no separate development set: LSTM hidden units and fully connected size, epoch count, mini-batch size, learning rate, and the minLength lower bound, all reported in a single results table with the best configuration carried forward. The stimulus-discriminability ranking used to argue that 60 images suffice was likewise computed on the same data, so the proposed shortened protocol is selected in-sample. Third, no majority-class floor (57.6%) or confidence interval is given. None of these undermine the subject-level split, which is the hard part and is done correctly; they mean the 96.73% is a mildly optimistic estimate under a transductively chosen threshold rather than a fully prospective one. [RQ5.1] Index terms: Autism spectrum disorder, deep autoencoder, deep learning, dynamic viewing patterns, long short-term memory (LSTM) network. Four of the five are architectural or methodological, and the one novel construct - dynamic viewing patterns - is the paper's own coinage, which the abstract, title and body use consistently as a named attribute (abbreviated DVP throughout). Terms carried through the body: weakly supervised learning, between-group and intra-class difference, time-delay embedding, Hausdorff distance, superpixel, semantic hashing code, maximum between-class variance, AI-marker, scalable screening, medical cloud service centers. Neither 'diagnosis' nor 'classification' appears among the index terms despite both being performed, and 'screening' appears only in the title. [RQ5.2] IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering 70(5):1622-1632, May 2023 - a high-profile biomedical engineering journal, submitted 17 June 2022, revised 15 October 2022, accepted 14 November 2022, published online 21 November 2022. The venue accounts for the paper's characteristic asymmetry: the signal-processing and machine-learning pipeline is specified to a standard that would permit reimplementation, complete with LSTM gate equations, a parameter sensitivity table, reimplemented baselines, ablations and a reported negative result, while the clinical apparatus that generated the labels is not described at all. Supplementary material comprising ten figures and three tables is hosted by the publisher. The paper adopts the journal's structured abstract format (Objective, Methods, Results, Conclusion, Significance), which is unusual in this corpus and enforces an explicit statement of clinical significance. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 by Northwestern Polytechnical University's School of Automation with the Institute of Artificial Intelligence at the Hefei Comprehensive National Science Center, in collaboration with the Children Healthcare Department of the Affiliated Hospital of Northwest University, the Children Rehabilitation Center of Shaanxi Rehabilitation Hospital, Beijing University of Chinese Medicine and Nanchang University - a broad engineering-clinical consortium, funded by three National Natural Science Foundation of China grants. The framing is health-equity infrastructure and is stated with more precision than most: the introduction identifies three specific barriers to screening in remote areas - affordability, child-friendliness and the availability of professionals - and every subsequent design choice is justified against one of them, including the explicit contrast with fMRI as an unaffordable alternative and the proposal that storage and analysis run on a cloud computing centre. The prevalence trajectory is cited precisely (1/68 in 2014, 1/59 in 2018, 1/44 in 2021 per US CDC), with the claim that developing-country prevalence is comparable. Two aspects of the positioning are notable for the synthesis. The paper explicitly criticises the small-sample norm in this literature, arguing from its own visualisation that 'when the number of subjects is less than 100, the test cannot accurately reflect the performance of the model' - a methodological argument that a 333-child multi-site study is entitled to make and that indicts much of the surrounding corpus. And the burden framing in the opening paragraph ('most patients diagnosed with ASD cannot independently live, study and work when they grow up, which places a heavy burden on their families and society') is the starkest deficit language encountered in this review, sitting uncomfortably beside an otherwise child-centred and access-oriented design. |
| S-102 | Retrospective classification study on scraped social-media text, conducted at Universidad de Leon, Spain. Two hundred and fifty-two public Twitter accounts were assembled: 221 whose biography states that the user is autistic, found by manually searching for the keywords 'Autism', 'ASD', 'Asperger', 'Aspie', 'Autistic' and 'ActuallyAutistic' and then reviewing each profile by hand to exclude organisations, self-described 'ASD advocates' and family members using phrases such as 'father of an ASD kid'; and 31 comparison accounts whose selection is never described. No user was recruited, contacted or aware of the study, and no demographic, cognitive, language or severity information exists for anyone. Tweets from 1 January 2017 to 31 January 2022 were harvested through the Twitter developer API, yielding 1,014,723 posts, reduced to 404,627 after removing duplicates, retweets, incompletely extracted tweets and cross-platform auto-posts, and subsampled to a balanced 90,000 with 45,000 per class - which means each of the 31 comparison users contributes about 1,450 modelled tweets against about 200 per autistic user. No ethics approval, ethics committee or consent is reported anywhere in the paper. | Each tweet was classified independently, with the user's biography-derived label propagated automatically to all of their posts. Four models were compared: a decision tree (max depth 9, min samples leaf 2, min samples split 4), XGBoost (colsample_bytree 0.8, gamma 5, max depth 5, min child weight 1, subsample 0.8), k-nearest neighbours with k = 1, and BERT-base-multilingual-cased. Hyperparameters for the three classical models were selected by GridSearchCV; BERT was deliberately left at defaults in order to test whether an untuned deep model would beat tuned classical ones. The text representation supplied to the classical models is not described anywhere. Evaluation used a single random 75/25 split over the 90,000 tweets - the unit is the tweet, not the user - with no cross-validation, no repeated splits and no held-out authors. Analysis ran in Python 3.9 on a single workstation. | BERT achieved 84.3% accuracy and F1 0.84 (tp 9,252, fp 1,515, tn 9,715, fn 2,018), corresponding to sensitivity 82.1% and specificity 86.5%. XGBoost reached 71.6% and F1 0.74, the decision tree 61.2% and F1 0.72, and k-nearest neighbours 60.8% and F1 0.67. The published confusion matrices show more than the headline figures: the decision tree recorded 11,229 true positives against just 41 false negatives, meaning it assigned nearly every tweet to the autistic class, giving 99.6% sensitivity at 22.6% specificity - near-degenerate behaviour that its accuracy and F1 conceal. The authors present the untuned BERT beating the tuned classical models as the paper's principal finding and describe it as 'quite astonishing'. No user-level result, confidence interval, chance baseline or feature analysis of any kind is reported for any model. | The 90,000 tweets were split at random by tweet rather than by author, so every writer in the test set has the great majority of their own posts in training. For the negative class this is extreme: 31 people supply all 45,000 non-autistic tweets, roughly 1,090 of each user's posts sitting in training alongside the 360 used to test them, so a transformer that simply learned to recognise 31 individual writing styles would score very well while learning nothing about autism. No estimate of performance on an unseen writer exists. Separately, the positive class was assembled by searching biographies for autism keywords, no autism-related vocabulary was removed from the tweets, and no topic analysis or feature inspection of any kind was performed - so the classifier may be detecting subject matter rather than communication style, and nothing in the paper can distinguish the two. The label is unverified self-disclosure with no clinical component; the 31 comparison users are undescribed, unmatched and unscreened for undisclosed autism; no demographic data exist; hyperparameters were grid-searched without a validation set separate from the test data; no user-level metric is reported although per-user aggregation is the only form in which such a system could be applied; and a paper titled 'Early Detection', motivated in its introduction by identifying children before the age of three, is trained entirely on adult social-media users. Finally, there is no ethics approval, no consent and no discussion of the ethics of building an autism classifier from identifiable individuals' public health disclosures. | The only study in this review whose modality is written language and whose data are entirely naturalistic and self-initiated, which makes it worth charting despite its weaknesses: social-media text is ecologically valid in a way no laboratory task is, longitudinal by default, and essentially free to collect at scale, and the authors are right that it is under-explored relative to imaging and eye tracking. It is also the corpus's clearest illustration of two failure modes that appear elsewhere in milder form. The first is unit-of-analysis leakage taken to its limit: where other studies here split segments or trials within participants, this one splits tweets within a negative class of 31 people, so the model's most efficient route to high accuracy is author recognition. It is the study that most sharply demonstrates why the split unit, not the sample size, governs what an accuracy figure means - 22,500 test tweets confer no more generalisation evidence than 252 writers would, and rather less, since none of those writers is new. The second is proxy-label drift: the quantity actually predicted is whether an account's biography contains an autism keyword, and because the keyword search that defined the positive class also selects for people who write about autism, topic and label cannot be separated by anything reported. Two further points belong in the discussion. The terminological contradiction is instructive: the study takes its ground truth from #ActuallyAutistic, a hashtag the autistic community coined specifically to assert its own voice and to reject pathologising framing, and then reports on the people who wrote it as 'ASD patients' who 'suffer from ASD'. And it is the only included study that builds a health classifier from identifiable individuals' unwitting public disclosures with no ethics approval, no consent and no discussion of either - which, for a review that must say something about how this technology should be developed, is the more important observation of the two. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of Twitter accounts rather than of assessed people: 221 users whose public biography states that they are autistic and 31 users who do not, totalling 252. The imbalance is severe and consequential. Because the modelled dataset was balanced at the tweet level - 45,000 per class from a cleaned pool of 404,627 - each of the 31 comparison users contributes on average about 1,450 tweets while each of the 221 autistic users contributes about 200, a sevenfold difference in per-user concentration. The entire negative class is therefore the writing of 31 individuals. No user was recruited, contacted or aware of the study; the data are historical public posts from 1 January 2017 to 31 January 2022. Cleaning removed 60% of the raw corpus (1,014,723 to 404,627 tweets) by deleting duplicates, retweets, incompletely extracted tweets and cross-platform auto-posts, which is a substantial and appropriately reported reduction, though it is not broken down by user or by group. [RQ1.2] The terminology is the most internally contradictory in this corpus, and the contradiction is instructive. The search keywords include 'ActuallyAutistic' and 'Aspie' - terms coined and used by autistic people themselves, the first being an identity hashtag that exists precisely to distinguish autistic voices from those speaking about autism, and one that carries an explicit rejection of pathologising language. The paper harvests those self-identifications and then describes the people who wrote them as 'ASD patients', as 'individuals who suffer from ASD', and as 'people that suffer from ASD'; the comparison group is 'people that do not suffer from ASD'. Autism is 'a developmental disability' that 'affects the social and interactive skills of those who have it', which 'appears before the age of three and can last a lifetime'. The framing of value is entirely deficit-and-outcome: 'people who are not diagnosed in childhood have a poorer quality of life'. So the study takes its ground truth from a community that names itself in one register and reports its findings in the opposite one, without noticing. There is no neurodiversity framing, no autistic-community involvement, and no acknowledgement that the data subjects are a self-organised community with stated views about how they are described - or about being classified by algorithms trained on their own posts. [RQ1.3] None whatsoever. No age, sex, race or ethnicity, socioeconomic status, education, nationality, language background, comorbidity or medication is available for any of the 252 users in either group, and none is estimated or discussed. Three consequences follow. First, the sample is necessarily adolescents and adults, since Twitter requires account holders to be at least 13 - which sits at odds with a paper titled 'Early Detection' and motivated in its opening pages entirely by the value of diagnosing children before the age of three, a mismatch the text never addresses. Second, no matching of any kind was possible between the 221 autistic and 31 comparison users, and none was attempted, so any demographic difference between the groups - in age, sex, nationality, education, topic interests, or how much they tweet - is fully confounded with the label. Third, the only English-language requirement is stated for the tweets, but the chosen model is BERT-base-multilingual-cased, a multilingual checkpoint, which suggests the corpus may not be uniformly English. The one participant characteristic that is described in detail is not demographic but procedural: the manual exclusion of organisational accounts, self-described advocates and family members from the autistic group, which is careful work and is the paper's strongest methodological passage. [RQ1.4] Self-disclosure in a public social-media biography, with no clinical component of any kind. Users were located by keyword search over biographies for 'Autism', 'ASD', 'Asperger', 'Aspie', 'Autistic' and 'ActuallyAutistic', and each candidate profile was then reviewed by hand and discarded if it belonged to an organisation or society, to someone describing themselves as an 'ASD advocate', or to a family member using phrasing such as 'father of an ASD kid' or 'mother of an ASD kid'. That filtering is thoughtful, is described in enough detail to repeat, and removes the most obvious sources of false positives - it is the best-executed part of the study. What it cannot do is establish that anyone is autistic. There is no diagnosis, no instrument, no criterion, no date and no verification, and the authors themselves note that biographies may contain false information and that tweets may be written by someone other than the account holder. The comparison label is weaker still and is not described at all: the paper never states how the 31 non-autistic users were found or chosen, whether they were sampled at random or selected for any property, or whether any effort was made to exclude autistic people who simply do not disclose - which, given that undiagnosed and undisclosed autism is common, means the negative class is defined by the absence of a public statement rather than by the absence of the condition. What the models therefore predict is whether a tweet came from an account whose biography contains an autism keyword. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure exists, and none could exist given the data source. This matters more than in most studies here because language is the entire modality: a paper classifying people by their writing reports no lexical, syntactic, readability or pragmatic measure of that writing, and no characterisation of how the two corpora differ. Severity appears only in the introduction, where Asperger syndrome is described as 'the one that is labelled as severity 1' and is included among the search keywords, but no severity information is extracted, used or reported. The absence has a specific analytical cost: because self-disclosure of autism on social media is likely to be associated with particular parts of the spectrum - verbally fluent, self-aware, digitally engaged, often diagnosed later in life - the sample is drawn from a narrow and self-selected slice of the autistic population, and nothing in the study characterises which slice. [RQ2.1] The stated objective is to build models 'capable of diagnosing ASD through the analysis of texts posted by users who disclose their condition in their biographies', motivated by the scarcity of specialists and the value of early diagnosis. Three contributions are claimed: a new Twitter dataset of 404,627 tweets from 252 users of whom 221 disclose autism; application of several machine-learning techniques to build predictive models; and comparison of classical machine learning against deep learning. Findings: BERT-base-multilingual-cased, used untuned, reached 84.3% accuracy and F1 0.84, outperforming XGBoost at 71.6% (F1 0.74), decision trees at 61.2% (F1 0.72) and k-nearest neighbours at 60.8% (F1 0.67), all three of which were hyperparameter-tuned by grid search. The authors present this as the paper's headline - that a default deep model beats optimised classical ones - and describe the result as 'quite astonishing'. The confusion matrices they report, to their credit, reveal more than the accuracies do: the decision tree produced 11,229 true positives against just 41 false negatives, meaning it labelled nearly every tweet autistic and achieved 99.6% sensitivity at 22.6% specificity - close to a degenerate classifier, which its 61.2% accuracy and 0.72 F1 conceal. BERT's counts correspond to sensitivity 82.1% and specificity 86.5%. No user-level result is reported for any model. [RQ2.2] There is no setting in the usual sense. No participants were recruited, contacted, assessed or informed; the study consists of harvesting five years of public posts from 252 identifiable Twitter accounts through the developer API and classifying them offline. The research group is at Universidad de Leon in Spain, and the compute is a single desktop workstation. Two features of this design deserve comment for the review. It is the only study in the corpus with no acquisition protocol at all, which means it is free of every acquisition confound that troubles the video and audio studies here - no equipment differences, no examiner effects, no laboratory artificiality - and simultaneously free of every control those protocols provide, since nothing about who wrote what, when, why, or to whom is known or standardised. And it is the only study here whose data subjects are neither aware of nor consenting to their participation, on a topic they disclosed publicly about themselves, which raises governance questions the paper does not engage with at all. [RQ2.3] None. This is the only included study with no elicitation paradigm: the behavioural sample is whatever 252 people chose to post on Twitter over five years, unconstrained in topic, audience, purpose, length or timing. The consequence that matters most is topic confounding, and it goes unaddressed throughout. The autistic group was assembled by searching biographies for autism-related keywords including 'ActuallyAutistic', a hashtag whose function is to mark autistic people's own commentary on autism; people who identify that way in their profile will frequently tweet about autism, disability, sensory experience, diagnosis, accommodation and advocacy. No preprocessing step removed autism-related vocabulary from the tweets, no topic model or lexical analysis was run, and no ablation tested whether the classifier still works with such terms masked. So the most parsimonious explanation of the 84.3% figure - that BERT is detecting subject matter rather than communication style - is neither tested nor mentioned. The paper's own framing invites this reading, since its introduction speaks of identifying 'linguistic patterns, emotional expressions, and communication styles', which is a style hypothesis, while its method offers nothing that could separate style from topic. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional in analysis though the data span five years, with no temporal modelling: tweets from 2017 and 2022 are pooled and classified independently, so nothing is learned about stability or change over time, and no test-retest or within-user consistency is examined. Ethics is the study's most serious deficiency and is entirely absent. There is no institutional review board approval, no ethics committee, no research-ethics statement, no consent, and no discussion of the ethics of the enterprise. The data are health-related disclosures made by identifiable individuals about themselves, harvested without their knowledge and used to train a classifier whose stated purpose is to identify people who may be autistic. The only privacy measure described is the redaction of username, location and date of birth from two example biographies reproduced as a figure, done 'in compliance with Twitter's policies' - a platform-terms consideration rather than a research-ethics one. The paper does not consider whether the autistic Twitter community, which is organised and vocal, would regard such a classifier as acceptable; whether a model that infers autism from public text could be used against the people it identifies; or whether public availability implies availability for this purpose. Given that several of the search keywords are terms this community coined for itself, the omission is conspicuous. [RQ2.5] Data collection used a Python script against the Twitter developer API, exporting to CSV. Analysis ran in two Jupyter notebooks under Python 3.9 on a single workstation (Intel Core i7-9700K at 3.60 GHz, 32 GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080). The models are named with their selected hyperparameters - decision tree (max depth 9, min samples leaf 2, min samples split 4), XGBoost (colsample_bytree 0.8, gamma 5, max depth 5, min child weight 1, subsample 0.8), k-nearest neighbours with k = 1 - and the deep model is identified precisely as BERT-base-multilingual-cased, used without tuning by deliberate design. GridSearchCV is named as the search tool. What is conspicuously missing is the representation layer for the three classical models: the paper states that natural language processing techniques were combined with the models but never says how text became numbers - no tokenisation, no bag of words, no TF-IDF, no n-gram range, no embedding - so it is not possible to say what the decision tree, XGBoost and k-nearest neighbours were actually fitted to, which makes their comparison against BERT uninterpretable as a claim about model families. [RQ2.6] Partial, and unusually asymmetric. The data-collection procedure is described well enough to repeat in principle: the six search keywords are listed, the three manual exclusion rules (organisations, advocates, family members) are stated with examples, the four cleaning steps are enumerated, the date range is given, and the tweet counts before and after cleaning are reported. Model configuration is also specified, with selected hyperparameters for all three classical models, the exact BERT checkpoint, the split ratio and the compute hardware. Against this: how the 31 comparison users were chosen is never stated, which alone prevents reconstruction of the dataset; the text representation for the classical models is undescribed; BERT's fine-tuning regime (epochs, learning rate, batch size, maximum sequence length) is not given; no random seed is reported for a study whose single result rests on one random split; and neither code nor data is available. The data could not straightforwardly be shared in any case, since they consist of identifiable individuals' posts, which is a reason to have addressed data governance rather than a reason to omit it. [RQ2.7] The two stated limitations are correctly identified and concern label validity: users may give false information in their biographies, and tweets may be written by someone other than the account owner. Everything else is unaddressed, and several of the omissions are decisive. The split is random over 90,000 tweets, not over the 252 users, so every author in the test set has the great majority of their own tweets in training; for the comparison class this is extreme, since 31 people supply all 45,000 negative tweets, meaning roughly 1,090 of each comparison user's tweets are available to help classify their remaining 360. A model that learned to recognise 31 individual writing styles would score very well and would have learned nothing about autism. There is no control for topic, in a design where the positive class was assembled by searching for autism keywords and no autism vocabulary was removed from the text. The 31 comparison users are undescribed, unmatched and unscreened, so undisclosed autistic people may sit in the negative class and any group difference in age, nationality, profession or interests is confounded with the label. No demographic data exist. Hyperparameters were grid-searched with no separate validation set. No user-level metric is reported although per-user aggregation is the only form in which such a system could be used. And the framing gap is never acknowledged: a paper titled 'Early Detection', motivated by diagnosing children before age three, is trained entirely on adult social-media users. [RQ2.9] Two directions, both narrow: tune BERT's hyperparameters, since it was deliberately left at defaults and might improve further; and train additional deep and classical models 'to ensure that no high-performing models are overlooked'. Both extend the leaderboard rather than test the finding. The steps that would matter are absent from the list: splitting by user rather than by tweet, masking autism-related vocabulary to separate topic from style, describing and expanding the comparison group, reporting user-level performance, and obtaining any form of clinical validation for the label. So is any consideration of research ethics or of engagement with the community whose posts constitute the dataset. [RQ3.1] Written language produced spontaneously on social media - the only study in this corpus whose behavioural sample is entirely self-initiated public communication rather than behaviour elicited under a protocol. That is genuinely interesting as a modality: it is ecologically valid in a way no laboratory task can be, it is longitudinal by default (five years per user), it costs nothing to collect at scale, and it captures communication in its natural social context with real audiences and real stakes. But the study does nothing to characterise the behaviour it collects. No linguistic construct is named or measured - not lexical diversity, sentence length, pronoun use, sentiment, pragmatic markers, disfluency, figurative language or any of the features the autism-language literature has examined - and no analysis reports how the two corpora differ. The introduction gestures at 'linguistic patterns, emotional expressions, and communication styles' but nothing in the method operationalises any of these. The result is a study in which the behavioural target is left entirely to the classifier to define, with no account of what it found. Given that the positive class was assembled by searching for autism keywords and that no autism vocabulary was removed from the tweets, the behaviour actually being detected may be talking about autism rather than any property of autistic communication. [RQ3.2] No fusion, and no possibility of it in this design - text alone, one tweet at a time. Two structural forms of integration that the data support were also not used. The first is user-level aggregation: 252 users each contribute hundreds or thousands of tweets, and pooling per-tweet predictions into a per-user decision would be the natural analogue of the multi-stimulus aggregation used to good effect by several eye-tracking studies in this corpus, and is the only form in which a screening application could work, since no one would be assessed on a single tweet. It is neither performed nor discussed, and no user-level metric appears. The second is metadata: the Twitter API returns posting time, reply and thread structure, follower and following counts, engagement figures and interaction partners, all of which are behavioural signals about social communication and all of which are discarded in favour of raw text. The paper's own framing - that social media offers insight into 'the social experiences and challenges faced by individuals with ASD' - points directly at interaction structure, which is precisely what is thrown away. [RQ4.1] Four models compared: a decision tree, XGBoost, k-nearest neighbours with k = 1, and BERT-base-multilingual-cased. The comparison is framed as a deliberate test - the three classical models were hyperparameter-tuned by grid search while BERT was left entirely at defaults, 'to see if the DL model just with the basic model gives more accurate results than ML models that have been optimised' - and BERT won by 13 accuracy points over the best classical model. Setting up an asymmetric comparison and reporting it transparently is a reasonable framing, but the comparison is not interpretable as stated, because the text representation given to the classical models is never described. BERT builds its own contextual representation from subword tokens; the decision tree, XGBoost and k-nearest neighbours must have been given something, and what that was is unstated. If it was a sparse bag-of-words vector, then the finding is about representation rather than model family, and the paper cannot tell the two apart. Two of the classical results also look near-degenerate rather than merely weak: k = 1 nearest neighbours over a high-dimensional text representation is close to a memorisation baseline, and the decision tree assigned nearly everything to the positive class. Neither observation is drawn out. [RQ4.2] For BERT, subword tokens and contextual embeddings from the multilingual cased checkpoint, applied to one tweet at a time. For the three classical models, unspecified - the paper says natural language processing techniques were used but names no tokenisation, vectorisation or feature scheme, so the representation those models consumed is unknown. In every case the unit is a single tweet treated independently: no thread context, no reply structure, no temporal ordering, no user-level aggregation, and no metadata. The maximum sequence length is not stated, which matters because tweets in the 2017-2022 window span both the 140- and 280-character limits. Nothing was masked or normalised beyond the four corpus-cleaning steps, so hashtags, mentions, URLs, emoji and autism-related vocabulary all remain in the text the models see - the last of these being the reason the results cannot be read as evidence about communication style. [RQ4.3] Accuracy and F1 for each model, together with full confusion matrices giving true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives - and the confusion matrices are the most valuable thing in the results, because they expose behaviour the summary metrics hide. The decision tree's counts (tp 11,229, fn 41, tn 2,540, fp 8,690) show a model that assigned almost every tweet to the autistic class: 99.6% sensitivity against 22.6% specificity, reported as 61.2% accuracy and F1 0.72, both of which make it look like a mediocre classifier rather than a near-degenerate one. BERT's counts give sensitivity 82.1% and specificity 86.5%, reasonably balanced. Publishing the raw counts for all four models is good practice and lets a reader recover what the headline numbers conceal. What is missing: sensitivity, specificity, precision and recall are never named or computed even though the counts are present; there is no AUC; there are no confidence intervals; there is no majority-class baseline, though the balanced tweet-level design makes it 50%; and there is no user-level metric, which is the only level at which the proposed application would operate. F1 is also computed with the autistic class as positive, which given the balanced tweet-level design is defensible but is never stated. [RQ4.4] None. No feature importance for the tree-based models, despite decision trees and XGBoost both supporting it natively and both having been fitted; no attention or probing analysis for BERT; no error analysis; no inspection of misclassified examples; no lexical comparison between the two corpora; no topic modelling. The paper's entire interpretive content is the observation that BERT 'utilizes neural networks to recognize intricate patterns within the input data' and that this 'demonstrates the potential of deep learning models to extract relevant patterns'. The absence is not merely a missed opportunity but the reason the study's central claim cannot be assessed: the difference between a classifier that has learned something about autistic communication and one that has learned that certain accounts discuss autism, or that has memorised 31 people's writing styles, would be visible in even a cursory look at the most predictive tokens, and no such look is reported. [RQ4.5] The weakest validation design in the corpus, and the failure is structural rather than marginal. A single random 75/25 split was applied to 90,000 tweets, with the tweet as the unit.
