Those tweets come from 252 users, so every user is represented on both sides of the split, and the imbalance makes this acute for the negative class: 31 comparison users supply all 45,000 non-autistic tweets, roughly 1,450 each, of which about 1,090 land in training and 360 in test. A model needs only to recognise those 31 writing styles - vocabulary, topics, habitual phrasings, recurring names, professional jargon, regional idiom - to classify the negative test set almost perfectly, and BERT is exactly the kind of model that will do so. The positive class is less concentrated at roughly 200 tweets per user but is leaky by the same mechanism. Nothing in the paper estimates performance on a writer the model has never seen, which is the only quantity relevant to the stated application. Compounding this: there is no cross-validation and no repeated split, so the single reported figure carries no stability estimate; hyperparameters were grid-searched with no validation set distinct from the test set; no chance baseline or confidence interval is given; and no user-level aggregation is performed, so the study never reports the metric its own use case requires. The corrective is simple and would be a genuinely informative experiment: hold out entire users, expand the comparison group well beyond 31 people, mask autism-related vocabulary, and report user-level sensitivity and specificity. On the current design, the 84.3% cannot be interpreted as evidence about autism at all. [RQ5.1] Index terms: Machine Learning, Deep Learning, ASD, tweets, NLP. Four of the five are method or data-source labels and the fifth is the condition; no term describes a behaviour, a linguistic construct or a clinical application, which accurately reflects a paper with no behavioural hypothesis. Terms carried through the body: early detection, early diagnosis, social media texts, biographies, ActuallyAutistic, Aspie, hyperparameters search, BERT-base-multilingual-cased, GridSearchCV. The title's 'AI-Powered' is doing rhetorical rather than descriptive work. [RQ5.2] 2023 IEEE 36th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS), pages 235-238 - a four-page conference paper at a computer-science venue oriented to medical systems. The format explains some of the compression, though not the absence of an ethics statement, which conference length limits do not excuse. The venue also explains the paper's evaluative frame: the result is presented as a model comparison with a winner, in the idiom of a benchmark leaderboard, rather than as a clinical or linguistic finding. Two DOIs appear in the retrieved text (10.1109/CBMS58004.2023.00051 and .00223), an artefact of the proceedings metadata. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 by the SALBIS and SECOMUCI research groups in the Department of Electric, Systems and Automatics Engineering at Universidad de Leon, Spain, partially supported by a university internal research programme. The framing is the familiar access-and-scarcity argument - diagnosis 'remains a challenge due to the resources and specialized professionals needed', existing methods rest on interviews and questionnaires that 'take too much time' - combined with a strongly stated case for early diagnosis occupying most of the introduction. The positioning within the field is explicitly as a gap-filler: the authors note that prior autism machine-learning work has used images and eye tracking, that 'few have focused on detecting ASD using text as input', and that there is 'a notable gap in research utilizing the information found in Twitter users' biographies'. That gap is real, and social-media language is a legitimate and under-explored modality. What makes the paper a cautionary case for this review is the distance between its framing and its evidence: a study motivated in its opening pages by identifying autistic children before the age of three, using adult self-disclosure on a platform with a minimum age of 13, claiming to 'pave the way' for diagnosis on the basis of a tweet-level classification whose validation design cannot distinguish autism from authorship. It is also the only study in the corpus that builds a health classifier from identifiable individuals' public disclosures with no ethics approval, no consent and no discussion of either. |
| S-103 | Cross-sectional two-group study embedded in routine paediatric primary care at four Duke Children's Primary Care clinics. Four hundred and thirty-six toddlers aged 17-36 months took part during well-child visits: 40 autistic and 396 typically developing, a 9.2% prevalence reflecting prospective ascertainment rather than case-control recruitment. All children received the caregiver-completed M-CHAT-R/F as part of standard care, and any child screening positive or prompting caregiver or clinician developmental concern was evaluated by a child psychologist using the ADOS-Toddler module; mean ADOS-T total in the autistic group was 7.64 +/- 1.69, and one typically developing child who screened positive was evaluated and not diagnosed. Exclusion criteria were practical: known hearing or vision impairment, child too upset, caregiver unwilling or without time or unable to consent in English or Spanish, procedures not completed, or clinical information missing. Demographics are reported in full per group and show three substantial imbalances - the autistic group is 3.6 months older (24.21 +/- 4.72 versus 20.62 +/- 3.21 months), markedly more male (77.5% versus 48.9%) and considerably less White (47.5% versus 77.7%) with four times the proportion of Hispanic/Latino children (32.5% versus 7.3%). Caregiver education is high across the sample (82.8% college degree). No cognitive or language measure was obtained. The study was approved under two Duke University Health System IRB protocols with written caregiver consent. | Each child sat on a caregiver's lap with an iPad at 60 cm while six short movies played and the front camera recorded at 30 fps; all other family members and practitioners stood behind the pair. Four movies were social - actors making eye contact, smiling, gesturing, reciting rhymes, acting silly, with both successful and failed attempts - and two were non-social, showing dynamic toys or animations. The child's face was isolated from those of caregiver, siblings and clinicians using a facial embedding, and 49 landmarks were tracked. Global head motion was removed by affine alignment to a canonical face using eye-corner and nose points, with head-pose angles estimated separately; signal above 15 Hz was filtered as noise on the grounds that a facial expression requires at least 260 ms; and intervals of inattention were excised. Landmarks within the eyebrow and mouth regions were averaged into one-dimensional series, and multiscale entropy computed by coarse-graining over 30 scales with sample entropy at m = 2 and r = 0.15 sigma. Two methodological modifications are presented as contributions: missing data are handled by admitting only fully observed embedding vectors into the coefficient counts, since concatenating across gaps would inflate one coefficient but not the other; and the measure is normalised per participant to permit across-subject comparison, a problem the authors note is generally unaddressed in the health-research use of multiscale entropy. Integrated entropy - the cumulative sum across the first 20 scales - was the summary feature; participants with under 40% valid data for a movie were dropped for that movie. In parallel, affect probabilities were estimated with the group's previously validated pose-invariant method and summarised as the energy of their first derivative. Groups were compared with Mann-Whitney U and effect size r, regions with Wilcoxon signed-rank, and confounds addressed by ANCOVA on missing-data percentage and landmark variation. A decision tree with Gini splitting was evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation, AUCs compared by DeLong's method, and logistic regression used for odds ratios. | Autistic toddlers showed significantly higher entropy in both eyebrow and mouth landmark dynamics across the first 20 scales, in four of six movies, with a clear social gradient: social movies gave p < .0001 with large to very large effect sizes (r = .51-.82), non-social movies gave significant differences with only medium effects (r = .32-.40). Integrated entropy differed at p < .00001 with large or very large effects for every social movie. Eyebrow and mouth complexity did not differ from each other within either group (p > .05, r < 0.1). The autistic group also showed a significantly wider range of integrated entropy across the six movies (eyebrows p = .001, r = .33; mouth p = .0002, r = .39). Both candidate confounds correlated only weakly with integrated entropy (0.2-0.42), the groups did not differ in missing-data percentage, and ANCOVA adjustment individually and jointly preserved the group difference (p < .0001 social, p < .001 non-social). On redundancy, integrated entropy correlated moderately with positive-affect energy for two movies (r up to .60) and negligibly for the other four (r = .01-.15). Decision-tree classification on social movies gave 76.6-78.3% accuracy with entropy alone, 61.6-75.0% with affect alone, and 63.3-79.5% with both, so affect added nothing; logistic-regression odds ratios reached 1.8 for entropy against 0.8 for affect. | The three demographic differences between groups - 3.6 months of age at a stage of rapid developmental change, 29 percentage points of sex ratio, and 30 points of racial composition with four times the proportion of Hispanic/Latino children in the autistic group - are all reported plainly and none is adjusted for, in a study that constructs ANCOVA models for two other covariates. The racial difference compounds the authors' own acknowledged limitation that the landmark and affect detectors were trained primarily on adults, since detector accuracy also varies with facial morphology and skin tone, so differential measurement error across groups cannot be ruled out. The secondary classification analysis was restricted to the four social movies on the basis of effect sizes computed in the same data. No class handling is described for the decision tree, yet the reported precision of around 70% with recall near 89% cannot arise from a 40:396 ratio, so an undisclosed balancing or subsampling step exists and, without knowing it, the accuracy figures cannot be placed against the correct baseline - which at 9.2% prevalence would be roughly 91% for majority-class prediction. Per-movie analysed sample sizes are shown only graphically. ADOS-T severity scores were obtained but never related to the entropy measure, so the biomarker's association with symptom severity is untested. And no test-retest reliability is reported for a measure proposed for treatment monitoring. The authors state that the sample lacked power to determine the impact of demographic characteristics on the results, which is an honest acknowledgement of the first problem without resolving it. | One of the two strongest studies in this review, and the one whose design most directly answers the corpus's dominant external-validity failure. Recruitment is from consecutive well-child visits at four primary care clinics with autism ascertained prospectively at 9.2% prevalence through routine screening and ADOS-T evaluation, so this is a screening cohort rather than a specialist-clinic case-control contrast, and the comparison group is screened rather than assumed non-autistic. Four further features earn it a central place in the synthesis. Its primary claims rest on non-parametric group comparisons with effect sizes reported and interpreted throughout, ANCOVA adjustment for two prespecified confounds, and an internal social/non-social control condition - a design where the finding is a graded, confound-adjusted effect rather than a cross-validated accuracy figure, and one that much of this corpus would have been better for adopting. Its treatment of missing data is the most careful here and is presented as a methodological contribution: missing points are excluded at the embedding-vector level with a worked example showing why concatenation biases the estimate, missing-data percentage is shown not to differ between groups, and it is additionally entered as a covariate - all in a study whose data come from toddlers moving freely in a clinic room. Its handling of head motion is the mirror image of what most video studies do: rather than modelling head movement as signal, it is estimated and removed by affine normalisation so that what remains is facial deformation. And it contains the corpus's cleanest test of measure redundancy, showing through correlation, classification and odds ratios that a complexity measure and an affect measure derived from the same video carry largely independent information - a discriminant-validity design more informative than the usual report that fusion raised accuracy. Two things should also be carried forward as cautions. The demographic imbalances are unadjusted in a paper that plainly knows how to adjust, and the racial difference interacts with an acknowledged detector limitation in a way that deserves attention across this literature. And this is the most commercially conflicted study charted here, with app technology licensed to Apple and authors holding patents and company directorships - which makes its disclosure practice the relevant model: the conflicts are itemised at length, and analysis is independently and continuously reviewed by a named conflict-free co-author, a safeguard no other study in the corpus reports. | [RQ1.1] Four hundred and thirty-six toddlers aged 17-36 months, comprising 40 with autism and 396 typically developing, recruited at four paediatric primary care clinics during routine well-child visits. The recruitment route is the defining feature and separates this study from almost every other in the corpus: children were not enrolled as known cases and known controls, but as consecutive clinic attenders who received the M-CHAT-R/F as part of standard care and were referred for ADOS-Toddler evaluation only if they screened positive or if a caregiver or clinician raised a developmental concern. The resulting 9.2% autism prevalence is far closer to a real screening population than the near-balanced designs elsewhere here. Exclusion criteria are stated in full and are practical rather than diagnostic: known hearing or vision impairment, child too upset, caregiver not interested or without time or needing to care for siblings or unable to consent in English or Spanish, child did not complete the procedures, and missing clinical information. The analysed sample varies by movie because only participants with at least 40% valid landmark data for a given movie were included, and those per-movie counts are shown graphically rather than tabulated - the one place where the participant accounting is less transparent than the rest of the paper. [RQ1.2] 'Toddlers with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD) toddlers', used consistently and person-first throughout, with 'children with autism' also appearing. The register is notably measured for this literature. Autistic children are described as experiencing 'challenges in establishing social communication' and 'differences in use of facial expressions', and the paper speaks of 'atypical' and 'ambiguous' expressions rather than of deficits or abnormality - though 'atypical facial expression' is called an 'early symptom' and the language of biomarkers, symptoms and risk is used throughout. There is no burden framing, no cost-to-society argument, and no claim that autistic people cannot live independently, all of which appear in other papers charted here. Two interpretive passages are worth noting for their care. The explanation offered for the finding is framed as speculation and is symmetrical rather than deficit-laden: typically developing toddlers may respond more predictably because they share an understanding of the movies' social meaning, whereas autistic children's responses 'may be more idiosyncratic' - idiosyncrasy rather than impairment. And the authors note that neutral expressions 'might be interpreted by others as more ambiguous', locating the communicative difficulty in the interpretation as much as in the expression. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement statement. [RQ1.3] The most complete demographic reporting in this corpus, and the completeness is what makes the imbalances visible. Table 1 gives, per group: sex (autistic 77.5% male versus typically developing 48.9%), race (White/Caucasian 47.5% versus 77.7%; African American 15.0% versus 8.6%; other 37.5% versus 13.6%), Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (32.5% versus 7.3%), M-CHAT-R/F positivity (87.5% versus 0.25%), ADOS-T total (7.64 +/- 1.69 in the autistic group), and age in months (24.21 +/- 4.72 versus 20.62 +/- 3.21). Caregiver education is reported for the whole sample: 82.8% college degree, 15.5% more than high school, 1.8% no high school. Three of these differences matter and none is adjusted for. The age gap of 3.6 months is large at 17-36 months, a period of rapid change in facial expressivity, affect regulation and attention, and it runs in the direction that would be expected to produce more, not less, behavioural regulation in the older autistic group - so it does not obviously explain the finding, but it is a live confound in a study that goes to the trouble of ANCOVA-adjusting two other covariates. The sex difference reflects autism's true sex ratio rather than a sampling error, but sex differences in facial expressivity in toddlerhood are documented. The racial and ethnic difference is the one with a technical as well as a demographic dimension: the autistic group is 30 percentage points less White and over four times as likely to be Hispanic/Latino, and the paper's own stated limitation is that landmark and affect detectors were trained primarily on adults - detector accuracy is also known to vary by skin tone and facial morphology, so differential measurement error across groups cannot be excluded. The authors acknowledge the general problem, stating that the sample 'did not have sufficient power to determine the impact of demographic characteristics on the results'. [RQ1.4] Among the strongest in this review, and structurally different from the case-control norm because the diagnostic pathway is the clinical one rather than a research recruitment. Every toddler received the M-CHAT-R/F, a validated caregiver screening instrument, as part of routine well-child care. Children screening positive, and children about whom a caregiver or clinician expressed developmental concern, were then evaluated by a child psychologist using the ADOS-Toddler module, the age-appropriate observational gold standard. Mean ADOS-T total in the autistic group was 7.64 +/- 1.69. Two features deserve particular credit. The comparison group is screened rather than assumed: 396 typically developing toddlers all completed M-CHAT-R/F, so undetected autism in the comparison group is reduced (though not eliminated, since M-CHAT-R/F sensitivity is imperfect and only screen-positive or concern-flagged children received ADOS-T). And the single discordant case is reported explicitly - one typically developing child screened positive, was evaluated with ADOS-T, and was not diagnosed - a level of transparency about the reference-standard pathway that no other study charted here provides. The limitation is the one intrinsic to a two-stage design: children who screened negative and prompted no concern did not receive ADOS-T, so the comparison group's status rests on a screening instrument rather than on the diagnostic one. [RQ1.5] Partial, and better than most here on severity while silent on cognition. ADOS-Toddler total scores were obtained for the diagnosed children and are reported as a group mean of 7.64 +/- 1.69, giving a genuine quantitative severity index - the study is one of relatively few in this corpus where such a score exists at all. But it is used only descriptively. No analysis relates integrated entropy to ADOS-T score, so the question that would most strengthen the biomarker claim - whether facial-dynamics complexity tracks symptom severity within the autistic group, rather than merely separating groups - is not asked. The tight standard deviation (1.69) also indicates a fairly homogeneous severity range, which limits what such an analysis could have shown and constrains generalisation to more or less affected children. No cognitive, developmental or language measure was administered to either group, which matters for a paradigm requiring 17-36 month olds to attend to a screen for several minutes: developmental level governs sustained attention, and the paper's own 40% valid-data threshold removes children who looked away too much, so cognitive and attentional capacity silently shapes who is analysed. The authors partly address this by verifying that missing-data percentage does not differ significantly between groups and by entering it as an ANCOVA covariate, which is a good empirical substitute for a developmental measure but not a replacement for one. [RQ2.1] Three questions, stated as hypotheses in advance. Whether the complexity of facial landmark dynamics differentiates autistic from typically developing toddlers; whether that complexity is higher specifically in the eyebrow region, on the basis of prior work on eyebrow raising in this cohort, and the mouth region, on the basis of atypical vocalisation literature; and whether the complexity measure adds information beyond the group's own previously published affect-based analysis or merely duplicates it. Findings: autistic toddlers showed significantly higher multiscale entropy in both regions, with a clear social/non-social gradient - during social movies p < .0001 with large to very large effect sizes (r = .51-.82), during non-social movies still significant but only medium (r = .32-.40). Integrated entropy over the first 20 scales gave p < .00001 with large or very large effects for all social movies. Eyebrows and mouth did not differ from each other (p > .05, r < 0.1), so the hypothesis of regional specificity was not supported in the sense of one region dominating. The autistic group also showed a significantly wider range of integrated entropy across the six movies (eyebrows p = .001, r = .33; mouth p = .0002, r = .39), meaning their facial responsiveness varied more between contents. On the third question, correlations between integrated entropy and positive-affect energy were moderate for two movies and negligible for four, and adding affect to the classifier did not improve on entropy alone - while affect alone performed worse - so the measures are largely independent and the complexity measure is the more informative of the two. Classification with a decision tree on social movies gave 76.6-78.3% accuracy with entropy alone; logistic regression gave odds ratios up to 1.8 for entropy against 0.8 for affect. [RQ2.2] Four paediatric primary care clinics in the Duke Children's Primary Care network, with data captured during routine well-child visits. This is the study's most consequential design property and it addresses the corpus's most pervasive external-validity problem. Because recruitment is by clinic attendance rather than by diagnostic status, the sample is not a set of specialist-clinic cases contrasted with community controls but a screening cohort in which autism is identified prospectively at 9.2% prevalence. The measurement is embedded in the visit rather than added to it: the child sits on the caregiver's lap, an iPad is placed at 60 cm, and the movies play for a few minutes while the front camera records. Practical constraints of the setting are reported honestly as exclusion criteria - the child was too upset, the caregiver had no time or needed to mind siblings, consent could not be given in English or Spanish - which is a realistic account of what limits deployment in primary care and is more informative than a laboratory study's silence on the same issues. The one respect in which the setting is not fully representative is socioeconomic: 82.8% of caregivers held a college degree, which is far above the US population and reflects the catchment of an academic health system. [RQ2.3] Six short movies, each under 90 seconds, presented on a tablet during the clinic visit, with the social/non-social split used as an internal control rather than as incidental variety. The four social movies feature human actors making eye contact, smiling, gesturing, reciting nursery rhymes and behaving comically - Blowing Bubbles (64 s), Spinning Top (53 s), Rhymes and Toys (49 s) and Make Me Laugh (56 s) - and two of them deliberately include both successful and failed attempts, which creates natural moments for affective response. The two non-social movies show dynamic toys or animations: Mechanical Puppy (25 s) and Dog in Grass Right-Right-Left (40 s), the latter using a structured spatial sequence. The design has three strengths worth carrying into the synthesis. It is short, passive and requires nothing of the child, so it can be administered opportunistically to 17-36 month olds in a clinic room. The social/non-social contrast provides a within-subject test of whether the measured signal is specific to social content, and the answer - large effects for social movies, medium effects for non-social - is more informative than a single accuracy figure, because it shows the complexity difference is amplified by social content but not created by it. And the environment is controlled in a low-tech way that suits the setting: caregiver holds the child, tablet at a fixed 60 cm, everyone else stands behind the pair to reduce distraction. The limitation is that passive viewing elicits a narrower behavioural range than interaction, and the authors identify live interpersonal interaction as the natural next step. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up, and no test-retest reliability of the entropy measure - which matters for a biomarker proposed for treatment monitoring, since sensitivity to change requires knowing the measurement's stability. Governance is exemplary by the standards of this corpus. The study was approved by the Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board under two protocol numbers (Pro00085434, Pro00085435), written informed consent was obtained from caregivers or legal guardians, and inability to consent in English or Spanish is disclosed as an exclusion criterion rather than passed over. Funding from eight sources including four NIH grants and four technology companies is itemised, with an explicit statement that 'the funders had no direct role in the study design, data analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript'. The competing-interests statement is the longest in this corpus and is unusually forthcoming: several authors developed technology licensed to Apple and have benefited financially, one is CEO of a company and holds a granted patent plus three applications alongside numerous advisory and consulting relationships, and another was affiliated with Apple at publication. Crucially, a structural mitigation is described rather than merely asserted: 'Data analysis for this project is constantly independently reviewed by Scott Compton, who has no conflict of interest related to this work', and Compton is a named co-author. Given the commercial stakes attached to a tablet-based autism screening app, an independent analysis reviewer is the right safeguard and is worth noting as a practice other groups could adopt. [RQ2.5] An ordinary consumer iPad with its front-facing camera at 30 frames per second, running a purpose-built application - no research-grade sensor, no eye tracker, no wearable, no additional hardware. That choice is the point: the entire measurement chain is a device already present in most homes and clinics, which is what makes the scalability claim credible rather than aspirational. Analysis components are all published and cited: a face detection algorithm, a low-dimensional facial embedding used to identify and track the child's face specifically among those of caregiver, siblings and clinical staff, a 49-point landmark detector, and the group's own pose-invariant affect estimator, itself previously validated against human frame-by-frame coding of 136,450 frames with an intraclass correlation of 0.9. Statistical work used Python with pingouin (Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon, ANCOVA), scipy (Spearman) and scikit-learn (logistic regression), each named at function level. The one component with a stated weakness is the perception layer: the landmark and affect algorithms were trained primarily on adults, which the authors list as a limitation while noting their prior validation in toddlers. [RQ2.6] The strongest methods reporting encountered in this review. Reproducible from the text: the full recruitment and screening pathway, all five exclusion criteria, the seating and device arrangement with the 60 cm distance, all six movies with durations and content, the 30 fps capture, the complete preprocessing chain including the affine canonical-face normalisation, the 15 Hz low-pass cut-off with its physiological justification (260 ms to produce an expression, 150-250 ms for a valid one), the removal of non-attending intervals, the entropy parameters m = 2 and r = 0.15 sigma with their literature sources and a supplementary sensitivity analysis, the exact rule for handling missing data inside the entropy computation with a worked numerical example, the 40% validity threshold and its consequence for per-movie sample size, the 20-scale integration window, the affect-energy definition with its 10-frame moving average, and every statistical test named down to the Python function. Two methodological contributions are presented as such rather than buried: the modification of multiscale entropy to handle partially missing time series without concatenation artefacts, and its normalisation to permit across-subject comparison - the latter accompanied by the pointed footnote that despite MSE's popularity in health research 'this problem has never been addressed before, and often authors report lower MSE for data that is clearly more complex and vice-versa'. Not available: code, data, the movies, and the decision-tree configuration. Five supplementary appendices hold further analyses, including the developmental-delay comparison and the head-motion work. [RQ2.7] The three stated limitations are accurate and appropriately weighted: adult-trained landmark and affect detectors applied to toddlers, the possibility that other complexity measures would discriminate better, and insufficient power to determine how demographic characteristics affect the results. The last is an honest acknowledgement of a real problem, since the groups differ substantially on three demographic axes. The unstated limitations are fewer than in any other study charted here but include some that matter. The 3.6-month age gap between groups is never adjusted for, which is conspicuous in a paper that constructs ANCOVA models for two other covariates - the direction of the gap makes it an unlikely explanation of the finding, but it should have been modelled. The racial and ethnic composition differs sharply (47.5% versus 77.7% White; 32.5% versus 7.3% Hispanic/Latino), and this interacts with the acknowledged limitation about the detectors: landmark localisation accuracy varies with facial morphology and skin tone, so differential measurement error is a specific possibility, not a generic caveat. The decision to run the classification only on social movies was taken after seeing which movies produced larger effect sizes in the same data. No class handling is described for the decision tree, and the reported precision of about 70% with recall near 89% cannot arise from a 40:396 ratio without some balancing, so an undisclosed step exists in the classification pipeline. Per-movie analysed sample sizes appear only in figures. And ADOS-T totals were collected but never correlated with the entropy measure, leaving the biomarker's relationship to severity untested. [RQ2.9] Four directions, each following from a specific gap. Study complexity and coordination of facial dynamics during live interpersonal interaction rather than passive viewing, motivated by evidence that autistic people have difficulty with affect coordination in social exchange - the natural extension of a measure built on temporal predictability. Apply the same complexity analysis to head motion as an index of postural control, exploiting data the pipeline already produces. Pursue the preliminary supplementary finding that integrated entropy may separate autism from developmental or language delay, which is the differential-diagnosis question most of this corpus avoids. And combine the facial-complexity biomarker with gaze indices, response to name, motor signatures and other measures before any automated decision tool is deployed - stated as a precondition rather than an aspiration. Absent from the list, and worth adding: test-retest reliability, prospective external validation, and the relationship between entropy and ADOS-T severity. [RQ3.1] Spontaneous facial movement, characterised by its temporal predictability rather than its content - which is the study's conceptual contribution and distinguishes it from the affect-recognition tradition. Two regions were prespecified with stated rationales: the eyebrows, following the group's earlier finding about eyebrow raising in this cohort and the possibility that it indexes attentional engagement; and the mouth, on the basis of literature linking atypical vocalisation and mouth movement to autism. For each region the landmark points are averaged into a one-dimensional signal, head motion having first been removed by affine normalisation so that what remains is facial deformation rather than head movement. Multiscale entropy then quantifies how unpredictable that signal is across temporal scales. The authors are careful to explain what this does and does not capture, and the explanation is worth stating precisely because the distinction is often blurred elsewhere: a signal with large but highly periodic excursions gives low entropy, and so does a nearly stable signal with small excursions, while only irregular non-periodic movement gives high entropy. So the measure is not amplitude, not frequency and not variability, but predictability - and the paper backs this up empirically by showing that integrated entropy correlates only weakly (0.2-0.42) with landmark variation. The finding is that autistic toddlers' facial movement is less predictable in both regions, that the difference is amplified by social content, and that their responsiveness also varies more across different movies. The interpretation offered is that typically developing toddlers respond more predictably because they share an understanding of the movies' social meaning while autistic toddlers respond more idiosyncratically - explicitly labelled as speculation. [RQ3.2] No cross-sensor fusion, but the paper contains the corpus's cleanest test of whether two measures from the same modality carry redundant information, and the test is designed as discriminant validity rather than as an accuracy chase. The comparison measure is the group's own previously published affect analysis - the energy of the first derivative of neutral, positive and negative affect probability time series, computed as a 10-frame moving average of the rate of change followed by cumulative sum. Three lines of evidence are brought to bear. Correlation: Spearman r between integrated entropy and positive-affect energy is moderate for Blowing Bubbles (.49 eyebrows, .60 mouth) and Mechanical Puppy (.41, .49) but negligible for the other four movies (.01-.15), and the mouth correlates more strongly than the eyebrows, which the authors note is expected because smiling is a mouth event. Classification: decision trees using entropy alone reach 76.6-78.3% accuracy, using affect alone 61.6-75.0%, and using both 63.3-79.5% - so adding affect does not help and in two of four movies hurts, while AUCs compared by DeLong's method favour entropy alone in three of four movies. Logistic regression: entropy gives odds ratios up to 1.8 while affect gives 0.8, i.e. below unity. The conclusion that the two measures are largely independent and that entropy is the stronger is therefore supported by three convergent analyses rather than by a single accuracy comparison. The general lesson for the review is that a partially correlated second measure can be genuinely non-redundant, and that testing for redundancy explicitly - rather than reporting that fusion improved accuracy - is the more informative design. [RQ4.1] Deliberately simple, and the simplicity is appropriate to the claim. The primary analyses are conventional non-parametric statistics: Mann-Whitney U for between-group comparison, Wilcoxon signed-rank for within-group, with effect size r reported for every significant test, and ANCOVA to adjust for two prespecified confounds. The modelling contribution is not a classifier but the entropy estimator itself - a modification of multiscale entropy that handles partially missing time series by admitting only fully observed embedding vectors into the coefficient counts, and that normalises per participant so complexity can be compared across people. The authors flag the second point sharply, noting in a footnote that despite MSE's popularity in health research the across-subject comparison problem 'has never been addressed before, and often authors report lower MSE for data that is clearly more complex and vice-versa'. The classification component is a secondary demonstration using a decision tree with Gini splitting and leave-one-out cross-validation, plus logistic regression for odds ratios. No deep learning appears anywhere. Given 40 autistic participants and two features, this is the right choice, and the paper does not pretend otherwise - the classifier is presented as evidence of feasibility rather than as the result. [RQ4.2] Two scalar features per participant per movie: integrated entropy of the eyebrow region and of the mouth region, each being the cumulative sum of sample entropy across the first 20 coarse-grained scales of the landmark time series. The pipeline that produces them is where the work sits. Forty-nine landmarks are tracked at 30 fps; the child's face is isolated from those of caregiver, siblings and clinicians by facial embedding; eye-corner and nose landmarks drive an affine transform to a canonical face so that head motion is removed rather than confounded with expression; head-pose angles are estimated separately; signal above 15 Hz is filtered as noise on the physiologically motivated grounds that a facial expression takes at least 260 ms; non-attending intervals are excised; and the remaining landmark points within each region are averaged into a single time series. Sample entropy uses m = 2 and r = 0.15 sigma, both taken from prior literature with an appendix showing insensitivity to the choice. The missing-data rule is stated with a worked numerical example: only embedding vectors free of missing points contribute to the counts, because concatenating across gaps would inflate Cm without inflating Cm+1 and so bias the entropy. A minimum 40% valid-data requirement per movie applies. The representation deliberately discards expression identity, amplitude and timing, retaining only predictability - which is what makes it complementary to the affect measure rather than a variant of it. [RQ4.3] Two metric sets for two purposes, both appropriate. For the primary group comparisons: exact p-values with effect size r reported for every test at every scale and every movie, ANCOVA-adjusted significance after controlling for missing-data percentage and landmark variation individually and jointly, Spearman correlations for the redundancy analysis, and within-group Wilcoxon tests for the eyebrow-versus-mouth comparison. Reporting effect sizes systematically alongside p-values, and interpreting them (medium for non-social, large to very large for social), is better statistical practice than anything else in this corpus and is what allows the social/non-social gradient to be read as a graded finding rather than a binary significant/not-significant one. For the secondary classification: accuracy, precision and recall for three feature sets across four movies under leave-one-out cross-validation, ROC curves with AUCs compared by DeLong's method, and logistic-regression odds ratios. Gaps: no confidence intervals on any classification metric; AUC values are shown graphically but not quoted numerically in the retrieved text; no majority-class baseline, which at 9.2% prevalence would be about 91% and therefore above the reported accuracies; and no positive or negative predictive value at the study's own prevalence, which for a primary-care screening tool is the number that would matter most. The precision-recall combination reported (about 70% and about 89%) is also arithmetically incompatible with a 40:396 class ratio, implying an undisclosed balancing step. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is structural rather than added afterwards, because the feature is a single quantity with a stated physical meaning. The paper explains precisely what integrated entropy measures and, importantly, what it does not: not amplitude, not variability, not frequency, but predictability, with the specific consequence that both a highly periodic large-excursion signal and a nearly stable small-excursion signal yield low entropy. That distinction is then tested rather than asserted, through the weak correlation (0.2-0.42) between integrated entropy and landmark variation, and through ANCOVA adjustment for variation as a covariate. Region selection was hypothesis-driven and prespecified with citations, so the analysis is confirmatory rather than exploratory in its choice of features. The social/non-social contrast functions as an interpretive control, showing that the effect is amplified by social content but present without it. The redundancy analysis against affect is itself an interpretability exercise - establishing that the measure is not simply detecting smiles. And the substantive interpretation offered is clearly labelled as speculation and is symmetrical rather than deficit-framed. What is missing is individual-level explanation: no error analysis, no examination of which children were misclassified, and no link between entropy and ADOS-T severity, which would have been the strongest available evidence that the measure tracks the construct it claims to index. [RQ4.5] Sound at the level that matters most and loose at the margins. The classifier uses leave-one-out cross-validation over participants, so the split unit is the child and no within-participant leakage is possible - though this is easier to achieve here than elsewhere because each participant contributes a single feature vector per movie rather than many segments. More importantly, the paper's primary claims are not predictive at all: they are group comparisons with effect sizes, supported by ANCOVA adjustment for two prespecified confounds and by an internal control condition (non-social movies), which is a design where cross-validation is not the relevant safeguard and where the reported statistics carry their own uncertainty. Three looser points. The classification analysis was restricted to the four social movies because the group comparisons on the same data had shown larger effect sizes there, so that restriction is in-sample; the effect is modest, since the choice was made on a prespecified social/non-social distinction rather than by searching over movies individually, but it should be stated. No class handling is described for the decision tree, and reported precision near 70% with recall near 89% cannot be produced from 40 autistic against 396 typically developing participants - so an undisclosed balancing or subsampling step exists, and without knowing it the accuracy figures cannot be placed against the correct baseline. And no majority-class baseline is given, which at 9.2% prevalence would be about 91%, so the reported 76-79% accuracies would be below trivial on the unbalanced sample and are only meaningful under whatever balancing was applied. None of this affects the study's principal finding, which rests on non-parametric group comparisons with large effect sizes, confound adjustment and an internal control - a design that is more robust than a cross-validated accuracy figure and that this corpus contains too few of. [RQ5.1] Index terms: Autism spectrum disorder, affective state, facial dynamics, complexity, sample entropy, multiscale entropy. Four of the six name the measurement rather than the application, and neither 'machine learning', 'deep learning', 'classification' nor 'diagnosis' appears - which accurately reflects a paper whose contribution is a biomarker and its statistical characterisation rather than a classifier. 'Complexity' and 'sample entropy' locate the work in the physiological time-series tradition rather than the affective-computing one, despite the venue. Terms carried through the body: integrated entropy, landmarks' dynamics, coarse-graining, canonical face model, pose-invariant affect, social versus non-social movies, biomarker, well-child visit. [RQ5.2] IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing 14(2):919-928, April-June 2023; manuscript received 30 April 2021, revised 4 September 2021, accepted 16 September 2021, published online 20 September 2021 - so the work predates its issue date by nearly two years. The venue is an affective-computing journal, and the paper is in part an argument against that field's dominant framing: rather than recognising emotions, it discards expression identity entirely and measures only the predictability of movement, then demonstrates that this carries information the affect pipeline misses. Five supplementary appendices are hosted with the article, containing the entropy-parameter sensitivity analysis, the across-subject normalisation discussion, the developmental-delay comparison, the head-motion analysis and the confound correlation values. The paper is unusually well supplied with methodological detail for its length, and the appendices carry material that would otherwise have been omitted. [RQ5.3] Published 2021/2023 by the Duke University Electrical and Computer Engineering department with the Duke Center for Autism and Brain Development and Duke Children's Primary Care - an engineering-psychiatry-primary care collaboration, funded by an NIH Autism Center of Excellence award, two further NIMH R01s, the Marcus and Simons Foundations, NSF, ONR and NGA, plus Apple, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services and Google. The framing is scalability of assessment: standardised observational assessment requires highly trained clinicians, manual facial coding from video is complex and time-intensive, and neither deploys at scale, so computer vision is proposed to make quantification universal. The positioning within the group's own programme is explicit and unusually candid - the paper states that it replicates the affect-related analysis of its own prior work on a larger dataset with redesigned stimuli, and then argues that the new complexity measure is 'an independent and more powerful measure' than the group's earlier one. Self-supersession of this kind is rare in this literature. The paper also carries an internal methodological critique of its own field, noting in a footnote that multiscale entropy is widely used in health research without addressing the across-subject comparability problem, with the result that 'often authors report lower MSE for data that is clearly more complex and vice-versa'. Commercially, this is one of the most conflicted studies in the corpus - several authors have licensed the underlying app technology to Apple and benefited financially - and it is also the only one to describe a structural mitigation, with data analysis independently reviewed throughout by a named conflict-free co-author. |
| S-104 | Cross-sectional multi-group classification study conducted by Nara Institute of Science and Technology with the psychiatry department of Nara Medical University and Osaka Psychiatric Medical Center, Japan. Two independent datasets were collected. Adults: 15 with autism (9 male, 6 female, aged 32.1 +/- 9.13), 15 with schizophrenia (7 male, 8 female, 26.0 +/- 5.85) and 16 controls (8 male, 8 female, 29.3 +/- 3.72), the controls reduced from 26 to equalise group sizes by ranking on SRS-2 score. Children: 15 with autism (13 male, 2 female, 10.9 +/- 1.39) and 15 controls (7 male, 8 female, 10.0 +/- 1.55), reduced from 17 the same way. Diagnoses followed DSM-5 research criteria and were re-evaluated with ADOS-2 for autism (adult mean total 46.5 +/- 11.9) and PANSS for schizophrenia (67.1 +/- 13.0); controls were interviewed by physicians and psychologists and excluded for any psychiatric history, drug abuse, epilepsy, learning delay or communication problems. Phenotyping was extensive - SRS-2 in both datasets, Kikuchi's Scale of Social Skills for adults, ADHD-RS and CBCL for children - but no IQ was measured, and the authors state the sample comprises only mild, high-functioning cases. Ethics approval came from committees at both institutions with informed consent obtained. | Participants completed the Facial Emotion Identification Test while gaze was recorded on a Tobii Pro Fusion at 120 Hz from approximately 65 cm. Each trial began with a one-second fixation cross, then a morphed facial expression of varying intensity was shown for 5 seconds, after which the participant named the emotion aloud; adults saw 21 images spanning seven emotions and children 32 spanning four. Fixations and saccades were classified by Tobii Pro Lab's I-VT algorithm at a 100 degrees per second threshold, with areas of interest on the eyes (up to the eyebrows), nose and mouth, redrawn per image because mouth size varies with expression. Scan-path length was computed in Python by an algorithm published as pseudocode. Trials with zero scan-path length were excluded and all retained data preserved at least 40% of gaze samples, with the resulting per-emotion trial counts listed exactly. Two per-trial classifiers were compared: a three-layer multilayer perceptron on the three scalar gaze features, and a two-layer CNN on a 34 x 34 greyscale gaze heat map paired with the stimulus image. The paper's contribution is the aggregation of the 21 or 32 per-trial decisions into a participant-level decision, either by unweighted hard voting or by a random forest that learns which stimuli matter - motivated by the prior finding that group differences in gaze vary by which emotion is presented. Evaluation used nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with the learning rate optimised in the inner loop, and every accuracy was tested against chance with a binomial test. | For autistic adults versus controls the weighted CNN reached 0.710 accuracy (sensitivity 0.733, specificity 0.688), significantly above chance (p < .05) and ten points above the unweighted CNN. For autistic children the weighted models reached 0.667 (weighted CNN sensitivity 0.600, specificity 0.733), significant (p < .05) and 16.7 points above the unweighted CNN, with weighting raising the CNN's sensitivity from 0.286 to 0.600. For schizophrenia versus controls the best models reached 0.645, only marginally above chance (p = 0.052), and weighting gave no improvement. The accompanying statistical analysis is the more substantial result. In adults, reduced fixation at the eyes separated the schizophrenia group from controls for every one of the seven emotions (p < .0001 to p < .01), but separated the autistic group from controls for only two (anger and neutral); conversely, scan-path length separated autism from controls for six of seven emotions and mouth fixation for five, neither of which distinguished schizophrenia at all. In children almost nothing was significant - only eye fixation for anger. Emotion recognition accuracy was essentially identical across all groups in both datasets (adults 15.5, 14.5 and 14.3 of 21; children 22.1 and 22.2 of 32), so the gaze differences occur without any difference in task success. Random-forest importances placed neutral faces highest for adult autism and surprise and anger highest for child autism, each converging with the significant statistical comparisons, while for schizophrenia the authors declined to interpret the ranking because eye fixation differed uniformly across all emotions. | Sample sizes of 30-31 per classification problem mean a single participant moves accuracy by roughly three points, so the 10-point and 16.7-point gains attributed to weighting correspond to about three and five people, and no confidence intervals are reported. Control groups were selected from larger pools by ranking on SRS-2, conditioning the sample on a variable related to the classified construct, with the direction of selection ambiguous from the text. The adult groups differ by up to six years in mean age with very different variances, the children's groups are 87% versus 47% male, and autistic children score more than twice as high on the ADHD Rating Scale as controls - an unaddressed attentional confound in a task whose outcome is where the eyes go. No IQ was measured, which the authors acknowledge, so intellectual level cannot be separated from diagnosis and the sample is explicitly high-functioning. The per-emotion statistical analysis that motivates the whole method treats individual trials as independent units in Welch's t-tests, though they cluster within participants at two or three trials per person per emotion, so those p-values are anticonservative even after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Japanese participants viewed the Western FEIT stimuli, an other-race configuration in a face-scanning task, without comment. And eight participants whose gaze never left the centre were misclassified by every model - correctly diagnosed in the error analysis as probable peripheral-vision users, but retained and unhandled. | Valuable to this review out of proportion to its accuracies, for four reasons. First, it is one of very few studies here with a psychiatric rather than merely neurotypical comparison group, and the parallel analysis against a shared control group produces a finding that bears on the whole corpus: reduced fixation at the eyes - the signature most eye-tracking autism studies are built on - separated schizophrenia from controls for all seven emotions but separated autism from controls for only two, while what distinguished autistic adults was longer scan paths and more mouth fixation. If reduced eye-looking is at least as characteristic of schizophrenia as of autism, then studies that classify autism against typically developing controls on that feature cannot claim to have found something autism-specific, and this study supplies direct evidence to that effect within one dataset and one paradigm. Second, its accuracies are what a properly conducted evaluation of gaze features in 30 people looks like: nested leave-one-participant-out cross-validation with the learning rate tuned in the inner loop, equalised group sizes so chance is 50%, and binomial tests against chance with the failing result left visible at p = 0.052. Placed beside the 90-plus figures reported elsewhere in this corpus from segment-level splits and in-sample thresholds, the contrast is instructive. Third, the paper's methodological proposal is transferable and is tested against its own ablation across three problems with an explanatory result: weighting per-stimulus decisions helps when group differences are selective across stimuli, as in autism, and is useless when they are uniform, as in schizophrenia - a more useful statement about when multi-stimulus aggregation should be weighted than any accuracy comparison here. Fourth, its error analysis identifies a failure mode intrinsic to the modality that no other study in this corpus reports: a subset of participants complete the task using peripheral vision without moving their eyes, are misclassified by every model, and cannot be detected as non-compliant because their recognition scores are normal - affecting 6.5% of adults and 17% of children. Finally, the equivalence of FEIT recognition scores across all groups, with gaze differing but task performance identical, is a clean demonstration that the measured behaviour is a viewing strategy rather than a competence difference. | [RQ1.1] Two independent datasets and three diagnostic groups. Adults: 15 with autism (9 male, 6 female), 15 with schizophrenia (7 male, 8 female) and 16 controls (8 male, 8 female), the latter selected from 26 available controls in order to equalise group sizes, with the selection made by ranking on SRS-2 score in descending order. Children: 15 with autism (13 male, 2 female) and 15 controls (7 male, 8 female), again reduced from 17 by SRS-2 ranking. The presence of a schizophrenia group is what distinguishes this sample from almost every other in the corpus: it supplies a psychiatric rather than merely a neurotypical contrast, and although no autism-versus-schizophrenia classifier is built, the parallel analyses against a common control group produce the study's most useful finding. Note also that the modelled unit is the trial rather than the participant - each adult contributes 21 trials and each child 32 - but the cross-validation splits by participant, so the two levels are handled correctly in the modelling even though the statistical analysis treats trials as independent. [RQ1.2] 'People with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)' and 'people with schizophrenia (Sz)' predominate, person-first, with 'the ASDs' and 'the Szs' appearing as shorthand in the participants section and 'disorder groups' used throughout as the collective term for the clinical samples. The register is clinical-psychiatric and uses 'abnormalities' freely - 'ASD and Sz have abnormalities in cognitive functions, particularly social cognitive functions', 'abnormalities in eye movement during facial expression recognition have also been reported' - and 'atypical gaze patterns' and 'social cognitive deficits' elsewhere. Autism is described as 'a neurodevelopmental disorder, meaning that it does not appear in adulthood but is an innate trait', which is an accurate developmental statement rather than a deficit claim. One passage is notably person-centred in a way the corpus rarely manages: the introduction explains that some people 'have spent their childhood without being diagnosed with ASD' and that in adulthood 'difficulties in real social life may become emerged', sometimes with secondary depressive states leading to a first psychiatric presentation - a description of late diagnosis framed around the person's experience rather than around missed screening opportunities. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement, but there is also no burden or cost rhetoric and no overstated claim. [RQ1.3] Reported per group in two tables and more completely than most in this corpus, though with gaps. Adults: n and sex ratio, age, Kikuchi's Scale of Social Skills 18-item, SRS-2, FEIT score, ADOS-2 and PANSS as applicable. Children: n and sex ratio, age, SRS-2, FEIT score, ADHD-RS and CBCL. Three imbalances are visible and none is adjusted. The adult groups span six years of mean age (Sz 26.0 +/- 5.85, control 29.3 +/- 3.72, ASD 32.1 +/- 9.13) with very different variances, and age affects both gaze behaviour and face processing. The children's groups differ sharply in sex - 13:2 male:female in the autistic group against 7:8 in controls, so 87% versus 47% male - which is the largest sex imbalance in a matched-design study charted here. And autistic children scored more than twice as high on the ADHD Rating Scale as controls (17.6 +/- 10.2 versus 6.88 +/- 9.40), so attentional difficulty is confounded with diagnosis in a task whose outcome is where the eyes go. Not measured at all: IQ, which the authors identify as a limitation and which matters because they characterise the sample as high-functioning without being able to quantify it; and race or ethnicity, relevant here because Japanese participants viewed the FEIT's Western facial stimuli, an other-race configuration that goes unremarked. What is unusually well reported is the phenotypic battery: SRS-2 in both datasets, ADOS-2 totals for autistic adults, PANSS for schizophrenia, plus social-skills and behaviour-checklist measures, with a clear explanation of why SRS-2 was not administered to the schizophrenia group. [RQ1.4] Among the strongest in this review, and the only one applying condition-specific re-evaluation to two different diagnoses. Diagnoses were determined according to DSM-5 research criteria and then re-evaluated with the appropriate instrument: ADOS-2 for the autistic participants, with the adult group's mean total raw score reported (46.5 +/- 11.9), and the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale for the schizophrenia group (67.1 +/- 13.0). Controls were not merely assumed neurotypical but were actively screened - 'physicians and psychologists interviewed them and excluded' anyone with learning delays or communication problems, and no control had a history of psychiatric disorder, drug abuse or epilepsy. So all three groups have an explicit ascertainment procedure, the two clinical groups have quantified symptom measures, and the control group has a stated exclusion protocol applied by clinicians. The residual gaps are minor by comparison: no inter-rater reliability is reported for the ADOS-2 or PANSS administrations, no interval between diagnosis and testing is given, and the ADOS-2 figures are total raw scores rather than calibrated severity scores, which limits comparability with other studies. [RQ1.5] Rich on symptom severity and empty on cognition - an unusual combination in this corpus, where the reverse is more common. Severity and phenotype are measured with four or five instruments per dataset. Adults: SRS-2 total raw score (control 55.2 +/- 20.9, ASD 73.3 +/- 36.0 - note the very large SD in the autistic group, indicating wide variation in social-communication severity), ADOS-2 (46.5 +/- 11.9), PANSS for the schizophrenia group (67.1 +/- 13.0), and Kikuchi's Scale of Social Skills 18-item (control 64.7 +/- 11.0, ASD 45.3 +/- 9.46, Sz 59.1 +/- 9.14, so the autistic group scores lowest on self-reported social skill). Children: SRS-2 (control 19.2 +/- 11.5, ASD 74.7 +/- 26.9 - a very wide separation), ADHD-RS and CBCL. SRS-2 was deliberately not administered to the schizophrenia group because it has not been validated in that population, an omission explained rather than glossed. Against this, no IQ or developmental measure was obtained for anyone. The authors state the limitation squarely: participants were recruited without intellectual difficulties but 'we did not obtain any actual IQ values', so the study 'does not adequately take into account the influence of intellectual level', and the sample comprises 'only a small number of mild (high-functioning) cases'. Two consequences follow. Because the FEIT is a cognitive task with a correct answer, intellectual level plausibly affects both recognition accuracy and viewing strategy. And because SRS-2 was used to select which controls were retained, a severity-related variable enters the sampling as well as the description. Notably, no analysis relates any of these severity scores to model output, so the rich phenotyping is used descriptively rather than analytically. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to test whether modelling the specificity of gaze to particular facial expressions improves classification, on the premise - supported by prior basic research but not previously operationalised - that groups differ in gaze for some emotions and not others. The proposal is to classify each of the 21 or 32 FEIT images separately and then aggregate the per-image decisions with a random forest that learns which images matter, rather than by unweighted voting. Findings, all reported with binomial tests against chance and none oversold. For autistic adults versus controls the weighted CNN reached 0.710 accuracy (sensitivity 0.733, specificity 0.688), significantly above chance and 10 points above the unweighted CNN. For autistic children the weighted models reached 0.667 (weighted CNN sensitivity 0.600, specificity 0.733), significant and 16.7 points above the unweighted CNN, with the weighting raising sensitivity from 0.286 to 0.600. For schizophrenia the best models reached 0.645, only marginally above chance (p = 0.052), and weighting produced no improvement at all. The statistical analysis explains why the method behaves differently across conditions and is the more interesting result: in adults, reduced fixation at the eyes distinguished the schizophrenia group from controls for every one of the seven emotions, but the autistic group from controls for only two (anger and neutral), while scan-path length distinguished autism from controls for six of seven emotions. So the classic reduced-eye-looking signature was present uniformly in schizophrenia and only selectively in autism - which is exactly the condition under which per-image weighting helps for one and not the other. In children, almost no gaze feature reached significance at all, yet the weighted models still exceeded chance. [RQ2.2] Single-country, clinic-linked laboratory testing in Nara and Osaka, Japan, with participants recruited through the psychiatry department of Nara Medical University School of Medicine and Osaka Psychiatric Medical Center and tested on equipment at the Nara Institute of Science and Technology. The setting is a controlled screen-based assessment at a fixed 65 cm viewing distance rather than a naturalistic or point-of-care one, and no deployment scenario is proposed. Recruitment geometry is the standard clinical case-control arrangement, with the important qualification that both clinical groups come from psychiatric services and both are contrasted against the same actively screened control group, which is what makes the parallel comparison meaningful. One setting-related feature is unaddressed: the FEIT is a Western instrument and the participants are Japanese, so every trial involves other-race face processing, in a task whose entire outcome is where on a face the participant looks. Cross-cultural differences in face-scanning are well documented and the paper does not mention them. [RQ2.3] The Facial Emotion Identification Test, a validated instrument that uses morphing to generate expressions at varying intensity, including deliberately weak ones - which is central to the paper's argument, since the finding it converges on concerns subtle rather than prototypical expressions. Each trial: a one-second central fixation cross, then a face for 5 seconds, then a verbal response naming the emotion. Adults saw 21 images (three each of happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust, neutral) and children 32 (eight each of happiness, sadness, anger, surprise), all in random order. Three properties make this among the better paradigms in the corpus. It has an objectively correct answer on every trial, so task performance and gaze behaviour are separately measurable - and the result is striking: FEIT scores were essentially identical across groups (adults 15.5, 14.5 and 14.3 out of 21 for controls, autism and schizophrenia; children 22.1 and 22.2 out of 32), meaning the groups recognised the emotions equally well while looking at the faces differently. Any gaze difference therefore cannot be attributed to differential task success. The stimulus set is systematically structured by emotion, which is what makes per-image weighting meaningful and interpretable rather than an arbitrary ensemble. And the one-second fixation cross standardises the starting gaze position across trials and participants, so scan-path measures begin from a common origin. The paradigm's limitations are the short trial (5 seconds, giving at most 600 gaze samples), the static stimuli, and the copyright restriction that prevents the images being reproduced or shared. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session per participant, no follow-up and no test-retest reliability for any gaze feature. The two datasets are age-stratified rather than longitudinal - adults and children are separate samples, not the same people at two ages - although the introduction motivates the design partly by an interest in 'the developmental trajectory in processing emotional stimuli in neurodevelopmental conditions', and the parallel analysis does permit a cautious comparison across age groups, which the discussion makes: anger is highly weighted in both the adult and child autism models, suggesting a possible common specificity. Ethics reporting is complete for approval and consent: the data collection was approved by ethics committees at both Nara Medical University and Nara Institute of Science and Technology, the procedure was explained at the start of recording and informed consent obtained, and the formal ethics statement records written informed consent from participants' legal guardian or next of kin. Funding from a single CREST grant is stated, and competing interests are declared as none. [RQ2.5] A Tobii Pro Fusion eye tracker sampling at 120 Hz, with participants seated approximately 65 cm from a 1920 x 1080 display. Fixation and saccade classification used Tobii Pro Lab version 1.145 with its attention filter and the I-VT velocity-threshold algorithm, with the threshold stated explicitly at 100 degrees per second - a level of specificity about event detection that most eye-tracking papers in this corpus omit entirely, and one that matters because fixation counts are meaningless without it. Areas of interest were drawn on the eyes (extending up to the eyebrows), nose and mouth, and were redrawn for each image because mouth size varies with expression, which prevents a systematic bias in mouth-region measurement across emotions. Scan-path length was computed in Python with an algorithm published as pseudocode that segments rather than bridges invalid samples. Modelling used PyTorch with fully tabulated architectures. Clinical instruments: ADOS-2, PANSS, SRS-2, Kikuchi's Scale of Social Skills 18-item, ADHD-RS and CBCL. No calibration procedure is described. [RQ2.6] Among the best-specified studies in the review. Reproducible from the text: the full instrument battery per group, the FEIT protocol with image counts per emotion and exact trial timing, the eye tracker and sampling rate, the viewing distance, the I-VT algorithm with its velocity threshold, the area-of-interest definitions and the per-image redrawing rule, both trial-exclusion rules with the resulting per-emotion trial counts listed exactly, the scan-path computation as pseudocode, both model architectures in a table giving neuron counts and kernel sizes and channel counts, the optimiser, loss function, epoch cap and early-stopping patience, the heat-map construction including the Gaussian sigma and the 34 x 34 centre-cropped downscaling, the three-step strategy adopted specifically because the dataset is small, and the nested leave-one-participant-out scheme with its 8:2 inner split. Statistical procedures are equally explicit, including Welch's t-test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Not available: code, and the FEIT images, which are under copyright and could not even be reproduced as figures. Raw data are offered on request without undue reservation. [RQ2.7] The three stated limitations are well chosen and one is a genuine contribution. Small sample size is acknowledged first. The IQ limitation is stated with unusual candour - participants were recruited without intellectual difficulties but no actual values were obtained, so the study 'does not adequately take into account the influence of intellectual level', and the sample is 'only a small number of mild (high-functioning) cases'. Most valuable is the error analysis, which is the kind of work almost no study in this corpus performs: the authors identified the eight participants misclassified by all four models, inspected their raw data, found that their gaze did not move from the centre at all, checked whether they had simply not engaged with the task, and found that their FEIT recognition scores were normal (18 and 19 of 21 for two autistic adults; 19, 25, 22 and 17 of 32 for four autistic children). The conclusion - that some people complete the task using peripheral vision without moving their eyes - identifies a failure mode intrinsic to gaze-based assessment, quantifies it at 6.5% of adults and 17% of children, and names it as a target for future work. Unstated limitations remain. The statistical analysis treats trials as independent when they cluster within participants at roughly two or three per person per emotion, so Welch's t-tests on 101-172 trials overstate the effective sample size. Control selection by SRS-2 ranking introduces a construct-related variable into the sampling, and the direction of the selection is ambiguous from the text. The adult groups differ by up to six years in mean age and the children's groups by 40 percentage points in sex ratio, neither adjusted. Autistic children scored more than twice as high on the ADHD Rating Scale as controls, an unaddressed comorbidity confound in a gaze task. And Japanese participants viewed Western faces without comment. [RQ2.9] Three directions, each tied to a specific finding. Collect more data to establish validity, the standard response to a small sample. Develop a method that works for participants whose gaze barely moves - which follows directly from the error analysis and is a real methodological problem rather than a generic wish, since a gaze-based classifier that fails on 17% of children because they use peripheral vision has a systematic blind spot that more data alone will not close. And obtain actual IQ values and other individual characteristics so that the relationship between the model and the heterogeneity of the conditions can be examined - an acknowledgement that a high-functioning sample of 15 cannot speak for a spectrum. Not proposed, and worth noting: a direct autism-versus-schizophrenia classifier, which the dataset already supports and which would be the natural differential-diagnosis test; and validation on an independent cohort. [RQ3.1] Visual attention during facial emotion recognition, measured in three ways and analysed separately for each emotion presented. Fixation counts within anatomically defined areas of interest - the eyes region extending up to the eyebrows, the nose and the mouth - index where attention is allocated on the face. Saccade counts index how often gaze shifts. Scan-path length, defined as the mean displacement between consecutive gaze samples, indexes how far and how restlessly the eyes travel. The paper's behavioural hypothesis is the one the field takes for granted, that autistic people look less at the eyes; its finding is that this holds much more clearly for schizophrenia than for autism in these data. In adults, fixation at the eyes separated the schizophrenia group from controls for all seven emotions with p values from .0001 to .01, but separated the autistic group from controls for only two of seven (anger and neutral). What did separate autistic adults from controls, across six of seven emotions, was scan-path length - they moved their gaze further per sample. Fixation at the mouth separated autism from controls for five of seven emotions but never separated schizophrenia from controls. So the two conditions produce distinguishable gaze signatures: schizophrenia is characterised by uniformly reduced eye-region fixation, autism by increased mouth fixation and longer scan paths that vary with the expression shown. In children, almost nothing reached significance - only eye fixation for anger. A secondary behaviour is measured and turns out to be null: emotion recognition accuracy, which was essentially identical across all groups in both datasets, so the gaze differences occur without any difference in task success. [RQ3.2] No cross-sensor fusion, but two forms of within-study integration are central to the design. The first is the CNN's dual input: the gaze heat map is presented alongside the stimulus image, so the network can 'explicitly learn the facial regions and expressions' rather than treating gaze positions as coordinates divorced from what was at those coordinates. Since the same 21 or 32 images are shown to every participant, the image channel functions as a conditioning signal identifying which trial the heat map came from. The second, and the paper's actual contribution, is the aggregation layer: each of the 21 or 32 trials is classified independently and the per-trial decisions are then combined either by unweighted hard voting or by a random forest that learns which stimuli to trust. That is a form of stimulus-level fusion, and unlike most fusion claims in this corpus it is tested against its own ablation across three separate problems with informative results - weighting adds 10 points for autistic adults and 16.7 for autistic children but nothing for schizophrenia. The differential outcome is explained mechanistically rather than left as a number: weighting helps precisely when group differences are selective across stimuli, and is useless when they are uniform. That is a more transferable finding about when multi-stimulus aggregation should be weighted than any of the accuracy comparisons in this review. [RQ4.1] Deliberately small models with a classical aggregation layer, and the modesty is justified rather than incidental. The per-trial classifiers are a three-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron with five neurons per layer, taking three scalar gaze features, and a two-convolutional-layer CNN with 3 x 3 kernels and 8 and 16 channels plus one fully connected layer, taking a 34 x 34 greyscale heat map and the stimulus image. The authors describe a three-step strategy adopted explicitly because the dataset is small: downscale the images to 34 x 34 greyscale after centre-cropping, reduce the CNN to two layers plus one fully connected layer, and use leave-one-participant-out cross-validation to maximise training data. Above the per-trial classifier sits the paper's contribution, an aggregation over the 21 or 32 per-trial decisions by either hard voting or a random forest, the latter learning which stimuli should count. Training used Adam with cross-entropy loss, a 300-epoch cap and early stopping after 15 epochs without validation improvement, with the learning rate optimised inside the nested cross-validation. The authors also justify not using a support vector machine, on the grounds that the per-fold sample size of 630 or 651 trials is adequate relative to a cited prior study - an argument about sample adequacy rather than an unexamined preference for deep learning. [RQ4.2] Two parallel representations, compared directly. The baseline uses three interpretable scalars per trial: number of fixations, number of saccades and scan-path length.
