Low-level response to joint attention is the ability to follow and sustain attention on an object indicated near the child. High-level response requires following an indication to an object across the room, so the child must physically turn. The interpretability analysis then characterises what the model responded to in exactly these terms, and the descriptions are specific enough to be checked against the construct: comparison children showed the triadic shift in IJA while autistic children fixated neither toy nor examiner; comparison children sustained gaze on the indicated toy in low-level RJA while autistic children glanced briefly then looked away; comparison children turned immediately to the distant poster in high-level RJA and then back to the examiner as if seeking approval, while autistic children responded slowly or not at all. Two secondary behaviours are also measured. Task compliance across repeated trials, from which the authors establish that both groups habituate and that autistic children specifically disengage at the start of RJA tasks. And, implicitly, gaze itself - the Grad-CAM heatmaps localise to face and eyes - measured from ordinary video without an eye tracker, which is the study's quiet technical achievement. [RQ3.2] No cross-sensor fusion; a single camera. Two forms of internal integration are central. Architecturally, spatial features from a CNN are combined with temporal modelling by an LSTM and an attention mechanism over frames, so the system represents both what is in each frame and when in the sequence it matters - and the interpretability analysis exploits this composition directly, using attention weights to find the informative time points and Grad-CAM to localise within them, which is a genuinely joint spatial-temporal explanation rather than two separate ones. Conceptually, three separate task-specific models are built rather than one fused model, and the comparison across them is where the study's substantive findings lie: all three tasks detect autism near-perfectly, but only IJA carries severity information, and high-level RJA improves with age. Treating the three joint attention subtypes as separate models and comparing them, rather than pooling all video into one classifier, is what allows the paper to say something about which behaviour matters for which question - a design choice more informative than a fusion gain would have been. The unexploited channel is the compliance score, which is computed for every trial, shown to differ between groups in a diagnostically interesting way, and then used only descriptively rather than as a model input or covariate. [RQ4.1] A single custom architecture combining a convolutional neural network for spatial features, a long short-term memory network for temporal sequence modelling, and an attention mechanism over frames, applied end-to-end to raw video with no hand-crafted features, pose estimation or gaze tracking. The rationale for each component is given: the CNN for frame-level spatial content, the LSTM because it 'was developed to better process sequential data' and the video is time-dependent, and attention to make it possible 'to access and visualize the attention weights across each video sequence according to which frames or video time points contributed most to the model's decision-making' - so the attention mechanism is included at least partly for interpretability rather than purely for performance, which is a defensible and unusual justification. Three separate models are trained, one per joint attention task, with input dimensions matched to task duration (300 frames for the 10-second IJA clips, 150 for the 5-second RJA clips). No alternative architectures or baselines are compared, and no ablation of the CNN, LSTM or attention components is reported, so the contribution of each is unestablished. Grad-CAM, attention plots and agglomerative hierarchical clustering complete the analysis pipeline. [RQ4.2] Raw RGB video frames at 224 x 224, in sequences of 300 (IJA) or 150 (RJA) - a fully end-to-end representation with no intermediate abstraction whatsoever. This is a stronger commitment to learned representation than any other study in this corpus, most of which extract landmarks, poses, gaze coordinates or hand-crafted statistics before modelling. It has two consequences that pull in opposite directions. It removes an entire class of failure - no landmark detector to fail on a child who turns away, no gaze estimator to calibrate, no feature engineering to bias - and it is what allows the same pipeline to work on a task where the child physically turns around, which a face-based method could not handle. But it also means the model has access to everything in the frame: the child's appearance, clothing, posture, the examiner, the room, and anything that co-varies with recruitment site. With autistic children recruited exclusively from one hospital clinic and comparison children from day care centres, and with a 44-50 point IQ difference between groups, an end-to-end model on raw frames has many routes to near-perfect separation that have nothing to do with joint attention. The Grad-CAM analysis is the study's answer to this, and it is a good one as far as it goes - the heatmaps localise to faces and eyes and the described behaviours match the constructs - but it is illustrative rather than systematic, and no quantitative check on background or appearance confounds is reported. [RQ4.3] AUROC, accuracy, precision and recall, each with 95% confidence intervals estimated by the Hanley and McNeil method, reported for all three tasks in both the detection and severity problems - twenty-four interval-bounded estimates, and the most complete uncertainty reporting in this review. That completeness is a direct consequence of adopting the STARD reporting guideline and publishing in a journal that enforces it, and it makes the results checkable in a way that most of this corpus is not. The gaps are nonetheless significant for a diagnostic study. Specificity is never reported, which is an odd omission under STARD and matters because precision and recall alone do not characterise false-positive behaviour at a given prevalence; for the detection models precision is 95.5-98.9% at roughly balanced prevalence, so specificity is evidently high, but it should have been stated. No negative predictive value, no calibration, and no prevalence-adjusted predictive value are given, although the proposed use is referral support in a population where autism prevalence is a few per cent rather than 47%. For the three-class severity problem the class distribution is not reported, so the reader cannot compute a chance baseline, and no baseline is offered. And no permutation test or majority-class comparison accompanies the near-ceiling detection figures. [RQ4.4] The most thorough interpretability work in this review, and unusually it is used to verify the model's reasoning against an independent clinical account rather than to generate a post-hoc narrative. Three techniques operate in sequence. Attention weights across the frame sequence identify which time points drove the decision, plotted per participant. Grad-CAM is then applied specifically at those attention peaks, localising the spatially informative regions within the frames that mattered - so the spatial and temporal explanations are coupled rather than independent. Agglomerative hierarchical clustering of attention-weight trajectories across the test set, displayed as dendrograms with participant identifiers alongside the heatmaps, tests whether the model's temporal decision patterns cluster by class at the dataset level rather than only in selected examples. The results are behaviourally specific and, crucially, match the constructs the tasks were designed to elicit: triadic gaze shifting in IJA, sustained versus fleeting gaze on the indicated object in low-level RJA, and immediate turning with a return to the examiner in high-level RJA. The authors' claim that the system 'made predictions based on salient behavioral differences... in the same way trained specialists diagnose ASD' is therefore supported by evidence rather than asserted. The cluster maps also corroborate the quantitative severity finding independently, showing IJA separating the three severity classes more cleanly than the RJA tasks. Two limits remain. Grad-CAM and attention illustrations are presented for selected participants and time points, so they demonstrate that the model can attend to the right things without establishing that it always does. And no quantitative test rules out appearance, background or site confounds, which an end-to-end model on raw frames from differently recruited groups is exposed to. [RQ4.5] Correctly constructed at the split, and this deserves explicit credit: 'we used 10-fold group-wise (by individual) cross-validation', stated unambiguously, so all clips from a child fall in the same fold and no participant contributes to both training and testing. That is exactly the safeguard most of this corpus omits, and it matters here because each child supplies up to ten IJA and five RJA clips from a single continuous session, which under clip-level splitting would be near-duplicates. Confidence intervals are computed by a named method and reported for every metric, and the classification threshold is fixed at 0.5 rather than tuned. Within its own terms the evaluation is therefore sound, and the near-perfect detection figures cannot be attributed to participant leakage. The problem lies upstream, in what the evaluation is an evaluation of. The paper states that conservative criteria were used deliberately 'to select individuals belonging to clinically distinct groups to ensure development of an accurate and precise ASD vs TD classification model', and the participant table shows a 44-50 point IQ gap at p < .001 with an autism sample that is 62% preverbal or single-word. Separating those two groups is a far easier problem than the clinical question, and AUROCs of 99.5-99.8% are the expected result rather than a surprising one - so the honest reading is that the study demonstrates the protocol and pipeline work, not that the system would perform at this level on the children a referral tool would actually see. The severity analysis inherits the same issue in a specific form: its three classes include non-autism, so a large part of its 90.3% AUROC is the already-solved detection problem, and because no autism-only result is reported there is no evidence that the system grades severity within the spectrum. Further gaps: no external validation, which the authors acknowledge; no clinical comparison group; no specificity; no class distribution for the severity bands and hence no chance baseline; and no adjustment for the IQ difference despite ANCOVA being straightforward and the authors demonstrably comfortable with mixed ANOVA elsewhere in the paper. The corrective study is well specified by the authors themselves - an IQ-matched external cohort - and would be worth considerably more than the present numbers. [RQ5.1] No formal keyword list is carried in the retrieved text; the article is categorised under Psychiatry as an Original Investigation. Governing terms in the title and body: joint attention, deep learning, detection, symptom severity assessment, behavioural biomarker, explainable AI, initiation of joint attention, response to joint attention, Early Social Communication Scales, compliance score, Grad-CAM, attention weights, hierarchical clustering, digitalized measurement. The framing vocabulary is diagnostic-clinical rather than engineering - 'diagnostic study', 'criterion standard diagnostic tool', 'predictive performance' - and 'screening' appears only in reference to the K-CARS-2 stage. [RQ5.2] JAMA Network Open 6(5):e2315174, published 25 May 2023, accepted 10 April 2023, open access under CC-BY, with a correction issued 7 July 2023 for an author contact detail. This is the highest-profile clinical venue of any study in the corpus and the venue standards are visible throughout: adherence to the STARD reporting guideline is declared, the participant table carries formal group comparisons with p values for every characteristic, every performance metric is reported with a 95% confidence interval computed by a named method, funder role and author contributions are itemised, competing interests including issued patents are disclosed in full, and a data sharing statement is provided. Two supplements carry the enrolment flow diagram, task and acquisition procedures, compliance metric, architecture diagram, training and validation performance, age-stratified results and all interpretability figures. The contrast with the conference-proceedings papers elsewhere in this corpus is instructive: the same underlying study reported at a workshop would have shown none of the participant characterisation that makes its IQ confound visible. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 by the Department of Biomedical Systems Informatics at Yonsei University College of Medicine with the Division of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry at Seoul National University College of Medicine and LumanLab Inc, funded by an MD-PhD Physician-Scientist Training Program grant from the Korea Health Industry Development Institute. The framing is a critique of the existing computational literature rather than of clinical practice, and it is one of the sharpest such critiques in the corpus: prior autism-detection models are said to be unsuitable for tool development because of 'a lack of automation, the requirements for specialized and expensive equipment, calibration, trained personnel, dependence on human rating of autistic behaviors, and low precision and recall', with the low performance attributed to the absence of targeted behavioural biomarkers and of methods for quantitatively measuring hallmark autism behaviours. The response - instrument an already-validated clinical construct with a replicable protocol and a consumer camera, rather than search for a statistical signature in whatever data are available - is the study's real contribution and is a template the rest of this literature could usefully follow. Two contextual features should be carried into the synthesis. This is one of very few studies here whose autistic sample is predominantly minimally verbal with mean IQ in the 50s, a population systematically excluded elsewhere by paradigms requiring screen attention or conversation - and simultaneously the study whose groups differ most on IQ, so the two facts are the same fact. And the method is patented by its authors with a commercial entity involved in data management, disclosed fully but without the independent-analysis safeguard reported by the Duke group elsewhere in this corpus. |
| S-107 | Secondary computational analysis of a public eye-tracking scanpath image dataset, conducted at Vellore Institute of Technology in India with no new data collection. The dataset comprises 547 visualised scanpath images from 59 children, distributed as two folders - one for typically developing children and one for children diagnosed with autism. Nothing further about the participants is reported: no ages, no sexes, no group sizes, no IQ, no language level, no severity, no comorbidity, and no diagnostic instrument, criteria or clinician. The eliciting task, stimuli, eye tracker and the scheme by which gaze data were rendered into images are likewise not described. The images were split once into 382 training (70%), 108 validation (20%) and 57 test (10%), with the image as the unit of splitting; since 59 children produced 547 images, roughly nine per child, each test image is accompanied by around eight images from the same child in the training and validation sets. The test-set confusion matrix implies 34 typically developing and 23 autism images among the 57 held out. No ethics, funding or competing-interests statement appears. | Images were converted from RGBA to RGB and then handled along two paths. For a custom convolutional network they were resized to 100x100 and converted to greyscale using the standard luminance weighting, a choice adopted after RGB training proved slow and greyscale was observed to improve accuracy. That network has five levels - 16, 32, 64 and 128 3x3 filters with ReLU and 2x2 max pooling, then flatten to 2048, dense layers of 256 and 128, and a sigmoid output over two classes - and was trained with Adam at learning rate 0.001, binary cross-entropy loss, batch size 64 and 15 epochs. For the proposed pipeline, images were resized to 299x299 with pixel values normalised to [-1, 1] and passed through ImageNet-pretrained InceptionV3, with a 2048-dimensional feature vector taken from the last convolutional layer immediately before global average pooling on the stated rationale that layers near the classifier head carry the most distinctive representations. Those features were fed either to logistic regression or to a two-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron with 200 and 100 neurons. All implementation used TensorFlow on Google Colab. Evaluation was on the single fixed 57-image test set with accuracy, per-class precision, recall and F1, confusion matrices and ROC curves. | The custom CNN reached 71.9% accuracy, InceptionV3 features with logistic regression 78.9%, and InceptionV3 features with an MLP 81.0%. The per-class results are more informative than the headline figures and the authors report them prominently. The custom CNN classified 30 of 34 typically developing images correctly but only 11 of 23 autism images, giving class-wise recall of 0.88 versus 0.48 and F1 of 0.79 versus 0.58 - so a model reported at 71.9% accuracy detected fewer than half the autism cases, below the 59.6% majority-class baseline implied by the same matrix, and the authors state that its 'ability to classify the people affected by ASD was not upto the mark'. Both transfer-learning models were substantially more balanced: logistic regression achieved class-wise precision 0.84/0.72, recall 0.79/0.78 and F1 0.82/0.75, and the MLP 0.83/0.77, 0.85/0.74 and 0.84/0.76. ROC curves are plotted for both but no AUC value is quoted. The conclusion attributes the modest overall accuracy to the dataset containing only 547 images and proposes augmentation and dataset expansion. | The 547 images were split by image rather than by child, so with roughly nine images per child each test image has about eight siblings in training - the same leakage route that recurs across reuses of this dataset. The single fixed split leaves 57 test images with no cross-validation and no confidence intervals, so the 81.0% versus 78.9% comparison the paper draws corresponds to about one image, and no majority-class baseline is computed against an implied 59.6% floor. Greyscale conversion was adopted partly because it improved accuracy on this same data. Nothing at all is reported about the 59 children - no demographics, no clinical characteristics, no group sizes, and no diagnostic procedure - so the quantity being predicted is defined only by folder membership. The task that generated the gaze data is never described, so the paper's own rationale about looking at eyes and mouths cannot be connected to its data. And because the input is a rendered picture rather than a gaze time series, incidental graphical properties such as plotted extent, ink density and line-crossing count are available to the models and indistinguishable from behavioural signal, a question no interpretability analysis addresses. The authors state one limitation - the small dataset - and state it correctly. | The value of this study to the review is comparative rather than evidential. It is the fourth independent reuse of the 547-image scanpath dataset encountered here, and it is the one that reports the lowest accuracy: 81.0% at best, against roughly 97% and 99% reported by other groups on the identical images. Crucially, it shares the same methodological flaw as those higher-scoring reuses - splitting by image rather than by child, so that each of 59 children's roughly nine images straddle the split - yet does not achieve their results. The most plausible reading is that generic ImageNet features passed to a shallow classifier extract less individual-identity information from a rendered trajectory than an end-to-end network trained or fine-tuned on the same images, which means the gap between this paper and the higher-scoring ones is itself evidence about how much of those figures reflects within-child similarity rather than diagnostic signal. Read alongside the source authors' own participant-level correction to around 71% and another group's one-image-per-child leave-one-out figure of 72.88%, this study's 81% sits nearer the defensible end of the range. Two further observations are worth carrying forward. Its per-class reporting demonstrates concretely why aggregate accuracy is inadequate in this literature: a model reported at 71.9% detected 48% of autism cases, a fact visible only because the authors published the confusion matrix and reasoned explicitly that accuracy 'does not give much importance to the class imbalance'. And its recommendation to use generative adversarial networks to expand the dataset should be flagged as a hazard rather than a remedy, since synthesising images from a 547-image corpus and then evaluating on an image-level split would deepen the dependence between training and test data while making it harder to see. | [RQ1.1] Fifty-nine children contributing 547 scanpath images - the fourth independent reuse of this dataset encountered in this review. The study reports nothing further about who those children were: no counts per group, no ages, no sex, no diagnostic information. The dataset is described purely as two folders, 'TCImages' for typically developing children and 'TSImages' for children diagnosed with autism. The modelled unit is the image, and the split is 382 training, 108 validation and 57 test images with no indication that a child's images were kept together. Because 547 images come from 59 children, each child contributes roughly nine images, so under a random image-level split every test image is accompanied by around eight images from the same child in training or validation. The test-set confusion matrix implies 34 typically developing and 23 autism images among the 57 held out, which is the only class-composition information recoverable anywhere in the paper. [RQ1.2] 'Children with autism spectrum disorder' and 'ASD child' are used alongside 'normal child' and 'TD child', with the autism/normal contrast appearing repeatedly - 'the gaze patterns of a normal child and a child affected with autism', 'differentiate between a TD child and an ASD child'. The framing is medical-model and at times stronger than the evidence warrants: autism is 'a medical condition which is a result of abnormal brain development', characterised by 'abnormal behaviours' and 'fixation abnormality'. Autistic children are described as people who 'refrain from expressing their feeling in the form of facial expressions' and who 'indulge in various repetitive behaviours'. The intent is plainly not hostile - the paper's motivation is that the existing diagnostic process 'consumes a lot of time and energy of both the children and parents' - but the vocabulary of abnormality is used without qualification and the 'normal' contrast term is the one this review has flagged elsewhere as carrying an implication that 'typically developing' does not. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. [RQ1.3] None whatsoever. Not a single demographic or clinical characteristic of the 59 children is reported - no age, no sex, no IQ, no language level, no severity, no comorbidity, no socioeconomic status, no race or ethnicity, and not even the number of children or images in each group. The paper's participant description consists entirely of two folder names. This is the most complete absence of participant information among the included studies, and it follows from the study's nature as a pure dataset-reuse exercise: the authors downloaded images and classified them. The consequence is that nothing can be said about who the model works for, whether the groups were matched on anything, or whether the classification could be driven by an age or sex imbalance between folders - questions that a reader must go to the original dataset publication to answer, and which this paper does not flag as open. [RQ1.4] Absent. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, clinician or process is reported for the 59 children, and the labels are taken directly from the folder structure of the downloaded dataset. The introduction does contain a description of how autism is diagnosed in general practice - initial concern about developmental milestones, paediatrician assessment, referral to a psychologist, child neurologist, speech and language pathologist or developmental paediatrician, then behavioural observation, child and parent interviews, questionnaires and the CARS rating scale - and it correctly observes that 'there are no standard definitive tests like blood test to identify the condition'. But none of this is connected to the actual data. The target being predicted is therefore whichever folder an image sits in, and the study inherits without examination whatever ascertainment the source dataset applied. For a review comparing studies partly on the strength of their reference standards, this is the floor. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure appears, and none could, since no participants were assessed by these authors. The absence has a specific analytical cost in this design: the scanpath is a picture of where a child looked during an unreported task, and how much a child looks at all - the number of fixations, the spatial extent covered - varies with attention, developmental level and task compliance. Without any measure of those, a difference in the visual density or spread of the plotted trajectory cannot be separated from a difference in social attention. Since the models are given only the drawing, this is precisely the ambiguity that an interpretability analysis would have addressed, and none is performed. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to use eye-tracking scanpath images 'as a biological indicator to identify children with autism' and to compare a transfer-learning-plus-classical-classifier pipeline against an end-to-end custom CNN. Findings: the custom CNN reached 71.9% accuracy, InceptionV3 features with logistic regression 78.9%, and InceptionV3 features with an MLP 81.0%. The per-class analysis is the substantive result and the authors present it properly rather than resting on accuracy. The custom CNN's confusion matrix shows 30 of 34 typically developing images correct against only 11 of 23 autism images - class-wise recall of 0.88 versus 0.48, F1 of 0.79 versus 0.58 - so a model reported at 71.9% accuracy is in fact detecting fewer than half the autism cases, and the authors say so: its 'ability to classify the people affected by ASD was not upto the mark'. The transfer-learning models are markedly more balanced, with class-wise F1 of 0.82/0.75 for logistic regression and 0.84/0.76 for the MLP, and the authors conclude on that basis rather than on the accuracy difference alone. The conclusion attributes the modest overall performance to the small dataset and proposes augmentation and dataset expansion. [RQ2.2] There is no study setting: all work was performed on Google Colab using a downloaded public dataset, at Vellore Institute of Technology in India, on images collected elsewhere. No children were recruited, tested, observed or consented for this work. This matters for how the study should be weighted in the review: it contributes no new evidence about autistic children and no new data, and its value lies entirely in being an additional independent modelling attempt on a dataset that several other included studies also use - which makes it a comparison point rather than a primary source. [RQ2.3] Not reported. The paper never states what the children were looking at when the gaze data were recorded, how long the recording lasted, what the display or eye tracker were, or how the scanpaths were rendered into images. It describes only the general definitions of fixation, blink and saccade from the source experiment, and states that the source study 'provides these visualised scanpath images which is used in the work as a biomarker'. So the study models a representation of a behaviour elicited by an unknown task. Two consequences follow for interpretation. Nothing can be said about whether the discriminative signal is social - the whole rationale offered in the introduction concerns looking at eyes and mouths, but if the stimuli were not faces that rationale does not apply. And the rendering choices that turned gaze coordinates into pictures - line width, colour, marker size, axis scaling, whether fixation duration is encoded as circle radius - are properties of the source dataset that determine what a convolutional network can extract, and none is described. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional by inheritance; the study performs no temporal analysis and could not. No ethics statement of any kind appears, which for a secondary analysis of published de-identified images is defensible in substance but is still a reporting omission - the source dataset's approvals are not referenced. No funding statement and no competing-interests declaration appear either. The paper is a four-to-six page conference contribution and these omissions are typical of that format, but they are omissions nonetheless. [RQ2.5] Google Colab and TensorFlow; InceptionV3 pretrained on ImageNet. That is the entirety of the apparatus, because no data were collected. The eye tracker, display, stimuli and recording software that produced the underlying gaze data are not named, so a reader cannot evaluate the measurement chain at all - a striking situation for a study whose stated contribution is to use eye tracking as a biomarker. The description of InceptionV3's architectural innovations (factorised convolutions, asymmetric factorisation, auxiliary classifiers, efficient grid size reduction) is detailed and accurate but is standard exposition rather than anything specific to this application. [RQ2.6] Adequate for the modelling, absent for the data. Reproducible: the source dataset is cited and public; the split counts are given exactly (382/108/57); the preprocessing is fully specified including the RGBA-to-RGB conversion, the 100x100 resize, the greyscale luminance formula, the 299x299 resize for InceptionV3 and the [-1, 1] normalisation; the custom CNN is tabulated layer by layer with kernel counts, sizes and output dimensions at each of five levels; the extraction point in InceptionV3 is named; and the MLP hidden layer sizes, optimiser, learning rate, loss, batch size and epoch count are all given. Not reproducible: the specific train/validation/test split, the random seed, and the mapping from images to children - which is the one piece of information needed to determine whether the evaluation is participant-disjoint. There is also a transcription error in the greyscale formula, where the blue coefficient is given as 0.144 rather than the standard 0.114. [RQ2.7] The single stated limitation is correct and is stated without defensiveness: accuracy is not high, and this is attributed to the dataset containing only 547 images. The authors do not inflate their results - they describe them as promising for future research rather than as a demonstration of feasibility, and they report the custom CNN's poor autism-class performance rather than burying it. What is unaddressed is nonetheless substantial. The split is by image and not by child, so with roughly nine images per child each test image has around eight siblings in training - the mechanism that has produced very high accuracies in other reuses of this same dataset, and one this paper neither invokes nor guards against. A single fixed split of 57 test images cannot support the three-way accuracy comparison the paper draws, since a difference of 81.0% against 78.9% is a single image. No majority-class baseline is computed, though the confusion matrix implies 59.6%, so the custom CNN's 71.9% is roughly twelve points above trivial and its autism-class recall of 0.48 is below it. The greyscale conversion was adopted partly because it improved accuracy, a decision made against the same small dataset. Nothing is reported about the 59 children. And no analysis addresses what visual property of a drawn trajectory the models respond to. [RQ2.9] Two directions, both aimed at the sample-size constraint the authors identify: use data augmentation, specifically generative adversarial networks, to synthesise additional scanpath images, and expand the dataset itself. The first should be flagged as a hazard rather than a solution in this specific setting - generating synthetic scanpath images from a 547-image corpus and then evaluating on an image-level split would compound rather than mitigate the dependence between training and test data, and would do so invisibly. Expanding the dataset is the sound recommendation. Not proposed: splitting by participant, reporting participant-level accuracy, characterising the children, or examining what the models learn. [RQ3.1] Visual scanning behaviour, encoded as a picture. A scanpath is defined correctly in the paper as a spatiotemporal representation of consecutive fixations and saccades that may overlap, and the input to every model is a rendered image of that trajectory. The behavioural claim motivating the work is the standard eye-tracking account of autism - that autistic children look away from eyes and mouths and towards background, with the widely cited 2008 observation about a 15-month-old attending more to the mouth than the eyes given as the example. But the study cannot test that claim, because it never reports what the children were looking at and never inspects what the models attend to. What is actually modelled is the appearance of a line drawing, and the properties of that drawing that a convolutional network could exploit include several that are only indirectly behavioural: the total extent of the plotted region, the density of overplotting, the number of line crossings, the aspect ratio of the traversed area. Some of these are informative about looking behaviour; others would follow from a child simply producing more or fewer gaze samples. The representation makes them indistinguishable, and no analysis in the paper separates them. [RQ3.2] None. A single modality rendered as a single image type, with no fusion, no auxiliary features and no metadata. The three reported models are alternatives compared against each other rather than channels combined. What the comparison does establish, usefully, is a difference in error profile rather than merely in accuracy: the end-to-end CNN is heavily skewed towards the majority class (recall 0.88 versus 0.48) while the ImageNet-pretrained feature extractor plus a simple classifier is balanced (0.85 versus 0.74 for the MLP). That is a real observation about small-sample deep learning - a network trained from scratch on 382 images collapses towards the majority class, while generic pretrained features generalise better - and it is the study's most transferable finding, though the paper frames it in terms of accuracy rather than of what it reveals about training regime. [RQ4.1] Two contrasting approaches. The proposed pipeline uses ImageNet-pretrained InceptionV3 as a fixed feature extractor, taking the 2048-dimensional output of the last convolutional layer before global average pooling on the stated principle that layers close to the classifier head carry the most distinctive representations, and feeds these to either logistic regression or a two-hidden-layer MLP (200 and 100 neurons). The baseline is a custom five-level CNN trained from scratch (16, 32, 64 and 128 3x3 filters, ReLU, 2x2 max pooling at each level, flatten to 2048, dense 256, dense 128, sigmoid output) with Adam at learning rate 0.001, binary cross-entropy, batch size 64 and 15 epochs. The choice is appropriate to the data volume and the result vindicates it: with 382 training images, transfer learning outperforms training from scratch by 9 percentage points and, more importantly, produces a balanced rather than a majority-collapsed classifier. The paper describes InceptionV3 as 'fine-tuned' in one place while describing features as extracted from a fixed layer in another, an ambiguity about whether any weights were updated that is not resolved. [RQ4.2] A rendered scanpath image, resized either to 100x100 greyscale (custom CNN) or 299x299 RGB with pixel values normalised to [-1, 1] (InceptionV3). The greyscale conversion for the CNN is described candidly as an empirical choice: RGB training was slow and 'converting the images to grayscale proved to significantly reduce the training time and an improvement in classification accuracy was also noticed'. That is honest reporting of a decision made partly on observed accuracy, and it is worth noting that if the source rendering used colour to encode anything - fixation order, duration, or which eye - greyscale conversion would discard it, and the paper cannot say whether it did, because the rendering scheme is never described. The deeper representational point is that all temporal information in the original gaze data survives only as visual geometry: sequence order, fixation duration and saccade velocity are recoverable from a drawing only to the extent the renderer encoded them, and the model receives no time series at all. [RQ4.3] Better than the corpus norm for a paper of this scale. Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are reported per class rather than only in aggregate, confusion matrices are given for the CNN, and ROC curves are plotted for both transfer-learning classifiers. The per-class reporting is what makes the study useful, because it reveals that the custom CNN's 71.9% accuracy conceals autism-class recall of 0.48 - fewer than half the autism images detected, which is below the 59.6% majority-class baseline implied by the confusion matrix. The authors explicitly justify reporting beyond accuracy on the grounds that it 'does not give much importance to the class imbalance in a dataset if at all it exists', which is the right reasoning. Gaps: AUC values are plotted but never quoted numerically; no confidence intervals accompany any figure, although a 57-image test set makes one image worth 1.8 percentage points and therefore makes the 81.0% versus 78.9% comparison uninterpretable; no majority-class baseline is stated; and no participant-level metric is possible given the splitting scheme. [RQ4.4] None. No class activation mapping, saliency analysis, feature visualisation, error analysis or inspection of misclassified images is reported for any of the three models. The methods section instead provides several paragraphs of general exposition on how convolutional layers, pooling variants and InceptionV3's factorisation techniques work - accurate but generic. The absence is more consequential here than in studies that model interpretable features, because the input is a picture of a behaviour rather than the behaviour itself, so there is a genuine open question about whether the models respond to where the gaze went or to incidental graphical properties such as ink density, plotted extent or line crossing count. A single class activation map over a handful of correctly and incorrectly classified scanpaths would have addressed it directly and would have been the most informative addition the paper could have made. [RQ4.5] A single fixed 70/20/10 split of 547 images into 382 training, 108 validation and 57 test, with the image as the unit. Fifty-nine children produced those 547 images, so roughly nine images per child, and nothing in the paper indicates that a child's images were kept together - so on a random split each test image is accompanied by around eight siblings from the same child. This is the same design flaw that recurs across reuses of this dataset, and it is the reason the review treats the family of studies built on it as a triangulation problem rather than as independent evidence. What makes this particular paper informative is that the leakage does not produce a high number: 81.0% at best, against figures near 97-99% reported by other groups on the identical images. The most plausible reading is that generic ImageNet features plus a shallow classifier extract less individual-identity information from a rendered trajectory than an end-to-end network fine-tuned on the same data - so the gap between this study and the higher-scoring reuses is itself evidence about how much of those higher scores is identity rather than diagnosis. Read alongside the source authors' own participant-level correction to around 71% and another group's one-image-per-child leave-one-out result of 72.88%, this study's 81% sits closer to the honest end of the range than to the inflated one, despite sharing the flawed split. Other weaknesses compound the picture: a 57-image test set with no confidence intervals, so the three-way model comparison rests on differences of one or two images; no cross-validation or repeated splits; no chance baseline against an implied 59.6% floor; and one architectural choice (greyscale conversion) made with reference to observed accuracy on the same data. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, scan path, eye tracking, deep learning, transfer learning. Four of five name the method or modality and none names an application - neither screening, diagnosis nor classification appears, although the body text uses 'autism diagnosis technique' and 'second opinion'. Terms carried through the text: visualised scanpath images, biomarker, gaze disparities, fixation abnormality, hybrid classifier model, InceptionV3, feature extraction. [RQ5.2] 2023 2nd International Conference on Vision Towards Emerging Trends in Communication and Networking Technologies (ViTECoN), IEEE - a general communications and networking engineering conference, not a clinical, biomedical or machine-learning venue. That placement explains the paper's balance: substantial textbook exposition of convolutional networks and InceptionV3 architecture aimed at a non-specialist engineering audience, minimal clinical context, and no participant characterisation at all. It also explains the absence of ethics, funding and competing-interests statements, which such venues do not typically require. The paper is short and does not overreach; the reporting gaps are those of the format as much as of the authors. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 by the Department of Computer Science at Vellore Institute of Technology, India, with no reported funding. The framing is the standard workload-and-subjectivity argument: there is no definitive biological test for autism, diagnosis depends on a chain of specialist referrals and subjective instruments, and 'the process of diagnosis itself consumes a lot of time and energy of both the children and parents', so computer-aided methods offering a reliable 'second opinion' are attractive. The paper positions itself within an eye-tracking-for-diagnosis literature that it surveys across several conditions - Parkinson disease, dementia, dyslexia, schizophrenia - before turning to autism, which is a useful reminder that the same modality and often the same architectures are being applied across diagnoses, and that a scanpath classifier reported at 95% for dyslexia and 78.85% for schizophrenia in the cited work is not obviously measuring anything condition-specific. For this review the study's value is not its result but its position: it is the fourth independent reuse of the 547-image dataset encountered here, it applies a different modelling family from the others, and its comparatively modest 81% - obtained under the same image-level splitting that has yielded 97-99% elsewhere - is a useful data point on how much of those higher figures is attributable to method rather than to signal. |
| S-108 | Secondary computational analysis of pooled public child-language corpora, conducted at IIIT Delhi with no new data collection. Transcripts of 76 children were drawn from three independently assembled datasets in the CHILDES databank: Eigsti (16 autistic, 16 typically developing, aged 3-6 years, 30-minute free play), Nadig (13 autistic, 25 typically developing, aged 3-7 years, approximately 10 minutes of parent-child free play) and Flusberg (6 autistic, no comparison children, aged 12-26 months, natural mother-child interaction), giving 35 autistic and 41 typically developing children overall. Because Flusberg contributes autistic children exclusively and from an age band no comparison child occupies, corpus membership carries diagnostic information by construction. No individual-level information is reported for any child - no sex, IQ, language level, severity or comorbidity - and no diagnostic instrument, criteria or procedure is described, the labels being inherited as binary clinical status from the three sources. The Eigsti corpus additionally contains a developmental delay group, which is not used. No ethics statement, competing-interests declaration or limitations section appears; funding is acknowledged in full. | Seventy-seven linguistic features were extracted from the transcripts in three families. Nine semantic-pragmatic measures were specified explicitly against ADOS criteria: mean length of utterance in morphemes, number of distinct word roots, questions initiated by the child, proportion of immediately repeated phrases, child-child discourse coherence and child-partner discourse coherence (both cosine similarities between BERT embeddings of consecutive sentences), echolalia as immediate repetition of the partner's bigrams, proportion of unintelligible units, and unexpected words via TF-IDF. Forty-five part-of-speech tag frequencies formed the lexical family and 23 measures from L2SCA the syntactic complexity family, with CLAN supplying the morphosyntactic baseline. Count-based features were normalised over conversation length, which is necessary given that source sessions range from about 10 to 30 minutes. SHAP analysis on the initial feature set drove elimination to 63 features, apparently before the train-test split. Six classifier families were then compared using an AutoML tool under a stated 90:10 split, with an RBF-kernel SVM retained as best and its C and gamma tuned by grid search with 5-fold cross-validation inside the training data. Accuracy, macro precision, macro recall and macro F1 were reported for every classifier and for seven feature-set configurations, with a majority classifier as the baseline comparator. | The best model, an RBF SVM on all 63 features, reached 94.1% accuracy with macro precision 95%, recall 94% and F1 94%, against a majority-classifier baseline of 56.4% accuracy and 32% macro F1 - a 37.7% relative improvement. Across classifier families, k-nearest neighbours reached 64.7%, logistic regression and gradient boosting 76.5% each, and random forest 88.2%. The feature ablation is the substantive result: morphosyntactic baseline features alone gave 70.59%, syntactic complexity alone 70% (with macro F1 of only 55%, reflecting recall of 58%), part-of-speech frequencies alone 82%, the semantic-pragmatic set alone 82.3%, part-of-speech plus semantic-pragmatic 88.2%, and all three families together 94.1% - so the semantic-pragmatic family matches the lexical family on its own and the three combine additively rather than redundantly, which is precisely the question the study set out to answer. SHAP attribution placed the number of distinct word roots first, with unexpected words and both discourse-coherence measures in the top ten, and the authors related these to prior findings that vocabulary extent differentiates autistic children and that autistic children show reduced global coherence in conversation. | The three pooled corpora differ in age band, session length, conversation partner and transcription convention, and the differences are not label-neutral: Flusberg contributes 6 autistic children and no comparison children, from an age range of 12-26 months that no comparison child occupies, so corpus identity partially predicts diagnosis and corpus-specific artefacts are available to the classifier as diagnostic cues. Since every feature is a language measure in children and the top SHAP contributor is the number of distinct word roots - a canonical developmental index that changes dramatically between 12 months and 8 years - a developmental rather than autism-specific explanation of the result cannot be excluded, and no age, IQ or language-level data exist to adjust for it. The conversation partner varies across corpora and is referred to inconsistently within the paper as therapist, trainer and parent, while child-partner discourse coherence ranks among the top features. SHAP-based feature elimination from 77 to 63 appears to precede the train-test split, and six classifier families were compared with the best reported. All reported accuracies are exact multiples of 1/17, fixing the test set at 17 items rather than the 7 or 8 implied by the stated 90:10 split, so the difference between the headline 94.1% and the next configuration is one child, and no confidence intervals are offered. No reference standard is described for any participant, and the developmental delay group available in the Eigsti corpus - the material for the differential comparison the conclusion says is needed - was not used. | The most substantive feature-engineering contribution in this review's language-based studies, and the one that most directly tests a question the field has left open. Its design principle is worth carrying forward independently of its results: features are specified against ADOS, so every measure has a clinical referent, and the resulting model can be explained in terms a clinician would recognise - echolalia, discourse coherence, initiative in asking questions, vocabulary extent - rather than in embeddings or spectral coefficients. That places it with the joint-attention and facial-complexity studies charted here in the small group that treats interpretability as a design constraint rather than a reporting nicety. Its ablation is the finding to retain: semantic-pragmatic features alone match part-of-speech features (82.3% against 82%), and the three linguistic families combine additively to 94.1%, which establishes that pragmatic measures carry independent signal rather than restating lexical ones. Two of its features are also unusual in this corpus for being genuinely dyadic - echolalia and child-partner coherence are defined by the relation between what the partner said and what the child said next, so they encode interaction rather than individual output, which is what pragmatic assessment actually requires. Its evaluation practice is mixed in an instructive way: it reports a majority-classifier baseline as a named comparator with improvements quantified against it, which most of this corpus omits, while resting its headline on a 17-item test set with unnested feature selection and a six-way classifier search. And its central design decision - pooling three corpora one of which supplies autistic children exclusively, from an age band the comparison group does not reach - is the clearest example in the review of a confound created by dataset assembly rather than by measurement, in a study where the obvious corrective (leave-one-corpus-out validation) was available in the data and not performed. | [RQ1.1] Seventy-six children assembled from three independent corpora in the CHILDES databank: Eigsti (16 autistic, 16 typically developing, aged 3-6, 30-minute free play), Nadig (13 autistic, 25 typically developing, aged 3-7, approximately 10 minutes of parent-child free play) and Flusberg (6 autistic, no comparison children, aged 12-26 months, natural mother-child interaction), giving 35 autistic and 41 typically developing overall. The composition matters more than the totals. Flusberg contributes autistic children only, so corpus membership is partially informative about diagnosis by construction, and it contributes them from an age band - infancy and early toddlerhood - that no comparison child occupies. The three corpora also differ in session length by a factor of three, in conversation partner, and in transcription era and convention. The paper notes that the Eigsti corpus contains a developmental delay group alongside autism and typical development, but that group is not used. No child-level information beyond corpus, group and corpus-level age range is reported anywhere. [RQ1.2] 'Children with autism (CwA)' is used throughout as the working abbreviation, alongside 'typically developing (TD)' and 'neurotypical', which is a more current pairing than the 'normal' contrast used elsewhere in this corpus. The clinical framing is nonetheless firmly deficit-based and in one respect dated: autism is characterised by 'repetitive and stereotypic behaviours and impaired social and communicative skills collectively called the triads of impairments', a formulation superseded by DSM-5's two-domain structure a decade before this paper. Language differences are described as 'language and communication impairments', 'language atypicalities' and 'aberrant receptive and expressive language development', and the targeted behaviours are 'stereotypic language behaviours'. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. Against this, the paper's motivating concern is a reasonable one about assessment rather than about people - that quantifying behavioural traits 'is cumbersome, and the efficacy of such methods primarily depends on the evaluators' expertise' - and its stated goal is interpretable measurement that a non-expert could follow, which is a service orientation rather than a replacement one. [RQ1.3] Almost nothing at the individual level. Table 1 reports, per corpus, the number of autistic and typically developing participants and an age range: Eigsti 16/16 aged 3-6, Nadig 13/25 aged 3-7, Flusberg 6/0 aged 12-26 months. No sex, IQ, language level, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, comorbidity or severity is given for any child, and no group means or matching statistics of any kind are reported. Three consequences follow, all unaddressed. Because the pooled age range spans 12 months to 8 years while the comparison group is confined to 3-7 years, the two groups differ in age distribution by construction - and every feature in the study is a language measure, which in children is dominated by developmental stage. Mean length of utterance and number of distinct word roots, the latter identified by SHAP as the single largest contributor to the model's predictions, are canonical expressive-language milestones that change dramatically between 12 months and 8 years, so an age difference between groups is not a nuisance covariate here but a direct alternative explanation for the headline result. And without IQ or language-level data there is no way to separate an autism-specific pragmatic signature from a general language-delay one, which is precisely what the unused developmental delay group in the Eigsti corpus could have tested. [RQ1.4] Absent as a described procedure. The paper's entire statement on this point is that it 'considered the binary classification problem of classifying a child as having ASD or not, as all three datasets had binary labelling of the clinical status' - so the labels are inherited from three separately assembled research corpora with no account of how autism was diagnosed in any of them, by whom, against which criteria or in which era. Given that the Flusberg corpus records children aged 12-26 months, its labels must derive from a very different ascertainment process from corpora recruiting 3-7 year olds, and pooling them without comment means the target variable is heterogeneous in an unexamined way. ADOS is invoked repeatedly, but as the source of the behavioural constructs the features are designed to mirror - echolalia, back-and-forth interchange, building on statements - rather than as an instrument administered to these children. That is a legitimate and rather elegant use of a diagnostic instrument as a specification for feature engineering, and it should not be confused with having a reference standard. [RQ1.5] No external cognitive, language or severity measure exists, and the absence is more consequential here than in most studies because language is simultaneously the modality, the feature set and the plausible confound. The study computes mean length of utterance in morphemes and number of distinct word roots - both standard expressive-language indices used clinically to characterise developmental level - and uses them as classifier inputs, with the second identified by SHAP as the dominant predictor. In a sample where the autistic group extends down to 12 months and the comparison group does not go below 3 years, that finding is compatible with the model having learned a developmental-language gradient rather than an autism-specific one. Nothing in the analysis distinguishes the two, because no independent measure of language level exists to adjust for. Severity is likewise absent and is named as future work. The gap also blocks the more interesting question the feature set was built to answer: whether pragmatic atypicality - echolalia, poor discourse coherence, failure to initiate questions - is present over and above general language level, which is the clinically meaningful version of the claim. [RQ2.1] The stated objectives are threefold: to automatically extract semantic and pragmatic language features including echolalia, semantic coherence and repetitive language usage; to compare them systematically and identify the most significant; and to build an interpretable assessment system on that basis. The gap the paper identifies in the literature is specific and fair - prior work on semantic-pragmatic features for autism has examined individual measures such as echolalia or pronoun usage in isolation, and 'the cumulative effect of the features and how they complement the lexical, syntactic and other text-based features in the diagnosis of autism has not been analysed'. Findings: the best classifier, an RBF SVM on all 63 retained features, reached 94.1% accuracy with 94% macro F1 against a majority-classifier baseline of 56.4% accuracy and 32% macro F1. The feature-set ablation is the substantive result and is reported in full: morphosyntactic baseline 70.59%, syntactic complexity alone 70%, part-of-speech frequencies alone 82%, semantic-pragmatic features alone 82.3%, part-of-speech plus semantic-pragmatic 88.2%, and all three families 94.1%. So the semantic-pragmatic set matches the lexical set on its own and the three families are complementary rather than redundant, which is exactly the claim the study set out to test. SHAP attribution places the number of distinct word roots first, with unexpected words and both child-child and child-partner discourse coherence in the top ten, and the authors relate each to prior findings on vocabulary extent and on global coherence in autistic conversation. [RQ2.2] No study setting: this is a computational reanalysis conducted at IIIT Delhi on transcripts collected years earlier in North American research laboratories. The three source settings are described only briefly and differ substantially - 30-minute free play sessions in one corpus, roughly 10 minutes of parent-child play in another, and natural mother-child interaction with 12-26 month olds in the third. That heterogeneity is the study's central unexamined problem, because it is not random with respect to the label: one corpus supplies autistic children exclusively. Any systematic difference between the corpora - transcription conventions, how disfluency and unintelligibility were marked, who the partner was, how long the session ran, what era the recording belongs to - is therefore partially aligned with diagnosis. Length-dependent features are normalised over conversation length, which handles the most obvious component, but transcription and partner effects are not addressable by normalisation and are not discussed. [RQ2.3] Three different paradigms pooled as though equivalent. Eigsti recorded 30-minute free play sessions; Nadig recorded approximately 10 minutes of parent-child free play; Flusberg recorded natural mother-child interaction in infants and toddlers. The conversation partner is not held constant and the paper's own terminology drifts - the echolalia feature is defined by repetition of bigrams 'originally spoken by the therapist', the discourse-coherence feature is described as similarity 'between BERT embeddings of consecutive sentences of therapist and child', SHAP results refer to 'trainer-child (t-c) discourse', and the corpus descriptions say the partner was a parent or the mother. Whoever the partner was, they are a live participant whose own language shapes every child-partner feature, and pragmatic behaviour in a child differs systematically with whether the interlocutor is a parent or a clinician. Since child-partner discourse coherence ranks among the top contributing features, this is not a peripheral concern. The countervailing strength is the paradigm's ecological character: these are unstructured natural conversations rather than elicited tasks, so the pragmatic behaviours the features target - taking initiative, building on statements, sustaining a topic - had a genuine opportunity to occur. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional by inheritance, with one session per child and no temporal analysis. The pooling of corpora spanning 12 months to 8 years creates something that looks like developmental range but is not a developmental design, since age is confounded with corpus and with label. No ethics statement appears, which is defensible for a secondary analysis of a public research corpus but is still an omission - the CHILDES databank operates under its own conditions of use and no reference to the source studies' approvals is made. Funding from an Indian government start-up research grant with partial industry-linked centre support is acknowledged; no competing-interests statement is provided. [RQ2.5] An entirely software-based pipeline, well specified for its scale. CLAN, the standard CHILDES analysis toolkit, supplied the morphosyntactic baseline features. L2SCA, an established second-language syntactic complexity analyser, supplied the 23 syntactic complexity measures. BERT embeddings with cosine similarity supplied the two discourse-coherence measures. TF-IDF vectors supplied the unexpected-word count. An AutoML tool was used to compare classifier families, and SHAP for attribution and for feature elimination. Using off-the-shelf, community-standard tools throughout is appropriate and makes the pipeline reconstructible in outline, though the specific BERT variant is not named and no code is released. Notably absent, given publication at ICASSP and repeated reference to 'speech signals' and 'speech features', is any acoustic analysis: the study operates entirely on transcripts, and the prosodic properties the introduction cites from prior work - increased pitch range and variability in autistic children - are not measured. [RQ2.6] Better than most conference papers of this length. Reproducible: the three source corpora are public, named and cited with their participant counts and age ranges; every one of the 77 features is named with a definition in a two-column table, including the exact construction of the BERT-cosine coherence measures and the TF-IDF basis of unexpected words; the normalisation of count features over conversation length is stated; the tools are named; the reduction from 77 to 63 features and its SHAP basis is described; the classifier family, kernel and the grid-search-with-5-fold-CV procedure for C and gamma are given; and both the six-classifier comparison and the seven-configuration feature ablation are reported with four metrics each. Not available: code, the split or seed, the identity of the 63 retained features, the per-corpus composition of the training and test sets, the BERT variant, and the AutoML configuration. The stated 90:10 split is also inconsistent with the reported accuracies, all of which are exact multiples of 1/17. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section, and the omissions matter more than in most studies of this type because several are specific to the pooling strategy. The three corpora differ in age band, session length, conversation partner and transcription convention, and - decisively - the Flusberg corpus contributes 6 autistic children and no comparison children, so corpus membership is partially predictive of diagnosis and corpus-specific artefacts are available to the classifier as diagnostic cues. The autistic group therefore extends to 12 months while the comparison group starts at 3 years, in a study whose features are language measures and whose top SHAP contributor is the number of distinct word roots - a canonical developmental index. Feature elimination by SHAP from 77 to 63 features is described before the train-test split with no statement of nesting, so the retained set saw the evaluation data. Six classifiers were compared and the best reported. All accuracies are multiples of 1/17, implying a 17-item test set rather than the 7 or 8 that a 90:10 split of 76 children would give, and no confidence interval accompanies a comparison in which one child moves accuracy by 5.9 points - so the 94.1% versus 88.2% difference between the best model and the next is one child. No demographic or cognitive data exist for any participant. And the Eigsti corpus's developmental delay group, which would have supported the differential comparison the conclusion identifies as needed, was present in the source material and not used. What the paper does do well on the evaluation side is report a majority-classifier baseline as a named comparator in both results tables, which is better practice than most of this corpus. [RQ2.9] Two directions, both apt: identify autism severity from speech, and explore differential diagnosis using speech-based analysis. The second is the more important and is unusually actionable, because the Eigsti corpus the study already uses contains a developmental delay group alongside autism and typical development. Distinguishing autistic children from children with developmental delay on pragmatic features - rather than from typically developing children on measures dominated by general language level - is the clinically meaningful version of this study's claim, and the material for it was in hand. Not proposed, and needed: leave-one-corpus-out validation, which the three-corpus structure makes available and which would test whether the model generalises across settings rather than learning corpus identity; adjustment for age and language level; and nesting of feature selection. [RQ3.1] Conversational language, targeted at the pragmatic and semantic level rather than the acoustic or syntactic one, and specified against a clinical instrument rather than by exploration. The design principle is stated plainly: features were extracted 'following the standard diagnostic tool for ASD - Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule', and the resulting measures map onto behaviours ADOS actually rates - echolalia, the ability to sustain back-and-forth interchange, asking questions, building upon statements, use of pronouns. Operationally this yields nine semantic-pragmatic measures: mean length of utterance in morphemes, number of distinct word roots, questions initiated by the child, immediate phrase repetition, coherence between the child's own consecutive utterances, coherence between the partner's and the child's utterances, echolalia as immediate repetition of the partner's bigrams, proportion of unintelligible units, and unexpected word use. Two design decisions are worth noting. Echolalia and child-partner coherence are inherently dyadic, defined by the relationship between what the partner said and what the child said next - so unlike almost every other behavioural measure in this corpus, these features encode interaction rather than individual output. And unintelligibility is retained as a feature rather than discarded as noise, which is behaviourally defensible since articulation and intelligibility are clinically relevant, though it also means transcription-quality differences across corpora enter the model. [RQ3.2] No cross-modal fusion, and the absence is conspicuous for a paper at a speech-signal-processing venue: the introduction cites acoustic findings on pitch range and variability in autistic children, the abstract refers to 'diagnostic predictions made using speech signals', and the title names speech features - yet the study operates entirely on transcripts and computes nothing acoustic. What it does instead is a careful within-modality fusion across three linguistic levels, and reports the ablation in full: syntactic complexity alone 70%, part-of-speech frequencies alone 82%, semantic-pragmatic features alone 82.3%, the last two combined 88.2%, and all three 94.1%. That progression is the study's real contribution and is more informative than a single accuracy figure, because it establishes that the semantic-pragmatic family carries as much signal alone as the lexical family and that the three are complementary rather than overlapping - the specific question the authors identified as unanswered in the prior literature. The caution is that the ablation shares its data, its unnested feature selection and its 17-item test set with the headline result, so the ordering is more reliable than the individual numbers. [RQ4.1] Six classifier families compared by an AutoML tool - majority baseline, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting and support vector machine - with an RBF-kernel SVM retained on the basis of best accuracy and its C and gamma tuned by grid search with 5-fold cross-validation. The choice of simple, interpretable models is appropriate to 76 samples and 63 features and is consistent with the paper's stated priority of interpretability over raw performance. Two aspects of the comparison need stating. Selecting the best of six families on the same small evaluation set means the reported 94.1% is the maximum of a search, and the spread across families is wide (64.7% to 94.1%), so the choice is doing real work. And SHAP serves a dual role - as the feature-elimination criterion reducing 77 features to 63, and as the post-hoc attribution method interpreting the final model - which is efficient but means the interpretation is being read off a feature set that SHAP itself selected on the full data. [RQ4.2] One fixed-length vector per child summarising an entire conversational session, comprising 45 part-of-speech tag frequencies, 23 syntactic complexity measures and 9 semantic-pragmatic measures, reduced from 77 to 63 by SHAP-guided elimination that removed non-informative tags such as SYM and MD and an um-propagation artefact. Count-based features - echolalia, unintelligible units, unexpected words - are normalised over conversation length, which is a necessary and correctly applied step given that source sessions range from about 10 to 30 minutes. Two of the features are computed with contextual embeddings rather than surface statistics: child-child and child-partner discourse coherence are cosine similarities between BERT representations of consecutive sentences, which is a reasonable operationalisation of topic maintenance and is more sensitive than lexical overlap would be. The representation discards temporal structure beyond that local coherence, so trajectory across a session - whether a child warms up, disengages, or shifts topic progressively - is not represented. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, macro precision, macro recall and macro F1, reported for every one of six classifiers and every one of seven feature-set configurations, with a majority classifier as the first row of both tables. Macro averaging suits the near-balanced 35:41 split, and including the majority baseline as a named comparator - with improvements quantified against it - is better practice than most studies charted here, particularly given the authors' explicit rationale that inconsistency in the datasets used across the literature makes cross-study comparison unreliable. The gaps are nonetheless serious at this sample size. No confidence interval is reported anywhere, and since every accuracy is an exact multiple of 1/17 the test set contains 17 items, so one child is 5.9 percentage points and the difference between the headline 94.1% and the next-best 88.2% is a single child. No confusion matrix, no AUC, and no sensitivity or specificity named as such. The majority-classifier figure of 56.4% also does not correspond to the 53.9% implied by the overall class ratio, so it appears to be computed on a particular split, which is not stated. [RQ4.4] The study's strongest dimension, and interpretability is treated as the objective rather than as a diagnostic afterthought. Three layers support it. The feature set is specified against ADOS, so every measure has a clinical referent and the model's inputs are quantities a clinician would recognise - echolalia, discourse coherence, initiative in asking questions, vocabulary extent - rather than embeddings or spectral coefficients. The feature-family ablation quantifies what each level of linguistic description contributes, which is itself an interpretive result: semantic-pragmatic features alone reach 82.3%, matching part-of-speech features, and the families combine additively to 94.1%. And SHAP attribution identifies which individual features drive predictions, with the findings then checked against independent literature rather than asserted - the number of distinct word roots emerges as the largest contributor and is linked to prior work on vocabulary extent in autistic children, while the prominence of unexpected words and of both discourse-coherence measures is connected to evidence that autistic children show reduced global coherence in conversation. The authors' claim that these features are 'coherent and understandable to non-experts as well' is defensible. Two limits: no error analysis or per-child examination is performed, and no check is made on whether the top features differ systematically across the three source corpora - which, given that one corpus supplies only autistic children, is the analysis that would distinguish a linguistic finding from a corpus artefact. [RQ4.5] The weakest dimension, and the problems compound. The reported scheme is a single 90:10 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation used inside the training data only for SVM hyperparameter selection - which is the correct placement for hyperparameter tuning and is stated clearly. But three issues sit above it. First, the arithmetic does not match the description: every reported accuracy is an exact multiple of 1/17 (64.7, 70.59, 76.5, 82.3, 88.2, 94.1 per cent), which fixes the test set at 17 items, roughly 22% of 76 rather than the stated 10%, and the discrepancy is unexplained. Whatever the intended design, a 17-item test set means one child is worth 5.9 percentage points, so the headline 94.1% is 16 of 17 correct and its margin over the next-best configuration is one child - a difference no confidence interval is offered for and none would support. Second, SHAP-based elimination from 77 to 63 features is described as performed on the initially extracted set with no indication of nesting inside the split, so the retained feature set was chosen with sight of the evaluation data; on 76 samples and 77 candidate features this is exactly the regime in which unnested selection produces substantial optimism. Third, six classifier families were compared and the best retained, with a 30-point spread between the worst and best, so the reported figure is the maximum of a search. Beneath all of this lies the pooling problem, which no amount of correct splitting would fix: because the Flusberg corpus contributes autistic children only and from a much younger age band, corpus identity partially predicts diagnosis, and a random split across pooled corpora cannot separate a linguistic signature from a corpus signature. The corrective design is available in the data and would be far more informative - leave-one-corpus-out validation, which would show directly whether features learned on Eigsti and Flusberg transfer to Nadig and vice versa, together with nesting the SHAP elimination and reporting the ablation ordering rather than point accuracies. [RQ5.1] Index terms: speech analysis, autism spectrum disorder, human-computer interaction. All three are broad, and the third is a venue-fit choice rather than a description of the work. The acronym SPASHT is glossed in the abstract as meaning 'unambiguous', a deliberate reference to the paper's interpretability claim. Terms carried through the body: semantic and pragmatic features, echolalia, discourse coherence, repetitive language, stereotypic language behaviours, morphosyntactic features, syntactic complexity, CHILDES, CLAN, L2SCA, SHAP, majority classifier, interpretability. [RQ5.2] ICASSP 2023, the IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing - the principal venue for speech signal processing, and a slightly incongruous home for a study that performs no acoustic analysis at all. The paper operates entirely on transcripts, computing lexical, syntactic and semantic-pragmatic measures, while the abstract refers to 'diagnostic predictions made using speech signals' and the introduction reviews acoustic findings on pitch range and variability that the study does not build on. The four-page format accounts for the absence of a limitations section, an ethics statement and a competing-interests declaration, though not for the unexplained mismatch between the stated 90:10 split and the 17-item test set implied by the reported accuracies. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 by the Human-Machine Interaction Lab at IIIT Delhi, funded by an Indian government Science and Engineering Research Board start-up grant with partial support from a TCS Foundation centre and the Infosys Centre for Artificial Intelligence. The framing is the standard objectivity argument - autism diagnosis depends on behavioural assessment because 'the unavailability of genetic tests or biological markers' leaves no alternative, and 'quantifying these behavioural traits is cumbersome, and the efficacy of such methods primarily depends on the evaluators' expertise'. What distinguishes the paper's positioning is the specificity of the gap it claims: prior computational work on semantic-pragmatic language in autism has examined individual features such as echolalia or pronoun use in isolation and 'focused only on smaller feature sets', so 'the cumulative effect of the features and how they complement the lexical, syntactic and other text-based features in the diagnosis of autism has not been analysed'. That is a well-identified and genuinely open question, and the feature-family ablation is a direct answer to it.
