The paper's other distinctive commitment is to interpretability as a design constraint rather than a reporting nicety - features are specified against ADOS so that predictions can be explained in clinically recognisable terms - which puts it in the same small group as the joint-attention and facial-complexity studies charted here. For this review its main value is as the corpus's clearest demonstration that pragmatic language measures carry as much discriminative signal as lexical ones and combine with them additively; its main caution is that this was established on three pooled corpora, one of which contains autistic children exclusively. |
| S-109 | Cross-sectional classification study by a seven-institution United States consortium, framed around parsing heterogeneity within autism rather than detection alone. Ninety-nine children were enrolled and 86 had valid eye-gaze data - 54 autistic and 32 typically developing per Table 1, though the abstract states 55 autistic. Participants span infancy to adulthood in five age bands, with the autistic group distributed 3/11/23/13/4 across 0-1, 2-4, 5-9, 10-17 and 18+ years against 5/6/16/5/0 for the comparison group, and differ markedly in sex composition: 44 male and 10 female among autistic participants (81.5% male) against 15 male and 17 female among comparison participants (46.9% male). No diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician or procedure is reported for either group, and no IQ, language, severity or comorbidity measure appears anywhere. The modelled unit is the scan-path image, one per participant per video clip, giving 1,012 autistic and 380 typically developing images from 1,414 clip viewings - roughly sixteen per child - later expanded by rotation-based augmentation. No ethics approval, consent statement or competing-interests declaration appears in the retrieved text; funding is from an NIH K01 award and the Simons Foundation. | Four video-based eye-tracking tasks were used, selected for strong construct performance, demonstrated between-group discrimination and relation to autism symptoms, and noted to resemble the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials battery. Activity Monitoring shows two actresses playing with toys amid deliberate distractors; Dyadic Bid has an actor address the camera while two others either look silently at the viewer (a control against pure gaze-following and a competing-face distractor) or look down with subtle hand movements (a foil for mouth-movement salience); Social Referencing films escalating stressful episodes with a discrete critical event; Theory of Mind implements a naturalistic false-belief scenario. Gaze was rendered as trajectories on a 1680 x 1050 black background, resized to 100 x 100 greyscale. Three representations were compared: spatial scan-paths with no temporal encoding; spatio-temporal scan-paths restricted to non-overlapping 3-second windows across the first 15 seconds, or to 1-second sub-windows; and velocity-infused scan-paths in which average speed between consecutive gaze points, computed as Euclidean distance over time interval, is mapped to colour. Dense and convolutional neural networks were trained at 50 and 100 epochs with dropout of 0.2 or 0.5, evaluated on fixed 7:3 or 75:25 splits of images with rotation-based augmentation of the smaller class. Separate experiments classified age band and sex within the autistic group, ablated individual video clips, and varied augmentation level. | Diagnosis classification reached 74.4% test accuracy with AUC 0.68-0.72, against training accuracy of 100%. Within the autistic group, scan-paths separated 2-4 year olds from 10-17 year olds at 80.5% (AUC 0.868) and males from females at 78.0% (AUC 0.850); within the 5-9 year autistic subgroup, male-versus-female classification reached 98.8% at the highest augmentation level, falling to 85.8% and 85.1% at lower levels. Temporal windowing showed discrimination highest in the first three seconds (76.3% averaged over three repeats) and declining steadily to 70.2% by 12-15 seconds. Velocity-based colour coding raised the 3-6 second window from 71.74% to 80.25% with AUC improving from 0.790 to 0.839 - the paper's headline representational result. Per-clip ablation showed that removing individual videos changed test accuracy by up to about four points, with Theory of Mind and Dyadic Bid clips contributing most. A supplementary run on the separate public 547-image scan-path dataset used by several other studies in this corpus gave 76.97% with AUC 0.79. Training accuracy was 100% or within a fraction of it in essentially every reported configuration. | Splitting is by scan-path image rather than by participant, with roughly sixteen images per child, and no subject-disjoint evaluation appears anywhere in twenty pages - so each test image has around eleven siblings from the same child in training, sharing that child's habitual gaze extent and scanning style. Rotation-based augmentation compounds this: augmented counts are quoted for whole datasets rather than training partitions, and the sex-by-age experiment shows test accuracy rising monotonically with augmentation level, from 85.07% at 961/957 images to 98.84% at 3,121/2,905 - a pattern characteristic of augmented duplicates straddling the split, since a genuine signal does not strengthen with synthetic replication, yet the 98.8% is presented as evidence of substantial male-female difference. Training accuracy of 100% in almost every table confirms complete memorisation at every setting tried. Most consequentially, the study's own experiments establish that scan-path images encode age band at 80.5% and sex at 78.0% within the autistic group - both above the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis - while its diagnostic groups differ by 35 percentage points in sex composition and twofold in the proportion aged 10 or over; these findings appear four pages apart and are never connected, so the diagnostic result cannot be attributed to autism-related looking rather than to demographics. Beyond this: no diagnostic reference standard, no IQ or severity measure despite an abstract grounded in intellectual impairment, no eye tracker or sampling rate reported although the headline representation depends on velocity, no ethics or consent statement, no sensitivity, specificity or confidence intervals, uneven stimulus exposure ranging from 1 to 92 viewings per clip, and an unresolved discrepancy between 55 and 54 autistic participants. | The most useful study in this review for understanding what scan-path-image classification actually measures, and useful precisely because of a finding its authors present as a strength. By classifying age band and sex within the autistic group alone, the paper quantifies how much demographic information a rendered gaze trajectory carries: 80.5% for 2-4 versus 10-17 year olds and 78.0% for male versus female, both exceeding the 74.4% it achieves for diagnosis. Since its own diagnostic groups are 81.5% versus 46.9% male and differ twofold in the proportion aged 10 or over, this is direct internal evidence that a scan-path autism classifier can be substantially a demographic classifier - a caution that applies to the several other scan-path studies charted in this corpus, none of which performs the equivalent check. The paper also documents an augmentation artefact with unusual clarity: accuracy climbing from 85.1% to 98.8% as rotated copies are added, which is what duplicate leakage looks like and is worth citing wherever augmentation is used without partition-aware application. Three further contributions deserve to survive the methodological problems. Its stimulus battery is the best-designed in the review, with explicit controls and foils built into the Dyadic Bid task to distinguish genuine social responsiveness from gaze-following and from mouth-movement salience - design reasoning that most studies here replace with post-hoc statistics. Its temporal analysis establishes that discrimination is highest in the first three seconds of a clip and decays steadily thereafter, which is a substantive finding about orienting and has a direct implication for protocol length. And its velocity-infusion result - 8.5 accuracy points gained by colouring the trajectory with gaze speed - addresses head-on the central weakness of drawing gaze as a picture, namely that time is discarded, and shows that a derivative of the same signal recovers much of what the rendering throws away. Finally, the paper reports training accuracy alongside test accuracy in all fourteen tables, making its own overfitting plain; that transparency is what allows the reader to see 100% training accuracy against 74% test accuracy and draw the right conclusion. | [RQ1.1] Ninety-nine children were enrolled and 86 had valid eye-gaze data - 54 autistic and 32 typically developing according to Table 1 and the participant text, though the abstract states 55 autistic, an unresolved inconsistency. The 13 excluded participants are not characterised. Participants span the full paediatric age range and are grouped into five bands, with the autistic group distributed 3/11/23/13/4 across 0-1, 2-4, 5-9, 10-17 and 18+ years and the comparison group 5/6/16/5/0. Sex composition differs sharply: 44 male and 10 female among autistic participants (81.5% male) against 15 male and 17 female among comparison participants (46.9% male). The paper states plainly that 'each subject has a different number of recorded ET videos and the data is unbalanced with respect to diagnosis, age, and gender'. The modelled unit is not the child but the scan-path image, one per participant per video clip: 1,012 autistic and 380 typically developing images before augmentation, from 1,414 total clip viewings across 86 children - roughly sixteen images per child, unevenly distributed since Table 6 shows individual clips viewed anywhere from once to 92 times. [RQ1.2] 'Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)' and 'Typically Developing (TD)' throughout, person-first and consistent, in the register of a computational health-informatics paper. Clinical description is deficit-framed but restrained: autism is 'a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with social communication deficits and repetitive behaviors', with 'deficit in social attention' and 'atypicality in social attention' as the operative constructs. One passage uses 'ASD patients' when summarising prior work. The framing of purpose is unusual for this corpus in being oriented towards heterogeneity rather than detection: the stated motivation is that 'the observed heterogeneity in autism' compounds the subjectivity of clinical assessment, and that 'ASD heterogeneity and proven difficulty to identify generalizable markers of ASD have led to the presumption of the presence of multiple etiologies rather than a single disorder'. That is a defensible scientific position and it drives the study's most interesting experiments. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. One factual error should be noted: the paper states that 'ASD prevalence is found to have a gender bias with one in four individuals with ASD diagnosis being male', which inverts the well-established ratio. [RQ1.3] Age band and sex are reported per group in two tables and nothing else is. No IQ, language level, severity, comorbidity, medication, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity appears anywhere, and no exact ages, means or statistical comparisons are given. The two variables that are reported are the two that matter most here, and both are badly imbalanced. Sex: 81.5% male in the autistic group against 46.9% in the comparison group, a difference of nearly 35 percentage points. Age: 31.5% of autistic participants are aged 10 or over against 15.6% of comparison participants, and all four participants aged 18 or over are autistic while all remaining comparison participants are under 18. Ordinarily these would be recorded as uncontrolled confounds of unknown magnitude. What makes this study distinctive is that it measures their magnitude itself: its own experiments show that scan-path images predict sex within the autistic group at 78.0% accuracy with AUC 0.850, and age band within the autistic group at 80.5% with AUC 0.868. Both figures exceed the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis. So the study demonstrates that its input representation carries demographic information at least as strongly as diagnostic information, in a sample where the demographics differ substantially between diagnostic groups - and the two results are presented in consecutive sections without the connection being drawn. [RQ1.4] Not described. The retrieved text contains no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician, procedure, date or setting for either group; participants are simply designated ASD or TD. This is a notable omission for a study from a group closely associated with the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials, whose tasks the paper says its battery resembles, and it sits awkwardly with an introduction that criticises clinical assessment for being subjective and providing 'minimal information about the underlying mechanism of the disorder'. Whatever the actual ascertainment - and given the authorship it was very likely rigorous - the paper as published does not state it, so the target being predicted is undefined from the report alone. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, language, adaptive or severity measure is reported for any participant. The absence is more consequential here than in most studies because the paper's opening claim is explicitly about clinical gradation: 'in children with ASD, these patterns change with intellectual and social impairments, suggesting that patterns of social attention provide indices of clinically meaningful variation in ASD'. That is a claim about the relationship between looking patterns and intellectual and symptom severity, and the study collects no data with which to examine it. What it substitutes is demographic stratification - age and sex - which are sources of variation in autism but are not the clinically meaningful ones the abstract invokes. The result is a study framed around parsing heterogeneity that measures none of the clinical variables by which heterogeneity is defined, and which therefore cannot distinguish a scan-path difference that indexes symptom severity from one that indexes being a twelve-year-old rather than a three-year-old. [RQ2.1] The stated objective is to test whether scan-path images - spatial representations of gaze - can stratify autism from typical development, and then whether they also capture the age and sex variation that makes autism biomarkers hard to generalise. The two contributions claimed are incorporating temporal information into scan-path images and infusing gaze velocity into them. Findings, in the paper's own summary order: spatial scan-paths separate autism from typical development at 74.4% test accuracy (AUC 0.68-0.72); scan-paths separate 2-4 year old from 10-17 year old autistic children at 80.5% (AUC 0.868); scan-paths separate male from female autistic children at 78.0% (AUC 0.850); and within the 5-9 year autistic subgroup they separate male from female at 98.8%. Temporal windowing shows the first three seconds of viewing discriminate best (76.3%) with a monotone decline to 70.2% by 12-15 seconds. Velocity-based colour coding raises the 3-6 second window from 71.74% to 80.25% (AUC 0.839), the paper's headline representational result. Per-clip ablation ranks the contribution of individual videos, with Theory of Mind and Dyadic Bid clips mattering most. The authors read the age and sex results as evidence that scan-paths capture heterogeneity; they can equally be read as evidence that the diagnostic result is confounded, since the two groups differ substantially on both variables. [RQ2.2] Described only as a naturalistic study with a battery of eye-tracking video stimuli; no site, room, equipment or procedure is given in the retrieved text. The authorship spans seven United States institutions including the Yale Child Study Center and Seattle Children's Research Institute, and the paper notes that its paradigm 'share similarities with recent studies of autism biomarker Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT)', which locates the work within a serious clinical-research programme even though the report itself supplies no setting detail. The recruitment geometry cannot be assessed because recruitment is not described. [RQ2.3] The best-designed stimulus battery in this corpus, and described with a care that the rest of the methods does not match. Four tasks were chosen on three explicit criteria - strong construct performance, demonstrated between-group discrimination, and relation to autism symptoms in prior work with school-aged children. Activity Monitoring shows two actresses using child-directed speech and directing gaze to each other or to the activity between them, with clusters of colourful but irrelevant toys as deliberate distractors. Dyadic Bid is the most carefully constructed: an actor periodically addresses the camera while the two non-speaking actors either look silently at the viewer - included both as a control, to ensure the participant is not merely following a face that looks at them, and as a competing-face distractor - or look down with subtle hand movements, included as a foil controlling for the salience of the speaker's mouth movements. Social Referencing films escalating stressful episodes with distinct escalation, critical-event and resolution phases, such as a balloon inflated until it bursts. Theory of Mind implements a naturalistic false-belief scenario in which an antagonist repeatedly relocates objects unbeknown to a protagonist. Building explicit controls and foils into the stimuli rather than relying on post-hoc statistical adjustment is the kind of design reasoning that most studies here omit entirely. Against this, exposure to individual clips was extremely uneven - Table 6 shows clips viewed 92, 90, 62, 61 or 60 times alongside eighteen clips viewed exactly once - so the effective stimulus set is much smaller than the 43 clips listed, and participants did not all see the same material. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional with no follow-up and no test-retest assessment. The study is nonetheless the most thorough in this corpus on within-trial temporal structure: gaze is analysed in successive non-overlapping 3-second windows across the first 15 seconds, and separately in 1-second sub-windows, revealing that discrimination is highest in the first three seconds (76.3%) and declines steadily thereafter (71.7%, 69.3%, 71.0%, 70.2%). That is a substantive finding about when social attention differentiates, and it has a practical implication the paper does not draw out - that a shorter protocol may lose little. No ethics approval, consent statement, or competing-interests declaration appears in the retrieved text, which for a study of children including infants is a significant reporting omission whatever the underlying governance. Funding from an NIH K01 award and a Simons Foundation grant is stated. [RQ2.5] Not reported. The paper describes no eye tracker, sampling rate, display, viewing distance, calibration procedure or recording software - a striking gap in a study whose entire input is eye-tracking data and which computes gaze velocity, a quantity whose meaning depends directly on sampling rate. What is specified is the downstream rendering: scan-paths are drawn on a black background at 1680 x 1050, resized to 100 x 100 and converted to greyscale, with velocity encoded as colour in the final experiments through a stated threshold mapping. Modelling used DNN and CNN architectures shown only as a figure. [RQ2.6] Sharply uneven. The stimulus design, the per-clip view counts, the rendering resolution and downsampling, the temporal windowing scheme, the velocity formula and colour mapping, the dropout and epoch settings, the split ratios and the image counts for every one of fourteen experimental tables are all specified precisely - so the analysis pipeline is largely reconstructible. Almost everything about the data is not: no eye tracker or acquisition parameters, no diagnostic procedure, no demographics beyond age band and sex, no ethics or consent statement, no mapping from images to participants, no augmentation parameters, no seeds or split specifications, and no code or data. The mapping from images to participants is the single most consequential omission, because without it a reader cannot verify whether any evaluation in the paper is subject-disjoint - and nothing in the text suggests any of them is. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section, and the two constraints acknowledged in passing - too few female autistic participants for sex analysis outside the 5-9 band, and class imbalance depressing AUC - are both treated as problems that augmentation solves rather than as bounds on inference. The unaddressed issues are severe and partly self-documented. The splitting unit is the scan-path image, and with roughly sixteen images per child each test image has about eleven siblings from the same participant in training; no subject-disjoint result appears anywhere in the paper. Augmentation compounds this: image counts after augmentation are quoted for the whole dataset rather than for the training partition, and the sex-by-age experiment shows test accuracy rising monotonically with augmentation level - 85.07% at 961/957 images, 85.81% at 1,276/1,259, and 98.84% at 3,121/2,905 - which is the characteristic signature of rotated duplicates falling on both sides of the split, since a genuine signal does not strengthen with synthetic replication. The 98.8% is nonetheless presented as evidence of 'substantial difference' between male and female autistic children. Training accuracy is 100% or within a fraction of it in essentially every table while test accuracy ranges from 67% to 81%, a twenty-to-thirty point gap noted once as 'a gap in performance' and never analysed. And the study's own results contain the material for its strongest self-critique: it shows that scan-path images encode age at 80.5% and sex at 78.0% within the autistic group, both higher than the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis, in a sample where the autistic group is 81.5% male against 46.9% and twice as likely to be aged 10 or over. Those two facts are reported four pages apart and never brought together. Beyond this: no reference standard, no IQ or severity measure despite an abstract that invokes intellectual impairment, no ethics or consent statement, no eye-tracker description, no sensitivity or specificity, no confidence intervals, and an unresolved discrepancy between 55 and 54 autistic participants. [RQ2.9] No future-work section. The conclusion restates the finding that velocity-infused spatio-temporal scan-paths capture patterns associated with age, sex and their interaction, framed as progress on the heterogeneity problem. The steps the study's own results most clearly call for are absent from the paper: subject-disjoint evaluation, augmentation applied only within training folds, and - most importantly - a diagnosis classifier stratified or matched on age and sex, since the paper has itself established that both are strongly encoded in the representation and both differ substantially between its diagnostic groups. [RQ3.1] Social attention, decomposed into four constructs with distinct developmental and clinical significance rather than treated as a single quantity. Activity monitoring - attending to what others are doing together - is targeted with deliberate irrelevant distractors present. Dyadic bid sensitivity - responsiveness to another person's overture for engagement - is targeted with two built-in controls that distinguish genuine responsiveness from mere gaze-following and from mouth-movement salience. Social referencing - seeking clarifying information from others' faces in uncertain situations - is targeted with escalating stressful episodes containing a discrete critical event. Theory of mind - spontaneous processing of another's beliefs - is targeted with a naturalistic false-belief scenario. The measured behaviour is where and when the child looks within these scenes, rendered as a trajectory image. Two further behavioural findings emerge from the analysis rather than the design. Discrimination is strongest in the first three seconds of a clip and declines steadily thereafter, suggesting that the initial orienting response carries more diagnostic information than sustained viewing. And gaze velocity, added as colour, improves discrimination substantially over position alone in the same time window (71.74% to 80.25%), indicating that how fast the eyes move between points carries information the trajectory shape does not. [RQ3.2] No cross-sensor fusion, but the paper is one of the more informative in this corpus about fusing information types within a single modality, and it reports the ablation cleanly. Three representations are compared on the same data. Spatial scan-paths encode position only and give 74.4% for diagnosis. Spatio-temporal scan-paths encode position within bounded time windows, which allows the temporal locus of discrimination to be identified (76.3% in the first three seconds, declining to 70.2% by 12-15 seconds) but does not by itself improve peak performance. Velocity-infused spatio-temporal scan-paths encode position, time window and speed simultaneously by using velocity as the colour channel, and raise the 3-6 second window from 71.74% to 80.25% with AUC improving from 0.790 to 0.839 - a gain of 8.5 accuracy points from adding a derivative of the same underlying signal. That is a well-controlled demonstration that a rendered-image representation can be enriched with dynamics rather than discarding them, and it addresses head-on the central weakness of scan-path-image approaches, which is that drawing a trajectory throws away time. The caveat is that all three representations were evaluated under the same image-level splitting and the same whole-dataset augmentation, so the ordering is more trustworthy than the absolute values. [RQ4.1] A dense neural network and a convolutional neural network, compared throughout at two dropout rates (0.2, 0.5) and two epoch counts (50, 100), with both reported and the better bolded in each table. No classical baseline, no majority classifier, and no architecture search beyond dropout and epochs; the networks are shown only as a schematic figure. The modelling is deliberately simple and the paper's intellectual investment sits in the input representation rather than the classifier, which is a reasonable division for a study whose claimed contributions are representational. The consistent pattern across every table is diagnostic of the setup rather than of the models: training accuracy reaches 100% or 99.9% almost everywhere while test accuracy sits between 67% and 81%, so both architectures memorise the training images completely at every setting tried, and dropout at either level does not prevent it. [RQ4.2] A 100 x 100 image per participant per video clip, produced by drawing the gaze trajectory on a 1680 x 1050 black background and downsampling. The downsampling is aggressive - each output pixel spans roughly 17 x 11 input pixels - so fine spatial structure such as whether gaze fell on an eye or a cheek is not preserved, and what survives is the coarse geometry of the trajectory: its extent, its density, how many times it crosses itself. Three enrichments are then tested. Temporal restriction to 3-second or 1-second windows, which encodes time by segmentation rather than within the image. Velocity colour coding, which maps average speed between consecutive points - Euclidean distance over time interval - onto a colour scale with stated thresholds. And rotation-based augmentation, which generates additional images and is applied at three levels in one experiment. Two properties of this representation matter for interpretation. Because the image is a drawing, incidental graphical characteristics such as total ink and plotted extent are available to the network alongside behavioural ones, and no analysis distinguishes them. And because velocity depends on sampling rate, which is never stated, the velocity encoding cannot be reproduced or compared across studies. [RQ4.3] Training accuracy, test accuracy and AUC for every configuration across fourteen tables - and the decision to report training accuracy is worth crediting, because it makes visible what most papers in this corpus conceal: the models reach 100% training accuracy in essentially every experiment while testing between 67% and 81%. A reader can therefore see the overfitting directly rather than having to infer it. AUC is also reported throughout, which is better than accuracy alone, and the paper reasons about the gap between accuracy and AUC, correctly attributing the low AUC to class imbalance in the training data. Against this, no sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1 or confusion matrix appears anywhere, so nothing is known about the error profile or about which class the models fail on. No confidence intervals are given; the temporal experiments are repeated three times and averaged, which gives some sense of stability, but the diagnosis and stratification headlines rest on single splits. And no chance baseline is stated, although after augmentation the classes are near-balanced. [RQ4.4] No model interpretability whatsoever - no saliency, class activation, filter visualisation or error analysis is applied to either network, so the study cannot say what feature of a scan-path image produces a prediction. Its interpretive work is entirely at the input level and is systematic: individual video clips are removed one at a time and the models retrained, ranking each clip's contribution and showing that Theory of Mind and Dyadic Bid clips matter most while one Social Referencing clip matters least; scan-paths are restricted to successive temporal windows to locate when in a trial the discriminative information lies; and velocity encoding is added and removed to test whether dynamics contribute beyond position. These ablations yield findings a clinician could act on - that the first three seconds carry the most signal, that certain stimulus types are more informative than others - and are more useful than a saliency map would have been for stimulus design. But they say nothing about whether the network is responding to where the child looked or to how much of the canvas the drawing covers, which is the question a scan-path-image method most needs to answer. [RQ4.5] The weakest element, and the paper contains the evidence for its own strongest critique. The splitting unit is the scan-path image at 7:3 or 75:25, and no participant-level or subject-disjoint evaluation is reported anywhere in twenty pages. With 86 participants generating 1,414 clip viewings, each child contributes roughly sixteen images, so a random image-level split places about eleven of a test child's own scan-paths in training - and scan-paths from one child viewing different clips share that child's habitual gaze extent, saccade amplitude and scanning style. Rotation-based augmentation makes this worse rather than better, because augmented counts are quoted for the whole dataset rather than for training partitions, implying that rotated copies of a single scan-path can appear on both sides of the split. The sex-by-age experiment then supplies near-direct evidence of this: test accuracy rises monotonically with augmentation level, from 85.07% at 961/957 images through 85.81% at 1,276/1,259 to 98.84% at 3,121/2,905. A real signal does not strengthen when synthetic copies are added; a duplicate-leakage artefact does exactly this. The 98.8% is nevertheless reported as the paper's most striking stratification result. Training accuracy of 100% in almost every table confirms complete memorisation at every setting. Layered on top of the leakage is a confound the paper documents without recognising: it establishes that scan-path images predict age band at 80.5% and sex at 78.0% within the autistic group - both above the 74.4% achieved for diagnosis - while its diagnostic groups differ by 35 percentage points in sex composition and by a factor of two in the proportion aged 10 or over. Taken together these mean the headline diagnosis figure cannot be attributed to autism-related looking patterns rather than to age and sex. The corrective design is straightforward and would be genuinely valuable given the quality of the stimulus battery: split by participant, augment only within training folds, and evaluate diagnosis within age-and-sex-matched strata using the paper's own demographic classifiers as a check. [RQ5.1] CCS concepts: supervised learning by classification, neural networks, health informatics. Additional keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, eye tracking, eye-gaze scan-path, Convolution Neural Network. All are method or modality labels; no application term such as screening or diagnosis appears, consistent with a paper whose stated contribution is representational. The organising term throughout the body is 'stratification' rather than classification or detection - used both for separating autism from typical development and for separating subgroups within autism - which reflects the paper's heterogeneity framing. Other recurring terms: spatio-temporal scan-paths, velocity fusion, ASD heterogeneity, biomarker discovery, social attention. [RQ5.2] ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data 17(2), Article 25, published 20 February 2023; received 15 July 2021, accepted 8 May 2022, online 3 June 2022 - a ten-month review at a data-mining journal. The venue explains the paper's shape: twenty pages with fourteen results tables systematically varying representation, temporal window, stimulus subset and augmentation level, alongside almost no clinical reporting - no diagnostic procedure, no demographics beyond age band and sex, no ethics statement, no sensitivity or specificity. Open access support is provided by six institutions. The article had accumulated 18 citations and 2,645 downloads at retrieval. [RQ5.3] Published 2023 by a seven-institution United States consortium including the Yale Child Study Center, Seattle Children's Research Institute and the University of Washington, funded by an NIH K01 award and a Simons Foundation grant, with a first author who also leads the AAC-telemetry study charted elsewhere in this review and a senior author (Shic) whose eye-tracking work recurs throughout this literature. The framing is heterogeneity rather than detection, and it is argued rather than asserted: clinical assessment is subjective and expert-dependent, autism heterogeneity has 'led to the presumption of the presence of multiple etiologies rather than a single disorder', and the quest for personalised medicine is obstructed by it - so a method that can parse subgroups is more valuable than one that only separates cases from controls. The literature review is the most thorough of any study in this corpus on the specific question of scan-path classification, surveying Carette's LSTM work (83% on 32 children), Li's oculomotor behaviour framework (80% on 49 children), Elbattah's autoencoder clustering, the Saliency4ASD grand challenge submissions of Tao and Shyu (74.22% validation falling to 55.66% on test, attributed to overfitting) and Wu (65.41% and 55.13%), and Pusiol's Fragile X work - and it criticises several of them on exactly the right grounds, noting where validation-to-test performance collapsed and where the stratification comparisons needed to support a heterogeneity claim were not reported. The paper's own most valuable contribution to this review is an unintended one: by demonstrating that scan-path images classify age at 80.5% and sex at 78.0% within a single diagnostic group, it quantifies how much demographic information this widely used representation carries, and therefore how much caution the many scan-path autism classifiers in this corpus require. |
| S-110 | Secondary computational analysis of the public 547-image eye-tracking scan-path dataset from 59 children, conducted at the University of Jordan and Princess Sumaya University for Technology in Amman, with no new data collection. The source sample comprises 29 autistic and 30 typically developing children, 38 male and 21 female, mean age 7.88 years and median 8.1, with CARS mean 32.97 and median 34.50 - the only reuse of this dataset in the review to report severity information. The images divide 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic, roughly nine per child. No demographic or clinical variable is reported by diagnostic group. The autistic children were evaluated in specialised clinics with CARS used to gauge severity; comparison children were recruited from mainstream schools in the Hauts-de-France region with no screening instrument reported. Source acquisition used an SMI Red-m remote eye tracker at 250 Hz in a quiet university room with white barriers reducing distraction, the child seated alone or on a parent's lap about 60 cm from the screen, watching videos with balloons, animated characters and, in some cases, a live host speaking to the child and directing attention towards visible and hidden elements, all in French. The originating study's ethical approvals and Helsinki compliance are cited. | Images were downscaled from 640 x 480 to 100 x 100, converted from colour to greyscale and then flattened from three dimensions to one before entering the model - a step described and figured explicitly, and one that removes the spatial adjacency a convolutional network exploits, despite the model being named and described as convolutional throughout. The proposed T-CNN-ASD was then optimised across an extensive hyperparameter grid: kernel size (3, 6, 9), stride (1, 2), pooling, batch size, six optimisers (Adam, SGD, Adadelta, RMSprop, AdaMax, Nadam) and thirteen architecture configurations from a single layer of 50 neurons up to two layers of 500 and 250, with every cell scored by ten rounds of cross-validation at 100 epochs and 20% dropout, and the maximum carried forward. Data augmentation was deliberately not used, the authors stating that where earlier studies 'depended on augmenting image data to improve outcomes, we maintained the original image count'. Four classical classifiers - k-nearest neighbours, decision tree, random forest and multilayer perceptron - were run for comparison. Cross-validation partitions the 547 images; nothing indicates that a child's images were kept within a fold. | The headline result is 95.59% accuracy on greyscale images with two hidden layers of 300 and 150 neurons, kernel size 3, stride 1 and the Adam optimiser; the colour variant gives 94.69%. Comparators reach 61.3% for k-nearest neighbours, 67.7% for decision tree, 69.60% for random forest and 94.69% for the multilayer perceptron - the last within one point of the proposed model on flattened pixels. Optimiser choice dominates all other hyperparameters: Adam and Nadam give 81-95% across architectures while SGD and Adadelta collapse to 56-62%, a 35-point spread on identical data. Against prior work on the same images the paper tabulates Naive Bayes 61%, logistic regression 70%, SVM 77%, random forest 70% and the source study's own ANN 92%. The decisive result, however, is an internal contradiction: the same table that reports 95.59% accuracy for the proposed model reports 77.60% sensitivity and 79.91% specificity for it, and at 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images those values imply an accuracy of approximately 79.0%. The multilayer perceptron row shows the same pattern - 94.69% reported against about 73.6% implied. The quantity labelled F1 is defined as the harmonic mean of sensitivity and specificity rather than of precision and recall. | The reported accuracy cannot be reconciled with the reported sensitivity and specificity at the stated class sizes, and the paper offers no reconciliation, so two irreconcilable characterisations of the same classifier stand side by side in one table. Cross-validation partitions the 547 images rather than the 59 children, so with roughly nine images per child each held-out image has about eight siblings from the same child in training - the recurring leakage route across this dataset's reuse literature. More than a hundred hyperparameter configurations were evaluated on that same cross-validation with the maximum reported and no held-out confirmation, in a setting where optimiser choice alone moves accuracy by 35 points. Images are flattened to one dimension before entering a model described throughout as convolutional. No majority-class baseline is computed against an implied 60.0% floor, and no confidence intervals, AUC or confusion matrices are given. No demographic variable is reported by group, so matching cannot be checked; no diagnostic criteria are described; and the CARS severity data the dataset carries - and which the paper's own introduction invites using by discussing severity-linked eye-tracking subtypes - are reported and then ignored. There is no limitations section and no acknowledged constraint of any kind. | The fifth reuse of the 547-image scan-path dataset charted in this review, and the one that most clearly demonstrates why reported accuracies in this literature require arithmetic verification rather than acceptance. It is the only reuse to report sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy, and those class-conditional metrics imply roughly 79% - which sits close to the three most defensible estimates on these identical images: 81.0% from an independent transfer-learning reuse under the same image-level splitting, 72.88% from a one-image-per-child leave-one-out analysis, and approximately 71% from the source authors' own participant-level correction. The 95.59% headline is incompatible with the paper's own class-conditional numbers, and whichever column is in error, the episode illustrates that a synthesis of this dataset's reuse literature cannot treat reported accuracies as comparable quantities. Three further observations are worth carrying forward. The paper declines to use augmentation on explicit and correct grounds, stating that prior work depended on augmenting a small image set to improve outcomes - a judgement directly vindicated by another study in this corpus where accuracy climbs monotonically with augmentation level to 98.8%. Its optimiser sweep is inadvertently informative: a 35-point spread between Adam and SGD on fixed data and fixed architectures indicates that the reported performance is substantially a property of the optimisation trajectory rather than a robust property of the signal. And it is the only reuse to report the source dataset's CARS severity scores, which shows that severity information has been available in this widely reused dataset all along and that no study charted here has related it to model output. | [RQ1.1] Fifty-nine children producing 547 scan-path images - the fifth independent reuse of this dataset encountered in the review. Unlike the other reuses charted here, this paper reports the source participant statistics in a dedicated table: 29 autistic and 30 typically developing children, 38 male (64%) and 21 female (36%), mean age 7.88 years and median 8.1, with CARS mean 32.97 and median 34.50. The image split is 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic, so roughly nine images per child. None of the demographic or clinical variables is broken down by diagnostic group, so it cannot be determined whether the groups were matched on age or sex - the sex ratio of 64% male across the whole sample is compatible with anything from a balanced split to a heavily male autistic group and a balanced comparison group. The 547 images, not the 59 children, are the unit of cross-validation throughout. [RQ1.2] 'Children with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD) children' predominate, person-first, alongside 'individuals with ASD' and 'people with ASD'. Autism is 'a developmental disorder that encompasses difficulties in communication (both verbal and non-verbal), social skills, and repetitive behaviors' and 'a neurodevelopmental disorder that impacts the behavioral and cognitive abilities of children'. The register is medical-model but not pejorative, and the introduction is unusually attentive to autistic people's communicative experience for an engineering paper - it discusses difficulty grasping 'deeper implications in dialogues, resulting in literal understandings and struggles in recognizing indirect messages like sarcasm', and notes that 'clear and specific instructions are necessary for their understanding'. It also engages seriously with heterogeneity, comorbidity (ADHD, anxiety, mood disorders) and the interpersonal-coordination framing of diagnostic conversation. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. One framing choice should be flagged: early detection is motivated partly by 'reduced costs for both individuals and society as a whole', a cost-benefit argument that recurs across this corpus. [RQ1.3] Better than the other reuses of this dataset, which typically report nothing, but still incomplete and entirely inherited. Table 1 gives, for the sample as a whole: 59 participants, 38 male and 21 female (64%/36%), 29 autistic and 30 typically developing, mean age 7.88 years and median 8.1, and CARS mean 32.97 and median 34.50. No variable is reported by group, so age matching, sex balance between groups and the severity distribution within the autistic group are all unavailable. The CARS figures nonetheless carry information the paper does not use: a mean of 32.97 with median 34.50 places the autistic sample in the mild-to-moderate band on that instrument, which characterises the spectrum position of the group better than most studies in this corpus manage - and the paper's own introduction notes that eye-tracking markers have been linked to a more severely affected subtype, so relating CARS to model output was both possible and thematically invited. Nothing else is available: no IQ, language level, comorbidity, medication or socioeconomic data, and no race or ethnicity beyond the participants being French-speaking children from the Hauts-de-France region. [RQ1.4] Inherited and thinly reported, though better specified than in the other reuses of this dataset. The autistic children 'were evaluated in specialized clinics, and the level of autism in each child was gauged using the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS)', while typically developing children were recruited from mainstream French schools. Two distinctions matter. CARS is described as gauging the level of autism rather than establishing the diagnosis, so it functions here as a severity measure applied after specialist clinic evaluation - and that evaluation is named but not described, with no diagnostic criteria, DSM or ICD version, clinician discipline or procedure given. And the comparison group's status rests on school recruitment with no screening instrument reported, so undetected autistic traits in that group cannot be excluded. For the present study these are inherited rather than authored deficiencies, but they define the target being predicted and the paper does not flag them as open. [RQ1.5] CARS scores are available and reported at the sample level - mean 32.97, median 34.50 - which makes this the only reuse of this dataset in the corpus to carry any severity information at all. That is a genuine asset and it is entirely unused: no analysis relates CARS to model output, no within-autism severity gradient is examined, and no check is made on whether misclassified images belong to less severely affected children. The omission is more conspicuous because the paper's own introduction sets up exactly this question, noting that 'an atypical preference for geometric images can serve as an early indicator of a specific subtype of autism spectrum disorder, which is linked to more severe symptoms', and that comorbid ADHD alters fixation durations on faces. Both observations invite a severity or subtype analysis on data the study already holds. No cognitive, language or adaptive measure is available for any participant. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to build an enhanced convolutional deep network for autism identification from eye-tracking scan-path images, with an explicit methodological claim distinguishing it from prior work: 'we addressed the issue of working with a dataset containing a small number of images without utilizing augmentation. Whereas many earlier studies depended on augmenting image data to improve outcomes, we maintained the original image count and achieved superior performance.' That is a defensible and welcome position, since augmentation on a 547-image corpus split at image level compounds dependence between training and test data, as another study in this corpus demonstrates directly. Findings: 95.59% accuracy for greyscale images with two hidden layers of 300 and 150 neurons, kernel size 3, stride 1, Adam optimiser and 20% dropout; 94.69% with colour. Comparators on the same data reach 61.3% for k-nearest neighbours, 67.7% for decision tree, 69.60% for random forest and 94.69% for a multilayer perceptron. Optimiser choice dominates everything else: Adam and Nadam give 81-95%, RMSprop and AdaMax 85-94%, while SGD and Adadelta collapse to 56-62% - a 35-point spread that indicates the result is highly sensitive to optimisation rather than robustly present in the data. The decisive problem is that the same results table reports sensitivity 77.60% and specificity 79.91% alongside the 95.59% accuracy, and those three figures cannot describe the same classifier: with 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images they imply an accuracy near 79%. [RQ2.2] No study setting: a computational reanalysis at two universities in Amman, Jordan, of images collected in France. The source acquisition setting is described in more detail than in the other reuses of this dataset and is worth recording, because it bears on what the scan-paths represent: a quiet room at university premises, physical white barriers erected to reduce visual distraction, the child seated alone or on a parent's lap approximately 60 cm from the screen, and all interaction conducted in French, the participants' first language. Typically developing children came from schools in the Hauts-de-France region and autistic children from specialised clinics - the standard clinic-versus-school case-control geometry, inherited rather than chosen. [RQ2.3] Inherited and described at second hand, but more informatively than by the other reuses. Children watched videos built to attract them - colourful balloons, animated characters, elements whose position changed during the study - and some videos included a live host who spoke to the child and attempted to direct attention towards both visible and hidden elements. That last detail matters for interpretation: a live host issuing verbal direction makes the task partly a joint-attention and instruction-following probe rather than pure free viewing, so the resulting scan-paths reflect responsiveness to social direction as well as spontaneous visual preference. What is not stated in this paper is how many videos each child saw, how long they lasted, how a session was segmented into the roughly nine scan-paths per child, or how gaze coordinates were rendered into images - the last being the determinant of what a convolutional network can extract from the drawing. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional by inheritance, with no temporal analysis. Ethics is handled by reference to the source study: procedures 'were conducted following the ethical standards set by the institutional and/or national research committee, as well as in compliance with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its subsequent amendments'. Citing the originating study's ethical basis is appropriate practice for a secondary analysis and is more than most dataset-reuse papers in this corpus do. No funding statement and no competing-interests declaration appear in the retrieved text. [RQ2.5] Acquisition equipment is inherited and specified: SMI Experiment Center Software with a Red-m remote eye tracker sampling at 250 Hz, producing images at 640 x 480. That is a high sampling rate and a named commercial system, which is more than several primary studies in this corpus provide about their own equipment. The analysis stack is given in full: Python 3.6.8 with Keras on TensorFlow, OpenCV, scikit-learn and Matplotlib, running on an Intel Core i7 tenth-generation machine with 16 GB RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce MX230. No calibration procedure, tracking-quality criterion or rendering specification is available. [RQ2.6] Extensively reported on the computational side and unverifiable on the numerical side. Reproducible from the text: the public source dataset with participant statistics, stimulus description, eye tracker and native image size; the full preprocessing chain from 640 x 480 colour through 100 x 100 greyscale to a flattened one-dimensional vector, with figures; the complete hyperparameter grids for kernel size, stride, pooling, batch size, optimiser and architecture, each reporting accuracy for every cell; the winning configuration in full; and the software and hardware. Not reproducible: code, the cross-validation implementation and seed, the image-to-child mapping - the one fact needed to assess whether any evaluation is participant-disjoint - and, most seriously, the headline numbers themselves, since the reported accuracy cannot be derived from the reported sensitivity and specificity at the stated class sizes. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section and no constraint of any kind is acknowledged; the paper's self-assessment is uniformly favourable. The problems are correspondingly unaddressed and one is arithmetic rather than methodological. First, the reported metrics are mutually incompatible: Table 9 gives the proposed model 95.59% accuracy, 77.60% sensitivity and 79.91% specificity, but with 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images those sensitivity and specificity values imply an accuracy of approximately 79.0%. The same holds for the multilayer perceptron comparator (94.69% reported against an implied 73.6%). Either the accuracy figures come from a different computation than the class-conditional ones, or one set is in error; the paper does not reconcile them, and a reader cannot determine which number describes the model. Second, the quantity labelled F1 is defined in Equation (4) as the harmonic mean of sensitivity and specificity, which is not F1. Third, cross-validation partitions the 547 images rather than the 59 children, so each held-out image has roughly eight siblings from the same child in training - the recurring leakage route in this dataset's reuse literature. Fourth, more than a hundred hyperparameter configurations were evaluated on that same cross-validation and the maximum reported as the result, with no independent confirmation; the 35-point spread between optimisers shows how much of the outcome depends on that search. Fifth, images are flattened to one dimension before entering a model described throughout as convolutional. Sixth, no majority-class baseline is computed against an implied 60.0% floor. And the CARS severity data the dataset carries, and which the introduction's discussion of severity-linked subtypes invites using, are reported and then ignored. [RQ2.9] No dedicated future-work content in the retrieved text beyond the conclusion's framing that early-detection tools should be 'brief, easily understandable for parents, and easy to administer by healthcare professionals' and that eye tracking suits that purpose. Absent, and needed: reconciliation of the reported metrics, participant-level cross-validation, a held-out confirmation of the selected hyperparameter configuration, a majority-class baseline, and use of the available CARS scores to test whether classification tracks severity. [RQ3.1] Visual attention during video viewing, encoded as a drawn trajectory. The behavioural rationale offered is the standard one - that autistic children show atypical visual attention, particularly towards human faces - and the introduction develops it further than most reuses of this dataset, discussing atypical preference for geometric images as a marker of a more severely affected subtype and noting that children with both autism and ADHD show shorter fixation durations on faces than children with autism alone. None of this is operationalised: no areas of interest, no fixation durations, no face-versus-object contrast is computed, because the input is a picture of a path and the model receives nothing else. The source protocol's inclusion of a live host directing the child's attention means the recorded behaviour also reflects responsiveness to verbal social direction, which the paper does not discuss. As with the other scan-path-image studies in this corpus, the representation makes behavioural properties (where the child looked) and incidental graphical properties (how much of the canvas the drawing covers, how dense the overplotting is) indistinguishable to the model, and no analysis separates them. [RQ3.2] No fusion of any kind - a single modality rendered as a single image type, classified by a single network. The only representational variation tested is greyscale versus colour, with greyscale giving marginally better results (95.59% versus 94.69%). The paper's related-work section notes that others have combined eye tracking with kinematic data to gain 5-8 accuracy points, and that gaze features combined with demographic descriptors such as age improved classification with the observation that 'the average classification accuracy decreased when age was excluded as a feature in all tested classifiers' - a finding it reports without recognising its implication for its own work, namely that gaze-based classifiers in this literature draw part of their performance from age information. Since the present study's dataset carries age and CARS at the participant level and uses neither, both a fusion experiment and a confound check were available and not attempted. [RQ4.1] A network the paper calls T-CNN-ASD, described as a convolutional deep neural network but parameterised and reported entirely in terms of hidden-layer neuron counts, from a single layer of 50-600 neurons up to two layers of 500 and 250. The characterisation is internally confused: kernel size, stride and pooling are swept as hyperparameters, which implies convolution, yet the preprocessing explicitly flattens the 100 x 100 image 'from 3D to 1D' before the model, which removes the two-dimensional adjacency structure convolution operates on, and no layer diagram or channel specification is given. The comparison set is four classical classifiers - k-nearest neighbours, decision tree, random forest and multilayer perceptron - of which the multilayer perceptron reaches 94.69%, within one point of the proposed model, suggesting that whatever is driving performance is available to a plain feed-forward network on flattened pixels. The most informative modelling result is the optimiser sweep: Adam gives 95.59% and Nadam 95.07%, but SGD and Adadelta collapse to 56-62% across every architecture tried. A 35-point dependence on optimiser choice, on a fixed dataset with a fixed architecture family, indicates a result that is a property of the optimisation trajectory as much as of the data. [RQ4.2] A 100 x 100 greyscale image flattened to a 10,000-element vector, with a parallel colour variant. Three transformations separate the raw gaze data from the model input, each discarding information: rendering the coordinate time series as a static drawing removes temporal order, fixation duration and saccade velocity; downscaling from 640 x 480 to 100 x 100 means each output pixel spans roughly 6 x 5 source pixels, so fine spatial resolution of where on a face gaze landed is lost; and flattening removes spatial adjacency. What survives is the coarse geometry and density of the drawn path. The greyscale conversion is reported to work slightly better than colour, which is consistent with colour carrying no information in these renderings - but the rendering scheme is not described, so whether colour originally encoded anything (order, duration, which eye) cannot be determined. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and a mislabelled F1, reported for the proposed model and all four comparators in both greyscale and colour conditions - and this fuller metric set is what exposes the paper's central problem. Reporting sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy is good practice, but here the three quantities cannot describe the same classifier: at 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images, the reported 77.60% sensitivity and 79.91% specificity imply an accuracy of about 79.0%, not the 95.59% claimed, and the multilayer perceptron shows the same pattern (94.69% claimed against about 73.6% implied). The discrepancy is not small and is not reconciled anywhere. Separately, Equation (4) defines F1 as 2 x (Sensitivity x Specificity) / (Sensitivity + Specificity), which is the harmonic mean of sensitivity and specificity - a balanced-accuracy variant - rather than the F1 score, so the column labelled F1 does not mean what its name implies. Also missing: AUC, confusion matrices, confidence intervals, and any majority-class baseline against an implied 60.0% floor. [RQ4.4] None. No saliency map, class activation, filter visualisation, error analysis or example inspection is performed for any model. The discussion's account of why the proposed model outperforms the alternatives is entirely generic and borrowed from the image-processing literature - that convolutional networks are 'successfully used for image denoising' and that convolution 'reduces the high dimensionality of images without losing its information' - with no reference to anything observed in these scan-paths. The absence is compounded by the flattening step, which means the model is not exploiting spatial structure in the way that explanation assumes. For a study whose entire input is a picture of a behaviour, and where incidental graphical properties are as available to the network as behavioural ones, a single class activation map over correctly and incorrectly classified scan-paths would have been the most informative addition possible. [RQ4.5] Two problems compound, and a third makes the result difficult to interpret at all. First, cross-validation partitions the 547 images rather than the 59 children. With roughly nine images per child and no statement that a child's images were kept within a fold, each held-out image is accompanied by around eight siblings from the same child in training - the same route that has produced accuracies from 81% to over 99% across five reuses of this identical dataset, against the source authors' own participant-level figure near 71% and an independent one-image-per-child leave-one-out result of 72.88%. Second, the reported figure is the maximum of an extremely large hyperparameter search: separate sweeps over kernel size, stride, pooling, batch size, optimiser and thirteen architecture configurations, well over a hundred cells in total, every one scored on the same cross-validation with the best bolded and carried forward. No held-out confirmation of the selected configuration is performed, and the 35-point spread between optimisers on identical data shows how much room that search had to exploit. Third, and most consequentially, the headline accuracy cannot be reconciled with the sensitivity and specificity reported for the same model. At 219 autistic and 328 non-autistic images, 77.60% sensitivity and 79.91% specificity give approximately 79.0% accuracy. That implied figure is strikingly consistent with the other honest estimates on this dataset - 81.0% from an independent transfer-learning study, 72.88% from one-image-per-child leave-one-out, and roughly 71% from the source authors' own participant-level correction - which suggests the class-conditional metrics may be the trustworthy ones and the accuracy column an artefact. Either way, the paper reports two irreconcilable characterisations of its own classifier and reconciles neither, so no single number from it can be carried into a synthesis without that caveat. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder (ASD); convolutional neural network (CNN); deep learning; eye-tracking scan path; multi-layer perceptron (MLP); machine learning (ML). Five of six are method labels and none names an application, although the body text speaks of automatic classification, early detection and biomarkers throughout. The coined model name T-CNN-ASD appears in the title and abstract and functions as branding for what is architecturally a small feed-forward network over flattened pixels. [RQ5.2] Information 15(3), article 133, MDPI, open access under CC BY; received 22 January 2024, revised 21 February, accepted 26 February, published 28 February 2024 - a 37-day turnaround from submission to publication. The venue is a general information-science journal rather than a clinical, biomedical or specialist machine-learning one, which is consistent with the paper's shape: twelve tables of hyperparameter sweeps, extensive tutorial exposition of convolutional network components, and no limitations section, ethics statement of its own, funding declaration or competing-interests statement. The compressed review period is worth noting given that the paper's central results table contains an unreconciled arithmetic inconsistency between accuracy and the class-conditional metrics. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by the Department of Artificial Intelligence at the University of Jordan with Princess Sumaya University for Technology, Amman. The framing is the familiar cost-and-expertise argument, developed at unusual length: diagnosis requires specialised professionals using observation, interviews and questionnaires; current tools are time-consuming because of 'the extensive number of items that need to be checked by the specialist' and rely on 'static human-embedded rules'; and because 'each specialist relies on their own expertise and experience to diagnose autism spectrum disorder', the process suffers 'inconsistencies and a lack of reliability'. The introduction also engages with delayed diagnosis and its causes - limited resources in rural areas and low-income families, shortage of specialist referrals, parental awareness - which locates the work in the access literature. For this review the study's value is as the fifth reuse of the 547-image dataset and as the clearest instance of a specific reporting hazard. It is the only reuse to report sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy, and those class-conditional metrics imply roughly 79% - close to the independent transfer-learning reuse at 81%, to the one-image-per-child leave-one-out figure of 72.88%, and to the source authors' own participant-level correction near 71%. The 95.59% headline is irreconcilable with them. Whichever number is correct, the paper illustrates why a review of this literature must recompute rather than accept reported accuracies, and why the near-ceiling figures that dominate this dataset's reuse literature should be treated as claims requiring arithmetic verification. |
| S-111 | Retrospective national cohort study using electronic health records from Tipat Halav, the Israeli Ministry of Health's universal well-baby developmental surveillance programme, delivered by trained nurses and a developmental paediatrician across 503 clinics covering 75% of the population over roughly eleven visits from birth to age six. All 780,610 children born between January 2014 and December 2019 with at least two years of computerised records were included; 1,163 had an autism diagnosis recorded after age two and 774,778 formed the comparison group, giving a population incidence of 0.15%. Cases were ascertained by ICD-9 code (722 children) or by keyword search of provider free-text notes with manual verification that the reference concerned the child rather than a relative (553 children), with acronym collisions such as atrial septal defect screened out. Down syndrome was excluded from the comparison group but Fragile X, tuberous sclerosis and other autism-associated aetiologies were deliberately retained. The autism group was 78.3% male against 51.4% in the comparison group, with higher rates of preterm birth, older mothers, lower gestational age and birth weight, lower nursing rates and far higher parental concern. Mean age at recorded diagnosis was 37.5 months. Approval came from the Ministry of Health Helsinki committee with consent waived on anonymisation grounds; funding was from the Gertner Institute and no conflicts were declared. | One hundred candidate features were assembled from the records and reduced to 59 on clinical-relevance grounds before modelling, spanning developmental milestone attainment across gross motor, fine motor, language and personal-social domains, birth parameters, post-natal growth percentiles, familial variables and parent-reported concern. The surveillance protocol assesses 60 age-related milestones based partly on the Denver Developmental Screening Test, with 38 checked up to 24 months across nine age bins. Because checkup timing varies and children have multiple entries per milestone, each milestone was reduced to a binary of 'ever passed' versus 'only failed', chosen explicitly to avoid embedding developmental assumptions about never-tested and late-tested records, at the acknowledged cost of not distinguishing children who passed after several attempts. Predictors were capped at 24 months and the outcome restricted to diagnoses recorded after 24 months, a separation adopted deliberately to minimise leakage from diagnosis to predictors. A gradient boosting model was fitted with 3-fold cross-validation over children and compared against logistic regression, random forest and naive Bayes. The high-risk group was defined by the Youden threshold. SHAP quantified feature importance within each fold, with cross-fold stability reported, and the seven leading milestone predictors were tested independently with Fisher's exact tests. | Average test AUC was 0.86 (SD 0.009) with sensitivity 0.75 (SD 0.03) and specificity 0.81 (SD 0.02); training AUC was 0.88, which the authors report as indicating slight overfitting. At the Youden threshold 144,632 children (18.6% of the cohort) were flagged high risk, capturing 874 of the 1,163 cases - an autism incidence of 0.006 in that group against 0.001 in the cohort, a 4.3-fold enrichment, and a positive predictive value of 0.60% that the paper does not compute. The method comparison found almost no advantage for the tree ensemble: logistic regression matched gradient boosting at AUC 0.86 with marginally higher sensitivity (0.77 versus 0.75), random forest reached 0.84 and naive Bayes 0.83. The seven most important milestone predictors, all confirmed at p < 0.001 by independent testing, were vocabulary over ten words, building a tower from cubes, giving a kiss, eating independently with a spoon, knowing at least one body part, composing two-word sentences and saying 2-3 words - four language, two personal-social, one fine motor, all between 12 and 24 months. Male sex, parental developmental concern, non-nursing, older maternal age, lower gestational age and atypical growth percentiles were also key. SHAP rankings were stable across folds, with 15 of 24 unique top-20 features appearing in all three. A boys-only model performed comparably. Children flagged high risk had an odds ratio of 3.29 (95% CI 3.18-3.39) of independent referral for developmental assessment, a variable deliberately excluded from the model. | Outcome ascertainment is the binding constraint and the authors state it plainly: because diagnoses are captured only when reported during well-baby visits, 'based on the national incidence of ASD, the true positive ASD group is at least 10 times higher in the examined population', so the great majority of autistic children in the cohort sit in the comparison group. That misclassification adds substantial label noise, biases sensitivity and specificity in directions the data cannot resolve, and means the derivable positive predictive value of 0.60% is an underestimate by an unknown factor. Diagnoses also come from two routes with 43.4% ascertained from provider free-text notes, and recording practice varies across 503 clinics with no inter-rater data. Milestone binarisation to ever-passed versus only-failed discards the pattern of delay over repeated attempts, which is arguably the most informative aspect of longitudinal milestone data. The feature set is bounded by what the national protocol records, and plausible early markers outside it - head lag at three months, raising hands to be picked up at six months, nodding at twelve months - are named as missing. Paternal age and family history of autism, both established risk factors, are not routinely collected, and the authors note that the advanced-maternal-age effect may partly proxy paternal age. Positive predictive value is never stated despite the confusion counts making it computable, so the reader must derive that 165 children are flagged per recorded case. And maternal country of birth is reported as associated with diagnosis rate without discussion of whether it entered the model or of the equity implications of a risk score that could encode migration background. | The most important study in this review for translational interpretation, and the only one whose numbers describe deployment rather than a research contrast. Three contributions are decisive. First, it makes the prevalence problem concrete: a well-validated model with AUC 0.86 and 75% sensitivity, applied to a genuine population at 0.15% incidence, produces a high-risk group of 144,632 children containing 874 recorded cases - a positive predictive value of 0.60%, or 165 children flagged for every one with a recorded diagnosis. Every accuracy figure elsewhere in this corpus was obtained at prevalences between 40% and 60%, and this study shows what happens when the same order of discriminative performance meets the real base rate. Second, its method comparison undercuts the algorithmic framing that dominates the rest of the corpus: on real population data with 59 clinically chosen features, logistic regression matched gradient boosting exactly at AUC 0.86 with marginally better sensitivity, and the entire spread across four methods was 0.03 AUC - which suggests that the large algorithm-driven differences reported in small-sample studies elsewhere here are more likely properties of sample size and validation design than of modelling power. Third, its validation design solves problems the rest of the corpus does not have to face and solves them well: a population cohort with no recruitment or spectrum truncation, cross-validation over children, and temporal separation between predictors and outcome imposed explicitly to prevent leakage from diagnosis back to predictors. Two further features deserve emulation. Its limitations section quantifies its own outcome undercount at a factor of ten and states the cost of its representational choices in the same passage as their rationale. And its external validity check - showing that children flagged high risk were 3.29 times more likely to have been independently referred for developmental assessment, using a variable deliberately kept out of the model - is a model of how to interrogate what a high false-positive rate actually consists of. The study also sits at the boundary of the review's modality scope, since its behavioural data are nurse-recorded milestone attainment rather than sensor-derived measurement, and it is worth noting how far that coarse, binary, administratively captured signal goes: whether a two-year-old has ten words, builds a tower, gives a kiss or eats with a spoon. | [RQ1.1] A national population cohort rather than a recruited sample - 780,610 Israeli children born between 2014 and 2019 with at least two years of computerised well-baby records, of whom 775,941 entered the analysis: 1,163 with an autism diagnosis recorded after age two and 774,778 without autism or another pervasive developmental or medical condition. This is by four orders of magnitude the largest sample in the review and the only one drawn from an unselected population. Case ascertainment used two routes and both counts are given: 722 children (56.6%) identified by ICD-9 code and 553 (43.4%) by keyword search of provider free-text notes with manual verification that the reference concerned the child rather than a family member. A further 112 children with autism diagnosed before age two were excluded to preserve the temporal separation between predictors and outcome. Conditions sharing the ASD acronym, notably atrial septal defect, were screened out. Down syndrome was excluded from the comparison group but Fragile X, tuberous sclerosis and other autism-associated aetiologies were deliberately retained, on the reasoning that autism has multiple aetiologies and excluding them would narrow the target condition artificially. The resulting incidence of 0.0015 is roughly a tenth of Israel's reported national rate, and the authors state this openly as a limitation. [RQ1.2] 'Children with ASD' and 'typically developing (TD)' children, person-first and consistent. Autism 'manifests through social communication deficits and atypical behaviors' per DSM-5, and the vocabulary of red flags, risk, markers and screening runs throughout - appropriate to a public-health surveillance framing. The register is notably free of the burden and cost rhetoric found elsewhere in this corpus; the motivation offered is access and equity rather than economic saving. Two framing choices are worth recording. The paper repeatedly emphasises heterogeneity as the obstacle to early detection - 'the great heterogeneity in the red flags, onset, and progression of symptoms, and in the divergence of developmental trajectories in ASD' - and treats variation as something a model must accommodate rather than as noise. And it frames the problem partly as one of clinician support rather than clinician replacement, noting that some early signs 'can be easily missed by a healthcare provider during a short checkup visit due to their gradual deviation or subtlety, such as social reciprocity, social smile, and eye contact', and that 'disparities in healthcare screening resources and in provider awareness of individual developmental differences' are themselves barriers. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. [RQ1.3] Extensive and, uniquely in this review, describing a whole population rather than a matched sample. Reported with formal comparisons at a p < 0.001 threshold chosen for the large sample size and multiple comparisons: sex (78.3% male in the autism group against 51.4%), birth year distribution, maternal country of birth (with higher diagnosis rates for mothers born in Russia and Ethiopia), preterm birth rate, maternal age, gestational week, birth weight, nursing status, parental concern rates, and number of well-baby visits (13.7 in the autism group against 11.44, t(775,939) = -23.05, p < 0.001, d = 0.7).
