Twenty-nine pages, of which a substantial proportion is devoted to the linguistic theory, the annotation scheme and the interpretation of what the tags mean - so the balance is unusual for this corpus, with the machine learning occupying perhaps a quarter of the paper and the linguistic framework the rest. The venue's reporting requirements produce the data availability, funding and competing-interests statements, and the length permits the annotation scheme to be documented at a level that a conference paper could not accommodate. Two supplementary files carry the tag frequency comparisons between groups. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by the Department of Neuropsychiatry at Hirosaki University with Aomori Chuo Gakuin University and the Natural Language Processing Lab at Tohoku University, funded by two JSPS KAKENHI grants. The framing is diagnostic supplementation grounded in a specific, well-evidenced critique of the gold standard rather than in generic complaints about subjectivity: ADOS-2 does not clearly differentiate autism from ADHD or from the negative symptoms of schizophrenia and other psychiatric comorbidities; masking, compensation and camouflaging can conceal impairment; and adult diagnosis is further hampered because caregiver developmental reports are usually unavailable while self-insight is unreliable. That is a more precise diagnosis of what automated assessment is for than any other paper in this corpus offers, and it leads to a correspondingly bounded claim - language analysis as one input among several, not a replacement. Four features make the study particularly valuable to this review. It is the only one that applies a gold-standard instrument to both groups, so its comparison group is screened rather than assumed. It is the only one that nests a fitted preprocessing component inside its cross-validation. It is the only one that tests model comparisons statistically and then declines to over-read non-significant differences. And it is the only one that refuses to rank its models by accuracy, retaining an interpretable linear model on the explicit ground that interpretability is not commensurable with accuracy in clinical use. Set against these, its unmeasured comparison-group IQ is a real limitation, and its reliance on ADOS-2 transcripts means the speech analysed was produced inside the diagnostic encounter itself - a form of dependence between sample and label that no other language study here faces and that the paper does not discuss. |
| S-116 | Secondary computational analysis of a scraped public image dataset, conducted at Andhra University and GITAM Deemed to be University in Visakhapatnam with no data collection. The dataset comprises 2,936 colour facial photographs from Kaggle, evenly divided at 1,468 autistic and 1,468 non-autistic - the same publicly scraped 'Autistic Children Facial Dataset' already charted in this review from a companion study using a 2,836-image version, in which the autistic images were sourced from autism-focused online platforms and the non-autistic images gathered separately from the internet. Labels are the names of two subdirectories, and features were extracted by traversing the directory structure with a label column added to denote 'autistic' or 'non_autistic'. No age, sex, race, cognitive, language, comorbidity or severity information exists for any image, and the number of distinct children is unknown. No diagnostic verification of any kind underlies either class. No ethics approval, consent, funding or competing-interests statement appears. | Eight feature families were extracted with counts tabulated: 3,000 activations each from ImageNet-pretrained VGG16, ResNet and Inception with fully connected layers excluded; 100 HOG features encoding gradient distributions; 50 LBP features encoding local texture; 50 ORB keypoint and descriptor features; 65 perceptual hash features; and 50 SIFT features. These were combined into three feature vectors of 3,315 dimensions each, pairing the 315 handcrafted features with one backbone's deep features. Five classifiers - random forest, k-nearest neighbours, decision tree, support vector machine and logistic regression - were applied to the handcrafted features alone and to each fused vector. The extraction pipeline is narrated in step-by-step procedural detail down to directory traversal, DataFrame construction and CSV export. No evaluation protocol is described anywhere: the words 'split' and 'validation' do not appear, no cross-validation is reported, and no train-test partition or holdout proportion is stated for any of the twenty tabulated accuracies. No hyperparameters are given for any classifier. | Handcrafted image features alone gave 84.50% accuracy with random forest, 81.20% with logistic regression, 80.00% with decision tree, 78.50% with SVM and 78.00% with k-nearest neighbours. Fusing with ResNet features raised the range to 84.4-90.2%, with SVM and logistic regression best at 90.2% and 90.0%. Fusing with Inception features gave 83.2-94.6%, with SVM best at 94.6%, random forest 91.2% and logistic regression 90.0%. Precision, recall and F1 are reported as identical values to the percentage point in almost every row, without the underlying confusion counts. No AUC, confidence interval or chance baseline is given for any result, and no interpretability analysis of any kind is performed. | No evaluation protocol is described at all, so none of the twenty reported accuracies can be interpreted as an estimate of performance on unseen data, and the comparison the paper is organised around - handcrafted versus fused features, and among three backbones - cannot be evaluated either, since a resubstitution comparison would favour higher-dimensional representations regardless of generalisation. The dataset's two classes come from different internet sources, so photographic properties are confounded with the label; this matters more here than in the companion study because five of the eight feature families are descriptors that respond directly to gradient structure, texture, keypoint density and global image fingerprint - all functions of resolution, sharpness, compression and lighting - and that feature set alone reaches 84.5%, a result reported without comment. Labels are directory names with no diagnostic verification. The number of distinct children is unknown, so partition integrity could not be established even if a partition had been specified. No demographic information exists. No interpretability analysis is performed that could distinguish a face classifier from a photograph classifier. The title and introduction frame the work as emotion-based while no emotion or expression analysis appears anywhere. And there is no limitations section, no ethics approval, no consent and no discussion of either. | Charted as a second data point on the facial-photograph branch of this literature, and it strengthens three observations already recorded from the companion study on the same scraped dataset. First, the branch is substantial rather than marginal: two independent groups published on this collection in the same year, and this paper's own literature review cites at least half a dozen further facial-image autism classifiers using MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, VGG19 and hybrid vision transformers at accuracies from 88% to 92.5%. Second, its reported accuracies - up to 94.6% - are comparable to or higher than those of the best-conducted studies charted in this review, including the joint-attention system with ADOS-verified diagnoses and the human-benchmark comparison against expert clinicians, which is further evidence that reported accuracy in this literature does not order studies by evidential quality. Third, and specific to this paper, it can report twenty accuracy figures without stating anywhere how training and test data were separated, while narrating the feature-extraction pipeline down to CSV export - an asymmetry that is itself informative about what this branch's peer review is filtering on. One further observation is worth carrying forward as a methodological point rather than a criticism of this study alone. The handcrafted feature set used here consists of HOG, LBP, ORB, PHASH and SIFT: gradient histograms, texture patterns, keypoint descriptors and perceptual hashes. These are the standard toolkit for image retrieval and near-duplicate detection - that is, for telling photographs apart - and they achieve 84.5% on their own. In a dataset whose two classes were harvested from different parts of the internet, that is close to a demonstration of the confound, and it appears in the paper as an intermediate result on the way to a better one. | [RQ1.1] There are no participants - 2,936 facial photographs from a Kaggle collection, evenly divided at 1,468 per class, described only as colour images of autistic and non-autistic children. The number of distinct children behind them is unknown and unrecoverable. This is the same publicly scraped 'Autistic Children Facial Dataset' already charted in this review in a companion study which used a 2,836-image version, and the two counts imply different snapshots of a dataset that has been revised. The companion study documents the provenance that this one does not mention: autistic images sourced from online platforms focused on autism, non-autistic images gathered separately from the internet. [RQ1.2] 'Autistic children' and 'non-autistic children', person-first in most constructions but with 'normally developing youngsters' appearing when summarising prior work. The clinical description in the introduction is drawn accurately from DSM criteria and is comparatively careful - reduced sharing of emotions and interests, deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, difficulty adapting behaviour to social contexts, difficulty making friends. The framing of purpose includes an unusual note: technological advancement is described as 'a blessing to the parents who are clueless about managing the condition', which positions the work as parent-facing. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement - a notable absence given that the dataset's autistic images were collected from autism-focused online spaces created by and for that community. The premise that 'autistic children show distinctive patterns' in facial and emotional expression is asserted without citation to any evidence about facial morphology. [RQ1.3] None whatsoever - no age, sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, cognitive level, language, comorbidity or severity data for any image, and no statement that such information is unavailable. The paper does not report even the age range that the dataset's own description carries. As with the companion study, the omission is consequential because the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, and autism-focused online spaces will differ from general internet image collections in the demographics they represent as well as in photographic convention. [RQ1.4] Absent. The labels are the names of two subdirectories in a downloaded folder, and the methods section describes exactly this: features are extracted 'by traversing through the directory structure', with 'a label column added to denote the class label (autistic or non_autistic)'. No diagnosis, instrument, criterion, clinician or verification underlies either class. The quantity the models predict is therefore which folder an image was filed in, and given that the folders were populated from different parts of the internet, the reported accuracies are best read as measures of how distinguishable the two source collections are as image sets. [RQ1.5] None, and none is possible. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive information exists for any image. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to improve autism detection accuracy from facial images by combining transfer-learned deep features with handcrafted image descriptors, and to identify the best classifier and feature combination. Findings: handcrafted features alone gave 78.0-84.5% across five classifiers, with random forest best; adding ResNet features raised the range to 84.4-90.2%, with SVM best; and adding Inception features gave 83.2-94.6%, with SVM best at 94.6%. The reported progression - handcrafted alone, then fused with each backbone - is a systematic ablation and is the paper's substantive content. What it cannot establish is what the improvement means, because no evaluation protocol is stated: the words 'split' and 'validation' appear nowhere, no cross-validation is described, and no train-test partition is specified for any of the eighteen reported accuracies. Whether these are held-out figures, training figures, or something else is not determinable from the paper. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Work was performed on a downloaded Kaggle dataset at two universities in Visakhapatnam, India, with no contact with any participant and no acquisition of any kind. [RQ2.3] None. There is no task, protocol or elicitation - the data are photographs. The framing gap is worth stating plainly: the title announces 'Emotion-based Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection' and the introduction argues that 'facial expressions and emotional expressions can help in early detection and diagnosis of ASD', but no expression is labelled, detected, elicited or analysed anywhere in the paper. The features extracted are generic image descriptors, and the classification target is the image's folder. The word 'emotion' does not recur in the method, results or conclusion. So the study measures no behaviour at all while describing itself as behavioural, which places it further outside this review's modality scope than the companion study on the same dataset, that one at least having attached a genuine facial-expression module trained on AffectNet. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional in the trivial sense. No ethics statement, consent, funding declaration or competing-interests statement appears anywhere. As with the companion study, the dataset consists of identifiable photographs of children obtained without their families' knowledge, with one class assembled specifically because those images appeared in autism contexts - so the collection asserts a health status about identifiable minors, and training and publishing on it propagates that assertion. None of this is acknowledged. [RQ2.5] None. Pretrained VGG16, ResNet and Inception networks used as fixed feature extractors with fully connected layers excluded, and five classical classifiers. No hardware, software package, version or hyperparameter is reported. The imaging characteristics of the source photographs - the properties that differ between the two source collections and that HOG, LBP, PHASH and SIFT are designed to capture - are neither reported nor examined. [RQ2.6] Curiously uneven. The feature-extraction pipeline is described at unusual procedural length, narrating library imports, directory traversal, per-image processing, DataFrame construction, label-column addition, merging and CSV export, with exact feature counts tabulated for all eight families. The evaluation is described not at all. A reader is given enough to reconstruct how a 3,315-dimensional feature vector was built and nothing whatever about how the reported accuracies were computed. Also absent: the Kaggle dataset identifier and version, any classifier hyperparameters, any seed, and code. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section and no constraint is acknowledged. The unaddressed problems are the same as for the companion study on this dataset, plus one that is specific to this paper. The dataset's two classes come from different internet sources, so image provenance is confounded with the label - and here the confound is sharper than usual, because five of the eight feature families are handcrafted descriptors that respond directly to gradient structure, texture, keypoint density and perceptual hashing, all of which are functions of resolution, sharpness, compression and lighting rather than of anything about the child. That the handcrafted features alone reach 84.5% is therefore not evidence that facial morphology is informative; it is equally consistent with the two collections being distinguishable as image sets. No diagnostic verification exists for either class. The number of distinct children is unknown. No demographic data are available. Eighteen classifier-feature combinations were evaluated and the maximum reported. And, uniquely among included studies, no evaluation protocol of any kind is described. [RQ2.9] None proposed. The conclusion restates the method and the comparison without identifying any next step. [RQ3.1] None is measured. The paper's framing is behavioural - emotion, facial expression, distinctive patterns shown by autistic children - and its method is not. HOG captures gradient orientation distributions, LBP captures local texture, ORB captures keypoints and their descriptors, PHASH computes a perceptual fingerprint of the whole image, SIFT detects scale-invariant local features, and the three backbones supply generic ImageNet activations. None of these is a measure of expression, movement or any behaviour, and no expression labels exist in the dataset. For the review this study marks the far end of a boundary the companion paper already approached: automated autism detection that has left behaviour behind entirely while retaining behavioural vocabulary. [RQ3.2] Fusion within a single modality and across feature families, systematically ablated. Three feature vectors are constructed, each concatenating the same 315 handcrafted features with one backbone's 3,000 deep features, and results are reported for the handcrafted set alone and for each fused vector across five classifiers. The ablation shows a consistent gain from adding deep features - best accuracy rising from 84.5% with handcrafted features alone to 90.2% with ResNet and 94.6% with Inception - which is a clean comparison and is the paper's only methodological contribution. Its interpretability is destroyed by the absence of an evaluation protocol: without knowing how the accuracies were computed, the gain cannot be attributed to better representation rather than to greater capacity to fit the data. [RQ4.1] Three ImageNet-pretrained backbones used as fixed feature extractors with fully connected layers excluded, and five classical classifiers - random forest, k-nearest neighbours, decision tree, SVM and logistic regression - applied to each of four feature conditions, giving twenty reported model-condition combinations of which eighteen are tabulated. The design is a systematic grid rather than a single proposed model, which is reasonable for a comparison study. No hyperparameters are reported for any classifier, and no rationale is given for the choice of backbones or descriptors beyond their being commonly used. [RQ4.2] A 3,315-dimensional concatenation per image: 3,000 activations from one backbone plus 100 HOG, 50 LBP, 50 ORB, 65 PHASH and 50 SIFT features. The handcrafted component is worth characterising because it determines what a source-provenance confound would look like. HOG encodes gradient distributions, which depend on image sharpness; LBP encodes local texture, which depends on resolution and compression; PHASH is a whole-image fingerprint, which encodes global tone and layout; SIFT and ORB encode keypoint structure, which depends on contrast and focus. Every one of these is a property of the photograph rather than of the face, and all differ systematically between images collected from different sources. That this feature set alone achieves 84.5% is therefore the paper's most diagnostic result, and it is reported without comment. [RQ4.3] Precision, recall, F1 and accuracy, reported as whole percentages for five classifiers across four feature conditions. The set is nominally adequate, but three problems undercut it. Precision, recall and F1 are reported as identical values to the percentage point in almost every row, which for a balanced binary problem is arithmetically possible but is presented without the confusion counts that would let a reader verify it. No AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears. And most fundamentally, no evaluation protocol is stated, so it is not determinable what population any of these numbers estimates - they may be held-out, resubstitution, or cross-validated figures, and the paper provides no basis for choosing between those readings. [RQ4.4] None. No feature importance, saliency map, activation visualisation, error analysis or example inspection appears for any of the eighteen combinations. The absence is decisive rather than incidental in this design, because the study's own results contain the material for an interpretability check it does not perform: handcrafted descriptors sensitive to image quality reach 84.5% alone, and a single analysis of which descriptors carry that performance - or a single visualisation of what distinguishes the two classes - would establish whether the model responds to faces or to photographs. [RQ4.5] There is no validation strategy. This is not a case of an inadequate or leaky protocol but of no stated protocol at all: the words 'split' and 'validation' do not occur in the paper, no cross-validation is described, no holdout proportion is given, and no resampling scheme is mentioned, yet twenty accuracy figures are tabulated across four feature conditions and five classifiers. The methods section narrates the feature-extraction pipeline in step-by-step detail down to CSV export and then moves directly to results. Consequently none of the reported numbers can be interpreted as an estimate of performance on unseen data, and the comparison the paper is built around - handcrafted versus fused features, and among the three backbones - cannot be evaluated either, since a resubstitution comparison would favour the higher-dimensional representations regardless of their generalisation. Beneath this sits the same structural problem as in the companion study on this dataset: the two classes were assembled from different internet sources, so no split, however constructed, could separate a model that has learned about faces from one that has learned about photographs; and the number of distinct children is unknown, so images of one child may fall on both sides of any partition undetectably. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder; transfer learning; image features; VGG; ResNet; Inception. Five of six name architectures or feature types; no behavioural, clinical or application term appears. The title's 'Emotion-based' has no counterpart in the keywords, the method or the results, and is the paper's clearest instance of behavioural vocabulary applied to non-behavioural work. [RQ5.2] International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications 15(5), 2024, pages 566 onwards - a general computer-science journal published by The Science and Information Organization, outside the clinical and biomedical literature. The venue accounts for the reporting profile: extensive procedural description of feature extraction, a large comparison grid, and no ethics, funding, competing-interests or limitations statement. It does not account for the absence of an evaluation protocol, which is a scientific rather than a formatting omission. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by the Department of Computer Science and Systems Engineering at Andhra University with the Department of Applied Psychology at GITAM Deemed to be University, Visakhapatnam. The framing is early detection and parental support, with the observation that diagnosis 'depends predominantly on the aberrations in the functioning of the brain that may not surface in the very early stages' and that technology has been 'a blessing to the parents who are clueless about managing the condition'. The presence of a psychology co-author makes the absence of any diagnostic verification, demographic reporting or ethical consideration more striking rather than less. For this review the study's value is entirely as a second data point on the facial-photograph branch of the literature, and it strengthens three observations already recorded from the companion study on the same dataset. The branch is not small - two independent groups publishing in the same year on the same scraped collection, with a literature review here citing at least half a dozen further examples using facial images, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet and hybrid vision transformers at accuracies from 88% to 92.5%. Its reported accuracies are comparable to or higher than the best-conducted studies in this review, so accuracy in this literature does not order studies by evidential quality. And its methodological reporting can omit the evaluation protocol entirely without that omission preventing publication - which is the strongest available evidence that peer review in this branch is not filtering on the properties that determine whether a number means anything. |
| S-117 | Retrospective algorithm-development study by a computer science and engineering group at R.M.D. Engineering College, Thiruvallur, India. Two public affective-computing corpora were used: the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces corpus, comprising posed expressions photographed under fixed laboratory conditions with the subject's eyes and lips aligned to standard image coordinates, evaluated across four brightness variants; and the Extended Cohn-Kanade corpus, comprising 327 instructed expression sequences from 118 adult volunteers, of which only the peak frame of each sequence was used. Neither corpus contains autistic participants, autism labels or any clinical ascertainment, and no autism classification, screening or severity-estimation target is modelled anywhere in the paper. A single passing reference in the results to 'the Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression (ASD-FE) dataset and the Extended Cohn-Kanade (CK+) dataset adapted for ASD research' is unsupported by any description, citation, sizing or characterisation in the methods. | Images were converted to grayscale and resized to 120x110 for a Gabor filter stage and 100x100 for the convolutional network, after intensity normalisation, histogram equalisation, face detection with realignment and background removal, with landmark and local binary pattern descriptors described in the preprocessing account. The proposed architecture couples Weighted Quantum Particle Swarm Optimisation - which encodes the swarm in quaternion rather than Euclidean space, with the quaternion algebra set out through Hamilton's relations - to a Fast Mask Recurrent Convolutional Neural Network. Comparison baselines were a CNN, a linear support vector machine and k-nearest neighbours, with t-values and p-values reported for the differences. No train-test split, cross-validation scheme, held-out set size or partitioning unit is stated anywhere; CK+ is described as testing the model 'on unseen data' after KDEF, implying cross-corpus evaluation, but no cross-corpus result is reported separately. | The hybrid architecture achieved 99.8% accuracy, 99.8% precision, 100% recall and 94% specificity on six-way emotion classification, described as surpassing existing systems, with all baseline comparisons significant at p < 0.01. No confusion matrix, class-wise breakdown, confidence interval or chance baseline accompanies these figures, and the number of emotion classes is stated as six in the abstract, seven in the KDEF description and five in a CK+ figure caption listing 'happy, digest, angry, fear and sad'. | The paper contains no autistic participants, no autism labels and no autism classification target, while its title, keywords, abstract, introduction, problem statement and conclusion are all written in terms of autistic people and the failure of conventional systems to read their faces. The data are posed prototypical expressions from adult volunteers, captured at peak intensity, on a corpus geometrically standardised so that eyes and lips occupy fixed coordinates - the most favourable possible input for facial expression recognition and the furthest from the spontaneous, low-intensity, idiosyncratic expression the paper says it addresses. The introduction itself notes that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' and that the field lacks spontaneous-stimulus work, without connecting either observation to the study's own design. No validation scheme, split proportion, cross-validation arrangement or partitioning unit is described anywhere, so the reported figures cannot be located relative to any evaluation design. The metric combination of 100% recall with 94% specificity across six classes is unusual and is presented without confusion matrices, class-wise results or a definition of multi-class specificity, and without confidence intervals or a statement of how many runs contributed to the significance tests. The architecture narrative repeatedly describes the optimiser as encoding 'physiological signal characteristics' although no physiological signal is collected or used. And there is no limitations section. | The study contributes to the review not as evidence about autism detection - it contains none - but as its clearest instance of autism framing attached to work with no autism content, and as a marker of what high accuracy on the posed-expression benchmark actually signifies. Every framing element identifies the paper as autism research, and the underlying problem it names is real and under-addressed: autistic people's facial signalling may be atypical in ways that conventional recognition systems misread, with the consequence, as the introduction puts it, that 'these differences can lead to social withdrawal, especially when others react negatively to the atypical responses of individuals with ASD' - a formulation that locates the difficulty partly in others' reactions rather than solely in the autistic person, and which is better than most framing in this corpus. The executed work tests none of it. The evaluation uses instructed prototypical expressions from non-autistic adults, at peak frames, on geometrically standardised images, which is the canonical easy case for this task and one on which very high accuracies have long been achievable. The paper's own introduction supplies the reason this cannot support its stated aim, observing that staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones and that spontaneous-stimulus work is what the field lacks. Read alongside another study charted in this review, which tests the transfer question directly and finds that affect models trained on neurotypical faces estimate arousal and valence poorly in autistic children until fine-tuned on autistic data, the pair makes the synthesis point cleanly: the posed-expression benchmark is close to solved, the autism-relevant expression problem is not, and reported figures move between the two without the distinction being marked. Three procedural defects complete the record - no stated validation scheme of any kind, metrics reported without confusion matrices or class-wise results, and an emotion-class count given as six, seven and five in three different places. | [RQ1.1] There are no autistic participants. The Extended Cohn-Kanade corpus supplies 327 sequences from 118 adult volunteers, of which only the peak frame of each sequence is used, giving roughly 2.8 images per person; the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces corpus supplies posed adult expressions photographed under fixed conditions, with its sample size not stated in this paper. Both are general-population affective-computing resources with no autism component, no autism labels and no clinical ascertainment of any kind. The paper's results section mentions once, in passing, 'the Autism Spectrum Disorder Facial Expression (ASD-FE) dataset and the Extended Cohn-Kanade (CK+) dataset adapted for ASD research', but no such dataset is described, cited, sized or characterised anywhere in the methods and no adaptation procedure is specified, while the experiments reported in the results and figures are conducted on brightness variants of KDEF and on CK+ peak frames. The sample is therefore adult, non-autistic, and posed - three respects in which it differs from the population the study's stated purpose concerns, which is autistic children experiencing spontaneous distress. [RQ1.2] The framing is entirely autism-focused and the content is not, which is the record's central observation. The introduction is written with some care about autistic experience: it notes that autistic people 'frequently struggle with self-regulation, emotional interpretation, and understanding and labeling others' emotions', and that 'these differences can lead to social withdrawal, especially when others react negatively to the atypical responses of individuals with ASD' - which locates part of the difficulty in other people's reactions rather than solely in the autistic person, a formulation better than most in this corpus. The conclusion likewise frames the goal as addressing 'the existing challenges faced by conventional facial expression recognition systems when applied to ASD populations, where nuanced facial cues may be misinterpreted or overlooked', which correctly identifies a technology failure rather than a personal deficit. Against this, autism is described as 'a neurological illness', and the phrase 'the minor changes and quirks typical of the facial movements' of autistic people is dismissive. No autistic person is reported as involved, and no autistic person's face appears in the data. [RQ1.3] Not applicable to a study with no clinical groups, and unreported for the corpora used. No age distribution, sex composition or ancestry is given for either KDEF or CK+, although both are documented in their originating publications. The one demographic fact that matters here is implicit and unremarked: both corpora consist of adult volunteers, while the paper's motivating application concerns autistic children, so the modelled population differs from the target population by several decades of facial development as well as by diagnosis. [RQ1.4] None is required by the task as executed, since no autism classification is attempted - the labels are posed emotion categories, which are a strong ground truth for emotion recognition and carry no information about autism. The consequence for this review is that the study cannot contribute evidence on any of the diagnostic questions. Its relevance is instead to the review's treatment of how autism framing attaches to work containing no autism data: a reader relying on the title, abstract, keywords and conclusion would record this as an autism study, and it is not one. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists, and none could, since no clinical population was studied. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to improve recognition of altered facial expressions in autistic people, on the argument that conventional systems misread the nuanced cues that autistic faces produce - a real and under-addressed problem, and the strongest idea in the paper. The executed work is six-way emotion classification on KDEF and CK+, reporting 99.8% accuracy, 99.8% precision, 100% recall and 94% specificity, with significance tests against CNN, linear SVM and k-nearest-neighbour baselines at p < 0.01. The gap between the two is the study's defining feature. The paper's own introduction supplies the reason the executed task cannot address the stated aim, observing that 'research indicates a lack of studies utilizing static or dynamic facial stimuli displaying real, spontaneous emotions' and that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' - after which the evaluation uses only staged emotions from instructed adult volunteers. A separate study charted in this review tests the transfer question directly and finds that affect models trained on neurotypical faces perform poorly on autistic children and improve substantially only after fine-tuning on autistic data, which is the evidence this study would have needed and did not seek. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Both corpora were collected under laboratory conditions by their original creators, with KDEF in particular geometrically standardised so that eyes and lips fall at fixed image coordinates across all images. That standardisation is the opposite of the conditions the paper's motivating application would face - an autistic child in spontaneous distress, filmed at whatever angle and distance the situation allows - and the mismatch is not discussed. The one robustness check reported, evaluation across four brightness variants of KDEF, addresses illumination but not pose, spontaneity, age or population. [RQ2.3] Instructed posed expression production, as designed into both corpora. This is the canonical easy case for facial expression recognition: prototypical, maximally intense, produced deliberately, and captured at the peak frame - CK+ explicitly uses 'the peak frame of each sequence' because 'it includes the greatest information relating to emotions'. Selecting peak frames maximises separability and is standard practice for benchmarking, but it removes precisely the subtlety the paper claims to address. The paradigm gap is therefore twofold: posed rather than spontaneous, and peak rather than continuous. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics statement appears, which is conventional for secondary use of two established consented affective-computing corpora. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment. Preprocessing is described in reasonable detail - grayscale conversion, resizing to 120x110 for a Gabor filter stage and 100x100 for the convolutional network, intensity normalisation, histogram equalisation, face detection with realignment, and landmark or local binary pattern feature extraction. The two-resolution arrangement for the two processing stages is a specific and reproducible detail. [RQ2.6] Partial. Reported: both corpora by name, CK+'s 327 sequences from 118 individuals, the peak-frame selection rule, the full preprocessing chain with both working resolutions, the quaternion algebra underpinning the optimiser given as explicit Hamilton relations, the three baseline comparators, and t-values and p-values for the comparisons. Not reported: KDEF's sample size, class distributions for either corpus, any train-test split or cross-validation scheme, the swarm optimiser's own population size and iteration count, the network's hyperparameters, how many runs contributed to the reported means, over what units the t-tests were computed, code, funding and competing interests. The mathematical apparatus is documented and the experimental protocol is not. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section. The most consequential omission is the mismatch between the paper's framing and its content: every framing element - title, abstract, keywords, introduction, problem statement and conclusion - is written in terms of autistic people, while the data are posed expressions from non-autistic adults and no autism label, participant or classification target exists anywhere. The paper also identifies, in its own introduction, the reason its evaluation cannot support its aim - that staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones and that spontaneous stimuli are what the field lacks - without connecting that observation to its own design. Further unstated issues: no validation scheme, split proportion or partitioning unit is given anywhere; the reported metric combination (100% recall with 94% specificity in a six-class problem) is unusual and is presented without confusion matrices, class-wise results or a definition of multi-class specificity; the number of emotion classes is stated as six in the abstract, seven in the KDEF description and five in a CK+ figure caption; and the architecture narrative repeatedly describes the optimiser as encoding 'physiological signal characteristics' although no physiological signal is collected or used. [RQ2.9] None stated. The directions the study most needs are evident from its own framing: evaluate on autistic participants, evaluate on spontaneous rather than posed expression, and test whether a model optimised on posed adult faces transfers to autistic children's faces at all - the last being a question another study in this review answers negatively for a comparable pipeline. [RQ3.1] Prototypical posed emotion in adult volunteers - anger, fear, joy, sadness, surprise and disgust - captured at peak intensity. The construct the paper claims to address is different and considerably harder: the atypical, low-intensity, idiosyncratic facial signalling that autistic people may produce and that conventional recognition systems misread. The paper states that problem clearly and does not test it. For this review the distinction matters because the two constructs have opposite difficulty profiles: posed peak-frame expression is the benchmark case on which affect recognition has long achieved very high accuracy, whereas spontaneous atypical expression in autistic children is where every reported system in this corpus degrades. A 99.8% figure on the first tells a reader nothing about the second. [RQ3.2] None. A single static image modality throughout. The recurring references to encoding 'physiological signal characteristics' and 'physiological signal properties' in quaternion space describe the optimiser's original application domain rather than anything in this study, where no physiological signal is acquired. [RQ4.1] A hybrid of Weighted Quantum Particle Swarm Optimisation with a Fast Mask Recurrent Convolutional Neural Network. The optimiser's distinguishing feature is that it encodes the swarm in quaternion rather than Euclidean space, and the quaternion algebra is set out explicitly through Hamilton's relations, on the stated rationale that this concentrates the search on more productive regions. Comparison against CNN, linear SVM and k-nearest-neighbour baselines with significance tests is more than many papers in this branch offer. What is not reported is the optimiser's own configuration - population size, iteration count, inertia and weighting parameters - or the network's hyperparameters, so the mechanism credited with the improvement cannot be reproduced. [RQ4.2] Grayscale cropped faces at 120x110 for Gabor filtering and 100x100 for convolutional processing, after normalisation, histogram equalisation, face detection and realignment. KDEF images are additionally pre-standardised by the corpus creators so that eyes and lips occupy fixed coordinates, which removes pose and scale variation entirely - a property that raises accuracy and reduces the relevance of the result to any uncontrolled setting. [RQ4.3] Accuracy 99.8%, precision 99.8%, recall 100% and specificity 94%, with t-values and p-values against three baselines at p < 0.01. Three problems. The combination is unusual for a balanced multi-class problem - perfect recall alongside 94% specificity - and no confusion matrix, per-class breakdown or definition of multi-class specificity is supplied to make it interpretable. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, and the number of runs behind the reported means is not stated, so the significance tests cannot be assessed. And no chance baseline is given, though six-way classification would place it near 17% under balance. [RQ4.4] None. No attribution, saliency, feature-importance or error analysis is reported for the classifier. The quaternion formulation is presented in mathematical detail but is a search-space construct, not an explanation of what the network responds to, and the associated claim that it captures physiological signal properties has no referent in the data. [RQ4.5] Not assessable, because no validation scheme is described. The paper states no train-test split proportion, no cross-validation arrangement, no held-out set size and no partitioning unit anywhere. The one hint is that CK+ is used 'to test the WQPSO-FMRCNN model on unseen data' after KDEF, which would be cross-corpus evaluation - the design this review regards most highly, since it tests transfer across acquisition conditions and populations. It is not reported as a separate result, so what would have been the study's strongest methodological feature goes unquantified. Two further points bound the figures. CK+ contributes 327 peak frames from 118 individuals, roughly 2.8 images per person, and whether images of the same individual span any partition is unstated. And KDEF is geometrically standardised with eyes and lips at fixed coordinates, so a classifier operating on it faces none of the pose, scale or framing variation that any real deployment would present. A 99.8% accuracy on peak-frame posed expressions from geometrically aligned adult faces is close to the ceiling that this benchmark has long supported, and is not evidence about the harder problem the paper describes. [RQ5.1] Keywords: hybrid WQPSO, FMRCNN, facial expression recognition, ASD, computational intelligence, healthcare. The inclusion of ASD in the keyword list, alongside an autism-framed title, ensures the paper is indexed and retrieved as autism research - which is how it entered this corpus - although it contains no autism data. That indexing effect is itself a finding for the review: searches for computational autism work will return studies of this kind, and their reported accuracies will enter informal impressions of the field's performance without ever having concerned autistic people. [RQ5.2] Traitement du Signal 41(6), IIETA, open access under CC BY, doi 10.18280/ts.410628; received 12 April 2024, revised 7 August, accepted 20 August, available online 31 December 2024. A signal-processing venue. The review process accepted a paper whose title and abstract promise autism facial expression recognition while its experiments use two general-population posed-expression corpora; whose class count differs across three locations in the text; whose architecture narrative refers repeatedly to physiological signals that are never collected; and which states no validation scheme of any kind. [RQ5.3] Published December 2024 by a computer science and engineering group at R.M.D. Engineering College, Thiruvallur. For this review the study's value lies in what it illustrates rather than in what it measures, and two lessons carry into the synthesis. The first concerns the boundary between autism-framed and autism-evidenced work. Every framing element here - title, keywords, abstract, introduction, problem statement, conclusion - is written in terms of autistic people and the failure of conventional systems to read their faces, which is a real and under-addressed problem stated with some sympathy; and the entire experimental content is six-way emotion classification on posed expressions from non-autistic adult volunteers, evaluated at peak frames on a corpus whose images are geometrically standardised. A reader relying on title and abstract would record 99.8% as an autism result. The second concerns what such figures mean. The paper's own introduction notes that 'staged emotions are easier to detect than spontaneous ones' and that the field lacks work on spontaneous stimuli, which is precisely why 99.8% on peak-frame posed adult expressions is near the long-established ceiling for that benchmark and carries no implication for autistic children in spontaneous distress - the application the conclusion invokes. Another study charted in this review tests exactly that transfer and finds that affect models trained on neurotypical faces perform poorly on autistic children and improve materially only after fine-tuning on autistic data. Read together, the two studies make the point cleanly: the emotion-recognition benchmark is solved, the autism-relevant problem is not, and the two are frequently reported as though they were the same. Three further defects should be recorded: no validation scheme, split or partitioning unit is stated anywhere; the reported metrics (100% recall with 94% specificity across six classes) are presented without confusion matrices or class-wise results; and the number of emotion classes is given as six, seven and five in three different places. |
| S-118 | Cross-sectional two-group classification study at the Natural and Artificial Cognition Lab, University of Naples Federico II, with the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center. Twenty children aged 3-6 were recruited between 13 February and 21 March 2023: 10 autistic (mean age 4 years, SD 0.94) from the rehabilitation centre where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, and 10 typically developing (mean 3 years 9 months, SD 0.1) from a mainstream pre-primary and primary school in the province of Naples. Autism required a clinical diagnosis confirmed with ADOS-2, administered by healthcare professionals stated explicitly to be independent of the research laboratory and study, together with age 3-6 and absence of comorbid conditions; no ADOS-2 score is reported. Comparison children were selected only on parent and teacher report of no neurodevelopmental disorder and were recruited 'without specific assessment of their pre-existing abilities'. No sex, IQ, developmental, language or severity data exist for either group. The modelled dataset is 738 trajectories, roughly 37 per child, extended to 932 samples for the correlation analysis by adding simulated trajectories. Ethics approval, written parental consent, funder no-role statement and a competing-interests declaration are all reported, and the trajectory data are published openly on GitHub. | Children played a purpose-built Unity 2D drag-and-drop game on a 12.3-inch Dell Latitude tablet, raised and tilted at about 60 degrees, seated at a table 45-60 cm high with the experimenter 30 cm to their right. The task required dragging an image from the screen centre to a target at one of eight positions spaced 45 degrees apart while avoiding distractors, with identical settings for every participant. No verbal instructions were given: a video tutorial started on pressing play and the image to be moved vibrated as a cue, both introduced explicitly to avoid stressful social situations and improve engagement and autonomy. Finger coordinates were logged at 20 Hz, with recording restricted to completed drags from image to target and only trajectories of 20-69 points retained. Coordinates were then rotation-normalised so that trajectories to different targets became comparable, using the angle between consecutive points computed by atan2 and mapped into 0-360 degrees, with the transformation written out in three numbered equations. Two sequential artificial neural networks were compared, one receiving only the rotated x and y coordinates and one adding velocity and acceleration, evaluated by four-fold cross-validation with a 110-sample validation set described as 15% of the 738 trajectories. A simulation experiment then generated trajectories with average acceleration systematically varied between -5 and +5 cm/s squared, and a robustness analysis simplified trajectories at seven rates from 35% to 90%. | The four-feature model reached 0.90 accuracy against 0.76 for the two-feature model, with a consistently higher distribution across folds and a better ROC curve. The simulation analysis established the role of acceleration directly: across 932 samples, average trajectory acceleration correlated with the model's prediction at r = 0.69 for the two-feature model and r = 0.82 for the four-feature model, both at p < 0.001, with higher acceleration increasing the probability of an autism prediction. The two-feature model's correlation is the more informative of the two, since that model never receives acceleration as an input - so acceleration information is recoverable from the raw coordinate sequence, and the four-feature representation makes it easier to use rather than supplying anything new. The authors conclude accordingly that raw data analysis has potential while the four-feature model excels. No sensitivity, specificity, confusion matrix, AUC value, confidence interval or participant-level result is reported. | The 738 modelled trajectories come from 20 children at roughly 37 each, and four-fold cross-validation partitions trajectories rather than children, with the validation set quoted in samples out of 738 and nothing indicating that folds respected child boundaries. Each validation trajectory therefore has around 36 siblings produced by the same child in the same session with the same hand - and after rotation normalisation those siblings differ only in the noise of execution. Fine motor kinematics at this granularity function close to an individual motor signature, so the reported 0.90 is not an estimate of performance on a child the model has not seen, and no participant-level figure appears anywhere; with 20 children, leave-one-child-out validation would have been trivial to run. Neither group received any developmental or cognitive assessment, and the comparison children were recruited explicitly without assessment of pre-existing abilities, so a general developmental explanation for the motor difference cannot be separated from an autism-specific one in 3-6 year olds. The autistic group's age standard deviation is nearly ten times the comparison group's, so the groups differ in developmental spread even though their means are close. The autistic children were receiving psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre - direct motor intervention - while the comparison children were not. Comorbidity was excluded, narrowing the sample. No sex data are reported, no model architecture or training hyperparameters are specified, and no class-conditional metric or confidence interval accompanies either accuracy. | Three contributions make this study valuable to the review out of proportion to its sample size. It is the only included study to publish its data openly, at a stated GitHub URL, so its central claim can be independently rechecked - including, by anyone who wishes, under a participant-disjoint split that the paper itself did not perform. Its interpretability method is a template worth propagating: rather than applying post-hoc attribution, it generates synthetic trajectories with acceleration systematically varied across a stated range and measures how the models' predictions move, yielding causal, directional and quantified evidence about the decision function. And its incidental finding is a useful corrective to an assumption running through this literature - the two-feature model, which never receives acceleration as an input, nonetheless correlates with acceleration at r = 0.69, showing that the 14-point accuracy gain from adding derived kinematic features reflects easier access to information already present in the raw sequence rather than new information. Studies throughout this corpus report feature-engineering gains and read them as evidence that the added features capture something; this one shows a case where they do not, and shows it by manipulation. Its task design also deserves noting: the deliberate removal of verbal instruction, replaced by a video tutorial and a vibration cue explicitly to avoid stressful social situations, is the clearest instance in the review of an elicitation designed so that a motor measurement is not contaminated by social demand. Against all this, the study partitions 738 trajectories from 20 children by trajectory, and shares with its companion study from the same group the unaddressed confound that its autistic participants were receiving psychomotor therapy while its comparison participants were not. | [RQ1.1] Twenty children aged 3-6, recruited between 13 February and 21 March 2023: 10 autistic (mean age 4 years, SD 0.94) from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center where they were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, and 10 typically developing (mean 3 years 9 months, SD 0.1) from a pre-primary and primary educational institute in the province of Naples. Inclusion for the autistic group required a clinical diagnosis, age 3-6 and absence of comorbid conditions; the only criterion for the comparison group was parent and teacher report of no neurodevelopmental disorder, with the paper stating explicitly that they were recruited 'without specific assessment of their pre-existing abilities'. The modelled unit is not the child but the trajectory: 738 trajectories were retained after filtering, roughly 37 per child, and a further set of computationally generated trajectories brought the correlation analysis to 932 samples. Twenty children is the smallest sample of any included study in this review, and the discrepancy between 20 participants and 738 modelling units is the central interpretive issue. [RQ1.2] 'Children with autism', 'children with a diagnosis of autism' and 'individuals with ASD', person-first and consistent, alongside 'typically developing (TD) children'. Autism is 'a complex and heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder' with the standard two-domain description, and motor differences are called 'motor abnormalities' and 'motor disorders'. The framing is otherwise notably measured and contains one argument worth recording: the paper's opening critique is that autism diagnosis 'is based on subjective observations of behavior' focused on the two core domains, and that 'many other characteristics are overlooked in the diagnostic process, considered non-central to the disorder' - specifically motor characteristics, which 'have always been considered secondary symptoms and not closely related to the syndrome' despite evidence that they precede language and social difficulties. That is an argument for widening what is measured rather than for replacing clinicians, and it is grounded in embodied-cognition theory rather than in an appeal to objectivity alone. The paper also reports the literature on visuospatial ability in autism honestly as conflicting - some studies finding deficits, some no difference, some better performance - rather than selecting the supportive citations. There is no neurodiversity framing and no autistic-community involvement. [RQ1.3] Thin, and thinner for the comparison group than for the autistic group. Reported: group sizes, age means and standard deviations, recruitment source, and for the autistic group the requirement of an ADOS-2-confirmed diagnosis and absence of comorbidity. Not reported: sex, IQ, developmental level, language ability, socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, or any severity score. Two features of what is reported deserve attention. The autistic group's age standard deviation is 0.94 years against 0.1 for the comparison group - nearly a tenfold difference in spread - so although the means differ by only three months the autistic group spans a much wider developmental range, which matters for a fine-motor outcome in children aged 3 to 6 where motor control changes rapidly. And no cognitive or developmental assessment was performed on either group; the comparison children were recruited without any assessment of pre-existing abilities, and the autistic group's functioning is inferred rather than measured, from the fact that all 'were able to engage with a tablet, suggesting a moderate level of functioning'. Since the outcome is the smoothness and dynamics of a dragging movement, and both groups were selected without reference to developmental level, a general developmental explanation for the difference cannot be separated from an autism-specific one. A further asymmetry is that the autistic children were undergoing psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre - direct motor intervention - while the comparison children were not. [RQ1.4] Solid for the autistic group and absent for the comparison group. Autism required a clinical diagnosis confirmed with the ADOS-2, and the paper states something few in this review do: the diagnoses were made 'by healthcare professionals and industry experts who were independent of our research laboratory and study'. Explicit independence between the diagnosing clinicians and the research team removes one route by which knowledge of the study could influence the reference standard, and is worth crediting. Against this, no ADOS-2 score of any kind is reported, so the severity range the autistic group is said to span cannot be characterised; comorbidity was excluded by criterion, narrowing the sample relative to the clinical population; and typically developing status rests entirely on parent and teacher report of no neurodevelopmental disorder, with no screening instrument administered and no assessment of abilities - so undetected autistic traits or developmental difficulty in the comparison group cannot be ruled out. [RQ1.5] None for either group. No IQ, developmental quotient, language, adaptive or severity measure was obtained, and the paper says so implicitly by describing the autistic group's functioning as inferred from their ability to use a tablet. The absence has two specific costs in this design. Because the outcome is fine motor kinematics in 3-6 year olds and neither group was assessed developmentally, the difference between groups cannot be attributed to autism rather than to general developmental level - and the autistic group's much wider age spread makes this more rather than less pressing. And because the autistic group is described as covering 'a range of symptom severity levels within the spectrum' without any score, the natural question of whether the model's confidence tracks severity cannot be asked, even though the study's simulation methodology is well suited to it. [RQ2.1] Two objectives, both methodological rather than clinical. First, to test whether raw motion trajectories alone - unprocessed x and y coordinates - carry enough information to classify autistic from typically developing children, or whether derived kinematic features are needed; the comparison is motivated by the group's own prior work, which had found that maximum and minimum acceleration and standard deviations of speed and acceleration were the leading contributors in a feature-based model. Second, to test the specific role of acceleration by generating synthetic trajectories with systematically varied acceleration and observing how the models respond. Findings: the four-feature model reached 0.90 accuracy against 0.76 for the two-feature model, with a consistently higher fold-wise distribution and a better ROC curve, so derived features help substantially. But the simulation analysis complicates the simple reading: acceleration correlated with the two-feature model's predictions at r = 0.69 despite that model never receiving acceleration as an input, and with the four-feature model's at r = 0.82, both at p < 0.001 over 932 samples, with higher acceleration increasing the probability of an autism prediction in both. So the information is present in the raw coordinate sequence and the four-feature representation makes it easier to use rather than supplying something new - a conclusion the authors reach and state, writing that their findings 'support the potential of raw data analysis in objectively assessing motor behaviors related to autism' while the four-feature model 'excels'. [RQ2.2] Two recruitment sites in the Naples area with a familiar asymmetry: autistic children from the Neapolisanit S.R.L. Rehabilitation Center, which is also a co-author affiliation and where the children were receiving psychomotor and speech therapy, and comparison children from a mainstream pre-primary and primary school. The testing arrangement is described in unusual physical detail - table height 45-60 cm adjusted to the child's age, experimenter seated to the child's right at about 30 cm, a 12.3-inch tablet raised and tilted at approximately 60 degrees to give a full view of the game - and this level of specification is a genuine reproducibility asset. One element of it is also a small confound: adjusting table height by age introduces a systematic postural difference correlated with a variable whose spread differs sharply between groups. The wider recruitment geometry is the standard clinic-versus-school case-control arrangement, compounded here by the autistic group receiving active motor therapy at the recruiting site. [RQ2.3] A purpose-built drag-and-drop game, and the design reasoning behind it is the paradigm's most valuable feature. The child drags an image from the screen centre to a target at one of eight positions spaced 45 degrees apart while avoiding distractors, with the settings panel allowing category, scene count and distractor number to be varied - all held constant here. Three design decisions address problems that recur throughout this review. No verbal instructions were given: the examiner deliberately withheld them so the child could work out the game's logic independently, and the two support mechanisms provided - a video tutorial triggered by the play button and a vibration cue on the image to be moved - were introduced explicitly 'to avoid stressful social situations and improve engagement and autonomy'. Designing the elicitation to minimise social demand, in a study measuring motor rather than social behaviour, removes a confound that several other studies here carry unexamined. The eight-target arrangement at fixed angular spacing then makes rotation normalisation possible, so trajectories to different targets become comparable - a design choice that pays off directly in the analysis. And recording is restricted to completed drags from image to target, with incomplete drags and stray touches excluded, so the measured behaviour is well defined. The costs are that session duration varied between children without being modelled, and that a single session per child leaves no within-child stability estimate. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session per child, with recruitment compressed into five weeks. No follow-up and no test-retest reliability for any kinematic measure - which the authors identify as a limitation and address directly, recommending that 'the sample should be expanded and observed longitudinally'. Governance is complete: approval by the Ethical Committee of Psychological Research of the Department of Humanities at the University of Naples Federico II, written informed consent from parents of all participants described as guaranteeing full understanding, funding from two named sources with an explicit statement that the funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, publication decision or manuscript preparation, and a declaration of no competing interests. The data are deposited in a public GitHub repository, which is the only open data release among the included studies in this review. [RQ2.5] A 12.3-inch Dell Latitude tablet running purpose-built software written in Unity 2D and C#, logging finger x and y coordinates at 20 Hz with asynchronous programming used for storage so that recording did not degrade game performance. No sensor, marker, camera or wearable is involved. The 20 Hz sampling rate is modest - one sample every 50 ms - and bounds what can be said about rapid acceleration changes, though it is adequate for the trajectory-shape features the study models. No analysis software or framework is named, and the neural network architectures are not specified in the retrieved text, which is the one substantive gap in an otherwise well-documented apparatus. [RQ2.6] Among the strongest in this review, and uniquely so on data. Reproducible from the text: exact recruitment dates, inclusion criteria for both groups, the game platform and task geometry with eight targets at 45-degree spacing, the settings panel contents and the statement that identical settings were used for all participants, the tablet model and its 60-degree tilt, the table-height range and experimenter position, the 20 Hz sampling rate, all three data-inclusion rules including the 20-69 point trajectory-length window, the rotation normalisation written out across three numbered equations with the atan2 construction and the angle-range mapping, both feature sets, the four-fold cross-validation with its 110-sample validation size, the acceleration-variation range for the simulation, and the seven trajectory-simplification rates. The trajectory data are published on GitHub at a stated URL - the only open data release among included studies here, and one that makes the central claim independently checkable. Not reported: the network architectures, training hyperparameters, seeds, and, critically, whether cross-validation folds were constructed by child or by trajectory. [RQ2.7] The stated limitations are four and are well chosen: small sample size, exclusive reliance on a tablet as the tracking device, the absence of longitudinal observation, and the absence of complementary measures - with the specific and useful suggestion that manual and ocular movement data be coordinated to characterise hand-eye patterns. The authors also call for cross-validation against other diagnostic tools. What is not addressed is the relationship between 20 children and 738 modelling units. Cross-validation partitions trajectories, and with roughly 37 trajectories per child each validation trajectory has around 36 siblings from the same child in training; movement kinematics are close to an individual motor signature at this granularity, so a model can separate children rather than groups and report high accuracy. No participant-level result appears anywhere, and the paper does not state whether folds respected child boundaries. Three further omissions matter. Neither group received any developmental or cognitive assessment, and the comparison children were recruited explicitly without assessment of pre-existing abilities, so a general developmental explanation cannot be excluded in a fine-motor task with 3-6 year olds. The autistic group's age standard deviation is nearly ten times the comparison group's, so the groups differ in developmental spread. And the autistic children were receiving psychomotor therapy at the recruiting centre while the comparison children were not, confounding motor training with diagnosis in a study of motor kinematics - the same confound this review recorded in the group's companion study on a different sample, and unaddressed in both. [RQ2.9] Four directions, all concrete and following from stated limitations. Expand the sample and observe it longitudinally, to establish predictive capacity over time. Move beyond a single tablet as the tracking device, on the reasoning that richer data collection would improve analysis even from raw coordinates. Coordinate complementary measures, specifically manual and ocular movement data together, to characterise hand-eye patterns - a well-targeted proposal given that the drag-and-drop task is inherently visuomotor and the study measures only the manual half. And cross-validate against other diagnostic tools. Not proposed, and needed: participant-level validation, developmental assessment of both groups, and relating model output to the severity range the autistic sample is said to span. [RQ3.1] Fine motor control during goal-directed touchscreen dragging, represented as a full temporal sequence rather than as summary statistics. The behavioural claim is that motor differences in autism are prevalent, early-appearing - present 'even before the onset of language and social interaction difficulties' - and clinically neglected, with the paper stating that despite their relevance 'currently there are no adequate tools available to accurately assess motor function in children with autism'. The theoretical grounding is embodied cognition: how a person moves shapes how they learn from and explore the environment, so motor patterns are informative about cognition rather than peripheral to it. Empirically the study localises the signal to acceleration: synthetic trajectories with higher average acceleration are more likely to be classified as autistic, with correlations of 0.69 and 0.82 for the two models. That is a specific, directional and testable behavioural claim - faster or more abruptly accelerating dragging movements are associated with autism in this sample - and it is arrived at by manipulation rather than by correlation with observed data. Two things the representation does not capture: the visual half of the visuomotor task, since only finger position is recorded and gaze is not, which the authors identify as the priority extension; and any measure of task success beyond the requirement that a drag reach its target. [RQ3.2] No cross-sensor fusion. The study's ablation is between two representations of the same signal - raw coordinates alone versus coordinates plus velocity and acceleration - and its result is more interesting than a simple fusion gain. The four-feature model outperforms the two-feature model substantially (0.90 versus 0.76), which would ordinarily be read as the derived features adding information. But the simulation analysis shows that acceleration correlates with the two-feature model's predictions at r = 0.69 even though that model never receives acceleration as an input, so the information is already present in the raw coordinate sequence and is being recovered from it. The 14-point accuracy difference therefore reflects how easily a network of this size and training regime can extract a derivative from a 20 Hz position sequence, not what information the sequence contains. That is a genuinely useful distinction for the review's treatment of feature engineering: it shows a case where explicit derived features improve performance without adding information, which is the opposite of the usual assumption and is established by manipulation rather than asserted. The authors' own conclusion follows this reading, noting that raw data analysis has potential while the four-feature model excels. [RQ4.1] Two artificial neural networks trained on sequential data, differing only in input dimensionality - two features (rotated x and y coordinates) versus four (adding velocity and acceleration). No architecture details, layer counts, activation functions, optimiser or training hyperparameters are given in the retrieved text, which is the study's main reporting gap and is conspicuous against the exceptional specification of the task, the preprocessing and the simulation procedure. No alternative model families are compared and no baseline classifier is reported. The modelling is deliberately minimal because the study's question is representational rather than architectural: whether raw trajectories suffice. Given 20 children, keeping the model simple is the right choice, but the absence of any specification means the comparison between the two models cannot be checked for confounds such as differing capacity or training duration. [RQ4.2] A rotation-normalised sequence of 20-69 points per trajectory. The rotation step is the representational contribution and is worked out carefully: because targets sit at eight positions 45 degrees apart, raw trajectories to different targets are not comparable, so the angle between consecutive points relative to the origin is computed with atan2, mapped from the atan2 range into 0-360 degrees, and applied as a rotation - with all three steps written out as numbered equations and the resulting endpoint coordinates given. This makes trajectories to any target directly comparable while preserving their shape, and it is the kind of preprocessing that reflects thought about the construct rather than convention. The two-feature model then receives only these rotated coordinates and the four-feature model adds velocity and acceleration. Crucially, unlike the group's companion study on a different sample - which averaged twelve kinematic features across a task to give one vector per child - this study preserves the full temporal sequence, so the model sees the unfolding of the movement rather than its summary. The 20-69 point length window standardises comparability at the cost of discarding both very brief and very extended drags. [RQ4.3] Binary accuracy, reported as a distribution across cross-validation folds rather than as a single point, which conveys stability better than a bare figure; ROC curves for both models; and Pearson correlations with p-values for the acceleration analysis. Reporting the fold-wise distribution is good practice and is rare in this corpus. But the metric set is otherwise thin for a diagnostic claim: no sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1 or confusion matrix is given, so the error profile is unknown and it cannot be determined whether the models fail preferentially on autistic or comparison trajectories; no AUC value is quoted despite ROC curves being plotted; and no confidence interval accompanies either headline accuracy. No majority-class baseline is stated. Since the modelled unit is the trajectory rather than the child, no participant-level metric of any kind is available - which is the figure a clinical claim would require. [RQ4.4] The strongest element of the study, and methodologically distinctive. Rather than applying a post-hoc attribution method, the authors manipulate the input: synthetic trajectories are generated with average acceleration systematically varied between -5 and +5 cm/s squared, and the models' predictions are measured as a function of that variation, yielding correlations of r = 0.69 and r = 0.82 with a stated direction - higher acceleration increases the probability of an autism prediction. This is causal rather than correlational evidence about the model's decision function, it is quantified, and it is directional. A second robustness analysis simplifies trajectories at seven rates from 35% to 90% and re-tests, with generated trajectories under 20 points excluded. And the analysis produces an informative incidental finding: the two-feature model, which has no acceleration input, still correlates with acceleration at 0.69, showing that the raw sequence carries the information. What is absent is any individual-level interpretation - no error analysis, no examination of which children were misclassified, and no relation between predictions and the severity range the autistic group reportedly spans. [RQ4.5] The decisive weakness, and it is structural rather than procedural. The dataset is 738 trajectories from 20 children, roughly 37 each, and evaluation uses four-fold cross-validation with a 110-sample validation set described as 15% of the trajectory dataset. The unit is explicitly the trajectory: the validation size is quoted in samples out of 738, and nothing in the paper indicates that a child's trajectories were kept within a fold. Under a random trajectory-level split, each validation trajectory is accompanied by approximately 36 siblings produced by the same child in the same session with the same hand, differing only in which of eight targets was approached - and after rotation normalisation even that difference is removed. Fine motor kinematics at this granularity function close to an individual motor signature, so a model can separate children rather than groups and report high accuracy; the reported 0.90 is therefore not an estimate of performance on a child the model has not seen, and no participant-level figure appears anywhere. With only 20 children, a participant-disjoint scheme would have been straightforward - leave-one-child-out would give exactly 20 folds - and would have produced the number a clinical claim requires.
