The paper also flags the transition from two-legged to one-legged stance as a feed-forward process worth examining separately, which is a construct-level insight most balance studies do not articulate. [RQ3.2] Genuine two-sensor fusion, and the fusion is constitutive rather than additive. A pressure sensor supplies centre of pressure and a webcam supplies joint angles via pose estimation, synchronised at 20 Hz - and the study's proposed variables are precisely the correlations between the two streams, so neither sensor alone could produce them. The ablation is reported across three configurations and is informative: conventional variables derived from the pressure sensor alone gave the weakest accuracy and sensitivity, the proposed cross-sensor correlation variables reached perfect scores on their own, and the combined set also reached perfect scores. That ordering says that the information distinguishing the groups lies in the relationship between body movement and base-of-support movement rather than in either measured separately, which is a more specific and more mechanistically meaningful fusion result than the accuracy gains reported by most multimodal studies in this corpus. The caveat is that all three configurations share the same feature-selection procedure and the same evaluation, so the ordering is more trustworthy than the absolute values - and with two of the three reaching exactly 1.000, the comparison has no headroom to discriminate further. [RQ4.1] A linear-kernel support vector machine, with the cost parameter reported (0.01 for the two best models) and between three and five variables selected from sixteen per configuration. The choice of a linear SVM on interpretable biomechanical features is well matched to 126 participants with 19 positives, and the reported model equations - high autistic trait group as a function of named variables - make each fitted model fully transparent. Only one algorithm family was tried, which the authors identify as a limitation and propose remedying by comparison against random forests or deep learning. The more consequential modelling detail is that feature selection and hyperparameter optimisation were performed jointly in a single procedure described in one sentence, with the stated purpose of improving 'performance and generalization of all SVM classification models' - so the search is doing substantial work, reducing sixteen candidates to three to five while also fixing the regularisation, and its relationship to the cross-validation loop is not specified. [RQ4.2] A 16-dimensional summary vector per child. Time-series pressure and pose data are compressed into scalar descriptors: path length, mean speed, entropy and convex-hull area for centre-of-pressure; longest-trial duration for overall balance; and ten joint-wise correlations plus the centre-of-mass to centre-of-pressure difference for the body-pressure relationship. This is aggregation rather than sequence modelling, so the temporal unfolding of a stance is not represented except insofar as entropy and correlation capture it. The correlation features are nonetheless well chosen for the construct: a correlation between a joint angle and centre-of-pressure position is inherently relational and cannot be computed from either stream alone, and it summarises coordination in a single interpretable number. Every variable is named, categorised and explained, with the rationale and calculation method for each given in supplementary material. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for each of three variable sets, reported alongside the named variables and cost parameter of each best model; SHAP values displayed for all participants; and correlations between SRS-2 total and predicted probability. Reporting sensitivity and specificity separately is essential at 15.1% prevalence and is done. But three gaps matter. No majority-class baseline is stated, so the reported 1.000 is not placed against the 84.9% floor that a trivial all-negative classifier would achieve - although sensitivity of 1.000 does establish that all 19 positives were caught, which a trivial classifier could not do. No AUC, confusion matrix or confidence interval appears; on 19 positives, an exact binomial interval around a sensitivity of 1.000 would extend below 0.82, which is the figure a reader needs. And no positive predictive value is computed, despite the population-based design making it directly meaningful - at the observed 15.1% prevalence and perfect specificity it would be 1.000, but any realistic degradation in specificity would move it sharply, and that sensitivity analysis is exactly what a screening proposal requires. [RQ4.4] Strong, and directed at the study's substantive question rather than at post-hoc justification. Every one of the sixteen variables is a named biomechanical quantity with its rationale and calculation given in supplementary material, so an attribution is interpretable without further translation. SHAP values are computed for each of the three variable sets and displayed across all participants, and the variables selected by each model are named in the results table - so a reader can see not only which features mattered but which entered each fitted model. The convergent finding across SHAP and model selection, that shoulder, hip and trunk correlations dominate, supports a specific claim about where in the body the difference lies. Most valuable is the continuous check: predicted probability is correlated with SRS-2 total score for each variable set, testing whether the model tracks the underlying trait dimension or merely reproduces the imposed threshold, with a positive relationship reported in every case. That analysis is the one this review has repeatedly noted as absent elsewhere, and it is performed here on the study's own severity variable. What is missing is per-participant error analysis - though with perfect classification there are no errors to analyse, which is itself a reason for scepticism about the perfect scores. [RQ4.5] Correct on the split unit and ambiguous on the step that matters. The evaluation is leave-one-out cross-validation over 126 participants, each contributing one 16-dimensional vector, so the unit is the person and within-participant leakage is impossible. The class imbalance is acknowledged and drives the choice of scheme, with the authors stating that with around 20 above-threshold samples they 'were forced to use LOOCV to avoid polarization of prediction toward the Low autistic trait group'. They then state the risk this creates in their own words - that leave-one-out 'can also produce optimistic performance estimates due to the small test set in each iteration' and 'can be unstable when the dataset contains noise or outliers' - and conclude that their results need cautious interpretation. That is the right instinct, but it does not reach the decisive issue. The methods state that the procedure 'simultaneously selected the 16 explanatory variables and optimized the hyperparameter', and three to five variables plus a cost parameter were retained per model from sixteen candidates on 126 participants of whom 19 are positive. Whether that joint selection was repeated inside each of the 126 folds is not stated anywhere in the main text. If it was not - and the sentence's placement before the description of cross-validation suggests it may not have been - then the selection saw every participant's label, and on this configuration that alone is sufficient to produce accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of exactly 1.000. Perfect scores on all three metrics for a behavioural measurement in five-year-olds are not a plausible property of the phenomenon, and unnested selection is the most parsimonious explanation. Three further points: no majority-class baseline is given against an 84.9% floor; no confidence interval accompanies a sensitivity estimated on 19 positives; and the three variable sets were compared on the same 126 participants. The corrective is straightforward and would leave the study's substantive contribution intact - nest the selection, report the resulting accuracy with an interval, and add the positive predictive value that the population-based design uniquely permits. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autistic trait, machine learning, balance, one-legged standing, screening. The set is precise and honest - 'autistic trait' rather than autism, and 'screening' rather than diagnosis, both of which accurately describe what the study does. Terms carried through the body: centre of pressure, convex hull, sway entropy, centre of mass, joint angle correlation, feed-forward process, anticipatory postural control, SHAP, leave-one-out cross-validation, Social Responsiveness Scale. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Psychiatry 15:1464285, Original Research, open access under CC BY; received 13 July 2024, accepted 30 September 2024, published 17 October 2024. Editorial and review handling is disclosed by name as Frontiers requires, and the reviewers include a researcher whose own work on movement analysis in autism is cited in this review's corpus - an indication that the paper was assessed within the relevant specialist community. The venue's structure produces the ethics, funding, competing-interests and data-availability statements, and supplementary materials carry the per-variable rationale and calculation methods that would not fit the main text. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by informatics and engineering groups at Shizuoka and Gifu Universities with neuropsychiatry and medical sciences at Nagasaki University, funded by two JSPS Grants-in-Aid together with JST MIRAI and JST CREST. The framing is a timing gap stated with unusual precision: autism can be detected at 14 months and diagnosed with high accuracy by two years, yet more than 70% of affected children are not diagnosed until after 51 months, so identifying autistic traits before elementary school entry is the target. The chosen route is to instrument an assessment that already happens - the one-legged standing test within a routine preschool medical examination - which is why near-complete population coverage was achievable. For this review the study is valuable on four counts. It is one of only two with genuinely population-based sampling, and the only one whose comparison group is simply the rest of the same age cohort, so the spectrum-truncation problem that inflates the diagnostic studies does not arise at all. Its measurement is embedded in an existing examination with a consumer webcam and a single pressure mat, so the deployment claim is credible rather than aspirational. Its cross-sensor fusion is constitutive rather than additive, with the discriminative features being correlations between body movement and base-of-support movement that neither sensor could produce alone - and the ablation shows those features outperforming the conventional sway measures drawn from prior literature. And it correlates its model's output with the continuous SRS-2 score, testing whether the prediction tracks the trait dimension rather than only the imposed threshold. Against all this stands a single unresolved question: whether the joint feature-selection and hyperparameter-optimisation procedure was nested within the leave-one-out loop. On 126 children with 19 positives, selecting three to five of sixteen variables plus a cost parameter would by itself explain accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of exactly 1.000, and the paper does not say. The authors' own warning that their validation scheme 'can produce optimistic performance estimates' should be read as applying with more force than they intend. |
| S-122 | Retrospective algorithm-development study on two secondary web-sourced image corpora, conducted by information systems and computer science groups in Saudi Arabia and Egypt. Dataset 1 is the Piosenka Kaggle collection of 2,866 cropped facial photographs, 1,433 labelled autism and 1,433 control, described as ages 1-11 with the sex distribution recorded as unspecified; the paper states that the images were 'taken from websites and Facebook pages that included autism-related content'. Dataset 2 is the YTUIA corpus, 1,163 face crops extracted with MTCNN from the Self-Stimulatory Behaviours Dataset - frames from 100 videos, 50 publicly available on YouTube and 50 obtained from therapists and professional organisations - with controls drawn from unrelated YouTube videos of kindergarten activities. No child in either corpus is known to have received a diagnostic assessment, no diagnostic instrument or clinician judgement is cited, and the number of distinct individuals behind either image count is unknown. No ethics approval or consent statement appears anywhere in the paper. | Two architectures were compared - a squeeze-and-excitation CNN and a squeeze-and-excitation CNN with multiscale feature fusion - each with and without hyperparameter optimisation by the white shark optimisation algorithm, giving four configurations per dataset. The search covered learning rate, two layer widths, batch size, convolutional depth and kernel size, using ten agents over two iterations against a fitness combining accuracy, F1 and loss. Training used an NVIDIA Tesla T4 on Google Colab with early stopping at patience 5, checkpointing on best validation loss and learning-rate reduction by a factor of 0.1 on a three-epoch plateau. The validation design is the study's distinctive element. Recognising that frame-level splitting of a video-derived corpus risks subject-level and temporal leakage, the authors extracted ResNet-50 features for all 1,163 YTUIA images and measured the maximum training-test cosine similarity, obtaining 0.9714 - direct evidence of leakage. They applied K-Means clustering over the deep features, swept the cluster count from 30 to 150, split clusters rather than images into 80/10/10 partitions, and reassigned any test image exceeding 0.90 similarity to a training image back into training. The adopted 100-cluster configuration yielded 951 training, 144 validation and 68 test images at a final maximum similarity of 0.8989 with 28 images reassigned. The same check on the Piosenka corpus returned 0.90 and its original split was retained. Evaluation used accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Cohen's kappa, specificity, AUC and AUC-PR with confusion matrices and curves, McNemar's test and paired t-tests across model variants, Grad-CAM heatmaps for interpretability, a four-way ablation, and bidirectional cross-dataset evaluation. | Headline performance was 95.36% accuracy, 92.62% precision and 95.5% F1, a triple that is arithmetically consistent with a recall of 98.6% and a specificity of 92.2% at the reported 1:1 class ratio. The ablation is the more informative result: without the hyperparameter search, the squeeze-and-excitation CNN reached 0.89 accuracy while the multiscale variant reached only 0.85, so the paper's own architectural contribution degrades performance in isolation, and the authors state that 'adding multi-scale fusion may not have yielded better results'. Adding white shark optimisation reverses the ordering, with McNemar and paired t-tests returning p below 0.01 for the optimised against unoptimised comparison. Cross-dataset evaluation reached 90% accuracy and AUC 0.94 training on YTUIA and testing on Piosenka, and 89% with AUC 0.93 in the reverse direction. Grad-CAM heatmaps were produced for each attention module and are reported without clinical validation. | The labels in both corpora record where material was found on the internet rather than any assessment of the child depicted - a fact the paper states in its own methods and never revisits. No child is known to have been diagnosed, no reference standard is cited, and the paper nonetheless describes the positive class as 'individuals diagnosed with ASD'. Demographics are absent and the sex distribution is explicitly recorded as unspecified, so at a roughly four-to-one male-to-female diagnostic ratio and given that facial classifiers key strongly on sex-linked morphology, an unmeasured sex imbalance remains an untestable alternative explanation for the entire result. The leakage work, though the best in this branch, addresses only within-corpus duplication: a model that has learned to recognise images sourced from autism-related web content performs identically on perfectly subject-disjoint splits. The same reading applies to the cross-dataset result, which is presented as evidence of robustness - both corpora were assembled by the same principle, autism-labelled material from autism-associated sources against controls from general sources, so a shared confound transfers exactly as a shared phenotype would. Perceptual similarity is in any case a proxy for identity rather than a measurement of it, and the reassignment of high-similarity images out of the test set is a data-dependent edit using the model's own feature space. The reported confidence intervals are uniformly plus or minus 0.4 percentage points on a test set of 68 images, where one image is worth 1.47 points and an exact binomial interval around 95% accuracy runs from roughly 87% to 99%. The hyperparameter search does not state which partition its fitness was evaluated on. No positive predictive value is computed at any realistic prevalence despite an assembled 1:1 ratio. And no ethics or consent statement appears anywhere, in a study trained on identifiable photographs of children scraped from personal websites, Facebook pages and YouTube. | This is the fifth study in the review to build on the Piosenka Kaggle corpus and the most methodologically careful of them, which is exactly why it earns extended treatment. It is the only paper in the facial-photograph branch to test for leakage rather than assume its absence, and its test produced a concrete number that indicts the branch's standard practice: a maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714 in the video-derived corpus under conventional frame-level splitting. It archives its code on Zenodo with a DOI, reports a metric suite with significance testing, runs an ablation whose result contradicts its own headline contribution and says so, and evaluates across datasets in both directions. Set against the other Piosenka papers charted here - which report 98.8%, 99.8%, 97.0%, 95.59% and 81.0% under image-level splits with no leakage analysis at all - it demonstrates that the analytic standards of this branch are capable of improving. The lesson for the synthesis lies in what that improvement does not buy. Every one of these strengths operates downstream of a label that records image provenance rather than a diagnosis, and none of them can repair it: subject-disjoint splits do not help when the confound is the source of the image rather than the identity of the child, and transfer between two corpora built by the same harvesting principle is not independent confirmation but a demonstration that the confound is shared. The paper is therefore the review's clearest case of rigour applied to the wrong layer, and the most useful illustration of why methodological quality scores computed at the analysis stage can rank a study above less careful work whose data are sounder. Two further items belong in the discussion. The absence of any ethics or consent statement, in a paper whose data are identifiable images of children harvested from support and awareness pages, marks a gap in how computer science venues handle human-subjects material even when their declaration structures are otherwise thorough. And the conclusion's instruction that clinicians 'must recognize these facial traits or regions, as they indicate the condition' shows how a physiognomic claim reaches a clinical audience through a paper whose own interpretability caveat, stated three pages earlier, is that no clinician ever looked at the heatmaps. | [RQ1.1] There are no participants. The units are images: 2,866 in the Piosenka Kaggle collection, split 1,433 autism-labelled and 1,433 control, described as ages 1-11; and 1,163 face crops extracted with MTCNN from the YTUIA/SSBD video corpus, split after re-clustering into 951 training, 144 validation and 68 test. The number of distinct children behind either figure is unknown and unreported - the paper's own table labels the 2,866 images as 'Total individuals', which is the conflation this review has repeatedly recorded in the image-classification branch. The provenance of each class is stated plainly and is the decisive fact: the autism images were 'taken from websites and Facebook pages that included autism-related content', while the YTUIA positives derive from 100 videos assembled to depict self-stimulatory behaviour, of which 50 came from YouTube and 50 from therapists and professional organisations, with controls being 'YouTube videos featuring kindergarten activities within the relevant age range'. In both corpora, therefore, the class label records where material was found rather than any assessment of the child depicted. [RQ1.2] Consistently medical and deficit-framed, with the diagnostic label used as an attribute of appearance. Autism is 'a complex neurodevelopmental disorder that affects both cognitive and social development' posing 'a significant concern in modern healthcare'. The facial framing is the distinctive feature: the introduction assembles a physiognomic case - 'craniofacial anomalies make neuro-developmental disorders like ASD more likely to happen', autism severity 'has been associated with a wider intercanthal distance and a lower height of the facial midline', and 'facial asymmetry and facial masculinity are good signs that someone has significant ASD symptoms'. The conclusion instructs clinicians that they 'must recognize these facial traits or regions, as they indicate the condition'. Person-first phrasing appears alongside 'individuals diagnosed with ASD' and 'the non-ASD control group'. There is no neurodiversity framing, no autistic-community involvement, and no acknowledgement that a facial-appearance classifier trained on photographs of children scraped from support and awareness pages carries a different set of ethical questions from a behavioural measurement. [RQ1.3] Almost entirely absent, and the paper marks the absence in its own table. Age is given as a range of 1-11 for dataset 1 and not at all for dataset 2; the sex distribution is recorded as 'Females/Males: -' with the note 'Gender distribution unspecified'; and no information exists on ancestry, socioeconomic status, cognitive level, language, comorbidity or medication for either class. No between-class comparison of any characteristic is possible, and none is attempted. Two consequences follow directly. Because autism is diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys, and because facial classifiers are known to key strongly on sex-linked morphology, an unmeasured sex imbalance between classes is a live and untestable alternative explanation for the entire result. And because the two classes were harvested from different regions of the internet - autism advocacy and support content on one side, general and kindergarten content on the other - they are likely to differ in the geography, ancestry and photographic circumstances of the children depicted, none of which can be checked. The reported cross-dataset transfer does not resolve this, since both corpora were constructed on the same principle. [RQ1.4] There is none. No child in either corpus is known to the authors to have received a diagnostic assessment. In the Piosenka dataset the positive label means an image was found on a website or Facebook page with autism-related content; in the YTUIA dataset it means a video was collected into a corpus of self-stimulatory behaviour, half from YouTube and half from therapists and professional organisations. Neither carries a clinician judgement, a diagnostic instrument, a medical record or any documented ascertainment. The paper cites no reference standard, does not identify the absence as a limitation, and describes the positive class throughout as 'individuals diagnosed with ASD' - a description the data cannot support. The YTUIA positives at least depict a behaviour that is associated with autism, which places them a step above pure provenance labelling; but the modelling target is the face crop rather than the behaviour, so even that association does not transfer to what the model is trained on. This is the same reference-standard failure recorded for the other Piosenka-based papers in this review, and it bounds every figure the paper reports. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, severity, adaptive or language measure exists for any image in either corpus, and none could, given how the data were assembled. The introduction cites literature relating intercanthal distance and facial midline height to autism severity, which would make a severity analysis the natural test of whether the model has learned anything morphological - but no severity data exist to run it against, and the point is not raised. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to improve facial-image-based autism detection by combining squeeze-and-excitation channel attention, multiscale feature fusion and convolutional networks with automated hyperparameter search using the white shark optimisation algorithm, motivated by four claimed gaps in prior work: limited modelling of long-range dependencies by CNNs, insufficient local inductive bias when images are treated as token sequences, weak interpretability, and inadequate splitting strategies. The headline finding is 95.36% accuracy, 92.62% precision and 95.5% F1 - a triple that is arithmetically consistent with a recall of 98.6% and a specificity of 92.2% at the reported 1:1 ratio, which is worth noting because internal inconsistency is common in this branch. Three secondary findings carry more weight than the headline. The ablation shows that the paper's own multiscale fusion contribution reduces accuracy relative to squeeze-and-excitation alone when the hyperparameter search is removed (0.85 against 0.89), and the authors state this plainly rather than burying it. The leakage investigation on the video-derived corpus found a maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714 before intervention, which is direct evidence that naive frame-level splitting of that dataset - the standard practice in the papers it is drawn from - leaks. And bidirectional cross-dataset evaluation reached 89-90%, which the paper presents as robustness and which is better read as evidence that whatever the model has learned is common to two corpora built by the same web-scraping principle. [RQ2.2] No study setting exists. Both corpora are secondary web collections assembled by third parties, and the computational work was done on Google Colab. This matters more here than in most secondary-data studies in this review, because the setting is precisely what generates the labels: the Piosenka positive class is defined by having been found on autism-related websites and Facebook pages, and the YTUIA classes are defined by being drawn from a self-stimulatory-behaviour video corpus versus unrelated kindergarten videos. In a study where the data collection setting differs systematically between classes and no other ascertainment exists, the setting is the confound rather than a background detail. [RQ2.3] None. No task, paradigm or elicitation procedure exists in either corpus. The children in the Piosenka images were photographed for reasons unrelated to any study, and the YTUIA videos were recorded by families and organisations for their own purposes. This has a specific analytic consequence the paper does not draw: the introduction motivates the work through evidence about facial expression dynamics - that autistic infants 'exhibit more complex facial expressions than their typically developing classmates, particularly in the eyebrows and lips' - but nothing in an uncontrolled still photograph or an isolated video frame holds expression, pose, gaze, emotional context or elicitation constant, so a difference in expression between classes cannot be distinguished from a difference in the circumstances under which the two classes of image were taken. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional and retrospective, with no longitudinal element and no repeat measurement. The ethics reporting is the notable gap: the paper contains no ethics statement, no institutional review board approval and no consent statement of any kind - a full-text search returns no occurrence of 'ethic' or 'consent'. Analysis of public datasets frequently proceeds without fresh approval, and PeerJ's declaration structure elicited funding, competing-interests, author-contribution and data-availability statements from these authors, so the omission is specific to human-subjects considerations. The data are identifiable photographs and video frames of children, harvested from personal websites, Facebook pages and YouTube, whose families posted them to seek support or raise awareness and did not consent to their use as training data for an autism classifier. The paper's conclusion envisages clinical deployment of a model built on that material without touching the question. Funding from King Faisal University grant KFU250488 is declared with a no-role statement, competing interests are declared as none, and the authors disclose that generative AI was used to correct the English. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment exists. Computation used an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU on Google Colab under Python 3.8 with 12 GB RAM and 16 GB GPU memory, batch sizes between 32 and 128. MTCNN performed face detection on the video frames, followed by alignment, cropping and resizing; pixel values were normalised to [0, 1]. A pretrained ResNet-50 supplied the feature space for the leakage analysis. Because the images come from unknown consumer cameras and phones under unknown conditions, every acquisition variable that a purpose-built study would control - focal length, sensor, resolution, illumination, distance, compression - varies freely and, critically, may vary systematically with class, since the two classes were harvested from different kinds of online source. [RQ2.6] Better than most of this branch on the computational side and empty on the human side. Fully reported: both dataset URLs, the preprocessing pipeline, the final split sizes for both corpora, the leakage-detection procedure in pseudocode with its cosine thresholds, cluster sweep from 30 to 150 and reassignment rule, the training regime including early stopping with patience 5, checkpointing on best validation loss and learning-rate reduction by a factor of 0.1 on a plateau of 3, the hyperparameter search bounds, the white shark configuration, the hardware and software environment, and the full metric suite with McNemar and paired t-tests. Code is on GitHub and archived on Zenodo with a DOI, which places this paper in the minority of the corpus that permits computational replication. Not reported: the number of distinct individuals behind either image count, any demographic composition, which data partition the hyperparameter fitness was evaluated on, the number of runs behind the reported means, and how the confidence intervals were computed. The stated search dimension of 3 is also inconsistent with the six hyperparameter ranges tabulated. [RQ2.7] Two limitations are stated and both are real. The computational cost of a deep multiscale attention architecture combined with metaheuristic search is acknowledged as a barrier to real-time deployment. And the interpretability claim is qualified honestly: 'clinical users or experts did not validate our heatmaps, limiting our ability to assess their potential clinical utility', with a concrete remedy proposed. The ablation discussion adds a third, unprompted admission - that multiscale fusion alone did not improve on squeeze-and-excitation alone. What is not stated is more consequential. The provenance confound is never raised, although the paper supplies the evidence for it in its own description of where the images came from. No diagnostic reference standard exists for either corpus and this is not identified as a limitation. Demographics are absent and marked as absent, yet the possibility that age, sex or ancestry imbalance drives the result is not discussed. The 1:1 class ratio bears no relation to prevalence and no positive predictive value is computed. The confidence intervals - uniformly the mean plus or minus 0.4 points, on a test set of 68 images where one image is worth 1.47 points - cannot be describing the uncertainty in the accuracy estimate; an exact binomial interval around 95% on 68 images runs from roughly 87% to 99%. The cross-dataset result is offered as robustness without noting that both corpora were built the same way. And the ethics of the underlying images is untouched. [RQ2.9] Two directions are named: clinical validation of the Grad-CAM heatmaps by psychiatrists or autism specialists, which is the right next step for the interpretability claim; and reduction of the computational cost for real-time use. Not proposed, and needed before any of the reported figures could support the paper's clinical claims: evaluation on a cohort with documented diagnoses, reporting of the demographic composition of each class, a test of whether the model's output survives matching on age and sex, and an assessment of whether the classifier's decisions track image provenance rather than facial phenotype. [RQ3.1] Nominally facial morphology and expression; operationally, whatever separates two sets of internet images. The motivating literature is specific - intercanthal distance, facial midline height, facial asymmetry, facial masculinity, and increased complexity of eyebrow and lip movement in autistic infants - but none of it is operationalised. The representation is a raw RGB face crop, so no morphometric measurement is extracted, no landmark geometry is computed, and no temporal information is retained, which rules out expression dynamics entirely. What the network can key on is unconstrained: craniofacial shape, but equally facial expression at the captured instant, head pose, apparent age, ancestry, image resolution, compression artefacts, illumination, background and crop convention. The paper's leakage analysis inadvertently demonstrates how much non-diagnostic structure the images carry - a maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714 in a pretrained ResNet-50 feature space, on a corpus that supposedly contains different children. [RQ3.2] None in the sense this review uses the term. The paper's 'multiscale fusion' combines feature maps at different spatial resolutions within a single network operating on a single image modality, and the abstract's reference to 'both facial and multimodal datasets' is not borne out by the methods - both corpora are collections of still images. The multiscale ablation is nonetheless informative and is reported honestly: without the hyperparameter search, adding multiscale fusion lowered accuracy from 0.89 to 0.85, and the authors state that 'adding multi-scale fusion may not have yielded better results'. Only in combination with white shark optimisation does the fuller architecture win, which means the architectural contribution and the search contribution are not separable in the reported comparison. [RQ4.1] Deep convolutional networks with channel attention and multiscale feature fusion, in four configurations - SE-CNN and SE-MSF-CNN, each with and without white shark optimisation. White shark optimisation is a swarm metaheuristic that adjusts learning rate, layer widths, batch size, depth and kernel size against a fitness combining accuracy, F1 and loss. The reported configuration is ten agents over two iterations, roughly twenty fitness evaluations, which is a very shallow search for a six-dimensional space - and the tabulated dimension of 3 does not match the six ranges given. The evaluation partition for the fitness function is not stated, which matters: if fitness was computed on the test partition, the reported test performance is a selection maximum rather than a held-out estimate. Comparison across configurations is supported by McNemar's test and paired t-tests with p below 0.01, more statistical care than is usual in this branch, applied to a comparison whose foundation - the labels - is the unexamined part. [RQ4.2] RGB face crops, normalised to [0, 1], obtained by third-party cropping in dataset 1 and by MTCNN detection with alignment, cropping and resizing in dataset 2. No landmark coordinates, no morphometric derivations, no temporal sequence. The representation therefore cannot express any of the specific craniofacial or expression-dynamic constructs the introduction invokes, and it retains every source-dependent property of the image - resolution, compression, illumination, pose, background - that is free to vary with class given how the two classes were harvested. [RQ4.3] The broadest metric set in this branch: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Cohen's kappa, specificity, AUC and AUC-PR, with confusion matrices, ROC and precision-recall curves, means and standard deviations across runs, 95% intervals, McNemar's test and paired t-tests. The apparatus is well beyond what most facial-image papers in this review report, and the headline triple is internally coherent - 95.36% accuracy with 92.62% precision and 95.5% F1 implies recall 98.6% and specificity 92.2% at a 1:1 ratio, which reproduces the stated accuracy exactly. Two failures nonetheless undercut the reporting. The intervals are not compatible with the data: every one is the mean plus or minus 0.4 percentage points, accompanied by a standard deviation of 0.03, on test sets as small as 68 images where a single misclassification moves accuracy by 1.47 points; an exact binomial interval around 95% on 68 images spans roughly 87% to 99%. And no positive predictive value is computed for any realistic prevalence, despite a 1:1 class ratio that exists only because the datasets were assembled that way - at a population rate near 1-2%, a specificity of 92% would place the great majority of positive calls on non-autistic children. [RQ4.4] Grad-CAM heatmaps are computed over the attention-generated feature maps and presented as ensuring 'transparency and reliability in decision-making'. The authors then add the qualification that distinguishes this paper from others in the branch: the heatmaps were never shown to clinicians, so their diagnostic meaning is unassessed, and collaboration with psychiatrists or autism specialists is recommended to establish whether the highlighted regions are informative. That is the correct caveat and it is stated in the authors' own voice. Its limits should be clear, though. Saliency identifies where in the image the model looked, not what property it responded to, and every candidate explanation for the result - craniofacial shape, expression, apparent age, ancestry, image resolution, crop convention - is located in the same face region. A heatmap centred on the eyes and mouth is therefore equally consistent with a facial phenotype and with the model having learned to recognise the photographic style of images that appear on autism support pages. The conclusion nevertheless instructs clinicians that they 'must recognize these facial traits or regions, as they indicate the condition', which asserts precisely what the heatmaps cannot establish. [RQ4.5] The most developed validation section in the facial-image branch of this review, and worth recording carefully because it is the one place where a paper in that branch takes leakage seriously. The authors recognised that the video-derived corpus risks subject-level and temporal leakage under frame-level splitting, and rather than asserting the problem away they measured it: ResNet-50 features for all 1,163 images, maximum training-test cosine similarity of 0.9714, correctly interpreted as 'a substantial likelihood of leakage'. They then applied K-Means over the deep features, swept cluster counts from 30 to 150, split clusters rather than images 80/10/10, and reassigned test images exceeding 0.90 similarity to a training image back into the training set, adopting the 100-cluster configuration for its balance of test-set size (68 images), final similarity (0.8989) and reassignment count (28). The same check on the Piosenka corpus returned 0.90, and the original split was kept. Compared with the four other Piosenka-based papers charted here, all of which split images without comment, this is a substantial advance. Three qualifications bound it. Perceptual similarity is a proxy for identity and not a measurement of it - two images of one child under different lighting can fall below any threshold while two different children in matched conditions can exceed it - so the paper's claim to have confirmed 'the absence of subject- or frame-level leakage' asserts more than a cosine threshold can support. The reassignment step edits the test set using the model's own feature space, moving out precisely the images most similar to training data, which makes the reported performance conditional on a data-dependent curation rule. And the leakage machinery addresses only within-corpus duplication; it does nothing about the confound that determines what the labels mean, since a model that has learned to recognise images sourced from autism-related web content will do so equally well on perfectly disjoint subjects. The cross-dataset evaluation deserves the same reading. Training on one corpus and testing on the other reached 89-90% in both directions, which the paper offers as robustness. But both corpora were built by the same principle - autism-labelled material harvested from autism-associated online sources, controls from general online sources - so a confound common to both transfers exactly as a genuine phenotype would. Transfer between two datasets that share a construction bias is not independent confirmation; transfer to a clinically ascertained cohort would be, and is not attempted. The remaining gaps are the unstated evaluation partition for the hyperparameter fitness, the absence of any chance or prevalence baseline, and confidence intervals incompatible with the test set sizes. [RQ5.1] Keywords: artificial intelligence (misspelled as 'artificial intellgent' in the published keyword list), multi-scale view convolutional neural network (SE-MSF-CNN), autism spectrum disorder, white shark optimisation. The set is entirely method-facing - three of four terms name the architecture or the optimiser - with no term describing the population, the data source, the behaviour or the clinical question. That distribution is characteristic of the branch and is one reason these papers are hard to locate from a clinical search. Terms recurring in the body: squeeze-and-excitation, multiscale attention, Grad-CAM, explainable artificial intelligence, transfer learning, craniofacial anomalies, facial masculinity, cosine similarity, K-Means, leakage. [RQ5.2] PeerJ Computer Science 11:e3134, submitted 8 April 2025, accepted 29 July 2025, published 2 October 2025, open access under CC-BY 4.0, academic editor Davide Chicco, with subject areas listed as bioinformatics, algorithms, artificial intelligence and data science. The venue is a computer science journal, which shapes what the review process attended to: the paper's statistical comparison of model variants, its ablation design, its code archiving on Zenodo and its leakage analysis are all above the norm for this branch, while the absence of any ethics statement, any diagnostic reference standard and any demographic description passed without comment. PeerJ's declaration structure elicited funding, competing-interests, author-contribution and data-availability statements from these authors but has no field that would have prompted a human-subjects declaration. The bibliographic record also carries an inconsistency worth noting for the corpus: the supplied metadata dates the article to 2024 while the article itself is a 2025 publication. [RQ5.3] Published 2025 by information systems and computer science groups at Al Yamamah University Riyadh, Minia University and King Faisal University, funded by King Faisal University grant KFU250488. The framing is the standard early-detection appeal - screening is subjective, expertise is scarce, and a facial-image classifier would be objective, scalable and non-invasive - built on a physiognomic literature the introduction reviews approvingly and the conclusion endorses, telling clinicians that facial traits 'indicate the condition'. For this review the paper occupies an unusual position, and its value lies in the tension between its two halves. Methodologically it is the best-executed study in the facial-photograph branch: it is the only one to test for leakage rather than assume its absence, and it found a maximum training-test similarity of 0.9714 in the video-derived corpus, which is direct evidence that the naive frame-level splitting practised by the papers it draws on does leak; it is one of the few in the whole corpus to archive its code with a DOI; it reports a full metric suite with significance testing; its ablation honestly records that its own architectural contribution underperforms without the accompanying hyperparameter search; and it evaluates across datasets in both directions. Substantively, none of that reaches the problem, because the labels in both corpora encode where an image was found rather than any assessment of the child in it - a fact the paper states in its own methods and never revisits. The cross-dataset result sharpens rather than resolves this: two corpora built by the same principle, autism-labelled material from autism-associated online sources against controls from general online sources, will share their confounds, so 89-90% transfer between them is what a provenance-driven model would produce as readily as a phenotype-driven one. The lesson the review should carry from this paper is that methodological rigour applied downstream of a corrupted label does not repair it, and can make an uninterpretable result look better validated than the less careful papers alongside it. Two further points belong in the discussion: no ethics or consent statement appears anywhere in a paper whose training data are identifiable photographs of children scraped from personal websites, Facebook pages and YouTube; and the reported confidence intervals of plus or minus 0.4 percentage points on a 68-image test set are narrower than a single test image, which is a reporting failure that the journal's statistical framing did not catch. |
| S-123 | Retrospective algorithm-development study by the School of Computer Engineering and Mathematical Sciences at the Defence Institute of Advanced Technology, Pune, with a collaborator at Manipal University Jaipur, using the global autism EEG corpus held by the brain-computer interface group at King Abdulaziz University and accessed with permission. The sample is 17 boys: 13 autistic aged 10 to 16 and 4 typically developing aged 9 to 16. No diagnostic instrument, criteria or clinician qualification is described for the autistic group and no screening procedure for the comparison group; no age distribution, cognitive level, language ability, comorbidity or medication information is reported for either. The ethics declarations state that neither a human-rights statement nor informed consent is required for this type of study. | EEG was recorded during participants' relaxed states to minimise artefact, using a g.tec cap with 16 Ag/AgCl electrodes at FP1, FP2, F7, F3, Fz, F4, F8, T3, C4, Cz, C3, T5, Pz, O1, Oz and O2 under the international 10-20 system, with AFz as ground and the right earlobe as reference, through a g.tec GAMMAbox and USBamp driven by BCI2000. Signals were bandpass filtered 0.1-60 Hz, notch filtered at 60 Hz and digitised at 256 Hz. Eleven linear and non-linear features spanning time and frequency domains were extracted, and four neural architectures were compared: a convolutional network, a three-layer dense network (128 ReLU units, 64 ReLU units, single sigmoid output, with layer equations given explicitly), a long short-term memory network and a custom design. No train-test split, cross-validation scheme, partitioning unit, segment count or segment duration is stated anywhere in the paper. | The custom neural network reached 94.02% accuracy, the LSTM 93.83%, the deep neural network 91.98% and the convolutional network 89.02%, with precision, recall, specificity and F1 reported for each. The paper's own comparison table places the prior EEG literature at 56% to 93%, and lists participant counts alongside those accuracies. | No validation scheme of any kind is described - no split, no cross-validation, no partitioning unit and no segment count - so the reported figures cannot be located relative to any evaluation design. With 17 participants, accuracies of 89% to 94% cannot have been computed over people and must derive from EEG epochs; with only four control children, a participant-disjoint arrangement would place at most one control in any held-out set, so the natural reading is that epochs from the same children appear on both sides of the partition and the networks are separating individuals rather than groups. The participant-level majority-class baseline is 76.5% and is never stated, so the increment over a trivial classifier is far smaller than the headline figures suggest. The comparison group of four is too small to characterise typical EEG variation or to support the reported specificity. No age distribution by group is given across a 9-to-16 window in which EEG spectral characteristics mature substantially, and medication - which alters EEG directly and differs systematically between such groups - is unrecorded. No diagnostic ascertainment is described. No feature-importance analysis identifies which of the eleven descriptors or which electrode positions carry the signal. And there is no limitations section. | The review's representative of the electrophysiological branch, and useful for three things beyond its own numbers. It makes plain both the branch's structural advantage and its cost: a purpose-built corpus in which both groups were recorded on identical equipment under an identical protocol removes the acquisition confound that undermines the scraped-image, thermal and clinic-versus-school studies charted elsewhere here, and the acquisition itself is reported more completely than any behavioural instrument in this review - montage, ground, reference, filter settings and sampling rate all specified. Against that, a research EEG amplifier, a gel cap, a trained operator and a child willing to sit still is precisely the apparatus that the webcam-and-toys and free-play protocols exist to avoid, while the motivating argument is identical in both branches: that diagnosis depends on subjective and time-consuming behavioural assessment. Second, it reproduces in a fifth modality the pattern the review has traced through scanpath images, video frames, thermal images and cry recordings - a small sample, accuracies necessarily computed over segments rather than people, no stated partitioning rule, and an unmentioned majority-class baseline that here stands at 76.5%. Third, and most usefully, its own comparison table supplies independent corroboration of the review's central quantitative observation, assembled by authors with no intention of demonstrating it: six prior studies with 15 to 80 participants report 81% to 93%, while the one study in the table with 411 participants reports 56% to 64%. Within a summary the authors constructed themselves, the study with a sample an order of magnitude larger than the rest reports by far the lowest performance. | [RQ1.1] Seventeen boys: 13 autistic aged 10 to 16 and 4 typically developing aged 9 to 16, drawn from the global autism EEG corpus held by the brain-computer interface group at King Abdulaziz University and used with permission. The comparison group of four is the smallest in the review and is too small to characterise typical variation in any EEG measure, let alone to support a claim about detection. The sample is entirely male, which removes sex as a confound and means nothing reported can be assumed to apply to autistic girls. No age distribution by group is given beyond the two ranges, and none of the descriptors this review usually records - cognitive level, language ability, comorbidity, medication, socioeconomic background - is available. The 13:4 ratio also sets the participant-level majority-class baseline at 76.5%, against which the reported 89-94% should be read and never is. [RQ1.2] Conventional clinical framing, brief and largely accurate. Autism is 'a complex neurodevelopmental condition characterized by a spectrum of challenges, including difficulties in communication, response, attention, social behavior, and repetitive activities', with the addition that autistic people 'exhibit atypical neural activity patterns'. The diagnostic argument is the branch standard: current practice 'predominantly depends on subjective and time-consuming behavioral assessments', so an objective non-intrusive biomarker is needed. Person-first phrasing is used throughout and no pathologising excess appears. No neurodiversity framing is present and no autistic person is reported as involved. The framing is worth recording for the synthesis because it is identical to that of the behavioural studies charted elsewhere in this review - the same dissatisfaction with behavioural assessment motivates both branches, while the electrophysiological branch requires equipment and expertise that the behavioural work is generally chosen to avoid. [RQ1.3] Almost entirely absent. Sex is fully controlled by the sample being all-male; age is given only as two overlapping ranges (10-16 and 9-16) with no distribution or group comparison; and no cognitive, language, comorbidity, medication or socioeconomic information exists. Two specific risks follow. EEG spectral characteristics change substantially across the 9-to-16 window - the alpha peak rises in frequency, slow-wave power declines, and the maturational trajectory is well documented - so an age difference between a 13-child and a 4-child group would be sufficient to separate them on spectral features, and nothing reported allows the check. And medication is unrecorded, although antiepileptics and antipsychotics both alter EEG spectra and are more common in an autistic than in a comparison sample. [RQ1.4] None described. The 13 autistic participants are stated to be 'diagnosed with ASD' with no instrument, criteria, clinician qualification, setting or date, and no screening procedure is reported for the 4 comparison children. The labels derive from the originating corpus and this paper transmits none of its documentation. The consequence is the same as for several studies in this review: the quantity the models predict is a label of unknown provenance, and no reported figure can be located relative to any clinical standard. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for any participant, so no gradient analysis is possible and the models' outputs can be related only to group membership. [RQ2.1] The aim is to compare a broader range of neural architectures on EEG-derived features than prior work has done, on the argument that existing studies have explored a limited set of models and feature combinations. Four architectures were fitted to eleven linear and non-linear time- and frequency-domain features: a custom neural network reached 94.02% accuracy, an LSTM 93.83%, a deep neural network 91.98% and a convolutional network 89.02%, with precision, recall, specificity and F1 reported for each. The comparison is even-handed and includes the lowest performer rather than only the winner. What the study cannot establish is what those figures mean. With 17 participants the accuracies must have been computed over EEG epochs rather than people, no validation scheme of any kind is described, and with four control children a participant-disjoint evaluation would leave at most one control in any held-out set. The paper's own comparison table is the most useful thing in it for this review, and its pattern is discussed below. [RQ2.2] No primary collection. Recordings were made by the originating group under controlled laboratory conditions with participants at rest, described as ensuring artefact-free and reliable data. Both groups were recorded on the same equipment under the same protocol, so the acquisition asymmetry that undermines several branches of this review - clinic against school, autism websites against general internet - does not arise here. That is a genuine structural advantage of purpose-built physiological corpora over the assembled behavioural ones. [RQ2.3] None, by design. The EEG was recorded 'during participants' relaxed states to ensure artifact-free data', so no task was administered, no stimulus presented and no behaviour elicited. This is the defining difference between the electrophysiological branch and the behavioural studies charted elsewhere in this review, and it cuts both ways. Resting-state acquisition is maximally undemanding - it requires no cooperation with instructions, no verbal ability and no social engagement, which is why it reaches participants that task-based paradigms cannot - and it also means there is no behavioural or cognitive event to which any observed difference can be anchored. A group difference in resting spectral power is a difference in ambient neural state, interpretable only against a physiological literature, whereas a group difference in gaze during a social scene or in utterance length during play is interpretable directly. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. The ethics declarations read in full: 'For this type of study, statement of human rights is not required' and 'For this type of study, informed consent is not required.' The data are EEG recordings of identifiable children obtained from another institution's research group with permission, so the declaration concerns secondary use rather than the original collection - but the paper does not distinguish the two, gives no reference to the originating approvals, and states the exemption in absolute terms. The data provider is acknowledged by name with the corpus URL, and competing interests are declared as none. [RQ2.5] The most completely specified acquisition chain in the review. A g.tec EEG cap with 16 Ag/AgCl electrodes, a g.tec GAMMAbox and g.tec USBamp, driven by BCI2000; electrodes at FP1, FP2, F7, F3, Fz, F4, F8, T3, C4, Cz, C3, T5, Pz, O1, Oz and O2 under the international 10-20 system; AFz as ground and the right earlobe as reference; bandpass 0.1-60 Hz with a 60 Hz notch; digitised at 256 Hz. Montage, ground, reference, filter settings and sampling rate are all given, which is more acquisition detail than most behavioural studies in this review report for their own instruments and is exactly what would be needed to replicate the recording. The corresponding practical point is that this apparatus - a research EEG amplifier, a gel cap, a trained operator and a cooperative child who will sit still - is at the opposite end of the deployment spectrum from the webcam-and-toys protocols charted elsewhere, and the review's synthesis should note that the electrophysiological branch shares the behavioural branch's motivation while requiring the equipment that motivation exists to avoid. [RQ2.6] Sharply divided. Fully reported: the data source with its URL and a named acknowledgement of the provider, both group sizes and age ranges, the complete electrode montage with ground and reference positions, the filter settings and sampling rate, the recording condition, the count of features and their domain families, all four network architectures with layer sizes and activation functions given as explicit equations, and five performance metrics for each model. Entirely absent: any train-test split, cross-validation scheme or partitioning unit; the number of EEG segments analysed and how they distribute across the 17 participants; the identity of the eleven features; hyperparameters; and any account of how autism was ascertained. A reader could replicate the recording and the architectures and could not evaluate or reproduce the result. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section. What should have been stated, in order of consequence: no validation scheme of any kind is described, so the reported 89-94% cannot be placed relative to any evaluation design, and with 17 participants those figures must derive from epoch-level evaluation where a participant-disjoint arrangement is barely constructible from four controls. The participant-level majority-class baseline is 76.5% and is never stated. The comparison group of four children is too small to characterise typical EEG variation. No age distribution by group is given across a 9-to-16 window in which EEG spectra change substantially, and medication - which alters EEG directly and differs between such groups - is unrecorded. No diagnostic ascertainment is described. No feature-importance analysis identifies which of the eleven descriptors separates the groups, which would have been the study's most transferable finding. And the paper's own comparison table displays a pattern it does not comment on, discussed below. [RQ2.9] None stated. The steps this study most needs are participant-disjoint evaluation with the scheme reported, a stated majority-class baseline, feature-importance analysis over the eleven descriptors, and a comparison group larger than four. [RQ3.1] None. No behaviour is observed, elicited or measured at any point: the recordings capture spontaneous cortical electrical activity while participants rest. The construct is neurophysiological - spectral power, signal complexity, fractal and entropy characteristics of the resting EEG - and the paper's motivating premise is that 'individuals with ASD exhibit atypical neural activity patterns'. For the review this places the study in a parallel evidence stream: it addresses the same clinical problem as the behavioural work and answers it with a different kind of measurement, one that is more direct physiologically and further from anything a clinician, parent or teacher observes. The related-work section shows the branch's feature vocabulary clearly - recurrence quantification analysis, power spectrum, wavelet transform, fast Fourier transform, fractal dimension, correlation dimension, Lyapunov exponent, entropy, detrended fluctuation analysis and synchronisation likelihood - none of which corresponds to an observable behaviour. [RQ3.2] None. A single electrophysiological modality throughout, with no behavioural, imaging or clinical data fused. The eleven features span time and frequency domains, which is within-modality diversity rather than fusion. [RQ4.1] Four architectures compared on a common feature set: a convolutional network, a three-layer dense network (128 ReLU, 64 ReLU, single sigmoid, with the layer equations written out explicitly), an LSTM, and a custom design. Presenting four architectures with their formulations, and reporting the weakest alongside the strongest, is more even-handed than much of this corpus. The comparison's informativeness is limited by the spread being small - 89.02% to 94.02%, five points across four quite different architectures - which on a 17-participant sample is well within the range that resampling variation alone would produce, and by no hyperparameter or training detail being reported. The pattern nonetheless matches the one found in the skeleton-movement study charted elsewhere in this review, where six architectures spanned two percentage points on one dataset: in this literature the data determine the result and the architecture rarely does. [RQ4.2] An eleven-dimensional vector of linear and non-linear time- and frequency-domain descriptors per EEG segment. The features are individually interpretable and have an established electrophysiological literature, which makes the absence of any feature-importance analysis a real loss - identifying which descriptors and which electrode positions separate the groups would have produced a transferable finding independent of the classification accuracy. The number and duration of segments and their distribution across participants are not reported, which is the missing information needed to judge the sample structure. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 for all four architectures. Reporting specificity is appropriate at a 13:4 class ratio and more than several studies in this review provide. Three gaps: no confidence intervals on figures derived from 17 participants; no confusion matrices or class-wise breakdowns; and no chance or majority-class baseline, although the participant-level ratio places a trivial all-autistic classifier at 76.5%, so the reported 89-94% represents a much smaller increment over the trivial solution than the raw numbers suggest. [RQ4.4] None. No feature-importance, attribution, spectral-band or electrode-localisation analysis is reported. In a study whose features are interpretable physiological quantities and whose electrodes have known anatomical correspondences, this is the clearest missed opportunity: a ranking of the eleven descriptors, or a topographic map of discriminative channels, would have been comparable across the branch's literature and would have survived any subsequent revision of the accuracy figure. [RQ4.5] The study reports no validation scheme at all, and the sample structure makes the omission decisive. With 13 autistic and 4 typically developing participants, accuracies of 89.02% to 94.02% cannot have been computed over people - 17 cases cannot produce those percentages - so they must be computed over EEG epochs or windows, and the paper never states how many segments were extracted, how long they were, how they distribute across participants, or how they were partitioned. With four control children, any participant-disjoint evaluation would place at most one control in a held-out set, which would make the reported specificity uninterpretable; the natural reading is therefore that segments from the same children appear on both sides of the boundary, and that the networks are separating individuals rather than groups. This is the same failure the review has documented for scanpath images, video frames, thermal images and cry instances, arising here in a fifth modality, and it is compounded by the absence of a stated majority-class baseline: at 13 against 4, a classifier that predicts autism for everything scores 76.5% at participant level, so the headline numbers represent a far smaller gain than they appear to. The paper's own comparison table is the most useful evidence in the study and it points the same way. It lists participant counts of 16/46, 10/5, 34/11, 10/10, 15/0 and 13/4 alongside accuracies of 92.9%, 93%, 72.77%-90.57%, 81%, 91.12% and 89.02%-94.02% - and one outlier at 212/199 participants reporting 56% to 64%. The single study in the table with a sample an order of magnitude larger than the rest reports by far the lowest accuracy, and the authors reproduce this pattern without comment. That inverse relationship between sample size and reported performance is the same one this review has traced through the behavioural branches, and its appearance in a table assembled by the authors themselves makes it the study's most transferable contribution. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism, detection, EEG, machine learning, neural network. Compact and accurate, naming the population, the task, the modality and the method. The keyword set would place the study in searches for computational autism detection alongside the behavioural work, which is how it entered this corpus, and the review should note that the two branches are not distinguished at the indexing level. [RQ5.2] Advances in Technology Innovation 9(4):287-300, 2024, doi 10.46604/aiti.2024.13951; received 1 July 2024, revised 31 July, accepted 2 August 2024 - a 32-day cycle. A technology-innovation venue, and the reviewing pattern is consistent with that: the acquisition chain, the feature families and the four architectures with their layer equations are all documented, while the complete absence of any validation scheme, of any majority-class baseline, of a limitations section and of any account of diagnostic ascertainment passed without comment, as did an ethics declaration stating in absolute terms that no human-rights statement or informed consent is required. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by the School of Computer Engineering and Mathematical Sciences at the Defence Institute of Advanced Technology, Pune, with a collaborator at Manipal University Jaipur, using data provided by the brain-computer interface group at King Abdulaziz University. The framing is identical to that of the behavioural studies charted throughout this review - diagnosis 'predominantly depends on subjective and time-consuming behavioral assessments', so a 'reliable and non-intrusive biomarker' is needed - which is itself worth recording, because the two branches share a motivation while differing entirely in what they measure and in what they require. For the synthesis the study contributes three things. It is the review's representative of the electrophysiological branch, and it makes clear both that branch's advantage - a purpose-built corpus with both groups recorded on identical equipment under an identical protocol, removing the acquisition confound that undermines the scraped-image and clinic-versus-school studies - and its cost, since a research EEG amplifier, a gel cap, a trained operator and a child who will sit still is precisely the apparatus that the webcam-and-toys approaches exist to avoid. Second, it reproduces the methodological pattern the review has traced across five behavioural modalities: 17 participants, accuracies necessarily computed over epochs, no stated partitioning rule, and a majority-class baseline of 76.5% that goes unmentioned. Third, and most usefully, its own comparison table supplies independent evidence for the review's central quantitative observation. The table lists six prior studies with participant counts from 15 to 80 reporting accuracies of 81% to 93%, and one study with 411 participants reporting 56% to 64% - so within a table the authors assembled themselves, the single study with a sample an order of magnitude larger than the rest reports by far the lowest performance. The inverse relationship between sample size and reported accuracy that this review documents in the scanpath, facial-image and speech branches is therefore visible in the electrophysiological branch too, and visible in a summary constructed without any intention of demonstrating it. |
| S-124 | Prospective matched case-control prediction-model development study conducted in Beijing between January and August 2022 by the Peking University Sixth Hospital group with authors from ALSOLIFE, a Beijing autism-services company. Two hundred and forty-six children aged 1 to 6 took part: 123 autistic (105 male, 18 female, mean age 54.0 months, SD 9.9) recruited from a hospital and from autism intervention service centres, and 123 typically developing (103 male, 20 female, mean age 51.1 months, SD 13.5) recruited from a local kindergarten. Autism was established by best-estimate clinical diagnosis from senior child and adolescent psychiatrists under DSM-5, corroborated by CARS-2 with a required total of at least 30; 23 clinically diagnosed children scoring below that threshold were excluded, as were children with any other psychiatric diagnosis, major physical or neurological disease, or prior psychotropic medication. Groups were matched and formally tested on age (p = 0.0591) and sex (p = 0.860), with median CARS-2 of 37.0 against 15.0. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee, conducted under the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki with written caregiver consent, and received no funding; six of the eleven authors declare two patent applications arising from the work. | Each child was seated at a table in a playroom with warm-up toys while an instructor spent 5-10 minutes building rapport. The warm-up toys were then removed and a fixed set of play materials presented, spanning miniature or representational toys, cause-and-effect toys and construction toys. The child played independently for 90 seconds while the instructor gave neutral responses to child-initiated interaction but started none - an instruction reproduced verbatim in the paper. Sessions were videotaped and coded against a purpose-written manual for 19 autistic behaviours including functional and imaginative play, eye contact, facial expression, vocalisations with socially oriented and word-use subclasses, stereotyped language, repetitive movements, restricted behaviours and unusual sensory seeking, with onset and offset recorded on a timeline so that duration and overlap could be computed. Three coders with 3 months to 11 years of relevant experience were trained for a month under the manual's authors; all three independently coded the same 30 children, reaching inter-coder consistency of 83.7-91.7%. The coded behaviours were expanded arithmetically into 81 indicators of count, duration and proportion. Analysis proceeded from group-difference tests and clinical judgement to univariate logistic regression and then stepwise logistic regression, with the final model displayed as a nomogram and assessed by ROC analysis, the Hosmer-Lemeshow test, a bootstrap procedure and a calibration curve. | Autistic children showed less functional and less imaginative play and reduced eye contact, facial expression and vocalisation. Restricted and repetitive behaviour indicators did not separate the groups - the reported odds ratios for stereotyped language use, repetitive hand and body movements and unusual sensory seeking are numerically enormous with confidence intervals from zero to infinity and p-values near 1, reflecting near-total absence of these behaviours in 90 seconds and confirming a prediction the authors had stated in advance. Stepwise regression retained five predictors, all protective in direction: duration of socially oriented vocalisations and verbalisations (OR 0.940, 95% CI 0.907-0.970), total counts of functional play (OR 0.639, 0.529-0.760), total play time with miniature or representational toys (OR 0.985, 0.975-0.995), with cause-and-effect toys (OR 0.973, 0.960-0.985) and with construction toys (OR 0.958, 0.934-0.978). The nomogram achieved AUC 0.826 (95% CI 0.776-0.877), with sensitivity 85.4%, specificity 68.3%, positive predictive value 72.9% and negative predictive value 82.4% at a cut-off of 0.399. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test returned chi-square 15.329, p = 0.053, and the calibration curve showed good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities. | The five predictors were selected from 81 candidates and the operating threshold read off the same ROC curve, all using the 246 children whose data then supply the reported AUC, sensitivity and specificity - so the headline figures are apparent rather than validated, and although a bootstrap was run no optimism-corrected estimate is reported. The autistic group was restricted to CARS-2 at or above 30, removing 23 clinically diagnosed children from the milder end; the authors identify this and state that model performance may consequently be overestimated. Predictive values are computed at the 50% prevalence created by the matched design, and at any realistic screening base rate a specificity of 68.3% would place most positive calls on non-autistic children - a recalculation the paper's screening proposal requires and does not perform. No language or cognitive measure was obtained although the strongest predictor is the duration of socially directed speech, so expressive language level remains an unmeasured alternative explanation; the proportional vocalisation indicators that would have separated social direction from speech quantity had stronger univariate odds ratios but were not the ones retained. Age is matched at the mean but not adjusted for, in a sample spanning 1 to 6 years where four of five predictors are quantities of object play and the two groups' age variances differ. Coder blinding to group is not stated, and with autistic children recruited from clinical services and controls from a kindergarten the recordings may reveal group membership. The 90-second task cannot access restricted and repetitive behaviour at all, no non-autistic clinical comparison group was included, and predicted probability is never related to CARS-2, leaving the severity-gradient question untested on data already collected. | One of the most clinically careful studies in the review and the best available demonstration of what a brief structured observation can and cannot deliver. Its diagnostic ascertainment - psychiatrist best-estimate under DSM-5 with CARS-2 corroboration and cited psychometrics - is among the strongest here, its groups are deliberately matched on age and sex with the tests reported, its comorbidity and medication criteria are explicit, its task instruction is reproduced verbatim, its coding manual is published in full, and its three coders were trained for a month with inter-coder consistency verified on 30 shared cases. The reporting is correspondingly complete: AUC with an interval, sensitivity, specificity, both predictive values, a calibration curve, a goodness-of-fit test and per-predictor odds ratios at both analysis stages. The performance claimed - AUC 0.826, sensitivity 85.4%, specificity 68.3% - is modest, plausible and in a different register from the 95-100% figures that dominate this corpus, and the limitations section contains the clearest statement of spectrum truncation and its consequence anywhere in the review. Three contributions carry into the synthesis. The degenerate restricted-repetitive indicators, predicted in advance and confirmed, establish empirically that a 90-second sample accesses the social-communication and play dimensions of the phenotype while leaving the restricted-repetitive dimension unobserved - a boundary that applies to every short-observation study charted here and that this study makes visible where others leave it implicit. The five-predictor model shows that the discriminative information lies in reduced quantity of functional object play together with reduced socially directed speech, which is interpretable, clinically recognisable and could be discussed with a family in ordinary language. And the study's principal weakness is instructive precisely because everything else is sound: selecting five predictors from 81 on the development sample and reading the operating point off the same curve produces optimism of a known direction and modest size, which is what a well-conducted study's residual error looks like, in contrast to the uninterpretable figures produced elsewhere in this corpus by corrupted labels and leaked splits.
