The participant counts cannot both be right - 64 typically developing children within a corpus of 67 participants would leave three for all three atypical classes - and the number of children per diagnostic class is never given, so how many distinct speakers stand behind the 26 test samples per clinical class is unknown, and the value of speaker disjointness cannot be assessed. No age distribution is reported for any group in a corpus spanning 6 to 18 years, across which voice changes fundamentally. No diagnostic procedure is described for either corpus and the categories predate DSM-5. No language measure exists although one of the four classes is a specific language impairment. Nothing is stated about what the children were doing when recorded, which for a prosodic claim removes the ability to separate speaker characteristics from task demands. No uncertainty estimate accompanies any figure, on margins as small as 0.7 points and test sets as small as 26 samples per class. And the development-to-test inversion is noted but unexplained, though a test score sixteen points above development usually indicates that the partitions differ in composition. | Valuable to the review for reasons largely independent of its headline number. It is one of only two included studies whose comparison groups include another clinical population, and the only one to attempt a four-way separation of autism from dysphasia and PDD-NOS - the discrimination that clinical practice requires and that the rest of this corpus does not attempt. Its result on that task is the honest one: 60.9% against a 25% chance level, below the published baseline of 62.4% and below two prior methods on the same data, reported in a comparison table the authors supply themselves. It names the leakage problem precisely and splits by speaker to address it, in language sharper than almost any other paper here. And its equalised-odds fairness testing is the most searching subgroup analysis in the review, with a result that should propagate into the synthesis as a general warning: the same model that reaches 94.8% sensitivity on a pooled test set reaches 43.6% on girls and 61.5% on boys when evaluated on held-out gender partitions, and the second model falls to 24.4% on girls. Almost no other study in this corpus evaluates any subgroup at all, so the extent to which their pooled accuracies conceal comparable deficits is simply unknown - and this paper is the only evidence available on that question. Two cautions travel with it, and they mirror the pattern recorded for the multiscale-attention facial study charted nearby. The binary result rests on a corpus in which the clinical groups were recorded in clinics and the comparison group in schools, so the acoustic environment is a perfect proxy for the label, and none of the study's careful validation machinery addresses a confound at that layer. And the participant accounting is internally contradictory in a way that leaves the study's own leakage safeguard unquantifiable. Read together, the two studies make the review's clearest point about methodological quality: rigour applied downstream of a confounded label produces a well-validated number that cannot be interpreted, and can rank above less careful work whose data are sounder. | [RQ1.1] Two corpora combined, and the participant accounting is the weakest part of the description. De-Enigma contributes 55 autistic children aged 4 to 10, described as 25 from Serbia and 25 from the United Kingdom - a split that does not sum to 55 - with no control group at all, yielding 5,368 vocalisation samples over 115 minutes. The Child Pathological Speech Database contributes monolingual French-speaking children aged 6 to 18, recruited in Paris, carrying diagnoses of autism, dysphasia or PDD-NOS alongside a typically developing group, yielding 1,722 samples over 62 minutes. The CPSD participant counts cannot be reconciled: the control group is said to consist of 64 typically developing children (52 male, 12 female), while the corpus as a whole is said to have 13 female participants contributing 334 samples and 54 males contributing 1,388 - a total of 67, which would leave three children for the autism, dysphasia and PDD-NOS groups combined. The number of children in each atypical class is never stated anywhere in the paper. This is not a bookkeeping quibble. Speaker-disjoint splitting is the study's stated safeguard against leakage, and its protective value depends entirely on how many speakers each class contains: if the 26 autism, 26 dysphasia and 26 PDD-NOS samples in the diagnosis test partition come from one or two children each, then class membership and speaker identity are nearly the same variable, and disjointness across the split cannot separate them. The sex proportions are also stated inconsistently, as 78% and 81% male in the dataset section and as 95% and 90% male in the limitations. Age distributions per group are not reported for either corpus. [RQ1.2] Mixed, with the strongest and weakest language in this corpus sitting a few pages apart. The clinical framing in the introduction is dated and inaccurate: autism is 'a neurological disease correlated by imbalances in the brain', it is 'incurable' though it 'can be managed', and the population is characterised through what it lacks - 'a lack in verbal skills or continuing to be non-verbal'. 'Individuals with ASD' and 'children with ASD' are the standard usages, with 'atypically developing' as the analytic label. Against this, three passages show real care. The fairness section states that bias testing 'is crucial in our experiment, specially that we are adhering to a vulnerable group', and grounds the analysis in the observed male-to-female diagnostic ratio and in the 'female camouflage effect', which suggests females are better at masking autism - one of very few places in this review where under-identification of autistic women is treated as a methodological problem rather than a footnote. The limitations argue that 'non-verbal vocalisations are a form of speech and hold communicative value', which treats the sounds autistic children make as communication rather than as noise to be filtered - a substantive interpretive commitment. And the paper's reflection on research ethics committees as safeguards for child data, and on the difficulty of obtaining such data, shows awareness of the population's vulnerability even though the study's own ethics declaration is thin. No autistic person or community organisation is reported as involved. [RQ1.3] The weakest demographic reporting of any included study, and the gaps are consequential rather than cosmetic. No age distribution is given for any group in either corpus, though the combined range spans 4 to 18 years - the period across which voice undergoes its most profound changes, including the pubertal fall in male fundamental frequency, vocal-tract growth and the maturation of prosody and syntax. If the atypical and typical groups differ in age composition, an age classifier and a diagnosis classifier would be behaviourally identical, and nothing reported allows this to be tested. No IQ, language, adaptive or socioeconomic measure exists, which is particularly striking given that one of the four diagnostic classes is dysphasia - the task asks a model to separate autism from a specific language impairment with no independent measure of language ability in any group. Ancestry is not reported. Sex is reported but inconsistently, at 22% female in De-Enigma and 19% in CPSD in one section and at 5% and 10% in another. The one demographic variable that receives serious analytic attention is sex, through equalised-odds fairness testing - and that analysis returns the study's most important result, showing that performance measured on a mixed-gender partition conceals a substantial deficit for girls. That single finding does more for this review's understanding of demographic confounding than the descriptive tables of most other included studies. [RQ1.4] Absent as an independent element and inherited without description. De-Enigma children are stated to be 'diagnosed with ASD' and CPSD children to carry diagnoses of autism, dysphasia or PDD-NOS, but neither corpus's diagnostic process is described - no instrument, no criteria, no clinician qualification, no date. The typically developing group is characterised only by absence: 'no prior history of difficulties with learning, speech, hearing or general learning', which is a screening statement rather than an assessment. Two features compound this. The CPSD categories are pre-DSM-5, since PDD-NOS was eliminated as a diagnosis in 2013, so the labels encode a superseded nosology whose boundaries with autism were themselves contested - and the four-class task therefore asks a model to reproduce a distinction that the diagnostic system has since abandoned. And the atypical and typical children were recorded in different physical settings, clinic and school respectively, so the label is confounded with the circumstance of recording independently of whatever the diagnoses mean. The paper does not treat the reference standard as a topic at all. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, language or adaptive measure is available in either corpus as used here. De-Enigma carries additional annotations for emotion, autistic behaviour and non-verbal vocalisation type, which the authors explicitly set aside as outside their focus - and among these, the autistic-behaviour annotation would have permitted exactly the severity-gradient analysis this review has repeatedly found missing. The four-class diagnosis task partially substitutes for a severity measure by requiring differentiation among clinical categories rather than only from typical development, which is more informative than any single-group severity correlation would have been. [RQ2.1] The aim is to test whether deep transfer learning can compensate for the scarcity of labelled child speech data in autism recognition, by comparing two fine-tuning strategies - discriminative fine-tuning pre-trained on a related child corpus, and Wav2Vec 2.0 fine-tuning pre-trained on 960 hours of unrelated adult speech - across a binary typicality task and a four-class diagnosis task, with fairness testing by gender. The findings are best read against the study's own comparison tables, which the authors supply. On binary typicality, D-FT reached 94.8% unweighted average recall and W2V2-FT 91.5%, against a stated baseline of 94.1% and prior published results of 90.7% and 93.6% on the same corpus - an improvement of 0.7 points over baseline. On four-class diagnosis, D-FT reached 60.9% and W2V2-FT 54.3%, against a baseline of 62.4% and prior results of 67.1% and 69.4% - so both proposed models fall below the baseline and below prior work on the task that actually requires separating autism from other conditions. And the fairness analysis shows that the binary headline does not survive subgroup evaluation: D-FT sensitivity falls from 94.8% on the mixed-gender test set to 43.6% on the female set and 61.5% on the male, with W2V2-FT falling from 92.3% to 24.4% and 53.8%. Publishing a benchmark table showing one's own model below baseline on the harder task, and a fairness table showing a fifty-point sensitivity collapse, is a level of candour this review has encountered in very few papers. [RQ2.2] No primary collection, and the setting structure of the evaluation corpus is the study's central unexamined problem. The CPSD description states that 'recordings of all subjects were captured in their typical environment, i.e clinic for the LIC subjects and elementary, secondary, and high school for the TD subjects'. The atypical classes were therefore recorded in clinical rooms and the typical class in schools, so reverberation, background noise, microphone type and placement, examiner presence and recording protocol all covary perfectly with the binary label - and the entire binary result is trained and tested on this corpus. No acoustic normalisation, channel compensation or noise handling is reported that would mitigate it. The paper does discuss setting as a limitation, but the setting difference it examines is the one between its two corpora (De-Enigma at home, CPSD in laboratory conditions), which affects pre-training rather than the labelled contrast; the within-CPSD clinic-versus-school structure, which is the confound that directly threatens the headline, is never mentioned. This is a clean instance of a pattern the review has documented across modalities - a class label that is inseparable from the circumstances under which the two classes were recorded - arising here in audio rather than in images. [RQ2.3] Not described, for either corpus, and the omission is more damaging here than in most studies because the paper's substantive claim is prosodic. The motivating account is that autistic speech is monotonous, 'lacking the typical variations in pitch, intonation, and expressive elements' - but prosody is determined as much by what a speaker is doing as by who they are. Spontaneous conversation, responding to an adult's questions, reading aloud, repeating modelled utterances and playing all produce systematically different intonation contours. Nothing is stated about what the children in either corpus were doing when recorded, whether an adult or a robot was present, what was said to them, or whether the elicitation differed between the clinic-recorded atypical children and the school-recorded typical ones. De-Enigma was collected within a robot-assisted autism education project, so its vocalisations arise from a specific and unusual interactive context that is not characterised at all. Without a task description, a prosodic difference between groups cannot be attributed to speaker characteristics rather than to what each group was asked to do. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element and no repeat measurement. The ethics reporting is the thinnest of any included study that reports any at all: approval is attributed to 'The Child Pathological Speech Database and De-Engima Project administrations' - the dataset custodians rather than a named research ethics committee - and written informed consent was 'not required from the participants or the participants' legal guardians/next of kin in accordance with the national legislation and institutional requirements'. The contrast with the paper's own introduction is worth noting, since that section reflects specifically on research ethics committees and institutional review boards as safeguards for child data and presents transfer learning as a response to the difficulty of obtaining such data - the topic is raised seriously in the argument and handled formulaically in the declaration. The study received no funding and declares no competing interests, and author contributions are itemised. [RQ2.5] None reported, which is itself a finding. For a speech study, no microphone, sampling rate, channel configuration, recording environment specification or preprocessing chain is given for either corpus. Sample durations are not stated; the reported totals imply mean sample lengths of roughly 1.3 seconds in De-Enigma and 2.2 seconds in CPSD, which are short for prosodic analysis. Computation used two pre-trained model families - a discriminative fine-tuning architecture and Wav2Vec 2.0 with quantisation removed feeding a BLSTM classifier - but no hardware, framework or hyperparameter detail is provided. The absence of acoustic condition reporting is directly connected to the study's principal vulnerability: with the two classes recorded in different physical settings, the properties of the recording chain are exactly what a reader would need to judge whether the signal is speech or room. [RQ2.6] Reported: both corpora with their sources and project pages, sample and duration totals, complete partition tables giving class counts for training, development, test, female and male sets under both tasks, the 70/15/15 split proportions, the speaker-disjoint splitting rule with its stated rationale, the two architectures and their pre-training corpora, the decision to upsample the minority class in training while leaving development and test distributions intact, unweighted average recall as the primary metric, the equalised-odds procedure with its sensitivity and specificity formulae, confusion matrices for every model and partition, and comparison tables against a baseline and against published results on the same dataset. Not reported: code, hyperparameters, sample durations, recording equipment and conditions, the number of children per diagnostic class, age distributions by group, any diagnostic procedure for either corpus, and the number of runs behind each figure. Neither corpus is openly available. The partition tables are the strongest element - they let a reader compute the class balance of every evaluation set, which is what makes the fairness results interpretable and what reveals that the gender test sets differ in composition from the mixed-gender set. [RQ2.7] The limitations section is long, specific and unusually self-critical, covering six issues. The study's original aim - autism recognition in children aged 1 to 3 - was abandoned because data on that population could not be obtained, and the authors say so plainly. The two corpora were collected in different settings, creating domain-shift risk and possible bias toward the more heavily represented one. Class imbalance limited the models, and the authors note that the resampling remedies themselves affect classification performance. Gender imbalance is severe and the fairness testing demonstrates its consequence. The test sets are small and 'not fully representative of the real-world'. And the headline is explicitly qualified: a development UAR of 78.0% against a test UAR of 94.8% is flagged as reflecting corpus-specific characteristics and the additional partitioning, with the conclusion that 'due to the limitations in the dataset, the results reported herein must be carefully interpreted' - reinforced by a citation to a discussion of 'potential over-expectation in speech analysis tasks for real-world application'. What is not addressed is the recording-setting confound within CPSD, where atypical children were recorded in clinics and typical children in schools, which the paper's own dataset description states and which makes acoustic environment a perfect proxy for the binary label. Nor is the participant-count inconsistency resolved, or the number of children per diagnostic class stated - facts that determine how much protection speaker-disjoint splitting actually provides. No age data are available in a corpus spanning 6 to 18 years. No diagnostic procedure is described for either corpus, and the CPSD categories are pre-DSM-5. No language measure exists although one class is a language disorder. Nothing is said about what the children were doing when recorded. And the specific direction of the development-to-test discrepancy - test scoring sixteen points above development - is noted but not explained, though a test score well above a development score usually indicates that the partitions differ in composition rather than that the model improved. [RQ2.9] Four directions are named: stratified sampling to distribute class imbalance evenly across folds; generative adversarial networks for minority-class synthesis, argued to be more representative of real data than SMOTE or ADASYN; extension to children younger than four and to pre-linguistic vocalisations, which the authors argue is supported by their use of non-speech vocalisations from De-Enigma; and continued fairness work given the gender disparities. Not proposed, and needed before the binary result can be interpreted: acoustic normalisation or channel compensation to address the clinic-versus-school recording split, reporting of the number of children per diagnostic class, age distributions by group, and evaluation on a corpus in which both classes were recorded under matched conditions. [RQ3.1] Vocalisation and speech, with the target construct stated as prosodic. The motivating account is specific: autistic speech is monotonous and 'lacks the typical variations in pitch, intonation, and expressive elements that are commonly observed in the speech of typically developing children', a pattern reported to persist into school age. Both speech and non-speech vocalisations are used from De-Enigma, and the authors defend that choice on communicative grounds - 'non-verbal vocalisations are a form of speech and hold communicative value' - and argue it extends the approach toward pre-linguistic assessment in younger children. What the study cannot establish is whether its models respond to that construct. The representation is a learned embedding of the raw waveform, no acoustic analysis or attribution is performed, and prosody is not measured directly at any point, so the models' 94.8% could rest on fundamental-frequency variability, on vocal-tract length, on speaking rate, on the language spoken, on the age of the speaker, or on the reverberation of the room. The four-class task is more informative about the construct than the binary one, because separating autism from dysphasia requires something more specific than general atypicality of speech - and it is precisely there that performance falls to 60.9%, below the baseline of 62.4%. [RQ3.2] None. A single audio modality throughout, with no fusion across sensors, channels or annotation types. The transfer in this study is across datasets and tasks rather than across modalities - discriminative fine-tuning transfers from one child-vocalisation corpus to another, and Wav2Vec 2.0 transfers from 960 hours of unlabelled adult speech to child clinical speech. The comparison between these two transfer sources is the study's clearest methodological result and is worth recording for the review: pre-training on a small, closely related corpus of child autistic vocalisations (D-FT) outperformed pre-training on a vastly larger but unrelated adult speech corpus (W2V2-FT) on both tasks, by 3.3 points on typicality and 6.6 points on diagnosis. Domain proximity beat scale. The caveat is that D-FT's advantage may partly reflect its exposure to De-Enigma's autistic vocalisations, which are class-informative in a way the unlabelled adult corpus is not. [RQ4.1] Two transfer-learning approaches compared head to head. Discriminative fine-tuning pre-trains on De-Enigma child vocalisations and fine-tunes on CPSD - the first application of this technique to autism recognition from speech, according to the authors. Wav2Vec 2.0 fine-tuning uses self-supervised representations pre-trained on 960 hours of unlabelled speech, with the quantisation step removed so that context representations derive solely from the input signal, feeding a BLSTM classifier. Both are appropriate to the data-scarcity problem the study sets out to address, and the comparison is fairly constructed - identical folds for both models and both tasks, a separate development partition, and evaluation on the same test sets. The finding that the smaller, domain-matched pre-training corpus outperforms the much larger unrelated one is the substantive modelling result. Minority-class upsampling was applied in training only, with development and test distributions left intact - a deliberate choice, correctly explained, and one that this review has found in strikingly few papers, since rebalancing the evaluation set is a common and usually silent source of inflation. [RQ4.2] Raw waveform segments per vocalisation, encoded by learned representations - either the discriminatively fine-tuned model's features or Wav2Vec 2.0 context representations. No hand-crafted acoustic descriptors are used in the study's own models, though the ComParE feature set is discussed as background. Sample durations are not stated but can be inferred at roughly 1.3 seconds for De-Enigma and 2.2 seconds for CPSD from the reported totals. Short segments are a real constraint on a prosodic claim: intonation contour, pitch range and expressive variation are properties of utterances and turns rather than of one- to two-second fragments, so the representation may not span the timescale on which the hypothesised difference lives. [RQ4.3] Well chosen and honestly deployed. Unweighted average recall is the primary metric, which is the correct choice for imbalanced classes and sets chance at 50% and 25% for the two tasks. Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are reported for every model and every partition - mixed-gender, female and male - for both tasks, alongside confusion matrices and sensitivity and specificity by gender for the equalised-odds analysis. Most valuably, two comparison tables place the results in context: one against a baseline and two published studies on the same corpus, the other against published Wav2Vec 2.0 implementations. Those tables show that the study's typicality result exceeds the baseline by 0.7 points, and that its diagnosis result of 60.9% falls below the baseline of 62.4% and below prior results of 67.1% and 69.4%. Reporting a table in which one's own method loses on the harder task is rare in this corpus and should be recorded as such. What is missing is any uncertainty estimate - no confidence intervals, no variance across runs, no significance testing - which matters when the typicality margin over baseline is 0.7 points and when the diagnosis test partition contains 26 samples per clinical class. [RQ4.4] None attempted. No saliency, attribution, acoustic analysis or characterisation of the learned representations is presented, and none is claimed - the models are evaluated purely as classifiers. The only window onto behaviour is the confusion matrices, which the authors do interpret, observing that both models predict typically developing more successfully than atypically developing and attributing this to the class distribution. For a study whose motivating hypothesis is specific and acoustically measurable - reduced variation in pitch, intonation and expressive elements - the absence of any analysis connecting model decisions to prosody is the clearest missed opportunity in the paper, because it is the analysis that would distinguish a model responding to speech from one responding to the acoustics of a clinic room. The fairness analysis partially compensates by revealing something about the models that no saliency map would have: that their apparent competence does not extend to girls. [RQ4.5] Genuinely mixed, with the best-stated splitting principle in this corpus sitting alongside an unexamined confound that undercuts the headline. On the credit side, the splitting is speaker-disjoint and the reasoning is articulated precisely: samples from each child belong to one fold only, 'to prevent the model from over-fitting by learning speaker or recording idiosyncrasies, and therefore deceptively excelling'. That is the leakage problem named accurately, and it is the failure mode this review has documented across the scanpath-image, video-frame and EEG branches where it went unaddressed. A separate development partition is maintained, the same folds serve both tasks for comparability, unweighted average recall is used throughout, minority-class upsampling is confined to training with development and test distributions deliberately left intact, and the results are benchmarked against a baseline and against published work on the same corpus. On the debit side, three problems bound what the 94.8% means. First, speaker disjointness cannot address a confound operating at the class level, and the corpus description states that atypical children were recorded in clinics while typically developing children were recorded in schools - so a model that has learned clinic acoustics transfers perfectly across any speaker boundary, and no acoustic normalisation is reported. Second, the number of children in each atypical class is never stated and the two participant counts given are mutually incompatible; if the diagnostic classes rest on very few speakers, the 26 test samples per class may effectively be one or two voices, and speaker-disjoint splitting offers little protection when class and speaker are nearly the same variable. Third, the development UAR of 78.0% against a test UAR of 94.8% is an inversion that the authors flag but do not explain, and a test score sixteen points above development usually indicates that the partitions differ in composition rather than that the model generalises unusually well - a reading supported by the fairness analysis, in which the same model's sensitivity falls to 43.6% and 61.5% on the female and male partitions. The fairness testing is the most valuable validation act in the paper and deserves emphasis: by evaluating on gender-specific held-out sets rather than only on a pooled test set, it exposes a fifty-point sensitivity gap that pooled reporting concealed entirely. That is a generalisation check almost no other study in this review performs, and its result is a warning about every pooled accuracy in this corpus. Finally, the four-class result is the study's most trustworthy number precisely because it is its worst: 60.9% against a 25% chance level, below the published baseline, on the task that requires distinguishing autism from dysphasia and PDD-NOS rather than from typical development. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, child speech, artificial intelligence, deep learning, transformer, transfer learning, fairness in AI. The inclusion of 'fairness in AI' is the notable element and is earned rather than decorative - the fairness analysis occupies a full section, is grounded in the diagnostic sex ratio and in the female camouflage effect, uses a defined criterion (equalised odds) with stated formulae, and produces the paper's most consequential result. This is the only keyword set in the review to name fairness, and one of very few papers anywhere in the corpus to evaluate subgroup performance at all. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Digital Health 7:1274675, Original Research, open access under CC BY; received 8 August 2023, accepted 28 May 2025, published 18 August 2025, with editor and reviewers disclosed by name. The near two-year interval between submission and acceptance is unusual. The venue is a digital-health rather than a clinical journal, and the paper reads accordingly: the partitioning, metrics, benchmarking and fairness analysis are handled to a good computational standard while the clinical description of the corpora - diagnostic procedures, ages, per-class participant counts, recording conditions - is left almost entirely to the source datasets and is internally inconsistent where it is given. The supplied bibliographic metadata dates the article to 2024 while the article itself is a 2025 publication. [RQ5.3] Published 2025 by speech and behaviour-analysis groups at Imperial College London, the University of Augsburg and University Grenoble Alpes - the GLAM and iBUG laboratories, whose senior authors are central figures in computational paralinguistics and automatic behaviour understanding - with no funding and no declared conflicts. The framing is data-scarcity-driven: obtaining child speech data is hard because ethics committees rightly restrict it, so transfer learning is offered as a way to build usable models from small corpora. For this review the study earns its place on four counts, none of which is its headline. It is one of only two included studies whose comparison groups include another clinical population, and the only one to attempt a four-way separation of autism from dysphasia and PDD-NOS - the discrimination that clinical practice actually requires. It names the leakage problem precisely and splits by speaker to address it, in language sharper than most papers in this corpus manage. It performs equalised-odds fairness testing on held-out gender partitions and publishes a result that undermines its own headline: D-FT sensitivity falls from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls and 61.5% for boys, and W2V2-FT from 92.3% to 24.4% and 53.8% - which should be read as a general warning that pooled accuracies in this literature may conceal large subgroup deficits that nobody has looked for. And it benchmarks itself against a stated baseline and prior work on the same corpus, showing its four-class result at 60.9% against a baseline of 62.4% and prior results of 67.1% and 69.4%, so its own model loses on the harder task. Two cautions travel with it. The binary result rests on a corpus in which the atypical children were recorded in clinics and the typical children in schools - a recording-setting confound perfectly aligned with the class label, stated in the paper's own dataset description and never revisited - so 94.8% may be substantially a measure of room acoustics, and no normalisation is reported that would rule this out. And the participant accounting is internally contradictory, with the number of children in each diagnostic class never stated, which leaves the protective value of the speaker-disjoint splitting unquantifiable. The general lesson matches the one drawn from the multiscale-attention facial study charted nearby: careful validation methodology applied above a confounded data layer produces a well-validated uninterpretable number, and the review should treat the two together. |
| S-127 | Retrospective digital-phenotyping study by the Department of Information and Computer Sciences at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, using a purpose-built Twitter corpus. English-language tweets carrying #ActuallyAutistic and posted between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2022 were collected with snscrape; users whose profile descriptions contained 'autism', 'autistic' or 'neurodiverse' were identified, and their full timelines harvested, yielding 3,137,952 tweets from 17,323 users. A control corpus of 3,377,518 tweets from 171,273 users was assembled by excluding the hashtag and sampling 1,000 tweets per day over the same period. No demographic, clinical or diagnostic information exists for any user; the location field was discarded as largely missing or uninformative. The study holds University of Hawaii IRB approval 2023-00248 under expedited review and passed a separate institutional data governance determination of exemption on public-data grounds; user IDs were encrypted and mentions and email addresses anonymised as measures beyond regulatory requirement. Explicit consent was not obtained, which the authors identify as the study's primary limitation, and both the dataset and the trained models were deleted after analysis and never shared outside the author team. | Text was preprocessed by masking profanity, tokenising, removing non-alphanumeric characters, hyperlinks, user mentions and HTML tags, lowercasing, removing stop words, and applying stemming and lemmatisation, with padding and an unknown token for fixed-length input. Sixteen autism-related hashtags and keywords - including 'actuallyautistic', 'autism', 'autistic', 'neurodiversity', 'neurodivergent', 'adhd', 'diagnosis', 'autismpride' and 'autismspeaks' - were removed on the stated ground that they 'could introduce bias and lead to model overfitting'; since the label is defined by hashtag use, this closes the most direct leakage route. Sentiment was analysed with VADER on both the raw and profanity-censored corpora, and topics were examined for qualitative insight. For tweet-level classification, TF-IDF features were passed through support vector machines, naive Bayes, logistic regression and XGBoost with 5-fold cross-validation on accuracy to select the best algorithm, after which word2vec representations were trained with that algorithm; splitting was at user level, 85:15 for train and test with a further 85:15 division of training into training and validation, explicitly to prevent a user's tweets scattering across the split. For user-profile classification, users with at least five tweets had their preprocessed tweets concatenated into a single document, split 80:20 at user level, and classified by an attention-based bidirectional LSTM over a self-trained embedding layer. | The tweet-level classifier reached 73% accuracy, AUC 0.728 and F1 0.71 using word2vec representations with logistic regression. The user-profile classifier reached AUC 0.78 and F1 0.805 using the attention-based bidirectional LSTM, so aggregating a full timeline improved discrimination over individual posts. Sentiment polarity was almost unchanged between the raw and profanity-censored corpora, indicating that any group difference in polarity is not driven by swearing. Autism-related discussion rose across the nine-year window, which the authors read as increasing engagement of autistic people with the platform. The performance figures are modest by this corpus's standards and are reported identically in the abstract, results and conclusion without amplification. | There is no clinical validation of any diagnosis: the positive label is use of an advocacy hashtag plus profile keywords, which the authors describe in their own conclusion as 'an imperfect proxy for self-reported autism', and the control group is entirely unscreened. Beyond that, the two classes differ in ways no demographic variable would capture - the positive class is a self-selected community organised around a topic and the negative class is a background platform sample, so they differ in subject matter, audience, posting motivation and network position, and a classifier reaching 73% may be recognising the register of autism self-advocacy rather than any property of autistic language production; removing sixteen keywords attenuates but cannot eliminate this, and no feature analysis is reported that would help decide. The corpora were also assembled by different procedures, full timeline harvesting against daily sampling, so 17,323 users contribute nearly as many tweets as 171,273 and the classes differ in how material was selected as well as in who wrote it. No age, sex, ancestry or socioeconomic information exists for either group, and the #ActuallyAutistic community plausibly differs from a general platform sample on all of them. The authors' bound on control-group contamination assumes population prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones. No confidence intervals, calibration or predictive value at realistic prevalence are reported. And the English-only restriction over-represents younger and higher-socioeconomic users, which the authors state. | The most distinctive study in the review, and important for reasons that mostly do not concern its accuracy. It is the only included study whose behavioural data are naturally occurring and unelicited, at a scale no laboratory design can approach - 6.5 million posts from 188,596 people across nine years - which makes it the clearest available test of whether ecological validity and volume can substitute for measurement control. The answer is informative: 73% accuracy and AUC 0.728, modest against the 90-plus percent figures reported elsewhere in this corpus from far smaller samples collected under laboratory conditions, and a useful reminder that those higher figures are products of controlled contrasts rather than of stronger signal. It implements two deliberate leakage controls - user-level splitting with the reasoning articulated, and removal of the sixteen autism-related tokens that define its own label, which is the same target-leakage failure this review documents in the questionnaire studies, handled here rather than left in place. It states its label honestly in its own conclusion as hashtag use rather than autism. Its terminology is the most careful in the corpus, and uniquely it explains the community politics behind its inclusion criterion - that #AutismMom and #AutismParent hashtags 'represent the perspectives of neurotypical parents' and that autistic adults' own voices have been 'overshadowed' in research and policy, which is why #ActuallyAutistic exists and why the study samples from it. And it is the only paper anywhere in this review that argues against deploying what it built: having demonstrated feasibility, the authors restrict legitimate use to population-level inference, enumerate the misuse scenarios an individual-level classifier would enable - insurance profiling, university admissions, hiring decisions, government surveillance of citizens - delete both the dataset and the models, and caution researchers against building comparable systems without explicit consent and participatory community-centred design. Set beside the studies charted nearby that scrape identifiable photographs of children from autism support pages with no ethics statement at all, this paper demonstrates that the ethical questions this literature raises are tractable when researchers choose to engage them. The substantive caution is that the study's contrast has several sufficient explanations and it distinguishes none of them - a limitation the authors partly anticipate by declining to present the result as a finding about autistic language at all. The published record shows the article was issued in a corrected version and attracted a formal comment, making it the only included study whose approach generated a documented scholarly exchange. | [RQ1.1] The largest sample in this review by an order of magnitude, and the least clinically characterised. The autism corpus comprises 3,137,952 tweets from 17,323 users, identified by their use of #ActuallyAutistic in English-language posts between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2022 combined with 'autism', 'autistic' or 'neurodiverse' appearing in their profile description, after which all tweets from those users' timelines were collected. The control corpus comprises 3,377,518 tweets from 171,273 users, obtained by a search query excluding the hashtag and sampling 1,000 tweets per day over the same window. No demographic information of any kind exists for either group - no age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic status, cognitive level or comorbidity - and the location field was discarded as largely missing or uninformative, though the authors note that most of the top 20 stated locations were variants of the United Kingdom. Two structural features of the sample deserve emphasis. The tweet counts are near-balanced while the user counts differ tenfold, because the autism group's entire timelines were harvested while control posts were sampled from the platform's daily stream - so the two classes differ in how their material was selected as well as in who produced it, and this is not discussed. And the autism group is not a clinical population but a self-selected online community organised around a hashtag with an explicit advocacy stance, which the paper describes accurately and which bears on everything downstream. [RQ1.2] The most careful terminology in this review, and the only paper here that treats the politics of autism language as part of its subject matter rather than as background. Identity-first language is used throughout - 'millions of individuals are autistic', 'autistic community', 'autistic peers' - alongside 'individuals with autism' in places, and 'neurotypical' rather than 'normal' or 'healthy' for the comparison group. More substantively, the paper explains the origin of its own inclusion criterion in community terms: hashtags such as #AutismMom and #AutismParent 'have represented the perspectives of neurotypical parents, significantly influencing research and policies in this domain', but 'these advocacy groups often overshadow adults with autism, creating a gap in their representation within decision-making processes', and #ActuallyAutistic emerged as 'a paradigm shift ... in the autism rights movement', redirecting attention toward autistic people 'rather than solely focusing on caregivers'. That passage does something no other included study attempts: it recognises that the autism research literature has been shaped disproportionately by parents and professionals rather than by autistic people, and it selects its sample specifically from autistic voices for that reason. The conclusion follows through, calling for 'a more inclusive approach during the model development process that involves the autistic community directly in the ideation and consent processes' and referring to autistic people as a 'marginalized population' whose consent is at issue. The framing is not uniformly neurodiversity-aligned - the introduction still describes autism through misdiagnosis, delayed services and 'negative outcomes later in life' - but the paper is the only one in this corpus to treat the people it studies as a constituency with standing in how they are researched. The published record also shows that the article attracted a formal comment (JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e59794) and was issued as a corrected version, which indicates that its approach was contested in the literature. [RQ1.3] None available, and the authors are candid about what follows. There is no age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information for any of the 188,596 users, and location was dropped as unusable. The limitations section states the resulting representativeness problem directly: restricting to English 'raises concerns about the lack of diversity in the data, where only English-speaking users from higher socioeconomic groups or younger adults are represented in the data set, as they comprise a larger portion of Twitter users'. Two consequences go further than the paper takes them. The #ActuallyAutistic community is widely observed to include a high proportion of late-diagnosed and self-identifying autistic adults, and a higher proportion of women, than clinically ascertained autism samples - so the demographic distance between the two corpora is likely to be substantial and is entirely unmeasurable, meaning that a sex- or age-linked difference in writing style would be indistinguishable from an autism-linked one. And the two groups differ in a way that no demographic variable captures at all: one is defined by participation in a topic-organised community and the other is a background sample of the platform, so their tweets differ in subject matter, audience, posting motivation and network position before any question of authorship arises. [RQ1.4] None, and the paper's handling of this is the most precise in the review. The positive label is use of #ActuallyAutistic plus autism-related keywords in the profile description - self-identification within an online community. The authors do not claim otherwise at any point: their own conclusion states that the models predict 'use of the #ActuallyAutistic hashtag, an imperfect proxy for self-reported autism', and their first limitation is that 'while we focused on individuals who self-identified as autistic, there is no clinical validation for their diagnosis'. They then reason about contamination in both directions. Users of the hashtag might be parents, caregivers or advocacy organisations rather than autistic people, which they judge rare 'due to the negative social connotations of using #ActuallyAutistic without a diagnosis' - an appeal to community norms rather than evidence, but an informed one, since the hashtag's function within the autism rights movement is precisely to mark first-person testimony. And autistic users who do not self-identify will contaminate the control group, which they bound at roughly the population prevalence, arguing that 'with autism having a prevalence rate of <3%, the model performance should not degrade by more than 3%' - a bound that assumes population prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones, neither of which is established. What the paper does not consider is that its label might be a design choice rather than a defect: undiagnosed self-identifying autistic adults are precisely the population an access-oriented screening tool would most want to reach, and treating their self-identification as noise assumes that clinical ascertainment is the only valid criterion in a study whose framing elsewhere questions exactly that assumption. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for any user, and none could without linking to clinical records. The corpus retains rich behavioural metadata - account age, friend and follower counts, reply, retweet and like counts, posting source, timestamps - which the authors note could support network or statistical analysis but deliberately do not use. Some of these would function as crude proxies for social engagement and could have supported a gradient analysis of the kind this review has repeatedly found missing; the paper's decision not to pursue them is consistent with its overall restraint about extracting more from the data than it collected consent for. [RQ2.1] The stated objective was 'to study the feasibility of autism screening from Twitter data and discuss the ethical implications of such models' - the ethics being a co-equal aim from the outset rather than an appended caveat, which is unique in this corpus. The technical finding is modest and honestly reported: a tweet-level classifier reached 73% accuracy, AUC 0.728 and F1 0.71 using word2vec representations with logistic regression, and a user-profile classifier reached AUC 0.78 and F1 0.805 using an attention-based bidirectional LSTM. Aggregating a user's full timeline improved discrimination over single tweets, as expected if the signal is a property of a writer rather than of a post. Exploratory analysis found that sentiment polarity was nearly unchanged between the raw and profanity-censored corpora, and that autism-related discussion rose across 2014-2022. The conclusion the authors actually draw is not about accuracy: having demonstrated feasibility, they restrict the legitimate use of such models to 'a broader cross-sectional level' rather than individual prediction, enumerate the misuse scenarios the artefact would enable, delete the data and the models, and caution researchers against building comparable systems without explicit consent and participatory community-centred design. That is the study's contribution and it is a real one. [RQ2.2] No study setting exists in the ordinary sense - the data are public posts scraped from Twitter using snscrape, a library chosen because it avoids the need for platform API keys. The absence of a setting is the point: the data are naturally occurring, produced without observation effects, at a scale no laboratory could approach, at essentially zero collection cost. The corresponding costs are equally structural. Nobody knew they were being studied. The two classes were assembled by different procedures - full timeline harvesting for the autism group, daily sampling for controls - so the corpora differ in composition independently of authorship. The platform's user base is skewed by age, language, geography and socioeconomic status in ways the authors acknowledge. And the positive class is defined by membership in a community organised around a topic, so the contrast is between a self-advocacy discourse and general platform conversation rather than between two comparably situated populations. [RQ2.3] None, and this is the study's chief methodological attraction. There is no elicitation, no examiner, no instruction and no observation effect - people wrote what they wanted to write, at their own pace, over nine years. Against the 90-second free-play sample, the 3-minute video and the 40-minute standardised assessment charted elsewhere in this review, a user's full Twitter timeline is an enormous and ecologically valid behavioural record. What the absence of a paradigm removes is any control over what the two groups were writing about, and here the comparison is unfavourable: because the positive class was selected by participation in a hashtag community, its members were writing about autism, diagnosis, accommodation, sensory experience and ableism far more than a background sample would. Removing the explicit autism keyword list attenuates but cannot eliminate this, since topic pervades vocabulary, syntax and stance well beyond a list of sixteen terms. Naturalistic data therefore buys freedom from task effects at the price of losing any guarantee that the two samples are doing the same thing. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional in analysis but drawing on nine years of longitudinal record, since users' full timelines from 2014 to 2022 were collected - a temporal depth no other included study approaches. That depth is used only descriptively, to show a rising trend in autism-related discussion, and no within-user temporal modelling is attempted. Ethics reporting is by a distance the most thorough in this review. The study holds University of Hawaii Institutional Review Board approval 2023-00248 under expedited review and passed a separate institutional data governance review that deemed it exempt 'due to the inherently public nature of the study data'. The authors then describe measures 'not required by the Institutional Review Board': encrypting user IDs to reduce reidentification risk, and anonymising user mentions and personal information such as email addresses within tweet text. They engage with the consent question substantively rather than resting on the public-data exemption, citing survey evidence that 84% of users were not or only slightly concerned about university research use while observing that 'this leaves a considerable portion of the population who remains concerned', and noting that privacy policies are 'long, with complex legal terms that the users may fail to understand or authorize'. They call for large-scale consent procedures and a regulatory framework for social media data mining. And they act: 'the data set and the model that we built using those data have been deleted. When the data set did exist, it was never shared outside of the original authors.' Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation. snscrape for collection, better-profanity for masking swear words, VADER for lexicon-based sentiment, word2vec and TF-IDF for representation, and an attention-based bidirectional LSTM for user-level classification. The equipment cost of this study is zero and its collection cost is a scraping script - which is precisely why the ethical analysis matters more here than anywhere else in this review. Every other included study is bounded by what a research team can afford to collect from consenting participants; this one is bounded only by what a platform will serve, and the authors' response is to build the model, measure it, describe what it would enable, and destroy it. [RQ2.6] Deliberately partial, with the incompleteness explained rather than concealed. Fully reported: the scraping library, both search queries with their date range, the profile-keyword criterion defining the autism group, the 1,000-per-day sampling rate for controls, the complete preprocessing chain from profanity masking through tokenisation, stop-word removal, stemming and lemmatisation to padding, the full sixteen-item list of removed autism-related keywords, the sentiment tool and the censored-versus-uncensored comparison, the representation methods and model families, the 5-fold cross-validation used for algorithm selection, the 85:15 user-level split for tweet classification with a further 85:15 training-validation division, the 80:20 user split and five-tweet minimum for profile classification, and all corpus counts by group. Not available: the dataset and the trained models, both destroyed, and the code, which is not mentioned. The pipeline is therefore reconstructible and the corpus is not - which is the outcome the authors intend, since re-creating the corpus is the act they argue should not be undertaken without consent. [RQ2.7] Five limitations are stated and the reasoning behind each is unusually developed. There is no clinical validation for any diagnosis, and expert or crowdsourced annotation would help. Hashtag users may be family members, parents, caregivers or advocacy organisations rather than autistic people, though the authors judge this rare given the negative social connotations of using #ActuallyAutistic without a diagnosis. Autistic users who do not self-identify will contaminate the control group, bounded at roughly the population prevalence of under 3%. VADER sentiment may be less accurate than human labelling. And the English-only restriction limits diversity, over-representing younger and higher-socioeconomic users. The authors add a scope restriction that functions as a finding - 'the predictive power of social media is not to be used at an individual level but at a broader cross-sectional level' - and name the consent failure as 'the primary limitation of this study', enumerating misuse scenarios including university admissions, hiring, and government surveillance. What is not addressed is the group-definition confound: the positive class is a community organised around a topic and the negative class is a platform sample, so a classifier could reach 73% by recognising the register of autism self-advocacy rather than any property of autistic language production, and removing sixteen keywords does not close that route. Nor is the structural asymmetry addressed by which the autism group's full timelines were harvested while control posts were sampled daily, so that 17,323 users contribute nearly as many tweets as 171,273 - a difference in how material was selected that is confounded with the label. No demographic data exist for either group in a comparison where the communities plausibly differ in age and sex. No feature analysis is reported for the classifiers, so the interpretive question is left open where it could have been partly answered. And the contamination bound assumes that population prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones. [RQ2.9] The technical directions named are clinical or crowdsourced annotation to replace hashtag labels, extension beyond English, and use of the retained network metadata. But the direction the paper actually advocates is procedural: 'a more inclusive approach during the model development process that involves the autistic community directly in the ideation and consent processes', supported by research-community work to 'find ways to support large-scale consent procedures' and by 'a regulatory framework for social media data mining'. The paper closes by keeping itself 'as a case study of what is currently possible with publicly available' data rather than proposing a successor system. No other study in this review proposes participatory governance as its principal future work, and none argues against the further development of its own method. [RQ3.1] Written language produced in unconstrained public communication - the only such behaviour in the review, and the largest behavioural record it contains. Three analytic layers were applied: sentiment polarity via VADER, computed on both the raw corpus and a profanity-censored version with the two found to be almost identical; topic analysis for qualitative insight; and lexical-distributional modelling through TF-IDF and word2vec for classification. What the study cannot say is which linguistic properties distinguish the groups, because no feature analysis or attribution is reported for the classifiers. The behaviour targeted is therefore best described as 'written register' rather than any specific construct, and the ambiguity between two candidate constructs - autistic language production on the one hand, and participation in an advocacy discourse on the other - is the study's central unresolved question. It is worth noting against this that the authors' preprocessing removes a sixteen-item vocabulary specifically to prevent the second construct from being trivially detectable, which is more than most studies in this corpus do about their own confounds even when they name them. [RQ3.2] None modelled, though the opportunity was substantial and deliberately declined. The curated corpus retains account creation date, friend count, follower count, tweet timestamp, reply count, retweet count, like count, hashtag lists and posting source, and the authors observe that 'other supporting metadata could be used in the future for network analysis or statistical studies'. Fusing behavioural text with network position and engagement metrics would be a natural extension and would plausibly improve discrimination - which is precisely why not doing it, in a paper that concludes such models should not be built without consent, is consistent rather than an oversight. [RQ4.1] A sensible staged progression rather than a single architecture. TF-IDF features were first passed through four classical algorithms - support vector machines, naive Bayes, logistic regression and XGBoost - with 5-fold cross-validation on accuracy used to select the best; word2vec representations were then trained with the selected algorithm and evaluated on a fuller metric set; and an attention-based bidirectional LSTM over a self-trained embedding layer was used for the user-level task, with padding and an unknown token to handle variable tweet lengths. The final tweet-level result comes from word2vec with logistic regression, and the profile-level result from the BiLSTM. The modelling is proportionate: a corpus of 6.5 million tweets can support a deep sequence model, and the authors escalate to one only for the aggregated user-document task where sequence structure and attention have a plausible role. [RQ4.2] TF-IDF vectors and word2vec embeddings at tweet level; a self-trained embedding layer feeding an attention-based BiLSTM over a concatenation of all of a user's preprocessed tweets at profile level, restricted to users with at least five tweets. The representation is the product of aggressive normalisation - profanity masking, removal of non-alphanumerics, links, mentions and HTML, lowercasing, stop-word removal, stemming and lemmatisation - which strips much of the paralinguistic texture of social media writing (capitalisation, punctuation, emoji, elongation) that might itself carry the signal of interest. The most consequential representational decision is the removal of sixteen autism-related tokens including the hashtag that defines the label, on the explicit ground that they 'could introduce bias and lead to model overfitting'. That is a target-leakage control, correctly reasoned, and it is the same failure mode this review documents in the questionnaire-item studies where the label is an arithmetic function of the features - handled here rather than left in place. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, AUC and F1 for both classifiers, with 5-fold cross-validation accuracy for algorithm selection: 73% accuracy, AUC 0.728 and F1 0.71 at tweet level; AUC 0.78 and F1 0.805 at profile level. The figures are modest by this corpus's standards and are presented without inflation - the abstract, results and conclusion all carry the same numbers and none is described as high. What is absent is uncertainty and operating-point reporting: no confidence intervals despite a corpus that would support tight ones, no calibration, and no sensitivity or specificity at any threshold. For a paper that raises screening, the absent quantity is the positive predictive value at population prevalence - at roughly 1-2% base rate, a classifier with AUC 0.78 would place the overwhelming majority of its positive calls on non-autistic people. The authors reach a compatible conclusion by a different route, restricting legitimate use to cross-sectional rather than individual inference, but they do not compute the number that demonstrates why. [RQ4.4] Limited at the model level and thoughtful at the corpus level. Sentiment and topic analyses were run before classification to develop qualitative understanding of the data, and the comparison of sentiment polarity between raw and profanity-censored versions is a genuine methodological check - it establishes that any polarity difference between groups is not simply a difference in swearing. But no attribution, coefficient inspection, attention visualisation or error analysis is reported for either classifier, so what the models responded to is unknown. This is the study's clearest missed opportunity, because inspecting the highest-weighted terms in the word2vec logistic regression would have spoken directly to the interpretive question the paper leaves open - whether 73% reflects something about autistic language or about the vocabulary of a self-advocacy community - and because the prior removal of sixteen autism-related tokens means the answer would have been informative rather than circular. [RQ4.5] Careful on the mechanics and unresolved on the substance, which is the reverse of the pattern in most of this corpus. The mechanics are good. Splitting is at user level with the reasoning stated explicitly - tweets from one user must not scatter across training and test, 'potentially leading to overfitting by the model due to learning user-specific patterns' - and applied to both tasks, 85:15 for tweet classification with a further 85:15 training-validation division, 80:20 for profile classification. Algorithm selection used 5-fold cross-validation with a held-out test partition maintained separately. And the sixteen-token removal list closes the most obvious inflation route, since the label is defined by a hashtag whose presence in the text would otherwise make the task a lookup. Together these are more deliberate leakage controls than most studies in this review implement, and the modest performance obtained is consistent with the controls having worked. What remains unresolved is the construct. The positive class consists of users who chose to participate in a hashtag community organised around autism advocacy; the negative class is a daily sample of general platform conversation. These populations differ in topic, audience, community membership, posting motivation, network position and - plausibly, though unmeasurably - in age, sex and geography. A model reaching 73% accuracy on that contrast may be detecting autistic language production, or the discourse register of self-advocacy, or the difference between a topically coherent community and a background sample, and the study provides no evidence separating them. The corpus construction adds a further asymmetry that is not discussed: the autism group's complete timelines were harvested while control tweets were drawn at 1,000 per day, so 17,323 users supply almost as many tweets as 171,273, and the two classes differ in how their material was sampled as well as in who wrote it. The authors reason carefully about label contamination in both directions and bound the control-group error at the population prevalence, but that bound assumes prevalence transfers to Twitter's user base and that non-self-identifying autistic users write like non-autistic ones. The honest reading is that the study demonstrates a detectable difference between two corpora whose separation has several sufficient explanations, and that its authors' decision to treat the result as a feasibility demonstration rather than a finding about autistic language is the correct one. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism, autism spectrum disorder, machine learning, natural language processing, public health, sentiment analysis, social media analysis, Twitter. The set spans population, method and application domain and includes 'public health', which locates the work in population monitoring rather than individual diagnosis - consistent with the conclusion's restriction of legitimate use to the cross-sectional level. Terms carried through the body: digital phenotyping, #ActuallyAutistic, neurodiversity, weak supervision, VADER, word2vec, attention-based BiLSTM, data governance, participatory research, informed consent. [RQ5.2] JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e52660, Original Paper, open access. The record carries two notable annotations: the version retrieved is a corrected version, with the correction statement published at JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e59349, and a formal comment on the article appears at JMIR Formative Research 2024;8:e59794. A published comment on a paper of this kind indicates that its approach was contested in the literature, which is itself part of the paper's significance for this review - it is the only included study whose ethics generated a documented scholarly exchange. JMIR's formative-research track is intended for feasibility and early-stage work, which fits a study whose conclusion is that the thing is possible and should not be done without consent. The venue's structure produced the ethical-considerations section with its IRB number, data-governance determination and description of measures taken beyond regulatory requirement - a section that has no counterpart anywhere else in this corpus. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by the Department of Information and Computer Sciences at the University of Hawaii at Manoa. The framing is the standard access argument - limited availability of standard tests, misdiagnosis, delayed services, negative outcomes later in life - applied to a data source of unprecedented scale and zero collection cost, with the stated aim of 'enabling support for communities with limited access to diagnostic resources'. For this review the study matters on four counts, only one of which is its performance. It is the only included study whose behavioural data are naturally occurring and unelicited, at a scale - 6.5 million posts from 188,596 people over nine years - that no laboratory design can approach, which makes it the clearest available test of whether ecological validity and scale can substitute for measurement control. The answer it returns is instructive: 73% accuracy and AUC 0.728, modest against the 90-plus percent figures obtained elsewhere in this corpus under laboratory conditions with clinical ascertainment, and obtained despite the vastly larger sample. It implements two deliberate leakage controls - user-level splitting, with the reasoning stated, and removal of the sixteen autism-related tokens that define its own label - which places it among the more careful studies here on mechanics. It is the only paper in this review to discuss its own label honestly enough to state in its conclusion that the model predicts hashtag use rather than autism. And it is the only paper anywhere in the corpus that argues against the deployment of what it built: having demonstrated feasibility, the authors restrict legitimate use to population-level inference, enumerate the misuse scenarios an individual-level classifier would enable - insurance profiling, university admissions, hiring, government surveillance of citizens - delete the dataset and the models, note that the data were never shared outside the author team, and caution researchers against building comparable systems without explicit consent and participatory community-centred design. Set beside the studies charted nearby that scrape identifiable photographs of children from support pages with no ethics statement at all, or that ship an 'AI-driven assistive diagnostic tool' for at-home use on the strength of a model that recomputes a questionnaire's own scoring rule, this paper is the corpus's clearest demonstration that the ethical questions raised by this literature are tractable when researchers choose to engage with them. The substantive caution that travels with it is that its positive class is a self-selected advocacy community and its negative class a background platform sample, so the 73% has several sufficient explanations and the study does not distinguish them - a limitation the authors partially anticipate by declining to treat the result as a finding about autistic language at all. |
| S-128 | Prospective case-control classification study nested in the Geneva Autism Cohort at the University of Geneva, with participants recruited between 25 September 2012 and 10 September 2023. One hundred and sixty children aged 1.1 to 5.1 years took part: 80 autistic (48 male, 32 female, mean age 2.68 +/- 0.89 years) meeting DSM-5 criteria with diagnosis supported by gold-standard assessment, and 80 typically developing (48 male, 32 female, mean age 2.46 +/- 0.98 years) screened for absence of known neurological or psychiatric conditions and for no first-degree relative with autism. Both groups underwent the same ADOS assessment in the same setting, so recording context is matched across classes, and sex was matched exactly, giving 40% girls in each group - the highest female representation of any included study. The work was approved by the Faculty of Medicine Ethics Committee at the University of Geneva, with written parental consent for all children and separate specific consent from the child depicted in a figure, their guardian and the examiner for publication of identifying images. Six funding sources are itemised with grant numbers and a no-role statement, and no competing interests are declared. | ADOS sessions averaging about 46 minutes were recorded and processed through two independent pipelines. For video, OpenPose extracted skeletal keypoints which were plotted over a plain black background at 320x240 resolution - removing face, clothing, body habitus, room and lighting while preserving the interaction between child and examiner - and split into 5-second segments; an ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 with its dense layers removed extracted per-frame features feeding a 512-unit LSTM, 512 fully connected ReLU units and a softmax, with segment predictions retained only above 90% confidence and averaged across the session. For audio, the full undiarised band was normalised to 2-channel 44 kHz 192 kbps to homogenise across the different microphones used over eleven years, split into 10-second segments, and summarised by Librosa into mean MFCCs (150 retained), Mel spectrogram, chromagram, spectral contrast and tonal centroid, fed to a 1D convolutional network with dropout 0.5, trained with Adam at batch size 512 for 30 epochs. The 160 children were split 50-50 into training and test halves of 80, each containing 40 autistic and 40 typically developing children matched for age, sex and ADOS module, with 20% of the training half held out for validation and all hyperparameter selection confined there. Three late-fusion rules were compared: OR, AND, and a decision tree taking the video prediction when its confidence exceeded 60% and otherwise deferring to audio. For interpretation, random regression forests were fitted with all 27 ADOS-2 items as predictors and each network's confidence as outcome, with importance assessed by increase in mean squared error, increase in node purity and p-value, plus a third normalising forest to make the two modalities comparable. | On the held-out 80 children, the video model reached 80.0% accuracy (precision 0.833, recall 0.750, specificity 0.850, NPV 0.773, F1 0.789) and the audio model 78.8% (precision 0.811, recall 0.750, specificity 0.825, NPV 0.767, F1 0.779). The confidence-gated ensemble reached 82.5% (precision 0.861, recall 0.775, specificity 0.875, NPV 0.796, F1 0.816). The OR rule gave sensitivity 0.90 at specificity 0.75 with accuracy 82.5%; the AND rule gave specificity 0.925 at sensitivity 0.60 with accuracy 76.3%. Both networks were simultaneously wrong on only 8.75% of cases, indicating complementary errors despite the small accuracy gain. The interpretability analysis found video confidence most strongly related to initiation of joint attention, quality of social overtures, unusual eye contact and pointing gestures - a coherent nonverbal social-communication cluster - while audio confidence related most strongly to showing behaviour, pointing gesture, unusual sensory exploration and hand mannerisms, none of which is a vocal construct. | The reference standard's independence from the index test is not established: diagnosis was supported by unspecified 'gold standard diagnostic assessments' while the model input is the ADOS recording, so unless the diagnostic session differed from the recorded one the label is partly derived from the material - a milder circularity than in the questionnaire studies, since the model receives raw pose and audio rather than coded items, but one that a single sentence would resolve. No confidence intervals are reported on a test set of 80 children, where one case is worth 1.25 accuracy points and an exact interval around 82.5% spans roughly 72% to 90%; the ensemble's advantage over the video model alone amounts to two children and is not distinguishable from noise. No positive predictive value is computed at any realistic prevalence despite the screening framing, where a specificity of 0.875 would place most positive calls on non-autistic children at a population base rate. The 90% segment-confidence filter on video is an output-selection step whose effect on aggregate accuracy is unquantified. Cognitive and diagnostic-instrument details are deferred to supplementary material. No sex-stratified analysis is reported although the 40% female sample makes one uniquely feasible. The comparison group is typically developing only, so discrimination against other developmental conditions is untested. And the abstract contains two transposition errors - describing high specificity as producing few false negatives and high sensitivity as producing few false positives, and swapping the ensemble's precision and recall - though the results table is internally correct throughout. | One of the most useful included studies, and the review's clearest example of what an unconfounded design produces. Four features distinguish it. Both groups were recorded under the same ADOS protocol in the same setting, so acquisition context cannot proxy for diagnosis - which removes at a stroke the confound this synthesis has had to record against the scraped-photograph, video-frame and clinic-versus-school audio studies charted nearby. The video input is rendered as skeletal keypoints on a black background, architecturally excluding face, clothing, body habitus, room and lighting, so a video classifier that works must be using movement and interaction dynamics; this is a designed answer to the appearance confound rather than an assertion that none exists, and it is what made a de-identified data release possible when raw recordings could not be shared. Splitting is participant-level and matched on age, sex and ADOS module, with all tuning confined to a validation partition inside the training half. And the interpretability analysis - random regression forests over all 27 ADOS items for both modalities, with a normalisation model making them comparable - produces the review's most valuable methodological finding: the audio model's most predictive items are showing behaviour, pointing, unusual sensory exploration and hand mannerisms, none of them vocal, leading the authors to conclude in their own voice that ambient non-vocal sound from object manipulation contributed to classification, and to note prior evidence that examiners' prosody adapts to child severity such that a full-band model may be reading the adult rather than the child. That result generalises to every study in this corpus using undiarised interaction audio and is examined by none of the others.
