Not proposed, and needed: an independent language measure to separate delay from autism; reporting of age and sex composition by diagnostic group; model evaluation stratified by sex, given the interaction the paper itself reports; and reinstatement of the developmentally delayed children as a third class, since the source corpus contains them and the resulting three-way discrimination is what clinical practice requires. [RQ3.1] Structural and quantitative properties of spontaneous speech, operationalised as six standard psycholinguistic descriptors: mean length of utterance, mean length of turn, mean word length, number of utterances, total number of words and number of different words. Two design decisions distinguish this from a generic bag-of-features approach. Each feature was computed both for the child alone and as a ratio to the investigator's value in the same session, and the two versions were compared empirically to see which carried more information - a construct-level question about whether autistic children's speech differs absolutely or relative to their conversational partner's. And the count-based features were used only in ratio form to normalise for transcript length. The results locate the discriminative information in utterance and turn length and in the child's output relative to the adult's, with typically developing children higher on cMLU, rMLU, rMLT, rUtts and rTNW - a coherent picture of shorter utterances, shorter turns and proportionally less talk. Mean word length carried no signal, and the paper draws the right conclusion, that characters are a poor proxy for lexical complexity and that phonemes or morphemes would be the correct unit. The construct that this cannot separate from autism is expressive language level, of which MLU is a canonical index. [RQ3.2] None across modalities - text only, with no acoustic, prosodic or visual information. The ratio features constitute a form of dyadic fusion in that they combine the child's output with the investigator's within a session, which is conceptually similar to the interaction-level modelling in the pose-based studies charted elsewhere in this review and is more than most transcript-based work attempts. Its vulnerability is that the investigator's behaviour is not standardised across the four source corpora, so the denominator of every ratio feature varies by protocol. [RQ4.1] A systematic seven-model comparison spanning logistic regression, Gaussian naive Bayes, random forests, k-nearest neighbours, support vector machines, a multilayer perceptron and a small convolutional network. Comparing classical against neural models on the same features is the paper's stated purpose and is executed evenly - same features, same splits, same metrics. The scale is appropriate for 64 children and twelve features, and the classical models are the ones such data can support. The conclusion drawn from the comparison, however, exceeds it: a 5-to-10-point advantage for neural models on 64 children, with test folds of sixteen and no confidence intervals, is not a stable basis for the recommendation to use deep learning clinically, and the one-to-two-point margin between the multilayer perceptron and the convolutional network is certainly not. [RQ4.2] A vector of at most twelve interpretable linguistic values per child, reduced after a first round comparing the child-alone and ratio forms of each feature. This is the most parsimonious representation in the review and is well matched to the sample: every dimension is a quantity with a published psycholinguistic literature, computed by documented rules from a public archive, so the representation is auditable end to end. Its limitation is that transcript-level aggregation discards everything about how the speech unfolded - no sequence, no timing, no prosody - so constructs such as turn-taking latency or intonation, which the wider literature associates with autistic speech, are outside its reach. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for all seven models, with ROC curves that plot the individual splits, the mean curve and a one-standard-deviation band. That variability band is worth singling out: on 64 children with 50 repeated splits it conveys the instability of the estimate more honestly than a point figure, and it is a form of uncertainty reporting that almost no other study in this review provides. Precision and recall are also interpreted correctly in clinical terms, with recall of 80-81% read as a low false-negative rate 'important for ensuring that children with ASD are diagnosed correctly' and precision of 84-86% as protecting children without autism from being misdiagnosed. Missing: confidence intervals, confusion matrices, calibration, and any positive predictive value at a realistic prevalence - the last mattering because the reported precision holds only at the near-balanced sample ratio. [RQ4.4] Among the better-handled in the review, because the features are interpretable by construction and the interpretation is pursued rather than asserted. Feature-importance plots are given for logistic regression and random forests; mean length of utterance emerges as the top predictor in both; and the finding is compared explicitly against prior literature, confirming one study's MLU result and contradicting another's conclusion that total number of words does not differ. The stratified analysis goes beyond importance to describe how each feature behaves across diagnosis, age band and sex, producing the specific and testable claims recorded above. And the negative result on mean word length is interpreted correctly rather than ignored - characters are the wrong unit for lexical complexity, and phonemes or morphemes would be better. What interpretability cannot settle here is the identity of the underlying construct: MLU is a developmental language index and no independent measure of language ability exists in the data, so the models' leading signal is compatible with autism-specific pragmatic difference and with generic expressive language delay, and the paper does not raise the distinction. [RQ4.5] Sound on the mechanics for a study of this size, and unresolved on the confounds. Each child contributes one transcript and one feature vector, so the split unit is the person and no within-participant leakage is possible - which places this study among the minority in the review not exposed to the failure that dominates the image, frame and thermal branches. The evaluation is a 75/25 split repeated over 50 random draws with results averaged, and the choice is both explained and empirically justified: cross-validation was rejected because of small sample size, and 50 repetitions were selected because metrics stabilised, varying by no more than 1% as further splits were added. Stating a stability criterion for the number of repetitions is a level of care that very few papers in this corpus show, and the ROC plots with a one-standard-deviation band around the mean curve carry that honesty into the presentation. Three qualifications bound what this buys. Test folds contain sixteen children, so each averaged estimate rests on very small samples and no confidence interval is given; the headline 83-84% is stated elsewhere in the paper to have been obtained 'after the removal of certain features', a selection made on the same data, so it is a post-selection figure; and repeated random splitting addresses sampling variance and not the three confounds that determine what is being separated. Those are, in order of importance: that the top-ranked feature is a developmental language index with no independent language measure available and no age composition reported by group; that part of the typically developing class comes from corpora containing no autistic children, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class; and that the four source protocols differ in session length, structure and investigator role, while half the features are ratios to that investigator's output. None of these would be revealed by any splitting scheme, and none is addressed. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Natural Language Processing, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Linguistics. Balanced across population, modality and method, and 'Linguistics' in particular signals that the features are psycholinguistic constructs rather than learned embeddings. Terms carried through the body: mean length of utterance, mean length of turn, total number of words, number of different words, TalkBank, CHILDES, ASDBank, Stanza, feature importance, train-test split. [RQ5.2] 2024 IEEE 3rd International Conference on Computing and Machine Intelligence (ICMI), doi 10.1109/ICMI60790.2024.10585946. A short computing-conference paper, single-authored by a student at The Harker School in San Jose - a secondary school - which is worth recording factually because it contextualises both the scale and the character of the work. The paper is careful where a beginner might not be: it splits by participant, justifies its repeated-split design with a stated stability criterion, documents its token-cleaning rules against TalkBank's transcription guide, plots ROC variability bands, compares its feature findings explicitly against three named prior studies including where it contradicts them, and reports modest accuracies without inflation. It is weaker on the clinical reasoning that a conference in computing and machine intelligence would not have prompted: no independent language measure, no age composition by group, a non-autistic clinical comparison deliberately discarded, and a recommendation about clinical model choice resting on a one-to-two-point margin. Set beside several journal papers in this review that report 98-100% from image-level splits on web-scraped corpora, its 84% from a participant-level split on a consented research archive is the more informative result. [RQ5.3] Presented at an IEEE computing conference in 2024 by a single secondary-school author in California. The framing is the standard early-detection argument, stated accurately: 1 in 36 children affected, no medical test, professional diagnosis reliable from age 2, and many children diagnosed late or never. For this review the study is valuable on four counts that have little to do with its accuracy figure. It is one of a small number of included studies whose split unit is the participant and whose evaluation design is both explained and empirically justified - 50 repeated 75/25 splits chosen because metrics stabilised within 1% - and it reports estimate variability through ROC standard-deviation bands rather than a bare point figure. Its features are named psycholinguistic constructs with an established literature, so its results are directly comparable with prior findings, and it makes those comparisons explicitly, confirming one study's mean-length-of-utterance result and contradicting another's on total word count. Its accuracy of 83-84%, benchmarked against three prior studies at 70-80%, sits in a credible range for a genuinely hard task and provides a useful calibration point against the 95-100% figures produced elsewhere in this review by leaked or confounded designs. And its sex-stratified feature analysis reports a diagnosis-by-sex interaction - mean length of turn lower in autistic boys than typically developing boys but higher in autistic girls than typically developing girls - which, if real, means a classifier trained predominantly on boys would misread girls, exactly the failure another study in this review demonstrated empirically with sensitivity falling from 94.8% pooled to 43.6% for girls. Three cautions travel with it. The top-ranked predictor is mean length of utterance, a canonical index of expressive language development that the paper's own analysis shows rising with age, and with no independent language measure and no age composition reported by group, language delay and age cannot be separated from autism as explanations. Part of the typically developing class was drawn from corpora containing no autistic children and using different recording protocols, so corpus of origin is partly correlated with class, and the four protocols differ in session length, structure and investigator role while half the features are ratios to the investigator's output. And the developmentally delayed children present in one source corpus were deliberately excluded to keep the task binary, discarding the non-autistic clinical comparison that would have made the study far more informative and that the review has found almost nowhere else. |
| S-133 | Retrospective algorithm-development and architecture-comparison study by the School of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Aizu, Japan, funded by the university's Competitive Research Fund. Two public skeleton corpora were used in parallel. The Gait Fullbody Dataset contains 100 children aged 4 to 12 - 50 autistic and 50 typically developing - recorded with a Kinect v2 capturing 25 three-dimensional joint coordinates; each child performed ten walking trials, of which one was retained, 'the most optimal trial ... selected based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', giving 100 samples. The DREAM dataset contains 61 children aged 3 to 7 recorded with Kinect v1 during robot-assisted therapy, yielding 3,121 samples of which 1,833 were used after the non-spectrum class was excluded; only 10 upper-body joints are recorded. No age distribution by group, sex, cognitive, language or clinical characterisation is available for either corpus, and no diagnostic procedure is described. Both datasets are public and identified, one by Dryad DOI. | A dual-stream architecture derived from a prior design was optimised. Stream one converts skeleton sequences into Skepxels - spatial image-like encodings - processed by an image classification backbone; stream two embeds relative joint angles into the sequence and applies MSG3D, combining graph convolution over the skeletal topology with temporal convolution. A pairwise Euclidean distance loss aligns the two embeddings during training to promote complementary representations, and the streams are tested separately. Six image backbones were compared - ViT-B as the reference, ConvNeXt-Base, Swin-V2-B, ShuffleNetV2-X2, ResNet-152 and MaxViT-T - and MSG3D was compared against a Stack Transformer in the second stream. Training used SGD at learning rate 0.001 with batch size 12, initially for 30 epochs and extended to 100 after inspecting preliminary learning curves. Evaluation used 10-fold cross-validation: on the Gait dataset, 90 children training against 10 testing per fold, repeated five times for 50 runs; on DREAM, 1,650 samples training against 183 testing per fold, repeated three times, with no participant-level partitioning described. Mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation across runs were reported for every architecture, on an RTX 3090 under a fully versioned Python 3.10 software stack. | On the Gait Fullbody Dataset the six backbones spanned 93.2% to 95.4% average accuracy - ShuffleNetV2-X2 and MaxViT-T at 95.4%, ConvNeXt-Base 95.0%, the ViT-B reference 94.8%, ResNet-152 94.0%, Swin-V2-B 93.2% - with standard deviations of 0.71 to 1.82. On DREAM the same six spanned 68.92% to 70.19%, ConvNeXt-Base highest, with standard deviations of 0.15 to 0.96. Substituting a Stack Transformer for MSG3D in the second stream lowered accuracy, which the authors read as evidence for graph-based models in motion analysis. The most informative pattern in these tables is that architecture choice moves accuracy by 2.2 points on one dataset and 1.3 on the other, against a 25-point gap between the datasets - so performance here is determined by the data rather than the model. | The single modelled walking trial per child was chosen from ten 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the data were selected on the outcome before any model saw them, and no downstream splitting scheme can address this. On DREAM, 1,833 samples from 61 children were split without any participant-level partitioning described, leaving within-participant leakage unaddressed - though notably that leak-prone dataset produced the lower figure, so leakage does not explain the 25-point gap. Neither corpus reports age composition by diagnostic group or any sex information, in a domain where walking kinematics mature substantially between 4 and 12 years and differ by sex from middle childhood. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confusion matrix is reported for any proposed model, so a screening claim rests on accuracy alone. The headline 95.4% is a best-of-six architecture selection on test folds of ten children, where one child is worth ten percentage points and the six backbones span 2.2 points against run-to-run standard deviations reaching 1.82. The DREAM experiment discards the non-spectrum class, making it a discrimination among autism-related labels rather than autism versus non-autism, with the resulting class balance never quantified so no chance baseline exists. No interpretability analysis connects the models to any nameable gait characteristic, despite skeleton data making joint- and phase-level attribution straightforward. And the paper transmits without comment that the Gait dataset's own creators moved from approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation to 92% with seven augmentation techniques applied to 100 samples. | Contributes four things to the synthesis that are largely independent of its headline figure. Its modality argument fills a coverage gap the review has otherwise left open: diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests', yet at the early detection stage 'many young children may not yet be able to speak', so a movement-based measure reaches the youngest and least verbal children whom the transcript- and conversation-based studies charted elsewhere here cannot assess at all. Its skeleton representation functions as a designed confound control of the same kind used by the Geneva pose study - face, appearance, clothing, room and lighting are absent by construction - and the paper argues the accompanying privacy advantage explicitly, against anonymity concerns it cites for gaze and video data. Its six-architecture ablation produces a valuable negative result: accuracy spreads of 2.2 and 1.3 percentage points across backbones, against a 25-point gap between the two datasets, showing that in this branch the data and not the model determine performance - a direct corrective to a literature organised around architectural novelty, and reinforced by the paper reporting mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation for every configuration rather than a single best number. And the direction of that 25-point gap is instructive in its own right: the corpus with unaddressed within-participant leakage produced the lower figure, which is a counterexample to the assumption that leakage always explains the highest numbers in a branch, and points instead to sensor coverage - 25 full-body joints against 10 upper-body - as the operative difference. Three cautions travel with it. The Gait dataset's single modelled trial per child was selected on the basis of the diagnosis and a clinician's recommendation, a form of outcome-informed selection that the methods quote and never examine. No sensitivity or specificity is reported for any model, and no demographic data exist for either corpus in a domain where gait varies strongly with age and sex. And the paper supplies, as motivating background, the clearest single piece of evidence in this review for augmentation-driven inflation: a 32-point accuracy gain in the Gait dataset's originating study, from approximately 60% to 92%, produced by applying seven augmentation techniques to a 100-sample corpus. | [RQ1.1] Two public corpora used in parallel. The Gait Fullbody Dataset, created by Al-Jubouri and colleagues, contains 100 children aged 4 to 12 - 50 autistic and 50 typically developing - recorded with a Kinect v2 capturing 25 joint coordinates, with each child performing ten walking trials of which one was retained, giving 100 samples. A separate subset of nine children with severe symptoms is available and is not analysed here. The DREAM dataset contains 61 children aged 3 to 7, recorded with Kinect v1 during robot-assisted therapy, yielding 3,121 samples of which 1,833 were used after the non-spectrum class was excluded; only 10 upper-body joints are recorded, since Kinect v1 detects 20 joints and DREAM omits the lower body. No age distribution, sex, cognitive level, language ability or clinical characterisation is available for either corpus. Two structural facts shape everything downstream. In the Gait dataset each child contributes exactly one sample, so cross-validation necessarily partitions children - a property that arises from the data rather than from a design decision, but that gives this study the participant-level split unit most of the video branch lacks. And that single retained sample was chosen from ten trials 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the modelled data were selected with knowledge of the outcome. [RQ1.2] Predominantly medical, with 'patients with ASD' used repeatedly and autism described as a set of 'complex developmental disabilities' with symptoms such as 'a lack of eye contact and an obsession with certain behaviours'. Two passages show more thought than the register suggests. The introduction gives an accurate and unusually careful account of rising prevalence, noting that the doubling of diagnoses between 2015 and 2024 occurred despite the stricter DSM-5 criteria expected to reduce it, and attributing the net increase to awareness and earlier diagnosis - concluding that 'many patients with ASD have not yet surfaced'. That is the correct reading of the epidemiological trend and stands against the alarm framing used elsewhere in this corpus. And the account of the access barrier is concrete rather than rhetorical: 'the high barrier to visiting a hospital, along with the fact that many children are not yet able to speak. Deciding to visit a hospital often requires recognising signs within the household', with the proposed role for the technology being to give families 'a clearer motivation to visit a hospital' rather than to substitute for assessment. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved. [RQ1.3] Absent for both corpora beyond the stated age ranges of 4 to 12 and 3 to 7 years. No age distribution by diagnostic group, no sex, no cognitive or language measure, no ancestry and no comorbidity. Two of these are specifically damaging for a gait study. Walking kinematics mature substantially across 4 to 12 years - stride length, cadence, arm swing, double-support time and postural stability all change - so if the autistic and typically developing groups differ in age composition, a gait classifier and an age classifier would be behaviourally indistinguishable, and nothing reported allows the check. And gait differs by sex from middle childhood, with no sex information available in either corpus. The DREAM corpus additionally spans 3 to 7 years with ages recorded in months, so finer age information exists in the source data and is not used. The paper does not report demographic composition for either dataset or acknowledge these as confounds. [RQ1.4] Inherited and undescribed for both corpora - no diagnostic instrument, criteria, clinician qualification or assessment date appears anywhere. The Gait Fullbody Dataset carries binary autistic and typically developing labels from its creators; DREAM carries a three-level label - non-spectrum, ASD and AUT - of which the non-spectrum class was discarded, following the prior study whose architecture this work extends. Discarding the non-spectrum group has a consequence the paper does not draw: the DREAM experiment is then a discrimination between two autism-related categories rather than between autism and non-autism, so its 70.19% is not comparable to the Gait dataset's autism-versus-typical task and the two figures cannot be read as measurements of the same thing. The reference-standard issue that most affects validity, however, is procedural rather than definitional. The methods state that in the Gait dataset each child performed ten walking trials and 'the most optimal trial was selected based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation'. Selecting which of a child's trials enters the dataset on the basis of that child's diagnosis is selection on the outcome: it means the 100 modelled samples are not a random sample of each child's walking but the trial a clinician judged most suitable given what the child was known to have. Whatever separation the models achieve is conditioned on that choice, and no splitting scheme downstream can undo it. [RQ1.5] None used. The Gait Fullbody Dataset includes a subset of nine children with severe symptoms, and the paper's methodology section states that the architecture is proposed 'for ASD detection and severity assessment' - but no severity analysis is performed, no result for the severe subset is reported, and severity appears nowhere in the results. DREAM's three-level labelling likewise encodes a gradient that is collapsed by discarding one class. No cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for either corpus. [RQ2.1] The aim is to optimise a dual-stream skeleton architecture for autism detection, replacing the vision transformer of a prior design with a convolutional backbone to test whether CNN-based models capture gesture features effectively, and comparing MSG3D against a Stack Transformer in the temporal stream. The headline results are 95.4% on the Gait Fullbody Dataset and 70.19% on DREAM. The more informative findings are in the ablation tables. Across six image backbones the Gait results span 93.2% to 95.4% and the DREAM results 68.92% to 70.19% - so architecture choice moves accuracy by around two points on one dataset and one point on the other, while the gap between the two datasets is 25 points. That is a clean demonstration that in this branch the data determine performance and the model barely matters, which is a useful corrective to a literature organised around architectural novelty. The paper also reports that substituting a Stack Transformer for MSG3D lowered accuracy, and it reports its own reference implementation (ViT-B at 94.8%) alongside the alternatives rather than only the winner. What the study does not establish is what the 25-point gap means: the two corpora differ in sensor generation, joint coverage (25 full-body against 10 upper-body), task (walking against robot-assisted therapy), label structure (autism versus typical against two autism-related classes) and splitting unit (child against sample), and no analysis separates these. [RQ2.2] No study setting. The Gait Fullbody Dataset records walking trials captured by Kinect v2, and DREAM was collected during robot-assisted therapy sessions with Kinect v1. The paper documents the sensor difference carefully - Kinect v2 detects 25 joints, Kinect v1 detects 20, and DREAM omits the lower body leaving 10 - which is exactly the kind of acquisition detail that determines cross-corpus comparability and that most secondary-analysis studies in this review omit. It does not, however, examine the settings themselves: what the children were doing during DREAM sessions, how a robot's presence shapes movement, or whether the walking protocol was standardised in distance, speed or footwear. Within each corpus, both classes were recorded under the same conditions, so the acquisition confound that affects the photograph and clinic-versus-school audio studies charted elsewhere in this review does not arise here - a genuine structural advantage of using purpose-built research corpora. [RQ2.3] Walking trials in one corpus and robot-assisted therapy sessions in the other, neither described in detail. The gait paradigm is well chosen for the review's purposes: walking requires no verbal ability, imposes no social demand, is producible by very young children, and yields a motor signal that can be measured objectively - which the paper argues explicitly, noting that diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests' but 'at the early detection stage, many young children may not yet be able to speak'. That argument identifies a real gap in the assessment landscape, since the language-based measures charted elsewhere in this review are inapplicable to precisely the youngest and least verbal children for whom early detection matters most. Two things weaken the execution. Only one of ten walking trials per child is retained, and that trial was chosen with knowledge of the diagnosis, so within-child variability - which is itself a candidate marker in motor studies - is discarded by a non-blind procedure. And in DREAM the recorded movements arise from therapy interaction with only upper-body joints available, so the gait construct that motivates the paper is not measurable in the second dataset at all. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics statement appears, which is conventional for analysis of two public corpora collected under their originators' governance. The paper does address a related concern substantively, and its argument deserves recording: it notes that prior eye-tracking work 'raised concerns about ensuring anonymity' and identifies 'the issue of privacy protection associated with gaze data', then positions skeleton representation as the answer. Joint coordinates carry no face, appearance, clothing, room or lighting information, so a skeleton corpus is inherently less identifying than the video or photograph corpora that dominate this branch. That is a real privacy property of the modality, argued as a motivation rather than noted as a side effect, and it aligns with the same reasoning that led the Geneva group charted elsewhere in this review to render pose as skeleton-on-black and to release a de-identified pose subsample when raw video could not be shared. Funding from the University of Aizu Competitive Research Fund is declared, competing interests are declared as none, and both datasets are identified with public locations. [RQ2.5] Microsoft Kinect v2 for the Gait Fullbody Dataset, giving 25 three-dimensional joint coordinates, and Kinect v1 for DREAM, giving 20 joints of which 10 upper-body positions are recorded. The paper explains the difference and its consequence for comparability, with a figure contrasting the two joint layouts. Kinect-class depth sensing is consumer hardware, which matters for the deployment argument: skeleton capture requires no markers, no wearables, no calibration by the family and no clinical instrumentation, and produces data that cannot identify the child by appearance. Analysis used Python 3.10 with nine named packages at stated versions on an RTX 3090 with 48 GB RAM, trained with SGD at learning rate 0.001 and batch size 12 - a fuller software and hardware specification than almost any other study in this review provides. [RQ2.6] Among the more reproducible computational records in the corpus. Reported: both datasets with public access locations, one with a Dryad DOI and access date; sensor models, joint counts and the difference between the two Kinect generations with a figure; sample counts for both corpora; the exclusion of the non-spectrum class; the complete software stack with version numbers for nine packages; the hardware; optimiser, learning rate and batch size; the epoch schedule with the reason for its extension; the cross-validation scheme with fold sizes and repetition counts stated separately for each dataset, including why DREAM was run three times rather than five; mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation for every architecture on both datasets; and the specific configuration flag needed to enable Skepxels in the inherited codebase. Not reported: whether DREAM splitting respected participants, any demographic composition, per-class counts for DREAM, sensitivity and specificity, and the authors' own code. [RQ2.7] The conclusion names three limitations: generalisability requires further optimisation, 'particularly for datasets with biased label distributions'; 'the computational complexity of dual-stream models also poses challenges for real-time clinical applications'; and future work should pursue lightweight architectures, improved augmentation and pre-training. Naming one's own computational cost as an obstacle to the clinical use one proposes is candid, and identifying label imbalance as the source of the DREAM shortfall is a reasonable diagnosis even if not the only one. There is no separate limitations section, and several substantial issues go unaddressed. The Gait dataset's single retained trial per child was selected 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation' - the methods quote it and nothing follows. No participant-level partitioning is described for DREAM, where 1,833 samples come from 61 children. No demographic information exists for either corpus, in a domain where gait varies strongly with age and sex. No sensitivity, specificity, AUC or confusion matrix is reported for any proposed model, so a screening claim rests on accuracy alone. The 95.4% is a best-of-six architecture selection on test folds of ten children, where one child is worth ten percentage points and the six backbones span 2.2 points. And the paper reports, without comment, that the Gait dataset's own creators moved from approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation to 92% with seven augmentation techniques - a 32-point gain from augmentation alone, which is as clear a statement of augmentation-driven inflation as this review has found, quoted as background rather than treated as a warning. [RQ2.9] Lightweight architectures to make dual-stream inference tractable in real time; improved augmentation and pre-training; and multimodal extension combining audio and visual data with skeleton. Not proposed, and needed: participant-level partitioning for DREAM; sensitivity and specificity alongside accuracy; demographic reporting and age-stratified analysis; use of all ten walking trials per child rather than one clinician-selected trial, which would both remove the outcome-informed selection and make within-child movement variability available as a feature; and joint-level attribution, which skeleton data make straightforward and which would connect model behaviour to describable gait characteristics. [RQ3.1] Whole-body movement kinematics, and the construct argument is one of the better ones in this review. Gait and gesture are presented as 'prominent behavioural markers' that can be 'efficiently and non-intrusively captured', and the case for preferring them to language-based assessment is made explicitly: diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests', yet at the early detection stage 'many young children may not yet be able to speak'. That identifies a genuine coverage gap - the transcript-based and conversational measures charted elsewhere in this review are inapplicable to non-speaking and pre-verbal children, who are precisely the population early detection targets. The operationalisation is only partly matched to the argument. In the Gait dataset the construct is walking, measured across 25 full-body joints, which is the right instrument for the claim. In DREAM only 10 upper-body joints are available and the movements arise from therapy interaction, so gait is not measurable and the second experiment addresses a different construct under the same label. And no interpretability analysis connects the models to any nameable movement characteristic, so what aspect of gait the 95.4% reflects - stride variability, arm swing, postural sway, turning - is unknown, despite skeleton data making such an analysis unusually accessible. [RQ3.2] Two representational streams over one sensor, aligned by a pairwise Euclidean distance loss during training and then tested separately. Stream one encodes skeleton sequences as Skepxels for an image backbone; stream two embeds relative joint angles and applies MSG3D, combining graph convolution over the skeletal topology with temporal convolution over time. The design rationale is stated clearly - the loss 'minimises the distance between the Skepxel embedding, which captures spatiotemporal features, and the GCN embedding, which models structural joint relationships', promoting co-learning of complementary representations - and the ablation supports the graph component, with a Stack Transformer substitution lowering accuracy. This is representational rather than sensor fusion, but it is a coherent idea coherently tested. What is missing is a decomposition of how much each stream contributes to the final figure, which would be the natural complement to the architecture ablation that is reported. [RQ4.1] A dual-stream architecture derived from a prior design, with two deliberate substitutions tested: ConvNeXt-Base replacing the original ViT-B in the image stream to assess whether CNN backbones capture gesture features effectively, and a Stack Transformer trialled against MSG3D in the sequence stream. Six image backbones were compared in total - ViT-B, ConvNeXt-Base, Swin-V2-B, ShuffleNetV2-X2, ResNet-152 and MaxViT-T - spanning transformer, convolutional and hybrid families. The comparison is even-handed and the reference implementation is reported alongside the alternatives rather than only the winner. Its most valuable outcome is a negative one: across six architectures the accuracy spread is 2.2 points on one dataset and 1.3 on the other, against a 25-point gap between the datasets, so architectural choice is nearly irrelevant to performance here. For a literature in which most papers are organised around a new architecture, that is a finding worth propagating. [RQ4.2] Three-dimensional joint coordinate sequences, re-expressed two ways - as Skepxel images and as angle-augmented graph sequences. The skeleton representation functions as a designed confound control of the same kind used by the Geneva pose study charted elsewhere in this review: face, expression, clothing, body habitus, room, lighting and background are all absent by construction, so a classifier operating on it cannot exploit the appearance and setting confounds that dominate the photograph branch. It also carries the privacy property the paper argues for, since joint coordinates do not identify a child by appearance. The limitation is coverage: 25 full-body joints in one corpus against 10 upper-body joints in the other, so the two experiments do not measure the same thing, and the paper's own figure contrasting the joint layouts makes this visible without drawing the inference for the 25-point performance gap. [RQ4.3] Accuracy only, but reported with dispersion - average, maximum, minimum and standard deviation across repeated cross-validation cycles for every architecture on both datasets, plus per-epoch accuracy and loss curves. The dispersion reporting is a real strength and is what makes the architecture comparison interpretable: standard deviations of 0.71 to 1.82 on the Gait dataset against a 2.2-point spread between backbones show immediately that the architectural differences are barely larger than run-to-run noise, and the paper is able to note that ShuffleNet was more stable than MaxViT at the same mean accuracy. What is absent is everything a screening claim requires. No sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1, AUC or confusion matrix is reported for any proposed model, so the balance between missed cases and false alarms is unknown, and no positive predictive value at any realistic prevalence is computed. Accuracy on a 50:50 corpus tells a clinician very little, and on DREAM - where the class distribution is described as biased but never quantified - it tells them nothing at all. [RQ4.4] None attempted, and the omission is more notable here than in most of this review because the modality invites it. Skeleton data are inherently interpretable: joints have names, angles have physical meaning, and time is explicit, so a joint-level or phase-level attribution would map directly onto describable gait characteristics - stride variability, arm swing amplitude and asymmetry, trunk sway, turning smoothness - which are the terms in which the clinical motor literature the paper cites is written. The Geneva pose study charted elsewhere in this review shows what such an analysis yields when its model confidences are regressed on clinical item scores. Here nothing connects the 95.4% to any nameable property of how the children walked, so the study establishes that a classifier can separate the groups and contributes nothing to understanding what it separates them on. Given that no demographic data exist either, the possibility that the models respond to age- or sex-related gait maturation rather than to autism cannot be examined from any direction. [RQ4.5] Two arrangements with materially different properties, reported clearly enough that both can be assessed. On the Gait Fullbody Dataset the split unit is necessarily the child, because each of the 100 children contributes exactly one sample, so 10-fold cross-validation partitions 90 children against 10; each configuration was run through five complete cycles giving 50 training runs, with mean, maximum, minimum and standard deviation reported. That is sound practice and the dispersion reporting is better than most of this corpus. On DREAM, 1,833 samples from 61 children were split 1,650 against 183 per fold with no participant-level partitioning described - roughly 30 samples per child distributed across folds - so within-participant leakage is unaddressed. The instructive result is the direction of the difference: the leak-prone dataset produced the lower figure, 70.19% against 95.4%, which means the gap between them cannot be explained by leakage and must lie in sensor coverage, task, label structure or class balance. That inversion is worth carrying into the synthesis, because it is a counterexample to the assumption that leakage always explains the highest numbers in a branch. Three issues nonetheless bound the Gait figure despite its clean split unit. The single sample per child was chosen from ten trials 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation', so the modelled data were selected with knowledge of the outcome - a threat that operates entirely upstream of cross-validation and that no splitting scheme addresses. The 95.4% is the best of six architectures whose spread is 2.2 points against run-to-run standard deviations reaching 1.82, on test folds of ten children where a single child moves accuracy by ten percentage points, so the difference between the reported winner and the reference implementation's 94.8% is not resolvable. And the DREAM experiment discards the non-spectrum class, making it a two-way discrimination among autism-related labels rather than an autism-versus-non-autism task, with the resulting class balance never quantified so that no chance baseline exists for its 70.19%. Finally, the paper transmits without comment the single clearest piece of evidence in this review for augmentation-driven inflation: the Gait dataset's own creators reported approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation and 92% after applying seven augmentation techniques including noise addition, scaling and flipping. A 32-point gain from augmenting a 100-sample dataset is a statement about the augmentation, not about gait, and it is quoted here as motivating background. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism diagnosis; Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs); Convolutional Neural Network (CNN); Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs); effective feature extraction; MSG3D; skeleton points. Almost entirely architectural - six of seven terms name a method or component, with 'autism diagnosis' the only clinical term and no reference to gait, movement, children or screening. Terms carried through the body: Skepxels, dual-stream, pairwise Euclidean distance loss, Kinect, joint angles, gait, gesture, early detection. [RQ5.2] Electronics 14(11):2231, MDPI, open access under CC BY; received 26 April 2025, revised 21 May, accepted 26 May, published 30 May 2025 - a 34-day review cycle. An electronics and computing venue, and the profile matches: the software stack is versioned to nine packages, the hardware is specified, the cross-validation scheme is stated separately for each dataset with fold sizes and repetition counts, and every architecture is reported with mean, max, min and standard deviation. What a clinical venue would have required is absent: no sensitivity or specificity, no demographic composition, no examination of the outcome-informed trial selection quoted in the methods, and no discussion of what the 25-point gap between the two datasets implies about the construct being measured. [RQ5.3] Published May 2025 by the School of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Aizu, Japan, funded by the university's Competitive Research Fund. The framing is screening-oriented and modest in its target: because 'deciding to visit a hospital often requires recognising signs within the household', a video-based assessment could give families 'a clearer motivation to visit a hospital' - an aim scoped as prompting help-seeking rather than replacing assessment, which is among the better-calibrated translational positions in this review. For the synthesis the study contributes four things. Its modality argument fills a real gap: diagnosis 'often requires speech-based tests' yet 'many young children may not yet be able to speak', so a movement-based measure reaches the youngest and least verbal children whom the language-based studies charted elsewhere here cannot assess. Its skeleton representation is a designed confound control, discarding face, appearance, clothing, room and lighting entirely, and the paper argues the accompanying privacy advantage explicitly against the anonymity concerns raised for eye-tracking and video data - the same reasoning that led the Geneva group to render pose as skeleton-on-black. Its architecture comparison produces a valuable negative result: across six image backbones the accuracy spread is 2.2 points on one dataset and 1.3 on the other, against a 25-point gap between the two datasets, so in this branch the data determine performance and the architecture barely matters - a corrective to a literature organised around architectural novelty. And the direction of that 25-point gap is instructive, since the corpus with unaddressed within-participant leakage produced the lower figure, which is a counterexample to the assumption that leakage always explains the highest numbers. Three cautions travel with it. The Gait dataset's single modelled trial per child was chosen from ten 'based on the disease and the doctor's recommendation' - selection on the outcome, quoted in the methods and never examined. No sensitivity, specificity or confusion matrix is reported for any model, and no demographic data exist for either corpus in a domain where gait varies strongly with age and sex. And the paper transmits, as motivating background, the clearest evidence of augmentation-driven inflation in this review: the Gait dataset's own creators went from approximately 60% accuracy without augmentation to 92% with seven augmentation techniques applied to 100 samples. |
| S-134 | Secondary analysis of the publicly available Khozaei et al. cry corpus, collected in Iran under ethics approval from Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences and Health Services in Tehran with comprehensive informed consent from parents or legal guardians. Sixty-two children aged 18 to 54 months contributed: 31 autistic (mean age 35.6 months) and 31 typically developing (mean age 30.8 months), with 24 boys and 7 girls in each group. Autism was established through a four-stage process - the GARS-2 parental questionnaire, a DSM-5-based caregiver interview, direct evaluation and observation by two doctoral-level child clinical psychologists, and separate confirmation by at least one child psychiatrist in a different setting - with the authors noting that ADOS was not administered because no official Farsi version exists. Recordings were made with Sony UX560 and UX512F voice recorders (74.2%) and smartphones running a custom application (25.80%), in WAV at 16-bit and 44.1 kHz, at approximately 25 cm from the child's mouth in quiet environments. Recording settings differed by group: 87.10% of autistic cries came from autism centres and 12.90% from homes, while 54.84% of typically developing cries came from health centres and 45.16% from homes. After excluding pain cries and impure segments, 6.10 +/- 5.05 cry instances were retained per autistic child and 5.39 +/- 3.66 per comparison child. The research was funded by Zoundream AG, a commercial infant-cry-analysis company, with two authors employed by it, one a co-founder holding stock, and a third compensated as a scientific advisory board member. | Two parallel analyses. Praat computed pitch-based acoustic features per cry pattern, with jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio selected for their established clinical use in voice assessment, and groups compared statistically with means, standard errors and significance coded at three thresholds. Separately, cry audio was converted to 128x128 single-channel spectrogram images and a recurrent convolutional network was trained from scratch, combining three convolutional layers of kernel size 3 with 32 output channels for spatial features and LSTM layers for temporal structure, regularised by dropout of 0.2 in each LSTM layer and by frequency- and time-masking augmentation applied to the training split, optimised with Adam under a cyclic learning rate between 1e-6 and 1e-5 at batch size 16. Training ran for 2,000 epochs, and the model exhibiting the highest validation accuracy was designated the final classifier. No test partition, cross-validation or participant-level splitting is described, and the evaluation unit is the cry instance, as the results table confirms by defining sensitivity and specificity in terms of instance counts. | The statistical comparison found significantly higher jitter and shimmer in autistic children's cries (both p < 0.01) and significantly lower harmonics-to-noise ratio (p < 0.0001), a pattern indicating greater cycle-to-cycle instability in pitch and amplitude together with a noisier, less periodic voice signal, consistent with less stable laryngeal control and replicating the direction reported in prior cry research the authors cite. The recurrent convolutional network reached 90.28% validation accuracy with AUC 90.83%, sensitivity and specificity both 88.64%, precision 95.12% and F-score 91.75%. | The classification result carries no information about performance on a new child. There is no test partition of any kind; the final model was selected as the epoch with the best validation accuracy out of 2,000, so the reported figure is a maximum over 2,000 draws taken on the partition it is reported from; and the evaluation unit is the cry instance with no participant-level splitting described, so with roughly six instances per child from 62 children the network can recognise an individual voice and recover its fixed label. The sensitivity and specificity are likewise instance-level rather than per-child, so they are not the operating characteristics a screening tool would have. The statistical comparison is more defensible but faces three confounds that the paper reports and does not adjust for. The groups differ by 4.8 months in mean age - about 16% of the younger group's mean - during a period of rapid laryngeal and vocal-tract maturation, using measures known to change with that maturation, with no test or adjustment. Recording settings are strongly imbalanced, with 87.10% of autistic cries captured at autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes, and all three measures are sensitive to reverberation, background noise and microphone distance - harmonics-to-noise ratio, the strongest finding at p < 0.0001, being a direct measure of periodic-to-aperiodic energy that ambient noise depresses mechanically. And the eliciting causes of the cries differ between groups. Two device classes were used with no level normalisation reported; GARS-2 scores were collected and are not used for any severity analysis; and the statistical tests appear to be computed over cry instances rather than per-child summaries, leaving their effective sample size unclear. | The only study in the review to analyse pre-linguistic vocalisation, and its construct is its principal contribution. Cry is the earliest behaviour any included study measures: it precedes language, is produced by every child regardless of cognitive or verbal level, requires no cooperation, task compliance or social engagement, and can be captured on a phone at home and repeated indefinitely at no cost. That combination reaches a population nothing else charted here can assess - pre-verbal infants, and children whose developmental level precludes the eye-tracking, conversational and play-based paradigms used elsewhere in this corpus - and the physiological rationale is coherent, since jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio index the stability of laryngeal and respiratory control rather than any social construct. The diagnostic ascertainment behind the corpus is also among the strongest in the review, with four stages culminating in independent confirmation by a child psychiatrist in a separate setting, and the authors explain rather than conceal the absence of ADOS. The competing-interest declaration - itemising employment, co-founder status, stock ownership and advisory compensation by individual, alongside company funding - is the most complete in the corpus and is the standard other commercially sponsored work here should be held to. What the study cannot deliver is evidence about detection. Its classification figure has no held-out test, was taken as the best of 2,000 epochs on the validation set, and is computed over cry instances from children whose other cries were in training - the same failure this review has now documented in scanpath images, video frames, EEG epochs, thermal images and here in cry audio, a fifth modality. And its statistical findings, which are otherwise the more credible half of the paper, are confounded with a 4.8-month age difference and with a recording-setting imbalance in which nearly nine in ten autistic cries came from autism centres, using three measures that all respond to room acoustics. The corrective analyses are available from data the paper already reports - stratify by setting, adjust for age, aggregate per child, and relate the acoustic features to the GARS-2 scores already in hand - which makes this a case where a promising construct is undermined by analyses that were not run rather than by data that were not collected. | [RQ1.1] Sixty-two children aged 18 to 54 months drawn from the publicly available Khozaei cry corpus collected in Iran: 31 autistic and 31 typically developing, with 24 boys and 7 girls in each group, mean ages 35.6 and 30.8 months. The exact sex matching at 24:7 is a genuine design strength and gives the sample 22.6% girls, higher than most autism research samples in this review. Two features of the sample are less favourable and both are reported without being examined. The mean ages differ by 4.8 months - about 16% of the younger group's mean, in a period of rapid vocal-tract and laryngeal maturation - with no test or adjustment reported, which matters because jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio all vary with vocal development. And the recording settings differ sharply by group: 87.10% of the autistic children's cries were recorded at autism centres and 12.90% at home, while 54.84% of the typically developing children's were recorded at health centres and 45.16% at home. Roughly six cry instances were retained per child (6.10 +/- 5.05 for the autistic group, 5.39 +/- 3.66 for the comparison group), giving an instance-level dataset of around 355 cries from 62 children. No cognitive, language, socioeconomic or comorbidity information is available. [RQ1.2] Clinical and developmental, without pathologising excess. Autism is 'a neurodevelopmental condition', described through 'a wide range of cognitive, social, and communicative challenges' and framed in terms of impact on the child, the family and society across education, healthcare and employment - a systemic rather than individual framing. Person-first phrasing is used consistently ('children with ASD', 'individuals diagnosed with ASD'), and the early-detection argument is made in terms of neuroplasticity and long-term prognosis rather than urgency or alarm. One formulation deserves note for its restraint: the paper states that 'any behavioral cues that raise concerns should be diligently combined with clinical assessments to enable the early identification of atypical development', positioning the technology as an input to clinical judgement rather than a substitute for it. The phrase 'children at risk of ASD' recurs and carries the usual risk framing. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person or family organisation is reported as involved in the work, which is worth noting for a study whose proposed product is an at-home screening tool for caregivers. [RQ1.3] Better than most secondary analyses in this review on sex and worse on age. Sex is matched exactly - 24 boys and 7 girls in both groups - so it is fully controlled, and at 22.6% girls the sample is less male-skewed than most autism research. Mean ages are reported per group at 35.6 and 30.8 months, but no statistical comparison is made and no adjustment is applied, despite a 4.8-month difference spanning a developmental window in which laryngeal control, vocal-tract length and respiratory coordination all change substantially. The three features that reached significance - jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio - are exactly the measures known to vary with vocal maturation, so an age difference of this magnitude is a competing explanation for the group findings and no analysis distinguishes them. The authors come close to the point in their limitations, noting that 'cry characteristics may evolve as children grow, potentially influencing model accuracy, making it essential to explore age-specific models', but treat it as a generalisability issue rather than as a confound within their own comparison. No cognitive, language, adaptive, socioeconomic or comorbidity data are available, and the sample is entirely Iranian and Farsi-speaking, which the authors identify as limiting cultural generalisability. [RQ1.4] Among the stronger ascertainment procedures in this review and described with unusual completeness for a secondary analysis. The process ran in four stages: the Gilliam Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition completed by parents; a caregiver interview conducted against DSM-5 criteria; direct evaluation and observation of the child by two child clinical psychologists holding doctorates; and separate confirmation of the diagnosis by at least one child psychiatrist in a different setting. Independent confirmation by a second clinician working in a different setting is a real safeguard against single-assessor error and appears in almost no other study charted here. The authors also state plainly why ADOS was not administered - 'the official version of Autism Diagnostic Observational Schedule (ADOS) is not available for Farsi' - and repeat it in their limitations rather than leaving the omission unexplained. Two qualifications remain. The GARS-2 is a parental questionnaire, and its position at the front of the process means the pathway begins with parental report; and the typically developing group's status is not described as having been screened by any instrument. [RQ1.5] GARS-2 was administered to every autistic child as the first step of the diagnostic process, so a quantified severity measure exists in the source data - and no score is reported, no group summary is given, and no analysis relates severity to any acoustic feature or to the model's output. That is the analysis this review has repeatedly found missing where the data would support it, and here the data plainly do: correlating jitter, shimmer or harmonics-to-noise ratio with GARS-2 total would test whether the acoustic differences track autistic trait severity or only group membership, and would distinguish a graded biological signal from a categorical artefact. No cognitive, language or adaptive measure is available for either group. [RQ2.1] Two aims: to identify acoustic differences between autistic and typically developing children's cries, and to test whether deep learning can classify them. The statistical result is coherent and physiologically interpretable - significantly higher jitter (p < 0.01) and shimmer (p < 0.01) and significantly lower harmonics-to-noise ratio (p < 0.0001) in the autistic group, which together describe greater cycle-to-cycle instability in both pitch and amplitude and a noisier, less periodic voice signal, consistent with less stable laryngeal and respiratory control. The direction replicates prior cry work the authors cite. The classification result was 90.28% accuracy with AUC 90.83%, sensitivity and specificity both 88.64%, precision 95.12% and F-score 91.75%. The two halves of the study are of very different evidential weight. The acoustic comparison is a straightforward group contrast on prespecified clinical measures and stands or falls on the confounds - age, recording setting, cry cause - none of which is adjusted. The classification figure additionally rests on a validation-set maximum selected across 2,000 epochs with no held-out test partition and no participant-level splitting, so it carries essentially no information about performance on a new child, and the paper does not connect the network's behaviour to the interpretable acoustic features it identified. [RQ2.2] The recording settings are reported group by group and their distribution is the study's most consequential unexamined feature. For the autistic children, 87.10% of recordings came from autism centres and 12.90% from homes; for the typically developing children, 54.84% came from health centres and 45.16% from homes. The paper describes this variety as deliberate - 'a variety of devices and recording locations ... were used to avoid bias and increase generalizability' - but variety across a study is not the same as balance across groups, and here almost nine in ten autistic recordings come from one type of setting while the comparison recordings are split between two others. Jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio are all sensitive to reverberation, background noise and microphone distance, and harmonics-to-noise ratio in particular is a direct measure of the ratio of periodic to aperiodic energy, so ambient noise depresses it mechanically. The strongest statistical finding in the paper (HNR, p < 0.0001) is therefore in the direction that a noisier recording environment would produce. Partial standardisation was applied - a common WAV format at 16-bit and 44.1 kHz, a 25 cm microphone distance instruction, exclusion of recordings not made in quiet conditions - which mitigates but cannot remove the imbalance, and no per-setting stratified analysis is reported although the data to run one plainly exist. [RQ2.3] None, by the nature of the behaviour - cries were captured opportunistically when they occurred. That is appropriate and unavoidable, and the paper handles the resulting variability better than most: it excluded pain-associated cries, retained 'only pure crying sounds' with segments containing other vocalisations or non-empty-mouth cries eliminated, and recorded the eliciting cause for each cry. Reporting the cause distribution is genuinely good practice and appears nowhere else in this review. It also reveals a further imbalance: complaint or discomfort accounted for 74.20% of autistic and 67.75% of typically developing cries, with sleepiness, hunger and anxiety making up the remainder at 25.80% and 32.25%. Cry acoustics vary with what prompted the cry, so aetiology is a third variable covarying with class alongside age and setting, and it is not adjusted for. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element, though the paper argues that the modality would support one - cry 'allows for longitudinal assessment, enabling researchers to track developmental changes over time', which is a real advantage of a signal that can be captured repeatedly at home at no cost. Ethics reporting is complete for the original collection: approval by the ethics committee of Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences and Health Services in Tehran, with 'comprehensive informed consent ... acquired from the parents or legal guardians' before enrolment, specified as covering objectives, procedures and possible advantages and risks. The competing-interest declaration is the fullest in this review and is itemised by individual: two authors are employed by Zoundream AG, a commercial infant-cry-analysis company, one of them being a co-founder holding stock; a third received compensation as a member of its scientific advisory board; the fourth declares none; and the company funded the research alongside four public and quasi-public funders. Naming employment, founder status, equity and advisory compensation separately is exactly what a commercially sponsored diagnostic-technology study should do, and it allows a reader to weigh the translational claims accordingly. [RQ2.5] Sony UX560 and UX512F voice recorders for 74.2% of recordings and smartphones running a custom recording application for the remaining 25.80%, all captured in WAV at 16-bit and 44.1 kHz specifically 'to ensure consistency across devices', with parents and trained voice collectors instructed to record in quiet environments at approximately 25 cm from the child's mouth. Praat performed acoustic analysis. The equipment story is the strongest part of the translational argument: a smartphone recording of a cry costs nothing, requires no clinic visit, no specialist operator, no cooperation from the child and no language ability, and can be repeated indefinitely at home - which is why the authors propose 'continuous remote monitoring'. Two device classes with different microphones nonetheless introduce acoustic variation that no level normalisation or channel compensation is reported to address, and the device mix by group is not stated. [RQ2.6] Strong on the human and acoustic protocol, incomplete on the modelling. Reported: the source corpus with citation and public availability, group sizes with exactly matched sex composition, mean ages, the four-stage diagnostic procedure with instruments and clinician qualifications and the stated reason ADOS was unavailable, recorder models and their proportions, the audio format and sampling rate with the rationale, the 25 cm distance instruction, the recording-setting distribution by group, the cry-cause distribution by group, the exclusion rules for pain cries and impure segments, per-child cry yields with standard deviations, the acoustic software and the definitions of the perturbation measures, and the network architecture with layer counts, kernel size, channel count, dropout, augmentation methods, optimiser, cyclic learning-rate bounds, batch size and epoch count. Not reported: any test partition, the split proportions, whether splitting respected participants, the number of cry instances per partition, and code. A reader could reproduce the acoustic analysis and could not evaluate the classification result. [RQ2.7] Four limitations are stated in a dedicated section and they are reasonable as far as they go: generalisability limited by sample size, demographic variation and the 18-to-54-month age range; cry characteristics changing with growth, making age-specific models necessary; the absence of ADOS because no official Farsi version exists; and the need for larger datasets and refined diagnostic methods. The second of these comes close to identifying the age confound but treats it as a generalisability question rather than as a threat to the group comparison in hand. What is not addressed is more consequential. The classification result has no held-out test partition, the final model was selected as the best of 2,000 epochs on the validation set, and the evaluation unit is the cry instance with no participant-level splitting described - so with roughly six instances per child, the network can identify a voice and recover its fixed label, and 90.28% is a selection maximum on data it has partly seen. The recording-setting imbalance is reported in the methods and presented as a strength when 87.10% of autistic recordings came from autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes, and the three significant acoustic measures are all sensitive to room acoustics and background noise. The 4.8-month age difference is not tested or adjusted. Cry causes differ between groups and are not adjusted. Two device classes are used with no normalisation reported. GARS-2 scores exist and are not used for any severity analysis. And the statistical tests appear to be computed over cry instances rather than per-child summaries, so their effective sample size is unclear. [RQ2.9] The authors propose larger and more culturally diverse samples, age-specific models to accommodate developmental change in cry acoustics, refined diagnostic methodology, and real-world testing and integration - adding that implementation 'would require clinician training and addressing ethical considerations', which is an appropriate acknowledgement from a commercially sponsored group. Not proposed, and prerequisite to interpreting the classification result: a held-out test partition, participant-level splitting, and a model-selection rule that does not maximise over the evaluation set. Also needed and readily available: a stratified analysis by recording setting, an age-adjusted group comparison, and a correlation between the acoustic features and the GARS-2 scores already collected. [RQ3.1] Cry acoustics, and specifically voice quality rather than cry structure. Three perturbation measures were analysed - jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio - selected because of their established clinical use in voice assessment. The construct choice is the study's strongest conceptual contribution and is unique in this review: cry is available before any language develops, is produced by every child regardless of cognitive or verbal level, requires no cooperation, no task compliance and no social engagement, and directly reflects neuromuscular control of the larynx and respiratory system. The paper's formulation is apt - 'infant cries provide a unique window into the neurological and physiological state of the infant' - and it identifies prior work reporting atypical cry acoustics in autistic toddlers under 18 months, which is younger than any other behavioural measure charted here can reach. The findings are physiologically legible: higher jitter and shimmer mean greater cycle-to-cycle instability in the frequency and amplitude of vocal fold vibration, and lower harmonics-to-noise ratio means a greater proportion of aperiodic energy, so the composite picture is of less stable phonatory control. Two constructs are conspicuously not addressed: the temporal and prosodic structure of the cry, which prior work also implicates, and the communicative function of crying, which is discarded when only 'pure crying sounds' are retained. [RQ3.2] None. A single acoustic modality, with two analysis routes over the same signal - Praat-derived perturbation measures for the statistical comparison and spectrogram images for the network. The two routes are never joined: the paper does not test whether the network's confidence relates to jitter, shimmer or harmonics-to-noise ratio, which would have connected its interpretable finding to its opaque one and is the single most useful additional analysis the existing data would support. [RQ4.1] A recurrent convolutional network trained from scratch, combining three convolutional layers (kernel size 3, 32 output channels) for spatial feature extraction from spectrograms with LSTM layers for temporal structure - a standard and well-motivated architecture for audio, and the paper justifies the hybrid by reference to its success in video and speech recognition. Regularisation is taken seriously: dropout at 0.2 in each LSTM layer, and frequency masking and time masking augmentation applied specifically to the training split, which is the correct restriction. Optimisation used Adam with a cyclic learning rate between 1e-6 and 1e-5 and batch size 16. All of this is competently specified. The problem is not the model but the selection rule: training ran for 2,000 epochs and 'the model exhibiting superior validation accuracy being designated as the final trained classifier', so the reported figure is the maximum of 2,000 validation-accuracy draws, reported from the partition on which the maximum was taken. [RQ4.2] Two representations. For the statistical analysis, Praat-derived scalar features per cry pattern - jitter as the mean absolute difference between consecutive pitch periods, shimmer as the amplitude analogue, and harmonics-to-noise ratio - each with a clinical interpretation and an established literature. For the classification, 128x128 single-channel spectrogram images per cry instance. The spectrogram representation retains time-frequency structure that the scalar perturbation measures discard, which is the right complement in principle; but because each cry instance is treated as an independent observation and roughly six come from each child, the representation also carries whatever is idiosyncratic to an individual voice, which is what an instance-level split allows the model to exploit. [RQ4.3] A fuller metric set than most of this branch: accuracy 90.28%, AUC 90.83%, sensitivity 88.64%, specificity 88.64%, precision 95.12% and F-score 91.75%, with sensitivity and specificity reported separately and defined explicitly in the table as counts of autistic and typically developing instances. The statistical analysis reports means with standard errors and codes significance at three thresholds. Two problems limit what any of it means. Every classification figure is a validation-set value with no held-out test, taken at the best of 2,000 epochs, so all six metrics inherit the same selection optimism. And the instance-level definition of sensitivity and specificity means these are not per-child operating characteristics: a screening tool's sensitivity is the proportion of autistic children it flags, not the proportion of their individual cries, and with six cries per child the two quantities can differ substantially. No confidence intervals accompany any figure, on an effective sample of 62 children. [RQ4.4] Split between a well-interpreted feature analysis and an uninterpreted model. The three perturbation measures are clinical voice-quality metrics with direct physiological meaning, so the statistical result translates into a specific and evaluable claim about phonatory stability, and the paper articulates it correctly. The network is treated as a black box: no attribution over the spectrogram, no examination of which frequency bands or temporal regions drive its decisions, no error analysis by age, setting or cry cause, and - most importantly - no test of whether its confidence relates to the jitter, shimmer or harmonics-to-noise ratio the same study found significant. That last analysis is available from the data already collected and would have determined whether the network learned the acoustic phenomenon the paper identified or something else entirely, such as the recording environment. Its absence means the study's two halves neither corroborate nor constrain each other. [RQ4.5] Three compounding failures make the reported 90.28% uninterpretable, and none is discussed. First, there is no test partition: accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F-score are all validation-set figures, and no held-out evaluation of any kind appears in the paper. Second, the final model was chosen as the epoch with the best validation accuracy out of 2,000 - so the reported number is a maximum over 2,000 draws taken on the very partition it is reported from, an optimistic selection whose inflation on a small validation set is substantial. Third, the evaluation unit is the cry instance rather than the child, as Table 1's own definitions confirm, and no participant-level partitioning is described anywhere; with roughly six instances per child from 62 children, cries from the same child will fall on both sides of the boundary, so the network can recognise an individual voice and recover that child's fixed label. This is the same failure documented in this review for scanpath images, video frames, EEG epochs and thermal images, appearing here in a fifth modality. Set against this, the statistical analysis is a separate and more defensible piece of work - a prespecified comparison of three clinically established measures, replicating a direction reported in prior cry research, with significance at p < 0.01 and p < 0.0001. But it faces its own confounds, all reported in the paper and none adjusted: the groups differ by 4.8 months in mean age during a period of rapid vocal maturation, using measures that change with that maturation; 87.10% of autistic recordings came from autism centres against a comparison group split between health centres and homes, and all three measures are sensitive to room acoustics and background noise, with harmonics-to-noise ratio - the strongest finding - being a direct measure of periodic-to-aperiodic energy that ambient noise depresses mechanically; the eliciting causes of the cries differ between groups; two device classes were used; and the tests appear to be computed over cry instances rather than per-child means, leaving their effective sample size unclear. The corrective analyses are all available from data the paper already reports - stratify by recording setting, adjust for age, aggregate per child, and correlate the acoustic features with the GARS-2 scores already collected. [RQ5.1] Keywords: cry analysis, early childhood, autism spectrum disorder, deep learning. Compact and well balanced across modality, population, condition and method. Terms carried through the body: vocal biomarker, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio, fundamental frequency, spectrogram, R-CNN, Praat, GARS-2, at-home screening, continuous remote monitoring. [RQ5.2] Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, Brief Report, accepted 18 March 2025, open access under CC BY-NC-ND, doi 10.1007/s10803-025-06811-1. A clinical autism journal, and the venue's influence is visible in what is reported well: the four-stage diagnostic procedure with clinician qualifications, the explanation of why ADOS was unavailable in Farsi, the ethics and consent statements, the exclusion rules, the per-group recording-setting and cry-cause distributions, and above all a competing-interest declaration that itemises employment, founder status, equity holding and advisory compensation by individual.
