The authors do identify the absence of an external validation cohort, correctly noting that 10-fold cross-validation addresses overfitting but not generalisability. None of this touches the more basic issue that the autistic images were harvested from autism-related websites, so the label encodes provenance and no splitting scheme could separate that from a facial phenotype. For the gelotophobia task, the problem is not validation but the absence of anything to validate. The ethics section states that the GELOPH<15> 'was not directly administered to participants in this study' and that 'no direct contact with human participants occurred', which contradicts the abstract's assertion that it 'was administered to confirm the diagnosis' and means that no image in the corpus carries a gelotophobia label of any kind. There is therefore no ground truth, no held-out set, no metric and no result - and the conclusion nonetheless states that the study 'demonstrates the effectiveness of combining deep learning techniques with validated diagnostic tools for detecting gelotophobia'. Across this whole review, this is the only instance of a primary claim for which no measurement of any kind was performed, and it is worth distinguishing in the synthesis from the many studies whose measurements are confounded or inflated. [RQ5.1] Keywords: social anxiety; emotion recognition; machine learning; facial expression analysis; neurodevelopmental disorders; GELOPH<15>; residual network with 50 layers; ResNet-50; artificial intelligence. Two of the nine name ResNet-50, which the limitations section states was not implemented in this study and which appears only as future work - so the keyword list advertises a method the paper did not use. Terms carried through the body: DeepFace, multilayer perceptron, gelotophobia, comorbidity, high-functioning autism, data mining, computer-aided diagnosis. [RQ5.2] JMIR Formative Research 9:e72115, 2025, Original Paper, with a companion article listed at formative.jmir.org/2026/1/e91833. The formative-research track is intended for early-stage and feasibility work, which fits a study proposing a diagnostic architecture ahead of collecting the data to evaluate it. The venue's structure produced the ethics, funding, data-availability and competing-interest declarations, and the ethics statement is more detailed than most in this branch - it is also the statement that reveals the contradiction with the abstract about whether the GELOPH<15> was administered. That a paper whose abstract, objective and conclusion all centre on gelotophobia detection was published while its own ethics section records that no gelotophobia assessment took place is a reviewing gap that the structured declarations made visible rather than concealed. [RQ5.3] Published 2025 by the Information Systems department at Mansoura University, Egypt, with no funding and no declared conflicts. The framing identifies a genuinely under-researched problem: gelotophobia, the fear of being laughed at, affects around 6% of neurotypical people but up to 45% of autistic people, reaching 41.98% in adolescents with high-functioning autism, and the paper's account of the condition - internalised belief, heightened rejection sensitivity, shame, social withdrawal - is written from the experiencing person's perspective in a way that little else in this corpus manages. Identifying a comorbidity that shapes autistic people's social participation, and proposing to route ambiguous cases to a validated self-report instrument rather than forcing a facial judgement, are both good instincts. For the review the study contributes three things, all cautionary. It is the seventh built on the Kaggle facial-image corpus family, and its own description - images 'collected from platforms such as Kaggle and ASD-related websites' - restates the provenance confound that makes every figure in that branch uninterpretable, while its choice of DeepFace, a face-recognition library whose embeddings encode individual identity, maximises the exposure that an image-level split with an unreported number of distinct children creates. It applies an emotion classifier trained on neurotypical faces to autistic children without fine-tuning, which a study charted elsewhere in this review shows empirically to degrade substantially. And it is the only paper in the corpus whose headline contribution rests on no measurement at all: the abstract states that the GELOPH<15> 'was administered to confirm the diagnosis' while the ethics section states it 'was not directly administered to participants in this study' and that 'no direct contact with human participants occurred', so the gelotophobia system was never evaluated against any ground truth, no metric for it appears anywhere, and the conclusion nevertheless claims its effectiveness has been demonstrated. That distinction matters for the synthesis: most of the problems documented in this review concern measurements that are confounded or inflated, whereas here a diagnostic claim is advanced for a construct on which nothing was measured. The paper's own limitations section, which names uncontrolled demographics, the absence of external validation and the fact that its proposed architectures were never implemented, is candid enough to make clear that the authors understood the work as preliminary; the abstract and conclusion do not. |
| S-138 | Retrospective algorithm-development study by a group at Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology, Dhaka, presented as a five-page conference paper. The data are the public Kaggle autistic-children facial image corpus, comprising 2,940 images of autistic and non-autistic children - the eighth study in this review built on this dataset family. The number of distinct children is not stated, and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is available for either class. No diagnostic instrument, clinician judgement or record is cited for any image; the corpus's autistic class was assembled from autism-related online sources. Experiments ran in Jupyter Notebook on TensorFlow 2.10.0 with an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 Ti Max-Q. No train-test split proportion, cross-validation scheme, held-out set size or partitioning unit is stated anywhere in the retrieved text, although results are described as being obtained on test data. | The best combination of pretrained feature extraction and logistic-regression classification reached 88.33% accuracy on test data, with a confusion matrix for the binary classifier presented as a figure. No precision, recall, specificity, F1, AUC or confidence interval is reported, and no accuracy figures are broken out for the individual extractors or preprocessing configurations, so the two comparisons the study set up are not reported in a form that supports conclusions about them. | The corpus's autistic class is harvested from autism-related online sources, so the label encodes image provenance rather than diagnosis, and no diagnostic ascertainment exists for any image - neither point is raised. No validation scheme, split proportion or partitioning unit is described anywhere, and the number of distinct children behind 2,940 images is unreported, so the within-subject leakage route standard to this corpus family cannot be examined. Augmentation by zoom and brightness is applied without stating whether it preceded or followed splitting, and such variants of a single photograph are near-duplicates rather than independent observations - a distinction another study in this review shows to be decisive, reporting a 32-point accuracy gain from augmentation alone on a small corpus. No demographic information exists for either class, in a study whose motivating premise is morphometric and whose named quantities all vary with age, sex and ancestry. Only accuracy is reported, with no chance baseline. And the physiognomic claims that motivate the work are neither measured nor tested against model behaviour, although the frozen-extractor architecture would have made a coefficient analysis straightforward. | The eighth study in this review on the Kaggle facial-image corpus, and useful principally for where it sits in that group's distribution. Its reported 88.33% is the second-lowest of the eight, which span 81.0% to 99.8%, and its architecture is the one least able to memorise: five frozen ImageNet extractors feeding a logistic-regression head fit only a linear function of fixed embeddings, against the millions of end-to-end parameters tuned by the higher-scoring studies on the same images. That correspondence between model capacity and reported accuracy, across eight independent groups working from identical data, is direct evidence for the synthesis's position that figures in this branch track evaluation protocol and model capacity rather than any property of the children depicted. Its preprocessing work is also the most thoughtful in the branch: three configurations are compared, one of which converts to greyscale and applies contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalisation, thereby removing colour and normalising local illumination - the two appearance cues most likely to differ between images drawn from different online sources. That is the right experiment for this problem, though the per-configuration results are not broken out, so its answer goes unreported. And its accessibility argument states plainly why the branch is so heavily populated: 'since capturing a facial image is simpler compared to other detection methods, we anticipate a significant reduction in the difficulty of ASD detection', with the whole pipeline running on a laptop GPU and a free public dataset. Two framing points belong in the record. The abstract asserts that 'differentiating facial features from normally developing children is a clear way to identify children diagnosed with ASD', which is stronger than the craniofacial literature it cites supports. And it attributes diagnostic delay to families 'in denial and superstition' - the least sympathetic characterisation of parents anywhere in this corpus, and one contradicted by the paper's own conclusion, which describes families as encountering genuine difficulty in recognising and understanding autistic characteristics. | [RQ1.1] There are no participants. The units are 2,940 facial images from the Kaggle autistic-children corpus - the eighth study in this review built on this dataset family - with the number of distinct children never stated and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information available for either class. The corpus's construction is the determining fact: its autistic images were harvested from autism-related online sources and its comparison images from elsewhere, so the label records where an image was found rather than any assessment of the child in it. This study does not restate that provenance, but it inherits it. [RQ1.2] Physiognomic and, in one passage, dismissive of families. The premise is stated as fact: 'abnormal facial traits caused by impairment of embryonic development are significantly related to underlying neurological issues', with autistic infants said to show 'wider eyes, a larger mouth, a shorter middle face, a broader top face, and a pronounced philtrum', and the University of Missouri work cited for 'an atypically broad upper face, which includes wide-set eyes' and 'a shorter nose and cheekbones in the middle of their faces'. The abstract states that 'differentiating facial features from normally developing children is a clear way to identify children diagnosed with ASD' - a considerably stronger claim than the cited morphometric literature supports. 'Normal children' is used in the conclusion as the contrast term. The most unfortunate formulation is in the abstract: 'early detection is crucial to help the parents and families in denial and superstition', which attributes diagnostic delay to parental denial and superstition rather than to the access barriers the same paper elsewhere identifies. Against this, the conclusion's framing of the problem is sympathetic and accurate - 'families often encounter difficulties in recognizing and understanding the symptoms of ASD, resulting in delays in seeking diagnosis and treatment' - and the accessibility argument that follows is the paper's best reasoning. No autistic person is reported as involved. [RQ1.3] Entirely absent. No age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information exists for either image class, and none could, given how the corpus was assembled. The omission is consequential because the study's own motivating claims are morphometric - upper-face breadth, eye spacing, nose length, mid-face proportions, philtrum prominence - and every one of these varies systematically with age, sex and ancestry. A model reading whole face crops from two internet-sourced folders has access to all three, and nothing reported allows any of them to be excluded as the operative signal. [RQ1.4] None. The autism label reflects folder membership in a public collection whose positive class was harvested from autism-associated online content; no child is known to have received a diagnostic assessment, no instrument or clinician judgement is cited, and the paper does not identify the absence as a limitation. This is the eighth study in the review on this corpus family and the position is unchanged across all of them: whatever the models separate, they separate two collections of internet images. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for any image. [RQ2.1] The aim is autism detection from facial images alone, using pretrained convolutional networks as feature extractors with a simple downstream classifier. Five extractors - MobileNet, Xception, VGG16, VGG19 and EfficientNet - were compared across three preprocessing configurations, with augmentation applied, and the best combination reached 88.33% accuracy on test data, supported by a confusion matrix. The figure is the second-lowest among the eight Kaggle-corpus studies charted in this review, which range from 81.0% to 99.8%, and the architecture is the one least able to memorise: frozen pretrained extractors with a logistic-regression head have far fewer fitted parameters than the end-to-end fine-tuned networks used elsewhere on the same images. Whether the lower figure reflects that restraint or simply a different split cannot be determined, because no validation scheme is described. [RQ2.2] No study setting. The corpus is a public Kaggle assembly of children's photographs harvested from the internet, with the two classes drawn from different kinds of online source - the construction principle documented across this review's facial-image branch, in which collection route is the one respect in which the two image populations are known to differ. [RQ2.3] None. The children were photographed in unknown circumstances for purposes unrelated to any study. This matters for the study's own premise, since the morphometric literature it invokes - intercanthal distance, mid-face height, philtrum length - depends on controlled pose, distance and camera geometry, none of which is available in web-sourced photographs. Even if the morphometric claims were correct, the data could not test them. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics or consent statement appears anywhere in the paper, in work whose training data are identifiable photographs of children collected from the internet without their families' knowledge. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment. Analysis ran in Jupyter Notebook on TensorFlow 2.10.0 with an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 Ti Max-Q - a laptop GPU. Reporting the hardware is a small but genuine transparency, and it substantiates the accessibility argument the conclusion makes: this pipeline requires a consumer laptop and a public dataset, which is why the branch is so heavily populated. [RQ2.6] Reported: the corpus with its size and source, all five feature extractors by name, the logistic-regression classifier, the three preprocessing configurations with illustrative sample images, the augmentation parameters with explicit numeric ranges and an explanation of what each does, the software with version, and the hardware. Not reported: class distribution, the number of distinct children, any train-test split or validation arrangement, whether augmentation was applied only to the training partition, hyperparameters, any metric beyond accuracy and a confusion-matrix figure, ethics arrangements, funding and code. The preprocessing description is the most thorough element and is genuinely reusable. [RQ2.7] No limitations section exists. What should have been stated: the corpus's autistic class is harvested from autism-related online sources, so the label encodes provenance and no diagnostic ascertainment exists for any image; no validation scheme, split proportion or partitioning unit is described anywhere and the number of distinct children is unreported, leaving the standard leakage route for this corpus open and unexaminable; augmentation by zoom and brightness is applied without stating whether it was confined to training, and brightness or zoom variants of a single photograph appearing on both sides of a split are near-duplicates rather than independent observations; no demographic information exists for either class in a study classifying faces, while the study's own motivating morphometric quantities all vary with age, sex and ancestry; only accuracy is reported, with no sensitivity, specificity, interval or chance baseline; and the physiognomic premise is neither measured nor tested against model behaviour. [RQ2.9] Collaboration with others in the field, per the conclusion. The steps the study most needs are participant-level splitting with the number of distinct children reported, a stated validation scheme, per-class metrics, and - given the frozen-extractor architecture - a coefficient analysis showing which embedding dimensions carry the signal, which would at least locate the discriminative information. [RQ3.1] Nominally craniofacial morphology and operationally whatever separates two internet image folders. The motivating claims are unusually specific - wider eyes, larger mouth, shorter mid-face, broader upper face, pronounced philtrum, shorter nose - and none is measured: no landmarks are detected, no distances or ratios computed, and the models receive whole preprocessed face crops. The three preprocessing configurations do bear on this indirectly and constitute the study's most interesting technical choice: greyscale conversion removes colour and therefore skin tone, and CLAHE normalises local contrast, so the greyscale-plus-CLAHE configuration strips two of the appearance cues most likely to differ between image sources. Comparing configurations that differ in exactly which appearance information is retained is the right instinct for this problem, and a systematic report of accuracy across the three would have been informative about how much of the signal survives when colour and illumination are removed. That comparison is set up and its results are not broken out in the retrieved text. [RQ3.2] None. A single image modality throughout. [RQ4.1] Five ImageNet-pretrained networks used as frozen feature extractors with logistic regression as the binary classifier - a deliberate capacity restriction and the study's most defensible modelling decision. A linear classifier on frozen embeddings estimates only as many parameters as there are embedding dimensions, against the millions fitted by the end-to-end networks used on this same corpus elsewhere in the review, so it has far less scope to memorise individual images. Comparing five extractors also gives the architectural breadth that single-model papers lack. The corresponding limitation is that frozen ImageNet embeddings encode general visual appearance rather than anything face-specific or autism-specific, so the representation carries every source-dependent property of the photograph. [RQ4.2] Preprocessed face crops in one of three configurations - resize plus normalisation; resize plus normalisation plus CLAHE; resize plus normalisation plus greyscale plus CLAHE - encoded as pretrained CNN embeddings, with augmentation by zoom (1.0 to 1.2) and brightness (0.7 to 1.3). The augmentation parameters are explained rather than merely listed, which is good reporting; the concern is that zoom and brightness variants of one photograph are near-duplicates, so if augmentation preceded splitting the evaluation is compromised, and the paper does not say which order was used. [RQ4.3] Accuracy of 88.33% with a confusion matrix presented as a figure. No precision, recall, specificity, F1, AUC or confidence interval is reported in the retrieved text, and no chance baseline is stated - although a confusion matrix at least permits per-class errors to be read off, which several studies on this corpus do not provide. Notably, no accuracy figures are broken out for the five extractors or the three preprocessing configurations individually, so the comparisons the study set up are not reported in a form that supports conclusions about them. [RQ4.4] None. No attribution, saliency or coefficient analysis appears. This is a particular loss here because the architecture makes interpretation cheap: with frozen extractors and a linear classifier, inspecting the logistic-regression coefficients would identify which embedding dimensions carry the discriminative signal, and comparing those across the three preprocessing configurations would show whether the signal survives the removal of colour and the normalisation of contrast. That analysis would have spoken directly to the question of whether the model reads facial phenotype or photographic character, and it was one line of code away. [RQ4.5] No validation scheme is described anywhere. The retrieved text states no train-test split proportion, no cross-validation arrangement, no held-out set size and no partitioning unit, while reporting accuracy 'on test data' and presenting a confusion matrix - so a test partition existed and its construction is unstated. The number of distinct children behind 2,940 images is likewise unreported, so whether images of the same child appear on both sides of the boundary cannot be determined; this is the standard failure of the corpus family and is documented in this review for seven other studies on the same images. Augmentation compounds the concern: zoom and brightness variants of a single photograph are near-duplicates rather than independent observations, and the paper does not state whether augmentation preceded or followed splitting - a distinction that another study in this review makes decisive, reporting that its dataset's originators moved from roughly 60% to 92% accuracy by applying seven augmentation techniques to a 100-sample corpus. Two features nonetheless make this study's figure among the more plausible in its branch. Its 88.33% is the second-lowest of the eight Kaggle-corpus studies charted here, which span 81.0% to 99.8%. And its architecture is the one least able to memorise, since frozen pretrained extractors with a logistic-regression head fit only a linear function of fixed embeddings, whereas the higher-scoring studies on the same images fine-tune millions of parameters end to end. Neither observation can be confirmed without the split description, and none of it touches the provenance confound: a model that has learned to recognise images sourced from autism-related web content will perform identically on perfectly subject-disjoint partitions. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Kaggle Facial Image Dataset, Pre-trained CNN Model, Feature Extraction, Logistic Regression. Naming the dataset explicitly in the keyword list is a small transparency worth noting - it makes the corpus's reuse traceable, which is how this review has been able to identify eight studies built on the same images. [RQ5.2] Cognitive Models and Artificial Intelligence Conference (AICCONF '24), Istanbul, 25-26 May 2024, ACM, doi 10.1145/3660853.3660888; five pages. A short conference paper from an artificial-intelligence venue, and the profile follows: the preprocessing and augmentation are documented carefully, the software and hardware are versioned, and the five-extractor comparison is set up systematically, while no validation scheme, no class distribution, no per-configuration results, no ethics statement and no limitations section appear. [RQ5.3] Published 2024 by a group at Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology in Dhaka. The framing is physiognomic - autistic children are said to show wider eyes, a larger mouth, a shorter mid-face, a broader upper face and a pronounced philtrum, with the abstract asserting that 'differentiating facial features from normally developing children is a clear way to identify children diagnosed with ASD' - and the abstract also attributes diagnostic delay to families 'in denial and superstition', which is the least sympathetic characterisation of parents in this review. For the synthesis the study is the eighth built on the Kaggle facial-image corpus and contributes three observations. Its reported 88.33% is the second-lowest of those eight, which span 81.0% to 99.8%, and its architecture is the one least able to memorise - five frozen ImageNet extractors feeding a logistic-regression head, fitting only a linear function of fixed embeddings against the millions of end-to-end parameters used by the higher-scoring studies on the same images. That pattern is consistent with the review's broader finding that figures in this branch track model capacity and evaluation protocol rather than any signal in the data. Its preprocessing comparison is the most thoughtful in the branch, contrasting three configurations of which one strips colour and normalises local contrast - removing exactly the appearance cues most likely to differ between two image sources - though the per-configuration results are not broken out, so the comparison's answer is not reported. And its accessibility argument is the clearest statement of why this branch exists: 'since capturing a facial image is simpler compared to other detection methods, we anticipate a significant reduction in the difficulty of ASD detection', with the whole pipeline running on a laptop GPU and a public dataset. Against all of this stand the branch's standing problems, none addressed here: no diagnostic ascertainment for any image, no validation scheme or partitioning unit described anywhere, the number of distinct children unreported, augmentation applied without stating whether it preceded splitting, no demographic data in a study whose premise is morphometric, only accuracy reported, and no ethics or consent statement for identifiable photographs of children taken from the internet. |
| S-139 | Retrospective algorithm-development study by the Department of Computer Science at Bharathiar University, Coimbatore, using two public Kaggle corpora. The autism corpus comprises facial images labelled autism versus non-autism, partitioned by stratified random sampling into 2,526 training, 280 testing and 80 validation images - the standard split of the Piosenka autistic-children collection charted eight times elsewhere in this review - after poor-quality images were discarded to ensure each retained image showed a frontal face with eyes, nose and mouth visible. A separate emotion corpus supplied 703 training and 130 testing images across six emotion categories. The number of distinct children behind either corpus is not stated, and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive or clinical information is available - an absence the authors name as their first limitation. No diagnostic instrument, clinician judgement or record is cited for any image, and no ethics or consent statement appears anywhere in the paper. | Images were normalised and augmented. A hybrid architecture combining ResNet50V2 and InceptionV3 was fitted for autism classification, motivated by the argument that single-network approaches fail to obtain hierarchical fine-grained features; an enhanced MobileNet with global average pooling and fully connected layers was fitted for six-way emotion recognition, motivated by the observation that existing emotion models are trained on non-autistic faces and therefore miss atypical facial movement. Both were compared against baseline architectures including VGG16 with Random Forest. Stratified sampling preserved class proportions across partitions for both the autism labels and the emotion categories. The authors state that the dataset was split only once and the procedure not repeated, owing to the computational expense of training deep networks on CPU-based hardware. | For autism prediction the hybrid model is reported as 'accuracy = 95, precision = 0.96, sensitivity/recall = 0.94, Specificity = 42.5, F1 = 0.95 and AUC = 78'. This set is not arithmetically possible on the stated balanced 280-image test set: a recall of 0.94 with a specificity of 0.425 would give roughly 132 of 140 positives and 60 of 140 negatives correct, an accuracy near 68% rather than 95%, with about 80 false positives implying a precision near 0.62 rather than 0.96; and an AUC of 0.78 is incompatible with 95% accuracy. No reconciliation is offered. For emotion recognition the enhanced MobileNet reached 73.33% accuracy with precision 72.26, recall 73.33, specificity 83.90 and F1 70.38, against 57.33% for VGG16 with Random Forest, supported by confusion matrices - an internally consistent and modest result. | The autism model's reported metrics are mutually incompatible and no reconciliation is attempted, so the headline 95% cannot be interpreted; if the reported specificity of 42.5% is the accurate figure, the model correctly identifies fewer than half of non-autistic children, which is below chance. The corpus's autistic class was harvested from autism-related online sources, so the label records image provenance rather than diagnosis, and no diagnostic ascertainment exists for any image - neither point is raised. The split is at image level with the number of distinct children unreported, so subject overlap across partitions cannot be excluded; stratification preserves class balance but not subject separation. The quality filter, while genuine, introduces a selection whose size and class distribution are unreported. No chance baseline is stated. And there is no ethics or consent statement for identifiable photographs of children taken from the internet. The authors do name six limitations themselves - missing gender and ethnicity data, small sample size, restriction to static images, no external clinical validation, no explainable-AI component despite arguing for one, and CPU-limited training - and separately acknowledge the single split with its reason. | The ninth study in this review built on the Kaggle autistic-children facial corpus, and the one whose reporting is most complete - which is precisely what makes it valuable. By reporting specificity and AUC alongside accuracy, it exposes an internal contradiction that the eight earlier studies on the same images could not have revealed: its autism metrics cannot all be true, since 95% accuracy is incompatible with the 42.5% specificity and 94% recall stated beside it on a balanced 280-image test set. The synthesis point is general rather than specific to this paper - specificity functions as an arithmetic check on accuracy, and its near-universal absence from this branch removes the field's simplest safeguard against inconsistent reporting. If the 42.5% is the accurate figure, this study's real result is that the model performs below chance on non-autistic children, which would tell directly against the branch's claims. The emotion component is separately instructive. Its motivation is the best reasoning in the paper - existing emotion models are 'primarily trained for healthy ones and consequently missing abnormal facial movements', so one trained on autistic faces is required - and its 73.33% across six classes sits far below the 98-99% that posed neurotypical benchmarks support elsewhere in this review, corroborating the independent finding that affect recognition degrades substantially on autistic children's faces. Two further features are better than the branch norm and should be recorded: an explicit image-quality filter requiring a visible frontal face with eyes, nose and mouth, which is real quality control on a web-scraped corpus; and a candid limitations section naming missing demographics, small sample, static-image restriction, absent external validation, the absence of the explainable-AI component the introduction argues for, and CPU-limited training, alongside an open statement that only one split was used and why. What none of this touches is the corpus's provenance confound, which no splitting scheme or metric set can address. | [RQ1.1] There are no participants. The autism corpus comprises 2,886 images partitioned 2,526 training, 280 testing and 80 validation - the standard split of the Piosenka Kaggle autistic-children collection, which this review has now charted in eight other studies - after poor-quality images were discarded. The emotion corpus supplies 703 training and 130 testing images. The number of distinct children behind either count is never stated, and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is available for any class. The authors name this directly as their first limitation, observing that 'the absence of demographic information such as gender and ethnicity in the utilized Kaggle datasets might hinder the generalization across different populations' - which is a more explicit acknowledgement than most studies on this corpus offer, and which correctly identifies the consequence without identifying the deeper problem, that the corpus's autistic class was harvested from autism-related online sources so that the label records image provenance. [RQ1.2] Deficit-framed and, in one passage, seriously mischaracterising. Autism is 'a multifaceted neurological development disability' with 'deficits in social communication and emotion detection', and autistic children are described as 'noted for odd actions or hyper/hypo activity because of aggression, self-aggression, and stereotypical movements'. The most objectionable sentence conflates several distinct things: 'Individuals with a severe form of autism can erupt in dangerous outbursts caused by abnormal facial expressions associated with complex emotional states and mistreatment of autistic children'. Against this, two passages show genuine attention to autistic experience. The introduction observes that 'children with significant autism are non-verbal making it difficult for them to express or understand words' and that 'children who are unable to manage their feelings find it hard to express how they feel' - which frames the emotion-recognition task as serving communication rather than surveillance. And the paper's stated motivation for building a separate emotion model is the best reasoning in it: existing systems are 'primarily trained for healthy ones and consequently missing abnormal facial movements', so a model trained on autistic faces is needed. That is the correct diagnosis of a real problem, and one another study in this review confirms empirically by showing that affect models trained on neurotypical faces transfer poorly to autistic children. [RQ1.3] Absent, and identified as absent by the authors. No age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information exists for either corpus, and the limitations section names gender and ethnicity specifically as missing in a way that constrains generalisation. Two consequences go beyond what is acknowledged. Facial classifiers key strongly on apparent age and sex-linked morphology, and autism is diagnosed roughly four times more often in boys, so an unmeasured sex imbalance between a class harvested from autism-related sources and a class harvested elsewhere could produce the entire separation. And the paper's own motivating claim is morphological - that autistic children 'show morphological differences within their face' - which is precisely the kind of quantity that varies with age, sex and ancestry, none of which is recorded. [RQ1.4] None. The autism labels reflect folder membership in a public collection whose positive class was assembled from autism-associated online content; no child is known to have received a diagnostic assessment, and no instrument, clinician judgement or record is cited anywhere. The paper describes the corpus as 'large, well-labelled public data promoting reproducibility', which conflates consistent labelling with valid labelling - the labels are consistent in that every image in the autistic folder carries the same tag, and they are not diagnoses. This is the ninth study in the review resting on this corpus family and the position is unchanged. The emotion labels are category assignments from the source corpus and are adequate for what they measure, though nothing establishes that they were assigned by raters familiar with autistic facial expression, which is the very phenomenon the paper says general-population models miss. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for any image in either corpus. [RQ2.1] Two aims are pursued. The first is autism prediction from facial images using a hybrid architecture, justified by the argument that 'a single CNN is utilized within most studies which limits generalization. Therefore hierarchical features with fine grains are not obtained' - so combining ResNet50V2 and InceptionV3 should capture features at multiple granularities. The second, and the paper's better idea, is emotion recognition trained specifically on autistic children's faces, on the reasoning that existing systems are 'primarily trained for healthy ones and consequently missing abnormal facial movements'. The reported results diverge sharply in credibility. The emotion model reached 73.33% on six classes against a VGG16-plus-Random-Forest baseline at 57.33%, with precision 72.26, recall 73.33, specificity 83.90 and F1 70.38 - a modest, internally coherent figure on a genuinely hard task, and one consistent with the difficulty another study in this review documents for affect recognition in autistic children. The autism model's reported set is not coherent: 'accuracy = 95, precision = 0.96, sensitivity/recall = 0.94, Specificity = 42.5, F1 = 0.95 and AUC = 78'. On a balanced 280-image test set, recall 0.94 with specificity 0.425 yields roughly 68% accuracy, not 95%; precision 0.96 is impossible alongside specificity 0.425 at a 1:1 ratio, where the implied 80 false positives against 132 true positives would give precision near 0.62; and an AUC of 0.78 is incompatible with an accuracy of 0.95. The figures cannot all be right and no reconciliation is offered. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Both corpora are public Kaggle assemblies, with the autism images drawn from internet sources by a third party. The paper's stated reason for choosing Kaggle - 'large, well-labelled public data promoting reproducibility in work' - is a genuine consideration and explains why this corpus has attracted at least nine independent analyses, but it addresses reproducibility of the computation rather than validity of the labels. [RQ2.3] None. The children were photographed outside any study, in unknown circumstances. This is a specific problem for the emotion task, which the paper does not raise: an emotion label attached to a photograph taken for unknown reasons has no eliciting condition, so what the child was feeling, whether the expression was posed or spontaneous, and what prompted it are all unknown - and the paper's own argument is that autistic facial expression differs from the neurotypical patterns on which such labels are usually based, which makes the labelling process itself the thing most in need of scrutiny. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics or consent statement appears anywhere, for work whose training data are identifiable photographs of children collected from the internet without their families' knowledge. Funding and competing interests are not stated in the retrieved text. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment. Training ran on CPU-based hardware, which the authors identify as a limitation that 'limited more profound tuning and real-time optimization' - an honest disclosure, and one that also indicates how low the computational barrier to this branch is. [RQ2.6] Better than most of this branch on protocol. Reported: both corpora with their source, the exact partition sizes for both tasks (2,526/280/80 and 703/130), the stratified random sampling procedure with its stated purpose of preserving class proportions, the image quality-filtering criterion requiring a frontal face with eyes, nose and mouth visible, the preprocessing steps, both architectures with their constituent networks and layer types, the baseline comparators, a full six-metric set for each task, confusion matrices, the explicit statement that only one split was used and why, and the training hardware. Not reported: class counts within each partition, the number of distinct children, hyperparameters, code, ethics arrangements, funding and competing interests. [RQ2.7] A dedicated limitations section names six issues and is among the more candid in this branch: missing demographic information on gender and ethnicity limiting generalisation across populations; a small image count possibly yielding a less robust model; analysis restricted to static images so that 'facial cues that were dynamic like gaze direction and micro-expressions were not captured'; no validation on independent clinical datasets; no explainable-AI visualisation, limiting clinical interpretability; and CPU-based training restricting tuning. The methods add that only a single split was performed, with the computational reason given. What is not addressed is more consequential. The autism model's reported metrics are mutually inconsistent - accuracy 95% cannot hold alongside specificity 42.5% and recall 94% on a balanced test set, and precision 0.96 cannot hold alongside specificity 0.425 at a 1:1 ratio - and no reconciliation appears anywhere, so the headline figure is uninterpretable. If the specificity is the accurate value then the model misclassifies more than half of non-autistic children, which is below chance and would be the paper's most important result. The corpus's provenance confound is unmentioned, no diagnostic ascertainment exists, the image-level split leaves subject overlap unexaminable since the number of distinct children is unreported, the quality filter introduces an unreported selection, and no chance baseline is given. [RQ2.9] Multimodal inputs and explainable-AI methods are proposed in the abstract, and the limitations section implies five more: demographic diversity, larger datasets, dynamic rather than static analysis, external clinical validation, and GPU-based training. All are reasonable. The step the study most needs and does not propose is reconciliation of its own metric table, followed by participant-level splitting with the number of distinct children reported. [RQ3.1] Two constructs, of very different tractability. The autism task targets facial morphology, on the premise that autistic children 'show morphological differences within their face' - a physiognomic claim, unmeasured here, with the models receiving whole face images so that expression, pose, apparent age, ancestry and image provenance are all equally available. The emotion task targets six-way facial expression in autistic children specifically, and the construct argument for it is the paper's strongest contribution: general-population emotion models are 'primarily trained for healthy ones and consequently missing abnormal facial movements'. That correctly identifies a real gap, and the resulting 73.33% is instructive precisely because it is modest - emotion recognition on posed neurotypical adult faces reaches 98-99% in the benchmark literature charted elsewhere in this review, so a drop to the low seventies on autistic children's faces is consistent with the independent finding that affect models transfer poorly across this population. Read together with that study, this one supplies a second data point for the same conclusion. [RQ3.2] Architectural rather than modal fusion. The autism model combines ResNet50V2 and InceptionV3 at the feature level, with the rationale that single-network approaches fail to obtain 'hierarchical features with fine grains'. Combining backbones whose receptive-field structures differ - residual depth against inception-module width - is a coherent argument for multi-granularity feature capture, and it is stated rather than assumed. No ablation isolates what each backbone contributes, so whether the hybrid outperforms its components is not established, and given the inconsistency in the reported metric set the comparison could not be evaluated in any case. [RQ4.1] A hybrid ResNet50V2 plus InceptionV3 for autism classification, and an enhanced MobileNet - MobileNet layers followed by global average pooling and fully connected layers - for six-way emotion recognition, each compared against baseline architectures including VGG16 with Random Forest. Choosing MobileNet for the emotion task is sensible given CPU-only training, and the baseline comparisons with confusion matrices give the emotion result more support than the autism result receives. The hybrid's motivation is argued rather than asserted, which is more than most of this branch offers. [RQ4.2] Normalised and augmented face images, filtered to require a visible frontal face with eyes, nose and mouth. The quality filter is a genuine and unusual step for this branch, since web-scraped corpora contain profile shots, partial faces and heavy occlusion that add noise without adding signal - but it also selects a subset whose class balance is unreported, and if image quality differs systematically between two folders drawn from different online sources then the filter itself could shift the composition. [RQ4.3] The fullest metric reporting of any Kaggle-corpus study in this review - accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, F1 and AUC for the autism model, six measures plus confusion matrices for emotion - and that completeness is what makes the problem visible. The autism figures are 'accuracy = 95, precision = 0.96, sensitivity/recall = 0.94, Specificity = 42.5, F1 = 0.95 and AUC = 78'. These cannot all be correct. On the stated balanced 280-image test set, a recall of 0.94 recovers about 132 of 140 positives while a specificity of 0.425 recovers about 60 of 140 negatives, giving 192 correct and an accuracy near 68%. The same figures imply about 80 false positives, so precision would be near 0.62 rather than 0.96. And an AUC of 0.78 is not compatible with 95% accuracy on balanced classes. Reporting specificity at all is what exposes this - the seven other Kaggle-corpus studies charted here that report accuracy alone would have concealed an identical failure. If the specificity of 42.5% is the accurate figure, the model correctly identifies fewer than half of non-autistic children, which is worse than chance and is the study's most important result. The emotion metrics, by contrast, are internally consistent and modest. [RQ4.4] None implemented, and the gap is acknowledged. The introduction argues that 'clinicians find XAI models useful since the decision making process of AI models is easier to understand', and the limitations section records that 'the deep learning models were not provided with explainable AI visualization, thereby, limiting clinical interpretability'. Stating the value of interpretability, not delivering it, and then saying so is more honest than the several studies in this branch that claim interpretability analyses they do not perform. The absence nonetheless leaves the central question untouched: with no attribution, nothing indicates whether the autism model responds to facial phenotype or to the photographic character of images drawn from autism-related web sources. [RQ4.5] Two failures of different kinds, and the reporting quality that exposes the second is worth crediting. The first is standard for this corpus family: the split is at image level, 2,526 training against 280 testing and 80 validation, with the number of distinct children behind 2,886 images unreported, so in a web-assembled collection where a child may appear in several photographs, images of one child can fall on both sides of the boundary. Stratified random sampling was used and is correctly described as preserving class proportions across partitions - but stratification balances classes, not subjects, and the paper does not consider subject overlap. The authors do state candidly that 'the dataset was split only once, and the procedure was not repeated due to the high computational expense of training deep learning models', which names a real limitation with its reason and is more forthcoming than most of this branch. The second failure is arithmetic and more serious. The autism model's reported metrics - accuracy 95, precision 0.96, recall 0.94, specificity 42.5, F1 0.95, AUC 78 - are mutually incompatible on the stated balanced test set: recall 0.94 with specificity 0.425 gives roughly 68% accuracy, precision would be near 0.62 rather than 0.96, and an AUC of 0.78 cannot accompany 95% accuracy. No reconciliation is offered anywhere. The instructive point for the synthesis is that this inconsistency is detectable only because the study reported specificity and AUC alongside accuracy; the seven other studies charted here on the same corpus report accuracy alone or accuracy with precision and recall, and an identical internal contradiction in any of them would be invisible. If the specificity is the accurate figure, the model is below chance at identifying non-autistic children, and the paper's 95% headline conceals a result that would substantially undercut the branch's claims. The provenance confound in the corpus is untouched by any of this, since a model recognising autism-related web imagery would succeed on any partition. [RQ5.1] Keywords: Autism spectrum disorder, Emotion prediction, Facial expression analysis, Deep learning, Artificial intelligence. Balanced across population, both tasks and method. Terms carried through the body: hybrid architecture, hierarchical features, explainable AI, stratified sampling, non-invasive, morphological differences. [RQ5.2] Pattern Recognition 173:112906, Elsevier; received 13 June 2025, revised 11 November 2025, accepted 8 December 2025, online 9 December 2025, with a 2026 volume date. A pattern-recognition venue, and the profile is characteristic: the partition sizes, stratification procedure, quality filter, architectures and metric tables are all documented, while a metric set that is arithmetically impossible on its own stated test set was published without reconciliation, alongside no ethics statement, no diagnostic ascertainment and no chance baseline. The limitations section is nonetheless one of the better ones in the branch, which suggests the shortfall is in verification rather than in candour. [RQ5.3] Published 2025 by the Department of Computer Science at Bharathiar University, Coimbatore. For this review the study contributes three things. It is the ninth built on the Kaggle autistic-children facial corpus, using the standard 2,526/280/80 partition, and it reports the fullest metric set of any of them - which is precisely what makes its central problem visible: the autism model's figures cannot all be true, since accuracy of 95% is incompatible with the specificity of 42.5% and recall of 94% reported beside it on a balanced 280-image test set, and precision of 0.96 is incompatible with that specificity at a 1:1 ratio. The seven earlier studies on this corpus report accuracy alone or accuracy with precision and recall, and an identical contradiction in any of them would have been undetectable. The lesson for the synthesis is that specificity is not merely an additional metric but an arithmetic check, and its near-universal absence from this branch removes the field's simplest defence against inconsistent reporting. If the 42.5% is the accurate value, the model identifies fewer than half of non-autistic children correctly - below chance, and a finding that would tell against the whole branch. Second, the study's emotion component is genuinely well motivated and its result is instructive. The stated rationale is that existing emotion models are 'primarily trained for healthy ones and consequently missing abnormal facial movements', so a recogniser trained on autistic faces is needed - correctly identifying a real problem - and the resulting 73.33% on six classes sits far below the 98-99% that posed neurotypical benchmarks support, which corroborates the independent finding elsewhere in this review that affect models transfer poorly to autistic children. Third, its limitations section is among the more candid in the branch, naming missing gender and ethnicity data, small sample size, the restriction to static images, the absence of external clinical validation, the absence of any explainable-AI component despite having argued for one, and CPU-only training - and the methods separately state that only a single split was performed and why. That candour makes the unreconciled metric table the more conspicuous. What remains unaddressed throughout is the corpus's provenance: the autistic class was harvested from autism-related online sources, so the label records where an image was found, and no diagnostic ascertainment exists for any child depicted. |
| S-140 | Retrospective algorithm-development study by an electrical engineering group at Universitas Semarang with collaborators in Jakarta. The corpus comprises 2,936 facial images balanced at 1,468 labelled autistic and 1,468 labelled normal, described as 'obtained from Kaggle and data from an autism center in Semarang' - so it mixes the public web-assembled collection charted nine times elsewhere in this review with photographs from an Indonesian clinical service. The proportion of images from each source, and their distribution across the two classes, is never reported. No diagnostic instrument, criteria or clinician is described for either portion, the number of distinct children is unstated, and no age, sex, ancestry, cognitive or clinical information is available. No ethics or consent statement appears anywhere in the paper. | Images were resized, normalised and augmented by rotation, flipping and contrast adjustment, then split 80:20 into training and testing at image level with no cross-validation and no separately described validation partition. Five lightweight ensemble pairings were compared: MobileNetV2 with EfficientNetB0, EfficientNetB5 and EfficientNetB7; ResNet50 with EfficientNetB0; and VGG16 with EfficientNetB0. Each pairing classified independently and the outputs were combined either by averaging the predicted probabilities or by majority voting, with a softmax layer producing a probability and a threshold applied to reach a decision. The lightweight architectures were selected explicitly for deployment reasons, using depthwise separable convolutions and compound scaling so that inference would be fast enough for mobile phones or edge devices in clinical settings. | MobileNetV2 with EfficientNetB0 performed best, reaching accuracy 0.8299, precision 0.8514, recall 0.8182 and F1 0.8344 - an internally consistent set and among the lower figures in this branch. ResNet50 with EfficientNetB0 achieved higher precision but lower recall, which the authors correctly judge makes it 'less useful for finding all ASD cases'. Training and validation curves are reported for all five pairings and read for learning stability, with some pairings noted to show slower learning and greater fluctuation indicating models 'that might struggle with generalization'. A comparison table places the result against two prior studies reporting 0.7500 and 0.8050. | The corpus mixes two sources and the paper reports neither their proportions nor their distribution across classes - the single fact determining whether the mixed design mitigates the branch's provenance confound or introduces a sharper one, since a corpus in which autistic images come predominantly from an Indonesian autism centre and comparison images predominantly from an international web collection would be separable by ancestry, camera and setting alone. The paper's own statement that the network uses 'the texture of the skin' is consistent with that possibility, and a source-held-out evaluation, which the two identifiable sources make directly available, is not performed. No diagnostic ascertainment is described even for the clinic portion, forgoing the study's clearest opportunity to improve on its predecessors. The split is at image level with the number of distinct children unreported; augmentation ordering relative to splitting is unstated, and rotation, flip and contrast variants of one photograph are near-duplicates. No demographic information exists for either class. No specificity, AUC or confusion matrix is reported, so the error profile behind a recall of 0.8182 cannot be inspected, and no chance baseline is stated. There is no ethics or consent statement despite part of the corpus consisting of identifiable photographs of children attending a clinical service, and no limitations section. | The tenth study in this review on the Kaggle facial-image corpus family, and the only one to supplement it with images from a clinical service - which makes it simultaneously the branch's most interesting variation and its clearest missed opportunity. Adding photographs from an autism centre in Semarang could have anchored part of the corpus in genuine clinical diagnoses, addressing the labelling problem that undermines every other study on these images; instead no ascertainment is described and no source-by-class breakdown is given, so the addition may equally have introduced a sharper confound in which ancestry, camera and setting align with the label. The decisive experiment was in the authors' hands: with two identifiable sources, training on one and testing on the other would have established directly whether the models detect facial phenotype or image provenance, and that single result would have been the most informative in the entire facial-image branch of this review. Three features nonetheless place the study above the branch norm. Its reported 0.8299 is internally consistent and modest, and it benchmarks itself against comparators at 0.7500 and 0.8050 rather than against the high-nineties claims made elsewhere on the same corpus. Its precision-recall discussion is the best in the branch, correctly judging a high-precision low-recall pairing 'less useful for finding all ASD cases' - a screening-oriented reading that almost no other study here articulates. And its account of rising prevalence is accurate where most of this corpus is alarmist, attributing the change from 1 in 150 to 1 in 36 to diagnostic criteria, awareness and detection across a broader age range. Its description of what the network extracts - face shape, expression and skin texture - is also unusually candid about the range of information a whole-image classifier receives, and names precisely the property most likely to track image source rather than the child. | [RQ1.1] Two thousand nine hundred and thirty-six facial images, balanced at 1,468 labelled autistic and 1,468 labelled normal, drawn from two sources - Kaggle and 'data from an autism center in Semarang'. The mixed provenance is what distinguishes this study from the other nine Kaggle-corpus papers charted in this review, and it cuts both ways. Supplementing a web-scraped collection with images from an actual clinical service is in principle an improvement, since clinic-attending children have real diagnoses; but the paper never states how many images came from each source, nor whether the clinic contributed to the autistic class only or to both. If the autistic images are predominantly Indonesian clinic photographs while the comparison images are predominantly international web-scraped ones, the two classes would be separable by ancestry, camera and setting without any facial phenotype being involved - a sharper confound than the pure-Kaggle studies face. The paper's own account of provenance is loose enough to leave this open: the data 'could come from a variety of places, such as clinics, past research, or relevant public statistics'. No age, sex, ancestry, cognitive, language or clinical information is reported for either class, and the number of distinct children behind 2,936 images is never stated. [RQ1.2] Plain and largely accurate, with one notable feature. Autism is 'a developmental disorder that affects how a person talks, interacts with others, and thinks and acts', and the description of the spectrum is correct - conditions 'that used to be called classic autism, Asperger's syndrome, and undefined pervasive developmental disability are now part of ASD. This spectrum shows how different people can have very different symptoms'. 'Normal' is used as the class label for non-autistic children, which is the least careful terminology choice. What sets the framing apart is the treatment of rising prevalence: the paper records the increase from 1 in 150 in the early 2000s to 1 in 36 in 2023 and attributes it correctly to 'changes in how autism is diagnosed, more people and healthcare professionals being aware of it, and better detection of autism across a wider range of ages' - an accurate account that most papers in this corpus replace with an alarm narrative. The Indonesian framing is also specific rather than generic, noting the scarcity of national statistics and the reliance on Ministry of Health reports and local studies. No neurodiversity framing appears and no autistic person is reported as involved. [RQ1.3] Entirely absent, and unusually consequential here. No age, sex, ancestry, socioeconomic, cognitive or comorbidity information is reported for either class. The mixed-source corpus makes ancestry a specific rather than generic concern: a Kaggle collection assembled from international web sources and a set of photographs from an autism centre in Semarang would be expected to differ systematically in ancestry, in camera and lighting, and in photographic convention, and the paper's own description of the extracted features - 'the shape of the face, the expression on it, and the texture of the skin' - names skin texture explicitly as something the network uses. Without a source-wise breakdown of the classes, none of this can be examined, and a source-held-out evaluation, which the mixed corpus would have made straightforward, is not performed. [RQ1.4] None described for either source. For the Kaggle portion the labels are folder membership in a collection whose autistic class was harvested from autism-associated online content - the position documented across nine other studies in this review. For the Semarang autism-centre portion, children attending a clinical service would ordinarily carry clinical diagnoses, and this is the one point at which the study could have improved on its predecessors; but no instrument, criteria, clinician, assessment date or procedure is reported, and the paper's provenance sentence explicitly leaves the sources open, saying the data 'could come from a variety of places, such as clinics, past research, or relevant public statistics'. The opportunity to anchor part of the corpus in real diagnoses is therefore present and unrealised. [RQ1.5] None. No severity, cognitive, adaptive or language measure exists for any image. [RQ2.1] The aim is to identify a lightweight CNN ensemble that classifies autism from facial photographs accurately enough for deployment on mobile or edge devices. Five pairings were compared - MobileNetV2 with EfficientNetB0, B5 and B7; ResNet50 with EfficientNetB0; VGG16 with EfficientNetB0 - combined by probability averaging or majority voting. The best, MobileNetV2 with EfficientNetB0, reached accuracy 0.8299, precision 0.8514, recall 0.8182 and F1 0.8344, an internally consistent set and among the lower figures in this branch. Two aspects of the reporting are better than the branch norm. The precision-recall trade-off is interpreted in screening terms: ResNet50 with EfficientNetB0 achieved 'higher precision but lower recall, making them less useful for finding all ASD cases', which correctly identifies that a screening instrument's priority is not missing cases. And the learning curves are read substantively for stability and overfitting rather than displayed decoratively, with some pairings noted to show 'slower learning with more fluctuations, indicating less stable models that might struggle with generalization'. The comparison table places the result against two prior studies at 0.7500 and 0.8050 - modest comparators, and the study does not claim to have exceeded the high-nineties figures reported elsewhere in the branch. [RQ2.2] Two settings, imperfectly distinguished. Part of the corpus is the Kaggle collection, which has no setting - the images were harvested from internet sources by a third party. Part comes from an autism centre in Semarang, which is a clinical service setting and the same kind of environment in which the proposed edge-deployed tool would run. The mixture is potentially valuable and is undermined by the absence of any breakdown: without knowing how many images came from each source and how they distribute across the two classes, a reader cannot tell whether the clinic data broadens the corpus or introduces a setting confound aligned with the label. A source-held-out analysis would have answered this directly and is not attempted. [RQ2.3] None. The photographs were taken outside any study, in unknown circumstances, for both portions of the corpus. The paper's description of what the network extracts - face shape, expression and skin texture - underlines the consequence: with no task and no controlled acquisition, expression at the captured instant is free to vary with why the photograph was taken, and skin texture with the camera that took it. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary and clinic-sourced analysis with no longitudinal element. No ethics or consent statement appears anywhere in the paper. This is a more serious omission than for the purely Kaggle-based studies charted elsewhere in this review: part of the corpus consists of facial photographs of children attending an autism centre in Semarang, so identifiable images of clinically attending children were obtained and used with no reported institutional approval and no consent process. Funding and competing interests are not stated. [RQ2.5] No acquisition equipment is described. The architectural argument is explicitly about deployment hardware: MobileNetV2 and EfficientNetB0 were chosen 'because they are fast and have small models', using depthwise separable convolutions and compound scaling so that inference is quick enough for 'devices with limited processing power, like mobile phones or edge devices used in clinical settings'. That is a coherent design rationale for a low-resource context and connects the architecture choice to the stated Indonesian setting, where the paper notes national statistics are scarce. [RQ2.6] Adequate on the pipeline and deficient on the corpus. Reported: total image count and exact class balance, both sources by name, the 80:20 split ratio, the preprocessing and augmentation operations (resizing, normalisation, rotation, flipping, contrast adjustment), all five ensemble pairings with their constituent architectures, both combination rules, the softmax-plus-threshold decision structure, four metrics for each pairing, learning curves for each, and a comparison table against prior work. Not reported: the proportion of images from each source and their distribution across classes, the number of distinct children, whether augmentation preceded splitting, hyperparameters, per-class error breakdowns, ethics arrangements, funding and code. [RQ2.7] No limitations section exists, and the conclusion repeats the results paragraph almost verbatim without critical reflection. What should have been stated: the proportion of Kaggle against Semarang images and their distribution across classes is unreported, which is the single fact determining whether mixing sources mitigates the branch's provenance confound or creates a sharper one aligned with ancestry, camera and setting; no diagnostic ascertainment is described even for the clinic-sourced portion, forgoing the study's clearest opportunity to improve on its predecessors; the split is at image level with the number of distinct children unreported; augmentation ordering relative to splitting is unstated and rotation, flip and contrast variants of one photograph are near-duplicates; no demographic data exist in a study classifying faces; no specificity, AUC or confusion matrix is given, so the error profile behind a recall of 0.8182 is uninspectable; and there is no ethics or consent statement despite part of the corpus coming from a clinical service. [RQ2.9] None separately stated. The step this study most needs is a source-held-out evaluation - training on Kaggle images and testing on Semarang images, or the reverse - which its own mixed corpus makes available and which would establish directly whether the models detect a facial phenotype or the character of an image source. Reporting the source-by-class breakdown would be the prerequisite. [RQ3.1] Facial appearance, described more honestly than in most of this branch. Rather than asserting a specific craniofacial phenotype, the paper says the network finds 'important patterns in the image, such as the shape of the face, the expression on it, and the texture of the skin'. That enumeration is accurate about what a whole-image CNN actually receives, and it names two properties - expression and skin texture - that are not morphological and would vary with photographic circumstance rather than with the child. Naming skin texture as a used feature is particularly pointed in a corpus mixing an internationally scraped collection with photographs from an Indonesian clinic, since skin appearance in an image is jointly determined by ancestry, lighting and camera. No landmark geometry or morphometric quantity is computed anywhere. [RQ3.2] Decision-level ensembling rather than modality fusion. Two CNNs classify independently and their outputs are combined by probability averaging or majority voting, with the stated rationale that this 'makes the system more reliable and accurate by lowering the chance of errors from a single model and making it better at generalizing new data'. Five pairings are compared, which gives real architectural breadth, and the pairings deliberately combine a lightweight backbone with an EfficientNet variant of differing scale. No ablation reports single-model performance against the ensembles, so the claimed ensembling gain is asserted rather than demonstrated. [RQ4.1] Five ensemble pairings of pretrained convolutional networks, combined at the decision level by averaging or voting. The selection criterion is explicitly computational: lightweight architectures using depthwise separable convolutions and compound scaling, chosen for fast inference on constrained hardware. That is an appropriate design goal for a low-resource deployment context and is argued rather than assumed. Comparing five pairings with learning curves for each is more architectural breadth than most single-model papers in this branch offer, and the authors' reading of those curves for stability - identifying which pairings learn smoothly and which fluctuate - is a legitimate diagnostic use rather than a decorative one. [RQ4.2] Resized and normalised face images augmented by rotation, flipping and contrast adjustment. Contrast adjustment is worth noting because it partially normalises a property that would differ systematically between image sources; whether it is sufficient to remove a source signal is untested, and no source-wise analysis is performed. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for each of the five pairings, with training and validation curves. The metric set supports one genuinely useful observation - that a pairing with higher precision but lower recall is 'less useful for finding all ASD cases', which is the correct screening-oriented reading and is articulated in almost no other study in this branch. What is missing is specificity, AUC, confusion matrices and confidence intervals, and no chance baseline is stated despite the exactly balanced construction placing it at 50%. The comparison table cites two prior studies at 0.7500 and 0.8050 rather than the high-nineties figures reported by other Kaggle-corpus work, so the study positions itself against modest comparators. [RQ4.4] None. No attribution, saliency or feature analysis is reported. The omission is pointed here because the paper itself names skin texture among the features the network uses, and because the mixed-source corpus makes it directly testable whether the models respond to image source - a saliency or source-classification analysis would have addressed the study's central ambiguity and neither is attempted. [RQ4.5] An 80:20 image-level split with no cross-validation, no separately described validation partition, and no participant-level partitioning; the number of distinct children behind 2,936 images is never stated. Augmentation by rotation, flipping and contrast adjustment is applied without specifying whether it preceded the split, and such variants of a single photograph are near-duplicates rather than independent observations. These are the standard weaknesses of this branch. What is distinctive here is a confound the mixed corpus introduces and the paper leaves entirely unexamined. The images come from two sources - Kaggle and an autism centre in Semarang - and neither the proportion from each nor their distribution across the two classes is reported. If the clinic supplied predominantly autistic images while the comparison class came predominantly from the international web collection, the classes would be separable by ancestry, camera, lighting and photographic convention without any facial phenotype being involved, and the reported 0.8299 would measure source rather than diagnosis. The paper's own account of what the network extracts - face shape, expression and skin texture - is consistent with that reading. The remedy is available and unused: with two identifiable sources in hand, a source-held-out evaluation, or simply a source-by-class table, would settle the question directly. Two elements of the analysis nonetheless stand above the branch norm: the learning curves are interpreted for stability and overfitting rather than displayed without comment, and the precision-recall trade-off across pairings is read in screening terms, with a high-precision low-recall model correctly judged 'less useful for finding all ASD cases'. [RQ5.1] Keywords: autism spectrum disorder, early detection, ensemble convolutional neural network, facial images, classification, accuracy. Method- and task-facing, with the modality named. The leading keyword field contains the placeholder word 'Component', which suggests a template was not fully edited. [RQ5.2] International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications 16(7):229ff, 2025. An open-access computer science venue, and the profile follows: the ensemble pipeline, augmentation, split ratio and metric tables are documented, while the corpus's dual provenance is left unquantified, no ethics statement appears despite clinic-sourced images, no limitations section is provided, and the conclusion repeats the results paragraph verbatim. An unedited template placeholder survives in the keyword list. [RQ5.3] Published 2025 by an electrical engineering group at Universitas Semarang with collaborators at Institut Kesehatan Indonesia and a Jakarta stem-cell laboratory. For this review the study is the tenth built on the Kaggle facial-image corpus family and the only one to supplement it with images from a clinical service - an autism centre in Semarang - which makes it both the branch's most interesting variation and its clearest missed opportunity. Mixing a web-scraped collection with clinic photographs could have anchored part of the corpus in real diagnoses; instead the paper reports neither the proportion from each source nor how they distribute across the two classes, so a reader cannot tell whether the addition reduces the provenance confound documented across the other nine studies or replaces it with a sharper one, in which Indonesian clinic photographs and international web images are separable by ancestry, camera and setting alone. The paper's own description of what the network extracts - 'the shape of the face, the expression on it, and the texture of the skin' - is unusually candid about the range of information a whole-image CNN receives, and names skin texture, which is exactly the kind of property that tracks image source rather than the child. The remedy was in the study's hands: with two identifiable sources it could have trained on one and tested on the other, and that single experiment would have been the most informative result in the entire facial-image branch of this review. Three further observations. The reported 0.8299 accuracy with precision 0.8514, recall 0.8182 and F1 0.8344 is internally consistent and among the branch's lower figures, and the study benchmarks itself against comparators at 0.7500 and 0.8050 rather than against the high-nineties claims elsewhere. Its precision-recall discussion is the branch's best, correctly judging a high-precision low-recall model 'less useful for finding all ASD cases'. And its account of rising prevalence is accurate where most of this corpus is alarmist, attributing the change from 1 in 150 to 1 in 36 to diagnostic criteria, awareness and broader age-range detection. Against this: no ethics or consent statement anywhere, despite identifiable photographs of children attending a clinical service; no diagnostic ascertainment described even for that portion; no demographic data; image-level splitting with the number of children unreported; no specificity or confusion matrix; and no limitations section. |
| S-141 | Retrospective secondary analysis of the publicly archived Eye-tracking Dataset to Support the Research on Autism Spectrum Disorder (figshare 20113592, Cilia et al.): 59 children - 29 with ASD, 30 typically developing - viewing static images (faces, objects, scenes) and short videos (cartoon characters, balloons) for about five minutes each at ~60 cm from a 17-inch display, recorded on an SMI RED mobile tracker at 60 Hz. The analysed table holds 1,048,575 gaze-sample rows, one short of Excel's worksheet maximum. Sex composition is 25M/4F in the ASD group against 13M/17F in the TD group; age is given as a single pooled mean of 7.88 years. | Mean imputation of missing values, label encoding of categorical fields, mutual-information feature selection down to 16 features, min-max normalisation, and reshaping to a single-timestep tensor.
