Two architectures were fitted: a 64-unit LSTM and a hybrid 1-D CNN plus LSTM, both with dropout, binary cross-entropy, an adaptive optimiser and early stopping. Evaluation used stratified 5-fold cross-validation over the gaze-sample rows. | CNN-LSTM mean accuracy 99.78% (SD 0.11%), per-class precision/recall/F1 of 99.81/99.85/99.83 for non-ASD and 99.72/99.63/99.67 for ASD; the standalone LSTM was lower but still above 99%. A one-sample t-test of the fold accuracies against 95% gave t(4)=14.2, p<0.001. The authors conclude the system successfully diagnosed ASD and shows promise for clinical application. | The paper states none. In fact the result is uninterpretable as diagnostic accuracy for four compounding reasons. (1) The 16-feature input vector includes CARS_Score, the Childhood Autism Rating Scale - a clinician-administered measure of the target condition supplied to the model as a predictor. (2) Cross-validation partitions gaze samples, not children: with roughly 17,800 rows per child, every test fold contains rows recorded milliseconds apart from its own training rows, so the classifier can succeed by identifying individuals. (3) Mutual-information selection and mean imputation were both computed on the full dataset before splitting. (4) The 42.9-point sex gap between groups provides an independent route to high accuracy. No participant-level metric, no specificity, no AUC, no external validation, no ablation without CARS, no ethics statement, and no limitations section appear anywhere in the article. | This study is the review's cleanest single illustration of how several validation failures stack multiplicatively. It sits alongside local_3e88f3ce and local_8253c2ec/local_a0d73248 in the target-leakage group, and alongside the scanpath, video-frame, EEG-epoch, thermal-image, cry-instance and facial-image studies in the within-participant leakage group - but it is the only charted paper that belongs to both simultaneously, at the finest analysis granularity in the corpus. Its 99.78% should be read against local_cd7545e2, where the ADOS-2 itself reaches AUC 0.562 in a clinically relevant discrimination, and against local_7d7f1fcc, where a participant-level matched split over pose data yields 82.5%. It also extends the review's venue finding: an article with no ethics statement and no limitations section, using a diagnostic instrument as a model input, cleared peer review at a clinical journal in 32 days. | [RQ1.1] Two groups from a single archived dataset: 29 children with ASD and 30 typically developing children, 59 in total. The unit actually analysed is not the child but the gaze sample: 1,048,575 rows. That figure deserves attention - 1,048,576 is the maximum row count of a Microsoft Excel worksheet, so the analysed set is almost certainly a spreadsheet-truncated slice of the source recording rather than the complete data, and the paper never remarks on it. Per-child row counts, per-group row counts and per-fold composition are all unreported. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children diagnosed with ASD, autism group, non-ASD, typically developing (TD) children. Diagnosis-first, deficit-oriented phrasing predominates: children with ASD typically have difficulty focusing, reduced attention to important stimuli, autism and non-autism profiles. There is no mention of autistic community perspectives, no identity-first alternative, and no acknowledgement that the sample carries clinical labels assigned by others. [RQ1.3] Sparse and, where present, alarming. Table 2 reports sex and a single pooled mean age of 7.88 years - no SD, no range, no per-group age. Sex composition is 25 male / 4 female in ASD (86.2% male) versus 13 male / 17 female in TD (43.3% male), a 42.9-point gap. This is the largest sex imbalance in the review's charted corpus, exceeding the 32-point gap in local_4ceee075. Because sex systematically affects gaze behaviour towards faces, a classifier reading gaze coordinates can score highly by learning sex. No race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, language, geography or recruitment source is reported for either group. [RQ1.4] Not confirmed by this study. Labels are inherited wholesale from the figshare dataset. The presence of a CARS_Score field implies that the original collectors administered the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, but this paper reports no cut-off, no administrator qualification, no ADOS or ADI-R, no DSM or ICD criterion, and no statement of who made the diagnoses or when. The TD group's status as non-autistic is likewise asserted rather than evidenced - no screening instrument is named. [RQ1.5] CARS_Score is present in the data but is never reported as a participant characteristic - no mean, no range, no distribution by group. Instead it is consumed as a model input feature. No IQ, developmental quotient, adaptive-behaviour, language or comorbidity measure is reported for any participant. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to implement deep learning on eye-tracking data from social attention tasks to diagnose ASD, and to identify the feature-selection strategy that lets the model reach high accuracy. Note that maximising accuracy is written into the objectives themselves - one of the listed research questions asks for the feature selection strategy that can assist the deep learning model in achieving high accuracy, which is a statement of intent to optimise the reported number rather than to estimate a diagnostic property. The headline finding is CNN-LSTM accuracy 99.78% (SD 0.11%), reported as outperforming previous studies and showing promise for clinical application. [RQ2.2] Data collection setting is described second-hand: a dedicated experimental room, participant seated about 60 cm from a 17-inch display, session length about five minutes, stimulus order varied between participants, infrared reflection tracking. The country, clinic type, recruitment channel and date of the original collection are not stated. The analysis itself was run on a desktop workstation. [RQ2.3] Free viewing of mixed static and dynamic stimuli. Dynamic content comprised short videos with engaging elements such as cartoon characters and balloons designed to attract children's attention; static content comprised images of faces, objects and scenes. No areas of interest are defined, no fixation or saccade extraction is performed, and no social-versus-nonsocial contrast is computed - the abstract's framing as social attention tasks is inherited from the dataset description rather than operationalised in the analysis. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is absent entirely - no approval statement, no committee, no consent statement, and the word ethic does not appear in the article. This is a study of clinically labelled disabled children published in a medical journal with a full data-availability statement and no ethics statement of any kind. Only the public status of the source dataset is offered, which addresses data access, not the ethics of the analysis or of the diagnostic claim being made. [RQ2.5] SMI RED mobile eye tracker at 60 Hz with a 17-inch stimulus display, participant at ~60 cm. Compute: 7th-generation Intel Core i7, 8 GB RAM, 16 GB GPU. Software is described only as a suitable computational framework for neural network training - no library, no version, no seed. Calibration procedure, data-quality thresholds and drift handling are not described, which matters because Tracking_Ratio (a data-quality index) is one of the retained features. [RQ2.6] Partial and, on the decisive points, poor. Reproducible: the source dataset is openly archived on figshare with a resolvable URL, and the preprocessing sequence is narrated step by step. Not reproducible: no code, no software or version names, no random seed, no complete hyperparameter specification, no statement of the mutual-information threshold or scores that produced exactly 16 features, no per-fold row counts, and no per-child row counts. A reader cannot verify whether the 16 selected features are the same ones the mutual-information ranking would yield on their machine, nor reconstruct the folds. [RQ2.7] None acknowledged. There is no limitations section, no threats-to-validity paragraph, and no caveat anywhere in the discussion or conclusion. The paper moves directly from 99.78% to promise for clinical application. Every issue this review identifies - row-level splitting, unnested feature selection, CARS as an input, the sex imbalance, imputation before splitting, the Excel-shaped row count - passes unmentioned. [RQ2.9] Two directions: incorporating attention mechanisms into the deep learning models so the model focuses on the most relevant features, and extending to multimodal data combining eye-tracking with other behavioural or physiological signals. Neither addresses the validity problems in the present design; both propose adding capacity to a pipeline whose reported ceiling is already 99.78%. [RQ3.1] Visual attention allocation during free viewing - fixation position (point of regard, left and right eye), gaze direction vectors in three dimensions, and the categorical annotation of what was being looked at (Category_Right, Category_Left) alongside stimulus identity. The behavioural construct is therefore where the child looks, sampled instantaneously, with no aggregation into fixations, saccades, dwell times or AOI proportions. [RQ3.2] No fusion of behavioural modalities - eye tracking only. There is, however, an undeclared fusion of a different kind: the clinical instrument score (CARS) is concatenated with the behavioural features into a single input vector. That is not multimodal behavioural fusion; it is the insertion of the outcome's own measurement instrument into the predictor set. Multimodal work is named as future rather than present. [RQ4.1] Supervised deep learning for binary classification: a standalone LSTM (64 units, dropout, sigmoid) and a hybrid 1-D CNN plus LSTM. The recurrent framing is nominal - the input tensor has exactly one timestep, so the LSTM has no sequence to traverse and reduces to a gated dense transformation of a 16-dimensional vector. The paper says this explicitly (even though the input consisted of only a single timestep) without recognising that it removes the entire justification for the architecture. [RQ4.2] A 16-element tabular vector per gaze sample: trial and stimulus identifiers, Tracking_Ratio, Point_of_Regard right/left X and Y, six gaze-vector components, Category_Right, Category_Left, #Stimulus, and CARS_Score. Min-max scaled to [0,1], reshaped to (1,16). Two of these deserve separate note. CARS_Score is a clinician-administered autism severity instrument: within this dataset it is effectively a monotone function of the label, so its inclusion is direct target leakage and by itself can account for a near-perfect result. Tracking_Ratio is a signal-quality index that plausibly differs systematically between groups for reasons of compliance rather than social attention. Stimulus and trial identifiers encode session structure. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall/sensitivity, F1, per-class values and per-fold confusion matrices; means with standard deviations across the five folds. Missing: specificity as a separate figure, AUC or any threshold-free measure, calibration, positive and negative predictive value at a stated prevalence, and any participant-level metric. Because the analysis unit is the gaze sample, none of the reported numbers is a diagnostic accuracy in the clinical sense - not one figure in the paper describes how often a child would be correctly classified. [RQ4.4] None applied to the model. A Pearson correlation heatmap and the mutual-information ranking characterise the input data before fitting. No post-hoc attribution, no attention weights (attention is proposed as future work), no ablation showing performance with CARS_Score removed - the single experiment that would have settled what the model learned. [RQ4.5] Stratified 5-fold cross-validation on 1,048,575 gaze-sample rows, stratified by class only. This is the review's clearest instance of within-participant leakage at the finest possible granularity: with 59 children and roughly 17,800 rows each, every test fold is virtually guaranteed to contain samples drawn from the same recording session, the same child and the same stimulus presentation as the training rows, differing by fractions of a second. A model can reach 99.78% by recognising individual children rather than autism. Three further defects compound it. First, mutual-information feature selection was run on the whole dataset before cross-validation, so the folds were chosen using their own test labels. Second, mean imputation of missing values was likewise computed over the whole dataset. Third, early stopping restores the weights that minimise loss on the same partition whose accuracy is then reported. The 0.11% standard deviation across folds is presented as evidence of stability; it is better read as confirmation that the five folds are near-identical resamples of one recording set. No participant-level split, no external cohort, and no held-out site is attempted anywhere in the paper. [RQ5.1] autism spectrum disorder; eye-tracking; deep learning; diagnosing; ASD. Purely method-and-condition; nothing on validation, generalisation, participants or clinical deployment. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Medicine 12:1690177 - an open-access general medical journal, not a computing venue. This matters for the review's venue analysis: the paper's audience is clinical, its abstract advises healthcare professionals, and no clinical reviewer flagged the absence of an ethics statement, the absence of a limitations section, or the use of a diagnostic instrument as a model input. [RQ5.3] 2025, published 9 October, 32 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is unqualified diagnostic replacement: the system successfully diagnosed ASD, the approach shows promise for clinical application, assisting healthcare professionals in diagnosing ASD more accurately through advanced artificial intelligence technology. The comparison table positions the contribution purely as a higher accuracy number than nine listed predecessors, with no comparison of study design, split scheme or sample. It belongs to the review's leaderboard genre, in which the reported figure rather than the estimand is the unit of scientific progress. |
| S-142 | Primary cross-sectional questionnaire study in Pakistan. A Q-CHAT-10-based instrument was circulated through several rehabilitation centres, collected on paper and via Google Forms, and completed by parents, caregivers, medical staff or clinicians for children aged 2-4 years. The paper states 750 participants, though the reported sex counts (434 male, 308 female) and the split counts (593 train, 149 test) both sum to 742. The test set is 106 autistic-class and 43 non-autistic-class children. | After removing incomplete rows, binary-encoding categorical fields and deleting the case identifier and the who-completed-the-test field, the authors correlated each Q-CHAT item with the Q-CHAT-10 score and the class label and deleted items A1, A2, A6, A8 and A9 for high correlation. The remaining five items plus age, sex, jaundice and family history were passed to TPOT (10 generations, population 100) over a single random 80/20 split. TPOT returned a BernoulliNB plus RandomForestClassifier ensemble, which the authors then rebuilt manually with the published parameters to verify reproducibility, and compared against six hand-specified baselines. | Autistic class precision 0.83, recall 0.90, F1 0.86; non-autistic class 0.68, 0.53, 0.60; accuracy 0.83 in the results and comparison tables but 78% in the abstract; micro-average ROC 0.87, macro-average ROC 0.81; PR 0.892 and 0.728. Baselines ranged from 0.70 (decision tree) to 0.80 (naive Bayes). | The label is the Q-CHAT-10 scoring function applied to the same ten items that supply the features, so no clinical diagnosis enters the study and the task is reconstruction of a checklist threshold rather than detection of autism. The correlation-based deletion of five items is arithmetically self-defeating - those items correlate with the score because they are summed into it - and removing them is what pulls the result down from the near-perfect figures other checklist-label studies report to the low 80s. The test set is 71.1% positive, making the majority-class baseline 71.1%; the paper's own SVM row (recall 1.000, precision 0.718, accuracy 0.71) is that trivial classifier, printed without comment. Everything rests on one unseeded 80/20 split with no intervals, the dataset is not shared, respondents were recruited through autism rehabilitation services, comorbid neurological conditions were excluded, and the stated sample size exceeds the accounted-for participants by eight. The authors state only one limitation, the absence of public-dataset evaluation. | This paper is the informative middle term of the review's questionnaire-tabular branch. local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 retain all ten checklist items and report 100% on six metrics; this study deletes five of them and reports 0.83 - the same circular estimand, differing only in how much of the label's own arithmetic was left in the feature set. Read together, the three establish that reported accuracy in this branch is a function of how completely the label's summands survive preprocessing, and nothing else. It is also one of only two included studies (with local_7b468950) whose authors manually re-implemented and verified their own selected model, and its ethics reporting - named committee, protocol number, approval date, consent as an inclusion criterion - stands well above the corpus norm, though the reviewing body is a software engineering department. Its stated novelty, a locally collected Pakistani cohort rather than another reuse of a public high-income-country dataset, is a genuine and rare contribution to the corpus's geographic distribution. | [RQ1.1] One group of children aged 2-4 years recruited through Pakistani rehabilitation centres, split by questionnaire outcome rather than by recruitment stream. The paper states 750 participants, but 434 male plus 308 female is 742, and 593 training plus 149 test is also 742; eight children are unaccounted for and the inconsistency is not noted. Class sizes are never stated directly and must be recovered from the test-set support column (106 autistic, 43 non-autistic), implying about 71% positive overall. There is no separate typically developing comparison group in the design sense - both classes come from the same rehabilitation-centre respondent pool, and the questionnaire was described as circulated among trainers and parents of children with autism, which makes the non-autistic class a by-product of scoring rather than a recruited control group. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, ASD traits, autistic class, non-autistic class, children with autism, affected individuals. The introduction is unusually careful in one respect - it states that autism is not a sickness or disease but a lifelong neurological developmental disorder - and unusually careless elsewhere, describing symptoms as tiresome behaviors, deficits in public interactivity, and social disablement. The DSM-5 support levels are laid out at length, then never used. No autistic or community perspective is cited. [RQ1.3] Age band 2-4 years (recorded in months, no mean or SD); 434 male / 308 female overall with no per-class breakdown; jaundice at birth and family history of ASD recorded as binary fields. Nothing on socioeconomic status, urban/rural location, language, education or which rehabilitation centre each child came from - the last being important, since centre could act as a site effect in a dataset pooled across several centres. The paper does report a sex effect in the data (males give more positive Q-CHAT responses) and interprets it as males being more prone to autism, without considering respondent expectation or referral bias. [RQ1.4] Not confirmed for any participant. This is the defining feature of the study: there is no clinical diagnosis anywhere in the pipeline. The label Class/ASD Traits is generated by the Q-CHAT-10 scoring function applied to the same ten items that supply the features. What is modelled is therefore a scoring rule, not a condition. The one screening instrument used is a caregiver checklist completed variously by parents, caregivers, medical staff or clinicians - and the field recording which of those it was was deleted during preprocessing as irrelevant, discarding the only available indicator of measurement heterogeneity. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, developmental quotient, adaptive behaviour, language level or ASD severity measure. Q-CHAT-10 score is present but is the label's source. Comorbid neurological conditions were an exclusion criterion, so no comorbidity data exist. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to apply automated machine learning (TPOT) to a locally collected Pakistani dataset to determine the likelihood of ASD in children at early stages and to speed up diagnosis, with an explicit framing as one of the first uses of AUTOML for ASD detection on real-world non-high-income-country data. Headline findings: TPOT selected a BernoulliNB plus RandomForest ensemble; autistic-class precision 0.83, recall 0.90, F1 0.86; non-autistic-class precision 0.68, recall 0.53, F1 0.60; accuracy 0.83 in the results tables but reported as 78% in the abstract; micro-ROC 0.87, macro-ROC 0.81. [RQ2.2] Several rehabilitation centres across Pakistan, with responses collected on paper and via Google Forms into a Google Sheet. The authors are candid about the context: there is no proper reporting and tracking of ASD cases in the country, and the data had to be recorded from scratch. Neither the number of centres, their names, their catchment, nor the collection dates are given, so site cannot be treated as a variable and the pooled sample cannot be characterised. [RQ2.3] There is no task or paradigm. The instrument is the ten-item Quantitative Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (Q-CHAT-10) of Allison et al., reproduced in full in Table 2, plus seven auxiliary variables. Behaviour is entirely caregiver-reported and retrospective. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, no follow-up. Ethics reporting is among the better examples in this corpus in form: Declaration of Helsinki compliance, named committee, protocol number BUIC/H11/SE/46113 with an approval date of 3 April 2023, informed parental consent as an inclusion criterion, and exclusion of children with comorbid neurological disorders. The reviewing body is a Software Engineering Department ethical review committee rather than a clinical or psychological board, which is a mismatch given that the study collects health data on disabled children and advertises a diagnostic use. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation - Google Forms for capture, CSV export. Modelling used the TPOT library (10 generations, population 100, remaining parameters default) with scikit-learn estimators. No versions, no hardware, no seed. The full best-pipeline parameter set is given in Table 4, which is more than most papers in this corpus supply. [RQ2.6] Mixed, with one notable strength. The authors manually rebuilt the TPOT-selected pipeline using the exact reported parameters to verify that the automated result was reproducible - a deliberate replication step that almost no other study in this corpus performs, and the paper's best methodological instinct. Against that: the dataset is not deposited, no code is released, no library versions or random seed are given, the single 80/20 split is unseeded, the participant counts do not reconcile, and two different accuracies (78% and 0.83) appear for the same experiment. [RQ2.7] One limitation is stated - no evaluation on public datasets, and the Pakistani rehabilitation-centre sample's demographic and cultural specificity may limit generalisability, with a sensible note that direct comparison against UCI data would itself introduce socio-clinical bias. Unstated: that the label is a deterministic function of the predictors, that five of the ten items were deleted precisely because they predicted the label too well, that the majority-class baseline is 71.1%, that a single unrepeated split underpins every number, that the sample size does not add up, and that respondents were drawn from among parents of children already attending autism rehabilitation services. [RQ2.9] Compare other AUTOML libraries; benchmark the model on public datasets such as the UCI ASD screening data to test robustness across populations. Both are reasonable and directly address the stated limitation, but neither touches the circular label that governs the entire result. [RQ3.1] Early social-communication behaviours as reported by a caregiver: response to name, ease of eye contact, requesting gestures, declarative pointing, pretend play, gaze following, comforting a distressed family member, early speech quality, conventional gestures such as waving goodbye, and prolonged purposeless staring. After correlation-based deletion only five of these (A3 requesting gestures, A4 pointing, A5 pretend play, A7 comforting, A10 staring) remain as predictors. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single questionnaire modality, augmented by four static fields (age, sex, jaundice, family history). The study belongs to the corpus's questionnaire-tabular branch alongside local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 rather than to any sensor-based branch. [RQ4.1] Automated machine learning by genetic programming: TPOT searched pipelines over classical estimators and returned an ensemble of BernoulliNB and RandomForestClassifier. Six manually specified baselines (SVM, KNN, naive Bayes, logistic regression, decision tree, random forest) were fitted for comparison. No deep learning. [RQ4.2] A nine-field tabular row per child: five binary Q-CHAT items plus age in months, binary sex, binary jaundice and binary family history. The feature-selection step is the analytically decisive move and it runs in an unexpected direction. Items A1, A2, A6, A8 and A9 were removed because they correlated highly with the Q-CHAT-10 score - but the Q-CHAT-10 score is the sum of exactly those items, so high correlation is arithmetic necessity, not redundancy. Deleting them does not remove noise; it removes half of the summands that define the label. The reported 0.83 is thus an estimate of how well five items reconstruct the threshold on all ten, which is why this study lands in the low 80s while local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248, which retained all items, reach 100%. [RQ4.3] Per-class precision, recall and F1 with support, macro and weighted averages, accuracy, a confusion matrix, micro-average ROC 0.87 and macro-average ROC 0.81, and PR values of 0.892 and 0.728. This is a fuller metric set than most of the corpus offers, and unusually the weaker class is reported honestly (non-autistic recall 0.53). Missing: specificity named as such, calibration, predictive values at a stated prevalence, and any confidence interval. The abstract's 78% does not match the 0.83 in the results and comparison tables - the 0.78 in the table is the weighted-average precision/F1 row, so the headline accuracy has been read off the wrong line. [RQ4.4] Pearson item-label correlations guide feature deletion, and the correlation matrix is shown. No post-hoc model explanation - no permutation or Gini importance from the RandomForest component, no partial dependence, no per-case attribution - despite the model family making all of these trivially available. The discussion raises pipeline interpretability as a consideration for AUTOML users but does not act on it. [RQ4.5] A single random 80/20 split: 593 training, 149 test. No cross-validation of the final model, no repeats, no seed, no stratification statement, no interval estimate. TPOT's internal search cross-validates within the training portion, so the pipeline choice is not directly contaminated by the test rows - a cleaner arrangement than most of this corpus - and the manual re-fit with the reported parameters confirms the pipeline is what it claims to be. Two problems dominate nonetheless. First, the validation design cannot address the label's circularity: no split scheme can turn the reconstruction of a checklist threshold into diagnostic accuracy. Second, the test set is 71.1% positive and the paper never states the majority-class baseline, even though it prints it - the SVM comparator's recall of 1.000 at precision 0.718 and accuracy 0.71 is the all-positive classifier, sitting unremarked in the comparison table as though it were a genuine competitor. Read against that baseline, the AUTOML pipeline's contribution is about 12 accuracy points, and the non-autistic recall of 0.53 shows where its errors fall - on precisely the children a screening tool exists to reassure. [RQ5.1] autism spectrum disorder; AUTOML; TPOT. Three terms, one condition and two tooling names - no participants, no validation, no setting, and nothing marking the study's genuine distinguishing feature, which is that the data come from Pakistan. [RQ5.2] Diagnostics 15(15):1859 (MDPI) - an open-access clinical diagnostics journal, with academic editors drawn from the biomedical signal-processing community. The venue's clinical framing did not surface the label circularity or the abstract/table accuracy mismatch in review. [RQ5.3] 2025, published 24 July, 46 days from submission to acceptance including one revision round. Framing is assistive and comparatively restrained: an encouraging approach to improve detection, a first step towards early diagnosis within a few minutes saving time and expense. The novelty claim is placed on the population rather than the accuracy - unlike prior work relying on publicly available datasets from high-income countries, this study uses a locally developed dataset reflecting regional demographics and clinical practices - and that is the paper's real contribution to the corpus. The overreach is concentrated in one sentence claiming the system differentiates intellectual disability disorder from ASD using DSM-5-TR-derived questions, which nothing in the study tests. |
| S-143 | Retrospective analysis of 2,526 images (1,263 ASD, 1,263 non-ASD) from the Kaggle Autistic Children Facial Image Dataset (imrankhan77), an eleventh reuse in this corpus of the web-scraped autism face collection. An 80-20 stratified image-level split gave 2,020 training and 506 test images, with 5-fold cross-validation inside the training portion; the final evaluation used 200 images selected from the test set. Table 1 additionally reports age bands, sex, six ethnicity categories, urban/rural residence and a four-way facial-morphology partition, all summing exactly to 2,526, none of which exists in the source dataset and none of whose derivation is described. | Images were resized to 224x224 and augmented by rotation and scaling; landmarks were located with OpenCV and Dlib and refined by a CNN combined with an Active Shape Appearance Model; the landmark configuration was encoded as a Euclidean graph through graph encoder convolutional networks; Randomized Trees ranked geometric features (upper-face breadth, eye spacing, mid-face length) and XGBoost performed the classification. Training used Adam at learning rate 0.001, batch size 32, 500 epochs, on a Windows 10 desktop with 8 GB RAM and an Intel i3 CPU. | At 500 epochs: accuracy 0.985, precision 0.975, recall 0.987, F1 0.925, AUC 0.98, detection accuracy 0.99, miss rate 0.07, fall-out 0.07, and landmark localisation error 0.9 mm. At 100 epochs the same pipeline reports accuracy 0.60 and AUC 0.6. Comparator figures (SVM AUC 0.74, AdaBoost 0.66, MobileNet-V2 0.64) are quoted from one prior paper rather than measured. | The study's premise and its data are different things: every methodological argument concerns depth information available only from 3D scans, while the input is a folder of 2D web photographs processed with a 2D landmark detector, and the reported millimetre localisation error has no metric basis in such images. The labels are Kaggle folder names with no clinical diagnosis behind them. The demographic and facial-morphology table used to argue that the dataset reflects real-world diversity has no source and no described annotation procedure. The headline metrics come from an unexplained 200-image selection from the test set, while the accompanying confusion matrix totals 300 cases and implies accuracy 0.957, precision 0.940 and recall 0.972 - none matching the reported values - and the reported F1 of 0.925 is incompatible with the reported precision and recall. Feature importances, the one output that would show what the model uses, are described but never given. The limitations section is substantive but addresses 3D imaging hardware the study did not use. | This is the eleventh charted reuse of the web-scraped facial-image corpus, and it extends that branch's pattern in a new direction. The other ten vary in model capacity and split protocol while reporting the same kind of number on the same pictures; this one adds an entire imaging modality (3D scanning), a physical measurement (millimetre landmark error) and a demographic annotation layer that the underlying data cannot support. Alongside local_84bcd4ed, which claimed effectiveness for gelotophobia detection without measuring gelotophobia in anyone, it marks the branch's furthest drift between what is claimed and what was measured. Its 0.985 should be read against local_cd7545e2, where the ADOS-2 itself reaches AUC 0.562 in a clinically meaningful discrimination. Its future-work proposal to deploy facial ASD detection in classrooms, in a paper with no ethics statement and no account of where the children's photographs came from, is the corpus's clearest single example of the gap between the ethics gradient's two ends. | [RQ1.1] There are no participant groups in any meaningful sense. The unit is the image file: 2,526 images, 1,263 labelled ASD and 1,263 labelled non-ASD, downloaded from a Kaggle re-upload of the web-scraped autism face corpus. The number of distinct children behind those images is never asked, and because the corpus is known to contain multiple images of the same faces, the effective sample is unknown and certainly far below 2,526. An 80-20 split gives 2,020 training and 506 test images, but the headline evaluation is then run on 200 images selected from the test set - and the reported confusion matrix sums to 300 (146 + 141 + 9 + 4), agreeing with neither figure. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autism spectrum disease, autism spectrum condition, ASD patients, affected persons, neurotypical youngsters, non-ASD. The framing is medical-pathological throughout, opening with autism spectrum disease is a neurological disease and treating the face as a biomarker of brain abnormality under the phrase the face predicts the brain. Autistic people are described as patients diagnosed with ASD who often behave in the same way. There is no engagement with autistic perspectives, and no acknowledgement that the study is inferring a neurodevelopmental condition from the appearance of children's faces. [RQ1.3] Table 1 presents an unusually complete-looking demographic breakdown: age bands 2-5 / 6-9 / 10-12 years (850 / 880 / 796), sex 1,340 male and 1,186 female, ethnicity Caucasian 750, Asian 620, African 530, Hispanic 370, Middle Eastern 156 and Indigenous 100, urban 1,480 versus rural 1,046, and a partition by facial structure variation into broad upper face 505, wide-set eyes 725, shorter middle face 625 and narrow jawline 671. Every row sums exactly to 2,526. None of this metadata exists in the cited Kaggle dataset, which distributes only two folders of JPEGs; the paper describes no annotation procedure, no rater, and no automatic estimator for age, ethnicity, urban/rural residence or facial morphology category. The table is presented as evidence that the dataset adequately reflects real-world diversity, minimizing biases in ASD classification. Assigning every one of 2,526 web-scraped photographs - including all 1,263 non-ASD ones - to one of four ASD-associated facial morphology categories is not a description of a dataset; it is an unsourced annotation layer that cannot be verified and that the study's own conclusions then rest on. [RQ1.4] No diagnostic confirmation of any kind. The class labels are Kaggle folder names on images gathered from the open web. No clinical assessment, no instrument, no assessor, no date, and no record of who the children are. The paper does not mention this once, and instead treats the labels as ground truth adequate to support claims about automated ASD screening. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure - none is derivable from a photograph, and none is discussed as missing. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to overcome the failure of 2D face scans and eye tracking to capture subtle facial asymmetries by performing 3D facial landmark localisation with a CNN plus active shape appearance model, encoding inter-landmark geometry as a Euclidean graph, and classifying with Randomized-Trees-guided XGBoost. Headline findings at 500 epochs: accuracy 0.985, precision 0.975, recall 0.987, F1 0.925, AUC 0.98, detection accuracy 0.99, miss rate and fall-out both 0.07, and landmark localisation error 0.9 mm. The central problem is that the premise and the data do not meet: the entire methodological argument is about depth information that 3D scans obtain and 2D images lack, while the actual input is a Kaggle folder of 2D web photographs processed with Dlib's 2D 68-point detector at 224x224. A localisation error quoted in millimetres cannot be established from such images at all, since they carry no scale reference and no metric ground truth. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Images were downloaded; computation ran on a Windows 10 desktop with 8 GB RAM and an Intel i3 CPU. That configuration is worth recording because it is not plausible hardware for training a CNN, a shape model and a graph network for 500 epochs on 2,020 images, and no training time is reported. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Static photographs, no stimulus, no interaction, no session. The construct measured is facial morphology, though the abstract describes the target as ASD-related behaviours and the keyword list includes eye tracking, which appears nowhere in the method. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is absent: the declarations section contains only a conflict-of-interest line. There is no approval, no consent statement, and no consideration of the fact that the corpus consists of photographs of identifiable children scraped from the web and redistributed with an autism label attached. The limitations section does raise a genuine ethical point - that false positives cause unnecessary family stress and false negatives delay intervention - which makes the silence on image provenance more conspicuous rather than less. [RQ2.5] OpenCV and Dlib for landmark detection, Python for the pipeline, XGBoost for classification; Windows 10, 8 GB RAM, Intel i3, no GPU. Training settings: Adam, learning rate 0.001 chosen by grid search over [0.0001, 0.01], batch size 32, 500 epochs, 224x224 input, rotation and scaling augmentation. No versions, no seed, no runtime. [RQ2.6] Low. Positives: the source dataset is publicly linked, the split ratio is stated, and the main optimisation settings are listed. Negatives dominate: no code, no seed, no software versions, no architectural specification sufficient to rebuild CNN-ASAM or the GECN, no landmark count, no XGBoost parameters, no identification of which 200 test images produced the headline numbers, and a Table 1 whose annotations have no reconstructible source. Independent replication is impossible in principle, not merely inconvenient. [RQ2.7] Section 5.1 is a real limitations section and, judged in isolation, a thoughtful one: cost and technical barriers to 3D imaging in clinics, the asymmetric harms of false positives and false negatives, residual demographic bias from underrepresented facial morphologies, lighting effects on scan quality, and computational cost precluding real-time use. Judged against the study, it is misaddressed - four of the five items concern 3D scanning hardware the study never used. Nothing is said about the dataset's web provenance and absent diagnostic labels, about the unexplained demographic annotations, about evaluating on a hand-selected 200-image subset, about the confusion matrix that sums to 300, or about the fact that all comparator figures are quoted from another paper rather than measured. [RQ2.9] Multimodal extension (3D scans plus voice analysis, eye tracking and movement data); explainability to improve clinical trust and transparency; real-world deployment in classrooms and social interactions on mobile or edge devices; robustness to lighting, expression and morphological variation. The classroom-deployment proposal is worth flagging - it would place automated facial ASD screening in schools, applied to children who have not consented and on the basis of a model trained on web-scraped photographs with no diagnostic labels. [RQ3.1] Static facial morphology rather than behaviour: inter-landmark geometry and facial asymmetry, operationalised as upper-face breadth, eye spacing, mid-face length and jawline shape, over landmarks at the eye corners, eyebrows, nose tip, mouth corners and jaw outline. The theoretical warrant offered is that discrepancies in facial landmarks between those with ASD and those without indicate underlying variances in brain development. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single image modality. The architecture stacks several representations of the same photograph (CNN features, shape-appearance model, landmark graph, boosted trees), which the paper presents as integrating multiple facial features but which is pipeline depth rather than multimodality. Genuine multimodal fusion with voice, gaze and movement is deferred to future work. [RQ4.1] A four-stage hybrid: CNN with Active Shape Appearance Model for landmark localisation; a Euclidean graph over the landmarks encoded by graph encoder convolutional networks; Randomized Trees for feature importance; XGBoost for the final binary decision. Each stage is motivated by a stated deficiency of prior work, in the now-standard architecture-stacking rhetoric of this literature, but no ablation isolates any stage's contribution. [RQ4.2] Nominally a 3D landmark graph; actually a 2D landmark configuration from Dlib applied to 224x224 web photographs, with rotation and scaling augmentation. The depth channel that the entire introduction argues is essential does not exist in the data. This mismatch propagates into the results: the reported landmark localisation error falling from 2.5 mm at 100 epochs to 0.9 mm at 500 epochs is a physical measurement that no part of the input can support, since the images have neither metric calibration nor ground-truth 3D landmark positions. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, loss, AUC, detection accuracy (reported separately from accuracy and never defined), miss rate, fall-out, millimetre localisation error, and a confusion matrix. The abstract claims excellent specificity but no specificity value appears. The internal arithmetic does not hold: the confusion matrix reports 146 true non-ASD, 141 true ASD, 9 false positives and 4 false negatives, summing to 300 cases although the stated final evaluation set is 200 images and the test split is 506. Those cell counts give accuracy 287/300 = 0.957, precision 141/150 = 0.940 and recall 141/145 = 0.972 - none of which match the reported 0.985, 0.975 and 0.987. Separately, F1 is given as 0.925 while precision and recall are 0.975 and 0.987, whose harmonic mean is 0.981; no combination of the reported figures is mutually consistent. [RQ4.4] Claimed but not delivered. Randomized Trees are described at length as revealing which facial features are most relevant for distinguishing between ASD and non-ASD individuals, yet not a single importance value, ranking or plot is reported - the one output that would have shown whether the model attends to facial geometry or to image-provenance artefacts. Explainability is then listed as future work, in a paper whose central claim is that specific facial measurements carry diagnostic information. [RQ4.5] An 80-20 stratified image-level split (2,020 / 506) with 5-fold cross-validation inside the training portion. The cross-validation placement is correct in principle and better than most of this branch. Four problems undo it. First, the split is image-level, not child-level, on a corpus known to contain repeated faces, so the same child can appear on both sides. Second, augmentation by rotation and scaling is described as part of preprocessing rather than as applied within training folds only. Third, and most serious, the headline numbers do not come from the 506-image test set at all: 200 images (100 ASD, 100 non-ASD) were selected from the test set for the final evaluation, with no selection rule stated, which is the definition of a hand-picked evaluation subset - and the accompanying confusion matrix nonetheless totals 300. Fourth, every reported metric is presented as a monotone function of epoch count with the maximum always at the largest value tried (500), and no criterion determined where to stop, so the reported figures are the best point on a curve rather than the output of a prespecified procedure. The cross-validation folds, having been run, are never reported as a mean and standard deviation. [RQ5.1] Facial landmark detection; autism spectrum condition detection; 3D facial landmark; convolutional neural network; eye tracking. The last is a keyword for a modality the study does not use, and 3D facial landmark describes data the study does not have. [RQ5.2] Sadhana 51(1):30 - the Indian Academy of Sciences' general engineering-sciences journal, not a clinical or specialist vision venue. This is relevant to the review's venue analysis: the mismatch between a 2D Kaggle photo set and a paper about 3D scanning, the unsourced demographic table, the absent ethics statement and the internally inconsistent confusion matrix all survived a 324-day review cycle at a general engineering journal. [RQ5.3] Received 4 October 2024, revised 13 March 2025, accepted 24 August 2025 - the longest review cycle among the recently charted studies, and by far the least effective. Framing is diagnostic-replacement with an explicit efficiency argument: enabling more accurate and automated ASD screening, reducing reliance on subjective assessments, and facilitating timely interventions. Positioning is entirely comparative against numbers quoted from a single prior paper, with the contribution expressed as a higher AUC (0.98 against 0.74, 0.66 and 0.64) rather than as an estimate of anything. |
| S-144 | Prospective single-site study at Dakshinya Autistic School, Guntur, India. Forty children aged 8-12 with an existing ASD diagnosis (CARS >= 30, DSM-5 criteria applied by experienced physicians in the absence of locally available ADOS/ADI-R) were assigned to four severity classes of ten each. Gaze was recorded with an SMI RED250 at 250 Hz during a ten-second silent movie of a woman articulating English letters, after five-point calibration. Fifty frames per child were segmented and both eyes cropped, producing 4,000 images at 416x416, split 70:15:15. A secondary experiment reused the public Saliency4ASD data (14 ASD, 14 TD). | After noise removal, calibration drift correction and fixation/saccade segmentation, four scanpath features (x, y, fixation duration, velocity) were extracted and compared across severity levels using dynamic time warping and MultiMatch, with maximal information coefficient scoring. Sequences were padded and masked and passed to a hybrid CNN-RNN (128-unit LSTM layers, softmax output, batch 64, learning rate 0.0001), with GRU, two-layer LSTM, random forest and XGBoost as comparators across four feature combinations. Implementation in MATLAB on a Windows 10 machine with an Intel i5 and 4 GB RAM. | CNN-RNN with (x, d, y) reached accuracy 97.00%, recall 98.24%, F1 97.04%; (x,y,d,v) 95.23%, (y,x) 94.00%, (x,y,v) 90.00%. GRU and 2-LSTM reached 92%, XGBoost 80.25%, RFC 80.80%. The ablation supports the substantive claim that fixation duration and vertical gaze position discriminate severity while velocity does not. On Saliency4ASD the model is reported at 95.93% (full dataset) and 97.95% (eye dataset). | The 4,000 images derive from 40 children at exactly 100 images each, and the 70:15:15 split is at the image level, so every participant appears in training, validation and test - and the two eyes of a single video frame can fall on opposite sides. Augmentation precedes the split. Cross-validation is claimed four times but never quantified. There is no typically developing group, although the abstract reports gaze differences relative to TD children. The four severity bands in Table 3 are impossible as written: the High class requires CARS above 60 on a scale whose maximum is 60, and the Low and lower-Mild classes lie below the study's own CARS >= 30 eligibility threshold, so the four groups of ten cannot have been produced by the stated rule. Sex is never reported; the Gesell Developmental Scale is collected but never analysed; specificity, FDR and FOR are defined but never given; the stimulus is ten seconds in one section and two minutes in another; a placeholder reading 8-10 children aged x years survives in the introduction; and the literature review carries citations on building energy consumption and distributed generation that belong to a different manuscript. | This study occupies an unusual position in the review. Methodologically it repeats the corpus's dominant failure - a frame-level split that cannot separate participants, here in its most mechanical form, with a constant 100 crops per child - and its 97% belongs with the leakage-inflated figures rather than with local_7d7f1fcc's participant-level 82.5%. But it is also one of the few eye-tracking papers to do genuine behavioural analysis rather than benchmark chasing: the four-way feature ablation and the DTW/MultiMatch contrast produce a falsifiable claim about which aspect of gaze carries severity information (continuous attention, not transitions), and the paper is candid in its abstract that generalisability remains untested. Its ethics reporting - a named committee with a decision reference, parental consent, and a separate publication-specific consent for participants' details and images - places it near the responsible end of the review's ethics gradient with local_7d7f1fcc and local_4b02df7c, and its account of why ADOS and ADI-R were unavailable is the corpus's clearest statement of the infrastructural constraints under which much of this literature is produced. It is the best available illustration that leakage and scientific seriousness are independent axes. | [RQ1.1] Forty children, all with an existing ASD diagnosis, recruited from Dakshinya Autistic School in Guntur, India, and divided into four severity classes of exactly ten each: low, mild, medium and high. There is no typically developing comparison group, which matters because the abstract nonetheless reports that children with ASD exhibit unique and highly individualized gaze patterns when compared to TD children - a comparison the design cannot support. The only TD data in the paper belong to the separate public Saliency4ASD set (14 ASD, 14 TD) used in a side experiment. Two internal inconsistencies affect the count: the introduction states that in the initial training we enrolled a group of 8-10 children aged x years, with the placeholder x left in the published text, and the analysis unit is not the child but the cropped eye image - 50 frames x 2 eyes x 40 children = 4,000 images, which is what the 70:15:15 split partitions. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, ASD children, autism applicants, participants, TD children, neurotypical. The paper is one of the few in the corpus to define neurotypical explicitly and to note that it refers to individuals whose neurological development conforms to societal norms and expectations - a formulation that recognises the norm as social rather than natural. Elsewhere the register slips (autism applicants as a table heading; the severity ladder low/mild/medium/high applied to children rather than to symptoms). The introduction is unusual in this corpus for framing the research motivation partly around reducing stigma, promoting inclusion, and improving educational and employment outcomes rather than solely around detection. [RQ1.3] Thin. Age is given only as the 8-12 eligibility band, with no mean, SD or per-class distribution. Sex is not reported at all - not even a total male/female count - despite forty children being individually recruited and consented. Nothing on socioeconomic status, language, verbal ability or schooling level, and no per-severity-class characteristics of any kind. The Gesell Developmental Scale is said to have been used to relate eye-tracking data to behavioural and clinical outcomes, but no GDS number appears anywhere in the article. [RQ1.4] Well handled and honestly reported. Diagnoses were made by experienced physicians applying DSM-5 criteria together with CARS scores, and the paper states plainly why gold-standard instruments were not used: ADI-R and ADOS evaluations are not widely available in India. That candour about a real infrastructural constraint compares favourably with the many studies in this corpus that simply assert diagnosis or inherit labels from a download. What undermines it is the severity banding rather than the diagnosis: eligibility required CARS >=30, yet Table 3 assigns ten children to a Low class defined as CARS <=20 and ten more to a Mild class spanning 20 to 40, and a High class defined as CARS >60 when the scale's maximum is 60. The four equal groups cannot have been generated by the stated rule, and the actual CARS distribution is never shown. [RQ1.5] CARS is the only reported measure, and it is the label rather than a covariate. The Gesell Developmental Scale is named but never reported. No IQ, adaptive-behaviour, language or comorbidity data. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to replace largely manual, unscalable eye-tracking analysis with an automated scanpath-based method that classifies autism severity into four levels, and to characterise how gaze features vary across those levels using DTW and MultiMatch similarity. Headline findings: CNN-RNN with features (x, d, y) reaches accuracy 97.00%, recall 98.24%, F1 97.04%, against GRU 92%, 2-LSTM 92%, XGBoost 80.25% and RFC 80.80%. The more interesting finding is the feature ablation: velocity contributes least, and the authors conclude that it is the continuous attention process, as opposed to the transition phases, that reflects atypical visual behaviour - with differences concentrated in attention duration and vertical gaze distribution. [RQ2.2] A single special school (Dakshinya Autistic School, Guntur) supplying participants, with ethics oversight from Government Medical College, Guntur, and analysis at VIT-AP University. Recording used a five-point calibration then passive viewing. Setting is described adequately for the acquisition but the recording room, examiner and session conditions are not characterised, and there is no discussion of whether recording conditions varied across severity groups. [RQ2.3] Passive viewing of a ten-second silent movie in which a young Asian woman articulates the English letters, chosen on the reasoning - well argued from the prior literature reviewed - that a speaking face is a more discriminating stimulus than a static one, since gaze duration on inner facial features is reduced specifically while the face is speaking. The stimulus choice is one of the better-motivated in the corpus. Against that, the workflow section describes classifying autism severity from a 2-min ET video, which contradicts the ten-second stimulus and is never reconciled. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session, no follow-up. Ethics is a genuine strength: approval from the Government Medical College Guntur Ethics Committee with a stated decision reference (IRB-2024-0057), written parental informed consent before participation, and separate written consent for publication of participants' details and any accompanying images. That second, publication-specific consent places this study at the responsible end of the review's ethics gradient, alongside local_7d7f1fcc and well away from studies that report no ethics statement at all. [RQ2.5] SMI RED250 portable eye tracker at 250 Hz, 1024x768 display, stated spatial resolution 0.05, five-point calibration, with calibration drift correction applied in preprocessing. Fixation/saccade segmentation by dispersion-threshold and velocity-threshold algorithms. Classification implemented in MATLAB on Windows 10 with an Intel Core i5 and 4 GB RAM; frame segmentation in Python. The hardware is implausibly modest for the described deep models and no training time is given. [RQ2.6] Mixed. The acquisition protocol is reported in enough detail to be repeated - device, sampling rate, calibration procedure, stimulus, display parameters, eligibility criteria - and the four feature sets and their ablation are fully specified, so the study's most interesting result could be re-tested. Everything downstream is opaque: no code, no seed, no MATLAB version, no convolutional architecture, no epoch count, no fold count for the cross-validation that is repeatedly asserted but never reported, and no access route for the 4,000-image dataset the paper announces as a contribution for researchers and developers to leverage. A further reproducibility concern is the literature review, which contains a run of citations on building energy consumption, distributed generation, solar-equipped neighbourhoods and electric vehicles - and the abbreviation list correspondingly defines DB as Design builder, DG as Distributed generation and ICME as Integrated Computational Materials Engineering. These belong to a different paper and indicate that portions of the manuscript were assembled rather than written for this study. [RQ2.7] Three limitations are stated: small-scale datasets typical of ASD research; the practice of retaining valid scanpaths across paradigms, which produces inconsistent sample sizes across subjects; and eye-tracking reliability problems from calibration precision, subject cooperation and equipment limits. All three are real and specific. Unmentioned: that the 70:15:15 split is at the eye-image level so every participant appears in all three subsets; that there is no TD group despite the abstract's TD comparison; that the CARS bands defining the four classes are arithmetically impossible and inconsistent with the eligibility threshold; that the external comparison is against a different task on a different dataset; that specificity, FDR and FOR are defined but never reported; and that the asserted cross-validation is never quantified. [RQ2.9] Weight DTW by fixation duration to improve scanpath alignment; address calibration precision and data-integrity problems in eye-tracking to improve reliability and accessibility for screening; and evaluate on an independent dataset to assess generalizability and precision. The last is stated in the abstract itself, which is an unusually forthright acknowledgement that the reported figures are not yet generalisation estimates. [RQ3.1] Visual attention during viewing of a speaking face, decomposed into fixation position (x, y), fixation duration and inter-fixation velocity, and into scanpath shape compared by DTW and MultiMatch. The behavioural claims that emerge are specific and testable: attention duration and vertical gaze distribution differ most across severity levels, velocity least, and children with ASD show highly individualised rather than merely reduced gaze patterns. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion - eye tracking alone. There is a within-modality fusion of two representations of the same recording (scanpath sequences for the RNN path, cropped eye images for the CNN path), which is what the hybrid designation refers to. The Gesell Developmental Scale was collected and could have supported a genuine behavioural-clinical fusion, but no GDS result is reported. [RQ4.1] Supervised sequence classification. Primary model is a hybrid CNN-RNN combining convolutional feature extraction with GRU and LSTM recurrence; comparators are GRU, a two-layer LSTM, BiLSTM, random forest and XGBoost. LSTM layers use 128 hidden units into a fully connected softmax; batch size 64, cross-entropy loss, learning rate 0.0001. The classification section describes the output as softmax regression for class probability prediction in binary classification although the task is four-class throughout. [RQ4.2] Two representations. (i) Variable-length scanpath sequences over four features - x, y, fixation duration d, velocity v - padded to maximum length with a masking mechanism, evaluated in four combinations. (ii) 4,000 cropped eye images at 416x416, fifty frames per child times left and right eye, each labelled with subject ID, frame number, severity band and eye side. The image-level representation is what the 70:15:15 split partitions, and it is where the validity problem originates: with a fixed 100 images per child, the split cannot separate participants even in principle. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, false discovery rate, false omission rate and AUC are all defined by equation, which reads as thorough; only accuracy, recall and F1 are then reported for the within-study experiments, and specificity, FDR and FOR appear as numbers nowhere. A four-class confusion matrix is shown and discussed sensibly - low and medium separate better than mild and high. The Saliency4ASD table reports accuracy and AUC together (95.93/95.82 and 97.95/97.84). The 25% four-class chance level is never stated, and no metric carries an interval. [RQ4.4] The strongest interpretability work among the eye-tracking studies charted so far, and the reason this paper is worth more than its headline number. Maximal information coefficient scores rank individual scanpath features and the similarity measures; a systematic four-way feature-set ablation shows accuracy moving from 90.00% ((x,y,v)) to 97.00% ((x,d,y)) to 95.23% ((x,y,d,v)); and from that pattern the authors argue that velocity is uninformative for severity while fixation duration and vertical gaze position carry the signal. They further contrast the two similarity metrics, finding MultiMatch less sensitive to subtle temporal or spatial change and DTW more sensitive to vertical gaze distribution. These are claims about gaze behaviour that could be falsified by another laboratory, which is rare in this corpus. Their evidential weight is nonetheless limited by the same leakage that inflates the accuracies: an ablation computed under an image-level split ranks features by how well they support participant recognition as much as by how well they support severity discrimination. [RQ4.5] The design is a 70:15:15 partition of 4,000 eye images derived from 40 children at exactly 100 images per child (50 frames, left and right eye). Because the per-child image count is constant and the split is at the image level, every participant is present in the training, validation and test subsets simultaneously; more finely still, the left and right eye of the same video frame - two crops of one instant of one recording - can land on opposite sides. This is frame-level leakage of the same kind documented in the video, EEG-epoch, thermal, cry and facial-image branches, and it is sufficient to explain a 97% four-class result from 40 children. Three further weaknesses compound it. Augmentation by rotation and shearing is described as a dataset-preparation step applied before partitioning. Cross-validation is asserted four separate times as ensuring robustness, but no fold count, no per-fold result and no variance is ever reported, so it cannot be assessed and may not have been run on the final model. And the external comparison in Table 7 places this study's four-class severity accuracies (95.93%, 97.95%) beside Saliency4ASD entries (74.22%, 65.41%, 61.62%) that solve a different, binary ASD-versus-TD task on different data - the numbers are not commensurable, and the higher figure is not evidence of a better method. To the authors' credit, the abstract itself concedes that further evaluation on an independent dataset will assess the generalizability and precision of the model, which is the correct reading of their own result. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; CNN-RNN hybrid network; Early diagnosis; Eye-tracking data; Machine learning; Scanpath analysis. Method- and modality-centred, with scanpath analysis correctly signalling the paper's actual analytic contribution; nothing about severity, participants or validation. [RQ5.2] Neural Computing and Applications 37(33):27631-27654, in a special issue drawn from the 2023 India International Congress on Computational Intelligence. Special-issue routing is relevant to the review's venue analysis: the impossible CARS bands, the absent TD group behind a TD claim in the abstract, the surviving x placeholder in the participant count, and a literature review containing building-energy and distributed-generation citations all passed review in 53 days. [RQ5.3] Received 12 August 2024, accepted 4 October 2024, published online 4 December 2024, issued 2025. Framing is assistive-to-transformative: the work is said to show how ML and eye tracking can transform the diagnosis and treatment of autism and to set a new standard in the field, with the method described as capturing spatial and temporal dynamics with unprecedented accuracy. Set against that rhetoric, the paper is also one of the few in the corpus whose abstract states outright that generalisability has not yet been assessed, and whose introduction motivates the work partly by stigma reduction, inclusion and long-term quality of life rather than solely by detection throughput. |
| S-145 | Retrospective analysis of the Kaggle Autism Image Data set (cihan063, accessed 22 November 2024) - the twelfth charted reuse in this review of the web-scraped autism facial-image corpus. The paper states 2,926 images in two classes, Normal and Autism, with no demographic information of any kind and no diagnostic labelling behind the folder names. The confusion matrices imply approximately 1,400 images per class, about 2,800 in total. | Images were passed through Gabor filtering, MTCNN face detection, median denoising and Z-score colour normalisation, resized by bicubic interpolation to an unstated resolution, and augmented by rotation, horizontal flip, cropping and brightness variation, with inverse-frequency class weights applied. MobileNetV2 supplied features to an ensemble of an LSTM, a deep belief network of stacked restricted Boltzmann machines and a hybrid-kernel extreme learning machine, whose hyperparameters were selected by the Crested Porcupine Optimizer. Results are reported at 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500 epochs. | Best average performance at 1,000 epochs: accuracy 96.43%, precision 96.44%, recall 96.43%, F-score 96.43%, G-measure 96.43%. Per class: Normal accuracy 95.57%, Autism accuracy 97.29%. A Gabor ablation gives 96.43% with filtering against 92.80% without, at 10.5 versus 26.0 training-time units. Seven literature-quoted comparators fall between 89.55% and 92.64%. | The paper states none. Its reported performance cannot be attributed to a held-out evaluation: the confusion matrices account for essentially the whole dataset and the experimental section describes no train-test division, while a 5-fold cross-validation asserted later in the comparison discussion is reported without a single per-fold value, mean or standard deviation. The headline figure is the maximum over five epoch settings with no selection rule. Labels are Kaggle folder names on photographs of unknown children; the ethics statement declares the study exempt because publicly available datasets were used. The stated 2,926 images contradict the roughly 2,800 implied by the results. An LSTM is applied to single static images with no sequence to model. Image resolution is left as an unfilled placeholder. All seven comparators are quoted from other papers rather than measured. There is no limitations section and no future work. | This is the twelfth charted reuse of the web-scraped facial-image corpus and the branch's terminal case for architectural elaboration. Where local_b9e05a8f and local_0f5a351e used a frozen extractor with a linear classifier and reported around 81%, this study stacks Gabor filtering, MobileNetV2, three heterogeneous classifiers and a metaheuristic optimiser and reports 96.43% - and the branch pattern established across the ten earlier reuses holds exactly: reported accuracy tracks pipeline capacity and evaluation looseness, not signal. It pairs with local_986436f2 as the two most extreme cases in the branch, but in opposite directions: that paper invented demographic and 3D metadata the data cannot carry, while this one reports no participant information at all and never notes the absence. Its ethics statement - that no ethical review was needed because the study did not involve direct experiments on humans, only publicly available Kaggle datasets - is the corpus's most explicit articulation of the reasoning that makes this entire branch possible, and belongs directly beside local_45ef7022 (Ethical Approval. Not required.) at the permissive end of the review's ethics gradient. | [RQ1.1] No participants. The unit is the image: a stated 2,926 facial samples in two classes, Normal and Autism, downloaded from Kaggle. The number of distinct children is unknown and never raised. The stated total does not survive contact with the results: the confusion matrix at 1,000 epochs reports 1,338 correctly recognised normal and 1,362 correctly recognised autism images, which against the per-class accuracies of 95.57% and 97.29% implies about 1,400 images in each class and about 2,800 overall. Those counts also span essentially the whole dataset, which means the reported confusion matrices are not computed on a held-out subset at all. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic children, autistic patients, individuals with ASD, normal controls, Normal class, typically developing children. The pathologising register is unusually strong even for this branch: autism is described as a set of intricate neuro-developmental brain diseases, the comparison class is labelled Normal throughout, and the stated benefit of early recognition is to aid families and parents in superstition and denial. Elsewhere autistic people are said to require treatment and reintegration. There is no autistic or community perspective anywhere in the article. [RQ1.3] None whatsoever. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status or recruitment source - the dataset carries none and the paper requests none. This is notable in comparison with local_986436f2, which reused a sibling of the same corpus and supplied an elaborate demographic table that the data cannot support; here the same absence is simply left unremarked. The abstract's claim about the facial evolution of newborns with ASD is particularly untethered, since nothing in the data identifies any subject's age, let alone a neonate. [RQ1.4] None. Labels are Kaggle folder names on photographs of unknown origin. No clinical assessment, instrument, criterion, assessor, date or provenance record exists for a single image, and the paper does not acknowledge the issue at any point - including in its ethics statement, which cites the dataset's public availability as the reason no ethical review was required. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure, and none obtainable from photographs. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to distinguish facial images of individuals with ASD from normal controls with an ensemble pipeline: Gabor filtering, MobileNetV2 feature extraction, an ensemble of LSTM, deep belief network and hybrid-kernel extreme learning machine, and Crested Porcupine Optimizer hyperparameter selection. Headline findings: average accuracy 96.43%, precision 96.44%, recall 96.43%, F-score 96.43% and G-measure 96.43% at 1,000 epochs, against literature-quoted comparators between 89.55% and 92.64%. The Gabor ablation - the paper's one genuinely executed experiment - gives 96.43% with filtering against 92.80% without, at less than half the training time. [RQ2.2] No setting. Images were downloaded from Kaggle on 22 November 2024; the compute environment is not described at all, and the only timing information is an unlabelled training-time column (10.5 versus 26.0) in the Gabor ablation table. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Static photographs with no stimulus, interaction or session. The construct is facial morphology and texture, justified by the premise that developmental problems affecting face features are often associated with fundamental brain disorders. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics is handled by explicit exemption: the study did not involve direct experiments on humans or the use of human tissue samples, and publicly available Kaggle datasets were used instead. That reasoning treats identifiable photographs of children - carrying a disability label that no clinician assigned - as outside the scope of human-subjects consideration entirely. It is the clearest statement in the corpus of the assumption that makes this branch of the literature possible, and it is stated as a formal declaration rather than in passing. [RQ2.5] None for acquisition. Processing components named: Gabor filter bank, MTCNN face detection, median filter, Z-score colour normalisation, bicubic interpolation, MobileNetV2, LSTM, DBN built from restricted Boltzmann machines, hybrid-kernel ELM, Crested Porcupine Optimizer. No software, versions, seed, hardware or runtime environment is given, and the target image resolution is left as the literal placeholder (X, Y pixels). [RQ2.6] Very low. Some preprocessing choices are specified with real precision - rotation range -15 to 15 degrees, horizontal flips, random crops to 10%, brightness 0.8 to 1.2, inverse-frequency class weights, Z-score channel normalisation - and the source dataset is properly cited with an access date. Everything needed to actually rebuild the system is missing: no code, no libraries, no seed, no image size, no layer configuration, no ensemble combination rule, no CPO search space or budget, no split specification, and a stated sample size that the reported confusion matrices contradict. [RQ2.7] None. The article contains no limitations section, no threats-to-validity discussion, and no caveat of any kind. Nothing is said about the dataset's web provenance, the absence of diagnostic labels, the evaluation counts that span the whole dataset, the epoch-wise selection of the reported figure, or the fact that all comparator numbers are quoted rather than measured. [RQ2.9] None. There is no future-work section. The paper closes on the claim of superiority over existing methods. [RQ3.1] None. No behaviour is observed, elicited or measured. The target is static facial appearance - edges, contours and textures at multiple Gabor orientations and scales, described as capturing intricate details of face characteristics including the eyes, nose and mouth. [RQ3.2] No fusion of modalities - a single image source. What the paper calls an ensemble is three classifiers (LSTM, DBN, HKELM) over one shared MobileNetV2 feature vector from one photograph. The LSTM's inclusion is unexplained: there is no temporal or sequential structure in a single still image for a recurrent model to exploit, and the paper never addresses this. [RQ4.1] A four-stage pipeline: Gabor filtering, MobileNetV2 feature extraction, a heterogeneous ensemble of LSTM, deep belief network and hybrid-kernel extreme learning machine, and metaheuristic hyperparameter selection by the Crested Porcupine Optimizer. This is the corpus's most elaborate architecture stack applied to its simplest and least trustworthy data. Only one component's contribution is actually tested (Gabor filtering); the others are argued for in the conditional - removing MobileNetV2 may result in diminished performance, evaluating individual classifiers against the ensemble might reveal improvements - without those experiments being run. [RQ4.2] Gabor-filtered RGB face crops at an unstated resolution, passed through MTCNN detection, median denoising and Z-score channel normalisation, then encoded as MobileNetV2 features. Augmentation adds rotation, horizontal flip, cropping and brightness variation, described as a preprocessing stage rather than as a training-time operation. Class weighting is applied on the stated grounds of imbalance, although the source Kaggle corpus is balanced by construction and the paper's own confusion matrices imply near-equal class sizes. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F-score and G-measure, per class and averaged, at 500 through 2,500 epochs; ROC curves described qualitatively; a Gabor ablation with training time and a computational-cost index whose units are not given. No specificity, no numeric AUC, no calibration, no predictive values at a stated prevalence, and no confidence interval anywhere. The reported average of 96.43% is not one measurement but the best of five epoch settings, carried into both the abstract and the comparison table against baselines evaluated under unknown conditions in other papers. [RQ4.4] None of the trained model. The Gabor ablation shows that texture filtering helps (96.43% versus 92.80%) but says nothing about what the classifier attends to. No saliency, no attribution, no per-class error analysis beyond the raw confusion counts. In a study whose premise is that specific facial characteristics carry diagnostic information, no facial characteristic is ever identified. [RQ4.5] The validation account is internally contradictory, and this is the study's central defect. The experimental section reports confusion matrices at five epoch settings whose correct-classification counts - 1,338 normal plus 1,362 autism at 1,000 epochs, and comparable figures at the other settings - account for essentially the entire stated dataset. No train-test division is described anywhere in that section. If those matrices are computed over all available images, then every reported metric is a resubstitution figure on the training data. Separately and much later, the comparison discussion asserts that 5-fold cross-validation was applied with 80% training and 20% testing per fold, and that the model consistently attained elevated accuracy and F1 scores across all folds, exhibiting minimal variance - yet not one per-fold number, mean or standard deviation is given, so the claim cannot be checked and does not reconcile with the confusion-matrix counts. On top of that: the reported headline is the best of five epoch settings with no selection criterion or held-out basis; the Crested Porcupine Optimizer searched hyperparameters against an unstated objective on an unstated partition; augmentation is described before any split; and the split, whatever it is, is at the image rather than the child level on a corpus known to repeat faces.
