The comparison in Table 3 sets this study's figure against seven baselines taken from other publications on unstated data and protocols, which is a comparison of numbers rather than of methods. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; ensemble learning; crested porcupine optimizer; facial images; computer-aided diagnosis. Four of five terms name the machinery; none names participants, validation or setting. [RQ5.2] Computers, Materials & Continua 83(2) (Tech Science Press) - a broad-scope open-access computing journal covering materials, computing and engineering. This is the review's clearest venue-mismatch case: a diagnostic claim about children, resting on unlabelled web photographs and an explicit ethics exemption, published in a journal with no clinical review capacity, with no limitations section and no future work, in 81 days. [RQ5.3] 2025, published 16 April, 81 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is unqualified computer-aided diagnosis, with an unusual and revealing justification: early recognition is said to be significant to aid families and parents in superstition and denial, and AI is credited with aiding the treatment and reintegration of autistic patients. The contribution is expressed purely as a higher number than seven quoted baselines. There is no limitations section, no future work, and no acknowledgement that any part of the claim is provisional - the paper's closing position is that the method is superior, full stop. |
| S-146 | Retrospective secondary analysis of an uncited open-source movement dataset from Mendeley Data comprising 44 examples - 22 individuals diagnosed with ASD and 22 non-autistic individuals - with 120 kinematic features and 48 observational behavioural/eye-movement features per instructional segment, organised into four subsets (K_General, K_Attention, L_General, L_Attention). No age, sex or other characteristic of the 44 people is reported, and no acquisition task or setting is described. | Missing values were replaced with the mean of each respective class; the text both denies and asserts MinMax normalisation. Pearson correlation was used to screen multicollinearity, and an XGBoost model with SHAP summary plots ranked features for a reduced-feature scenario. A simulated federated setup ran three clients over three rounds with two local DNNs each (a shallow dense binary network and a five-hidden-layer network) aggregated by FedAvg into a global model, evaluated with all features and with SHAP-selected features. | The abstract reports L_General as best, with Client 2 at 99.99% accuracy and Client 1 at 88%; the contributions list gives 0.88 to Client 3; the results section reports the best configuration (Local Model 2, Client 2, L_General, all features) at accuracy 1.00 and F1 1.00. Across the full grid, all-features accuracies range from 0.01 to 0.88, and SHAP selection improves some client-subset pairs while sharply degrading others. | The study states none. Every reported figure rests on nine test cases: the confusion matrices contain nine cases (6 true negatives, 2 true positives, 1 false negative, 0 false positives) and every tabulated accuracy is a multiple of one ninth, so the 99.99% headline is nine of nine correct and the standard error on any of these estimates is about 17 percentage points. Missing values were imputed with the class mean, conditioning the predictor matrix on the outcome, and SHAP feature selection was run over the whole dataset - both before any split. No split ratio, seed, cross-validation or repetition is reported, and the client partition of the 44 examples is unstated. The preprocessing description contradicts itself on normalisation; the dataset is called openly available but is uncited and the formal statement says it is available on request; the headline is attributed to different clients in three places. There is no ethics or consent statement of any kind in a paper whose thesis is the privacy-preserving handling of sensitive health data. | This study is the review's sharpest illustration of metric density substituting for evidence: dozens of accuracy, precision, recall and F1 values across four feature subsets, three clients, two models and two scenarios, all generated from 44 people and evaluated nine cases at a time. It also supplies the corpus's only late-fusion multimodal architecture - separate kinematic and eye-movement branches merged into a global model - a design that is structurally better than the feature-concatenation approaches elsewhere but that cannot be assessed at this sample size. Its class-conditional mean imputation places it with local_3e88f3ce, local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 in the target-leakage group, by a mechanism none of those shares. Most distinctively, it inverts the corpus's usual ethics failure: rather than omitting ethics because the data came from the web, it builds an entire privacy-engineering framework around sensitive health data - invoking GDPR and HIPAA - while never stating any ethical basis, approval or consent for its own reuse of 44 identifiable people's behavioural recordings. Federated learning is offered as a governance solution in a paper with no governance statement. | [RQ1.1] Forty-four examples in total - 22 individuals diagnosed with ASD and 22 non-autistic individuals - taken from an open-source movement dataset on Mendeley Data that is neither named nor cited. Nothing else is known about them: not their age band (the introduction discusses both children and adults without saying which these are), not their sex, not their recruitment, not the country, not the year. The 44 examples were divided among three simulated federated clients by an unstated rule, and each client's evaluation rests on nine test cases - a figure that appears nowhere in the text and is recoverable only from the confusion matrices (6 true negatives, 2 true positives, 1 false negative, 0 false positives) and from the fact that every accuracy in Tables 2 through 5 is a multiple of one ninth. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, individuals with ASD, autistic individuals, non-autistic individuals, ASD patients. The register is comparatively neutral for this corpus: the comparison group is called non-autistic rather than normal, autistic individuals is used alongside person-first phrasing, and the introduction notes that the spectrum makes each individual's experience unique. There is no autistic-community engagement and no discussion of how the people in the dataset were labelled or whether they knew their data would be reused. [RQ1.3] None. Not a single demographic characteristic is reported for the 44 people - no age, sex, ethnicity, geography, language or clinical background. This is a striking omission in a paper whose entire argument concerns the responsible, privacy-preserving handling of sensitive personal health data: the study invokes GDPR and HIPAA in its abbreviation table while reporting nothing at all about the individuals whose data it processes, and without asking whether they consented to this reuse. [RQ1.4] Not described. Labels come as a binary field in the downloaded dataset (1 autistic, 0 non-autistic). No diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor, setting or date is reported for either group, and the source dataset's own procedures are not summarised. The comparison group's non-autistic status is likewise asserted with no screening evidence. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, adaptive behaviour, language, severity or comorbidity measure of any kind. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a secure, privacy-preserving ASD diagnostic framework combining multimodal kinematic and eye-movement data, deep neural networks, federated learning with FedAvg, and SHAP-based explanation, evaluated in two scenarios (all features versus SHAP-selected features) across three clients and three rounds. The reported headline is that L_General gives the best results with an accuracy of 99.99% and F1 of 99.99%, described as flawless classification performance. The substantive finding, once the tables are read, is different and more interesting: performance is wildly unstable. Across the four feature subsets and three clients, accuracies in the all-features scenario range from 0.01 to 0.88, and SHAP-based feature selection helps some client-subset combinations and badly hurts others (Client 2 on K_General rises from 0.22 to 0.66 while Client 2 on K_Attention falls from 0.55 to 0.33). The paper reports this variability but attributes it to data heterogeneity rather than to the estimator's variance at n=9. [RQ2.2] None described. No acquisition setting, no laboratory, no clinic, no country of origin for the data. The federated clients are simulated - the paper says they represent independent clients such as hospitals or personal devices, but all three run on the authors' own partition of one 44-row file, so no distributed data actually exists. [RQ2.3] Not reported. Features are said to be extracted per instructional segment, and the eye-movement subsets are labelled General and Attention, but no task, stimulus, instruction, session length or protocol is described anywhere in the article. A reader cannot say what the participants were doing when the kinematic and gaze data were recorded. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethics reporting is absent - no approval, no consent, no exemption statement, and the word ethic does not appear in the article. This absence is the paper's most consequential internal contradiction: the entire contribution is framed as a privacy-and-security advance for sensitive health data, invoking GDPR and HIPAA, yet the study reuses identifiable behavioural recordings of 44 people without stating any ethical basis for doing so. Federated learning here protects data from a hypothetical future adversary while the actual governance question - whether these 44 people agreed to this - is never raised. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation is named, because the data were downloaded and the source acquisition is not summarised. Computational components: a shallow DNN with dense layers, ReLU and dropout (Local Model 1), a five-hidden-layer DNN described as multi-class although the task is binary (Local Model 2), FedAvg aggregation, XGBoost with SHAP for feature ranking, MinMaxScaler. No library, version, seed, hardware or runtime. [RQ2.6] Very low, and internally contradictory on a basic point. The preprocessing section states that each feature is preserved in its original, continuous form without normalization and then, one paragraph later, that the MinMax scaler was employed for scaling and the dataset normalised; the pseudocode also calls MinMaxScaler. The dataset is described as openly available on Mendeley but is given no name, DOI or URL, and the formal data-availability statement instead says the data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. Code is available on demand only. No split ratio, no seed, no client partition rule, no layer widths, no learning rate, no epochs. The paper also refers to Pearson correlation analysis by the abbreviation PCA, which elsewhere denotes principal component analysis. [RQ2.7] None. There is no limitations section. Nothing is said about 44 examples being the entire dataset, about nine-case test sets, about accuracies quantised to multiples of one ninth, about class-mean imputation using the outcome label, about the contradictory normalisation account, about the absent ethics statement, or about the three federated clients being partitions of a single small file rather than independent institutions. [RQ2.9] A single paragraph proposing Physical Neural Networks based on stacked intelligent metasurfaces to process multimodal sensory data at the hardware level, reducing computational overhead and enhancing privacy through localised data handling. Computational overhead is not a difficulty encountered anywhere in a study that fits shallow networks to 44 rows, and the proposal addresses none of the study's actual weaknesses. [RQ3.1] Movement kinematics and eye-movement behaviour, split into general and attention-specific variants: 120 kinematic features and 48 observational-behavioural features per instructional segment, with the attention-specific eye subset described as covering fixation and saccade characteristics. Because no task is described and no feature is ever named, the behavioural content of the study is opaque - the reader cannot identify a single behaviour that distinguishes the groups. [RQ3.2] This is one of the few charted studies with genuine cross-modal structure, and its fusion design is worth recording precisely. Two local models operate on separate files, one specialising in kinematic features and one in eye-movement features; their outputs are merged and passed to a global model with its own dense layers and dropout. That is late fusion at the model level, in contrast to the feature-concatenation fusion used elsewhere in the corpus. The design is sound in outline. What it cannot support is inference: with 44 examples divided among three clients and evaluated on nine cases, no comparison between the unimodal and fused configurations is distinguishable from noise, and the paper never makes that comparison explicitly in any case. [RQ4.1] Supervised deep learning in a simulated federated architecture: two local DNNs per client (a shallow dense network for binary classification, and a five-hidden-layer network described as multi-class), three clients, three communication rounds, FedAvg aggregation into a global model. XGBoost with SHAP serves as a separate feature-ranking model. No classical baseline is fitted for comparison. [RQ4.2] Tabular vectors of 120 kinematic or 48 behavioural/eye features per instructional segment, organised into four named subsets (K_General, K_Attention, L_General, L_Attention). Preprocessing includes one step that deserves separate note: missing values and anomalies were replaced with the mean value of each respective class - imputation conditioned on the outcome label, computed over the whole dataset before any split. Where a feature has missing values at different rates in the two groups, that step writes the label into the feature matrix directly, and it is a sufficient mechanism to produce a nine-of-nine result on its own. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1, reported per client, per feature subset, per local model and for the global model in both scenarios. No specificity, no AUC, no calibration, no predictive values and no confidence interval anywhere. The metric grid is dense and the reported values are internally revealing: they take only the values 0.11, 0.22, 0.33, 0.44, 0.55, 0.66, 0.77, 0.88 and 1.00, which are the achievable accuracies on nine test cases. The headline of 99.99% is that same 9/9 restated, and the paper describes it as flawless classification performance. One tabulated value, Client 3 on L_Attention at 0.01, is not a multiple of one ninth and is presumably a typographic corruption of 0.11. [RQ4.4] SHAP over an XGBoost surrogate produces a summary plot ranking feature importance, and the ranked features define the second experimental scenario. The intent is right and the framework is one of the review's few genuine attempts at explanation before rather than after modelling. Two things undercut it. First, no feature is ever named in the text, so the explanation is reported as an activity rather than a result and nothing can be learned about which movements or gaze behaviours matter. Second, SHAP values estimated from 44 rows are not stable quantities, and the all-features versus selected-features comparison bears this out - selection helps some client-subset combinations and severely harms others with no interpretable pattern, which the paper attributes to data heterogeneity rather than to sampling variance. [RQ4.5] This is the review's clearest case of a metric grid resting on almost nothing. The entire empirical base is 44 examples. Those are divided among three simulated federated clients by a rule that is never stated, and each client's reported accuracy is computed on nine test cases - a number that appears nowhere in the text and must be reconstructed from the confusion matrices (6+2+1+0 = 9; 6+3 = 9) and from the quantisation of every tabulated accuracy to multiples of one ninth. On nine cases the standard error of an accuracy estimate is roughly 17 percentage points, so the difference between the paper's best result (1.00, reported as 99.99%) and its worst (0.11) is barely more than sampling noise, and the four-subset by three-client by two-scenario by two-model grid amounts to dozens of comparisons among estimates that cannot be distinguished from each other. Three further problems compound it. Class-conditional mean imputation was applied across the full dataset, writing outcome information into the predictor matrix. SHAP-based feature selection was likewise performed on the whole dataset before the federated runs. And no split ratio, seed, cross-validation or repetition is reported, so none of the figures carries a variance estimate. Finally, the headline itself is unstable across the paper: the abstract credits 99.99% to Client 2 and 88% to Client 1, the contributions list credits 88% to Client 3, and the results section reports the best configuration as accuracy 1.00 - three descriptions of the same experiment. The framing of nine correct classifications out of nine as flawless classification performance and as high diagnostic accuracy suitable for healthcare applications is not supportable at any sample size this study has. [RQ5.1] Multimodal data; Kinematic features; Eye movement; Federated learning; Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI); Security and privacy; Autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Seven terms, five of them naming machinery or infrastructure properties; the condition appears last and the participants not at all. [RQ5.2] Complex & Intelligent Systems 11:173 (Springer) - a computational-intelligence journal. Relevant to the review's venue analysis in a specific way: this is a privacy-and-governance paper by construction, invoking GDPR and HIPAA, published without an ethics statement of any kind, and its headline accuracy of 99.99% on nine test cases passed review over 126 days. [RQ5.3] 2025, published online 19 February, 126 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is infrastructural rather than clinical - the contribution is offered as a viable solution for healthcare applications involving sensitive data that preserves privacy and security while maintaining high diagnostic accuracy. The claim of high diagnostic accuracy rests on nine test cases; the claim of privacy preservation rests on a federated architecture simulated over a single downloaded file; and the paper's own governance obligations - stating an ethical basis for reusing 44 people's behavioural recordings - go unmet. It is the corpus's clearest example of privacy engineering standing in for research ethics. |
| S-147 | Prospective primary data collection in Banda Aceh, Indonesia. Thirty-five children with autism from a Special Elementary School and 35 typically developing children from a State Elementary School were photographed individually in a controlled studio - 2x2 m capture area, black curtains, 25-27 degrees C, sessions 09:00-12:00, subject one metre from a tripod-mounted Canon EOS M-100 at ISO 800, f/5.6, 1/25 s. Each child produced flat, smiling and sad expressions with five photographs each, giving 15 images per child and 1,050 in total (525 per class). Children with acute illness were excluded from both groups; autistic children with intellectual disability, cerebral palsy or Down syndrome were also excluded. | Images were cropped to 1:1, resized to 224x224, rescaled and augmented (rotation 20 degrees, shifts 0.2, shear 0.2, zoom 0.2, horizontal flip) on the training generator. A convolutional neural network with a sigmoid output was trained; no architecture, optimiser, learning rate, batch size or epoch count is reported. The data were divided 70/20/10 at the image level into 369/105/51 images per class. | On 102 test images the model achieved accuracy 0.90, precision 0.92, recall 0.88 and F1 0.90, from a confusion matrix of 47 and 45 correct with 4 false positives and 6 false negatives. Training and validation accuracy are reported as reaching nearly 100% within a few epochs. | The study states none. Two problems dominate. Labels are school placements, not diagnoses - the autism group is defined by attendance at a special school and the comparison group by attendance at a state school - so autism status is perfectly confounded with institution and no diagnostic instrument, criterion or assessor is reported for any child. And the 70/20/10 split is at the image level over a fixed 15 photographs per child, so five near-identical shots of the same child in the same expression under identical lighting are distributed across training, validation and test; with 70 children, a participant-level split was available and unused. Beyond these: the three deliberately elicited expressions are pooled and never analysed separately, discarding the study's only behavioural variable; the CNN architecture is entirely unspecified despite custom layer design being claimed as a contribution; the number of augmentations generated was not recorded; no confidence interval accompanies a 102-image estimate; acquisition parameters conflict between the narrative and Table I (age 3-14 versus 5-15, humidity 40-45% versus 50-60%, lighting 30 W versus 22 W, acclimation 10-15 minutes versus 3 minutes); and the testing workflow describes classifying a stunted child versus a normal child, terminology carried over from unrelated research. | This study matters to the review as the counterexample within the facial-image branch. Twelve charted papers reuse the same web-scraped Kaggle corpus with no provenance, no demographics and no consent; this one recruits 70 children through two schools, obtains ethics approval with a code number, takes parental consent, has teachers accompany the children, applies prespecified exclusion criteria, and publishes an acquisition protocol detailed enough to replicate - room, lighting, humidity, camera body, ISO, aperture, exposure, distance and session hours. It then reports 90%, squarely inside the 81-99.8% range the Kaggle reuses occupy, which is itself informative: careful acquisition does not by itself produce an interpretable number when the split is at the image level and the label is a school roll. It sits alongside local_7d7f1fcc as evidence that data-collection quality and validation validity are separable, and its unanalysed expression manipulation is the corpus's clearest instance of a designed behavioural factor being collected and then discarded. | [RQ1.1] Seventy children in two recruited groups: 35 with autism from a Special Elementary School in Banda Aceh and 35 typically developing children from a State Elementary School in the same city. Each contributed 15 photographs (three expressions x five shots), giving 1,050 images split evenly 525/525. The analysis unit throughout is the image, not the child: the 70/20/10 division yields 369/105/51 images per class, and the reported metrics rest on 102 test images drawn from the same 70 children who supplied the training images. This is genuine primary data collection with a real, separately recruited comparison group - which distinguishes it sharply from the twelve Kaggle-corpus reuses charted in this review - but the group difference is confounded with school of origin, since every autistic child comes from one institution and every comparison child from another. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with autism, autistic children, autistic condition, typically developing children, normal children, Normal class. The Normal/Autism class labelling runs throughout including in the figures and conclusion. One artefact of manuscript reuse is worth recording: the description of the testing workflow states that the output classifies the child as either a stunted child (label 1) or a normal child (label 0) - terminology from childhood stunting research that has no place in an autism study and that survived into the published text. [RQ1.3] Thin, and internally inconsistent where present. Age is given as 3 to 14 years in the acquisition narrative and 5 to 15 years in Table I and again in the results; no mean, SD or per-group distribution is provided. Sex is not reported at all. No socioeconomic, ethnic, linguistic or verbal-ability information. The exclusion criteria are unusually explicit for this corpus - children with colds, diarrhoea, lung infections, epilepsy or flu were excluded from both groups, and autistic participants with intellectual disability, cerebral palsy or Down syndrome were excluded - which controls the sample tightly but also removes the co-occurring conditions most likely to be present in a real screening population and narrows the autistic group to those without intellectual disability. [RQ1.4] None. Group membership is determined by school: the autism group is the set of children attending a Special Elementary School, the comparison group the set attending a State Elementary School. No diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor, date or record is reported for a single child, and the typically developing children were not screened with any instrument. The study's exclusion of intellectual disability, cerebral palsy and Down syndrome implies some clinical information was available, but its source is never described. School placement is a proxy for diagnosis that also carries administrative, geographic and socioeconomic structure into the label. [RQ1.5] None. No IQ, developmental, adaptive or language measure, and no autism severity instrument. Intellectual disability appears only as an exclusion criterion. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to address the limited variation and representativeness of existing autism facial-image datasets by building a new dataset with broader variation in facial characteristics, lighting and social context, and to refine a CNN classifier on it. Headline findings: accuracy 0.90, precision 0.92, recall 0.88, F1 0.90 on 102 test images, with 47 and 45 correct classifications against 4 false positives and 6 false negatives. The conclusion attributes the result principally to the choice of a 1:1 aspect ratio and 224x224 image size, which is a claim about preprocessing conventions rather than about autism. [RQ2.2] Reported in more detail than any other study in this corpus. A 7x7 m room with a 2x2 m capture area, black curtains over the windows, air conditioning at 25-27 degrees C, controlled humidity, fixed room lighting, sessions restricted to 09:00-12:00 to limit lighting and temperature variation, a fixed one-metre subject-to-camera distance, a tripod-mounted camera, and a stated acclimation period before capture. The two groups were photographed at different institutions, however - a special school and a state school - and the paper does not report whether the studio setup was physically identical at both sites or whether the same operator ran both. Given how completely the acquisition is otherwise specified, this is the one variable that matters most and is left open. [RQ2.3] Posed expression photography: each child produced flat, smiling and sad expressions on instruction, five photographs each. The paper states outright that the process focuses solely on the final classification between Normal and Autism without independently assessing the individual expressions. That is a striking design decision - the expression manipulation is the only behavioural content in the study, it was deliberately elicited, and it is then discarded as a variable. A per-expression analysis would have distinguished a model reading facial morphology from one reading expression production, which is precisely the question the design was built to answer. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session. Ethics reporting is solid: an ethics code number is given (036/EA/FK/2025, Faculty of Medicine), parents signed a consent form before collection, and children were accompanied by their teachers throughout - a safeguarding measure that no other study in this corpus mentions. What is missing is consent for publication of images, since sample photographs of identifiable children appear in Figures 3 and 6, and any statement about the dataset's future distribution, even though building a shareable dataset is presented as the study's primary contribution. [RQ2.5] Canon EOS M-100 on a tripod, 256 GB storage, ISO 800, f/5.6, 1/25 s, 6000x4000 capture cropped to 1:1 and resized to 224x224. Room instrumentation includes a 17-inch LCD screen and speakers, listed for video viewing although no video task is described. Analysis software is not named; only the Keras ImageDataGenerator augmentation block is printed. Several environmental parameters conflict between the narrative and Table I: lighting 30 W versus 22 W, humidity 40-45% versus 50-60%, acclimation 10-15 minutes versus 3 minutes. [RQ2.6] The most sharply divided reproducibility profile in the corpus. The data side is exemplary: room dimensions, temperature, humidity, lighting, session hours, camera body, ISO, aperture, exposure, capture and output resolution, subject distance, curtain arrangement, expression protocol, per-child photograph counts and the verbatim augmentation configuration are all published, so another laboratory could recreate the acquisition closely. The model side is empty: no architecture, no layer specification, no optimiser, no learning rate, no batch size, no epoch count, no seed, no code, and no deposit for the dataset that the paper exists to introduce. The internal contradictions between narrative and Table I further undercut the acquisition detail, and the survival of stunted child in the workflow description indicates text carried over from an unrelated manuscript. [RQ2.7] None stated. There is no limitations section. The image-level split across 15 photographs per child, the school-based group assignment standing in for diagnosis, the confounding of group with institution, the absence of any per-expression analysis, and the 102-image test set all pass without comment. The one candid admission is incidental: the study does not record the total number of augmentations applied in the code. [RQ2.9] A single sentence proposing augmentation technologies to generate larger and more diverse datasets, plus unspecified additional techniques. Given that the study's own contribution is a dataset built to address representativeness, proposing synthetic augmentation as the route to further diversity moves away from the recruitment-based solution the paper has just demonstrated. [RQ3.1] Posed facial expression - flat, smiling and sad - and, implicitly, static facial appearance. Because expressions are pooled before classification, the study cannot say whether the model distinguishes groups by how the children produce expressions or by how their faces look, and the paper does not raise the distinction. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion - a single photographic modality. The introduction reviews thermal-imaging work at length (ResNet-50 on facial skin temperature across emotional states) and a thermal branch would have been a natural pairing with this acquisition setup, given that the protocol already controls room temperature and includes a body-temperature acclimation period. Only RGB photographs are collected. [RQ4.1] A convolutional neural network with a sigmoid output, trained end to end. The architecture is never described. The introduction promises the design of custom layers to optimise detection of ASD-specific visual characteristics, and no custom layer, or indeed any layer, is ever specified. Prior architectures (VGG-19, ShuffleNet, MobileNet, ResNet-18/34/50, AlexNet, VGG16) are discussed only as literature figures. [RQ4.2] 224x224 RGB face crops at 1:1 aspect ratio, rescaled to [0,1], with training-time augmentation by rotation to 20 degrees, width and height shifts to 0.2, shear 0.2, zoom 0.2 and horizontal flip. Noise removal and contrast enhancement are mentioned without method. The conclusion treats the 1:1 ratio and 224x224 size as the study's principal finding, which places a preprocessing convention where an empirical result should be. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and a confusion matrix, with sensitivity and specificity defined by formula but specificity never reported numerically. The reported figures reconcile exactly with the confusion-matrix cells - 92 of 102 correct gives 0.902; 47 of 51 predicted-positive gives 0.922; 47 of 53 actual-positive gives 0.887 - which is a level of internal consistency several other studies in this corpus fail to achieve. What is absent is any interval: with 102 test images the 95% confidence interval around 0.90 runs from roughly 0.83 to 0.95, so the comparison against the quoted literature figures of 87%, 88%, 89.2%, 90% and 92% is not discriminating. The abstract also describes the evaluation as using a nuisance matrix. [RQ4.4] None. No saliency, attribution or ablation, and no per-expression error breakdown despite expression being a designed factor. In a study whose premise is that specific facial characteristics reflect social and emotional traits relevant to autism, no facial characteristic is identified anywhere. [RQ4.5] A single 70/20/10 division at the image level - 369, 105 and 51 images per class - applied to 1,050 photographs from 70 children at exactly 15 photographs each. Participant separation is therefore impossible: five near-identical shots of the same child pulling the same expression, taken minutes apart under fixed lighting at a fixed one-metre distance with the same camera settings, are distributed across training, validation and test. This is the same frame-level leakage documented across the video, EEG-epoch, thermal, cry and facial-image branches of this review, and it is the study's decisive methodological failure - the more so because the acquisition protocol is so tightly controlled that the only systematic variation left between images of different children is the children themselves. Three further points. The split is unrepeated and unseeded, with no cross-validation and no interval on any figure. Training and validation accuracy are reported as reaching nearly 100% within the first few epochs with loss near zero, described as optimal and stable performance without signs of overfitting, while held-out accuracy is 90% - a gap the paper reads as success rather than as evidence about the split. And group membership is perfectly confounded with institution, since all autistic children were photographed at a special school and all comparison children at a state school, so any residual site difference in setup, operator or child preparation is available to the classifier. What would have rescued the design is available and unused: with 70 children, a participant-level split holding out, say, 7 autistic and 7 typically developing children entirely would have cost nothing and produced an interpretable, if less impressive, number. [RQ5.1] ASD; Normal; CNN; Confusion Matrix; Dataset. Five terms, two of which name an evaluation artefact and a data structure rather than a subject; Normal appears as a keyword in its own right. [RQ5.2] 2025 10th International Conference on Computer and Communication Engineering (ICCCE), IEEE, pages 351-355. A short engineering conference paper. The venue explains but does not excuse the asymmetry between a fully specified acquisition protocol and a completely unspecified model, and the survival of unrelated stunting terminology in the workflow description. [RQ5.3] 2025 IEEE conference proceedings. Framing is optimistic but hedged more than most: the study is said to pave the way for further application of facial recognition technology in clinical contexts and the potential development of automated detection systems that can be used in daily diagnostic practice. The novelty claim is placed on the dataset rather than on the accuracy - the paper's stated purpose is to remedy the poor representativeness of existing autism face datasets, and it does so by actually recruiting and photographing 70 children under a controlled protocol rather than by downloading images. That is a real contribution to a branch of this literature that has otherwise recycled the same web-scraped corpus twelve times over. |
| S-148 | Single-author retrospective analysis of the public ASD Toddler (Q-CHAT-10) dataset obtained from Kaggle: 1,054 cases aged 12-36 months with 17 categorical variables - ten Q-CHAT-10 behavioural items plus demographic and history fields - of which 735 carry the ASD-traits label and 319 do not. SVM-SMOTE expanded the set to 1,456 instances, which was then partitioned 70/10/20 into training, validation and a 292-case test set (148 ASD, 144 non-ASD). | Preprocessing removed noisy records, label-encoded categorical fields including ethnicity, region and the class label, and min-max scaled the features. Chi-square tests ranked attributes against the class label to define a reduced feature subset. Six classifiers - LightGBM, Extra Trees, Decision Tree, KNN, RBF-SVM and a four-layer MLP - were tuned by Bayesian optimisation with cross-validation inside the training data and evaluated with and without feature selection. SHAP beeswarm and bar plots explained the best model. | Chi-square selection improved every classifier: DT 0.938 to 0.969, KNN 0.959 to 0.973, LGBM 0.976 to 0.980, ET 0.986 to 0.990, MLP 0.993 to 0.997. SVM reached 1.000 accuracy, precision, recall and F1 both with and without selection, with log loss falling from 0.011 to 0.008; all 148 ASD and all 144 non-ASD test cases were classified correctly. SHAP identified joint attention, simple gestures and empathy-related behaviours as dominant and sex and jaundice as negligible. | Two ordering and definition failures account for the perfect result. SVM-SMOTE was applied to the entire dataset before the train-test split, so synthetic instances in the training set are interpolations of real cases sitting in the test set and vice versa - the hold-out is not independent. And the outcome, Class/ASD_Traits, is the Q-CHAT-10 screening result, a deterministic threshold on the sum of the ten items supplied as predictors, so the task is reconstruction of a checklist rule rather than detection of autism; the paper nonetheless describes the 735 positive cases as diagnosed with ASD. Neither baseline is stated (50.7% on the balanced test set, 69.7% majority class in the original data), no confidence interval accompanies any figure, the number and identity of chi-square-selected features are never reported, and whether selection was nested inside the split is not stated. The limitations paragraph raises single-dataset dependence and the need for external validation but never questions the 100%. | This is the fourth charted study built on a Q-CHAT-derived checklist label and it completes the branch's pattern. local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 retain all ten items and report 100% on six metrics; local_8ff20c48 deletes five of the ten and falls to 0.83; this study retains them, adds SMOTE and Bayesian tuning, and reaches a flawless 292 of 292. Read together the four establish that reported accuracy in this branch is governed by how completely the label's own summands survive preprocessing and by whether resampling crosses the split - and by nothing else. What makes this paper distinctive is that it is the most methodologically careful of the four: hyperparameters fully published, partition roles explicitly stated, tuning correctly nested, a real limitations paragraph, and the only log-loss column in the entire charted corpus (which does genuine work, exposing the Decision Tree's 2.223 miscalibration behind a 0.938 accuracy). It is therefore the review's clearest demonstration that methodological rigour applied downstream of a circular estimand produces a more confident wrong answer, not a better one. Its SHAP analysis, presented as clinical corroboration because the important features align with established markers, is the same point in miniature. | [RQ1.1] No groups were recruited. The unit is the questionnaire record: 1,054 cases from the public ASD Toddler dataset (Thabtah, via Kaggle), of which 735 are labelled ASD and 319 non-ASD - a 69.7% positive rate. SVM-SMOTE then expanded the set to 1,456 instances, meaning 402 of the rows subsequently modelled and evaluated are synthetic interpolations rather than children. The 292-case test set (148 ASD, 144 non-ASD) therefore contains an unstated number of synthetic records, and the number of real children behind the reported 100% is never given. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, non-ASD, toddlers, children, ASD presentations. Register is clinical and restrained; the comparison class is called non-ASD rather than normal, and the limitations paragraph shows unusual awareness that ASD presentations vary across populations and cultural contexts. One phrase runs against this: the introduction describes ASD as a complex neuro-developmental abnormality. No autistic or community perspective is cited. [RQ1.3] Almost none reported, though several demographic variables are present in the data and used as predictors. Age is given only as the dataset's 12-36 month scope. Sex, ethnicity and region exist as columns - sex and jaundice are named in the SHAP analysis as low-importance features - but no counts, proportions or distributions are printed for any of them, and no subgroup breakdown is performed. Ethnicity and region are label-encoded into ordinal integers, a transformation that imposes an arbitrary ordering on nominal categories and is not discussed. [RQ1.4] None. The outcome is Class/ASD_Traits, the Q-CHAT-10 screening result, and no clinical diagnosis exists for any case. The paper describes this as 735 cases diagnosed with ASD, which overstates what the dataset contains: the ASD label here records that a caregiver's ten checklist answers summed above a cut-off, not that a clinician assessed the child. No assessor, criterion, instrument beyond Q-CHAT-10 or date is reported. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, developmental, adaptive, language or severity measure is available in the dataset or reported. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to improve early ASD detection for toddlers aged 12-36 months by combining chi-square feature selection with six machine learning classifiers, SVM-SMOTE balancing, Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation and SHAP explanation, claimed as the first study to combine all four. Headline findings: chi-square selection improved every classifier (DT 0.938 to 0.969, KNN 0.959 to 0.973, LGBM 0.976 to 0.980, ET 0.986 to 0.990, MLP 0.993 to 0.997), and SVM reached 1.000 on accuracy, precision, recall and F1 both before and after selection, with all 292 test cases classified correctly - zero false positives and zero false negatives, reported as 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity and as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening applications. [RQ2.2] No study setting. A single-author secondary analysis of a downloaded file; no computing environment or runtime is described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. The instrument is the ten-item Q-CHAT-10 caregiver checklist, completed retrospectively about a toddler; the paper does not reproduce the items but names three of them via the SHAP results. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. There is no ethics or consent statement for this study. The single occurrence of the word ethical is in the XAI section, which argues that interpretability is needed in healthcare for clinical adoption, risk reduction, ethical compliance, informed consent and patient engagement - the paper names informed consent as a value that explainable AI supports, while providing no consent or governance statement for its own reuse of 1,054 toddlers' screening records. [RQ2.5] None for acquisition. Analytical components: label encoding, MinMaxScaler, SVM-SMOTE, chi-square selection, six scikit-learn-family classifiers, Bayesian optimisation and SHAP. No library, version, seed, hardware or runtime is reported. [RQ2.6] The strongest reporting in this review's questionnaire branch, with one structural gap. The dataset is public and cited; the preprocessing sequence is given step by step in order; the split proportions and the exact test-set composition (292 cases: 148 ASD, 144 non-ASD) are stated; and Table I lists every tuned hyperparameter for all six classifiers to four significant figures, including C = 635.2340 and alpha = 0.0002816. Against that: no code, no seed, no versions, and - most consequentially - the number of features chi-square retained is never given, the selected features are never listed, and whether selection was fitted inside or outside the split is never stated. The paper's headline claim concerns the effect of feature selection, and the reader cannot determine how many or which features that selection produced. [RQ2.7] A real limitations paragraph, and better than most: the results rest on a single public dataset which may not capture the full diversity of ASD presentations across populations and cultural contexts, real-world deployment would require external validation on larger and more heterogeneous cohorts, and additional modalities such as genetic or neuroimaging data could be integrated. What it does not question is the result itself. A model that classifies 292 consecutive cases without a single error is treated as an achievement to be explained by good feature selection rather than as a signal that the target is recoverable from the inputs by construction. Also unmentioned: that SMOTE preceded the split, that the label is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome rather than a diagnosis, and that a fifth of the evaluated instances are synthetic. [RQ2.9] External validation on larger and more heterogeneous cohorts, and integration of genetic or neuroimaging modalities. The first directly addresses the stated limitation; the second proposes adding expensive modalities to a pipeline whose reported ceiling is already 100%, which is the characteristic move of this literature - scaling up inputs rather than questioning the estimand. [RQ3.1] Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours drawn from Q-CHAT-10. The SHAP analysis names three specifically: joint attention (does your child follow where you are looking), use of simple gestures, and empathy-related behaviours. These are clinically sensible early markers, and the paper notes correctly that they correspond to established clinical markers - but their prominence in the model is a property of how the label was constructed, not independent evidence about them. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single questionnaire modality plus static demographic covariates. Multimodal extension with genetic and neuroimaging data is proposed as future work only. [RQ4.1] Six classical supervised learners - LightGBM, Extra Trees, Decision Tree, KNN, RBF-kernel SVM and a four-layer MLP - each evaluated with the full feature set and with a chi-square-selected subset, all tuned by Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation with cross-validation inside the training data. No deep learning on raw signals; no ensemble of the six. [RQ4.2] A tabular row per toddler: ten binary Q-CHAT-10 items plus sex, ethnicity, jaundice, family history, region, respondent and age, label-encoded and min-max scaled. Two features of this representation matter. First, the ten items are the constituents of the Q-CHAT-10 score whose threshold defines the label, so the predictor set arithmetically determines the outcome - the same structure as local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 (which reach 100% on six metrics) and the inverse of local_8ff20c48 (which deleted five of the ten items and consequently fell to 0.83). Second, ethnicity and region are nominal categories converted to ordered integers by label encoding, imposing an artificial ordering that the paper does not remark on. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and log loss for all twelve configurations, plus a confusion matrix and SHAP plots for the best model. The log loss column deserves credit: it is the only calibration-sensitive measure reported by any study charted in this review, and it does real work here - Decision Tree posts 0.938 accuracy with a log loss of 2.223, exposing badly miscalibrated probabilities that accuracy alone would hide. Against that, no confidence interval accompanies any figure, and neither baseline is stated (50.7% on the balanced test set, 69.7% majority-class on the original data). The F1 score is also described as the geometric mean of precision and recall, when it is the harmonic mean. [RQ4.4] SHAP beeswarm and bar plots for the SVM with chi-square selection, showing joint attention, simple gestures and empathy-related behaviours as the dominant predictors and sex and jaundice as negligible. This is properly executed explainability, presented as evidence of clinical trustworthiness on the grounds that the model's important features align with established clinical markers. The alignment is real but uninformative: the label is a threshold on the sum of exactly those items, so any model that recovers the label must weight them heavily, and any model that recovered the label from sex or jaundice instead would be the anomaly. SHAP here confirms that the pipeline learned the arithmetic it was given, and the paper reads that confirmation as external validation of the behavioural markers. [RQ4.5] The validation section is, in most respects, the most carefully constructed in this review's questionnaire branch. A stratified 70/10/20 split is used, the roles of the three partitions are stated explicitly (fitting, hyperparameter tuning and model selection, final reporting), Bayesian optimisation is cross-validated inside the training data only, the test set is described as never used during training or tuning, and the author pre-empts the overfitting objection directly, listing four mitigations. Two problems defeat all of that care. The first is ordering: SVM-SMOTE was applied to the whole 1,054-case dataset before partitioning, expanding it to 1,456 instances, and only then was the balanced dataset randomly partitioned. Synthetic minority instances are interpolations between real minority cases, so synthetic rows in the training set are constructed from real rows that ended up in the test set, and synthetic rows in the test set are constructed from real training rows. The hold-out is therefore not independent, and this alone can produce near-perfect minority-class recall. The second is the estimand: the label Class/ASD_Traits is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome, a deterministic threshold on the sum of ten items that are supplied as features. No split scheme can make the reconstruction of that threshold into a diagnostic accuracy. Together these explain a result that the paper instead attributes to methodological quality - 292 of 292 test cases correct, zero false positives and zero false negatives, reported as 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity and as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening. The external comparison in Table III compounds this by ranking the 100% against literature figures of 97.15%, 97.82% and 93.69% from other datasets and protocols, presenting the gap as a methodological advance. [RQ5.1] Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); chi-square feature selection; machine learning; explainable AI. Four terms, three naming technique. Neither the instrument (Q-CHAT-10) nor the population (toddlers) appears, despite both being central. [RQ5.2] Engineering, Technology & Applied Science Research 15(5):27954-27959 - an open-access general engineering journal. A 100% diagnostic accuracy claim, a hold-out contaminated by pre-split synthetic oversampling, and a label that is a threshold on its own predictors passed review there in 48 days including a revision round. [RQ5.3] 2025, accepted 14 August, 48 days from submission. Framing is screening-tool improvement rather than diagnostic replacement, and is comparatively measured: integrating robust feature selection with explainable ML models can significantly advance the reliability of early ASD screening tools. The overreach is concentrated in one sentence - that 100% sensitivity and specificity confirm the model's suitability for reliable clinical screening applications - and in a comparison table that ranks the perfect score above three published figures from unrelated datasets. The paper's genuine contributions are its hyperparameter transparency, its inclusion of log loss, and a limitations paragraph that correctly identifies single-dataset dependence. |
| S-149 | Retrospective analysis merging two public toddler ASD screening datasets - the Kaggle ASD Toddler set (1,054 instances, 17 columns, ten Q-CHAT-10 items plus demographics) and an online questionnaire dataset covering toddlers aged 12-36 months across regions of Saudi Arabia. Neither the size of the second dataset, the merged total, the post-SMOTE total, the class counts nor the split sizes is reported anywhere. The Phase I label is stated explicitly as the Q-CHAT-10 cut-off: one point per item answered Always, Usually or Sometimes, with a total above 3 indicating potential ASD traits. | SMOTE balancing, then three feature-selection techniques (Bi-Directional Elimination, Boruta, ML-based selection), seven classifiers (RF, DT, LR, KNN, SVM, GBM, XGBoost) and a proposed RF-XG voting ensemble, evaluated on an 80:20 split and by 10-fold cross-validation. In Phase II a Teaching Method column was created by the authors with numpy - integers 1 to 6 for six specialised interventions plus 0 for none - assigned by binning the Q-CHAT-10 total into five severity levels, and the same models were trained to predict it from the remaining columns. | Phase I RF-XG: 0.94 on original features, 0.92 with Bi-Directional Elimination, 0.98 with Boruta, 0.99 with ML-based selection; 10-fold cross-validation averaging 0.986. Phase II RF-XG: accuracy 0.9917 with precision, recall and F1 all 0.99. The state-of-the-art comparison table claims 99.99% for the proposed approach against quoted figures of 98.77%, 97.82%, 99.25% and 99.85%. | The study states none. Phase I predicts a threshold on the sum of the ten items it is given as features, with SMOTE and feature selection of unstated ordering and no row counts at any stage. Phase II predicts a target the authors manufactured with numpy by binning that same Q-CHAT-10 total, from the very features the total is computed on - so 0.9917 measures a classifier reproducing the authors' own arithmetic, and a lookup table would score 1.00. The severity-to-intervention mapping is uncited, has no evidence base, and assigns Intensive Behavioral Intervention to the low-severity band and Pivotal Response Training to the high, inverting the usual intensity gradient. No physical, verbal or behavioural performance measure exists in the data despite Phase II claiming to assess them. The headline 99.99% appears in no results table and exceeds the study's own best figure of 0.99; the printed 10-fold average of 0.986 does not match the mean of the printed folds (0.9876). There is no ethics or consent statement, and no limitations or future-work section. The merged two-region design offered a free external validation - train on one cohort, test on the other - and it is not taken. | This is the fifth charted study built on a Q-CHAT-derived label and the branch's endpoint. local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 reach 100% with all ten items retained; local_ed30e24c reaches a flawless 292 of 292 by adding pre-split SMOTE; local_8ff20c48 falls to 0.83 after deleting five items; and this study reaches 0.99 in Phase I and 0.9917 in Phase II. What distinguishes it is Phase II, which is unique in the corpus: the target variable was written by the authors with numpy as a deterministic function of the predictors, and the resulting accuracy is offered to educators as a basis for real decisions about which intervention an individual autistic child should receive. The rest of the corpus produces uninterpretable diagnostic probabilities; this study produces an uninterpretable placement recommendation, which is a category of harm the review should record separately. The uncited severity-to-intervention mapping - assigning the most intensive intervention to the least affected band - is the clearest instance of clinical content asserted without any clinical input. Its position beside local_7b468950, the Play.Care phase III protocol with a locked algorithm and blinded prospective validation, marks the full range of what this literature currently contains. | [RQ1.1] No participants were recruited. Two public toddler screening datasets are merged: the Kaggle ASD Toddler set (1,054 instances, 17 columns) and an online questionnaire dataset covering toddlers aged 12-36 months across regions of Saudi Arabia. The size of the second dataset is never given, the size of the merged set is never given, and the size after SMOTE oversampling is never given - so the number of rows behind every table in the paper is unknown, and it cannot be determined how many are real records and how many synthetic. Class counts are likewise absent. The stated motivation for merging - improving diversity by combining two regions - is the paper's best idea and is never exploited: the two cohorts are pooled rather than used as development and held-out sets. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic children, children with ASD, individuals affected by ASD, high-level and low-level autistic children, autism students. The abstract opens with a genuinely thoughtful observation - that ASD is highly diverse, each affected child is unique, no two autistic children are alike, and what benefits one child may not suit another - and the whole paper is then organised around assigning children to one of six teaching methods on the basis of a checklist total. The severity vocabulary (high-level, moderate-to-high, low-level autistic children) applies the label to the child rather than to support needs, and the framing describes ASD as having a primary origin that is genetic and as significantly affecting cognitive abilities and object recognition. [RQ1.3] None reported. Gender is present as a variable and is named as a factor in the Phase II rationale; ethnicity, region and jaundice exist as columns; no counts, proportions or distributions are printed for any of them. The absence of a regional breakdown is the notable one, since regional diversity is the stated reason for merging the two datasets and the merged column would have made a two-cohort comparison immediate. [RQ1.4] None, and the paper states the label rule plainly enough that this is not in doubt: a 1 is scored for each Q-CHAT-10 item answered Always, Usually or Sometimes, and a total above 3 indicates the presence of potential ASD traits. That threshold is the outcome variable. No clinician, diagnostic instrument, criterion or assessment date exists for any record in either dataset, and the online questionnaire origin of the Saudi data means the respondents were not verified either. [RQ1.5] No validated cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. The Q-CHAT-10 total is repurposed as a severity index in Phase II, binning children into five severity levels. Q-CHAT-10 is a binary screening instrument with a single cut-off; it was neither designed nor validated to grade severity, and using its total as a severity scale is an unsupported extension that Phase II then rests on entirely. [RQ2.1] Two goals. Phase I: identify ASD from merged toddler screening data using seven classifiers plus a proposed RF-XG voting ensemble, under three feature-selection schemes. Phase II: recommend an appropriate teaching method for each child from their physical, verbal and behavioural performance. Headline findings: RF-XG reaches 0.94 on original features, 0.92 with Bi-Directional Elimination, 0.98 with Boruta and 0.99 with ML-based feature selection; 10-fold cross-validation averages 0.986; and Phase II predicts the teaching-method label at 0.9917. The comparison table separately claims 99.99%, a number that appears in none of the results tables and exceeds every figure the study actually reports. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Two downloaded or pre-existing questionnaire datasets, analysed in Python. No computing environment, runtime or data-handling arrangement is described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm - an online caregiver questionnaire. Phase II claims to assess children's physical, verbal and behavioural performance, and this claim is unsupported at the most basic level: the dataset contains ten checklist items and a handful of demographic fields, and no physical, verbal or behavioural performance measure of any kind. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. There is no ethics statement, no consent statement and no data-governance statement anywhere in the article. That absence is more consequential here than in most of this corpus, because the output is not a screening probability but a specific educational placement recommendation for individual children, offered to educators as a basis for decisions affecting their learning and development. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation. Python with scikit-learn for modelling; numpy is named specifically as the library used to create the Phase II teaching-method column. No versions, seed, hardware or runtime. [RQ2.6] Low. The one Kaggle dataset is linked and the Q-CHAT-10 label rule is stated explicitly, which is better than most of the branch. Everything else is missing: the second dataset has no accession, the merged dataset that is claimed as a contribution is not deposited, no row counts are reported at any stage (pre-merge, post-merge, post-SMOTE, per class, per split), no hyperparameters are given for any of eight models, no seed or library versions appear, the number and identity of features retained by each of the three selection methods are never stated, and the order of SMOTE relative to the split is unspecified. The manuscript is also visibly an unedited accepted version - the header retains Date of publication xxxx 00, 0000 and the placeholder DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2017.DOI, and the running footer reads VOLUME 4, 2016 throughout. [RQ2.7] None. There is no limitations section and no caveat anywhere. Unmentioned: that the label is a threshold on the summed predictors; that the Phase II target was manufactured by the authors from that same total; that the reported 99.99% appears in no table; that the printed cross-validation average does not equal the mean of the printed folds; that row counts are absent throughout; and that no ethics approval was sought for a study producing educational placement recommendations. [RQ2.9] None stated. There is no future-work section. [RQ3.1] Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours from Q-CHAT-10 - response to name, eye contact, gestures, pointing, pretend play, gaze following, comforting, early speech, staring. No behaviour is observed, and the physical and verbal performance invoked in the Phase II framing does not exist in the data. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion. The only fusion is the merging of two questionnaire datasets from different regions, which is dataset pooling rather than multimodal integration - and, as noted, the regional structure created by that merge is then discarded rather than used for cross-cohort validation. [RQ4.1] Seven classical classifiers - random forest, decision tree, logistic regression, KNN, SVM, gradient boosting, XGBoost - plus an RF-XG voting ensemble presented as the novel contribution. Three feature-selection techniques (Bi-Directional Elimination, Boruta, ML-based selection) are compared. No hyperparameter is reported for any model. [RQ4.2] Tabular rows of ten binary Q-CHAT-10 items plus demographic and history fields, SMOTE-augmented and feature-selected. The ten items are the constituents of the Q-CHAT-10 total whose threshold defines the Phase I label and whose bands define the Phase II label, so in both phases the predictor set arithmetically determines the outcome. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 across four feature conditions, seven classifiers and an ensemble; per-fold cross-validation values; Phase II results; and a state-of-the-art comparison. No AUC, no specificity, no calibration, no confidence interval, and no chance level for either the binary Phase I task or the seven-class Phase II task. Two internal inconsistencies matter. The 10-fold table prints an average accuracy of 0.986 while the ten listed fold accuracies average 0.9876, and it contains a fold reporting recall 0.999 against accuracy 0.988 and another reporting accuracy 0.999 - values out of line with their neighbours. More seriously, the comparison table credits the proposed approach with 99.99% accuracy, positioning it above four quoted literature figures (98.77%, 97.82%, 99.25%, 99.85%), when the study's own best tabulated result is 0.99 and its cross-validated average is 0.986. The headline claim of surpassing the state of the art rests on a number the paper never produced. [RQ4.4] A single feature-ranking figure from the ML-based selection method. No attribution analysis, no examination of which features drive the teaching-method assignment, and no interrogation of why three different feature-selection methods produce accuracies spanning 0.92 to 0.99 on the same data. [RQ4.5] Phase I follows the familiar pattern: an 80:20 split plus 10-fold cross-validation over data whose label is a threshold on the summed predictors, with SMOTE applied at an unstated point relative to the split and feature selection of unstated nesting. Row counts are absent at every stage, so no reported figure can be located to a sample. That much places the study alongside local_ed30e24c, local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 in the circular-label group. Phase II is a different and more serious matter, and it is the reason this record exists. The teaching-method target did not come from any school, therapist, assessment or record: the paper states that a new column named Teaching Method was added to the dataset using the numpy library, containing integers 1 to 6 for six specialised teaching methods plus 0 for no special education needed, and that these were assigned on the basis of severity as analysed from the Q-CHAT-10 score, which is the count of the A1-A10 values. The models are then trained to predict that manufactured column from the other columns - including A1 to A10 themselves. The reported 0.9917 accuracy therefore measures how well a classifier reproduces an arithmetic rule that the authors wrote, applied to the very features they wrote it from. It is not an estimate of anything about children, education or autism; a lookup table would score 1.00. Compounding this, the mapping from severity band to intervention (Pivotal Response Training for high-level, technology-aided instruction for moderate-to-high, PECS for moderate, task analysis for low-to-moderate, Intensive Behavioral Intervention for low) is asserted with no evidence base, no clinical input and no citation, and it inverts the usual intensity gradient by assigning the most intensive intervention to the least affected group. The results are then offered to educators and professionals as a basis for informed decisions about teaching methods that can have a significant impact on the children's learning and development. The merged two-region design offered a genuine external-validation opportunity - train on one cohort, test on the other - and it is not taken. [RQ5.1] Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); Autism Students Learning; SMOTE; Multi-model Learning; Feature Engineering. Three of five terms name technique; the educational claim that occupies half the paper appears only as Autism Students Learning. [RQ5.2] IEEE Access - a high-volume open-access multidisciplinary engineering journal. The published PDF is the unedited accepted version, retaining template placeholders in the header (Date of publication xxxx 00, 0000; DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2017.DOI) and a VOLUME 4, 2016 footer throughout. No reviewer questioned a fabricated educational-placement target, a 99.99% figure absent from the results, or the absence of any ethics statement in a paper recommending educational interventions for individual children. [RQ5.3] 2025 (accepted version, citation DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3349988). Framing moves beyond diagnosis into intervention allocation: the aim is personalised educational approaches for individuals with ASD, harnessing machine learning to enhance precision in addressing their unique needs, with results said to help educators make informed decisions. The paper opens by insisting that no two autistic children are alike and closes by assigning them to six intervention categories on the basis of a ten-item checklist total that the authors themselves binned. It is the corpus's clearest example of a pipeline whose output is an action taken on a child rather than a probability, built on a target the authors wrote with numpy. |
| S-150 | Single-author retrospective analysis of the public toddler Q-CHAT dataset: 1,054 app-submitted records with 19 attributes, 728 labelled autism and 326 control, mean age 25-28 months, 69.7% male within the autism group, spanning eleven ethnic groups. The outcome is the Class/ASD traits field - the Q-CHAT-10 screening result - and the predictor pool contains the ten Q-CHAT items, the Q-CHAT total and demographic fields. | Preprocessing is published as a numbered algorithm (drop Case_no, handle missing values, one-hot encode ethnicity and respondent, label-encode binary fields, standardise). Three selection methods - chi-squared SelectKBest, RF/Extra Trees importance, and correlation analysis with Pearson, Spearman and VIF - produce four feature subsets, compared against the default set and against Q1-Q10 alone. Four classifiers (LR, KNN, ANN, LR-KNN ensemble) were tuned and evaluated with k-fold cross-validation; no resampling was applied to the 69/31 imbalance. Kruskal-Wallis tests related each item to the class variable, and an iterative analysis tracked sensitivity and specificity as Q1 through Q10 were added one at a time. | With Q1-Q10 alone (41% feature reduction), LR-KNN reached accuracy 0.99, precision 1.00, F1 0.99, MCC 0.98, sensitivity 0.99, specificity 1.00; ANN 0.98/0.98/1.00/0.98/1.00/0.98; LR 0.97 with specificity 0.90; KNN 0.94. Q9, Q6 and Q5 ranked highest across all three selection methods and Q8 and Q10 lowest. In the iterative analysis, age and sex alone gave 99.5% sensitivity. | The label is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome and the predictors are its own items and total, so the reported figures measure recovery of a checklist rule rather than detection of autism. The validation design is under-reported: no split proportions, no value of k, no per-fold results, no statement of whether selection and tuning were nested inside the training partition, and a passage describing tuning followed by training and evaluation on the dataset. The four confusion matrices imply a 317-record test set but disagree on its composition (105/212 for LR, KNN and LR-KNN; 110/207 for the ANN). No chance level is stated, although with 728 of 1,054 positive the majority-class baseline is 69.1% accuracy and 100% sensitivity - which is what the reported 99.5% sensitivity from age and sex alone actually reflects. The ethics statement treats absence of direct human interaction as itself constituting ethical approval. There is no limitations section, and the extracted text ends mid-discussion with no conclusion. | This is the sixth and analytically most useful of the review's Q-CHAT-labelled studies. Where local_8253c2ec and local_a0d73248 retain all ten items and hit 100%, local_ed30e24c adds pre-split SMOTE and classifies 292 of 292 correctly, local_b9de0d7f manufactures a second target from the same total, and local_8ff20c48 deletes five items and falls to 0.83, this study systematically varies which part of the Q-CHAT arithmetic enters the feature set and reports the result for each configuration. Its subsets separate the total from its summands and combine them, and every configuration containing either performs well - which is the branch's governing mechanism laid out experimentally. The author comes closer than anyone else to naming it, observing that Subset 2 included both the Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10 features, which could sometimes mislead the model results, and then treats it as a redundancy problem. Its 99.5% sensitivity from age and sex alone is the corpus's cleanest demonstration that sensitivity without a stated prevalence baseline is uninformative. It is also the branch's most careful study in reporting terms - MCC with an explicit rationale, confusion matrices for all four models, a published preprocessing algorithm, no resampling, an honest title, and a discussion willing to say the results were not entirely satisfactory. | [RQ1.1] No participants. 1,054 records from the public toddler Q-CHAT dataset, 728 labelled autism and 326 control - a 69.1% positive rate that the paper reports and, unusually for this branch, leaves in place rather than resampling. The records were submitted through an ASD screening application by parents and other stakeholders, so neither respondent nor child was verified. The confusion matrices imply a test partition of 317 records, though no split proportion is stated; the row totals also differ across models within the same table (105/212 for LR, KNN and LR-KNN but 110/207 for the ANN), which they should not if all four were evaluated on the same partition. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autism traits, ASD traits, toddlers, individuals with ASD, controls, non-ASD individuals. The register is careful and the title is the most honest in this branch of the corpus: predicting autism traits, not diagnosing autism. ASD is described as a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition, controls rather than normals are used for the comparison class, and the stated motivation includes that incorrect diagnoses can have significant implications for families. One slip: the opening sentence calls ASD a complex neuropsychiatric developmental condition. [RQ1.3] Better than most of the branch, though still descriptive only. Age averages 25 to 28 months with a note that labelled cases rise between 25 and 30 months and become more noticeable by 35-36 months. Sex is given only as 69.7% male within the autism group, with no control-group figure. Ethnicity is reported across eleven groups with White Europeans most represented followed by Asians, and the paper states there were no significant ethnic differences in diagnosis rates - the one ethnicity analysis in this branch. Jaundice, family history and respondent type are present. No performance is broken down by any of these, so the demographic detail informs the sample description but not the evaluation. [RQ1.4] None. The outcome is the Class/ASD traits field, the Q-CHAT-10 screening result, applied to app-submitted responses with no clinical assessment, no clinician, no instrument beyond the checklist and no verification of who completed it. The paper's title and abstract are accurate about this - it predicts autism traits, not autism - and that accuracy distinguishes it from several neighbours in the corpus that describe the same label as a diagnosis. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity instrument. The Qchat-10-Score total appears as a predictor in two feature subsets rather than as a participant characteristic. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to identify a minimal feature subset for ASD trait screening in toddlers through systematic feature selection and hyperparameter tuning, and to map Q1-Q10 and the Q-CHAT total onto DSM-5 behavioural domains. Headline findings: using Q1-Q10 alone (a 41% feature reduction) gives the best performance across all classifiers, with the LR-KNN ensemble at accuracy 0.99, precision 1.00, specificity 1.00 and MCC 0.98, followed by ANN 0.98, LR 0.97 and KNN 0.94. Q9, Q6 and Q5 rank consistently highest across chi-squared, tree-importance and correlation methods; Q8 and Q10 lowest. [RQ2.2] No setting. A single-author secondary analysis of a downloaded file; no computing environment or runtime is described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. The instrument is the ten-item Quantitative Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, administered through a screening app on a five-point frequency scale from never to always, collapsed to binary. Table 1 maps each question to its behavioural construct - response to name, eye contact, finger pointing and so on - which is more transparency about the instrument than most of the branch offers. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. The ethics statement is the notable feature: the dataset was collected via an ASD test screening application, with no direct human interaction, with responses submitted by parents and other stakeholders, ensuring ethical approval for research purposes. Absence of contact between researcher and participant is presented as itself supplying ethical approval. No committee, protocol number, consent statement or data-governance arrangement appears, and no consideration is given to whether app users agreed to research reuse of their children's screening responses. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation. Analytical components: StandardScaler, one-hot and label encoding, SelectKBest with chi-squared, RF and Extra Trees importance, Pearson and Spearman correlation, variance inflation factor, Kruskal-Wallis tests, logistic regression, KNN, a feed-forward ANN and an LR-KNN ensemble. No library names, versions, seed or hardware. [RQ2.6] Moderate, and the strongest in this branch alongside local_ed30e24c. The preprocessing is published as a numbered algorithm specifying every encoding and column operation; the dataset is public; the composition of each of the four feature subsets is listed; the statistical tests and their exact p-values are tabulated; and confusion matrices are printed for all four final models. Missing: split proportions, the value of k in the cross-validation, any per-fold result, final hyperparameter values, the ANN architecture, the ensemble's combination rule, a seed, and code. The extracted PDF also ends mid-discussion after Table 7, so no conclusion or funding statement is available. [RQ2.7] No limitations section, but two candid remarks stand out. The author writes that on reviewing performance across multiple feature subsets, the results obtained were not entirely satisfactory - an unusual admission in a literature where every result is a success. And, discussing Subset 2, that it included both the Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10 features, which could sometimes mislead the model results. That second sentence is the closest any of the six Q-CHAT-based studies charted in this review comes to naming the circularity at the centre of the branch: the total and its own summands are both in the feature set, and the label is a threshold on the total. Having noticed it, the paper treats it as a redundancy nuisance and moves on. [RQ2.9] Not available - the extracted text ends mid-discussion and contains no conclusion or future-work section. [RQ3.1] Parent-reported early social-communication behaviours from the Q-CHAT: response to name, ease of eye contact, pointing to express desires, and the remaining seven items, each mapped to a DSM-5 behavioural domain. The item-level analysis produces a consistent ordering - Q9, Q6 and Q5 most informative, Q8 and Q10 least - which is the paper's substantive behavioural claim.
