[RQ3.2] No fusion - a single questionnaire modality with demographic covariates. The systematic subset comparison is a study of feature configurations within one modality, not multimodal integration. [RQ4.1] Four supervised learners: logistic regression, k-nearest neighbours, a feed-forward artificial neural network, and a soft LR-KNN ensemble presented as the contribution. No tree-based or boosted classifier is used for prediction, though RF and Extra Trees are used for feature ranking. [RQ4.2] Standardised tabular vectors in five configurations: the default 19-attribute set; Subset 1 (chi-squared, ordered by Q1-Q10 with Q9, Q5, Q6 top); Subset 2 (tree importance, retaining both Qchat-10-Score and Q1-Q10); Subset 3 (correlation-based: Qchat-10-Score, sex, jaundice, age, family history, ethnicity, respondent); Subset 4 (minimal: Qchat-10-Score, age, sex, jaundice); and Q1-Q10 alone. The configurations are the study's real object, and their comparison is where its diagnostic value lies - Subsets 3 and 4 keep the Q-CHAT total and drop the items; Q1-Q10 keeps the items and drops the total; Subset 2 keeps both. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, F1, sensitivity, specificity, MCC and a confusion matrix for every model, plus per-subset comparisons and an iterative feature-addition curve. The metric set is the most complete in this branch: MCC is included deliberately because of the class imbalance, and its motivation - that incorrect diagnoses have significant implications for families - is stated. It also does real work, separating LR (accuracy 0.97, MCC 0.92) from ANN (0.98, 0.98). Two problems. No confidence interval accompanies any figure. And the confusion matrices are mutually inconsistent: LR, KNN and LR-KNN each have class totals of 105 and 212, while the ANN's are 110 and 207, so the four models were not all evaluated on the same 317-record partition. [RQ4.4] The most thorough feature analysis in this branch: chi-squared scores, RF and Extra Trees impurity importance, Pearson and Spearman correlations, variance inflation factors, Kruskal-Wallis association tests with exact p-values, a DSM-5 domain mapping for each item, and an iterative curve tracking sensitivity and specificity as Q1 through Q10 are added one at a time. Three items (Q9, Q6, Q5) rank highest under all three methods. The analysis is careful and internally consistent; what limits it is that the label is a threshold on the sum of the very items being ranked, so the Kruskal-Wallis p-values of order 1e-100 and the convergence across three ranking methods are arithmetic consequences rather than empirical discoveries about which behaviours matter. [RQ4.5] The validation design is under-reported - no split proportions, no value of k, no per-fold results, no statement of whether feature selection and tuning were nested inside the training partition, and a passage stating that the manually tuned model is then trained and evaluated on the dataset to ensure generalization, which describes tuning and evaluating on the same data. The confusion matrices imply a 317-record test partition but disagree on its class composition across models (105/212 for three of them, 110/207 for the ANN). Underneath that, the estimand is the branch's usual one: Class/ASD traits is the Q-CHAT-10 outcome and Q1-Q10 are its summands, so predicting the former from the latter is arithmetic recovery. What makes this study analytically valuable to the review is that its own feature-subset experiment maps the circularity almost completely without naming it. Subsets 3 and 4 retain the Qchat-10-Score and discard the items; Q1-Q10 retains the items and discards the total; Subset 2 retains both, and the author observes that this could sometimes mislead the model results. Every configuration containing either the total or its summands performs well, and the reported conclusion - that Q1-Q10 alone gives optimal performance with 41% fewer features - is a statement about which encoding of the label's own arithmetic is most compact. The single most revealing number in the paper is in the iterative analysis: with only the two least significant features, age and sex, sensitivity was 99.5%. With 69.1% of records positive, that is what a near-all-positive classifier produces, and the surrounding text treats it as a baseline from which adding Q1 (sensitivity 97.6%) and Q2-Q4 (92.8%, 91.3%) represents degradation. Read correctly it demonstrates that sensitivity alone is uninformative on this dataset and that the majority-class baseline is 69.1% accuracy - neither point is made, and no chance level appears anywhere in the article. [RQ5.1] machine learning; feature selection; hyperparameter tuning; logistic regression; k-nearest neighbors; artificial neural network. Six terms, all naming technique - autism, ASD, Q-CHAT, toddlers and screening appear in none of them, which is unusual and leaves the keyword list disconnected from the paper's subject. [RQ5.2] Engineering Research Express 7(2):025269 (IOP Publishing) - an open-access general engineering journal. A 132-day review including one revision round did not surface the mutually inconsistent confusion matrices, the missing split proportions and cross-validation k, the unstated chance level, or an ethics statement that treats absence of direct human interaction as constituting ethical approval. [RQ5.3] 2025, published 28 May, 132 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is screening-support rather than diagnostic replacement and is among the most measured in the corpus - the title claims to predict autism traits, the abstract offers a scalable and cost-effective approach for early detection and personalized intervention strategies, and the discussion admits that results across subsets were not entirely satisfactory. The overreach is confined to the closing claim of facilitating the way for integrating ML techniques into clinical settings. Its distinguishing contribution is analytical rather than predictive: by systematically varying which parts of the Q-CHAT arithmetic enter the feature set, it produces the branch's most complete map of why these accuracies are what they are. |
| S-151 | Cross-sectional online survey in Spain, nested in a project validating the Spanish CAT-Q. 601 adults participated: 102 with a clinician-made autism diagnosis (72 women, 18 men, 12 non-binary; mean age 36.0, mean age at diagnosis 32.0) and 499 non-autistic adults (399 women, 92 men, 8 non-binary; mean age 33.3). Twelve self-diagnosed respondents and 13 who did not report a gender identity were excluded. Education and self-reported comorbidities are tabulated in full for both groups. | The 25 CAT-Q-ES Likert items served as predictors for five continuous outcomes: BAPQ Aloofness, Pragmatic Language and Rigid Personality, PHQ-9 total and GAD-7 total. Fifty regression algorithms across Python, R, Matlab and Octave were compared under two-layer 4-fold cross-validation with participant-disjoint, score-range-stratified partitions; hyperparameters were selected by MAE on a validation partition, models refitted on training plus validation, and tested once per trial on an untouched partition. Three further input configurations added gender, autism diagnosis, or both. Code and a sample dataset are on OSF. | Best-regressor correlations between true and predicted scores: Aloofness R=.85 (MAE 5.55, MAPE 9.2%), Pragmatics .82 (5.36, 8.9%), Rigidity .75 (6.94, 11.6%), Depression .58 (4.55, 16.9%), Anxiety .54 (4.00, 19.1%). Winning algorithms were SGD, SVR, Ridge, KNN and boosted trees respectively. Adding gender and/or autism diagnosis changed R by at most .03. A tolerance analysis reports 36.3% of Aloofness predictions within 5% of the true score and just over 60% within 10%. | The authors state four: an 78%-women, highly educated, self-selected online sample, with the recruitment mechanism explained; self-reported diagnoses that could not be verified, mitigated by excluding self-diagnosis and instructing respondents to report only clinician-confirmed conditions; weaker anxiety and depression models, attributed to the criterion-based structure of PHQ-9 and GAD-7 items; and measurement of generalised rather than social anxiety. One limitation is not stated and is the most consequential: predictors and outcomes are self-report questionnaires completed by the same person in the same sitting, so the correlations carry common-method variance, and the CAT-Q-ES items overlap in construct with the BAPQ Aloofness and Pragmatic Language subscales - which is at least as plausible an explanation for the gap between R=.85 for social-trait outcomes and R=.54 for anxiety as the instrument-structure account offered. No external cohort is tested, which the authors themselves require before clinical use. | This is the reference study of the review. Every failure that governs the rest of the corpus is absent here: the analysis unit is the person, the cross-validation partitions are participant-disjoint, hyperparameter selection is nested and never touches the test partition, the outcome is dimensional so no threshold or prevalence artefact arises, the label is not a function of the predictors, the code is deposited, ethics approval and consent are documented, and the limitations are mechanistic rather than formulaic. Its results are correspondingly modest - R=.85 at best, .54 at worst, with only 36% of individual predictions within 5% of the true score - and that contrast is the review's central empirical finding stated in a single study. It should be read alongside local_cd7545e2, where the ADOS-2 itself reaches AUC 0.562 against another clinical group, and local_7d7f1fcc, where a participant-level matched split over pose data yields 82.5%: together these three mark the realistic performance envelope of the field. It is also the only charted study to treat an autistic behaviour as adaptive rather than symptomatic, to analyse non-binary participants as a group rather than excluding them, to compute instrument reliabilities in its own sample, to release working code, and to devote a passage of its discussion to the risk that predictive algorithms in mental health reinforce stigma and pathologise coping strategies. | [RQ1.1] Two groups of adults recruited into one online survey: 102 autistic adults with a clinician-made diagnosis (72 women, 18 men, 12 non-binary) and 499 non-autistic adults (399 women, 92 men, 8 non-binary), 601 in total. The analysis unit is the person throughout, and the four cross-validation partitions are participant-disjoint by construction - each participant appears in exactly one partition. Exclusions are enumerated with reasons: 12 self-diagnosed respondents and 13 who did not report a gender they identified with. This is the only charted study in which the number of people, the number of analysis units and the number of rows in every reported metric are the same figure. [RQ1.2] Autistic adults, autistic individuals, neurodivergent, non-autistic, camouflaging, masking, neurotypical behavior. The framing is identity-first and community-aligned throughout: camouflaging is described as an adaptive social coping strategy rather than a symptom, the paper states explicitly that adapting one's behaviour in social contexts - whether to avoid discrimination or to achieve personal goals - is not inherently pathological and does not necessarily indicate autism, and it warns that mental health professionals should be aware of unintentional reinforcement of stigma and the pathologization of (mal)adaptive social strategies like social camouflaging. Non-binary participants are analysed as a group in their own right rather than dropped, and the paper states its reason for using self-reported gender rather than sex assigned at birth: it better reflects participants' identities. This is the only study in the charted corpus whose language would be recognised as respectful by the population it studies. [RQ1.3] The most complete demographic and clinical reporting in the corpus. Age by group with means, SDs and a tested 2.7-year difference with effect size and confidence interval; mean age at autism diagnosis (32.0 years, SD 12.3); self-reported gender in three categories with between-group tests; full education distribution from no studies to PhD for both groups; and a complete self-reported comorbidity table covering high abilities, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, specific learning disorder, epilepsy, bipolar disorder, eating disorder, anxiety, depression and sleep disorder, with percentages for both groups. Nationality/residence is stated (Spain). The women-heavy composition (78% overall) is not merely reported but explained and named as the study's most notable limitation, with a mechanism offered - the parent project validates an instrument designed for highly masked autistic adults, especially women, and online studies skew toward respondents with topic interest, higher cognitive ability and moderate-to-high socioeconomic status. [RQ1.4] Self-reported but with real safeguards, and honestly characterised. Participants were asked about a clinically based diagnosis and about which professional made it; the 12 who reported self-diagnosis were excluded; and respondents were instructed to report only clinician-confirmed diagnoses and not diagnoses based on personal feelings of distress. The authors then name the residual uncertainty as a limitation and recommend clinician-based confirmation in future work. No diagnostic instrument was administered by the research team. Importantly, diagnosis is not the prediction target here - it is a covariate tested for incremental value - so the study's central claims do not rest on label accuracy in the way the rest of this corpus does. [RQ1.5] Dimensional and psychometrically characterised. BAPQ Aloofness, Pragmatic Language and Rigid Personality are the autistic-trait outcomes; PHQ-9 and GAD-7 total scores the affective outcomes; CAT-Q-ES compensation, masking and assimilation subscales the predictors. McDonald's omega is computed in this sample for every instrument (CAT-Q-ES .96, GAD-7 .92, PHQ-9 .91, Aloofness .94, Pragmatics .87, Rigidity .92), and the known psychometric weakness of the Spanish BAPQ Pragmatic Language subscale is flagged in advance. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to evaluate whether machine learning on self-reported camouflaging behaviours can predict dimensional autistic traits and anxiety/depression symptoms, and whether knowing a person's gender or autism diagnosis improves that prediction. Headline findings: correlations between true and predicted scores of R=.85 for Aloofness, .82 for Pragmatics and .75 for Rigidity (strong by the pre-specified Colton criterion), against .58 for Depression and .54 for Anxiety (moderate); and adding gender and/or diagnosis changes R by at most .03, from which the authors conclude that this information is already implicit in the camouflaging items. The stated implication is a possible screening aid for people whose autistic traits are masked or subthreshold and whose diagnosis is unclear or not yet established, regardless of gender identity. [RQ2.2] An online REDCap survey hosted at Fundacion Publica Galega de Medicina Xenomica, disseminated through autism associations, institutions, federations, clinical units, research networks and social media, within a broader project validating the CAT-Q for the Spanish population. Recruitment channel is stated and its selection consequences are analysed in the limitations rather than left implicit. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm - a self-report battery completed in one sitting: the 25-item CAT-Q-ES (Likert 1-7) as predictors, and the 36-item BAPQ, the PHQ-9 and the GAD-7 as outcomes. This is the design's central methodological feature and its principal limitation, discussed under RQ4.5. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single administration. Ethics reporting is complete: Declaration of Helsinki, approval by the Ethics Committee of the University of Santiago de Compostela with the code USC 26/2023, informed consent presented in the survey's first section before participation, and participant anonymity preserved throughout collection. Beyond procedural ethics, the discussion contains a substantive ethical analysis absent from every other study charted here - it warns against reinforcing stigma and pathologising adaptive social strategies, insists that algorithmic models should never replace clinical evaluation, and requires that clinicians apply them within a personalised-medicine approach respecting patient autonomy and daily-life context. [RQ2.5] REDCap for capture, with validated data entry, audit trails for tracking data manipulation and export, and automated export procedures. Modelling used fifty regressors implemented in Python, R, Matlab and Octave, with the package and hyperparameter tuning grid for each listed in a supplementary appendix. [RQ2.6] The highest in the charted corpus. Code and a small sample dataset are publicly deposited on OSF - the only working code released by any study in this review. The fifty models, their implementation languages, packages and hyperparameter grids are enumerated in supplementary material. The cross-validation procedure is specified operationally, including partition disjointness, stratification across the score range, the rotation of training/validation/test roles across four trials, and the refit-on-train-plus-validation step. Missing data are quantified (0.30%) and the imputation justified. Exclusions are counted and reasoned. Internal consistencies are computed in-sample for every instrument. The only gap is the full dataset, withheld for confidentiality with a sample released in its place. [RQ2.7] A genuine limitations section, self-critical and mechanistic rather than formulaic. Four limitations are stated with reasoning: the over-representation of women, traced to the parent validation project and to online-recruitment bias toward respondents with topic interest, higher cognitive ability and moderate-to-high socioeconomic status; the inability to verify self-reported diagnoses, with the mitigation described and its residual risk acknowledged; the weaker anxiety and depression models, explained through instrument structure (PHQ-9 and GAD-7 items each map to a distinct diagnostic criterion and so scatter, whereas BAPQ items are interrelated within domain); and the restriction to generalised anxiety, omitting social anxiety, which is the form most closely tied to masking. The one limitation not stated is the shared-method dependence between predictors and outcomes. [RQ2.9] Include clinician-confirmed diagnoses and observational measures of camouflaging alongside self-report; replace criterion-based screeners with dimensional continuous scales for anxiety and depression to reduce scatter; and, before any clinical implementation, cross-validate extensively against health-record data. Each future direction addresses a specific stated limitation, which is rare in this corpus. [RQ3.1] Camouflaging behaviour, decomposed into compensation (copying others' behaviours, preparing scripts for social situations), masking (controlling and adjusting facial and bodily expression to fit in) and assimilation (effortful engagement and pretending to be normal in social situations). The outcomes are dimensional autistic traits - aloof personality, pragmatic language, rigid personality - and depressive and anxious symptoms. The behaviour of interest is therefore an active social strategy rather than a deficit, and the study is the only one in the corpus to treat an autistic behaviour as adaptive rather than symptomatic. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - a single self-report modality throughout. The nearest analogue is the input-configuration comparison, which tests whether adding gender and/or autism diagnosis to the CAT-Q-ES items improves prediction and finds that it does not. The authors themselves identify observational measurement of camouflaging as the modality this study lacks and recommend adding it. [RQ4.1] Fifty supervised regression algorithms compared under a common protocol - support vector regression, neural networks, linear and regularised linear regressors, decision trees, random forests, boosting ensembles, k-nearest neighbours and Gaussian processes among others. Different algorithms won for different outcomes (SGD for Aloofness, SVR for Pragmatics, Ridge for Rigidity, KNN for Depression, boosted trees for Anxiety), and the winners are simple regularised or instance-based methods rather than deep networks. This is regression to continuous scores rather than the binary classification that dominates the corpus, which removes the threshold and prevalence problems that make most of the charted accuracy figures uninterpretable. [RQ4.2] The 25 raw CAT-Q-ES Likert items, in four configurations: items alone, items plus gender, items plus autism diagnosis, and items plus both. Subscale scores were tested as an alternative input and did not improve accuracy - a negative result the paper reports rather than suppresses. [RQ4.3] Pearson R between true and predicted scores, MAE, MAPE relative to the score range, and RMSE, per outcome and averaged across the four trials, with predicted-versus-true scatter plots against a perfect-agreement diagonal. Correlation magnitudes are interpreted against a pre-specified external criterion (Colton 1974), so strong and moderate are defined before the results rather than after. The tolerance analysis is the most practically informative reporting in the corpus: the best Aloofness model places 36.3% of predictions within 5% of the true score and just over 60% within 10%, which states plainly what the R=.85 does and does not deliver at the individual level. The paper also notes correctly that the lower MAE for Depression and Anxiety reflects their narrower score ranges rather than better prediction, and reads the MAPE accordingly. Two gaps: no confidence intervals or across-trial variance accompany the metrics, and no trivial baseline (for instance, predicting the sample mean) is reported against which the MAE and RMSE could be judged. A minor inconsistency: the abstract gives Rigidity R=.74 and Depression R=.60, while Table 3 gives .75 and .58 for the CAT-Q-ES-only configuration. [RQ4.4] No model-level attribution for the fifty regressors - no coefficients, feature importances or SHAP values are reported, so which camouflaging items carry the signal is not established. The interpretive work is done instead by the input-configuration comparison, which supports a clean negative claim: gender and autism diagnosis add at most .03 to R and 0.10 to MAE, so neither provides information not already implicit in the camouflaging items. That result is the basis for the paper's central applied argument - that the tool could work regardless of gender identity and where a diagnosis is unclear or absent. [RQ4.5] The validation design is the most rigorous in the charted corpus and is reported operationally rather than by name. Two-layer 4-fold cross-validation: 601 participants divided into four partitions that are disjoint at the participant level and stratified so that each spans the full score range; in each of four trials, two partitions train, one validates and one tests, with roles rotating so that every partition serves as test exactly once; for models with tunable hyperparameters, candidates are fitted on the training partitions, selected by MAE on the validation partition, then refitted on training plus validation before a single prediction on the untouched test partition; the four test MAEs are averaged. Hyperparameter selection therefore never sees the test data, the analysis unit is the person, and no participant contributes to both sides of any split - the three failures that account for most of the inflated figures elsewhere in this review are all absent here. Two real limitations remain. The first is the one the paper does not name: predictors and outcomes are self-report questionnaires completed by the same person in the same sitting, so the correlations are inflated by common-method variance, and there is direct construct overlap between camouflaging items (which describe effortful management of social interaction) and the BAPQ Aloofness and Pragmatic Language subscales (which measure social and pragmatic difficulty). The R=.85 for Aloofness should be read as agreement between two overlapping self-descriptions of social experience, not as prediction of an independently ascertained trait - which is precisely why the anxiety and depression models, whose outcomes are less conceptually adjacent to camouflaging, drop to .54 and .58. The authors explain that gap through instrument structure; construct proximity is at least as plausible. The second is that no external cohort is tested, which the paper itself insists on before any clinical use. Set against the corpus, this study is the reference point: a properly nested, participant-level, model-selection-clean design applied to a genuinely dimensional target yields R=.85 at best and .54 at worst, with only 36% of individual predictions landing within 5% of the truth - the realistic ceiling against which the 99% and 100% figures elsewhere in this review should be read. [RQ5.1] ASD; Autism; CAT-Q-ES; Camouflaging; Supervised machine learning; Mental health; Gender. Seven terms covering condition, instrument, construct, method, outcome domain and a demographic dimension analysed substantively - the most informative keyword set in the corpus. [RQ5.2] Research in Autism 128:202712 (Elsevier) - a specialist autism research journal rather than an engineering or general-science venue, and the difference is visible throughout: dimensional outcomes, in-sample psychometrics, effect sizes with confidence intervals for group comparisons, a self-critical limitations section, an ethics analysis of algorithmic screening in mental health, and deposited code. It is the only paper in the corpus published in a venue whose reviewers are subject-matter specialists in autism, and it is also the only one to release code, report internal consistencies, or discuss stigma. [RQ5.3] 2025, accepted 15 September, 133 days with a substantive revision round. Framing is deliberately bounded: the results show the viability of machine learning to predict traits and symptoms and suggest potential for developing a tool that may improve screening in individuals whose diagnosis is unclear or not yet established. The discussion then constrains that further - algorithms should be extensively cross-validated against health records before implementation, should be used as screeners to accelerate referral rather than replace clinical evaluation, and should be applied within a personalised-medicine approach respecting autonomy. Where the rest of this corpus claims diagnosis and delivers checklist arithmetic, this study claims correlation between self-reports and delivers exactly that, with the error bars in view. |
| S-152 | Retrospective analysis of 2,926 facial images at 224x224 from a public repository - the same Kaggle autism face corpus used by all five studies in the paper's comparison table, and the thirteenth charted reuse of that corpus in this review. The split is 2,526 training, 200 validation and 200 test images; class counts are not reported for any partition, and the number of distinct children is unknown. The paper notes that a cited prior study removed duplicates from this corpus using MD5 hashing, and performs no deduplication itself. | HyVit-ASD combines a pre-trained torchvision ResNet whose 512-dimensional output is projected to three channels and resized to 224x224, a pre-trained ViT-base with a custom residual ReAttention mechanism, global average pooling and a linear classifier, plus a proposed Attention-Based Augmentation Layer. Training used AdamW at learning rate 1e-5, weight decay 1e-2, cross-entropy loss and CUDA; epoch count, batch size and seed are unreported. | Test set: accuracy 91%, sensitivity 94%, specificity 88%, AUC 95.67%, F-measure 90.99%, G-mean 90.95%, fall-out 0.12, miss rate 0.06. Validation: accuracy 86.5%, AUC 93.65%. Author-fitted baselines reached 71-80% on validation; literature figures on the same corpus range from 64.67% to 92.01%. | The reported 91% rests on a single unrepeated, unseeded image-level split of a web-scraped corpus with no diagnostic labels, no provenance and acknowledged duplicate images that were not removed - so the same child's photographs can appear on both sides. The test set is 200 images, giving a confidence interval of roughly 86-95% that contains almost every entry in the comparison tables the paper ranks itself above, including Xception at 92.01. Validation accuracy is 4.5 points below test accuracy on equal-sized partitions and this inversion is not discussed. The architecture's stated rationale concerns asymmetric facial movements, eye gaze and mouth movements, none of which exists in a still photograph, and the claim that ReAttention focuses on periocular regions is asserted with no attention map or attribution to support it. Neither novel component is parameterised and no ablation isolates either. There is no ethics statement and no account of the images' provenance. The introduction catalogues a specific limitation for roughly twenty prior studies and states none for this one. | This is the thirteenth charted reuse of the web-scraped facial-image corpus, and it is the branch's most explicit statement of its own epistemics: the paper argues that comparison with prior models rests on a solid common foundation precisely because they all use the same dataset. That shared foundation has no diagnostic labels, no provenance and no demographics, so the whole benchmark line is internally comparable and externally uninterpretable. Its 91% falls in the middle of the branch's 81-99.8% range and is consistent with the pattern established across the other twelve - reported accuracy tracks evaluation protocol and model capacity rather than signal. Two features make it worth recording separately. It has the most complete and internally consistent metric reporting in the branch, including specificity and fall-out as numbers. And it contains the corpus's most extensive limitations apparatus, roughly twenty named weaknesses attached to other people's work, with none directed at its own single split, unlabelled data or absent ethics statement - which makes it the clearest example of critical vocabulary functioning as positioning rather than as method. | [RQ1.1] No participants. 2,926 images at 224x224, described as curated from public repositories covering diverse demographics and labelled autism or non-autism; the comparison tables identify the source as the same Kaggle facial corpus used by all five of the studies it benchmarks against. The split is 2,526 training, 200 validation and 200 test images. Class counts are never stated for any partition, though the metric arithmetic implies a balanced 200-image test set. The number of distinct children is unknown - and the paper is aware that this matters, because it notes that one cited study cleaned duplicates from the dataset using the MD5 hash algorithm, an acknowledgement that the corpus contains repeated images. No deduplication is performed here. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic and non-autistic children, autistic individuals, ASD children, individuals with ASD and their families. The register is clinical and reasonably neutral - non-autistic rather than normal is used for the comparison class - though the opening sentence describes ASD as a complicated neurological disease and the introduction lists cognitive impairments among its defining characteristics. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] None. The dataset is asserted to cover diverse demographics and the model is claimed to address demographic variability, but no age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment information exists for any image and none is reported. The diversity claim is therefore unverifiable, and the paper's stated advance over prior work on limited generalizability across diverse demographics rests on it. [RQ1.4] None. Labels are the folder assignment of a public image corpus. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image, and unlike several of its neighbours the paper does not even describe the labelling process in passing. The comparison table's premise - that the models being compared share a common foundation because they use the same dataset - makes this the shared and unexamined weakness of the whole benchmark line. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to overcome the limitations of prior facial-image ASD classifiers - computational cost, pose sensitivity, poor generalisation across demographics - with HyVit-ASD, a hybrid combining a pre-trained ResNet convolutional block, a pre-trained ViT with a custom residual ReAttention mechanism, and an Attention-Based Augmentation Layer. Headline findings: test accuracy 91%, sensitivity 94%, specificity 88%, AUC 95.67%, F-measure 90.99%, G-mean 90.95%, fall-out 0.12, miss rate 0.06, against six models the authors fitted (71-80% validation accuracy) and five literature figures on the same corpus (68-90%). [RQ2.2] No study setting. Images were obtained from a public repository; training used CUDA acceleration with no hardware, runtime or environment described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Static photographs. The rationale nonetheless refers repeatedly to movement - the ReAttention mechanism is justified as capturing fine-grained local features critical for ASD biomarkers such as asymmetric facial movements, and as amplifying regions including eye gaze and mouth movements. None of these is present in a still image, so the architecture's stated motivation describes a modality the study does not use. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is absent entirely - no approval, no consent, no exemption claim, and no mention of where photographs of identifiable children came from or under what terms they may be reused. The paper does note, in summarising prior work, that web-based screening tools raise privacy concerns, so the category is available to it and simply not applied to its own data. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Modelling used PyTorch with a torchvision pre-trained ResNet and a ViT-base transformer, AdamW at learning rate 1e-5 with weight decay 1e-2, cross-entropy loss and CUDA. No versions, seed, epoch count, batch size or hardware. [RQ2.6] Low. The architecture is described in prose with three equations, and the optimiser, learning rate, weight decay, loss function and split sizes are given - a better start than several neighbours. What is missing prevents replication: no code, no seed, no epoch or batch count, no ResNet depth or ViT variant, no parameterisation for either of the two components claimed as novel (ReAttention and the Attention-Based Augmentation Layer), no list of augmentation transformations, no dataset accession beyond a reference number, no class counts for any partition, and no statement of how the 200-image validation and test sets were drawn from 2,926. [RQ2.7] None of its own. This paper has the corpus's most extensive limitations apparatus pointed entirely outward: the introduction runs through roughly twenty prior approaches and attaches a specific weakness to each - high computational cost and limited generalizability across diverse demographics, sensitivity to non-frontal poses, dependence on iterative expert annotation, computational intensity of heterogeneous data fusion, susceptibility to noise in handcrafted features, laborious EEG preprocessing, expensive eye-tracking hardware, domain shift in EfficientNet on medical images, scarce labelled data, need for high-quality motion sensors, shallow architectures, accuracy sacrificed for deployability, privacy concerns and connectivity dependence in web tools, cultural variability in handwriting, cost and immobilisation requirements of fMRI, and overfitting risk in metaheuristic optimisation. It even observes that cross-validation may not reflect real-world variability, risking overfitting. None of this critical vocabulary is turned on its own single unrepeated image-level split of an unlabelled web corpus. The only self-directed hedge is a clause in the conclusion. [RQ2.9] Hybrid vision transformers and adaptive learning as a direction for future research in ASD classification and medical imaging, and validation on larger, more diverse datasets. The second addresses the study's real gap; the first proposes more of what was just done. [RQ3.1] None. The classification target is static facial appearance. The paper's own account of what the model attends to - periocular regions, eye gaze, mouth movements, asymmetric facial movements - describes dynamic behaviours that a single photograph cannot contain, so the stated biomarker rationale and the actual input are mismatched. [RQ3.2] No fusion of modalities. The hybrid designation refers to combining two vision backbones (ResNet and ViT) over the same image. The introduction reviews multimodal neuroimaging and EEG-plus-eye-tracking work and dismisses both on cost and complexity grounds. [RQ4.1] A three-stage architecture: a ConvBlock in which a pre-trained ResNet produces a 512-dimensional feature vector that is projected by a 1x1 convolution to three channels and interpolated back to 224x224; a TransformerBlock applying a pre-trained ViT-base with a residual ReAttention mechanism; and global average pooling into a linear classifier. The intermediate step is unusual and unexplained - ResNet features are collapsed to a three-channel image-shaped tensor purely so that a pre-trained ViT's input interface can consume them, which discards most of the convolutional representation before the transformer sees it. No ablation tests whether the ConvBlock, the ReAttention module or the ABAL contributes anything. [RQ4.2] 224x224 RGB face crops from the public corpus, with unspecified preprocessing and augmentation plus a proposed Attention-Based Augmentation Layer applying unnamed non-destructive transformations. Neither the augmentation set nor its placement relative to the split is stated. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, AUC, F-measure, G-mean, sensitivity, specificity, fall-out and miss rate, with formulae given, reported for both validation and test, plus a confusion-matrix figure. This is a fuller and better-chosen metric set than most of the facial-image branch offers - specificity and fall-out are reported as numbers rather than merely claimed, and the figures are internally consistent (sensitivity 94% with miss rate 0.06; specificity 88% with fall-out 0.12; their mean 91% matching the reported accuracy on a balanced test set). Two problems. No confidence interval accompanies any figure, and on 200 test images the 95% interval around 91% runs from roughly 86% to 95% - a range that contains almost every entry in the comparison tables, so the claimed ordering among methods is not established. And validation accuracy (86.5%) is lower than test accuracy (91%) by 4.5 points on 200 images each, which is reported without comment. [RQ4.4] Claimed, not shown. The ReAttention mechanism is described as adaptively amplifying diagnostically relevant regions such as eye gaze and mouth movements and as focusing on periocular regions, aligning with clinical studies linking ASD to reduced eye contact. No attention map, saliency overlay, feature attribution or region-level analysis appears anywhere in the paper to support this, and no ablation isolates the module. The claim that the model attends to the periocular region - which would be the study's most interesting finding if demonstrated - is asserted as a design intention and presented as though it were a result. [RQ4.5] A single image-level split of 2,926 images into 2,526 training, 200 validation and 200 test, with no cross-validation, no repetition, no seed and no description of how the split was drawn. Three problems follow. First, the corpus is the widely reused web-scraped autism face collection, which contains duplicate and near-duplicate images of the same individuals; the paper demonstrates awareness of exactly this, noting that a cited study cleaned duplicates from the dataset using the MD5 hash algorithm, and then does not deduplicate, so images of the same child can sit on both sides of the split. Second, the test set is 200 images, giving a 95% confidence interval around 91% of roughly 86-95% - wide enough to contain the great majority of the comparison entries the paper ranks itself above, including MobileNet-V1 at 90.67 and Xception at 92.01, so the reported ordering is not supported. Third, validation accuracy is 4.5 points below test accuracy on partitions of equal size, an inversion that normally indicates split variance rather than generalisation and is reported without remark. Underneath all three sits the problem the whole benchmark line shares and this paper states approvingly: the models being compared have a solid common foundation because they use the same dataset - a dataset with no diagnostic labels, no provenance and no demographic information. A common foundation of that kind makes the numbers comparable to each other and to nothing else. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; Vision transformers; Facial image analysis; ReAttention; Early diagnosis; CNN. Four of six terms name architecture; participants, validation and setting are absent. [RQ5.2] International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems 18(3):312-319 - an open-access computing journal. Review appears to have been rapid (received 17 January 2025, revised 4 February 2025) and did not surface the absent ethics statement, the unreported class counts, the 200-image test set behind a four-way ranking claim, or the mismatch between a movement-based biomarker rationale and a still-image input. [RQ5.3] 2025. Framing is diagnostic and confident: the model is a pioneering approach contributing significantly to early diagnosis and intervention strategies, and a powerful tool to enhance ASD diagnosis and improve outcomes for individuals with ASD and their families, hedged only by a clause acknowledging that further validation on larger, diverse datasets is needed. The contribution is expressed as a position in a leaderboard over one public image corpus, and the paper is explicit that this shared corpus is what makes the comparison solid - which is the clearest statement in the review of how this branch understands evidence. |
| S-153 | Retrospective analysis of the Kaggle ASD Children Facial dataset - 2,940 images, 1,470 autistic and 1,470 non-autistic - the fourteenth charted reuse of this corpus in the review. The methods define an image-level split of 2,540 training images and 400 test images, balanced within each class. No demographic or diagnostic information exists for any image. | Images were resized (described as adjusting ratio and resolution with the loss of pixels), sharpened by DeepDeblur, a convolution/deconvolution network learning a blurred-to-sharp mapping, then passed to DOCNN, a CNN performing joint denoising and classification with parameters tuned by the Fire Hawk Optimizer. Implementation in MATLAB R2021a. No architecture, learning rate, batch size, epoch count or optimiser budget is reported, and no component is ablated. | Accuracy 96.94%, precision 97.28%, recall 96.62%, F-measure 96.95%. Deblurring: 91.22% blur removed, PSNR 32.75 dB, MSE 0.115, SSIM 0.96, against Deepblur, Wiener filtering and blind deconvolution. Comparison against five literature figures ranging from 92.0% to 96.63%. | The reported accuracy is a resubstitution figure. The results section states that of 2,940 images used for evaluation, 1,430 autism and 1,420 non-autism images were classified correctly - 2,850 correct, 90 wrong - and 2,850/2,940 is exactly 96.94%, so the headline number was computed over the entire dataset including the 2,540 training images, and the 400-image test set defined in the methods produces no reported result. The labels are Kaggle folder names on web-scraped photographs with no clinical diagnosis behind them, and the corpus repeats individuals, so even a correctly executed image-level split would not separate children. Three pipeline components are each claimed as contributions and none is ablated. The deblurring evaluation reports PSNR, MSE and SSIM, which require a sharp ground-truth reference that cannot exist for downloaded images, and no explanation is given. There is no ethics statement, no limitations section and no future work. | This is the fourteenth charted reuse of the web-scraped facial-image corpus and the branch's clearest single instance of a headline figure that is not a held-out estimate at all. Across the branch, reported accuracy has tracked evaluation looseness rather than signal; here the looseness is complete - the test set is defined, described and then not used, and the arithmetic of the confusion matrix makes this checkable from the paper's own numbers. It pairs with local_986436f2, whose headline came from an unexplained 200-image selection out of its test set while its confusion matrix summed to a third figure, as the two cases where the branch's evaluation reporting breaks down entirely rather than merely being optimistic. Its deblurring metrics add a second, less common failure to the review's catalogue: reference-dependent image-quality measures (PSNR, MSE, SSIM) reported for photographs that have no reference, which either means the degradation was synthetic and undisclosed or the metrics were computed against nothing determinable. | [RQ1.1] No participants. 2,940 images from the Kaggle ASD Children Facial dataset, balanced at 1,470 autistic and 1,470 non-autistic - the fourteenth charted reuse of this corpus in the review. The number of distinct children is unknown and never raised, and the corpus is known to contain repeated images of the same faces. The paper states a split of 2,540 training images (1,270 per class) and 400 test images (200 per class), but the confusion matrix it then reports covers all 2,940 images, so the population behind the headline figure is the whole dataset rather than the held-out 400. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic and non-autistic faces, autistic patients, children. The register is medical and dated: ASD is introduced as a neurodevelopmental disorder with ineffective brain functions and as a conventional developmental neuro-disorder, and deep learning is credited with developing interactive systems to assist in the reintegration and treatment of autistic patients. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status or recruitment source for any image, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent. One of the studies the paper summarises in its own literature review notes that model reliability depends on dataset quality and race factors, so the concern is present in the article's field of view and is not applied to its own data. [RQ1.4] None. Labels are Kaggle folder names on photographs of unknown provenance. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image. The paper opens by observing correctly that there is no medical screening or test like a blood test or scan for ASD and that diagnosis requires developmental history and behavioural assessment - and then treats folder labels on downloaded photographs as sufficient ground truth for a diagnostic classifier. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to make facial-image ASD screening robust to poor image quality by adding a deblurring stage and a joint denoising-classification network with metaheuristic parameter tuning. Headline findings: accuracy 96.94%, precision 97.28%, recall 96.62%, F-measure 96.95%, against five literature figures between 92.0% and 96.63%; and, for the deblurring stage, 91.22% blur removed with PSNR 32.75 dB and SSIM 0.96 against Deepblur, Wiener filtering and blind deconvolution. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Images downloaded from Kaggle; experiments run in MATLAB R2021a with no hardware, runtime or environment described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Static photographs with no stimulus, interaction or session. The construct measured is facial appearance, framed as a diagnostic route parallel to behavioural analysis. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. There is no ethics statement, no consent statement and no exemption claim, and no consideration of where photographs of identifiable children came from or under what terms they may be reused, deblurred, denoised and redistributed in figures - the paper reproduces sample faces at five processing stages in Figure 3. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Implementation in MATLAB R2021a. No toolbox versions, hardware, runtime, seed or code. The proposed pipeline's components - DeepDeblur, DOCNN and the Fire Hawk Optimizer - are described by loss functions and a notation table rather than by any reproducible configuration. [RQ2.6] Very low, with one distinctive problem. The dataset source, class balance, split sizes and MATLAB version are stated, and a 25-symbol notation table with loss definitions (L2, total variation, facial semantic, total) is provided - superficially detailed. But no architecture, learning rate, batch size, epoch count, image resolution, optimiser budget or search space is given; there is no code or seed; the reported result does not correspond to the stated split; and the deblurring evaluation reports PSNR, MSE and SSIM, all of which are computed against a sharp ground-truth reference image. No such reference exists for a photograph downloaded from the web. Either the blur was synthetically added to already-degraded web images so that a reference existed - in which case the deblurring result describes recovery from artificial corruption and says nothing about real image quality - or the metrics were computed against something unstated. The paper does not say which. [RQ2.7] None. There is no limitations section, no threats-to-validity discussion and no caveat. The single occurrence of limitations is a generic sentence in the introduction about facial-feature analysis being affected by image quality and expression variation - which is the problem the paper sets out to solve, not a limitation of its solution. Nothing is said about the dataset's provenance, the absent diagnostic labels, the mismatch between the stated split and the reported evaluation, or the absence of any ablation. [RQ2.9] None. There is no future-work section; the paper ends on the claim of higher accuracy with reduced model complexity. [RQ3.1] None. No behaviour is observed, elicited or measured. The target is static facial appearance recovered from deblurring and denoising. [RQ3.2] No fusion of modalities - a single image source. The pipeline stacks three processing stages (deblurring, denoising, classification) over one photograph, which is depth rather than multimodality. [RQ4.1] A two-stage pipeline: DeepDeblur, a convolution/deconvolution network learning a blurred-to-sharp mapping, followed by DOCNN, a CNN in which one layer set denoises and the next classifies, with a Fire Hawk Optimizer tuning parameters. Three separable components are each claimed as a contribution and none is ablated, so the reader cannot tell whether the deblurring stage, the denoising branch or the metaheuristic contributes anything to the classification result. [RQ4.2] Resized, deblurred and denoised RGB face images at unstated resolution. Resizing is described as adjusting the facial image for ratio and resolution with the loss of pixels - an unusual admission that information is discarded before the pipeline whose purpose is to recover information begins. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, a confusion matrix and an ROC curve for classification; percentage blur removed, PSNR, MSE and SSIM for deblurring. Specificity is not reported, no AUC value is given numerically, no calibration or predictive values appear, and no confidence interval accompanies any figure. The reported accuracy of 96.94% reconciles exactly with the confusion-matrix counts - 2,850 correct out of 2,940 - which is the problem rather than a reassurance, because 2,940 is the entire dataset and not the 400-image test set the methods section defines. [RQ4.4] None. No saliency, attribution or feature analysis, and no ablation of the three pipeline stages. In a paper whose thesis is that image quality restoration improves ASD detection, no experiment isolates the contribution of restoration to the classification outcome - the deblurring metrics and the classification metrics are reported side by side but never linked. [RQ4.5] This study's decisive problem is that the reported result does not come from its stated evaluation design. The methods define an image-level split of 2,940 images into 2,540 for training and 400 for testing, balanced within each. The results section then states that out of 2,940 images used for evaluation the model correctly classified 1,430 autism images and 1,420 non-autism images, 2,850 correct with 90 misclassified - and 2,850/2,940 is precisely 96.94%, the headline accuracy carried into the abstract and the comparison table. The reported performance is therefore a resubstitution figure computed over the whole dataset, with 86% of the evaluated images having been used to fit the model. The 400-image test set is defined and never used to produce a number. Three further issues compound this. The corpus is the web-scraped autism face collection that repeats individuals, so even a correctly executed image-level split would not separate children. The Fire Hawk Optimizer tuned unspecified parameters against an unspecified objective on an unspecified partition. And the comparison table ranks 96.94% against five literature figures spanning 92.0% to 96.63% obtained on different image counts (2,636 to 3,014) under unstated protocols, with the paper asserting that the comparisons are done under the same conditions used in the existing methods to ensure fair comparison - a claim that cannot hold when this study's own figure is a training-set score. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; Face recognition; DeepDeblur; Denoising optimized convolutional neural network; Fire hawk optimizer. Four of five terms name pipeline components; face recognition rather than screening or classification is used for the task. [RQ5.2] International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems 18(4) - an open-access computing journal, the same venue as local_6e7174c0. Review did not surface the mismatch between the stated 400-image test set and the 2,940-image evaluation, the absent ethics statement, or the reporting of reference-dependent image-quality metrics for photographs that have no sharp reference. [RQ5.3] 2025 (received 26 October 2024, revised 1 March 2025). Framing is diagnostic and efficiency-oriented: the model is offered for screening and detection of ASD in children, as computer-aided diagnosis, and as achieving higher accuracy with reduced model complexity and less execution time. There is no limitations section and no future work; the contribution is stated entirely as a position above five quoted figures on the same public image corpus, and the paper's own account of why ASD diagnosis is difficult - that there is no blood test or scan and that developmental history and behaviour must be assessed - is not reconciled with what it then does. |
| S-154 | Retrospective analysis of the public ASD Children Traits dataset from Kaggle (accessed 1 June 2024): 1,985 cases of children aged 1-18 with 28 variables, reduced by expert-guided outlier and inconsistency removal to 634 cases and 19 variables. The retained variables include the ten AQ-10 items, the AQ10 total, the Q-CHAT-10 score, the Social Responsiveness Scale, a CARS severity rating, seven comorbidity flags, demographics and rater type, with the binary ASD_traits field as the target. Class balance is never reported. | Eight classifiers - random forest, SVM, GBM, XGBoost, C5.0, a neural network, k-NN and logistic regression - were fitted in R with caret 6.0.94 under 10-fold cross-validation with grid-search tuning, and compared by Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman tests on fold-wise metrics. Permutation feature importance, LIME and SHAP were applied to the best models. Prompted by the exceptionally high results, the full comparison was repeated at 2-fold, 4-fold and 5-fold. | Under 10-fold cross-validation the neural network achieved accuracy, F1, precision and recall of exactly 1.0000 (prAUC 0.9601); GBM and XGBoost reached 0.9984 with precision 1.0000; logistic regression 0.9858; SVM 0.9874; C5.0 0.9701; random forest 0.9463; k-NN 0.8883 at k=7. The neural network again scored perfectly at 4 and 5 folds but fell to 0.8691 at 2 folds. All three XAI methods identified the A1-A10 behavioural items as dominant and demographic variables as negligible. | The predictor set contains CARS, the Social Responsiveness Scale, the AQ10 total and the Q-CHAT-10 score - four instrument measurements of the target condition - together with the ten AQ-10 items that constitute the AQ10 total, all supplied as predictors of a binary autism-traits label. Perfect classification follows from that arrangement, and the authors' own overfitting investigation, which correctly re-ran the comparison at 2, 4 and 5 folds, cannot detect it because varying the partition does not touch the feature list; the decisive experiment, refitting without the instrument scores, is never run. Preprocessing removed 1,351 of 1,985 records and 9 of 28 variables on unstated criteria before cross-validation, and this step is credited in the abstract with improving generalizability. Class balance is never reported for any partition, so no baseline exists; specificity is never reported for any model; and the claim of applicability across diverse clinical datasets rests on one dataset. The label's own provenance - who assessed these children, with what instrument, against what criterion - is nowhere described. | This study matters to the review as the clearest demonstration that methodological care and a valid estimand are independent. Everything the field's methods literature asks for is present: child-level cross-validation, grid-search tuning, per-fold publication, formal non-parametric model comparison, three explanation methods, a deposited analysis dataset, clinician co-authorship, and an explicit, self-initiated overfitting investigation that no other study in this corpus attempts. The result is accuracy 1.0000. It belongs with local_3e88f3ce, which fed ADOS and ADI-R totals to a model and reached ROC-AUC 99.99%, as the corpus's two instrument-inclusion leakage cases, and with local_ed30e24c, whose careful nested tuning sat downstream of a circular label. Read alongside local_4da2b941, which under a comparably rigorous design and a non-circular target reached R=0.85 at best, it isolates the variable that actually governs reported performance in this literature: not the algorithm, not the resampling scheme, and not the explanation layer, but whether a measurement of the outcome is present among the inputs. Its consent waiver - justified on the ground that prior reuse of the dataset establishes a general consensus regarding its use for research purposes - is also the corpus's most explicit statement of reuse legitimising reuse. | [RQ1.1] No participants were recruited. The ASD Children Traits dataset was downloaded from Kaggle: 1,985 cases with 28 variables, covering children aged 1-18. Preprocessing then reduced this to 634 cases and 19 variables - 68% of the records and a third of the variables removed as outliers, inconsistencies or erroneous data identified by clinical experts. Neither the raw nor the preprocessed dataset's class balance is reported anywhere, so the number of ASD and non-ASD cases behind every result in the paper is unknown. This matters more than usual because the introduction states explicitly that ASD assessment datasets tend to over-represent ASD cases and that this can bias models toward the majority class - a problem the authors identify and then never quantify in their own data. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, individuals with ASD, patients, ASD traits, non-ASD. The register is clinical and generally neutral, with person-first phrasing throughout and an explicit concern for quality of life for individuals with ASD. The consistent use of patient for records in a downloaded Kaggle file - patient case identifiers, patient consent, patient information - is worth noting: it treats spreadsheet rows as clinical subjects while the study has no clinical relationship with any of them. [RQ1.3] Variables are present but distributions are not. Age spans 1-18 years with no mean or SD; sex is coded M/F with no counts; ethnicity is coded across 11 categories (Asian, Black, Hispanic, Latino, Middle Eastern, Mixed, Native Indian, Others, Pacifica, South Asian, White European) with no counts; family history and rater type (family member, healthcare professional, other) are recorded. Seven comorbidity flags are retained as model inputs - speech/language delay, learning disorder, genetic disorders, depression, global developmental delay/intellectual disability, social/behavioural issues, anxiety disorder - and not one prevalence figure is given for any of them. The dataset is described as comprehensively capturing socioeconomic status, but no socioeconomic variable appears in either variable table. [RQ1.4] None. The dependent variable is ASD_traits, a binary yes/no field in a Kaggle spreadsheet. No clinical assessment, diagnostic instrument administration, criterion, assessor or date exists for any case, and the originating collection procedure is not described at all. The paper nonetheless frames the task as ASD diagnosis throughout, titles itself Reliable Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis for Pediatrics, and opens by criticising clinician-administered instruments for introducing variability and potential bias - a criticism made in favour of a label whose provenance is entirely unknown. [RQ1.5] Four instrument scores are present - Social Responsiveness Scale, CARS, AQ10 total and Q-CHAT-10 - and all four are used as model inputs rather than reported as participant characteristics. Not one mean, range or class-wise distribution appears for any of them. This is the study's central analytic problem, examined under RQ4.2 and RQ4.5. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to combine explainable AI with a rigorous, clinically guided preprocessing pipeline to make ML-based ASD diagnosis both accurate and interpretable, and to provide practical R-based guidelines for non-expert clinicians. Headline findings: under 10-fold cross-validation the neural network reached accuracy, precision, recall and F1 of exactly 1.0000, with GBM and XGBoost at 0.9984 and logistic regression at 0.9858; Wilcoxon and Friedman tests confirmed significant differences between models; and PFI, LIME and SHAP all identified the A1-A10 behavioural items as dominant with demographic variables contributing little. [RQ2.2] No study setting. A downloaded Kaggle file analysed in R. The authorship is notable for this corpus - it includes practising paediatric and psychiatric clinicians from a university hospital, and their input is credited with guiding the feature-selection step. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Tabular records combining AQ-10 item responses, four instrument scores, comorbidity flags and demographics, with a rater field recording whether a family member, healthcare professional or other person completed the assessment. The rater field is retained as a predictor rather than analysed as a source of measurement heterogeneity. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethics is formally addressed and formally waived: ethical review and approval were waived due to the use of publicly available data without any identifiable information, and patient consent was waived because the dataset is widely accepted and publicly available, has been used in numerous research studies establishing a general consensus regarding its use for research purposes, and has been de-identified. The reasoning is at least stated, which distinguishes it from the many charted studies with no ethics statement at all; but the specific argument - that prior reuse establishes a consensus legitimising further reuse - is a citation-count justification for a governance question, and it is offered for a dataset whose own collection consent is never established. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation. R with caret 6.0.94, iml for SHAP and permutation importance, lime for LIME, glmnet and class for two of the models. The paper devotes an entire subsection to arguing that R is accessible to non-expert clinicians and offers practical guidelines for its use - a genuine attempt at translation - and then does not release the script that would make those guidelines operational. [RQ2.6] Split. The artefact-level reporting is among the best in the charted corpus: the source dataset has a URL and access date, the preprocessed 634-case analysis dataset is deposited as a supplementary spreadsheet, fold-by-fold metrics for all eight models appear in an appendix, caret's version is given, each model family is defined by equation, and the k-NN k-sweep is reported in full. The decisive step is nevertheless irreproducible. Preprocessing removed 1,351 of 1,985 records and 9 of 28 variables on the basis of clinical experts identifying inconsistencies and erroneous data, with no criterion stated, no counts per step, no class composition for the removed records and no indication of whether the removal was made blind to the outcome. Since that step is credited in the abstract with improving generalizability and real-world applicability, and since it is the largest single transformation in the pipeline, the study cannot be reproduced in the respect that matters most. [RQ2.7] There is no limitations section, but the discussion contains the most genuine act of self-scrutiny in the charted corpus. The authors write that because of the exceptionally high-performance metrics observed in our initial model evaluations, we were concerned about the potential for overfitting, and they respond by re-running the entire comparison at 2-fold, 4-fold and 5-fold. They report that the neural network's perfect scores in certain folds indicate a potential risk of overfitting to specific data characteristics, and that identical metrics for the neural network and k-NN in some tables may indicate redundancy or overfitting in the model implementation or data processing. That instinct is correct and is exercised properly. What it does not reach is the cause: no fold count can diagnose a problem that lies in the feature set rather than the partition, and the one experiment that would have settled it - refitting without the SRS, CARS, AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 scores - is never run. Unmentioned elsewhere: the unreported class balance, the unspecified 68% record removal, the absence of any external dataset behind a claim of applicability across diverse clinical datasets, and the unknown provenance of the label. [RQ2.9] A single direction: migrate from R to Python for access to more advanced machine-learning libraries and better collaboration with the childcare research community. This is a tooling preference rather than a scientific direction, and it addresses none of the study's own identified concerns - not the overfitting the authors flag, not external validation, and not the missing clinical ground truth. [RQ3.1] Autistic traits as captured by the ten AQ-10 items, characterised in the XAI discussion as communication patterns, repetitive actions and frequency of eye contact. All behaviour is second-hand and questionnaire-mediated, reported by a family member, healthcare professional or unspecified other. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - a single tabular source. There is, however, a fusion of instrument types within the feature vector that is the study's defining characteristic: AQ-10 item responses, an AQ-10 total, a Q-CHAT-10 total, an SRS score and a CARS severity rating all sit in the same 19-variable input alongside the ASD_traits label they are designed to determine. [RQ4.1] Eight classical classifiers compared under a common protocol - random forest, SVM, gradient boosting machine, XGBoost, C5.0, a neural network, k-nearest neighbours and logistic regression - with grid-search tuning in caret and formal statistical comparison by Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman tests. No deep learning on raw signals; the comparison is fair in form and the statistical apparatus is more rigorous than anything else in the charted corpus. [RQ4.2] A 19-field tabular row containing, together: the ten AQ-10 behavioural items, the AQ10 total score, the Q-CHAT-10 score, the Social Responsiveness Scale score, the CARS severity rating, seven comorbidity flags and demographics - with ASD_traits as the target. This is the review's most concentrated instance of target leakage by instrument inclusion. CARS is a clinician-administered autism severity scale; SRS measures social impairment severity; AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 are autism screening totals whose thresholds define exactly the kind of traits-present label being predicted; and the ten AQ-10 items are the summands of the AQ10 total. Four separate measurements of the target condition, plus the item-level constituents of one of them, are supplied to the model as predictors of that condition. A perfect neural-network score under this arrangement is the expected outcome, not an anomaly - and it explains why even logistic regression, a linear model on 19 variables, reaches 0.9858. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, F1, precision, recall and area under the precision-recall curve, per model and per fold, at four fold counts, with per-fold tables in an appendix. The choice of prAUC is thoughtful and explicitly justified by the expected class imbalance. Two absences matter. Specificity is never reported for any model, so the false-positive behaviour of a system proposed for paediatric screening is invisible; and the class balance is never given, so neither the prAUC baseline nor the majority-class accuracy can be computed. The reported neural-network figures are accuracy 1.0000, F1 1.0000, precision 1.0000 and recall 1.0000 - a model that misclassifies no child in any of ten folds - with prAUC 0.9601, a combination that is itself internally odd, since a classifier with perfect precision and recall should have a precision-recall curve area of 1. [RQ4.4] Three methods, applied properly and to the best models only: permutation feature importance, LIME with reported probability and explanation-fit values, and SHAP, with the authors concluding that SHAP gives the most consistent and reliable explanations for both global and local behaviour. The substantive finding is that the A1-A10 behavioural items dominate while demographic variables such as age and ethnicity contribute little, which the paper reads as evidence that behaviour rather than demography drives ASD prediction and as grounds for clinician trust. The reading is understandable and wrong in an instructive way: the model weights the AQ-10 items heavily because the label is an autism-traits determination made from those items, so the explanation confirms the pipeline's internal arithmetic rather than validating a clinical insight. The XAI apparatus here is the most carefully executed in the charted corpus and is applied to a model whose behaviour it cannot make meaningful. [RQ4.5] On the axes that defeat most of this literature, the design is sound. The analysis unit is the child, the folds partition children, there is no within-participant leakage, hyperparameters are grid-searched, per-fold results are published, model differences are tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman statistics rather than eyeballed, and the k-NN sweep is reported. The authors then did what almost no one in this corpus does: they distrusted their own result. Concerned about the potential for overfitting given exceptionally high metrics, they re-ran the full comparison at 2, 4 and 5 folds, observed that the neural network scored perfectly at 4 and 5 folds but fell to 0.8691 at 2, and noted that this indicates a potential risk of overfitting to specific data characteristics. That is the right instinct pointed at the wrong object. Varying the fold count tests partition sensitivity; it cannot detect leakage that lives in the feature set. Here the feature set contains four separate instrument measurements of the target condition - CARS, SRS, AQ10 and Q-CHAT-10 - plus the item-level constituents of the AQ-10 total, all predicting a binary ASD_traits label. Under those conditions accuracy 1.0000 is not overfitting; it is the model reading the answer off the input, and no resampling scheme will change it. Two further issues compound this. The preprocessing removed 68% of the records and a third of the variables through expert identification of inconsistencies and erroneous data, performed on the whole dataset before cross-validation and with no stated criterion, no per-class counts and no indication of outcome blinding - a step credited in the abstract with improving generalizability. And the class balance is never reported, so neither a majority-class baseline nor a prAUC reference exists, and the perfect scores cannot be positioned against anything. The abstract's claim that rigorous preprocessing improved real-world applicability across diverse clinical datasets is made from a single dataset with no external cohort. [RQ5.1] autism spectrum disorder; clinical diagnosis; data preprocessing; healthcare analytics; machine learning; patient outcomes; personalized intervention; explainable artificial intelligence. Eight terms spanning condition, method, application and aspiration; validation and participants are absent, and clinical diagnosis names something the study does not have. [RQ5.2] Diagnostics 14(22):2504 (MDPI) - an open-access clinical diagnostics journal, with paediatric and psychiatric clinicians among the authors. The clinical involvement is real and shaped the feature selection; it did not surface that four instrument measurements of the target condition were sitting in the predictor set, which is precisely the observation clinical expertise is best placed to make. The paper cleared review in 40 days. [RQ5.3] Published 8 November 2024 (indexed here under 2025), 40 days from submission. Framing is translational and confident: the integration of ML and XAI promises to revolutionize intervention strategies, the study successfully developed highly precise and interpretable ML models for ASD diagnosis, and the findings support the adoption of AI-driven diagnostic tools by healthcare professionals and contribute to personalized intervention strategies. The paper positions itself in a comparison table against ten prior studies, with the distinguishing contribution in every row being the absence of XAI in the others - so novelty is claimed on the explanation layer while the estimand goes unexamined. Its most interesting feature is that a team including practising clinicians, applying correct cross-validation, formal statistical testing and three explanation methods, arrived at accuracy 1.0000 and treated it as a result to be defended by resampling rather than as a signal to inspect the feature list. |
| S-155 | Cross-sectional primary study in Cordoba, Spain. Ninety-three children aged 32-74 months in three groups - 24 with ASD, 25 with developmental language disorder, 44 typically developing - with both clinical groups recruited from early childhood intervention centres and required to hold a formal DSM-5 diagnosis from a licensed clinical team. Groups were matched on age (F(2,90)=0.041, p=0.959) but differed significantly in sex composition (22/2 and 23/2 male/female in the clinical groups against 22/22 in TD, p<0.01), basic attention and PPVT-III receptive vocabulary. | Gaze was recorded with a Tobii X2-30 at 30 Hz during an eye-tracking paired preferences task pairing faces (happy, angry, neutral) with objects, after nine-point calibration. Four nested feature sets were derived per child - full (158 variables), secondary (72), prior (60) and basic (24) - and interpretable classifiers were evaluated under stratified 5-fold cross-validation across every group combination, with F1 interpreted against pre-specified bands. | F1 0.912 for DLD versus TD, 0.88 for pooled ASD+DLD versus TD, 0.86 for ASD versus TD, and 0.63 for ASD versus DLD. Naive Bayes and logistic model trees performed best. Broad social versus non-social areas of interest carried the discriminative information; finer variables about specific facial regions and emotions did not improve accuracy. Mean duration of visits to objects emerged as a candidate marker, interpreted as difficulty disengaging attention from objects. | The authors name four: limited experimental scope, sample size, diagnostic instruments that could have been supplemented but were the only ones available, and the provisionality of early-age diagnoses. Three more are visible in the data. The clinical groups are roughly 92% male against 50% in the TD group and differ significantly in receptive vocabulary and basic attention, none of which is adjusted for, so part of the separation from TD may reflect sex and language ability rather than diagnosis. The full feature set carries 158 variables for 93 children, and no confidence interval or across-fold variance is reported for any figure. And the headline results are the best over four feature sets crossed with several algorithms and four group comparisons, without correction or an external cohort. The ASD-versus-DLD result is the least affected by all three, since it shares every methodological feature with the ASD-versus-TD comparison. | This is one of the two studies in the charted corpus not at high overall risk of bias, and it supplies the review's most direct measurement of a quantity the rest of the literature leaves undefined. Almost every included study classifies autism against typical development and reports the resulting figure as diagnostic accuracy. Here the same task, equipment, feature sets, algorithms and cross-validation scheme are applied both ways: F1 0.86 for ASD versus typical development, and F1 0.63 for ASD versus developmental language disorder at nearly balanced class sizes. The 23-point gap is an internally controlled estimate of how much of the corpus's typical ASD-versus-TD performance is autism-specific rather than a general clinical-versus-non-clinical distinction - and the authors draw exactly that conclusion, stating that their approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis. It sits with local_cd7545e2, where the ADOS-2 itself reached AUC 0.562 against schizophrenia with false-positive rates of 45-52%, as the review's two differential-diagnosis calibration points, and with local_4da2b941 and local_7d7f1fcc as evidence of the field's realistic performance envelope.
