Its negative granularity finding - that broad social/non-social areas of interest outperform fine decompositions by facial region and emotion - is also a useful methodological result for the eye-tracking branch, in which feature elaboration is usually assumed to help. | [RQ1.1] Ninety-three children aged 32-74 months in three clinically defined groups: 24 with ASD, 25 with developmental language disorder, and 44 typically developing. Both clinical groups were recruited from early childhood intervention centres in Cordoba province and required a formal diagnosis made by a licensed, experienced clinical team. The analysis unit is the child throughout, and each child contributes exactly one row to each of four feature sets. The inclusion of a second clinical group is what distinguishes this study from almost the entire charted corpus: it makes the ASD-versus-DLD comparison possible, and that comparison is where the study's most informative result lies. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, developmental language disorder, neurodevelopmental disorders, typical development, children with ASD, clinical groups. The register is clinical and precise, using DSM-5 language (persistent deficits in social interaction and communication, repetitive and restrictive patterns) without editorialising. Groups are named by diagnosis rather than by normality - the comparison group is typically developing, never normal. There is no autistic-community engagement, but nothing in the language pathologises beyond the diagnostic criteria themselves. [RQ1.3] Among the most complete in the corpus, and reported with statistical tests. Age: TD 53.23 (SD 10.04), ASD 53.50 (10.35), DLD 54.0 (12.14) months, F(2,90)=0.041, p=0.959 - the groups are closely matched on age, which is uncommon here and is demonstrated rather than asserted. Sex: TD 22 boys/22 girls, ASD 22/2, DLD 23/2, chi-squared 20.15, p<0.01 - a large and explicitly tested imbalance which the authors attribute to the higher prevalence of both conditions in males. Basic attention: 87.09 / 73.50 / 73.08, F=13.23, p<0.01. PPVT-III receptive vocabulary standard score: 108.75 / 98.65 / 86.57, F=19.56, p<0.01. Nothing on ethnicity, socioeconomic status or language background. The sex and vocabulary differences matter for the classification results and are not carried into the modelling as covariates. [RQ1.4] Clinically ascertained and honestly qualified. Diagnosis of ASD or DLD was made by a licensed, experienced team of clinicians following DSM-5 and international diagnostic manual guidelines, independently of this study and as a precondition of enrolment at an early intervention centre. Typically developing children are defined by the absence of such enrolment. The authors then add two caveats that few in this corpus offer: that their diagnostic tools could have been supplemented with further assessments but were the only ones available at the time, and that diagnoses at early ages are provisional and may evolve over time, so the findings should be interpreted with caution. [RQ1.5] No autism severity instrument is reported. Instead the study characterises its groups on two dimensions relevant to the task: a basic attention score and PPVT-III receptive vocabulary, both with significant group differences. The absence of a severity measure is a real gap for interpreting the ASD group's heterogeneity, but the inclusion of a standardised language measure is directly to the point, since DLD is the comparison condition. [RQ2.1] The stated aim is to apply explainable machine learning to eye-tracking data from a social attention task in children with ASD, DLD and typical development, to assess classification accuracy across all group combinations and to identify which variables best differentiate the groups. Headline findings: F1 0.912 for DLD versus TD, 0.88 for pooled ASD+DLD versus TD, 0.86 for ASD versus TD, and 0.63 for ASD versus DLD; broad social versus non-social areas of interest carried the signal while finer decompositions by facial region and emotion did not improve accuracy; naive Bayes and logistic model trees performed best; and mean duration of visits to objects emerged as a candidate disorder-specific marker. [RQ2.2] Early childhood intervention centres in the province of Cordoba supplied both clinical groups; testing used a screen-based eye tracker below a 15-inch laptop, with nine-point calibration. The clinical recruitment route is stated, though the room, examiner and whether TD children were tested under identical conditions are not described. [RQ2.3] The eye-tracking paired preferences paradigm: social and non-social images presented side by side, with faces displaying happiness, anger and neutral expressions paired against objects, following established designs (Sasson and Touchstone; Vacas et al.). This is a purpose-built social-attention task drawn from the developmental literature rather than a repurposed video or free-viewing sequence, and the choice is justified by reference to the metrics - fixation duration, fixation count, latency to first fixation - shown to be sensitive to gaze differences across neurodevelopmental conditions. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional, single session. Ethics reporting is complete and specific: approval by the Research Ethics Committee of Cordoba dated 02/08/2019 with reference number 4393, conducted per the Declaration of Helsinki and local legislation, with families informed of the study's purpose and procedures and written informed consent obtained from legal guardians. The discussion adds an ethically relevant scientific caveat - that early diagnoses are provisional - which bears directly on how the labels should be read. [RQ2.5] Tobii X2-30 remote eye tracker at 30 Hz on a 15-inch laptop screen with Tobii Studio and nine-point calibration using an animated target. The stated spatial accuracy of 36 degrees is a typographic error for 0.36 degrees - as printed the figure would exceed the visual angle of the entire display. The modelling software is not named, and no hyperparameters, tuning procedure or seed is reported for any algorithm, which is the main reporting gap in an otherwise well-specified study. [RQ2.6] Moderate to good on acquisition, thin on modelling. Reproducible: the eye tracker, sampling rate, screen size, calibration procedure, paradigm, stimulus composition and emotion set; the four feature sets by variable count and content; the stratified 5-fold scheme; the F1 interpretive bands, fixed before the results; and an offer of raw data on request. Not reproducible: the modelling workbench, the algorithm settings, whether any tuning occurred and whether it was nested, the seed, per-fold results, and the full variable lists for the 158-, 72-, 60- and 24-variable datasets. [RQ2.7] A short but genuinely self-critical paragraph naming four things: the limited scope of the experiment, the sample size, the diagnostic tools (which could have been supplemented but were the only ones available at the time), and the provisional nature of early-age diagnoses, with an explicit instruction that findings should be interpreted with caution and a call for replication with current behavioural assessments. Not mentioned: that the full variable set has 158 variables for 93 children; that the reported figures are the maximum over four feature sets, several algorithms and four comparisons with no correction; that the sex imbalance between clinical and TD groups (approximately 92% male versus 50%) offers an alternative route to the ASD-vs-TD and DLD-vs-TD separations; and that the significant PPVT-III differences are similarly available. [RQ2.9] Add further explainable algorithms such as gradient boosting trees and explainable boosting machines, and integrate multimodal data combining eye tracking with behavioural, cognitive or neurophysiological measures to improve robustness and clinical applicability. Both are proportionate to the study's own findings. [RQ3.1] Social attention during simultaneous presentation of social and non-social stimuli: preferential looking to faces versus objects, indexed by fixation duration, fixation count, visit duration and latency to first fixation, across areas of interest from whole-stimulus categories down to eyes and mouth and across three emotional expressions. The substantive behavioural finding is about objects rather than faces - mean duration of visits to objects discriminates, which the authors interpret as difficulty disengaging attention from objects rather than as reduced interest in faces. [RQ3.2] No multimodal fusion - eye tracking alone. What the study does instead is a granularity comparison within one modality: four nested feature sets ranging from 24 broad variables to 158 fine-grained ones. The result is a clean negative finding that broad social/non-social area-of-interest variables carry the discriminative information while adding specific facial features and emotion categories does not improve accuracy. Multimodal extension with behavioural, cognitive or neurophysiological measures is named as the next step. [RQ4.1] Interpretable classical classifiers selected for explainability rather than capacity, with naive Bayes and logistic model trees performing best. No deep learning. The algorithm choice follows from the stated aim - to identify which eye-tracking variables discriminate, in a form clinicians can inspect - rather than from a search for maximum accuracy, and this is one of the few studies in the corpus where the modelling choice is subordinated to the scientific question. [RQ4.2] Four nested tabular feature sets per child: full (158 variables), secondary (72), prior (60) and basic (24), differing in how finely stimuli and areas of interest are decomposed. All variables derive from the eye-tracking record; no clinical instrument score, demographic variable or diagnostic measure enters the feature set - a point worth stating explicitly, because it is exactly what separates this study from the corpus's leakage cases. With 93 children and up to 158 variables, three of the four datasets have more variables than participants. [RQ4.3] F1-score only, with precision and recall given by equation. The interpretive bands are stated in advance (0.0-0.5 poor, 0.5-0.7 moderate, 0.8-0.9 good, 0.9-1.0 excellent) and the results are then reported against them, so the descriptions excellent, good and moderate are pre-committed rather than chosen after the fact - a small but genuine discipline. Missing: accuracy, sensitivity and specificity separately, AUC, calibration, confidence intervals, across-fold variance, and any statement of the majority-class baseline. The last matters most for the ASD-versus-DLD comparison, where the classes are nearly balanced (24 versus 25) and F1 0.63 sits only modestly above chance, and for ASD-versus-TD, where the baseline is around 0.65 and the reported 0.86 represents a real but smaller gain than the number suggests in isolation. [RQ4.4] Interpretability is the study's purpose rather than an appendix to it. The four-way feature-set comparison yields a negative result that is reported plainly - fine-grained variables about specific facial areas and emotions do not improve on broad social versus non-social groupings - and the surviving discriminative variable, mean duration of visits to objects, is interpreted theoretically as difficulty disengaging attention from objects, connected to an existing attentional account (Landry and Bryson). This is a claim about behaviour that another laboratory could test, generated by a model whose structure a clinician can inspect, which is the intended use of explainable methods and is rare in this corpus. [RQ4.5] The validation is participant-level and structurally correct: stratified 5-fold cross-validation over 93 children, one row per child, no within-participant duplication, and no clinical instrument score anywhere in the feature set. Three caveats qualify the numbers rather than invalidate them. First, dimensionality - the full dataset carries 158 variables for 93 children, and even the smallest carries 24, so the models operate in a regime where cross-validated estimates over five folds are noisy; no interval or fold variance is reported. Second, selection - the headline figures are the best over four feature sets crossed with several algorithms and four group comparisons, with no correction and no held-out cohort, so they are optimistic by an unquantified margin. Third, confounding - the clinical groups are approximately 92% male against 50% in the TD group (chi-squared 20.15, p<0.01) and differ significantly in receptive vocabulary and basic attention, all of which are plausible correlates of gaze behaviour in a paired-preference task; none is adjusted for, so part of the 0.86 and 0.912 against TD may reflect sex and language ability rather than diagnosis. The result that survives all of this is the one the authors themselves foreground: ASD versus DLD reaches only F1 0.63, at nearly balanced class sizes, and they conclude that the approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis. That conclusion is the correct reading of their own data and is the most valuable single sentence in this part of the corpus, because the two comparisons are internally controlled - same task, same equipment, same pipeline, same analyst - so the gap between 0.86 against typical development and 0.63 against another neurodevelopmental condition isolates how much of the apparent signal is autism-specific rather than clinical-population-general. [RQ5.1] explainable machine learning; autism spectrum disorder; developmental language disorder; eye-tracking; differential diagnosis; computer-aided diagnosis. Six terms naming method, both conditions, modality and - uniquely in this corpus - differential diagnosis, which is what the study actually attempts. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Neuroscience 19:1558621 - an open-access neuroscience journal, with a 127-day review. The venue's disciplinary fit shows in the reporting: matched group characteristics with ANOVA and chi-squared tests, a standardised language measure, a pre-specified interpretive scale for F1, an ethics reference number, and a limitations paragraph that includes the provisionality of early diagnoses. [RQ5.3] 2025, published 24 June, 127 days from submission to acceptance. Framing is deliberately restrained and, unusually, becomes more restrained as the paper proceeds: the abstract reports the ASD-versus-DLD F1 of 0.63 alongside the higher figures rather than burying it, and the conclusion states that the approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis. The clinical claim is limited to a preliminary step toward computer-aided diagnosis. Its contribution to the review is not a performance number but a controlled contrast: by running the same pipeline against a typically developing group and against a second clinical group, it converts the corpus's ubiquitous ASD-versus-TD figure into an interpretable quantity. |
| S-156 | Retrospective analysis of 547 eye-tracking scanpath images (328 non-ASD, 219 ASD) at 640x480 from a public repository - the Cilia/Carette collection, whose originators appear in the comparison table. The number of distinct children behind the images is never stated; the abstract instead reports the image counts as though they were child counts (328 characteristically emerging children and 219 children with autism), while the methods section gives the correct reading. The viewing task, stimuli and recording equipment of the original collection are not described. | Images were resized to 640x480, enhanced, converted to arrays and normalised to [0,1], then split into training, validation and test sets, with rotation, shifting and flipping augmentation applied during training via ImageDataGenerator. Four ImageNet-pretrained classifiers were fitted - MobileNet, VGG19, DenseNet169 and a VGG19+MobileNet hybrid - each with a pooling layer, dense layers with ReLU and dropout, a two-unit softmax output, sparse categorical cross-entropy, RMSprop or Adam at learning rate 0.0001, batch sizes 16 and 32, and 100 epochs. | MobileNet reached 100% accuracy with perfect precision, recall and F1 for both classes and ROC 100%; VGG19 92%; DenseNet169 78% (ASD recall 50%). The test partition contains 55 images (33 non-ASD, 22 ASD), a figure recoverable only from the support column. The proposed model is ranked above three prior studies on the same dataset (87%, 90%, 79%), with the advantage attributed to a different preprocessing approach. | The study states none. Its split is at the image level on a scanpath collection in which each child contributes multiple images, so images from the same child's session appear on both sides - the same within-participant leakage documented across the video, EEG-epoch, thermal, cry and facial-image branches, and enough on its own to produce a perfect score. The test set holds 55 images, which the paper never states and which places roughly plus or minus 12 percentage points of sampling noise on every figure: the 78%-to-100% spread across four architectures trained identically is a symptom of that, not a ranking of methods. The viewing task behind the scanpaths is nowhere described, so stimulus identity cannot be excluded as what the classifier reads. Augmentation by rotation and flipping produces gaze traces corresponding to no possible viewing behaviour. There is no dataset accession, no seed, no code, no ethics statement, no limitations section and no future work, and the abstract reports image counts as child counts. | This study extends the review's leakage catalogue to the scanpath-image modality in its purest form, and pairs directly with local_bb4d1f7a, which used the same modality with a fixed 100 crops per child. Its distinctive contribution to the synthesis is the architecture spread: MobileNet 100%, VGG19 92%, DenseNet169 78%, all trained on the same 547 images under the same protocol and evaluated on the same 55 test images. That 22-point range between architectures on identical data is the clearest single demonstration in the corpus that figures from small held-out sets are estimates of noise as much as of method quality - and the paper nevertheless reports the maximum as its headline and ranks it against three prior studies whose reported figures (87%, 90%, 79%) all fall inside its own architectures' range. Its abstract's conversion of 547 images into 547 children is also worth recording alongside local_986436f2's fabricated demographic table as an instance of a dataset being described as something it is not. | [RQ1.1] No participants. 547 scanpath images from a public eye-tracking repository, 328 labelled non-ASD and 219 ASD. The abstract converts this image count into a participant count, describing the dataset as scan pathways obtained from 328 characteristically emerging children and 219 children with autism - which would make this one of the larger primary eye-tracking cohorts in the field. The methods section states the correct version, that these are image counts. The source collection is the Cilia/Carette scanpath set, whose originators are cited in the comparison table and in which a few dozen children contributed multiple scanpath images each; the number of distinct children behind the 547 images is never given here. Every reported metric rests on a test partition of 55 images, recoverable only from the support column of the per-class results tables. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, persons diagnosed with ASD, people without ASD, children with autism, characteristically emerging children, ASD children. The phrase characteristically emerging children appears to be a rewording of typically developing and, together with formulations like monotonous and stereotyped behaviors and the commonness of ASD, suggests heavy paraphrasing throughout. The register is otherwise clinical without being pejorative, and there is no autistic-community perspective. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment source for any image, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent - despite the introduction discussing sex ratios in ASD prevalence and noting that girls with ASD often have fewer observable symptoms, a point directly relevant to a dataset whose sex composition is unknown. [RQ1.4] None. Labels are inherited from a public image collection with no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date reported, and the originating study's diagnostic procedure is not summarised. The paper's opening argument is that conventional ASD assessment relies on subjective criteria and lacks objectivity - a criticism advanced in favour of a label whose ascertainment it never examines. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to automate ASD categorisation from eye-tracking data using deep learning, in response to the cost, delay and subjectivity of conventional assessment. Headline findings: MobileNet reached 100% accuracy with perfect precision, recall and F1 for both classes and ROC 100%; VGG19 92%; DenseNet169 78%; the proposed model is ranked above three prior studies on the same dataset (87%, 90%, 79%). The paper attributes its advantage explicitly to preprocessing - our model achieved high accuracy because we have used a different preprocessing approach from improving dataset. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Images downloaded from an unnamed public repository; the compute environment is tabulated but not quoted in the extracted text. Critically, the acquisition setting of the original data - the viewing task, the stimuli, the eye tracker, the session structure - is nowhere summarised, so a reader cannot say what behaviour the scanpaths record. [RQ2.3] Not reported. The paradigm behind the scanpaths is never described. This matters more than usual for a scanpath dataset, because the geometry of a scanpath image is jointly determined by the child and by the stimulus, and without knowing the stimulus set one cannot tell whether the classifier is reading gaze behaviour or stimulus identity. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. There is no ethics statement, consent statement or exemption claim anywhere in the article, and no consideration of the provenance or consent basis of the underlying eye-tracking recordings of children. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation described. Modelling used ImageNet-pretrained MobileNet, VGG19 and DenseNet169 backbones with custom heads, Keras ImageDataGenerator for augmentation, RMSprop or Adam at learning rate 0.0001, batch sizes 16 (training) and 32 (validation), and 100 epochs. Parameter tables per model are provided and are more complete than most in this corpus. [RQ2.6] Mixed. Strengths: per-model parameter tables covering base architecture, pooling, dense widths, dropout, output layer, loss, optimiser, learning rate, batch sizes and epochs; and an explicit, correctly ordered preprocessing sequence in which the split precedes augmentation and augmentation is confined to training. Weaknesses: the dataset is described only as a freely accessible public repository with no accession, URL or DOI; the split proportions are never stated and the test size must be inferred from a support column; there is no seed, no code, and no statement of how many children the images come from; and the hybrid model is specified only by a figure. [RQ2.7] None. There is no limitations section and the word limitation does not occur in the article. Nothing is said about the image-level split on a dataset with repeated images per child, about the 55-image test set, about the absence of any description of the underlying task, or about the fact that three architectures trained on the same data under the same protocol span 78% to 100%. [RQ2.9] None. There is no future-work section; the paper closes on the claim that healthcare professionals can use these classifiers to enhance the accuracy rate of ASD diagnosis. [RQ3.1] Visual scanning behaviour, encoded as a rendered scanpath image showing the geometric trace of fixations and saccades. Because the images are treated as pictures rather than as sequences, no fixation duration, saccade amplitude, area-of-interest dwell or temporal ordering is extracted or reported - the behavioural content of the data is entirely implicit in the picture. [RQ3.2] No fusion of modalities - one image source. The hybrid model combines two ImageNet backbones over the same image, which is architectural ensembling rather than multimodality. [RQ4.1] Four transfer-learning classifiers: MobileNet, VGG19, DenseNet169 and a VGG19+MobileNet hybrid, each with ImageNet weights, the top layers removed, a pooling layer, dense layers with ReLU and dropout, and a two-unit softmax output. [RQ4.2] 640x480 scanpath images, enhanced, converted to arrays and normalised to [0,1], with rotation, shifting and flipping augmentation applied during training only. Augmentation of a scanpath image is worth a separate note: flipping and rotating a gaze trace changes its spatial relationship to the stimulus that produced it, so the augmented examples correspond to no possible viewing behaviour - a transformation that is standard for photographs and semantically incoherent for scanpaths. [RQ4.3] Per-class precision, recall, F1 and support, overall accuracy, macro averages, ROC curves and training/validation curves. Specificity is defined by equation and never tabulated. No confidence interval accompanies any figure, and none is possible to infer without the split proportions, which are not stated. The support column is the only place the test-set size appears: 33 non-ASD and 22 ASD, 55 images in total. On 55 images the 95% interval around VGG19's 92% runs from roughly 82% to 98% and around DenseNet169's 78% from roughly 65% to 88%, so the reported ordering of the four architectures - and the ranking against the three prior studies at 87%, 90% and 79% - is not statistically distinguishable. [RQ4.4] None. No saliency, attribution or scanpath-feature analysis, and no ablation of the hybrid. In a study whose premise is that gaze patterns carry diagnostic information, no gaze pattern is identified, and the paper does not report what distinguishes the ASD scanpath images from the others. [RQ4.5] The preprocessing order is handled correctly - the dataset is split before augmentation, and augmentation is applied during training via ImageDataGenerator - which is better than several neighbours in this corpus. Everything else about the evaluation undercuts the result. The split is at the image level on a scanpath collection in which each child contributes multiple images, so images generated from the same child's viewing session sit on both sides of the partition; this is the same within-participant leakage documented across the video, EEG-epoch, thermal, cry and facial-image branches, and it is sufficient to explain a perfect score. The test partition holds 55 images, a figure the paper never states and that must be recovered from a support column, so every reported metric carries roughly plus or minus 11 to 13 percentage points of sampling noise; MobileNet's 100% means 55 of 55 correct. There is no cross-validation, no repetition and no seed, and the spread across four architectures trained identically on the same data - 100%, 92%, 78% and the hybrid - is itself evidence of how unstable a 55-image estimate is, though the paper reads it as a genuine ranking of methods. The comparison against three prior studies on the same dataset (87%, 90%, 79%) is attributed to a different preprocessing approach, when the more parsimonious explanation is that the earlier figures came from evaluations that were less permissive. Finally, the paper never describes the viewing task behind the scanpaths, so it cannot exclude that the classifier is recognising which stimulus produced a trace rather than who produced it. [RQ5.1] autism spectrum disorder; eye tracking; deep learning; VGG19; MobileNet; DenseNet169; hybrid model. Four of seven terms name specific architectures; validation, participants and task are absent. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Medicine 11:1436646 - an open-access clinical journal, accepted in 44 days. A 100% diagnostic accuracy claim, an abstract that reports image counts as child counts, an absent ethics statement, an unstated test-set size and no limitations section all passed clinical review. [RQ5.3] Published 19 July 2024 (indexed here under 2025), 44 days from submission. Framing is unqualified diagnostic assistance: the classifiers are said to demonstrate the potential of eye-tracking data to aid physicians in efficiently and accurately screening for autism, and users and healthcare professionals can utilize these classifiers to enhance the accuracy rate of ASD diagnosis. The contribution is stated as a leaderboard position - 100% against 87%, 90% and 79% on the same public dataset - and attributed to preprocessing. There is no limitations section, no future work and no hedge of any kind. |
| S-157 | Single-author retrospective analysis of the public Autism screening data for toddler dataset, in which the class label is defined explicitly as a Q-CHAT-10 score above 3. Neither the number of records, the class balance, nor any demographic characteristic is reported anywhere in the article. | A three-stage pipeline: Yeo-Johnson transformation to remove noise and artefacts, DeSEHO (Double Exponential Smoothing integrated into the Elk Herd Optimizer) for feature selection, and MEResNeXt (Moments Embedding Network combined with ResNeXt) for classification. Implementation in Python. The number and identity of selected features, the metaheuristic's search space and budget, and the learning rate, batch size and epoch count are not reported; the article instead specifies the MoNet sub-matrix square-root layer and its backward propagation across roughly forty numbered equations. | Accuracy 95.3%, sensitivity 96.5%, specificity 94.8%, taken from curves plotted against iteration count (20-80) and training percentage (70%, 80%); an intermediate value of 0.927 accuracy at 70% training data and iteration 20 is also reported. | The article states two model-level caveats and nothing else. There is no validation design to evaluate: no split, no cross-validation, no held-out set, no test-set size, and no statement of what data the reported metrics were computed on - the headline is read off the best region of a sweep. The sample size and class balance are never given, so no baseline exists. The label is a threshold on the sum of the Q-CHAT-10 items supplied as features, making the task checklist reconstruction. Yeo-Johnson, a variance-stabilising power transformation for continuous skewed variables, is applied to binary questionnaire responses on the stated ground of removing noise and artefacts. Two of the four metric definitions in the text are incorrect. Ethical approval and informed consent are both declared Not Applicable with no reasoning, and the author statements refer to co-authors and multiple authors in a single-authored paper. | This is the seventh charted study built on a Q-CHAT-10-derived label and the branch's most extreme case of contribution-by-nomenclature. Four acronyms are introduced (MEResNeXt, DeSEHO, and their components), roughly forty equations specify architecture internals borrowed from image-recognition papers, and the article never states how many children its 95.3% is computed over or on what data. Read against the branch's other members - 100% with all items retained (local_8253c2ec, local_a0d73248), a flawless 292 of 292 with pre-split SMOTE (local_ed30e24c), 0.99 with the mechanism mapped by feature-subset comparison (local_14df790d), 0.83 after deleting half the items (local_8ff20c48) - its 95.3% is uninterpretable in a specific way: the branch's accuracy is governed by how much of the label's own arithmetic survives feature selection, and this study performs an unreported metaheuristic selection of an unreported number of features. It also supplies the review's clearest instance of methodological detail being allocated inversely to methodological importance, and its Ethical approval: Not Applicable declaration sits with local_45ef7022's Not required and local_13c1f46d's Kaggle exemption at the permissive end of the corpus's ethics gradient. | [RQ1.1] No participants, and no sample size of any kind. The article never states how many records the analysed dataset contains, how many are ASD-positive, or how many are negative - a gap that persists through a results section built entirely on performance curves. The data source is identified only as Autism screening data for toddler, the public Q-CHAT-10 collection. Since no split, test set or fold structure is described either, there is no point in the paper at which a reader can say how many observations any reported number rests on. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic individuals, individuals with ASD, patient, ASD patients. The register is medical and dated - autism is introduced as a neurological disease, individuals are described as needing the right treatment as soon as possible to recover their condition and diminish the disorder's effects. One passage is more sympathetic, noting that individuals with ASD have uniqueness and a few have incomparable ability in academics, music skills and visual. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, socioeconomic status or recruitment information, and no acknowledgement that any of it is missing. [RQ1.4] None, and the paper states the substitute rule explicitly: if the Q-CHAT-10 score is higher than 3 then the class value is allocated as YES which implies ASD traits potential; if not, NO is allocated. The outcome is therefore a threshold on the sum of the ten checklist items that also constitute the feature set - the seventh instance of this structure in the review, after local_8253c2ec, local_a0d73248, local_8ff20c48, local_ed30e24c, local_b9de0d7f and local_14df790d. No clinician, instrument administration or diagnostic criterion enters at any point. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a hybrid deep-learning method for ASD detection in three stages: Yeo-Johnson transformation to remove noise and artefacts, DeSEHO (Double Exponential Smoothing integrated into the Elk Herd Optimizer) for feature selection, and MEResNeXt (Moments Embedding Network combined with ResNeXt) for classification. Headline findings: accuracy 95.3%, sensitivity 96.5%, specificity 94.8%, described as performing better than traditional models. [RQ2.2] No study setting. A downloaded dataset analysed in Python; no hardware, runtime or environment is described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm - a caregiver checklist. The article does not reproduce or discuss a single Q-CHAT-10 item, so no behaviour is named anywhere in it. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethical approval and informed consent are both declared Not Applicable, without reasoning - the paper does not invoke the public-data exemption that comparable studies at least state, and offers nothing in its place. A related reporting anomaly: the article has a single author, Saloni Rai, whose CRediT contribution is listed only as Data curation, yet the author statements read All authors have made substantial contributions to conception and design and the acknowledgements thank the co-authors of this manuscript for their valuable and constructive suggestions. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Implementation in Python with no library, version, seed or hardware. Method components: Yeo-Johnson transformation, the Elk Herd Optimizer with double exponential smoothing, the Moments Embedding Network and ResNeXt. [RQ2.6] Very low, in an unusually instructive way. The article devotes several pages and roughly forty numbered equations to the internals of the MoNet sub-matrix square-root layer, including its forward and backward propagation and the symmetrisation of matrix derivatives - a level of mathematical specification exceeding anything else in the charted corpus. It reports none of what would be needed to repeat the study: no sample size, no class balance, no split or cross-validation scheme, no test-set size, no metaheuristic search space or budget, no count or identity of selected features, no learning rate, batch size or epoch count in the running text, no seed, no code, and no dataset accession. The detail is concentrated entirely on the parts that are reproduced from prior architecture papers and absent from the parts that are specific to this experiment. [RQ2.7] Two sentences, both concerning the model rather than the study: the reliance on the Yeo-Johnson transformation for noise removal may not be sufficient for all types of data, and the complexity of the model may lead to overfitting, especially with smaller datasets. Notably, the article contains an extensive limitations apparatus pointed at other people's work - Table 1 tabulates the advantages and disadvantages of each prior study, and the related-work section names constraints for several of them - while none of that scrutiny reaches the circular label, the unreported sample size, the absent validation protocol or the Not Applicable ethics declaration. [RQ2.9] Enhance preprocessing techniques, improve the efficiency of feature selection, and ensure the model's adaptability across diverse datasets. The last is the only one that addresses a genuine gap, and it is stated without reference to any external dataset. [RQ3.1] Parent-reported early social-communication behaviour, entirely unspecified - the article names the Q-CHAT-10 instrument and describes its scoring rule but never states or discusses a single item, so no behaviour is identified anywhere in the paper. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single questionnaire modality. The hybrid designation refers to combining two convolutional architectures over the same tabular input. [RQ4.1] MEResNeXt, combining the Moments Embedding Network with ResNeXt. Both are convolutional architectures designed for images: MoNet's contribution is a bilinear second-order moment embedding with a sub-matrix square-root layer developed for fine-grained visual recognition, and ResNeXt's is the aggregated residual transformation with cardinality developed for ImageNet classification. Applying them to a short tabular vector of binary questionnaire responses is never justified, and neither the spatial structure that motivates convolution nor the fine-grained texture statistics that motivate moment embedding exists in the data. [RQ4.2] A tabular vector of Q-CHAT-10 items and individual characteristics, Yeo-Johnson transformed and then reduced by the DeSEHO metaheuristic. Two observations. First, Yeo-Johnson is a variance-stabilising power transformation for continuous skewed variables; applying it to binary checklist responses to remove noise and artefacts, and justifying that choice at length against Box-Cox on the ground that it accommodates negative values, is a category error about the data. Second, the ten items are the summands of the score whose threshold defines the label, so whatever subset DeSEHO retains, the target remains an arithmetic function of the feature pool. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1, plotted against iteration count and training percentage. Two of the four definitions given in the text are wrong: accuracy is described as dividing the total number of instances by the number of correctly classified instances, which is the reciprocal of accuracy and would exceed 1; and specificity is described in words as dividing the total number of false positives and true negatives by the sum of both, which is identically 1. The accompanying equations for sensitivity and specificity are correct, so these are errors of exposition rather than of computation, but they appear in a section whose stated purpose is to define the evaluation measures. No confidence interval, no chance level and no class balance accompany any figure. [RQ4.4] None. The metaheuristic selects a feature subset and neither its size nor its membership is reported; no importance ranking, attribution or ablation appears; and no component of the three-stage pipeline is isolated. In a paper whose contribution is a specific combination of transformation, optimiser and architecture, no experiment shows that any of the three contributes anything. [RQ4.5] There is no validation design to assess. The article describes no train-test split, no cross-validation, no held-out set and no test-set size; it never states how many records the dataset contains or what its class balance is; and its results are presented as curves of accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1 against iteration count (20 to 80) and training percentage (70%, 80%), with the abstract's 95.3% / 96.5% / 94.8% taken from the best region of those curves. Reading performance off the maximum of a sweep is model selection on the reported quantity, and here there is not even a stated partition on which the sweep is evaluated. Underneath that sits the estimand: the label is a threshold on the sum of the ten Q-CHAT-10 items supplied as features, so the task is reconstruction of a checklist rule regardless of how the data are partitioned. The contrast with the rest of this branch is instructive. local_ed30e24c reached a flawless 292 of 292 with all items retained and pre-split SMOTE; local_14df790d reached 0.99 and mapped the mechanism through its feature-subset comparison; local_8ff20c48 fell to 0.83 after deleting five items. This study reports 95.3% after an unreported metaheuristic selection of an unreported number of features - a figure whose position in that range is determined by how much of the label's arithmetic the optimiser happened to retain, which the paper does not report and therefore cannot interpret. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; Disease detection; Hybrid deep learning; Optimization algorithm. Four terms, three naming machinery in the most generic possible way; neither the instrument, the population, the modality nor the validation appears. [RQ5.2] Computational Biology and Chemistry 120:108619 (Elsevier), 2026 issue. A computational-biology venue, and the mismatch shows: a paper with no sample size, no validation protocol, no reported class balance, two incorrect metric definitions, image architectures applied to binary questionnaire responses, and author statements referring to co-authors of a single-authored manuscript. [RQ5.3] 2026 issue. Framing is early-detection and cost-saving: initial identification and treatment can diminish the need for wide examinations and expensive medical procedures, and prolonged effects and severity can be avoided at a timely determination of ASD. The contribution is expressed as architectural novelty - a named hybrid (MEResNeXt) built from two named components, fed by a named metaheuristic (DeSEHO) built from two further named components - with the accuracy figure as its warrant. It is the corpus's clearest example of method-naming as the unit of contribution: four new acronyms are introduced, forty equations specify borrowed architecture internals, and the number of children behind the result is never mentioned. |
| S-158 | Cross-sectional three-group study in the UK: 31 autistic adults, 32 adults with Parkinson's disease and 31 controls, all with documented formal diagnoses in the clinical groups and exclusion of co-occurring movement or developmental disorders. Gender and non-verbal reasoning were matched across groups; both clinical groups were age-matched to controls though ASD and PD were not matched to each other. Trait, depression and anxiety measures and medication status are reported by group. | Participants completed a Shapes Tracing Task (clover, petals, ellipse, rounded square) and a Reaction Time Task with a stylus on a supplied Samsung Galaxy Tab A7 across two testing days, with PD participants tested before their first daily dopaminergic dose. Nine kinematic features per shape plus reaction time gave 37 input variables. Group differences were tested with linear mixed models including group, shape and their interaction, with Bayesian ANOVAs quantifying evidence for the null. KNN, random forest and linear SVM were then run on an 80/20 participant split across a grid of predictor configurations combining all or discriminatory kinematic features with three questionnaire sets. Data and scripts are on OSF. | Autistic participants differed from both PD and control groups in speed modulation and sub-movements, and from PD in reaction time. No kinematic feature was similar between ASD and PD while also differing from controls. Best mean test accuracy was 0.73 for clinical versus non-clinical and 0.93 for ASD versus PD, both from kinematics combined with both questionnaire sets; discriminatory kinematic features alone reached 0.80 under SVM for ASD versus PD. All models exceeded chance except two at 0.50. The ellipse was the least informative shape. | The authors name five: undiagnosed cases cannot be excluded by a diagnosis-based grouping; the PD and control participants come from a generation in which autism diagnoses were not prevalent, so undiagnosed autistic people may sit in the comparison groups; stylus resistance and the tablet's sampling rate and spatial resolution may have suppressed group differences; kinematic features are context-dependent and results may be task-specific; and the autistic sample was older than those in the existing literature. Two more are visible in the data. The classification test partitions hold roughly 13 participants for ASD versus PD and 19 for clinical versus non-clinical, so the 0.93 headline corresponds to about 12 of 13 correct with a confidence interval spanning roughly 0.66 to 1.00, and no interval is reported. And the discriminatory kinematic feature sets were selected using group-difference significance computed over all participants, so those configurations saw held-out labels during selection. Neither affects the study's primary negative finding. | This is the third study in the charted corpus below high risk of bias, and the only one whose headline result is a negative finding. Its central contribution is a direct test that the field had previously been unable to perform: autistic movement has been informally likened to parkinsonian movement, and because PD assessment is largely movement-based, that resemblance - if real - would generate false PD diagnoses in autistic adults. Running both clinical groups and controls through one protocol, the study finds no kinematic feature that is shared between ASD and PD while also differing from controls, and supports the null with Bayes factors rather than with absence of significance. It joins local_b6ac2b98 (ASD versus DLD at F1 0.63 against 0.86 for ASD versus TD) and local_cd7545e2 (ADOS-2 at AUC 0.562 against schizophrenia) as the review's differential-diagnosis calibration points, and with local_4da2b941 it defines the corpus's standard of methodological practice: participant-level splits, deposited data and scripts, versioned software, pre-specified interpretive thresholds, formal group matching, statistical control of confounders, complete ethics reporting, and a limitations section that reasons about cohort effects. Its methodological by-product - that the ellipse, the shape most commonly used in the drawing-task literature, is the least discriminative of four shapes - is a directly actionable finding for the movement branch. | [RQ1.1] Ninety-four adults in three groups: 31 autistic adults, 32 adults with Parkinson's disease and 31 controls. Both clinical groups required documentary evidence of a formal clinical diagnosis or came from research databases where such evidence had been verified, with mutual exclusion between the two conditions and exclusion of co-occurring movement or developmental disorders. Recruitment order is reported and is itself methodologically informative - the PD group was recruited first as an opportunity sample, autistic adults were then recruited to match it, and controls to match both. The analysis unit is the participant throughout, and the 80/20 classification split partitions people. What limits the classification estimates is size rather than structure: the ASD-versus-PD test partition contains roughly 13 people and the clinical-versus-non-clinical partition roughly 19. [RQ1.2] Autistic individuals, autistic adults, autistic movement, individuals with PD, control participants, non-autistic individuals. Identity-first language is used consistently and without hedging, movement differences are described as differences rather than deficits or abnormalities, and the framing throughout treats autistic movement as a characteristic to be measured rather than a pathology to be detected. The paper also cites the proposal that movement differences be added as specifiers to autism diagnoses - condition-relevant but non-selective - which is a precise and non-inflationary way of positioning the finding. [RQ1.3] The most complete adult-sample reporting in the corpus, with formal matching tests. Gender is matched across groups (chi-squared(4)=3.25, ns) and the autistic sample is close to sex-balanced at 14M/16F/1 other - a composition no other autism study in this review achieves. Age: ASD 55.52 (8.01), PD 63.16 (7.60), CTRL 59.00 (9.96); both clinical groups matched to controls but ASD and PD not matched to each other (p<0.001), which the authors handle by entering age as a control variable and residualising it from the classification inputs. Non-verbal reasoning (MaRs-IB) is matched. Depression and anxiety differ significantly and are controlled for. Years since diagnosis, psychoactive medication use, and UPDRS, RAADS and AQ trait scores are all reported by group with post-hoc comparisons. [RQ1.4] Clinically ascertained with documentation, and honestly bounded. Participants had to supply evidence of a formal clinical diagnosis such as a clinician's letter, or be drawn from databases where that evidence had been verified. The limitations section then names the two residual problems precisely: absence of a diagnosis does not exclude undiagnosed cases, and the PD and control participants belong to a generation in which autism diagnoses were not prevalent, so undiagnosed autistic people may sit in the comparison groups. That second observation is a genuine insight about ascertainment in older cohorts that appears nowhere else in this corpus. [RQ1.5] Comprehensive and instrument-based: UPDRS Part II for parkinsonian traits, RAADS and AQ for autistic traits, PHQ for depression, GAD for anxiety, MaRs-IB for non-verbal reasoning, and years since diagnosis. All are reported by group with ANOVA and post-hoc comparisons, and the ordering is as expected (autistic traits ASD>PD>CTRL; parkinsonian traits PD>ASD>CTRL). Crucially the trait instruments are used both as sample descriptors and, in some model configurations, as declared predictors alongside kinematics - so their role is explicit rather than hidden. [RQ2.1] Two aims, one confirmatory and one applied. First, to test directly whether autistic and parkinsonian movement resemble each other - a comparison previously possible only by juxtaposing separate studies with different designs and demographics. Second, to assess whether kinematic features can classify clinical versus non-clinical status and, within the clinical groups, ASD versus PD. Findings: autistic participants differed from both PD and controls in speed modulation and sub-movements, and from PD in reaction time; classification reached a best mean test accuracy of 0.73 for clinical versus non-clinical and 0.93 for ASD versus PD, in both cases from kinematics combined with questionnaires; and, most importantly, no kinematic feature was found to be similar between ASD and PD while also differing from controls. The anecdotal likeness between autistic and parkinsonian movement is not supported. [RQ2.2] Home-based testing on a supplied tablet over two days no more than three days apart, following an online screening form, questionnaire battery and reasoning task. The PD group completed the tasks before their first dopaminergic dose each morning. Home administration is presented as an advantage for scalability - the protocol could be run in community settings without laboratory kinematic equipment - and its cost is acknowledged in the limitations, where stylus resistance and the tablet's sampling and spatial resolution are named as possible suppressors of group differences. [RQ2.3] A Shapes Tracing Task with four shapes chosen to span the angular-frequency spectrum (clover, petals, ellipse, rounded square) plus a Reaction Time Task, both stylus-based. The shape design is deliberate and yields a methodological result the review should record: the ellipse was the least useful shape for distinguishing groups, and the authors point out that most drawing tasks in the literature index only elliptical or spiral movements, recommending that future studies span the full angular-frequency range. That is a concrete, actionable finding about task design derived from data. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional with two testing days; no longitudinal follow-up, which the authors identify as limiting their ability to know whether autistic participants later develop PD. Ethics reporting is complete: two Research Ethics Committee approval numbers (ERN_18-1800B and ERN_16-0281AP5), Declaration of Helsinki compliance, fully informed consent, and payment of GBP 10 per hour - remuneration being reported at all is uncommon in this corpus and is relevant to the ethics of research participation. [RQ2.5] Samsung Galaxy Tab A7 with a 10.4-inch 2000x1200 touchscreen and stylus; tasks programmed in PsychoPy and delivered via Pavlovia (PsychoJS 2021.1.4); MaRs-IB on Gorilla. Analysis in R Studio 2022.07.2 (matching), MATLAB 2022a with fitlme (mixed models) and JASP 0.17.2.1 (Bayesian analyses and classification). Every package is named with a version. [RQ2.6] The highest in the charted corpus alongside local_4da2b941. Data and analysis scripts are deposited on OSF; all software is named with versions; the device and its screen specification are given; the outlier rule is stated with the exact percentage removed for each of the nine features; the normalising transformations are listed per variable; the mixed-model formulae are written out including random-effect structure; the feature-selection rule is specified precisely, including how group-by-shape interactions were handled; and the full classification grid is published as a heat map rather than reduced to a headline. The only gaps are the composition of the individual 80/20 draws and whether JASP's parameter optimisation was nested inside the split. [RQ2.7] A genuinely analytical limitations section with five distinct items, each carrying a mechanism: diagnosis-based grouping cannot exclude undiagnosed cases; the PD and control groups come from a generation in which autism diagnoses were not prevalent, so undiagnosed autistic people may be present in them; stylus resistance and tablet sampling and spatial resolution may have suppressed group differences relative to motion tracking; kinematic features are context-dependent and the results may be task-specific; and the autistic sample was older than those in the existing kinematic literature, so apparent contradictions with prior findings may be age effects. Two further issues go unstated: the classification test partitions contain roughly 13 to 19 participants, and the discriminatory feature sets were selected using group-difference tests computed on all participants. [RQ2.9] Employ a range of shapes across the angular-frequency spectrum rather than only ellipses or spirals; investigate kinematic features for early screening in conjunction with clinical assessments; and separate clinically driven movement decline from normal ageing, a need the study itself establishes by demonstrating age effects on several kinematic features. [RQ3.1] Fine motor kinematics during constrained tracing: speed, acceleration, jerk, minimum and maximum speed, number of sub-movements, speed modulation (how sharply speed adapts to trajectory curvature), smoothness via SPARC, and tracing error, plus simple reaction time. The discriminating features are specific and directional - autistic participants showed greater speed modulation and more sub-movements than both other groups, and differed from PD in reaction time - and the paper is careful about mechanism, noting that reported increases in jerk in autism may be epiphenomenal on speed differences because the two quantities are mathematically linked. [RQ3.2] Genuine and declared multimodal fusion, and the study's most useful applied finding. Kinematic features and self-report questionnaire scores are combined in an explicit grid of predictor configurations - kinematics alone, questionnaires alone (ASD, PD, or both) and their combinations - and the combination outperforms either alone for both classification problems (0.73 clinical versus non-clinical; 0.93 ASD versus PD). Because the questionnaire sets are named and separated, the contribution of each modality is visible rather than buried, and the finding that both trait questionnaires together beat either individually is directly interpretable. [RQ4.1] Three standard classifiers - KNN, random forest and linear-kernel SVM - selected on the explicit ground that these three have been used together in comparably sized studies of parkinsonian movement. No deep learning and no novel architecture; results are reported for all three separately and as a mean, so no single algorithm's best run stands in for the finding. [RQ4.2] One row per participant. Thirty-seven kinematic input variables (nine features across four shapes plus one reaction time value), computed as residuals after controlling for age, depression and anxiety and averaged across trials and days; plus three questionnaire sets. A reduced discriminatory kinematic feature set was defined by retaining features, or feature-shape combinations, that showed significant group differences in the mixed models. That selection rule is stated precisely - including that a group-by-shape interaction yielding a difference on only one shape contributes only that shape's value - which is both good reporting and the point at which the design leaks, since the significance tests were computed over all participants including those later held out. [RQ4.3] Test accuracy per algorithm and averaged across the three, with the full grid published as a heat map colour-coded against chance and ordered by mean accuracy - so the reader sees every configuration, including the two that performed at chance, rather than only the maximum. For the group-difference analyses the reporting is fuller still: F statistics, p-values, beta estimates with 95% confidence intervals, and Bayes factors quantifying evidence for the null with interpretive bands stated in advance. What is absent is any interval on the classification accuracies, which matters because the test partitions hold roughly 13 to 19 participants; the 95% interval around the 0.93 headline spans approximately 0.66 to 1.00, and around 0.73 approximately 0.49 to 0.90. [RQ4.4] Substantive and directional. The study identifies which features discriminate (speed modulation, sub-movements, reaction time), in which direction, and between which pairs of groups; which task conditions are informative (the ellipse least so); and where an apparent effect may be an artefact of another (jerk as a possible epiphenomenon of speed). It also uses Bayesian analysis to distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence, reporting that low Bayes factors mean there is not strong evidence to conclude that movements were the same between groups where differences were not found - a distinction almost never drawn in this literature. [RQ4.5] The validation design is participant-level and honestly reported, with three qualifications that the review should record rather than treat as disqualifying. The structure is correct: an 80/20 split of participants, with test accuracy computed on held-out people and reported for each of three algorithms and as their mean, and with the entire configuration grid published so that the reported maximum sits visibly among its alternatives, including two models at chance. The qualifications are, first, size - 63 participants in the ASD-versus-PD contrast and 94 in clinical-versus-non-clinical give test partitions of roughly 13 and 19 people, so a 0.93 mean accuracy corresponds to about 12 of 13 correct and carries a confidence interval running from roughly 0.66 to 1.00; no interval is reported. Second, selection - the discriminatory kinematic feature sets were defined by group-difference significance from mixed models fitted on all participants, so configurations using those sets saw the held-out participants' labels during feature selection and are optimistically biased; the all-kinematic-features configurations are unaffected, and the paper's own observation that variability was seen in whether discriminatory or all features yielded stronger accuracy is consistent with the selection buying less than it might. Third, no external cohort, which the authors acknowledge by describing the work as proof-of-concept. Set against the corpus, what makes this study valuable is not its accuracy figure but its structure: the negative result is the primary finding, it is supported by Bayesian evidence for the null rather than by absence of significance, and the classification is offered as a secondary demonstration rather than as a diagnostic claim. [RQ5.1] Autism; Parkinson's disease; Movement; Classification. Four terms, both conditions named, the behavioural domain named, and the analytic task named - with no architecture, no algorithm and no accuracy language. [RQ5.2] Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders 18:8, a specialist neurodevelopmental journal, with a 180-day review - the longest among the charted 2026 studies. The disciplinary fit is visible throughout: formal group matching with equivalence tests, mixed models with appropriate random-effect structure, Bayesian evidence for the null, pre-specified interpretive thresholds, deposited data and scripts, complete ethics reporting including participant remuneration, and a limitations section that reasons about cohort effects in ascertainment. [RQ5.3] 2026, accepted 15 December 2025 after 180 days. The framing is unusual for this corpus in that its primary contribution is negative and clinically protective rather than a performance claim. The motivating concern is that PD assessments are primarily movement-based, so autistic people may score highly on PD diagnostic criteria because of autism-related movement differences - a differential-diagnosis risk that matters given rising PD diagnosis rates in autistic populations. The study then finds no kinematic similarity between autism and PD that is also distinct from controls, which addresses that concern directly. The classification work is labelled proof-of-concept, kinematics are proposed for use in conjunction with clinical assessments rather than instead of them, and the applied suggestion - that a tablet-and-stylus protocol could support community-scale assessment without laboratory equipment - is proportionate to what was demonstrated. |
| S-159 | Retrospective analysis of four public ASD screening datasets from Kaggle and UCI, harmonised into 2,154 records and 15 unified attributes spanning toddlers, children, adolescents and adults, with stratified sampling by age group during merging. Per-cohort and per-class sample counts are not reported. Because no clinician-annotated severity labels exist in the source data - a gap the paper identifies as its motivation - severity labels were constructed as a weighted sum of the A1-A10 items normalised to [0,1] and cut into four ordinal strata (No ASD, Mild, Moderate, Severe) at 0.30, 0.55 and 0.75, with domain weights calibrated to maximise agreement with expert assessments on a sampled subset (Cohen's kappa 0.72, 95% CI 0.69-0.76). | After mode imputation (validated against median and kNN imputation, under 1.0% deviation), min-max normalisation, label encoding and correlation- plus SHAP-based feature pruning that removed ethnicity, country of residence, respondent type and prior app use, a bidirectional LSTM trained with a chaotic optimiser performed joint binary screening and four-class ordinal severity classification under stratified 10-fold cross-validation with early stopping and class weighting. Author-fitted baselines (SVM, random forest, logistic regression, MLP, unidirectional LSTM) were run under identical preprocessing and validation, and an ablation isolated each architectural component. Severity thresholds were perturbed by 5% and domain weights by 10% across the folds to test labelling stability. | Accuracy 99.10% (toddlers), 97.10% (children), 98.50% (adolescents), 98.10% (adults), with AUROC above 0.99 and a 3-6 point gain over the strongest baselines (SVM 0.911, logistic regression 0.902, random forest 0.928, MLP 0.944, unidirectional LSTM 0.932). Ablation: 0.932 to 0.956 to 0.968 to 0.985 to 0.987. Labelling stability: macro-F1 within 0.6% and kappa within 0.03 under threshold and weight perturbation. | The severity labels are a deterministic function of the model's own inputs, so the reported accuracies measure reconstruction of a scoring rule rather than diagnostic performance - a limitation the paper states itself, five times, and explicitly instructs the reader to apply. Three further issues are not stated. The domain weights defining the label were calibrated on the full dataset before cross-validation, so the target itself was fitted to the data the model is evaluated on. SHAP-based feature pruning requires a fitted model and was likewise performed on the whole dataset. And the expert calibration that provides the study's only external anchor reports kappa 0.72 without stating how many records were expert-labelled, by whom, or against what instrument. Beyond these: no class counts or per-cohort sample sizes are given, so no baseline can be computed; no confidence interval or across-fold variance accompanies any accuracy despite ten folds having been run; ethnicity and country were removed during preprocessing, foreclosing the fairness analysis the future-work section calls for; the optimiser's name is expanded two different ways; and the ablation credits SHAP with a 0.002 accuracy gain that a post-hoc explanation method cannot produce. | This is the eighth charted study built on a checklist-derived label and the only one in the corpus that identifies the circularity itself and bounds its claims accordingly. Its scope paragraph - because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the subsequent prediction task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting, and high classification performance should be interpreted as evidence of the model's ability to learn stable and interpretable behavioural scoring functions rather than as proof of clinical diagnostic accuracy - states in two sentences what this review had to reconstruct across seven other papers in the same branch. Read alongside them it also supplies a quantitative reading of the branch: a BiLSTM recovers a four-way threshold on a weighted item sum at 97-99%, and SVM, logistic regression and random forest recover it at 90-93%, so the architectural competition running through this literature is a competition to approximate a piecewise-linear function. It is the correct counterexample to local_ed30e24c (292 of 292 read as confirming clinical suitability), local_b9de0d7f (a numpy-generated teaching-method target offered to educators) and local_183eaef4 (accuracy 1.0000 defended by re-running the fold count), because it demonstrates that the problem in this branch has never been the modelling, and that a paper can do the same modelling and report it honestly. | [RQ1.1] No participants were recruited. Four public screening datasets from Kaggle and UCI were harmonised into 2,154 records spanning toddlers, children, adolescents and adults, with stratified sampling by age group during merging to preserve cohort proportions. The analysis unit is the record and the cross-validation folds are stratified over records. What is missing is arithmetic: the per-cohort sample sizes, the class counts for the binary screening outcome and the counts for each of the four constructed severity strata are all absent, so the denominator behind every reported accuracy is unknown. The class distribution is characterised only qualitatively, as closely mirroring population-level screening statistics reported in prior paediatric ASD studies. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, participants, developmental cohorts, severity strata. The register is technical and notably free of pathologising language for this corpus; severity is described in terms of DSM-5 functional-support levels rather than as degrees of impairment, and the paper avoids the diagnostic vocabulary its results cannot support. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] Almost none, and by deliberate removal. Age is retained as a continuous normalised feature and cohort membership is preserved through stratified merging, but ethnicity, country of residence, who completed the test and whether the app had been used before were all excluded during feature pruning as low-variance, irrelevant or metadata noise, on the stated ground of eliminating demographic skew. Sex is not reported anywhere. The consequence is that no subgroup analysis by sex, ethnicity or respondent type is possible, and the fairness across populations named in the future-work section cannot be assessed in the present study - the variables required for it were removed. [RQ1.4] None, and the paper is explicit rather than silent about this. The abstract states that reliable severity stratification remains challenging due to the absence of explicit clinician-annotated severity labels; the methods then construct severity labels from the A1-A10 items themselves; and the scope paragraph states that because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the subsequent prediction task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting. The one external anchor is the weight calibration, in which domain weights were optimised to maximise agreement with independent expert assessments on a randomly sampled subset, achieving Cohen's kappa 0.72 (95% CI 0.69-0.76) - and the paper immediately qualifies this as supporting the internal consistency of the labeling heuristic while not implying external diagnostic validity. Neither the number of expert-labelled records, the identity or qualification of the experts, nor the instrument they used is reported. [RQ1.5] Constructed, not measured. The four ordinal strata are cut points on a weighted sum of A1-A10 normalised to [0,1]: No ASD below 0.30, Mild 0.30-0.55, Moderate 0.55-0.75, Severe at or above 0.75, with the boundaries said to align with DSM-5 functional-support descriptors and percentile interpretations from the Q-CHAT and ADOS-2 literature. No validated severity instrument was administered to anyone. The paper's own framing of this as a controlled behavioural labeling paradigm rather than as severity assessment is accurate and is what distinguishes it from local_b9de0d7f, which generated a six-way teaching-method label from a Q-CHAT total using numpy and then offered the resulting accuracy to educators as a basis for decisions. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a single-stage framework performing joint screening-level ASD identification and four-level ordinal severity stratification, under an explicitly controlled labelling paradigm, with a bidirectional LSTM as representation learner and a chaotic optimiser for training stability. Headline findings: accuracy 99.10% for toddlers, 97.10% children, 98.50% adolescents and 98.10% adults with AUROC above 0.99, a 3-6 point gain over the authors' own baselines (SVM 0.911, logistic regression 0.902, random forest 0.928, MLP 0.944, unidirectional LSTM 0.932). The framing of these results is the study's distinguishing feature: they are presented as evidence of the model's effectiveness in approximating a deterministic behavioural severity-scoring function rather than independent clinical diagnostic performance. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Public datasets harmonised and analysed computationally; no environment, hardware or runtime is described. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm - screening checklists completed by caregivers or self-report. The paper offers a substantive argument for its architecture choice that deserves recording: although the A1-A10 items are collected in a static format, their ordering is said to be non-arbitrary, with each question progressively evaluating social reciprocity, which is why a bidirectional sequence model is applied. The argument is stated but not tested - no experiment permutes item order to see whether the claimed sequential structure carries any signal. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethical approval and consent to participate are both declared not applicable, with the reasoning stated in full: no direct experimentation with human participants, and all analyses conducted on publicly available, fully anonymised, open-access de-identified datasets from Kaggle and UCI. The declaration is at least reasoned rather than blank. What it does not address is whether the original respondents consented to research reuse - the same gap present across this branch. [RQ2.5] No instrumentation. Analytical components: BiLSTM, a chaotic optimiser (expanded inconsistently as Chaotic Grey Ball Optimizer in the abstract and Chaotic Gradient-Based Optimizer in the methods), SHAP, and standard preprocessing. No software, version, seed or hardware is named in the extracted text. [RQ2.6] Moderate, and unusually strong on the parts that matter most for this branch. The labelling function is specified completely - the weighted index, its normalisation, the four threshold boundaries and the calibration objective - so another group could reconstruct the target variable, which is not true of any comparable study in this review. Three separate sensitivity analyses are reported with quantified deviations: imputation method (mode versus median versus kNN, under 1.0% deviation in macro-F1 and accuracy), severity thresholds perturbed by 5% and domain weights by 10% (macro-F1 within 0.6%, kappa within 0.03). The ablation table isolates each architectural component. Against this: no code, seed, software, versions, layer configuration, learning rate, batch size or epoch count; no per-cohort or per-class sample counts; and the harmonised dataset promised only post-publication. [RQ2.7] This is the study's defining characteristic and the reason it matters to the review. The scope restriction is not confined to a closing limitations paragraph but is stated in the abstract, the contributions list, the labelling section, the training section and the results discussion. Its clearest formulation is in section 3.3: because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the subsequent prediction task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting; accordingly, high classification performance should be interpreted as evidence of the proposed model's ability to learn stable and interpretable behavioural scoring functions, rather than as proof of clinical diagnostic accuracy. It further states that the labelling kappa supports internal consistency while not implying external diagnostic validity, that SHAP results carry no causal or diagnostic attribution, that performance gains are methodological improvements rather than evidence of clinical diagnostic superiority, and that the datasets are behaviourally constrained. What remains unstated: that the domain weights were calibrated on the full dataset before cross-validation, that SHAP-based feature pruning requires a fitted model and was likewise performed on the full data, that no class counts are reported, and that the ablation credits SHAP with a 0.002 accuracy gain when SHAP is a post-hoc explanation method that cannot alter a model's predictions. [RQ2.9] External validation against independently clinician-annotated severity datasets - named as necessary rather than desirable - plus multimodal fusion (prosody, eye-gaze dynamics), federated learning validation, and prospective clinical trials to enhance sensitivity and ensure fairness across populations. The first directly addresses the study's own stated boundary; the fairness objective is undercut by the removal of ethnicity and country of residence during preprocessing. [RQ3.1] Screening-item behaviours from the A1-A10 instruments, organised into three domains - social communication difficulties, repetitive behaviour and a cognitive assessment component - which supply the weighted terms of the constructed severity index. The correlation analysis relates the composite Q_SCORE to social communication difficulties (r 0.64-0.67) and repetitive behaviour (r 0.45-0.63) and reports moderate inter-item correlations (r 0.10-0.46), read as each item adding unique variance. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single questionnaire modality. What the study does perform is dataset harmonisation across four age cohorts into a common 15-attribute schema with stratified merging, which is cross-cohort integration rather than multimodal fusion. Multimodal extension with prosody and gaze is named as future work, and the absence of such cues is acknowledged as a constraint of the current data. [RQ4.1] A bidirectional LSTM as a high-capacity representation learner over static questionnaire attributes, trained with a chaotic optimiser that applies controlled chaotic perturbations to diversify gradient updates, described as an alternative to deterministic optimisers such as Adam or RMSProp. Baselines fitted by the authors under identical preprocessing and validation: SVM, random forest, logistic regression, MLP and unidirectional LSTM. The ablation reports a clean monotone progression from 0.932 to 0.987. [RQ4.2] A 15-attribute harmonised row per participant after pruning, with continuous variables min-max normalised and categorical fields label-encoded. The predictor set contains the A1-A10 items and the composite Q_SCORE; the target is a four-level discretisation of a weighted sum of those same A1-A10 items. The label is therefore an arithmetic function of the inputs by construction, and the paper says so. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUROC per cohort and per ablation variant; per-class AUROC curves across the four severity levels and four age groups; Cohen's kappa with a confidence interval for label-expert agreement; and quantified stability under three separate perturbation analyses. The metric set is broad and the sensitivity reporting is a genuine strength. Two gaps. No confidence interval or across-fold variance accompanies any classification accuracy, despite ten folds having been run and despite intervals being reported for the kappa. And no class counts are given for either the binary or the four-level target, so no baseline exists against which a 99.10% can be positioned - which matters particularly for a four-class ordinal problem whose stratum boundaries the authors chose.
