[RQ4.4] SHAP is applied with its scope explicitly bounded, and the bounding is the point: the contributions list describes it as methodologically bounded explainability, applied to analyse feature utilisation and model consistency without asserting independent clinical causality. That is the correct use of the method under a constructed label, and it is unique in this corpus - the six other Q-CHAT-labelled studies charted here all read their SHAP or feature-importance output as clinical corroboration. Two problems remain. SHAP was also used upstream, as a feature-pruning criterion, which requires a fitted model and was performed on the full dataset before cross-validation. And the ablation table lists BiLSTM + CGBO + SHAP at accuracy 0.987 against BiLSTM + CGBO at 0.985, attributing a 0.002 gain to the addition of SHAP - which is not possible, since a post-hoc explanation method computes attributions for an already-trained model and cannot change its predictions. [RQ4.5] The evaluation is stratified 10-fold cross-validation at the record level with early stopping and class weighting, supported by three quantified sensitivity analyses - imputation method, severity thresholds perturbed by 5%, domain weights perturbed by 10% - showing macro-F1 stable within 0.6% and kappa within 0.03. That is more robustness checking than any other study in this branch performs. But the estimand is settled before any of it, and the paper states the conclusion itself: the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, so the task is function approximation and the accuracy figures are not diagnostic accuracy. Read that way, the results are internally coherent and even informative - a BiLSTM recovers a four-way threshold on a weighted sum of ten items with 97-99% accuracy, and simpler models recover it with 90-94%, which quantifies how much architectural capacity the reconstruction of a piecewise-linear scoring rule requires. Three residual issues qualify even that reading. The domain weights were calibrated on the full dataset by optimising kappa against expert labels before cross-validation, so the labelling function itself was fitted to the data the model is then evaluated on. SHAP-based feature pruning was likewise applied to the whole dataset and necessarily requires a fitted model. And the expert calibration - the only external anchor in the study - reports kappa 0.72 without stating how many records were expert-labelled, by whom, or with what instrument, so the one bridge between the constructed label and clinical severity is itself unspecified. Compared against the branch, the difference is not in the estimand but in the interpretation: local_ed30e24c reported 292 of 292 correct as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening; local_b9de0d7f offered a numpy-generated teaching-method label at 0.9917 to educators; this study reports 99.10% and states in four separate places that it does not mean what it appears to mean. [RQ5.1] Not captured in the extracted text. [RQ5.2] Discover Applied Sciences 8(4):363 (Springer) - an open-access multidisciplinary applied-sciences journal. The venue is not clinical, yet the paper is the most careful in the branch about the boundary between computational and clinical claims, which suggests the discipline of the authors rather than of the reviewers is doing the work here. [RQ5.3] 2026. The framing is the study's principal contribution to this review. Where the rest of the questionnaire branch presents reconstruction of a checklist threshold as diagnostic accuracy, this paper presents the same task as what it is - approximation of a deterministic behavioural scoring function - and repeats that restriction in the abstract, the contributions, the methods, the results and the conclusion. It describes its own labelling as a heuristic with internal consistency but no external diagnostic validity, bounds its SHAP interpretation against causal claims, calls external validation against clinician-annotated data necessary rather than desirable, and requires human oversight for any deployment. The overreach that remains is modest and confined to the discussion, which speaks of diagnostic precision and of stratifying ASD into four functional levels, and to the clinical-integration proposal for electronic health records and e-learning platforms. It is the only study in the branch whose stated conclusions a reader could act on safely. |
| S-160 | A proposed algorithmic framework (MUXAI-ASDBD) evaluated in what the article repeatedly calls simulation across named developmental screening datasets (ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT, STAT) and imaging modalities (MRI, EEG), with code and data cited to a GitHub repository. The sample description is internally contradictory: 10,000 MRI samples in one sentence, 25,000 positive and 1,200 negative cases described as class-balanced in the next, 500 subjects in the CSBS description, and study-population ages given as 0-36 months, 12-36 months and 3-6 years in three separate passages. | Each modality is split into non-overlapping partitions (six in the methodology, four in the parameter table), each processed by a CNN (ResNet-50 or InceptionV3, 224x224 input, Adam at 0.003, batch 64, 150 epochs, binary cross-entropy), with features aggregated per modality and fused for a softmax classifier. A machine-unlearning mechanism at the summation layer supports subject-level deletion, with an audit protocol requiring the unlearned model to be statistically indistinguishable from one retrained without the deleted subject. The stated evaluation is a 70/15/15 subject-level split with Youden-index thresholding, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, AUC and calibration, paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and an MRI-only ablation. | Maximum diagnostic accuracy of 98%, a 23% reduction in overall error rate, reduced false positives and reduced processing time; unlearning and retraining times of 3.2 s and 5.6 s per partition. None of the named clinical metrics is reported as a number, no confusion matrix appears, and the presented results are bar charts of error rate, false-positive count and precision binned into low, medium and high before and after unlearning. | The two stated limitations concern dataset availability and unlearning overhead. The substantive problems are elsewhere. The sample description contradicts itself - 25,000 positive cases from a 10,000-sample dataset, a 21-to-1 ratio called class balance - and the study population's age is given three incompatible ways in a paper whose entire claim is to address a gap in newborns specifically. No diagnostic label ascertainment is described for any dataset. The evaluation protocol is described in exemplary detail and reports no value from any of its named metrics, while the headline 98% has no denominator and, under the stated class ratio, would sit 2.6 points above a majority-class baseline. Ethics and consent are declared unnecessary because no hospital deployment occurred, and the same passage states the datasets were fully identified. Cybersecurity vocabulary about malicious and fraudulent events survives in the results section, as does a sentence from the response to reviewers. | This study contributes two things to the review, one substantive and one diagnostic. The substantive contribution is its motivating argument, which no other charted study makes: that once a newborn's data enters a training set, most systems have no mechanism to remove its influence if parents withdraw consent, and that this is an obligation under GDPR and HIPAA rather than a courtesy - a point that bears directly on the fourteen studies in this corpus built on web-scraped children's photographs and on the several that waive consent because a dataset is public. The diagnostic contribution is the gap between that framing and the work: the paper obtains no ethical review or consent for its own use of newborn data, reports no value from any of the clinical metrics it names, and contradicts itself about how many children it studied and how old they were. It sits alongside local_e771fb69, which built a federated privacy framework with no ethics statement and evaluated it on nine test cases, as the review's two instances of privacy and governance machinery standing in for research governance. | [RQ1.1] No participants and no coherent sample. The methods state within four consecutive sentences that the study utilised MRI datasets of newborns comprising 10,000 samples and that the final dataset included 25,000 positive cases and 1200 negative cases, with class balance maintained. Both claims cannot hold: 25,000 positives cannot come from 10,000 samples, and a ratio of nearly 21 to 1 is not balance. Elsewhere the CSBS description reports 500 subjects, and Table 4, labelled Standard dataset, lists the same identifier range 01-1000 five times over with different family relationships (son, daughter, niece) and a different algorithm name in each row, so it is a results table presented as a data description. No consistent count of children exists anywhere in the article. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, newborns, newborn babies, infants, children, brain disabilities, brain disorder. Autism is grouped throughout with brain disabilities and brain disorders as a single detection target, and the abstract describes ASD as a rising disorder in the brain among newborns. No autistic or community perspective appears. A distinct register intrudes in the results, where false positives are explained as occurring when the system flags safe/normal data as malicious or abnormal, and precision is explained in terms of how likely a nominated event is to be true when the model declares it malicious, fraudulent, or different from the expected behaviour - vocabulary from cybersecurity or fraud detection that has been carried into a paper about newborns. [RQ1.3] None. No sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic or geographic information for any dataset. Age is reported three incompatible ways: newborns aged 0 to 36 months in the title and abstract, children aged 12-36 months in the MRI inclusion criteria, and aged 3-6 years in the CSBS description. Since the paper's central claim is that existing tools are restricted to toddlers above 18 months and that it addresses the gap in newborns, the age of the analysed population is the single most consequential fact in the study and it is stated three different ways. [RQ1.4] None. No diagnostic instrument administration, criterion, assessor or record is described for any dataset. The named sources - ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT and STAT - are developmental screening instruments, not diagnoses, and the paper does not describe how any label was assigned. One results passage categorises outcomes as yes (Y), random (R) - indicating a 50% probability of yes and a 50% probability of no - and not detected (N), which introduces a coin-flip category into what is presented as a diagnostic output. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a machine-unlearning-integrated explainable AI framework for early ASD and brain-disability detection in newborns, motivated by a genuinely important argument: once a newborn's data is used in training, most models provide no mechanism to remove it if parents withdraw consent, which raises ethical and legal problems under GDPR and HIPAA. Headline findings: a 23% reduction in error rates, reduced false positives, accuracy improved to 98%, and reduced processing time. The results are described as simulation results. [RQ2.2] No study setting. Datasets are said to have been processed in different computing laboratories; a testbed with 32 GB RAM and 2 TB storage is named for timing measurements. The paper states that the work involved no hospital deployments while also claiming, in its contributions list, past experience implementing the system in clinical settings and that the framework can effectively validate itself in real-world clinical implementations. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Developmental screening instruments and archived imaging. The most concrete behavioural description concerns CSBS items on communication via eye movements (straight, upward, leftward, downward) and repetitive hand and finger movements, recorded as binary responses over 30-second monitoring windows. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics and consent are declared unnecessary on the stated ground that the work involved no hospital deployments, and the same passage claims that the datasets were fully identified and processed with strict subject-level partitioning, with fully authorised controlled access, audit logging and standard encryption. Fully identified is the opposite of de-identified and appears in a sentence listing privacy safeguards, so it is presumably an error - but it is the operative word in the article's only statement about the identifiability of newborn data. The irony is structural rather than incidental: the paper's entire motivation is that models must be able to forget a newborn's data when parents withdraw consent, and it obtains no consent and no ethical review for its own use of that data. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Model components: ResNet-50 (50 layers) or InceptionV3 (48 layers) at 224x224 input, Adam at learning rate 0.003 (described as increasing), batch size 64, 150 epochs, binary cross-entropy; unlearning and retraining times of 3.2 s and 5.6 s per partition; an inter-modality correlation threshold of 0.65. A testbed with 32 GB RAM and 2 TB storage is named. [RQ2.6] The article makes strong reproducibility claims - a public GitHub repository for both code and data, frozen configuration files, and an explicit statement that the entire pipeline can be replicated end-to-end - and simultaneously makes reproduction impossible by contradicting itself about what was run. The partition count is six in the methodology and four in the parameter table; the sample is 10,000 MRI scans and also 25,000 positives plus 1,200 negatives; the age band is 0-36 months, 12-36 months and 3-6 years in three places; the modality set is MRI, video, audio, text and EEG in one section and MRI, video and text in another. Feature vectors are printed as illustrative example values rather than as results. A sentence from the revision process also survives in the published text, reporting that figures are revised with corrected captions, algorithm numbering is standardized, and placeholder references are replaced with accurate citations. [RQ2.7] Two sentences, both about deployment: the framework depends on the availability and quality of multimodal datasets, which may vary across clinical settings, and repeated unlearning operations can incur overhead at scale. Neither addresses the evidence. Unmentioned: the contradictory sample sizes, the three different age ranges, the absence of any diagnostic label description, the absence of any numeric result table for the headline accuracy, the majority-class baseline implied by the reported class ratio, and the fact that the experiments are described as simulations. [RQ2.9] Not separately developed beyond the deployment limitations. The paper closes on the claim that the framework improved interpretability and diagnostic reliability. [RQ3.1] Developmental screening behaviours as captured by ASQ, CSBS, PEDS, M-CHAT and STAT items - communication through eye movements and repetitive hand and finger movements are the only behaviours described concretely - together with imaging and physiological modalities named but not characterised. [RQ3.2] Multimodal fusion is the framework's structural claim: each modality is partitioned, processed by per-partition CNNs, aggregated into a modality representation, and fused into a single feature vector for a softmax classifier. The claim cannot be evaluated. The modality set differs between sections (MRI, video, audio, text and EEG versus MRI, video and text); no dataset is characterised well enough to know what any modality contains; the fused feature vectors are printed as illustrative example numbers; and no ablation isolates any modality's contribution except a reference to an MRI-only ablation whose results are not shown in the extracted text. [RQ4.1] MUXAI-ASDBD, described as a partitioning-based explainable CNN framework with layer-wise explainability and a machine-unlearning mechanism at the summation layer, using ResNet-50 or InceptionV3 as per-partition feature extractors. Baselines named are CNN, GNN, ACNN, SVM, LSTM and a proposed FCNN-LSTM - a list that does not match the framework the paper is proposing, since the title framework is a partitioned CNN and the proposed baseline is a fully connected LSTM. [RQ4.2] 224x224 images for the CNN backbones; the representation of questionnaire data is never specified, which matters because five of the seven named datasets are questionnaires and a 224x224 convolutional backbone cannot consume a checklist without a stated encoding. Aggregated feature vectors appear in the text as literal illustrative values such as [0.5, 0.6, ..., 0.8] and [0.45, 0.55, ..., 0.75]. [RQ4.3] The named metric set is clinically appropriate and unusually complete for this corpus - sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, ROC AUC and calibration, with thresholds set by the Youden index and significance assessed by paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. None of it is reported. No sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, AUC or calibration value appears in the extracted text, no test statistic or p-value is given, and the phrase all reported with 95 to 98% confidence intervals conflates a confidence level with an interval width. What is actually presented is bar charts of error rate, false-positive count and precision binned into low, medium and high before and after unlearning, plus a headline accuracy of 98% and a 23% error reduction with no denominator. If the stated class ratio of 25,000 positives to 1,200 negatives held, the majority-class baseline would be 95.4% and the headline would be 2.6 points above it. [RQ4.4] Layer-wise explainability is the framework's named contribution and no explainability result is presented. Modality-specific outputs are described in a single sentence as gradient spectrogram features for audio and spatiotemporal attention maps for video, each demonstrating interpretability in a clinically meaningful context, with no figure, attribution or quantitative measure to support the claim in the extracted text. [RQ4.5] The validation section contains, in isolation, the most methodologically literate paragraph of any weak study in this review: a 70/15/15 partition with strict subject-level separation to avoid leakage across folds, stratified sampling to preserve class distribution, Youden-index thresholding on validation data, clinically meaningful metrics including PPV and NPV and calibration, paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, ablation of the MRI-only modality, runtime measurement with means and standard deviations, and a subject-level deletion threat model under which the unlearned model should remain statistically indistinguishable from one retrained without the deleted data, audited by removing specified subjects and validating forgetting against deletion audit sets. Every element of that is the right thing to do. None of it can be assessed, because the article does not report a single number from any of it and because the data description it would apply to is self-contradicting - 10,000 MRI samples yielding 25,000 positive cases, a 25,000-to-1,200 split called class balance, six partitions in one section and four in another, three mutually exclusive age ranges. The experiments are moreover described throughout as simulation results, and the only quantitative outputs shown are before-and-after bar charts binned into low, medium and high. The gap between the methodological vocabulary and the reported evidence is the finding here: this is the corpus's clearest instance of validation language functioning as a genre convention rather than as a description of work performed. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; Newborn babies; Machine un-learning; Convolutional neural network; Explainable artificial intelligence. Five terms; the population claim (newborn babies) is the one the article's own data description contradicts three times. [RQ5.2] Alexandria Engineering Journal 145 (2026) 164-181 (Elsevier) - a general engineering journal. Review did not surface a sample description in which 25,000 positive cases are drawn from 10,000 samples and a 21-to-1 ratio is called balanced, three incompatible age ranges for the study population, partition counts differing between sections, a named metric set none of whose values are reported, cybersecurity vocabulary about malicious and fraudulent events in a paper about infants, or a surviving response-to-reviewers sentence in the body text. [RQ5.3] 2026. The framing rests on a genuinely important and under-addressed problem: that once a newborn's data enters a training set there is usually no mechanism to remove it when parents withdraw consent, and that this is a live obligation under GDPR and HIPAA. That argument is correct and is made nowhere else in this corpus. What follows it does not support any of the claims made from it - accuracy improved to 98%, error rates reduced by 23%, false positives reduced, and a framework said to be able to validate itself in real-world clinical implementations and to be implementable in hospital settings. The study reports no confusion matrix, no metric values from its own named metric set, no consistent sample size and no ethics approval, in a paper whose organising principle is the ethical handling of newborns' data. |
| S-161 | Retrospective analysis of the Self-Stimulatory Behaviour Dataset: 75 YouTube videos of roughly 90 seconds each, uploaded by parents and caretakers of autistic children and annotated by the dataset's originators for the start and finish of each behaviour episode. Frames were extracted with OpenCV, cropped by region-of-interest detection and augmented. The number of distinct children is never reported; the k-fold confusion matrix covers 303 samples. All four target classes - arm flapping, head banging, spinning and normal behaviour - come from videos of autistic children, so there is no non-autistic comparison group. | A custom CNN-GRU was trained to classify the four behaviour categories, with GRU chosen over LSTM for simpler gating and greater stability under repeated k-fold retraining. VGG16, MobileNet, EfficientNet-B7 and 3D-CNN+LSTM were trained on the same data under identical hyperparameters for comparison. Evaluation used k-fold cross-validation with per-fold means and standard deviations, plus a separate held-out test with its own confusion matrix, and paired t-tests against each baseline at a corrected threshold of 0.0125. | CNN-GRU k-fold accuracy 0.9294 +/- 0.0038 (validation accuracy 0.96, loss 0.16; precision 0.96, recall 0.95-0.96, F1 0.96), against MobileNet 0.9193, 3D-CNN+LSTM 0.8912 and EfficientNet-B7 0.8808, with all four paired comparisons significant. Per class, arm flapping and head banging reached F1 0.98 while spinning and normal behaviour reached 0.94 and 0.93; errors concentrated between spinning and the repetitive classes. | The folds are formed over clips extracted from only 75 videos with no video-level or child-level grouping, so clips sharing a child, room, camera and clothing appear on both sides of every fold - and the per-fold standard deviations below 0.004, presented as evidence of robustness, are better read as evidence that the folds contain much the same material. The number of distinct children is unreported, as are per-class counts and the value of k, so neither the effective sample size nor the chance level can be established. Most fundamentally, the task performed is four-way movement classification within a dataset containing only autistic children, which cannot support the screening and diagnostic claims made in the title and abstract; the paper's own statement that the system is a clinical decision support system and not an independent diagnostic system is the accurate description. There is no ethics or consent statement for the reuse of identifiable children's home videos, whose parent-posted provenance the paper describes explicitly, and a detailed limitations column is applied to eleven prior studies while none is applied to this one. | This study occupies a distinctive position in the review. Its data are the most ecologically valid in the entire corpus - spontaneous self-stimulatory behaviour recorded by families in children's own homes, annotated for when it occurs, with no laboratory, stimulus or instruction - and its comparative design is among the better controlled, with five architectures trained under identical hyperparameters, per-fold standard deviations for every model and paired significance tests at a corrected threshold. It nonetheless repeats the corpus's dominant failure in the video modality, splitting at the clip level over 75 recordings, and it makes the review's clearest category error of a different kind: a within-population behaviour-recognition result presented as ASD screening, when the dataset contains no non-autistic person at all. Read alongside local_b6ac2b98 and local_69b10fe4, which both defined their comparison groups explicitly, it shows that the presence or absence of a meaningful contrast group is a separate axis from validation design, and that a study can be careful about architecture comparison while being silent about what its classes actually contrast. Its ethics silence is also the corpus's sharpest, because the paper itself states that the videos were posted by parents and caretakers on publicly accessible websites and then does not ask whether that constitutes consent to machine learning reuse. | [RQ1.1] No participants and no groups. The data are 75 YouTube videos of approximately 90 seconds each from the Self-Stimulatory Behaviour Dataset, uploaded by parents and caretakers, segmented into frame clips by behaviour type using the dataset's original annotations. The number of distinct children is never stated - a consequential omission, since 75 videos may represent fewer than 75 children and the k-fold confusion matrix reports 303 samples, so the analysis unit is the clip. Crucially there is no non-autistic comparison group: all four classes, including normal Behavior, are drawn from videos of autistic children, so the study is a behaviour-recognition problem within one population rather than a diagnostic contrast between populations. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, autistic children, ASD children, ASD youngsters, abnormal Behavioral patterns, stereotypical Behaviors, normal Behavior. The stereotyped/normal opposition is applied to movements rather than to children, which is the more defensible usage, but the framing describes self-stimulatory behaviours as abnormal throughout and the fourth class as normal. No autistic or community perspective appears, and there is no discussion of self-stimulatory behaviour as regulatory rather than pathological. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or setting information for any child. The videos are consumer home recordings of unknown provenance, and the paper does not report even the age range of the children whose behaviour it classifies. [RQ1.4] None, and not required by the task as executed - but required by the task as described. The videos are annotated for when a behaviour occurs, not for whether the child has a diagnosis; no clinical assessment, instrument or assessor exists for anyone in the dataset. The paper's title nonetheless places the work in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder and its abstract states that the approach facilitates quick, accurate and effective screening of ASD. Those claims do not follow from a four-way discrimination among arm flapping, head banging, spinning and other movement in videos of children who are all autistic. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to classify four behaviour categories - arm flapping, spinning, head banging and normal behaviour - from naturalistic, unstructured video, using a CNN-GRU architecture, in order to help clinicians monitor behavioural trends. Headline findings: CNN-GRU reaches k-fold accuracy 0.9294 +/- 0.0038 and validation accuracy 0.96, outperforming MobileNet (0.9193), 3D-CNN+LSTM (0.8912), EfficientNet-B7 (0.8808) and VGG16, with paired t-tests significant against all four at a corrected threshold of 0.0125. Per class, the two clearly distinct repetitive behaviours (arm flapping, head banging) reach F1 0.98 while spinning and normal behaviour reach 0.94 and 0.93. [RQ2.2] No study setting - the defining property of the data is precisely that there is none. The videos are unstructured home recordings made by families in everyday environments, which is the source of both the design's principal strength (ecological validity, behaviours observed rather than reported) and its principal uncontrolled variance (camera, framing, lighting, distance and activity all vary by video and are perfectly confounded with the child). [RQ2.3] No imposed task. Naturalistic recordings of children engaged in everyday activities, with behaviour episodes delimited by the SSBD annotations of start and finish times. This is the most ecologically valid data source in the charted corpus - no laboratory, no stimulus, no instruction, and behaviours that occurred spontaneously in the child's own environment. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. There is no ethics statement, consent statement or exemption claim anywhere in the article. The omission is more pointed than in the questionnaire studies because the paper itself describes the data's provenance: parents and caretakers posted their videos on websites that are accessible to the public, and the dataset consists of URLs to 75 YouTube videos of identifiable autistic children. Whether a parent posting a home video to YouTube thereby consents to its use as machine learning training data is exactly the question the study needed to address and does not raise. [RQ2.5] No controlled acquisition equipment - the recordings are consumer video of unknown origin. Python OpenCV was used for frame extraction. Region-of-interest detection and cropping were applied to remove background objects, which is the appropriate response to uncontrolled framing. No deep learning framework, version, seed or hardware is named. [RQ2.6] Mixed, with real strengths on the comparative design. Reproducible: the source dataset is public and correctly attributed to its originators, the preprocessing chain is described in order, all five architectures were deliberately trained under identical hyperparameters to make the comparison fair, per-fold standard deviations are reported for every model and metric, and paired t-tests with a corrected significance threshold of 0.0125 are tabulated. Not reproducible: the value of k, the number of frames or clips extracted, the number of distinct children, per-class sample counts, the unit at which folds were formed, the learning rate, batch size and epoch count, any seed, and any code or data-availability statement. [RQ2.7] The paper announces that it will discuss its weaknesses, and the only self-directed remarks concern the data - that SSBD is the sole freely available dataset of its kind, that it is somewhat helpful but does not fully meet the study's conditions, and that no existing dataset does. Against that, a full column of Table 1 assigns a specific limitation to each of eleven prior studies (did not describe the pre-processing and model development steps; need to improve results; implemented a basic CNN model that performs binary classification and was tested on a small dataset). Unmentioned for this study: that folds are formed over clips from 75 videos with no video-level or child-level grouping; that the number of distinct children is unknown; that there is no non-autistic comparison group behind a screening claim; that no ethics statement accompanies the reuse of identifiable children's home videos; and that per-class counts and the chance level are unreported. [RQ2.9] Announced in the paper's structure but not developed in the extracted text. [RQ3.1] Self-stimulatory motor behaviour observed in natural settings: arm flapping, head banging and spinning, against a fourth class of non-stereotyped movement. This is the corpus's clearest instance of behaviour being observed directly rather than inferred from a photograph, a checklist or a questionnaire - the behaviours are the ones clinicians actually watch for, recorded where they actually occur. The confusion-matrix analysis adds a substantive behavioural observation: errors concentrate between spinning and the two repetitive classes, attributed to overlap in motion dynamics, and normal behaviour is moderately confused with the repetitive classes in the held-out test. [RQ3.2] No fusion - video only. The CNN-GRU combination is spatial-plus-temporal modelling within one modality, and the architectural rationale is stated properly: convolutional layers extract spatial features from single frames while autism-related behaviour is a temporal phenomenon requiring sequence modelling across frames. That is a correct justification for a recurrent component, unlike the several studies in this corpus that apply LSTMs to single static inputs. [RQ4.1] A custom CNN-GRU hybrid, with GRU selected over LSTM on the stated grounds of simpler gating, fewer parameters, greater training stability and less overfitting under repeated k-fold retraining. Four comparators - VGG16, MobileNet, EfficientNet-B7 and 3D-CNN+LSTM - were fitted by the authors on the same data under identical hyperparameters, which makes this one of the few architecture comparisons in the corpus that is actually controlled. [RQ4.2] Cropped frame sequences from annotated behaviour segments, after region-of-interest detection to remove irrelevant background and augmentation to reduce overfitting. The ROI step is well motivated for uncontrolled home video, where background and framing differ systematically between recordings. [RQ4.3] Validation accuracy and loss, precision, recall and F1 per architecture; per-fold means with standard deviations for every model and metric; per-class F1; two confusion matrices; learning curves; and paired t-tests with a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.0125. The statistical reporting is among the better examples in this corpus - the standard deviations are given rather than implied, and the multiple-comparison correction is stated explicitly. What is missing bears directly on interpretation: per-class sample counts are not reported, so the 25% chance level for a four-class problem cannot be checked against the actual class balance; the value of k is never given; and the very small per-fold standard deviations (under 0.004 across five architectures) are read as evidence that the model is robust and consistent across the folds when, over clips drawn from only 75 videos, near-identical fold results are equally consistent with folds that are near-identical resamples of the same recordings. [RQ4.4] No model interpretability, but a genuine and clinically sensible error analysis. Spinning is confused with the repetitive classes because of overlapping motion dynamics, and normal behaviour is confused with the repetitive classes in the independent test set - both of which are the errors one would predict from the physics of the behaviours, and both of which point at the harder discrimination (is this movement stereotyped or not?) rather than the easier one (is this flapping or banging?). [RQ4.5] The evaluation is better constructed than most in this corpus and still cannot support the claim the title makes. On the credit side: k-fold cross-validation with per-fold standard deviations reported for all five architectures, an independent test evaluation with its own confusion matrix, identical hyperparameters across models to make the comparison fair, and paired t-tests against every baseline at a corrected threshold. On the debit side, three things. First, the unit: 75 source videos are segmented into clips and the k-fold matrix covers 303 samples, with no video-level or child-level grouping described, so clips from the same recording - same child, same room, same camera, same clothing - fall on both sides of every fold. In naturalistic video this is the strongest available shortcut, because recording identity is far easier to learn than movement type. Second, the reported stability is read backwards: standard deviations below 0.004 across five different architectures are presented as robustness, whereas over clips from 75 videos they indicate that the folds contain much the same material. Third, and separately from any of this, the task is not the task claimed. Four-way discrimination among arm flapping, head banging, spinning and other movement, in videos of children who are all autistic, cannot yield screening for ASD, because no non-autistic person appears anywhere in the data - a screening claim requires a comparison the design does not contain. The paper's own hedge, that the system is intended as a clinical decision support system and not an independent diagnostic system, is the correct reading and sits uneasily beside a title placing the work in diagnoses of ASD and an abstract promising effective screening. [RQ5.1] Autism Spectrum Disorder; Behavior analysis; CNN-GRU; deep learning; naturalistic video. Five terms, and naturalistic video is the one that matters - it names the study's genuine distinguishing property in a corpus dominated by downloaded photographs and checklists. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience 20:1626315, with a 174-day review including a substantial revision. The review did not surface the absent ethics statement for reuse of identifiable children's home videos, the unreported number of distinct children, the absence of a non-autistic comparison behind a screening claim, or the reading of near-zero fold variance as robustness. [RQ5.3] 2026, published 18 March, 174 days from submission with one revision round. The framing is internally split. The objectives section states that the system should be used as a clinical decision support system and not an independent diagnostic system - an accurate and unusually explicit limit. The title, abstract and conclusion pull the other way, placing the work in diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder, claiming it facilitates the quick, accurate, and effective screening of ASD, and asserting tremendous potential for real-world clinical implementation. What the study actually demonstrates is that a CNN-GRU distinguishes four movement categories in home video at about 93% under a clip-level split, which is a behaviour-recognition result and a useful one; the screening language is added on top of it. |
| S-162 | Secondary analysis of the Spanish BeGaze eye-tracking corpus: 45 children aged roughly 5-8 years, comprising 19 with an ASD diagnosis made externally by neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists before inclusion and 26 typically developing children. Group characteristics are tabulated - age 75.9 versus 78.1 months, SCQ 12.6 versus 4.7, KBIT-2 108.78 versus 104.3, PPVT-III 50.0 versus 67.3 - and the corpus's ethics approval (Ethics Committee of the Universitat de Valencia, Declaration of Helsinki, guardian informed consent) is reported. | Children watched a professional storyteller narrating short stories with the face visible, then answered comprehension questions. Six stories were presented, three audio-only and three audio-visual, counterbalanced across participants, with each instance segmented into pre-speech, speech and post-speech phases. Eighteen temporal gaze features were computed over eyes, mouth and nose areas of interest. Six interpretable classifiers were evaluated under five-fold nested cross-validation with participant-independent splits, per-fold class balancing, inner-loop grid search and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, against a per-fold majority-class baseline. Feature importance and SHAP were computed on each fold's test set and averaged. | Best performance 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC (logistic regression, audio-visual speech phase), with roughly 55% F1 in the speech phase across both modalities and all models exceeding the majority-class lower bound. Audio-visual stimuli significantly outperformed audio-only in the pre-speech phase but not during or after speech. Per-story means were 57.7 (SD 9.8) audio-only and 64.1 (SD 9.1) audio-visual, with no consistent clustering by narrative content. Feature importance and SHAP converged on mouth fixation time and cross-AOI revisits as the leading discriminators. | The authors state three - a small sample for specific modality/phase pairings limiting generalisation and increasing overfitting risk, the context-specific storytelling task potentially not transferring, and predefined AOIs and fixed intervals limiting granularity - plus separate treatments of the Castilian/Valencian bilingual confound and of clinical viability. The one substantive omission is that the ASD group's receptive vocabulary is markedly lower and is not adjusted for in a task requiring comprehension of narrated stories, so part of the gaze difference may reflect comprehension rather than social attention. No external cohort is tested, and the sample of 45 children means several modality comparisons could not reach significance, which the paper notes each time. | This is the fourth charted study below high risk of bias and the corpus's clearest calibration point for the eye-tracking branch. Its validation design is the most complete in the review - nested five-fold cross-validation with participant-independent splits, inner-loop hyperparameter selection, per-fold class balancing, bootstrap confidence intervals on every estimate, and a per-fold majority-class baseline built in specifically to test whether the gaze features beat class distribution. Under those conditions, with clinician-made diagnoses and a purpose-designed social-attention paradigm, the best result is 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC. That figure should be set against the eye-tracking studies charted elsewhere in this review reporting 99.78% (local_7432ffd7, sample-level splits with CARS in the feature set), 100% (local_44d3aef5, 55 scanpath images from a repeated-image collection) and 97% (local_bb4d1f7a, 100 eye crops per child): the difference between them and this study is not the modality, the algorithm or the year, but whether the same child can appear on both sides of the split. It also joins local_b6ac2b98 and local_69b10fe4 in the group of studies that manipulate their stimulus systematically rather than presenting one fixed condition, and its finding that the audio-visual advantage is concentrated before speech onset is a behavioural result rather than a benchmark entry. | [RQ1.1] Forty-five Spanish children from the BeGaze corpus: 19 with an ASD diagnosis made externally by neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists before inclusion, and 26 typically developing children, focused on the 5-8 year preschool-to-primary transition. Each child contributed multiple samples - one per story, under two modality conditions and segmented into three temporal phases - and the cross-validation folds are explicitly participant-independent, so the multiplication of samples per child does not leak across the split. This is the correct handling of a repeated-measures design and it is rare in this corpus. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing children, TYP. The register is measured and clinical without pathologising; gaze differences are framed as attentional and perceptual patterns and as potential biomarkers rather than as deficits, and the comparison group is typically developing throughout. One inherited phrase from the literature review describes eye tracking as quantifying social attention deficits. There is no autistic or community perspective, but nothing in the language overstates. [RQ1.3] Well reported for the variables collected. Group sizes, mean ages with standard deviations, SCQ, KBIT-2 nonverbal intelligence and PPVT-III receptive vocabulary are all tabulated by group, and the pattern is described accurately: nonverbal intelligence comparable across groups (104.3 versus 108.78) while the ASD group shows higher SCQ (12.6 versus 4.7) and markedly lower receptive vocabulary (50.0 versus 67.3). Sex is not reported. Two features deserve note for interpretation. The ASD group's age variability is more than double the comparison group's (SD 19.4 versus 8.8 months), and the receptive-vocabulary gap is large and not adjusted for in the models - in a task whose stimulus is a narrated story, receptive vocabulary is a plausible driver of where a child looks. The paper does address linguistic background separately, devoting a discussion section to the Castilian/Valencian bilingual environment of the recordings. [RQ1.4] Independent and clinician-made: diagnostic classification was conducted externally by qualified specialists (neuropaediatricians or clinical psychologists) prior to inclusion in the corpus, with the SCQ administered separately as a symptomatology measure. The label therefore predates and is unrelated to the gaze data - the property that separates this study from the checklist-threshold and folder-label branches of this review. [RQ1.5] SCQ for autism symptomatology, KBIT-2 for nonverbal intelligence and PPVT-III for receptive vocabulary, all administered by the research team using Spanish-adapted standardised instruments and reported by group with standard deviations. No ADOS or calibrated severity score. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to investigate eye-tracking-based ASD detection during audio-visual storytelling using traditional but explainable machine learning, and to identify which gaze features and which phases of speech carry discriminative information. Headline findings: best performance 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC (logistic regression, audio-visual speech phase); around 55% F1 in the speech phase across both modalities; a statistically significant advantage for audio-visual over audio-only stimuli in the pre-speech phase but not during or after speech; and convergent feature-importance and SHAP evidence that mouth fixation time and revisits across facial areas of interest are the most informative features. The abstract states in its second-to-last sentence that performance remains modest. [RQ2.2] The BeGaze corpus was collected in a Spanish research setting with children viewing pre-recorded storytelling clips on screen with AOIs defined over the narrator's face. The bilingual Castilian/Valencian environment of the recorded participants is treated as a methodological factor in its own right rather than left unmentioned. [RQ2.3] A well-designed and unusually informative paradigm. Children watched a professional storyteller narrating short children's stories with the face clearly visible, then answered comprehension questions. Six stories were used, three audio-only and three audio-visual, counterbalanced across participants, and each instance was segmented into pre-speech, speech and post-speech phases. This yields a factorial design in which modality and temporal phase can be varied independently, and it is the only study in the charted corpus that manipulates the stimulus systematically rather than presenting a single fixed stimulus set. The paper also notes what it did not control - that the data were not stratified by story content - and then tests that concern directly in a per-story analysis. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is complete for the corpus: approval by the Ethics Committee of the Universitat de Valencia, conduct in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and informed consent from the legal guardians of all participants. Funding is fully itemised across six grants. [RQ2.5] Screen-based eye tracking with predefined AOIs over eyes, nose and mouth; the device model is not named, which is the study's one notable acquisition-reporting gap. Analysis used Scikit-learn, XGBoost and PyTorch on an Intel i7 desktop with 16 GB RAM and no GPU, a configuration the authors highlight deliberately as evidence that the pipeline is deployable without specialised hardware. [RQ2.6] High. The corpus is cited to its source with its ethics approval; participant characteristics are tabulated with standard deviations on four measures; the 18 features are enumerated by area of interest; the factorial design is described in full including story counterbalancing; the grid-search space is published for every algorithm; the nested cross-validation, participant independence, per-fold class balancing and bootstrap interval procedure are all specified; the software stack is named; and per-story and per-condition results are tabulated with variability. Missing: the eye-tracking device, a code or data availability statement, and the number of instances contributing to each modality/phase cell. [RQ2.7] A dedicated limitations section naming three constraints - small sample for specific modality/phase pairings limiting generalisation and increasing overfitting risk; the context-specific storytelling task potentially not transferring to other situations; and predefined AOIs and fixed time intervals limiting analytic granularity - plus a separate section on cultural and linguistic constraints addressing the Castilian/Valencian bilingual environment, and a further section (7.3) that positions the work explicitly against clinical viability benchmarks. The self-assessment is distributed through the discussion rather than confined to a closing paragraph, and it is accurate. The one limitation not raised is the substantial receptive-vocabulary difference between groups, which is measured, reported, and then not adjusted for in a task built on comprehending narrated stories. [RQ2.9] Sequential models that exploit the temporal structure of AOI fixations rather than aggregating them into summary features; larger cross-linguistic cohorts to assess bilingual exposure; and cost-benefit analysis of false positives to define what performance threshold would count as meaningful in low-stakes screening. The last of these is a form of future work no other study in this review proposes - defining the target rather than raising the number. [RQ3.1] Social attention to a speaking face, decomposed by facial region and by time relative to speech onset: fixation count, average fixation duration, dwell-time and fixation-time percentages, normalised dwell coverage and revisits, for the eyes, mouth and nose separately. The substantive behavioural findings are specific and testable - eye revisits and mouth fixation count rank highest in importance, mouth fixation time and cross-AOI revisits emerge as candidate biomarkers under both attribution methods, and the audio-visual advantage is concentrated in the pre-speech phase, which the authors read as anticipatory attention to the mouth before speech begins. [RQ3.2] Modality is manipulated experimentally rather than fused computationally, which is a different and arguably more informative use of the term. By presenting the same storytelling task audio-only and audio-visually and comparing gaze features across the two, the study isolates what the visual speech channel contributes to group discrimination - and finds that it contributes most before speech onset. That is a designed contrast producing an interpretable answer, in contrast to the corpus's several studies that concatenate modalities and report only the combined figure. [RQ4.1] Six classical interpretable classifiers - SVM (linear kernel only, chosen deliberately to preserve interpretability), logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost and a shallow MLP among them - selected explicitly because the study prioritises explainability over capacity. SVM was most consistent across conditions; logistic regression gave the single best result. No deep sequence model is used, and the authors give the reason: the corpus is small and the features are lightweight. [RQ4.2] Eighteen AOI-based temporal gaze features per experimental instance, where an instance is one participant viewing one story under one modality in one speech phase. No clinical instrument score, demographic variable or diagnostic measure enters the feature set - the SCQ, KBIT-2 and PPVT-III are reported as sample characteristics and kept out of the model. [RQ4.3] Macro F1 and AUC, chosen explicitly because the data are small and imbalanced, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every estimate; per-condition, per-phase and per-story breakdowns with standard deviations; paired t-tests between modalities within each phase with full statistics; and - critically - a per-fold majority-class baseline built into the design as a lower bound to test whether the gaze features add anything beyond class distribution. That last element is present in only one other charted study. The reported numbers are correspondingly modest and are described as such: about 55% F1 in the speech phase, 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC at best, with the paper noting where differences fail to reach significance and attributing that to the limited number of observations. [RQ4.4] Two attribution methods - model feature importance and SHAP - applied convergently, and computed on each cross-validation fold's test set before averaging, which is the correct placement and is stated explicitly. The result is a ranked feature list dominated by eye revisits, mouth fixation count and mouth fixation-time percentage, interpreted against existing cognitive literature on social attention rather than presented as a novel discovery. The authors also note honestly where interpretation fails: for features beyond the leading ones no clear pattern emerged, which they attribute to the modest performance of the classifiers rather than explaining away. [RQ4.5] This is the most rigorously validated study in the charted corpus, and its result is the corpus's most useful single number. The design is five-fold nested cross-validation with participant-independent splits, class balance preserved within folds, hyperparameter selection confined to the inner loop, retraining on the full training portion before a single outer-fold evaluation, bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every estimate, and a per-fold majority-class baseline included specifically to test whether the features beat class distribution. Each child contributes multiple samples across stories, modalities and phases, and the participant-independent split is what prevents that from becoming the leakage that inflates most of this literature. The outcome is 64.1% F1 and 64.5% AUC at best and around 55% in most conditions - and the authors state plainly that this positions the work as a research exploration rather than a deployable diagnostic tool, given that benchmarks for clinical viability often exceed 80-90%. Two qualifications remain. The sample is 45 children, and the paper repeatedly notes that the limited number of observations prevents modality differences from reaching significance. And the ASD group's receptive vocabulary is markedly lower (PPVT-III 50.0 versus 67.3), which is measured and reported but not adjusted for in a task requiring comprehension of narrated stories - so part of the gaze difference may be a comprehension difference. Neither qualification changes the study's value to this review, which is calibrative: run with correct participant-level nesting, an explicit trivial baseline, confidence intervals and a purpose-designed social-attention paradigm, eye-tracking classification of autism in children reaches the low sixties. [RQ5.1] Autism spectrum disorder; Early identification in children; Eye-tracking; Audio-visual speech comprehension; Explainable Artificial Intelligence. Five terms covering condition, application, modality, task and method, with the task - audio-visual speech comprehension - named specifically rather than generically. [RQ5.2] Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 10(3), Article ETRA012, the ETRA eye-tracking venue. The disciplinary fit shows in the reporting: participant-independent nested cross-validation, bootstrap intervals, a majority-class lower bound, paired significance testing between conditions, fold-level attribution computation, and an explicit comparison of the achieved performance against published clinical-viability thresholds. [RQ5.3] 2026 (May). The framing is the most disciplined in the review. The abstract concedes in its own body that performance remains modest; the results section opens by observing that the modest overall performances underscore the inherent challenges of detecting ASD from gaze-based features in data-scarce naturalistic settings; and section 7.3 states that roughly 64% F1/AUC positions the work as a research exploration rather than a deployable diagnostic tool, given benchmarks for clinical viability often exceed 80-90%. Value is claimed only for preliminary screening as a complement to human judgement, and the proposed future work includes defining, by cost-benefit analysis, what performance threshold would count as meaningful for low-stakes screening. Set beside the studies in this corpus reporting 99% and 100% from checklist thresholds and web-scraped photographs, its contribution is not a method but a demonstration of what the honest number looks like. |
| S-163 | Two datasets analysed under a common ensemble pipeline. Dataset 1 is the public 1,985-record ASD Children Traits collection with 28 attributes - including the Autism Spectrum Quotient, Social Responsiveness Scale, Q-CHAT score and Childhood Autism Rating Scale - and a binary ASD-traits target, with 729 positive (36.72%) and 1,256 negative (63.28%) instances and 283 records carrying missing values. Dataset 2 consists of 100 original clinical samples augmented fourfold to 400, evenly distributed across four severity categories (Mild, Moderate, Severe, Very Severe) with no non-ASD class, and with 4,220 features spanning facial images, voice, motion and physiological signals. No source, citation, country or institution is given for Dataset 2. | A published algorithm specifies label encoding, z-score normalisation, correlation filtering above 0.90, a stratified 60:20:20 split, conditional SMOTE applied only to the training partition when the class ratio falls below 0.8, and ANOVA F-test feature selection. Five base learners (RF, XGBoost, GB, SVM, LR) plus soft-voting and stacking ensembles and two neural networks were trained, with SHAP and LIME applied to Dataset 1 only. Dataset 2 used a stratified 80/10/10 split and 5-fold stratified cross-validation over the augmented set of 400. | Dataset 1: regularised neural network 97.60% (ROC-AUC 0.998), voting 96.90%, SVM/LR/stacking 96.10%, RF and GB 94.50%, XGBoost 93.70%; logistic regression reports recall 100.00% with ROC-AUC 1.000. Dataset 2: 98.2%. Ablation on Dataset 1 rises from 89.40% (no feature selection, no resampling) to 97.60% through feature selection, SMOTE, ensemble fusion and neural-network regularisation. | The paper states none. Dataset 1's predictor set contains four instruments used to determine autism status - AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS - alongside the autism-traits label, the same structure that produced accuracy 1.0000 for local_183eaef4 on the identical collection. Its 63.28% majority-class baseline is computable from the paper's own table and never stated. Dataset 2 is unsourced: no citation, country, institution or ethics committee accompanies its 100 clinical samples, and its 80/10/10 split and cross-validation were applied after fourfold augmentation, so transformed copies of the same sample fall on both sides and the 40-sample test partition faces 4,220 features. Dataset 2 also contains no non-ASD class, making its 98.2% a four-class severity result presented in the abstract alongside a binary detection figure. SHAP and LIME are applied only to Dataset 1, omitting the multimodal case where modality attribution would have been informative; precision, recall and F1 are omitted for both neural-network rows; and no confidence interval accompanies any value. | This study is the second charted analysis of the 1,985-record ASD Children Traits dataset, and reading it against local_183eaef4 is instructive: the same collection, the same four embedded instruments, and accuracies of 97.60% here against 1.0000 there, with the difference produced by preprocessing rather than by anything about the data. It also supplies the class balance (63.28% negative) that local_183eaef4 omitted, allowing that study's perfect result to be positioned for the first time. Its own distinctive contributions to the review run in opposite directions. On the positive side it is one of the few studies in this branch to state explicitly that SMOTE was applied only on the training set, preventing data leakage - the exact ordering error that invalidated local_ed30e24c's hold-out - and to publish its whole pipeline as a numbered algorithm. On the negative side, Dataset 2 is the corpus's clearest case of augmentation-crossing-the-split combined with an unsourced dataset: 100 clinical samples of unstated origin inflated to 400, partitioned after augmentation, evaluated on 40 rows against 4,220 features, with an IRB and consent claim that names no committee, institution or country. | [RQ1.1] Two datasets with very different standing. Dataset 1 is 1,985 instances with 28 attributes from public ASD screening databases - the same 1,985-record ASD Children Traits collection analysed by local_183eaef4 - and here, unlike there, its class balance is reported: 729 ASD-positive (36.72%) against 1,256 negative (63.28%), with 283 instances carrying missing values. Dataset 2 consists of 100 original clinical samples augmented fourfold to 400, distributed evenly across four severity categories with no non-ASD class at all, and with no source, citation, country or institution given for the original 100. The number of distinct children behind either dataset is never stated. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, ASD traits. The register is clinical and unremarkable; the framing is service-oriented, opening on the need for clinicians to trust AI tools and closing on healthcare trustworthiness. One sentence in the introduction overreaches in a way worth recording - that machine learning algorithms assess the likelihood of a child being diagnosed with autism from behavioural information, making them a suitable replacement for routine and expensive screening tests. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] Thin for Dataset 1 and absent for Dataset 2. Dataset 1 lists age, sex, ethnicity, jaundice and family history among its features and reports none of their distributions; seven comorbidity indicators are similarly listed as features with no prevalences. Dataset 2 reports no demographic information of any kind for its 100 clinical samples, despite claiming IRB approval and caregiver consent for their collection. [RQ1.4] None for either dataset. Dataset 1's target is a binary ASD-traits field with no diagnostic procedure described, and the dataset's own feature list includes the Autism Spectrum Quotient, Social Responsiveness Scale, Q-CHAT score and Childhood Autism Rating Scale - four instruments used to determine autism status, supplied as predictors of it. This is the same instrument-inclusion leakage documented in local_183eaef4, which used the same 1,985-record dataset and reached accuracy 1.0000. Dataset 2's four severity categories are asserted with no instrument named; clinical experts are said to have verified annotation consistency at Cohen's kappa 0.92, but what they were rating and against what standard is not stated. [RQ1.5] Dataset 1 carries AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS as features rather than as reported participant characteristics - no mean, range or class-wise distribution appears for any of them. Dataset 2's severity categories are the prediction target with no underlying measure described. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is an ensemble framework that is both accurate and interpretable enough for clinicians to trust, evaluated on a behavioural dataset and a multimodal one. Headline findings: 97.6% accuracy on behavioural data from a regularised neural network (ROC-AUC 0.998) and 98.2% on multimodal data, with all other models above 93%; and an ablation showing accuracy rising from 89.40% (no feature selection, no resampling) through feature selection, SMOTE and ensemble fusion to 97.60% with neural-network regularisation. [RQ2.2] No setting is described for either dataset. Dataset 1 is a public download; Dataset 2's 100 original clinical samples have no stated collection site, country, institution or period, which is difficult to reconcile with the claim that an Institutional Review Board granted approval for their collection. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm for either dataset. Dataset 2's modality descriptions imply that facial images, 10-30 second voice recordings, body-keypoint motion and wearable physiological signals were captured simultaneously with synchronisation errors below 100 ms, which requires a structured session protocol - none is described. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics is claimed only for Dataset 2, in a short paragraph stating that all participant data were anonymised, written consent was obtained from caregivers, and IRB approval was granted for data collection and analysis, with secure storage, encryption and restricted access. No committee, protocol number, institution or country accompanies any of this, and no ethics statement covers Dataset 1 at all. Given that Dataset 2 is otherwise entirely unsourced, the ethics paragraph is the only evidence offered that its 100 clinical samples exist as described. [RQ2.5] For Dataset 2, vision-based pose estimation and wearable sensors are named without models; ResNet50, VGG16 and MobileNetV2 supply image features at 224x224 with ImageNet normalisation; audio features include MFCC, spectral, temporal, rhythmic and voice-quality measures such as jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio. No software, version, seed or compute environment is given anywhere. [RQ2.6] Sharply divided between the two datasets. Dataset 1's pipeline is one of the better-documented in this branch: the whole sequence is published as a numbered algorithm specifying label encoding, z-score normalisation, the 0.90 correlation-filtering threshold and its retention rule, the 60:20:20 stratified split, the exact SMOTE trigger condition (minority-to-majority ratio below 0.8) with the interpolation formula, the ANOVA F-score expression, and the SHAP and LIME definitions - and the dataset's instance count, feature count, missing-value count and class balance are all tabulated. Dataset 2 is unreproducible in principle: no source, citation, country, institution, ethics committee, participant description or access route exists for the 100 original samples, and its characteristics are conveyed entirely through asserted quality figures (complete data availability, synchronisation below 100 ms, inter-rater kappa 0.92). Neither dataset is accompanied by code, seeds, base-learner hyperparameters or a stated fold count. [RQ2.7] No limitations section appears in the extracted text. A comparison table instead assigns a named limitation to each of roughly fifteen prior studies (few participants, results may not apply widely; tested only in lab settings, not in daily life situations; works best only on similar data, not tested in real-world settings). None of that scrutiny is turned inward. Unmentioned: that four autism instruments sit in Dataset 1's feature set alongside the autism label; that Dataset 2's split partitions augmented copies rather than original samples; that Dataset 2's test partition holds 40 samples against 4,220 features; that Dataset 2 contains no non-ASD class, so its 98.2% is four-class severity rather than detection; that the 63.28% majority-class baseline on Dataset 1 is never stated; and that Dataset 2 has no provenance. [RQ2.9] Not captured in the extracted text. [RQ3.1] Dataset 1: screening-questionnaire responses and comorbidity flags, none of them examined individually. Dataset 2: the most behaviourally specific description in the paper - velocity, acceleration, jerk, movement range, coordination and repetitive behavioural patterns from body keypoints, alongside voice quality and autonomic arousal - describing exactly the kind of multimodal behavioural measurement this literature needs, for a dataset whose existence the paper does not evidence. [RQ3.2] Dataset 2 is presented as genuine four-modality fusion - image, audio, motion and physiological features concatenated into a 4,220-dimensional vector - and the ablation attributes the final gain from 97.80% to 98.2% to multimodal integration. Three things make that uninterpretable. There are 4,220 features for 400 samples, of which only 100 are original. The 400 include augmented copies split across training and test, so the multimodal gain is measured on partly duplicated data. And no modality-level attribution is reported: SHAP and LIME are applied to Dataset 1 only, so the paper cannot say what any modality contributed. A 0.4-point accuracy gain on a 40-sample test set is a single case reclassified. [RQ4.1] Five base learners (random forest, XGBoost, gradient boosting, SVM, logistic regression), soft-voting and stacking ensembles with a logistic-regression meta-learner, and two neural networks - a regularised MLP with L2, batch normalisation and dropout, and a deeper variant with early stopping and adaptive learning-rate scheduling. Predictions are combined by ensemble weighting proportional to validation performance. [RQ4.2] Dataset 1: a reduced tabular vector after correlation filtering above 0.90 and ANOVA F-test selection, drawn from 28 attributes that include the AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS scores alongside the ASD-traits target. Dataset 2: a 4,220-dimensional concatenation dominated by 4,040 image features, against 400 samples - a ratio of more than ten features per sample, and more than forty per original clinical sample. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC for eight configurations on Dataset 1, plus accuracy and F1 for six ablation configurations on both datasets. Three problems. Precision, recall and F1 are omitted for both neural-network rows, so the two models carrying the headline figures are reported on accuracy and AUC alone. No confidence interval or cross-validation variance accompanies any value. And the reported logistic-regression row - recall 100.00%, precision 87.20%, ROC-AUC 1.000 - is the signature of a model that separates the classes perfectly on the test partition, which on a dataset containing four autism instruments as features is expected rather than notable, and which the paper reads as displaying more false-positive tendencies. The 63.28% majority-class baseline is computable from the paper's own table and is never stated. [RQ4.4] SHAP and LIME are applied, and applied only to Dataset 1 - a choice the abstract states plainly. The consequence is that the paper's interpretability contribution covers the dataset where the answer is predetermined by the presence of AQ, SRS, Q-CHAT and CARS among the features, and omits the dataset where attribution would have been genuinely informative, namely which of four fused modalities carries the signal. No SHAP or LIME output is described in the extracted text. [RQ4.5] The two datasets require separate verdicts. On Dataset 1 the pipeline ordering is right and is unusually well documented: a stratified 60:20:20 split precedes SMOTE, SMOTE is applied only to the training portion and only when the class ratio falls below 0.8, and the paper states this explicitly as preventing data leakage - the ordering that local_ed30e24c got wrong and that most of this branch does not discuss. What the ordering cannot repair is the feature set, which contains the Autism Spectrum Quotient, the Social Responsiveness Scale, the Q-CHAT score and the Childhood Autism Rating Scale as predictors of a binary ASD-traits label. The same dataset produced accuracy 1.0000 for local_183eaef4; here it produces 97.60%, and the difference is attributable to preprocessing choices rather than to anything about autism. Dataset 2 is worse in kind. Its 100 original clinical samples were augmented fourfold to 400, and the stratified 80/10/10 split and 5-fold cross-validation were applied to the augmented set - so rotated, pitch-shifted, coordinate-scaled and noise-added copies of the same clinical sample sit on both sides of the split. The test partition therefore holds 40 samples, of which perhaps ten correspond to distinct originals, evaluated against a 4,220-dimensional feature vector. The reported 98.2% is roughly 39 of 40 correct on data the model has seen transformed versions of. It is also not a detection result: Dataset 2 contains four severity classes and no non-ASD class, so the abstract's presentation of 98.2% accuracy alongside the behavioural detection figure conflates a four-way severity task with binary ASD identification. Neither dataset carries a confidence interval, and the 63.28% majority-class baseline available in the paper's own Table 2 is never used. [RQ5.1] Twelve keywords including ethical AI and healthcare trustworthiness. The list is longer than any other in the corpus and names trust, interpretability, ethics and reliability - all values the paper's Dataset 2 handling does not exemplify. [RQ5.2] Computer Modeling in Engineering & Sciences 146(1):41 (Tech Science Press), 55 days from submission to acceptance. A modelling and engineering venue; review did not surface an entirely unsourced clinical dataset carrying an IRB claim with no committee or institution, a split performed over augmented copies, a four-class severity result reported alongside a binary detection result, or four autism instruments sitting in the predictor set. [RQ5.3] 2026, published 29 January. The framing is trust-centred - the stated goal is a model that is not only good at predicting ASD but also clear in its reasoning, with the title promising to enhance trust, interpretability and reliability in AI-driven healthcare. Against that, the paper reports a 98.2% figure from a dataset it does not source, whose split partitions augmented duplicates, and whose task is not the one the abstract implies; it applies its interpretability methods only to the dataset where they are least informative; and it reproduces the branch's characteristic overreach in describing machine learning as a suitable replacement for routine and expensive screening tests. Its genuine methodological contribution - explicitly confining SMOTE to the training partition and publishing the whole pipeline as an algorithm - is real and is the part of the paper most worth borrowing. |
| S-164 | Secondary analysis pooling three prior online experiments with overlapping participants, conducted in the Netherlands. From 959 recruited adults (538 autistic via the Netherlands Autism Register, 421 non-autistic mainly via Prolific Academic), 407 were excluded for missing data from at least one experiment, leaving 286 autistic and 266 non-autistic participants. The autistic group was older (44.2 versus 32.2 years), more often female (71.0% versus 48.9%) and late-diagnosed (mean age at diagnosis 35.6 years); cognitive ability (ICAR-16) was matched. A fully age- and gender-matched subsample of 125 per group was drawn and used as the primary analysis. | Fifty-four dependent variables from online tasks measuring multisensory perception, emotion recognition and executive function were used to train a random forest, with hyperparameters tuned by GridSearchCV under 3-fold cross-validation and overfitting monitored by the train-test performance gap. No resampling was applied. Three predictor configurations were compared - tasks alone, AQ alone, and both combined - alongside a label-randomisation control. Group differences were tested with Mann-Whitney U and Bonferroni correction. The analysis script is on OSF. | Full sample: accuracy 81.8%, sensitivity 77.1%, specificity 84.1%, F1 77.9%. Age- and gender-matched sample (primary): accuracy 74.0%, sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 79.2%, F1 73.5%. On the matched sample, the AQ alone reached 83% and the combination reached 92%. The label-randomised model performed at chance. Several variables showing no significant group difference under Bonferroni correction carried predictive value in combination; reaction-time variables ranked consistently high. | The authors state the most important one themselves: performance in the unmatched sample is inflated by including age and gender as features given the group disparity, so the matched figure of 74.0% - rather than 81.8% - is the better estimate. They also note that the feature ranking may not generalise across participant ages and that the work is an initial effort. Remaining: diagnosis is self-reported, albeit as a clinician-made diagnosis obtained through a national research register; 407 of 959 recruited participants were excluded for missing data, which may not be at random; the matched subsample is 250 people; and no confidence intervals or cross-validation variance accompany the final estimates. | This study is one of the review's principal calibration points and contributes two things no other charted study does. First, it quantifies demographic confounding directly: the same models reach 81.8% accuracy on the unbalanced sample and 74.0% once age and gender are matched, so roughly eight accuracy points were attributable to demographics alone - a number that bears directly on the many studies in this corpus reporting large unadjusted sex imbalances between groups, including local_7432ffd7 (43-point gap) and local_4ceee075 (32-point gap). Second, it diagnoses the questionnaire branch's two failure modes explicitly and in print: that higher published accuracies were obtained either by predicting whether participants fell above or below an AQ cut-off rather than whether they received an official diagnosis, or by using groups unbalanced on demographic features that were themselves included as predictors, both of which risk sampling biases inflating performance. That is a published statement of exactly what this review reconstructed across seven Q-CHAT-labelled studies. Its own results also set an honest ceiling for adult autism prediction: 74% from a 54-variable performance battery, 83% from the AQ alone, and 92% from both together, in a late-diagnosed, majority-female sample that existing instruments identify least well. It joins local_4da2b941, local_5f57ba19, local_b6ac2b98 and local_69b10fe4 as the studies defining what careful work in this field actually yields, and it is the only one to report the fusion increment in a form that can be checked. | [RQ1.1] Two recruited groups of adults: 286 autistic and 266 non-autistic in the final dataset, from 959 initially recruited, with 407 excluded for missing data from at least one contributing experiment (per-study exclusion criteria, technical issues, attrition). Autistic participants came from the Netherlands Autism Register and non-autistic participants principally from Prolific Academic.
