A second, fully age- and gender-matched subsample of 125 per group was drawn by random selection from the unbalanced sample, and it is this matched analysis the paper reports as its primary result. The analysis unit is the person throughout. The attrition is large and is stated plainly with its causes. [RQ1.2] The most carefully handled in the entire corpus, and explicitly so. The paper inserts a parenthetical statement in its opening paragraph that it alternates between person-first and identity-first language to address the varying preferences of the international autism community, citing a published recommendation. Its terminology is consistently difference-based rather than deficit-based - behavioural differences, differences from the norms seen in the non-autistic population - and it justifies its choice of algorithm partly in those terms, noting that random forests capture any patterns that exist in the data and are therefore difference focused rather than deficit focused. It is the only study in the review to make a language decision explicitly, to cite community preference as the reason, and to connect that framing to a methodological choice. [RQ1.3] Complete and analytically load-bearing. Age, gender, ICAR-16 abbreviated IQ, AQ total and age at diagnosis are tabulated for both samples with means, standard deviations and Mann-Whitney tests. The full sample carries large group differences in age (44.2 versus 32.2 years) and gender (71.0% versus 48.9% women), both significant at p<0.001; the matched subsample is exact on both. Cognitive ability is matched in both samples (ICAR 0.54 versus 0.53). The autistic sample is 71% women and late-diagnosed at a mean of 35.6 years - a demographic profile that is the opposite of almost every other autism study in this corpus, and one the paper identifies as particularly difficult to identify. Nothing on ethnicity or socioeconomic status. [RQ1.4] Self-reported formal diagnosis by a registered clinician, with participants drawn from a national research register (NAR) rather than a convenience sample, and non-autistic participants reporting no autism diagnosis. Diagnosis therefore predates and is independent of the task data. The population is explicitly characterised as late-diagnosed, which the paper treats as a strength for the research question - it is precisely the group that existing screening instruments miss - rather than glossing over it. [RQ1.5] AQ-28 total, ICAR-16 abbreviated intelligence, and age at diagnosis, all reported by group with standard deviations and significance tests. The AQ is additionally used as a comparator predictor and a fusion partner, so its role in the modelling is explicit rather than hidden inside a feature vector - the distinction that separates this study from the corpus's instrument-inclusion leakage cases. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to test whether online performance-based measures can predict adult autism diagnosis, whether they add to the most widely used screening questionnaire, and which behavioural variables carry the predictive signal. Headline findings on the age- and gender-matched sample: objective task measures alone reach 74% accuracy (sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 79.2%, F1 73.5%); the AQ alone reaches 83%; the two combined reach 92%. On the unmatched full sample the objective measures reach 81.8%, which the paper states is inflated by including age and gender as features. A label-randomised control performs at chance. Several variables with no significant group difference under Bonferroni correction nevertheless contributed predictive value in combination. [RQ2.2] Entirely online, in Dutch, via the Neurotask platform, on participants' own devices - which the paper presents as the point rather than a compromise, arguing that online performance-based measures offer a marriage of more objective data types with the accessibility of surveys, against neuroimaging approaches that are costly, time-consuming and require laboratory attendance. The battery is described as briefer than a typical movie. [RQ2.3] A battery of online tasks spanning three neuropsychological domains - multisensory perception, emotion recognition and executive function - reused from three prior published experiments with overlapping participants, yielding 54 dependent variables. The design rationale is stated clearly: because autism is heterogeneous, differences in any one neuropsychological domain are inconsistently detected, so the study looks across domains rather than within one. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics reporting is complete: ethical committee approval from the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam with reference VCWE-2020-041R1, compliance with the Netherlands Code of Conduct for Research Integrity and the revised Declaration of Helsinki, and informed consent from all participants prior to the experiments. Data governance is also handled properly - the register data are restricted for privacy reasons, and the procedure for requesting access through a research proposal and Data Sharing Agreement is documented. [RQ2.5] Participants' own devices, with tasks programmed and delivered online through Neurotask. Analysis in Python with scikit-learn's RandomForest and GridSearchCV, with the script deposited on OSF. [RQ2.6] High, and complete on the axes that matter. The analysis script is publicly deposited; the recruitment sources are named with a justification for the platform chosen; the 407 exclusions are counted with their reasons; the matching procedure is described; demographic, cognitive and AQ characteristics are tabulated with standard deviations and significance tests for both samples; the tuned hyperparameters are enumerated; the tuning procedure and the overfitting criterion are stated; the decision not to resample is stated with its reasoning; and a label-randomisation control is reported. The primary data are restricted by register privacy rules, with the request procedure documented - the correct handling for a national register rather than a gap. [RQ2.7] Distributed through the discussion rather than isolated, and unusually incisive. The paper states that the unmatched sample's higher accuracy is inflated by including age and gender as features and that the matched estimate should be preferred; that the feature ranking may not generalise across participant ages; and that the work represents initial efforts with limits on what can be concluded. Its most valuable limitation, though, is directed outward and applies to a large part of this review's corpus: it notes that studies reporting higher accuracy did so either by using the AQ-10 items to predict whether participants fell above or below an AQ cut-off score rather than whether they received an official diagnosis, or by using groups that were not balanced on demographic features included as predictors - and that this risks sampling biases inflating performance, which the authors accounted for through their matched analysis. That is a precise, published statement of the two mechanisms this review has documented across the questionnaire branch. [RQ2.9] Use feature ranking to remove uninformative measures and shorten the battery; design manipulations that accentuate reaction-time differences in the most sensitive domains, since certain emotional categories and stimulus types are harder to categorise and leave more room for RT differences; and test whether the sensitive measures differ across age groups. [RQ3.1] Neuropsychological performance across three domains rather than a single behavioural marker: multisensory perceptual integration, emotion recognition (with accuracy and reaction time varying by emotional category and stimulus type), and executive function. The substantive behavioural findings are specific - reaction-time variables consistently ranked high in predictive value, and executive function emerged as informative in this adult sample - and the paper is careful that the ranking is sample-dependent. [RQ3.2] Genuine, declared and quantified multimodal fusion, and the study's central result. Objective task measures and the AQ questionnaire are evaluated separately and together on the same matched sample: 74% for tasks alone, 83% for the AQ alone, 92% combined. Because each configuration is reported, the increment attributable to fusion is visible (9 points over the questionnaire alone), and because the feature-importance profile is very similar with and without the AQ, the authors can argue that the two data types contribute information in different ways rather than merely duplicating each other. This is the only study in the charted corpus to report all three configurations and thereby make the fusion claim checkable. [RQ4.1] Random forest, selected with reasons given: capacity to detect sparse signals in high-dimensional data, provision of feature-importance rankings usable for battery optimisation, and the property of being difference-focused rather than deficit-focused. No deep learning and no architecture competition - the modelling is subordinated to the scientific question. [RQ4.2] One row per participant containing 54 task-derived dependent variables, with AQ total and demographic variables added in specified configurations. No dimensionality reduction or feature selection is applied, and no clinical instrument is smuggled in - the AQ's presence is the explicit object of one of the three comparisons. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1 for both samples and each configuration, plus a label-randomised control model. The specificity/sensitivity split is reported rather than collapsed into accuracy (matched sample: sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 79.2%), which shows that the model misses roughly a third of autistic adults at the reported operating point - visible precisely because the paper reports it. Missing: confidence intervals, cross-validation variance on the final estimates, and calibration. The chance level is established empirically by the randomisation control rather than asserted. [RQ4.4] Feature importance is used as a scientific instrument rather than as decoration. The headline interpretive result is that several variables showing no significant group difference even under highly conservative Bonferroni correction nonetheless carried predictive value in combination - a finding that only a multivariate model can produce and that the authors read as evidence of complex latent relationships associated with autism rather than as a discovery of new markers. Reaction-time variables ranked consistently high; executive function was informative in this adult sample; and the near-identical importance profile with and without the AQ supports the claim that objective and subjective measures contribute differently. The authors also state the limit: the ranking may not generalise across ages. [RQ4.5] This is one of the two most rigorously evaluated studies in the charted corpus, and its distinctive contribution is the demographic-confounding analysis. The design uses a train/test split with 3-fold cross-validated grid search for hyperparameters and monitors overfitting by the train-test performance gap; adds a label-randomisation control that falls to chance, empirically establishing the baseline rather than assuming it; and declines to resample, stating that neither SMOTE nor undersampling was used. Its decisive move is to run the entire analysis twice - once on the full unbalanced sample and once on a subsample matched 100% on age and gender at 125 per group - and then to report the matched result as primary, stating that performance in the unmatched sample is inflated by the inclusion of age and gender as features given the disparity between groups in those factors. The difference is large: 81.8% unmatched against 74.0% matched, so roughly eight accuracy points in this study were attributable to demographic confounding alone. That number is directly relevant to the rest of this review, in which sex imbalances of 32 points (local_4ceee075) and 43 points (local_7432ffd7) between groups are reported and left unadjusted, and it is the only quantification of that effect anywhere in the corpus. Residual limitations: no confidence intervals or fold variance accompany the final estimates; the matched subsample is 250 people; diagnosis is self-reported rather than verified, albeit through a national register; and 407 of 959 recruited participants were excluded for missing data, which may not be at random. None of these undermines the study's central results, and the authors identify the most important of them themselves. [RQ5.1] Not captured in the extracted text. [RQ5.2] Translational Psychiatry 16:129 (Nature Portfolio) - a clinical and translational psychiatry journal, and the only such venue in the charted corpus. The disciplinary fit is evident throughout: matched-subsample analysis, Bonferroni-corrected group comparisons, a label-randomisation control, sensitivity and specificity reported separately, deposited analysis code, documented data-access procedures, an explicit language statement citing community preference, and a discussion that diagnoses the methodological failures of the prior literature it is compared against. [RQ5.3] 2026. The framing is screening-support and is bounded at every point: the measures may be a promising means of predicting autism, providing complementary information to existing screening questionnaires; the value proposition is triage for expedited assessment given protracted diagnostic wait times, not replacement of clinical assessment; and the reported gain is stated as 9 percentage points over the most popular adult screening questionnaire, with the authors noting that this matters in the context of an estimated 1% population prevalence. The paper is also unusual in reporting a result that undercuts its own headline - that the same models reach 81.8% on the unmatched sample and 74.0% once age and gender are matched - and in choosing the lower figure as its primary estimate. |
| S-165 | Retrospective analysis of a public eye-tracking scanpath dataset of 28 participants (14 ASD, 14 typically developing), released in anonymised form on Zenodo. No age, sex, cognitive ability, recruitment source, viewing task, eye tracker or diagnostic procedure is reported for the source cohort. | Each scanpath was truncated or zero-padded to 20 fixations, and nine handcrafted descriptors were computed per trial - fixation count, mean/first/maximum/total fixation duration, total path length, mean saccade amplitude, dispersion and fixation-duration entropy. These were aggregated to one vector per participant via mean and standard deviation, standardised, and classified by a hybrid ensemble combining bagging, boosting and stacking over five base learners. Evaluation used five-fold cross-validation with an explicitly subject-wise protocol adopted to prevent data leakage, a Friedman test on fold-wise F1 scores, and permutation-based feature relevance used solely for interpretation. | Stacking ensemble accuracy 0.9600 (SD 0.0800), precision 0.9750 (0.0500), recall 0.9500 (0.1000), F1 0.9524 (0.0952). Base learners: AdaBoost 0.9267/0.9181, KNN 0.8867/0.8781, random forest 0.8533/0.8374, decision tree 0.8200/0.7657, gradient boosting 0.7800/0.7181. | The authors state the principal one themselves - a single small-scale dataset of 28 participants limits statistical generalisability and the results should be read as a proof-of-concept demonstration. Two further issues are not raised. The within-subject resampling that generates additional subject-level samples is described as occurring during model training without stating whether it precedes or follows the fold split; if it precedes, several vectors derived from the same participant would cross the partition and undermine the subject-wise protocol that is the design's main safeguard. And nothing whatever is reported about the source cohort - no demographics, no viewing task, no equipment, no diagnostic procedure - so what the classifier separates cannot be assessed, and stimulus identity cannot be excluded as a contributor to scanpath geometry. With five folds over 28 people, each test set holds five or six participants, which is what the reported standard deviations of 0.08 on accuracy and 0.095 on F1 record. | This study matters to the review as the eye-tracking branch's counterexample on validation design. Where local_44d3aef5 split 547 scanpath images from a repeated-image collection and reached 100%, local_bb4d1f7a split 100 eye crops per child and reached 97%, and local_7432ffd7 split gaze samples from 59 children and reached 99.78%, this study aggregates to the participant, evaluates subject-wise, and lists leakage prevention among its four stated contributions - and reaches 0.96 with a standard deviation of 0.08 on 28 people, which it labels a proof of concept. It thus demonstrates that participant-level evaluation is straightforward in this modality and that the branch's near-perfect figures are a choice rather than a consequence. Its own weakness is different in kind: an entirely uncharacterised source cohort, with no task, equipment, demographics or diagnostic procedure reported, in a paper co-authored by clinicians. It also reports its fold-wise standard deviations rather than only means, which makes the imprecision of a 28-person estimate visible - and reading those standard deviations against the near-zero fold variance claimed as robustness in local_8d43288c is instructive about what small honest folds actually look like. | [RQ1.1] Twenty-eight participants, 14 with ASD and 14 typically developing, from a public benchmark eye-tracking dataset released on Zenodo. This is the smallest participant base of any charted study apart from local_e771fb69, and it is the only quantity the paper reports about the people involved - no age, sex, cognitive ability, recruitment source, country or diagnostic procedure appears. Crucially, the analysis unit is the participant: scanpath-level features are aggregated to one vector per person by taking the mean and standard deviation across that person's trials, and the evaluation is described as subject-wise specifically to prevent data leakage. With 28 people and five folds, each test fold holds roughly five or six participants. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, TD, individuals with ASD. The register is clinical and unremarkable; the opening characterisation uses deficits in social communication and the presence of restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, standard DSM phrasing. No autistic or community perspective appears, and no demographic or personal description of the participants is offered at any point. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography, cognitive ability or recruitment information for any of the 28 participants, and no acknowledgement that this information is absent. The paper's own discussion notes that generalisation across demographics and hardware platforms remains a pressing issue in this literature - a concern it identifies and then cannot address, because it reports no demographic variable at all. [RQ1.4] Not described. Labels are inherited from the public dataset with no diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date reported, and the originating collection's ascertainment procedure is not summarised. This is the study's largest unforced omission, since two of its authors are clinicians - one at a psychiatric hospital and one at a clinical medicine school - and a paragraph characterising the source cohort would have been straightforward. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a hybrid ensemble integrating bagging, boosting and stacking that operates directly on raw scanpath features rather than on scanpath images, so as to reduce preprocessing overhead and improve interpretability for real-time screening. Headline findings: the stacking ensemble reached accuracy 0.9600 (SD 0.0800), precision 0.9750, recall 0.9500 and F1 0.9524, above every base learner (AdaBoost 0.9267, KNN 0.8867, random forest 0.8533, decision tree 0.8200, gradient boosting 0.7800), and comparable to image-based deep learning models on the same dataset at a fraction of the preprocessing cost. [RQ2.2] No study setting. A public dataset analysed computationally, with no compute environment, runtime or hardware described - which sits awkwardly with a contribution framed around computational efficiency and real-time deployment, since no timing measurement supports it. [RQ2.3] Not reported. The viewing task, stimuli, eye tracker and session structure of the originating collection are nowhere summarised, so a reader cannot say what the participants were looking at when the scanpaths were recorded. For a scanpath analysis this matters, because scanpath geometry is jointly determined by the viewer and the stimulus, and without knowing the stimulus set one cannot exclude stimulus identity as a source of the signal. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethics is declared not required, with reasoning given: the dataset is publicly available, was released in anonymised form by its creators, contains no identifiable personal information, and no new data were collected. The declaration is at least argued rather than blank, and the paper additionally discloses that one author is an editorial board member of the journal and was excluded from the editorial decision - a disclosure no other charted study makes. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation is described. Modelling components: decision tree, random forest, KNN (k=3), AdaBoost, gradient boosting and a stacking meta-learner. No software, version, seed or hardware. [RQ2.6] Moderate. Reproducible: the source dataset has a DOI; the nine handcrafted scanpath descriptors are enumerated with definitions; the 20-fixation truncation/padding rule, the mean-and-standard-deviation aggregation to participant level, and z-score standardisation are all specified; fold-wise means and standard deviations are tabulated for every model; and the permutation-importance procedure is described with its intended scope. Not reproducible: no code or seed, no software or versions, no hyperparameters beyond k=3, no count of scanpaths per participant, no description of the source task, and no statement of where in the pipeline the within-subject resampling occurs relative to the fold split. [RQ2.7] Stated plainly and correctly, in the discussion rather than in a boilerplate paragraph: although the framework achieved high accuracy, it was evaluated on a single small-scale dataset of 28 participants, which limits the statistical generalizability of the findings, so the reported results should be interpreted as a proof-of-concept demonstration pending validation on larger and more diverse populations. That is the right reading of a 28-person study and it is offered without hedging. What is not raised: that the fold-wise standard deviations (0.08 on accuracy, 0.095 on F1) are large precisely because each fold holds five or six people; that no demographic, task or diagnostic information about the source cohort is reported; and that the within-subject resampling step is not located relative to the split. [RQ2.9] Validation on larger and more diverse datasets, and integration into an end-to-end screening platform. Both follow directly from the stated limitation. [RQ3.1] Visual scanning behaviour reduced to nine interpretable descriptors: number of fixations, mean and maximum and first fixation duration, total fixation duration, total path length, mean saccade amplitude, spatial dispersion of fixations, and fixation-duration entropy as a measure of irregularity in gaze allocation. Operating on these rather than on rendered scanpath images is the paper's central methodological claim, and it is a defensible one - the features are inspectable and the permutation analysis can name which of them matter. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - eye tracking alone. What is fused is classifiers rather than data: bagging, boosting and stacking are combined within one architecture, with base learners selected by a stated diversity criterion to promote complementary decision boundaries. [RQ4.1] A three-strategy ensemble - bagging, boosting and stacking - over five base learners (decision tree, random forest, KNN k=3, AdaBoost, gradient boosting) with a stacking meta-learner. The base-learner set is chosen by an explicit diversity-aware strategy rather than assembled arbitrarily, and every constituent's performance is reported separately so the ensemble's increment is visible: the best base learner reaches 0.9267 accuracy and the stack 0.9600, a gain of about 3.3 points. [RQ4.2] One vector per participant, formed by aggregating nine scanpath descriptors across that person's trials via mean and standard deviation, after each scanpath was truncated or zero-padded to 20 fixations and before z-score standardisation. The 20-fixation cap is a substantive modelling decision - it discards everything after the twentieth fixation in longer scanpaths and pads shorter ones - and its effect is not tested. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 with fold-wise means and standard deviations for all six models, plus a Friedman test on fold-wise F1 and a permutation-importance ranking. Reporting the standard deviations is a real strength and is also where the study's honest signal lies: an accuracy standard deviation of 0.0800 and an F1 standard deviation of 0.0952 on a five-fold split of 28 people means individual folds ranged widely, which is what five- or six-person test sets produce. On such folds, 0.9600 accuracy corresponds to roughly 27 of 28 participants classified correctly across the full cross-validation, and a single reclassification moves the figure by about 3.6 points. No confidence interval accompanies any estimate and the 50% chance level is never stated. [RQ4.4] Permutation-based feature relevance, with an unusually precise statement of scope: the analysis was performed independently of model selection procedures and served solely as an interpretability tool rather than as a feature selection mechanism. That distinction matters and is drawn correctly - permutation importance computed for interpretation cannot leak into the model, whereas the same computation used to select features would. A full ranking is presented, though the extracted text does not name which descriptors dominated. [RQ4.5] The design gets the structural question right and is limited by size rather than by construction. Subject-wise aggregation and evaluation are adopted explicitly to prevent data leakage and to provide a more realistic estimate of generalisation in clinical settings, and this is listed as one of the paper's four stated contributions - a rare instance in the eye-tracking branch of participant-level splitting being treated as a design requirement rather than overlooked. Set against the branch, that choice is what separates this study's 0.96 on 28 people from local_44d3aef5's 1.00 on 55 scanpath images and local_bb4d1f7a's 0.97 on 100 eye crops per child. Three qualifications remain. First, size: 28 participants across five folds gives test sets of five or six, and the reported standard deviations (0.08 accuracy, 0.095 F1) reflect that directly - the estimate is not wrong, it is imprecise, and the paper says as much in calling the work a proof of concept. Second, the within-subject resampling: additional subject-level samples were generated by resampling scanpaths within each subject and recomputing the aggregated representation, described as occurring during model training; if that augmentation was performed before the fold split rather than inside it, several aggregated vectors derived from the same participant's scanpaths would cross the partition and the subject-wise protocol would be undermined by the very step intended to increase sample diversity. The paper's wording suggests the correct placement but does not state it unambiguously. Third, the source cohort is uncharacterised - no task, no equipment, no diagnostic procedure, no demographics - so what the classifier separates cannot be independently assessed. [RQ5.1] Autism Spectrum Disorder; Bagging; Boosting; Stacking; Ensemble learning; Eye-tracking. Four of six terms name ensemble strategies; participants, task and validation are absent. [RQ5.2] Array 30 (2026) 100753 (Elsevier) - an open-access computer science journal. The author list spans engineering and clinical institutions including a psychiatric hospital, which makes the absence of any description of the source cohort's diagnosis or demographics more notable rather than less. The paper discloses an editorial conflict of interest for one author, which is good practice and uncommon in this corpus. [RQ5.3] 2026. The framing is proportionate and, on the point that matters, correct: the reported results should be interpreted as a proof-of-concept demonstration, pending validation on larger and more diverse populations. The claims that go beyond that are about engineering rather than clinical accuracy - reduced preprocessing overhead by eliminating scanpath-to-image conversion, suitability for real-time screening environments, and a more direct and deployable solution bridging the gap between research prototypes and practical clinical tools - and even those are asserted without any timing measurement. Its contribution to the review is as the eye-tracking branch's demonstration that participant-level evaluation is achievable in this modality and that when it is applied, the resulting figure comes with a standard deviation of eight accuracy points on 28 people. |
| S-166 | Retrospective analysis of 14,352 annotated facial images of children obtained from the Roboflow platform, labelled autistic or non-autistic with bounding-box annotations. No class counts, split proportions, partition sizes, demographic information or count of distinct children is reported, and the originating collection is not described. Roboflow's export pipeline supplied resizing to 640x640, RGB conversion, normalisation and augmentation for illumination, expression and pose. | YOLOv8n and YOLOv9c were trained with the Ultralytics framework for 50 epochs at 640x640, with the dataset divided into training, validation and testing groups. Performance was assessed by precision, recall, F1, mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95, with normalised confusion matrices including a Background class, precision-recall and F1-confidence curves, and an informal probe on non-human images. | YOLOv8n: precision 91.95%, recall 92.77%, F1 92.36%, mAP@0.5 94.76%, mAP@0.5:0.95 94.73%. YOLOv9c: 91.29%, 90.29%, 90.79%, 93.32%, 93.21%. In the out-of-distribution probe, YOLOv8n rejected a dog and a leaf while YOLOv9c classified the dog as Autistic and the leaf as Nonautistic. | The study states none. Labels are platform annotations on photographs with no clinical diagnosis behind them. No class counts, split ratios or partition sizes are reported, so no result can be located to a sample, and no chance level can be computed. Augmentation was applied through the Roboflow export pipeline rather than during training, so transformed variants of the same photograph may cross the split - and a 14,352-image set most plausibly derives from a much smaller pool of originals, given that the paper's own literature table cites the roughly 3,000-image public autism face corpus repeatedly. The reported mAP figures are mutually inconsistent: mAP@0.5:0.95 averages precision over IoU thresholds up to 0.95 and cannot sit within 0.11 points of mAP@0.5 for a detector trained on uncalibrated images. An object-detection architecture with a Background class is applied to a single-face whole-image binary question without rationale. And real-time screening is the central claim with no latency or throughput figure anywhere in the paper. | This is the fifteenth charted study in the facial-image branch and it contributes one finding the other fourteen do not. In an informal robustness comparison, one of its two models labelled a photograph of a dog as Autistic and a leaf as Nonautistic. The authors present this as evidence that YOLOv8n filters irrelevant inputs better than YOLOv9c; read as a fact about the task, it demonstrates that a model trained to detect autism from a face will assign an autism label to arbitrary objects unless a background-rejection mechanism intervenes, and that the difference between the two architectures on this dataset is a difference in background handling rather than in anything about autism. No other study in the branch tests a non-face input. Its second distinctive feature is its ethics paragraph, which - alone among the fifteen - states explicitly that given the child's facial data aspect, there is ethical sensitivity, before proceeding on the presumption that a hosting platform's sharing policy implies the original curators obtained consent. Its reported mAP@0.5:0.95 sitting 0.03 points below mAP@0.5 places it with local_986436f2 and local_e04bcd32 among the branch's arithmetically unreconcilable results. | [RQ1.1] No participants. 14,352 annotated facial images of children obtained from the Roboflow platform, labelled autistic or non-autistic and carrying bounding-box annotations. No class counts, no split sizes and no count of distinct children appear anywhere. The scale is worth noting against the branch: the paper's own literature table cites the Kaggle autism face corpus repeatedly, and that corpus contains roughly 3,000 images, so a 14,352-image Roboflow set is most plausibly an augmented export of the same underlying photographs - which the paper's description of Roboflow's built-in augmentation at export time supports but never states. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with autism, autistic, non-autistic. The introduction is unusually careful in one respect - it notes that while certain individuals with ASD may also experience cognitive impairment, the majority possess average to above-average intelligence, and that symptoms vary so that some face mild difficulties while others require full-time care. Elsewhere the register is standard for this branch. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] None. No age, sex, ethnicity, geography or recruitment information for any image, and no acknowledgement of the absence - although the paper's own literature table repeatedly lists limited dataset diversity and poor generalization as limitations of prior studies using the same kind of data. [RQ1.4] None. Labels are annotations attached to a Roboflow dataset. No clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date exists for a single image, and the originating collection is not described. The paper's introduction gives an accurate account of how ASD is actually diagnosed - paediatricians or psychologists using developmental history, behavioural observation and instruments including CARS for severity - and then treats platform annotations on downloaded photographs as an adequate substitute. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is real-time ASD screening from facial images using object detection, with YOLOv8n compared against YOLOv9c to identify the more effective solution. Headline findings: YOLOv8n reached precision 91.95%, recall 92.77%, F1 92.36% and mAP@0.5 94.76%, against YOLOv9c at 91.29%, 90.29%, 90.79% and 93.32%; YOLOv8n showed higher true-positive rates for both classes with fewer misclassifications into the Background class; and, in an out-of-distribution probe, YOLOv8n rejected non-human inputs while YOLOv9c classified a dog as Autistic and a leaf as Nonautistic. [RQ2.2] No setting. Images exported from Roboflow and models trained with the Ultralytics framework; no hardware, runtime or environment is described, which is a notable gap in a paper whose central claim is real-time deployability. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Static photographs. The construct is facial morphology, with the backbone described as extracting facial symmetry, eye spacing, philtrum width and face shape - a list of dysmorphology features that would require calibrated measurement rather than a detection head trained on uncalibrated web images. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. Ethics is not obtained but is genuinely reasoned about, which distinguishes this study from most of its branch: the authors note that the data comprise only de-identified facial images with no personally identifiable information, state that according to Roboflow dataset sharing policies it is understood that the curators obtained adequate consent and ethical clearance before publication, confirm that no personal or clinical collection took place, and - unusually - write explicitly that given the child's facial data aspect, there is ethical sensitivity. That last sentence is the only acknowledgement anywhere in the fifteen-study facial-image branch that photographing and labelling children's faces raises a question at all. Its weakness is the inference immediately preceding it: consent is presumed from a hosting platform's sharing policy rather than verified. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Roboflow supplied preprocessing (640x640 resize, RGB conversion, normalisation) and augmentation (horizontal flipping and transformations for illumination, expression and pose variation) at export; training used the Ultralytics YOLO framework for 50 epochs. No learning rate, batch size, optimiser, seed or hardware. [RQ2.6] Low. Named: the source platform, the export-time preprocessing and augmentation, the image size, the epoch count and the training framework. Missing: the dataset URL, accession or version; class counts and split proportions; the number of distinct children; optimiser, learning rate, batch size and seed; and any code. The reported metrics also contain an internal inconsistency that cannot be reconciled - mAP@0.5:0.95 sits within 0.11 points of mAP@0.5 for both models, which no genuine detection evaluation produces. [RQ2.7] None for this study. The literature table (Table 2) is unusually thorough in the opposite direction, assigning each of roughly ten prior works a named weakness - limited dataset diversity and challenges generalizing to real-world conditions; overfitting risk with limited data; overfitting in small datasets and poor generalization; low model interpretability and high training time; small and limited dataset, lack of clinical validation, no multimodal analysis. Every one of those applies to the present study and none is claimed by it. Unmentioned: the absent class counts and split ratios, the unstated number of distinct children, the impossible mAP relationship, and the fact that a model trained to detect autism from a face assigned a class label to a dog. [RQ2.9] None stated. [RQ3.1] None. No behaviour is observed or measured; the target is static facial appearance, described in terms of symmetry, eye spacing, philtrum width and face shape. [RQ3.2] No fusion - a single image modality. The paper's own literature table lists no multimodal analysis as a limitation of a cited prior study and does not apply it to itself. [RQ4.1] YOLOv8n and YOLOv9c, single-stage object detectors, applied to a whole-image binary classification problem. The architectural choice is consequential and unexamined: an object detector localises instances within a scene and scores them against a Background class, so the confusion matrices contain Autistic, Non-Autistic and Background categories, and the reported mAP is a localisation-plus-classification measure rather than a diagnostic accuracy. Nothing in the task requires detection - each image contains one face - so the apparatus adds a spatial estimation problem and a third class to a two-class question. [RQ4.2] 640x640 RGB images with bounding boxes, preprocessed and augmented by Roboflow's export pipeline. Because augmentation is applied at export rather than at training time, augmented variants of an image may be distributed across the train, validation and test partitions - the paper gives no information that would exclude this, and gives no split ratio either. [RQ4.3] Precision, recall, F1, mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 for both models, with normalised confusion matrices, precision-recall curves and F1-confidence curves. The reporting looks complete and contains an impossibility. For YOLOv8n, mAP@0.5 is 94.76% and mAP@0.5:0.95 is 94.73%; for YOLOv9c, 93.32% and 93.21%. mAP@0.5:0.95 averages average precision across ten IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95, so it is bounded above by mAP@0.5 and in practice falls well below it - gaps of twenty to forty points are typical for face-scale objects. A gap of 0.03 points implies that localisation quality is perfect at every threshold up to 0.95, which no detector trained for 50 epochs on uncalibrated web photographs achieves. The two numbers are therefore not both genuine mAP values. No class counts, no split sizes, no chance level and no variance across the repeated runs the paper claims to have performed are reported. [RQ4.4] No formal attribution, but the paper contains an out-of-distribution probe that is the single most informative result in it and is presented only as a robustness comparison between architectures. Given a picture of a dog and a picture of a leaf, YOLOv9c classified the dog as Autistic and the leaf as Nonautistic, while YOLOv8n rejected both. The authors read this as evidence of YOLOv8n's superior filtering. The more important reading is what it reveals about the task: a model trained to detect autism from a photograph will assign an autism label to whatever is placed in front of it unless something else stops it, and the difference between the two architectures here is a difference in background rejection rather than in anything about autism. No other study in this fifteen-strong branch tests its model on a non-face input, and this one does so almost incidentally. [RQ4.5] The evaluation is thinly described and internally inconsistent. The dataset is said to be divided into three groups for testing, validation and training, with the reasoning that such splitting reduces the bias and overfitting possibility - and no ratio, no partition size, no seed and no cross-validation follows. The split is at the image level on a corpus whose per-child composition is unknown, and whose 14,352 images most plausibly derive by augmentation from a much smaller set of underlying photographs, since Roboflow's augmentation was applied at export rather than during training; if so, transformed variants of the same photograph sit on both sides of the partition. Training and evaluation are said to have been carried out multiple times with highly consistent results, and no variance figure supports that claim. Most concretely, the two mAP figures cannot both be genuine: mAP@0.5:0.95 within 0.11 points of mAP@0.5 is arithmetically achievable only under near-perfect localisation at IoU 0.95, which is not attainable here. And the informal robustness probe demonstrates directly that the system's decision surface extends to objects that are not faces, which no reported metric captures. [RQ5.1] Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); Facial Image Analysis; YOLO; Real-time screening; AI-based Diagnostics. Five terms, two of them deployment claims (real-time screening, AI-based diagnostics) that the paper does not measure - no inference latency or throughput figure appears anywhere despite real-time being the central selling point. [RQ5.2] Journal of Pioneering Medical Sciences 15(1):137-145, a medical sciences journal, 90 days from submission to acceptance. Clinical review did not surface the absent class counts and split ratios, the mAP inconsistency, or the reported finding that one of the two models labels a dog as autistic. [RQ5.3] 2026, published 5 February. Framing is real-time clinical screening: the study is said to facilitate real-time ASD screening, providing healthcare professionals with timely and effective interventions in clinical environments, with mobile and web deployment proposed to reach remote areas. There is no limitations section and no future work, and the contribution is expressed as a position above one quoted prior YOLO result. Its distinguishing features within the branch are two: an ethics paragraph that at least names the sensitivity of children's facial data before proceeding, and an out-of-distribution test that inadvertently shows the model assigning an autism label to a photograph of a dog. |
| S-167 | Retrospective analysis of 2,940 facial images balanced at 1,470 per class - the sixteenth charted reuse of the public autism facial-image corpus, identified here only by reference number. No demographic, diagnostic or provenance information accompanies any image, and the number of distinct children is unknown. Results are reported separately for a 70% training phase and a 30% testing phase, with no partition counts or seed. | Gaussian Gabor filtering enhanced facial features; deep features from VGG16, DenseNet-121 and XceptionNet were concatenated; a wavelet neural network performed classification with parameters tuned by the chimp optimisation algorithm; and Grad-CAM++ produced visual interpretations. Training used ReLU, learning rate 0.01, dropout 0.5, batch size 5 and a stated 50 epochs, on a desktop with an i5-8600K and a GTX 1050 Ti. | Testing phase: average accuracy 98.42%, precision 98.40%, recall 98.42%, F-measure 98.41%, AUC 98.42%. Training phase: 97.75%, 97.80%, 97.75%, 97.76%, 97.75%. Quoted comparators (CONCAT-SDAE, ViT-B, EfficientNet-B4, VGG-19, GBM, RF, KNN) range from 92.10% to 97.76% on precision. | The labels are folder assignments with no diagnostic basis, and the split is a single unseeded image-level partition of a corpus that repeats individuals, so it does not separate children. No component of the four-stage pipeline is ablated, and the chimp optimiser tuned parameters against an unstated objective on an unidentified partition. The testing-phase accuracy exceeds the training-phase accuracy, and the same inversion in the learning curves is read as good generalisation without overfitting rather than as a question about partition independence; the stated 50 epochs also disagree with the 25-epoch curves. Two formal declarations contradict the article: ethics states that it contains no studies with human participants, and data availability states that no datasets were generated or analysed. Privacy preservation is claimed as part of the research gap with no privacy mechanism described. Against all this the paper does state one accurate limitation - that the dataset's lack of demographic information prevents any examination of how facial morphology and expression vary across populations. | This is the sixteenth and final charted reuse of the public autism facial-image corpus, and it closes the branch on two notes worth recording. Its 98.42% sits at the upper end of the branch's 81.0-99.8% range and is produced by the branch's now-standard formula - stack more stages (Gabor filtering, three-backbone fusion, a wavelet classifier, a metaheuristic optimiser, a saliency method), split at the image level, ablate nothing, and report the maximum. Its testing accuracy exceeding its training accuracy, read as good generalisation, is the branch's clearest instance of an anomaly being interpreted as a virtue. But it also contains the branch's most accurate self-diagnosis: a limitation paragraph stating that because the dataset carries no demographic information and because facial morphology and expression vary across demographic groups, the influence of those factors on classification cannot be examined - which is precisely the objection that applies to all sixteen studies, stated plainly by the last of them, in the same article whose formal declarations assert that it involved no human participants and analysed no data. | [RQ1.1] No participants. 2,940 images in two balanced classes of 1,470 - the sixteenth charted reuse of the public autism facial-image corpus, identifiable from that exact composition although the paper names only a reference number rather than a repository. The number of distinct children is unknown and never discussed. Results are reported for a 70% training partition and a 30% testing partition with no counts, no seed and no statement of how the split was drawn. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, individuals with ASD, children with ASD. The register is medical and dated - ASD is introduced as a complex psychological disease and later as a critical neurodevelopmental condition with excessive medical expenses - and the symptom list includes repetitive and aggressive behaviours, hyperactivity, and cognitive impairment. Grad-CAM++ is described as providing abnormality detection, which frames the highlighted facial regions as abnormalities rather than as model attention. No autistic or community perspective appears. [RQ1.3] None reported, and the paper is one of the few in this branch to say so and to explain why it matters: expression patterns and facial morphology differ across demographic factors, and because the dataset carries no such information, their influence on ASD classification and on facial-feature learning cannot be clearly examined. That is an accurate statement of the branch's central data problem, made by a study that then proceeds anyway. [RQ1.4] None. Labels are the folder assignments of a public image corpus, with no clinical diagnosis, instrument, criterion, assessor or date for any image, and no description of how the collection was assembled. The introduction gives a conventional account of ASD as requiring thorough clinical testing and then treats folder labels as sufficient ground truth for a system offered as a diagnostic aid in clinical settings. [RQ1.5] None. No cognitive, adaptive, language or severity measure; none obtainable from photographs. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a computationally efficient, privacy-preserving and optimised framework for ASD detection from facial images, combining Gaussian Gabor filtering, fused deep features from VGG16, DenseNet-121 and XceptionNet, a wavelet neural network classifier tuned by the chimp optimisation algorithm, and Grad-CAM++ for visual interpretation. Headline findings: average accuracy 98.42% with precision 98.40%, recall 98.42%, F-measure 98.41% and AUC 98.42% in the 30% testing phase, against quoted comparators from 92.10% to 97.76%. [RQ2.2] No setting. A downloaded dataset analysed in Python 3.6.5 on a desktop with an i5-8600K, 16 GB RAM and a GeForce GTX 1050 Ti - a configuration reported in unusual detail for a study whose stated contribution includes computational efficiency, though no runtime or inference-time measurement accompanies it. [RQ2.3] No task or paradigm. Static photographs with no stimulus, interaction or session; the construct is facial morphology and expression. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional. The ethics declaration is factually wrong rather than merely permissive: this article does not contain any studies with human participants performed by any of the authors, stated for an analysis of 2,940 photographs of children, with consent to participate and consent to publish both marked not applicable. It is paired with a data-availability statement asserting that no datasets were generated or analysed during the current study, in an article whose results section reports a full metric grid computed on a 2,940-image dataset. Together the two declarations describe a paper that did not use any data, which is the opposite of what the article reports. The framing also claims the framework is privacy-preserving, with no privacy mechanism of any kind described. [RQ2.5] No acquisition instrumentation. Compute fully specified (Python 3.6.5, i5-8600K, 16 GB RAM, GTX 1050 Ti 4 GB, 250 GB SSD, 1 TB HDD). Training settings: ReLU, learning rate 0.01, dropout 0.5, 50 epochs, batch size 5 - though the accuracy and loss curves are described over 25 epochs, which does not match. [RQ2.6] Low. The compute environment, the four principal training hyperparameters, the class composition and the pipeline order are all given, which is more than several neighbours provide. Against that: the dataset is identified only by a reference number while the formal data statement denies that any dataset was analysed; no split procedure, partition counts or seed appear; the wavelet basis and network topology are unspecified; the chimp optimiser has no stated objective, search space or budget; no code is released; and the epoch count in the text contradicts the epoch axis of the learning curves. [RQ2.7] One stated limitation, and it is the right one: the dataset lacks demographic information, expression patterns and facial morphology vary across demographic factors, and their influence on classification and feature learning therefore cannot be examined - with future work directed at demographically different datasets to assess fairness and generalisability. Within the facial-image branch this is the clearest statement of the problem that undermines all sixteen of its members. What is not stated: that the labels have no diagnostic basis, that the split is at the image level on a corpus that repeats individuals, that the testing-phase accuracy exceeds the training-phase accuracy, that the epoch counts disagree, and that the ethics and data-availability declarations contradict the article's own contents. [RQ2.9] Assessment on demographically different and stable datasets to evaluate fairness and generalisability - proportionate to the stated limitation and the only future direction offered. [RQ3.1] None. No behaviour is observed or measured. The targets are static facial features enhanced by Gabor filtering, with the paper referring to facial cues relevant to ASD and to expression patterns and facial morphology without identifying any specific feature. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - a single image source. The paper's fusion is across three ImageNet backbones (VGG16, DenseNet-121, XceptionNet) applied to the same photograph, which is representational concatenation rather than multimodality, and no ablation isolates any backbone's contribution. [RQ4.1] A four-stage pipeline: Gaussian Gabor filtering, concatenated features from three pretrained CNNs, a wavelet neural network classifier, and chimp-optimisation parameter tuning, with Grad-CAM++ appended for visualisation. Each stage is named as a contribution and none is ablated, so the reader cannot tell whether the Gabor stage, the three-way fusion, the wavelet classifier or the metaheuristic contributes anything to the reported figure. [RQ4.2] Gabor-filtered facial images encoded as a concatenation of three backbone feature vectors. Neither the input resolution, the fused vector dimensionality, nor the wavelet basis is stated. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure and AUC, per class and averaged, for both phases, with confusion matrices, precision-recall and ROC curves. The reporting is dense and contains one telling relationship: the 30% testing-phase average accuracy (98.42%) is higher than the 70% training-phase average accuracy (97.75%), and the per-class figures move in the same direction. A model that performs better on held-out data than on the data it was fitted to is normally a signal that the partition is not independent - shared or near-duplicate images across the split being the usual cause on this corpus - or that the reported training figure is not a resubstitution score. The paper reads the same inversion in its learning curves as good generalisation without overfitting. No confidence interval, no chance level and no variance across runs accompanies any value. [RQ4.4] Grad-CAM++ is applied and a visual interpretation figure is shown, described as highlighting the most significant facial regions and improving model transparency. The description also calls this abnormality detection, which reframes model attention as pathology. No quantitative attribution is reported, no facial region is named as consistently salient across images, and no test establishes whether the highlighted regions correspond to anything anatomically meaningful rather than to image-provenance artefacts - the question the branch most needs answered and the one a saliency method is least able to settle on unlabelled web photographs. [RQ4.5] The evaluation rests on a single image-level partition of 2,940 photographs into 70% training and 30% testing, with no cross-validation, no repetition, no seed and no statement of how the split was drawn. The corpus repeats individuals, so an image-level split does not separate children, and the number of distinct children is unknown - the same defect documented across the other fifteen members of this branch. Two further features are specific to this paper. First, the accuracy inversion: the testing phase reports 98.42% against the training phase's 97.75%, and the learning curves show validation accuracy exceeding training accuracy, which the authors interpret as evidence of good generalisation. The more usual explanation on this corpus is that the partitions are not independent. Second, the chimp optimisation algorithm tuned the classifier's parameters against an unstated objective on an unstated partition, so the reported test figure may be the outcome of a search evaluated on the data it is then reported against. On top of this, the comparison against seven quoted literature figures (92.10% to 97.76%) is drawn from other papers under unknown protocols, and no component of the four-stage pipeline is ablated. [RQ5.1] Autism Spectrum Disorder; Facial Images; Wavelet Neural Network; Deep Learning; Chimp Optimisation Algorithm. Three of five terms name pipeline machinery; validation, participants and setting are absent. [RQ5.2] Multimedia Tools and Applications 85:300 (Springer), 218 days with a revision round. A multimedia and computing venue. Review did not surface an ethics declaration stating that no human participants were involved in a study of 2,940 children's photographs, a data-availability statement denying that any dataset was analysed, a test accuracy above training accuracy read as good generalisation, or the mismatch between the stated 50 epochs and the 25-epoch learning curves. [RQ5.3] 2026. Framing is diagnostic-aid: the technique is offered as a promising diagnostic aid in clinical settings for the early and non-invasive detection of autism, and the stated research gap is a computationally efficient, privacy-preserving and accurately optimised framework - with no privacy mechanism described and no runtime measured. The contribution is expressed as a position above seven quoted figures. Its one substantive merit within the branch is its limitation paragraph, which states plainly that the dataset's lack of demographic information prevents any assessment of how facial morphology and expression vary across populations, and commits future work to demographically diverse data - the clearest statement of the branch's central problem made by any of its sixteen members, sitting alongside declarations asserting that the study used no data and involved no human participants. |
| S-168 | Secondary analysis of the public Kinect V2 dataset Three-dimensional dataset combining gait and full-body movement of children with autism spectrum disorders, available on Zenodo and Dryad: 109 children comprising 50 typically developing, 50 moderate ASD and 9 severe ASD. The typical and moderate groups have real 3D recordings from 25 Kinect joint points with 463 pre-calculated motor features each; the nine severe-ASD children have only 2D phone video, because the original collectors could not deploy Kinect V2 in controlled settings for them. Severe-class feature vectors were therefore synthesised by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise. | A random forest classified three severity levels from 463-dimensional per-child vectors after z-score normalisation, with the repository's seven geometric augmentations deliberately unused. Evaluation combined 5-fold cross-validation with two 20% held-out test sets, one reserved solely for final validation, and the paper states that both are reserved subsets from the same data distribution rather than independent external validation. SHAP produced per-class importance, summary and waterfall analyses. | 84.6 +/- 10.9% accuracy under 5-fold cross-validation and 86.4% on the held-out sets. For the severe class, 100% accuracy on 4 of 4 synthetic cases with a 95% confidence interval of 39.8% to 100.0%. SHAP identified wrist movements, knee trajectories and elbow-to-foot distances as leading biomarkers, with Y-axis features declining and X-axis features increasing across severity levels. | The author states them comprehensively. The severe-ASD class contains no real measurements: its features were generated by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise, so the 100% result reflects the ability to distinguish real moderate ASD data from an artificially constructed distribution rather than true clinical severity, its 95% confidence interval runs from 39.8% to 100.0%, and a single misclassification would reduce recall to 75%. The overall sample of 109 is small, and neither held-out set constitutes external validation. Two limitations are not raised: the severity labels' own provenance and instrument are never established, and the three-class majority baseline of approximately 45.9% is never stated against which the 84.6% should be read. The dimensionality - 463 features for roughly 87 training cases - is also unremarked. | This study earns its place in the review not for its accuracy but for its reporting. It is the only charted paper that produces a 100% result and, in the same abstract sentence, explains that the result means nothing clinically and why - because the class in question was synthesised from another class. It computes an exact confidence interval on a 4-of-4 outcome (39.8% to 100.0%), states that one misclassification would move recall to 75%, specifies a minimum sample of 20 to 50 for genuine validation, declines available data augmentation that would have inflated its numbers, and states explicitly that its held-out sets are reserved subsets from the same distribution rather than independent external validation. Read against local_ed30e24c (292 of 292 read as confirming clinical suitability), local_183eaef4 (accuracy 1.0000 defended by re-running fold counts) and local_b9de0d7f (a numpy-generated target offered to educators), it demonstrates that the corpus's characteristic failure is not statistical but rhetorical. Its substantive finding is also worth carrying into the synthesis: Kinect V2 could not be deployed at all for children with severe autism, so the modality that this branch proposes as an objective severity measure is unavailable precisely for the children whose severity most needs measuring. | [RQ1.1] One hundred and nine children from a public Kinect V2 dataset: 50 typically developing, 50 moderate ASD and 9 severe ASD. The composition is uneven in a way that determines everything else about the study - the nine severe-ASD children have no Kinect recordings at all, only 2D phone video, because the original collectors could not set up Kinect V2 in controlled laboratory settings for children with severe autism. The severe class in the analysis therefore contains no real motor measurements from any child; its feature vectors were synthesised by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise. The analysis unit is the child, one 463-dimensional vector each, and the paper reports this structure openly rather than presenting three comparable groups. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typical development, moderate ASD, severe ASD. The register is clinical and neutral; motor differences are described as impairments in line with the cited literature, and severity terms are applied to groups rather than to children as labels. One artefact intrudes: the keyword list ends with violence level classification, evidently carried over from an unrelated manuscript. [RQ1.3] Not reported in the extracted text - no age, sex, ethnicity or socioeconomic information for any of the 109 children. The author names this as a gap prospectively rather than leaving it implicit, listing age groups, genders and cultural backgrounds among the dimensions on which generalisation must be tested in future work. [RQ1.4] Inherited from the original collection and not independently established. The three-level grouping (typical, moderate, severe) is used as the classification target and the instrument behind the moderate/severe distinction is not named in the extracted text. What the paper does establish clearly is the provenance chain: ethics approval was obtained by the original collectors from their institutional review board before collection, guardian consent was given, and this study is a secondary analysis of de-identified public data. [RQ1.5] The severity grouping is the outcome rather than a covariate, and no validated severity instrument is named. Given that the study's subject is severity classification, the absence of a stated instrument behind the labels is its largest unaddressed gap - the synthetic-data problem is discussed at length, the label-provenance problem is not. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is objective classification of three ASD severity levels from 3D motor features, identification of the contributing motor biomarkers through SHAP, and evaluation across multiple validation strategies. Headline findings: 84.6 +/- 10.9% accuracy under 5-fold cross-validation and 86.4% on the held-out sets; 100% on the severe class (4 of 4) with a 95% confidence interval of 39.8% to 100.0%; and wrist movements, knee trajectories and elbow-to-foot distances as the leading biomarkers. The abstract itself states that the severe-class result is a methodological proof-of-concept rather than clinical validation because the severe features were synthetically generated. [RQ2.2] The original recordings were made in a controlled laboratory environment for the typical and moderate groups and in clinical settings for the severe group. The reason for that difference is reported and is substantive: Kinect V2 could not be deployed in controlled conditions for children with severe autism, so only phone video was obtained. That is a real, generalisable observation about who this class of technology can and cannot measure, and it is stated plainly rather than worked around silently. [RQ2.3] Gait and full-body movement recorded with 25 Kinect V2 joint points at X, Y and Z coordinates, from which the dataset creators pre-calculated 463 features: inter-joint Euclidean distances, range-of-motion metrics, gait parameters (speed, step length, cycle time) and temporal characteristics. The severe-ASD group was recorded on a Samsung Note 9 in clinical settings, and the paper explains why extracting the same 463 features from that video was technically impossible - missing 3D coordinates, depth information and time-series data. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional secondary analysis. Ethics is documented at both levels - institutional review board approval obtained by the original collectors before data collection, guardian written informed consent, and a secondary analysis of publicly available de-identified data in accordance with local legislation and institutional requirements. Both repository locations are given. This is complete provenance reporting for a secondary analysis and is among the best in the corpus. [RQ2.5] Microsoft Kinect V2 capturing 25 joints in three dimensions in real time for the typical and moderate groups; a Samsung Note 9 phone camera for the nine severe-ASD children. The analysis software, versions and seed are not reported. [RQ2.6] High for a secondary analysis. Both repository URLs are given with the note that they contain the same data with full documentation and metadata; the six preprocessing stages are enumerated with exact dataframe dimensions (109 x 466) and class encodings; the decision to use only original rather than the repository's seven geometric augmentations is stated explicitly; the synthetic-generation rule is described precisely enough to reproduce; and both a fold standard deviation and a 95% confidence interval are reported. Missing: model hyperparameters, software and versions, seed and code. [RQ2.7] The most thorough and self-critical limitations discussion in the charted corpus, and the only one in which the paper's own headline result is dismantled by its author. The severe-class analysis is described as the most critical limitation of the study; the reason no real data exist is explained; the synthetic-generation method is named; and the consequence is stated in full - that the reported 100% reflects the model's ability to distinguish between real moderate ASD motor data and an artificially constructed distribution, not between true clinical severity levels. The author further notes that the extremely wide confidence interval indicates high statistical uncertainty and that a single misclassification would reduce recall to 75%, sets a minimum target of 20 to 50 real severe-ASD cases for future work, and states that the two test sets are reserved subsets from the same data distribution rather than independent external validation. The one limitation not raised is the provenance of the severity labels themselves. [RQ2.9] Collect real Kinect-derived severe-ASD data with a stated minimum sample of 20 to 50; test generalisation across age groups, genders and cultural backgrounds on larger datasets from multiple institutions; and run longitudinal studies of how motor biomarkers track severity change, framed as a way to evaluate intervention effectiveness. Each addresses a specific stated limitation. [RQ3.1] Motor function measured directly in three dimensions: inter-joint distances, range of motion, gait speed, step length and cycle time, and temporal characteristics, over 25 skeletal joints. The behavioural claims arising from SHAP are anatomically specific - wrist movements, knee trajectories and elbow-to-foot distances - and are related to motor impairments reported in the prior ASD literature rather than presented as novel discoveries. A structural pattern is also reported: Y-axis features decline (30% to 10% to 0%) and X-axis features increase (70% to 90% to 100%) with increasing severity, though the severe end of that gradient is synthetic. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - 3D skeletal motion alone. The study's most interesting observation is instead about modality availability: the severe-ASD group could not be captured with the same sensor as the other two, so the modality itself is unavailable for the group whose severity the study most wants to classify. That is a genuine finding about the deployability of depth-sensor assessment and it applies well beyond this paper. [RQ4.1] Random forest, chosen for performance, flexibility and compatibility with SHAP-based interpretation. No architecture competition, no metaheuristic and no deep learning - the modelling is subordinated to the interpretability aim. [RQ4.2] One 463-dimensional feature vector per child, pre-calculated by the dataset creators, z-score normalised, with timestamps omitted. Two aspects deserve note. The dimensionality is high relative to the sample - 463 features for 109 children, of whom roughly 87 are available for training - so the model operates in a regime where a random forest's variable selection is doing most of the work. And the repository's seven geometric augmentations (rotation, mirroring, scaling) were available and deliberately not used, a restraint that several studies in this corpus do not exercise. [RQ4.3] Accuracy with a fold-wise standard deviation (84.6 +/- 10.9%), held-out accuracy (86.4%), per-class results and, for the severe class, an exact binomial confidence interval (39.8%-100.0%) on a 4-of-4 result. Computing and reporting that interval is the single most useful reporting decision in this part of the corpus: it converts an apparently perfect result into a statement that the true accuracy could be anywhere above 40%, and the author draws exactly that inference. The fold standard deviation of 10.9 points is likewise reported rather than smoothed. What is missing: the three-class majority baseline (approximately 45.9%) is never stated, and no per-class sensitivity or specificity is given for the two real classes. [RQ4.4] SHAP applied per class with importance, summary and waterfall plots, yielding anatomically interpretable biomarkers (wrist, knee, elbow-to-foot) that the author relates to established motor findings in autism. The interpretation is properly bounded for the two real classes - the author states that for typical and moderate ASD the approach relies on biomarkers that are anatomically interpretable and reflect systematic motor patterns consistent with the literature - and implicitly withheld for the severe class, whose SHAP profile describes a distribution the author constructed. The reported axis gradient across severity is the clearest illustration: its severe endpoint (X-axis features 100%) is a property of the synthesis procedure rather than of any child. [RQ4.5] The evaluation is competently constructed at the child level - 5-fold cross-validation with a fold standard deviation reported, plus two 20% held-out sets one of which is reserved solely for final validation, and an explicit statement that neither constitutes independent external validation because both are reserved subsets from the same data distribution with the same sensor, protocol and feature pipeline. Against most of this corpus that is exemplary. The decisive issue is the severe class, and the paper states it before any reader could raise it: because no Kinect recordings exist for the nine severe-ASD children, the severe class's feature vectors were created by averaging moderate ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise. A classifier separating that construction from real moderate data is separating a smoothed, noise-perturbed version of one distribution from the distribution itself, which is a task with a known answer and no clinical content - and the author says so, writing that the 100% result reflects the ability to distinguish real moderate ASD motor data from an artificially constructed distribution, not true clinical severity levels. The 4-of-4 result carries a 95% confidence interval from 39.8% to 100.0%, which the author computes, reports and interprets. Two further qualifications apply to the real two-class portion: 463 features for 109 children is a high-dimensional regime with roughly 87 training cases, and the three-class majority baseline of about 45.9% is never stated against which 84.6% should be read. The study is nonetheless the corpus's clearest demonstration that a near-perfect number can be reported and simultaneously explained away by the person reporting it. [RQ5.1] autism spectrum disorder; motor biomarkers; random forest; SHAP analysis; violence level classification. The last term belongs to a different paper and survives in the published keyword list. [RQ5.2] Frontiers in Psychiatry 17:1751654, 107 days with a revision round. A psychiatry venue, and the fit shows in the reporting - confidence intervals on a small-sample result, an explicit statement that held-out sets are not external validation, full provenance for a secondary analysis, and a limitations discussion that identifies the study's own most striking result as uninterpretable. The revision round appears to have strengthened rather than softened these statements, since the synthetic-data caveat appears in the abstract itself. [RQ5.3] 2026, published 23 March. The framing is the most restrained in the charted corpus relative to the numbers reported. The abstract states 100% accuracy for the severe class and, in the same sentence, that this represents a methodological proof-of-concept rather than clinical validation because the features were synthetically generated; the discussion adds that a single misclassification would reduce recall to 75%; the conclusion describes the work as proof-of-concept demonstrating methodological feasibility pending validation on independent datasets; and future work is specified with a minimum sample target. Its contribution to this review is therefore not its accuracy but its demonstration that an author can report a perfect score and simultaneously explain, in the abstract, why it means nothing - the exact move that the corpus's fifteen facial-image studies and seven checklist studies do not make. |
| S-169 | Secondary analysis of two public TalkBank child-language corpora: Eigsti et al. (48 children aged 3-6 in three balanced groups of 16 - typically developing, developmental delay, ASD - recorded in 30-minute free-play sessions, with ethnic composition reported) and Nadig and Bang (38 children, 26 typically developing and 12 with ASD, sampled at three time points over a year in parent-child interactions). Participant counts, sex, mean ages, total words and utterance statistics are tabulated by group. In the Nadig corpus the typically developing children average 29-34 months against 53-61 months for the ASD children. | Transcripts were retrieved via TalkBank APIs and reduced to 52 features covering participant details, utterance statistics, stem words and parts of speech. Logistic regression, a depth-2 random forest and TabNet were tuned by grid search under 5-fold stratified cross-validation and evaluated on Nadig binary, Eigsti binary, the merged data and Eigsti three-class, with six metrics each. SMOTE was applied to the Nadig corpus only and validated by Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests (KS below 0.15, p around 0.99). Overfitting was checked by a train-validation accuracy gap of no more than 4%. Logistic-regression coefficients were averaged across folds for the importance analysis. | Logistic regression reached ROC-AUC 0.93 on Nadig and 0.87 on Eigsti binary; TabNet approximately 0.96 on the merged data; random forest 0.71 on the three-class Eigsti task including developmental delay. Accuracy exceeded 86% on both binary datasets, and a model using only the top four non-part-of-speech features - Mean Length of Utterance, Mean Length of Turn Ratio, age and total words - reproduced nearly the same 86%. | The authors state several: the small size and narrow 3-6 year age range of the corpora, the loss of prosodic information (pitch, rhythm, intonation) that text cannot capture, the overfitting risk from 38-48 participants, and the markedly weaker three-class performance, which they read as showing the need for features specific to developmental delay to reduce misdiagnosis risk. One limitation is documented in their own table and not addressed: in the Nadig corpus the ASD children average roughly two years older than the typically developing children and are more male-weighted, and age is included among the features and named as one of the four carrying the result - so the 0.93 there partly measures developmental stage. The placement of SMOTE relative to the cross-validation folds is unstated, no confidence intervals or fold variance are reported, and the 68.4% majority-class baseline for the imbalanced Nadig corpus is never given. | This study contributes two things to the review. First, it makes privacy the design criterion and states the critique that the rest of the corpus does not: that a major drawback of facial-image approaches is the invasion of privacy, especially for minors, and the need to collect their images over prolonged periods of childhood.
