That is a direct assessment of the sixteen facial-image studies charted here, several of which reuse web-scraped photographs of identifiable children with no ethics statement, and it is made by a study that then accepts the information cost of its own choice - acknowledging that prosodic markers of atypical speech cannot be represented in text. Its privacy claim is also properly qualified, stating in the abstract that no differential privacy or encryption was implemented. Second, its three-class analysis provides another differential-diagnosis calibration point: the same features and pipeline give ROC-AUC 0.87-0.93 for ASD against typical development and 0.71 once developmental delay is included, joining local_b6ac2b98 (F1 0.86 versus 0.63) and local_69b10fe4 in quantifying how much apparent autism signal is a general clinical-versus-typical distinction. Its own weakness is a clean illustration of the confound local_7b19a959 measured directly: with a two-year age gap between groups and age in the feature set, part of its best result is developmental rather than diagnostic. | [RQ1.1] Eighty-six children across two independently collected public corpora. Eigsti et al.: 48 children aged 3-6 in three balanced groups of 16 - typically developing, developmental delay and ASD - each recorded in a 30-minute free-play session, with ethnic composition reported (39 White, 3 LatinX, 6 African-American). Nadig and Bang: 38 children, 26 typically developing and 12 with ASD, sampled at three time points over a year in parent-child interactions. The analysis unit is the child throughout, and the two corpora are analysed separately, merged, and - for Eigsti - as a three-class problem. The presence of a developmental-delay group is the design's most valuable feature and is the reason this study can say something the rest of the speech branch cannot. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing, delayed development. The register is neutral and the paper's framing is unusually ethics-forward: it argues that a major drawback of facial-image approaches is the invasion of privacy, especially for minors, and the need to collect their images over prolonged periods of their childhood, and that MRI-based approaches rely on invasive data collection raising ethical and privacy concerns. One phrase slips - facial features recorded at the onset of the disease - but the overall orientation treats the children's data as something requiring protection rather than as a resource. [RQ1.3] The most complete demographic reporting in the speech branch. Sex, participant counts, mean ages, total words and mean and median utterance lengths are tabulated by group and by sex for both corpora, and Eigsti's ethnic composition is given. That reporting is what makes the study's central confound visible: in the Nadig corpus the typically developing children have mean ages of 29 and 34 months while the ASD children have mean ages of 61 and 53 months, a gap of roughly two years, and the ASD group is 83% male against 58% in the TD group. The authors note the age difference explicitly, attributing it to the significant language delays typically observed in children with ASD - but they then include age in the feature set. [RQ1.4] Inherited from two peer-reviewed developmental-language studies, whose own diagnostic procedures are cited but not summarised. Governance is handled by reference to TalkBank's contribution requirements, which oblige contributing researchers to obtain informed consent from participants or guardians and the necessary ethical approvals before sharing. That is a reasonable basis for secondary analysis of a curated academic repository and is stated rather than assumed - a different situation from the web-scraped and platform-hosted collections elsewhere in this review. [RQ1.5] No severity or cognitive instrument is reported. The Eigsti developmental-delay group provides a partial control for general developmental level in the three-class analysis, which is the closest the study comes to separating autism-specific from delay-general language differences. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is to test whether privacy-preserving machine learning on speech transcripts can screen for ASD, on the argument that structured text avoids identifiable biometric data such as raw audio or video. Headline findings: ROC-AUC 0.93 on Nadig and 0.87 on Eigsti binary with logistic regression, approximately 0.96 on the merged data with TabNet, accuracy above 86% on both binary datasets, and a four-feature model reproducing nearly the same 86%. The result the authors themselves flag as important is the three-class Eigsti task, where the best ROC-AUC falls to 0.71. [RQ2.2] No setting of the authors' own. The source recordings were 30-minute free-play sessions (Eigsti) and parent-child interactions at three time points over a year (Nadig), both naturalistic language-sampling protocols from developmental research rather than screening paradigms. [RQ2.3] Naturalistic language sampling rather than a designed classification task, which is a strength - the speech is spontaneous interaction, not an elicited response to a stimulus. The features derived from it are conversational as well as lexical: Mean Length of Turn Ratio measures the child's turn length relative to the adult's, capturing conversational participation rather than isolated production. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional analysis of longitudinally collected data. Ethics rests on TalkBank's stated requirement that contributors obtain informed consent and ethical approval before sharing, which the paper cites explicitly. The privacy argument is the paper's organising claim and it is stated with appropriate qualification: the authors acknowledge that they have not implemented explicit cryptographic privacy measures such as differential privacy or encryption, and claim only that text-based inputs inherently avoid identifiable biometric data. That qualification, placed in the abstract, is more careful than the unqualified privacy-preserving claims made elsewhere in this corpus. [RQ2.5] None for acquisition; transcripts retrieved through TalkBank APIs. Modelling used logistic regression, random forest and TabNet with grid-searched hyperparameters; no software, version or seed is named. [RQ2.6] Moderate to high. Both corpora are public and linked with their source studies cited; participant counts, sex, mean ages, total words and utterance statistics are tabulated by group; the feature count is given; the selected hyperparameters are reported for all three models; the SMOTE validation is quantified with KS statistics and p-values; and the overfitting check is reported as a numerical train-validation gap. Missing: code, seed, software versions, the complete 52-feature list, and the placement of SMOTE relative to the folds. [RQ2.7] Substantive and mostly well aimed. Stated: the small size and limited diversity of the corpora, particularly the narrow 3-6 year age range; the absence of prosodic information - pitch, rhythm, intonation - which text cannot represent and which is indicative of atypical speech in autism, an honest acknowledgement that the privacy advantage carries an information cost; the risk of overfitting given 48 and 38 participants, addressed by a quantified train-validation comparison; and the markedly lower performance on the three-class task, read as showing that features specific to developmental delay are needed to reduce misdiagnosis risk. Not stated: that the ASD and TD groups in the Nadig corpus differ in mean age by roughly two years and that age is one of the four features the paper identifies as carrying the signal. [RQ2.9] Broader age ranges, more diverse environments and dialects, transfer learning from larger speech corpora, features capturing developmental-delay-specific nuances, conversational agents or robotic assistants for scalable screening, and a multimodal extension adding limited prosodic cues while preserving the privacy advantage of text. The last is a considered trade-off rather than a generic call for more modalities. [RQ3.1] Expressive language and conversational participation in spontaneous interaction. The two leading features are behaviourally specific and directionally interpretable: Mean Length of Utterance, where lower values indicate shorter and simpler utterances and are associated with higher ASD likelihood, and Mean Length of Turn Ratio, the child's turn length relative to the adult's, where lower values indicate that the child contributes less to conversational exchange. Both correspond to well-established clinical observations, and the paper relates them accordingly rather than presenting them as discoveries. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - text alone, deliberately. The paper's argument is that excluding audio and video is the point, since transcripts avoid identifiable biometric data, and it acknowledges the cost: prosodic features indicative of atypical speech cannot be captured in text. Its future-work proposal to add limited prosodic cues while preserving text-level privacy is an explicit privacy-information trade-off, which no other study in this corpus formulates. [RQ4.1] Three classifiers - logistic regression, random forest at maximum depth 2, and TabNet - with logistic regression selected for the interpretability analysis on the basis of its performance. The depth-2 random forest is an appropriate constraint for 38-48 cases and is reported rather than left implicit. [RQ4.2] Fifty-two tabular features per child spanning participant details, utterance statistics, stem words and parts of speech. The inclusion of age among the predictors is the study's principal unaddressed problem: the two groups in the Nadig corpus differ in mean age by roughly two years by the authors' own table, and age is reported as one of the four features that carry the result. [RQ4.3] Six metrics per model per configuration - accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and p-values - with the rationale for each stated. The reporting is complete and the paper draws the right comparison from it: ROC-AUC 0.93 for ASD versus TD in Nadig, 0.87 in Eigsti, roughly 0.96 merged, and 0.71 for the three-class task including developmental delay. Missing: confidence intervals, fold variance, and the majority-class baselines - which matter particularly for Nadig, where 26 TD against 12 ASD gives a 68.4% baseline against a reported accuracy above 86%. [RQ4.4] Well executed. Logistic-regression coefficients were accumulated across all five cross-validation folds and averaged rather than taken from a single fit, and the resulting ranking was then tested by refitting on the top four non-part-of-speech features alone, which reproduced nearly the same 86% accuracy. That reduced-model check is a genuine validation of the importance ranking rather than an assertion, and it supports the paper's privacy argument directly - fewer features means less data collection. The named features are clinically interpretable, and their directions are stated. The one problem is that age is among them, and age is confounded with group. [RQ4.5] The design is sound in structure and limited by two things the paper handles unevenly. Structurally: 5-fold stratified cross-validation at the child level, grid-searched hyperparameters under the same scheme, an explicit overfitting check reporting a train-validation gap of no more than 4% with the small sample sizes named as the reason for checking, SMOTE confined to the one imbalanced corpus and validated by Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests showing near-identical distributions, and six metrics reported for every configuration. That is careful work. Two problems remain. The first is confounding, and it is visible in the paper's own table: in the Nadig corpus the typically developing children average 29 and 34 months while the ASD children average 61 and 53 months - roughly a two-year gap - and the ASD group is 83% male against 58%. Age is then included as a feature and identified as one of the four that carry the signal. A classifier separating a four-year-old from a two-and-a-half-year-old on utterance length and vocabulary is doing developmental rather than diagnostic work, and the Nadig ROC-AUC of 0.93 cannot be separated from that. The Eigsti corpus is better matched (TD 40-45 months, ASD 55-56) and yields a lower 0.87. The second is the placement of SMOTE relative to the folds, which is not stated - though the distributional validation is more than most studies provide. Against these, the study's most valuable number is the one it foregrounds itself: 0.71 for the three-class task including developmental delay, against 0.87-0.93 for ASD versus typical development. The gap is internally controlled - same features, same corpus, same pipeline - and it quantifies how much of the binary performance is autism-specific rather than a general clinical-versus-typical distinction. [RQ5.1] Computational linguistics; Machine learning; Artificial intelligence; Feature importance; Autism spectrum disorder (ASD); Privacy. Privacy as a keyword reflects the paper's organising argument rather than being decorative. [RQ5.2] Scientific Reports 15(1):34134 (Nature Portfolio). A multidisciplinary venue. The reporting reflects it: demographic tables by group and sex, six metrics with stated rationales, a quantified overfitting check, KS validation of the oversampling, and a limitations section that names the information cost of the privacy choice. [RQ5.3] Framing is screening-support and privacy-forward, and both claims are qualified in the abstract itself - the models are described as a foundation for future applications in clinical and educational contexts, and the privacy claim is explicitly limited to the absence of biometric data rather than to any cryptographic guarantee, with the authors stating that they have not implemented differential privacy or encryption. The paper's contribution to this review is twofold. It is the only study in the corpus to make privacy the design criterion and to argue explicitly that facial-image approaches invade the privacy of minors - a critique that applies directly to the sixteen facial-image studies charted here, several of which reuse web-scraped photographs of identifiable children with no ethics statement. And its three-class result (ROC-AUC 0.71 including developmental delay, against 0.87-0.93 against typical development) joins local_b6ac2b98 and local_69b10fe4 as the review's differential-diagnosis calibration points. |
| S-170 | Prospective primary study in Brazilian inclusive-education settings. Three trained education professionals supervised 12 children aged 3-6 - six with a clinical ASD diagnosis and six without, matched across age bands - who completed 640 sessions of a purpose-built three-game tablet application over three months. Guardians gave written informed consent for every child and the administering professional signed a consent form after training; children with co-occurring disorders or with disabilities impairing application use were excluded under enumerated criteria. | Session telemetry (duration, game identity, task-performance fields) was compiled into a tabular dataset partitioned 20% validation with the remaining 80% split 70/30 into training and testing. Seven algorithms - random forest, MLP, deep MLP, KNN, logistic regression, SVM and naive Bayes - were tuned by exhaustive grid search with 5-fold cross-validation, with the complete search space and selected values published, and learning curves plotted for each. Code and dataset are publicly deposited on GitHub. | Random forest 96% accuracy; MLP, deep MLP and SVM 94%; KNN 90%; logistic regression 82%; naive Bayes lower. Learning curves show training accuracy above validation accuracy with no abrupt decline, which the authors read as strong generalisation. | The authors name six threats - small sample, convenience sampling and selection bias, scope restricted to ASD signs alone, overfitting risk from the reduced sample, absence of longitudinal data, and the ethical implications of school-based screening including stigmatisation and the need for professional training. They do not name the one that determines the result: 640 game sessions come from 12 children, roughly 53 each, and both the initial partition and the 5-fold cross-validation operate on sessions with no participant grouping, so every test fold contains sessions from children whose other sessions trained the model. With six children per class, a session-level split cannot yield a participant-level estimate, and leave-one-child-out validation was available. Compounding this, the paper argues that the high accuracy observed in the models and the robust metrics reinforce the low likelihood of overfitting, and reads high validation accuracy as generalisation - inverting the inference. No feature importance is reported, so nothing establishes which executive-function variables carry the 96%. | This study is the review's clearest example of a well-designed study undone by a single validation choice. Almost everything about it is what the field's methods literature asks for: primary collection over three months in the actual deployment setting rather than a laboratory or a download; a purpose-built task grounded in the executive-dysfunction literature rather than a repurposed dataset; age-matched groups with enumerated inclusion and exclusion criteria for both children and staff; dual written consent; the complete hyperparameter search space published for seven algorithms; code and data deposited for replication; claims bounded explicitly to screening rather than diagnosis; and a threats section that raises the risk of stigmatisation from school-based screening and the need for professional training - an ethical concern no other study in this corpus articulates. And the reported 96% is a within-participant figure from 12 children, because the 640 game sessions were split by session. It belongs alongside local_bb4d1f7a (100 eye crops per child), local_8d43288c (frame clips from 75 videos) and local_945300a5 (15 photographs per child) in the corpus's frame-level leakage group, and it is the case where that failure costs the most, since with 12 children leave-one-child-out validation was both obvious and free. | [RQ1.1] Twelve children aged 3-6 years - six with a clinical ASD diagnosis and six without, matched across the same age bands - who together completed 640 game sessions over three months in their own school setting. The recruitment structure is documented in unusual detail: three inclusive-education professionals were recruited with stated inclusion and exclusion criteria, trained on the tool, and supervised the children's use of it, with guardians absent during play. The gap between the number of children and the number of analysis rows is the study's decisive feature: 640 sessions from 12 children is roughly 53 per child, and the dataset is partitioned by session rather than by child. [RQ1.2] ASD, autism spectrum disorder, children with ASD, typically developing children, atypical and typical children, neurotypicals. The register is educational rather than clinical and the orientation is inclusive - the stated purpose is to let educators tailor teaching to individual needs and promote inclusive education, and the discussion warns against stigmatisation. One phrase dates the framing (ASD as a neuropsychiatric disorder), and the keyword list begins with Phishing, an artefact from an unrelated manuscript. [RQ1.3] Age is reported and controlled by design - children were organised into groups G3, G4 and G5 by age, and the ASD and control groups were matched across those bands specifically to make the samples more homogeneous. Sex is not reported. Nothing on socioeconomic status or ethnicity, though the school-based recruitment in a Brazilian public inclusive-education setting is described. Guardians completed a behavioural anamnesis questionnaire whose contents are not reported. [RQ1.4] Clinical diagnosis is an inclusion criterion - children with a diagnosis form the ASD group and children without form the control group - but the diagnosing procedure, instrument and assessor are not described. The framing is honest about why this matters in context: the study's motivating problem is that a significant number of children with ASD in Brazilian early and primary education remain without an appropriate clinical diagnosis, which leaves educators without information to tailor teaching. The tool is proposed for exactly those undiagnosed children, and is trained on children whose diagnostic status is already known. [RQ1.5] None. Comorbidity and severity are handled by exclusion rather than measurement: three participant profiles are defined - ASD alone, ASD with co-occurring disorders, and children whose disabilities would impair application use - and the scope is restricted to signs of ASD exclusively, with each exclusion criterion enumerated and justified. That is transparent design, and it also means the sample excludes the children for whom screening decisions are hardest. [RQ2.1] The stated goal is a serious-game tablet application combining inclusive-design requirements with machine learning, to give educators a playful, non-invasive ASD screening aid usable inside the school day. Headline findings: random forest reached 96% accuracy, MLP, deep MLP and SVM 94%, KNN 90%, logistic regression 82% and naive Bayes lower, with learning curves showing training accuracy above validation accuracy and no abrupt decline. [RQ2.2] A specialised educational service setting within Brazilian full-day schools, with the games administered by a trained education professional during the child's normal activities and guardians not present. This is the only study in the charted corpus whose data were collected in the setting where the resulting tool would actually be used, and the choice is argued: full-day schools provide a convenient setting, the professional's existing daily relationship with the children was leveraged, and the application was incorporated into planned educational demands. [RQ2.3] Three classical games on a tablet, purpose-designed around executive functions - planning, cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control, working memory and performance monitoring - with the theoretical grounding cited to Pennington and Ozonoff and to Hill. The paradigm is genuinely constructed for the question rather than repurposed, and the games' accessibility and usability requirements were derived from a prior review stage documented in the methodology flowchart. [RQ2.4] Cross-sectional analysis of three months of collection. Consent is documented at both levels - guardians signed an Informed Consent Form as the precondition for each child's participation, and the administering professional signed a Free and Informed Consent Form after training - though no ethics committee reference appears in the extracted text. The paper also contains an ethical discussion that no other study in this corpus offers: it states that the ethical implications of early screening in educational settings must be considered, including the risk of stigmatisation and the responsible use of the generated information; that screening should be understood as an initial support for identifying warning signs and guiding the search for specialised clinical evaluation, not as a definitive diagnosis; and that use of the tool should be accompanied by appropriate training for education professionals to reduce misinterpretations and promote an inclusive and respectful approach to differences. For a tool intended to be operated by teachers on undiagnosed children, that is the right set of concerns and it is stated without prompting. [RQ2.5] A tablet running the study's own serious-game application. Modelling used seven standard algorithms with grid-searched hyperparameters; no software, version, seed or compute environment is named. [RQ2.6] High on artefacts. Code and dataset are publicly deposited on GitHub with replication named as the explicit purpose - the second study in the charted corpus to release working code. The full hyperparameter grid and selected values are tabulated for all seven models; the collected data fields are listed with types and example values; inclusion and exclusion criteria are enumerated for both children and professionals; the consent procedure is described at both levels; and the game design and its executive-function rationale are documented through a methodology flowchart. Missing: an ethics committee reference, sex composition, a random seed, software versions, and - most consequentially - any statement of how the 640 sessions were assigned to the training, testing and validation partitions. [RQ2.7] One of the fullest threats-to-validity sections in the corpus, with six distinct items: small sample size as a major constraint on generalisation given the variability among individuals with ASD; convenience sampling as a source of selection bias restricting profile diversity and compromising external validity; the restriction of scope to ASD signs alone, with each exclusion criterion enumerated and justified; overfitting risk from the reduced sample; the absence of longitudinal data, with repeated collections recommended; and the ethical implications of school-based screening including stigmatisation risk. The one thing not identified is the thing that governs the result: that 640 sessions come from 12 children and are partitioned by session. The paper instead argues in the opposite direction, stating that the high accuracy observed in the models and the robust metrics reinforce the low likelihood of overfitting - which reads a symptom as reassurance. [RQ2.9] Longitudinal protocols with additional collections at different time points to assess response stability and tool robustness; larger and more diverse samples to address the convenience-sampling limitation; and training for education professionals as a condition of deployment. Each addresses a stated threat. [RQ3.1] Executive function as elicited by three purpose-built games - planning, cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control, working memory and performance monitoring - captured through session-level telemetry including duration and task-performance fields. This is behaviour observed during a designed task rather than reported on a checklist or inferred from an appearance, and the construct is theoretically motivated rather than chosen for convenience. What the paper does not do is say which behaviours distinguished the groups: no feature importance is reported, so the executive-function framing that justifies the whole design is never connected to a result. [RQ3.2] No modality fusion - game telemetry alone. The behavioural anamnesis questionnaire completed by guardians is collected and not used as a predictor, which keeps the model's inputs clean of parent-report information but also leaves an available modality unexploited. [RQ4.1] Seven algorithms under a single protocol - random forest, MLP, deep MLP, KNN, logistic regression, SVM and naive Bayes - with the full grid search published. The comparison is genuinely controlled and the spread it produces (96% down to 82% and lower) is informative in itself. [RQ4.2] One row per game session, with fields covering session duration in seconds, game identity and task-performance variables, tabulated with data types and examples. The row is a session, not a child, and the paper does not remark on the distinction anywhere. [RQ4.3] Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for all seven models, plus learning curves plotting training and cross-validation accuracy against training-set size. The learning curves are read carefully - training accuracy above validation accuracy is correctly described as expected, and the absence of an abrupt decline is noted - but the reading stops short of asking why validation accuracy is so high at all. No confidence interval, no fold variance and no chance level appears; and the 96% is not related to the effective sample of 12 children. [RQ4.4] None. Random forest was the best model and supplies feature importances at no cost, and none is reported. The study's entire justification is that specific executive functions are impaired in autism and that a game can measure them, so the identification of which game-derived variables carried the signal was both available and central - and it is absent. [RQ4.5] The design is careful everywhere except the one place that determines the answer. Careful: three months of primary collection in the real deployment setting; age-matched groups organised into bands; enumerated inclusion and exclusion criteria for children and professionals; guardian and professional consent; a purpose-built task grounded in the executive-function literature; grid search with 5-fold cross-validation and the full search space published; seven algorithms under one protocol; learning curves inspected per model; code and data deposited; and a six-item threats section including the ethics of school-based screening. Decisive: the analysis unit is the game session. Six hundred and forty sessions from 12 children give roughly 53 sessions per child, and the partition into 20% validation and an 80/70/30 training-testing split - together with 5-fold cross-validation - is performed over sessions with no participant grouping described. Every fold therefore contains sessions from the same children as its training data, played on the same device in the same room with the same supervising professional, so a classifier can reach 96% by recognising individual children rather than autism. With six children per class, no session-level partition can produce a participant-level estimate. Two further points compound this. The learning curves showing high training and validation accuracy are read as suggesting a strong generalization capability, and the paper states elsewhere that the high accuracy observed in the models and the robust metrics reinforce the low likelihood of overfitting - inverting the inference, since under session-level splitting high validation accuracy is what leakage produces. And no feature importance is reported, so there is no evidence about what the 96% is built on. The remedy was available and cheap: with 12 children, leave-one-child-out validation would have given twelve honest folds. [RQ5.1] Phishing; ASD screening; Machine learning; Serious game. The first keyword belongs to an unrelated manuscript and survives in the published article. [RQ5.2] Expert Systems With Applications 295 (2026) 128884 (Elsevier) - an applied AI journal. Review did not surface that 640 analysis rows come from 12 children with no participant-level partitioning, nor the Phishing keyword. [RQ5.3] 2026. The framing is the most appropriately bounded in the primary-data group: the tool is offered as laying the groundwork for future research and practical applications to screen for suspected ASD among children in school settings, and the discussion states explicitly that screening should be understood as an initial support for identifying warning signs and guiding the search for specialised clinical evaluation, not as a definitive diagnosis, with professional training required to reduce misinterpretation and the risk of stigmatisation named. Its contribution to this review is a study that gets almost everything right about design, ethics, transparency and scope - primary collection in the real setting, matched groups, published code and data, a full hyperparameter grid, enumerated criteria, dual consent, and an unprompted discussion of screening ethics - and then reports a 96% that its own validation design cannot support, because 640 game sessions from 12 children were split by session rather than by child. |

### 3.4 Synthesis

This review charted 170 computation-based autism prediction studies that use behavioural data, published between 2013 and 2026, and extracted for each one the same 23 review questions on participants, study conduct and reporting, behaviours, computational methods, and publishing trends. What follows synthesises those 170 charts. It is organised around the finding that emerged from them: that reported performance in this literature is governed almost entirely by how the evaluation was constructed and how the outcome was defined, and only marginally by the modality, the algorithm or the year.

**1. The performance distribution and what produces it.** Reported headline accuracies span roughly 50% to 100%, and the distribution is bimodal. One mode sits between 90% and 100%; the other between 55% and 85%. The separating variable is not the behavioural signal but the analysis unit. Where the unit of analysis is smaller than the person - an image, a video frame, a gaze sample, an EEG epoch, a cry instance, a thermal frame, a game session, an eye crop - and the data are partitioned at that unit rather than by participant, reported accuracy clusters in the upper mode. Where the unit is the person and folds separate people, it clusters in the lower one. The review found this pattern in every modality it examined. In eye tracking, Al-Adhaileh et al. (local_7432ffd7) partitioned 1,048,575 gaze samples from 59 children by sample and reported 99.78%; Alsharif et al. (local_44d3aef5) partitioned 547 scanpath images by image and reported 100% on 55 test images; Cheekaty and Muneeswari (local_bb4d1f7a) generated exactly 100 eye crops per child from 40 children and reported 97%. Against these, Zaragoza-Portoles et al. (local_5f57ba19) used participant-independent nested cross-validation on 45 children with a purpose-built social-attention paradigm and reported F1 0.641; Alagha et al. (local_d7b6fa00) aggregated scanpaths to the participant, listed leakage prevention among their contributions, and reported 0.96 with a fold standard deviation of 0.08 on 28 people. The same contrast appears in video (Jabbar et al., local_8d43288c: clip-level folds over 75 YouTube videos, 0.929 with fold standard deviations below 0.004), in facial photography (Zainal et al., local_945300a5: 15 photographs per child from 70 children split at image level, 90%), and in serious-game telemetry (Martins et al., local_b26db2f2: 640 sessions from 12 children split by session, 96%, where leave-one-child-out validation was available and unused).

**2. Circular and instrument-contaminated outcomes.** A second mechanism produces near-perfect figures independently of the split. In twelve charted studies the outcome variable is a deterministic function of the predictors. The clearest form is the checklist-threshold label: the Q-CHAT-10, AQ-10 and M-CHAT datasets encode a class as the thresholded sum of the ten items that are then supplied as features. Abu-Errub (local_ed30e24c) classified 292 of 292 test cases correctly and read this as confirming suitability for reliable clinical screening; Hajjej et al. (local_b9de0d7f) additionally manufactured a six-way teaching-method target with numpy by binning the same Q-CHAT total, predicted it at 0.9917 from the items the total is computed from, and offered the result to educators as a basis for decisions about individual children's education. Sankari (local_14df790d) mapped the mechanism without naming it, showing that every feature subset containing either the total or its summands performs well, and that with only age and sex as predictors sensitivity reaches 99.5% on a 69%-positive dataset. Rathod et al. (local_af9f4c12) is the only study in the corpus to identify the structure explicitly, writing that because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the prediction task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting and high classification performance should not be read as diagnostic accuracy. A related form is instrument inclusion: Jeon et al. (local_183eaef4) supplied CARS, the Social Responsiveness Scale, the AQ-10 total and the Q-CHAT-10 score as predictors of an autism-traits label and obtained accuracy, precision, recall and F1 of exactly 1.0000, then investigated the result by re-running the cross-validation at 2, 4 and 5 folds - the correct instinct aimed at the partition rather than at the feature list.

**3. Data provenance.** Sixteen of the 170 studies reuse the same web-scraped corpus of children's facial photographs, reporting accuracies from 81.0% to 99.8% on it. Across those sixteen, reported accuracy tracks model capacity and evaluation looseness rather than signal: frozen-extractor designs with linear classifiers occupy the low end, end-to-end fine-tuning under image-level splits the high end. Several of the papers state the provenance confound in their own methods sections - images randomly retrieved from web searches, or from websites and Facebook pages that included autism-related content - and none tests a source-held-out evaluation. Two members of this branch describe the corpus as something it is not: Attar and Paygude (local_986436f2) report age bands, six ethnicity categories, urban/rural residence and a four-way facial-morphology partition for a Kaggle image folder that carries no metadata, and describe 2D photographs as 3D scans with a 0.9 mm landmark localisation error; Alsharif et al. (local_44d3aef5) report 547 images as 547 children in their abstract. The branch's own terminal case, Vasundhara et al. (local_e54c304c), inadvertently supplies its most informative result: in an out-of-distribution probe, one of its two detectors classified a photograph of a dog as Autistic and a leaf as Nonautistic. No other study in the branch tests a non-face input.

**4. Differential diagnosis.** The review's most consequential quantitative findings come from the small number of studies that included a second clinical group. Antoli et al. (local_b6ac2b98) ran one pipeline against both a typically developing group and a developmental-language-disorder group: F1 0.86 for ASD versus TD, and 0.63 for ASD versus DLD at near-balanced class sizes, concluding that the approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis. Assaf et al. (local_1b457442) found the same shape in speech transcripts - ROC-AUC 0.87 to 0.93 against typical development, 0.71 once developmental delay was included. Hickman et al. (local_69b10fe4) compared autistic and parkinsonian movement directly and found no kinematic feature that was shared between the two conditions while also differing from controls, refuting the anecdotal resemblance that motivates part of this literature. And local_cd7545e2 supplies the field's reference point: the ADOS-2 itself reaches AUC 0.562 and 0.569 when asked to discriminate autism from schizophrenia, with false-positive rates of 45.0% and 52.5%. Read together, these establish that a substantial part of the ASD-versus-typical-development performance reported across the corpus is a clinical-versus-non-clinical distinction rather than an autism-specific one.

**5. Demographic confounding.** Van der Burg et al. (local_7b19a959) quantified this directly, and are the only study to do so: the same models reached 81.8% accuracy on their unbalanced sample and 74.0% once age and gender were matched, and they reported the matched figure as primary. Roughly eight accuracy points were attributable to demographics alone. That number bears on many studies in this corpus that report large unadjusted between-group imbalances - a 42.9-point sex gap in local_7432ffd7 (86.2% male ASD against 43.3% male TD), a 32-point gap in local_4ceee075, an approximately two-year age gap between groups in the Nadig corpus used by local_1b457442 with age entered as a predictor, and a 22-point sex gap alongside significant receptive-vocabulary differences in local_b6ac2b98. Van der Burg et al. also diagnose the questionnaire branch's two failure modes in print: that higher published accuracies were obtained either by predicting an AQ cut-off rather than an official diagnosis, or by using groups unbalanced on demographic features that were themselves included as predictors.

**6. Reference standards.** Across the corpus, outcome ascertainment ranges from documented clinician diagnosis to a folder name. At the strong end, local_b6ac2b98 required formal DSM-5 diagnoses from licensed clinical teams and stated that early-age diagnoses are provisional and may evolve; local_bb4d1f7a diagnosed with DSM-5 criteria and CARS scores and explained candidly that ADI-R and ADOS evaluations are not widely available in India; local_7b19a959 drew participants from a national autism register. At the weak end, sixteen facial-image studies inherit labels from image folders with no diagnostic procedure of any kind, and twelve questionnaire studies use a checklist threshold. A distinct third category is the constructed label: local_b9de0d7f generated a teaching-method target with numpy, local_af9f4c12 constructed four severity strata as cut points on a weighted item sum, and Firat (local_231757c7) synthesised an entire severity class by averaging another class's feature vectors and adding Gaussian noise - and said so in the abstract.

**7. Ethics and governance.** Reporting is bimodal and the split does not follow the modality. Complete reporting - named committee, reference number, guardian consent, and in two cases separate consent for publication of images - appears in local_bb4d1f7a (IRB-2024-0057, with publication-specific consent), local_b6ac2b98 (Cordoba REC 4393), local_4da2b941 (USC 26/2023), local_7b19a959 (VCWE-2020-041R1), local_69b10fe4 (ERN_18-1800B and ERN_16-0281AP5) and local_945300a5 (036/EA/FK/2025, with teacher accompaniment during data collection). At the other end sit explicit exemptions granted on the ground that data are public: local_13c1f46d states that the study did not involve direct experiments on humans because publicly available Kaggle datasets were used; local_183eaef4 waives consent on the ground that prior reuse of a dataset establishes a general consensus regarding its use for research; local_24fefc5f declares ethical approval Not Applicable without reasoning; local_e4c2a776 declares that the article contains no studies with human participants while analysing 2,940 photographs of children, alongside a data-availability statement asserting that no dataset was analysed. Two studies invert the pattern in an instructive way. Lakhan et al. (local_367db0b6) build an entire machine-unlearning framework on the correct observation that once a newborn's data enters a training set there is usually no mechanism to remove it when parents withdraw consent - and obtain no ethical review or consent for their own use of that data. Almadhor et al. (local_e771fb69) propose a federated privacy architecture invoking GDPR and HIPAA, with no ethics statement and nine test cases. Against these, Assaf et al. (local_1b457442) make privacy the design criterion and state plainly that a major drawback of facial-image approaches is the invasion of privacy, especially for minors - a critique that applies directly to sixteen studies in this same corpus.

**8. What the careful studies find.** Fifty-three studies were rated below high overall risk of bias (17 low, 36 some concerns). The five whose designs most directly support a generalisation claim - participant-level or participant-disjoint partitioning, clinician-ascertained outcomes, and an explicit baseline or control - converge on a narrow range. local_4da2b941 (601 adults, participant-disjoint two-layer cross-validation, deposited code) reached R = 0.85 at best and 0.54 at worst on dimensional targets, with only 36.3% of individual predictions within 5% of the true score. local_7b19a959 reached 74.0% on matched data from performance tasks, 83% from the AQ alone, and 92% combined. local_5f57ba19 reached F1 0.641 with a majority-class baseline built into the design. local_b6ac2b98 reached F1 0.86 against typical development and 0.63 against another neurodevelopmental condition. local_69b10fe4 reached mean test accuracy 0.73 for clinical versus non-clinical and 0.93 for ASD versus Parkinson's on test partitions of roughly 13 to 19 people. The envelope these define - roughly 0.6 to 0.9 depending on the comparison, with wide uncertainty at realistic sample sizes - is the field's actual current performance, and it is not the envelope the corpus as a whole reports.

**9. Behaviours and modalities.** Where the behavioural analysis is done well it produces falsifiable claims rather than leaderboard entries. local_bb4d1f7a's feature ablation concluded that continuous attention rather than transition phases carries severity information; local_b6ac2b98 found that broad social/non-social areas of interest outperform fine decomposition by facial region and emotion; local_5f57ba19 localised the audio-visual advantage to the pre-speech phase; local_69b10fe4 found the ellipse - the shape most used in the drawing-task literature - the least discriminative of four; local_7d7f1fcc found that its audio model's top ADOS items were non-vocal (showing, pointing, sensory exploration, hand mannerisms); local_1b457442 identified mean length of utterance and mean length of turn ratio, the child's conversational share, as the leading discriminators. Against these, a large fraction of the corpus - and nearly all of the facial-image branch - reports no interpretable behavioural finding at all, and several studies name interpretability as a contribution while reporting no attribution output.

**10. Publishing trends.** Output rises steadily across the window (1 study in 2013, 17 in 2019, 22 in each of 2021 and 2022, 27 in 2025, 14 in the partial 2026), and venue composition shifts with it. Clinical and specialist journals in the corpus (Translational Psychiatry, Research in Autism, Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders, Frontiers in Psychiatry, Frontiers in Neuroscience) contain most of the well-designed studies; general engineering and computing venues contain most of the near-perfect ones. Review cycles are correspondingly short in the second group - 32 days for a paper with no ethics statement and no limitations section (local_7432ffd7), 40 days for one reporting accuracy 1.0000 (local_183eaef4), 44 days for one reporting 100% on 55 images (local_44d3aef5) - and long in the first (180 days for local_69b10fe4, 133 for local_4da2b941, 127 for local_b6ac2b98). Framing follows the same division: the specialist venues produce abstracts that concede modest performance, benchmark against published clinical-viability thresholds, and label the work proof-of-concept; the computing venues produce claims of clinical deployment, real-time screening and diagnostic replacement, expressed as a position above quoted figures from other papers.

### 3.6 Risk of Bias Assessment (Items 18, 21)

Overall risk of bias was rated high for 108 of the 170 included studies, moderate for 36, low for 17 and unclear for 9, using QUADAS-2 domains supplemented by four PROBAST-derived appraisal domains.

The distribution is not evenly spread across the four QUADAS-2 domains. Patient selection was rated high in the great majority of studies, driven by convenience or secondary use of public corpora with no recruitment, eligibility or demographic reporting; by comparison groups that were not recruited but produced by scoring; and by unadjusted between-group differences in age, sex and language ability. The index test domain was rated high wherever preprocessing steps that use outcome information preceded the split - class-conditional mean imputation (local_e771fb69), feature selection or SHAP-based pruning computed on the full dataset (local_7432ffd7, local_183eaef4, local_af9f4c12), pre-split synthetic oversampling (local_ed30e24c), and augmentation applied before partitioning (local_1d856900). Reference standard was the most consistently high-risk domain: in sixteen studies the outcome is a folder name on a web-scraped photograph, in twelve it is a checklist threshold on the predictors, and in three it is a variable the authors constructed. Flow and timing was rated high wherever the analysis unit was smaller than the participant, which was the single most frequent defect in the corpus.

Three cross-cutting patterns deserve separate statement. First, methodological care and estimand validity are independent: local_183eaef4 applied child-level cross-validation, grid search, Wilcoxon and Friedman model comparison and three explanation methods, and obtained accuracy 1.0000 because four autism instruments were in its feature set. Second, several studies read the symptoms of leakage as evidence against it - near-zero fold variance treated as robustness (local_8d43288c), test accuracy exceeding training accuracy treated as good generalisation (local_e4c2a776), high accuracy treated as reducing the likelihood of overfitting (local_b26db2f2). Third, internal arithmetic frequently fails: confusion matrices that do not match the stated evaluation size (local_986436f2), a headline accuracy computed over the whole dataset including the training portion (local_e04bcd32), mAP@0.5:0.95 within 0.03 points of mAP@0.5 (local_e54c304c), 25,000 positive cases drawn from a 10,000-sample dataset and described as class-balanced (local_367db0b6), and a stated total exceeding the accounted-for participants (local_8ff20c48).

Against this, a minority of studies were assessed as low or moderate risk on design grounds, and they share identifiable features: clinician-ascertained diagnoses obtained independently of the data, participant-level or participant-disjoint partitioning, hyperparameter selection nested inside the training portion, an explicit trivial baseline or label-randomisation control, confidence intervals or fold variance reported, and limitations sections that reason about mechanisms rather than listing generic caveats.

### 3.7 Certainty of Evidence - GRADE (Item 22)

**Diagnostic accuracy of behavioural computational models for autism (reported):** Very Low
  Very low certainty that reported accuracies estimate diagnostic performance. The subset of studies with participant-level partitioning, clinician-ascertained outcomes and clinically meaningful comparison groups supports a screening-aid level of performance (roughly 0.6-0.9 depending on the comparison) with low to moderate certainty.

**Discrimination of autism from other clinical conditions:** Moderate
  Moderate certainty that computational behavioural models discriminate autism from other neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions substantially less well than from typical development (F1 0.63 versus 0.86; ROC-AUC 0.71 versus 0.87-0.93), and that the gold-standard ADOS-2 also performs near chance against a comparison clinical population (AUC 0.562).


### 3.8 Per-Behavioural Modality (Approximate, Derived From Charted Data Type) Analysis

*9 groups · 170 included articles · 0 unlabeled (excluded from analysis).*

**Overall caveats:** Groups are loosely defined families, not exhaustive mutually exclusive categories; several studies combine modalities and are assigned to the family matching their charted primary data type. Group-level statements describe tendencies and name exemplars rather than asserting properties of every member.


#### Eye tracking and gaze *(n = 49)*

Largest group in the corpus. Reported accuracy is bimodal and tracks the analysis unit: studies partitioning gaze samples, scanpath images or eye crops report 97-100%, while the two studies using participant-independent partitions report F1 0.641 and 0.96 with a fold standard deviation of 0.08 on 28 people. Where interpretability is done properly the group produces its most valuable output - falsifiable claims about which gaze parameters carry information.

*Representative studies:* PMID:local_863980f8, PMID:local_40cd7d53, PMID:local_54954c19, PMID:local_88ddfdd1, PMID:local_96c87d36

*Caveats:* Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

**Group-specific Q&A:**

- **Q:** What determines reported performance in this group?
  **A:** The unit of analysis, not the paradigm. local_7432ffd7 split 1,048,575 gaze samples from 59 children by sample (99.78%, with CARS additionally in the feature vector); local_44d3aef5 split 547 scanpath images by image and reported 100% on 55 test images; local_bb4d1f7a generated exactly 100 eye crops per child from 40 children (97%). local_5f57ba19 used participant-independent nested cross-validation with a majority-class baseline built in (F1 0.641) and local_d7b6fa00 aggregated to the participant and listed leakage prevention as a contribution (0.96 ± 0.08 on 28 people).
  *Sources:* PMID:local_863980f8, PMID:local_40cd7d53, PMID:local_54954c19, PMID:local_88ddfdd1, PMID:local_96c87d36
- **Q:** What behavioural findings does the group produce?
  **A:** Where feature analysis is performed: fixation duration and vertical gaze distribution discriminate severity while velocity does not (local_bb4d1f7a); broad social/non-social areas of interest outperform fine decomposition by facial region and emotion (local_b6ac2b98); mouth fixation time and cross-AOI revisits are the leading discriminators, with the audio-visual advantage concentrated before speech onset (local_5f57ba19); mean duration of visits to objects distinguishes groups, read as difficulty disengaging attention (local_b6ac2b98).
  *Sources:* PMID:local_863980f8, PMID:local_40cd7d53, PMID:local_54954c19, PMID:local_88ddfdd1, PMID:local_96c87d36
- **Q:** How is the comparison group defined?
  **A:** Almost always typically developing children. The one study including a second clinical group (local_b6ac2b98, developmental language disorder) found F1 falling from 0.86 to 0.63, and concluded that the approach is more effective as a screening tool than for differential diagnosis.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_863980f8, PMID:local_40cd7d53, PMID:local_54954c19, PMID:local_88ddfdd1, PMID:local_96c87d36


#### Movement, kinematics and interaction traces *(n = 31)*

Contains the corpus's strongest differential-diagnosis study and its most honest handling of a perfect result, alongside frame- and session-level leakage of the same kind found elsewhere.

*Representative studies:* PMID:local_0dbc5018, PMID:local_dc5fc4bb, PMID:local_e404a2a3, PMID:local_780141fc, PMID:local_3a331973

*Caveats:* Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

**Group-specific Q&A:**

- **Q:** What does direct comparison with another movement disorder show?
  **A:** local_69b10fe4 compared autistic and parkinsonian movement with matched controls and found no kinematic feature shared between the two conditions that also differed from controls, refuting the anecdotal resemblance; classification reached mean test accuracy 0.73 for clinical versus non-clinical and 0.93 for ASD versus Parkinson's on test partitions of roughly 13 to 19 people.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_0dbc5018, PMID:local_dc5fc4bb, PMID:local_e404a2a3, PMID:local_780141fc, PMID:local_3a331973
- **Q:** How is a perfect result handled?
  **A:** local_231757c7 reported 100% for its severe-ASD class and stated in the same abstract sentence that the class's features were synthesised by averaging moderate-ASD vectors and adding Gaussian noise, computed the 95% interval (39.8-100.0%), noted that one misclassification would reduce recall to 75%, and set a minimum sample of 20-50 real cases for validation. It also reports that Kinect could not be deployed at all for children with severe autism.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_0dbc5018, PMID:local_dc5fc4bb, PMID:local_e404a2a3, PMID:local_780141fc, PMID:local_3a331973
- **Q:** What leakage patterns appear?
  **A:** local_b26db2f2 split 640 game sessions from 12 children by session and reported 96%, with leave-one-child-out available and unused; local_e771fb69 evaluated a four-modality federated framework on nine test cases with class-conditional mean imputation.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_0dbc5018, PMID:local_dc5fc4bb, PMID:local_e404a2a3, PMID:local_780141fc, PMID:local_3a331973


#### Speech, voice and language *(n = 26)*

The group contains both the corpus's most privacy-considered design and clear instances of demographic confounding. Where a second clinical group is included, performance falls markedly.

*Representative studies:* PMID:local_76fc33d0, PMID:local_be8aa62f, PMID:local_7b3e6b3a, PMID:local_36aa3ace, PMID:local_5b1d0b36

*Caveats:* Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

**Group-specific Q&A:**

- **Q:** What does the group find when a clinical comparison group is added?
  **A:** local_1b457442 reports ROC-AUC 0.87-0.93 for ASD versus typical development and 0.71 once developmental delay is included, reading the gap as showing the risk of misdiagnosis.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_76fc33d0, PMID:local_be8aa62f, PMID:local_7b3e6b3a, PMID:local_36aa3ace, PMID:local_5b1d0b36
- **Q:** What confounds the binary results?
  **A:** Age. In the Nadig corpus used by local_1b457442 the ASD children average roughly two years older than the typically developing children, and age is one of the four features the paper identifies as carrying the result.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_76fc33d0, PMID:local_be8aa62f, PMID:local_7b3e6b3a, PMID:local_36aa3ace, PMID:local_5b1d0b36
- **Q:** What behavioural markers emerge?
  **A:** Mean length of utterance and mean length of turn ratio - the child's conversational share relative to the adult - both directionally interpretable and consistent with established clinical observation.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_76fc33d0, PMID:local_be8aa62f, PMID:local_7b3e6b3a, PMID:local_36aa3ace, PMID:local_5b1d0b36


#### Multimodal and other *(n = 19)*

Heterogeneous group containing the corpus's best-validated adult study and several of its clearest reporting failures.

*Representative studies:* PMID:local_7b468950, PMID:local_7547db68, PMID:local_6249bd63, PMID:local_8b9e0e8a, PMID:local_0e476686

*Caveats:* Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

**Group-specific Q&A:**

- **Q:** What does the best-validated study in this group report?
  **A:** local_7b19a959: 74.0% accuracy on an age- and gender-matched sample against 81.8% unmatched, with the matched figure reported as primary and the eight-point difference attributed explicitly to demographic features; 83% for the AQ alone and 92% combined; and a label-randomisation control that falls to chance.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_7b468950, PMID:local_7547db68, PMID:local_6249bd63, PMID:local_8b9e0e8a, PMID:local_0e476686
- **Q:** What are the group's principal failures?
  **A:** local_367db0b6 reports 25,000 positive cases drawn from a 10,000-sample dataset and describes the result as class-balanced, names an exemplary metric set and reports no value from it, and declares no ethics approval necessary in a paper premised on parental consent withdrawal for newborns' data. local_1d856900 splits an unsourced 100-sample clinical dataset after fourfold augmentation and reports 98.2% on 40 rows against 4,220 features.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_7b468950, PMID:local_7547db68, PMID:local_6249bd63, PMID:local_8b9e0e8a, PMID:local_0e476686


#### Facial images (still photographs) *(n = 16)*

Sixteen studies, all reusing the same web-scraped corpus of children's facial photographs, reporting 81.0% to 99.8%. Reported accuracy tracks model capacity and evaluation looseness rather than signal. No study performs a source-held-out evaluation, none establishes the number of distinct children, and none reports a diagnostic procedure for any image.

*Representative studies:* PMID:local_261afa51, PMID:local_948fa8d0, PMID:local_b9e05a8f, PMID:local_5a331ffe, PMID:local_0f5a351e

*Caveats:* Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

**Group-specific Q&A:**

- **Q:** What is the provenance of the data?
  **A:** A public corpus assembled from web searches and social-media pages with autism-related content, redistributed through Kaggle and Roboflow. Several papers state the provenance confound in their own methods sections and none tests it. Two describe the corpus as something it is not: local_986436f2 supplies age, ethnicity, urban/rural and facial-morphology annotations that the dataset does not contain and reports 2D photographs as 3D scans with 0.9 mm landmark error; local_44d3aef5 reports 547 images as 547 children.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_261afa51, PMID:local_948fa8d0, PMID:local_b9e05a8f, PMID:local_5a331ffe, PMID:local_0f5a351e
- **Q:** How are outcomes ascertained?
  **A:** By folder name. No study in this group reports a diagnostic instrument, criterion, assessor or date for any image.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_261afa51, PMID:local_948fa8d0, PMID:local_b9e05a8f, PMID:local_5a331ffe, PMID:local_0f5a351e
- **Q:** What does the group's own evidence say about what the models decide?
  **A:** local_e54c304c ran the only out-of-distribution probe in the branch: one of its two detectors classified a photograph of a dog as Autistic and a leaf as Nonautistic. Separately, local_e04bcd32's headline 96.94% is a resubstitution figure computed over all 2,940 images including the 2,540 used for training, and local_986436f2's confusion matrix sums to 300 cases against a stated 200-image evaluation.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_261afa51, PMID:local_948fa8d0, PMID:local_b9e05a8f, PMID:local_5a331ffe, PMID:local_0f5a351e
- **Q:** How is ethics handled?
  **A:** Mostly by exemption or silence. local_13c1f46d states that the study did not involve direct experiments on humans because publicly available Kaggle datasets were used; local_e4c2a776 declares that the article contains no studies with human participants. The exceptions are local_945300a5, which recruited and photographed 70 children under an ethics code with parental consent and teacher accompaniment, and local_e54c304c, which is the only study in the branch to state that given the child's facial data aspect, there is ethical sensitivity.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_261afa51, PMID:local_948fa8d0, PMID:local_b9e05a8f, PMID:local_5a331ffe, PMID:local_0f5a351e


#### Questionnaire and checklist data *(n = 15)*

Reported accuracy in this group is governed by how much of the label's own arithmetic survives preprocessing. Where all checklist items are retained the models reach 99-100%; where half are deleted performance falls to 0.83. No study in the group predicts a clinician diagnosis.

*Representative studies:* PMID:local_9c4af7a3, PMID:local_02fa4215, PMID:local_361b59fb, PMID:local_8ff20c48, PMID:local_ed30e24c

*Caveats:* Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

**Group-specific Q&A:**

- **Q:** What is the outcome variable?
  **A:** In every case a threshold on the sum of the items supplied as features. local_ed30e24c classified 292 of 292 correctly; local_183eaef4 reached accuracy 1.0000 with CARS, SRS, AQ-10 and Q-CHAT-10 scores all in the predictor set; local_8ff20c48 deleted five of ten items for correlating with the score they are summed into and fell to 0.83; local_14df790d showed that every subset containing the total or its summands performs well.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_9c4af7a3, PMID:local_02fa4215, PMID:local_361b59fb, PMID:local_8ff20c48, PMID:local_ed30e24c
- **Q:** Does any study identify the circularity?
  **A:** One. local_af9f4c12 states that because the severity labels are deterministically derived from the same behavioural attributes used as model inputs, the task constitutes a structured function-approximation setting and high performance should not be read as diagnostic accuracy - and repeats the restriction in five sections. local_14df790d comes closest without naming it, observing that retaining both the total and its items could mislead the model.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_9c4af7a3, PMID:local_02fa4215, PMID:local_361b59fb, PMID:local_8ff20c48, PMID:local_ed30e24c
- **Q:** What use is proposed for the outputs?
  **A:** local_b9de0d7f is the extreme case: a six-way teaching-method target generated with numpy from the Q-CHAT total, predicted at 0.9917 from the items that total is computed from, with an uncited severity-to-intervention mapping offered to educators as a basis for decisions about individual children's education.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_9c4af7a3, PMID:local_02fa4215, PMID:local_361b59fb, PMID:local_8ff20c48, PMID:local_ed30e24c


#### Robot-mediated and interactive-system data *(n = 8)*

Small group characterised by primary data collection in interactive settings, and containing the corpus's methodological benchmark for prospective validation.

*Representative studies:* PMID:local_cb9a5b48, PMID:local_9528024b, PMID:local_d587f9cd, PMID:local_c6f1209b, PMID:local_1579c85a

*Caveats:* Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

**Group-specific Q&A:**

- **Q:** What is the strongest design in the corpus?
  **A:** local_7b468950, the Play.Care phase III protocol (NCT03438994): a locked algorithm, blinded prospective external validation, sensitivity and specificity as prespecified primary outcomes, a 200-child cohort with other neurodevelopmental disorders for differential diagnosis, and a design powered to detect underperformance. It states of its own pilot that it only trained and tested patterns on that particular dataset.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_cb9a5b48, PMID:local_9528024b, PMID:local_d587f9cd, PMID:local_c6f1209b, PMID:local_1579c85a


#### Video of naturalistic behaviour *(n = 4)*

The most ecologically valid data in the corpus - spontaneous behaviour recorded in children's homes - undermined by clip-level partitioning and, in one case, by a task that contains no non-autistic comparison at all.

*Representative studies:* PMID:local_4b031d44, PMID:local_83b99e73, PMID:local_5b7ea7dc, PMID:local_3e88f3ce

*Caveats:* Modality assignment is approximate, derived from each record's charted data-type field rather than from a categorisation applied by the original authors.

- **Q:** What is the validation problem?
  **A:** local_8d43288c formed folds over clips extracted from 75 parent-posted YouTube videos with no video- or child-level grouping, and read fold standard deviations below 0.004 as robustness.
  *Sources:* PMID:local_4b031d44, PMID:local_83b99e73, PMID:local_5b7ea7dc, PMID:local_3e88f3ce

  **A:** In local_8d43288c, four movement categories within a dataset containing only autistic children - so the study's screening and diagnostic framing cannot follow from its result, as its own decision-support hedge implicitly concedes.

## 4. Discussion

### 4.1 Limitations

This review has five limitations that bear on how its conclusions should be read.

First, the corpus was supplied rather than searched. The 170 records are a human-verified set assembled by the reviewer requesting this synthesis, not the output of a documented database strategy, so no recall claim can be made and the search-provenance fields of the PRISMA flow are necessarily incomplete. Identification counts, database queries and date filters were not available; one duplicate was detected and removed during corpus construction, giving 171 records identified and 170 after deduplication. All 170 were assessed on full text, and none was excluded on eligibility grounds, per the reviewer's instruction that the set was already human-verified.

Second, screening and charting were performed by a single assessor without independent duplicate extraction, so no inter-rater reliability can be reported. The charting instrument was applied uniformly - all 170 records carry the same 23 review questions, the same QUADAS-2 domains and the same four appraisal domains - but consistency is internal rather than externally verified.

Third, no meta-analysis was attempted and none would be defensible. The reported performance figures are not commensurable: they are computed over different analysis units (persons, images, frames, gaze samples, sessions), against outcomes of radically different provenance (clinician diagnosis, checklist threshold, folder label, author-constructed variable), under evaluation designs that differ in whether participants can appear on both sides of a split. Pooling them would produce a number whose principal determinant is the prevalence of leakage in the corpus.

Fourth, the review charts what studies report, and reporting quality is itself a variable under study. Where a paper does not state its class balance, its split proportions or the number of distinct participants behind its images, the charting records that absence but cannot recover the missing quantity. Several conclusions in this review - particularly about the number of distinct children behind reused image corpora - therefore rest on inference from arithmetic rather than on stated fact.

Fifth, the modality grouping used in the per-group analysis is an approximate assignment derived from each record's charted data-type field, not a categorisation applied by the original authors. Studies that combine modalities, or that describe their data in the terms of an adjacent literature, may be assigned to a group that does not fit them well; the group-level statements should be read as descriptions of tendencies within loosely defined families rather than as properties of exhaustive, mutually exclusive categories.

- **PMID:local_0dbc5018** (score: 0.95): "The classification accuracy reached a maximum accuracy of 96.7 % (specificity 93.8 % and sensitivity 100 %) by using seven features selected by the Fisher discriminant ratio-based technique.
